_childDocuments_.review: If I could only tell you only one thing about this game, I'd warn you: You'll probably enjoy this game the most if you really want to do both - build AND raid. You'll need knowledge from both to improve in both aspects.I really enjoy this game. I did play the Open Beta a bit during NextFest, and I got right back in after it released.The controls are good, the graphics are pretty good, it runs well even on my slightly aged machine, loading times aren't too bad. It can be a bit grindy, but in general, you play some, you get some stuff. The time to raid a base is usually pretty short... depending on size and how methodical or daring you are, between 30 seconds and 20 minutes. The balance between raider equipment and traps feels pretty good, the selection of both is limited, but they're recognizable and have enough differences to matter - mods offer some nice additional variety and make a ton of sense. Being able to destroy traps is great. Oh, and I love the Second Wave mod and that your default traps start with the mod unlocked.Weaknesses are mostly limited building block selections (only 2-3 per style category) and the fact that Forsaken Tombs aren't properly tutorialised. Also, while it fits the underlying story and theme, the visuals are a bit niche.The game can be played in 2-player-coop, but playing solo almost has an abstract cooperative quality to it: As a builder, you want to build a base you'd enjoy (and feel challenged while) playing. As a raider, you want to really test the defenses and explore the base built for you... and if you did enjoy a good challenge as a raider, give it an accolade or two!The fact that you don't lose anything when a raid is successful (and dying also doesn't cost you anything as a raider, unless you used consumables) plays nicely into this notion. (And I know some people view this differently, but I am very happy with this game having this perspective on it.)I am NOT an elite player. I can not claim that I have never seen a base I couldn't beat, but from what I've seen from raids on my bases, I do believe those who say they haven't. Most bases I've raided were somewhere along the lines of serviceable to good, some standard fare, some tricky ones, some easy, some challenging... but there have been more utterly brilliant, great bases than annoying / frustrating ones that felt unbeatable to me, or at least not worth the effort.I had THREE of the latter, among ALL bases I raided, and I did quit two of them.Most of the best bases I raided, that I enjoyed the most, did kill me at least once.I have built three bases myself, two small, one medium. One rated normal, two dangerous.All of them have been beaten by players with 0 deaths, both in a speedy fashion and while thoroughly destroying most or all traps for the loot.All of them had at least one instance with one player attempting it dying 4 or more times. Only one player has ever quit a raid on one of my bases (after one death, 1:08 minutes in, dying to the second trap they encountered, before even getting to the fully trapped areas).One of my bases killed a raider 5 times over, and they still made it through, taking 15 minutes to do so, but awarding the base two accolades, so they seemingly enjoyed the experience. (I get it, though: My favorite raid thus far was very similar - 3 deaths, 11 minutes, but two accolades well earned. I tip my hat to the builder.)Some people claim that the game only rewards kills (and this is why everyone builds death traps and kill boxes), but accolades count more than kills for prestige purposes (and that's  important for the longevity of a base). I'm also against the requirement to validate a base. This mechanic has proven pretty insufficient in comparable games, and I think the mechanisms in place in this game might be more useful long-term. That said, if I had to, I could validate my bases, pretty easily. I could probably make them a fair bit more deadly and still validate them without too much of a hassle. But the mechanisms currently in place (limited runtime for bases and accolades > kills for prestige points) really make me want to create bases that, yes, genuinely try to kill you, but also kinda want to be a thrilling experience for you that you will be able to beat in the end....just the kind of bases I'd like to play myself.See you in the wasteland, Custodian.

_childDocuments_.review: Terrific game, one I feel like I could keep coming back to for a long time. I've only ran Normal Outposts so far, not quite ready to attempt Dangerous or Brutal, but the more risk you take the higher the reward. Anyone going into a Dangerous or Brutal Outpost knows they are likely to die, a lot. For someone like me who loves building things I'll sometimes spend hours building an Outpost. An outpost may only last around 10 days or so but building them is the fun part for me and any that have been mastered can still be made into social Outposts. You may only be able to have 5 Outposts active at a time but you can keep up to 200.One tip I can give after playing for a while is try to build smaller Outposts at the start. That way while building up a large one you can still have others active.When encountering killboxes there is usually a good way to solve them, though some may require a massive amount of skill. You can always abandon an Outpost if it's too difficult. There are all types of people so there will be all types of Outposts, just be patient and you'll find ones you can complete. I have one small killbox myself, though it's a baby compared to ones I've seen and can easily enough be cleared if you are careful. A good variety of maps is nice, from nearly impossible killboxes to long ones where death could be around every corner. While I may get frustrated from dying a lot to some Outposts it doesn't take away from the fun of the game itself. Some people will be better raiders and some better builders and you can get the same resources either way.I can hardly wait for the new stuff coming and hope they continue to add more to the game. I even bought Dead by Daylight just to get the special decor pack as I like to have as many options as I can get when building.

_childDocuments_.review: I'm giving this a thumbs up although I did not buy it after the free trial. I'll come back when it's $15. To me it's currently 7/10, but could be 10/10 with some improvements. Very fun core mechanics and pieces to build with. First of all though, add vaulting up onto blocks! Grappling *almost* high enough and falling, or grappling onto something further away and getting stuck on a block in front of you is very frustrating. Also with the grappling hook there is no way to deal with death pits that are full of mobs or acid.Most importantly, I agree with many players that you should have to play through your own outpost before you activate it and whenever some number of changes are made. Beating another player's outpost after 1-3 deaths is the sweet spot imo, and more brutal outposts and "kill boxes" are the worst part of the experience. They tried to award accolades more highly than base kills, but I think it's not enough. You should only get any rewards from someone raiding your base if they end up beating it - and you shouldn't be able to give accolades to outposts that you forfeit (unplayable bases get rewarded like this). Better metrics for builders would be amazing as well: "heat map" style outlines of paths all the recent players took and where they died, kill counters on individual traps/monsters, average number of accolades given to you per raid, etc.Alongside that, I think it needs more granular difficulty tiers, such as more advanced traps putting outposts straight into the Dangerous level so new players are unlikely to encounter them.The other issue as people are mentioning is the progression system. Everything simply costs currency which is hard to remember the names of, and unlocks aren't gated behind your level so it feels more like a grind than you're "leveling up" and becoming a better raider/builder. Maybe if suits/weapons/consumables were related to your "raider level" and guards/traps were related to your "builder level" they could more properly match raiders to the appropriate bases (I'm a level 5 raider, this base was made by a level 5 builder, etc). Alongside this, while trap and guard mods are fantastic (second wave is a blast), suit/gear/weapon mods are very lackluster. I was expecting more functional mods like: you can't hang on your grapple anymore but it launches you much farther / your grenades do less damage but split after throwing/launching them / your bolts fly slower but penetrate 1-2 targets, ricochet off surfaces, curve after firing, etc. Also, why are we feeding and leveling up the chimera? Is there nothing gated by your player level at all?Lastly, the advisor levels and boost system are pretty unsatisfying. You "level up" your advisors but it doesn't feel impactful at all, since they very slightly increase the duration of boosts which aren't worth their cost anyway - at least in my first 10 hours of playing. Some more meaningful level up rewards such as cheaper unlocks, cheaper boosts, a free boost at a certain level, or a random rotating discounted boost, would make it much more enticing to even open the boost menu. After a few hours, I ended up raiding any outposts that looked fun rather than aiming to level up any particular advisor.P.S. If you guys could crack crossplay raiding and building I would absolutely get this game to play with my console buddies.

_childDocuments_.review: Maybe you remember "the mighty quest for epic loot" before Ubisoft bought and ruined it. Meet your maker has the same premise but changes up a few things:Neutral Changes:-Meet your Maker is a fps rpg. Mighty quest was a hack and slay rpgPros:-Vertical movement. As a raider you are super agile with no-cooldown grappling hook and double jumps. The movement in general feels really smooth.-Everything deals 1 damage. Everything has 1 Hp. You. Traps. Guards. Everything. This makes the information that you have to process a lot simpler and the gameplay more dynamic.-Freedom of Building. You can get very creative with your outposts. (though some players don't use this potential)-Caring Devs, that already reacted to community feedback.Cons:-Gore. The guards are very distorted and killing them results in beheadings etc. If you like stuff like that, than thats a pro for you... I guess.-Limited Content. This term is relative. The game has only 4 different guards and 9 different traps. However, each of these do fundametally different things and can be equipped with 2 different mods each. There are 4-6 different Mods per trap and 7 Mods per Guard. I guess their use and diversity depends on the way they are positioned/set on patrol.-Slow Unlocks. The game is very grind intensive - especially at the start. Some say this is to increase the runtime due to the limited content. I am neutral to this. You should do some informed choices what to unlock first. But after you got the basic everything gets smoother and faster.

_childDocuments_.review: Before I go into this review:This game is being actively developed. Don't let my or any other review let you think this is the guaranteed final product, If you think this game could be worth it in the future, it's worth considering. The only reason I have my review as not recommended is the current state of the game being.... incomplete feeling. Which makes sense, the game isn't finished yet, and the devs haven't necessarily put everything they want in the game yet.Review:Admittedly, this game struggles to hold my attention. But not for a lack of effort. The game is the most fun when you aren't trying to optimize everything as a raider at the start. Some reviews miss the point of raiding, slowly going through bases rather than rushing and figuring out the layout through repetition, changing your load out in between deaths, and fun movement mechanics. The opposite can be said of the base building however. You have to be very careful about the choices you make and working around the restrictions placed on you. It's interesting and honestly I far prefer it over the raiding, which is ironic because most people seem to have the opposite opinion. There are content updates coming which will solve my main issue with the game: There's only so much to do. To comparing it to their other game dead by daylight, something I am loathing since they are so different, the amount of customization is sorely lacking compared to the perk and addon system simply because of how little there is in the game so far. I hope that the devs will add some non-Premium ways to get new traps and minions on the base building front, along with new suits and weapons for raiders. As it is now there isn't enough content to justify the 30 dollar price tag, along with the cost of dlc to make the game feel more robust. I only hope some of their future content updates focus on giving the player more to do at base without a hard monetary blocker. I want to love this game, but I've already unlocked a good portion of what is available and as you can see from this review I am not that far in. That doesn't mean I've run out of enjoyment for the game, but I feel like that enjoyment is on borrowed time right now.

_childDocuments_.review: Meet your maker is a game where you build a map for other players to go through, or go through a map other players have built for you. If you are building, your objective is to not only kill the player, but make the player enjoy the map you have built. Building a map intended to be 'impossible', isn't favorable to a map that can be beaten, but is challenging and rewarding.The building system is entirely reliant on a grid-based system with blocks. This makes it easy to build whatever you want without sinking hours and hours into it, though if you're like me this will end up happening anyway.Along with the building system is a replay system, which allows you to look back on who raided your base, and where they, or your traps, failed.A complaint i see very frequently is the lack of trap variety. As of writing there are 9 (6 of which can kill) traps in the game.The Boltshot, which acts similar to a dart trap.The Bomb Ejector, which 'ejects' a large number of bombs in a path.The Corrosive Cube, which acts akin to any kill barrier in any other game. Think lava in minecraft.The Death Piston, which is a, well, piston, which continually expands and retracts, killing anyone if it squishes them against a wall.The Holocube, A fake block which can be used to hide traps.The Impaler, Which is simply a spike trap.The Incinerator, which spews flame in a long line.The Iron Claw, which is a grappling hook that grabs players and pulls them toward it.Lastly, the Plasma Sentinel, which acts as a turret.Each trap has a set of modifications that can be applied, individually, to each trap placed. These can make them faster, have longer reach, ect. It is important to note that the Holocube, Bomb Ejector, Boltshot, and Impaler will only activate once, then never work again unless given a mod that lets them activate more than once, of which only the Boltshot and Impaler have.A complaint i commonly see is that there are few traps. While i am somewhat confident more traps may be added in the future, the main way these traps are used interacts with eachother, not functioning individually. A single trap, or even a single mod for a trap, could very well make a combination of any set of traps very, very strong.Further reinforcing this, all traps, excepting the holocube and corrosion cube, all take at minimum one second to activate. Using one trap by itself will rarely get anyone. When they do, it is due to clever placement.In addition to the traps, the game has a set of enemies you can place in your maps.The Cannonback, which launches a single bomb at the player.The Enforcer, which launches a single bolt in a straight line at the player.The Hornet, which flies and fires a single, slow, homing projectile.And the Warmonger, which charges at the player with two swords.All of these enemies die in one hit from any weapon the player has, with one exception. A modifier can be put on them, just like any trap, which gives them armor. If given armor, they can only be be killed if hit in spots where the armor does not cover, or the player breaks the armor first with a heavy weapon. A personal gripe of mine is that there are only three blocks. A cube, A wedge, and a square corner. In addition to this, the way the game checks if a player can complete a level, is by having an npc that walks in a straight path to the objective of the map, then back out to the player spawn.This npc requires about one half block of space to either side, and one full block above it to reach the objective. This limits what kind of pathways you can make, and often results in players making long wedge paths that go up and down repeatedly. I would prefer to see this npc capable of going through smaller spaces, a bit larger than what the player can go through. This would enable players to make better looking, and more dangerous, corridors and rooms.In addition, i would like to see the list of blocks expanded upon from the existing three. Even a simple, normal corner piece, would be extremely appreciated, but some other frequently seen blocks in other block games such as ramp pieces and inverse corners would also be very nice to see, and would enable players to, yet again, make better looking outposts, rooms, and corridors, and give players going through the map a better challenge.Finally, i would like to see the game have a larger pool of decorative props to choose from. Currently, the list of props is acceptably large, but all of them can only go inside of a wall. Props that can go in the world space could add much needed detail to the standard 1x1 hallway often seen.Now for the part i'm sure most of you were waiting for, raiding.At first, raiding in the game is very daunting, as other players know much more than you do when you first start, and are likely to get you with the traps several times, especially if they are good with how they set them up. However, the small pool of traps and enemies lets you get used to them very quickly. The key things to learn are what sounds each one makes when they activate, and the range, as well as effect, of each one. Each enemy, trap, and even props in the game make noise. Often very distinct from eachother, and easy to hear. This gives you important information on how to handle each one before you see it, or if you've triggered it.After your first few raids into other players maps, you'll gain some of the resources in the game, which you can use to upgrade your equipment, or get new ones. This loop is continual, and feeds into building as-well, building acting as an idle component of this game. The better your base preforms, the more resources you will get out of it over time.There are four weapons, and one shield in the game. Two crossbows, two swords, and the 'arc shield', which i will explain soon.The crossbows are the 'Volt Lancer', and the 'Falconic Plasmabow', being a heavy and light variants of the crossbow respectively. The Volt Lancer can break traps, and armor on enemies, but only gets two to three shots. The Falconic Crossbow can only kill enemies, and won't break armor or traps, but gets between six to fifteen shots. The high ammo count of the Falconic Crossbow makes it desirable, but it is highly situational.The swords are the 'Sledgeblade', and the 'Fury's Edge', being the Heavy and Light variants of the sword respectively.Both swords can break traps, and most importantly,  Deflecting projectiles is a mechanic many newer players miss, but the swords can both deflect *any* projectile if you swing them as the projectile gets within range.The only difference between the two, is that the sledgeblade is slower, but can break armor, while Fury's Edge is faster, but cannot.The arc shield is a unique 'weapon', that acts much like a sword that can only deflect. The difference being that this deflect lasts a full second and a half, and makes you completely immortal for the duration.Of these weapons you can only equip two, so choose wisely.In addition to the weapon you have four 'utility' items, which are used up when you use them. These are the Grenade, Flash Barrier, Phoenix Pod, and Spike Drive. The Grenade is as it says on the tin, you throw it and it explodes. You get them from the start of the game, and they are always useful as they can disable traps around corners.The Flash Barrier acts much like the Bubble Shield from halo. It provides a dome, in which traps cannot hit you though. It can also break traps if the trap is inside the Bubble. Enemies cannot shoot through the bubble, but can walk inside.The Phoenix Pod acts as a respawn point you can place down.The Spike Drive makes you 20% faster, which doesn't sound like much, but this small boost lets you simply walk away from more or less any trap in the game due to the added speed.The game is as fast or slow as you make of it. If you want to go fast, try speedrunning, if not, go slow and check every corner.

I'd suggest this game to folks who like building lethal outposts or who like playing fast-paced, violent raider games. _childDocuments_.review: This game is awesome! It's basically a mature mario maker extraction game focused on trap bases and shooting. You build bases and get rewards for them killing other people. You play other people's bases and get rewards for beating them. You use these rewards to buy new traps, new abilities and lots of stuff to upgrade your character and your base. It's a fun and rewarding gameplay loop. This is not a platforming game, it's about trying to maneuver through a kill house and escape with the treasure. You won't be doing pixel perfect jumps or crazy obstacle courses. You'll mostly be trying to figure out how to get past/destroy X trap without Y and Z trap killing you. Before any trap is triggered, you'll see a red alert flash and have about 1 second to react. For the most part, you can dodge or avoid almost every trap fairly easily. I'v seen people complain about traps in the back but you quickly learn to lookout for those and you still get a red alert to help you avoid them.More difficult bases will use a combination of traps to bait you into moving the wrong way or something and it can be fun to try and figure out the proper way to avoid the combination of traps A few of the higher difficulty maps can be extremely difficult but they are not impossible, especially once you have upgraded your character and abilities some. It's a great game and definitely worth a try!

_childDocuments_.review: Meet your Maker is a game that puts you in the role of both level designer and playtester. You can design outposts full of traps and monsters, and try to get through the outposts designed by other players.  If you want to build as a creative outlet, just to see all the variety of levels you can make, you will probably enjoy the game for a few days. The raiding is also pretty fun. Everything dies with one hit, including you, so raids tend to be a fun challenge and you have a grappling hook which makes things more exciting.  The aesthetic is cool and there are the beginnings of an interesting story, but then the game doesn't really expand on it, and what you do in the game doesn't really make sense for the story.However, the game has tons of problems with it.1. The UI is overly complicated. You have to press like six buttons to end a level, and you need to visit each base to collect resources from it, prestige it, or activate it, rather than being able to do this all from a main menu.2. The progression system is overly complicated. There are tons of different resources and progression mechanics: synthite, parts, cells, genmat, character experience, chimera experience, and experience levels for each individual advisor. You get most of them by doing the same things, some of them do nothing except give you the other ones, and the ones you can choose to focus on hardly make any difference. The game could easily get by with just one or two resources.3. The devs keep insisting that they don't want to force players to be good at both raiding and building, but at the same time, you cannot just be a builder, because you can't gain enough resources from your outposts to maintain them or buy new ones. Building a good outpost is a huge time commitment, and then you hardly get any reward from it.4. The game crashes a lot.5. It seems a bit expensive for a game that you'll likely get tired of pretty quickly.6. The forums are full of people giving feedback and suggestions to the devs on this game that's still pretty early in development, and I have yet to see a single developer response, which is disappointing.  7. I don't think many people are even playing this game any more. It needs a community of both builders and raiders in order to thrive, and doesn't have one.8. And what bothers me most about the game is that it has the foundation to be a really non-toxic multiplayer game, in that you can design challenging but solvable levels just for other people to enjoy, and yet you are not incentivized to do so. The game incentivizes builders to kill raiders as many times as possible, and incentivizes raiders to abandon raids and block builders if they don't like one of their bases. This is all toxic, and is a huge wasted opportunity to build a friendly community-based game.

Very quickly. The biggest culprit is that damn worker. I think that's why i found the labyrinth map so refreshing and creative. Their mere existance is exactly why the game is full of braindead design. It always led to shortest path to the genmats and you have no complete control over it. sure, people don't really follow him. But builder are still forced to having to make level design around letting him into the destination. He can't climb, jump or crawl around without proper platform, that means no multiple pathway to the genmats, no platforming-based level, no upper-verticality play (it's so stupid, you have grappling hook that can go pretty much any direction without cooldown, and then you have builder mode that forced you to create corridor map? absolutely baffling.) and the worst part? you can't change where the genmats should be. you are literally building a level inside a box. on a game that demand your creativity.... i have no words. _childDocuments_.review: Fantastic Game, With a Few Caveats. MYM(Meet Your Maker) has a very simple game play loop; you raid another player's base and gain materials, you build a base for other players to raid and if they die in your base you collect more materials, rinse and repeat. This loop is appealing because it is all built around player made content, but this is also where the game falls flat. Some players build bases that are easy, some players build bases that are difficult, and other players build bases that look pretty. Many players consider raiding to be too easy while others see it as too challenging. Some players think the game should focus more on building and other players opt not to build at all. This game is what you make of it. One issue that stands out with this game is the price and the live service model. Every "season" of this game brings about new DLC that comes in 2 packs, a cosmetic pack, and a pack that features new items for players to use in raiding or building. If you do not buy these DLCs you may be at a disadvantage compared to other players depending on the strength of these seasonal offerings. Understanding this, the game is still very solid game that offers a new experience with every login but has an ever increasing "buy-in", waiting for a sale to pick this game up is more than a good idea.

_childDocuments_.review: We had a good thing going, but BHVR thought it would be a good idea to effectively abandon the game's development since "we had fully see the world that Meet Your Maker has to offer"... in reality they are too lazy to actually flush out this world and would rather just cash out while they have the chance.This game had massive potential but they threw it away early on.If you want a rough timeline of events, continue reading, if you dont care, just skip past...The game was riddled with bugs early on and the developers did too little too late to actually fix it. The Second Wave (augment) lets traps be activated once the Genmat was collected, but there was a bug that let other traps see the player and trigger through Corrosive Cubes (with the Second Wave augment) and potentially kill the player. It resulted in almost every base being full of traps that you had to waste crossbow bolts to destroy but could not actually retrieve the bolts.As a result players left the game. The developers took months to actually fix it.Content releases were slow, we received little to no communication or community support. The final straw was them effectively just releasing a battlepass while also not really addressing the community issues or adding content that was actually meaningful for both sides. It felt like the game was trying to cash out on whatever it could without actually trying to support the community in a slightest.To put it as bluntly as possible, the game did not earn the right to monetize itself further, and the community was pissed.Now here we are. Almost everyone left. BHVR is stopping development on the game. The official forums for Meet Your Maker got deleted by BHVR and instead just redirects you to the Steam page. Please, just avoid this game.
_childDocuments_.name: Meet Your Maker

_childDocuments_.review: On principle and for the first 3-4 hours this game has a satisfying loop. Beyond this, you soon get the sinking feeling that there's not a great deal there.2 classes for a game where you spend 90% of your time raiding as that class?7-9 traps (depending on your definition) in a game entirely reliant on traps. This game has two parts, building and raiding. Let's talk about raiding first.What is it?You get resources by attempting to steal X McGuffin from Y map. The "Y map" being one that is user created with traps and enemies designed to stop you.What's fun about it?What's not fun about it?What is it?You in turn build your own deathtrap dungeons for other users to attempt to raid. You get resources for each player you kill.What's fun about it?What's not fun about it?The developers are very focused on "creating a balanced player ecosystem". And the way they have gone about it almost seems like they're about to add microtransactions to buy resources at any moment. The whole game feels like it's squeezing you for resources. Forcing you to play as many levels as possible regardless of quality. And to a certain degree this makes sense, they need to maximize the ratio of level plays to levels, otherwise, builders wouldn't get plays on their levels.I would say I am more of a builder, and usually only sign on to replenish/prestige my levels and watch some replays. But now I think, what's the point? It's getting more and more expensive and I have to sink more and more time just to keep my level active for what, 6 hours?I don't want to build a kill box, I want to build something fair, fun, and pretty. Yet the current state of the game encourages maximum kill at the cost of all other features.I don't want to play the 100th "drop bombs on you from above on a ramp" level. I have seen it.I understand that the developers want to release with less, so it's easier to balance and maintain this "player ecosystem", but honestly I feel this game needed to release with 3x times the content. Whether or not you feel that this game has enough content, as it stands it's gone from an average peak of 3000 concurrent Steam players to 1000. 1/3rd in two weeks. That's 2000 less players that are part of the player ecosystem, playing levels, and giving builders resources. 2000 fewer players innovating and building interesting levels. If the developers really are cautiously trying to optimize the player economy, I'd say they may need to up the ante.The developers plan to release 1 more trap, class, gun, and map theme in June. I personally feel that's a plaster over a gaping wound.If that's the rate of content additions, then this game will be prime to pick up on sale after 5 years of content. Who can say if it will survive it that long.EDIT 18/10: After two "content updates" I signed in to see if things have improved. - 1 new trap which I can't afford without another 6 hours.- My outpost only got 4 plays before needing a refill. - Levelling up the prestige of your outpost still only allows you to add one upgraded trap.- Higher skill and more tools mean fair levels don't get kills, further encouraging killboxes.Developers.This type of game is made for me. But this game needs more than drip-feed of cosmetics.It needs doors, timers, traps, block pushers, rotators; .

_childDocuments_.review: Honestly a really good game. Smooth game.. The difficulty can be brutal but all of it is a learning curve. Love the progression system for the variety of traps/enemies/weapons/suits. Makes you wanna play more to upgrade them.Big brain is needed for some of the playermaps and there is variety in the ways to dismantle or rush an enemy outpost!
_childDocuments_.name: Meet Your Maker

_childDocuments_.review: Im reluctant to not recommend, but the devs clearly need to be forced to read the overwhelming consistent thoughts of their community. Things need to change to make this game a success, and these changes being implemented would have me change my review immediately. Most important is #1, which I guarantee if the devs dont implement this game will be dead within a few months. 1. Players need to beat their own maps before publishing. This is obvious and from what ive seen, 9/10 of the community is demanding it. 2. Costs of things need to be adjusted. Its weird leveling up so much but never being able to upgrade/unlock anything because the same resources are shared across everything. 3. Bases should not reset their points if they failed to get enough kills to prestige. My favorite/most accoladed base never gets to grow because the kill points dont stack. 4. Leveling up individual vendors doesnt have any benefit aside from the material rewards of leveling up the chimera. Weird that a level 18 vendor has the same prices/options as a level 1.
_childDocuments_.name: Meet Your Maker

_childDocuments_.review: The game is fairly decent, don't get me wrong. Loading into other people's levels, seeing what unique twists, combos, and ways people design their bases is amazing.  The progression is worth the reward, and its fairly easy to get the resources you need to buy the upgrades for your attacker or base upgrades for defender. So, good job there.However, the deal breaker for me is the way the base design works. Just discovered that artistic map I made for an hour and half filled with traps, strategy, and a theme (some maps i was getting onwards of 6 kills so it was working) ran out of its map resource, making the map no longer accessible.  Having to constantly remake maps and spend my currencies on buying new land is a bit of a deal breaker for me.  I'm someone who likes map design, spending hours on Divinity's campaign makers, Far Cry 5's maps, Halo Forge (back in the day), so i'm someone who likes my creations to be permanent and repeatedly played on.If you're like me, and are heavily invested in the base building part, maybe think twice, as you'll be forced to remake your creations as they become irrelevant.
_childDocuments_.name: Meet Your Maker

_childDocuments_.review: Nice concept but kinda odd that they don't require the maker to beat their own outpost to make it active. The fact we have grappling hooks but are required to build an outpost that caters to a robot on a fixed path also limits on the creativity we can do for the map. Map difficuly is solely based on enemies and traps so brutal maps are almost always just boring kill boxes instead of creative and fun maps.Game might be more fun after a few updates and they allow people ot be more creative.
_childDocuments_.name: Meet Your Maker

_childDocuments_.review: A lot of people complaining are missing the entire point of the game. They want it to be like mario maker, and that was never the intention to begin with. They complain that the game encourages builders to make elaborate death traps instead of making "carefree and relaxed maps". They'll go on to say that these elaborate death traps are impossible or really difficult to beat, when the game gives raiders several different tools to completely cheese everything. The game is not meant to be played like Quake or Doom, it's almost like a puzzle game in disguise.Raiders have a shield that blocks all damage.They have deployable domes that block all projectiles and can be shot out of.They have a grappling hook that can be used to latch on to walls to get away from traps.The default melee weapon can deflect most projectiles in the game.They have a deployable respawn beacon.And best of all, co op players can keep reviving each other as long as one of them stays alive.The game is actually surprisingly well balanced all things considered. Just don't expect to go into a brutal ranked outpost with the default loadout and expect it to be a cakewalk. Unlock the different tools and use them.I think a lot of the screeching is carrying over from the DBD community to. Who also, funnily enough complain when they have to rub 2 brain cells together to outplay someone. But that's a different rabbit hole entirely.
_childDocuments_.name: Meet Your Maker

_childDocuments_.review: Played a bunch in the beta, and it's just as fun now if not moreso with the bigger playerbase. Struggle your way through a house of horrors someone else made for a rush of joy as you sneak your way out past the second wave traps. Then sit back and relax as you enjoy the replays of people struggling through a hell of your own design.
_childDocuments_.name: Meet Your Maker

_childDocuments_.review: this game is fun, challenging and promotes creativity and varied play styles. it's still new, and doesn't have the biggest player base yet. it's very open to differing opinions and creativity to the point it is inevitable to encounter styles that you don't enjoy as much, and with the smaller player base it might be easier at first for new players to feel overwhelmed. but most of the people i talk to who play are very helpful, go at your own pace, learn, play have fun play with friends or people you meet through the game. i learned alot and had alot of fun on my own, i also can say the same about playing with people who are new, or waaay above my skill level, every frustration has just let me learn if nothing else then my current limits, don't be afraid to collaborate for ideas, either strategies on how to get passed certain obstacles while raiding, or ideas for your own bases. you can be sneaky or bold, i and many others have died to tricky, diabolical hard, or even just simple traps we shouldn't have gotten caught by so don't be discouraged and just try if you want to build, or be as reckless or careful as you want while raiding. find what you enjoy!

You really get to dive deep down both rabbit holes.Customization galore: You find you have a favorite trap? Upgrade the crap out of it. You got a favorite gun? UPGRADES FOR DAYS!Overall art style has a real great feel to it. _childDocuments_.review: I strongly reccomend this game. _childDocuments_.review: There is some sick pleasure derived from watching real people suffer at the hands of your diabolical creations. Amazing game. Scratches an itch i didn't even know i had. _childDocuments_.review: I really think this game is going a right direction, but I have one problem with it and it's how good levels are over shadowed by more "kill box" hodgepodge levels.  I think that a level that's hard, but is well designed, should be the main type of levels that players should experience as it best shows how good this game is.  I think, right now, the game rewards both deaths and accolades a little too evenly.  Because of this, it's more efficient to create a level that kills players over and over again forcing them to run the exact same loop than to create creative traps, that may or may not kill a player, giving the level accolades.  Quality or quantity should be the name of the game.  However, with the number of "kill box" type levels that I play, it seems it's just more efficient to go for kills.  Granted I play in "Brutal" difficulty and if that's just how that difficulty is then fine, but I still think that even Brutal levels can be creative and challenging.  If this changes, then I'll change this review to be a recommend.  Until then, accolade levels that make creative traps and try to fake you out rather than one large arena with the same three traps over and over again.

_childDocuments_.review: TLDR: This game IS FUN! But it's only fun for so long before you start seeing it's faults, and these faults really take away a lot. This is a long review because I REALLY like the core concept for this game and want to recommend it, but there are several key things that I feel need to be changed or added to the game, otherwise I think it's at risk of an early death. #1: "killboxes"/unbeatable maps- You don't have to beat your own map before publishing it so players are encouraged to just stack a huge room full of traps that are near impossible to get through. 9/10 brutal maps I come across are killboxes and it makes me not want to play the higher difficulty maps, however the lower difficulty maps are too easy. Adding the requirement that the publisher has to beat their own map (or upload it socially for someone else to beat) to be able to add it to the main story roster feels like a necessary step to keep this game from dying. #2: Trap timings- The delay on trap activation is way too long. I can play almost any map and just speed run through it, and as long as I have a place to sidestep/backstep I can ALWAYS get out of the way of the trap. You should not have enough time to hear the trap activate, locate it, and then shoot a relatively slow moving arrow at it BEFORE it goes off. Traps need to be more punishing in their timing or at least a way to hide their visibility via upgrades or something to offset their insanely long buildup. #3: Lack of "triggers"- I have many trap ideas that are ineffective because there is no way to set their activation based on a trigger. I like to set AI to chase the players after a set amount of time via the patrol recording, however if a player steps off the main platform and doesn't enter the map the timing is completely ruined and the surprise is lost. I need a way to activate certain things when a player touches a specific spot. Balance wise you could set the trigger to only activate a single trap or a set number of traps so people can't just activate an entire room of flamethrowers when you get to the middle of it. It could also be made expensive to build so having a triggered trap costs 3x more than a standard visible trap. A trigger would also stop people from just corner peaking constantly and taking out every single thing.#4: Slow/Bad progression/currency earnings- I have so many levels on the AI characters in my main base and I have no idea what those levels are for. As far as I can tell, all unlocks are just stuck behind an earned currency paywall and currency is earned excruciatingly slow. Particularly the orange currency which is necessary for upgrading traps and creatures, as well as purchasing and prestiging your maps. The main problem comes down to having to use orange currency for everything useful, and how little you get outside of leveling up. On each map is a node that has a chance to drop currency and if you are able to find every node you may get up to 150 or more. However the map doesn't require that these nodes are accessible, and most players don't even realize those nodes are on their maps and don't design maps around them. The majority of the time the node is blocked off and I can't even get to them which means I get a whopping ZERO orange currency that run. And the only other decent way to get it (that I've found) is having players die on your map which leads me to my next and I feel most important aspect that ruins this game for me.#5: 24 hour map life- If you make a map it only stays in rotation for 24 hours before depleting and you have to spend ORANGE CURRENCY to prestige it and reupload it. That means double your investment just to have a CHANCE to earn your money back. I've had one map that I prestiged twice and when I first made it, about 8 different players tried it out, then I prestiged it and about the same amount of people played it, and I prestiged a third time and 1 person played it. 24 hours is not nearly enough time for a map to be active, and if you get especially unlucky you won't have a single person play it. I spent about 3 hours making a map that had zero players try it out likely because it was a monday. And when having players try your map is the main way to make decent money it's insane that you don't get to keep it for more than a day. The timer should at LEAST be based on how long players are on your map, otherwise you just get unlucky and nobody plays it, and then you can't afford to prestige it.Some small gripes: Why are boosts only active for like, 20 minutes? You spend 100+ of a currency for a chance at more of a different currency and it's only active for 1 or 2 runs? This especially doesn't make sense for currencies earned when players die on your map. If I only get one player over the course of 24 hours why would I ever spend money to have a small boost for 20 minutes that's almost guaranteed to be completely wasted. Leveling up the character makes the boost longer but my guys are like 10+ and it's still around the half hour mark. Not worth the money at all.The grappling hook should have weighted physics to it, or an alternate version that has physics. It would just be way more fun being able to swing around instead of ziplining straight forward. Replays are super laggy/glitchy. Half the fun of this game is watching people play your map for the first time but there's a lot of desync and visual glitches that hinder that experience a lot. I assume this will be fixed in a future patch but it's a pretty big deal. Having to load into your building mode to collect dropped loot from dead players is unnecessary. I feel like it's a holdover from a previous build that didn't have the replay system so you could see which traps were killing players but I already watched the replay so having to manually collect it is just tedious. The tombstones are helpful as reminders but just give me my loot. Upgrades are expensive and feel pretty worthless. I get 1 extra arrow and a shorter reload for the same currency that upgrades my traps which have a way higher return on investment so why bother with them. I haven't even bought the other suit yet because I can't see what it does and it's too expensive to throw money at just to try it out. The little guy that walks through the map makes sense in concept so that you're always guaranteed a path to the objective. It really stifles creativity though in terms of jump puzzles and verticality when you have a grappling hook for movement but everything needs to be wheelchair accessible. It also limits secret paths and mazes because you just watch where he goes and he leads you directly to it.
_childDocuments_.name: Meet Your Maker

_childDocuments_.review: Okay so, 5 hours in... Meet Your Maker is a fun combination of dungeon building and trap defence (similar to Orcs Must Die!) and raiding other players' bases. The game runs smoothly and all the features feel very intuitive - the developers have obviously looked at how other games do base building and have taken a lot of good features. After a player raids your base, you have the option to watch their replay to see where you outsmarted them... and where you need to do more work!It's a visually pleasing game - the grimy "Mad Max" aesthetic is done well and, alongside the near-constant paranoia of looking out for traps and monsters, you feel quite immersed in the universe of the game. Where this gets muddled though is in the progression. There's no "story" to speak of, only the grind for resources to improve your equipment, traps, base or buy new land to create new bases. The upgrades though feel overly-expensive and having glanced through most of them I find myself uninspired to pursue any of the different areas mentioned above. It feels like it's a technique to add longevity to the game, but it's over-extended and actually feels disheartening. Even the most minor of upgrades means a sizeable grind, or sacrificing buying that new plot of land you've been working towards. I'd like to see 10 times as many upgrades at half the cost, and upgrades which actually effect play style - as it is, almost everyone plays the same way because there's little you can do to TRULY change your load-out.Is it a AAA title? No. What it does, does it do well? Yes!It's important to remember that MYM has only just been released and personally I'm eager to see where this game goes.
_childDocuments_.name: Meet Your Maker

_childDocuments_.review: This game fills a niche of something i've always wanted in a game, the ability to setup an outpost with guards and traps, setup patrol paths with those guards and then see other players interact with it via replays is absolutely incredible.  For builders and raiders alike there is a hub that lets you buy new weapons, suits, armor, traps, guards and upgrades/modifications for all of them via resources you earn buy base building and raiding.  Everything you play is player created content, and if you run into a base thats an absolute pain in the ass to beat with the gear you have you can leave and abandon that outpost to get another one.  While i'm not the best raider your gear loadout may allow for more optimal clearing of these harder outpost..seriously try buying the shield, throwing grenades etc on harder outposts etc.
_childDocuments_.name: Meet Your Maker

_childDocuments_.review: It reminds me of building a mob farm on Minecraft...except instead of zombies, skeles, and creepers...its real-life humans that fuel you with their peril....and their peril is sweet.Runs excellent (8700K, 3080Ti FTW3, 32GB Ram, 3840x1600)Rewards strategy, both for raiding and building. Both cautious and reflexive playstyles are required in a delicate dance to avoid death.
_childDocuments_.name: Meet Your Maker

_childDocuments_.review: An absolutely fantastic and brutal marriage of Mario Maker and Quake. Building is satisfying as you get to see all of the would be thieves die to your traps in replays. Progression is simple with bursts of bonuses from running Champion outposts. Lots of little upgrades and different ways to configure your outposts, traps and minions.Love it.
_childDocuments_.name: Meet Your Maker

_childDocuments_.review: Really fun game. Puts level design in the player's hands, bringing out all kinds of devious ideas that are so fun to be challenged by, not to mention people coming up with all sorts of cool aesthetics and themes to their maps (Giant prison? Eerie tomb? Circus tent?). Gameplay is extremely satisfying. You have a grapple and double jump, cool katana, and electric rifle with limited ammo that challenges you to use your bullets, and your movement, strategically. Cyborg guards get split in half, bombs drop from the ceiling, you can slice through incoming arrows. It's really cool.Overall, I love it and I would recommend it to anyone who likes FPS-style building trapped up bases, watching people attempt them (the game has a replay feature for everyone who plays your map), and running through the gauntlet yourself to fly out of a trap-infested ruin like Indiana Jones.
_childDocuments_.name: Meet Your Maker

_childDocuments_.review: Found it a lot more fun to actually play than the gameplay videos led on.Watched a few reviews and thought it would be ok/fun but once I started playing, the hook of beating someones base, watching your base destroy players and upgrading gear was far more enjoyable than I expectedCurrently the content for me personally is enough to justify the price, but the game will only keep getting better as content gets added. Especially enjoy knowing that my bases are raking in resources and XP for me while I'm not playing the game. This just adds to the base building enjoyment and satisfaction of the game

_childDocuments_.review: I think the negative reviews are warranted. I really think that the game is great to play with friends and solo when you get a few mods(upgrades). The killboxes people talk about are not fun while playing solo but are a lot more manageable with a friend or two. I think that if they made the player SOLO their base/dungeon before it goes active it could prevent a lot of these "impossible killboxes". Currently the only thing you need to do is allow the robot/human to walk to the objective and back. This means you can't have any jump/vertical puzzles in the game. This is a disappointment just because they built such good mobility into the game. There would be no need for this robot-chicken-man IF you made the player solo their own dungeon from start to finish successfully. It would also allow for a lot more creativity in the map creation.I do think this game is great! The bones are solid and with time it will be an amazing niche game that you can't get anywhere else. Its worth the money as it is right now. But do remember that "Brutal" difficulty is just that, dying 10+ times to figure the map, then dying 10+ more times to get it done. Its a great game. Play it and bring a friend!

_childDocuments_.review: This is a changed review from Positive to Negative. The core concept of this game is great and the game play is fluid and smooth. This game is a classic example of what could have been but never was.Original idea, great core mechanics and fun game play loop.So why the thumbs down you ask?Simple, the game has exploits and like all games that have them gamers will abuse them because that's human nature sadly, and the Dev's not fixing it or addressing the issue only serves to show how invested they are in making a fun experience for the player vs make money in the short term. i have 125 hours in this game and the first 100 were fun, now the servers have degraded into exploited bases nearly every time and it's not enjoyable anymore.Also the grind is pointless, you level up all your stuff and it honestly makes little difference to the game play at all, I would suggest giving it a few years until it either has more content or they fix all the issues, but for the player base that supported this early I think the damage has been done and people will move on.Also you won't get all the content unless you spend money on other games / products to unlock it all which just stinks of greed and VERY poor marketing choices. When will dev's learn that games should be inclusive and fun, that is what you pay for, not this piece meal garbage that has been served up here.Anyway I hope this helps  you make a choice about it, for me I am moving on to other games and won't be returning.

_childDocuments_.review: Thoroughly enjoying this game and high hopes for its future.The loop of needing to raid to be able to build is clever and though the 'retiring' of level 10 bases seems unpopular with some i see it as perfectly sensible if you want to let new maps have room to be found and played.I spent 100s of hours in various TrackMania games that had similar building mechanics and I expect to do the same with MYM.I'm hoping we get to see maybe some more 'props' in game, maybe some thing like doors that aren't necessarily one of the only three shapes available for building. _childDocuments_.review: The game is not bad overall but I wouldn't advise a game of this style for general audiences, it suffers from a critical flaw.It relies purely on players to carry the entire weight of the game. By large people are not used to ingenuity or creativity (they can learn it) and as a result, levels are not fun or challenging more often than not. Player's time is more wasted than engaged and there is no content the player engages in outside player content or making content themselves.There is also no gate to players being forced into maps when the maps prohibitively are designed to only allow some builds to win. The base gear is 2 bullets and a sword base, if I have not upgraded, there are designs I literally cannot do anything against, but I have to try them to cycle them. 2 armored Warmongers, with 2 more behind me, with pistons and a flamethrower and all this trap density that goes off in second phase. It's too much. 2 bullets is not enough, the sword prioritizes wall traps over guards. There's no real way to dismantle it, or enjoy this without the tools. Since the game gates your progress behind playing levels to unlock those tools, players can spend hours trying to handle these setups to get the tools to handle them, it's all uphill, there's no skill, it's bashing your head against a wall and some players definitely have to be experiencing that.There's a lot of various smaller issues too. EasyAntiCheat for starters. Beyond that are weird glitches, terrain that catches, player grapple not disengaging reliably, traps shooting through terrain edges, bullets not going through open air, bullets not destroying traps on direct hits, traps not detecting a player in range and direct line of sight, a lack of corner block holograms, all second wave blocks are instead grey blocks that don't match, second wave corrosive cubes still glow in first wave, ammo being stolen by dead guards into irretrievable locations, players blocking off tombstones intentionally, jumps having different physics not related to mods (sometimes you can jump up 1 block, sometimes you can't, might be a spacebar input issue, shouldn't be inconsistent though).The game needs a way of flagging maps for repetitiveness (when seeing too many map clones) and for being "unfun", which while subjective feels prudent to internally figuring out what players are really not enjoying. I don't think things are "unfun" because they're hard to be clear. I think "unfun" is stuff like a map where an enemy glitches your ammo into 3 layers of corrosive cubes intentionally or a featureless grey hallway of nothing except spike traps. It's subjective again, but allowing players to flag those maps would give them positive feedback for what they didn't want to engage with, while giving Devs internal stats to help the game improve.

_childDocuments_.review: I wish there was a [Meh] or a [Neutral Opinion] option, but there isn't so i'll just have to go to the one I lean on the most.This game is great for a few hours, then you slowly start to realize a lot of the numbers are useless and don't go anywhere. Like most cookie cutter games of our time. This has a unique premise, but pretty stupidly executed.First the story is your basic apocalyptic mad-max with kill houses instead of regular houses, your boss is a giant fetus that everyone takes orders from because.... That's right. Because. The Chimera doesn't strike me as something that should lead an operation into humanities salvation, it strikes me as a science project that became self aware and started to build a savior complex.The game itself is pretty simple. You are a created thing, that goes into buildings made by other created things and then you create things to kill other things or protect you from things trying to kill you. I say things a lot because that is exactly what everything is. There is no overarching faction or enemy at large, it's just mutated things built from test-tubes or traps built from mutated test tube people.The fun factor varies. Do you like beating your head against a wall and trying to solve 1 map? Do you like killboxes?I've played this game a lot and did some metrics. I played 200ish raids, of those 200 every other one, was a killbox. A map that was less a level in Doom or some other forge-style game. And more of a; throw everything into a small room.But you know people are going to do that if killing nets you rewards, also the point of the game is tomb raiding and security needs to be tight? Well it's hard to be a locksmith in the era of plastic explosives, and the explosives used to crack most maps are.1) Shield2) Adrenaline3) Free Space.95% of the time you can just speed run a level that was meant to take 10-15 mins, just by popping a 3-4 second shield and some go-go juice then running through the map. Taking the prize, then doing the same exact thing out of it. Sure you might die 1-2 times while you get the feel of it. But you'd complete a lot of maps this way.Someone made an elaborate bomb puzzle? Rush through it. Warbringer Spam? Grenade as equipable, rush through the armor or even back-stabbing them through the front like a TF2 spy. Firewalls? Shield and rush through it.Gotta problem? Shield and rush through it.The traps take 1-2 seconds to trip, now I know that doesn't sound like a lot. But when you're actually walking through it the time gives you plenty of space to just waltz right through it. The fastest trap is a spike-trap that pierces you with sharpened rods and you can just go through it at default running pace. Tack on other traps that take 2-3 seconds LONGER to trip and you wonder why people aren't dying left and right to good positioned traps. Make the shield have limited uses so that the sword deflection is actually used on some traps and increase the AoE of grenades if you're only going to give out 3. Make mods for the equipment so grenades can glide ontop of acid too. If builders have mods for their stuff, why can't raiders?So if map makers can't reliably use the traps what do they do to get rewards via kills?Killboxes and spam. Oh i'm sorry you want your 2-3 hour thought out build to be up to speed with the meta of shield and speed? Don't care. Here is a room full of eyes that shoot the same damn AoE bolt, riddled with pistons that take 6 years to get through and flames instead.Oh you want your ammunition back after it was lost in an acid cube? Or perhaps it is too far away in the killbox for you to reliably get some? Too bad, guess you should use the Sword + shield meta and get the new suit ASAP so you aren't behind. The direction here is all over the place and easily fixable. Give raiders more equipment to mess around with [3 Equipables instead of 2], make traps proc faster and harder to spot around corners so it is a guessing game of whether or not what you are shooting is an actual trap and actually reward players for incorporating Lost Tombs in their maps. Give a mod for creatures so they can't friendly fire [Cannonball] and make some of the other traps more viable so we don't spam Bolt + Homing or Eye + Field. Allow trappers to tweak traps in different ways like proc-time [For bombs] and give like 30-50 points for free in the creator for cosmetic purposes.BHVR I know from looking at DBD that you're not exactly keen on Balancing, but I am begging you. This game is going to nose-dive fast if you don't make it [FUN]. Not everything has to be a competition, I'm going to reliably say that no one cares about what rank they are in a tomb-raider game alright?

_childDocuments_.review: This game is really fun raiding and base building wise, but I simply cannot recommend people play this game as is. Lots of text ahead:Base building seems to have a large part of RNG to it. Layouts of the maps you get are seemingly randomly generated, which can make building a base you had in mind completely impossible, on top of this you don't get to choose where the end-goal (genmat) is, nor where any of the side-goals (tombs) are either. This can be extremely annoying, and can cause some builders to just either completely block off or ignore side-goals all together. Edit, this is sorta better since their matchmaking update, but the amount of raiders you get is still way too low on average.  Edit, after prestige and matchmaking reworks it's much easier and consistent to prestige your bases.Raiding can range from fun to infuriating. I've seen a lot of creative, inventive, and super fun bases while I've played, but on top of this I've also encountered a very large amount of the same type of base you've probably seen referenced in other reviews, killboxes.I've never found a killbox I couldn't beat, but that doesn't mean that killboxes are fine or even enjoyable. They're tedious, waste time, and waste your resources in the form of gear. Simply put, there is no base that can't be beat, but there are MANY bases that are extremely awful and boring to raid. Because of this, playing on harder difficulties only prove a challenge because of how much of your time they waste. The harder the difficulty, the less creative, inventive, and fun the bases get. Not because the bases are actually harder, but because there's a very clear cookie-cutter meta at the higher difficulties that cut out the creativity that is present at other difficulties where it's more difficult to fill rooms with traps: Death pistons with flamethrowers behind them, rooms full of plasma sentinels, armored cannonbacks that line the walls, acid cubes and grapples as far as the eye can see, and sometimes all of these are used and combined in the same raid, or even in the same room.Rant aside, raiding has potential to be fun, but steps need to be taken in order to ensure that it's fun for the raider to play the game, otherwise you're purposefully killing half of the gameplay loop. And no, I don't think that forcing builders to complete their own base is the solution, because the only road that'll lead down are hidden holo-blocks that allow the builder to easily complete the base while leaving the actual raider in the dark. (I think the quickest way to deal with the issue is to force trap uniqueness, making raiders only able to use so many of one type of trap, but this also comes with its own set of issues.) Edit, after roughly 65~ hours of gameplay (including time from the open beta), I have maxed out all advisors, armor, biolinks, weapons, equipment, guards, traps, and the chimera. tl;dr it takes about 65 hours to max everything outGame has lots of potential, can be really fun, but building has a surprising amount of RNG and raiding devolves into tedious time-wasters at higher difficulties.I'll change my review if any of the things I have talked about change in the future.

_childDocuments_.review: Level creators don't have to actually beat their own stage before posting, and the game incentivizes you to create brutal stages because you get currency for every person you kill.  This results in any stage you try to play either being incredibly hard for no reason, downright unfair, or specifically created to waste your time.I've had stages with giant arenas with a ton of enemies slapped on it that takes around 20 minutes to fight through because the combat in this game is simplistic and clunky.  I've had stages that spawn-kill the NPC that walks from the start of the stage to the end so you have to walk through a gigantic maze with no guidance.  I've had literal walking sims where you spend 5-10 minutes walking to the goal, only for tons of traps to spring up on you and instantly kill you as soon as you grab the materials.  So you then have to do the beginning part all over again just to try again.Every single person is trying to make a ♥♥♥♥♥♥ kaizo mario level.  This isn't an enjoyable mario-maker style game where you can find fun, casual levels, challenging but fair levels, etc.  The levels are encouraged to be unfair, and as a result, it makes the game incredibly un-fun.Edit: Found out that the reasons the stages are like this is because the stage creator has needless limitations that essentially forces makers to create bland, uninspired stages.  There's an NPC called "The Harvester" that needs to have a clear path from start to finish in order to upload the map.  Issue is, the Harvester can't jump, and walks very slowly.  So despite having a double jump and grappling hook, EVERY SINGLE STAGE needs to be completable without jumping a single time. Needless to say, this limits what makers can do significantly, and forces them to spam traps or enemies and create actual horrible stages in order to compensate.  If they try to make a normal, fair level, you can actually run through the entire stage by just holding forward and running through the whole thing. I've tested this on around 20 different stages, and 18 of them were completable with this method.Would not recommend. It's a game that is entirely focused on user-generated content.  The user-generated content is bad and not fun to play, and the creation tools are so limited and hard to work with that it's hard to actually create anything fun or good.  It fails on both aspects.

_childDocuments_.review: This game has a really interesting concept. You build a base, or bases (or outposts, as they're called here) in a Minecraft fashion - all the items you can place are cubes. People can raid your base, with the objective of finding their way the the precious Genmat, which you have hopefully fiendishly hidden in your trap-filled maze. Most outposts end up looking quite like oldschool Doom levels, and there are some truly inventive designs out there already, even though the game has only just released.Of course, you should raid other bases too, because all the resources you manage to collect in someone's outpost are yours to keep and put towards upgrading your own outpost, or upgrading your traps and guards.Your character comes with a grappling hook, gun and sword as standard. Your weapons are for killing guards, and destroying traps. Traps are flat plains that you can stick to any surface of any cube, and they range from  spikes that shoot out on contact, or projectile traps that will shoot arrows or bombs at you (and a bunch of other devious things), depending on their configuration. Your weapons can be upgraded to have more ammo, or a faster lunge or swing with the sword, for example. Currently there are 2 different suits you can choose from - a more ranged type and a more melee type. Like everything else, the suits are upgradeable with perks.The absolute best feature about Meet your Maker is the replay system. Anyone who attempts a raid on your base has their run saved for your viewing pleasure, and it's a real thrill watching people trying to navigate your base, and seeing how some people obliviously pass by obvious areas where you've left easy access to resources for them (players stealing your resources doesn't subtract those resources from your stash - you lose nothing if someone beats your outpost (unless you opt for the ability to let your stuff be actually stolen, but the default settings loses you nothing).It's a great new morning ritual for me, to sit with a coffee and some of the devil's lettuce and watch people trying to raid my outpost.Since I also own Dead By Daylight, made by the same devs, I got a cool extra tileset of blocks with the DBD theme. Very nice touch.This game is already a firm favourite of mine, and by the looks of things there's a lot more cool stuff on the way. I bought this here on Steam, and then it went free on PS+, and I don't even care. It's worth the price and it's far more suited to mouse & keyboard than a controller. I've noticed that console players generally have a much tougher time, especially when trying to line up split-second panic shots against guards. But hey, if you don't feel like shelling out cash for this game, I'd say go grab it for your PS5. Meet your Maker is something that really has to be experienced, and seriously, the replay system is a stroke of genius.There is one gripe that many people have an issue with though, which is your outpost has an expiry date. While active it generates Genmats for you, but when they dry up the base goes offline. You can use some of your in-game currency (earned by playing, not bought with cash), and "prestige" your outpost, making it live for everyone else again. After 10 prestiges (which will take a while), your outpost is removed from circulation, but it's still not the end. If you're particularly fond of your outpost you can set it to "social" instead of simply "active", and it'll stay up for ever. Only thing is you won't generate any more resources from Social outposts, but at least you can technically keep it up and running purely for the enjoyment of other players.Solid 9/10 from me.Edit: Typos.

Either way…When two dungeons called “easy” have a cakewalk right next to a deathbox-- I realized rolling the dice on raiding wasn’t worth the fun of building. I’m not here to drown. I’m here to build. But with the currency needed to build mostly locked behind raiding, the rising water level I just faced was not one I want to repeat.Thank you for the hours spent. _childDocuments_.review: I played a lot of the beta so my hours here may not reflect that. Calling this a First Person Shooter is a stretch.  This is more of a player-generated puzzler played in a first person view where occasionally you may need to "shoot" something with a harpoon gun.  The entire point is that another player creates a building full out of different blocks, fills said building with traps and enemies, and places an "End" point somewhere inside of it.  Once you find the end point, a second layer of the building opens up which could potentially contain more traps, more enemies, or a more complex layout.  It's fairly simple but can get fairly addicting, and the premise of infinite user generated content makes the $30 very enticing.  The main issue you may run into on more difficult missions is people creating "killboxes" where the entire point is to immediately kill the player rather than provide a more unique challenge/puzzle to solve.  Besides that I'm having a great time finding unique and intricate maze with puzzles to solve and obstacles to overcome, with extra resources (used to unlock consumable items, permanent upgrades, and additional Tiles for your custom buildings) being available to pick up.  I'm curious how they'll expand upon this in the future, but for now it's a nice little thing to plug away at.

_childDocuments_.review: The game is just fundamentally flawed. It has a cool concept, but the game designed in an unfun way and there isn't enough content to justify the $30 price tag. It will be in the Death Garden in no time.Reasons it's flawed:1. Bad performing bases are incentivized: You build a base. If that base does well in terms of kills and accolades, it eventually goes inactive and must be prestiged to the next level to reactivate it. Once you hit Prestige 10, your base can never be reactivated in the normal matchmaking pool again, it can only be put into "Social" mode. But there is no incentive to ever raid social mode bases because you don't get resources from doing it, and simply trying to browse social mode bases is a mess and basically broken unless you know the author/base you want to raid.However, if your base DOESN'T do well in terms of kills and accolades, then your base doesn't prestige, but it still goes inactive, but you can reactivate it and attempt to get enough prestige points again. So effectively, a base that performs poorly can exist in the matchmaking pool indefinitely compared to a good performing base. It's not that hard to get the resources required to reactivate a base through raiding, which brings me to my next point:2. The game punishes builders who don't want to raid. You don't get nearly enough resources from raiders dying to your base to afford all the upgrades. And you barely start with any traps/guards. I've seen multiple comments from people who were discouraged by the game because they were essentially forced to raid for resources. Personally I like raiding more than building, but that leads me to my next point:3. The lack of block types lead to uninteresting bases. Cube. Ramp. Corner block. That's all you get. I'm glad they're adding more decals and block textures, but the game really needs new geometry available. The more you play this game, the rarer it gets to see an interesting base. And that happens a bit too quickly.
