_childDocuments_.review: I thought this game might have potential, but it is hamstrung by both the developers design philosophy, and the games lack of actual content.In short, the game is a simple community driven game divided into two main parts: raiding, and building. Builders create levels consisting of traps and a few basic enemies, while raiders play through levels for some minor resources and progression rewards. Meet Your Maker in concept is similar to a game like Mario Maker, but plays like a slower paced Doom title. This on paper sounds good, and if executed differently, it probably would be. So if the game is conceptually sound where do things go wrong?The biggest issue, is that all of the incentive and reward for building a level lies with how many people you kill. The developers even leaned into this in their marketing and trailers which for me is the most concerning part of it. This simple design concept snowballs into lots of other issues that I'll get into.Because builders from the get go are encouraged to kill the raiders above all else, it means that zero regard for player enjoyment is put in place. 95% of levels you will come across will be complete garbage, and there is no way to filter the quality of levels you play.So if every level is designed to be as miserable and unfair as possible, does this mean the raiding feels impossible and hopeless?Surprisingly, the answer is no.The developers knew that this would happen, but instead of changing the incentive and rewards for building, they made the building tools ineffective. The game puts many features in to protect the raiders from the atrocities getting thrown their way. The danger indicators are so overly generous, that traps are extremely trivial to avoid. Even the most effective traps are extremely one dimensional, and over half of the tiles and perks are completely useless.The second biggest issue with Meet Your Maker, is the games lack of content.As a raider, the tool and weapon variety is so scarce that they might as well not have custom loadouts to begin with. This doesn't pose too much of an issue, and clearly was done on purpose to make the game easier to balance.Building on the other hand, is unforgivably shallow. There is only four total enemies, and nine total trap tiles. Typing nine feels disingenuous because in reality you are only using five of these tiles. The tile and enemy perks, while interesting at a glance, barely add any depth to the gameplay, and less than half of them are effective in any way.The lack of content is exacerbated by the games horrible progression system. The developers were worried that players had nothing to work towards and the game would have no longevity, so you start off the game with about 10-20% of the games already limited tools. This means that the majority of the levels you are going to play through are going to have the exact same three trap tiles and basic ranged enemy with no perks. There is some irony to this, because by locking building tools behind a progression system, the levels as a result feel even more repetitive. This in turn is going to do more harm to player retention than not having a "DING DING LEVEL UP HERE'S YOUR PRIZE" style incentive.In conclusion, Meet Your Maker is a conceptually interesting game that doesn't live up to its potential. The games only content is what was created by the players/builders themselves, but the developers chopped off the builders arms, resulting in a monotonous gameplay loop. Good co-op fun for a day, but there's no meat on the game's bones to keep you coming for more.

_childDocuments_.review: Meet Your Maker is a good concept that has been tried many, many times, and it, like so many other games before it, fell prey to the same issues that plagued every other game. The game struggled to find a healthy balance making people want to play levels and create levels. They incentivized kill box designs that encouraged unsatisfying levels, because those were the most profitable, and in turn made it a hassle to play, meanwhile you were unable to create levels because of the miniscule amount of drops that you received which were necessary to create levels.The only successful game of this type was likely Mario Maker, and this game is unfortunately a far cry from it. There's fun to be had, the actual gameplay mechanics were solid, but unfortunately the developers were too blind, deaf or confident in their vision to budge to community demands, to the point where they've now decided to abandon ship.Do not buy the game, it's neither worth the money (even after the price drop), nor worth your time.

_childDocuments_.review: First off, I actually like this game. That being said, I'd be a jerk recommending it to anyone in its current state. There are SO many great tools, both for raiding and building, but the game is structured around incentives that encourage players to use these tools in ONE way. It has been said and then echoed that switching to a mario-maker-style map verification system would improve most of the game's core issues. I'm not going to break from the pack on that one. There is the obvious upside of keeping people who are bad at the game from challenging the people who are the best at it. The unending tide of kill boxes would turn into a trickle, and each one would go from being an arresting speed bump in the gameplay loop to a seriously impressive feat by whoever made it. That would be nice—really nice—but there's a bit more of a benefit than that.The current way MYM determines whether or not a map is beatable is by checking if a small cargo guy can waddle across an uninterrupted path between the base's central goal and the outside. In a very literal sense, that works, but it causes bases to all follow the same claustrophobic theme as raiders are bound to the track of the NPC that cannot even jump. Juxtaposed against that, the raider has a double jump and grappling hook, allowing for a degree of fun and responsive mobility that you can only currently experience by hopping around the outside walls of the trap-laden labyrinth with its 1 by 1 corridors that you just loaded in to. A jumping puzzle map was one of my first ideas when I saw the trailers for this game, so while I'm disappointed on a personal level, the regimented nature of drawing a straight line to the goal flies in the face of potential level diversity as a whole. Conversely, opting for the 'mario maker' style of letting the map maker prove their map is beatable by doing it themselves would let builders embrace more unique level ideas and keep the game unpredictable and give people—and I mean me—a constant reason to come back. Clearly, though, that isn't currently the case. There's a very 'samey' feeling to nearly all bases, and while the current map verification is a contributor to that fact, it's not nearly the biggest.Before I mentioned the tools players are given in MYM. There's a small but actually really varied arsenal that raiders can get their hands on: High ammo guns that can only kill enemies, swords for deflecting bullets and swords for crushing enemies' armor, and an invulnerability shield that rewards you for perfect parrying instant death. You get to bring two of these in at a time which leads to interesting builds and fundamentally changes your relationship with the map you're on. One build I like is the samurai that just runs around dual wielding blades and slashing everything to pieces. It's the same on the builders' side: there are grapple traps that reposition raiders, hologram walls that drop raiders and let you do some seriously creative stuff with monster positioning. But for all of that, raiders get rewarded for doing one thing: escaping the map. And builders? They get rewarded for one thing: killing raiders. The current state of the game shows how in-game incentives warp a playerbase's actions.Now what I say next is just my experience. It's anecdotal, and doesn't exactly represent a perfect picture of the game. If anyone reading this wants to form their own opinion without sinking money into a game that might die before it has a chance to live, steam has refunds for a reason. With that said, personal experience is still the  kind of experience anyone is going to have with this game, and mine is the reason this review exists at all. That experience not only ends with the kill box but begins with it too.When I booted up the MYM beta a month ago, the first thing I did was try to build a base. I found the land plot purchasing menu and noticed they cost in-game currency. I just loaded up the game; of course it was going to be at zero. So I raided—went from level to level collecting orange boxes and ruby red cylinders—until I could afford my first map. When I got it, though, I was worried—worried that a map that flippantly followed my creative interests wouldn't kill enough players to earn me the points I needed for my second map. I think you can guess what I did, but I'll say it anyway. I made a kill box—a lazy, blocky, mess with uncountable traps and monsters all pointed at the entrance the players have no choice but to walk in to. The worst part is that I was right. My first map is about to expire for good, and it sits around 3700 player deaths. That map funded all the weird and wacky building I pulled off. I could afford my hologram wall because of it, I got the beefy guards that make close quarters combat exciting and terrifying. But when I make my creative maps now, there's that worry that I can't afford to keep it all running, and it literally costs currency JUST to keep a map running, if it wasn't deadly enough. So my maps are all a little aggravating—not as much as the first, which I'm actually glad is about to go offline, but there's a bit of my first in all of them now.My time as a raider was like Dante's Inferno. I truly think it was a very minor and almost comical microcosm of going to hell for my sins. Every map was a kill box. Every. Single. One. And in this I could only be frustrated with myself and the other builders for bending to the currents of digital currency. I didn't quit, however, I optimized my build instead. For the fun sucking, soul crushing kill box, there is an equally unfair and unbelievable raiders build. With a deflecting sword, invulnerability bubble, and a speed boost, you can race past the cramped and unimaginative dungeons faster than they were built. I didn't feel like I was missing something by crushing a person's base in a minute flat. You can take one look at the map you load into and see the stagnant lineage of every map that came before it. And when you know how that map will look and how it will play, the only thing left for a player to enjoy is winning, and I want you to remember how a raider wins:Imagine that. The two playstyle's simplistic and diametrically opposed incentives between keeping a raider as bogged down in your base and, as a raider, running through other players' bases so fast you couldn't remember what color the  were leaves us in a game state where the only fun—which is a word I am stretching to its limit—is when you are done playing. Meet Your Maker is so uncompromisingly geared towards results that there is no room for anything else.Now I can't really stomach playing much more. I know it says fifteen hours now, but I played the beta for ninety, and the game is very much unchanged since then. I only hope that MYM's dev team breaks with their mother-company's tradition of ignoring their players. Right now, this game doesn't even have the player base to survive that kind of belligerence. I've said it before—it's even my title—the community is right. They're giving advice and feedback freely after buying the game.I'd like to believe that the devs will implement at least some of the community's suggestions, but their hesitance to speak about it on AMAs and streams leaves me doubtful. And for everyone on the fence about buying this game, I say wishlist it. . If they structure their game around results and raw numbers, chances are they'll respond to them too.Anyway, i understand that was a massive wall of text. If you made it to the end, thanks for reading.

_childDocuments_.review: PROS:- Pretty unique gameplay, I don't think there's anything similar on the market at the moment.- Graphics look ok. Enemy designs are interesting.- Good sound design, can tell what traps are firing based off sound.- Combat and mobility feels good, although everything being a 1shot kill can take some time to get used to.- Co-op Rading is a blast with a friend, co-op building can also be fun.CONS:- The games progression system is extremely one sided. If you don't raid you'll not be able to get anywhere with progression, which is pretty unfortunate since I enjoy building the deathtraps a bit more then Raiding the deathtraps.- Resource gain feels too slow. I really hope they increase how much resources you get soon, especially Synthite. Parts are the only resource that feels about right.- The content feels a bit light, I feel like there should be many more enemy types, traps, suits and weapons to choose from. So it can feel a bit stale after a while.VERDICT:I think MYM has a lot of potential to go from a good game to a great game, it just needs more content and time to mature. If support is kept up and new content keeps coming, I think this will be a great game in a year or so. Would I recommend to buy it? Yes, but get it on sale if at all possible, the base price is a bit high for what you get in my opinion.

It is however really enjoyable to see tricks that others  have come up with and find your own way to mix techniques to make your own frustrating death trap.  I find myself watching the replays often of the attempts made on my base and find better ways to bypass those who are successful. The one thing I will say as the most important would be that this game does lose its luster after awhile.  That being said, if I can get at least 20 hours of enjoyment out of a game the price is worth it.  Its also one of those games you can easily pick up and put down at will, so replay value will always be there so long as there is a player base.

_childDocuments_.review: I have greatly enjoyed playing this game and likely I'll continue to enjoy it for a while.It's great to see the deadly designs that other players have come up with, and it's crazy how different individual bases can feel. The main weaknesses of the game currently is that there are somewhat limited gear options for the Raiders, and although there are many more trap types I feel like there could be way more. The decoration options are also somewhat limited, with only 3 shapes being supported currently. The Dev has a roadmap of what they plan for the game, and if this is maintained as planned this game should be playable for quite a while.

_childDocuments_.review: Has a cool enough concept, but fumbles a good bit of it. It's like Mario Maker, but creators aren't subjected to their own course prior to publishing, which leads to some frustrating challenges that are less challenge and more grief. Performance for this relatively simple game is rather poor, and the loading times between retries makes it a slog to continue. The NPCs in the main hub area are swiftly introduced and barely distinguishable from one another. The price is steep for the shallowness of the product--it may be worth it at $15-20, but at $30 ($40 with the "DLC"), it's insultingly high. I returned this product. I hope it gets better in the future, but I don't feel like my investment was worth it for the potential the game MAY achieve. Until then, I'll wait for improvements and a sale.

_childDocuments_.review: Played the hell out of the beta and picked the full game up late last night (thought it was out the following day)I think I have built a "kill box" that people are complaining about but I've only played 1 map before that's kind of like mine. To build a "kill box" is hard. If you just put traps everywhere, when a trap is triggered it can destroy another trap or kill a guard. You need to watch the replays of how people beat your map and improve it. Because of the time I've put into building my base, I get alot of kills, but 9 out of 10 co op players complete it and 6 out of 10 solos complete it. They just die alot and that's the point of building a base. I've played some maps that have some amazing ideas, using traps in ways I didn't think possible. I wish there was a way to leave a message to the builder to say what you liked and thought about parts of it. The whole game is a action puzzle that you have to work out when to run and when to take it slow. The people complaining need to learn that. People who grappling hook though my base fast and non stop, do it in 2 or 3 life's. People  who move slow trying to take out all the traps do it in 20 30 40 life's. Every map requires you to change your play style and that's what the hook of the game is.

_childDocuments_.review: The game can't be played for more than 10 to 15 minutes at a time without crashing to desktop and it's a common occurrence across varied hardware specs. I'm on a 3070 with 64gb RAM and it took me 3 hours to build my first base because it kept crashing and then deleting all my base building changes.It's also overrun with cheaters already. Most of the replays you see in bases involve people with infinite ammo who can either see your traps with an ESP cheat, or who skip the formalities and simply phase through your walls to get in and out in less than a minute.More importantly, and not as easy to fix, the bases themselves are a waste of time to build. They grant you resources but theyre on a timer where at the end of it they have to be "prestiged" or go inactive. This means your base can run out entirely without ever seeing a raider if you're unlucky. Once it reaches prestige 10 the base is permanently taken offline and all your work is lost. All in all, you get about 1 week per base before it either goes inactive forever OR can be made a "social raid" which means you can share it with your friends and it does nothing besides.Leveling, upgrading, etc is all meaningless. Your progression system is tied to collecting "GenMat" and leveling your advisors (merchants who provide weapons, gear, traps, etc) but leveling them does nothing but slightly increase the duration of boosts they provide. These boosts however cost money each time you use them and are by and large useless so progression feels, for the most part, like a meaningless treadmill designed to send you on endless raids for no benefit. Not that endless raids are that difficult because there's such a startling lack of trap diversity that if you've played about 10 to 15 bases, you've seen every combination of them. Don't get me wrong, every 1 in 30 bases you'll find something truly unique but most often you'll see the exact same configuration of killbox over and over and over until beating them becomes second nature. Sadly this means that unless you play on the highest difficulty (Where people can spam as many ridiculous and unwieldy traps combinations as they want) you get maybe 3 hours of challenge out of the game before you realize that you can use the grappling hook to zoom past literally everything untouched.In fact, the difficulty system is meaningless in itself. It has nothing to do with how difficult a given base actually is, instead it's based purely on how many trap blocks are placed down. This means that some Normal (easy level) bases are filled with completely unavoidable death traps and some Brutal (hard level) bases are just bizarre open rooms filled with a seemingly random assortment of ill-placed traps that you can walk straight through.The game also seems to be catering to the worst kind of PvP player. Trolls who intentionally wall off resource nodes called "Tombs" in such a way that it prevents players from ever accessing them all. Others still will intentionally use the games "Second Wave" mechanic to turn the room in which you acquire the GenMat, the games raiding goal point, into an inescapable death trap. This isn't possible before you acquire the Genmat because the Harvester (an NPC that leads players to the Genmat through the maze of traps) has to have a clear path from entrance to GenMat, however once the GenMat is acquired all bets are off and they can more or less turn every surface of the room into a giant trap that fires all the same time and decimates the player......Unless of course you use the item called the "Arc Barrier" which gives you god mode and once upgraded can basically be used to waltz through almost any base completely unscathed unless you choose to intentionally step into a giant glowing orange acid cube. (They glow. You can literally see them from a mile away and there's no logical reason anyone would be killed by one.)Edit: Also if you own Dead by Daylight, you get a special cosmetic block in a Dead by Daylight style. The issue is that the blocks are intentionally designed to perfectly mimic the texture of the traps. This means that players who own Dead by Daylight are at a distinct advantage against any legitimate raider because their traps are almost completely camouflaged.The Harvester is also frequently a target for trolls who intentionally kill him as soon as they enter their base. The base itself is then made into a giant 4K+ piece box filled with endless mazes that lead nowhere and take players an hour to navigate only to encounter a final room that spells instant death, designed solely to waste peoples time and then collect resources from their corpse when they rage quit.

_childDocuments_.review: I enjoy the game, both as a builder and a raider. There's a lot of people making remarks that builders are only rewarded for killing, so people make unfun killbox-style maps where they focus almost all their points in a dense fashion. Firstly. accolades are worth something to the builder, as it helps them prestige. Secondly: These types of maps can simply be left. If you walk into a map and go "Wow, this isn't fun" then just... leave. They miss out on the points they would get from you.Secondly, I recommend unlocking player tools such as the shield, upgrading your gun of choice to get extra ammo, or getting the armor-breaking alternate sword before getting base upgrades, especially if you want to raid more than you build. Many traps can only go off once. Pop out to trigger them, shield yourself, and simply back off to wait for your shield cooldown if you must. Purchase consumables such as the phoenix item that allows a respawn in single player. There ARE builds that are VERY frustrating to play with the basic starter gear, I totally agree with that criticism. I enjoyed the beta, and have been enjoying it on release. It's a recommendation for those interested in this sort of game, but it's not perfect, As of time of posting I do still occasionally crash trying to view a replay, or something similar, but hopefully that can be worked out.

Some items are 100% harder to unlock than others.I understand making the character gear hard to unlock, but do not understand making base upgrades so hard to unlock? _childDocuments_.review: I really have no idea how most of the game works but I do enjoy it.  I feel like it's excellent if you like building, it's also fun if you liked games like Mario maker.  It's less fun for the tiny corridor style everyone takes instead of making cool multilevel tombs but if you put the effort in, you can make something fun and dangerous.Edit:Got a bit more time under my belt now and I feel like everyone is starting to make real stages now.    Few things that I learned during my time that will make the experience smoother. Always want to keep at least 1 base up killing people, preferably 5 if you play a lot.  Without the bases, you will have to raid a lot more.  The bases help you get an extra upgrade each day(roughly), which is basically for free for the time investment(only needing to be prestiged once a day) once you build a base and it last for like a week.  You do need to pay currency to prestige the base but I don't think I've used it for anything else and have plenty of it always.Co op makes the game much more enjoyable. Since you can rez each other, you can play a lot more recklessly.  While this does make the game a lot easier, it also kind of inspires you to be more reckless and die a lot which rewards the base owners.Some stages cannot be beat with starter equipment and solo.  In my experience, I've only seen a few like this and exclusively on brutal difficulty.  I have experienced none on normal and difficult.Each stage has forbidden tombs which most people put decals to guide you to.  These drop extra resources.

_childDocuments_.review: This is an excellent game, I've already recommended it to a few friends. It's fun solo, and it's an absolute delight in co-op.Will you like Meet your Maker? That depends on what you're looking for.This is not a good skinner box, numbers go up, kind of game. If you're looking for limitless unlocks to spend your in-game currencies on you won't find them here. There is a small set of unlocks and they all contribute to gameplay directly. If you're looking for a gameplay loop where you run through levels quickly to grind XP you will be disappointed. Grinding will get you nowhere, each level is only worth the fun you had playing through it.This game's main strength is the player generated content. You just don't run out of content and you never stop being surprised. There are absolutely memes that you see frequently, trap A always followed by trap B in a certain configuration, but frankly I really like that. I've been playing since the beta and it's been really enjoyable to see what ideas phase in and out. You'll also see the same archetypes fairly often, but again I really like that. After a little while you can look at a level and tell how you're expected to engage with it. Is this level a maze? Is it an outdoor fight? Is it a kill box? etc.That said, you will certainly come across levels you don't enjoy. Sometimes these levels are so hard they aren't fun, other times they're so easy they aren't fun. Sometimes they're just entirely uninteresting, or exhausting to play. Fortunately there is NO PENALTY for leaving a level you aren't enjoying. If you aren't having fun just bounce.That's a recurring theme too, the game never punishes you for playing it, not playing it, playing it poorly, w/e. If you don't like building you don't have to do it. If you don't like raiding you don't have to do that either. If you like raiding but you find it too hard you can choose to play easy levels exclusively. If you run into levels that just swarm you with bad guys, etc. you can bring defensive gear and just run passed the hard parts. It's really up to you how much you want to engage with the game.Frankly I'm impressed overall with the design decisions the developers made. There were a lot of things that struck me as odd at first, but the more I played the more I realized that they made the right call. For example, this game doesn't do the traditional "the builder must complete the level to prove its possible" thing. Instead there's an NPC (Harvey) that has to be able to path through the level. At first I was like "boo, I don't like that, it limits the things I can build." And it does, but as a result you can always find your way to the goal by asking "what could Harvey do?" This is streets ahead of having a time limit and praying that you can find the path the builder memorized to complete the level in time.There's also a mechanic in the game called "forsaken tombs." These provide a tiny bonus if you find them, but there is no requirement that Harvey has to be able to reach them. This allows builders to put in additional, unconstrained challenges that you are under no obligation to complete.If you decide to give this game a try and find you aren't having fun stop and ask yourself "What's the fun way to approach this?" If you can't come up with an answer leave the level and pick another one, or take a break to build something instead. Throwing yourself into a level you aren't enjoying again and again is an easy way to burn yourself out.Oh, one other thing. If you build and publish levels you can access a replay console that will show you people's runs through your levels in first person. Honestly, watching these replays is some of the most fun you can have in this game. The moment where someone clears the difficult part of your level just to get sniped by something you forgot you left in? The moment when someone runs through your level EXACTLY the way you wanted them to? The moment when someone does something really cool that you didn't expect? It's just the best.

_childDocuments_.review: This game is addictive as hell. I love it.That said, its very niche. Think Doom meets Mario Maker. Also, if you love building bases in games like Rust, but hate getting offlined, this will definitely scratch an itch for diabolical trap building. I do wish there was some more cosmetic building options instead of just blocks and decals, but those may come with time.It's also snappy and quick. You can easily hop in for a 10-15 minute stab at a base and then hop off, and still farm up materials while people are attempting to raid your creation. Overall it seems to respect your time. Kudos to that.In sum, this is a nice, albeit extremely original take on a lot of other ideas done by other games, and I'm excited to keep raiding well into the future. I can easily see myself dumping a ton of time into this.

_childDocuments_.review: I want to love this game, but this game won't love itself. It is a victim of it's own design. My bases receive 1 maybe 2 Visitors a day, I have to refill my base once a day This costs 650-1,300. The number of visitors doesn't garnish enough experience to prestige. This leaves me to raid, and I come to bases that seem to be built the same, Long empty hallways that lead to a kill room it has 3-4 Plasma eyes, Units arranged along the sides, with flamethrowers covering them, Bolters set in the crevices, with bombs arranged to drop and fall along the way. I'm bored, Variety doesn't seem to be on the horizon just cosmetics, I'm holding out hope, but my experience asks how long before they need more money, and when they do will they offer a DLC that will change the game enough to ward away the feeling of repetition?

_childDocuments_.review: I did have to think on this one. I've had hours of fun with it originally, and even more fun once one of my friends joined me in the raids. Looking at Steam stats, the player base did drop, but it seems there are many, many more on console, so it's far from the dead game it might look like on Steam stats. Developer keep updating and adding.. balancing out new traps, items and guards that seemed particular  unbalanced or un-fun. So why is it a did I have to think? All that is great, but you will need to be prepared that the initial grind is real. There is a new raiding difficulty sorting, and it needs work.. some of the "Easy" one are really.. really not.. As a new player, there will be outposts you just can not survive until you upgrade your items. While many outposts are well though out and fun to play, there are maybe deathboxes, that may sap some enjoyment. You can abandon these though with no penalty (a great improvement from launch) I do recommend though. Frequently updated, and new reward track keeps things interesting when you have unlocked everything else. :)

_childDocuments_.review: Base building games like this are a rare treat, only a few I have seen close to this "Flavor" of the genre. But, where it does great in advertising, and teasing my hopes, it absolutely fell through in actual gameplay. The biggest limiting factor is the transporter that needs a perfect red carpet to get to the "Checkpoint" and back out. Combined with the absolute massive size of each individual unit you can place, it severely limits the possibilities of bases able to be made and absolutely rips creativity. Then, to compound this issue even further, by trying to compensate for the complete lack of content, they make every. single. possible. thing incredibly expensive, meaning you have to spend well over 100 hours to unlock everything. This game doesn't even have enough content to justify that. I could go on, writing a complete essay on everything thats ♥♥♥♥ with this game. Its a fantastic premise, but the executioin fails miserably, and I regret letting myself get excited about this game. And Im far from the only one that feels this way considering the game in a manner of months, went from 3000 players, down to 80-200, its such a disappointment.

_childDocuments_.review: great game idea terrible implementation, For one the game is not stable. I have a mid to high end PC and game will crash on launch screen. Base building is fun, getting people to try your base isn't. I've bought multiple bases and the only one i got close to prestige 10 was my first base. Kills mean almost nothing in the base which is a bummer since the point of the game is to make a map. Acolytes have too much value also if someone alt f4's while raiding your base you get nothing but time is still taken away from your bases lifespan. Raiding is easy and straightforward not very fun though, you can fly by most traps in a base with your zip line, if you get stuck don't worry there's a shield that give you immunity for a few seconds, also there a re spawn beacon you can throw down oh and there's another shield. You can literally zip-line from start to gen-mat capture and back to the exit and if your fast enough none of the traps can catch you. _childDocuments_.review: It's a fun game, but it crashes a LOT.  Once an hour, maybe more.  Also, there seems to be a bit of an incentive problem with building vs raiding.  Raiders don't have much of an incentive to play "Harder" outposts, since it's more likely to kill them and tank their ranking.  Even easier outposts don't get very many plays any more, as building seems to be far more popular than raiding.Honestly I could forgive the incentive problems if the game didn't crash literally every single time I played it, but until they fix the crashing issue I couldn't rightly recommend this to a friend.

_childDocuments_.review: The Game has fun and flexible core game mechanics and a give you good back and forth between Raiding an Outpost and Building you own one, if you like both!In the beginning the gameplay loop is exciting and interesting but after 100h in, I see that there are some grinds that need to balanced. Also, the game has definitely some problems with nearly unbeatable levels and player who trying to abuse the game mechanics to the extreme (like exploiting trap to kill harvester).Imho I can’t see that you can play as Builder only in the end game, even with cheesy outpost or KillBoxes which I don’t like so I don’t build such kind of Maps i can't see it.The Ranking System is a little bit clunky and only a real ranking system if you reach the Mastered Rank. Before that it is only getting point when your successful raid an outpost or loosing point when you get to much deaths or leaving a frustrating Map.I got enough Playtime for the money I paid (35€) and it was fun, but I think the content is only good for around 80-100 hours.At the moment I can’t recommend the game and I think the following things need to be changed before I will come back:-	The earning of Synthetic needs to be increased for Builder so that you also can as Builder Only. At the moment you Raid more then you Build your own Outposts.  -	QoL Feature that you can collect resources and see the remaining time of an Outpost without entering an Outpost over and over again.-	The Ranking System need to be clear for everybody-	Quicker Response to Exploits -	Filter for the Size of a Map-	Skip a base

_childDocuments_.review: I want to give this game a thumbs up. I do; it does so many things right; the look, the feel, and the entire idea is fantastic, but there isn't enough content to justify the price. Unless I'm missing something, you have a single unlockable ranged weapon, a single unlockable melee weapon, a single unlockable suit, 5-6 unlockable mutants to guard your outposts, and a handful of traps. Sure, all of these things have their own upgrades to go with them, and when it comes to the mutants and traps, I'll admit there's a nice selection, but suit and weapon upgrades are dull at best, and suit upgrades can be ignored. Sure, they're nice, but due to the nature of the game, there aren't major walls to overcome that require upgrades. I would have rather had skins or more suits in general. One of the game's primary goals has you "evolve" the chimera, something I thought would have a significant impact on the status/look of the sanctuary, but nope, you press a button and listen while the Chimera yells one of the few, repetitive voice lines at you. Leveling up vendors does... Well, I'm not sure what it does besides pulling them into the floor for several seconds, rendering them unusable for that time. No visual changes to them, maybe changes to the level of upgrade you can buy. Evolving the Chimera is made to look like you're doing something. When in reality, you're just opening a box of bonus resources. Several other reviews have already covered the issue with Killboxes, so I wont bother with that here, but it is a huge issue that needs to be resolved if the devs want any longevity out of this game. Once again, I could be missing something. There could be more content I still have yet to discover. Still, as of now, I see no signs of any extra unlocks, unless you count day one DLC (included in the deluxe edition) as extra unlockables. I'll happily change my review once the raiding side of the game gets some much-needed support and is no longer a content desert. If you must try the game, I remind you to keep and eye on your play time, and keep in mind that what you see in the level 1 vendor will be the exact same thing you see eight hours later in a much higher leveled vendor.

_childDocuments_.review: This was not a fun time in the slightest. There are different difficulties and "Normal" is the lowest. Many of the "Normal" difficulty maps are horrendously overblown with traps and obstacles. I had a decent time during the first few maps because they were neat little challenges, but then every other map I encountered was nothing but kill boxes. Just traps, traps, and traps. I understand the point is to kill players raiding, but when that's the goal, then what's the incentive to be creative? The game is so grindy that most people, especially the higher level players, are just making kill boxes, so they don't have to play the game as much and can farm resources that way. What a goofy ahh system.These kill boxes are what a lot of newer players will encounter as well because the game gives incentive to design kill boxes because the person who made the map gets money per player death trying to complete the map. They can even overclock their map to give them more money per player death, but lose money upon successes. Which is even more incentive for kill boxes. Newer players will also have a horrible time because there are 20+ traps in these kill boxes, but the player will have a sword and a weapon with 2 total shots to take it all out. That's it. Keep in mind, this is the start of the game, the lowest difficulty, and the first things a new player will see. There is also no way to report a map at all, so if you come across a map that is unbeatable, then too bad. All you're able to do is give 2 out of 4 different commendations. Just leave and try another. Oh, it's another kill box. Yippee.New players will have 3 traps to use and the only tweak is to hide until the crystal is picked up. Spikes, Bolts, and a red corrosive block that kills the player if they stay in it too long. Within the first 3 maps I had played, I had encountered a kill box that had many, many traps in a single room. Also, the difficulty is decided on the complexity of the pathway to the crystal that you have to grab is, not based on the rooms themselves. People just build tight corridors with traps outlining the walls and obstruct them being visible by putting the corrosive thick red blocks in front, so you have no idea what killed you or where it came from. People will also build a giant open area that has traps all over that just kill the player over and over again because they don't have the ammo or resources to deal with it all as a new player. The game's "difficulty" of maps means next to nothing and don't let that fool you in to thinking that the normal difficulty maps will be easier than other maps. It's awful and there is no real sense of difficulty in the game. No difficulty is harder than other difficulty because it just depends on who made the map and how they made it. It's just that the easiest difficulty will still stump a lot of players because of how riddled the rooms can be. A level 80+ player makes a killbox on "Normal" difficulty to farm rewards and can easily do it because they simply have access to more traps and better options for killing players and designing rooms. I understand the mechanic, but it's done so poorly that it just kills all/any fun.I have had an eye on this title since launch and was expecting a fun time with creative maps, some poorly designed maps, and a bit of difficulty, but I got an awful experience and more disappointment than Cyberpunk's launch. I'm glad they're letting people try this for free because I now have easily decided to never pick up this monstrosity.

_childDocuments_.review: I really like this game, but I recommend against it. Here's why.This is super mario maker meets quake. And its actually a really, really good idea. The problem is that it has harmstrung level designers.Every level will boil down to a straight line to the finish. This is because the way the game ensures you don't make unbeatable levels is to make a requirement that the Harvester, a lil dude that walks in and out of your base, can reach the objective and get back out. He can't jump, he can only walk on flat surfaces and slopes.You can't build a maze, because people will just follow the Harvester.You can't build platforming challenges, because the Harvester will not be able to reach the goal if you do.So the only thing you can do is try to blindside people, overwhelm them with enemy spam, or make the most frustrating killbox designs.Even the options they give you for trickery, like the Holocube which are fake walls/floors are way too obvious. Especially since the Holocube will mostly be used as a fake wall/ceiling because it can never be in the harvester's path if its just a corridor.The game needs more content, or to loosen up on a builder's ability to make more interesting level designs.

_childDocuments_.review: This game has a great concept and it's good enough for me to keep playing it, but it needs more time in the oven. When I started playing I really thought it was an early access release. For starters they LOVE loading screens,Every time you want to change an outpost status, collect resources from kills or prestige/reset an outpost you have to go into build mode, which requires a loading screen to get in and a loading screen to get out just to press one button. All of these options should be do-able from the hub. We're constantly changing maps to social so our friends can try them out, you have to then change it back to active after they're done, that's four loading screens. Loading is reasonably quick, but so unnecessary. There's usually very little reason to go back to the hub after a completing a map unless you want to upgrade or change to build mode, It'd be better if you were able to go into another map without loading back into the hub, there's no reason why you shouldn't be able to access the maps menu after I've finished the map.Watching a replay of someone playing your map is fun also requires loading into the replay and back to the hub, again no reason not to let us load into a different replay or a map to play. The Replay system also has a lot of issues, lot of lagging and freezing, especially when trying to jump forward or backwards.Going into a map to collect resources from your kills where the kills happen is cool but it gets pretty old fast, give us an option to collect all from the hub.There's currently four Accolades, they're fine but more would be better, especially negative ratings like "Boring" or "Long" I can guess the  reason for doing it this way but it feels bad to go into a ♥♥♥♥ map and the only option is to not play it and give no accolade. There's a LOT of really ♥♥♥♥♥♥ maps and no "This is a bad map" option.Having the little guide robot slowly lead the way and be able to be killed is really stupid, you can't have it both ways. Either don't show the path or show it all the time. You want people to be able to use the robot as a guide but you also want to slow down the pace of the game and make it boring.Being able to kill the little guide robot at the start of the map (or at all for that matter) shouldn't be possible, people do it and create boring ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ mazes with infinite paths and barely any traps, they take forever, they're not hard. It's just boring.Selling $20 DLC that give access to textures with the same colour as the traps is pretty ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ weak ¯\_(ツ)_/¯The game is fun and I'll get a decent amount of hours out of it, it's a little pricey for what you get and there are a lot of other minor problems not important enough to mention, I dunno how much work they're gonna put into refining this game, but until they do I can't recommend it.

_childDocuments_.review: This is a fantastically executed concept with a few minor issues. The core gameplay loop is FANTASTIC. Having user created maps makes the new content literally endless. The construction and traps systems is nearly perfect, and my only issue is the presence of the Genmat "gremlin" for level validation. The player has a much larger skill set when it comes to movement mechanics and being forced to make maps that this little box dude can navigate will feel like you're "dumbing down" the concepts you'd really like to execute. However, box dude's presence kinda makes a new playstyle, as some map makers will set alternate routes, hidden paths or trap setups based on the "guaranteed path", making it more dangerous to follow the gremlin or more rewarding to deviate. Plus it makes it so that no level is unwinnable. There's a good variety of enemy types, traps and player mechanics/abilities. All of those have a small catalog of mods that can radically change how the modded item behaves, adding tension for raiders and offering new strategies for map makers. The core movement and combat mechanics are nice and tight, and fit the game's atmosphere and pace well. However, I'd love wallrunning or at least walljumping (which you kinda have if you grapple hook good) at some point in later updates. One of the best features in here is the replay system. Not only can you replay your own attempts at storming people's bases, but all attempts on your bases are saved as well, for your viewing pleasure. You can learn the strengths and weaknesses of your design by watching how others navigate your deathtrap. Or at the least you can watch the player slowly descend into madness as the death room you built pushes their aim, patience and timing into the dirt.ALSO, the devs have outlined their DLC roadmap, and not only are they gonna be adding more content over the game's lifetime, but it seems like only cosmetic items will be purchase exclusive, everything else can be earned through gameplay (see: warframe).My only other gripe with this game is that, at least for me, it crashes a LOT. It never does it when im in the actual maps, but it really likes to crash when I enter/exit a menu in the main hub. Overall, I give this a 9/10, with a 10/10 if they change the level validator and fix the crashes. Buy this game, support this level of content quality, murder your friends and internet strangers with an egyptian pyramid filled with flamethrowers,

It needs a way to express that a map needs work or that you didn't like the map to the owner, currently it only has options to show that you liked it. I don't want it to be toxic, but just a "hey this is a little rusty, I'd put some more work into it".If you are willing to grind thru the not so great or the super easy levels, you will come across some absolute masterpieces that will leave YOU wanting to crawl back to mommy for muscle milkies. :(9/10

_childDocuments_.review: "Meet your maker," construct nefarious lairs of torment to safeguard the unholy artifact from the feeble grasp of lesser beings, and revel in their anguish as you witness their futile struggles within your malevolent fortress of despair. There is no pleasure more delectable than observing the helpless souls ensnared by your meticulously crafted snares, as they perish again and again in their pitiful endeavors to seize what is yours. Fortify your sanctum of suffering by unlocking new upgrades and traps, each imbued with the power to inflict exquisite agony upon any wretched fool who dares to trespass within the shadowy recesses of your wicked, twisted domain. As the bodies of your enemies accumulate, your reputation will grow, instilling dread in the hearts of those who hear whispers of your merciless cruelty. Let your reign of terror be unrelenting, as you continue to refine and expand your labyrinth of despair, ensuring that none shall ever escape the clutches of your ruthless mastery.10/10

_childDocuments_.review: I really recommend this game but be warned it's a niche genre and some people might buy it thinking it's a fast paced survival/builder fps and be disappointed, it might seem like that at first glance but it's not.  This game is a building-and-raiding game at its core, similar to the cancelled "The Mighty Quest for Epic Loot", "Mario Maker" or "Clash of Clans" but with a Doom twist. You build Outposts full of traps and guards while you can also raid other players’ creations, going in guns blazing will most likely get you killed since everything can one shot you but keep in mind that you can also one shot traps and enemies that are unarmored(except for head shots) and you have to take it slowly and watch your step at every corner because you'll die, a lot, before getting out with the "loot" but the good part is that you can respawn indefinitely with no repercussion. As for the base building, it's really simple and intuitive and it's addicting to fine-tune your outpost after watching replays of raids where you noticed the flaws.The game is not without its cons tho, you'll find generic kill boxes that aren't fun to raid, made by players with no incentive to create fun maps, just trying get as many kills as possible, haven't seen that many in over 10 hours but you'll see them, although you can always exit them and joins others.For now the game is a 8.5/10 for me, the cons being the generic kill box bases, some minor bugs(Replay function fast-forward/backward being broken) and a small variety of guards, weapons and suits but the pros outweigh them easily.

_childDocuments_.review: A very fun and addictive game! Most negative reviews here are complaining about "killbox" style bases, but I honestly enjoy trying to find a methodical way to take those on and I haven't found any base that's truly impossible. With every raid I complete, I feel like I'm learning new techniques to take back to my own builds.

_childDocuments_.review: Very fun and original concept BUT falls short of greatness on almost every aspects other than the core gameplay.Ressources and upgrades:To build a base and to upgrade your character/your traps and guard you need ressources. This, to me, is the biggest problem with this game. There are 3 types of ressources which I'll just call red orange and blue here but the difference between what they can be used to buy will only matter for the first few hours of you playing the game. You will quickly find yourself always lacking red and having an abundance of blue and orange. This is an issue because every traps/guards/character upgrades that you can buy always requires red + either blue or orange. Red can only be acquired by leveling your chimera(this is a long process that takes more or less 10 raids), completing daily challenges or by encountering reward nodes on the new expedition raiding system. Completing any of the above will typically only reward you with enough red to buy a single upgrade. Upgrades are very strong, very fun to use while raiding and building bases and should be rewarded to hard working players, but as it currently stands the process of obtaining upgrades is way to slow and repetitive. It completely breaks the flow of the game and will have you raid for hours before you can afford enough upgrades that you want to go back and rework existing bases or create new ones.Building bases:The controls of the base editor are pleasant and easy to use. There are several environment in which to build and they can have different weather conditions, sizes and flavor, providing players with a decent amount of choice to be creative with. A good palet of block styles and colors to choose from. Generally new environments and blocks are added with updates.Traps:While there isn't a massive selection of traps offered, They can all be customized with 2 upgrades that range from a simple rate of activation acceleration to fully altering the way in which they function. That being said some traps and upgrade are obviously a lot weaker than some others but the developers have made balance changes in the past.Guards:offer a wide variety of attack style and are in my opinion fun and interesting to fight against in raids. I will mention two things that I don't like about them: The upgrades for guards feel generic and unexciting, they are more or less the exact same on every types of guards with 1-2 actually gameplay changing mechanics included.The armor lack visual clarity especially from a distance. I think the armor upgrades provide interesting challenge but it's often hard to tell what part of the guard is being shielded when far away from them.Collecter/harvester/base generation:When building a base you have to create a valid path for the collector npc to walk from the spawn point of your base to the "objective" of the base. Bases are randomly generated but come with some amount of obligatory blocks that cannot be deleted. This along with the valid path restriction can often hinder creative freedom when making bases. Note that this was originally meant as a resctriction to keep the builder from making an impossible to complete base(validly so), but it's now become clear that such bases can exist even with this restriction which is mostly why I have a problem with it.Story/visual style/ambiance:I love the creepy dystopian wasteland in which the game takes place. I was very excited to explore the world when i first started playing. I wondered about what caused humanity to go nearly extinct, I was excited to meet/kill other player's chimeras, the advisor all seemed like they had interesting backstories and the player lobby seemed like it held secrets and upgrades that I would unlock along the way. All this potential is fully wasted, there is no story in this game, the player hub serves no purpose and could easily be replace with a menu and the NPCs constantly say the exact same lines adding nothing to a world that seemed like it was designed with a lot of taught and interest. I hope this will be expended upon at some point.Newly added expedition system:I personally think this brings little more or nothing more to the raid gameplay loop. You have to complete every raid in order to complete the expedition so why even add paths to the expedition? It's as if this was meant to give the palyer more agency on what raids they want to do and create a danger VS reward tension but at the end of the day it feels even more restricting than the old system.In short, Meet your maker is a game with a great concept and a fun and interesting core gameplay (raiding/building system) where every other system feels like incomplete fillers. It's truly a shame to see such potential being wasted.

_childDocuments_.review: Played this game on PS5 when it came out and it was so much fun!! You used to be able to build all sorts of bases. I liked to build back-rooms inspired mazes and watch people try to solve them. However they have since added a suit into the game that just SHOWS YOU THE DIRECT PATH TO THE GOAL. I even thought the players going through my maze were using mods or hacks to show the path. BUT NO it's an ACTUAL FEATURE put into the game by the developers!!! Completely ruining any maze bases and boxing players into only building trap-spam and kill-room bases.These types of bases are not fun to build, or raid as players can just rush through them with no issue.Disappointed that my base building options were limited by the developers. Can't recommend this game. It's just sad now.

_childDocuments_.review: I played this game on the free weekend. I frankly loved it. It has so many mechanics that allow for long term projects and fun experiences. It needs to improve a little on the speed of constring bases, kind of a mess at the moment. It fantastic to raid and to build bases. I do recommend buying this game. All that being said... I was *this* close from NOT buying the game because...A) Maps only last about 12hrs up before you need to upgrade them or they are 'inactive' until you do... wtf? Its annoying AF just to have to login to 'prestige them' maybe if they lasted 24 - 36 hrs it would be better but atm is a pain. Especially with a playerbase that is active only on some specific hours. Which leads to your map being unused for 8hrs and having few the other 4hrs. B) once you reach prestige 10 with a map you created, its permanently down/unavailable for the public. This is the biggest idiocy Ive ever seen in my life. Imagine if you reached max level in any game and it locked your character forever except for private games without any further rewards. I frankly dont want to see my 10hr+ maps get sh!t on by some random policy that DISCOURAGES long term quality creations. I would settle for "reduced gains" for mastered maps, and with settle I mean debuff 50% of gained resources from kills as max penalty. This review was written with the patch released before July 2 2023.

_childDocuments_.review: Meet your Maker had such potential to be good but the game flopped real quick. One of my biggest complaints is the building in this game and how you can publish it without beating it. In most games like this, the player has to do a run and beat the level in order for it to be playable, games like Mario Maker. But this game is far from that. The building in this game is so frustrating and limiting and it's all because of one mechanic in the game. When building, you have a harvester and you have to be able to path the harvester to and from your objective and from. But here's the problem, the harvester can only walk, so if you're trying to create a path that requires you to jump, grapple, etc, good luck with that.Now let's talk about maps being published. There are a lot of times that people don't play your map and your map remains active for a certain amount of times before you have to spend points to be able to activate it again. I personally think it's stupid, why am I having to spend points in order to keep a map I spent a lot of time active?I had such high hopes for this game and as someone who loves to build in video games, I'm very disappointed. I understand Behaviour taking risks creating something new but I feel the execution was poor. Graphically it looks nice but gameplay just sucks. Behaviour, in their words, did a good job with the game so far. Might as well stick with Dead By Daylight

_childDocuments_.review: Players are allowed to create outposts without limitation and without having to complete them themselves. I want to see challenging-as-hell and creative outposts. I want to be challenged by other players. Instead, you're spammed, and the difficulty rating makes no sense. I can't trust that there is a way to beat some outposts, so I'm left wasting my time trying all sorts of trickery or speed run nonsense to try and make simple progression. If they added the requirement that authors have to beat their own outposts, and some sort of proximity limitations, this game would become great for me because I love the concept and the gameplay foundation is solid.That being said, I am enjoying it. The loop of raiding other's outposts and creating your own is addictive. If you encounter outposts you can't get through I've learned to just abandon them and move on.

_childDocuments_.review: In a world with rules, a red button is a common symbol associated with emergency or danger, often used to activate a critical function or alert.However, the rush you get from pressing it is a feeling like no other. In a world without rules... some may find the constant presence of a red button anxiety-inducing or unsettling. Ultimately, the perception of a red button depends on the individual's context and experiences.What are your experiences like?Do You press the button?Maybe it's an act of extreme pleasure denial and all you can think of is the fact that you haven't pressed the button, nay, cannot press the button without exclusive permission?Are you slowly slipping in and out of reality?Is it now you ask?When, you ask...How will you press it, and will it feel the same as the last time?Is THIS the LAST time I will press it?!If I press it right now, will it end it all or will there be more future presses?The very existence of the button is driving you insane... or is it the button itself that's mad and you're just living in it's world. Are you under some type of spell. I love you button, I'm coming for you. This can't be the last time. Press me. I need you. I love you. I miss you. You started out as nothing and became my everything. You are all I obsess over and all I need in life.Just...PRESS....THE BUTTON!!!

_childDocuments_.review: Gruesome artstyle and quite a nice gameloop.However the introduction of reflex mechanics (parry anything with the sword) actually makes me leave the game.You are no longer trying to make a smart dungeon (mislead the player, make them pay attention to something else with good decoration and monster placement). You drop as much things as possible into the pile and see the bodies ramp up.Not what I was expecting from this game.It is not a puzzle, it is a reflex contest.But, if you are okay with that, you are going to have a great timeP.S.: The DLC costs way too much
_childDocuments_.name: Meet Your Maker

_childDocuments_.review: Combine MGSV multiplayer with DOOM gameplay and a Tarkov-esque progression system and mash it all together into a writing cube of steel-ridden flesh and you have Meet Your Maker. Raid bases for resources to upgrade your gear while building your own bases that will passively earn you income as people get murdered inside of them. There are some issues with people making borderline unwinnable mazes, but patches will inevitably iron things out and there are plenty of enjoyable ones to tackle outside of that.Highly recommended, and made even better by being an asynchronous PvP experience where concurrent player numbers are less of an issue. There will always be thousands of mazes to raid and I'm very much looking forward to future updates.
_childDocuments_.name: Meet Your Maker

_childDocuments_.review: I like this game, I can have fun in this game and I like the idea that they were going for. But I wouldn't recommend it, not even on sale, because it is a live service and its player count is barely 100 peak players on steam so at any point you could get the "I'm sorry" Jpeg from the dev's saying they're shutting down service on the game. Also the state of the game is piss poor. Again I like this game, but thats the bottom line.    I'll go further into my opinion below but I've had fun and I appreciate that the Dev's stuck to their vision despite the community voicing desire for changes to how maps dole out rewards and are considered for matchmaking.         Almost a year after release I don't think it was the right choice, people asked for changes for a reason. The system that existed led to the same map with the same goal and 0 creativity no matter what difficulty you were on.  Kill boxes, maps whose only goal was to kill a player as many time as possible with as small a chance of success for the one playing the map as possible. These maps were close to never fun to play against and crazy easy to make yourself because you never had to actually complete a map yourself, unlike in similar concept game Mario maker, leading to a feedback loop no one wanted which in turn led to the fore-mentioned requests from the community only to fall on disinterested ears. On top of 2-3 new items to unlock every 3 months some of which might be irrelevant to you because you just build, or just run maps. Itd kill anyone's motivation to keep playing.Playing now you don't see any kill rooms. Not because they don't work, they would if they were still made they never changed the system, but because the only people left playing are playing with the mentality of "If i die more than 2 times its not worth completing" and will leave long before a kill room has any chance to work. On top of that if your map takes too long people will also leave, because its just not worth it to complete it.  I am also guilty of this mentality because of how rewards are still doled out. it has nothing to do with time, or deaths in a level its all about completion. A flat reward upon completion. so spending 30 min trying to beat the map you died 60 times in rewards the same if not LESS than the map you completed in 30 seconds to 1 minute. Sure there are Vaults you can find in a level but sometimes a map creator will just block them off so is it really worth it to spend another 2 minutes looking on the off chance they have just for an extra 10-20 currency?     This thought is just permanently stuck in your mind while your making any gameplay decision because to make maps you need currency to buy them, which you get from running maps. To get new gear to run maps you need currency, so you have to run maps. To get new traps to put in your maps you need currency, so you have to run maps and so on.    Not to say that you cant get currency from deaths in your created maps but because of the mentality of efficiency that permeates the games systems at large anything you'd get from a map in 24 hours real time is outclassed by an hour of playing.  All that on top of 1-2 new traps or weapons every 6 months
_childDocuments_.name: Meet Your Maker

_childDocuments_.review: When I first got into it I was expecting a lot of unfun bases that try their best to kill you through overwhelming you with quantity, but I was pleasantly surprised when I started playing. About 90% of bases are actually decently designed with plenty of unique designs that are fun to go through. The leftover 10% are ones that either put you in a death chamber at the end when you pick up the material or a mess of small corridors with multiple traps around every corner with the occasionall big room with 30+ traps aiming at every step you walk forward.Luckily there is a simple solution for both problems. For the death chambers at the end you can use the shield consumable to get your bearing and then play the map out normally as you head back. As for the bases that are unfun and try to make your life hell around every corner, you can abandon them! You do not lose anything for just leaving the map and abandoning it, look for greener pastures instead.Watching replays in the bases I am proud of building is also very fun. Watching how different people fall for different traps so you can fine tune it a bit to give them more breathing room or to adjust the traps or layout a bit to create different challenges feel very rewarding when you see the next runner go through.The main thing I wish that the game had would be emotes. It would be fun to see back in replays when people emote out of frustration or because they approve of a design. Perhaps with an emote icon in the timeline for replay watchers so they can see where the action is happening.Another interesting thing would be the ability for the attacker to put down a sign with a comment that you can see when you go into building mode and that would disappear once you leave building mode again similar to the death beacons they leave behind.

_childDocuments_.review: The general idea is "Mario Maker vs Doom" but for me it's mostly reminiscent of Portal! a lot of fun once you get going and work out what you're supposed to be doing and how everything works, my favourite feature is being able to watch back people attempts at raiding your base, it's almost as fun as playing yourself and helps you work out whats working and whats not! progression is a little bit of a grind but i guess that's mostly for longevity and building is slightly more limited than i'd like it to be but still fun non the less.I see there are a few negative reviews because of people creating "kill boxes" or troll raids designed to be impossible to escape from and i haven't seen any yet but the obvious solution to this would be the same solution mario maker implemented, make it so you cannot activate the raid or make it public without first completing it yourself!i love that this game has a duo's feature but I think duos should only be allowed to complete brutal level raids, otherwise it's too easy for a duo with double the ammo, double the equipment & double the brain power to speed run your baseand finally i think if it's possible maybe a LIVE raid feature could be a fun addition in the future, matchmaking & watching someone raid your base live whilst you lay down traps and move mobs around so you can adapt to peoples playstyle if they're being too careless or too cautious, or perhaps even take control of the mobs yourself & having the power to set off traps when you want instead of them automatically activating! TL:DR = I like it!

_childDocuments_.review: Quite fun. If you're up for challenging yourself and mastering a games skills there is a lot here. The game is split into two parts. Part One -Attacking bases for resources, Part Two -Making bases to collect resources. For most players I think part 1 is likely what you are getting the game for, so I'll spend a bit more time on this than part 2, largely because while you can play the game without making bases, but I don't think it is entirely realistic to try and play exclusively as a base builder, you will eventually need to attack at least a few bases. The Bases are split into 3 difficulties, Normal, Dangerous, and Brutal. The difficulty seems to be based partially on number of traps and enemies, with a multiplier based on how close they are to the pathway. Because of this some bases, particularly larger bases will try to lure you off the path where their dangers are cheaper for them to place down. The primary method of this is that maps will have between one and three locations on the map, marked by a fairly loud rumble, if you can make it to these locations they give you extra loot to collect. This is most likely to be used on Dangerous and Normal maps as the map creators are trying to keep their danger rating bellow a certain level. Do remember that all bases are made by players, so do expect even normal ones to be a decent challenge at time, though the low number of options means you should be through sooner than others, that just means that players have to make what traps they do have count.Your goal is to follow the path, reach the end, and then escape the base. Traps all have a wind up time and a warning indicator to tell you their direction to guarantee you have time to either back away to safety the way you came, or to instantly turn and destroy the threat. Because of this there are two obvious playstyles you may gravitate towards. 1 Spec Ops, making sure to sweep and clear out threats one by one, checking every corner, this will often get you extra resources as you will gain resources from destroyed traps. 2 Jedi, where you just rush on through trying to get ahead of the traps before they can even activate, relying on quick reflexes and skilled movement, often in combination with the sword or shield, to try and get in and out as quickly as possible. Now while you are likely to prefer one or the other, some maps will be designed specifically with one of these two styles in mind, sometimes having traps activate in long halls or with a homing property to reduce your ability to get ahead of them, or alternatively having a large room with multiple projectiles to try and make it more difficult for you to dodge everything, other bases might try to counter more methodical play by having guards with patrol paths to surprise you from behind or otherwise make the base less predictable and try to force you to hurry along faster and out of your comfort range. For bases that are designed to throw off your style it is recommended that you try to get used to both of them for when you need them. That said, while switching to other styles of play can make bases easier, it is still quite possible to win with either if you really want to force the issue, even the largest rooms filled with the most enemies will still just be firing and where you just were, so if you are quick enough, or willing to keep at it long enough you should be able to work out a path that lets you whittle down the enemy, or otherwise just ignore and get past them, the same with roaming guards, if you can figure out their path can always ambush them back, afterwards letting you get back to a calm sweep and clear. If you are looking for, or trying to avoid specific experiences you have some tools in game to learn what sort of traps or guards maps have before you even enter them, so if you want to play a Doom or Quake sort of level look for lots of enemies to fight.That's most of the important stuff on attacking the bases, there are of course bits of gear, upgrades and such you can get to make missions significantly easier, but they are fairly easy to understand once you get them, the only thing left to mention is that if you feel a base will take too long to beat, you can always hit escape and exit that level.Part 2 of the game is map creation, and there is only really a few things to mention here as it grants you a lot of freedom to make what you like and thus is a bit much to try and pin down to a few points. The main thing to know is just the threat rating mentioned above, that having traps on or very near the path multiplier their threat rating, pushing you towards Brutal more quickly, in addition to that, having guards within live of sight of the path also increases their threat, giving them any patrol paths at all increases their threat, and having that patrol bring them within line of sight of the path is is similar if not the same as having them start that way. Your best tool to improve your maps, besides raiding other peoples and copying what works, is watching players Replays as they run through your base, and noting what traps never work as is, and what traps seem very effective, then going in to experiment with new placements. Overall the game is, as I said at the start, quite fun. I've had to learn a lot of skills to get good at this, patience, get at least decent with the zipline, had to focus on my reaction time, but thus far, while I have had a few missions I didn't think were worth the time to finish, I've yet to run into one that seemed impossible, the most difficult and annoying one was a player using a current bug, and even that one I got eventually.

_childDocuments_.review: This game is great! The Tutorial is intuitive and quick. The player made bases are really challenging most of the time. The building system is really cool. They seem to have thought of everything for balancing. You can't upload a map that has no traps just to make garbo. _childDocuments_.review: After reading a lot of the reviews, i wanted to share my own thoughts. For the price and quality of the game itself, i think it is worth buying. The game is fun, its amazing seeing what players come up with for traps and being devious, and the game has a lot of replayability. Now with that being said, there are two major things that do need to be addressed. 1 is the content. The base building and raiding is a fun loop, but there isnt a lot of customization and builds to choose from. I understand the game release just a few days ago, but the amount of content would make you think it was still in beta. But im sure itll be updated (hopefully free) soon. The other is the killboxes, bases that are almost impossible to complete, co op or cheese included. Now i dont know for sure what a good answer would be to it, maybe after a few tries the game saves your progression in the base and leaves destroyed traps destroyed up to a point at the cost of how much you'd collect after the game. A lot of people say that the creator should be able to complete the level for it to be fair, but i dont think that would work. If they build it, i can imagine them just making a very secret route hidden somewhere with holo cubes or behind dead ends the player wouldnt look at that lead to the genmat and make it "beatable" by proxy. Again i dont know what the fix for this would be, but i still think the game itself is worth the price

_childDocuments_.review: MIXED Great game, tons of fun, unique concept, but ultimately a failure in its core design.They posted a survey for feedback that was very detailed, so hopefully we see some sweeping changes soon. UPDATE: Devs confirm no changes will be made. Ironside suit skills are bugged, max level skills gone and locked at lower levels =) Nothing will ever change, done with this game. Second AMA: Still doubled down, no good changes coming. This game peaks at 180 players daily, dead.This is due to some baffling design decisions:- Players don't have to beat their own levels before publishing them.- Player created levels have TIMED PLAYABILITY, after a certain number of plays they are only able to be raided in 'Social' mode (with no earnable resources, having to manually find and enter the map name, etc). Why spend any length of time making the coolest base ever?- Another effect of the above is that levels are impossible to share or play socially like Mario Maker etc? Saw a cool level a Youtuber played? Want to replay/show off a level you played previously? Want to speedrun a level you liked? Too bad! Play the new levels!- Maps are focused on # of kills, so most levels become kill boxes with 10+ threats at once to untangle rather than cohesive levels.- Unreal amounts of grind to pad out content.- Every time I try to get the least bit creative with a level I am restricted on block or trap placement. Lots of hard, artificial rules that end up limiting trap setups. This limitation also extends to play as I see the same "tricks" in every map.- Overly complex progression system with three currencies and four 'leveling' meters, but it all means close to nothing, barely anything to unlock or earn. "Leveling up" just gets more small resource drops and doesn't actually gate any content.- Week into launch, maps get maybe 2-3 plays in 24 hours.This genre already had a design standard in Mario Maker, the answers were right in front of them.
