_childDocuments_.review: Overall great experience, with or without friends. This is pretty much exactly what I wanted from a base-building game, straight to the point with good customization of both your raiding equipment and the outposts that you build. It isn't a perfect game; there are some aspects that the tutorial fails to cover, and as of launch the amount of equipment options feels slightly lacking, but the game is well worth its pricetag regardless and more content updates are planned for the future.The gameplay, while great on its own, is even better in co-op, which is enabled for up to two players. The progression feels smooth and rewarding, and while you may bottleneck on resources here and there, there are ways to bypass this; simply playing more is also always a solution (and a fun one at that). I definitely recommend this game to anyone interested by the premise.

_childDocuments_.review: Really fun, polished game with very few bugs for a modern game. There are some negative reviews complaining about not having to raid your own base to verify it, but the developers explained that no outpost is impossible given all the (fully upgraded) tools available and at 37 hours, I have yet to prove them wrong.There were certainly times where I died many times attempting some brutal raids, but, I was able to solve all of them by coming back later with more experience, better gear, and the right consumables. The choice not to have to verify your own raid map is intentional as you are often required to modify and tinker with your map after watching replays or watching players succeed on your map, and having to validate it every time would be tedious as a lot of the modification is iterative. It also allows players who are not strong fps players to still compete in a meaningful way via their devious base building.You can also choose different difficulty maps and the devs have recently greatly improved the match making system to make it more fun overall. It is immensely satisfying watching replays of players die in your bases, and completing challenging raids yourself.It's worth noting that you can also do any raid co-op which makes it much easier.

_childDocuments_.review: After spending 26h in the game, my thoughts are as follows: In general the game will be worth buying after a few months provided some things will be addressed, namely:- Killboxes: it ruins the fun big time but can be easily dealt with, as other reviews pointed, the creator should be forced to complete his own map before allowing players to go through it. Currently there are tons and tons of outposts created with sole purpose of providing you enough frustration to last for a decade.- Pathings: no sophisticated design is possible due to limitations connected with the robot that has 0 mobility, just walks straight down the shortest path. This should be changed as it severly limits and interesting designs- Lacking content in terms of traps/blocks to useI believe the gameplay loop is good, the idea is terrific and the game has tons of potential, just in it's current state, I would simply recommend waiting for sale or (hopefully) for devs addressing the core issues. _childDocuments_.review: (Original positive review at the bottom)NEGATIVE REVIEW:Late game sucks. I have a couple outposts that after building them and prestiging them once gained enough points to be max rank which is great because I don't have to worry about them not making it to prestige.However as you prestige the outpost and your outpost gets closer and closer to lvl 10 you need more and more yellow currency (synthite) this yellow currency is earned how? Primarily by raiding. This ruins the ability to jump into the game watch a couple funny replays and prestige your base and come back to it later. It forces you to either spend a couple hours doing normal or dangerous maps or at least a while doing Brutal maps.For reference all of my advisers are around lvl 50 at this point I need to do at least 2 brutal maps which give 3750 genmat (adviser xp) each which means I need 7500+ xp to level those advisers and I need to do that 5 times in order to get a chimera level which only gives you 250 synthite which means I need to level my chimera 3-4 times if my outpost is level 8-9 which all adds up to about 30-40 brutal raids or roughly 5x that in dangerous or roughly 8x that in normal raids. If they fix the late game then yes I will change it back to positive but right now I've hit 41 hours and I am kinda done playing unless you absolutely love raiding you will be too and even then I enjoy raiding and it gets repetitive after a while because there's only so much you can build and a lot of meta recycled designs.(Original positive review)I was skeptical at first about the not having to complete your own maps etc but I now see why the developers are not concerned with it. It is actually more beneficial to force people to have a walkable path than to complete their own because it would be too easy to make insanely hard parkour maps with massively long jumps etc without the little robot having to complete the course.As far as killboxes go yes there are lots of maps that are garbage killboxes for no reason that are basically impossible to complete, To those maps I say just don't play them. You get the choice of 15 maps that are sorted based on size and number of traps in Normal Hard or Brutal. Some of the Normal ones are killboxes. some of the Brutal ones are easy. It's not an exact science or difficulty scale but it helps AND if you know a map is a killbox then after going into the map and trying it even if you only go in and look and die once (not sure if you have to die or not) and say no this map isnt for me you can abandon it and go in your list of maps and delete it in the bottom left corner and it will give you a new map.It is lots of fun to make maps. _childDocuments_.review: CURRENTLY EXPERIENCING MULTIPLE CRASHES W/ NO RHYME OR REASON THAT FORCES A HARD RESTART ON MY PC.Enjoyed the open beta and the official release is the same. Important thing to point out is the necessary right mindset for this game. It's Super Meat Boy trial and error 1st. You will die over and over, so that demands patience, anticipation, and reflexes. You will creep around corners, fearing for what you can see and panicking what you can't see. You will frantically run, hook, and deflect in ground and aerial combat w/ enemies that may be fast, armored, or freaking explode upon death. There are levels that may have both! It really helps the game has a very simple control scheme: run, slash, shoot, and grapple. This makes playing almost wholly reliant on YOUR abilities and reflexes, and it feels fair 99% of the time.Essentially if you can gel w/ the process of either quickly figuring out a base's traps and defenses or carefully dissecting them 1-by-1, then the satisfaction of successfully escaping is repeating nice feeling; especially w/ some devious or straight-up brutal base designs.What's also great about raiding is even failed attempts slowly increases your EXP and resources, if you play smart enough. Always search the outside for free loot walls. Half the time, (respectable) builders will even help you out and designate where they are. To be fair, though, sometimes they'll also booby-trap them. I should know. I've done it every other base. When you attempt a raid, you get rewards/EXP for enemy you kill, trap you destroy, or even barely surviving either. Each raid attempt is essentially a farming opportunity, and the only consequence is your time and patience.The 2nd thing is the base-building, that's my favorite. When I acquire a new area, I'm always excited to test a new concept or theme around a new trap or upgrade. It's a really robust building system and works perfectly on M&K or controller.1 unfortunate MAJOR issue I'm having is the occasional HARD crash almost every other play session w/ no rhyme or reason. My PC hasn't been upgraded in 2yrs but I haven't had any similar issue in awhile so something is probably buggy w/ engine at the moment.Some nitpick complaints are the rare moments where an action doesn't respond in time because a few other things in the game got triggered at the same, killing me. And (for artistic building) applying colors is limited around and on traps, so artistry can conflict w/ hidden trap design occasionally. But those only come up every so often, and you can easily work around them.While I don't care for (or agree) w/ the $$$ of the DLC for only cosmetics (at least how relatively expensive they're starting out w/), the base game for $30 is well worth it. This game has become a nice daily/semi-daily loop of check my base kill progress, raid for resources, and build a new base.

The result is you either willingly play extremely easy bases or you play extremely cheesy bases on "brutal". It removes and sense of challenge or accomplishment from raiding. You can try to build your own fun base but there is no reason to when the META is just to use the cheap costing corrosive cubes as a means to deny ammo retrieval as well as create entire floors made of lava. this was already an major issue in the beta and wasn't addressed in anyway. Maybe like DBD it will get better with time but just like DBD it's first iteration is deeply flawed and easily exploited.TLDR: not worth buying in it's current state. the only options for raiding bases are basically baby's first base or a kill box spammed with lava cubes and tracking plasma eye traps in a large open room. _childDocuments_.review: TLDR - Game has a great look and vibe, but makes focusing on base building impractical and discourages fun at every turn by design.Behaviour, as usual, nails the aesthetic. Navigation and movement feels quick and responsive and there is certainly a lot of potential to this game. Sadly, that is where my praise for this game ends.The overwhelming focus on raiding rather than building kills this for me, though. The reason games like Super Mario Maker or King of Thieves can function is because there is adequate space for both people who enjoy building and people who enjoy playing/raiding. In Meet Your Maker, however, building is costly and time-consuming. In return, your base might get very few plays and is likely not to even return the resources you put into it. To add insult to injury, your creation won't even persist - it will eventually be rendered defunct and destroyed. Raiding is an absolute necessity to the game - even if you play the game primarily to make bases, raiding will take up a significant portion of your time. To make matters worse...The entire model seems to punish fun or artistic levels, instead encouraging builders to make tedious, boring, cruel bases that you then have to hope someone is bone-headed enough to die in a few dozen times. This, in turn, hurts the raiding experience - since the game doesn't reward making something people might actually want to play, most of the bases you raid will be of the same miserable, ghoulish design. This is great for the people who like that brutal difficulty, and I am glad that sort of experience is available, but making it the only profitable design is a misstep that sours both building and raiding for me.I continue to hope that some significant change down the road will fix this, at which point I will amend my review, but until then there are better games for making or challenging fun, creative designs.

_childDocuments_.review: The definition of a neutral review. As it stands I don't think it's super worth it, but assuming the game doesn't die within a year, content additions will likely make it substantially better.While most negatove reviews complain about "impossible" levels, I've yet to run into one. The worst I've seen was one where essentially all traps were in the first 2 rooms, with primarily flamethrowers and eye sentinels. There's not enough ammo to tale out the sentinels, and not enough rool to maneuver to pick your bolts up again, but it only took me a few tries to realize you can just take out 2 key targets and just, grapple to the exit as fast as possible. A lot of harder levels are like that, and with some upgrades you get more offensive and defensive options for raiding, so it becomes even easier.I'm sure people have found ways to make actually impossible levels; it's inevitable, really. But I haven't seen one, it'll likely get patched quickly, and there's no penalty for quitting a map.The actual problems the game has is a lack of content and an agonizing grind. 2 suits, 2 crossbows with one being flesh only so it doesn't break traps or armor which makes it useless, and 2 melees, which aren't particularly different enough imo. As for bases; 4 enemy types and like 8-9 traps. There just isn't much to work with since there's nothing that can be used to create emergent gameplay in the way mario maker does with things like shells hitting on off blocks or anit-jump mechanisms etc. Even worse is that you likely wont want to make a base till you unlock way more stuff, but the grind is kind of atrocious. Badically everything gives you parts and synthite. 2-3 tombs per map, enemies and traps drop it, it's the reward for completing a level, etc. etc. Cells though, you ONLY get from a select few things, but EVERY SINGLE PURCHASE needs them. Unlock a trap, guard, weapon, suit, or utility item? Cells. Upgrade said items? Sells. Thd only thing that doesn't cost cells are utility refills, buying a new map, and boosts, which are frankly useless for quite a long time because by default they only last 9 minutes, with maybe 2 minutes added on per level. 20 minutes for at best a 30% increase in resources (which most of them only affect things that give synthite/parts) for a ton of resources is laughable. You can maybe do 2 missions in that time. Thing is, if the grind wasn't that arduous, you'd be done in no time, and legitimately good, fun levels are rare. Most levels just suck, even if they aren't raider pov rimworld killboxes or recreations of the worst boomer shooter arenas ever conceived. I've enjoyed some but it's maybe ~30% because there just isn't enough to work with yet.I'll keep playing for now, but this is a game that could be forgotten about within 3 months, or one that grows just enough to get the updates it needs like Dead by Daylight did. Guess we'll see.

_childDocuments_.review: I want to start out by saying I feel like I got my money worth out of this game but I only reluctantly recommend it. I started at release and it was a buggy mess that crashed constantly. I love this genre so I stuck with it and the experience has been mixed. BHVR have since issued patches to fix the stability issues and the 10-15 minute crashes have been greatly reduced, but right before my review I had a hard crash that rebooted my PC so there's still a lot of work to be done. The game is in mostly working condition though but it's still one of the most unstable games I have played in years.The controls are smooth, the atmosphere is great, the concept is fun.Raiding is hit and miss. It can feel like a chore because there isn't a requirement for Maker's to clear their own base before activating it (a feature the community and reviewers have passionately asked for) leading to an out-pour of tedious bases that are easy to make and only 'technically' beatable. Raiding can also feel adrenaline pumping and exciting! It all depends on the base you are raiding. Base building feels smooth and easily accessible. Having a replay feature to watch raider attempts is incredibly satisfying. Bases do expire though, and become socially accessible after 10 ranks so don't get attached to your creations.All the upgrades are lackluster, giving you a .1 reduction to reload speed or .1 reduction to swing speed and they take a lot of grinding to get. The traps are basic but they get the job done. Everything feel very generic and nothing feel rewarding to unlock or activate.Overall, the game feels unpolished but the core game play is fun. If BHVR manages to utilize all the feedback they have been getting there is a lot of potential for MYM.

_childDocuments_.review: Was really excited to try this game. It has an excellent idea to go off of. What couldn't be loved more than a super-mario maker style game, but in 3D, with various game progression mechanics to boot.Unfortunately, the execution of the game feels, lackluster, if not straight up terrible. And I'll explain why.- You don't have to beat your levels in order to put them out there. This, coupled with the reward mechanic for if your level kills someone, encourages players to create levels that are cheesy kill rooms, often feeling unfair and infuriating. Given that this is the PRIMARY reason to play this game, it feels unplayable in it's current state.- More often then not, you are forced to run through a long level, only to be met by a death room rife with traps that can hit you at literally every angle, accompanied by enemies. You can't even slowly clear these rooms, because they are often activated entirely at once, while you are standing in the middle of it, from grabbing the GenMat. Again, the people who build these levels, never have to beat the level, no, they don't even need to attempt to beat it if they do not want to, so they can sadistically place you in a situation like this, without ever experiencing it themselves.- Perhaps in a vacuum with some friends, where you build levels and see if you/your friends can beat each other's maps, you could have a lot of fun in this game, but unfortunately it is widely a troll map creator, and I can't recommend it to anyone.

_childDocuments_.review: The game has an insanely cool concept but a terribly unsuccessful implementation. It's fun to play, the asymmetry constantly forces you to switch between game modes. The builder allows you to construct genuinely beautiful structures, which challenges other players to figure out how to conquer the next peak. HOWEVER! The online experience is just dreadful. Firstly, to maintain 5 bases, you need, on average, about 3900 in-game currency, which is earned in approximately 1.5 hours by raiding other bases. That might not sound critical, as it opens up access to the third appealing aspect of the project - watching replays of other players raiding your base.Unfortunately, the online community is so negligible that you spend 2 hours farming every day (plus about 30 hours on construction, give or take a reasonable 5 bases). That's the minimum, but only about 10 unique individuals will see your base, if you're lucky.I'll give the game a plus in hopes of improvement, but if bhvr doesn't change their marketing strategy and methods of sustaining the online community, it'll be a big fat minus

_childDocuments_.review: Too many levels are not fun.  There is no way to find the kinds of maps you personally enjoy.  There is no way to give feedback to builders in the form of criticism.  They can see that you abandoned the raid presumably due to frustration at least.  Maps end up being functionally removed from the pool which considering I have multiple times been randomly given the same maps (that I already didn't like) is silly.They really should develop an ELO system for levels.  Good levels get bumped up the algorithm and more players get to experience them.  Levels with a lot of abandons or rated poorly get moved down the algorithm and less players have to suffer.  The game does not encourage builders to make the best, most fun levels.  It encourages builders to put as little time as possible in a level for as many kills (fun or not) they can get.  I have no issue dying.  I have an issue with tedious deaths.Fixes:Don't give players the option of which outposts to raid.  15 outposts to choose from where you get no real information about them is pointless and means 14/15 outposts won't be raided as players just pick the first one that is automatically selected.  Instead just give players an outpost to raid which they can skip if it's bad.That or have a filter system to only play maps that fit your criteria.  I still think players shouldn't get to pick which outposts to raid as most are just going to raid whatever is the first one selected by the game.Creating an ELO system for outposts would then filter out the crap.

_childDocuments_.review: Im leaving a positive review, but the game is good, not perfect.There is a lot that I hope to see improved or change in this game so I can recommend it to anyone.First of all, not needing to clear your own level is good in the artistic sense that if you have an idea on your mind, you can build it and share it. But at the same time you have the game incentivizing you to kill even if it makes your level completely unfun to play (the so called kill boxes, which are rooms full of traps and guards). They even added this dumb rank system (Im Bronze 2 so far, didnt play that much, a lot of hours were me AFK) which if someone completes your level without dying once, even if they accolade your level, you lose ranking points. All systems in this game are aimed towards killing the player and not making fun levels, and at the end of the run we cant boo a level like in Mario Maker.The grind is a bit annoying as well, it aims to keep making you coming back everyday for a boost of resources, so spamming the game too much is not that efficient. Not the worst thing in the world, but I think it could be slightly improved, specially because day 1 was the most boring to play this game with all levels being too simple and your kit while raiding being too simple as well.The levels requiring a clear path for the HRV from start to finish is kinda bummer. We have insane mobility, why not allow us to have a different type of level that incentivizes the parkour aspect of the grappling hook and the double jump? Or make a level with no traps but higher guard limit to make an arena. There is so much more we could be building in this game.Now, the good part: building levels. There is a lot of freedom with what to build, with some bedrock blocks serving as a canvas to start an initial shape of what your level is gonna be. Guards can have their patrol route recorded by you, making them patrol or you can just leave them at a better strategic point. Its awesome.The replay system is a godsend. My God, its so fun and interesting so see how and why your traps worked, or what didnt work. Since the game makes you reiterate your levels trough the Prestige system, its literally the perfect solution to allow us to improve our levels, be it to make it better or deadlier.The only thing I hope we get are tripwires, so we can activate traps earlier and thus allowing a more strategic use of the traps rather than just hiding them or making a cross fire.Raiding is fun too, all traps and guards give a warning that they saw you and are going to try to kill you. This giving enough reaction time to adapt to the situation and thus make it fair. If you die its probably because the level maker surprised you.All in all, its a good game and I hope Behavior listens to feedback and has a roadmap to move forward and bring more features to make this game great.

_childDocuments_.review: Took a look at this along with a few friends for the summer sale update. The 6-screen UELA should have been a warning, but the concept was very cool at first. Very interesting introduction and premise, as well as a promising build-up to what you would be raiding and creating yourself. The buildings themselves were very basic by design, but the sound editing and enemy design really had me thinking of Quake 2 Strogg as inspiration which was great.However, after the first hour, that's pretty much it. The signs of the Dead By Daylight development pitfalls begin to fall into place, as time sink investments, time limited events for something as basic as the actual stages themselves, and leader boards take priority over actually building up your home base, your arsenal, or your raid bases. You can get the majority of suits and weapons within the first two hours, but a lot of them feel underwhelming or a downgrade to your initial gear. Same goes for traps and guards, which will require them to be manually upgraded to do such basic things as 'pay attention to the guard next to you' and 'aim where someone is moving rather than where they are'.Building is simple enough, but with very pointless limiting. Limiting blocks and traps with a limited point system makes sense, as better buildings are considered more difficult for people who choose to raid you, but limiting ALL buildings to be relegated by a M.U.L.E cosplayer who needs to walk from Point A to Point B unhindered severely kneecaps any creativity or deviousness you could come up with. Every Raider comes equipped with a grappling hook and a double jump, but these facts can not be utilized in a way for base builders to create specialized courses made specifically to enforce more advanced movement. This means seeing a lot of rehashed buildings with long, cramped hallways with flames, bomb throwers, and other traps surrounded by an acid block to make retrieving your trap disabling tools that much more unlikely. Extremely effective, but only because it's as tedious as it is predictable to circumvent.With a user pool this low, I'm surprised to learn they're still using a system where, after a certain amount of real life time, your buildings are just destroyed. Gone. Not only do you have randomly generated foundations with floating bedrock that you can't remove for added lack of builder freedom, you are encouraged through force to start over. This kind of ephemeral gameplay doesn't affect me, but even I can see why most people would rather have a limited slot of possible bases, and only have even just one of them activated at a time, rather than outright destroying the bases every week. I've seen some very neat looking designs with this very limiting editor, and I cannot fathom that same person coming back every week just to make something of that same quality again, for a number of people who will actually see it in that amount of time that you can count on all fingers and toes.The early access feeling of the lacking story, building, and arsenal content makes me think that they want to go the DBD "add as you go approach". It worked out for them before, and they had 20% of the content of every aspect that have now compared to the beta days. I don't see people wanting to get behind this idea, considering that people have already been pinched dry by DBD's DLC prices for almost a decade already. Even if this game has more years down the line and more things are ready to be introduced by then, I am not looking forward to what I am going to have to shell out to get more out of an already frustrating base game experience.

_childDocuments_.review: Closed and open beta participant here, just getting back into the game for this free weekend (June 27th - July 3rd), and beyond disappointed to find my  suggestion to make this game  more enjoyable has been ignored after all this time. At present, many of you may find that some traps are overpowered, but this is not quite so--the true problem with this game is that  on what can be published aside from the basic rule that the harvester must have an unobstructed route to and from the objective within an outpost. What this means is that you can make wall-to-wall, floor-to-ceiling repeating ranged traps without any consequence (in fact, players are strictly rewarded for this)! The  change this game needs to immediately fix this issue of players constructing levels strictly designed to be impossible to survive is to force playtesting to be a requirement to publish, as I stated during the beta testing exit surveys. If you cannot extract from your own outpost successfully, you should be made to work on that outpost until you can. It is extremely disheartening to see this game's potential to be really fun utterly squandered by a severe lack of foresight on the part of the developers, as someone who has been excited for this game from the onset, and I hope to see that corrected in the near future. Should that happen, I'll update this review, but until then I can't recommend the game in good faith.

_childDocuments_.review: Meet your Maker... What an incredible experience this game was. I can confidently say that this is a one of a kind game. I love this game and will recommend it to everyone, with the admission that you missed the best possible time to play the game (aka when it came out). There is still a community for this game however, the discord for this game is filled with some of the most helpful and positive people Ive ever met. For a game that (largely) comes from DBD, our little community is tight knit. I've made some very good friends via this game. The discord also hosts a few competitions (at least one a month), as well as the submissions for the Pantheon of Builders whenever we manage to get enough submissions to it. So if you do pick up the game (or hell, if you wanna ask pointed questions about the game to the people who know the most about it before buying), please feel free to join! I would absolutely recommend this wonderful game.

_childDocuments_.review: It's a great core concept of a game, with a few very odd design choices.I can understand the dev's reasoning behind not wanting level creators to have to re-play their levels over and over again just because they changed one block or decal. The flip side of this though is that creators can make and publish levels that are essentially impossible to beat, or at least impossible without having a very specific loadout of gear that isn't unlocked for newer players.The difference in difficulty between single players and multiplayer groups is also staggering. As a solo player, any damage at all will send you back to the start of the level, while a 2 player team can keep triggering traps, dying, and resurrecting each other with no limit to "lives" or anything. Seems to trivialize a lot of more challenging levels, even the well designed ones.As someone who primarily likes to build rather than raid, I feel like the 12 - 18 hour expiration on maps I've made is rather grindy and feels like I spend a lot of my time just raiding to try and get enough material to keep a level I made going for another half-day. Even a full 24 hours would feel like this game was less of a second job at times. I play test my own maps to make sure they are challenging, yet completely beatable and hopefully fun to play, so I don't wind up with the massive resource farm that a killbox map can generate.

_childDocuments_.review: It's a well made asymmetric FPS and base builder that can dance the line between tense dungeon crawling and frantic movement shooter chaos. The game is split between building your own outposts and raiding outposts made by others. Both are appealing for different reasons and can be rewarding but it is not mandatory to do both if you find yourself gravitating towards one over the other.Raiding sees you entering another player's outpost and trying to steal a key resource (referred to in-game as GenMat) while avoiding all of the traps and guards the opposing player has set up to kill you. Everything in this game operates on a one-hit-kill basis so raiding is based predominantly on quick reactions and carefully taking stock of your surroundings. Something that should be said is that while I quite enjoy the raiding, Meet Your Maker is  the game for you if you get easily frustrated when having to repeat a challenging level over and over. Many of the outposts available to raid are brutally difficult and you will be reminded constantly that the builder's goal is the kill you as many times as possible. If you find that kind of challenge rewarding, you'll have a very satisfying experience with this game. There's an undeniable joy to finally finishing a difficult outpost that's had you tensely moving around every corner desperately on edge because you've made it further than you ever had before and don't want to lose your progress.The gameplay options available to you as a raider are simple yet efficient. You can only carry two weapons and a couple special items. These can range from guns to swords to grenades to shields. This is in addition to passive buffs you can apply to your character via either your suit abilities or single use enhancements. The game's received a few updates by this point and the options for equipment loadout now offer a decent variety of playstyles. The systems aren't overly complicated but that's because most outposts are designed to be completed in only a few minutes (provided that you don't die. In practice some of the harder outposts can taken considerably longer to finish as you go through multiple attempts)Something that is remarkably strong is the movement system for the raider. You can use a grappling hook (seemingly a necessity in all sci-fi FPS games now) and can move around an environment very fast, zipping around enemies and traps dodging dozens of projectiles as you try to clear a room. My one major criticism of the raiding experience is that while this type of movement is , it is only viable in specific circumstances. In most outposts, it's much more reliable to take it slow and only put yourself in least amount of danger at a time, which feels like a waste of the movement mechanics. Rushing in, especially when you don't know the trap layout will certainly get you killed. The other half of the game is building outposts for other players to raid. While the raiding can be equal parts tense and chaotic, the building is obviously much more relaxed and almost meditative. The layout of each outpost is based on a 3D grid of blocks, looking very much like a high-res version of minecraft but also including 45 degree slopes. You can place blocks or create entire walls/floors at a time. Traps and guards can also be easily dotted around your environment. Everything has to be placed manually though. There is no way to copy entire sections and paste them or rotate them elsewhere. This can make certain features like repeated decorations or trap layouts a bit tedious, but the tradeoff is that that building system is very . There's a very low learning curve to the technical side of building, although the more creative side both in terms of visuals as well as good trap placement and level design will take quite a bit of practice to become really proficient with.There are several limitations to the building system. The main one is that there needs to be a clear path from the entrance of the level to the GenMat for the raider to collect. This path needs to be navigable by the Harvester Unit (HRV) which cannot jump or climb walls. This means that the path must be continuous. This can feel a bit limiting, but it's vital for ensuring that the raider has some idea of where to go. If you could put the entrance to the GenMat down a hole or tucked away in a wall somewhere, the raiding experience would be defined more by boredom from trying to find out where he/she is supposed to go rather than by the challenge of contending with your traps. Another limitation is that the plot of land you can build on is auto-populated by immovable bedrock which shows up in random patterns for every outpost you create. Once the bedrock is generated it is impossible to remove it and you must build around it. I understand that this was done to force builders to use different layouts for each outpost they make, but sometimes the amount of bedrock generated can get frankly obnoxious.Something else I want to highlight though is the possibility for artistic expression. Having to build exclusively with cubes and 45 degree slopes may sound limiting, but Meet Your Maker provides a lot of cosmetic options for customizing your outpost. These are all entirely optional, but there's a lot of flexibility for some visually impressive maps as demonstrated by the community. Not every outpost you run into will have that kind of love put into it, but some of the ones that do really shine.Up until very recently, this was something the game really struggled with. It's improved significantly with recent updates, but it's still in my opinion the game's weakest part. This mostly stems from how there isn't much to spend the different types of currency on. You'll find that unless you are building and activating/reactivating outposts a , you'll quickly find yourself with a buildup of currency. Something you can spend the money on are boosts that result in you getting slightly more money for a short duration (only an hour or so depending on your level) which seems baffling and like the kind of thing that would be done in a free-2-play game... except Meet Your Maker isn't free-2-playRecently though, there's been a collection of cosmetics you can unlock by raiding a lot. These help provide some more incentive to raid more outposts (which in turn gives the builders more rewards, as they earn progress for kills and accolades given to their outposts) but it doesn't solve the aforementioned currency issue. The cosmetics themselves are pretty good. Given the game's very serious tone they can't go into wild territory for suit/weapon skins like a more cartoony game could, but it's still a welcome addition.Meet Your Maker is a game that tries and  succeeds at balancing both fast paced and tense first person combat with more relaxing and user friendly base building. The raiding can lend to frustration sometimes and the building takes a while to develop as a skill, but both offer a satisfying gameplay loop, even if the meta-game progression still needs to be ironed out a bit as the development progresses.

_childDocuments_.review: I probably played this more than I should during the free trial. The core idea could have been fun but it's half cooked and aims to retain players in grindy and unrewarding ways. Game trailers are rather deceptive because they show fast-paced action gameplay (like ) while in reality running and jumping around means dying in 5 seconds. Your objective as a Custodian is to steal an important resource from online outposts built by other players and use it to feed an experimental Chimera, which is humanity's last chance for survival. Despite feeding her multiple times, there isn't really a story or a sense of progression. The Chimera never evolves, so nothing changes. You are basically told to continue indefinitely to feed her, with no reward waiting for you at the end.Nearly half of my playtime went into carefully building my own outpost (which I unlocked after grinding resources for a few hours), only to later discover that I must grind again to keep it online. Only 5 players visited my outpost before it went offline within a day. The building part seemed fun at first, until I saw that the options were very limited. There are only 3 types of trap and 1 type of enemy at the beginning. Other types can be unlocked after grinding enough materials and resources. The customization options for your outpost are also not enough, so despite players efforts to make distinctive outposts at the end they all look nearly the same. A 2015 single player game called  did a better job with base-building and that wasn't even the game's main mechanic. Customizing your outpost too much could actually reveal your traps location, for example you can't set traps if a block is decorated, which means players who are smart enough can just look at the blocks that aren't decorated to understand where the traps are hidden.Before the free trial there were like 100 active players, which doesn't look good for a newly released multiplayer game (there are no outposts created by developers). The game is clearly overpriced for the amount of content and the unnecessary level of grind. It will probably follow 's fate (for those who remember it) and become free to play until they decide to shut down the servers.

_childDocuments_.review: I met my maker.FUN:Raiding is fast paced (if you're cocky) and slow paced (if you're smart). Raiding is def the best aspect of the game, and being able to raid outpost created by other players is cool. With only 7 hours, I've seen so many different outpost. Building, on the other hand, is still fun, but its a lot more slow. You get to use your brain to find ways to stop the raiders.With each outpost being created by other players, you have unlimited content. STORY:The story is pretty bare bones. Besides the cutscene in the beginning and what you read on the store page, theres not too much else to the story. However, the setting is nice and the game itself is fun. CONTENT:Theres not too much at the current moment. In terms of traps and guards, theres quite a good bit of content. Theres a lot of different decor as well. Dont worry though, almost everything has upgrades so it'll still take a while to 100% everything. _childDocuments_.review: One of the most addictive and fresh games I've played in a long time. While it's only been a week since release, it has a LOT of potential. If I had to describe the gameplay, it's like one half frantic speedrun and another half evil dark souls levels full of illusory walls, hidden traps, and rooms full of ranged enemies waiting behind the corner. As a raider, you can either tiptoe your way carefully through a level, checking around corners and taking your time dismantling the carefully laid traps that another player has hidden for you... Or you can go full speed with a grappling hook and blaze through dozens of traps, literally breaking levels. I don't know how to describe it, but it feels unfair for both sides, but its INSANELY fun. The general gameplay loop is raid, build, upgrade repeat. I hate comparing the game to Mario Maker, it's not really comparable in anything apart from building levels for other players. When players die in your levels, you see little markers that give info but you also get in game resources which is tons of fun. Whether raiders succeed or fail, the base owner will recieve passively generated resources while they're active. The REAL joy is coming back to the game after being away for the night only to come back to a flood of kills in the levels you make. Logging in to see 26 deaths in a single level and being able to WATCH THE REPLAYS of two players stumbling through and falling into the traps I designed is probably some of the most fun I've ever had in a multiplayer game. AMAZING 10/10 would recommend. Even when all of your traps fail, its an interesting learning moment and gives you insight for future levels...*Negatives: I will say, I have encountered probably like 5 crashes so far but this never resulted in any loss of progress. Not a huge deal, this is to be expected. A down side to raiding is sometimes you get these really boring levels where someone just creates a massive warehouse filled with like 100 plasma turrets and the only way to beat it is to brute force it or spend an hour shooting everything one by one. It's frustrating, but you also get some genuinely awesome levels that have a lot of love and creativity put into it.This game feels very different and I genuinely hope that the devs continue to pour love into it. I cant stop playing.

_childDocuments_.review: The visuals look amazing, the enemy designs are well-made, the game runs pretty smoothly, and you do have a choice between 3 difficulty levels, kill-room or otherwise.Before you start throwing Jester awards at me (which gives me free points), I am not inhaling copium when I say this.The people writing negative reviews have never played a community-curated online game. This is a very solid co-op game, which is rare in recent years. Me and my friend; while we took a break for a bit, have always enjoyed most of the time we've played this.While this has a dwindling player base and a lack of creativity for most of the levels, the Outposts weren't designed with "make fun" in mind. It was "kill people" for the sake of gaining resources.Even if the devs' incentive was for people to make fun levels, nothing would have changed. It would just be Mario Maker's Fallout cousin.We just need to give this game another chance, guys. If you had any expectation other than troll levels in a game like this, you are the wrong audience.

_childDocuments_.review: This is my first time writing a review; however, the potential for this game makes it that much more of a reason to write one!Positives: -The Building:The building feels smooth, and developing ideas to make traps against other players almost feels effortless. By progressing through this game and challenging against other people's bases, you pick up tricks and ways to target other players. Making, it easy to find a challenging base or create such a base. With this, the building aspect is amazing, making it easy for anyone to pick it up. - THE NPC within this game is amazing!     #5 guards: Cannonback(Shots grenades in a sense), Enforcer(Shots one arrow), Hornet(Flys in the sky, shoots one arrow), warmonger(Swings with swords), Augments(Shots multiple arrows).Yes, while the selection is a little, your versatility is wide. This largely contributed to controlling each AI and controlling them to do whatever formation you want from them. If the time is right, you could have a player trapped between two foes, or make it to each corner an enemy is waiting. I have not had any problem with their target tracking, or glitches. It feels well-polished!Feedback videos:You get to watch how people raid your base! Understanding what traps seem useless and how to improve your base is great. Watching the other player admire your base or struggle with it makes it much more fun.How Feature Works: Player's Aspect or go in a creative mood flying around watching the player raid your base.Negatives:The game Crashes:While this will not have a problem with gameplay, it isn't very unpleasant. It typically crashes when watching feedback, and you skip 30 seconds ahead. Besides this, it will happen rarely, however, never when raiding someone else base. So NO this will not affect GAMEPLAY.Versatility: Five guards and 10 traps; however, there are 12 of which that will kill a player. Because of this going through so many bases, you see a repetition of traps laid out to kill a player. This is also to consider that you can walk past most traps before they activate. Yes, that's right walk pass traps, making it very easy for a player to just speed run through your base. Having more of a selection of guards/traps will tremendously improve the game.There is No Reason to Progress:Yes, while they have a ranking system, in reality, you don't know what it's for. There's no leaderboard, and there are no best bases. However, the only reason you might progress is to create the best base...Ok, then what?How to fix this:Create a separate list of bases that you can raid. From this, have it where it will show what rank base you are going against. Make each difficulty on its own rank so that players can progress in each difficulty differently. Then a player can take the rewards for each difficulty, which will have different proportions. How will bases be ranked:Have bases be ranked based on players' deaths and the completion of grabbing the core. For exampleKills avg: 10.3Core Remaining 3.6Base rank: Diamond There are two approaches. First, have it that after a certain amount of deaths, the player is not allowed to compete against the base, making the base go up in rank. Second, to a value where deaths go over, let us say, 30, then, if they grab the core, it doesn't even count. Both of these can be adjusted to the rank of the player.With rank bases, have it where the player does not have to watch it non-stop. Rather, have it where the player is allowed to put one base into rank. Each time the core is stolen, the base losses health. It can be gained back through a series of methods. You buy a revive. It absorbs the fallen players, if the core does get stolen it naturally heals, and so on.       For example:Step 1-Create signs just like in Minecraft, books, or anything where a player can make a story. While you create your storyline, let other players do it for you. Players spend so much effort into their base there will be a great amount that would want to create their own story behind it. Next, please make it so players can do a series from their bases. From this, people could post their bases on TikTok with their story behind the base, giving you traffic and allowing other players to enjoy other people's work that much more.Step 2-Do you want the game to have a scary vibe, touch up on the graphics, or have monsters meant to scare players? For example, a spider's lower torso, a human upper torso that crawls on the roof, jumps down on the player, jump scaring them, then kills them. Step 3-Have decorations! Paintings, red handprints, skeletons, anything! Allow the player to create their own story this will improve the game. If done right, you would have people downloading the game to play against someone's storyline. This also means that you have to up the build limit for such an idea.Once again, there are so many ways this game can improve and become something much more. It just needs work and a big community to help them grow. This can be perhaps be done through the methods listed, just ideas, though. However, great game over all. Love the concept.

_childDocuments_.review: If you’re interested and want to try Meet Your Maker then the time is . There’s no guarantee this game will hold its audience, and this game is also very at risk of degeneracy taking root and causing everyone’s base designs to become soulless charnel houses. I’ve exclusively played solo Raider so far, and, right now, killbox bases are both infrequent and haven’t been perfected yet. The few I have encountered have been a bit fiddly in places, but the tools you have (particularly if you’ve levelled up your gear) give you ample options to take them down. Patience, using all the gadgets available, and learning from your mistakes will typically get you through tough bases. And, if you’re not in the mood for that, you can just abandon for an almost meaningless penalty and remove the map from your listings.Having said that, while killboxes are the current fearmongering buzzword for the playerbase, as someone that’s got a few Raider hours under their belt, I actually think Builders getting a bit more experienced would improve the challenge at the easier end of the base design spectrum a lot. Right now, we’re still at the stage where most bases are either a killbox or a series of corridors with traps hidden behind each corner. I’m not always in the mood for a killbox, but the other base type is overwhelmingly easy unless you deliberately hamstring yourself by attempting to blitz through it with minimal caution. I’m not sure what the midpoint between killboxes and the current easy corridor bases would look like, but I hope the community can evolve in that direction.I’ve read a lot of criticism, particularly from Builders, which I don’t have any opinion on as I’ve skipped all the building so far, but I do wonder what the Raider incentive to keep playing will be once I’ve maxed all the equipment. There’re cosmetic season rewards (which are essentially based on playtime), but other than that I don’t really know what will give me purpose after I’ve upgraded everything.Overall, I really like Meet Your Maker’s foundations, but the direction this game goes in, and how the community evolves, will make or break this game over the course of the next year or so. If you want to try it then now’s the only guarantee of a decent experience.P.S. - if you like Meet Your Maker's Raider gameplay, but want something less player-driven, then Phantom Abyss is very, very similar but with procedurally generated levels.

_childDocuments_.review: My issues with the game started from the beginning, all I wanted to do was build instead of raid, but the game incentives you to raid to get material to build. It's an issue I can deal with, but at the time the economy (imo) was too much, and raiding can be a pain considering the devs don't make it so you have to beat your own level, which leaves almost impossible/unfun raiding experiences. Along with that, the playback to see players raid your base was abysmal (which I heard they fixed at least?) But all this leads to being too little too late. I had my fun playing the game, not the grind, and didn't decide to come back. According to steam DB at the time of writing, the 24 hour player base stands close to 39 on steam. With a game that requires a large player base for any fun and unique experiences, I think this game should be skipped. They should have hit the ground running at launch, but oh well.

_childDocuments_.review: You get punished for building good maps. Once you prestige 10 a map you can no longer add it to the public map pool. This means that is a map does extraordinarily well, gets tons of accolades, tons of kills, is one of the better maps in the game, it gets removed once its proved itself.Co-Op gameplay is OP, you get unlimited revives, making most maps very easy.There is no reward for playing a map fast, as many people like to do, this is in part because the game has no idea what fast is, because the author of a map does not need to beat a level to publish it. Taking a map very slowly is encouraged, as every trap has a delay to activation. Making killboxes a common sight.Needs to make it so authors have to beat their own level, and do away with the collector robot. If I want to make a base that blocks off one route when the flag is captured, and opens up another, keeping my layout fresh and giving me more options with the space I have.

_childDocuments_.review: After playing through it some more i changed my review to negative since there are some disgusting practices at play here.First of all: the DLC content (both the 15 dollar pack, though in a lesser degree, as well as the content you get for owning DBD on the same platform) is basically pay to win. Especially the DBD content has tiles that look exactly like the trap, something you can't achieve with the normal content in the game. The Scorched content has items that will make your game lag (the rotating clock thing, which some people spam to achieve exactly that). Cosmetic items should never have an inherent gameplay benefit, but yet they do. That alone made me change this review to a negative. besides that the game is inherently skewed towards Raiding. Raiding gets you way more ranked points, to the point that you have to have like 400 something kills in your base to gain rank points equal to one raid. On top of that your base is automatically rendered useless once you get it to prestige  10. It is no longer activatable. So your hard work as a builder creating a fun, engaging base is rendered null and void because... well i don't know why they did that it's just stupid. Another thing that is stupid as hell is that you don't gain any resources for receiving accolades, just from kills. So all that supports is the killboxes the community likes to cry about. Yes, the killboxes are beatable, yes they are annoying as hell to play through and simply uninspired and not fun, and yes you could just leave those raids. However something like 90% of the raids i undertake are those same rooms full of pistons, incinerators, sentinels and corrosive cubes. But why bother making something people enjoy raiding when the accolades don't provide the builder anything? Bad game design there. Not that you get many resources from the kills anyways, you barely make enough to sustain the uptime on your base. Adding to that is the fact that there's also no reason to buy smaller bases (they are separated into small, medium, large) all you want is a base with high capacity and most importantly 9000 genmat so you only have to pay the refresh once per day. And anything well thought out traps get nullified by raiders running the arc shield which is basically a big undo button on any mistake the raider makes. It barely has cooldown, has a base 1.5s of complete invulnerability (no it's not direction based, go figure) and goes up to 2 seconds if you "perfect block". And if that is not enough to save yourself from all the mistakes you should be getting punished for, use a flash barrier. At least you're only limited to 2 of those per raid. Yes, these things are necessary in the current environment because the devs decided to only incentivize builders making killboxes, but they are completely overpowered if those things were to be changed. ---TL;DR.Right now i'd definitely recommend waiting for a sale if you're interested (thought by that point the game might be dead, considering there's been no advertisement for it that i've seen and it's currently only at a pop of 1.5k players or so, so that doesn't bode well). Because the pay to win aspects, the poor incentives and the actual incredible grind it takes to get anywhere (especially if you want to focus on building) is just not good. ---Lastly, be careful of the community discord server. It's owned by elitist snobs that have played since beta, especially the owner of the discord server who will personally attack you for "leaving raids". No casuals allowed in there.

_childDocuments_.review: Changing my review to negative for now.The gameplay has devolved into two styles of outpost creation:1. Killboxes: Most outposts you will find have these rooms that are just stuffed full of traps and/or guards. One might argue that "iT iS tOtALly pOSsiBlE" to beat these outposts, but it really isn't worth it. If you have all the time in the world to waste on one outpost, then by all means, torture yourself with it. I'm not spending 30 minutes or more, dying over and over on some garbage smashed together by masochists who have no intention to make a fun experience.2. Mazes: The point of a fun maze has always been to find the way and get through to the end. What makes 99% of the mazes in this game unbearable is that once you get the genmat, you have to find your way back to where you started! Basically, doing a maze twice. Then even worse, you have to battle your way through second wave traps on the way out.It's also worth mentioning that I enjoyed the first 4 outposts I built, but when they deactivate for good one by one, it becomes tedious. I don't really want to make more outposts. I liked the ones I had and now they're done. Hardly anyone raids my latest outpost, so I just wonder what's the point? Put all the work into making a new outpost for very little reward. This whole system needs a huge rework!

_childDocuments_.review: Absolute joy of a game to play! I typically stick to playing brutal (the hardest difficulty) levels and while I do run into the occasional "killbox" people are mentioning, I mostly am playing really fun levels. Don't get me wrong though, I get a lot of levels that are really hard, but not impossible as those select few killbox levels. That being said, it took me a solid few hours to really master the movement mechanics in order to consistently enjoy these levels, it may be more enjoyable for certain players to stay away from brutal levels...Speaking of the movement, it's really fluid and fun! There's some slight bugs here and there but overall I don't encounter them often at all. It's really fun to go around a level and combo the grapple with the various weapons and double jump!As for base building, I'm loving all the different ways I'm able to challenge raiders. However, the prestige system only allows your base to stay active in the level pool for about 5 and a half days if I did my math right? After that, you're able to move it to the "social" status where it can be played forever without giving rewards. I understand the thought process behind keeping the level pool fresh, but I feel like levels should stay active for longer... maybe adding 10 extra prestige levels would do the trick there.Excited for all the upcoming new content, I feel like I'll probably be sticking with this game for a long time as long as the community stays active as well!

_childDocuments_.review: The gameplay itself is very fun. It primarily splits into building and raiding and I have a bit of feedback regarding both.Raiding solo can be hard but rewarding when you finish, but raiding co-op sometimes feels like a joke and there should be separate categories of bases for it. I feel like the raiding is bit better balanced and slightly harder solo now than during the beta which is good. In the beta it felt like traps had too long of a delay to activate and now they activate fast enough that most of the time you can't just walk throughOne thing I would love is if when a map runs out of genmat it should have the option to automatically enable social mode so friends can check it out instead of having to manually enable it. _childDocuments_.review: I personally really like this game. It offers 2 types of gameplay -base building and raiding-. While I am more in favour of the raiding, there are still alot of problems in the current version.-Builders dont need to complete their own maps: You sometimes get nearly or fully impssible maps, where you just enter a single room with 30 traps stacked upon each other. No way to reach them with a sword, nor a way to recover your bolts.-Content: I know it's still a very early version, but having a weapon system and only 2 sword 2 ranged weapons and a shield as well as 2 armours is honestly not that much, especially as soon as you reach 10+ hours you basically already know your own preferred setup, as you dont really have that much choice anyways-Hardware: Your expandables are used, even if you die, which sometimes leads to having not enough of them and forces players to abandon missions and return later-Mission choice: As I have already written about it, there are some maps, that are generally impossible to do. If you abandon them and return to your base, they will just stay in your selection for ever, blocking that spot.I still recommend this game, especially if you are playing with friends (unfortunately I dont have any :,( ). _childDocuments_.review: Tips to make ultra crispy smashed potatoes:Ultra Crispy Smashed Potatoes are straight forward to make – boil, squish, drizzle, bake – but there are two little tips I’ve discovered along the way:Let the potatoes steam dry a bit after smashing them. This ensures optimum crispiness!Use butter and a touch of oil. Because butter = flavour, oil ensures more even and better browning and crispiness. Can’t use just butter because it burns in the oven at high temperatures.Also, you can totally feel free to add flavourings like garlic and dried herbs, but they do burn a bit so you’ll get little black bits on the surface. In all honesty, these are so tasty as they are, they don’t need anything more! (In my personal, potato-opinion)I hope this will help you for the decision to buy and play the game.

_childDocuments_.review: It is truly a wonderful thing to invest time into building a death trap base and watching others challenge your creation.  Of course to make a deadlier base you have to raid other bases to get the necessary materials to make such a deadly base.  That is the basic synopsis of Meet your Maker.Overall I found the game to be well balanced between base builders and raiders.  Raiders have a pretty deep upgrade pool to choose from when plotting your raids.  Should you dual wield range weapons or a mix of range and melee.  Only one of the ranged weapons can destroy traps and its ammo is severely limited.  The melee swords are very powerful against traps and NPC guards but is limited in range.  Base builds have many tools and traps to design their bases with. I have been truly amazed by what the community can built thus far. One example is a Egyptian themed pyramid of death and beauty. I was in awe as I raided it. There are also resource points a base builder can choose to incorporate into their build or just helpfully point them out to your raiders. I chose the latter because I know full well how challenging it is to learn how to raid properly. After getting "good" at raiding and leveling up my ranged raider (increased ammo, ammo pickup range and ammo finder) I am actually have a blast now. At first it was learning the hard way and dying over a dozen times, but laughing at myself all the while doing it.  I would highly recommend this game.

_childDocuments_.review: I have been enjoying the game. It's a fun concept that keeps you coming back. There are two games here. A raiding mode and a building mode. Each is tied to the other in the game play loop to keep the other active. It's a decent enough design and it works, though I do believe it could be improved upon. A game like this will live and die based on its player base and I believe its too early to see how that will play out, but I do have hope that the developers can add enough fresh content to keep the game exciting enough to keep players coming back. As is its a easy recommend at this point in time.

_childDocuments_.review: Look, can I just be real with you for a moment?GenMat is a zero-sum game - we need it, everybody needs it, and it's either us or them. We can harvest it, but so can they, so what I need you to do is go out, find GenMat sites, and loot them. Bring back as much material as you can get your hot little post-apocalyptic hands on.Of course, they're not going to make it easy for you - GenMat is the most valuable substance remaining on this planet, and if you're smart, you're going to fortify your source with walls, traps, and guards. We can do some upgrades on your gear, but for the most part, you're going to have to rely on intuition and quick thinking to get you into the center of their base. Don't worry about it if you die a couple times along the way - we can just build you a new body. Plenty of mutant material laying around for that.Our own source of GenMat needs to be similarly protected, so I'm going to need you to design a whole gauntlet of deadly devices to surround the source. Harvey the harvester can pick his way through without triggering anything, but other players trying to raid our fortress should be hosed. We can upgrade your traps too, and give you some big beefy dudes walking around with blades on their arms, and little waspy dudes that fly and shoot homing bolts - that sort of thing.Build up your own base. Raid other people's bases. And you know what? If you liked it, give them a nice rating. Let them know it was fun, or artistic, or particularly brutal. Hopefully they'll return the favour. Just because we live in the charred husk of civilization doesn't mean we can't be civilized.I know I look like a big ugly science experiment in a bacta tank, but trust me bro, I've got your back. Oh and next time you manage to scavenge enough materials to upgrade me, come hit the big red button next to my aquarium, it really helps me out.

_childDocuments_.review: IMO the trailers and marketing didn't do the game justice, it's amazing and I'm glad I took another look.It's an fps/platformer/puzzle game where you have to find the most optimal route in a base filled with traps, built by another player, or build one yourself and get rewarded depending on how many raiders you kill. You can speedrun and evade most traps or take your time and disable them.The movement feels great, you have a grappling hook a double jump and a sword dash which you can combine in any way. If you use both swords you can animation cancel and keep dashing around the level like a madman."Killboxes" are fine you will learn some tricks to deal with them.Spend the red mats wisely, you acquire it much slower than the other two and it becomes a bottleneck to your upgrades/items.

_childDocuments_.review: This game is ruined by the lack of integrity of the community. However, the game was doomed to fail by its own design,  Players have proven that they do not want to be challenged they want to win or they will just quit..  the game launched with all sorts of bugs which became exploited by the majority of the community.  The fixes for those bugs took to long and brought along new bugs that are being exploited.  The game launched with minimal content and a 20 cad expansion pack that was way overpriced.  Due to the ranking system even after it was patched, provides little value to this kind of game, plus behaviour Interactive must have known how many of their DBD survivor mentality players would join this game and ruin it as well, in the name of preserving their own fun. So if you play the game, and build an outpost that does what the game wanted you to do, kill raiders most of them will just rage quit and give up and block you, even without exploiting bugs. When you raid, every other outpost will be using some kind of exploit, the first month it was the 2nd wave corrosive cube exploit (traps could target players without line of site if placed behind a second wave corrosive cube.) Once that was fixed then it was traps can target you and fire through solid blocks, once that was fixed, now traps placed behind 2nd wave holo cubes will trigger without line of sight, but will not be able to go through the 2nd wave holo cube..   Look how many hours I have.. man I love this game, but i am done playing it, bugs, exploits, poor sportsmanship, crappy grinding, bad economy, pointless ranking system,  I was having fun, but there are so many things that are bringing this game down. _childDocuments_.review: Game seems incomplete and the balance is awful. Only people who challenged my map are fully geared with end game items making all traps useless. Which even if I had end game traps cant actually beat end game gear. Grenade launcher with bullets that can be picked up? The GL is broken, the shield that blocks all damage is broken, the fact you can skip traps without actually having to play the map is broken too. There are no chain reaction traps either which is crazy for a game like this. What can I say? They attempted something, failed, and its not really worth the money. I recommend something else within the same genre.Only thing this game does right is the skill gap, but even that doesn't matter eventually due to end game items being broken and how easily you can get them. If this game wants to improve then it needs rebalance the gear and traps, would also be interesting to have more than the normal building blocks, such as blocks that arrows can pass through or half blocks. Not sure why the devs decided that stuns and freeze traps shouldn't exist but its what ever, probably not playing this game anymore than I already have, was fun for the first few hours but I'm bored of it now. _childDocuments_.review: I highly recommend this game, for anyone even remotely interested.If you enjoy spelunking dungeons that are random and fresh every time, this might be your new favourite thing.Game controls feel very tight and simple, and don't feel like the reason you may trip up.Building your own death traps is also very fun, and super rewarding when you get to profit off of those you kill.Using the kill replay section, you can see which of your hazards are most effective, or not at all, providing good insight into optimising your builds.Play your way, with the game rewarding you very well if you choose to either Raid or Build, or both!Both modes allow Co-op with one friend, which is also extremely fun and makes for great moments.Progression feels great, as you continue to unlock more things to help you raid smarter, build up even deadlier bases, and so on.Simple 10/10 from me. I hope to see the player base grow as this game continues to expand and refine itself.

_childDocuments_.review:
You are the Custodian of the Chimera, a living experiment created as a last resort to save life on Earth. Enter a tactical battle for the planet's most coveted resource and the key to your Chimera's evolution: pure Genetic Material. Construct and fortify brutal Outposts to extract and guard your Genmat. Infiltrate and outsmart other players' Outposts to gather more.

Adapt, upgrade, and evolve... or die trying.

Meet Your Maker is a post-apocalyptic first-person building-and-raiding game where every level is designed by players. Switch between roles as you mastermind devious maze-like Outposts filled with traps and guards, then gear up for methodical fast-paced combat raiding other players' creations.
_childDocuments_.name: Meet Your Maker

name: Moncage
detailed_description: FOLLOW US We're a small team creating artistic games with dreamlike experiences for our players! Follow us here: Twitter: Discord: Awards About the Game Moncage is a stunning vignette puzzle adventure developed by Optillusion. The game takes place inside a mysterious cube, with each side of the cube housing a unique world: be it an old factory, a light tower, an amusement park, or a church, etc. At first sight, they may seem random and unrelated, but upon closer look, you will become mesmerized by the subtle and intricate ways of how these worlds connect…… 【Solve Puzzles with Mind-Boggling Optical Illusions】 Use your imagination and spare no brain cells to find the connection and pinpoint every possible interaction between different sides of the cube, then watch as the magic unfold in front of you. 【Collect All Photos to Unveil the Story】 Behind the puzzles, there lies a story with a surprising twist for the player to uncover. Collect the photos from obscure corners and angles to reveal the underlying story, one photo at a time. 【Get Unstuck with Thoughtful Hints】 There is a multitude of guidance systems to help prevent players from getting stuck. Focus can be activated to highlight the key items to the solution, while hint texts are available to provide further clarity. And, if all else fails, video walkthroughs can be unlocked as the ultimate safety plan. 【Prove Your Puzzle-Solving Skills with Medals】 There are a total of 15 achievements in the game, each corresponding with a Medal that has been crafted with a uniquely stunning design. A complete collection of the 15 Medals could be the perfect evidence to attest to your master puzzle-solving skills~

Focus can be activated to highlight the key items to the solution, while hint texts are available to provide further clarity. And, if all else fails, video walkthroughs can be unlocked as the ultimate safety plan. 【Prove Your Puzzle-Solving Skills with Medals】 There are a total of 15 achievements in the game, each corresponding with a Medal that has been crafted with a uniquely stunning design. A complete collection of the 15 Medals could be the perfect evidence to attest to your master puzzle-solving skills~
short_description: Moncage is a unique puzzle adventure game where you explore a fascinating world trapped inside a mysterious cube. With each face displaying a unique scene, you’ll have to leverage the illusions and discover the hidden links to solve the puzzle.

_childDocuments_.review: Masterfully crafted puzzle game that takes place on five sides of a cube as you piece together the story through interconnecting scenes.  is a relaxing perspective-based puzzle game with pleasant visuals, touching story told without words, and relaxing soundtrack. There is an alternate ending that requires players to find all hidden photos and replay the story a second time while keeping an eye out for ways "to think outside the cube".  About 2 to 5 hours to complete depending on how often you use the hint system or unlocking achievements.  A must try for puzzle enthusiast [10/10]
_childDocuments_.name: Moncage

_childDocuments_.review: Puzzle games or sequences in games built around perspective and optical illusions are tricky to do well. You have to direct player view to the patterns you wish them to see, but without robbing them of the eureka moment of finding it, provide them with a goal without turning the process into just solving problems, keeping the joy of discovery intact. Antichamber, Gorogoa or even The Witness (for all of its countless issues) are great examples of titles that do that well, at least for the most part. Moncage isn’t. It’s not bad, but playing it isn’t particularly fun.The concept is pretty simple – you look at a cube where each of its 5 available sides can show a different scene. Elements of those scenes, however can be interacted with or even combined, if you look at them from a correct perspective. So, say, a ladder on one side and a grate of the same overall form and color on the other side might actually connect between the two sides and change something on the scene. It’s a very simple, but fun mechanic that provides some fun during the first ten or so minutes of the game.Then it stops being fun. Mostly because the game never provides any understandable goals or reasons for combining elements – you just randomly rotate the perspective, shifting between different zoomed in elements of the scenes, until randomly stumbling upon something that connects and you can proceed further. Most of the time I couldn’t understand why I did what I did even after doing it and understanding what visual story it’s trying to tell. The game also sometimes hides elements that can be interacted with under odd perspective angles with no clear reason as to why that’s there and why interacting should do anything, but until you do, you’re stuck.I had some fun during the opening moments of the game and it isn’t a terrible execution of the idea. But it’s extremely undercooked, often poorly handled and in the end there are simply far better and more exciting titles that explore similar, if maybe not exactly the same, ideas.
_childDocuments_.name: Moncage
