_childDocuments_.review: So let's talk about some of the out-of-game things off the bat. This game and its prequel, Nexomon (also just released on Steam) are both ports of mobile games, and you can kind of tell. There's no option to rebind controls, there's no screen resolution setting, and it defaults to fullscreen (use Alt+Enter to window the game and drag to resize). Apparently there were microtransactions in some version of these games - there are none here, and I have no idea what you would have originally even paid money for. Despite taking place 1000 years after the first game, almost every single major character in this game is from the first game, and it's supposed to feel good to see them again. There's even one or two character reveals that fall totally flat if you've never played the first game. It's also a Pokemon clone through-and-through, down to some of the designs veering pretty close to plagiarism territory. If you don't mind those things, this game is really fun for what it is. The pitch is "Open-World Pokemon," but done in the traditional route-based style instead of Sword/Shield's Wild Area approach. As soon as you finish the tutorial, you can go pretty much anywhere you want. The characters said "Hey, we need to go east!" but then a random NPC told me about an island to the west that has every type of Nexomon on it. I think, cool, I want some ghost types or whatever, so I ignore the plot to go west, and I get to the docks. I'm expecting to be told, hey, can't go this way yet, but the guy takes me to the island and I snag a ton of cool monsters for my team before I even get to the first town. I meet up with the plot again, and get told "Hey, make sure you go North to town. Please don't go farther east, the Badlands are there." So you go east and sure enough, you can stroll into the Badlands and do stuff there. The gameplay mechanic of going wherever you want is also reinforced by the way the game works. This game has enemies that scale in difficulty, which can be done really poorly, but it works fine here. Normally, the mistake is scaling enemies to the player's level, because then you never get any leg up on the enemy. Here, enemies scale based on story progression, so every boss battle has a scripted level of difficulty. Which means that, yes, you could just powerlevel to surpass any challenge. However, you could also do what I did, which is to never stick with the same team and to constantly grab new party members. The first real boss in the game is a Water type, and I lost the fight kind of bad. I realized my team was underleveled, so I went back over to the forest to pick up some wild grass types that were now scaled just about to the bosses level and I won the fight much easier. Having trouble against a Grass boss? Go to the volcano and grab a few fire types. I basically never had to fight a trainer battle to level up in my entire playthrough because every time my team got too weak for a fight, I just caught new ones. But, if you did want to level up, trainers scale also, and are re-fightable after a short amount of time. There's also other things to do in the world as well that will help you sale up in power. Elemental shards can be mined from rocks around the world, and can be traded for numerous things. Most quest NPCs will ask you to bring them some combination of shards and will give you special rewards in return. Greed Wallets increase your gold gained from random Nexomon encounters and trainer fights by 3%, and they stack, so the more you find, the more gold you get. EXP Boosters do the same but for EXP, and elemental Whistles increase the capture rate of Nexomon of the corresponding element. You can also trade shards for Cores, which are equippable items. There are cores that increase stats, but also cores that increase your money and EXP gain as well. Four EXP III cores mean you're gaining +80% EXP per fight, which makes grinding VERY fast, even at high levels. Plus, four is all you'll ever need, since you can just swap them out to whoever you're leveling. There's also tons of rare Nexomon to find and hidden areas that you'll gain access to as you progress in the game and unlock more exploration tools. There's a series of postgame quests to get legendaries that are reminiscent of old-school JRPG world-exploration quests like Chrono Trigger or FF7. The game skews a little on the harder side, but honestly, this might have been a result of my playstle of never sticking with one team. By the 3/4 mark I was really relying on items, and I straight-up couldn't win the final boss rush. I spent one hour grinding my whole team up from 58 to 65 and I re-beat all the same fights and eventually the game, and didn't need to use a single item from that point on. However, during the main game, the way the difficulty manifests itself is your team getting mostly knocked out during a fight and then not getting any EXP, since all EXP from trainer battles is awarded at the end of a fight, not after each KO. So, if one monster defeats every enemy but the last enemy uses explosion and takes you down, you gain no EXP for the whole fight. This also means that there can be a LOT of time spent running back from a dungeon to a healing center, since you'll sometimes have to do multiple boss fights one after another. In that sense, it's very important to be prepared. You can see your and your opponent's stats in battle, so you can size up a Nexomon to see if it's worth catching and adding to your team. Evolutions are a huge power spike just like in Pokemon, but Nexomon also has an in-game Database that tells you exactly what the base stats for each monster is, so you can directly compare power levels. However, almost all Nexomon end up being in a very similar power range - there's no outright bad monsters whose stats make them significantly worse than other monsters, like comparing a Butterfree to a Salamance. My only complaint on this front is that movepools are very small, despite a large number of moves. One Electric type I was using never got a thunder move that did above 85 damage, so I trained up another one that had a move that did up to 150 damage. Late-game bosses are DPS races, so those differences in power are REALLY noticeable. That being said, I had one Nexomon who solo'd the final three fights, and it was a non-legendary grass type who had three healing move (two healed you at the end of every turn like Leftovers but they stacked) and only one attack move, so there's a lot of viable options. However, specific bosses are usually immune to status ailments, so those strategies can be dice rolls.The story itself is neat, but like I said, my enjoyment was slightly kneecapped by not knowing any of the characters. It's a direct sequel in all regards, basically. The game is also "funny," and whether or not you think meta-jokes are funny is gonna have a big sway on how you feel. Like, at least once per big cutscene, a character will look at the camera and say "man, I thought this was a kids game." I don't mind it, and thought some of the jokes were funny, but if you really hate that it might grate on you. That being said, the story actually tries to be something unique, which it really didn't have to, all things considered. I actually enjoyed it, and didn't expect what ended up happening. It was way more interesting than anything Pokemon has tried in the main series games. Anyways, if you're looking for something that feels like Pokemon but tries something new, this game is definitely worth a shot. I think this game answers the question of what an open-world creature collection game looks like much more than the Wild Area does, and I enjoyed the whole experience much more than I enjoyed the campaign of any Pokemon game since Black2/White2. It's got some RPGMaker crust to it (yes I know it's made in Unity), but if you're willing to look past some minor rough spots, this is a really fun 30-40 hour game.

_childDocuments_.review: Okay so after 35hrs I finished the main story & I have to say it was a pretty great play through the end was pretty damn difficult I'd say I cut it pretty close, the last boss almost wiped my team & my inventory LOLTLDR: Great story, good game mechanics, lackluster move pools, I loved the scaling difficulty, worth the price 100%!I've played my fair share of pokemon "knockoffs" & clones & this is definitely one of the better ones, I'd say it's right up there with Insurgence, but unlike many of the others, Nexomon isn't really a clone it's more like an inspired work. I think they do a lot of things better than traditional pokemon, such as the entire catching mechanics & imo cores are infinitely better than putting iv/evs into the game. I’ll also say that stamina is far superior to PP.One of & imo the strongest aspects of this game is the story & dialogue, coco is SO GREAT. That said I think that there are areas where it is lacking for sure, but I mean even pokemon has its own issues. That said I think an area where this game is poor is the nexomon move pool.A lot of the time it feels like you go 10-15 levels without getting a new move that could even replace the old ones, & when you get to 40+ & you start relearning old moves sometimes you relearn the same move back to back. The support or utility moves are also too niche & pretty underwhelming, I mean there is a ghost move that requires you to be 15 levels up to work but the way the difficulty works in this game there is never a point where there is more than a 3-5 level difference between nexomon.A suggestion I would make for future titles is to make utility or supportive moves into passive skills if what they provide is so niche & miniscule or in some cases are trade offs like the water move that gives you 40% crit but lowers your def by 20% or something close to that.I’ve seen a lot of complaints about the difficulty, people say that the leveling up of wild nexomon & opponents is too much but I really don't understand how that’s an issue, I got through the game without blacking out once & I switched my roster plenty of times throughout my 35hrs of gameplay, if anything it makes the game easier since you don't have to catch low level nexomons & train them from scratch.If you keep a balanced roster & don’t allow some of you nexomon to be under leveled relative to each other then you really should not be having any issues with the difficulty. (exp cores are your friend)

_childDocuments_.review: I haven't quite finished the game yet, but that is also precisely why i chose to write a review now. This game does a lot of things right, innovates on some things, but also struggles in other areas. Despite my review I will finish this game, although mainly to see where its going. Now hear me out on why:-  So far this game has a well written story, intriguing and funny. Unlike your traditional Pokemon title, you will find that some characters grow on you, you will be able to relate to them, while loathing other characters. The pacing is well done, unless you chose to actively grind/catch Nexomon. There are plot twists, some more obvious than others (even at this point in the game I am impressed by the story, which is why I will finish it).-  The music in this game is really good. It has individual tracks for areas, that fit the theme and set the mood. The battle themes are catchy and you will quickly find yourself humming along the tune.-  The art is quite breathtaking in my opinion. Its fairly unique from what games I've played so far in this genre, the animations are crisp and look cool. Every Nexomon really has a unique feel to it and evolutions make sense + you start to look forward to them.-  There are things other than music, story and artstyle that make this game different and one of the most interesting ones in my opinion, are "passive" items. There are also items called Cores, that boost the stats of your Mon, and you can equip more than 1 (4 in total). Throughout the game you will find items, that permanently increase money/EXP, or other things, you get. These are usually rewarded through side quests, which can often times be turned in immediatly when you arrive, or after a little bit of time investment, depending on how thoroughly you play through certain areas. I have probably invested about 1/4 of my time playing, trying to finish side quests and quite enjoyed it. Now despite all those points you might wonder, why I can't quite recommend this game. My main reason for that is the games actual main mechanic, the battle system. If you have played through other monster catching games, there are certain things you might have gotten used to, or grown to like. Nexomon, in my opinion, has a very shallow battle system, and heres why:-  As any other monster catching game, Nexomon also has types, with certain Weaknesses, or Strengths. Now oddly enough, I have not found information in the actual game, that tells you "hey, this is weak against that, while that is strong against this. I had to look it up on the "wiki". There are no multitype Nexomon either.Another thing that felt weird, was the actual amount of damage "effective" or "ineffective" moves did. Effective moves deal +25% damage, while ineffective moves deal 35% less damage and yes, that wasn't a typo, +25%/-35%.STAB (Same Type Attack Bonus) also seems to be a thing, albeit very minor, I could barely ever tell the difference.-  There are none. No Nexomon have any abilities, that can give them an advantage like causing rain, levitating etc..-  Nexomon have little base stats. Theres HP, ATT, DEF, Speed and "Stamina". This means a Mon with high base stats, can often win despite having a type disadvantage, while using a move that is ineffective. Mons of the same species also dont seem to have different stats (like IVs/EVs in Pokemon), meaning 2 Mon of the same species will have the same stats with an equel Level.On top of that, there are no Attack/Defense moves in the traditional sense. You can't buff your Mons attack to +6 like in Pokemon. While there are moves (like Barrier) that increase your DEF by 25%, nothing on the actual game screen, tells you that you have that buff, so better keep that in mind when you use it. You use it once during battle and its permanent (no clue if switching it in and out during one battle loses you that buff though, since the game just keeps it hidden from you). These things alone, cause battles to go one of 2 ways. You can chose to level a complete team, and will often find yourself looking for a type advantage on the field, OR, you will always fall back to that one Nexomon (most likely a Psychic type), that will quickly overlevel. In fact, you can  easily pick up a Mon called Divette early on, and sweep through everything in your path, if you have 10+ levels on the area you are in.Regardless of my negative review, this game has things to offer. In fact, maybe if you play monster catching games very casual, and haven't heard about deeper statistics (like EVs/IVs, SpD/SpA, abilites) and dont care about them, you might just enjoy this.

_childDocuments_.review: Nexomon: Extinction is a Pokemon knock-off, but a fairly good one I think that does enough to distinguish itself and make it worth a buy.The gameplay of Nexomon Extinction is very similar to the main-series of Pokemon games. You go around the world battling Nexomon, of which you have a team of up to six on you, each of which has up to four moves. It's not  identical though, there are some minor differences. In battle, rather than having PP, moves all have a certain stamina cost which use up some of your Nexomon's stamina bar. Personally, I prefer this system actually, first it's a bit more realistic, for what that's worth. It is also a bit more strategic since there is a drawback to using more powerful moves. They use more stamina, and that will limit the amount of moves total you'll be able to use. There are fewer types than in Pokemon, also (9), and there are no dual-types. One thing that I quite liked was that you had a choice of 9 starters, one for each type. If anyone's curious I picked the Noki when I played through the game, though I was torn between it, Mara, and Lume.In terms of the general gameplay, however, Nexomon: Extinction is much-more story focused than Pokemon. Rather than traveling around the region collecting badges with the goal of becoming the champion with some bad guys doing bad stuff in between as filler, in Nexomon your reason for going around the world accomplishing tasks is for direct story reasons, or for side-quests of which there are a few, though not a great deal.Unlike Pokemon or Nexomon 1, this is an open world game. Most of the map is available for you to explore from the beginning, though some areas have to be unlocked over the course of the story. To maintain balance, wild and opposing tamer's Nexomon's levels scale to the player. It has it's advantages and disadvantages. Its advantages are, of course that you are able to go around freely and not generally have to worry about being under leveled for an area, and also and wild Nexomon you catch will be fairly close to your team's level, so getting them up to a viable level is not a tremendously tedious task (unless you stow them in storage for a while). Its disadvantages are myriad, however. Firstly, and this is the same in pretty much every game that does this, leveling up isn't really making you any stronger, since it is as difficult to defeat an enemy at level 50 as it is at level 5 since they level with you. Also, raising a Nexomon that you might have put into storage for a while is a pain since they will certainly be massively under-leveled compared to every other Nexomon in the game, meaning that you have to use other Nexomon to battle and use the switch-out method or exp-sharing cores to raise it. Personally, I would suggest to the devs a compromise for the next game. Make tamer's Nexomon scale with the player, but don't scale the wild Nexomon so that training up a weaker Nexomon isn't impossible without the use of a stronger one. While the system Extinction uses has its flaws, though, it doesn't break the game or anything of the sort.The post-game though is very sparse. There are a few quests to capture legendary Nexomon, but since there isn't anything like the Battle Frontier or multiplayer there isn't much reason to do this other than completing the database. In terms of replayability there isn't a whole lot either other than using a different team.The story of Nexomon: Extinction is the reason to play this game, I think. While not on the level of  or , or to compare it to other games,  or  the story is competently written, and I found it to be quite enjoyable, with plenty of memorable characters (though there were a couple which just appeared and then were summarily thrown away) and twists and turns in the story. I did have a couple of complaints at first, mainly having to do the game taking a while to explain the central conflict of the game, and the reasons you should even be in opposition to the game's antagonist (which seem to be intentional, as some of the in-game characters even complain about this), though these were remedied midway through the game by the big twist there that occurs.Overall, the story is a bit more mature than Pokemon, while it isn't an adult game topics such as death are broached, and through the course of the story you do end up doing some morally dubious things in pursuit of your goals.That's not to say that the game is super-serious however, It liberally sprinkles in moments of levity throughout. The game has that sense of typical anime humor (I say this as someone who doesn't really watch that stuff) where the game constantly makes self-deprecating jokes about the writers/devs. There are also times when characters (well, mostly Coco, you're erstwhile sidekick) will point out the absurdities laden in the game world or in situations. Personally, I found the game to be fairly humorous, but it's easy to make me laugh. Perhaps you have higher standards than I do.Do you need to have played Nexomon 1 in order to understand the plot of Extinction? No, I did not and I was able to understand what was going on perfectly well. Everything you need to know is explained by the game (eventually).Nexomon: Extinction uses animated 2D sprites for both the overworld and battle scenes, like classic Pokemon games. For "cut-scenes" it uses still drawings to show what is going on. Overall, the game is pleasant to look at. The only criticism I have here is that the animations during battle-scenes don't change at all. For instance, if a Nexomon falls asleep or is at low health or the like the animation doesn't change to reflect that.The Nexomon designs are mostly strong. There were a few I wasn't fond of but most of them I liked.Overall pretty good. While not on the level of Wagner or Verdi, or the Pokemon games, the music in Nexomon: Extinction is still good in its own right. I only encountered on track which I wasn't really fond of but even then it wasn't that bad. Some of the music though I really quite like, and I look forward to hearing it when I boot up the game.The game does not allow you to rebind keys, unfortunately. The game uses the arrow keys for movement and I,J,K, and L for various actions. Also, there is a sprint button (backspace), but as far as I can recall the game didn't inform me of this. I didn't really encounter many bugs, there were a couple of moments when I tried to talk to someone and the wrong dialogue popped up, but that only happened twice and in neither instance did it I miss anything important.Also from what I can tell the devs are not native English speakers (Spanish, I think), so the game had to be translated in to English. How is the translation? Well, fine for the most part. There were a few lines of dialogue which had awkward grammar, but they were rare.Personally, I love this game. It uses the same tried-and-true gameplay formula as Pokemon with a few minor modifications, and adds in a fun and engaging story. The presentation, the Nexomon designs, and music are all strong too. It's not without its flaws, such as the inability to rebind keys, the incomplete explanation of the controls, or the lack of side content, but despite these flaws I would heartily recommend this game to anyone who is a fan of Pokemon-type games. I actually enjoyed this more than the games GameFreak has been releasing recently, and in fact would call this my favorite game of 2020. Personally, I rate this game a "Very Good" (scale below). As I said, if you're a fan of these sorts of games, I think this one is well worth your time.My scale (from worst to best): Atrocious, Very Poor, Poor, Mediocre, Below Average, Average, Above Average, Good, Very Good, Outstanding, Near-Perfect.

_childDocuments_.review: Nexomon: Extinction feels like a lackluster attempt at recreating the Pokémon formula. While it does deliver a monster-collecting experience, it struggles to stand out. Compared to similar titles like Coromon, Nexomon falls short in almost every aspect—except for puzzles, which it notably lacks. Ironically, this absence is its only advantage over Coromon.The most underwhelming part of the game is its art style, with monsters that fail to leave a lasting impression. Furthermore, the decision to balance the stats of rare and common monsters diminishes the thrill of finding rare ones. While this design choice might aim to encourage players to pick favorites based on personal preference rather than efficiency, it ultimately feels unfulfilling.If you're looking for a great monster-collecting experience, I’d recommend Coromon or Monster Sanctuary over this title. _childDocuments_.review: First time I've written a review for something.I do think this game has a lot of charm to it. The world has a level of non linearity and exploration elements that was very refreshing after the last few pokemon entries, the cast and story is actually pretty fun in a weird way (though I think it could do with less 'THIS IS A VIDEOGAME' meta humor) and has some good attempts at pokemon like dungeons. Unfortunately, this all gives way.Nexomon unfortunately starts to get very grindy out of complete no where. I can't really place how far in the game I was before writing this, but while being comfortably even with most of the trainers/wild nexomon, one boss fight just had an entire team of mons at a 4-5 level advantage over me, requiring me to just sit in the bushes and grind up to it. Fine, whatever. Level spikes at gyms have happened at some pokemon games aswell. But at the time, there was no exp share, and the way the battle system works means that you're likely only going to be fainting a few nexomon at a time before needing to run back to the center to get healed (which thank god  has no pokemon center healing animation). I was willing to grind through it at first, but its happened a second time now, demanding another long wave of bush grinding, center healing, then bush grinding again, all to fight a boss that out of complete no where massively over levels my team without any sort of level curve to it. And I just don't want to do grind in bushes for another hour or so to hit 5 levels over where I was.The second major problem I have is, despite the extremely numerous amount of Nexomon, I find they all homogenize themselves pretty quickly, the only real difference between them being what status (that seems to never get an explanation for what any of them do) they apply, and what element they are. No natures, no dual types, no items besides cores (which are just stat ups) and pretty little move diversity that isn't fast fire move, slow but strong fire move, etc etc. Their designs are very good aesthetically, but they all feel the same.So, yeah. I think the game has some potential, and I was honestly willing to look past some of the more minor issues, but the games combat has just lost its lustre and become monotonous, much worse than pokemon has. I'd like to see more of the story and explore around more, but I don't think it's worth it.

Single. Time. I find some new area, I'd have so much more fun with the game.This despite how unimpactful the actual collecting feels, it's more of a chore than a fun experience to find new Nexomon, because 99% of them are the same apart from art and element.And initially it feels like you get a shotgun blast of Nexomon straight to your face, takes out a lot of fun when there's 50 to get in the very first area, making it a fulltime job if you want to try out even half of them. _childDocuments_.review: TLDR: 6.5/10, it's a decent game, and if you are a fan of the genre you will probably enjoy it. That being said, it has some major flaws which I will detail below.*Now for the long version, I’ll be comparing this game to some of its contemporaries in the genre but you should still get the idea even if you are unfamiliar with them. Let's start with the positives because Nexomon: Extinction (NE) did some things well:- The monster designs and animations were fantastic. As a fan of this genre for over 20 years, it's always nice to see new creature ideas...that aren't just a ring of keys or a pile of garbage that is...- The story didn't take itself too seriously (the fourth wall was more of a fourth sheet of paper), which I personally don't mind. I much prefer an rpg story like this to the naval gazing, pretentious style that is all too common. In spite of the goofy writing style however, the pacing and exposition were excellent, building up to an epic conclusion. -The stamina system is a big improvement over pp. Other new games in the genre (like Temtem) are employing stamina as well and I hope more devs will follow suit.*Now for the negatives, this game really could have been fantastic. I'm hopeful that the devs will make improvements for the sequel:- NE essentially watered down or removed many of the deep customization and strategy elements that are present in other games in the genre. They are no passive abilities, doubles battles, hold items, EVs, or IVs. I wouldn’t mind if these systems were updated or replaced, but instead most of them are just gone, which leads to boring one dimensional combat. Each mon in NE can have 4 cores, which are sort of a hybrid between EVs and hold items, and are an interesting idea. The issue, however, is that this system removes the feeling of having a unique team, and working with their strengths and weaknesses. Instead, you can just catch higher level versions of your team as you level and they will be exactly the same. - The way mons learn new skills makes no sense to me. Every few levels, they keep relearning the same handful of boring skills, with no skill relearner npc. The vast majority of the skills in the game are just minor variations of typing, accuracy, damage, crit, speed, and hax. This is my biggest gripe with the game and just flat out LAZY game design. It is impossible to balance around hax. Of all the things to copy from pokemon, NE picked literally the worst thing about that franchise without even copying any of the interesting support moves. This game does have some support moves, but most of them are unusable, with only a 30% chance to not waste your turn. In fact, NE takes the rng/hax even further, emphasizing luck instead of strategy more than any other game I’ve played. It just isn’t fun. There are also a couple moves that are game breakingly OP (invincibility). My suggestion to the devs is to remove all hax like Temtem. No accuracy, no crit chance, no hax chance. That way you will be forced to come up with moves that are ACTUALLY INTERESTING, and players will get to come up with fun strategies.- The pc moves excruciatingly slowly, and for some god forsaken reason you don’t get running shoes until half way into the game. Beyond that, the battle speed also goes by at a snails pace. I was able to get past this by using a speed hack to play at 3x speed but if it weren’t for that, I honestly would not have had the patience to play.

_childDocuments_.review: I'm writing this review right after beating the game, to say that I had a lot of fun with it. Nexomon: Extinction was a good game. Good, but not without its flaws. Not enough flaws to put me off from playing the game, but enough for me to call out some of my biggest gripes in this review.For starters, the scaled leveling system. It's tied to your main story progress, which in theory is a good idea. It gives you the freedom to level wherever you want, and capture any Nexomon you want at any time at an appropriate level. However, sometimes the completion of several quicker story quests in a row can raise the level of wild Nexomon so rapidly, you'll be forced to stop and grind for EXP due to wild Nexomon overleveling your own team. This becomes especially notable near the end of the game, where you can potentially hit a wall due to wild Nexomon overleveling your own core team by at least 10 levels. Although the EXP cores and the recently introduced Synergy cores can do a lot of alleviate these grind walls, they will nonetheless end up taking several hours of your total gameplay time.As for the Nexomon themselves, although many of them have unique and compelling designs, the same can't really be said about their stats and movepools. Many Nexomon of the same type feel like they play exactly the same. The most notable exceptions to this are the Starters and the Legendaries, the former of which are capable of learning their type's most powerful attacking moves and the latter of which simply have very high stats. Additionally, the lack of dual typing means that every type of Nexomon always has the same weaknesses and counters. It ends up with every battle turning into rock-paper-scissors, and you'll most likely end up structuring your team around that fact. This additionally means that the Normal type is rather underpowered, as it doesn't resist or is super effective against any other type, but is weak against Ghost and Psychic types.And lastly, the story. To say the least, I didn't expect such a dark story from a game that looks so cute, bright and colourful. However, the game seems to struggle with taking its own story seriously. Whether that is by design or not could be up for debate, but what began to bother me the most is the amount of fourth wall jokes that the game employs. And it's not very subtle about it either. You can barely progress a step in the game without a character either calling out some kind of trope or even blatantly telling you they're in a video game. Such kinds of jokes can be fun in small amounts, but this case they really overstay their welcome to the point that it becomes a little obnoxious.However, in spite of these gripes, there is a lot of good about this game. Disregarding its more obnoxious fourth wall jokes, the story of this game genuinely engaged me and hit me with several twists and turns that I did not see coming. The graphics are pretty, the music is excellent, and while the gameplay is relatively simple, it does offer you enough to work with like in any other kind of Pokémon-esque game. Speaking of which, all in all this game just has a charm that the recent generations of Pokémon have lacked, and I'm glad that Nexomon was there to scratch that itch.My personal rating for this game? 7/10. It's a bit flawed and it could use a bit of polish, but overall it's well worth the experience. And for a price of only €20, I can guarentee you'll get your money's worth.

_childDocuments_.review: If you're taking a break from Pokémon but miss that series' specific vibe and atmosphere, this game might be a hard sell for you. It kind of feels like a Pokémon game written by jaded 28-to-32 Pokémon fans; sometimes it almost seems more concerned with dissing Pokémon and being meta than telling an actual story.But if you can get past that, what you'll find is a well-polished take on the mon collecting concept that competently and confidently delivers on the gameplay, with moderate levels of grind and the in-game economy kind of taking the piss being the only flaws. A solid choice, especially if you can get it on sale.

_childDocuments_.review: tldr: amazing game, because amazing story, but a bit let down by the battle mechanics.Let me preface this by saying: This is an absolute masterpiece of story telling; charming, funny, surprisingly witty and a great arc of suspense with a healthy dose of expected and *very* unexpected plot twists. Also nice to see a not completely black-and-white good against evil story! Characters had believable motivations, even the "bad" ones could be understood and sympathized with. I like stories with grey areas and some moral ambiguity ("Are we the bad guys?")I've finished the main story but haven't engaged with post story content as of writing. Now let's get to the not so great parts:I think it's not surprising to say that this game is *very* inspired by Pokemon and personally: I like this game *way* more than any of the Pokemon games I've played. But that's not because of the gameplay.- The (visual) designs of the Nexomons are great and there's plenty you Nexomons to choose from - but they feel like they're all the same. They barely have any unique attacks, most are shared between pretty much all of the Nexomons of the same type and even the attacks they do have, have very similar effects and visuals. There's almost no fancy leeching, "always first" attacks, charge up mechanics, ... It's almost always "you hit this hard with this accuracy at this speed" and you can choose between a hard hitting attack and a not as hard hitting but less stamina draining and faster one. On every single Nexomon. Yay.- The "trainer" (guild tamer) battles are more exciting, they usually have a wider variety of elements than Pokemon does and switch around more often so you need to also strategically switch. At least at first it was more exciting. Sometimes it got to the point of 2-3 switches from both sides after another which just gets tedious. Pokemon didn't have enough switching to combat type advantage, Nexomon uses it a bit too liberally. Not game breaking but on the verge of annoying.- Difficulty is a hard one: I've found most of the game fairly easy, but the difficulty scales with your own Nexomon's levels (or so it seemed to me) - but on (after) important story beats difficulty usually ramped back up. So after a big story event you kind of got weak which you then overcame to the point of it being easy, then next story section, rinse and repeat. Mind you, that's not a bad thing, I regularly felt like being challenged and then feeling the rewards for training by curbstomping my opponents. But! Together with the not so engaging battle system due to aforementioned lack of variety in attacks and uniqueness of Nexomon all the hard parts mostly got tedious and not actually hard. There was little to strategize apart from putting the right Nexomon type against your opponents, almost no "which attack will I use?", just "I'll take the hardest hitting one until my enemy is one shot, then I'll take the fastest one to be first and not get hit again". It's not bad. But it's also not great. Also, difficulty on the (story) end part was a bit whack, it rose rather dramatically which could have been overcome by a bit more training/side quest, but: While in the first half you got tons of compelling and rewarding side quests, that completely fell aside in the latter half of the story, which is great because the story was so captivating and well told I'd probably have wanted to ignore most side quests anyways! But... it killed the pacing. The end felt rushed and felt like a handful of side quests would have made the actual story end difficulty and pacing more in line the rest of the game. Again, it wasn't bad, but it wasn't great- The UI was cumbersome in some places. Animations always took a bit too long for my liking (I do like my animations *very* fast, so YMMV), some stuff was annoying like menus that don't wrap around so I had to move down 10 menu elements instead of going up 1 and wrapping to the bottom, the list of minor inconveniences goes on. Nothing truly bad but always a bit of a pain.And all of this brings us back to the story: It was absolutely amazing and it pains me having to write such long paragraphs about what I didn't like as much because this story deserved better. I still absolutely love this game and I *100%* would take Nexomon over any Pokemon game any day because for me the story is so much more important than the battles, but for someone who is more into the collection and fighting aspect that's going to be a brown stain on an otherwise masterpiece of a game.The good part is: From an outside perspective these issues seem like the easiest things to fix/improve upon in a sequel, so I'm definitely hyped for that! Having another Nexomon title with undoubtedly another amazing story but more sophisticated/more varied battle system sounds great!I'll also most likely take a gander at the post-story content which is rare for me to do.PS: Just thought of this and don't know how to get this in the flow of the review so have it at the end: Nexomon has a lot of very minor but very welcome small quality of life features that make it much less grindy than Pokemon, from "healing stones" spread throughout the world to passive heal after each battle so you don't need to run back after each battle to heal and collecting whistles to get better at catching Nexomon instead of buying increasingly expensive Pokeballs that serve no purpose besides being "better". Overall a lot of annoying pain points from playing Pokemon have been addressed here and I appreciate that a lot.PPS: I praised the story and humor, but this is a *very* subjective thing, especially the humor will not be everyone's cup of tea (4th wall breaks, sometimes a bit forced jokes) - I absolutely loved it and laughed a lot (Coco is the best sassy companion!), but it could easily cross over to cringe for others.PPPS: There's a lot more tiny things I could write about but either cut because this is already extremely long or I just didn't think about it - most of these tiny things are positive as well, so definitely do look at other reviews, I'm sure they have mentioned some of the stuff as well!PPPPS: I keep thinking of new stuff! One thing I'd like to mention about the very end of the story (trying to not spoiler, but if you haven't played you may want to skip this, this is mostly feedback for the developer): It felt a bit poo that the last battle felt so incredibly scripted. It was... fine that some sections were made that you couldn't possibly lose or couldn't possibly win just based on level and attack setups, but right at the very end that I was forced to win against the main adversary with a "very special Nexomon" (it makes sense why, it just feels a bit poo about how "I'm losing but suddenly all the enemie's attacks magically miss so I do win unless I use the other Nexomons which just get curbstomped"). I get that it should be a "oh wow this was such a close fight" moment, but... I just didn't have this feeling at all because it was super obvious it was scripted to be this way. It just didn't feel as if I just had a close fight because I knew this was the only possible outcome - I legit think that the very last section of the last fight (maybe even the entire last fight?) would have been better and more a climatic end if it was just a cutscene. Because effectively this is what it was anyways: Almost no matter my choices in the fight the outcome was pretty much guaranteed to be a very specific way, so why even bother with having the fight be an "interactive" thing if nothing about my input (apart from maybe actually actively trying to lose) would change anything? From a story telling perspective the end was absolutely amazing if a bit stereotypical, but the gameplay *severely* let down the suspense of the story at this point. Thinking about the content and story of the end makes me think fondly of it. Thinking about the medium (the fight) that told this story does not make me think fondly of it.

_childDocuments_.review: is basically a  game with a few different mechanics, but never strays too far away from  original form. The battles are fun, the world is amazingly designed and exciting to explore, there are tons of Nexomon to  capture and the story is intriguing. Even though there are a few problems here and there they don’t fault the enjoyment of this game all that much.• The game has quite a sense of humor• The story was compelling and well written throughout• 9 different starters to choose from, however they don’t feel unique• 381 unique Nexomon to capture and train• Capturing Nexamons has some depth to it• Different pre-made characters to choose from• Battles are quite difficult since the wild Nexomon and Tamers scale with your level•  isn’t as tediously grindy as • Sometimes jokes feel forced into more serious moments• The EXP system is can be annoying• New moves are boring and practically worthless at higher levels• Because you can’t fight several trainers at once without tons of healing supplies you’ll more than likely avoid a lot of them and you’ll eventually find yourself under-leveled• No feature to show you where Nexomon you’ve seen in the wild previously, so catching all 381 Nexomon will be frustrating• End game is just catching legendaries, unless you’re trying to complete the Nexodex there isn’t much pointYou are a young child in an orphanage who is picked out to be a Nexomon Tamer one day, a few escalated scenes later and you're given the choice of a Nexomon starter. With that under your belt you set off into the world, finding out about the Tyrant war that the human race seems to be caught in the middle of and so you selfless help to try and put a stop to this war even though it seems way out of your league.The story was interesting enough to hold my attention for the entire 30-ish hours and gave me a reason to read through all the dialogue. There’s a lot of humour as well that almost always hits at the right time, only a few times the jokes seemed forced since it was in the middle of a serious scene. It’s clear which characters had more thought put into them than others, but overall all the characters were decent.You can’t overlook the fact that a lot of work went into this game, it doesn’t try to hide that it’s a  type game even though it crosses the fuzzy line of being a clone, with different names for things and some new mechanics to make it feel a little different from . However, you’re probably interested in this game  you want to play a new  type game and that doesn’t necessarily mean  is bad, it tries to be different in a number of ways. However, some of these differences cause more problems that weren’t in .Picking your starter is probably one of the more memorable aspects of , they’re unique since you can’t find them in the wild so it becomes a valuable asset to your team that you can’t replace. Even though  gives you 9 different starters to choose from, these aren’t as unique or valuable as a starter should be. Without much effort, you can easily find these starters in the wild and some of them don’t really have good stats either. I suppose this flexibility gives you the option to change your starter if you find another but then you don’t have that attachment with the starter you chose in the first place.Battles are practically the same as  but with a stamina bar added instead of PP points for each individual skill. Each skill takes a specific amount of stamina points and each Nexomon has a stamina stat to determine how much stamina they have. It does change the mechanics slightly, but it also adds to the annoyance of having to refill their stamina bar either by healing or using potions.Mechanically, every fight in  is a lot more even than in . You won’t be able to bust your way through several Tamers before having to heal, even if you have a type advantage. Thankfully the Tamers can easily be avoided as you explore the world but that then leads to your Nexomon eventually being under-leveled because you’ve had to avoid them to try and make it to the next town. You can fight every Tamer, but unless you have a bunch of money to spend on healing supplies you’ll constantly be going back and forth to healing centers. Tamers do scale with your level as do the wild Nexomon so even if you have to grind it isn’t much of a problem. None of this really hinders the battles too much to make it unenjoyable, more of a slight inconvenience that you'll occasionally be reminded about now and then during the game.There is a diverse and large variety of different Nexomon to catch in the wild and the annoyance of being randomly encountered by them in the grass has been replaced compared to the older  games. You can now see the grass moving to indicate where the encounters are which move to different spots every 20 - 30 seconds. Even though there are still parts in the game where you’ll have random encounters (in caves and specific locations) the encounter rate is small enough to not get annoying.Capturing Nexomon has some added depth to it to increase the chances of a successful capture, lowering their health, giving them status effects, feeding them their favorite foods and capturing them in specific Nexotraps that correlate to their type will all help increase the chances of capturing them. It even goes as far as showing the percentage of how likely you will capture that Nexomon. There’s also a small mini-game every time you try to capture a Nexomon where you have 5 seconds to press the buttons in the correct order.The music is very  like but still sets the tone for more serious scenes as well as the more light-hearted and humorous ones too. Each town has its own unique soundtrack that really suits the place that you’re exploring, even though it’s simplistic it really does set the atmosphere well throughout the game. does a brilliant job at making each area you discover feel and look completely different. From an extremely vibrant and colourful floating island to a more gloomy and haunted abandoned town, each area feels exciting and new to explore. The character and Nexomon designs have clearly been worked on a lot with a lot of attention to detail which is surprising since there are 381 different Nexomon to catch.If you like  then  will definitely feel familiar to you, you might even get a sense of nostalgia from the old  games. It definitely has the upper hand with specific things that  doesn’t, but that does however bring its own problems. But these problems don’t really hinder the enjoyment of the game all that much. It’s quite easy to look past these flaws and enjoy the game from start to finish, if you’re a  fan then this is a must buy.

_childDocuments_.review: TLDR: (95/100) Buy this game.Let's not pretend most of us weren't interested in this game because of our love for Pokemon. That being said, there are lots of alternatives these days. I would put Pokemon, TemTem, and this game all together at the top. This game streamlines a lot of the things that have been added to the Pokemon games over the years and makes it (in my opinion) a more enjoyable experience. I'm going to do a pro/con list just to make it easier...that being said I want to touch on the difficulty. It is more difficult than Pokemon and less difficult than TemTem...has a good balance going for it.PRO'S: (water beats fire which beats plant which beats water). Pokemon long past over complicated it. You have different types of traps, food to increase your capture chances, status effects, and a  bonus quick-time game to improve your odds further. Everything is broken down in percentages plain as day for you. I don't think I've seen a better mechanic in any monster capture game. Quality characters, all with their own personality, and varied enough that anyone should be able to find a team they enjoy using. System is unlocked early, is straightforward and useful, and doesn't rely on specific conditions to work  (f'ing FLY) You definitely have a grind if you want to get to the point where you can one shot most things. At  that  point the world levels up with you. All trainers and every Nexemon level up as you progress  through the game, meaning that going through previous areas actually feels worthwhile.   Great story, and amazing writing...the writers keep it interesting and fun, and constantly poke fun at  themselves and the cliches that are found in this genre of game. Has SOMETHING to do once the credits roll. The game is fair when it comes to getting you paid. If you buy 5k worth of potions to go grind in the forest, then you will return to town with 5k and a stronger team. It has always been completely fair to me-not too much or too little. Every Nexemon you catch will have the same stats as any other one with the same name. There a color variations to find (rare Cosmic versions). However, the grind of catching fifty of the same monster just to see slight stat differences has been eliminated. Pokemon has constantly added                                more and more bloat to their games with every generation that make them less about fun and  more about min/maxing stats. This one has a few components:   1) In the world you instigate every battle with a Nexemon by walking into shaking grass. this means that   you can avoid any fights you don't want to get in. 2) Each patch of  grass has different sets of Nexemon. If you are hunting something specific you just have to go to a   patch that it spawns in. this helps reduce the number of Nexemon you have to fight through before you   get to something Mega Rare .3) Caves and buildings still contain the old "walk until something surprises you" mechanic. I don't see how they would change this, but if that's your thing it's still there. Here's a list for you: 4) All trainer battles can be avoided, and they reset after a time, which allows you to grind experience and money, as well as fight against teams often. There is a slight stat difference in Nexemon depending on the rarity, but it's not a huge enough one to through away a common monster you really love. They also make your starters EXTREMELY viable the entire game.PROS/CONS: It's more fair than TemTem with your constant running back to stores for healing. Pokemon gives you stamina for each  Nexemon it's all in one pool. This means that you can't pull the big moves out for hard fights, and save the smaller ones for trash grind...the differences between the stamina cost isn't enough in my opinion to bother. You will CONSTANTLY be popping stamina regenerating potions, because only a select few Nexemon have a move to recover it themselves. This is a chore at first, but because every encounter pays you, it has been balanced out for me during my playthrough. I always had enough money to buy the potions I needed to heal and recharge my team. In pokemon, it wasn't necessary, and in TemTem it's taken to such an extreme it's frustrating. In most games they are either useless or over powered. In this game they are mostly overpowered, but they have such a low hit chance it's kind of balanced. Want to freeze your enemy, which totally ruins their chances to do anything? Well here's a move that does a little damage and only has a 15% chance of freezing them. It's good and bad. Generally, the higher level you are, the less they matter. Big moves, a boost move, and a healing move will always be your go to's. Everything else is useful only in capturing or big fights. Four Cores replace any other equipment system, and add a small amount of customization. They help a lot, especially in leveling or money grind, but aren't a big addition.CONS:

_childDocuments_.review: Now that I've gone through the main story I think I can give this a proper review.My TL/DR would be some of the other bad reviews are misleading, it has real flaws, but it has refreshing aspects for the mon-catch genre and I want to see how they improve and grow with the sequel. And Old Scientist boi better be in the sequel like he wanted.Gameplay: I'll start with the positives. Usually you choose when to fight wild mons and tamers, huge quality of life for these kinds of games before you have the ability to teleport around. You can get/make "cores" which can be slotted into mons to increase stats or exp/money gain, or share exp etc. You can get special items exploring or doing quests that stack benefits like catch rate, exp or money boosting, etc. You can also get QoL items like an infinite repel spray to turn off/on, or the ability to access your storage box from anywhere. You can also change nicknames freely at any time, easily get back old moves, and other little things that just make it nicer than Mon-catch games that try to follow too closely to pokemon. Also there are actual boss battles that feel good...or as good as they can be, given the simplicity of the game.As for the negatives, these will probably make or break your intentions to pick this game up if you only care about the gameplay and nothing else. Firstly, outside of combat (where all options are labeled) you are never told the controls, and never will be. WASD/arrow keys work for movement, Q/E switches columns in menus, i is menu, J/U/O has special menu effects which are -sometimes- labeled, K is your standard interaction and yes button, L is your standard cancel and no button. Again, you wont be told this so if you are going to play it, there you go. Then there is typing, movesets, and stats. I like the type matchups as they are, feels right for the most part, and certainly more balanced out than pokemon. But there are no dual types so there is no brain power use in your decision making, made all the worse by the movesets. The movesets are baffling. Mons almost never have damage types outside Normal and their own type (I believe I saw 2 mons with an off type elemental move). So it usually really is easiest to just switch to type advantage and spam attack.  There are a bunch of moves that are just worse speed/power/accuracy versions of other moves, with little sense in when they are distributed in a mon's lvls. Most of the non-attack moves are far too situational, like a series of "take less damage from [element] for x turns except they are only learned by mons of said element which means they already resist said element. There are mons that can pick up objectively best moves at lvl 10 (which you can always get back if they are missing from a higher level catch) making the choice between 2 mons you are considering painfully obvious when the other wont learn said move til lvl 61 (or never), made all the worse by the issue with stats. And That issue is: They aren't different enough to matter. At low lvls every mon is only 1 or 2 points different in any given stat. By the very late game you can finally start to feel that a mon has low defense or good speed, and at that point you are beating the end of the story (maybe sooner, if you don't do any side stuff and avoid battles and catching mons like the plague, since the game has adaptive difficulty scaling you can probably beat the end of the game at a lower level than I did.)Art/Music: I think the art is very good personally, and I even like a lot of the designs. Obviously these are highly subjective things so I suggest looking at the database (pokedex equivalent) yourself before buying. I can't comment on the music as it was turned off for my playthrough (played casually with podcasts and stuff in the background)Story: If you really don't like it and you aren't here for it, spamming K and L at the same time will BLAST through dialogue, so I wouldn't worry about that. If you do care about the story, then I'd say in my opinion its actually good. I didn't play the first game, which has impact on this, but that didn't stop me from getting what was going on. I think its got a good number of twists, can be funny, and its leagues better than a standard pokemon game.Beyond that praise though, I have to say: The writer for the dev has contempt for themselves, the people they work for, and the players, and they need to stop and get help. Make friends and touch grass. The number of meta jokes are too high, sure, but thats not my real issue here. The real issue is its clear someone working on this has been badly hurt by negative, non-constructive criticism and is constantly injecting put downs to the game, and to gripes players may have against it or perhaps the previous game. If there was something making the story bad, it was this. Stop attacking the reader. Stop attacking yourself. The game, you, and the players will be better for it.Previous Review for transparency:Still gonna play it for some mindless time kill listening to podcasts/streams. But I don't recommend.You can't lower the volume until you've entered the title screen, chosen a save slot, watched a long intro, picked your character avatar and name, watched a cutscene, and told where to go. THEN you can change settings. The gradient for change is like 8 steps or so, so the music was too loud on the lowest setting and I still had to regulate it via windows volume mixer.Speaking of settings. You also can't change the resolution. You can change between fullscreen or not fullscreen (after going through all the same hoops required to change sound settings). You can force a resolution change while in windowed mode by haphazardly squishing the box as it'll 'pop' into the closest resolution to that, but this just makes everything smaller, it does not balance UI elements for legibility.Finally the controls. I already read from other reviews that you can't change them. Its annoying and dumb, but they are a serviceable. The much more pressing matter with them is they aren't told to you. Ever. They you a non-standard IJKL with I being the equivalent of a "start" button, opening your menu of options. K is you standard interaction and yes button. L is your standard cancel action and no or back out button. Holding L also lets you run, ala pokemon running shoes etc. If you read this review and still want to play it, then this is the only time you'll be told. I repeat, the game will never tell you any of this. And whats more, some characters WILL mention buttons...But they just call them "action button". The characters want to complain with meta humor about not having budget? Maybe don't pay for that Loud intro and put a settings option at the main menu, and show the ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ controls. Its borderline contempt for players.

_childDocuments_.review: The World: Very well fleshed out, and the story pays into it in full. Each area is explained and has meaning for why it is there, and has reasons to visit. You never feel like you just visit a place and never have to go back. Like its just there to fill in a spot and is nonsense. Each area is also very dynamic in how its is laid out as well.The Story: Brilliant. There is substance, and even after beating it twice I was finding myself slowing down in some parts so I could re-experience the chills I felt on my first run. The characters are expanded on and actually bring depth to not only the game but the story. I feel like the humor is fantastic, but it needs to be slimmed down slightly in some places, especially in the ending parts of the game so it doesn't feel like the story is being held hostage.Gameplay: We'll start off with traversing the world. The movement is clean and as you progress it gets even easier to move around, you don't have to just go to cities and find yourself having to run like crazy. It also allows you the option of shortcuts between areas if you so choose so you can revisit the landscape and enjoy the sights and experiences.Battling is very plain, I love the one typing system, with no skills to weigh down the gameplay. It's very simple and straight forward. I would like typings to have a larger impact with less impact from level. Moves should also be fleshed out more, I want more options. A lot of the moves have the same benefits, so you'll find yourself using the same good moves across mons just reflavored. However, some moves are used less by mons and can be more favorable (ie. stat increasing moves that are busted good that only a handful get.) I also noticed a lot of the stats are very similar. We need to see more mons with amped up defense, or hp. It will diversify the viability of mons without diminishing the combat.Powers are not used enough on the overworld. We need more opportunities to adventure, it would be cool to see previous areas have off shoots that have meaning. It would add even more options for world building and item locations. Or maybe for DLC placement later on. Idk, I just felt like some powers are completely useless outside of like three areas.Areas: Usually very good, I feel like the ending almost gets impatient with itself. It could use maybe another city or two to rehouse some of the story. I'd like to see sequel(s) with a larger group of people which can boast more unique shops and etiquette between nations.Items: The items are super impactful throughout the game. Most items I find can be insanely beneficial across the board. Some focus on support like cores, some focus on helping with resources. Others help with quality of life and traversal of the world.Ui/controls: Controls could be more focused and changeable for quality of life. I was lucky enough to find them on my own. But, for the first minute of the game, I found myself fumbling around the keyboard to find which key to press. I recommend a popup showing controls for a few moments and for the love of god. We need a type vs type chart in game. I couldn't find one in over 70+ hours on phone/pc. Both can be put in the journal in an interactive menu to show both typings and controls you can name it "Info Con."DLC: This was honestly the most grindy and irritating nonsense I have felt in a long time. I made it through in spades because I came prepared, and love puzzles. The end game shouldn't have scaled so damn hard. It can be made challenging in others ways instead of everyhign getting and exta idduno 100-10k hp and damage. Instead, you should have focused on buffing their defense and making them show up two at a time rather than one at a time. I felt like I was walking up a 90 degree incline. Keep in mind I had over 50 potions that would heal everything and I have 13 left. I spent 50k coins for my goods and had nearly nothing by the end of it. Base game was fabulous and I wanted to replay it for a third time. Once I found the DLC. I am finding it hard to get back on since it will require me to fight such absurd battles yet again. The capture rate in the end game also needs to be buffed slightly. If I hadn't come prepared I would have lost at least 2 mons per wild encounter. God forbid the boss fights and capturing stuff all while trying to stay healthy enough for the next. TL;DR: Game is fantastic and has great depth with excellent challenge definitely worth the money. However, the DLC is horrible to play through even for hardcore play. It's also excruciatingly plain. It's better to play the base game and completely skip the DLC.

_childDocuments_.review: I would like to state, first, that I am writing this review not as a kid that grew up with Pokemon, but as a teenager hugging her Pokemon Red to her chest the whole way home before popping new batteries into her gameboy so she could play the game on its green screen. I'm writing this as someone who sat for hours with friends, connected by a little wire, waiting for the transfer to be over to fill her pokedex. I am writing this as someone who has watched her own son learn to read with his very first copy of Pokemon on his DS system. I am writing this as someone who grew... underwhelmed with the Pokemon story as each game was produced and only led to more pokemon to capture but felt as if it were the same old story each game. Go from point A to point B and become the pokemon master. Perhaps there will be extraneous story along the way, but that was the real goal and storyline.I purchased Nexomon: Extinction on a whim, though, as the art style and music brought me back to being a teenager, when Pokemon felt fresh and had me enamored. Within the first few hours, I could tell this game was a labor of love. It is impossible not to compare it to Pokemon, but it is also impossible not to feel as though this game were created by those who saw Pokemon as a stepping stone but wanted so much more.At first, I was simply tickled. The music had me humming. The creatures delighted me. The writing was impeccable and made me smile and giggle time and time again.But then something about this game struck me to the very core. It was the story. It was everything I wanted, everything I needed, and suddenly I was binging the game and holding my breath after each new reveal. Sometimes I could call it, but other times I was simply blown away. Every time I felt I knew what was happening, there was a wrench thrown into the system and I was delighted by each twist and turn. This, in the end, is what had me completely sold on the game.Other delights that differ from Pokemon in a delightful breath of fresh air are things such as:- The world is completely open. The Nexomon and trainers all seem to level along with you, so there is no fear in simply traveling the world. You are not shuffled to go from on city to another and are encouraged to explore. Not just explore, but return to areas and re-explore. It seems there is always a little extra content and some special different interactions from characters you can get as you move your way up in the story.- The ability to see where the Nexomon are. It means you can walk directly towards your prey instead of needing to move back and forth and back and forth.- Since everything levels along with you, there is never a concern of going back to a lower area and being inundated by tiny level 4 creatures that you look at funny and they squeak out a single xp for you. It also means trainers will not simply constantly have the same level nexomon in their stash every time you fight them. It makes for a much more fair leveling system.- A database that actually tells you whether a creature evolves, when they evolve, or if it is their final evolution. Good lord, this saves so much time and makes me delighted.There were very few things that I wasn't fond of, and I felt it more of a knit picky notion than anything else. Such as how I would like for there to be a button you can press that will bring up information on your party members without needing to go to the database, switching back and forth every time. I would also like some kind of search button for the database to save time when you are looking for a certain creature, without needing to scroll all the way through. I am sad there is no manner of creating young Nexomon as often I find myself finding/capturing the mid or final evolution and struggle to find their pre-evolved state.All in all, the pros sincerely weight out the cons and I am pleased and delighted to have picked up a copy of this game. I anticipate the sequel and look forward to where further stories will lead.

_childDocuments_.review: Nexomon extinction is a labor of love- the devs are clearly fans of the pokemon series and have clearly put their heart and soul in the game's visual style, characters' designs, and original soundtrack. Everything about this game is brimming with personality, and the game's $20 asking price is a bargain for what you get.So why the bad review? There's a critical flaw in the design philosophy of the current state of the game that prevents me from enjoying what I know the game CAN be- the devs think making the gameplay loop TEDIOUS is the same thing as making the gameplay HARD.No, this game isn't hard. I know this is a common complaint in the negative reviews, but the game can be beaten quite easily with just one nexomon: Gekoko. Make sure your Gekoko knows these 3 moves: Absolute Barrier, Heal, and Drain. The last move can be any attack move of your choice. If you pick Gekoko as your stater, this can be done by the time it is level 25. To beat any nexomon in the game, you simply rotate using absolute barrier and drain until the enemy runs out of stamina, then cast Heal and use your attack move. Nothing hard about this. This does, however, sucks out the joy out of the "pokemon experience"- if you play like this, you are not having fun building your team but are just exploiting on the game's 1 op combo. From the game's latest update as of this writing, the devs talk about the game's "Dynamic Difficulty"- the game's fancy way of saying the wild pokemon you face will scale with your pokemons' level, citing the reason being "We don't want an easy game." While the intent of this enemy level scaling is to make the game "hard," this actually simply creates 2 issues- (1) it makes a tedious backtrack-and-heal gameplay loop and (2) it takes away the enjoyment of grinding levels.   Because of level scaling, wild nexomon hits your mons like a truck. It is common to have to back track and heal after 3-4 battles. Even if you can somehow 1 shot the enemy, you run out of stamina FAST.  You are forced to make 1 of 2 choices: backtrack to the pokemon center for some universal free health care or start making trump proud by using your potion$ and ether$ and revive$. This brings us to another questionable design choice in this game: you are always broke. If you are playing the game the way it's meant to be playedTM, you spent most of your hard earned money buying pokeballs (nexotraps). Long story short, the typical gameplay loop requires you to spend half your time grinding (for either gold or levels) and the other half backtracking to heal. Is this fun? Well, actually, the grinding part CAN be- but the backtracking part DEFINITELY ISN'T. I don' know what focus group the devs were consulting with, but they are clearly paying them TOO WELL if the devs are in anyway led to believe that THE ONE FEATURE fans of the pokemon series DESPERATELY WANTS BUT THEY COULD NEVER GET FROM THE MAIN SERIES is the INEXPLICABLE NEED TO RUN BACK TO THE POKEMON CENTER EVERY 3 BATTLES.  I actually love grinding in rpgs a lot. What makes it fun for me ISN'T the process of the grind, but the RESULT of the grind- by being over leveled, I am able to clear content MUCH FASTER or able to beat optional bosses that were CLEARLY NOT meant to be cleared at the point of the story I am at. By scaling my pokemons' level with the wild ones, I never get this sense of accomplishment out of my grind. Instead, I am caught in a cycle of constantly having to play "catch-up" to the level requirement the story content requires while feeling my team is never "good enough" to last longer than 3 battles with wild pokemon. The game's current design constantly makes my team feel under leveled and the need to grind, BUT takes away the joy of grinding from me by constantly scaling my enemy levels with my party's. The devs seems to think the game is "hard" and "rewarding" by forcing me to constantly grind levels in order to progress through the story- in my opinion, this is just an artificial way of lengthening the game. It does not take skill to numbing-ly grind for levels to increase my party's stats- it just takes time- time I would rather spend ENJOYING playing your game. Fights with other trainers (tamers) in this game is actually quite fun. They are usually at a similar level to your party and the tamer AI does a good job of switching into mons that has a type advantage over you. This forces me to make a balanced team (when not using the gekoko exploit) and all in all the most enjoyable part of the game for me. Of course, the diffulty of these battles causes the same problem as the level scaling- backtrack trips to the Pokemon center. The GOOD THING is that many tamers will not challenge you to a battle unless you initiate it. The FRUSTRATING part is that SOME tamers DOES NOT ASK FOR YOUR CONSENT- they just walk up to you if your eyes meet. What is double frustrating is that tamers you defeat will want to challenge you again WITHIN MINUTES of play time- effectively "blocking" you from going back to the pokemon center. My party wipe several times because half my team were dead and I forgot THAT ONE GUY really wanted a piece of me for the 500th time when I was making my way back to heal.  (1) consider CLEARLY marking tamers that will challenge you on sight and differentiate them from passive tamers. (2) consider having an "EASY" mode- one without the enemy level scaling(3) consider giving enemy tamer the option to HEAL YOUR PARTY after defeating him/her- let's face it, we are basically forced to backtrack and heal after ANY tamer battles. This will be a major QOL improvement. This actually provides incentives for beating the tamer, as unlocking the tamer heal will make that area that much easier to "grind" and catch nexmon- you know.. actually playing and enjoying your game. Phew, wow thanks for making it to the end. If you read this far, you can tell I actually really like this game. I really hope the devs consider to make the changes I suggested so other players like myself can enjoy and wholeheartedly recommenced this game to others.

_childDocuments_.review: So you're telling me I can play "Almost Pokemon" without Nintendo threatening to sue me every time you play it?!A Pokémon-like that plays like a Souls? HELL YEAH. My wife’s boyfriend says it’s like Neopets and Digimon had a toxic relationship so Pokemon raised their kid.Extinction is far beyond Pokemon. It evolves every aspect of the game and makes Pokemon retroactively a worse experience. It was reminiscent of Pokemon, but it was it's own unique thing. I really liked the challenge. I loved everything about it. No hand holding, somewhat high difficulty, absolutely gorgeous world, brilliant characters and dialogue(the humor in particular is top notch) and there is so much content for only $20. The Nexomon designs are really impressive to me. I would be totally convinced if you told me they were new Pokemon. The game is self aware, it knows it's a game so it makes some of the dialogue very funny.  The story is interesting as well. It has some subtle set ups with some great pay offs.Nexomon is like a pure old fashioned Pokemon turn based game but with updated graphics (camera above looking down) and a better story than just becoming Pokemon Grand Master by going to all the Pokemon gyms in every city. The story is far more compelling than Pokémon's simple plot, and it has lore behind the character you play as, as well as almost everyone you encounter. Hell your main character in the game has more personality than frankly every Pokemon MC ever. I found myself wanting to learn more about the game's history after I was done with the main story because I was genuinely interested in the world they had built. It again made me laugh a lot, especially the talking cat sidekick Cocoa. And the ending was great. The gameplay is, overall, fairly similar to Pokémon, but simpler in just the right way.Nine types, with no dual-types, and nothing is outright immune to another type, which makes it easier to remember what's effective against what without needing a convoluted chart. The amount of debuffs is interesting also. With Pokémon, I mostly remember asleep, paralyzed, burned, poisoned. There might be frozen as well IIRC. But with Nexomon, there's also things like demotivated, provoked, nervous, frail, and sick, some of which make for interesting dynamic battles. I also liked that instead of having IV and EV stats, you just have base stats that can be modified by cores. Yeah, you mostly will probably use the HP, Stamina, Attack, and Defense cores, but it still provides some more interesting ways to set up your team without feeling too complicated.Haven't explored any of the post game yet, but I could totally see myself jumping back in to finish collecting all the Nexomon. If you are starting the game, don't worry about trying to collect ALL the Nexomon right away. You'll definitely want to explore and collect a variety of types in the beginning (fire, plant, electric, water, etc). But the game and wild areas level up with you. So if you caught a Nexomon at level 10 and its been sitting in storage and now you're at level 60, you could just go back to the area you found it in and catch one at level 52. I'm not sure if you'll be able to get all the same upgrades as you would if you raised it from level 10, but it could potentially save you from leveling any unnecessary Nexomon you wouldn't otherwise have to. Overall I'm thrilled with the game. Everything I dislike about current Pokemon games does not exist here and it's wonderful. It's a shame it's very unlikely to become popular. I know I'll be recommending it to everyone. For $20 it is a no-brainer. Even if you're happy with current Pokemon there are enough differences to make it worth playing.I wholeheartedly recommend the game to any Pokemon fan or people who have fun with Monster Collection RPG's in general. In my opinion, it is better than the recent Pokemon games and shows what can be done with less money, less developers and when someone has a fresh vision that is not blurred by $ signs. The game wears it's heart on it's sleeves and it shows in what love has been put into it. I seriously hope that the developers will make another game. I personally can't wait!10/10
