_childDocuments_.review: This game title is an absolute blast given its extremely low retail price. I had been a fan of Pokemon since Red & Blue, and now playing Nexomon really brings back a lot of good memories in 2020. Instead of being a clone, Nexomon is a pure traditional RPG built on monster catching mechanics, but the pacing, QOL and story line is strong enough to make Nexomon worth a play. Below are the strongest points i felt Nexomon had delivered extremely well:[Story & Characters]The story writing, suspense and mystery is surprisingly funny and mature at the same time. Characters felt unique and held enough weight for players to actually care and remember. Even random NPC design in town area all look distinct and unique rather than generic makes the immersion of game world felt alive. Addition of CoCo as talking companion with the protagonist really makes it felt very different from traditional story telling.[Graphics]For 1/5 price of standard Pokemon, the 2D background couple with animation and bright coloring really blends and mesh well in overall presentation. Battle animation is flashy yet smooth and fast, makes the grinding a lot more fast pace and enjoyable. The character design are also very cute and funny at times, giving a very enjoyable feel throughout game play.[Music]It is smooth and soothing, yet creative enough for the ear to remember. [Quality of Life]There are so many improvement if you compare this to standard Pokemon. One example is healing center, instead of  making a pointless NPC dialogue and animation of laying down your monster on the healing pod, Nexomon reduces this whole process to around 3 seconds. Fighting is also much smooth as attack animation is fast and direct. Since players are expected to grind & repeat, healing and battle should be fast to facilitate it. The Developers are also very generous in providing free loot throughout the world, which makes exploration very encouraging.[Progression]This game certainly packs a punch, which is much welcome. Wild monsters and NPC will gain scaling and Bosses are actually tough to challenge. But because of the QoL, grinding is definitely not an issue, and players are encourage to prepare which is the essences of RPG. Scaling is also very welcome because players can now actually catch a higher level monster with less grind to reach next evolution stage instead of getting a level 5 monster when your main party is already 50s. Making the completion of dex much more manageable and players can also easily make line-up changes without having to re-grind the new member too much.There are also alot of interesting side quests (500++), lots of chest and loots that rewards players for exploration. The crafting system utilizing shards is also engaging and purposeful, which is motivating for players who puts in effort to collect and do everything the game has to offer.Highly recommended title!

Have to think more as to whether this is a good thing.* Level scaling is very controversial, on one hand it makes progression feels a little pointless at times, on the other it does help with the mindless X spamming that comes with its predecessorsCons:* Very simplified stat system* Rather grindy in placesOverall, very recommended if you're into this type of game.

_childDocuments_.review: Pros--------------Interesting story full of TONS of unexpected developments-Hundreds of creatures that all feet unique in design-Memorable characters with a good level of personality -Many battles actually feel challenging and tense -Gorgeous environments that all feet different from the last-Gives the PC lots of room to free roam early on, while still never leaving you lost on what's next-Optional exploration out the wazoo. Quality of life items, rare Nexomon, cosmetic companions, and plenty more. Including an entire region that's untouched by the main story.-Good balance of goofy humor thrown everywhere, while still having emotional tense moments throughout -Balanced money economy and level scaling-Plenty of optional quests, most of which are unique and interesting. There's also citizens all over that have useful rare items if you're willing to trade.-Unique Cores>Held Items system brings a nice bit of change to the usual system-Option to do a customized run after finishing the story (individual Nuzlocke mechanics, randomizer, no level cap, carry over a team from a used save, general easy/hardmode settings, etc.)-Each area is a habitat for new Nexomon. While some common ones show up in multiple areas, the majority are fresh, which makes exploring each new place feel worthwhile-Minimal hand-holding the PC through mechanics. Not every obvious system is expounded upon by a 5 minute NPC dialogue. -On that note, not once did I feel the need to spam through text boxes while slamming my head in a George Foreman. The game keeps a good pace throughout the whole story.-Enough good music variety to keep the adventure feeling fresh. Each area definitely has a vibe to match.-Smooth, quick animations. Combat related, cutscenes, screen transitions, idles, environment ambiance, etc. While nothing is elaborate per-say, nothing ever felt jarring, too robotic, or too slow.Cons--------------Maybe more of a personal gripe, but in order to fully enjoy it, I felt the need to trash my starter, and only use mons with varied rarities until I finished the main story. Some of the best designed monsters are of the lower rarities, and are still used on opponents' teams the entire game, so why not yours? "The rarer the better stats" system feels unbalanced when it's possible to get a full team of Mega Rares within the first couple hours with enough exploration.-Move variety/balance. The move list fell really flat for me. More often than not, when a move is learned while leveling: you'll skip it. Too many moves learned later on (across ALL rarities) that are just intrinsically worse than what was learned 20 levels back. A related aside: all but the occasional normal type mon will ONLY have attacking moves of their own type. No coverage moves, there's hardly any decent setup moves, and most status moves are too inaccurate/situational to feel worth keeping around. While battles were still fun, the lack of viable combat variety grew stale about halfway through my playthrough.Final Word-------------Definitely try it out if you like the genre! There's 20-30 hours of game here, depending on if you enjoy the exploration and sidequests or just beeline through the story. More with endgame. The engaging story, design, personality, and the creatures themselves shine through the negatives here. For the size of the team behind it, the polish and storytelling was worth every bit of time and money put into it. The first game I felt compelled to 100% in years :)

_childDocuments_.review: Barely passable as a creature collecting game, nothing noteworthy to justify a playthrough. The major thing i was missing here is a good sense of progress. You don't get that from levels, those scale anyways. Most areas are accessible from very early on, so you don't get anything out of travel and exploration either (there is not even a map, what gives?). The main storyline exists, but is nothing to write home about.I disliked the art style quite a bit. I'm not entirely sure if that's only due to preexisting mobile game trauma, or there is something inherently not good about it, but i'll settle on the latter for now. Overly bright colors, stiff animation. A lot of generic elements randomly mixed together. The creature designs themselves have anything from aweful to it's-just-a-pokemon to actually great, but too few of those last ones. The legendaries in particular are rather underwhelming, throwing more stuff on top usually doesn't improve anything. In terms of gameplay there isn't enough to distinguish creatures from each other.Again, the level scaling - at the point where anything wild and tamer owned is just the same level as your team anyways, one has to ask, why even have levels. I'd rather someone do away with the thing entirely and innovate, instead of cludge together something based an established system that usually was included because it worked better than other things. Being able to access a new area and defeat new foes because you became powerful enough for it is something central to the RPG experience. I appreciate the difficulty from not simply being able to outlevel challenges, but that is very little gain from something undermining mechanics to this degree.Lastly, the meta jokes. Why. It's not a good fit for this genre and extremely immersion breaking, just to save a few minutes spent coming up with good character writing instead, some of which - extra tragically - actually exists. Not every game has to be portal in order to be good.

_childDocuments_.review: The game mechanics are too shallow. There are over 300 monsters, but most of them have functionally identical stats and movepools, and abilities don't exist so the only thing setting them apart is their type. The open world is very nice, but once you that there are barely any differences between monsters of the same type, it loses its meaning.Moreover, this game does not try to be more than a shallow pokemon clone. It does not try to add anything new to the formula and has no redeeming qualities. It is just pokemon with fewer types and moves, a less intricate stat system, no abilities, no strategy, etc.Unfortunately, I only understood all this after playing other, more original monster catchers, e.g. Cassette Beasts or Disc Creatures. Even Coromon, which is also just a pokemon clone, is better than this, because it actually tries to be as good as pokemon once was. This game is just lacking in every way that matters, and I can not recommend it over any other monster catcher.

_childDocuments_.review: Nexomon: Extinction is a pokemon style game, but while it tries to emulate the original pokemon formula as much as possible, it adds many improvements to make the game more enjoyable.I have not played any pokemon games past diamond (4th generation) but those I did play, I played a lot. While I can’t say whether the current generation of pokemon is faithful to those older games, I can say that Nexomon definitely is, and it brings some much needed improvements as well. I have little desire to reenter the world of Pokemon because I think it is starting to be crushed under the weight of its own backlog. I think pokemon is due for a complete overhaul, but I kind of doubt it will happen. Nexomon kept the simple battle system, the simple RPG mechanics, even things like Mons being limited to 4 moves and trainers/tamers being limited to 6 Mons, a lot of the other details have been changed. I think Nexomon is the sort of overhaul Pokemon needs.We have all new creatures to collect, of course, but if you threw pictures of Nexomon and Pokemon together and presented them to someone who knows neither, they would not be able to tell them apart. They kept that cute, anime monster, aesthetic. I don’t like all of the Nexomon designs (I especially hate the ones that look too human, like Puggard, Cadeto, and Volpressor) but about 80% of them are either fine or good. There is almost 400 Nexomon to collect now, and they are ALL present in the game, which is nice. I hate how we have just accepted that in Pokemon they get released in two versions, neither of which has all of the pokemon. And apparently Sword and Shield will now be the first version of Pokemon that even with both copies, not all the pokemon from previous generations will be included. Another improvement, no contrived evolutions like trading, happiness, or stones, just leveling. We now have 9 types that are well balanced, instead of the 18 types Pokemon has, and all Nexomon are just 1 type.Generally Nexomon is simpler, more streamlined… and I will say better. They thought about how to improve the core gameplay of Pokemon, and I think they succeeded.But not everything is perfect. I actually dislike the art design of the game. The 3D-ish chibi people of the world, I think look kind of ugly, even if their anime splash art counterparts are good. In simplifying things and making the Nexomon all relevant, there isn’t actually too much difference between any of the Nexomon. Status effects, while powerful, don’t see much use because of their low proc rate, pushing you to use just damaging moves. The music is fine, but some songs I found kind of grating. It can get grindy at times. Story wise the game is also a bit of a rollercoaster. I think it really flubs its introduction, as you thrown straight into world ending, time stopping, nonsense without taking any time to introduce the world. There are also a TON of 4th wall breaking jokes while at the same time this sense of hopelessness in the world and characters. While the game gets better as you go along, I didn’t know AT ALL what sort of tone the game was trying to set at the beginning. And while it gets better, the tone never quite gets… good. Which is a pity, because the writing is actually quite good. There are genuinely funny moments and genuinely epic moments, and the story is much grander than any pokemon title I’ve played. A for effort, but C in execution. The bottom line is, if you want a pokemon style game, or a simple monster taming RPG, then this is for you.EDIT: After talking with Pokemon fans, I realize that Pokemon has a lot more depth than Nexomon at the higher levels of play. If your goal is not just to collect all pokemon and beat the game, but rather to master the mechanics and be able to beat other human players, Pokemon delivers a lot more than Necomon.

_childDocuments_.review: It's been a long time since I've finished a game and actually felt "achieved". It is extremely easy to make a path for players, do this, do that, bam, you completed the game! A lot of games fall into this trap where a player isn't really being given anything of substance for this. I worried this game might be the same but it blew me away from start to finish.Looking back on the Pokemon games I find them unplayable for me. Each gym battle practically forces you to do an aggravating amount of grinding with little to no reward for completing them, not to mention purposefully putting the odds against you to deplete your team before that point. There are only bare bone stories to keep you continuing and the characters are forgettable. I began to realize I love the idea of Pokemon, of collecting adorable/cool creatures and bonding with them, but not the execution. Why do I bring up Pokemon? Because, for the casual player, Nexomon does everything Pokemon did wrong Nexomon doesn't force a play style, and the game is beatable for those who just want to fill their team with cute/cool Nexomon or people who are super into strategy. As long as you continue to level up your team on the way and stay well stocked on supplies. The game actively rewards you for investing in your Nexomon with pretty great abilities. It's all thanks to the combat system. Instead of PP, Nexomon uses a system similar to a stamina or mana bar, so essentially you can use any moves as many times as you want, they simply will lower that bar. Just like health, the bar can be refilled with a potion. Having this be a bar makes it much easier to manage. Switching between Nexomon is also a wonderfully seamless and quick process, helping you spread out exp and manage health. It's easy and simple and, after some trail and error, I really got the hang of it. The wild Nexomon in the area are usually what you can pretty much expect from the bosses there, so you can get used to their abilities and counteracting their status effects. The level of wild Nexomon and those in trainer encounters also serve as a little hint at what level the game expects you to be at in that point in the game, so you know what to shoot for. This makes any "grinding" much easier, and you can actively feel the changes in your Nexomon as they level and evolve rather than it just feeling like a cosmetic change. The game doesn't want you to fail, it's not an up hill battle but a curve it does its best to lead you down without holding your hand. Trainers level up to match with where you should be as well. Add the addition of cores, items your Nexomon can hold to increase a variety of things, and you have a battle system that is fun but challenging in the right ways.Nexomon realizes fighting is part of the genre, but not the be all end all. It lets its story drive its fights, not the other way around. Whenever you are fighting, it is for a good reason. There are actual stakes to your fights, characters you care about are either cheering for you or on the line, and the story constantly intrigues you with shocking twists and turns. It also knows that if it is going to put its players through several battles, it needs to make it worth their while and reward them for it. After big fights, you are not only given big rewards, but also increase your ranking in the organization you are a part of. This gives you more access to materials, locations, and so on. The addition of side quest and treasure gives the player more to do as well.Now the story; Nexomon aims for an older audience, presenting a Pokemon like world with a dark spin. You see, creatures called Tyrants have been raging a war ever since their king died in search for another heir. Humans have been left in the crossfire of this, and what we're left with is a torn apart world. Its compelling and while it isn't a high graphics game, a lot of the places just look gorgeous honestly. The lore behind each location is definitely fun and imaginative. But I haven't even mentioned the player yet, and for once they actually have relevance instead of just being a completely blank slate. Nexomone recognizes that, in a game, it's fun to have importance  You feel like you are a part of this story rather than being an observer or willing participant, watching everything blow up around you. The twists are extremely well written, the story in inventive and spins the genre on its head, and your character is someone worth getting invested in. It's the type of story that blew me away and has to be experienced to fully appreciate it. The ending  I'm thrilled to see there is plenty of worthwhile after game content to explore.The characters are also very lovable, including Cocoa. He's supportive, yet makes funny comments along the way, and his sarcasm was pretty entertaining. The other characters have their own charm to keep dialogue interesting. The inside jokes based on your playthrough only make it better. Heck, even NPCs remember when you saved them and some of your other exploits. But dialogue is hardly forced down your throat and, with this and the teleportation system, you are freely allowed to explore the world in anyway you want.There are also a lot of fun, quality of life features. You're able to select your avatar and change this and your name whenever you want. You can collect followers, cute little Nexomon to follow you around. Cocoa always asks you if you're ready before fast traveling you somewhere else, and lots of other characters do this as well before a mission so you can make sure you are completely prepared. Even after starting a mission, you can sometimes still teleport away for materials and there is in-between time to heal your Nexomon or take a break. You can rebattle trainers to help get exp. There is plenty explanation of the story of the first game, so you don't have to play it to understand this one. The Nexomon designs are great! They're wonderfully creative with plenty to chose from. Even the humanoid ones, something I usually hate, just look really cool and cute. Finally, and my favorite features, there are crystals around the world that replenish your team without you having to use your resources, and they respawn after some time. They are great to use in a pinch or when battling trainers to level up.To summarize, Nexomon, in my opinion, is a very good game that goes above and beyond its genre. It's great for players that have always wanted to be a fan of Pokemon, but found the gameplay too grindy and unrewarding. It is also great for casual players and there is a lot for them to love here. That being said, if you struggle to grasp even the basic concepts of Pokemon, Nexomon is probably going to be too hard for you. If you like Pokemon, well, it just depends. Either way, I love this game and would highly recommend it. It's very underappreciated for how great its writing is and fun/smooth its gameplay is.

_childDocuments_.review: I had this game on my wishlist for ages and recently finally got it. It looks like a cheap pokemon copy at the first glance but this thought ended up being far from the truth. The story was really impressive for the genre. I don't think I played any other monster catching game with such a nice story. I constantly wanted to know more about the characters and the world. The characters were not static and the story did have some turning points and plot twists. I even stopped after the first few hours and picked up the first game since many events and characters were referenced. It is worth playing the first game even though the first game is bad compared to this one. It is not required to play the first one though. It actually even spoils some twists. In addition to that you get to see some pretty dope artwork at certain key points during the story. The quality of those varies for some reason though. The artwork for getting your first Nexomon was one of the best for example. While the characters lines were usually well written and funny, they did force 4th wall breaking jokes a bit too often tbh.The fights were not really impressive imho.. you basically just spam the strongest move with type advantage you have against the current enemy. You can bring some strategy to fights in the form of healing your Nexomon but that's probably it. Maybe I am not "competetive" enough to rate the combat system though. Otherwise the gameplay was awesome though. TONS of quality of life features. Travelling is easy but not too easy, as in you can't just teleport everywhere from anywhere. Exp share is a thing but you have a lot of control over it, as in which Nexomon receives how much shared exp. In addition to that there are other QoL items in the game like a monster repel which stays active as long as you want it to stay active, allowing you to ignore random encounters entirely. If you do want to encounter monsters, however you don't want to fight all of them, there is an item that guarantees the flee options from battles. There is actually a quite decent post game in Nexomon. Except the generic "catch all Nexomon" thing you do unlock some post game quest lines and I even heard of an bigger upcoming update that is coming soon. Since there are over 300 Nexomon you can train you will have enough things to do anyways. You can battle trainers you have beaten again as often as you want and there is a lot to explore even after you are done with the main story line! Engaging story, tons of (mostly) interesting Nexomon to catch, impressive QoL features and decent post game. Totally worth the price if you like the genre or want to get into it!

_childDocuments_.review: Sorry for my english, its not my main language!In the first few hours this game was so tedious. But after my gold was not so limited anymore, i stocked up on healing items and i had a blast.Just a little story: At the beginning i went to an area i was not supposed to go yet and guards blocked my path. I got the option "Try to stop me!" or "Alright i go back...". I chose the first one, obliterated their mons and proceeded walking around, searching for cool mons to catch there. I think that was super fun and gave me a big feeling of freedom. Enemy-Levels scale with your story progress, so i didnt struggle too much by going off-road. Had a nice "open-world"-feeling!The story doesnt take itself very serious but at the same time it does. There is actually a good story in there and dialogue is very well written, while managing to ruin my immersion every few minutes by breaking the fourth wall. Its like a crazy rollercoaster, especially towards the end. Some plot-twists just came out of nowhere. I loved it!The graphics look clunky. Dont know how else to describe it. There is definitely room for improvements. I loved the battle-backgrounds though. Also, there are some reeeally cool mon designs! (And some really weird ones, i guess...)Music was a mixed bag for me, similar to the graphics. I hated it when it tried to be generic "Spooky-Music", "Beach-Music" and so on. I loved it when it tried to be original and unique.I will be honest, the mechanics could be better, but at least it works. Its very simple and there is not much depth. Nexomon with the same element are almost identical. Cores (equipment items) are a bit bland/grindy and equipping them to your mons is tedious, especially if you use more than 6 mons, like me. I liked the cores that helped me gain more Exp though! Its very fun to see your Exp-gain going crazy, also it safes a lot of time.Balancing is all over the place. For example, some of the mons learn Scratch (one of the weakest attacks) as their second-last move at Level 50 or so, while at the same time learning their already strongest move at Level 10. Its weird and almost feels randomly-generated.Forging your individual strategy felt unrewarding. Since the game is actually very unforgiving, you have little space to go "out of the meta" which is simply spamming your strongest attack. I had some success with Healing-focused strategies, to some degree. I tried really hard to make useful and interesting strategies, but it was unrewarding and just didnt work out. There are also not that many options to work with.I missed a in-battle status-check. I mean, you can check the stats of your Nexomon, but you cant check if your "This attack has a 30% chance to decrease opponents Defense" actually triggered or not. There is literally no feedback and some things you can only find out by tedious testing. I still dont know if buffs or debuffs stack. An in-game explanation for special-effects would also be very nice (what does "puzzled" even mean?!)I criticised a lot here, but in the end its crazy how much content and fun i got out of this, its a steal, especially when its on sale!A sequel is already announced and i hope they will look over the mechanics, gameplay and balancing a bit more this time. But only if that unique charm isnt lost in the process! Wouldnt be worth it.

_childDocuments_.review: *UPDATE: 70 HOURS LATER*Full cleared the game and 56/56 achievementsPROS:-A simplified Pokemon-style game with "Metroidvania"-lite elements that offers a solid story and gameplay without taking itself too seriously. (Catch, fight, evolve, win. Nine elements instead of forty or whatever Pokemon is up to now)-Great dry, sarcastic humor that kept things fresh and lively throughout. Coco is a breakout character that needs to reappear. He reminds me of Kazooie from Banjo & Kazooie. Videll was also hilarious and memorable.-You feel strong yet engaged/challenged from the start. It isn't two or three hours of spamming tackle and growl.-Nexomon designs were on point. Range from cute to cool, with some real standouts (Psychic Ghost, Electric-types were almost all homeruns). Animations were very well done for the art style.-Music was well done and didn't wear on the ears while farming an area. Some real bangers.-Leveling system is rewarding and doesn't feel like a grinding slog even at 90+ thanks to the core system.-The movement skills you unlock (similar to Surf, Strength, etc.) are perfect and adds the "Metroidvania" feel. I had a great time going back to previous areas with new powers to unlock secrets.-Zones are compact but don't feel rushed at all. Great level layout for the most part, feeding into that Metroidvania thing.-Tamers "level up" several times and allow you to challenge them again and again.CONS:Note: None of these ruined any aspect of the game for me. They're just my personal opinion on where I feel it could be improved.-Nexomon lack individuality and investment.In Pokemon you have things like IVs, EVs, Natures, Abilities, dual element monsters.I think Nexomon actually sold itself a bit short by not incorporating at least one version of their own.There is the core system that can boost attack, defense, HP, stamina, status resist. It doesn't go far enough though and the fact that you can remove cores from one Nexomon to give to another makes the monsters themselves expendable. You don't have any investment that you leveled a monster to 65 and don't want to replace it for one in the wild you find at 75 (I did this many times).Speaking to individuality, Nexomon of a given element all feel the same regardless of rarity and the stat spread is too tame. Common or Legendary, their stats don't differ enough to standout. There is no iconic bulky Chansey or super sweeper Alakazam. There is SO MUCH POTENTIAL here though. Seriously, when I saw Glunch or Blimpapa I thought "that's a big boi." and expected some massive HP to chew through, which wasn't the case. Everything dies in 2-3 hits on average assuming correct typing.Devs if you're reading this: The core system would be the perfect place to introduce "legendary cores" or "unique cores" that work only for a specific evolution line and give a special ability.Another remedy to this would be to add a slight variable on base stats akin to Pokemon IVs so more invested players can feel they caught a "good one" (without the insane rarity of it being cosmic/shiny).-Most Nexomon only learn abilities of their element or the neutral "Normal" type.Only Normal-types themselves and a legendary learn anything else. There is tons of potential here without breaking the game balance to give some Ghost-types a Psychic move, or a Fire-type a Mineral move (looking at you Meteor Shower)Maybe there can be some buyable or quested scrolls to teach cross-element abilities.-On the topic of learned abilities. The leveling progression for unlocking them is totally jumbled. A few times I've had my final ability, or even last few, be a lackluster weak normal move. -I'd love a multiplayer, but if not, at least include some post-game tamers you can challenge at level 99 in Cadium's stadium or something! There isn't much to do with your legendaries after you catch them or with a team you took the time to build in post-game.**MOST IMPORTANT: There needs to be Glunch and Zumble plushies for sale.

_childDocuments_.review: No... just no. 1. The humor. Oh god, the humor. I have never seen worse. Fourth wall breaking isn't always funny. Jokes about how the developer was too lazy to change sprites or is too poor to do something arent funny. Jokes about how something doesnt make sense arent funny. It just takes me out of the game experience and I wanted to vomit each time a character made another "joke". There are exceptions, but they are exactly that, not the rule.2. The story. One of the more enjoyable parts of this game. Unfortunately no meaningful way to influence it. Some good scenes and genuinely good ideas, but that's all. At one point you meet a spooky~ character who has potential and he vanishes after... one battle.3. German localization. I don't know what convinced me to play this game in my mother tongue. In germany we would say "Welcher Teufel hat mich denn da geritten?" - It's ♥♥♥♥. Like... One Nexomon was spelled wrong and appearently I was the only person to google that specific monster, because google had literally _Zero_ search results under that name. And then there is "Kabsel"... Who did this translation of "capsule"? A fiver year old?4. Difficulty and Combat System. If you thought Pokemon games were easy in the story mode, think again. Just level your first Nexomon to ♥♥♥♥ and kill everything with your strongest attack. It seems like there are so, so many useless attacks and abilities. Some are waaaay to underpowered.5. The logic. If you thought the antagonist of Black/White made lowkey sense, don't even play this one. She has a point, you know? Funny that some guild tamers are able to capture me, when I'm pretty sure I could have taken all of them without breaking into a sweat. How are there characters displayed as powerful as ♥♥♥♥ when they are suddenly downgraded for story convenience?6. The Nexomon. Some interesting designs. SOME (Couplet, Duh, Lunabelle, Muh). The others are forgettable at best, and ridicolous at worst (Caninui, Lamparos, Ponic, Mallark, Hydrip, Lovinu...). If you think a garbage bag or an icecream cone are idiotic, don't play this game. Where do they get their ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ clothes? (Poyal, Chowser, Volprofessor) Not everything has to be a dragon or some weird bastard-T-Rex you know? Don't expect me to get hyped over a walking hydrant. Some have way too much ♥♥♥♥ going on, some not enough. 7. Legendaries. Yes, let us catch all the interesting and powerful Nexomon (almost all of them dragons btw) in the post game, great idea. And let us grind for all of them, even greater idea! I have all required tributes but I will never touch this game again and all except four or five will remain uncaught.8. The quests and the grind: Stupid. One small tip: Buy everything at least ten times so you dont have to walk as much. Grind shards for like five hours and you are good to go. And even then I would have to revisit every area like ten times. Annoying as ♥♥♥♥. I couldn't take it any more. And don't think you can go around and just buy the shards or, dare I even say, cheat your way around the grind, no, no. For some reason the option to buy shards doesn't exist and although I bought enough items for my next ten playthroughs I can sit on my money and do nothing with it. The developer thought he was clever with multiple anti-cheat systems ... in a solo-player game. Let that sink in. If they focussed on making the gameplay more enjoyable, maybe this game would even be fun! Oh, by the way: One tip: Challenge every trainer twice as soon as you can if you want the achievement, because if you find out afterwards, good luck finding the exact trainers you're missing!The bottom line is that this game is a simple copy of the Pokemon games with the rare good idea, some good moments, an interesting world, but way simpler, less polished and with far less FUN. I wouldn't even recommend on sale. I just want my 24 hours back.BUT if you're looking for a game for your 5-year old brother or sibling, this is it.

_childDocuments_.review: Some background context before I explain why I'm not recommending this game. First, I played every pokemon game from blue/red up until sun/moon. I don't have a switch so that's why I stopped. I love pokemon. However, I'm also very aware that pokemon as a game has flaws. Playing it so much makes these flaws very clear to me. Considering Nexomon is a hard copycat of pokemon, I expected some of the flaws to be improved on but they are not, and in some cases, the flaws are actually worse in Nexomon. Let's start with the most egregious flaw of Nexomon; the controls. Nexomon has absolute trash keyboard controls and almost no mouse capability. The button you will be pressing the most is "K." Hello? What? Why? The controls are hard coded and can't be rebinded. Again, for a pc game, why? That's basic stuff and a serious drawback of this game. I wish I knew this before I bought it.  In fact, when it comes to settings, Nexomon is sorely lacking. I'm not exaggerating when I say that the very first pokemon game, Pokemon Blue, has more settings that can be changed by the user than Nexomon does. Pokemon Blue had options like to turn off battle sfx and changing text scrolling speed. Nexomon has nothing. There's no options to change resolution and/or window size. The only options are fullscreen and windowed but you can't drag the window without cutting off part of the game. Again, this is basic stuff for a pc game that is inexplicably missing. From reading about it, Nexomon is a console game ported to PC and it's a half-hearted effort. There are basically none of the QOL features you'd expect from a modern pc game. I like to watch something in the background when I'm grinding levels in pokemon. Having a smaller resolution and window size setting for Nexomon would facilitate that but it's not an option. Another major flaw of Pokemon also present in Nexomon is the slow game speed. The pace of the game is very slow. I prefer playing pokemon on emulator because I can speed it up. Again, this isn't an option in Nexomon so it's a substandard experience. So far, and I'm only a few hours in, there's no sprint button and no bicycle. I'm sure something will show up later but it's still a flaw of the game. The animations, transition screens, dialogue and cutscenes all feel extremely sluggish and slow. There are a very few improvements I feel I should mention. The open world format is nice and so far you don't get soft locked from exploring new regions like in the Pokemon games. I like the idea of stacking items a lot even though I've barely scratched the surface of the feature. I'm curious to see how it works but currently there's items that add a stacking increase to catching certain 'types' of Nexomon as well as a stacking xp boost item. Cool idea. I'm not sure it will be implemented well but hopefully. I think it will depend on just how high the numbers can stack. The monster design is all right. It's definitely not as inspired as early pokemon games but it's pretty good. Overall, I will keep playing the game to see where it goes. It's only 10 bucks on sale after all. However, I wanted to highlight some of the serious technical problems with the game as I would've liked to know myself that they existed before I purchased and I saw no mention of these in the reviews I read. There are also complaints about a lack of keybindings dating back to the games release so there's next to no chance that these issues are ever fixed.

_childDocuments_.review: I like Pokemon, and I think this game has potential to be a good Pokemon-like, but if I had a time machine and had to tell myself whether or not to play it as it is currently, it would be a soft no. The game is an unambiguous Pokemon clone—I’ll just call the monsters pokemon from now on. It’s single player, so the core of the game is pokemon battles vs NPCs. Unfortunately, the battle system is cruder and less interesting than even Pokemon Gen I. There are fewer types, and no dual-typing, so the rock-paper-scissors mechanic is simple, even with the 6 mon party limit. Because creating a favorable type matchup is trivial, the devs are forced to set the effectiveness multipliers much lower than in Pokemon: +25% bonus for supereffective, -35% for non-effective. In Pokemon, consistently generating favorable matchups against different trainers with different mons requires knowledge of a complex type chart, careful team building, and thoughtful play. The reward is an explosive advantage over even much stronger enemies. In Nexomon, there’s no challenge in forcing a favorable matchup and the reward for doing so is barely worth it—if your enemy is a few levels above you they’ll still beat you 1-on-1.There are plenty of pokemon to catch, but there is little variety in how they play beyond type advantages. Nexomon drops the physical/special distinction, and base stats don’t vary that much. Nexomon also drops abilities, so mons are defined exclusively by their BST and movepool. EV spreads do have an equivalent in “cores”, which give you 4 slots to put stat buffs. Sadly the movepools are very small, and there is no analogue to TMs. Generally, mons get access to the a small set of moves from their typing, plus a few normal type moves for neutral coverage, making battles extremely predictable—enemies will hit you with normal moves if you have a type advantage and their own type otherwise. There are very few strategically interesting moves when compared to Pokemon. Most useful moves vary only in terms of base power, accuracy, crit chance, and mana cost. Status moves have very low proc chances, making them difficult to use outside of boss battles, which feature high HP, low damage enemies and therefore long fights that benefit from permanent status effects. Buffs and debuffs are generally quite weak, e.g. a move that decreases an opponent’s attack stat by 15%. Battles boil down to clicking your best attack until your enemy is dead and switching to an appropriate counter if your current mon can’t win 1-on-1. While Pokemon has experimented with a variety of single-player battle formats, Nexomon exclusively features the classic format-- 1-on-1 battles with 6 mon parties. The upshot of all this is that almost every battle you fight in Nexomon reduces to the mindless attack spamming and potion quaffing of the most basic JRPGs. There are also many QoL problems and other design oversights, but those are frequently mentioned in other reviews.This is all a shame, because Pokemon games have many shortcomings that could be addressed in an indie like this. Pokemon has always set the single-player difficulty to 0 in order to appeal to small children, and a pokemon-like that featured NPC trainers with a broad range of challenging strategies and creative moves and abilities that might be imbalanced in competitive play but fun and rewarding in single player could be a big step forward for the genre. Instead, Nexomon's method of upping the difficulty is to simply overlevel your opponents. A game with uninspired combat can still be good if it has a great setting and story, but NE has some shortcomings here, too. I said NE is a Pokemon clone, but it’s really halfway between an early gen Pokemon game and a generic 90’s JRPG. Many of the features that distinguished Pokemon from its JRPG forebears are rolled back here—Pokemon (at least initially) replaced warfare with a competitive sport and hopeless quests to avert apocalypse with what is essentially a sports story—rising to the top of your game. NE tries to present a more mature, grittier take on the classic kid’s game—this isn’t about having fun with your pokemon and being the very best, this is life and death!—but this inversion of the Pokemon formula is simply the generic portentous JRPG story that Pokemon itself inverted. This extends to gameplay—mana (in the form of stamina) replaces PP and RPG-style plot-based battles replace the structured gym challenges of Pokemon.Despite having a lot of JRPG boilerplate, the story has some interesting twists. However, the writing often falls short. Characters act in ways that serve to further the plot through its twists and to its climax but seem bizarre in the moment, only becoming rationalizable based on information the characters themselves learn later. The story is totally linear, so this includes your own choices, which often seem insane or evil when you’re making them. The story’s big shounen payoff moments—former enemies and old friends taking dramatic stands with you against the world—feel unearned, as most characters get little development or interaction with your silent protag. Besides your sassy narrator/silent-protag-interpreter Coco, only the last boss seems to have any real rapport with you—he rails off an endless stream of ponderous JRPG anti-villain dialogue during your final battle. In contrast, in this story your orphaned character finds out their mother is alive and has set the entire plot in motion—everything that happens to you, everything that you do—loses her again, and has the chance to get her back in the postgame. If you do, the resolution to the biggest thread in the story and the presumably most emotionally charged experience your character has is a single line of dialogue and a pokemon battle.Nexomon hedges its bet on the gritty story with plenty of humor, but its approach is quantity over quality. Characters constantly break the fourth wall and lampshade both the tropes of the genre and most of the shortcomings I’ve described above, but the jokes are very perfunctory—the lowest of low hanging fruit. E.g. “The game’s over, someone roll the credits!” “The developers didn’t have money to animate me properly lol”. There aren’t any laugh-out-loud moments or memorable punchlines. Nexomon Extinction is a simple and sometimes fun Pokemon-like that is frank about its own shortcomings, but wryly acknowledging those problems doesn't fix them.

_childDocuments_.review: Good story, mechanically meh.First thing I'd like to note is this is a very slight thumbs down, I actually enjoyed the majority of my time with the game, but the game simply doesn't give me enough incentive to finish it.Nexomon is a heavily Pokemon inspired monster tamer RPG which has quite a few things going for it. It's main strength is that it has decent writing, a coherent somewhat unpredictable story and a large open world to explore from the get go.Your companion Coco is pretty hilarious and the game never takes itself to seriously, the whole "WHERE ARE YOUR PARENTS" common complaint is actually factored into the story and the world has a structure that makes sense in terms of broad strokes, tamers are organized, Nexomon are seen as dangerous animals and the world is in peril. NPCs update their dialog frequently when certain story beats happen. The story does become formulaic later on after you get a certain mcguffin but its never as simple and straightforward as "get the badges, elite four, win gaem".Side quests are interesting and varied considering the genre, the world is large and has varied locales from deserts, forests, mines, labs, vaults, multiple cities and just feels large and put together. The in battle animations and visuals are fantastic, with great animations on the movement of the Nexomon which is doubly impressive when you consider how many of them there are. Combat animations are also great, being short enough to not get repetitive but expressive and flash enough to be entertaining.So why didn't I finish it? Simply put, the meat and potatoes of the game,  monsters bopping each other, is under cooked. Catching monsters has some annoying fluff that doesn't really add anything to the experience. Most if not all the games mechanical hooks seem interesting at first glance, but are shallow and don't really pique your curiosity or have you theory crafting like other monster tamers.Firstly catching a monster means feeding it something it likes, OK, interesting concept, but what does that mean game-play wise? It means buying a bunch of stuff, scrolling through a menu until a higher percentage comes up and clicking on it... so its not really engaging and kinda just wastes time. Maybe if there was a way to figure out organically what monsters like or food had an actual effect on the battle such as causing status effects or healing the monster so you can get it fully restored after capturing it then maybe...but still kinda half baked.Then you need to do a button press minigame, which is interesting the first 3 times you do it, but quickly devolves into busywork because it never really changes that much. In a turn based RPG based on knowledge why have a twitch based timing puzzle? It seems so out of place.Then we get to the Nexomon themselves, they have no special quirks or unique abilities and their stats are so similar that using any Nexomon of the same type basically yields the same result, so why are there 381 of them? Once you have a strong water type all other water types are moot unless you like the different looking sprites, because they have the same stats, most likely the same movepool and catching them means you lose out on exp. There are no special evolutions, no item based evolutions, no location based ones, time based ones, quest based ones, special event based ones, combat based ones, moveset based ones, zip, nada, nill.Speaking of movepools the game is remarkably shallow, maybe my viewpoint is tainted because I used to be into competitive pokemon battling and love the Shin Megami Tensei battle systems but there just doesn't seem to be much there. Status effects aren't explained anywhere, moves that inflict status have about a 30% chance to proc, buffing stats does next to nothing, de-buffing also does next to nothing and your Nexomon can learn stronger moves earlier or not its completely random! Nexomon also only learn their base element with the exception of normal which learn normal and one extra element, so the basic rock-paper-scissors gameplay just means switching since type coverage isn't a thing. This means movepools require zero thought .The stamina system means you should swap out mons between fights before they become useless, or just take a turn off and use the extremely cheap ether to heal it up. This isn't necessarily a "bad" in theory, they just didn't use it in a strategic way, its just a meter that drains. Why not have really high costing stamina moves but have it completely heal on switch out or at the end of the battle, meaning you really have to plan your moves instead of just healing every now and then.The only interesting moves are healing and absolute barrier which makes you invincible for a couple of turns, there is a speed system which subs in for priority from pokemon, but it never matters because you never outspeed barrier or healing. These aren't even that interesting because you can just use items to substitute for them.The battle system is literally, learn the type chart, hit the guy, swap frequently because your mons can't cover more than one element and use healing/absolute barrier to cheese the simplistic AI, or just potion spam because there isn't much else to do. Bosses are also just big dudes, normal mons with more HP and stamina, no unqiue strategies, no buffing/de-buffing, no in battle conversations they are all the same.Why not some high dps glass cannon bosses, some tank bosses, some sneaky bosses, bosses that rely on status effects, stallers, sweepers, item abusers?There is an equipment system but its literally just flat boosts to exp/damage/defense/status resistance with the only interesting one being exp share, a huge missed opportunity, I know they didn't want to copy pokemons item system but if they were gonna go the raw stat equips why not sets of cores, with bonuses like special effects or even special stats? Use the cores costing a lot of stamina like a heal or burst of damage?The crafting system is also pretty basic, you mine rocks and make nexotraps and cores, that's it, it's always a rock that looks exactly the same, which makes it just seem like busywork, maybe having a nexomon harvest from different looking resources? Getting resources from beating certain types of nexomon (eg: grass mon drops sap, earth mon drops clay, water drops fish scales etc) which gives you an excuse to move around the environment but it just feels like it has nothing to do with taming or Nexomon at all.Items are also pretty boring, there is no TM system to teach moves, no berry or held item systems, no There are item trades that give things that reduce prices by a certain small percent, boost exp by a percent, give discounts or increase coin gain but the problem is tiny percent increases are just BORING, did anyone really think "YES 3 PERCENT MORE EXP, WORTH IT", NPCS also trade items that includes special type based nexo traps, food and other things but it highlights the fact that there are zero Nexomon based trades, but there really couldn't be because there isn't much special about the Nexomon.There isn't any PVP but honestly the battle system isn't deep enough to support PVP.Overall I'm more disappointed in Nexomon than anything, it's clear the developers put a lot of love into the product, they are listening to the community and patching things in at a quick pace and I honestly don't regret my purchase if only to fund Nexomon 3. I sincerely hope that they add more depth to the core game play because the story and novelty/world alone carried me through 20+ hours of gameplay, its just now that my mons are reaching lvl 40 and I've fought enough tamers and bosses to realize that I'm just going through the motions, there isn't really anything to look forward to besides more damage sponge bosses and statistically identical Nexomon.

_childDocuments_.review: This game was absolutely phenomenal and I'm looking forward to its sequel.  In this review, I'm going to mention what this game excels at, some factors that could further amplify the game, as well as some suggestions of my own.  This is simply my opinion and it's entirely up to the incredible developers what to leave or take.+ As for what Nexomon excels at.  It an engaging story that pulls you in and keeps you on the edge of your seat, begging for more.  Where this truly shines is that it doesn't take the typical black/white approach of "we are good and they are evil," rather, it has the player questioning their OWN position in the story whether what they are doing is truly right - very much like how we live our own lives.  This is especially present when the "antagonist" is made clear and we are questioning our actions against them, as they haven't technically done something wrong.+  Compared to Pokemon, the functionality of Nexomon is astronomically simpler.  There are no EVs or IVs, there is only 1 defensive stat to track (just defense, no special defense), you can explore a large portion of the map before even beginning the story (it's not aggressively holding your hand), and the game scales in level (mapwide) as you progress the story.  Some combination of these factors can be unappealing to some, but ultimately simplifies the game, making it much more casual friendly, which I find is a huge plus, drawing in casual players by eliminating the "necessity" for micromanaging team-building.- As for what could be improved on.  I felt the many of the Nexomon were relatively bland, outside of appearances, specifically the learnsets and similar behavior of a plethora of the skills in the game.  For example, for the former, most plant-type Nexomon learn mostly the exact same moves, but at different levels (the learnsets).  That's not to say there weren't some signature moves (such as one for the mon that carried me through the story, Odiborg the lightning 'spider'), it just felt like most of the nexomon lacked uniqueness for their absence of signature moves (or abilities - which aren't in the game).  - On a lesser note, there are several moves that a blatantly useless.  For example, why would I use a move that deals no damage but has a 40% chance to confuse, when I could instead use a move that has 50 base-power with a 30% chance to confuse?  Similarly, why would I use an 75 base-power move with a 25% chance to crit and 80% accuracy, when I can use a 100 base-power move with a 5% chance to crit and 100% accuracy?  However, if the reason for this is to have players figure out what makes a better move to pick, then this is perfectly acceptable, as I fully understand the need for "new player's traps."~ As for what to challenge you with, I suggest focusing on the uniqueness factor of Nexomon (the monsters, not the game).  That was the main thing that bugged me the most, as many other monster catchers set their way of defining a unique creature is by having an ability that no other species can have, which might be something to consider.  If that deviates too much from Nexomon's intentions, then I would simply suggest signature moves for each Nexomon, preferably earlier in the game (if it learns them at 50+, then that means for 80%+ of the game, it isn't unique).  I'm aware this isn't easy to do, because to make 3 unique skills for each species, that's roughly 500 skills to come up with, which is no simple task.  Regardless of what Nexomon decides to change for its sequel, I am fully confident it will be the right decision, with another banger of a game to play once more.

_childDocuments_.review: It should be no surprise that you're being sent out into the world at a young age, all on your own. What was surprising was having a legendary--I mean, a dragon--attack out of nowhere.If you want to see Nexomon: Extinction in action for yourself, watch my video. A nice art style, self-aware humor, a focus on action, and a sense of freedom to explore in the direction you want to go combine to make this a distinct experience from its Pokemon clone roots. You'll be plunged into epic scale plot right from the start and RPG tropes will make sure you don't have a clear sense of what's going on, but perhaps someday you'll destroy the world. Having a loyal companion alongside you to deliver wit instead of exposition and to say the things that you might say as a player will be something you either love or hate. And you don't have to worry which of the 9 starters you choose: I stumbled across one of the others in the wild very early on. And that's something that bears repeating: while the plot pushes you in a specific direction, the world leaves you with several dead-ends open to explore first. You have the feeling of freedom despite the plot's direction.The battle system has its pros and cons. You capture chance is revealed before you throw a Nexotrap. There's also a weird button combination prompt that isn't quite clear on which button to start with (answer: upper-left) or what it adds to capturing. Moves have individual priority, decreasing the importance of levels. Accuracy claims to be par for the course, but of course you'll wonder if it's lying to you. One of my Nexomon evaded three or four attacks in a row. It happens, of course, but it always makes you give it the side eye. The most bizarre part is that you're forced to fight the Level 40-some odd Dragon right off the bat, and somehow your Nexomon is able to survive a single hit.All in all, if you're sick of the direction Pokemon has gone in in recent years, Nexomon is worth checking out. It has a different soul to it, being back in 2D will make you feel right at home.

_childDocuments_.review: One of the best games I have ever played.  It may not be as intensive or complex with the combat as Pokemon is, but it makes up for that with ACTUALLY having a story.  It also includes a great deal of humor that at times left me with stomach pains.  The monsters available for capture may be a bit... "inspired" at times, but many are unique as well.  So would I recommend this game?  Absolutely!  This is one of the most criminally underplayed games out there and I believe everyone should play this game at least once through.

_childDocuments_.review: DISCLAIMER - Play the first game! I unfortunately doubted that there was a first game, but there is. go play that one first. You don't HAVE TO to enjoy the game but I think its better if you did.Yes. Yes. Yes. YESThis game is epic. If you have felt unhappy with the newer Pokemon games you will LOVE this. Mind you this isn't a Pokemon Clone or ripoff. This is a Monster Catching Game. It fits within a sub-genre of RPG similar to how "Battle Royal" is a sub-genre of shooters. The story, the mechanics and the strategies you use are going to be fairly different than in Pokemon. First off there is no power point system for each individual move. Nexomon have stamina and each move or skill they have requires a set amount of stamina. Many of these skills inflict damage but some inflict statuses as well. Some skills only inflict statuses while others change how damage is dealt. There is a type system that I believe is more balanced than Pokemon's MASSIVE list of all the different types. Nexomon have 7(?) types i believe. Fire, Water, Wind, Mineral, Lightening, Ghost and Psychic. I may have missed one there. But anyway, different strategies include - trying to outlast your enemy by exhausting all their stamina, this causes them to have to take a whole turn to recharge some of it. It may also render some skills useless as they'd need to wait 2 or even 3 turns (the latter being rare) to recharge enough stamina to use that skill effectively. Another strategy is letting a nexomon die to get a free switch in. Now this strategy has been seen in pokemon I will admit but, Nexomon health fells more precious. There are fewer skills to restore your health and the ones that do don't do it in large enough quantities to really make a huge difference or require a large chunk of your stamina to activate. So, at least in my experience, health is more valuable in Nexomon and deciding to sacrifice one near-death Nexomon to conserve health for another that might have type-advantage is a calculated loss. So the story, this story (about 15-20 hours in) honestly beats out any story of any Pokemon game I've been exposed to. Now I haven't played the mystery dungeon series or the Pokemon Ranger series but as far as the main games go? They don't ever come close to this. Pokemon Black and White had a grand story that is very good but it just doesn't match the scale of this one. I have yet to finish the game but so far I have gotten to the biggest plot twist and MY GOD that was wild. This game doesn't hold your hand either. Even if you are even leveled with type-advantage, RNG might be your doom. I make sure to grind all my Nexomon up to where they are all equal level and at least 2 levels above what I think the game will throw at me next.Lastly, If you don't like 4th wall humor, this game may not be your cup of tea. This game will break the 4th wall for a joke at the drop of a hat, at one point it will make fun of you for laughing at 4th wall breaks. I adore this game's incredibly sarcastic humor. It doesn't take itself too seriously but it still has an awesome tone to it and honestly? So far this is my best game of 2020.Now with all those pros there's gotta be some cons right? Yeah....- graphical glitches (rare)- 4th wall humor can get a little old but they typically try to space it out-  Wind Nexomon in particular seem just kinda weak in general.- I think when you lose a fight you should be punished more harshly than just being sent back to your last save with all Nexomon at half health and half stamina- the moves aren't big and flashy like you see in later stage Pokemon games like Black and White, not really something i think everyone cares about but its a personal gripe- Wild Nexomon scaling with you. i prefer how pokemon handles wild levelsIt was difficult for me to get into this game but.... just finish the first quest you get as a Bronze tamer. That's where I was hooked.PS: this game has samurai riding dragons in sky island japan. Pokemon does not have that. Checkmate.

_childDocuments_.review: This game has good graphics, good designs and a nice premise but it lacks a soul and that is mostly because of the weak writing.The constant use of meta humor really throws you off and breaks the immersion. The character Coco, who is your companion, makes a lot of these jokes and is really annoying. A small little meta joke in a interaction with a NPC or an item, I can accept but really? So many meta jokes at the start of the game? During events that are so important for the story? I couldn't really feel the impact of any scene or feel like I was in a different world because the game itself reminded constantly that it was a game and that there are cliches used in this genre. If pointing out cliches was enough to make something funny, tvtropes would be the best comedy work of all times. I also really lamented not seeing little texts in the objects around the world to give you some additional knowledge about how people live their day-to-day lives and to give the game a bit more charm. You can only interact with itens that directly affect the gameplay, which is a bit of a shame. I would love to have more pieces of lore for me to discover by interacting with the enviroment.  I played for a hour and watched my boyfriend playing for two hours and I could never overcome my boredom, although I wish I did since I won't be asking for a refund. My boyfriend did like the game, although he cares much less about writing in games than I do. Maybe if your favorite thing about Pokemon is seeing cool monsters and making them duel, this game will work for you. My favorite part was the cozy and immersive universe and charming characters and these elements are absent from this game so I can't recommend it.

_childDocuments_.review: Pretty solid game overall. Wild encounters and trainers being scaled up based on story progress means that grinding is a very quick affair, if it's even necessary. Story is interesting, and characters are fun, though the dialogue breaks the fourth wall a little bit too often. The biggest flaw with the game is that the "Pokedex" of this game doesn't list possible locations for each Nexomon, so if you really want to catch 'em all, you're going to be spending a LOT of time wandering around aimlessly just hoping for that rare encounter you need.Gameplay: 8/10 - Typings and moves are relatively balanced, and this game, like many other monster catching games, uses a stamina system for moves that is well-implementedStory: 8/10 - The game actually has some interesting moral conflicts, and the dialogue is for the most part charmingArt: 7/10 - Animated 2D art for every Nexomon is fantastic, and while the move animations can be a bit lackluster, they're at least quick enough that it makes sense. Nexomon designs are good overall, with only a few of them looking like obvious Pokemon ripoffs.Overall: 8/10 - If you enjoy Pokemon or similar monster catching games, definitely pick this one up when you get the chance!

_childDocuments_.review: Overall I think the game is fairly good. At the end of the day it's what you'd expect from Fakemon game, though some monsters are more Pokemon ripoffs than Pokemon-inspired. The combat is simpler than Pokemon's, but this causes a lack of diversity in its rather large monster lineup. It's worth trying out if it's on sale at least. Definitely not a BAD game, and it is competently made, but some creative choices leave me kinda puzzled. Before I get into that though, there are some things it does that I'm quite a fan of. The capture mechanics are slightly more detailed than Pokemon's, and wild monsters are level-scaled to you.It feels like there's plenty of passion and effort put into it, but perhaps having around 400 creatures was not to its benefit. The monster lineups of games like this (such as Coromon or TemTem) are generally composed of fakemon of mixed quality, and there are definitely some pretty good ones in there, but I feel like there's plenty of filler. And that's fair enough, but some of them are unrepentant ripoffs of existing Pokemon.There's a ghost that is just a Duskull but as a sheet ghost with the same eye gimmick, a blue Krokorok, but the most blatant one I've seen was literally just a worse Vikavolt. There was a cool little electric stag beetle, and then it evolved into a ripoff Vikavolt and I never felt so disappointed by a Fakemon game evolution. At least change the typing! It's just like... if you're gonna put effort into the game then at least also put in more effort with the creature design and don't just blatantly rip stuff off!On another note, mechanics-wise the game is simpler than Pokemon, with fewer stats, no dual-typing and no passive abilities, and this makes the ~400 monsters less distinct from each other, as they mostly vary by movesets. While the simplified combat may be welcome, I think it does not mesh well with the quantity of creatures. The lack of IV and EV equivalents is very welcome though, at least if you catch one monster you won't end up with the possibility of just having it be straight up worse than another one.Storywise it seems to at least want to go in a different direction than Pokemon and many games derivative of it. It's slightly edgier and darker, but not in the "hey dude what if someone just shot the pokemon??" kinda crude video-game parody way. It doesn't take itself too seriously most of the time, but also personally I think it's REALLY overdoing it with the 4th wall break humour. Actually a lot of the comedy is either just 4th wall breaks or trying to point out that something that's normal in a video game should be kind of absurd or messed up. It gets old pretty fast imo.

_childDocuments_.review: After 100%'ing the first Nexomon I was excited to get into this one.There are more changes than similarities, but most of them I think are improvements. The game feels very 'open world'. After you get your first nexomon and a pickaxe you're free to go almost wherever you want! I explored every area I could while still being a "Bronze" tamer and caught over 100 nexomon, which felt awesome (but was also time consuming and required money grinding for nexotraps).Because of this 'open world' aspect, the level of the wild nexomon increases as you progress through the story. I had read about this so was prepared and made sure to catch as many nexomon at low level as I could. If I didn't know about this I think I would have been really frustrated and sad since I enjoy leveling up the monsters and having their evolved forms be a surprise. Definitely make a conscious decision how you want to handle this ahead of time! This is probably the number one debated feature of the game that I've seen and I agree why.The story itself so far seems just a great as the first with the same humor that doesn't take itself too seriously. The monsters are all high quality and there are A LOT of them! Really hard to pick which ones I want on my team.For the amount of gameplay and quality this game is EASILY worth 20$.

_childDocuments_.review: Is this a Pokemon clone?Yes.Is it better than Pokemon?Yes.(This comes from someone who has really only played Pokemon Firered FYI)Pros:-Random Grass encounters are significantly less annoying because in Nexomon you can see when the Nexomon are rustling in the tall grass and avoid them.(There is also a repel spray you can get in the late game that negates random encounters period.)-In Pokemon Firered you need to beat the first gym leader in order to gain the ability to run however in Nexomon you simply run as soon as the campaign starts-In **ALL** pokemon games you have 3 different choices to pick as your starter vs nexomon you get a choice of I believe 9 different Nexomon-Grinding doesn't feel as tedious or annoying in this game because it's alot easier to level up(In Firered you get the EXP share sometime in the mid-game if you catch about 50 pokemon but in the early game of Nexomon you can easily craft an EXP share)-In pokemon there are 18 different types vs Nexomon which has 9 types,it keeps things alot simplier with the rock paper scissors system-You can re-battle other trainers which is very fun and makes it more enjoyable for grinding-You can interact more with the overworld I'd like to say-Catching Nexomon is much more complex compared to Pokemon as you need to implement more strategy to it-Writing wise it's significantly funnier than pokemon although they aren't as limited to what they can say due to this being an indie game-Story wise it has a pretty thick lore and is not just 10 year old kid wakes up and goes out on a journey to become the champion of this regionCons:-It makes too many 4th wall jokes in my opinion not to the point where it's unbearable but to the point where I just don't laugh-I think it's easy get lost sometimes in certain areas-Sidequests aren't the most fun thing to do-More of a personal complaint but I do kinda prefer the 18 types of Pokemon vs the 9 of Nexomon

_childDocuments_.review: If you enjoyed Pokémon, then chances are you'll probably enjoy this. I went into this game initially thinking it was just a watered down Pokémon clone. But as I played, I found myself warming up to the game very quickly. Overall, I had a good time raising my Nexomon and I had an enjoyable time with the game as well. Since this game was clearly inspired by Pokémon though, do be warned that there will be a lot of comparisons to it. Also, for the 6 people who'll maybe read this review and the 2 of you who will care, I didn't play the first Nexomon game. Frankly I wasn't aware that this was a sequel, so take that however you will. I'll start with graphics, then go into gameplay/things I liked and hated, and end off with story, so that way people who read this in a blurb don't immediately get spoiled.As far as graphics are concerned, they're decent. By no means are the graphics reminiscent of Picasso, but it's also not 3rd grade tier art either. The colors are very vibrant, I thought the character art in some instances was cool, not too impressive but still servicable. I did like some of the character and creature art. Deena and Amelie stood out to me as really good. The Scooptor line of Nexomon is really interesting. My favorite Nexomon were probably Rapilux, Rapnux, Voltaic, and Volta. A lot of the other creature designs were pretty "eh", but none of them were really god awful. And for every "Oh, Bulbrit is just a lightbulb" thought that popped into my head, I also thought "Well, Voltorb is literally just a Pokéball so I'll cut them some slack." Some of their names are also wierd, but again, Pokémon also probably had unusual names at the time. So, how's the gameplay? Not to be one of those armchair game designers/developers, but it certainly has its highs and lows when it comes to design decisions. -The Good- One of the things I found pretty great right off the bat is that once you reach the main city and do your first mission, the game really opens up from there. You can go just about anywhere on the world map and run into minimal progress walls. I caught over 100 different Nexomon (there are 381 in total) before I even started the second mission, if that gives you an idea of how open the world is. I definitely liked that aspect about the game! I like the fact that wild Nexomon and trainers scale with you. When I first saw this advertised on the store page, I was concerned that they would scale all the time, meaning levels were essentially not that useful in the grand scheme of things. But, fortunately, they do scale to a point and eventually you can overtake trainers and wild encounters in level. As someone who actually doesn't mind grinding and investing time into a game, that was reassuring to see. I like the fact that trainers want to rematch you as well. I also like the stamina mechanic. Unlike in Pokémon where you can only use a move a certain amount of times, in Nexomon, you can use a move as many times as you like, but this is limited by the mon's stamina and certain moves have different stamina costs. Different moves also have different speeds and crit rates. So there's a strategic element to where you can purposefully use a slow but powerful move to deal massive damage, then use a weak but faster move to try and hurry and finish off your opponnet.  -The Bad, or How I Learned to Huff Sulfur- Unfortunately, there were a lot of things about this game that drove me up a wall as well, or things that I thought they could do better. I'll try to list my groans about the game in order of annoyance. Despite there being more cons than pros, keep in mind I actually really did like this game and enjoyed it, there are just quirks about it that annoy me. The biggest gripe for me was that the Nexodex or the Database or whatever doesn't show where a Nexomon can be found in the world. In the Pokémon games, when you checked the Pokédex, you had an "area" section that lets you get a general idea of where you could find said Pokémon on the world map. Nexomon doesn't have that. You shouldn't have to go to the Steam Guides or Google to look up where you can find certain mons. Speaking of Steam Guides and Google, I had to look up not only the type advantage chart, but also what the status ailments did.  Now, maybe I missed a tutorial or something, but I don't remember any of that stuff being explained. A really underrated thing about the Pokémon games is that they had a Trainer School or something to that effect. This is so dumb 7 year olds (basically me, mentally) could see what status ailments did. Yes, things like Poison were obvious. But you had to be paying a bit more attention to know stuff like Burn reduces your attack by half in Pokémon. In this game I would've never figured out what status ailments like Frail does without looking it up. A lot of the trainers have "Lance Syndrome" and have fully evolved mons. I remember being around the early-ish middle of the game when this was happening. I'm not sure if that's the result of scaling or if that's just what they naturally have, because admittedly I was pretty over-leveled, I was in my early to mid-30s and people were still in their mid 20s in terms of level. Either way, I think trainers having mons in their final evolution before you've even seen the final evolution ruins a bit of the mystery and charm of trying to raise a mon and find out what it looks like. Not that big of a deal though. The lack of encounter variety was also a bit disappointing. For example, and hopefully this will clarify what I mean, in Pokémon you also found mons in tall grass and caves. But, you could also do stuff like headbutt trees and smash rocks. You could also find mons in the sand, in the water, and in even taller grass. In 4th gen you could slather honey on a tree and attract them. If you were really zany, you could use Sweet Scent to attract wild mons...there were a ton of ways to encounter mons! And while these were small bits, they helped flesh out the world and immerse you. In this game it's kind of disappointingly shallow. You only ever find mons in grass or in caves. Another thing that dreadfully needs variety is the evolution method. All of them are level-based in this game. And look, I get it. At this point you're probably just like "damn dude, just play Pokémon", but in my defense, I don't want this game to be just like Pokémon. I do want it to take what Pokémon did well and expand on it further, and this is one of the things that it did well. Different methods of evolution adds an extra layer of character and uniqueness to each mon. Nexomon doesn't have to have Water, Fire, and Thunder stones. Maybe it could have Nexomon evolve in certain locations, maybe the mons could evolve at a certain happiness threshold (which this game doesn't have either. Your Nexomon don't grow more or less friendly with you, there's no friendship) but either way, there needs to be something other than levels.   Finally, I didn't like the fact that animations can't be turned off, at least that I know of. I looked at the options and didn't see a setting. Turning the animations off, would've made level grinding a lot more convenient and expedient. Thankfully, most of the animations are very brief. So let's talk story. It's pretty decent. It's at least on par with the plots of most Pokémon games, though probably a bit better. If anything, it's actually closer to Mystery Dungeon in terms of story structure. Especially in the fact that the guild you're working for turns out to be a bit evil. Well, they're not evil, they just hate renegades who aren't in the guild. And considering you eventually become a renegade...yeah. There's a bit of a twist to where it's revealed you're actually a tyrant yourself and not a human, which I thought was pretty neat. Then you fight the final boss as yourself and the tyrants you revived, which was pretty awesome. The parts leading up to the end does have a "muh friendship" aspect to
