_childDocuments_.review: Very good price point, great systems, non-stop entertaining. An amazing entry for the monster-trainer genre.A game where you set out to do a quest and get side tracked by new Mons, new quests, new areas, new mechanics, etc. on the way for an hour or two does something right.NPCs offering you trades and side-quests offers a lot to do. Battle animations are fast and snappy so they don't get old even after seeing them a hundred times.Big props to how type advantages are designed! If you min-max you can get a counter for any type with a team of just 4 out of 6 Nexomons. Which means that you have a lot of flexibility when building your team because type match-ups can overlap without leaving holes in your team. That's a really smart way to design your rock-paper-scissors table. It shifts the focus of teambuilding from "optimal and solved" to a matter of preference, how it should be in a game with so many Mons.What I definitely didn't like is that there are SO MANY completely useless moves. Especially status effect inducing skills are just horrible. Like a 30% chance to put the enemy to sleep. You could kill the enemy Mon in the time it might take you to even proc the sleep. Your choices when it comes to move sets are very limited because the vast majority of skills are so abhorrently bad that in reality most Nexomon only learn like 4 to 6 usable ones in total. I sometimes even found myself struggling to fill all 4 move slots because the choices were so bad. Sometimes Nexomon even learn a skill at higher levels that has just straight up worse numbers than a skill they already knew.The good thing is that you can switch moves at a move-trainer at any point for a small price. Additional means to traverse the environment are directly learned by the main character, not your Mons.The fact that Nexomon has level scaling is a bit unconventional but really not an issue. You can still overlevel and underlevel depending on your playstyle. And you can pick up any Mon at any level at any point and get it up to speed with the rest of your team in a reasonable amount of time thanks to XP share items.The humor is great! It's pretty rare to get more than a soft, short chuckle in media these days but Coco, the cat sidekick, has some absolute zingers that had me legitimately laughing. As do some other NPCs and quests.The story is nice, even offers moral ambiguity. And there are several moments where you have to do dubious things to achieve your goals, which is a nice touch for this genre.A bit barren. Would've loved additional info on where to find Nexomons in the wild that you already saw.If there ever is a Nexomon 3, I am here for it.

_childDocuments_.review: Nexomon: Extinction is a fun and engaging delve into the Pokemon/Monster Catching genre. If the game looks appealing, I can strongly recommend it for anyone that likes casually playing monster catching games. That being said, there are a few shortcomings it has in comparison to Pokemon I feel.Pros:-The story is very well thought out and has some nice twists and turns here and there. A lot of the pokemon games' stories have gone stale because they always use the same formula of X team of bad guys wants to harness the power of some legendary pokemon to take over the entire world etc. In this game's story, not everyone is who they seem at first glance.-The writing is also very well done. Most of the dialogue is rather engaging, and the devs have littered the game with self-aware jokes that break the fourth wall all the time. I get a good laugh just about every 10 minutes of dialogue I read.-Almost all Nexomon have three stage evolutions, but if they don't their final stage evolution will generally be just as viable as any other third stage evolution. You can therefore make teams of just about any of the nexomon that you want.-Permanent Progression items. In Nexomon Extinction, you can collect certain key items that permanently increase things such as catch rates, money earned, EXP earned, and the effectiveness of all food items. I feel like this is done flawlessly throughout the game and it really incentivizes the player to explore every nook and cranny of the world to get all those sweet bonuses.Neutrals:-The music is quite decent, but nothing to write home about.-The graphics are rather nice but more on the cartoon-ish side. Some people may be repelled by the art style, but it doesn't bother me personally.-The nexomon designs themselves aren't great but they aren't bad either. A few of the evolutions do seem to just be bigger versions of their pre-evos though, which is never a good thing.Cons:-The combat system is quite generic, and, although the devs have stated they want to make all moves equally viable, some are just downright useless and some moves are god tier. This con can be discounted by the engaging storyline and progression though.-The nexomon. There's nothing inherently flawed about the systems Nexomon Extinction uses to flesh out each nexomon in its own right, but nexomon feel much less unique apart from each other due to some of the differences between Pokemon. Nexomon have no ability, cannot have held items (there are cores which I'll cover in a bit), and can't have more than one typing. Nexomon don't have special/physical attack/defense split, but this is more of a preference than an advantage or disadvantage.-The core system. In Nexomon Extinction, instead of held items, nexomon can have up to four "cores" equipped at a time that will provide your nexomon with various stat bonuses. Admittedly, it isn't a terrible system, but I feel that much more could have been done with it. All of the cores provide generic bonuses like attack, defense, health, exp, etc, but as far as I know, there are no cores that have unique effects that would make it much more fun to play around with. The core system isn't terrible, but it could have been much more fulfilling.Final Rating: 8 / 10Overall the game is quite fun in spite of a few of the flaws I feel it has. If you feel like taking some time out of your day to play a monster catcher where you don't have to do much thinking and can just relax, this is the perfect game for it. In that sense, it might be a better buy on Nintendo Switch, but is quite nice either way. You can easily get over 50 hours of gameplay with the 381 Nexomon to find and collect and the overarching story and post-game.Suggestions:-Add an option to disable battle animations to make leveling/grinding a bit easier.-Add two or three permanent progression items for the pickax that give you an extra elemental shard per rock broken.

_childDocuments_.review: A wonderful pokemon style game with a lot of love in it. The visuals looks great, as does the music and the gameplay. There are a ton of nexomon to collect with over 300 of them to grab including training them and evolving them. The nexomon themselves have some really cool designs and are very cute as well. Nine different starters to choose from, i myself chose the fire type. Because it is inspired by pokemon it obviously plays like it, though it is really enjoyable. It has an interesting adventurous story with great characters and the gameplay is really fun as well. Capturing the nexomon is also quite unique as there is an added element to it. After tossing your trap, a quick time event pops up where it is required to press a series of buttons within a short period of time. Though it does have controller support, the mainly keyboard and mouse controls are excellent to play with. It is basically just w,a,s,d for movement; i,j,k,l for the different actions when fighting; and q and e together for capturing so it does have an easy control scheme to play with. Plenty of areas and biomes to go through as well as an cool story and lore to explore so there is quite a lot of content to get through. Some great humour and meta dialogue is had as well like one time a character was questioning the fantasy of dragon but they were called out by a talking cat. It is definitely a great rpg and can recommend it to those who want to scratch that pokemon itch.

_childDocuments_.review: Nexomon: Extinction is a monster tamer game, like temtem or pokemon, and is overall a good game.Pros: - The game has a good amount of nexomons (what the monsters are called), and the designs are overall pretty good.- This games version of EV's/IV's (from pokemon), I would consider better, since you dont have to grind for every single Nexomon you want to use (you dont need to go after a specific type of monster, nor try and breed what you need, to have it be as good as any other one)- * The humor. Here comes one of my personal oppinions. I personally really like meta humor, and thus i liked a good deal of the humor here, though it is propably far from everyone that would like it.- Story. this one intersects with the humor a bit, as it is somewhat meta. Its also a bit darker than these games usually become, though its not grim dark. also has some interesting consepts in it, and the world is pretty interesting, though not too tied to the original game, only giving references and explains everything from there that is needed to know.- Catch-rates are shown, when you choose your nexotrap.Cons- explaining. The game does not do the best at explaining some of the things that happen in it, mainly with status conditions (does not tell you what they do), and as far as i remember also dont really tell you how the stamina system works.- end game. The endgame is extremely lackluster. you get 3 quests, that is "catch the legendaries", and since there is no multiplayer (at this point at least), there isn't really that much to do, when you beat the game, other than completing the nexopedia (this games version of the pokédex), or hunting for the rare versions of each nexomon.- only one elemet pr. mon: This is one of my biggest grapes with the gameplay of this game. each mon only has one type (which im actually ok with), and then gains 1 type of elemental move, and normal moves (elemental moves are either based on its type, or for normal nexomons, is different for each kind). Overall i would say its a good and fun game, with some problems.

_childDocuments_.review: I have invested 20 hours in it in a span of 4 days, i only do that if the game is really fun, so there we go.It is a very well done pokemon clone, after a few minutes of gameplay, the game lets you free, this is the very first difference with Pokemon, you can actually explore and go to diferent places every time, it has many side quests, which of course you can do or ignore them completely. There are less elements in Nexomon than there is in Pokemon, and there are not mixed element (ex: grass/poison) so it simplifies your strategy, this ia a downside for me, it doesn't have double battles either, so it ends up being a bit simplistic. Every fight (wild nexomon and trainers) are scaled up to your team (around your highest level in party), this is a double edged sword, the challenge will keep up throughout the game, it won't allow you to have a beast and 5 punching bags that buys you time to heal the beast, but it kills that feeling of having an op party. Battling is fast, menus are designed to use a few clicks to perform an action (ex: A opens combat, Y opens your Nexomon party) and animations are very fast, i really liked this because otherwise it would get tedious after a few battles (we all have skipped changing our Pokemon to a better type in a battle due to being a long process), it also has an energy system, your combat moves will drain that energy (there are potions to refill it) so you need to use more than one in each battle. Trainers are not as dumb as they are in Pokemon, they usually have a lot of Nexomons, with various types and they will try to counter your Nexomon. It has a "core" system that lets you buff your nexomon, you need to craft them by mining ores and refining them, each core has 3 tier, ex: atk +5%, +8%, +10%, you can stack them, so you could add +40% atk in a Nexomon, there are more buffs (atk,def,hp,exp gained, exp shared and so on). Since the very beginning you will be able to catch all types as well, this leads us to the catching system, which i think it is way better than Pokemon. It has a few bars (feeding, tireness, states, Nexotrap, other), each bar fills a total % of catching rate, ex: feeding a nexomon will increase it by x% depending if it likes the food or not, it caps at 30%, getting it to low HP will add another % and so on.I think the art is pretty, and the music is fantastic but i have noticed a few moments in which the music didn't fit the mood of the game, but i think this is a very tiny detail. i like Nexomon's art as well, but sometimes they feel a bit generic or a straight up copy of a Pokemon design.It doesn't have the gym formula we all know either, you will fight bosses, which personally i enjoyed more than fighting a gym. It doesn't have any kind of online, devs have said that it may be implemented in the future, but no promises, so take this with a grain of salt. Also, 300+ Nexomons to catch.

It's a very well made game, it's got a kicker good soundtrack, attractive settings and atmosphere, monster designs and animations are unique and fun, and the story is intriguing, though I have yet to finish it yet due to the grind involved. After a while it gets tiring. After every story advancing event, the whole world gets stronger. Wild nexomons and trainers all scale in difficulty based on your story progress, and in order to keep up you have to spend literal hours grinding every nexomon up to a competitive level before and after you advance the story in any way. You could also just catch wild Nexomons that are already leveled up competitively, but that kind of ruins the fun of having a "team" if you're always replacing everyone in your lineup.I wouldn't say it's a good Pokemon alternative. It's a decent enough game on it's own, if you can survive the grinding. But I don't think it really compares to pokemon at all. It has none of the sense of adventure that old pokemon games give you, no element of exploration, no massive dungeons that take hours to find your way through. It's really just "go here, talk to these people, go here, fight this boss, grind your party, repeat". If you're looking for a pokemon clone, prepare to be underwhelmed, as no game has ever come close to be honest, and trust me I've looked for years for another game like that. But on it's own, Nexomon Extinction is an above average, well-put-together game with a good story and lots of monsters to catch.

_childDocuments_.review: In short, there are some missing quality of life features and the variety of moves isn't very good, but it's a fun enough game if you're looking for something like traditional Pokemon but with a different feel. In long, I'll go over some of the things that stand out to me:Nexomon almost never have more than one type of elemental attack. If you have a Plant type, it'll know Plant (Grass) moves and Physical (Normal) moves and that's it. The lack of coverage makes the battles switch-heavy. You'll constantly be switching your Nexomon to match up well into theirs, and for the most part, types that are effective against something also resist that type which makes the switch safer. This isn't really a bad thing and promotes using your whole team in each battle, though you feel punished for duplicating types on your team sometimes. Physical types usually have an elemental attack, but don't resist anything so they generally just feel inferior.However, because switching happens so much, it's hard to justify using moves that buff yourself, or debuff the opponent. The pure status moves are also generally very weak. For example, making the enemy use 25% more stamina (PP), reflecting 20% damage, reducing the enemy attack and defense by 15%, a move learned by Mineral (Rock) types that nullifies Mineral damage, and so on. Ones that apply statuses are also quite inaccurate, like a 30% chance to sleep or a 50% chance to curse. Others have odd decisions, such as a very fast move that increases crit rate but lowers defense, which means you go first and get hit with your lowered defense before your next action. I find very few of the non-attacking moves appealing.Some attacking moves are also hardly different at all. My Lunabelle leveled up and had the chance to learn Drill. It has 100 Power, 100% Accuracy, 44 Speed, 5% crit rate, and costs 15 Stamina. She already knew Rocknite Burst, which has 110 Power, 95% Accuracy, 44 Speed, 8% crit rate, and costs 15 Stamina. There are many such cases through the game. Many moves also have a very low chance to apply a status, like 10~20%, which adds a lot of unpredictable randomness, which can be seen as good or bad. Statuses seem to tick down even if the Nexomon isn't on the field, so you can switch out for some of them to get rid of it.The statuses aren't explained in game as far as I can tell, and Stunned doesn't have an icon, so you don't know when your opponent is stunned and can't move. Combine that lack of icon with the low chance of applying it and it's troublesome.Grinding on wild mobs is very not lucrative. It's much better to grind through rematch trainer battles. You can get the ability to run away from wild mobs with 100% chance early on by visiting the Drake Isles and then never have to bother with something you don't want to catch. These are good things for me.The level curve is rather sharp at times. At one point, the enemy levels go from around 18 to around 28 over the course of around three battles. The game levels up as you progress it, so the wild mobs and rematches will match your current progress.There are also some places where it doesn't heal your party despite having multiple battles in a row, so you have to run back to town between battles or be well-stocked on healing items. Escape Ropes are something I miss a lot. There are fast travel waypoints, but I haven't yet found a way to go from anywhere back to the town, which would make a lot of things more convenient.The in-game "Pokedex" doesn't tell you where to capture the Nexomon, so you'll have to look online if you're searching for something specific, and then their locations will be communicated in things like "South-east of the Frozen Tundra waypoint" and you'll have to compare what you're seeing in the grass to what they say should be there to confirm you're in the right place. The filters on their online Nexopedia don't work so you're better off using fan sites like Nexopad if you want to see information on them.Also you can't set settings on the main menu, so if you lower the volume in the settings of your save file a lot, the menu is going to hurt your ears each time you launch the game. Maybe lower the game's volume on your computer's volume mixer instead.All that aside, it's pretty enjoyable and has most of the things you'd expect from a Pokemon game. Metroidvania elements to get new stuff in old areas (like HMs), shinies, 1v1 battles with type matchups, catching a team, evolving them, and so on. But, it does feel distinct from Pokemon. There are no IVs or EVs, and Nexomon don't have genders so I doubt there is breeding, and all battles have been 1v1.

_childDocuments_.review: What can I say, I grew up with Pokémon. But I'm sure a lot of you are already familiar with that series. Anyway, nostalgia was the reason I was immediately interested in checking out Nexomon: Extinction. The important question here is: Is it just another Pokémon clone? Or is it actually very different? To be honest, whilst I wouldn't mind a game that plays out like the Pokémon series, I went into the game expecting a generic monster training game without any substance regardless. However, I couldn't be more wrong. Nexomon: Extinction turned out to be such a wonderful ride I never wanted to get off.Whilst Nexomon: Extinction is technically the second game in the Nexomon series, both games are not related to each other at all. The story is independent, although there are references available throughout the game about the previous entry. However, as I didn't get to play the first game yet, this review will be solely based on my experience with Nexomon: Extinction.Nexomon: Extinction opens with introducing the main character who grew up in an orphanage. The protagonist is about to begin their journey and have to select their first Nexomon. However, as the journey advances, it's evident that there is something terribly wrong. Tyrant Nexomon are becoming a threat to humans, and monsters, as they start to go rampage. The main character joins a guild and tries help with the fight, however, there might be more into it than it seems at first glance. During the long journey, the main character will discover a lot of secrets along the way.Yes, yes, and yes! This quote perfectly describes my experience with Nexomon: Extinction. The story seemed generic, at first, with the main character obtaining a Nexomon, starting to collect various other ones, all while having the main objective of eliminating the Tyrants. Well, admittedly, the player usually fights against the main villain but I guess it's more or less the same anyway.I'll keep this short, as I'm positive everyone knows how monster training games work. Nexomon: Extinction implements turn-based combats where the player can either fight against other tamers or random Nexomon. In addition to that, it's possible to catch wild Nexomon with so-called Nexomon traps, as well as giving them snacks, and complete a small mini-game of pressing specific buttons in the right order, to increase the chance for being successful. There are different types of Nexomon available such as water, fire, psycho, etc., as well as different rarity types which made it more challenging if the player wants to obtain every single Nexomon.I would strongly advise to level up the whole party instead of single Nexomon as Nexomon: Extinction implements an unusual system of level scaling so other tamers, and wild Nexomon, are catching up to the player. This feature depends on the player's three highest Nexomons and might become a problem later on when the player has to go through multiple battles without being able to heal in between. I feel quite mixed about this feature as it adds more challenge to the playthrough, however, I found it slightly annoying as I just wanted to experience the story at some point. Regardless, it's not impossible to beat the game, so it didn't bother me a lot.Graphic-wise, Nexomon: Extinction is beautiful. The environment reminds me of the Pokémon series with being able to find wild Nexomon in the grass or caves. Anyway, each city was so different from each other and had a completely different theme — Although I ended up loving each design. Fortunately, the Nexomon itself have a great design too and there are over 300 for the player to catch. I found the legendary ones especially memorable, although it's evident that they're more special. To top it off, when the player gets into a battle the environment doesn't only change depending on which location they're fighting but is also animated with leaves or wind moving around.The cutscenes itself work like a typical visual novel where each character has their own sprite and facial expressions. In the actual game, the expressions don't change, however, there are bubbles appearing above the characters that indicate what they are feeling — And it works out well. Something that really stood out here is that Nexomon: Extinction actually implements CGs for special scenes. Unfortunately, there is no way to look them up in a gallery, but as the character's design is selectable at the beginning of the game, the CGs are slightly altered as well.I expected Nexomon: Extinction to be a clone of the Pokémon series, however, it's much more than that. To my surprise, this game managed to catch me off guard with its well-executed plot and excellent comedic character writing. As a result, I ended up being more interested in experiencing the story than to hunt for Nexomon. Sure, a lot of things are very similar to Pokémon, however, Nexomon: Extinction does its own thing and adds its own charm, along the way, and managed to stand out, delivering an unforgettable experience to me. That being said, I can highly recommend Nexomon: Extinction to all fans of Pokémon, as well as newcomers who are looking for a game with a memorable story.

_childDocuments_.review: This is the best monster catching game I have ever played!In case you only read the first line I want to stress that point more than any other. I tried to keep this review spoiler free. Just in case this a spoiler warning. I have had SO MUCH FUN playing this game and I want to make sure people wont miss out on this experience. Nexomon is as far from being “Just another Pokemon clone” as you can get. I will include some information for those who are undecided about Nexomon Extinction.Now there are some similarities to other monster catching games but that is sticking to the genre. You need locations to heal your Nexomon. You need people to battle and strengthen your team. But the Nexomon team have included many unique elements to their game that I feel truly sets it apart from other games.Firstly the game revolves around a huge Immersive storyline. The story is a continuation from Nexomon One so while it's possible to enjoy Nexomon Extinction as a standalone game I would recommend starting with Nexomon One. The game begins similaar to most others. You are a young person ready to head off into the world and catch your first Nexomon. You're thrown into a world that has seen much hardship. Whole cities are in ruin. Through the story you can affect change and create a brighter future. You are ready to join the Guild of Tamers. The Guild are a global organisation who are tasked with helping out the population by maintaining peace. Each member of the Guild is ranked according to their accomplishments.  This is represented by two factors. Your Guild rank and Reputation level. Once you get your first Nexomon that is where any similarity to other games ends. The games storyline literally lands in your lap with a giant explosion. From here on you will find yourself hooked by the ever changing story elements and engaged until the very last battle, including the HUGE TWIST which I did not see coming. In addition to the main story there are currently over 500 side quests available. So you will find yourself with plenty to do as you can see from my time spent on the game.Reputation is another unique game feature. Reputation is a persistent measure of your progress and ability as a tamer. Your reputation will increase as you perform deeds for others, complete missions set by the guild and catch unique Nexomon. This affects the world around you too. As you improve your reputation you will notice that interactions reflect your higher standing. Along with this you will find the interactions with many characters, chief among them Coco your friend and companion show you a development team that really cares about the game they have created and they don’t take themselves too seriously.The grinding in this game is more than just earning EXP. There is a lot more effort involved in Nexomon Extinction but the harder something is to achieve the better it feels when you do. So in addition to grinding for EXP you can farm shards. These have multiple uses, chief among them is being combined to form Cores. Each Nexomon can have up to four equipped which provide a boost in battle. These include EXP gained, gold gained and attack power among others. The first two add that extra depth to grinding as I often found myself equipping gold cores to grind for gold one minute and EXP cores another minute. Then you may find yourself hunting for shards to build cores to increase your Nexomon’s abilities in battle.The game contains 381 different Nexomon, all of which can be caught in a single playthrough. I like almost all of the Nexomon designs including Legendary Nexomon however I do understand that this is all a matter of taste. You will need to explore every corner of the world to catch them all too. Within a single area different patches of grass will spawn different Nexomon.The game presents you with a bright, colourful and vibrant world. The graphics are still 2D but this is technically only the second game in the series. Players of Nexomon will note that there are graphical improvements. The world feels much more alive. The game doesn’t have a gym system. In Nexomon Extinction things are different. As the story unfolds you will learn who are going to be your most powerful enemies. There are more boss battles than I can count and a persistent all powerful threat, a final boss that your journey eventually leads to.This game is far more open world than any other game of its type. Almost from the first time you leave your home you are free to explore most of the world around you and there is certainly plenty to explore. I almost did not want to include anything negative but it isn’t fair to present a biased opinion. Without giving too much away the final battle has a section where it feels choreographed. The fight goes a specific way regardless of what you have done in the lead up to it. It does feel like you can lose this battle  but it just feels like the game is holding your hand and telling you which buttons to press. I would have preferred to fight with the team I had chosen and developed over the game.Another area for improvement is the move sets of certain Nexomon were quite limited. For example each type has one strongest attack move. But not all Nexomon are able to learn it. This is fine in the early game but towards the late game Nexomon will have stronger moves and it may leave you at an unnecessary disadvantage. I'm not saying that all Nexomon should have the same moves but they should have the option to have the strongest move of their type.While there are lots of fantastic looking Legendary Nexomon almost all of them are not available for you until after the main story. Now while I understand I would actually have preferred the chance to catch them sooner. When you play through the storyline there is one part where catching Legendary Nexomon would line up with current events.The game uses a dynamic system that governs the strength of encounters. As you progress along the story Nexomon and Tamers become stronger. This can feel like the progress has not amounted to much. Fortunately the system was revamped soon after launch and improved. The fact that Tamers get stronger over time is actually more realistic. Facing the same tamer multiple times and them having the same level Nexomon all the time would make no sense.To sum up how I feel about this game: Good Points•	A deep Immersive storyline that will keep you entertained for hours.•	A beautiful vibrant open world to explore.•	Character interactions that change dynamically according to reputation and achievements.•	A monster catching game doing its own thing and standing out.•	Numerous side quests to give you plenty to do.•	Added depth to characters development beyond simple EXP Gain.•	381 unique and mostly well designed Nexomon to tame and train.•	Lots of fun and humour woven into character interactions.•	Plenty of boss battles.•	Every Tamer can be fought again. This makes level grinding far easier.•	Fantastic sound design. High octane during Epic battles, calm during forest walks•	A game with a development team who really care about the quality of their game and the opinions of those who play and support it.Areas for Improvement•	The final battle feels in places choreographed and preset.•	Certain Nexomon lack a comprehensive moveset.•	The dynamic encounters can make progress feel less effective as enemies get stronger with you. But you can level up faster than others do with effort.I honestly cannot recommend this game enough. This is a fantastic monster catching game and much more than a clone of anything. I can safely say that you will have a hell of a time playing this game. The fantastic storyline is a fun ride from start to finish. Please give these guys a try. You will not be disappointed. You can tell that I really mean it too with almost 400 hours of play time. A new update is coming that will make this game better than it already is. I absolutely love NEXOMON EXTINCTION!

_childDocuments_.review: If you're looking for a less kiddy approach to pokemon with alot of QOL changes as well as alot of little bits and bobs to chase then look no further.- Art Style is adorable but is appropriately creepy on the proper mons.- Story is way better than expected.  Not Oscar material, but I've been interested and did not predict where it would go.  Definitely a more mature/grim world but counterbalanced by constant humor.  I want to see where it ends up!- Humor is generally quite good, game knows when to mock itself and the genre.  4th wall breaks are definitely a thing.- Combat is harder than standard pokemon and there are "full heal" mechanics scattered throughout the world to keep fights a threat without making you constantly go heal.   - Catching minigame is an improvement on pokemon.  I know my chances, how to improve them, and it's more than just "beat on the mob until it's low and use a higher ball"- Alot of passive items to find and collect that enhance your progression or QOL.- Elemental strengths/weaknesses matter but it's not utter suicide to fight into your weakness.  Bonus damage is only +25%, reduced damage only -35%.  This goes both ways, just because you elementally counter something doesn't mean it can't chunk you.- "core system" lets you customize your mon stats to a degree and also solve the leveling problem as some cores copy a % of exp from any defeat and if you explore/quest you get some free pretty early.- Tons of unique critters, I'm still finding a some new ones 40+ hours in.Only con is that while it does a good job of weighting accuracy vs damage vs speed and etc I feel like status effects are generally balanced to be a bit weak and the overall move library could use more variety.  Each element gets template moves and variety outside of that exists,  but im not sure how viable alot of the other stuff is.
_childDocuments_.name: Nexomon: Extinction

_childDocuments_.review: "Hey look, another Pokémon clone!" will be the first thought into most people's heads.Not many will get to try Nexomon and will quickly brush it away as a copy.Their loss..This game has excellent battle mechanics, astounding music, splendid creativity, wonderful visuals and caring devs that look to improve this already amazing game into something better and better.As someone who grew up with all the Pokémon games I absolutely love them to their core and have been looking for a creature-collector that can measure up to it for a long time.This "wow!" comes from Nexomon. It's arguably much better than Pokémon itself while introducing many new mechanics. A game I would've been sad to have skipped over. Onwards to the next game in this series! Keep up the great work devs!
_childDocuments_.name: Nexomon: Extinction

_childDocuments_.review: Nexomon Extinction is what one might call a "side-line" of the classic Pokémon JRPG-style monster catcher. Which is to say, it has its own direction and flow, while still feeling in-line with what you already know and love. There's a lot of Quality of Life improvements over Pokémon, and it'll be too long to list them here, but know that there are some nice takes this game has over what you might have come to expect in this genre.I enjoyed the story, the world-building and the overall feel of the game. I liked the humour too. The graphics are vibrant, the music is good, and the combat is what you'd expect, with a slight twist in that "stamina" is required to use moves. I also liked the catching mechanics; it tells you your capture chances as well as offering ways of increasing said chances (like feeding a nexomon their favourite treat for example).There's a nice focus on exploration and adventure in this game too which is awesome, I enjoyed going around and finding all sorts of areas and loot during my journey, doing side quests and catching nexomon as I went. Speaking of, the nexomon themselves are unique: from the cute to the monstrous - you get some awesome, as well as some bland - but well, with over 400 Nexomon, this is to be expected.Overall, a solid game and especially if it's on sale and you're a fan of this style of game give it a go!
_childDocuments_.name: Nexomon: Extinction

_childDocuments_.review: Enjoyable Pokemon-like! Just deep enough to keep you entertained, but fixes a lot of the issues I have with Pokemon as well. It's nice that not every single thing one-shots you, even on weakness, for example. The monster designs are stellar!The only cons I can think of are movement being rather clunky, and the game does force you to grind occasionally. There's a heavy reliance on 4th-wall-breaking jokes as well, but the writing's good enough to keep you interested. Highly recommended!

_childDocuments_.review: As someone who enjoyed the Pokemon franchise for years, it feels like the series has focused on multiplayer battles at the expense of everything else.  Not so with Nexomon: Extinction, which has all the single-player charm of old-school Pokemon games, combined with great visuals, creative creature designs that blow newer Pokemon out of the water, fun characters, and some witty writing that had me chuckling. With that witty writing comes a story much better than its Pokemon equivalent, with less bland moralizing and forgettable side characters. I can't help but make so many comparisons to Pokemon, because the game feels like the designers were fed up with Pokemon's descent into laziness and wanted to show the jaded heads at Game Freak how it's done, and succeeded at doing so.Having played the first Nexomon game, I have to say that this game is decided improvement in every regard, and well worth the price tag.
_childDocuments_.name: Nexomon: Extinction

_childDocuments_.review: I went in expecting a Pokemon knock-off. I looked at the reviews that praised the writing, design, and story. I bought the game on sale for half off. I regret the purchase.Nexomon Extinction would have been a decent game in a vacuum, but with Pokemon to compare it to it just falls short on almost every measure. The creature designs are passable, the writing self-derogatory, the combat system one gimmick (stamina instead of move points) from a copy of older Pokemon games, the world is constrained to a grid which even Pokemon has moved away from... I expected a Pokemon knock-off, and the game disappointed even that.

_childDocuments_.review: This is like if Neopets made a pokemon clone that poked fun at other games. The designs for a majority of the nexomon have potential to be really cool but then too often fall flat. After 14 hours of grinding out levels to try and see what all my nexomon look like evolved I gave up and looked up the dex on their website. Out of the 18 pages of nexomon only like 3 pages (the last 3) of them look really cool. Even so, when those cool ones are enlarged for cut scenes they really do not age well and just look so flat. Shading can go a long way.The writing is forgetable and the best of it is jokes from your cat companion breaking the 4th wall. The game is way more open than a pokemon game so you can go to a majority of areas before you need to for the story and farm materials and xp. Speaking of XP the game has scaling for enemies. Each zone has a minimum level starting but then scales based primarily on story progress with a little from the highest level nexomon in your party. There is exp share but you have to make it and it in the form of special orbs you can equip (4 per nexomon) and equip it to whoever is getting leveled. Need to swap them to a different nexomon? unequip all and then equip them on a new one one at a time. Tedious and and grind just to start grinding. Since they did this grid based layout that also means there is only up, down, left, right when moving around. It felt jarring for a while when not in grass moving around because you feel like diagonals should be possible. At first between the UI and the navigation handling I thought it felt like it should have been a mobile game instead. Turns out it was put out on mobile and the PC version feels like a mobile port. If the game is on sale for really cheap and after watching someone else play it looks like something you wanna put time into it you could do a lot worse. I think what is frustrating is how I can see a lot of potential and I want to like it more.

_childDocuments_.review: The game has similar elements to pokemon, you are allowed to have up to 6 Nexomon at a time in your party and there are capture devices. The capture rate is affected by damage done to the Nexomon, food fed to the Nexomon and status effects and also a random button combination, all of this shows up as a % for the capture rate. I personally prefer the way Pokemon does this but its an interesting change of pace. The graphics and animations are really good and polished. The story line is interesting and funny and you have many character models to pick from initially both male or female depending on preference. The Nexomon all have a single element but can use moves from other elements similar to how Pokemon can do so. Its worth giving the game a shot. Some might say the game is more difficult than Pokemon and it seems to be so far but its better if its abit more difficult because Pokemon is overly easy IMO.

_childDocuments_.review: Why I love this game:- Very easy to 'pick up and play' or 'put down'- A very streamlined experience where battles don't feel tedious/long and I can explore the game world- Interesting decisions in the 'core experience' (or battles) where I have a limited number of monsters, moves, and items I can throw at any challenge- Fun decisions with picking various monster types/teams to battle with (and choosing cores to customise my monster battle stats)Why I dislike this game:- At the time of writing this review, this game does not have enough replayability.Once I've beaten the main story once, I would like a 'New Game Plus' mode so I can try different monsters/teams in new playthroughs OR unlock some end-game 'arena' so I can endlessly challenge my team(s) in battle.I like this game so much I want to be able to replay this as much as humanly possible.- Not enough challenges or content when I reach 'the end of the game'. After the main story, I would like some way to discover more things I can use in battles or have a way to endlessly challenge any team of monsters I have

_childDocuments_.review: is a monster collecting RPG game that comes as the second entry in the series. It is not necessary to have played the first in order to jump into this game, even though there are some references back to the first game.It's a fairly standard monster-catching/taming/battling game where you take the role of a young Nexomon tamer and follow the storyline events, through the process you will earn money, find loot, fight and trap Nexomon, and fight against trainers and gradually progress. There are Tyrants to face on your journey as bosses. You will end up facing against the same trainers with increased difficulty later on. You will be able to take on side quests as well. There are different regions in the game that have effects on your monsters because of their types and you have to manage things to best suit the situations that you are in.I have a lot of experience playing  games and so with that also comes certain expectations for games that have a similar gameplay and even a similar name. I have not been able to really enjoy this game all that much because this game tries so hard to be  but just falls short a bit in several major ways.+ You can fight trainers multiple times, this allows you to earn some additional money when needed.+ The artwork looks really good, the creatures are designed well.+ There are many Nexomon to collect, over 300 (closer to 400 actually).+ You can find a lot of loot throughout the game.+ There are no game editions restricting specific monsters like you see in - Unfairness in battles,  unfair for the player. When you fight against another trainer you or the opposing trainer can switch out Nexomon accordingly. If you switch a monster, the opposing trainer can hurt your monster that turn. If the AI trainer does a switch, you cannot do the same to them. It just does not make sense to me and feels unfair. It leaves a sour taste in the mouth.- The monster catching process involves a bit of button mashing on the controller to increase your chances. I really do not like that at all. And in turn, you will likely need multiple traps to catch any one Nexomon.- The world is populated with too many NPCs that it feels quite overwhelming. I ended up skipping by most of them instead of trying to talk to them, to get their stories, etc.- No trading system.- No Nexomon breeding.- No shinies.- Overall the game just feels like it's trying to be  but it ends up falling short and leaves a bit of disappointment for a true  fan.The artwork is pretty good, and the battle screens/animations resemble the  styles, just not as good.These are very nice aspects of the game.This game is meant to be played with a controller, but it can also be played with a keyboard.It is 19.99 Euro/USD base price. It's double the price of the original in USD, but more than double in Euros because of lack of regional pricing for the EU.I did try to like  for what it is, but its flaws kept wearing away at my patience. Being a hardcore  fan, I was not very impressed. For people who enjoyed the first game, you will probably find a similar amount of enjoyment in this installment. For people who have never played  or maybe even dislike it, but still want a monster-taming adventure, this is perhaps a title to reach for.I cannot recommend it for people who, like me, have thoroughly enjoyed all of the  games. I was rather disappointed, and I think you might be too, in just some of the game aspects that have become integral to the monster-taming games. It just whet my appetite for the next actual  installment without offering any significant satisfaction in the gameplay. The battles in their unfair nature also left a bitter feel.

_childDocuments_.review: Very worthy sequel to an already excellent Pokemon-like game.Unfortunately Nexomons are still mono types, although they did introduce two more. They have more stat variety, but you'll end up using only the starters and legendaries, because they are the only ones that get the strongest damaging moves.Speaking of moves, status effects went from broken in the first game to almost useless here, low proc chance and no / very weak damage on the move itself. So there's almost no strategy, just use your strongest attack and hit your opponent weakness.The post-game is also imo a bit worse than in the first game, shorter and it's almost just a capture fest with very very low catch rates (but there are now ways to improve it).Overall though, the story is fun, soundtrack is great, graphics look good, plays perfectly on Steam Deck and I hope we get another sequel!

_childDocuments_.name: Nexomon: Extinction

_childDocuments_.review: So take Pokemon, add some much-needed quality of life tweaks to the capture formula, include elements like items to improve capture rate, and then have nearly 400 damn creatures available in one title -- you get Nexomon. This is a solid Pokemon-like that improves on a few ways on the original. It's got more challenge, it actually demands you change your party around or even (gasp) focus on leveling up your monsters before taking on a big challenge. The story/setting are interesting and unique and the writing can be at times a bit meh, but it often manages to be at least compelling, creating a mystery you'd like to uncover more of and fleshing out a world very, very different from the Pokemon standard. Overall, I think this game not only delivers on its stated goal (a Pokemon-like adventure) but it also manages to stand on its own two feet. It has a big world, a big bestiary and a lot to uncover. Don't expect this to have the graphical polish of a big Pokemon title, but if you're looking for a fun and meaty RPG with a very nice price tag, this is a great choice. I hope we see more games in the future!

_childDocuments_.review: Note: This is my first review, my first time playing any Nexomon game - I wasn't aware there was a prequel - therefore I'm a complete newbie both game/review wise, however it made a new fan in me and made me want to backtrack to it's prequel so I wrote this.If you love the handheld Pokémon games it is very likely you will enjoy Nexomon: Extinction as game-play wise it has similarities to Pokémon and could almost be called the meme version of Pokémon thanks to it's running commentary of fourth-wall jokes. However the two games are not the same as Nexomon: Extinction stands on it's own feet as a traditional RPG, and does so successfully, but happily flaunts that it was very likely inspired by Pokémon with it's critter catcher base. Instead I'd recommend people to try not to go in expecting it to be exactly the as Pokémon same mechanics wise, but instead to expect it to have similarities and give you some nostalgia - especially difficulty wise - whilst being an entirely different game.✔️ It's a game that is fairly cheap and overall will be smooth running game even for lower spec users like myself. (I do find when I boot up the game and use my first attack against an opponent in a battle it freezes for a short time, but it unfreezes pretty quick and runs perfectly fine after that so it's minor.)✔️ It's both colourful and visually appealing in all aspects. In particular I like the backgrounds over the Nexomon but the designs of the Nexomon are also well done. (And yes shiny ones are available and are called "cosmic".)✔️ The main story is fairly large (I completed it in about 30+ hours) and well paced. The world is also a nice size and very explorable as it's a semi open world from the get go. ✔️ All the characters are likeable and I love the silly fourth wall breaking humour. I have laughed at this game several times. However this will very much depends on the player though and will get old for some.✔️ Alongside your main slot there are 3 extra save slots for multiple playthroughs.✔️ It's fairly difficult and doesn't hand everything to you on a spoon. Be prepared for some grinding, buying potions, running back to the Nexostop (health centre) and the opponents switching out Nexomon strong against yours.✔️ Additional side quests are not only there but they don't feel forced into the game for no reason. There's also plenty of them as well which makes the game fairly playable even after finishing.✔️ All Nexomon, including starters, can be caught in the game and the game certainly makes it feel doable. No DLCs or anything of the sorts are needed. ✔️ Level scaling can be a make or break feature for some, but I personally enjoyed that the Nexomon and Tamers (who you can re-battle anytime) in world got tougher and it increased the difficulty nicely.✔️ Customisation is pretty good. You can customise your character whenever you want with a nice selection of sprite choices, find a few different Nexomon sprites that can follow you if you wish (and is entirely optional) and use a custom mode once you complete the game to change the game-play entirely.  ❌ No ability to change the keyboard mapping made it much more awkward for playing on a keyboard as did have odd controls. When I switched to controller I found it far easier for this game in particular. ❌ Whilst I enjoyed them at first and they're not terrible, some of the mechanisms got a bit repetitive for me. The mini game as you catch the Nexomon, the boulder smashing to farm shards and looking for higher percentages when throwing food at the Nexomon are some that just got repetitive after a while.❌ There was no tutorial about the type and status system so knowing what they did was pretty much a guessing game unless you googled it. An NPC or something explaining what the all types and status system are would've been really helpful for both old and new players.❌ Exploring is fun but without an on the go in-game map and no route names I found it hard to find/remember places sometimes (warpstones do help but you have to find it first). Maybe my sense of direction is bad though.❌ There just seemed like a lot of scrolling. Need to buy 50 potions? You're adding all of them 1 at a time. Same goes for things like throwing food at Nexomon and searching for a Nexomon in the Database. I personally think a bulk option and a few shortcuts would help out for some of it.❌ For those collecting them all there is no feature in the Database telling you where Nexomon was last seen/where to find them or any sort of hint. Right now it's a lot of wandering aimlessly and/or being reliant on online guides.❌ Move pool was fairly small but it felt even smaller since many of the non attacking moves just don't feel worth the slot they take up because the percentage of them hitting is just so low. Sadly this made the Nexomon kinda feel the same strategy wise for me since they also didn't have any unique abilities, stats and whatnot, then also all had similar move pools.❌ Minor but no selling items at the store was a shame. It would've been nice to be able to sell those excess Nexotraps I wasn't using for some money. All in all it very much embraces the fact it is Pokémon like but manages to change up those core features a just tad bit to make them feel different for both new and old players of the critter catcher genre. The game is most certainly not a masterpiece and could use with some things changing up a little, however considering how cheap it is and it's still receiving updates regularly I would most certainly recommend this game for anyone who loves critter catcher and RPG games or wants to play a Pokémon-esque game with a different take.

_childDocuments_.review: I've got 8 hours playtime right now and I must say that I am thoroughly impressed so far. Most people would assume this is a Pokemon rip-off but it's much more than that and so far I am enjoying it more than any Pokemon game I've played. It has a lot of similarities to Pokemon but also has a lot of it's own features. It also has a much more vibrant world filled with charm and much better written characters. The characters and vibe have a nice sense of humour too. It doesn't take itself too seriously which is nice for a game of this style. The game actually has a story which seems thought out and well written, so far there are plenty of mysteries that I am looking forward to discovering and seeing where the adventure takes me and my character. The creatures are really well designed and you can tell that time and passion was put into creating them. The mix of abilities that I've encountered so far is good but I know I have many more to discover. The combat is really engaging and fun. The effects look nice and all the moves are explained. I couldn't see a list of weakness and strengths or a list of status effects but these can be found easily online. It's nice to be able to see exactly what each move does while in combat with a list of stats to help you compare them too. I've only played 8 hours but so far I would definitely recommend this game as I'm having a great time and looking forward to playing more!!

_childDocuments_.review: Wish Pokemon went to this level of quality. The story was an absolute blast with some fantastic twists. The stamina and catching systems are entertaining. _childDocuments_.review: I grew up with Pokemon and played all the games so a friend recommended this game. I wasn't super sold on it at the beginning of the game because the game mechanics are different from Pokemon, like you can't switch between your Nexomon every time you defeat an opponent and the type matchups aren't super clear (or maybe I just missed the part where they explain it??). Also you have to run back and forth between warpstones instead of being able to just teleport to last one (the running was a bit of a waste of time for me). But I think some of the differences actually made the game harder than Pokemon, which I thought was a nice challenge, like the fact that you can re-battle opponents and their Nexomon are also scaled to match your level, as well as all the wild Nexomon. As the story progressed I actually found myself really enjoying myself and I wished that I had played the first Nexomon! There's a bit of post-game material too, but I found some of it to be mostly just grinding wild Nexomon encounters. So in all, I think that it's a unique game that has a good story but could definitely use some QoL updates. But the game is still relatively new so I think a lot can be said about how good the game is right now.

_childDocuments_.review: This is the good stuff. It's not perfect, but going toe-to-toe with a franchise like Pokemon is hard, and it's impressive to see something pull that off on what I'm assuming is the rpgmaker engine.But I'm getting ahead of myself.What is Nexomon? It's a *long* narrative-driven pokemonlike.Balance-wise, it's at the Red/Blue/Yellow level. Everything is mono type, but there's STAB bonuses and some interesting moves and you don't automatically get a free switch when you KO an opposing monster. There's also a universal stamina meter instead of PP, and big moves take a lot, but you can skip turns to recover it. There's a definite metagame here, even if it's not *super* complicated.Nexomon is also very convenience oriented. You can free-roam a *lot* more than in pokemon. The safari zone is open right from the jump. There's no HMs---just items that your trainer holds. There's no EVs and IVs or other hidden build information (that I'm aware of, at least.) When you approach a patch of grass, you can see where the encounters are in it. You can tell your capture chance based on a monster's status, HP, and other factors. Capturing involves some button inputs, rather than just watching an orb wiggle. You can also find tons of collectible items that boost your overall capture chance and encounter odds for certain elements and rarities, which is a really welcome addition to the formula.In terms of the individual monsters, a lot of them look a little we-have-pokemon-at-home, but there's *tons* of them, and some have fantastic visual design. The concepts get pretty inventive, too. There's bower birds and fire hydrants and ice cream sundaes. It's neat.As for complaints, I can really only muster up a few.The internal logic to the elemental weaknesses in Nexomon feels a little hard to wrap my head around sometimes. Sure, water beats fire. But plant beats...lightning? And psychic seems like it genuinely rolls a dice to decide what it cares about.The writing is also *very* fourth wall breaking. This keeps the mood light, but it's kind of a shame, because the actual plot is genuinely engaging. There's decent worldbuilding and character writing and a few solid twists, but the game tries very hard to keep reminding you that it's just a game. You don't get to really sink in and enjoy the setting.So overall: if you like monster-catching games and you don't need them to be too complex, definitely give this a try. I'd love to see more in this series, but even as a standalone Nexomon: Extinction is great.

_childDocuments_.review: Interested in seeing some gameplay? see below!TL:DR: Nexomon Extinction is charming. The catching system in this game is top notch, cute graphics and a very anime-styled story make for a fun experience. My main problem is the amount of exposition and cutscenes throughout the game. 8/10I know what your first question is: Is this better than Pokemon? Well I think it's very different to Pokemon and therefore it's hard to compare, but it does have a nice 2D Pokemon style feeling which the newer games may be missing.Nexomon Extinction is a great addition to the pet-battling genre of games, it takes the world built up in the first game, adds a bunch of cool new Nexomon and throws players into a new story experience. The game begins by offering you a whopping NINE different starters to choose from, this is an awesome change from other games like this, you are also able to catch all of these Nexomon later, which means you don't have to worry about starter FOMO! There is so much story and exposition at the start of this, it rivals Pokemon Sun and Moon in the annoying amount of cutscenes, it took about 10-15 minutes to reach the first battle of the game, which was also part of the story . The huge assortment of different Nexomon you can catch and battle is a treat, there's a huge array of different options, whether you're into cute animals or edgy dragons, there's something for everyone.The battle system is great, there are 9 different Nexomon typings and an array of different moves and status conditions to try out, the stamina bar is an interesting addition to this genre, forcing you to make complex decisions about how you want to manage the resource. The catching system is much more complex and interesting than others in the genre, there are 5 different ways of increasing your catch chance, and a Bop-it! style minigame in the end. Graphics: 10/10Absolutely adorable pets and chibi style characters make the game a charming experience.Audio: 7/10The audio is nice and chill, easy to listen to while playing.Gameplay: 8/10The gameplay is fun and interesting. There are some major differences to other games of the genre which allow this game to stand on its own.Overall: 8/10This game is extremely charming and the battles are loads of fun. The story can be silly but is still more engaging than certain other weapon based games released in the past year.

_childDocuments_.review: If you miss when Pokémon was good you'll enjoy this. _childDocuments_.review: Don't listen to the review that complains about level scaling!  There are cores that work like Exp Shares and give 25% of the exp gained without having to battle.  You can equip 4 of them per Nexomon and they don't reduce the experience any of them gain from battle.  So basically, your entire team can be gaining 100% of the experience per fight.I almost didn't buy the game because of that one review, but I'm glad that I just bought it anyway.  It's a really fun game with a beautiful art style, tons of Nexomon to collect, a good story, and lots of things to do.  Highly recommended for fans of monster catching games like Pokemon.Edit:  I completed the game and I can say that having only one Nexomon leveled up is a really bad idea.  Plenty of fights have enemies of multiple types and you'd be at a huge disadvantage in terms of type weaknesses and resistances with only one Nexomon.  I didn't have any trouble beating the game though, because I leveled up a team with more than one type of Nexomon to counter whatever was thrown at me.  Anyway, it was a really enjoyable experience and I recommend the game even more now.

_childDocuments_.review: Edit having finished the game: Did not find the humor in some of the dialogue throughout the game insulting or mocking the players. Really put a bad taste in my mouth over the entire game and made talking to all the npcs or actually journeying around feel like a huge waste of time, which is annoying since it was easy to get lost of have to back track constantly. Edited/tldr: I would recommend you only buy this game while it is on sale/discount. Story less then half way thru feels super rushed and certain expected features just fall off/are ignored and forgotten about, or not utilized as well as they could have been. Hoping to see improvement as I am relatively close to completing the story now and am saddened by the parts that fell short of what the game was laying the ground work to expect. Truly love this game so far as a creature collector and story teller. Love most of the creatures, huge variety for a single game and keeps most areas feeling fresh. There is a level scale, but it follows the story, so you can stop in an area and become over powered if you want, you can keep fighting trainers over and over every few minutes so it goes super fast too. The story feels fresh to me personally, and I absolutely love the big world and its building blocks that make it interesting to play and explore in, I actually want to talk to npcs and I am usually a person who skips all cut scenes and dialogue. There are just some in this game that work so well, though also sometimes silly/cringy in the story/for our character lol. The art, animations, and UI feel pretty smooth and put together OK if you don't mind using WASD and IJKL keys for left and right hand set up, if you don't it's a little jank-y since there's no way to Re-bind your hot keys. You spend most of your time running around rather then in your menu so it's not too bad really. Traversing the menu is a little much since it doesn't feel like the game actually shows you how to use the Cores within a reasonable time to help you get multiple Nexomon and level them all up together a little easier, but this could be because once you're past the tutorial the world is practical an Open World with so many zones to explore. The game will tell you ' hey we weren't suppose to go this way-- but that wont hurt!' and lets you go anyways, so you never feel that trapped. There's the occasional npc wall and 'you can't go this way yet, you're not strong enough' so you don't totally skip sections in the story. Which the big map is fun- the lack of a minimap/map I can pull up and properly see where I am in the sections- is a little frustrating so far, keep hoping I might unlock that if it's in the game. Really looking forward to playing this more every day so far.

Battle Trainers and Tyrants

Train hard to become the greatest

detailed_description: An aunt and uncle take their middle-school niece and her boyfriend on an overnight camping trip in WIDE OCEAN BIG JACKET Take part in a classic camping trip: Roast hot dogs on the fire, go birdwatching, tell ghost stories, grab a beverage from the cooler and do cartwheels on the beach. WOBJ is a short story game including 20 chapters, 4 playable characters, 10,000 words of dialog and 8 explorable areas, all rendered in a beautiful 2D/3D art style. \ Playtime: 60-90 minutes (like watching a good movie with friends or curling up to read a book) \ Made in 2019 by Turnfollow \\ CW: Includes a scene in which an adult and a tween have a (platonic) conversation about sex and consent. Also a scene depicting older teenagers verbally assaulting tweens.

short_description: A Camping Story starring: Uncle Brad, Aunt Cloanne, Mord (and Ben)

_childDocuments_.review: Brad and Cloanne take their niece and her new boyfriend on their first camping adventure. Mord and Ben are quite reluctant to begin with. They’re not quite sure what to expect but it’s been a long time since Mord spent time with her Auntie, especially as a blossoming adult, and she is keen for them to get to know her new partner.Brad and Cloanne are quite comfortable in the outdoor environment but less familiar with teenage angst and problems. It seems like everyone will be learning new things on this adventure.Wide Ocean Big Jacket is a short and linear narrative adventure revolving around life in the wilderness, relationships and growing up.If you liked the video and found it useful, I'd appreciate it if you could subscribe to my You Tube channel so that I could make more.👍This was a lovely way to spend ninety minutes of my evening, and the time just flew by. There was something mesmerizing about this game, with its abundance of charm and witty moments. The characters were very likable and the writing was engaging, light-hearted and entertaining.Events are never farcical, they’re just things that could easily happen on a camping trick, but they’re wonderfully presented and uplifting. The relationships between the four are cleverly constructed. Conversations flow between the characters effortlessly and we get to see a range of different topics discussed and evaluated. It’s all kept brief and punchy but it’s testament to the excellent writing that the short exchanges between characters leave such a memorable impression.I think this is partly down to the ambiance of the game. The graphics are striking in their simplicity, with bold colours and loosely drawn environments, and the music is so jaunty and spirited that it invokes happiness. It really is a feel-good game and you can’t help chuckle and smile whilst their adventure pans out.There isn’t much game play. Initiating conversations drives the story forward but this is quite linear and we have no choice who to speak to, just when we would like to start. You’ll find yourself bouncing between dialogue exchanges quite quickly. Sentences are very short but conversations still seem meaningful and often very witty. These short interchanges keep the pace high which holds your attention. At moments you will control each character and sometimes more than one at the same time. Everyone seems to get their moment and viewer’s attention. Moving around the environments is restricted but you will have the opportunity to complete very basic tasks as the game instructs, like lighting a fire, setting up a tent etc. None of these tasks are taxing in the slightest but it is a nice way to get involved rather than just watch events unfold.

_childDocuments_.review: If you've played Firewatch, then WOBJ will feel like a familiar but fresh take on walking around the woods and campgrounds. A little slow to start story/action-wise. You will love the characters, though, especially Mord. Some very poignant and unexpected moments in the game that make the most of the limited mechanics. Definitely recommend and it'll only take about 60 - 90 minutes depending on how long you want to linger...
_childDocuments_.name: Wide Ocean Big Jacket

_childDocuments_.review: Wide Ocean Big Jacket is outstanding. I had a grin on my face for almost the entirety of my playtime. Although the events of the game could easily be described as mundane, they are presented with so much charm and character. The game could easily translate into an excellent film; however, the player would then not be so involved in the comedic timing.The text overlays corresponding to various actions often made me laugh, and Mord (the teenage girl) is so refreshingly exuberant about EVERYTHING - it's one of the things I've lost a bit as I've gotten older, and I would like to get back in touch with that part of myself. Although there aren't any real "bombshell" life-changing moments for the characters in the game, I certainly found myself thinking about why and how we develop traditions and about the various "milestones" of life.If you don't require a particularly high stimulation threshold and need your games to be challenging above all, you should absolutely play Wide Ocean Big Jacket. It will make your day.
_childDocuments_.name: Wide Ocean Big Jacket

_childDocuments_.review: I have to admit that I first thought Wide Ocean Big Jacket was a bit too twee for its own good. I liked the writing and characters, but it all felt very slight. Not that the game or its plot became more weighty, but I came to see its light touch and its decision not to introduce major stakes or conflict as an asset. There are exchanges that are beautifully sweet without ever becoming sentimental, and there's a conversation towards the end that is handled wonderfully well. (Chances are you'll know it when you get there.) The juxtaposition between the kids and the grownups is done very nicely without making either seem phony or twee. If you like walking sims, indie comics and the tone of, say, Night in the Woods, this one is well worth checking out.

_childDocuments_.review: First played this in 2019 and loved it, and I was recently reminiscing about it with a friend so of course I had to play it again, and it truly continues to be one of my favorite games. Like, it really is exactly as long as it needs to be, but at the same time I would love to spend more time with these characters. Or at least Mord. Mord will forever be my spirit animal.Also, they even included a chapter select if you want to go back to any of the scenes! I hadn't expected it since the game isn't super long, but it's really nice to have the option since there are some parts where you have different (minor) choices you can pick between.

_childDocuments_.review: If you love travelling, then Wide Ocean Big Jacket is a small charming trip you can take part in without a doubt.I personally, being used to travel a lot, miss travelling while studying at university. With all the fun and all the small shades of family relationships, this game is what brought me to that unique atmosphere back again. And yeah, this was the feeling.I was a part of every of them, a bit of Mord, and a bit of Ben, and, of course, a bit of Brad and Cloanne. There were those two old men, the staff of this lovely camping, and their own pleasant story. There were lots of mean teens, but they weren't so mean in fact. When you travel, everything changes.There were birds singing, and there was the strong wind. Then, the sun was shining, and then it went down the sea horizon. I felt sand under my feet while standing by the seaside at night. I heard squeaking of the trees walking down the woods. I heard noises of burning wood sitting by the campfire. It's kind of a walking sim I should probably warn, and there are no achievements as well, but you'll dive into it in no time realising you don't need them at all. After all, you'll surely never notice it's time to head back home. With grin on your face and a bit of regret in your heart you'll realise that you'd like to stay for a little bit more. No long reviews, it's something you'd rather try for yourself than hear or read about it. If you are ford of traveling – it doesn't matter what you like more, sea or mountains, hitchhiking or hiking, as well as it doesn't matter if you prefer to hit the road alone or with a company of friends – this is the game just for you.And remember, if you see a random bush in the forest–

_childDocuments_.review: As the car hums past different scenery everyone fidgets slightly. The young girl and boy in the back seats look around, bored probably, as the car zooms along towards a destination unknown to the player. Steering the bright red convertible, a brunette woman in shades shifts her gaze slightly, accompanied by a man that lets his arms hang outside the car every now and then. This is the beginning of a quiet little camping trip. From the store page alone the expectations for Wide Ocean Big Jacket should be set: it’s a short camping trip about a niece, her new boyfriend, her aunt and her uncle. But this simple premise houses lots of simple, slice of life moments that add up to something more. The feelings it’s able to portray with bold colors and sparse lines of dialogue is impressive. The design of the game, from just the menu alone, speaks volumes in terms of the artistic approach of the game. The story isn’t necessarily led by 1 of the 4 in particular and even the setting itself is an important part of how the narrative feels. Mord, a wild, headstrong girl is easily quotable in her silly dialogue but also in the way she is thrusting herself into the role of growing up; she is trying so hard to find out what love and relationships mean and even approaches “the talk” with her aunt in such an honest way  Seeing lines as sincere as this is quite a treat.[/caption] Mord's timid, bespectacled, sesquipedalian boyfriend  gets to have his own touching moments as he discusses his family life. Then there’s Cloanne and Brad who are trying to entertain and protect their precocious niece while deciding where their own relationship should go.  The stylized cinematography, eye-catching color choices, family centric themes, and off kilter comedy are probably familiar. The title card introduction and jangly pop and strings of the soundtrack alone would make it easy to jump to Wes Anderson, but there is more just beneath the bright surface of WOBJ. At times it feels like WOBJ is only a hair away from sliding into an early Noah Baumbach-esque tragicomic breakdown. The dialogue, told with intertitle cards featuring a cartoon rendition of the speaker, manages to be silly and serious at different times. The little details of Wide Ocean Big Jacket also stand out.The color palette is striking, but there is also the sound design. The sound of the road, the ocean waves lapping against the shore, or the zipper of a tent, these sounds seem to pop. When characters speak they each get their own little chime, which just adds onto the charm.This is a very cinematic game with a strong sense of art style. Outside of film influences it is easy to find WOBJ’s kinfolk in games like , though this game foregoes the lack of dialogue. A low poly style with careful color choice is shared among them, but WOBJ opts for a more lighthearted look as it isn’t dealing with murder and mystery like Virgina. They all make interesting animation cuts between interaction or dialogue: for example a character might sit happily with a bottle in his hand, but after another character makes fun of him, the scene changes to him slouching and sad. These jump cuts don’t quite match the erraticism of Goddard, but they do give the game a good sense of pace and playfulness. This humor bleeds into the bold title font that prompts the player, such as when Mord tries to go to the bathroom. As a walking simulator, there are only some moments of interaction. You make a few choices that result in slightly different dialogue playing, there is a small quest to pee in a bush that you can opt out of (you coward),and you can wander around freely in a scene, though these scenes are contained quite closely. There is a nice serene moment of watching the moon on the beach or birdwatching with optional commentary through button prompt. It’s all minimal with no lose condition. WOBJ is meant to be played in full. The brief time the player spends on the camping trip is not meant to linger: the pivot of the camera as characters exchange banter or tell a ghost story all feel special. Wide Ocean Big Jacket doesn’t waste a moment of its short playtime. If there is one criticism I have, it’s that you cannot replay dialogue or go back. This certainly fits the movement of speaking and life, but some lines deserve a second look. Wide Ocean Big Jacket is a short slice of life that is full of charm and heart. It feels like a movie I could easily share with friends or family to chat about. Some of the moments in the game are completely relatable, and a few parts feel quirky and entertaining. It’s wholesome, sweet, and playful. On nearly every front Wide Ocean Big Jacket feels like a special little game that I want to keep talking about, even long after the tents are all packed up.
