_childDocuments_.review: Surprisingly good StS-like deckbuilder with a few new twists and takes.  The standout addition is the setting, lore, and overall vibe of the Arthurian version of purgatory you're tasked with saving (by Death himself, of course).  The voice work and writing are both surprisingly excellent and really make you want to keep plugging away.  A few of the classes are quite unique and interesting in their own ways as well.  The downsides are poor graphics performance (for not anything special) and a decent amount of grind (you cannot win a run without at least a failed runs to unlock 'the good stuff').  Overall, 9/10.Be warned: if you want to get all of the story, it took me about 50 hours of play, but could've been 30... if I had realized earlier that a good chunk of the story requires you to wander around without a wyrdcandle lit to trigger specific events.

_childDocuments_.review: The idea of the game is great, I'm a fan of roguelikes, rpg, and card games which makes it a perfect mix for me personally.-Music in the game is great, I really like it.-Story is okay, quite interesting, dark, and at the same time not too intrusive for this type of gameplay.-Combat is okay, although not very challenging, especially on some stronger characters.(but I got to difficulty 8 only)-Graphic isn't anything crazy, but my GPU certainly thinks it is, I don't own crazy machine, but im pretty sure my gtx 970 is either dying or turning into Wyrdspawn.Overall i'd very much advise this game.. but not in this state, for now, it's the buggiest mess I've seen in a long tome, questlines are getting stuck in place making you unable to progress, passive traits, or equipment runes are going crazy, a lot of them isn't functioning properly.. Characters are actually 3, not 9 - 3 warriors/summoners/archers , with the same cards as others in group, but slightly diffrent twist, to them (unbalanced for such similar archetypes, although necromancer is the best one i've seen in games). Game often crashes my pc with bluescreens and freezes. Today I decided to stop playing it, till it gets fixed, last update(today) I lost my 36h progress due to game corrupting my save with no way of backup, forcing me to start over grinding up all characters unlocks (terribly unnecessary feature), all village npc, storyline, resources, cards.. etc. As much as I enjoyed the game, I'm not going to risk losing almost 40h of gameplay again. (devs actually tried to help me with it, to no avail)All in all, Game is looking good, but not as relase, but beta at best, unpolished, buggy and unbalanced, I wish I could return it and buy at better time, for better price. I can't recomend it in this state, will gladly switch my review to positive if the game gets fixed.

_childDocuments_.review: Sooo I usually don't like deckbuilding games. _childDocuments_.review: Short version: If you like roguelites or card battlers, this difficult and highly replayable game will satisfy.Long Version: A grim and fascinating card battler / roguelite mashup, Tainted Grail tosses you face first into an unforgiving hellscape that offers quite a bit more story than most games in either genre. It’s difficult to progress in the beginning, but this is by design. You’ll need to make friends, collect currencies, unlock abilities, and get to know the boss fights before you can expect to move forward. As you explore farther into the game, new mechanics emerge, new cards unlock, and new classes become available. It’s a solid game that consistently presents meaningful choices, so even as your strength increases you might find yourself dying early in a run after making a boneheaded decision.There are significant differences between the available classes, each offering unique playstyles and synergies. While it’s certainly true that some of the classes are simply more powerful than the others, finding this out is part of the fun. I’d recommend jumping in without reading a guide so that you can enjoy the different playstyles of each class. The reality is that you’re going to need to do a lot of runs before you can expect to take on the final boss, so checking out the different classes gives you a change to switch things up.The art and story are dark and delicious, and the voice acting is professional. What perhaps surprised me even more was the score – it’s atmospheric and haunting in a way I’ve never heard.Bottom line: If you like card battlers and/or incremental roguelite progress, and if you can handle an interesting if somewhat twisted story, Tainted Grail will satisfy.

_childDocuments_.review: This game...It is one of my most mislead frustration I've recently bought.As you can clearly see on the store, the game was released in 2021, so it's not beta, not early access or anything, it is a finished game you can assume right?Well, it is not. It has one of the worst walking controllers i've ever seen. You get used to it, but it felt as bad as early 90s 3d games bad.The voice-over is clearly made by their own team, its not a bad team, but they can't act so all you hear is people reading text, and that turns anyone down.The animations are so bad, awful. all of them skip to idle animation when they are supposed to finish, its not a smooth transition, its not polished as it should be.The fights and enemies are always overwhelmingly hard. "But the game is supposed to be hard", don't shove that crap unto people...being hard is one thing, unfair, unplayable is another thing. YOUR FIRST FIGHT on the open world can be randomly against 3 monster which, buff themselves, debuff you (and the debuff you have to spend energy on that round or you will be ♥♥♥♥♥♥ on the next), damage you and almost leaving no way for you to retaliate them. So every fight feels like and endurance chore instead of being something challenging that you want to beat.In all, the game feels like it is still in early access and has tons of things to polish and be revisited.One last thing:The videos and dialogues are just some [image.jpg] images with almost no animations and tons of pixels, it is horrible. The first video played was very hard to see due to the massive low quality of it, it was like 144p of any 90's game's intro.

_childDocuments_.review: tldr; If you do well in Slay the Spire/Monster Train, you might not enjoy how easy this game is. This game is way easier than both of those.Solid game, with a decent story, interesting mechanics, and unique classes. But, simply put, the game is too easy. And this isn't me trying to big flex on anyone. EVERY class can become very powerful very easily, after only a few smart choices. You don't even need very many upgrades to your persistent village area; such upgrades only make you even more overpowered. And while the ascending difficulty system may help with this eventually, it doesn't feel like it solves the issue.I truly believe that any veteran of Slay the Spire or Monster Train can breeze through this game, as well as both the false and true final bosses.Overall, I feel no excitement from the game, and no clutch moments that made Slay the Spire/Monster Train fun. I just feel like I'm going through the motions of a deck-builder without any of the thrill. I suppose you could say the fun of the game is from how broken you can make each class, but I'd rather fight for my life than lifelessly mow down opponent after opponent.I'd only recommend this game to people who just can't get enough of deck-builders, or that can overlook how easy it is. Maybe even to people that haven't played any other deck-building rogue-likes, but even then I'd probably just recommend them the other two games mentioned above instead.If you want to see for yourself, I'd recommend you buy the game and see if you can beat it in your first run. If you can, you should then refund the game, because it doesn't get much harder afterward.
_childDocuments_.name: Tainted Grail: Conquest

_childDocuments_.review: Pretty decent deck-building game. The game's biggest strengths are the variety in classes, skills, decks, and enemies; the art-style and music, and the atmosphere.The animations are quite clunky though, and the voice-acting can be hit and miss. The rouge-like element of building up your village is also a bit weak (especially visually). Although I really like deck-building games, I am mediocre to poor in actually playing them, yet I find the gameplay aspect of Tainted Grail somewhat limited and easy.Overall, I'd say a decent game, but with the notable caveat that there are considerably better deck-builders out there.

_childDocuments_.review: The game has astonishing visuals, especially in battles, however not everybody will find it always nice due to some game mechanics outside of fight, that's true. Wasn't a problem for me as there is a way to have it always nice looking.To be able to enjoy the game you have to play and learn, and learning the game is actually a key element here to enjoyment as when you only start the game, the world around you totally unknown and everything is trying to kill you and you don't know yet what to do with that crap, lol.Story telling is in nice grim setting, you feel feeble traces of lurking anxiety in this world, sometimes it's a bit over the edge, but overall pretty comfortable. It's like Dark Souls in general in terms of atmosphere. You'll die, and die a lot. Literally. Till the moment you learn.Also all dialogues are voiced with very beautiful voices.

_childDocuments_.review: Don't sleep on this deckbuilder roguelite! I couldn't recommend it early on because of frequent crashes, but patches have fixed those and the game truly shines now. What differentiates this from every other deckbuilder? It's in 3D, for one. Graphics aren't amazing but the atmosphere is great. You have 9 classes to choose from, with each having unique cards and playstyles. There are quests that persist between runs, that give you persistent rewards, too. The combat is challenging but fair. And the Arthurian legends on offer here are of the lesser known variety, so you may pick up some interesting bits of story along the way.

_childDocuments_.review: So I got the game 2 days ago, and I've already put in over 12 hours.  It had been on my radar as a deckbuilder game, and I decided to pick it up while it was on sale.  Hadn't played a deckbuilder in a while, and hoped it would scratch that itch.....For the past 2 days, I've GRUMPILY turned the game off, late at night, because I needed to go to sleep, because I had work in the morning.  Both nights however, I seriously debated just calling in sick to keep playing, because I'm enjoying it that much.  I love deckbuilders, and this one has a really cool setup.  I love that it's got so many different classes, that play significantly different to each other.  I like how it's got a feeling of Diablo, and that I'm in the town of Tristram, running around doing missions for the various villagers.  I like how they all have fairly deep quest lines, with multiple stages, that have some interesting writing to them.  I enjoy the music in the boss fights, even though that isn't usually my jam, it does make the boss fights feel intense.This game is a hybrid of deckbuilders with progression like StS, Darkest Dungeon with the Wyrdlight/Dark mechanic as you explore/fight, Diablo in it's aesthetic and tone.   And it really works!  I definitely feel I've already got my money's worth out of this purchase, and I'll keep playing it.  I've technically "beaten" the content so far, or...at least the game actually broke the 4th wall to say "thanks for playing, keep playing if you want and we will be making more content later."  But, there's still plenty of quests to do, permanent upgrades for my character to unlock through repeat playthroughs, new classes to try out.   There is a lot in this game already, and it's quality content as far as I'm concerned.Cons:   There are some rough edges however, but it's a work in progress so that's kind of to be expected.1.  The voice/text REALLY don't match up half the time.  Just, completely different words are being said, compared to what is being written.  The context is the same, but totally different words will be on the screen.  Like, the voice dialogue will say "Hey there traveler, how fare you this evening?"   and the text on screen will say "Ho there stranger, how be ye this night?"    It's a bit off putting, and derails my investment in the game a bit.   Also, the voice won't match the tone of the dialogue sometimes either.   For example, the text will say "You hear a panicked voice, SHRIEK at you from the shadows"   but the voice actor, in a particularly bored sounding voice will say "Stay away stranger, don't come near me."  Like the person is totally calm, and wasn't just described as SHRIEKING at me.     So I think either a rework of the text to more accurately match the voice lines is in order, or redo the voice lines to more accurately reflect the tone of the script.  If you tell me the woman is shrieking at me, then have the next line out of their mouths be a shriek please.  Also, some of the overworld textures for the various npcs are very place holder.  Clearly not matching the actual image once you get into dialogue with them, and you see their picture.   I hope this will change, and we will see the various npc's actually look like their portraits, when we see them on the overmap.  Because I've seen several identical, shirtless bald dudes, who all look REALLY different when I go talk to them  :D But yeah, for the most part, my cons are only superficial things, and chunky writing here and there.  Stuff that can be easily polished up as development continues.  The core game loop, the combat, that is solid work, and really fun.  I keep playing it for hours on end.  I'm probably going to load it back up after posting this...though I guess I should probably go EAT something first.    If you like deckbuilders like I do, this is a REALLY good addition to your library.

_childDocuments_.review: Hello Awaken Realms. It is now time for a review.First, let's state this review goes for the Conquest mode. I did'nt want to play the campaign until I get to play the board game. Cuz reasons.Now I have to compare Conquest with two greatly beloved games: Slay the Spire and Darkest dungeon.Darkest dungeon similarities are easier and so let's just say in DD a great deal of your performance is based upon the interactions you do with the objects you find. I know this is a very early version, but locations found during exploration lack this depth. Some of them actually benefit you more if you choose the right dialog options, but once you know the right ones, the fun is over.Adding context to those encounters, based on the character you picked, the deck arquitecture, the options you choosed with prior encounters, etc... I'm not a big fan of probabilities but perhaps mild randomens could also add some spice to it (Fountain of health already does, for example), but making best-performant options  for one encounter cut even better performant options on possible future encounters could be something real nice. Or just pivot arounf everything I said. Something. But left as it is, encounters turn dull and mechanical after 3-4 playthrougths, if not sooner.Now, Slay the spire. That game really breaks your mind. And there are MANY (if not most) things they do better. Again, That's an already polished game and this is very early acces, not to say Conquest is a spin-off from the campaign... but delivering perfect abalance on Conquest I think would translate on a much more polished experience on campaign mode.So, talking about broken mechanics? I played 5 runs. First brawler. Easy to understand. Straightforward. The kind of deck you build your first runs to get to know the game. Then a berseker "High risk-high reward" says the description. Ok. That sounds fun and hard to master. I die without opportunity to use the rune more than once with little effect. I should learn.Then I try the Guardian. And beat all the bosses. Even the final boss. He does not touch me so I finish with full health the game. WTF??The guardian is OP. Broken. Lets summarize it in a few reasons:- The only rune which makes a turn fully invested in defense profitable, as you charge your "ultimate".- This rune makes easier and more powerfull the use of 3-cost cards and support cards as "All in" due to the fact you will have a turn with +4 energy + 3 draw every 2-3-4 turns. Also, you can keep the key card required for combo until you charge your rune high enough.- If you draw more blocks than required for a turn, you can keep it, reducing drastically bad draws which make you eat damage.- If you level up and get "Natural blocker", which gives you 1 free block per turn, last reasoning gets doble true.- If you get a perk that carries your rune charges between combats, once you have your foe at 1 hit, you can max your charges then rush next combat turn 1. All combats. Cuz you recharge by defending.- You can even get a perk to heal 10% each time you activate your rune. So basically you get infinite sustain if you are patient.So, guardian rune idea is great but... insanely broken.Now, about the berseker... 4 and 5 runs going for it. Totally unable to use it, even going for high armor, taunting weak attack enemies and stunning one hitters and promoting enemy multihits... there is virtually no way you get more health by lifestealing 25% one turn than what you loose by getting hit 4 times... not unitl you get a very decent 50% armor damage redution or so, and that is not until late game.Some other thoughs...- "Final strike" should not increase DMG when defeating totems. I raised such card with guardian up to 600% DMG by defeating totems until it basically one hitted most weak enemies.- Probably (IMO) part of the problem with balancing is getting hit consumes too much health, so blocking almost everything is vital, but then with the rigth deck of blocks and stunnings there is a point in which is possible to block ALL attacks except very specific combats/situations.All in all, a very promising combat experience but with tons of rebalancing ahead.Keep the good work! Eagerly awaiting the board game :)

_childDocuments_.review: If you like other Rogue-lite deckbuiding games like Slay the Spire(StS) then this is a fun game to check out. I don't see myself putting in quite the same number of hours into the game as StS, but I can see myself putting in 25-50. I don't find myself playing just to try out different builds like I did in StS. Instead I'm trying out the different characters which just has the feel that replayabiltiy isn't quite as high.DISCLAIMER: I haven't fully beaten the game. Just beaten the first run-through. There is apparently significantly more content after winning the first time, so replayability may be higher than I'm guessing.Pros:- Quirky Graphics: The weird causes a blur on the screen which makes the world look like a painting.- 9 Different characters. As of this review I've unlocked all but 2- Challenging but interesting gameplay- Characters meet power fantasies. I won with the blood mage, and I felt all powerful as I gave up life to gain power.Cons:- Confusing interactions: This may get better the more times I play, but starting out on a few characters it was difficult to see how they flowed. I found myself suddenly dead multiple times because of interactions between my mobs attacking on top of enemy buffs. Calculating how much damage you will take as the summoner left me confused.- Deckbuilding isn't clean. Again this may get better the more I play, but I find understanding if removing a card from the deck helps is murky. This isn't like Slay the Spire or Monster Train where there are more obvious choices.- Unbalanced characters. This is hard to fault the developers, but I went from struggling but getting slightly better with some characters to rolling the entire game with one. It was so easy I had to stop. The only way to lose was to get super unlucky.Overall I am enjoying the game. Its much easier to find issues, but the game just came out which means growing pains for both the developer and the players.

_childDocuments_.review: 6 hours in and I don't really have much of a desire to play any longer.In one word, this game is meh. Adequately designed. The setting, art, and voice acting are very well done, but the gameplay just isn't interesting. It seems like it's replaying the same few levels with the same few enemies over and over with the hope that you'll get a unique interaction and progress the story along. Everything except the core gameplay loop is executed extremely well, though. It runs well, looks nice, UI is solid, etc.I picked the pathfinder, finished a run easily, and since then I haven't had much motivation to keep going. I'm fighting the exact same enemies as before, in the same places, with a weaker deck. Even if I complete multiple runs I'll still need to keep searching for interactions until I get them all. The combat is mostly building up combos and unleashing them. You just delay until you get strong enough to win. Every fight drags on even when it's clear you will win, you can't just crush them as every combo takes ages.In Slay the Spire, after you beat the game, that was it. You actually progressed and the gameplay and story prrogressed with you. You didn't have to do the same thing over and over hoping for a random interaction to spawn so you could progress. Not so much in this game. It feels like padding. I would like to see where the plot goes, but it's become too tedious to continue. Maybe I'll return in a few months.Other things:The wyrdness mechanic is cool, although it seems to only affect you in fights so you can safely walk around with the candles out and light one before you start a fight. This game didn't really need to be 3d. It doesn't really add much. The music is good, especially the boss music with the chanting.

_childDocuments_.review: An addictive roguelite deckbuilder with lots of voiced content and paths you walk around like an RPG. Basically, imagine Slay the Spire by way of Diablo. You might well ask, "There are so many roguelike deckbuilders, why would I want this one?" Well, Tainted Grail adds a bit more storytelling RPG flair to the standard formula. Most events are narrated, lots of voiced NPCs, and it lends the game more of a different character. Not inherently a better one -- indeed, some deckbuilding purists will certainly prefer the streamlined speed of pure gaming in Slay the Spire and Monster Train -- but for those looking for a game that's more of a story you're playing through rather than just pure cardplay, this does hit a sweet spot, like Griftlands.Tainted Grail also leans more roguelite than like, which is to say, you can earn various currencies towards upgrades that persist between runs. Even your quests persist between runs -- I started a quest with a Summoner, and had another three runs with different characters before finally finishing the quest with my Berserker. There's a nice balance here between the usual tuning of the deck (and passive skills), and the fact that bosses behave very differently from each other, which means a setup that can crush one boss might get crushed by another, so you need to adapt, be lucky, or have a deck strong enough that it doesn't matter.In short, it's an interesting and enjoyable take on the roguelite deckbuilder genre, and if the idea of having dark fantasy encounters narrated to you like a storybook sounds appealing rather than appalling, Tainted Grail is definitely worth a look.

_childDocuments_.review: The short answer is, this is a great game with a lot of potential but this is the type of game where, if you're like me, you can quickly burn out. I enjoyed my 10ish hours and I am interested to play more when more content/rebalance hits but there are some significant issues which will only somewhat be addressed over time. The game itself has good bones. (I will compare it to Slay the Spire as its commonly considered the definitive game for the genre) There are runes for swappable/collectable buffs (no equivalent), items for small intermittent aids to play (potions), passives (relics from StS), and the tried and true mechanic of collecting cards after battles (from level up this time instead of from each win). I’ll list some aspects of the game, generally spoiler free, in which is my assessment at the current stage of the game.Runes – MediocreThese seem a lot cooler than they actually are. You start with one weapon and one armor slot and can theoretically unlock up to 3 slots of each. Each rune type has two effects, one of which will take effect at a time based on the slot you place it in. You can combine multiple runes of the same type to make stronger runes. At first it seems like there are a lot of possible builds which would utilize different runes and that's exciting. What it ends up boiling down to, however, is that there are a handful of runes that are crazy strong and the rest tend to be very weak by comparison. You're going to find a ton of runes over the course of a run and because the pool of rune types is small, I never had any trouble gathering the ones I wanted. There will be variance in the Mythical tier as you will generally only find 1-2 in a run and a couple of them can massively overpower a build/playstyle. There is a random encounter mechanic which allows you to open more slots which is very useful (so you can pack in more of the same runes) and because it often weighted against removing cards from your deck, I don't have multiple slots often. Usable items – Good enoughThese are about as good as potions in StS. Diverse effects, upgradeable through an unlockable NPC. Due to the general imbalance in the game, I didn’t use these very often outside of the early game of a run. They don’t add a ton to the game but I’m glad they’re there. It is nice when special events interact with your inventory, it helps add a little more connection between your character and world around him.Passives – Good-GreatThese are half the game. There a lot of very interesting passives they are the exciting part of leveling up. They often define your build and play style. The big difference between StS relics and here is there seem to be a lot less passives overall but the generally have more of an impact. The mechanic of constantly being able to pick them out of a smaller pool means you will be going for a lot of the same ones playing a character multiple time. It’s still enjoyable but the once you know the whole pool it can feel a little shallow. Deckbuilding – Good enoughThis are not, in my opinion, where the game shines which is weird to say in a deckbuilding game. There are some neat cards but through the over prevalence of card removal mechanics (through an unlockable npc in town, frequently an option during special events and 2 after killing the each of the first 3 bosses) you don’t have much of a reason to use most of them. You assemble an engine which draws out your deck every turn, with virtually every class, and create a combination of broken effects to generate massive damage, negate enemy attacks, stack hoards of debuffs, etc. There are quest cards which you have to do various things to unlock in their useful forms. There are a small number of powerful ones, slightly more/less depending on your build/class, and the rest aren’t worth the space in your deck. This concept of cards not being worth the space is a constant issue and kills what should be a more dynamic experience. There should always be overpowered and underpowered cards, that keeps things interesting and it is a lot of fun figuring out the best choice in the available options. The dynamic that while many cards are mediocre, your starting deck is always trash should make you wonder if you add in a mediocre card since most of your other cards are worse? In here, the answer is usually no. You only add in cards which fit in your specific, drawable each turn engine and you skip everything else. Sometimes you have the handful of cards you need during the first area and will not even look at the options the rest of the game. For this aspect to take off, we need more cards, a little rebalancing on a few and mainly a reduction in card removal/incentive to take more cards. Balance – PoorMainly for the reasons stated in Deckbuilding, you can readily assemble an engine that breaks the game fairly quickly in most runs. Each class I’ve played has a definitive way to play and you will build towards this repetitively when you figure it out. Other than the starting class, which is just a dull trashy mess. One of the big issues here is the power level of several prominent mechanics. The first and most often abused is stun. 90% of the games enemies/bosses can be stunned, which negates their turn. Using duplication or multiple copies of stun cards with a raw your deck each round engine, you can keep most important enemies, or even large groups, chain stunned. Sometimes you will stack stun 4-5 times in a single turn to keep them locked long into their deaths. This is a mechanic that tends to trivialize content and will aid any given class until it gets massive damage combos rolling. The next silly set of cards are the enemy damage reduction 50% cards. If you hit your opponents with two of these, instead of adding more turns to the effect, they stack and reduce your opponents damage to 1 point. This is as good as a stun, works on everything in the game and in the case of summoner classes comes with the added effect of greatly amplifying your damage. Lastly, armor is quite easy to stack and cap at 75% with runes or cards. I really only bothered with the beserker because he likes to get hit, but realistically the cap should be more fluid, with diminishing returns or with smaller buff values so stacking more of it is difficult. Graphics/Story – ExcellentThis piece blows StS out of the water. The story progresses very slowly, but encounters/dialogue are interesting and so far the writing is consistently good quality. The theme is good and the writing ties in nicely with the graphics. My only gripe here would be that the story is really only experienced by the hardcore players that are going to go on hundreds of runs. After my 10+ hours, all but two of which were wins, I’m still left feeling like not enough has happened but I can’t experience more without slogging through another full playthrough with the same strategies. Conclusion:I think this game is worth playing, even in its current form. This game sets itself apart from many other games well. It is nothing groundbreaking with most of its’ deckbuilding/cardplay elements, but the theme, writing, graphics, and handful of unique mechanics which I won’t spoil carry it through. I think it has the potential to become a fantastic game when they add more content and address some of the issues present. I think the difficulty is too high to just mess around and you will be required to utilize the variety of broken mechanics to win.  If you aren’t the kind of person who figures these out themselves or is willing to check online for guides, I think your longevity will be limited without switching to easy mode (I haven’t tested it, so I won’t comment there). That said, 20$ is a very reasonable price for what’s here and you should know well within the return window whether or not it’s going to be for you.

Great for casual gaming because you can just stop whenever.. and you don't need to spend time "getting back into it". You know what you're doing.Cons:This isn't so much a con as a caution. That little description tag up there says "DARK". That means a lot of failures, a lot of dying and unsuccessful attempts. If this puts you off, then this is not the game for you. You will fail. You're NOT a Hero. You're just the closest thing there is to it... so expect to struggle.But was the ride while you played fun? Satisfying? I think so.

Not all encounters show up in all runs, I assume it's randomly generated from the seed when the run starts. This would be OK if the quests wouldn't be tied to encounters. _childDocuments_.review: A great deckbuilder with some great ideas, very straightforward if you played a deckbuilder before and an overall great time waster. A few issues keep it from the being among the greats though.Classes are overall boring and very similar. The mages all summon things, the archers rapid fire things, the melees all hit like trucks. Maybe your mileage will vary, but i found the first class to be the most consistent and quickest to win with. It seems the other classes reward long drawn out fights, while the Wyrd hunter is just gogogogogo.Despite being a roguelike, it doesnt "feel" roguelikey. Cards are very similar in design regardless of class, and events get stale quick. The side missions are neat, but its not like you need to do anything special to complete them, just play and the occasional progression with a decent reward at the end.Overall though, fun game. The lore is VERY interesting to me, and the story takes a neat turn after the first completed run. $20 is fair, and they seem to be expanding on the Wyrdness with an FPS game in early access currently. Only thing i actually want is workshop support, considering the animations are so limited and the exploration ripe with possibles, workshop support should have been a priority in my opinion. Missed opportunity.

_childDocuments_.review: Tainted Grail is a card game roguelike title similar to Slay the Spire. To keep things interesting while playing through the same areas over and over again, the game offers sidequests to complete for NPCs that populate the world that continue through each subsequent run that expand the world and lore. _childDocuments_.review: Ok, this game is a mashup of a few different genres, at it's core it seems to be a CCG rpg.  This game has come a LONG way from it's infancy.  It was poorly optimized and ran pretty sluggishly for what it was.  These things have been drastically improved.  The camera angles are better, the choppiness is completely gone, and the difficulty seems to have been increased. (Very ok with me, the earlier versions had some deck builds that made the game seriously easy).  From what I've seen, the devs planned on this being a big world rpg with CCG battles at it's core.  The game we have now is merely a roguelike ccg game (like slay the spire), only you move around on a map instead of choosing locations or points on a map.  One cool thing is the big open rpg they have planned is still coming, and if you buy this game (last i checked) you will get the big version for free upon release.  All in All, I find this to be a pretty good game as it is, it's an original world with original characters, the story is interesting (told to you by a Faun), there's plenty of unlocks for current and future runs, you build a small village by finding lost citizens in the Wyrd (a strange blurriness that envelops the map, you can get torches to get rid of it, another decent game mechanic).  There are several classes to unlock as of right now with a couple more still locked (I may be mistaken).  My most recent play of the game was about 5 months before the last, and it had gotten so much better that i felt i should leave a comment.  It's a pretty good CCG and i am happy to see where it goes.
_childDocuments_.name: Tainted Grail: Conquest

_childDocuments_.review: Judgement -> An overthinker's dream. Turn based strategy lover here - So what does this game offer that's different? (to keep those of us that usually find a trick to beat the AI in these types of games) 1) It feels like a turn based dark souls. You die, you come back a bit stronger, wiser but your enemies also scale with you lol - Do not think they are the same everytime... Imagine playing dark souls, when you go back to earlier levels and you are buff....Enemies are all in the same place and do the same things, same combinations...Not here.2) For a couple of fights you think you are unbeatable, this feeling happens quite a lot! The enemy combinations are excellent and will tear your "unbeatable deck" apart (in a pinhead voice) IF you don't think ahead. The bosses also create havoc and you must pay attention. One boss took me 2 hours because my strategy was slow and steady....3) Every turn is a puzzleTo succeed you have to plan ahead by many turns. (but it's also fun just to go crazy and die a few runs in row just to explore etc)4) Card combos and different characters. Being honest, my 18 hours so far have all been with the default character. I like to push it until I find that limit then move to the next. The cards really start popping later in the game once you learn to count. Yes count.ie you have 10 perks that are on different counters - 3 hits for one to activate, 4 hits to make this enemy vulnerable, 2 turns before max damage, you ultimate counter is 4 hits from 300%, you deck draw has 10 cards left and you are waiting for a certain card or combo.....BOOOOOOOOOOM 1000 damage. Oops, I forgot about the other 2 enemies, uh oh! This game will make us overthinkers greedy.What is different to slay the spire? You have a base camp that you populate and upgrade. It is really tactical and not just for show! If you're like me and want to get the perfect strategy or die the least amount of times, this is a great addition to the genre. The story and creatures are so f'kin dark it's pure evil++++, I love it. The people you meet, the little stories are completely new - none of this "omg there's a girl who needs rescue, omg I found her, yay happy ending" .... It's all so dark that you actually start appreciating any good news for you or the people lolWhat else?EXPLORATION. Since you have a map and you move around it with your character, other stuff can happen in between fights. Be careful, plan ahead. Yes you can kill everyone and loop back before you fight the boss. What would I like to see in a follow up? Fights in Tight spaces style of play - Where you have decks but also move around a map, so location matters too

_childDocuments_.review: Definitely one for the MAYBE PILE at this point in early access. This game is almost completed, but still, a lot is lacking imo. The fighter class cards are similar to StS, but unique enough to be different and interesting. The summoner classes are all different variants of the same thing, and imo a total letdown. They all summon the same monsters but with different restrictions. The walking around part of this game should be removed and replaced with a isometric view, and be mouse driven. Besides pretending that you're playing The Witcher between card battles, there is no point in wasd'ing around. There's absolutely no point. It's a gimmick as the battles are completely static and cards are played using the mouse. _childDocuments_.review: 6.5/10 - It's ok.In short:Good ideas overall with a lot of unlocks and permanent progression, a bit on the easier side (after I won my first game I had a winning streak with all characters one after another with upping difficulty every time. Eventually, I won a game with them all in this winning train which is kind of crazy for a card game). Performance is unreasonably low for what this game is, tiny map with not that great graphics and effects.Pros:- atmosphere, art, setting is great, really an arthurian nightmare- 3 factions divided into 9 character classes- a lot of permanent progression and card unlocks- overall good design of enemies and game loop- gorgeous 2d art for quests, characters and cards- fun quests that are quite original, writing wiseCons:- this game does not look good tbh, on a glance it's ok but there is nothing to compliment when you take a closer look graphics wise + animations are super stiff and janky in battle but that's a minor problem, it just looks not great- performance is unreasonably high for what this game is, entirety of the game is a small map with a tiny village hub at the center and 3 zones connected to it, that's it. And yet it is rather taxing on the CPU. My old 1060 GPU would max out and currently ryzen 5800x is also getting high usage but why? I guess it is just made to be as inefficient as possible. Don't expect stable 60 fps on mid range system.- ascensions/difficulty scales a bit too slowly,- starting class (Wyrdhunter) feels kind of underpowered compared to the rest, it just feels like a bait to present the game as harder than it actually is,- environmental objects like statues, trees, crystals etc. spawns in town and paths but player can walk through those so it's not that bad but it just looks bad, is annoying and well, immersion breaking- character quests result in permanent resolutions which might be bad for the player and this is a roguelite so basically play with a guide or be ready to start a new save to "fix" your choices on a new slot or stick with bad/sub-optimal NPC interactions in your every run when you meet them in the field

_childDocuments_.review: Fantastic dark take on the Arhurian lore in a rogue-lite deck building manner.At a glance, it's a challenging card-based combat mixed in with 3D world map exploration. The learning curve is steep, but oh-so satisfying once one learn the ropes, allowing builds and optimizations.For fans of the rogue-lite genre, game play is a mixture of darkest dungeon and monster train.The replay value comes in the form of NPC stories and lore that spawns randomly per run.  Narration and NPC's are fully voiced - a stellar job of voice acting no less. Would recommend!

_childDocuments_.review: A game much in the style of Slay The Spire or Monster Train, Tainted Grail is quickly becoming my favorite of the genre. Rather that click on the path you want to take in between fights, you run around a map, looking for treasure, fights, and NPCs who will help or hurt on your journey.The most interesting change from others in the genre is implementation of grind. Not nearly as tedious as something like in a mobile game or an MMO, TG has permanent upgrades that are unlocked over the course of multiple playthroughs. These can be more slots for the runes you find on each playthrough to get offensive and defensive bonuses, increase the amount of difficulty-lowering "candles" you start with, or increase the healing on your health potions.All in all, I would say TG's mechanics probably make it less appealing to the more casual players who might only want a quick run, but if you like playing these kinds of games for a large length of time, I think TG is the best in the genre currently.
_childDocuments_.name: Tainted Grail: Conquest

_childDocuments_.review: + dark atmosphere+ music+ different characters and different styles of playing them+ good combat system- unbalanced difficulty, some classes are extremely strong- opponents and their abilities is not very differentTainted Grail is a roguelike deckbuilding turn-based game in the dark world of Arthur legend. The player in the skin of one of the 9 classes discovers the mysteries of the world covered by the strange fog, solves the problems of its inhabitants, whom he recruits to his settlement to help him in various endless cycles of transitions.The characters are from 3 different factions, where each has its own set of types of combat cards, but each of the 3 classes within the faction uses them a differently and has a different ultimate ability and skills that he gains through levels. In addition to basic cards, combat runes are used to modify character abilities and other various items. Using random encounters on a relatively small map, the player develops the story and improves his parameters. To conquer one map, it is necessary to kill its guard. The game has nice graphics with well-designed monsters, the combat system is good, it offers a lot of variants, but over time it will start to repeat itself as with all games of this style. The sound music page is good, it supports the dark tuning of the game.The difficulty is a bit unbalanced, some late unlocked classes and factions are much easier to play than others and one transition, which consists of 3 guards and one final boss, can be passed quite easily.For lovers of deck building games such as Slay the Spire or Monster Train, it can be recommended, for cheap money, it's fun.
_childDocuments_.name: Tainted Grail: Conquest

_childDocuments_.review: An incredibly well-made deckbuilding roguelite that takes a lot of different inspirations and wraps them up into a wholly unique and very enjoyable package. So far, I've only played three of the nine classes, each of which has been completely different in playstyle. Gameplay wise, I'd say fans of Slay the Spire or Monster Train will find a lot to like here, but the narrative and progression elements make the game welcoming for newcomers to roguelites. Difficulty here is solid so far - you'll likely not win immediately, but the buffs you get from progression make later runs slightly easier and create a good difficulty curve. Really solid pickup for fans of roguelites, especially with the easy to swallow price.

_childDocuments_.review: I bought this over a year ago during early access. Only now that the final version has been released do I feel the need to post this. The  final version of the game is filled with an enormous number of bugs. It should never have been given approval to go gold in this state. In less than 29 minutes worth of play in the final version it crashed twice before completing the most basic part of the tutorial. A third attempt to play got part way through the first battle with the one unlocked character you're given at the beginning, then I got a black screen that I was unable to get out of. I tried Alt-Tab, the Windows key, and Control-Alt-Delete to bring up the task manager. Nothing worked. I had to result in using the Reset button on the computer, which resulted in a message that the C: drive was corrupted and needed to be scanned and repaired. After an additional reboot it seems that Windows has successfully recovered from that, but it has lead me to deleting this program from my system.I can NOT recommend this game to anybody. You're in danger of losing your data if you install it, based on my experience with it. My hardware goes well beyond the published requirements to run it so that's not a possible problem. Maybe in another year the devs will have worked out the bugs but I won't be trying it again for some time.

_childDocuments_.review: OK, first I have to say that I have NEVER been a fan of these type of card game video games.  I got this digital copy because I backed the physical game on Kickstarter and I LOVE playing it.  I can play this game when I want to relax and not have to constantly be focusing on the action like I do with my FPS games.  Don't get me wrong, its not a mindless game at all.  You need to have some strategy when fighting your enemies, especially because each class of hero you use has different abilities.  I find myself swapping out my character regularly to both level them up as well as see how powerful they can get.Unlike other games, you are SUPPOSED to die over and over and you go thru the quests.  And each time you die, you respawn back in your village only to have to go back into the EXACT same landscape outside of the village to die again.  The strategy comes into play so that you can live longer each time.While I haven't made it out of the first area yet, I HAVE unlocked almost all of the character classes so far.  I can't wait to see what comes next.Altho I received this game for free, I honestly would pay for it if I had to.  I think it's a great way to play without having to deal with the frenetic action of many of the other games I play.  Highly recommend if you like card type games or if you want something to play while you are doing some work.
_childDocuments_.name: Tainted Grail: Conquest

There are tons of different classes to unlock and play and it will take a while to get through it.  I have only successfully completed a single run in my 15 hours, and that doesn't include the true final boss.  Highly recommend.

_childDocuments_.name: Tainted Grail: Conquest

_childDocuments_.review: While this game has some interesting characters and does fairly well in the deckbuilding mechanics, the rest of the game is just not very good.It has a severe lack of polish for example: bad voiceacting, bad graphics (looks like a 16-bit color graphic setting is always on), does not run well and most importantly all the elements are implemented in a sluggish way.... they are just placed on the map like indifferent objects. There are buildings which are just sized too small, evil monsters stand next to civilians clipping into each other, character models which look nothing like the character in the dialogue window you see after speaking to them... it is so bad. I just have the feeling that the whole presentation is just randomly chosen Unity Engine models thrown into a lackluster game.The devs could have at least tried to polish it up a bit. I mean once you enter the world map there are just some odd models standing around in place and you run around lightning up torches which have a silly amount of particle effects? Feels more like an alpha.The characters and deckbuilding works mostly well. Eventhough some classes are smoother than others. Summoners are very complicated at first because you don't know where the enemy strikes apparently?At last I also want to say that these body horror types of games are so overdone. I mean besides the background story (which is barely existent) this game has zero connections to the King Arthur myth. And seeing those grotesque and disgusting enemys I'd rather watch The Thing or Hellraiser then playing this game.
_childDocuments_.name: Tainted Grail: Conquest

_childDocuments_.review: Only a handful of hours in, but for a lover of rogue-lites, this is a refreshing take.The ambience is incredible. The map is dark and oppressive, fitting in nicely with the story. The narration is on point, with each voice actor nailing the gravity of the situation and the essence of their character.The different classes are fun to experiment with and keep each loop fresh.The deck building feels easy and intuitive, allowing for plenty of experimenting.I recommend you give this a try if you like dark, gritty RPGs, a different take on the Arthurian Legend and are not afraid of having terrible runs in-between incredible runs where you feel like a force of nature.

Hope feels all but gone and as usual everyones problems are yours to solve. I adore the art in this game and honestly the voice acting is quite good. _childDocuments_.review: It was fairly buggy in the past, at times which has been its only real downside. It's essentially a card game but I actually think it's a better 3D-Slay the Spire (if you enjoyed that, you should enjoy this), and unlike STS you actually make tangible progress between playthroughs using ingame items to level up your HP/Defence/Quantity or Quality of acquired runes (so it's not just run after run based on RNG). So if you have a bad run, you can work towards the next one being easier! (You have to 'find' NPCs to bring back to town who have separate currencies to upgrade your deck/self/map.)The music is also pretty damn good (it was what first intrigued me to the game and builds a convincingly gritty and mysterious world. Think Arthurian and Norse/Celtic themes. The sound design and visuals are very cohesive. Danheim!)Came for the music, stayed for the playstyles and the engrossing ministories/narration. One or two cheesy character voices like the ghost lol but otherwise captivating.The classes are quite varied with totally different moves and styles (one is "take as much damage as possible to become stronger"; another "avoid getting hit and you do more damage"; "get stronger the more hits you land". There are 3 summoner style classes, again all with slightly different mechanics (one of which can turn into a lich as their special lol) I was surprised how much fun I was having between even 4 different roles, and selecting which new cards would best suit the approach.You might really struggle one run and soon after upping your def/HP enjoy thrashing an enemy. You can up the difficulty to get more/better loot but beyond a certain point, even with max stats it can become hellishly difficult!Intrigued to see what comes next for the series, as the story starts off and is kind of left open ended at the end of the game (even if you break the loop).

_childDocuments_.review: This is actually pretty good even in its current Early Access state, I am curious to see how it improves over time. This is a sort of Slay-the-Spire like deck builder game but also an RPG. Instead of having a map where you choose your next encounter you  play a character on the field and can move around to the events/encounters directly which is pretty cool, though I feel it controls a little awkward at times, and a sore sight on the eyes at other times due to the fog. I think there could be some polish graphics and performance wise.That said, the gameplay is pretty good. There's a handful of classes available already. I tried our a warrior class and a summoner and they played really differently. Summoner uses cards to summon monsters and can't deal any direct damage. Can use the cards to buff/activate his summons instead or add more summons to the field. The more warrior focused classes on the other hands can be about building up damage combos or status effects and so on. Instead of relics, there are perks chosen upon milestone level ups and runestones you can find and upgrade throughout the run.There is also overall progression in the form of the starting area. This sort of home base is permanent and any NPCs you locate on the runs and move there will remain there on new runs. You can then purchase upgrades for these NPCs that will last throughout the next runs too. For example the first NPC can heal you and you can upgrade him to heal for more quality and quantity.The game does seem a bit easy early on, I never really felt like I was in danger except maybe the final encounter but I was able to scale with the encounter and do fine.  However, the game does have "corruption" similar to Slay the Spire's ascension levels. I have not tried these out to a high level yet so it could get quite a bit harder. I think the game is decent. Personally, something feels a little off and thus I put it off for now in favor of other card games and RPGs. I think it just needs a bit more polishing all around. But it's a good game and I'm willing to pick it up again when it fully releases to check it out!

_childDocuments_.review: The game is fine, but due to a combination of traits, not as good as some other deckbuilders. Slay the Spire is incredibly straightforward and thus elegant. Monster train is complicated, but it does all the math for you upfront so you make informed choices. This is neither; it is both complicated and inelegant in how it presents the outcome of your turn.The dreary Souls-like aesthetic is... okay. It does it well in presenting a consistent theme, and the story is one of the stronger aspects of the game. A few core classes with several variants on each class makes for lots of playstyles, but for some reason I'm just not that enthusiastic when I nail a combo, which is crucial for deckbuilder engagement.That being said, if you love deckbuilders, it's a a perfectly fine game. it's well-balanced with lots of replayability and scaling difficulty. I got it in a Humble Bundle and it was worth my time.

_childDocuments_.review: This game actually got me into deck builders with its grimdark theme and simplicity. Every other class, though? Amazing. Numerous ways to build them and enough cards and passives to keep you coming back for more, especially with NG+ to test you with every victory. The UI can be a bit finicky at times, but overall, I don't have any major complaints or concerns with the game. Additional Notes:This is one of the only games I played enough to collect all of the achievements on, and while none of them were particularly difficult to get, I'd say almost all of them were at least enjoyable to go after instead of tedious. Quite a positive for people interested in achievement hunting without the need to be bored to tears.Another note.. this game's story, writing, and voice acting are all oddly compelling. I don't know who did the writing for this game, but you should give yourself a pat on the back. Tainted Grail is a hidden gem in terms of lore and narrative, and I'd absolutely read or watch content based on what they've built.

_childDocuments_.review: All hero deckbuilding games ultimately fall back on comparison to the original hero deckbuilder: Slay The Spire. It's impossible to ignore because Slay The Spire did it first and, arguably, is still doing it best. Each new challenger touts its own USP and Tainted Grail's is that it has a story set to a gritty, Arthurian backdrop, which, honestly, is pretty damn good. The environments ooze murkiness, with corruption having twisted all the land's inhabitants. Everyone you meet is eccentric and warped in some way, and they all have a story to tell with voice acting galore in every interaction. The village segment carries some serious Diablo 1 vibes, even containing a guitar strum in the opening soundtrack that sounds almost a direct copy of the one used in the Diablo village theme. All in all, the ambience of the game really captures the "weird Arthur" theme that it's aiming for, and if you’ve been looking for a more story-focused, thematic deckbuilding experience then Tainted Grail has you covered.However, mechanically I feel like the jury's a bit out so far. I'm not deep enough into the game to know if it has the creative deckbuilding staying power compared to Slay The Spire. My reason for this concern is best explained by comparison.In Slay The Spire you're given a basic class template that can go in any number of directions during a run. Each class has its own mechanics and keywords that it plays off of, but the path you end up down depends on which combinations you build into courtesy of the RNG. One game you'll play a thousand armour Ironclad that tanks every hit and smacks back in giant one shot wallops that stomp the enemies flat. In another, you might play a HP-loss focused Ironclad that juggles HP sacrifice to fuel a series of quick and powerful attacks. Each game with the same character will feel vastly different, and your strategy and approach for handling each fight will need to adjust depending on how you’ve built in a given run.By comparison, Tainted Grail tries to load more upfront elements into each character to predefine your build strategy. The current nine characters belong to one of three factions (fighters, archers, mages), and characters in the same faction share the same pool of cards that they'll draft from as they level up. Straight off the bat this means the variety of having nine heroes to play is really a falsehood because, with the exception of their starting differences, there're really only three separate "classes" of character to play. However, to do the system some justice, each character focuses on different aspects of the class card pool, so they will play out meaningfully differently to each other by valuing cards in the shared card pool higher or lower relative to another hero in the same faction. Same-faction characters use the same starter deck (with one or two differences) and are distinguished by each having their own ultimate ability (which is charged up in its own unique way), their own passive ability, and a specific starter card that will always be in your hand each round. These three changes doesn't seem like much of an addition, but they really guide the build strategy of each character.For instance, in the melee class, the Wyldhunter gets a strong, single target attack as their ultimate, which is charged every time they make an attack, and their passive stacks a vulnerability effect on enemies that are hit multiple times in the same turn. This means you're heavily incentivised to take card effects that let you make multiple attacks in a single action because that's how to make the most of those starting abilities. Comparatively, the Pathfinder (also in the melee faction) has a passive that gives them stacking bonus damage for every round they don’t take a hit. Furthermore, their ultimate lets them draw a larger number of cards and gives them additional actions to have big attack turns to make use of the stacked damage they’ve received over turns of blocking, thus they value defensive cards much higher than the multi attack cards a Wyldhunter wants.The result of this design is that you have to play to your hero’s basic synergies regardless of what comes up in the drafting options; ignoring the innate abilities of the hero to try and build something different is inevitably hamstringing yourself. Admittedly, how you implement a build that plays off of those innate abilities will play out a little differently each time, but you’re locking yourself into a style of play at the character selection screen. By comparison, in Slay The Spire you’re handed a much blanker slate and given the freedom to build into whatever comes your way, figuring out a specialisation on the fly.All this said, I don’t know if this is necessarily a bad thing. Tainted Grail is trying to go for theme, so giving each hero its own vibe means you know what you’re building for and perhaps have a greater immersion in the build design process. However, I suspect that repeat playing a character might feel more stale than the myriad possibilities and unknowns you can get from a Slay The Spire run.Back on the positive, there’s no shortage of complexity in Tainted Grail’s tactical card play during fights, which makes it very engaging and, I suspect, holds a sizeable skill ceiling for players to finesse. For instance, each hero’s ultimate can theoretically be activated every turn, but they get stronger if you choose to hold off and allow more charges to accumulate. Knowing when to hold and when to fire are key decisions that don’t always have clear answers to them.Another less fun area of complexity comes from damage calculation. For some heroes this is no issue whatsoever, but classes like the Necromancer and the archer faction heroes would really benefit from a combat calculator to do some of the work for you because there can be a lot to keep track of and its easy to overlook something that ends up hurting you a lot.Overall, I like Tainted Grail. I worry that it doesn’t really have the strength of deckbuilding possibilities that defines the genre, but Tainted Grail is trying to sell you a story as well. When a company splits its resources in this way then the result can be a half-baked product in both areas. Developer Klei tried this with Griftlands and ended up with merely okay RPG mechanics and okay deckbuilding, but I think that Tainted Grail has got decent enough deckbuilding and excellent world-building that justifies the division of resources in its production. Is it the strongest game in its genre? For sure no, but it’s a decent enough entry if you want to take a different hero deckbuilder out for a spin.Edited for Steam Awards task.

_childDocuments_.review: If you liked "Slay the Spire" you will love Tainted Grail. And if you didn't like "Slay the Spire", or don't know it at all, chances are you will love Tainted Grail, too!Seriously, I follow this game since the first days in early access and now that it's finished I'm amazed at what the devs turned it into. A lot of love (and work!) went into this project and it shows. For a first title of a small indie studio this is impressive!The 3D world you move around in freely and the RPG part are a breath of fresh air in the deckbuilder/roguelite genre. The game grips you from the very first line of the story. Writing and voice acting are stellar, soundtrack is fantastic and the new graphics are gorgeous. Yes, graphics and animations are still not AAA material but as it turns out, that's not needed for a dark, dense atmosphere! Tainted Grail pulls you into this creepy re-imagination of the Arthurian legend and you probably won't want to leave anytime soon.Be aware there is a learning curve though and if you're not used to rogue-like games the difficulty might discourage you. But every run you get resources and points to unlock more stuff that will help you in future runs. Dying is part of the process! But as your understanding of the game mechanics grows and you unlock more cards you discover new strategies even for fights that before seemed impossible to win. Be aware: The gameplay loop is addictive - in the best possible way!The game explains the basics, but leaves you to discover much of the game on your own - this can be a downside for some. As a new player I know I'd like more handholding. To be fair, for the card game part there is a ton of tooltips so you get all the information you need. And for the rest you can always ask on the very friendly discord server or consult the wiki so this shouldn't be much of a problem.Devs are quick to fix bugs and really listen to feedback of the community. If you're still reading this, I recommend you buy this game immediately! Check your hardware specs though, because from the reviews I take that if you want to experience TG in its full glory it seems you will need more GPU power than you might expect (runs smooth on my RX480).

_childDocuments_.review: I am really sad that I have to down vote this game as I think in some aspects it is a masterpiece. It really is outstanding where it comes to NPCS, voice acting, atmosphere and story-telling and I would love to recommend it. The reason I am not doing this it is because I am bored out of my mind with repetitive combat and the same enemies over and over again. I would love to meet more characters and know the world - see what happens to all of the encountered NPCs and solve their dilemmas. However I wont because the grind is just too much.some minor SPOILERS BELOWPROS: - Outstanding music when fighting gives vibes and great atmosphere- Good graphics- Story telling is awesome and the actors are doing great job. All the lines are voiced in a phenomenal way. You just want more and more story and encounters.- World and Lore is interesting- The village thing and collecting NPC is great too- The fighting system, gaining new cards, runes, items and skills is great throughout your first run, then just good-ish in a 2nd run maybe 3rd if you really like it but then it becomes super tedious (This is a Pro that becomes a Con after a while for me) - There are many classes and each class is different from each other with different cards. All classes are more or less equally strong (maybe except for the first one and Blood mage seems like a poor copy of druid) but you have to adjust your play style to win. However once you get used to the cards the class has to offer there is no more strategy. Every fight you just use the same cards over and over again hoping that you will get good draws and that when you level up you will be able to pick upgraded better cards to add to your deck or skills which will let you heal.CONS:- World is super small and consists of only 3 areas. I am not sure but they are probably randomly generated as much as land and paths are concerned but each area always consists of the same enemy types and the same boss. You have to beat those areas every time you play. All the enemies are the same and there are 4 (the 4th final boss you can chose from 2 which one to fight)  bosses - Through every run there are different encounters with NPCs and all their quests carry over from run to run. So for example if you started some quest on run 2, you may finish it on run 4 or 6. Depends. That means if you started a quest on run 1 and potentially it finishes on run 4 you will then have to go through the same enemies and bosses 4 times to see how it ends. - Too many enemy encounter. Each (out of the 3) game area is packed with enemies. Each NPC encounter is guarded by enemies. Each fight is very similar. You have to kill ALL or nearly all enemies in the area to level up and stand a chance against the boss. ALL THIS MAKES THIS GAME A HUGE SLOG unfortunately. Playing with different classes gives it a bit variations but only for a first few fights.- Every new run you start anew from scratch and you have to level up your character every time from 0 to level 20So to conclude everything I really want to finish all those interesting quests and exhaust all the NPC encounters this game has to offer but I am giving up. Wasting so much time on fighting with the same enemies is not worth it for me. I think they should introduce AUTO-BATTLE mode (like maybe from when you reach level 10 each run) for people who just want to experience the story and skip at least some part of the very repetitive combat.

_childDocuments_.review: Updated=It's finally here! Full release! Well, of the roguelite deckbuilder mode anyway, the main board game campaign is still later this year. The game is much more polished now, though jank ability interactions can still happen occasionally. The biggest strength of this game imo, is how lore and character heavy it is. The other games in this genre(StS, Monster Train, etc) technically have plots, but that really is not their focus. Tainted Grail has npcs you get to know, and the game does a good job of entwining their storylines with each other in a way that makes them very engaging. Yes many of their plot lines are fetch quests at heart, but I genuinely wanted to see where each characters little side story would go. Combat has been expanded a lot since early access also. The third class group has been released and they are really strong. I don't think all 3 class groups are equally strong but it's possible I'm just really bad at playing mages. There's many more abilities added to the pool and there are interesting decisions in every run. There are enough enemy varieties that target a specific playstyle that you have to think and not always just formula min-max. Upgrades that carry over between runs do sometimes feel overly grindy, but I suppose it would be boring if you just got them all too fast as some of them are extremely powerful.Overall Tainted Grail is up there among the greats of the genre and well worth the price of entry. I look forward to the campaign and hope they continue supporting the game.Original=Watched a review of the board game and thought it was something I wanted to play. The plot is basically King Arthur and the Knights went off and never returned, so now you play as a C-tier warrior setting off to see what happened to them. Sadly the game wasn't in stores so it was unlikely for me to get a copy and when I heard there was going to be a digital implementation it perked my interest. My brother gifted it to me so hey I got to give it a shot. As of this writing the campaign is not done and the only mode is this roguelike deckbuilder mode. It's decent enough, but I feel it gates some stuff a bit too much behind villages unlocks. The first few runs were pretty brutal before scrimping enough to unlock some stuff. It's got a few classes with their own mechanics that focus on varying playstyles but the cards you can add to your deck are shared(I actually like this, it makes you think of the possibilities when you see a new card of what the other classes can do with it). The mode is competent but I don't think right now it has anything right now that would make me recommend it over the many games in the genre. But I am excited for the stuff they are continuing to add , optimization hopefully and the campaign eventually. I would say wait awhile for more updates or the campaign before buying it. Or just get it if you really like the theme or setting.

_childDocuments_.review: On the scale of Yuck to Feast, I'd rate this one "Wor Wonton Soup + mystery leftovers"This is mighty tasty so far, but I'm more than a little disturbed by the ingredients. Draws heavily from StS inspiration, but in my opinion is a worthy addition to the top tier of this genre. The DD inspiration is also apparent in the base/town, less so in the fighting mechanics, and very much so in the dirty dark themes. The Arthurian lore and 3D branching paths add significantly to the presentation. The music is DANK, with shades of viking menace and spine-chilling tones without being death-metal-obnoxious (please add more). The voice-acting ranges from pretty good to outstanding.The progression is interesting, and not entirely explained, but so far I like it. The core gameplay/battles/card synergy are familiar enough to not need explaining, and like all games in this genre will be the ultimate decider of StS glory vs. pretender, but so far I like it. Difficulty settings are odd, but seem manageable. The pace is pretty good (faster than Griftlands slower than StS?), and I didn't have major issues with brain-drain or over-analysis.Only minor complaint is that the 3D presentation comes with a performance price. I am guessing (I'm no techie and my rig is ok?) that some optimization would help with the minor stuttering and lengthy load times.Money well spent, and exceeding all expectations. Thank you ARD.

You'll face a variety of formidable enemies, each with their own strengths and weaknesses. The game offers a range of character classes and abilities, allowing for diverse playstyles and strategies.Visually, the game is a masterpiece, with its dark and atmospheric art style bringing the world of Avalon to life. The attention to detail and the haunting soundtrack further enhance the immersive experience.Overall, Tainted Grail: Conquest is a remarkable RPG that combines deep storytelling and strategic combat. _childDocuments_.review: Lazy game design, you play one very simplified level over and over again to increase corruption. The voice acting, role play aspect and graphics are good but this game is the equivalent of completing Diablo to the butcher (catacombs) over and over again to try and compete for score. Being a card based system this is mostly just luck to repeat over and over again, I like the idea of escalating difficulty by corruption but there's a total of 5 bosses and one level which you just play around and around in a circle.Has the potential to be something good if content was expanded, but I don't know why this is getting such high reviews. Card based combat is lazy, a single level to replay on repeat till you increase corruption which is easy to exploit via card abuse (e.g. duplicate, draw) is just slack.Value at about 7-15 dollars or free.

_childDocuments_.review: This is the first Review I have ever written cause I never want to deter someone from making the wrong choice. However this game fully deserves a good one. I've played tons of deck builders both video games and physical ones. This is hands down one of the best if not the best I have ever played. I've also played tons of rouge likes as well, roughly about the same for both. I love practically every aspect of this game. From having 9 different classes to choose from, with 3 different card types for each branch of classes. You have summoners, archers, and warriors/melee classes. Each class has it's own fairly massive difference from it's branch. The biggest thing by fair about this game however is the ability to make almost any combo of cards work. From being able to select between 3 randomly selected passives that help any cards you pick or drive the cards you will pick. You get passives every couple of times you level, then massive passives every 10. Every level you get a choice of a card, which all are quite useful depending on your build, not an easy choice sometimes cause they're all quite good. If by any chance you don't like them you can pass them up to hope for something better next level. The game does a fantastic and I mean fantastic job building up slow progress to make each run more and more feasible. This comes from new cards as well as passives being unlocked for the branch you use after your run to finding a plethora of different npcs, some of which join your village and offer huge permanent upgrades. The story is basically fully narrated and voiced for every event and person you run across, each having their own voice actor. The game does a great job of fully immersing you in it's story and everything both the npcs and your character is dealing with.      I mean this wholeheartedly that I would be willing to pay 60$ for this game. I got it for 18$ due to it being recently released so I would pay it's normal full price of 20$ any day. There's so much content in this game I'm astonished these fantastic game developers released it so low. I look incredibly forward to all future content and any other games they might work on for the future. These guys are seriously going places making a game like this.      Just so everyone is aware this game is not easy and it will take quite the astute and strategic mind to overcome it's challenges, but with the increased chance to find runes to buff yourself as well as consumables to help you make it through tough fights you will overcome the challenge while fully enjoying every minute.
