_childDocuments_.review: After the success of games like Slay the Spire, which were able to create a new approach to card games where you control your character(s) directly using the cards you draw. Normally this kind of games have one thing in common: they start out very slowly and get progressively more exciting the more cards you gather, both inside runs and in between them, simply due to the fact that more powerful cards give you access to often crazy combos. In this regard, Tainted Grail: Conquest follows the games that came before it, adding a dark atmosphere and tons of content to the mix. Will it be able to succeed?Tainted Grail follows the legends of Arthur, although re-imagined in a dark way: an incredibly powerful force called the Wyrdness has overcome the lands, killing and corrupting everything it touches. Weird and dangerous creatures started roaming these lands, while lost souls seek shelter from the darkness. Powerful ancient way stones could be able to keep this corruption at bay, but they are few, scattered and dying, as the druids that could have helped in restoring them were killed. The future is not looking good and the present is getting grimmer: heroes must rise against this dark force.Luckily, Tainted Grail: Conquest provides a great diversity of classes: whereas in this kind of games you get three of four classes, this title provides you with 9, each one with completely different playstyles and cards. These classes are divided into three different factions: the Children Of Morrigan focuses on melee fighters with direct approaches, the Moonring faction can instead use magic and bend the Wyrdness to their favour by summoning a number of different creatures. Last but not least, the Watchers of Tuathan focus on ranged fighting, shooting arrows at their enemies and making thoughtful preparations to empower them. The best aspect of these classes is, again, how much they play differently even inside a faction: taking the Moonring classes (they are my favourites, hands down), they are all able to summon the same creatures, but while the Summoner uses its energy to improve them and make them as big as possible, the Blood Mage uses instead its HP and the Necromancer doesn’t really improve them, sacrificing them instead to gain energy for its lich form.This doesn’t mean that all classes are made equal though, as balancing isn’t always perfect. Balancing 9 different classes in a card game can quickly become a very daunting task as more cards are added to the game and personally I found the game to be way easier with some classes: starting with the Wyrdhunter, the only available class in the beginning, I found the game to be very hard and was barely able to defeat the first boss, whereas in my first run with the Summoner I was able to steamroll through packs of enemies, losing my fight against the third boss only because of a misplay.Outside combat you will get a chance to explore the tainted land and to speak with the lost souls that inhabit it. At the start of each run, you will find yourself in the village, a place spared from the Wyrdness thanks to the presence of a grim statue overlooking the center of the place: here you will find a lot of empty buildings, that will eventually return to life when you will find and save different characters that you will find in the Wyrdness. These characters will help you during your runs and represent, along with the earning of new cards, the rogue-lite aspect of the game. Besides providing new items and cards, you will also be able to have interesting conversations with them from time to time.When not in the village, you will venture into the Wyrdness to find and slay four different guardians: the Wyrdness is not a safe place and you will be provided with Wyrd candles to help you in your journey: these make for an interesting gameplay mechanic where you can light a candle (that will burn over time) and cast away the Wyrdness from around you. The utility in doing this is that the Wyrdness makes encounters more dangerous, so these effectively act as difficulty-lowering candles, lowering the dangerousness of the enemies the brighter the candle is burning. Speaking of exploration, into the Wyrdness you will not only find monsters to fight, but also different NPCs to interact with: they will sometimes sell interesting items, stats boost or cards… while sometimes they will just have an interesting story to tell.Tainted Grail’s setting is truly fascinating, similarly to Darkest Dungeon’s: wandering a land filled with corrupting energy and horrible creatures ready to devour you certainly has its… charm we could say. Most of the creatures during combats resemble very well the corrupting power of the Wyrdness by showing monster of horror resembling tortured souls, tentacle-like creatures and totems to dark gods. Venturing in the Wyrdness feels dangerous, especially when you don’t have a Wyrdcandle lit, but the world outside combat does also feel a little bit dead, with you exploring what effectively are maps made out of corridors where enemies are sitting still waiting for you. Exploration is still enjoyable, don’t get me wrong, but overall it would have been a better experience if the whole thing felt more alive.Tainted Grail is a really well built deckbuilding roguelite game with a few unpolished edges. Overall, it offers a really great experience for players that appreciated games like Slay the Spire or Monster Train, featuring a lot of different classes and in general a lot of content. The dark setting is either love or hate, so follow your taste in this regard and, if you suits you, give Tainted Grail a go, you won’t be disappointed!

_childDocuments_.review: I'm playing Tainted Grail: Fall of Avalon (Board game) alongside this and there are no spoilers. Feel free to pick this up :)I love this game and can strongly recommendPros:- Really immersive world, lost of mystery and suspense. Great voice acting and interesting characters really add to this- Classes feel unique and meaningful. There are 3 major classes if you like, Archer, Warrior, Summoner but they each have 3 sub classes. They all play differently and all feel rewarding. You're encouraged to experiment- Combat feels great. It's turn based Card game which I'm really enjoying. You can really personalise your deck to meet your style of fighting- Straight forward to pick up and understand, also easy to take a break and come back to and still know where you're up toCons:- Turn based combat/Deck building games are not for everyone- UI and graphics sometimes feel a little tacky/still Early Access- Game can become repetitive, at its heart its' quite a shallow, simple game. This may not be for everyone- RNG with drawing cards, deck building, NPCs and events which may frustrate people- It is kinda difficult. There is an easy mode but I've not tried it but this may put people offOverall strongly recommend. It's cheap too!

_childDocuments_.review: tl,dr Now that you got the message, we can go a little deeper:Tainted Grail: Conquest is a little gem and a surprise but with a few flaws. The first impression is striking because it has fully 3D graphics and high production value. Every character is fully voiced (shout-out to voice acting team because they did a hell of job). The grimdark tone of the setting is a nice change of pace from big daddy Slay the Spire and similar games who go for a more comic-bookish, stylized approach.In my opinion the 3D overworld doesn't really add much and  The overall roguelite progression is a bit grindy, but I understand the reason, in TG:C the permanent upgrades are really really powerful and if they made it easier you could crush the game before even exploring the whopping nine classes you can play with. Also the class you start with is possibly the most boring one of them all, so this and the general  of the 3D map can make the first few hours a little bit rough.I might repeat myself but the game really clicked for me when I started exploring the various classes, they all feel unique and they feel broken in their very own way once you get deep in the deckbuilding and start figuring out possible archetypes. 20 hours in, I just finished the game with 2 of the 9 classes and I am just on the second of the 10+ (!) difficulty settings you can unlock. I can easily see myself sinking a hundred hours into Tainted Grail: Conquest without really getting bored. This amount of variety and content makes it stand out and a really easy recommend if you are a fan of roguelites and deckbuilders.

_childDocuments_.review: I'm having a tough time with this one. It has great reviews, cool voice-acting and a story. I should love this game. I am just so absolutely bored. It's not the repetition of content that's the problem. It's the quality of content being repeated that's the issue here. I've killed the 3rd boss. According to the achievements, only 38% of players have gotten that far.. clearly I'm not the only one who's bored..In the description in the top-right of the store page the devs defined this (as of this review) as a roguelike. It's not. It's a rogueLITE. They're not the same thing, A roguelike means you carry nothing over into your future runs, you just try to do better or hope for better rng. Roguelite, is a 'light' version with 'elements' of a roguelike except you have have unlockables for future runs, and carry some items/skills over into future runs so it gets easier the more you play. That's this. How this is mislabeled by its own creator is beyond me. I mean, do you know the difference? Do you know what you even made here...?Well anyway, with that out of the way, why am I bored by this game? With many rogue-type games you repeat content, a lot. I get that. But this is slooooow, very, very limited, content. It's the exact same enemies time, and time again with very, very little variation. Yes it's dressed up very nice, but it's same few, boring enemies, over, and over and over. RNG of new runs doesn't change the enemies, just where they are. So you still face the same ones, all over again.I'm at almost 12 hours with some classes unlocked, and I honestly don't care about the other (unlockable) classes, because no matter what class I am, it's the exact same enemies, fight after fight, that I'm already bored to tears with. At 10 hours in, I struggled to click the play button. Finally after a few days away I made myself play just now, for an hour and was just not enjoying it. Yes, re-read that, I had to 'force' myself to play this. Maybe others are more easily amused. Maybe I'm missing the 'excitement' of such a slow paced game. Maybe it's just me. What little action there is gets interrupted by something quest-related 2 out of every 3 fights, and many times is pointless until you randomly run into the 2nd half of it's quest, then back to the 1st part again in another future, random run. Repeating content is fine, that's the heart of a rogue-type game, but when it's the same slow, boring content for 10+ hours, it doesn't hold my interest, no matter how well dressed it is, no matter how well voiced it is.. And by the way, yes it still has some optimization issues. When I play this game, and only this game, on a mid-level rig, all the fans on my gfx card kick on and it vibrates - I mean, dayum.  Obviously I am in the minority, but this game is just going to sit until I see more content updates, which, you might be interested to know, it had just before I bought it. I can't even imagine how it was before... holy cow.

_childDocuments_.review: Yeah, this one deserves a review.I've played quite a few deckbuilder games in my time, and it's always a pleasant surprise when I find one that manages to engage me with new, interesting and varied mechanics. Tainted Grail is such a one.The forty hours playtime are across the last four or five days or so, and given the retail price of this game that makes it an absolute banger. Tainted Grail is a fascinating take on the deckbuilder genre, with a full blown macabre gothic Arthurian-Legend-Gone-Wrong-Police-Called storyline attached to it. You travel through increasingly difficult areas of an insidious forest filled with deformed, demonic bad guys, building up your character to get them ready to face each area's final boss.The first great aspect of Tainted Grail is the story and characters. As you explore these areas, you will meet a variety of messed up, fully voiced individuals who can trade things with you, give you quests to complete, fight you or even join your settlement and provide permanent legacy bonuses that persist even when your run ends. This is certainly a deckbuilder with all the juicy meta-progression elements one could hope for to keep replayability at max, and it's all implemented in a logical yet thematic way. The voice acting quality varies but is generally between C to A tier, nothing hammy, nothing lifeless.The second great aspect is the nine different character classes you can unlock and choose from when you start a new run. Given that the core gameplay loop is Draw Cards/Play Cards/Kill Stuff, the playstyle variety between each and every class is almost poetic. I nearly started typing an entire paragraph spoiling the classes here, but I'll hold off in the hope that you'll want to discover them for yourself. Suffice to say that not only is each class's deck different, but the WAY you play that deck is also completely different, and this makes experimenting with each one a total joy.The third great aspect is the Candle mechanic. Similar to Darkest Dungeon, you have a limited supply of candles that you light as you explore the monster areas. When you encounter monsters, you will receive bonus cards into your hand every other round or so. When you receive one of these bonus cards, you can either play it for an immediate effect, or leave it in your hand and receive an alternative effect at the start of your next turn. Sometimes the choice will be obvious, but occasionally this will prove a fascinating tactical dilemma. In addition, the effect of these cards is dependent on your candlelight level. At maximum light, their effects can change the course of the entire battle in your favour, but at low levels, these cards will actually punish you in battle if you DON'T play them (such as increasing the cost of your other cards etc). In the early game, this presents a crunchy issue of resource management - do you risk heading into the next fight with low light because you're saving the last candle for the boss? What if you don't make it that far?In addition addition, your candlelight burns down the longer you spend in battles. So if you think you're really clever spending 100 rounds lifestealing off the last mob you've caught in a damage loop, think again. You cannot afford to dilly dally, either on the world hub or in battles. Time is against you, and I love it.Sadly no game is perfect, and Tainted Grail does have a couple of flaws. First one is some UI issues - occasionally cards lag out when you click on them, and sometimes animations of selecting cards is alarming slow, making me believe I've accidentally clicked on the wrong one while skimming through my hand at the bottom of the screen.The other slight gripe I have with this game is the obfuscation of key information which can result in a run ending. Sometimes mechanics just don't work the way you might assume they would, and while the tooltips are generally very good, they sometimes don't tell you the whole story. Here are some things I found out "when it was too late":- Armour is capped at 75- Minions with Taunt multiply damage taken from AOE affecting allies- Duplicating the effect of a card that flips does not activate the same flipped side twice- "Lose 5% Max health" does not mean permanent max health- Enemies can trigger each others' damage procsThese circumstances are annoying, particularly when they don't kill you outright, but rather render your deck build impotent in some way, but in the case of Tainted Grail, the prospect of Game Over was simply an exciting opportunity to try another class, another build.Love it. Still playing it. Go get it.

_childDocuments_.review: Nice game, but not a great "rogue-lite" to be honest. Too slow and tedious for that imho.You get to pick out of 9 classes (eventually after unlocking), 3 melee, 3 ranged and 3 mages. Each archetype shares a common play type, but each class uses their shared cards differently, has a different ultimate ability and has different passives that you get when you level up. That's quite interesting.The battles themselves are strategic and interesting, often requiring quite a bit of finesse. The story and lore is also interesting ... at first at least, but towards the end it gets bogged down. I can't bring myself to go on however many more runs fighting the same battles over and over again to complete the final quest ... and get, what? Nothing, because the world obviously has to go on, I think. Voice acting ranges from great (narrator/death) to rather terrible, but that's fine. Tainted Grail is too meandering to be a good rogue-lite, where you can jump in and play a run in 30 to 60 minutes tops. No, a typical run takes anything from 2 to 3 hours. That's just too long. The upgrades in-between suffer from a similar issue then. I at least don't FEEL like playing more of this game, because I think I've basically seen it all. Yes, there are more cards to unlock and maybe some different builds of course ... and higher difficulty modes. But are they worth it after almost 30 hours? Not sure.In this case there is maybe too much. Games like Slay the Spire or Monster Train offer more motivation in that regard imho, because they offer more RNG, but shorter play times for each run. They also offer a better presentation. Nevertheless TG is a good game, especially for its bargain price!It's just not a game I think I'll continue playing to "the end" ("final boss" is a joke).I'm not even sure how to finish the final quest, as what is on the map and what isn't is predetermined in a run. So, you might waste another 3 hours to get nowhere. Upgrading isn't fun anymore either. So yeah.

_childDocuments_.review: The people who cooked up this game clearly tried to merge: 1. Dark Souls (all of ‘em), 2. Slay the Spire, and 3. Diablo (all of ‘em) into a single game.  It kind of works, better than expected, but the end results are simply not as good as Slay the Spire or any of the Dark Souls games – to its credit it does play better than the Diablos IMHO but that is the least of those games by far.  If you ever wanted to play Dark Souls as a shorter “time loop” deck builder ala Slay the Spire, this is probably going to be the best offering in that mixed genre for quite some time.In terms of the story and the setting, I feel it is a little overbaked and overwritten especially the dialogue.  Tainted Grail wants to be Dark Souls, but both Dark Souls and even Slay the Spire know how to “say more by saying less;” too much bumbly dialogue and needless backstory is more of a burden then an immersion factor.  That said the goat who helps orient you is generally done very well, which is important as especially at the beginning you get a lot of him.  One significant and repeated writing failure:  multiple times for no discernable reason or motivation is frankly terrible.  One could counterargue that this game really doesn’t need plot at all to work and be fun, and I would agree, but if one then bothers to put plot in it is going to be judged, and if it is bad it just shouldn’t have been put in.  The intro and setup are good, but the major twists from there are just random and unexplained in a way that only 12 year olds and certain Hollywood writers that have failed-upwards think is acceptable writing.Tainted Grail’s devotion to maximizing “grim dark” occasionally moves into a slightly cringy “trying too hard” category.  That said the art is really good IMHO and successfully fulfills their “Grim Dark” aspirations. This goes for the music too, though there is one legendary boss track with angry chanting that definitely has moments in the “trying too hard” category and was occasionally cracking me up as a result.I have an army of little nitpicks, but I’ll just mention the bigger ones.  First it is pretty easy to get enough cards in hand that the cards cover your energy counter which can really ruin things at the most critical of moments.   Second wandering around in the world on silly little hard-to-see jaunts between encounters is clearly a step back from the clean concise “move directly to the next accessible point of interest” from Slay the Spire that they are copying.  It feels like the developers of Tainted Grail were starting with but trying to improve on the “Slay the Spire” paradigm there, but their approach actually makes the world feel smaller than it would via a “Slay the Spire” world traversal approach if done properly, and their approach also slows down the pace of the game as the action and interaction are now broken up with what feel like janky, awkward, slightly-slow walking interludes.  Walking around in the mostly static tiny-feeling world has such a different feel from the rest of the game that it really is a bit of a set-back to the immersion and aspirations.My whining and nitpicking aside, overall Tainted Grail is definitely fun, interesting, and well produced; the strategy and play I find immensely satisfying with very high replay value.  I had to play it for a while before I fully appreciated the richness of diversity across the full range of different class play styles – it is one of the few areas where this game has actually beaten Slay the Spire in design at its own game and this is quite commendable and key to its replayability.

_childDocuments_.review: This is a weird one. There's a really great and fun card game here, if the game could get out of its own way. When I say that I mean, it's a card game that paces itself to be played 300+ hours, when I beat the game and got 100% achievements in 49 hours. It would take me, no ♥♥♥♥, another 200 hours to unlock all the cards on every class, and maybe complete every side quest (not from difficulty, but because there is absolutely no information in-game to assist you). That's the baffling thing- I beat the game, and I still don't even have half the cards unlocked for a class. HALF. The cards seem really cool, too. It would have been great to have them and build better decks, but they drip-feed them after long runs. Why would I want to do an hour-long run to unlock ONE card? (A card you then have to get as a random drop after a battle) I love the game, honestly, in spite of it's weird balance and style, but it hides its best qualities behind lack of information and an absurd, ABSURD, level of grind that most players won't get through.

_childDocuments_.review: The world of this game hooked me instantly and made me care about why my character was doing what they were doing in this Rouge-like deck-building RPG. With 9 playable classes each with a different mindset on how best to build a deck and what cards to use from a pool of "Faction" cards, and RNG keeping things fresh, no two runs will be exactly the same. That is unless you have the wealth to really fine tune your deck and minimize RNG. That is part of the fun!Each "event" that happens seems to have multiple purposes depending on if you are on a quest or not, which is exciting when you come across it and see what secrets it was hiding locked behind finding another "event" to lead to the quest. All of this leads to an enriched world with mystery, sadness, but hope that you can do something in this world twisted by the Wyrdness.I am 46 hours in as of writing this, and I am no where near done enjoying and discovering new aspects of this game. For $20 this game is definitely worth every cent as it respects your time and doesn't feel too grindy. It has short term and long term goals to reach. I imagine the power boost when they are all complete will be intoxicating. I hope to reach that level and see what it means to conquer this land.I have a couple small things I would like to see addressed at some point. Firstly, The game will lag the first time new assets are introduced or when many things happen in a single turn of combat like when many blood mage minions all do their last attacks plus overcharge abilities. Secondly, spells and attacks aren't as noticeable or flashy as I would have thought at first. For example: the Necromancer's spell that looks like a bolt of energy on the card, has little or no animation when it goes off. It is underwhelming. I don't need huge bombastic explosions or blinding spell effects, but something would be nicer than practically nothing. Keep the theme and art style the same dark and gritty, but please make it so magic feels like magic. Otherwise the game is really enjoyable and i'm curious where things will go from here.

_childDocuments_.review: This game grew on me. At first I was a bit iffy and didn't like the wyrd candle system, but after a while I've really grown to like it. _childDocuments_.review: This one is definitely one of my favorites, I dare say it goes in my top 5, mostly because of the rich story similar to a dark fairy tale.You are a poor lost soul, lingering between life and death in an environment corrupted by Wyrdness, this strange ambient thing that manifests physically your thoughts, emotions, memories into all sorts of things and events. Timeline are intertwined, as everything happens decades apart or all at once. You are without a vessel... until a friendly (and shady, let's be honest) saves you! Your task is simple, you want to get out of there, and for that, you need to defeat 3 guardians and fore-dweller, an ancient being. Your journey begins, you will meet characters that will save you, or in need to be saved. You will meet formidable enemies, or allies depending on your responses. You will trigger events after events, gaining power... or an additional death. You will finally fight the guardians, but whether your will or you lose, it is not the end. After all, did your victory really happened if there is no time to anchor it?Story : 9.5/10As shown above, this is a complete original idea with a few interesting hints from popular legends, such as the Knights of the Round Table. In this timeless universe, everything and nothing happens and each turns bring a new surprises.Narrative: 9/10I just love the voices that brings life to the characters, they are diverse, rich and fit the universe the game is set in.Gameplay: 8/10While you may be an experienced player who likes cards and turn by turn action, skills will not be your best ally here. Patience is key. This game is designed for you to die a couple of times before achieving some form of victory (because yes, in this game, the concept of victory and defeat is very blur). A single wrong turn of cards can change the whole game and sometimes sheer bad luck could be your downfall. However, dying over and over allows you to explore the universe as a whole, since you need MANY playthroughs to find the missing NPCs that requires your help and also unlock bonus and characters. As for myself, it took me around 12 hours to complete 1 playthrough without dying, and this is far from finishing the game. Again, patience is key.Graphics : 7/10It's not as good as the popular top games currently out but overall it's very good and I love the dark fantasy thematic. They did a very good job with the universe design.Conclusion :This game is worth it, if you like Divinity Original Sins 2 you will probably like this one as well. There is not as much liberty of movements but the story is as rich. You will greatly enjoy this game.

_childDocuments_.review: Pretty fun deckbuilder, albeit still a very obvious work in progress. The world, mini side-stories, and voice acting are fantastic and the clear shining point of the game. Enemy designs and battle themes are also stellar, even if the quality of the actual enemy battles can be inconsistent. The card-based combat revolves around the typical 3-energy "Slay the Spire" style, and is passable but not particularly innovative. My main issues with the combat are the balance and huge amount of meta-progression. I won my first run pretty easily, and have fully beaten six of the nine runs I've played, with lots of passive abilities seeming very obviously overtuned. There are nine different classes (from 3 class archetypes), and they have interesting and unique differences. While the individual classes keep combat fresh, enemy variety is pretty poor and the final boss (and unlockable, "true" final boss) are very underwhelming.The main hub of the game includes a number of unlockable vendors that have tons of meta-progressing abilities bought with persistent currencies, ranging from things like more health potions to straight up flat damage and max health upgrades. I played for about 12 hours, and was nowhere near to unlocking most of these upgrades, and am not really sure what the point of including such grindy upgrades is in the first place. Overall, if you enjoy the deckbuilding genre I would definitely recommend checking this game out. It's enjoyable, and has a larger emphasis on presentation and story than its contemporaries, but can't quite compete with the top dogs of the genre like Slay the Spire and Monster Train.

_childDocuments_.review: A thoroughly enjoyable roguelite type game in the vein of Slay The Spire.The basics are similar - you have your deck, you get a set amount of energy each turn to use on cards that attack or defend, you add new cards as you kill enemy encounters and level up, you grab loot which can be more cards, stat boosts, money, consumables and whatnot, and you kill the boss on each level to get to the next one.  Beat a final boss and you "win" the run, and get to start again.  Runs are quick, often thirty or forty minutes to complete.One twist on the formula is there's two types of defense in this game - barrier which are flat damage reduction against incoming attacks, and "blocks" which negate attacks entirely (but are more vulnerable to multi-hit attacks).  Different builds and encounters call for using each type differently and it's a smart inclusion.There's three main class archetypes, warrior, summoner, and archer, and each archetype has three subclasses.  Each subclass has a slightly different starting deck and a different passive skill and ultimate skill that vastly change how each class plays.  The subclasses also have a unique pool of passive abilities you pick on level up that can provide serious synergy to your build.  Each of the three archetypes shares a pool of common cards however, so the three Warrior classes are all offered the same cards from a random pool when they level up.  After each run is over your achievements are converted into score which then unlocks both new cards for your archetype's pool, new passive abilities for your selected subclass, and sometimes new outfits or subclasses.  Once you run out of those to unlock you get other random things you can use like resources.There's a major focus on incremental progression in this game.  You start with a mere one class available, base stats, an empty town with one lonely bum by the fire, weak healing potions, and a bare minimum of card options.  However, once you step out in the world, each enemy encounter is guarding something.  That something is often an NPC character, most of which have their own personal quests and some of which you can recruit back to your base after completing them.  Once at your base, NPCs offer new customization options, like permanently boosting your base stats over runs, permanently improving the effectiveness of each type of consumable item, removing cards from your deck, and more.Each NPC in your town usually also unlocks the ability to start gathering a passive resource exclusive to them.  The seamstress improves your passive stats with blood that now starts dropping from every encounter.  The scientist converts your remaining gold at the end of each run into tokens that she uses to improve item drop rates.  You can improve pretty much everything permanently, from the amount of health your healing potions restore, how many cards you draw each turn, and more.The NPCs outside town have a lot going on too.  They might give you a small reward normally, but after you complete their quest their rewards become magnified.As a result, once you get a hang of the game and start amassing wealth, your power level rises exponentially and things feel very good.  The game counters this by a steadily rising difficulty curve that unlocks the next level each time you successfully complete a run, although you can play on any difficulty level you've unlocked prior so you can go through a quick run stomping everything on base difficulty if you want to have fun or are just looking to complete quests and amass resources.The story is nothing to write home about.  NPCs are mildly interesting, and voice acting is decent (with some of them being pretty good, like whoever did Death)While the game is an immense amount of fun, there are a few issues.  The fact that which NPCs and locations show up each run is random makes things rather frustrating once you start running out of quests that you stumble on and want to complete something specific.  Like the Armed Wanderer needs you to talk to the Scavenger who needs you to get something from the Old Merchant who needs two items from shrines and then back to the Scavenger and yadda yadda - but that might take you 6-7 runs total even if each of your targets show up each run due to the sequencing in which you encounter them.  Also, since you don't start gathering the specific NPC resource type until you recruit them into your town, the ones that you pick up last sort of come at a disadvantage since you're behind on their scaling.There's also a bit of, let's say, balancing issues between the classes, in that some of the subclasses are very very clearly better than others.  The base Summoner class for instance seems far inferior to its other two subclass counterparts.  The archer archetype in general is super weak compared to the other two as well - while I could still win runs regularly with them I was never able to assemble a completely broken deck like I could with the Warrior (and the Pathfinder subclass specifically is bonkers).There's also I've found a bit of exploitation you can do with being able to avoid enemy encounters and steal their rewards by creeping close to their encounter zone and taking the loot they're guarding without triggering the fight, which certainly can't be what the developers intended.  Combat typically runs quite smoothly, but if you use too many cards too quickly (as you very often start doing once you get huge synergies going that let you play half your deck or more in a turn) the game starts getting confused and stutters, especially when you duplicate a card's effect.Those issue are all minor though.  If you enjoy this type of game Tainted Grail is well worth your money and time as it's immensely fun.

_childDocuments_.review: Tainted Grail (not to be confused with the board game by the same name) is a rogue-like deck builder with a grim dark, Arthurian legend inspired fantasy world. The models and atmosphere in the game is very dark souls like, which also means some pretty gross and grotesque imagery.You start your runs by picking one of the 9 available classes (all but 1 need to be unlocked). This gives you a starter deck, and as you level up you gain passive bonuses and new cards to add to your deck. What is impressive is that all the classes feel very, very different. While they split up into 3 types (summoner, archer and melee fighter) each class has its own take. The game starts of very difficulty, as you have few meta upgrades but for me I fairly quickly got to a point where I could assume I could win every run. Every victory unlocks a slightly higher difficulty, which means eventually the game does get very hard (its fairly easy till level 15 or so). There are also a TON of upgrades, meta progression and things to unlock. You have like 9 different currencies to spend on various upgrades, and it can be a bit overwhelming, but it does an excellent job of always giving you some kind of reward. There is also a lot to explore, as you meet characters on your runs that give you quests that unfold over several runs and encounters.Story wise the game is also quite impressive for a rogue-like. You are trapped in the wyrdness, a strange fog where horrible and impossible things happen, and you are not the only one. You encounter people with all sorts of problems, you encounter monsters, and even locations. Most of this is done through text, with the overworld just containing a simple representation fo what you are meeting, but the idea is good. And the goal within the story is to encounter all the different characters and help them out.Other production values are quite high as well. There is not much in the way of animation, aside from the barebones basics, but the various models look creepy, gross, and good. The music is standout, with inclusion of celtic and norse influences that really place you into the setting.The only real letdown is the voice acting. The narrator is pretty much the only good voice actor, with everyone else's performances being off in some way. Sometimes they are clearly not familiar with the context and put emphasize on the wrong words, sometimes they put on hokey accents, and the entire cast is laughable small with voices often sounding the same. Sometimes voices are also just horribly mismatched to what they are trying to accomplish, like the goat (you'll notice that within 5 minutes of playing the game).Lastly, I really appreciate the representation of women in this game. So often the fantasy genre has a problem with having to make women sexy or just ignoring them, but this time all the women feel like they are part of the world. How many times have you played a game with a dozen male characters ranging from beautiful to ugly, from cool to gross, and then have like one either sexy or generic female character. In Tainted Grail, just like the men, many of the women are disfigured and transformed, some are victims, some are powerful, some strange... there is just a pleasant variety. So A+ there.Bottomline, Tainted Grail is an excellent rogue-like, and while I can complain about things like the voice acting and lack of animations, everything still pulls together for a fun experience.

_childDocuments_.review: ✔ 9 classes sharing 3 separate decks. Each class is quite different from others and plays differently. On the other hand your class strongly defines how you are going to play, so there are more or less about 9 builds✔ meaningful choices in new cards and passives happen every combat on average ✔ it is possible to make your build completely ineffective by getting wrong cards/runes❔ many different permanent progression currencies - it's interesting that there are so many, but some are very easy to get and others ridiculously hard and grindy. As an example there is one, which improves mechanics of injectable runes, including major drop rates increases, but first you need to drop A LOT of them to get the related currency from combining them. The only thing that makes the system work is another currency, which you get for discovering new content, which can be exchanged to other currencies. I think that 80% of my currency came from that source and that was enough for the game to become too easy. Nevertheless reaching 100% unlocks would be a major grind❔ stories and setting - nothing amazing, but matches very well with the roguelite gameplay✘ in terms of difficulty it starts strong, but becomes easy and then very easy as both your understanding of the mechanics and perma-progression increases. E.g. there is a light mechanic, which forces you to use and manage torches, which are extremely difficult to come by at the beginning. In my last run I had more than enough of them at the last boss to go through the game again without any drops while liberally using them. All of it because of permanent upgrades✘ legendary cards have charges, after which they are gone. This results in making you weaker as long as you hold on to them. It's the old problem of keeping the best consumables for an entire RPG and never using them, but worse✘ NPCs you find have a tendency to disappear after talking to them. Sometimes. So you never know if leaving the dialogue to check your stats/equipment is an option. Will choosing quest progression make them disappear? Probably, who knows?Overall it's good experience when discovering how the classes work, but the game becomes far too easy and repetitive over time. So my advice is to play each class once, defeat the bosses and move on.

_childDocuments_.review: It's Slay the Spire with a pinch of Darkest Dungeon served with a dark fantasy setting based on Arthurian lore. There a ton of classes and each one I've unlocked thus far is mechanically interesting, adds a ton of variety, and provide a great incentive to continue playing and unlock more content. The art and music is great, and this game absolutely worth $20 if you like rogue-lite/deck builders.High points thus far- Your "Wyrdcandle", (very similar mechanically to how torches work in darkest dungeon), can add different cards to your hand each turn and add an incredibly interesting risk/reward mechanic. They have two effects that occur either when played or when they aren't played; typically buffing enemies the turn they're played and then providing you a significant buff afterward. Similarly the boss encounters are well designed and also provide their own unique risk/reward cards depending on your actions in the fight. Drawing one of these cards can completely change the course of the fight and the strategy you're using to deal with it. Very cool. There are layers on layers of mechanics, but everything is well explained and the tool tips are designed very well. You may have to take your time and read over effects/crunch numbers when several cards and buffs are all interacting during a turn but you never feel that you're missing information. This game can be very punishing, but rewards you significantly for utilizing your classes mechanics to their full effectiveness. A bad hand can definitely ruin your day, but if you pay attention and play carefully you'll be fine.

_childDocuments_.review: Tainted Grail is hands down the best deck-building rogue-like I have ever played. The world is dark and gritty, the stories are amusing and offer a nice side progression, but most importantly the core game play has been polished to something nearing perfection. (Unsurprisingly for a game that just came out, some bugs exist, but the devs are Extremely Active in the discord, responding to our bug reports.)The game has different classes and variants within those classes, each with their own decks, passives, and ultimates, and this provides a framework for exponential options that each feel stylistically compelling.My one and only real criticism isn't actually with the game itself, but rather the marketing. It is touted as having 9 different classes when in fact is actually has 3, each with 3 archetypes. As you play through the game and unlock something that, mechanically, seems quite similar to something that you already unlocked (and even shares the same starting cards) this can feel like a bit of a letdown as you find less options than what you were expecting to find.Speaking to the game's progression, it has been handled very intelligently in a way that adds to the experience without feeling like you are engaged in a grind.Not only do you unlock new characters and cards, but you also rescue NPCs who then work in your village and can each be upgraded with their respective resources. When I initially realized the large number of different resources I was worried, but they are implemented in a completely streamlined manner that requires no managing on your part. The resources are garnered passively through standard gameplay, and can be used to increase the potency and quality of life of your subsequent runs.Lastly, there are cosmetics that automatically unlock, and I am a real sucker for playing dressup. The character customization aspect, while still somewhat sparse, again feels stylistically compelling and reinforces the world that you are entering into.Over the course of about two weeks I have spent 55 hours playing this game, so I can definitely say that I heartily recommend it and am looking forward to further expansions.

_childDocuments_.review: Great voice acting. Impressive illustrative artwork. Interesting enemy models. Classes differ widely from one another. Classic deckbuilding roguelike powerfantasy executed fairly. It's got a dark tone that I like.Unsatisfactory(Stock?) animations. UI is hard for the eyes. Narrative blatantly sways to "Old-School RPG" at times. No FPS limiter ingame. The class acquisition and progression system is very unsatisfactory.You have to move your character in a 3D environment without restrictions. I mean torch diminishing as you travel mechanic would be much better if they implemented it without a 3D environment. I'd rather not use WASD to move my character in a card game. Another thing about 3D environment in this game is that you can shuffle and skitter around a combat encounter zone to interact with the event triggers they are trying to blanket. First, It breaks immersion when that prideful knight is just beside some ghouls and does nothing about them, and when you activate the event Its as if you didn't just clear the area around him of monsters. I'd much rather kill the beasts or whatever, walk some more, find a decrepit old ruin, search the place and find the guy there. This experience can be enhanced by obscuring the event I will encounter in some way. Darkest Dungeon does this by twisting and turning the pathways and not letting you move your camera away from the caravan that's carrying you.TLDR: satisfactory art content, good battle gameplay, stock animations, unsatisfactory progression loop, bad UI, could be better tenfold if it were a 2D game, devs love you please improve

_childDocuments_.review: Fantastic atmosphere.Great pace.Amazing soundtrack - especially the didgeridoo bits.Very accessible user-interface.Interesting progression system with nice dopamine hits.Good art-style with fine variety of classes and enemies.Easy-to-understand text and keywords on the cards - all well-presented.An absorbing challenge - engrossing game-play.Runs can seem rather long.Some encounters can seem a tad "cut and paste."EVERY encounter has an accompanying dialogue / an event.No Run History feature. (All the greats have this.)Can heat up PC like an oven on a hot day.Slight stutter / mild optimisation issues.Apart from over-reaching themselves a little with the production values, and that it's positively crying out for a Run History feature, TG is an absolute blast to play and rightly joins the ranks with the other leading contenders of the genre such as Griftlands and Gordian Quest (behind Slay the Spire and Monster Train of course). Helped particularly by its pumping soundtrack it also stands as one of the most gripping and immersive for sure. Did I mention it needs a Run History feature though?

_childDocuments_.review: Early Access:I Played the demo for just over an hour this morning and tried some conquest. First I really did enjoy the campaign and i want more.  The game is very intuitive and really does not need a lot of explanation.  Combat was fine, if you have experience with Slay the Spire or other games like that, there should be no issue for most players regardless of whether you have played similar games.  The game story sucked me in, which is what is going to make this game shine.  The narrative style reminds of board games like Dragonholt where you make choices and then get a paragraph that is based on some choice you make.  The combat card system is akin to most deck builders.  So as a hybrid board/PC game it does work.Conquest seemed easy enough at this time, I have to explore more of it to really judge but based on what I am seeing, they are going in the right direction.

_childDocuments_.review: ive never heard of tainted grail before this. i found this just browsing through steam and its the best purchase ive made in  long while. very happy i decided to click and buy.  really great bang for the buck.  i assume this is based off a real card game? ive never heard of it but im familiar with magic the gathering and at first glance on the steam page i was just excited to see a card game like this. where your playing the cards and you actually see whats going on with monsters on a battlefield, i honestly dont understand why there isnt more games like this considering how popular those irl card games are. when i play magic.. my imagination goes wild and.. i love that.. but ive been dying to find games that match my imagination instead of just a simulation of the tabletop game. i mean ive never really looked too hard but the ones i have seen were.., nice... but my imagination was still doing most of the work. this game here.. quenches that thirst and then some! it reminds me of some of my favorite games.. mixed into one with a unique twist of the card play. the soundtrack is AMAZING btw. i blast my speakers and rock out playing this game.  i hope they add more songs. it has  cycled between maybe 5 different songs so far. they are amazing compositions. would just love more! the lore to this game is awesome too, very interesting encounters in the wyrdness. i am hooked! and its been a very long time since i could say that. not sure why ive never heard of tainted grail if it is an actual tabletop card game aswell but i hope this is just the start of a very awesome line of games from these devs. very well done

_childDocuments_.review: I just now got around to playing this game, and I am sorely disappointed.I just spend almost 10 hours leveling up a Wyrdhunter, and despite having over 50% of passives/skills unlocked, I cannot for the life of me get the right combination of abilities to beat the VERY FIRST boss golem!I have it on difficulty 1, and I should be able to handle this no problem. I play all games on the hardest or 2nd down from that. The fact that I have grinding this long and still can't do it means it is bad game design. I shouldnt have to switch from a Wydhunter or get just the right combinations of abilities to beat the golem.They dont even truly let you grind your way up by allowing you to keep more stuff like runes. Whats crazy is despite ALL of the passives that I have, the mobs do not feel like that have ever gotten any easier than the first time I ran down the hill from town!THEN, they close the gates off so that you cannot use the utility of the town to heal. What a joke!I refuse to go down to normal difficulty or roll a mage so that I can abuse Barrier abilities. I really wanted to like this game. I actually started off not liking the very beginning (felt cheesy), and then the setting grew on me, but now that I have spent 10 hours and I am still at the beginning, again... this is just ridiculous.P.S. -- After serious grinding. _childDocuments_.review: Great game but few things could be improved:Font size bar. We can scale UI and we can scale Cards - but not the Font size. For a player (like me) that sits in front of a 50" TV that is a problem. I don't want my UI and Cards to obscure most of the screen, but I'd like to read the cards description. Shouldn't be that much of an issue to implement.Outdoor wyrdness. While I understand that it's supposed to distort reality and that I can use wyrd candless to dispell it (which I usually save for later) after just 2 runs that effect filter makes the game look ugly. Unnecasarily. I think that another slider to determine how much of that effect a player wants to see would be a good idea. Something like: "full", "obscured enemies only" and "disabled" EDIT: After several succesfull runs in the game I managed to unlock Candlemaker for the village. At that point Outdoor wyrdness stopped being a thing at all. The first impression of it sucks but it resolves itself automatically so... judge it yourself.Other than those ? Great card game. Great lore. Overall very enjoyable. Very replayable.

_childDocuments_.review: First off, I like this spin on the Arthurian legend with a giant heap of "weird". Atmosphere & setting are interesting, it really has a believable vibe of ruin/apocalypse imminent/"♥♥♥♥ this i'm out".  Music and visuals are creepy and unique, lots of crazy chanting and screaming type music ahahaha I was quite pleased with it and felt like it was complementary to the world.  Combat system has a lot of potential, you get a bunch of cards to use on a turn by turn basis and you can build your deck to suit your strategy.  Game still needs a ton of work, but it feels like there is a solid foundation and that there is a clear and unified vision in place for a final product.  What is available right now is a very limited "teaser", but is enough to allow the player to get a feel for the systems and a hint of what the full game could be.  I am interested enough to return periodically, or for the finished product.

_childDocuments_.review: “Cuanact is dying, its barren fields provide little food and its crumbling walls offer no protection. As the power of the guardian mehnir fails, the wyrdness creeps ever closer. Twisting places, breaches and even space its self, despite this the people of the farmhold refuse to leave. Instead Lord Yvain lead four of their best on a desperate mission to Kamelot. They promised to bring back help, they never returned. Now those left behind are growing desperate, they will try to bestow the burden their fate on someone else, new heroes, with even slimmer chance of success.”  There are two game modes currently, the Tainted Grail Campaign and the Tainted Grail Conquest. Currently the Campaign is just a teaser of the story-driven experience where your choices will affect the fate of Avalon. The Conquest mode is for hardcore players, slaying beasts while developing your village and skills. You will die plenty in Conquest, and each time you fail you’ll begin back at your village with what you first started with. Selecting to continue will open a window asking you to choose a slot for your game saves (there is three slots) after which you’ll be able to create your character. The options of your character consist of Gender, Skin and Hair Colour along with Hair and Beard Styles. Once you’ve chosen your characters look, next you can choose your Class and Rune. Currently though there is only one class you can choose, a Warrior (more will be available in the future). You have the choice of three Runes, Brawler, Guardian and Berserker. The Brawler Rune focuses on inflicting heavy damage against single opponents. The Guardian Rune is an energy-efficient rune which focuses on sequencing cards into advanced combos. The Berserker Rune is a high-risk high-reward which gains more power the less Health points you have. Once you’ve done deciding hit Create will start the game. Beginning a new quest, you find yourself in a clearing standing beside a huge Menhir statue, ruined buildings around the edge of the clearing. To one side there’s some tents around a camp fire and nearby is a Milestone. There’s only one path leading out of the village, however, surrounding the village is a strange blue fog … the Wyrdness! Entering the Wyrdness is a very dangerous environment to be in, things won’t always be as they seem on the map. While in the Wyrdness you’ll become weaker, engaging in combat will become much harder than normal but the rewards should you survive are more profitable. Stay too long in the Wyrdness and it will transform and corrupt your body and mind. You begin with a Sword, Leather Armour, WyrdCandles and Travel Map, the wyrdcandles will allow you to move through the Wyrdness without any problems. However, the candles only last for a short time, so after leaving the safety of your village you’ll need to find a Milestone. These mysterious stones light up and hold the wyrdness at bay, runes are inscribed into them. Some say that Merlin invented the runes, while others believe they hold a darker notion. If you find a Milestone you can activate it by carving your name into it, this will disperse Wyrdness around the Milestone. It will cost you One Health, if you have enough wyrdcandles then you can light one and this will increase the Milestones protective range from the Wyrdness. Once you have activated a Milestone, you’ll be able to travel between any other activated Milestone.  This will then allow you to move about and search the surrounding area without any problems. In the top right corner is a mini map which will detail the current quest path with red dots. The map is partially covered with a fog of war and will become visible as you make your way around the area. Also, on the map you’ll uncover new Milestones, Buildings, Enemy’s and Loot (Hidden Wealth and Chests).  As you make your way throughout the map, you’ll come across some enemies. You will see the enemies and be able to hover your cursor over them to get some details on them. Moving towards them will instigate combat which will open the battle screen. Along the bottom centre of the screen are your cards for your current turn, on the right side of your cards is the Energy Count and End Turn. In the opposite corner are your Combat Quick Slot items and your Weapon and Armour stats. The top left corner is your Rune Ultimate status, this will increase during combat and be able to use it once its full. In the top right corner is any Passive Skills you currently have.  Tainted Grail is a turn-based and you will go first when combat starts. Each turn you’ll have cards placed in your hand from your deck. Every card has in the top left corner the Energy Cost to play that card, there is also some information on the type of card and what it does. While in combat if you hover your cursor over the enemy, you’ll gain some information on their behavior such as if they’re immune to something. Above the enemy are some Icons, these will show what their intent is to be on their next turn. Keep an eye on the icons underneath an enemy’s health bar as you can gain valuable information to help you towards victory. Upon defeating the enemy you’ll have the choice to pick one of three cards to add to your deck. If you don’t fancy any of the cards you can skip the process and gain some gold instead. You will also get the chance to choose one of three new Passive Skills and again should you wish to skip a new passive skill then you’ll gain some gold. You will also gain some Experience Points, Gold and may be some random items to help you on your quest. You will come across some characters who you can interact with and maybe they’ll join you in your village. These characters will take over one of the ruined buildings, although they will require some resources to rebuild them.  When you die and you will die, your game stats will be displayed, Total Wealth Gained, Total Wyrdshards Gained, Total Damage Dealt, Enemies Killed, Rounds Fought and Total Cards Played. You will then have the options to carry on or to quit. If you carry on you will find yourself back in your village, you will have lost any items you had collected before dying. However, any character who you have added to your village will still be there as would any pathways you may have unlocked. If you decide not to carry on then you’ll lose any characters or pathways unlocked and start from scratch. The Campaign Mode takes place in Cuanacht, the Wyrdness is closing in around the city. You will have to complete quests and protect Cuanacht. You will have the choice of playing as two characters, although currently they play the same. The campaign story hasn’t been completed yet; you can play for a few hours currently. After which you may find some bugs, unfinished work and story. The game is in Early Access and they plan to have the campaign completed when the game comes out of early access. Positives + Fantastic graphics + Good story so far + Two game modes  + Choices matter Negatives - No achievements currently - No cards currently The Wyrdness is spreading across the land, soon it will envelope everything unless you find a way to push back the Wyrdness and save everyone. 8/10

_childDocuments_.review: Once again I am hunting for a great roguelite deckbuilder and this one came across my eye. My first impression was that it's very grotesque and gory, but after a few runs, you get used to it and there's a fun game in all this dreariness.The story starts with your village getting destroyed but then upon you dying, you return to life but notice that time seems to be stopped or stuck in place. There's this strange stuff known as the Wyrdness that you are stuck in. People don't seem to notice that time has stopped and strange things are happening. In order to break out of this nonsense you have to defeat guardians, save people who have things they need to get done, and bring some of them back safely to your village. Can you break free of this cycle?As stated before, the game is very gory and grotesque. It takes some getting used to, but it fits the theme and setting of the game. You start off as one class and slowly unlock more as you play more and more runs. Just like other roguelite deckbuilders, don't expect to get crazy far on your first few runs. Once you level up and unlock new cards and classes, then the fun really begins.Each class has their own special cards and an ultimate ability. They each gain charges for the ultimate in different way. Some gain it by dealing damage, some get it by taking damage, etc. It's important to figure out the gimmick of each one so you can maximize their effectiveness and know what cards to add to your deck. Some classes are definitely more easier to play than others. Some take awhile before they get stronger and more viable like the Summoner class. It's nice that there is variety to keep you on your toes to increase the replayability.If I can be completely honest however, I think what kept me hooked on this game was the storytelling and the worldbuilding. Throughout the game you will run into a lot of characters. Some will join you in your village so you can buy permanent upgrades to your character. Others will usually have a side quest for you to do to help them live out their lives in the Wyrdness, or escape it. A lot of the stories were really nice and kept me wanting to replay runs so I could see how the individual stories ended.I unfortunately do have some gripes with the game. The map movement outside of combat was a lil clunky and really hard to see if you don't have the Wyrd candles to help you see better. I wish it had just some fog of war or something, but be mindful that it may strain your eyes a bit when you are exploring without the candle. While there are many classes to choose from, the majority of them are just "echo fighters". They are copies of another class just with a slight variation. Like one fighter class works by you dealing damage, while another fighter class is the same thing, except it works by you blocking and not getting hit. Only some of the cards and the passive abilities change so it makes the gameplay sorta stale after awhile. Lastly, there is a lot of stuff you have to get to get the "true ending" to the game. Unfortunately due to how same-y the game feels after a couple of runs, I didn't have the urge to push for the true ending anymore, but I did save a lot of villagers and completed a ton of runs before I stopped.Final verdict? This was a super fun deckbuilder game. Despite the gameplay growing stale after awhile, the story and good writing kept me hooked for a lil longer. The aesthetic takes some getting used to at first but it's worth it for the fun combos and overall package you're getting. I think the asking price of 20 is fair for the amount of gameplay you get for this game, but if you're on the fence, getting it on sale is just as good. Thanks for reading!

_childDocuments_.review: I am on the borderline between recommending this game and not, don’t get it wrong, it is a decent deck-builder but compared to something like Slay the Spire, it feels off.First of all, there is the grind. The whole game revolves around the cycle: start a new game -> get as far as possible -> collect resources during your run -> use them to unlock perma bonuses -> die and start another game. Process is the standard rouge-lite but this can take a lot of time, especially if you wana try all the classes, because the more you level one of them, the more you will get stronger cards for that class. There are 9 in total so either stick and level up one of them, or take your time with multiple or all of them. By this point you might see where boredom starts building up, starting runs with the same class, over and over again, just to get some bland upgrade for it. Die and repeat.Speaking of the perma upgrades (which are shared between all runs and classes) you buy with the resources you gather; I have to say, they are too bland. You get stuff like +1 to attack/defense, extra slots for runes (which I found the most useful), a few bonuses for consumables and some other minor passives, that’s about it… Well, since it mentions that is also an RPG; I gotta speak a bit about that. There is a level up system which gives you the choice to pick a passive, there is also up to 6 runes (3 for weapon and 3 for armor), you need to unlock slots for them (you start with 1 for each) and (depending on the rune you equip) they provide the best bonuses. AND that’s it! That is the whole RPG elements you will get; no skill tree, no weapon/armor you can equip (you get some consumables though), nothing you got used to from other RPGs. Even StS has those relics you can get, BUT is not labeling itself as an RPG.Anyway, a positive, what keeps the reruns fresh is the story, every time you make progress you unlock all kinds of NPCs or events which help growing your small town, you also get to complete different quests and quests chains which lead up to saving those NPCs as well as others you run into.Another positive is the atmosphere, it builds a dark fantasy setting very well. Ohh and you can customize your character.In the end, the game is decent enough to give it a try but get ready to grind off your class and those bonuses. And if you do not get bored in 2-3 runs with the same class, and actually do not mind the grind then all the power to you.

_childDocuments_.review: The really good:+ Art: This game's art style looks awesome! Grim, bleak, unsettling and totally wyrd. Slay the Spire meets Dark Souls.+ Music: I can't praise the music enough, it's absolutely perfect and I love it.+ Gameplay: Difficult, but in the good way these deck-builder roguelikes need to be. It's just hard enough to keep you coming back for one more game without crushing your spirits. Lots of variety from the wide selection of classes, though there are a couple that feel a bit repetitive - especially with the blood mage using the same summons as the summoner, except they're red now.Some minor gripes:- Voice acting: It's really bad. The devs should pay for some professional VAs. Would be nice if we could mute the voices and just read the text, because as it stands I just find myself clicking through everything to avoid the voice acting and I end up missing story.- Story: Might be because I'm skipping a lot of the spoken dialogue portions but for the first few hours where I was paying attention it was a very uninspired retread of other games that have done the same recently, like Loop Hero. - Central Hub: I'm just not feeling it. The permanent upgrades are kind of boring (+10hp here or +1 potions per run there), navigating it is kind of clunky, and I usually just want to leave asap and get on with the actual combat.Overall:Minor gripes aside this is a fantastic game and I can see myself pouring a lot of hours into this. I've played a ton of deck-builder rogue-likes and I'm tempted to put this in my top three after Slay the Spire and Monster Train.

_childDocuments_.review: Tainted Grail is a lot of fun. There are a whopping 9 characters and the metaprogression is very rewarding. It is difficult at first, but once you figure out how to use each character properly, it is incredibly satisfying. The intriguing story and immersive graphics make it easy to sink a lot of time in the game. I highly recommend the game for players who enjoy deckbuilders. The cards and synergies are pretty awesome, but difficult to master. For beginners, this game might get a little overwhelming because the simple block and attack mechanics are much weaker if you don't build the synergies well. The game punishes you, even early on, for not utilizing the character's full kit. The first character, in my experience, is actually very difficult to use when compared to some of the others. Still, if you stick with it and follow along with the game, the metaprogression will do a ton to make the game easier. You just have to find the right NPCs. In conclusion, Tainted Grail is a challenging and intense deckbuilder with many fun and unique characters that grant the game lots of replayability. Difficult for beginners but awesome for deckbuilding veterans. 9.5/10

_childDocuments_.review: You died and then spawned in another dimension. The goal is to find and save all the missing villagers to rebuild the village and figure out how to save Avalon from the curse of Wyrdness. During the journey there are many random encounters that either help or harm you. Every character has a little background and story to tell, most of the dialogues have a deep meaning and the voice acting is top notch considering this is an indie game. I also love the dark fantasy/ gothic atmosphere, it is definitely one of the things that pulled me into the game and kept me playing. The soundtrack contributes to that a lot as well.Though Tainted Grail is a card game, it actually plays like a typical turn based RPG game. You can move in an open world area and choose which fights to do, in the order you want to do them. Skipping fights is also an option. The character can level up, use consumables and his stats have an impact in fights. Attacks, buffs and summons are played by using cards. I like the variety of classes and their designs, there is also a bit of character customization. As someone who isn't that good at card games, I'd say that the RNG is perfectly balanced and well thought out. Most tough fights are a fair challenge as long as you figure out some of the hidden gameplay mechanics. The procedural generated levels and events make it a bit immersive too.

_childDocuments_.review: Death slough with reskined same-ish champs.Three main stays of the classeswarrior, archer and magic user. each has flaw(s) and a theoretical way to be played.warrior: cards can hit hard. Best built class towards new players. Stack Hp buffs and Buy potions. Put up with the death and get to bezerker, I had fun with the life drain it does fall off as overkill doesn't always give you the full Hp refill.Archers: death by 1000 cuts, this archetype felt so action-to-damage starved. Plenty to do, nothing getting done. I suggest aiming your build toward on kill effects or towards stacking buffs and using free arrows. The lack of actions in the early game severely hampers set up builds.magic user: you summon stuff and it fights/blocks/buffs/debuffs for you in one of three styles and requires you to manage the creatures with your action pool. Skulls and concentration oil are your friends. The necromancer felt the most fun, the druid did better against bosses and legends.The Stagfather is a D*ck and hold onto your candles, using them before you go into fight can help change battle in your favor.Over-all this isn't a game meant to be fun. It is a patience test in disguise. Some heroes have no early game viability but to get their stride you need to survive to late game or die multiple times, I suggest the later, just kill the first three battles and die, repeat till the cool and better abilities are unlocked and hope they appear in the current run. (the worst offenders being the way-finder, apostate and druid). The action/energy pool you get is best described as stingy and makes you choose between damage and set up, often rewarding neither skill, memory or ability, only dumb Rng card luck and overwhelming cheese.bosses are huge health pools that do allot of damage. most summon brutes or defenders to Debuff you. champs without a hard punch attack or an adequate action/expenditure scheme will find themselves struggling,The Npcs are best ignored, they're supposed to help you make your deck stronger or allow you to use items. I think the idea was there, however the currency exchange system is paced very slowly and requires hard grinding for little reward.perseverance, a good guide and the willingness to cheese everything without shame is needed to enjoy this game.4/10 will update as I play more,Current boss 3/?8/no/1-13

_childDocuments_.review: I really wanted to like Tainted Grail; it has a really nice dark fantasy vibe, story telling is on point as is the voice actors delivering the lines, and in theory I was excited for a deck-builder that tried something new. In practice, however, so much of TG feels hollow or unfinished. The enemy designs are creative but the models look rushed and suffer from clunky animations. The game's tutorial is near nonexistent, so the player has to sus out what the game wants them to do, all the while introducing mechanics layered on top of each other that are rarely highlighted. At first I was concerned this would lead to difficulty and frustration, but I was surprised to find all this chaos was in the player's favor (for the most part) but lacked any sense of accomplishment. The helter skelter of the game's lack of balance didn't encourage me to continue, unfortunately, as it just began to devolve into a grinding sprint for permanent upgrades. Nothing really feels cohesive and it feels better suited as an Early Access title with room for fine tuning, IMO.

_childDocuments_.review: Really fun game! I'm on lvl6 difficulty so not late game but beyond early game now. Beaten it with one of each of the main classes.The aesthetics are superior to any deck builder I've ever played. The grim diabloesque style works really well here. The progression system is a lot more engaging here than in other similar games since you're slowly building you village. Also, there is actual voice acting which makes the game feel more involved. Overall look and feel of the game is top notch!Gameplay itself is also fantastic! The classes feel varied enough to make it interesting and among the 3 mains classes are 3 subclasses each with their own nuances. I've played my fair share of card games, rogue-likes, and deckbuilders and I'd say in terms of fun I rank this one pretty high. I definately prefer it to Griftlands which is actually the game which got me into this genre. This game isn't without its faults though. One thing I dislike is that a typical run in this game takes over 2 hours. As a rogue-like I don't want my runs to take that long, especially in later difficulties where I suspect you will die a lot. Also, there seem to be far too many cards that are utterly useless or simply worse versions of other cards. This results in a lot of skips for card selection which means my deck feels almost the same at the end as it was in the beginning of my run. Also, my decks seem to always end up the exact same every run. Another aspect I don't really like is how the damage dealt is in a min-max range. Part of the appeal of card games is the precision of planning a deck and executing a specific plan per turn. This can be very difficult to do if you don't know if you're going to be able to finish off an enemy or not. It just adds a layer of RNG that doesn't play into the game well and the devs didn't really implement into the game in a meaningful way. Overall I really enjoy the game and appreciate what the devs made here. You can really feel the production value and the art style and progression system are fantastic. From a deck-building gameplay purist perspective, I will say there are some redundancies that make it less fun than something like slay the spire but still way better than something like the negotiation rounds of Griftlands (bleh). In the end, if you like deck-builders, you should definitely try it out! If you never tried any deckbuilders before, this should serve to be a great segway into them since it has the feel of traditional rpg. 8/10 from me!

_childDocuments_.review: Welcome to Tainted Grail: Conquest, where Death isn't the end, rather, he's your boss!Tasked with punching, gouging, clawing and biting whatever goes bump in the night, lurks in the shadows, and bursts out of the mist born from your darkest fears, Death sends you on your merry way to gain the strength you need to be a reliable pawn in his little chess game.  Your only refuge from the fighting is your village, which you will slowly upgrade as you unlock new NPCs and bring them what they need to help you on your way.  As for the rest of the world?  It's constantly changing, warping and twisting.  Outside of the safety your village provides, only truly powerful beings will remember you even exist, if they can be bothered to remember you at all!Each of my runs tends to last about an hour and a half.  You can save and quit at any point to come back when you have more time, so you don't have to do it all in one sitting.  As you fight enemies and explore the world, you'll gain access to level-up rewards, event encounters and loot.  Things like adding/removing cards to your deck, gaining passive skills, asking the Gods for power, etc.  Use whatever you can to help build your character up from your basic starting point.  With 9 unique classes to pick from across 3 archetypes, there's a ton of versatility in playstyle to grab anyone's attention.I can't end this review without mentioning the music though!  Absolutely love it!  I'm waiting to see if a full OST will be released here, or if I'll have to pick up the main album used in this game off of Amazon later!

_childDocuments_.review: A good challenge that unlocks harder modes to test yourself.   It is slay the spire like.  Each game is a few hours and is around 30 fights with 4 bosses, with some mini type bosses.  What separates this from other card games?They put a lot more thought into replay-ability than any other game in this genre.  There are quests you complete that can take several runs to complete, which unlocks more things.  There are also several types of currency you collect that are saved between runs to unlock more upgrades for the vendors in your town.My biggest critiques are that there are several hero's and the base one feels way overpowered compared to the others.   Certain hero's have a very difficult time fighting certain enemies and your better off avoiding certain fights, which also means you have to memorize the head pictures of enemies so that when you walk up to the fight and it shows you their mini image you know what to expect, which is a pain to remember all of them and their abilities.Overall a fun and challenging game that is worth playing just to experience one of the most replayable games in this genre.
