_childDocuments_.review: A poignant narrative unfolded as I immersed myself in the story of a young girl grappling with autism and depression, bringing me to tears multiple times. Up until Chapter 5, I had rated it an eight, but the depth of emotion and revelation in that chapter elevated it to a solid ten in my book. Beyond the psychological aspects, the game masterfully depicted how we often shy away from confronting our true selves, succumbing to the fear of meeting our own expectations. The journey of redemption, discovering one's true essence, and finding solid ground resonated profoundly with me. Life isn't always a smooth sail, and this game beautifully conveyed that it's alright to stumble along the way. The imagery of sitting together on the roof, gazing at the stars as the world seemingly crumbles, was a powerful metaphor for cherishing our emotions and memories. I'm sincerely grateful for the experience of playing such a remarkable game.

_childDocuments_.review: A Space for the Unbound is more than a game; it's an emotional journey. From the moment I played the demo, I knew it was something special. I couldn't even describe the extent to which this game resonates with me and how much I can relate do Raya in almost all aspects of her character. I cried nonstop at the end, and I know that I won't forget the experience I had while playing - it was perfect, coming at a time when needed the most, when I needed to feel understood and empowered to overcome a bunch of stuff that was holding me back.I really recommend A Space for the Unbound to everyone who wants to be touched by a great story, incredible characters and beautiful art. Also, if you are a cat person, you'll love to pet all the cats in the game as much as I did. Absolute masterpiece.

_childDocuments_.review: A Space for the Unbound is a beautiful story about loss; the way we cope with it,  and self acceptance; the journey we take to feel at one with ourselves. The game takes us through this journey, and the steps we encounter along the way.The graphic style is beautifully rendered, really making a good effort of making you feel in Indonesia. The characters are believable and make you feel part of the story.Gameplay sets you on a 2D adventure, with puzzles, collectibles, and some fight encounters.The music was beautiful, helping set the scene. The puzzles were on the whole well realised, with the solutions in the environment to be found. The fight scenes revolved around a sequence of QTEs. Although infrequent, I would say these were the weaker elements of the game.Exploration takes you across the map, however there are occasions where you are restricted on where you can go, due to story beats. It can also take a bit of time to work out where each section leads, but gets easier over time.Overall, a lovely story to experience.

_childDocuments_.review: 11.3h (100% achievement, finished the game) No. Yes (18 achievements). No. is a sidescroller adventure game about a high school girl and boy in the 90s era. Set in Indonesia, it tries to depict a rural region as closely as possible with some fantasies mixed in it.- Gorgeous art with a lot of new, close-up scenes in each chapter- Various minigames- Some sections are dragged out for too longIntel Core i5-9300H 2.40GHz, 8GB RAM, NVIDIA GeForce GTX 1650Games with pixel art are usually depicted as low-budget games with a lot of limited and reused images. Well, the same can't be said for . It will show a fresh cutscene detailing a close-up look at the characters during the story most of the time, sometimes with simple animations that follow. The animation gives so much life to the characters that it even feels odd when there is none.The game always tries to break your perception of a 2D game - it uses a lot of parallax techniques to make the sky look alive or even make it so that the camera seems as if it was distorted to show you a vision from a different angle. I can't imagine how many times my mind was blown away by the artwork shown in the game.The story is not linear. It uses a storytelling type where you are given the facts bit by bit, and you need to reconstruct what really happened from them. A lot of symbolism will be used to tie the story with the in-game one made by one of the characters. Despite the fantasy theme, what the character experienced is not that far from what people might experience in real life, especially in that era.Honestly, describing the story here will just ruin your experience if you haven't played it. Without giving much about it, it's a story of encouragement, telling how you need to keep going even though everything is tough. Some dialogues might be convoluted, but there are a lot of subtle messages given by the time you reach the end. And that's when everything gets emotional. The build-up for it is very long and can be boring to some people though, especially since some sections can be dragged out for too long. Most of the game's gameplay revolves around quests. You'll need to take them and do what they say, traveling between locations to finish it. And then you take the next quest. Some will require you to , a technique to go inside people's minds to solve their problems. This gameplay is usually mixed with a bit of puzzle element where you either need to bring some items or solve some lock combinations based on some hints.You'll travel between places and interact with objects. The sidescroller format works well in this regard since it makes it easier to find items. Some objects might look useless at first, but the ones that are marked in yellow tend to be important, whether it's now or later. The exit of an area blends so well with the environment. Each area is designed just like any other rural village, with some empty spaces at the intersections. I always changed screens by instinct, thinking that I might just move my character a little bit to the north when I did that. Sometimes, I even forgot that it's a sidescroller game. That's just how great the design is.It seems to derive its minigames from some games, albeit simplified. The most noticeable one is the -like gameplay where you need to do an objection to someone's statement. Another one is a rhythm one similar to  where you need to press a bunch of keyboard keys within a certain amount of time, except that this one is to fight other people instead to dance. Those two, the QTE one where you need to press a button when a moving pointer is on the green color, and the stealth sections are the most commonly used, but there are also other smaller minigames for you to play. The game tends to drag out some things, though. The fighting gameplay tends to be reused a lot—you need to do this so many times in the final boss. The boss was easy to beat, but the lengthy fight just tires me out. Moreover, it also tries to prolong some cutscenes to no end. I understand that the cutscenes look great, but I don't want to wait for 5+ minutes just to see a scene of someone floating in the sky. Some cutscenes also tend to be reused—not that I had an issue with it, but it can take quite a long time to finish and is unskippable. All of it just numbs my brain and breaks my immersion at times.I finished the game in 11.3h. The game isn't difficult to beat—the time-based minigame might give issues to some people, but the game is quite forgiving of mistakes. Also, there is no chapter selection, so it can take a long time to redo the game again if you miss any achievements—you can't fast-forward any scenes!With its gorgeous pixel art and animation,  will blow your mind with its presentation. It also touches on some heavy topics about life, with some mysteries mixed in them. It'll try to drag you slowly to the game, to make you in love with its characters. Some parts might look dragged out, but it won't completely detract you from enjoying the story as long as you manage to get through to the end.

_childDocuments_.review: It's very difficult to rate this game. On one hand, the pixel art is amazing, and the story is so heartfelt and touching. _childDocuments_.name: A Space for the Unbound

_childDocuments_.review: I was drawn to A Space For The Unbound by its lovely pixel art, and after playing the demo, I waited with bathed breath for half a year for its release. I bought the game immediately when it came out, then proceeded to forget about it for the next couple of months, until I finally pulled myself together to play itIt's a masterpiece, it's emotional and honest, exploring many themes, that a lot of people can relate to, to some extent for better or for worse. The story is very linear, but the game still gives you enough freedom to explore at your own will, where the game nails the vibe of the setting and the atmosphere. The gameplay is mainly dialogue and fetch quests running back and forth, but the story and the art, as well as the soundtrack work well to make sure this doesn't feel like a chore, and in my case, I found it extremely satisfying.My one criticism, is that if you miss a collectible, there's a high chance that you won't be able to get it later after you've advanced the story too much, this might be okay for people who don't mind replaying chapters or even the entire game, but for me it was frustrating, and more than once resulted in me going back and skipping through stuff that I'd previously spent 2 hours playing through.Going back to the story itself, yes, it did make me cry towards the end. It's bittersweet, relieving, painful and joyous. I highly recommend this game, and if you decide to play it, do so with no prior knowledge.
_childDocuments_.name: A Space for the Unbound

_childDocuments_.review: Inspired by the works of Makoto Shinkai (), A Space for the Unbound tells the story of two high school students with seemingly supernatural powers in Loka City, a town based on Surabaya, East Java. What could possibly happen?The  involves you exploring Loka City. Most of the chapters are spent free roaming the town, solving puzzles, and petting cats (and other animals). There will be quick time events to do certain things like fighting or doing certain puzzles and minigames. You can fail these, but you can retry as much as you want. Near the end of a chapter, the game will ask you if you want to proceed to a “point of no return” of that chapter. The  looks better than I expected. The characters are expressive, and the backgrounds in particular look gorgeous too, parts of the game is basically wallpaper material.The  is the best part, and quite difficult to explain without spoiling it. Go experience it and try not to get spoiled!Also, so many cats to pet.
_childDocuments_.name: A Space for the Unbound

_childDocuments_.review: As someone who has previously played and enjoyed games such as Coffee Talk and When The Past Was Around, published by Toge Productions, I knew that this game would affect my feelings, so my expectations were quite high. It's the best 2D scrolling game I've ever tried. The story, art, and music describe this game perfectly. Even though the gameplay in this game is a bit slow, you will feel what is called loneliness, sadness and anxiety.
_childDocuments_.name: A Space for the Unbound

_childDocuments_.review: A story about two high school sweethearts at the end of the school year, and the end of the world. Slowly, the world starts to fall apart as Atma searches through the town for his girlfriend, Raya, who has the power to manipulate reality. A narrative puzzle adventure where you help heal the emotional pains of the townsfolk to progress the story.Set in late '90s Indonesia in a pixel art style, there are so many nostalgia-provoking references that call back to a simpler time. Armed with his determination to solve the mystery (and his magical book that allows him to 'space dive' into the minds of others), Atma must save his girlfriend and save the world. Oh, and pet a lot of cats… soooooo many cats.
_childDocuments_.name: A Space for the Unbound

_childDocuments_.review: This game will keep you on your toes; there's so much to explore, puzzles, solving psychological problems by seeing what it's like inside their hearts/minds (my personal favorite), and completing a bucket list with your supernatural girlfriend along the journey. Also half the time, you won't know if you're dreaming or not. I highly recommend this game!!

_childDocuments_.review: You know when you come across something so amazing, so incredible, that you just don't even know what to say about it? Like no words you can ever put on a paper, or speak, will be enough to do the product justice? For me, A Space for the Unbound is one of those games. I know I won’t manage to fully convey why I related to this experience so much, but if my ramblings here are enough to get even one of you to try this out, then it will have been worth it. And on that note, I will start with my strongest argument in favor of the game:  You can also pet a duck and a couple of other animals. I know, I know, you’re already sold and probably buying the game right now, but since I like to write, I’ll just continue my review anyway! You play as Atma, a high school senior in the late 90s rural Indonesia. As such, you get to walk around and interact with many elements from both that time period AND that location, which was an incredible experience. From jokes such as a computer getting disconnected in an internet café because the owner got a phone call to cultural references like Keroncong music,  Exploring the town is a joy, and it’s all thanks to the extreme care put into even the smallest of details.  The store page says that the game “tells a story about overcoming anxiety, depression, and about the relationship between a boy and a girl with supernatural powers”. This is very accurate. Atma and his girlfriend, Raya, are at the center of the story. Most things revolve around them and the powers they have. The store page even lists one of them: the power to dive into people’s minds. And just like in games like Psychonauts, this is a concept that is explored extremely well in this game, with the player constantly diving into minds to advance the plot and help the characters as needed., employing both dramatic bits regarding the supernatural elements and threats, as well as deeply personal ones, such as the aforementioned anxiety, depression and overall uncertainty of life. The story started off good, and it only got better and better. It’s rare for something to get me this emotionally invested to the point of just… feeling empty by the end, but A Space for the Unbound did it. And the positive steam reviews echo this sentiment, with plenty of folks saying they were very emotional or crying. The story does make use of some storytelling clichés that you might not be a fan of, but I’m of the belief that, as long as clichés are used correctly and do not feel like a cheap way out of a situation, then it’s totally fine. It’s hard to be entirely original. And before you ask, yes, this game did use them well., with some well thought out jokes and believable dialogues. As for the  You move Atma in his mostly 2D plane, and you interact with people and objects. When you do, you bring up a context menu to choose your action, such as talk, interact or use an item. There are lots of interactable things throughout the game, and quite a few are just for worldbuilding, which I appreciate. You can also find shiny objects on the ground that work as collectibles for the game. The first one is bottle caps, of which there are 20. The second are YOMAN letters: a bubble gum brand running a promotion in which you have to get letters from wrappers. Last but not least, you have tales, which are pages from a fairy tale that is deeply interconnected with the story. You mostly get these from story events and from completing your bucket list, which you get in chapter 1. Some of the items there are story related, but a few are optional. There’s also a motivation for completing all this past just achievements and trophies, which is that  Or you can just wait until it pops up on youtube. And while not formally a collectible, there are 25 animals you must pet throughout the game if you want to complete all bucket list items. The horror, I know, petting animals. All of these collectibles, and more, can be seen in the game’s excellent menu, which takes the form of a red book. In there, you can also find a map of the city and your inventory. It’s very nifty!  You’ll find yourself eating popcorn with your girlfriend, beating people up in self defense in and out of arcade games, and even taking part in court trials. Some of the minigames, especially the fights, can be tricky at times, but it’s mostly very easy. Plus, if you fail, you just automatically go back to right before you entered the minigame.  None of them are hard either, so don’t worry about that. However, do expect quite a bit of running around or backtracking for items.Normally, I would mind backtracking and running through the town multiple times, but… not here. Why? Partly because of the fact that the map is small, but mostly because of  The game is an absolute JOY to look at! This is legitimately one of the best looking games I have had the pleasure to play recently. I could honestly gush about this for this entire review. But I won’t. …but I could. At times it’s very calming, at times upbeat, at times it urges you to continue to your objective as fast as possible, and at times it’s just… silent. However the background music presents itself, you can be certain of one thing: it will always fit the mood the game is trying to go for. And in fact, the game’s attention to detail extends even to where the soundtrack is employed! For example: as soon as I enter the library, a place in which we are supposed to be silent, the soundtrack stops., such as the puzzle thing I mentioned, the fact you can’t hand in multiple items to NPCs at once, and the stealth sections (the game does have those) which are a bit of a drag. If you’re interested in the title, you should know that the  so I highly recommend checking that out before you make any decisions about your purchase! Again, I can not state this enough: this game was an incredible experience, and unless 2023 is absolutely phenomenal, I can safely say I already found one of my top 10 games of the year. I really did like it that much.

_childDocuments_.review: I really wanted to like it, but i can't, in good faith, recommend A Space for the Unbound to anyone. It's a crying shame, because i deeply respect the intention behind the project. I love the whimsical, yet somewhat grounded premise: anyone who likes Makoto Shinkai movies will feel right at home. The intrigue, even though the plot twists are fairly obvious, still creates an unsettling feeling of uncertainty and dread that clashes (in a good way) with cheerful, bright colors of youth. A Space for the Unbound is mainly a point-and-click quest, but the developers still tried to spice the gameplay up a little with mini-games and little one-off mechanics that successfully break up the monotony.And yet... For every memorable, emotional peak A Space for the Unbound presents an hour of pure, unadulterated filler. Almost every "puzzle" is a multi-step fetch quest that requires you to backtrack multiple times with no other reason than to pad the length of the gameplay sections. It also indulges in "gotcha" moments, where the game deliberately fools you into the wrong solution, while the right one, of course, requires you to back track somewhere. Yes, the hometown of our main heroes is not that big, but that's hardly an excuse. Even more so in numerous dream sequences, where you are often times forced to go back and forth between someone's mind and reality to collect key items. Spacedives represent a wonderful opportunity to do something different, but A Space for the Unbound rarely delivers on that front.Most people praise the game for the story, the characters and the fact that it was made in Indonesia -- an under-represented region when it comes to games. But neither of those three have any solid writing to stand on their own. Sure, Atma and Raya can be sweet, but developers never allow their relationship to truly blossom. There's almost no banter, she's not even a constant presence in the story. Raya is important to the world of A Space for the Unbound, but doesn't really feel important to the player. Yes, the game tries really hard to tug at your heartstrings, but more often than not does so in a terribly hamfisted manner. It's supposed to be so profound and melodramatic that, at a certain point, it becomes difficult to take the game seriously.Oh, and speaking of representing the community, A Space for the Unbound doesn't do a good job. The town itself is cute and full of life, there's no argument about that, but all of its inhabintants are either nameless mannequins with a so-so pixel-art, or just item bots. You speak to them once or twice, they give you what you need to advance the plot, and that's it. The fact that the game forces you to run laps around the town on an endless search for items doesn't make it any more charming or cozy. While, on the other hand, the authors only briefly touch on real societal issues, so as not to spoil the whimsy. In short, it's a huge nothingburger of a letdown, despite the fact that the whole setting is clearly supposed to be warm and nostalgic.Yes, you can excuse some of those flaws by the main plot twist, which i will not spoild. But while it does make certain things more clear in hindsight, again, it does not portray the story in a good light. A Space for the Unbound really wants to be a Makoto Shinkai movie by way of Night in the Woods, but falls tragically short wherever you look. However, despite my criticisms, i hope Mojiken will not stop making games. It is very clear that the devs have tremendous passion and some talent on display -- it just needs refinement.

_childDocuments_.review: I might cheat here since this game is from a fellow Indonesian developer (I visited their office years ago) so my review might be positively biased, so I think I'll have two reviews. This is an early review (only 4 hours and 2 chapters deep), so things may change as I discover new things during my playthrough.Cheating review follows.They nailed the nostalgia of 90s Indonesia culture, so many references here and there (I think I knew one of the bridges...). I giggled here and there (obviously I am playing in Bahasa Indonesia), the casual conversations are not too rigid as I expected, so I guess this time they prepared the script also in Bahasa Indonesia and not translating it from English at the last minutes (I plan to replay the whole game in English to see what global players receive this game, so I may be wrong here). Some of the music resembles Indonesian music (I don't regret at all buying all DLC, one of which is digital soundtracks), although so far I haven't found dangdut music (just two chapters in the game). If you are Indonesian, please do support them; buy it on full price (it's even discounted right now), 90/100 ribu apalah artinya 😁Non-cheating review then.The puzzles are just at the right complexity. At least for my 4 hrs playthrough, they are relatively simple (the staple of adventure game): just collect the correct items to solve them. You might have stumbled the items before you need them, so you won't really struggle to collect later. They might be more complex in later chapters, I'll update this once I finished the game.The minigames are simple enough. The stealth minigame is okay, but right when you think this minigame might be too tedious because you'll need to pass the "enemies" undetected again to reach the same location, they removed it so you can finally pass without worrying to do stealth. Game over is non-existant as far as I know, unless for the arcade one (obviously it's no fun if there's no game over). The maps are not too big, so if you fail the minigames (I did failed for my first stealth minigame since I didn't discover the exact mechanic of it), you are not severely punished to retry the whole map. The fighting game resembles another game which was very popular in Indonesia (or probably SEA), but it's approachable (they only ramp up the difficulty at the arcade game, which is optional unless you are aiming to finish the optional quest). I don't know if they introduce other minigames beyond Chapter 3; I'll update my review once I find them.The visual is breathtaking. I love the vibrant color, and the pixel art is not too pixelated. Sometimes simpler is better (yes I am biased again here, since I grew up with bad graphic games, so this is another nostalgic theme they take advantage on this game). Music is great. Characters have their own personality. Storywise, I can't tell too much, but so far I enjoy the story and some plot twists make me craving to play the game more (without spoiling too much: at the end of Chapter 2 I feel sorry for one of the character and starting to wonder if one of the protagonists is actually bad).Overall, a great game to start 2023. I'm halting my other games to finish this game first 😁PS: You can pet the cat and even name them (although there are predetermined and you can't change them afterwards)

_childDocuments_.review: A Space For The Unbound follows a tale set in 90s Indonesian about two highschool students, named Atma and Raya. ASFTU tells a story about overcoming depression, anxiety, and the connection between people. Gameplay mechanics are pretty straightforward and simple. It's a side scrolling narrative game with (ofc) a lot of dialogues and also few dialogue options. It also offers inventory system and collectibles that you can get throughout the game. There are also side objectives. The story itself is exquisite. Very beautifully written and wholesome. It takes a slow pace through the chapters, but it was a perfect pace. The theme of depression, self-esteem, and bullying is really what makes the story special. I can't say much bcs of spoilers, but it did make me cry. Characters in ASFTU are also memorable and well-written. The music is also wonderful addition to create the game's tone, a very genius composer I'd say. Art in this game is also brilliant with their take of using pixel art-style with amazing world-building. Aside from the narrative side of the game, ATSFU also offers some puzzles that you have to solve to progress the story. It also offers few minigames that you can play, like arcade. _childDocuments_.review: A beautiful story-driven game that's just a few small missteps short of being an undisputable masterpiece. The gameplay can be a drag at times and the early chapters are a bit too slow-paced (partly due to said gameplay), but stick with it and you'll find a deep, emotional experience that's sure to leave a lasting impression. Normally when I write a review about a game, I like to start with a brief synopsis of the story; but I think  is one of those games where the less you know going into it, the better. I'd even go so far as to say that the store page gives a little too much away, to say nothing about the trigger warnings in the opening that led me to predict a major plot point a full chapter before it happened. To attempt to explain the story with as little detail as possible, it follows two high school sweethearts, Atma and Raya, who find themselves struggling with their plans for the future and decide to create a bucket list of things they'd like to do together. What starts with such monumental goals as "watch a movie together" and "eat an entire cake" quickly becomes a supernatural journey of self-discovery, diving deep into the psyche of these two characters to uncover secrets that will change the course of their lives forever. I know that's not a very helpful summary, but like I said: the less you know, the better.When it comes to presentation, it does a fantastic job across the board. The story takes place in the late 1990s, in a small rural town somewhere around Surabaya, Indonesia; and to make it feel as authentic as possible, it's filled to the brim with cultural references and even recreations of regional landmarks. The town you explore is one of those tight-knit communities where everyone knows everyone, and over time you'll learn more about the residents and help many of them overcome their insecurities just like Atma and Raya. The pixel art used for the environments is incredibly detailed to make each location feel that much more alive, almost like the town itself could be a character of its own; and it's punctuated by a beautiful soundtrack that gives an almost ethereal quality to it all.In contrast, I'd say the gameplay is the weakest part of the whole experience—not outright bad, but more noticeably flawed. While it does sprinkle in mechanics like stealth segments or QTE combat, most of your playtime is dedicated to increasingly complex fetch quests in a semi-open map almost like a classic point-and-click adventure game, which feels like a fitting choice given the late 90s setting. You'll typically be given an overarching objective (e.g. find the ingredients to make a cake), and each individual task will, for one reason or another, cascade into a multi-step fetch quest of its own. While I wouldn't call these quests hard, they can be tedious by demanding a lot of running around and a lot of backtracking, sometimes for contrived reasons that at times can feel like unneeded filler. I've seen it argued that the gameplay isn't really the point, but it's a barrier standing between you and the story nonetheless, and I can't blame the players that were put off of finishing the game as a result—especially because I was almost one of them.Something I wouldn't normally bother to mention for this kind of game is the achievements, but I should note while I'm still on the topic of gameplay that there's a little bit of story content locked behind the completion of Atma and Raya's bucket list. Some of that list includes collectibles or other interactions that can be missed entirely if you don't find them before moving to the next chapter, and the only way to go back and get them is to either restart the whole game or take advantage of multiple save files. It does not-so-subtly tell you each time you're about to hit a point of no return, so take advantage of that and don't be afraid to pull up a  if you're afraid that you're missing something.While the story is absolutely the game's greatest strength, the early hours have a bit of a pacing problem, at least in my opinion. The prologue and Chapter 1 (of 6) made a good first impression, setting up the supernatural mystery that drives the rest of the story in just a little over an hour. Chapters 2 and 3, by comparison, moved at a frustratingly slow pace, spending a combined 3+ hours dropping crumbs of information in-between lengthy gameplay segments that just raised more questions without answering the ones I already had. It was around this time that I considered dropping the game entirely because completing drawn-out fetch quests for little to no payoff was starting to test my patience—but I kept going, and I'm very glad that I stuck with it.Chapter 4 onward is where the game puts its best foot forward. The story quickly picks up in pace, and it stops dangling question after question over your head to finally start giving you the pieces needed to put the proverbial puzzle together; all while showcasing some of the best visuals and music the game has to offer. You're introduced to a new gameplay mechanic that adds another layer of sorts to the maps you explore; and despite the fact that this can lead to even more convoluted puzzles, the payoff is so much better and faster than earlier chapters that it doesn't feel as annoying to work through as before. The supernatural elements are expanded in both the gameplay and the narrative; but as the world around our two main characters gets more and more fantastical, their deepest traumas are laid bare with an almost uncomfortable realism, exploring the subjects that lie at the core of the story in a much more grounded and mature way than I anticipated. It balances an overwhelming sense of despair with a message of hope, culminating into a story of triumph over adversity that left me with a feeling that I don't know how to properly articulate—all I can say is that I'm glad I got to experience it.In the end, it struck a certain chord with me that I wasn't expecting; and for all my gripes about the pacing and the tedious gameplay during my 8-hour playthrough, the only thought that ran through my head as the credits rolled was "it was worth it."

_childDocuments_.review: Space for the Unbound" is nothing short of a celestial masterpiece that effortlessly transcends the boundaries of conventional gaming. Developed by Mojiken Studio and published by Toge Productions, this visually stunning and emotionally resonant experience takes players on a journey that seamlessly blends nostalgia, wonder, and a touch of the surreal.At its core, "Space for the Unbound" is a captivating narrative-driven adventure set against the backdrop of 90s Indonesia. The game explores themes of love, friendship, and the universal quest for understanding in a poignant and relatable manner. The narrative unfolds with grace, delicately weaving together the lives of its endearing characters, Atma and Raya.One of the standout features of the game is its breathtaking art direction. The hand-drawn visuals are nothing short of breathtaking, immersing players in a world that feels like a living, breathing canvas. Each frame is a work of art, capturing the essence of the 90s with a nostalgic charm that adds a layer of authenticity to the experience. The attention to detail is impeccable, from the vibrant landscapes to the subtle expressions of the characters.The soundtrack deserves special mention, as it complements the emotional beats of the story flawlessly. The music, composed by Masdito "Ittou" Bachtiar, is a melodic journey that enhances the atmosphere, evoking a wide range of emotions. The sound design, coupled with the captivating visuals, creates an immersive synergy that is rarely found in gaming.Gameplay in "Space for the Unbound" is intuitive and engaging. The point-and-click mechanics allow for a seamless exploration of the richly detailed environments, while the puzzles are cleverly integrated into the narrative, serving as a natural progression rather than a forced interruption. The game strikes a perfect balance between interactivity and storytelling, ensuring that players remain engrossed from start to finish.What truly sets this game apart is its ability to resonate on a deep emotional level. The characters are masterfully developed, and their personal stories intertwine with the overarching narrative, creating a tapestry of emotions that stays with players long after the credits roll. The writing is poignant, introspective, and at times, whimsically philosophical, adding layers of depth to an already rich narrative.In conclusion, "Space for the Unbound" is a triumph in storytelling, artistry, and emotional impact. It transcends the boundaries of the medium, offering an experience that is not just a game but a profound journey through the complexities of the human heart. Mojiken Studio has created a timeless piece of art that will undoubtedly be remembered as a landmark achievement in the world of indie gaming. If you're a fan of emotionally charged narratives, breathtaking visuals, and a soul-stirring soundtrack, "Space for the Unbound" is an absolute must-play.

_childDocuments_.review: I'm leaving this to give a bit of a counter to the other reviews here which I think are a bit more positive than the game deserves.  It's not a bad game, but it really wasn't worth my time.  It may be worth it for other people though.  It starts off strong, but unfortunately ends up losing a lot of it's steam past the prologue/first chapter.One of the bigger issues is just that it's a visual novel trying to justify why it's not a visual novel...even though it would have probably been better had it just stuck with that.  This means for a 10 hour game nearly half of it is essentially fetch quests that may unlock a couple lines of dialogue relevant to the characters and the story which makes it feel like it drag on and by the time you get to the unlocks you kind of don't care anymore.  It also has a really forced combat system I don't really understand why they included as it felt like it took you more out of the story just to add more time to the game without any real challenge.  While I don't think it'd be a great game either way, It'd definitely be a 7/10 for me had they cut out the fluff or at least made it a lot more meaningful.The story is okay, it's nothing we haven't seen many times before.  It was clear what the surprise reveal was early in chapter 1.  It's major problem is being too on the nose, I love surrealism and weirdness but it needs to have a purpose and not beat me over the head.  For example good weirdness might be you dealing with a bull character that does bull-like things that certain types of people would do to that symbolizes a real character and maybe even eventually showing them turn back if you really want to make sure the player gets it, it ends up feeling more meaningful and natural...this game does the full reverse, instead of revealing the bull was a symbol all along at the end of the bull characters arch the person is just a human, acts like a human, and then randomly turns into a bull at the end for only very tenuous symbolism (because they didn't tie the person to the bull persona all along.)  It also tends to be randomly weird without much purpose, there honestly wasn't much reason to dive into people, it was rare that it felt more impact than a gimmick to get you into a puzzle.  In something like Psychonauts it's a bit on the nose with the symbolism inside the persons head, but you do feel like you naturally get to know them  this game you basically enter in and immediately the character monologues about why their there and then you solve a puzzle and a few minutes later you forget about that character entirely.The art suffers from the same problem, I love pixel art and this is passable, but especially in the weirder parts it just feels like they drew random artifacts to seem weird, there's not a lot of cohesiveness to it.  That being said, some of their higher detailed still images had very expressive characters.That all being said, about a third of players complete the game, if you like games like this enough to be in that third I'm sure you'll enjoy it a lot.  I personally feel every story beat was done significantly better in other games.  It ends up being like one of those movies where you don't hate it, but it's just mimicking things that were better and in a week you'll forget everything about it.

_childDocuments_.review: A Space for the Unbound is a mix between slice of life and magic, exploration, relatively easy puzzle solving, with a beautiful pixel art style!------You're playing as a high schooler from Indonesia, and his name is Atma. Chapter 0 is such a great opening in my opinion, and straight away you can explore the world and kinda get the premise of the game.The game loop of A Space for the Unbound is, to proceed the story, you have to solve a problem, and to solve the problem you have to explore the "stage" of the chapter.For me as I'm Indonesian myself, A Space for the Unbound is really touching and emotional. It brings a lot of nostalgia, from the street food like Cimol, the set that's so Indonesian every second, the Keroncong music and easter eggs, the plants hanging on the roof in the hallway of your school, everything made me happy.It's really amazing, as a gamer, that you can experience something like this in a video game. A game that's really close to your life, representing it, and feel really relatable.Everything in the game feels real and close to my heart.If you like indie games like Rakuen, Backbone, To the Moon, and Night in the Woods, I feel like you'll enjoy this game a lot!Thank you Mojiken Studio and Toge Productions for making this, and I hope more Indonesian games like this will be produced in the future. A personal one, that spark that kind of feeling whenever you play it.---p.s. You can give nickname to every stray cats you met. Game of the year 2023 lol.

_childDocuments_.review: Yep, this one got me.The gameplay is your standard "logic puzzle mind dive" affair, nothing terrible but somewhat bland. Objectives necessary to complete the bucket list are very easily missable... There was one objective that I missed by one (1) interaction and it was quite frustrating. The combat is super-bland but I can't see any other way they could have done it without ruining the game's vibe.But that's where my complaints end. This game - no, this story - is an obvious labor of love of those who put it together, and while it is set in Indonesia, you can make the connection of being a high school student pressured by your family and peers regardless of where you are in the world. The expectations that society puts on children and teenagers are very real, even in the 2020s. The characters' struggles with their life choices and finding their identities are also very real.Structurally, the narrative is "formulaic" but engaging throughout most of the game's run until the very end, when it grabs you by the arm and never lets you go. It's equal parts optimistic and sad, and if you have a shred of emotion in your psyche, you will absolutely feel it.The art direction is fantastic as well, deliberately limiting color palettes and making spritework just crunchy enough. Again, a labor of love here.I put A Space for the Unbound alongside other short, cozy story-based games I love like Gris, OneShot, and OPUS Echo of Starsong. Will I play it again myself? Probably not, at least for a while. But I am very glad I played it at all.

_childDocuments_.review: Out of everything I was expecting for this game, I was not disappointed in the slightest. This game has one of the coziest aesthetics I've ever experienced, and each moment in this game is a treat. Puzzles are pretty neat and straightforward, and it really does feel like a whole world, like I'm immersing myself in a "90s Indonesian town" as the game describes.It really does feel like an outstanding experience to just take in all the sights, all of the music and scenery. My best memory of this game so far is in Chapter 1 (on Chapter 2), and it involved just failing the popcorn minigame enough to the point where it's just a still image on the screen with the text "Press A to eat popcorn" on it. The little things in this game really make it charming and unforgettable, and you GET TO PET THE CATS AND GIVE THEM NAMES.Ultimately recommend this game, even at full price.

_childDocuments_.review: If I had to describe this game in one word, it's marvelous.The story is absolutely astounding, the music is great, the characters are great, and although the gameplay is standard, it's nothing bad by no means. Make sure to go into this fully blind if you're set on buying it, it's one of those games where experiencing everything blind makes it even more enjoyable. The best aspect of the game is definitely the story, which I don't want to give away in the slightest as it's that good. The only piece of advice I will give is to make sure you complete all of the Bucket List, and the best way to do that is by checking/exploring every area in each chapter. Talk to every NPC, pet every cat (Dead serious), and check the ground, all furniture, and all objects to gain bottle caps. If you're able to get everything checked, trust me it'll be worth it. The game is formatted in five core chapters with a prologue at the start and an epilogue at the end, and from my play time the game's about eight to maybe ten hours long, so not super long. Overall it's a very solid 8/10, which to me means it's great. Highly recommend! I hope this game gets more attention and for the development team to keep making high quality gems like this.

_childDocuments_.review: The most beautifully heartbreaking game I have EVER played!A Space for the Unbound was the best 10 hours I've spent gaming this year.Some of the puzzles in the main story became unpredictably tougher and chaotic towards the end of Chapter 4, which maybe fun for some players, but slowed down the story progress in that segment. Still, nothing that can't be enjoyable.This game is a walk down memory lane for anyone who has struggled with trauma, pain and forgiveness, and it handles these issues with such careful detail, that even those who haven't seen such trouble will be able to understand the lives of their peers who's struggles they may have failed to understand.As someone who is learning to write for story-rich video games, this is one I will always remember, and come back to. Nothing is more important in a story game, over and above the story. And in such a game, because it is interactive, and choices matter, a powerful and well researched story hits home much harder than anything else.Thank you, Mojiken and Toge. This game is truly a treasure.

_childDocuments_.review: ( full review with screenshots:  )A Space for the Unbound is the latest game from Indonesian developers Mojiken, who previously made great games like She and the Light Bearer and When the Past was Around. ASFTU is another adventure-style game, but it breaks from most of their previous work in that it is unashamedly about a specific time and place that won't be familiar to the vast majority of players. Its small 1990s Indonesian town plays as central a role in the story as any of the characters, and it has been lovingly realized from the gorgeous pixel art to the detailed backstories of its inhabitants. It's wonderful that the team were able to make what was clearly a passion project about their home without having to make Phoenix Wright-style localization compromises. Gameplay in ASFTU comes in roughly three forms. Most of the time, you're moving about the town, talking to people, and finding random items that are scattered around. This is not a point and click game, but it very much feels like one without all the moon logic that genre is famous for. Puzzles in the adventure mode typically consist of finding the right items and bringing them to the correct characters or places. The more detailed puzzles are reserved for the "Spacedive" mode, where you jump into surreal representations of other character's psyches and solve their problems with thematic puzzles. Most of these aren't terribly difficult, but they can be quite intricate and require several layers or even screens worth of tasks. Outside of those two modes, there are the minigame-type breaks. These are easily the weakest part of the game. Although there are a couple of one-off events, most of the time this either means combat or something that is mechanically identical to combat. That in turn means you need to enter a sequence of button presses within the time limit, then stop a moving bar within the right zone in order to avoid damage. This system isn't really bad per se, but it gets a bit tiresome since it's used so often and is so simplistic. I would have preferred either less combat overall or a slightly deeper system. Although this is not and should not be an action game, it could have used more interesting fighting considering how much of it there is.Next, the graphics and music. For graphics, I'll let the screenshots speak for themselves. ASFTU has some of the best pixel art I've ever seen, particularly when it comes to the special cutscenes and late-game backgrounds. The music is mostly not as impressive, but it'll probably be a unique experience unless you're already familiar with the Indonesian genres and instruments it's inspired by. Still, even though I probably won't remember most of the music in a year, there are a couple of special tracks in it that I loved, and at worst the music is still perfectly serviceable. Finally, the story. This is what takes ASFTU from being a solid adventure game with great art to being an absolute masterpiece. It has an incredible ability to make you care (if not always in a positive way) about even characters who play only a minor role in the story. It goes to some dark places by the end and has a couple of truly terrible people, but the overall experience is still a thoroughly heartwarming one thanks to the personalities and relationships of its core cast. Even though I had a pretty good idea of where it was going long before the end, I was still blown away by just how well it ultimately sticks the landing. Even though very few players will have personal experience growing up in rural Indonesia, the plot is still intensely relatable and inspiring. It's a very local story with universal themes. I really can't praise the writing enough. --------For more reviews, see

I should have read the few negative ones.The art is serviceable and the sound is OK (I can't remember the music.)How shall I explain the first 30 minutes.It's an story with some interactive element in it.I was so much crushed by the complete void of anything interesting to do that I was gasping for air, drowned in boredom.The character moves incredibly slowly by default, you have to double tap a direction to make him move at an acceptable pace.Most of what he can do is to "speak" to people, pet a cat and do "puzzles" a.k.a interacting with whatever is on screen. (Yes, that one will not tire your brain.)After finishing the prologue, I'm pretty sure I got the gist of what it will be about : a tragedy.  The hints aren't exactly subtle. I've played a bit further because, being impervious to sob stories, I was still hoping for something interesting to do.I had to give up and cut my losses, my time pointlessly wasted.Reading the reviews, I believe people who recommended this like it solely for the obviously depressing story and the feelings it gave them. (The are comments about tears.)  To each his own.  This is absolutely not for me.If you want tears, just watch Grave of the Fireflies : it's a guarantee and you'll not have to mindlessly touch a gamepad to progress the story.

_childDocuments_.review: After 7 years in development with ups and downs, A Space for the Unbound is finally here.Really hyped for this game since they showed the prologue, and I can say it was really worth the wait. This game is a masterpiece of it's own.The good stuff:- The art. Honestly I'm not much of a pixel graphic games fan, but dang this looks so nice to my eyes. I also love how they added the little details in the background (the moving cars, motorbikes, kid with a bicycle - they even set the speed so it looks realistic, like the motorbike/car would move faster than Atma running). And as an Indonesian, this does feel like the 90's atmosphere (even though I don't know much or feel it in real life because 2000-ish so dunno if it counts, heh).It feels more "alive" in some way, I can tell the developers put so much love and care into this game.- The story. Can't say much about this without spoilers, but it does contain lots of nostalgia and relatable stories that slaps you hard in reality. They also added some Easter eggs and a small tribute to Fahmi, which was a really nice touch.- The music. It's just too good. Unbound, Chasing Truth, and Klambi Abang are my favorites.- Cats. YOU CAN PET THE CATS AND NAME THEM, PEOPLE! Do I need to say more?- Game made me cry like a baby :(The bad stuff - nothing, but;- Wish we can have a "Free Roam Mode" where we can finish the bucket list. If you're a perfectionist and planning to get all the achievements, make sure to save your progress every chapter (maybe?) before you move on into the next chapter (or well, check Steam/YouTube guides) - usually the NPC asks if you're ready to do the next move, because it's  when you press "Yes", so you can't go back exploring around again. Don't be a dummy like me thinking "save slots are useless" and ended up restarting the whole game to get all the achievements.- You need to trigger a dialogue first before you can grab the items/do the things you need. It's kind of a hassle having to go back and forth, but I guess it's not a big deal.- Atma already got a gf at highschool? Unrealistic /j

_childDocuments_.review: Review A Space for the Unbound.After taking enough rest for a cooldown and thinking about it with a clear head, let's start the review.First, I want to say that I played this game in English. So my criticism may only be valid in the English version.Ok, before that, A Space for the Unbound is a game made by Mojiken and Toge Production, an Indonesian game developer that won an award (I forget what award), this developer previously made games like Coffee Talk. Basically, their biggest selling point is beautiful pixel art and "heavy" stories. In this game, they managed to maintain that and their music scoring is also better than their previous game, Coffee Talk, in my opinion. Also, in terms of gameplay, I have mixed feelings about it.Yeah, maybe from my tone, you already guessed it. Yes, in my opinion, this game is overrated.My biggest criticism is probably from its ineffective dialogue. Maybe it's our culture or the Indonesian language itself that, in my opinion, when translated into English, there are many inefficient uses of dialogue. Maybe the writer didn't check it first, there were many dialogue tags in the script.My second criticism is in the logic of the story. Yep, the story is more focused on emotions than logic, which for me is a drawback. For those who don't understand. Basically, it's like the story prioritizes the emotions of the audience regardless of whether a situation is logical or not. I'll explain it in the spoiler section later.Let's skip the story narration for now. For the gameplay, I think they were too accepting of the criticism of Coffee Talk, which had less gameplay...In this latest game, I think the gameplay is too much. Like when we're watching anime / movie / other media, we just enjoyed 30 seconds, we're immediately served with a mini-game that I find annoying. This game is very puzzle-like and for me who is not used to puzzles. the game can still be enjoyed even though there are some puzzles that I wouldn't be able to answer if I didn't see walkthrough or ask someone.What I mean is that the puzzles aren't boring, but I think they're too overdone. It's like it's just padding to make the game longer. For example, to open a locked library door, we're asked to find three keys from three different people. And it turns out these three people also have additional quests that need to be completed. After collecting the three keys and completing the quest, my reward for all this is just a 30-second cut scene? Just wtf. Luckily, this chapter is short, otherwise, I would have dropped it in chapter 5.This is also exacerbated by the fact that the puzzles are not always intuitive and often require a lot of backtracking and fetching items. It feels like the puzzles were added just to make the game longer, rather than to enhance the story or gameplay experience.Additionally, the characters in the game are not very well developed and their motivations and actions often feel inconsistent and unrealistic. The game also suffers from a lack of direction and clear objectives, leaving the player feeling lost and confused.I want to complain a bit of story so yeah, Spoiler ahead** Spoiler Begin **My problem with the story is 100% pure from Raya. I get that, he wants to be made relatable but it's silly. And in the end, it's not even made into a serious conflict. For a game that is bold in giving warnings about depression, etc., I think this is too tame. The story is too shounen-like but I don't want to criticize it in that aspect because honestly, the writer seems to like playing the shounen cliche like Naruto. It's not wrong, such a story also touches many reviewers and their pixel art target market which I am sure is more mature than me.I've mentioned before that the story only plays with emotional feelings without any logic at all. This makes the story become fail to be dark as the warning should be. For example, I actually relate to Raya's problems. But because I relate to it, I am a bit meh about Raya's illogical actions. For example, if you get scolded by your parents because of your bad grades, you should STUDY, not act like you're depressed. Damn.Even worse, Raya talks to a stranger (by the way, the stranger is a high school student and Raya is still a kid) and gets more depressed when he dies. I understand that she probably has guilty feelings. But why does the narration make it seem like Raya has imaginary friends and is bullied because of that? That just doesn't make any sense in my book. I know indonesia isn't that cruel to any accident survivor. Seriously. Suddenly, there's a boy who likes her but of course he's the one bullying Raya and she's fine with it. And then she hates him when he accidentally killed her favorite cat? Like, wtf cat lovers really doesn't make any sense. Her actions in the illusion world are really prick and freakish, making it "oh no wonder she's bullied". There's no characteristic of Raya that explains why the main character likes her so much.Oh, and one last complaint about the story is the amount of infodump and loredump, which is forced. Imagine, from the beginning to the end, there are so many infodumps to explain the phenomenon of magic, and even then the scenes are only 1-2 times, then forgotten.For the storymaker in Mojiken, I hope they read Kinug*sa's light novel or at least play Mete*r W*rld Act*r. That's the best way to give infodumps according to me. Sorry, not meant to be a promotion.** Spoiler End **Overall, while A Space for the Unbound has beautiful pixel art and a unique setting, the game falls short in terms of story, dialogue, and gameplay. The puzzles feel like a chore, the characters are underdeveloped, and the story lacks logic and direction. While it may appeal to those who enjoy puzzle games, it may not be the best choice for those looking for a well-rounded and engaging gaming experience.Despite that, I still think that the game is worth buying if you like Mojiken's previous works. I'm 100% sure that this game is an improvement from the previous one. I hope this isn't Mojiken's masterpiece because they have the potential to make even better games.

_childDocuments_.review: A Space for the Unbound is a heavy yet beautiful narrative-driven adventure about overcoming your fears and growing up, set in a rather unique setting of the 90s rural Indonesia. The game contains depictions of abuse, bullying, animal death, anxiety, depression and trauma so it may not be suitable for everyone.You play as Atma, a high school boy who has a very close friend named Raya. They’re both a bit ambivalent about graduating but together they map out a bucket list of things they want to do before the responsabilities of adulthood take over. While starting out on their adventure, Atma discovers a red book that grants him the ability to “space dive” into a person’s subconscious to help them face past trauma and make life-changing decisions. He soon discovers, however, that Raya has a similar but more destructive superpower that can alter reality itself. I’d say the story is one of those that are quite difficult to explain without spoiling it, but I assure you that it is one emotionally heavy story with many twists and interesting characters, one that will definitely make of you an emotioanl wreck by the end.Visually, A Space for the Unbound is a stunningly gorgeous game if you enjoy pixel art. There are some jaw-dropping images to be seen here, especially when the story starts going in very different directions than you initially thought it would. The character design is highly detailed and I loved the added expressiveness at times with emoji comic bubbles. The script is localized wonderfully and helps bring the characters and the emotions of a given scene to life. The soundtrack is catchy and relaxing and sets the mood for every scene and character. There are also vocal tracks that perfectly capture the game’s themes of sadness and loss and I would gladly listen to every one of these again. My only critique is that the music rarely shuts off, as if the game doesn’t trust the player to stay engaged with the world’s natural ambience. I can’t praise the soundtrack enough for the powerful emotion it conveys. It communicates the emotion behind the game’s setting and twists just as much as the story itself does.Most of the game's chapters are spent free roaming a town and the game will ask you if you want to proceed to a “point of no return” of that chapter. Save before this, since there is missable content. You will encounter tricky puzzles, but I don’t find them overly cryptic, since the hint is usually nearby. The game does not have a lose condition but there will be things like quick time events that require some reflexes. You can fail these but you can try again as many times as you need. The gameplay is fairly standard as you walk around Loka City, interact with townsfolk, pick up objects, name and pet every adorable kitty in town. The side-scrolling, story-driven adventure supports both gamepad and keyboard and both are pretty seamless. There are plenty of arcade-like mini-games that I found to be a bit easier on the gamepad.A Space for the Unbound is an intensely rewarding experience that pulls all the right heartstrings. It may not be perfect, but it has an incredibly touching story that will keep you guessing until the very end. It is truly a memorable gaming experience you don’t want to miss. A true masterpiece that every story rich indie game fan should play at least once. 10/10 recommended.
_childDocuments_.name: A Space for the Unbound

_childDocuments_.review: This is my second time playing something by this team and, once again, I am very conflicted as I write this review.Let's take some things out of the way first: The art in this game is astounding, it's honestly, truly beautiful. The story is filled with mysteries that keep you motivated to keep going and figure what the hell is going on and it's set on the 90s in Indonesia, which is definitely something you don't see everyday. It has cats, LOTS of cats (which you can name from a few set of names and also pet!!!) and overall it's something that you start and immediately get absorbed into. But that only last for the first half or so. There are so many characters that don't really matter. Why are they given the time of the day? Atma, our mc, enters the mind of some people to fix some of their trauma, "fix" them and stuff. But it always demands too much time for such a scratch on the mysteries. The gameplay is also not very creative, the fight scenes are a mix of fishing in Stardew Valley and pressing the right keys in the keyboard. If it was minimal that would be okay, but it's there just for the sake of it. What I mean is there is a great story in play, but so many things that feel like they're there just to make you play for a longer amount of time. I played When the past was around by the same team and it made me feel the exactly same (great story; not so great gameplay). The puzzles are better and more intuitive in this one, though, so that's an improvement from the last I played.The characters that aren't Raya, Nirmala, Atma and Lulu are also pretty whatever honestly. Lulu was a great companion for Atma during the game, but there isn't much effort in the other characters. And the whole beating around the bush to explain what was truly happening made me dislike Raya for a great part of the game as well. I feel if the game just focused on Atma/Raya more it could've been so much better! Because it was great at first, but as soon as it became a "where is Raya?" it started going off the trails. If this game was 6 hours long it could've told everything it wanted, but in a better way, I guess.The ending is what made me give this a positive review, however. That was beautiful. A viewer came to me at some point, commenting that Ollie from Hololive had almost dropped this game for the same reasons I was bored with it (I wasn't dropping though because I was already 12 hours on it or so), but that the ending was worth it. And yeah, it was. Made me cry and everything, and the art was great. Also the best OST of the game play next to the end as well. There were still some questions left unanswered but that didn't really bother me, I thought it was okay to leave it up to the player imagination. But if people get discouraged to play because of boring segments and feel like dropping it in the middle... That's just sad, isn't it? And it deals with important themes as well, such a domestic violence. I really wish it wouldn't beat around the bush with boring characters and boring storylines so much. Oh. And the very last scene (1 minute or so) can only be unlocked if you got all the achievements or all the pages of the book or whatever. If you didn't, the very last scene is extremely anticlimatic and makes no sense (the true ending scene isn't that great either honestly). I tried looking for it on youtube but most people that put up a full walkthrough didn't get the scene either... I did find it later though. But yeah. If it hasn't ended with the credits it would've been so much better! Argh! It's a good game that doesn't feel polished enough, I guess. It's a 5.5~6/10 for me.

_childDocuments_.review: Wow. This game will forever have a special place in my heart. The story and characters were amazing and the ending was so powerful. It made me cry but left me full of hope. As someone who has struggled with depression on and off for my whole life, the themes of self-destruction, isolation, and healing resonated with me. The music was amazing and supported the story in such an enchanting way.There was times in the middle that get a little bit of a slog, but the beautiful art and characters you meet are enough to keep it interesting. The endings of the middle chapters make you forget about any tedium you just experienced and keep you going toward the most inspiring ending. If you are thinking about quitting halfway through the story -- keep going. It's worth it, I promise.I've heard some criticism about this game's gameplay -- I just want to point out that this is basically a point-and-click game (but in such a way that works great with a controller) and this game is about the characters. There are small combat mini games that are worked in in a clever way and puzzles that are mostly easy but I did have to look up a walkthrough a couple times.Play this game. It's worth the full price. It's one of those games I wish I could wipe my memory clean of and experience again.

_childDocuments_.review: A project that proves that video games, along with films, painting, music, and so on, are art. But can we call all video games art? Do all video games catch the strings of your pathetic soul like that? Or are video games just a way to pump out money? This is a unique game, an example of real game art, not ♥♥♥♥ from Ubisoft, EA and others. It makes me extremely sad that the culture that I have lived in for so many years, and that has literally created me myself, is now just a fast-growing business. Every time a game like this comes along, I start to believe again. Into yourself, into people, into culture as a whole, and that's wonderful. Art should evoke emotions, real emotions, should make you feel something... to feel the echo of your soul. A space for the Unbound is a game that evoked a huge range of emotions in me, from sadness, worry and mild depression to joy, faith and hope. A game that tells a story as if you're there, as if it's all with you. A game that shows a believable outcome and development of a person, under the pressure of society, family, his inner demons and the struggle with these same demons. This is the merit of many talented people, just like the author of this review, who love games and respect them as art. It pains me to admit that over time such games will clearly lose popularity and lose all status in the world, but as long as they exist, I believe that large companies will have their own little garage geeks who create great worlds and unforgettable stories, worlds that evoke sincere emotions. Thank you for this piece of art, I will never forget it.  I wish peace to all, because we are citizens of the same world.

_childDocuments_.review: This game is really, really special.  It gets a lot of recognition for it's '90's Indonesia setting, and that certainly adds to it's charm, but this is way more than just a game set in Indonesia.   It tells a beautiful, meaningful story with perfect pacing and storytelling.   The characters and the writing are really fantastic, and the music perfectly complements it.  It plays like an old-school point-and-click adventure game, but it completely avoids the weird moon-logic puzzles that sometimes happen in that style of game.  It has a deep narrative that will keep you thinking about it, but it avoids being the common problem of being so convoluted that it's hard to follow or makes no sense.  It has a good number of side-quests and optional content, but it's set up in such a way that if you choose to, you can easily do it all without resorting to using a guide or spending hours completing collections.  It's rich in symbolism and touches on many important topics including bullying, anxiety, depression, abuse, trauma, and loss.  The game is very emotional and can make players cry at points, but I wouldn't call it a sad game - it's uplifting and bittersweet.  Combine all that with it's simple pleasures: a cute art style, catchy music, unique cultural references, petting and naming all the stray cats in town - it's just an all around wonderful and special game.

_childDocuments_.review: is one of those masterpieces that are very difficult to describe in words; they have to be personally experienced, ardently felt and actively lived. One of its characters mentions at some point in the game, “As a writer, I want to be able to move my readers with the things I create. Change them”;  is the embodiment of this quote: it’s a deeply emotional work of art that will move you and change you.Atma and Raya are two high-school sweethearts who one day decide to make a bucket list of fun things they want to accomplish in the near future. While this acts like a premise for the story, it’s in fact just a way to guide the player step by step into various circumstances that will slowly reveal the actual core of the game: Raya is a young girl having the superpower of altering the reality, while Atma possesses a book that allows him to dive into people’s hearts / minds and help them overcome their inner troubles. Strange incidents start to happen around them as Raya keeps misusing her powers to change little things to their advantage in an attempt to facilitate the completion of the bucket list. Soon enough the line between reality and fantasy is completely abolished and the player is transported into a series of unpredictable events as the world around the two main characters starts to destabilize. The story remains enveloped in mystery right until the end, keeping the player wondering what the actual meaning of all these incidents could be, but at the same time revealing new layers with every chapter. is a gripping tale about reconnecting with your true nature and finding the will to overcome all the obstacles that life throws at you. It deals with sensitive topics like emotional traumas caused by school bullying, depression, social anxiety, domestic violence and to some extent suicidal thoughts.As far as the gameplay goes,  takes the shape of a sidescroller point & click adventure. As Atma, you will explore the streets of the small Loka City, enter buildings or interact with the people you encounter. The linear gameplay and the fact that the game always makes it obvious what the player is expected to do allows them to deeply immerse themselves in the story. Unlike in other point & click games, where you just roam around without knowing where to go, talking to everyone just because you can, collecting every object you can find just because you can pick it up and because it will probably be used in a puzzle,  tightly guides the player through its wonderful story, leaving very little space for mindless experimentation and time-wasting conversation. You will pick up objects only at the right moment when they’re needed, all dialogues are on point and Atma’s inventory is filtered and populated with the only 2-3 items that you can and  to use when interacting with a character. In addition to that, all puzzles are clear and straightforward, usually encountered in the form of fetch-quests, but there are also a couple of light math riddles. Some of the dialogues have multiple choices, and in some cases these are mutually exclusive, other times not. The mutually-exclusive ones do not affect the outcome of the story in any way, and only provide a few alternative dialogue lines.From time to time, Atma will have to use a fighting mechanic which involves reproducing a sequence of keys in a limited amount of time in a QTE style (attack), followed by stopping a moving cursor at a precise location (block / defend). The minigame is designed so that it is accessible for pretty much everyone (there’s enough time to complete it in a rather relaxed mode), even though throughout the game its difficulty increases (you get longer sequences and tighter times of reaction). In case you fail to complete a sequence three times, you will be able to give it a new try starting from the current stage. While the game keeps the difficulty rather casual, for two specific achievements you will need to survive through 17 of these stages without failing, and beyond the first 10 of them you’ll be required to have extremely quick reaction times.In  you will encounter lots of cats, in fact, more than 25 of them. You can name and pet them all, which is obviously optional for completing the game but necessary for a certain achievement. While these sadly aren’t tracked, the other type of collectibles (the 20 bottle caps) are all listed in your inventory. Apart from a couple of cases they are all easily spottable in the environment through a spark that indicates their location. Unfortunately, the collectibles are missable in the sense that you won’t be able to go back to a previous chapter and pick them up in case you didn’t do so the first time. Aside from these, there are a few other missable achievements awarded for interacting with certain items in the world or doing specific actions at the right moment. One playthrough is enough for 100% completion, but due to the fact that you can’t replay previous chapters, using a guide will likely be needed.The game excels not only through the captivating story that it conveys, but also through the stunning (and very detailed) pixel art style, and an equally impressive soundtrack. In all these aspects, the developers included lots of Indonesian cultural and lifestyle references, which give the game a lot of flavor. Voice-acting is not present, yet this doesn’t diminish the warm experience that  provides.Do I recommend the game? Absolutely - I love  for its charm, for its fantastic story with a good character build-up, for its lively art and great presentation. It’s a one-of-a-kind game that deserves every penny for the 12-15 hours of joy that it offers.

_childDocuments_.review: It's hard to review this game in a way that truly makes it justice, without any spoilers, and I'd rather not do that.It's a game about escapism, friendship, regrets, loss, and so much more. The story is pretty out there, but it delivers an interesting narrative, that feels like a breath of fresh air among the stale and lifeless backdrop of modern mainstream gaming.The soundtrack is quite enjoyable. It's nostalgic, sweet and relaxing, and goes well with the game's setting.Pretty much everything about the game brims with nostalgia. The nice pixel art visuals, the 90s small town setting.Most of the pixel art is great, even though it's a bit simplistic at times and it's lacking in detail, and there are some scenes where it's clear that they didn't put as much effort, compared to other ones.Unfortunately, the game has its fair share of drawbacks.The action consists of some rudimentary mini-games; mostly basic quick time events. There are a lot of them, and they are rather repetitive and tedious.Most puzzles are easy, logical, but some, are tedious, requiring quite a bit of trial and error.There are too many errands with a ton of back and forth. For example, in order to get a simple cake, you have to jump through so many hoops, it's ridiculous; the worst part is that these errands are bland and simplistic in nature (basically, bad fetch quests), and most do not tie into the world or the story almost at all, just being isolated and contained. Would have been great if you would get more insight into the world, characters, lore, through these errands.While for the most part, the writing is pretty good, it has its gutter moments, with some of the dialog feeling forced and unnatural (will not go into details, to avoid spoilers).You can remap most keys, except for the movement keys, for some reason. Interestingly enough, in the 1st demo, you were able to move using WASD as well as the arrow keys. In the 2nd demo and the full game, you can only use the arrow keys. It's not that big of a deal, since you can use AutoHotKey to remap any keys however you want, but still, it would have been nice to have the option to be able to remap all keys.It has some wasted potential. With a bit more polish to its writing, characters, lore, and mechanics, the game could have been a brilliant masterpiece.Even so, despite all of these gripes, the game is enjoyable and well worth playing, ultimately delivering a unique and memorable experience.
