_childDocuments_.review: Finished it today.... Oh man... Such a sweet and paradoxical world. It's like a nonlinear puzzle about one's self, conflict, identity and recovery. I am at a lost of words right now. It is so beautiful, I can't even talk. Still crying. It is a story packed with everything for anyone. It has sensible issues, it has courage to face one's fears, it has action (fighting scenes, fighting for loved ones), it has good and satirical humour, it belongs on those unique shelves for great games. PROS:- Story is fabulous;- Character change at the end;- Wonderful art style and graphics;- Music fits every part of the story;- Book for inventory and map;- Collecting coins, letters and pages;- Petting cats and giving them names.CONS: (I must say sorry for this!)- The one thing that really drives me crazy are save points. The save point in this game is bad. When you save and load, it makes you start from the beginning of the checkpoint chapter, rather than the very minute you have saved the game. And this is frustrating because back in 1990s you could save on the spot in a SNES emulated game, but not in this 2023 game. This is bad! - A quick tip: The kid with the ball (letter M) needs to offer a quick tutorial for how to juggle the ball (i.e. press X when ball is on the leg - or something like that);- I cannot think of other issues right now.Forgive my rage for the save point. Because of my 1990s knowledge of games, I'm comparing mechanics of the past with mechanics of the present. You devs of the present have yet to please me. Well, some games like True Fear: Forsaken Souls, Guilty Gear, Legacy of Kain, God of War: Ragnarok, etc. have a special place in my heart. And I think I'm not alone in this statement. What I want to say is that A Space For The Unbound has become right now one of my favorites. It turned out a gem of a game, a must play for sensible hearts. In this light, I must thank my friend for giving this game for my birthday. Thank you, friend!

_childDocuments_.review: A Space for the Unbound is a story driven game based around fetch quests and relatively simple puzzles, and actually pretty well made for what it is. I can't say I didn't expect the ending (because it relies on known tropes), but I enjoyed the overall storytelling.However, there is one big flaw, and that is the lack of a chapter select, which means missing out on some stuff from as early as chapter 2 permanently locks you out from further content in the later chapters. And because you can't skip certain dialogue and cutscenes, I decided to look up the additional content on YouTube rather than play through the entire game again. As such, I would highly recommend following a guide (something I should've done earlier) to avoid missing content.Do also note that if you want the additional content at the end, you will need some degree of proficiency with QTE prompts, so I wouldn't necessarily consider this a "sit back and relax" game.I don't think this game is necessarily for everyone, but if you like retro, story-rich games that invoke nostalgia, this game should be right up your alley.

_childDocuments_.review: Quick:5/5  This game is amazing.  It has a great story with awesome characters.  The art is gorgeous and the music is fantastic.  I had such a good time playing this game, and I am so happy that I did.  Congratulations to the developers.  You have made something special.More:Ever since the demo / prologue for this game came out, a little over 2 years ago, I have been eagerly awaiting its release.  It's here now, and it has far exceeded my expectations.  A Space for the Unbound was well worth the wait.The best thing about this game is the story.  It is very deep and engaging.  Every time a chapter ended, I was left wondering where the story would go next.  There are lots of twists and turns, but the writing is so good that it doesn't seem cliche or over-done.  Lots of heavy and serious topics are touched on during the course of this game.  It is not at all juvenille, and does have some emotional as well as disturbing moments.  However, most of the time the story is a feel-good ride with a decent amount of humor in it as well.The majority of time in the game will be spent reading dialogue.  While characters are not having conversations with each-other, there are mini-games and puzzles.  I find the mini-games to be very fun and the puzzles, though easy enough, are well crafted and varied.  I can honestly say that I was never bored playing this game.  It changes so often that you always feel like there is something new to do and experience.All of the characters that you meet throughout the game have personality and charm.  Even the characters that you hate are crafted in such a way that you love to hate them.  They all have their place, in other words, and you will remember them and probably enjoy seeing most of them from time to time.If you enjoy story driven games such as RPGs then this game might be for you.  I recommend that you play A Space for the Unbound, and I hope that you enjoy it as much as I did.

_childDocuments_.review: I played the game in Bahasa. A lot of references are geared more towards Indonesian audience, and I personally like it. I like the overall idea of the concept, the world, the characters, and I respect the fact that no one is a "true protagonist": every one is eerily human, with all their complex background and personality. The story also doesn't end/close in a typical trope, but rather, choose to have a very "mature" conclusion with the "villains". Gameplay wise, this game is a fetch quest game through and through, with mini games in between. If you're looking for a story heavy game with complex, difficult gameplay (maybe like Undertale), this game is not it. But if you want to experience a more relaxed gameplay, with beautiful pixel arts, good musics, and follow a touching story of trying to understand people and their past, this game is definitely it.Kudos for the creators, this is a very beautiful game

_childDocuments_.review: It was a deeply personal experience for me, as someone with clinical depression and anti-social tendencies. Some moments felt like a mirror. It's not a pleasant feeling to be so vulnerable from seeing myself in video games, especially the ugly parts of me, but that's what makes this game special and dear in my heart. Really, some scenes felt like a memory, something I've been through in my darkest days.I love how the developer portrayed depression, very respectful and realistic. It doesn't glorifies nor vilifies mental illness at all. This game also highlights trauma, struggles, family issues, coping mechanisms and everything else humankind experience in an honest and bare way. Gosh, I even almost cried again while writing this review. I do admit, this game hits too close to home because I'm Indonesian too. Now, to other aspects of this game.I LOVE every single detail the developer had made for world-building, visually or through script. The close-knit neighborhood, food stalls, pop culture references, the shops, school, EVERYTHING screams Indonesia in a genuine, nostalgic way. Like c'mon. Warnet. Tambal ban. School as haunted site. The abandoned train cart as secret base. The freaking toko kelontong and batu akik. The story is interesting and not too predictable. Dramatic, but doesn't make me cringe. The ending made me feel like, "damn, someone actually experience this too, just like me." Don't let the fantasy aspect of this game fool you, even the "side stories" could be found in day-to-day life of Indonesian people. The visual and sound style is very gorgeous, it fits the narrative perfectly. I was actually speechless in some scenes from how beautiful everything felt. The 16-bit art and color palette made it so freaking nostalgic. The visual effects, transition, every trinkets and small sound effects. I love it so much. The art director and artists behind the visuals really experimented with lots of perspectives and lighting effects, too.The characters are perfectly flawed in their own ways. Some of them are likable, some are not, depends on your culture, views and morality. They felt real, even down to the minor characters. From visuals to the way they talk, and how they interact with each other. Literally, I could imagine them as part of my own life as Indonesian. I don't want to go too deep in this aspect because I might spoil it too much.P.s : the way CATS dominated this game made it 100000x more awesome. The game mechanics is not the main focus of this game, but it was quite fun and frustating at times. My favorite part is how one of the game mechanics referenced my favorite game, **e Attorney. Like, at this point, this game felt like it was made for me.I could probably talk about this game for hours and hours. But all in all, I just want to give my highest gratitude to Mojiken and Toge Productions for bringing this game to life. This game and all of you inspired me to pursue my passion more from now on,I finished this game in about 10 hours total with 2 achievements left, about to replay it in English because my first run was in Indonesian to get all achievements. See ya!

_childDocuments_.review: I like this game a lot. Really touching and personal story where you can really tell how much love the devs have for it. Thematically and structurally it's very similar to games like Omori or Rakuen, so if you're familiar with those you'll have a sense for what you're in for. The story has a really intriguing start and a real banger of a final third, really moving. The older I get the more value I put in things having good endings and this game certainly delivers.It isn't without its faults, the actual gameplay I'd say is just straight up dull. The puzzle design has issue where all the puzzles are either over-engineered or just tedious, most of them just being a series of "get these three things to make this one thing". It's very obviously just a vessel to move you through the world, and hinges a lot on you enjoying the time capsule-y 90's rural Indonesia setting to get through, luckily that's very easy to do with how nice it looks so it ends up not being too bad. The game's short anyway so it's never that big a deal.So yeah, it's really good. The type of release that just makes me love video games. Glad it exists.

_childDocuments_.review: Very cute, nostalgic sidescroller with a message about processing trauma that just... stays with you for a while. I knew going into this game that it would be a bit feelsy, and I saw the "big" twist coming, but I wasn't prepared for the suckerpunch of the game's final chapter. Woof.Lots of references to Indonesian culture that I didn't quite get, being an uncultured American, but these gave the game and its characters lots of color and life. I love the pixel art style used in both the sprites and cut scenes, and the way that the world moves in general. The story is well told and each of the characters (even the NPCs) are given a lot of personality that makes you want to root for each of them. An atmospheric and fitting OST also helps bring this vibrant world to life.The only bummer is that I missed two items on the bucket list, and I'd have to replay the whole game to get those achievements, because you can't travel between chapters to get them. Navigating between areas is also a bit of a headache, and because of that, I missed out on a couple of areas where there were additional cats to pet, and the music side quest — hence the missed achievements. Because the pace of the game is a bit slow, I'm not sure I want to replay it any time soon, but I'd like to finish all the achievements I also really disliked the fighting video game lmao... _childDocuments_.review: 9,5/10Bought this game a year ago and finally managed to finish it this year just a few hours ago.With a total playtime of 10.7 hours, spending money on this game last year when it was newly released was not in vain to play "A Space For The Unbound," even though I just completed it today because there was no time, hehe.So, "A Space For The Unbound" is a game created by Mojiken Studio and Toge Production, released on January 19, 2023.Here, Mojiken uses pixel graphics, which I am comfortable with, given the art in this game. You can see it on my previous instastory, and that's just a small part. You must try this game to experience other eye-pleasing pixel arts.In terms of gameplay mechanics, we are presented with a 2D side-scrolling mechanic that makes the game easy and more relaxed to play. Additionally, there are some simple puzzles and side games that add variety to the game.As for the story, we follow a high school boy named Atma to solve the mystery of his girlfriend, Raya. At the beginning, I was a bit confused about how the story would develop, but as the story progressed, many unexpected things happened, such as Raya also having supernatural powers, among other unexpected twists.So, that's my short review. I apologize if it seems messy, and I also apologize for any inaccuracies in my writing because I still have much more to learn.

_childDocuments_.review: A Space for the Unbound is a heartfelt story wrapped around gorgeous pixel art, a nice soundtrack, but frustrating gameplay, extremely on the nose hints that ruin surprises, and endless padding. Ultimately this is a "story game", it is the main focus, and as such is the most important thing for this game. Overall, the game tells a beautiful story about inner struggles, depression, anxiety, self reflection, abuse, loss, bullying, and more. The main character's struggles are sure to be relatable, especially if you play this while you're still in school. The main issue I have with the story itself is that every hint is so on the nose, you'll know most twists and turns before they happen, while not really looking out for or thinking about trying to solve the game's story. This section will contain spoilers: The game opens with the South Star Princess dying, yellow (warm colored) flower petals used for magic, and a dark colored cat. One chapter later you hear of the North Star Princess, but you don't know much about her. You then see Raya's light blue (cold colored) flower petals used for magic, and she has a light colored cat. Complete opposites, totally not the North Star Princess. You know Nirmala wrote these stories, so either you are in her story, or Nirmala has a new identity and taken on the role as the North Star Princess. The game reveales both of these are true. Shocker.This goes for a lot of the twists in the story. They're always very clearly explained before they even happen, and the only sense of mystery the game has comes from the game realizing they're being too obvious, so they have a cat tell you very ominously that "You don't know what's happening, fool, I am very mysteryous, nothing is as it seems". Then in the end the cat just gives up and starts explaining that it didn't want to be mysterious after all, they're all just here to help. This part of the narrative just felt and still feels out of place even after completing the game. The hints are so on the nose, that when you launch the game, the first thing you see is a trigger-warning list. "Animal death", I haven't even played the game yet, and my first thought is "The main character's cat will die, ok". This alone ruined any emotional impact this scene would have had otherwise.Other than that, the story itself is mostly fantastic, and handles the heavy topics with grace. The only thing that really took me out of the immersion was that they made the teenage characters censor themselves during fights. A late teenager would not censor themselves and say "You're such a B-!" when they're in a fight. It's not how people would speak, especially not a high school jock who isn't afraid to beat up people he doesn't like. This happens fairly often, so I thought I should bring it up. Writing aside, the game's biggest issue is the padding. Everything you do has padding. I think the developers were scared that just writing a good story wouldn't be enough, so they needed to insert a ridiculous amount of steps to do literally antything in the game, and it's simply not fun. For example, you need to go buy a cake, but you need to run around every part of town to gather each of the ingrediants. Fair enough. Actually, this wasn't enough, the chef is having a mental breakdown, so you need to sabotage her dream-food by pouring oil into it. The steps finding the oil alone is:Leave dream > Find Oil > Can't buy it, so you find a secret password to get free oil > You need your own container > Find container > Actually the container is dirty, find the one place in town you can clean it lol > Get free oil > Finally sabotage the dish. This was one of three foods you have to sabotage before the chef will help you. So to get the cake you need to run around town a minimum of 3 times. Doing this adds nothing to the story, you can barely call it gameplay, and it makes for an incredibly dragged out experience. It's simply not fun to run around the whole town looking for a random button to press, often with no hint. If it was just a few times, sure, but it happens almost every time you need to get anything done. The worst part is that you can't pick up items before you need them. For example that container you need for the oil, I found that ages before I needed it in a quest, but I wasn't allowed to pick it up.Adding these extra steps is something the game does any chance it gets. You need to break into the school? Cool, find a hammer to break wall (we'll skip every step it takes to find the hammer) > Run back to the wall > Break it > Actually you can't break it now, run for 3 whole minutes to the same wall in the past, then break it > Run for 3 minutes to get back > Finally, breaking it in the past made it decay, so it's broken for real now. What did this add? Another 6 minutes of holding left on the control stick? It wasn't a puzzle because the game literally told you to do it. It's just frustrating. I think if you take away this padding, keep the missions and dialogue generally the same, but without all the extra steps that add nothing, you'd probably save 3 or 4 hours of the game, and nothing would be changed otherwise.Something else that is baffeling to me is when the game introduces combat. You have a quest to beat the "Future Fighter" high score. This is the first time you will fight. Funnily enough, this high score is the absolute most difficult fighting you will do in the entire game. Why make the hardest fight the first? Everything after that is easier by a long shot. It is honestly ridiculous. Sure, you can try it once and skip doing the high score, but the high score isn't difficult to begin with, I did it first try, but it's still weird that they choose to make it the first fight the most difficult.This review is getting quite long, so I will end it here. In conclusion, the game features a fantastic story, gorgeous pixel art, nice music, but ultimately fails in the gameplay department. They should have toned down the gameplay and settled for a shorter playstime more focused on the story instead of tedious tasks, and they should be a bit more careful with the hints. Not saying a game can't be "figured out" before everything is revealed, but it should not be figured out without trying to pay attention to the finer details and without giving it much thought. I am glad I played it, I overall enjoyed the story a lot, but I can only hope they learn from their mistakes when their next game comes out.

_childDocuments_.review: Dislcaimer: I played this on my Steam Deck offline, so it says I've only played it for like two hours despite the fact that I'm in the final section of the game.Actual review: I bought this game on a whim based on the fact that it had such positive reviews and knowing absolutely nothing about it. It was a great decision.This is a charming indie game that's part old-school pixel art RPG, part old school point and click adventure, and part something else uniquely its own.It has a bit of everything. Engaging characters, a good story, humor, drama, magic (or at least superpowers), teenage angst, mental health issues, Inception-style dreamwalking, and a ton of cats you can pet and name. Oh, and ambiance. So much ambiance.I was wondering why I felt so attached to these characters and why the setting felt so familiar given that I'm not remotely Indonesian, when I found out that the main story is supposed to be set during the '90's. That was it. What I felt was familiarity and nostalgia because I'm roughly the same age as Atma and Raya and what I was recognizing was the very authentic feeling of what it was like to be a teenager in a small town in those long gone days of the late 20th century before the internet was everywhere and cellphones were even a thing. I don't think I had ever felt like that except when reading a good book or watching a good movie, but never while playing a video game. What an unexpected and interesting experience.

_childDocuments_.review: As someone who played the To the Moon series, I had a very high expectation of this game when I saw the trailer. And boy, it met my expectations magnificently and beyond!The game did a great job at what it wanted to do: tell you a good story. Its narration is easy to follow and enjoyable. As you follow Atma through his adventure, you can't help but be invested in him and the characters around him. The more the story unfolds, the more you are intrigued. It is one of the stories that you want to keep reading and see through to the end.Accompanying the beautifully woven story are lovely pixel art and soundtrack. Just like the To the Moon series, pixel art doesn't affect the delivery at all. Rather, its simplicity lets you focus more on the story. The beautifully composed soundtrack significantly amplifies your experience and helps with the immersion as you go through the game.The setting, which is Indonesia, might be a little bit foreign to many but fear not! You will get used to it in no time. I am sure that you can relate to many situations that occur in the game. Trust me.But none of this would matter if you can't relate to the characters. As I said above, you will get invested in Atma and the people around him. The characters are well-written and well-thought-out. Each of them has a unique character and is memorable.The only flaw I could say about the game is how it handle its fetch quest in the late game. Having layers of those is nice. But it can break immersion and the continuation of storytelling sometimes.Overall, I can recommend this game to anyone who loves narrative adventure. Its story and characters are well-written. The art and the soundtrack are perfect. It will be one of the games you will never forget.PS. I might be overthinking about this but the reference to the platypus in the game might be a reference to the To the Moon series.

_childDocuments_.review: 9/10, would cry againLoved the characters.  Good story, fantastic ending.  I know virtually nothing about Indonesia, but the game world felt very fleshed out.I do not recommend trying to get all achievements on the first run. I started enjoying it again when I let go of 100%ing the bucket list + achievements.The writers deserve an award for how hard some of those lines + scenes hit.  It's the kind of stuff that makes you stop and sit back for a moment.WHAT GAMEPLAY TO EXPECT (since the store page does not articulate it well):Where you can go and what you can do is tied to where you are in the story-line (chapters), which is pretty linear.  There is some side-content, but it's either tied to the bucket list or just achievements (though it does add to the  immersion as well).  Gameplay revolves around exploring (interacting with objects/animals/people) and minigames.  Minigames range from "stealth" (sneaking past people) to problem solving "puzzles" and even combat (mainly a back-and-forth cycle of quick-time events).  I don't usually like this kind of stuff but they pull it off perfectly and it avoids having to implement yet another RPG level/skill system, thus keeping it simpler and story-focused!

_childDocuments_.review: If you are looking for a game with good storytelling and whimsical, bittersweet themes, A Space for the Unbound could be appropriate. Gameplay is not particularly original, and there are very few parts that could be qualified as "challenging": It's more of a mellow experience, and the main focus is the story. If you are looking for a more challenging point-and-click adventure, stuff like Machinarium or the Phoenix Wright series might be more up your alley.Still, the storytelling is delicate and touching, and the aesthetics are definitely interesting: Probably designed by/for someone that was young in the nineties, sometimes it plays lightly on nostalgia. It is still somehow has a unique flavor, at least for people like me who are not familiar with Indonesian culture.I enjoyed it enough to play it through a second time. A recommend.

_childDocuments_.review: Content Warnings for A Space for the Unbound as provided by Mojiken Studio: abuse, depression, suicide, trauma, animal death, flashing lightsTackling coming of age and the YA register in a way that games frequently struggle to meet, Space for the Unbound is a 2D adventure game taking flavors from life sims, JRPGs, and Shenmue-style "♥♥♥♥ around and talk to people" puzzle routing. 90s Indonesia depicted in lush pixel art gives a nostalgic sense of place to this Mamoru Hosoda-y fantasy-realism piece. While sometimes a bit verbose or hung up on challenge based sideshows, A Space for the Unbound nails a sense of scale and gravity in its handling of teens on the fringe of their own life where something like the Life is Strange franchise constantly seems to struggle with.This game conducts itself without a huge dependence on melodrama to synthesize character beats with its fantasy elements. While it can be heavy-handed in writing or slightly off with timing or duration, the vital scenes and lock-and-key puzzle moments are meticulous and conservative. The palette and approach to line and weight in the animation give so much life to every second and the frequency at which the team at Mojiken knows when to let that speak is enlightening. I think some of the ways in which abuse are depicted and resolved is a little too simple, but the game doesn't claim at any point to be interested in making larger claims about the subjects. This is an incredibly charming game that delivers on everything it promise in its most gorgeous stills.

_childDocuments_.review: A Space for the Unbound caught me by complete surprise. Especially because I didn't think it deserved the hype even half way through the game. I was wrong, and I highly recommend this experience. Even the price of 20 Dollars is worth it.Reviews for ASftU are Overwhelmingly Positive on Steam, which - along with its promise of a good story -prompted me to purchase this game. I had never bought anything by Mojiken before and from the looks of the trailer and screenshots, it seemed to pay homage to classic arcade style games and point and click gameplay, which it does.Now, being perfectly clear. I don't think Space Unbound is a great game, or at least, does not have great gameplay. It is a good game, but not great. The puzzles are a bit too easy at times, the pacing is off at various points, and the back tracking didn't really settle me in the atmosphere like it seems to for others.The options in the main menu seemed a bit limited to me as well. No chapter jumps after completion, no artwork unlocked for finding hidden achievements... Little things like this would improve the game a bit in my opinion.Half way through I thought, "Yeah this is a good game. But a masterpiece? No, I don't see that."...I was wrong. I finished the second half.Despite my nitpicking of gameplay and my doubts, I can confirm A Space for the Unbound tells a beautiful, masterful story. It is obvious the creators were careful in their research of depicting the emotions of the depressed, the anxious and anger, that comes from someone suffering. What's even more impressive is that anyone can relate, to some level, what these characters are going through, and how they feel.I was very impressed. And that ending, that incredibly moving, gosh darn ending had me re-watching on youtube many times.Well worth everything, the hours and money spent.Is A Space for the Unbound a great game? No. But I don't believe it could be told correctly in another form of media either.Does A Space for the Unbound tell one of the most beautiful, down to earth stories about depression that I have ever played? Yes. And it is done masterfully.I look forward to your next game Mojiken. We need more video games like these. Highly recommend.

_childDocuments_.review: I played the demo and felt this game is a charming one with some potential. However I see the storytelling being very problematic when the plot in the demo so far established a somewhat serious undertone: establishing rapport with an anxious young girl who faces domestic violence from her father. The plot of the demo ended with a huge cliffhanger where the protagonist faces mortal danger… yet all these are forgotten when the main chapter starts. There’s a girlfriend who is basically a new character, and no attempt to address what happened in the demo is made. Essentially, the game starts telling a new story without resolving the existing plot. Even more egregious is the undertone change from serious to flippant, and then arbitrary superpower was introduced, and the game lost me when it started to demand me doing random chores to please the girlfriend.I want to like this game. The art style is gorgeous and the animation is stylish. However the story seems to be a train wreck that sapped every ounce of my desire to keep going. A lesson to be learned: Nostalgia isn’t a panacea, because it’s not material to those who can’t be nostalgic to the backdrop of the game’s settings.

_childDocuments_.review: A decent game with a fair price.It starts with a mystery but the story is actually predictable, you know what's going on half way and the rest is about sticking to the plan and being a hero sacrifice for the princess.A Space for the Unbound is made with beautiful pixel arts, using a fairy tale throughout the story to help player to understand what really happens. It also jumps between time and space, using a magic wand to look into the NPC's mind (mini games) to understand, and eventually to change the reactions so to pass certain events.The warm color in the game made it feels relaxing, however, the stories are dark with school bullying, family issues, self-doubt, antisocial revenge, conspiracy on power etc, due to the wideness of the problems the game tried to display, I personally think that this game has reached at a certain point but failed to give a throughout idea of how to face and deal with it. However, I take it as an important game, besides developers giving players a general idea that "you don't need to care about everyone's idea of you" and "learn to forgive yourself and accept your imperfections", sort of positive and right thinking while you are treated unfairly.I finished this game in 6 hours but it feels long. On one hand traveling back and forth trying to save a lost soul, and dealing with multiple issues while seeing the world crumbling down is tiring. On the other hand, all the battles are all about pressing simple keys they are repetitive and tedious and make me sleepy. Good thing is the ending is well made, the art elevates the entire story, however the bitterness is in the air.Honestly I don't feel much for the characters but I think there are quite a few players who do. I hope they find answers.

_childDocuments_.review: This game caught my attention when I saw its trailer some time ago, and I was captivated by its anime-esque art and character design, as well as the supernatural aspects that were shown. Adding to that, I also got really curious about how they would show Indonesian culture, something I haven’t experienced at all before and kinda looked forward to. A Space for the Unbound is a fantastic adventure set in the late 90s in rural Indonesia, wrapped in a magical and mysterious atmosphere, where our protagonist will be able to dive deep into the heart of people and their feelings, in order to help them with their problems and worries; this is all thanks to an enigmatic and curious red book, which grants him such abilities, and alongside them, a really important duty that he’ll come to know little by little.The  begins by presenting a tale about a princess and her faithful feline companion, which is told through its author, Nirmala; she’s a young cartoonist who, together with the main character, is working on a very emotional and peculiar fantasy book. However, she is unable to come up with a good ending, as she is burdened by doubts, insecurities and fear. It is here that we will learn about the special ability of our protagonist, Atma, who will be able to get into people's hearts thanks to the aforementioned red book; and, using this power, we will try to help our friend with her negative thoughts. One thing will lead to another, and we will then be able to wander around the town a bit. However, in the middle of our errand, a torrential rain begins, and after some somewhat dangerous events, the prologue will culminate. I don't want to comment much about it, since I think it's better not to ruin this part of the story by telling it; besides, it's possible to play it totally free since it has its own demo.Leaving aside the prologue, the story will introduce us to a new character: Raya, Atma's girlfriend, and the story will take a course around their school time, where we can see a bit of the typical student concerns, such as the future and the careers that could follow; something quite realistic and with which many can relate. But these kinds of things are a bit overwhelming and boring for a teenager, so Raya comes up with a list of "things to do'' before graduating; and after filling the list with goals to complete, they plan their next days accordingly. From here on, we will enjoy an adventure both pleasant and tense, with plot twists and more mystical or mysterious moments, such as the constant mention of an enigmatic comet, or the magical abilities that Raya also seems to possess. I found the plot very interesting and fun to follow, especially for the different scenes presented throughout our quest to complete the to-do list, and for the interactions between the protagonists and the different characters that are presented along the way. There are several twists and surprises that I'm obviously not going to tell, but it's a story that goes beyond what it seems at first.As far as the  aspect is concerned, A Place for the Unbound is presented to us in a pixel art style that is very pretty and pleasing to the eye. Both the landscapes in the distance, as well as the nearest buildings or pastures of the rural town, look very elaborate and detailed, and feel very in harmony with each other, thus creating a perfect setting. The characters feature fairly large sprites, designed in a somewhat anime style that I liked a lot, and they are also shown in a more detailed way when the perspective is changed to scenes with larger art. I want to add that simple animations such as lip movements or different facial expressions are something that is very appreciated, at least for people like me who are fans of these details. Without a doubt, one of the most charming aspects of the title. Another thing I found interesting was that Atma's red book is our menu that connects the different interfaces of the game, such as the mission log, the inventory and the map. I must say that I really liked the creativity and implementation of this detail.The  is also very nice and immersive, featuring several different and captivating tracks as expected. Tense, lively, calm tunes; few melodies are lacking, and none of them seemed repetitive or overwhelming to me, quite the opposite, as they aroused various emotions in me as the story progressed, and that’s one of the reasons why I play games. At a certain point there is a violinist, the first of several artists that we will be able to meet, and she will play one of the compositions that I liked the most in the game. The songs with vocals were also phenomenal, I would like to add. The music was a great accompaniment throughout the adventure, and I greatly appreciate the work and love that the developers put into this section. Moving on to the , the game is a 2D adventure game, where we will move from left to right through the town while interacting with the environment, be it talking to the different inhabitants of the town, petting cats scattered everywhere, or activating objects. Following the story and exploring around, we will find different puzzles and mini-games to deal with, highlighting two systems especially: the combat, and the "Spacedive". The combat is turn-based, and quite simple, since all we have to do is defend and attack, but I still found it entertaining. When defending, we are presented with a red and green bar in which a cursor moves, and we have to press the interact button at the right time (hitting on the green part) to successfully take cover. On the other hand, in the attack, you have to follow a pattern of keys between the directional and other buttons to hit our enemy, which reminded me a bit of rhythm games, but only for its appearance. It's a nice addition and gives a little more action to some scenes.As for the "Spacedive", it's the main mechanic and obviously a key part of the story, as it's the name of our ability to dive into people's souls, so to say. There will be various situations or mini-games depending on the individual we are trying to help with their afflictions, and it really is like every person is their own world; so we will have to look for different ways to find the solutions to their problems. I thought it was very neat and creative, a perfect touch in the setting. Expanding a little more on the mini-games, we can find a great variety of them, such as moments where we must use stealth, remember patterns or numbers, and answer some trivia of both the game universe and the real world, among others. I quite enjoyed most of them, although some made me wrack my brains (like a certain part where I had to decipher a mathematical formula, asking for help from my friends in Discord because I'm horrible with numbers), but I especially liked how they were implemented in the different points of the game.In , I want to say that I thought the game was excellent. It exceeded all my expectations, and left me very satisfied. Although I must say that the ending gave me mixed feelings, as it is bittersweet but touching (in my opinion). I really enjoyed the game a lot, accompanying Raya and Atma in their adventure, and gradually unveiling the themes it was addressing, such as bullying, depression, and the courage to accept oneself. The incredible soundtrack, the beautiful art and the cool scenes gave me a very nice and unforgettable experience; it is a game that I consider to be highly emotional in many aspects, and I would like to recommend it to anyone looking for emotiveness, and that wish to enjoy a fantastic story that has its roots firmly rooted in reality.

As the story unfolded, especially towards the end, I found myself tearing up—more than I expected. Those final scenes were incredibly powerful, and they’ll stay with me for a long time.Everything about this game is filled with love and care. The pixel art is gorgeous, the soundtrack is beautiful, and the gameplay is simple yet deeply engaging. You can tell that the creators poured their hearts into every detail.Even though I couldn’t personally relate to everything the characters went through, the game still managed to move me deeply. It made me feel connected to their struggles and emotions in a way that few games do. And for the parts that hit close to home—those moments were especially impactful.This game touched my heart in a way I didn’t expect, and I can only hope to find more experiences like this in the future. Thank you for creating such a beautiful, heartfelt game. ♥

_childDocuments_.review: TL;DR: Gorgeous narrative-driven game with great story and a strong message. Can be a bit repetitive but the game's beautiful pixel art and its simple and linear gameplay override that. As an Indonesian myself, I am generally skeptical about Indonesian-made video games which depict the country. But ASFTU, despite the mouthful title, is in my opinion objectively a fantastic game. It does not "force" its Indonesian-ness to the player; rather, the game uses it simply as a backdrop to a much stronger narrative. The game is  about Indonesia, it is simply  in Indonesia (huge difference!). I really respect the devs' decision to do it this way, as it makes the game relatable to worldwide audience instead of only catering to over zealous Indonesians (#adaindonesiacoy anyone?).The main theme of the game carries a strong message about mental health and it was delivered in a very beautiful manner. The allegorical representation of mental states in the form of fantastical elements in the game is spot on. It may have several plot holes (I won't state them to spare you the spoilers. ASFTU is best played cold, neither knowing nor expecting anything from it), but who cares? The overarching message is much more important than the petty details.Gameplay is very simple. While you can control the main character using multiple buttons, most of the interactions will remind players of old school point-and-click adventures, akin to the Monkey Island series. It does get a bit more variation as the game goes, with the Ace Attorney-style court gameplay and the obviously Street Fighter II inspired battle sessions. They remain simple, but they get the game running smoothly enough. Some mechanics like the stealth scenes can be a bit repetitive and even annoying, but never to the point of you yelling at your monitor.Graphics can only be described by one word: gorgeous. Makoto Shinkai and Ghibli-level gorgeous. Sure, not everyone may like the old school pixel art style, but I guess it was a creative choice which, for me personally who grew up with pixellated PS1 RPGs, paid off immensely. And I suppose ASFTU's intended market is exactly my profile: millenials growing up during the 90s. I always consider that Ghibli's strength is in its attention to detail, and ASFTU definitely shines on this one. Cigarette ads, postal boxes, Javanese blangkon, the details in the game is fascinating. Music is an achievement of its own. I do not think it is the best video game music I have had, but it's still a strong and memorable soundtrack. More than anything, it fits the scenes and themes of the game nicely. Slipping some traditional instrument and musical styles to some of its music is well appreciated. The theme songs also resonate to me as strongly "Indonesian indie music", with all the best meanings that come with the term.Overall, if you like gorgeous pixel art and narrative-driven games with a great and tear-jerking story, ASFTU is definitely for you. It just so happens that the story happens in Indonesia during the 90s; for some people that is reason enough to grab this game.

_childDocuments_.review: I’m conflicted.  I don’t quite know how to feel after finishing A Space for the Unbound.  I sure knew what I would be getting myself into when approaching Mojiken’s (of Banyu Lintar Angin and When the Past was Around fame) newest narrative piece, but I’ll be honest, by the time I was done I was concerned.  There’s a lot of things I found wrong and a lot of things that I didn’t like.  But like Atma’s and Raya’s journey: We see something in its worst, but must bear through the experiences to see the light at the end of the tunnel.  And let me tell you, A Space for the Unbound, despite all its flaws, is worth playing.I don’t want to delve too hard into the plot because the less you know about it the more interesting everything later becomes.  For Atma, a high school student with an aspiration to become a writer, and Raya, his better half with supernatural talents and personality, their lives become a topsy-turvy road to self-discovery and self-understanding baked into a point-and-click style based in a slice-of-life 1990s Indonesia.You’ll rummage around your small rural town in a 2D side scroll, taking in the sights with Mojiken’s beautiful pixel art.  Each section of the town is bursting with color, lovingly handcrafted with a real passion to show off the best qualities of a tightly knit community.  When we start getting into the meat and potatoes of the story, the double shots of beauty continue with a vast range of different areas, each providing an incredible amount of emotion that really sucks you into each frame.  These moments start off fast and furious, as a beautiful intro scene after a tense moment of mystery ties our shoes extra tight for the long road ahead.  From here, you get to learn about the hustle and bustle of the town around you: populated schoolyards and cramped storefronts to internet cafes and multi-theater megaplexes. The town is about 10 or so areas, which you’ll get used to quickly as the main story does not deviate too far from here.The art department really flexes their muscles in conjunction with Unbound’s main plot mechanic: The Spacedive.  Spacediving, done from reading through a mysterious red book that doubles as your Map/Inventory/etc. Hub, allows you to delve into the minds of townsfolk and use intellect and puzzle-solving to help solve internal struggles within the person.  Spacediving puzzles are usually small 1-2 step processes to complete and none are ever too difficult to complete.  The design of gathering items for objectives by fiddling with people’s heads is a very interesting, albeit exploitative mechanic (one the game fully realizes at a certain point).  Need chocolate for a cake but the general store is sold out?  Get the kid who’s hounding it to like veggies more ala a puzzle literally tipping the scales of obsessing to a healthier alternative.  Trying to get someone to stop making fake apocalypse necklaces?  Make him love his kid more!  I’m not kidding.Spacediving is leaned on a lot to move the story throughout its 11-13hr runtime, which becomes a lingering problem as the game progresses.  With Spacediving being used to gather items, a lot of time is spent solely in fetch-quest loops for the majority of the game.  You’ll be provided a list of what items you need, run around town at a brisk-not-fast pace, find the item but realize it’s blocked by something or someone.  You’ll then Spacedive to complete a character-specific puzzle that lasts roughly 2-3 minutes to get the item.  You’ll repeat this process a couple more times to gather the group of items you need to complete the main objective.  And then you’ll do it again.  And again.  And again.  The core gameplay loop is this and it stretches the game to the point of snapping.What makes this even more aggravating is that there’s some good plot development squeezed in between forced filler.  You’ll get 30-40 minutes of some focused character development and tantalizing crumbs to future prospects of current actions, the chapter will end, and then you’ll do the fetch-quest loop for another 2 hours before you can get back into it.  It’s like the game forces you to complete every side-quest in order to play the main mission.  And while the fetch-quests serve their purpose in providing context and buildup to the task at hand, there’s just too much of it that it deflates the tension of each chapter’s cliffhanger with such a long cooldown period.Unbound, funny enough, does have side quests to do as well.  These side quests are tied to the main plotline of the game.  Side quests like collecting certain items require a keen eye around random spots of the town, completing off-beat fetch-quests around random interactions from citizens, and naming cats that are placed randomly around the town.  These things are missable in specific chapters, so you can see the molasses-like speed this game takes when you’re expected to talk to every person in every part of town while looking for every sparkle on the ground and finding every cat while going through the fetch-quests above just to get a morsel of the main plot, and then doing it again for the 4 of the 6 chapters.  I was about halfway through the game when I started to just lose interest, which I guess I only have myself to blame when I realized all of the above is tied to a secret ending and if you miss anything you don’t get the epilogue and you just have to play the whole game over again and not miss anything.  Tall ask.But, after all this: why am I recommending A Space for the Unbound?  Because if you get past the first 4 chapters and get to the leaner, more focused final 2 chapters: you’ll be rewarded with some of the most heart-wrenching, tear-inducing, spirit-lifting writing you’ll get this year.  I cannot express how well the story pays off in the final act, I sat speechless for the last few hours as questions were answered and ends were tied.  It made everything I’ve talked about worth every moment of it, and the impeccable writing, the vibrant art filled with an ungodly amount of personality, and the musical score to tie it all in…dude I can’t even explain it.  It’s so ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ good.  It fires on all cylinders and slams it home so well that it almost makes me feel bad about how much I did not enjoy the rest of the game.So here I am.  I’m conflicted.  I don’t quite know how to feel after finishing A Space for the Unbound.  The first half of the game is a disastrous case of doing-too-much to keep you in your seat: repetitive objectives, an overabundance of similar puzzles, and missable items that can ruin the full experience of the story if not found.  But the final third puts together a narrative tour de force of emotion and the quality of the writing, tempo, and atmosphere is something that should be celebrated at year’s end.  I fully endorse taking the time to experience this story, just know the long road ahead will be worth it.

Perhaps the biggest gripe most people will likely have is that the "puzzles" require a lot of backtracking and "fetch quests". That said, some certainly tickled the brain more than others and I had a fair bit of fun with. Other mechanics are clearly inspired from other games such as classic fighting games and even Ace Attorney. The spacedive mechanic is also pretty unique and feels reminiscent of Inception (one of my personal fav movies). Run time is pretty decent for the price point at about 8-10 hours. It's absolutely worth picking up.

_childDocuments_.review: A Space for the Unbound opens with a fairytale, one about friendship, loss, and self-acceptance that quickly frames a big-brother relationship between small town teenager Atma and budding storyteller Nirmala. Soon, Atma is thrust out of his routine and into a dream-induced series of surreal breaks in reality, forcing him to find the truth about the many people in his quaint waterfront city and his supposed girlfriend Raya. A Space for the Unbound spares no time creating a suspenseful mystery adventure, but paces its 11 hour runtime with surprisingly emotional and complex beats that tell a larger narrative that culminates in one of the more subtle powerhouses of 2023.Mainly, A Space for the Unbound takes the form of a traditional point and click adventure game, running around the small, but dense town in order to pick up various items and clues to progress your investigation into the truth behind strange events. Apart from the standard dialogue and item interactions, Atma can use an ability called Spacedive, which allows him to inhabit the subconscious mind of its target and change their heart not unlike the Persona series. In contrast to the charming tight-knit community of the town, Spacedives present a more raw and unhinged interpretation of the psyche of your neighbors and enemies. Many of the game's most inventive ideas are explored within the depths of the mind and Atma as a vessel for change transforms him into an engaging protagonist, especially as he begins to consider if changing the desires of those around him is manipulative and wrong. The entire game wrestles with difficult moral dillemmas and despite a seemingly singular ending, the game give you the shadow of choice and agency.One of the most staggering elements of A Space for the Unbound is in its presentation; a gorgeous rendition of 1980s Indonesia portrayed in a variety of pixel art setpieces and sonic landscapes. The soundtrack is an absolute standout, with incredible range from catchy earworms to heart-wrenching supporting pieces to the game's heavier moments. The dialogue is a masterclass in realistic conversation, while not losing some goofy and downright hilarious beats of writing (a standout is a quiz-obsessed trio of fellow students). The only exception to the game's flawless exterior is a lack of voice acting, which in my opinion could have been the setup to one of the most incredible performances in games.A Space for the Unbound is not a game I really want to talk much about in premise. It's much more worth taking it all in on blind faith and discovering the charm on your own terms. Whether you fall in love with the charming cast or just like one of the many side activities like collecting bottle caps or petting every cat, there is a lot to love with this game, and it's something you need to check off your bucket list.

_childDocuments_.review: Wow... as a person who had similar family dynamics to Raya, and had that one dear, kind, patient friend who changed the trajectory of my life... I'm blown away. This game hit me HARD towards the end when everything becomes clear. Gameplay, sure, it was fun to collect things, pet animals, figure out puzzles, get achievements. Yes, sometimes the fights do feel a little bit long, but not so much that it feels like I'm wasting my time, and besides, the game makes you forget about the gameplay, because the story is just that engaging. Was it confusing at the beginning? Maybe, but it's very obvious from the beginning that reality and your perception of it is... off, and that mystery is what drives the plot forward. It's weird that some reviewers state this as if it's a detriment to the game when it's literally just... the story/plot that was already established. Like most games of this genre, all becomes clear the more you progress.If you enjoy adventure games and are seeking an emotional, heartfelt story with a little bit of a mystery, play this game. It deserves all the good reviews.

_childDocuments_.review: Is this game a masterpiece? Hm, no, but quite a soulful adventure.The mechanics are simple - walk left or right (or inside houses) and interact with hotspots using a dial with the available options - examine, talk, interact, use with an object from the inventory. You move rather slow (running is possible) and you can't jump, this is not a platformer. You carry a book with you that contains your current objectives, a map, your inventory and your collectibles.The story is taking place in Indonesia and shows a little of the life there, which is always interesting for me as a Westener. You play a young boy, still going to high school, who awakes from a dream and is now doing what kids do in this age, like skipping school to meet with his girlfriend Raya. You pet every cat you find (kicking them is not even possible), talk to everyone, collect various items either to use in puzzles later or just as collectibles. Collectibles are often at remote edges, but they flash so they are easier to spot. You flirt with other girls, build a cat shelter, meet a bully... but somehow you sense that it is not all as beautiful and perfect as it looks. When humans turn into cat zombies and you begin to spacedive into other people's mind, the story becomes a bit... darker.The game works fine with controller, the puzzles are not too difficult (also due to the limited interface - there are not THAT many options to try out).Wholesome, slow adventure, that is a BIT more doleful than it looks at first sight. With lots of cats. And you might weep.

_childDocuments_.review: I have to say this is probably one of the best psychological adventure game I've ever played. The part that always amazes me is the story. This is not just a good game with good story; this is A STORY that portrayed beautifully into a game.There are more than just story. It was so sad that I'm in tears, but I'm also relieved that I was able to finish the story. It was heartwarming even if it was very hard and we had to go through many traumatic events. It's just like in real life where we always have to move on, no matter how hard it is or how painful it's gonna get. I could relate to the psychological side of the story that basically told us that even if everything is a mess, we could always be brave, sort out our minds, and move on. I could say for sure that the story is the best part of this game.I really love the fact that this game is not just a simple 2D sidescroller. It has a lot of cool mechanics that make this game unique in its own way.The first thing I'd like to mention is The Rift. I like how they implement a time-travel mechanic into a rift that could be opened by a Magic Wand. It allowed us to travel through dimensions and timelines. I remember playing a game that had this advanced time-travel mechanic just like this. It's called The Silent Age and it was a very good game. Since then, I can never get enough of this amazing mechanic that actually has influence on what would happen in the future if we change the past. This is one of the best time-travel mechanic I encountered in a game, and this game has managed to implement it perfectly.Spacedive is also a great mechanic. I like how they portrayed the inside of people's mind in the spacedive world. It looked so random but it's actually a great representation of how the thoughts conflicting in their own heads. It subtly explained the depression and the desperation that the people experienced through the stories and mission we should accomplish as the player that go through their minds.There are more interesting mechanics in the game, but The Rift and Spacedive definitely are unique in the game and I really like those.I'm not an art person. I can't draw, I can't sing, I can't play music. However, I can say for sure that this pixel-art with calming music is a perfect combination that blends sweetly with the story. I really LOVE the environment in the game! The setting of this game is in a city called Loka. Loka City is a very beautiful small town with neatly lined local houses; stalls; shops that always stock all the necessities; bridge; beautiful trees and flowers; a community center with a mosque, internet cafe, arcade, etc. For those of you who live in Indonesia, this Loka City is set to be located in Indonesia. So it was a very familiar environment that brings us to nostalgia. I also recommend to play in Indonesian Language if you speak that language, it feels much more authentic.Cats are always the winner. The fact that they chose to put cats in this game is such a great decision. It's a perfect addition to the game! Animals are always the best, cats especially. They also put dog, rooster, hen, rat, goose, duck, and finally the legend Kebo Bule and Barong. We can pet them, name them, and they also played a big part in the game.I love puzzles. Puzzles are always one of the best elements in a game. I always like to solve a puzzle. Unfortunately, no matter how much I like puzzles, this is a bit tiring for me. There are no multiple ways to solve the puzzle, which means most puzzles only has a single solution. And this becomes tiring because completing an objective takes a long time and needs to go through so many steps. Those are actually good puzzles. But one chapter for one puzzle? I ended up got tired that I almost didn't want to do the objectives anymore. There's this objective that needs to be done in a very long way and took a surprisingly very long steps: the single objective in Chapter 2. The rest is still fine, I guess. But this puzzle in Chapter 2 took too long to solve, because it went to another objective, and onto the other objectives, again and again to the point it became tiring.Nevertheless, I still like how the story turned out, and it blends well with the objectives and puzzles. So, I guess this will only be a small criticism for this game. I still like it though, don't get me wrong. But yeah, that Chapter 2 puzzle is something else for me.This game is a masterpiece, I could say for sure. I encountered a crucial bug that wouldn't let me finish this game because I really couldn't progress. However, the Dev Team contacted me and give a really helpful solution to install a beta patch in order to fix the bug. I sincerely appreciate the Dev Team for responding to me and actually give a proper solution. Apart from that bug (and maybe the puzzles I mentioned), this is a very good game. The story is told beautifully. It has a perfect execution of how a story-rich adventure game should be. And the cats! Those are the great "addition" which made the game flawless.

_childDocuments_.review: Mojiken's New Game: Hype High, Delivery...Not So MuchOkay, Mojiken fans, gather 'round. Let's talk about their latest release, shall we? I jumped on this bandwagon the week it dropped (i think), fueled by Mojiken magic from past games. I was hyped, picture me bouncing off the walls like a caffeinated chihuahua. The art? Gorgeous. The music? Banging. The whole vibe? Perfection personified. I was ready to devour this game whole.And devour I did...the first few minutes, anyway. But then, I hit a snag. It wasn't the gameplay (though let's be honest, it wasn't exactly groundbreaking). It was the dialogue. Oh, the dialogue. Longwinded monologues that felt like reading Tolstoy after chugging five espressos. The structure? Wonky in both English and Bahasa, like a sentence got lost in Google Translate and returned wearing clown shoes.Look, I tried. I switched languages like a frantic tourist, hoping one would click. I pushed through, fueled by my initial excitement and a desperate hope for redemption. But alas, the dialogue was a dragon I couldn't slay. It just kept droning on, sucking the joy out of the game like a Dementor with a thesaurus.So, I tapped out right around the time Atma woke up in the school and started chatting with Raya. Dialogue coma, I tell you. Maybe someday, when the Baldur's Gate itch is scratched, the Valorant dailies are done, and Skyrim's frozen wastes have lost their allure, and the lure of taming cute yet deadly beasties in Palworld has faded, I'll give this Mojiken gem another go. Who knows, maybe with fresh eyes and a pot of strong tea, I'll unlock the secrets of its wordy world. Until then, it slumbers on my backlog shelf, a beautiful mystery waiting to be unraveled. And mark my words, if that day ever comes and the game redeems itself in my eyes, I promise I'll be back to rewrite this review with a chorus of praise. Until then, consider this a placeholder, a testament to my ever-growing backlog and the ever-present hope that hidden gems still await discovery.

_childDocuments_.review: "Whispers of Remembrance: An Sojourn in 'A Space for the Unbound"In the labyrinth of our minds, memories lie scattered like fractured glass, each piece a reminder of past pain and buried emotions. "A Space for the Unbound" invites players to delve into this inner landscape, confronting their deepest fears and finding solace in the act of self-discovery.The game's narrative serves as a poignant exploration of the human psyche, touching on themes of identity, trauma, and the power of self-acceptance. Through the eyes of its protagonists, players are taken on a journey of introspection and growth, where the facade of mental wellness gives way to the raw, unfiltered truth of their innermost selves.At its core, "A Space for the Unbound" delivers a powerful message about the nature of healing and the importance of confronting one's past. The protagonist's struggle with high school bullying and the subsequent suppression of painful memories resonates deeply with anyone who has grappled with trauma. The game's portrayal of the protagonist's journey towards acceptance is both heartfelt and impactful, reminding players that true healing comes from acknowledging and embracing their pain.But "A Space for the Unbound" is more than just a tale of overcoming adversity; it's also a celebration of life's simple joys and the beauty of human connection. From baking cakes to petting cats, the game's charming moments of nostalgia serve as a reminder that even in the darkest of times, there is light to be found.In contrast to other media that may approach bullying from a more realistic or societal perspective, "A Space for the Unbound" offers a unique and deeply personal exploration of the subject matter. Through its blend of introspective storytelling and interactive gameplay mechanics, the game provides players with a space for reflection and self-discovery.In the end, "A Space for the Unbound" is a testament to the resilience of the human spirit and the transformative power of self-acceptance. As players journey through the game's emotional landscape, they are reminded that while the road to healing may be fraught with challenges, it is also filled with moments of beauty, tenderness, and hope. So open the door, embrace your true self, and let the journey begin.

_childDocuments_.review: Much like South Korea has been very effectively exporting music, telly shows and more to a wider global audience for some years now, Southeast Asia is on a roll when it comes to . I'd go out and wager that  and others will continue to spearhead this for years to come. 's non-linearly told story puts you in control of a high school student who collaborates with his girlfriend on a bucket list of things to do before graduation, and then  and it's into figuring out what's going on: is the world ending, are there parallel universes, who is the real villain, and other questions that come up in your typical young-adult-with-superpowers story. At the same time, you get to meet plenty of town inhabitants and help them solve various problems.The developers manage not only to convey the distinct culture, architecture, lifestyle of Indonesia in the age before ubiquitous cellphones, but also to always keep the experience and character relationships perfectly relatable for a global audience. Expect to find mentions of various dishes of the local cuisine, though usually without explanation as to what they actually are or how they taste.The gameplay itself consists of walking (or usually running) through game screens with the arrow keys and interacting with everything around. Getting to all the right places in town will have you memorize the layout (or frequently consult the ingame map). There's a timed action system used frequently, which for the majority of the game is not too difficult. Objectives usually just amount to doing the right thing in the right place, with occasional puzzles to clue together from nearby items.As you would expect, as you interact with the world and the characters, you learn the various NPCs backstories and their worries (that you might help address). Especially the central more fleshed out ones will remain vivid in your mind. The game's themes include family, friendship, bullying, forgiveness, self-discovery. From time to time, there is this unfortunate game design antipattern that I call the "", heavily used in Odyssey and Valhalla so they can pretend they qualify as RPGs: in a conversation you get to pick between two or very rarely three mutually exclusive options that result in maybe two or three lines of dialogue without any other further impact or relevance, and there is no way to access the lines hidden behind the choice you did not take (beyond reloading the latest save and perhaps replaying a few minutes of the game).Depending on your pace and completionism levels, I'd estimate 8–12 hours to finish the game. While you cannot alter how the story unfolds, the bucket list mechanic essentially amounts to missable Steam Achievements. At the time of writing, only about a seventh of the users who finished the story also did everything else (to reach the "true ending"). For that, you truly must play with a guide at hand to know where to find collectibles (cats to pet, and name!, as well as bottle caps of Indonesian drinks) and when to go look for some other NPCs. At least one of these achievements is also frustratingly difficult: in the town's arcade, the previously mentioned timed action system has you execute fighting game combos with very tight timing. Theoretically you could write them down or memorize them ahead of time, but neither is a pleasant idea. The arcade machine is only accessible in the first third or so of the game, and successfully braving this challenge will make most of the other upcoming timed input sequences feel like a walk in the park. There is another slightly frustrating achievement where you must press the interact button with the right rhythm 70 times, and if you exceed 50 but don't reach 70 you have to reload your latest save. (I used  and additionally  and using those avoided what I would consider excessive story spoilers.)I think even the song interludes you get from time to time are missable, so only a fraction of players (again judging by achievement stats) have even reached them.Personally, I wasn't a particular fan of where the overall story went about halfway through the game (from chapter 4 on), but as I don't think my complaints will be shared by too many readers, I won't hold it against the game.I would recommend the game to people who enjoy touching storytelling and don't mind QTE-like action & dodging sequences. Pretty much every time you interact with a cat (or other animal) in town, you get a little speech bubble with a heart emoticon, so if you find that sort of thing heartwarming, go and press that buy button.However,  does not attempt to be /. If you want to solve truly complex puzzles, abhor any real-time keyboarding challenges, expect laugh-out-loud comedy, or want either a branching story or otherwise non-linear gameplay, you won't find these here.

_childDocuments_.review: I just finished a space for the unbound yesterday, and my heart still feels heavy. I found myself relating to Raya on some way. I shed tears multiple times, and each moment touched my heart in unexpected ways. The endgame in particular was the peak of emotion for me. As the story progressed to its climax, my tears poured uncontrollably, capturing emotions that i can't quite explainThere's something about it that struck me. Maybe it because of the plot or just simply because it was set in Indonesia. It felt eerily familiar as if it reflected some of my own experiences.Accepting things as they are has always been one of the hardest things for me. I often find myself trapped in a situation where I still yearning for the past, unable to fully embrace the present because I can't let go of what once was. There's a comfort in the past, in the memories that I simply refuse to let go—that those moments were gone. I realize now that it's this refusal—this stupidity to accept that leaving me stuck in a state of limboIn hindsight, my ignorance was the root of this mess. Instead of accepting that the past cannot be changed, I clung to the pleasant recollections of what once was and made a valiant effort to bring them back. Though deep down, I knew it was simply impossible to make things "go back to how they used to be" to mend things and this denial of reality only led to more pain and suffering because I'm just struggling to accept that some things are out of control and that's completely okay.I remember reading this quote somewhere, It sounds like "healing come when you allow it to happen". Perhaps, I was so profoundly wounded and could not see a way out, I wrote off this thought as naive at the time. I know it may sound stupid but there was a part of me that refuse to heal—that I don't mind feel this way for god knows how long. Perhaps I was afraid of what's coming on would entail, of having to let go of the old pain's comfort.However, I've been making an effort lately to be more accepting of the idea. I've been trying to accept that the past is the past and clinging to it would only hinder my growth. I've come to understand that it's simply not just unhealthy but also unfair to myself to keep living in the shadow of what once was.From this game, I've learned that no matter how much we cherish the past, It reminds me that I eventually have to let it go. The difficulty of clinging to memories we hold dear and the significance of moving on are both captured beautifully in the game. I have to let go of what once was and just can't linger there anymore. No matter uncertain the future may seem, I have to welcome the present and the future. For what's past is pastI could go on and on about this game but I'm afraid to say too much because I don't want to spoil the story to you who haven't played it yet. With all of its nuances and intricacies, best experienced firsthand. It's more than just a game, it's a journey of self discovery, acceptance, and ultimately, healing. I'll remember this story for a very long time because for the lack of better term, beautiful.

_childDocuments_.review: It's a nice and well-written game whose premise has been seen before and you can make out in the prologue, but it's still handled very well. A typical adventure game fare of doing things in the right order with specific items, but the story and its pacing is the driving force to completion and the world(s) is(/are) charming that it's a nice escape into modern era Indonesia with very well done music. The art direction itself as well as the subtle detailing within the pixel art with animations and impacts add nice touches of life which can look very simplified even for pixel art at points but enough detail is there to place emphasis on the emotional points of the game that the game shines from.It can take until the second or third chapter for things to start rolling, especially if you're aware of the type of 'game based on depression and anxiety in a cutesy aesthetic' genre of adventure games, but it's a charming and well-written indie title that's worth a playthrough or two.At the point of whether you'd want to play it would come down to how well you like slice-of-life, supernatural vibe-y adventure games before the story can hook you in.

_childDocuments_.review: A Space for the Unbound is a very, very beautiful game.The pixel art is outstandingly gorgeous, and manages to shine both in countryside landscapes and more surreal environments. The colors are both vibrant and nostalgic, and I particularly liked that the shading was done with pink instead of black. The sound design is also really good, and the music excellent.The story is good, yet not exceptional. It truly kicks in a quite late, and sometimes felt a little """"""easy"""""" if that makes sense, but what was there was done well -especially with the side-characters. The whole supernatural part is very good, if not very present in the early game. Special applause for the dev team who hired a psychology consultant. Real cool!The gameplay however…So much, way too much of this game is just running back and forth to trigger events so Atma can pick the damn things off the ground, or open a door, or a lock. Yes the world is beautiful, but I wish it was more linear or the map clearer because I got lost so often. The last three acts seldom have this problem, but the first three are a slog to go through Overall, this game should accept to be slightly shorter. We would all be better for it.A Space for the Unbound is, before all, unpolished. Still a bit rough, a bit jagged around the edges, but the jankiness almost makes it all the more endearing. It was made with love, for the characters and the obviously real people who inspired them, for the craft, and for Indonesia about which I learned a lot playing this game. If not a perfect time, it was a lovely one.

_childDocuments_.review: I wish I could give this game a thumbs up, I really wish I could. Not only because of the fact that it's an indie game where obvious effort and love was put into it, but also the music and atmosphere are really beautiful and moving. And you don't often see Indonesia as a location for video games, so representation is really great as you learn more about different cultures and realities of life that aren't always Eurocentric or Western-oriented. However, as the game progressed, I found several things to be visibly annoying until they completely detracted from the gaming experience and I just wanted it to come to an end merely for the sake of finishing it. Overall, it felt like a complete chore to me and my completionist maniac mind had to get it done with.Although the prologue and the first chapter were more than promising, the fetch-quests-esque features of the game got on my nerves very quickly. You are transported from one place to the next with forced routes for a lot of the time, the dialogues are not really profound, the game mechanics are exhausting and tedious after a while and even the story, which is actually quite profound and emotional, was not really innovative or earth-shattering to me. It doesn't have to be, but I couldn't really empathize with the characters, especially the protagonist Atma. He seems a bit passive and pseudo-heroic in everything and I couldn't really come to terms with this narrative. The game is artificially drawn out and the gameplay quickly becomes repetitive and boring. The worst thing for me was the fact that the game often doesn't even take my manual save into account and simply transports me to where it was automatically saved for the last time. I constantly had to intuitively assess when I could leave the game for good to avoid having to replay certain events and dialogues that had already taken place. I often don't have the attention span to play games for that long at a time, especially when I get bored with the gameplay and am forced to continue until the next chapter or checkpoint (neither of which I can predict). The game had nice aspects and features, but unfortunately it wasn't for me.
