_childDocuments_.review: The art and music are gorgeous. The story is so rich. So many "your choices matter" games are lying or overselling and since those sort of psychological implications are my favorite kind of games I find that really frustrating. But gotdangit Pentiment makes it HARD to do the right thing, the wrong thing, the smart thing, the saucy thing, the faithful thing, all the things... The writing is brilliant and I think it's because it is so deeply human. The story taps into a lot of really powerful emotions as it builds this little world around you. Sometimes it's hard simply because you're in a small town and people talk. The creators went for historical accuracy and tapped into so much of the human psyche by including so many little aspects of us and it made me uncomfy sometimes. And so the outcomes aren't always obvious. At least not in the first play through I thought.At times walking around to talk to everyone and make sure I had *all* the info could be a little tedious, but you don't even have to. Your choices are yours. And it's a small world so you're not going very far anyway. The scrolling is smooth and again the art is stunning. You can always stop to talk to a neighbor (or pet a cat or dog!!!) and sometimes those stops are more fruitful than initially anticipated.Aside from the main character, all the side characters are well thought out and developed. They all have a purpose. They are consistent as the story progresses. Their development makes sense. The dialogue is well written and gives each character their own voice. The more you talk to them, the more you see it. I like the changing scripts and typefaces in the speech bubbles, it's a wonderful touch. The corrections to letters is a small thing but those little details are part of what makes the game so rich. It is an extremely well researched historical setting (with references!!!!) and just utterly delightful for a medieval manuscript and early printed book nerd. I'm definitely going to play it again (and probably again and again and...) to see what changes as I pick different traits and snark at different people.And because I have to pet all the cats and dogs again.
_childDocuments_.name: Pentiment

_childDocuments_.review: I really really wanted to enjoy this game. Like others have posted, the first 1-2 hours of the game really seems to pull you in and make you think there are some larger RPG mechanics at work, but alas, there are not.It desperately tries to succeed in the way that Disco Elysium did but falls short.The artwork is great, but the story just drags and drags and drags. There is no reward for exploration, youend up longing for the end of the end of the game. Its about 6 hours too long. I am 11 hours in and still not at the end of the game. I really want to finish but at this point it is incredibly boring.
_childDocuments_.name: Pentiment

_childDocuments_.review: Pentiment is a fresh, authentic gaming experience that really impressed me.If you have even just an inkling of interest in history, it's 100x even more incredible.The setting is grounded, well-researched, educational, and wonderfully immersive - you really feel like you're stepping into the lives of ordinary people in the 1500s.The game has a decent mystery, but don't come in expecting a full-blown detective game. The story is the main focus.I was pleasantly surprised by the ways my choices had consequences.There's a lot of tedious walking from point A to point B.
_childDocuments_.name: Pentiment

_childDocuments_.review: An amazing point and click murder mystery.At first i was interested in the game because it was DiScO eLyIsIuM iN tHe MiDdLe AgEs. This is kinda like that but more lore oriented. And the characters are great.You will love this if you are a medieval history nerd. There is a lot of text though, so don't play this if you can't read
_childDocuments_.name: Pentiment

_childDocuments_.review: It took a bit for me to get into, I'll be honest. Everything about this world is dripping with historical detail that I couldn't hope to fully comprehend. But when the ball got rolling, I cared deeply for this little town and its inhabitants, its rich history and how that relates to the ongoing string of crimes. This was a truly wonderful experience, and I feel wiser for having played it.A criticism I've heard is that your choices don't matter, so I hope anyone going into this game understands one thing: yes, there is a linear narrative at play that will not be derailed despite your actions. However, all decisions, from the choices of the main character's background and personality to the simple conversations with townsfolk to the big accusations at various climactic points, allow each player to slightly influence how the town looks in future acts, discover secrets that they otherwise wouldn't have, and above all else, immerse themselves in and engage with the game in a way that feels completely personal. That type of player freedom speaks to me far more than adding several different story routes that exist only for the sake of replay value, and in that way I think this game's choices matter just fine.
_childDocuments_.name: Pentiment

_childDocuments_.review: Perhaps the best game I have played all year. The clear love of history, attention to detail and historical accuracy really makes this a must buy for any history nerd. The storytelling is magnificent, with complex moral quandaries and difficult choices, and few right answers that really makes you think about your decision making. The dialogue system is extremely fun and witty and Obsidian manages to thread the needle on making Andreas both his own distinct character beyond a blank slate for the player, while also giving the player the ability to make their own unique version of Andreas, the background and education selections are a stroke of genius in this regard, giving Andreas different worldviews to pull off, every Andreas believes they are doing the right thing by trying to solve the mystery and attempting to save the day, yet an Andreas who spent his years in Switzerland reading books and studying imperial law and an Andreas who spent time travelling through Italy studying the Occult and getting into fights will have completely different understandings of why what they are doing is right.  Pentiment is a game of deep meaning, elegant storytelling, complex themes and thoughtful characters in a package that I believe is the best story certainly of any game this year at least.The art style of the game is exquisite and really manages to capture and evoke the imagery and style of early modern woodcuts, early print and medieval manuscript artistry. The dialogue bubbles themselves, with each character having a unique font based on their social class and Andreas' perception of them is fantastic at giving characters a sense of identity without any VO, and the sound of quill on vellum parchment is like ASMR (tho this may be a turnoff for some). If all this can't convince you of Obsidian's attention to detail then this should, they have period accurate pigs! yes that's right proper long snouted tusked trotters take the stage, none of that modern short-snouted ♥♥♥♥♥. Now that is proper attention to detail.Always been wondering whether that knowledge of banned french religious books, obscure latin sayings, or complex medieval bavarian inheritance laws would ever come in handy? Then Pentiment is the game for you!
_childDocuments_.name: Pentiment

_childDocuments_.review: I've been intrigued by the art style since Pentiment's release but before playing I was a little hesitant of the game, enough so to leave it on my wishlist up until it was gifted to me by a friend. However, as soon as I started I was immeadiately hooked, the excellent writing you can expect from an Obsidian title really shines through, and I found myself caring about almost every minor character I ran across no matter their station or social standing. The art style continues to be a delight, and the references to European history feel rewarding if you're at all familiar with it. The choices & consequences mechanic is well implemented as well, requiring you to organically piece together what might be an important interaction and to whom but letting you know right after that it was to someone, and when the time comes where their views of you matter in how the plot develops you are reminded of the interactions that caused them to view you in this way.If you are at all intrigued by the premise or just looking for a good dialogue and character driven mystery adventure, Pentiment will reward you.
_childDocuments_.name: Pentiment

_childDocuments_.review: Several times in the game people quote, "blessed are those that believe but do not see." And I can't think of a better way to describe a game that gives you puzzles to solve but never a solution. As the characters in the game are beset with doubt, whether that be doubt in a higher power, a loved one, or oneself, so too is the player left to question the choices that they make. Many times will you make a choice that relies on faith without having clear sight, and as the narrative unfolds, you'll question your faith in yourself when the results of your actions aren't perhaps what you intended- but never unfair. For the game to click, you have to abandon yourself to faith- and like so many in the game and in our everyday lives, quiet your doubts in pursuit of a higher ideal.
_childDocuments_.name: Pentiment

_childDocuments_.review: A lovingly painted VN-style game in which the words are literally handwritten before your eyes.A thoughtful adventure, played in front of the tectonic plates of history, in which thoughts, feelings, and conversations are more important than clicking on an object.Pet a dog or a cat, pick flowers, fall in love, tell people off when they need it.  Bravo.
_childDocuments_.name: Pentiment

_childDocuments_.review: Taking place in an old Alpine town across generations of inhabitants, Pentiment has players engage with the local history, customs, and people to not only solve mysteries currently plaguing the inhabitants of Tassing, but discover the complex and evolving nature of History.  Pentiment does intersperse minigames to diversify the gameplay, but at its core it is a beautifully artistic narrative focused role-playing game so players should expect a lot of dialog with the citizens in gorgeous scenery. While an amazing experience, players should be aware that there's not enough time to do everything in a singe play through, as the first acts are time limited to several in-game days leading to a feeling of playing under pressure. However, by the end of the journey, you'll doubtfully will want to play again to see how things could be different.
_childDocuments_.name: Pentiment

_childDocuments_.review: I really enjoyed this game, although I felt like Act 3 was really drawn out with not a lot of game play. If you like the Enlightenment period, you'll enjoy this game. Lots of history, religious information, art, etc. I could tell while playing that the devs researched a ton for this game.This game was a bit of a beast to stream just because of how much dialogue there was. I wouldn't recommend it for streaming personally because of that, my throat hurt after every stream. However, genuinely really enjoyed the game, the mystery, etc.
_childDocuments_.name: Pentiment

_childDocuments_.review: I believe it is now safe to call the novel a dated vehicle for good fiction writing.I've been playing Obsidian/Troika/Black Isle games for a long time and if you have too, you also enjoy an engaging and immersive story book-ended by some clever rpg gameplay.   This is just a a story with dialogue choices exactly like you would expect from a great game by these folks, only instead of bookending it with throwing abilities and attacks at an endless array of random foes, they have left it to just be a story.  Having the world to walk around in also reminds me a lot of point-n-click adventure games from the 90s, but the story is a lot more linear than those kind of games.But getting back to my original claim, Pentiment is not just a great story, it is a wonderful piece of writing, a highly researched historical fiction which immerses the reader in the time period just like Kingdom Come: Deliverance, but with even less fudging to make it a fun game.  It is full of allegory and historical observations.  The art is simple but highly effective.  The effects uncomplex, but well done.I think, maybe, this might have been designed to be portable.  You could easily play this on a steam deck on a bus trip like reading a book.  My only complaint is that the kbm setup is kind of clunky.  I usually play with a controller, but its not an action game so it doesn't really matter if its clunky.
_childDocuments_.name: Pentiment

_childDocuments_.review: I really love history and also mystery games, and this is an amazing combo of both. The amount of detail that went into this game is incredible, from the art style to the historical setting. The characters truly feel like real people. Amazing game 10/10 would recommend it for people who love stories about how things change over time and also solving murders
_childDocuments_.name: Pentiment

_childDocuments_.review: Pentiment gives the player a magnifying glass to look into how communities in the Middle Ages may have operated, into their ideas about science, religion, politics, and these people's reactions to their own history and how it formed their society over time. At face value, the game's characters look like your typical Medieval peasant, noble, priest, etc., yet I came to find each of them to have their own individual "voice", through the unique stylisation of each character's dialogue text and how they are written. I think this game shows that civilisation evolves not on a linear scale, but experiences a complex and variable growth. Wonderful game, but know it's not interesting for everyone (lots of reading and history)
_childDocuments_.name: Pentiment

_childDocuments_.review: Josh Sawyer and team have done an amazing job bringing to life this German medieval village. The art, writing, and sound effects are perfect.  The twists and turns in the story are are as engrossing as most of Obsidian/Black Isle Studios previous endeavors.  A great Story to unravel over a few nights of play and will have you reaching for Wikipedia more time than you can count.  Very well referenced and accurate source material.  It is my deepest hope they continue to use this art style in a future RPG set in the same realistic time and locale (Southern German, Prauge or Vienna.)
_childDocuments_.name: Pentiment

_childDocuments_.review: The sheer level of research, passion, and attention to detail in this game is brilliant. Pentiment practically oozez love and care from every mechanic, every asset, and every line of dialogue. The cast is large and varied, and even though the dialogue system is barebones compared to something like, say, Disco Elysium, it serves its purpose in allowing you to really immerse yourself in the village of Tassing, and allowing you to feel like you're a part of this little community. It's a real emotional journey, following these people over the course of 25 years, feeling the tumult of change in their lives as the Medieval period is gradually overtaken by the ideas of the Renaissance. The themes of legacy, guilt, and coping with change are woven into the story in a way that feels purposeful and natural.The advice I'd give to people playing Pentiment for the first time is much the same as the advice I'd give to someone playing Disco Elysium for the first time. Your goal in playing Pentiment should not be to win, or to maximise the efficiency of every interaction. It should not be to solve the mystery as quick as possible or to calculate your actions to always get the best outcomes. Although the mystery in Pentiment is well written and is fun to follow, and has a pretty solid resolution, it was not the high point of the game for me. Pentiment's real strength is in its characters and setting. Just engage with people, explore, and immerse yourself in this slice of 16th century life. The rest will follow.It's worth noting that, for a game set in a christian town in the 1500s, the commitment to showcasing marginalised and minority histories in Europe is really exceptional. This game is proof that being historically accurate and being diverse are not mutually exclusive, and in fact go hand-in-hand. Working women, Jewish people, queer people, and people of colour have always existed in Europe to some extent, and this game takes pains to highlight their experiences. I know this won't matter to many people, and that's fine, but as a queer person and a Jewish person, i can't really stress how refreshing it is to see my own identity reflected in a medium that so often ignores and sidelines minority perspectives.I would also be remiss to not talk about the level of research that went into the game. I am not a medieval scholar, so I'm not in a position to comment on the accuracy of small details, but the amount of care that went into depicting the everyday lives of peasants and of monks, as well as the wider political and social climate of the period is very very clear. Pentiment does not only use it's setting as an aesthetically interesting backdrop for it's story, but rather has baked it integrally into every aspect of its story and themes. Even small aspects of the UI - the glossary function made to look like an illuminated manuscript, the different typefaces used to reflect the backrounds and social caste of various characters, the measuring of time by the hours of prayer eventually changing to hours of the clock as Tassing is pulled into the modern era - go a long way towards making the player feel like they're really living through this story. And the tiny details of the dialogue boxes - the moment where the ink settles into the page, the times when characters make typos which they scratch out and correct, the way the ink splatters when a character is especially upset or emotional - I mean, they didn't have to do that. They aren't at all relevant to the plot and nobody would have noticed if they weren't there. But they did it anyways, because, for once, an AA studio decided to not cut corners, not prioritise scale over quality, and commit to putting thought, attention, and love into every detail of a game.This is the second steam review I've ever written, and was typed out in a frenzy after finishing the game. I'm not really a video game guy, so take some of this with a grain of salt. But like. ♥♥♥♥, guys. Go play Pentiment.
_childDocuments_.name: Pentiment

_childDocuments_.review: Not an art history buff, but the story was engaging enough to keep me going. _childDocuments_.name: Pentiment

_childDocuments_.review: Pentiment presents a rich and fascinating view of life in the 16th century. The art is beautiful, and there are a great many little touches placed throughout the game that sell the immersion. The story it tells is interesting, and puts a lot of nuance into each struggle. It is unafraid to let you make the incorrect choices (and somehow I made a lot of incorrect choices), but it does still hold you to an on-rails overarching plot and you will never miss the most important pieces.My only major complaint with the game is that of the bugs. As you are presented with a staggering number of choices throughout the game, it is inevitable that there will be a slip-up somewhere. But in Pentiment, characters often reference events which never happened and discoveries that were never made. It was rather frustrating every time I encountered one of these, especially when it spoiled something.

_childDocuments_.review: Loved the historical themes of this game and the art style is really fun and unique. _childDocuments_.review: Pentiment’s existence is an astounding one. This is not because it’s a game developed by Obsidian, as they have been celebrated for nearly twenty years as one of the premiere WRPG devs, nor it is because it’s the passion project of Josh Sawyer, who was one of the lead devs for Fallout: New Vegas and Pillars of Eternity 2, which are among Obsidian’s best games. This game is astounding in that such a clear labor of love that goes so hard against the grain of the mainstream game industry would have not existed if not for the support of the largest AAA publisher, Microsoft. Pentiment isn’t a traditional RPG, even more so than fellow detective RPG Disco Elysium, as it’s more of an adventure game as it has no stats. I would still consider it a RPG though as the background and skills you choose for the protagonist, Andreas Maler, shapes what he can do and his relationships with the characters around him and the choices you make. Pentiment is also not a traditional detective game either for reasons that are bit spoilery, but one of them is that Andreas is not actually a detective. Andreas is not Sherlock Holmes, Harry DuBois, or Lady Love Dies; he is merely an artist completely out of his depth dragged into the rural Bavarian town of Tassing’s turmoil and forced to try and maintain the peace between the town and Kiersau, the Benedictine abbey who governs them. Andreas can’t Columbo his way to the truth, his and your choices are tinged with uncertainty as you try to uncover the culprits. Ultimately, the murders are a backdrop to the main theme of the game, history.Pentiment is foremost a game about history, a rumination of the past and how society is built on the foundations of older ones, how they evolve and change over time, and how the past and its truths can be obfuscated through multiple means. The game take place in the Holy Roman Empire in the early 1500’s at the dawn of the great societal upheavals of the Early Modern period in Europe. Martin Luther has published his 95 Theses only a few years prior to the start of the game’s narrative, which will eventually lead to the greatest schism in Christianity, The Protestant Reformation, and more than a century of bloodshed and strife across the continent. Johannes Gutenberg’s printing press has revolutionized society as now the proliferation of books and the ability to read them are no longer only in the realm of the aristocracy and clergy. The growing education of the peasantry leads to class conflicts with their noble and clerical lords who desire to keep the underclasses under heel. The old traditions of the medieval era are dying away, this is initially illustrated with Keirsau and its monks, who are the very few still writing and illustrating books by hand. All of these events tie into the events of the game’s narrative and its setting and characters, and what a fantastic job the game does bringing them to life.Pentiment’s attention to detail both to its historical time period, setting, and art design is wondrous. The game drops references left and right to historical people, places, and concepts of the era which deftly manages to give the uninitiated player a trove of information in the in-game glossary for clarification, an expansion of the similar systems that previous Obsidian RPGs, Tyranny and PoE2 had. As a lover of history and games that immerse themselves into the subject, Pentiment is one of the very finest, it not the most. The game is mostly a slow burn, letting you get to really learn about the daily lives of the townsfolk and the monks and nuns, before ♥♥♥♥ starts hitting the fan. This works so well for the game because you really get a sense of place with Tassing and its people. The writing is fantastic as its fleshes out its cast and setting splendidly. The game also manages to balance having its light-hearted moments with serious drama and the narrative ends up being a powerful journey. The game’s art design is absolutely beautiful, crafted akin to the style of the manuscript illustrations of the era. The characters have just so much lively detail to them and the backgrounds are so scenic. The UI is also so creative as well. Characters’ dialogue boxes are expressed through the writing of a quill complete with sound effects and typos in the dialogue that get corrected like someone was actually writing them by hand. There’s even another facet of this UI where the town printer, Klaus’, dialogue boxes are instead expressed in the style of printing press block prints complete with printing press sound effects. All of this sheer attention to detail are testament to how much love was clearly poured into this game. The soundtrack is also beautiful, though the game uses it more sparingly than most games. Just one of the most aesthetically beautiful and creative games I’ve played.Pentiment is a masterpiece of the medium and hopefully will stand as inspiration for other game developers in the years to come. If you have an interest in it, I highly recommend it, it’s fast become my GOTY and one of my absolute favorite games of all time. It truly is an amazing joy that this game exists.
_childDocuments_.name: Pentiment

_childDocuments_.review: A beautiful adventure game in the vein of Umberto Eco stories. The artstyle is gorgeous and fits perfectly with the time period and the themes the game conveys. The writing is stellar, from character motivations to grand themes about history, collective and personal memory, religious syncretism, the passage of time and how all of these impact the lives of people who experience them. An absolute must play for anyone interested in history but also in good writing and brilliant touching stories.
_childDocuments_.name: Pentiment

_childDocuments_.review: Welcome to Disco Elysium: Renaissance Bavaria editionLook, this game is good. It has a unique art style and an excellent way of making your decisions meaningful, which I think is what all adventure games need. The ramifications of your decisions may be a bit bryptic, but not to the point of not making sense or betraying your intentions. It also explains a very mature story in a serious manner, and lets you experience the lives of the characters close to what they actually experience, without sugarcoating hardships of peasant live in the liwer renaissance (well, maybe a little)An here comes the but, because there needed to be a but: But, the story makes you wonder a bit aimlessly during most of the game. Not like I want quest markers (you have them if you look for them), just that the main characters seem to have little idea of what to do themselves, and instead just decide to spend time on advancing quests that spend time when they stumble on them. As you have very limited time slots to advance the story, you'll feel that the game hasn't let you investigate enough before railroading you into the next story bottleneck, and forcing you to take story changing decisions without having had the chance to unveil all the secrets. I mean, that feels like real life, but I have real life at home already, I wanted to have not-so-real-life in my game.Finally, I'm dreading replaying the game. The idea seems to be to start the game a second and third time with different backgrounds (similar to Disco Elysium), but the dialogue is very slow and difficult to skip because of the (otherwise beatifully made) annoying text effect on the dialogue boxes, and I fear to see how the story will crack when seeing what part of my decisions is actually reflected or not on the consequencesI picked it shortly after launch, and if you're an avid point and click adventure gamer I guess the full price is okay. If you are just looking for something to fill time, pick it up in half a year when the first discounts start

_childDocuments_.review: This game is so good it feels like it shouldn't exist. It is an absolute masterpiece. Yes, there is a lot of reading and the gameplay is basically speaking to people and walking around (there are a few mini-games here and there which are amusing but simple). Still, it is a work of art and love with fascinating characters and incredible historical accuracy.
_childDocuments_.name: Pentiment

_childDocuments_.review: Above all, this game is a historically accurate representation of what life was like in early 16th century Bavaria. Historically accurate in terms of setting, people, lifestyles, music, art, and even writing. It has a  in its credits. To me, the primary reason to play this game is to immerse yourself in its representation of history as a new way to understand what life was like in that time.However, this game is also a story of a rural village and how your actions impact its future. As the player, you make meaningful choices and can see the impact of those choices years or decades down the line through the game's several-year time skips. Many of those actions will be through helping the town solve murders that draw up into a broader conspiracy. However, it's worth noting that these mysteries are generally "no wrong answer" outcomes. If you gather enough evidence against a suspect, you can make that accusation and the game will basically make that choice correct. So, if you're looking for a detective story where you can find the one "right" answer, keep looking.
_childDocuments_.name: Pentiment

_childDocuments_.review: This game is a masterpiece of storytelling, art, and gameplay. Despite being billed as a medieval story, the gameplay takes place at the post-Medieval end of the Early Modern Period in Germany during the rule of the Holy Roman Empire. To put it into better context— during the period of years that the game spans, the Renaissance ended in Italy, Henry VIII made himself the head of the English Church, and Copernicus theorized that the Earth revolved around the Sun. Of course many aspects of Medieval life were still around by this point, but to simply call it the Medieval period is quite misleading.The setting of the game is a fictional village called Tassing that is inspired by real-world locations but allows the developers to tell their own story which fits into actual history based on what was going on at the time (I won't spoil anything) but gives creative license with the details. The game is immersive, using different writing and printing styles for the speech of different characters based on class and profession, as well as multiple languages (all of which the game translates). The folk native to Germany speak in English (though their language is Early New High German, think the German equivalent of King James Bible English) though written materials you find in game are in ENHG (among other languages like Latin) but they are translated for you by your character.The story centers around a series of murders, but it is more than that. This is the story of a village and its people over a period of change and unrest. Your actions might just influence how things unfold, for good or ill. Fans of the Murder Mystery genre should know, however, that while this game features murder mystery investigation in a good portion of the gameplay, the gameplay does not exclusively involve solving murders. Overall, you will be talking to various people throughout the village, looking for clues, doing tasks associated with daily life in the Early Modern Period (centered around the Benedictine canonical hours from Matins to Compline). One thing to note, if the game warns you a task will take some time to complete, do that task last as it will usually end the day or at least advance the clock by a lot. Also, keep in mind you will not have time to do all tasks especially in the earlier parts of the game so some avenues of the story may go unexplored.Gameplay is simple. There is nothing in the game that requires a knowledge of an advanced control scheme, and no quick time events or other similar abrupt shifts in game play. The game is more or less point and click, and you do get to customize your character by choosing elements of their studies which gives you new options during dialog (such as knowing a particular language). As far as I know there are no right or wrong choices that end the game early, the game will simply progress and you will have to live with the outcome of your choices.The only thing that could be considered a downside in my opinion is the shift in pace and direction at the beginning of the third act (I won't go into spoilers). The pace ramps up from the beginning of the game up to a climactic second act finish and then abruptly slows down until the last third or so of the third act. It almost feels like a different game set in the same setting for a while. The game is still fun at this point, don't get me wrong, but the game had me missing the gameplay that had lead up to that point for a few hours of game time. It does eventually ramp back up by the end and in my opinion it is definitely worth it.I'm hoping we'll get another game in this style from Obsidian, perhaps set in another part of Europe or in a different time period.
_childDocuments_.name: Pentiment

_childDocuments_.review: As I regularly play story-driven games since the premiere of the first Baldur's Gate, I have to admit that Pentiment is one of the best games I have ever played. A mind-blowing tribute to point&click games, though focused much more on dialogues and choices than logical tasks. Obsidian, as always, provides us a deep and thought-provoking story that will haunt you some time after you finish the game. The story takes place in the 16th century, but the problems are discussed very universal and time-independent. In the game you explore well-written personal stories of many characters, but also you track the history of a particular space and community over the period of time, which is a brilliant idea, so well introduced in the game by the story and game mechanics.Graphics, music, animations - everything top quality. The only problem is that the Polish translation that I played has some minor issues and sometimes improper spelling appears.
_childDocuments_.name: Pentiment

_childDocuments_.review: This is a brilliantly researched, wonderfully written point-and-click adventure. It's a bit of a riff on Umberto Eco's Name of the Rose, but set in 16th-century alpine Germany, in the epoch of Martin Luther and Albrecht Dürer. The historical research done for this game is impeccable, the period portrayed is a truly inspired setting, much overlooked so far. The game begins in a sleepy Bavarian village where medieval times refuse to pass - yet. Andreas Maler, a young painter, is working on an illuminated manuscript at the local abbey to finish his professional education. He is however soon drawn into investigating a murder. The game does a brilliant job of showing how modern times slowly break into this still-medieval environment, the story taking place over several decades. The Printing Press, Martin Luther, Renaissance Art and peasant upheavals all herald the future, while Tassing (the village) still hold some secrets from its Roman and Heathen past. It's thrilling to play such a well crafted game, which suceeds at portraying the regional alpine peculiarities (local festivities like the Perchtenlauf) - you get to meet people from a wide variety of backgrounds, including Bohemians, Hungarians, Italians, French, Jews among others, portraying the cultural realities of the early modern Holy Roman Empire. Religion, Society, Art and Technology are all given their due, some of the jokes are geared at people with a high amount of knowledge about the period. It is however educational in of itself and a great introduction to a whole plethora of topics. Above and beyond its historical accuracy the game also features an exceptionally beautiful, stylized art-style, inspired by late medieval and early modern book illustrations and woodcuts. The game's heart however are it's endearing (and engaging) characters and story, rarely have I cared so much about my actions or even rued them hours afterwards. Although the story is in some ways fairly linear, the game offers great opprtunity for replayability, as there are a number of important junctions and decisions with weighty consequences. The dialogue is often witty and funny (without feeling out of place) and sometimes moving. All dialogue is presented in written form, in various fonts according to the speaker - i.e. the monks "speak" in elaborate handwriting, the printers' dialogue looks as if it were straight out of early prints. 10/10
_childDocuments_.name: Pentiment

_childDocuments_.review: All the embellishments - music, sound-design and obviously all the visuals - are stellar and went a long way towards keeping me engaged long enough to finish the game. Some other aspects are at least noteworthy, with the background/research and character realizations coming to mind. It is obvious that a lot of love, dedication and hard work went into the game. I think, if you play games for experiencing stories and soak in athmosphere (especially medieval), you'd probably like this. I didn't have much fun, though and can't recommend it as a "videogame".*MINOR SPOILERS FROM HERE*Unfortunately, the core-gameplay is just not doing it for me. This game is mostly a railroad - things happen and actions are taken because the script says so. In all this detective-work, which is the framing of this game, barely any deductions from your part are even possibly. You don't have to be overly attentive, exploring doesn't usually yield much and logic is usually the wrong angle. The game puts up signposts and you are expected to follow. Your choices have impact, but in the grand scheme of things, those feel minute. So from a videogame-standpoint, i.e. the extent to which the medium allows you interactivity and agency, I don't see much value here.Unfortunately, even just approached on a story-level, this piece of artistic expression does not really legitimize itself. The plot is okay, but you'd find much better in many books, where the story is artistically curated and assembled for you rather than you, as the player, haphazardly fumbling it together. Also, I thought the ending was disappointing and not worth the journey.By choosing to tell this story as a videogame rather than in a book, this gets diluted even further. Hitchcock famously said: "What is drama but life with the dull bits cut out!?" Welp, this game just puts the dull bits back in, by letting you actually walk back and forth across town to get to the interesting setpieces for much of the game's runtime. If on the way you'd have to explore or figure out by creative reasoning where you have to go next, then I'm on board. But as established earlier, you don't; there's a marker on your map and going anywhere else is nearly always just a waste of time.So yeah, even though it breaks my heart and I applaud the effort and creativity of the devs, I can't say the project was a success in the sense that I enjoyed it. For an engaging, detective-style murder mystery-videogame - play "Her story" or "Return of the Obra Dinn". For a great story of the same - at the danger of sounding snooty - read books like "The name of the rose" or Dürrenmatt's "The judge and his hangman".

_childDocuments_.review: So a game that's not too dependant on quick reaction speeds, lets you solve mysteries using dialogue to ascertain suspicions and adds in awesome historical side info in case you've never heard of what's being referred to in the story but your character would know about said thing. _childDocuments_.name: Pentiment

_childDocuments_.review: This game was a gigantic disappointment.The first act was so fun. Great writing, beautiful art, fun investigation mechanics. But I played it through two and a half times before realizing that the game was forcing you to accuse someone who was not guilty of the crime at hand (even if they may be guilty of other things). That was kind of frustrating, but I moved on to the second act.The second act is even worse. The game keeps preventing you from asking the right people about the obvious key piece of evidence that would solve everything. Even if you, as the player, figure out exactly what happened in the first two acts, you again have to accuse an innocent.The third act is just maudlin make work. All meaningful choice disappears, you just run around getting people to talk about their recollections of the first two acts. Again there's no way to ask about that one piece of evidence, until the very end of the game where everything is neatly revealed in a sequence you had no real hand in making happen.I was so excited for the game at the beginning but I'm just so sad about the missed potential now. It's possible that if I had gone into it not expecting meaningful game mechanics but just treating it as interactive fiction I could have enjoyed it more. For sure the production values are amazing. But as a game I can't bring myself to recommend it.

People used to walk by placing the front of their foot down first. (Instead of today where we step on our heel first) 10/10Something that I dislike in games is when it doesn't let you solve its puzzles. _childDocuments_.review: Having just finished Pentiment, I wholeheartedly recommend it, if you like stories.  It's by no means any type of action game, much more of a point-and-click (with cool art style), but is primarily about relationships and interaction.   There's a lot of "what is truth, what is the past, how do you know these things, how sure are you of your deductions".  Twice I thought the game was over, and it wasn't (there are 3 Acts).   The style of text used for character's writing is an important artistic point, and ties to the character's life/experience/personality.    While it's fictional, it's very much a period piece and really drops you into it - to the point when it was over, I had to check to make sure it wasn't based on real events (pieces of it are borrowed from real events/people, though).  And pretty emotional; you really feel like these are real characters/people, not cardboard cutouts you often see in games.

_childDocuments_.review: This game will not appeal to everyone, that much is pretty abundantly clear. I think its a bit of a shame how many people will never give it a chance, though. This has got to be one of the most all around well written games I've ever seen, right up there with the likes of Disco Elysium. Now I don't think its quite the masterpiece that Disco was, but its damn close, and I found the reading to be much easier to consume than Disco which is very dense. If you dont like reading, of course you wont like this. That's pretty much the entire game. But if you like to read even a little, give it a shot. The characters, dialogue, and overall plot have all been great so far. The characters are likable and distinct without just feeling like modern people, which is a problem I think the majority of period-piece media fails at. Either the characters are just modern humans in a historical setting, or overly bland and stoic with dry archaic dialogue. Josh Sawyer and his team at Obsidian managed to craft a cast of memorable 16th century Bavarians who feel like they come from the time while not being bland. The writing, combined with the gorgeous art derived from the period's own manuscripts, combine to create an experience that really draws you into the story being told. I was eager to hear each and every conversation, somehow they were almost never boring to me. Choices also seem to have a tangible effect and come up regularly in dialogue and affect the flow of the story. I definitely think I'll at least play it through twice. Also, I see many people saying you've gotta be a history nerd to like this. I may be a bit ignorant, because I am pretty well versed in history, but I'm not sure this is true. While having knowledge of the major events of the timeframe (Martin Luther, Protestant schism, spead of literacy and printing, ect) will definitely increase your appreciation of the game, I think the characters and central mystery plot would be enough to draw in anyone who likes a good story.

_childDocuments_.review: This game was so unique, unlike anything I've played before! The art and design are incredible, the storyline is captivating, and I love all the attention to detail. There are so many little details and surprises throughout the game that make it extra charming. As someone who likes to get a perfect ending, I was a little frustrated to have to be stuck with my choices lol, but it did add to the weight of all my decisions and make me think things through a bit more. Highly, highly recommend.

_childDocuments_.review: Beautiful game, very complex and well written story.In this game, set in the XVI century, you will explore a small village and its history. Set in Bavaria, you'll have the chance to interact with a multitude of characters and get to learn their stories, motivations and passions. Uncover a mystery, solve 2 homicides and watch the past unravel in front of your eyes.Highly recommended
_childDocuments_.name: Pentiment

_childDocuments_.review: I heard about this game and was interested, but I didn't think it would do very well. I am, to be frank, a _massive_ history nerd. I love little details, and stories of people's lives from beginning to end. I'm familiar with a thousand archaic little details and variations of words. And I firmly believe that there are a lot of people in the world who just don't have the attention span for this kind of stuff. I absolutely adored this game - I wish there were fewer loading screens, but that's a minor quibble - and I loved the depth of research that went into it, plus the easy glossary and who's who that made it so much easier to keep faces with names. But I also adore how much love this is getting - that others see the charm and the fairly universal themes of this game, and seem to identify. It genuinely brings me joy to share something that has such niche appeal with so many others. (Also, can we have another game, or maybe a DLC, with a certain character's adventures in Prague with their friend? Please? :D)

_childDocuments_.review: I am on the hunt for story-rich games with RPG elements and lots of style. Pentiment game checked all of those boxes! I'd recommend trying it if you enjoyed Disco Elysium, Roadwarden, Spiritfarer, or Kingdom Come: Deliverance. The game is text-heavy, but it's well-written with interesting and diverse characters. Your goal is to unravel the mysteries of a small Bavarian town in the 16th century. Political intrigue and character development abound. I cried a few times throughout the game.The RPG elements include making frequent dialogue choices that impact the story and customizing your character through four different background features (each with a range of options). I'd recommend selecting the following backgrounds: Italy / Bookworm / Medicine / Latinist / Orator on the first play through to maximize what you can glean from the characters and world. On my next play through, I plan to run the main character as a hot-headed, know-it-all occultist. I'm excited to see how it changes the gameplay!
_childDocuments_.name: Pentiment

_childDocuments_.review: As a lover of narrative driven games and an unrelenting history nerd, Pentiment was always something I would have enjoyed. However, its fully realized characters, gorgeous art, and clever writing surpassed my expectations.Pentiment is ostensibly a murder mystery, but that is really just a framing device to explore what it actually is about: this is the story of a town and its inhabitants going through a period of great change. As the Reformation rages in surrounding lands, Tassing must confront difficult questions like "what role should the abbey, and Catholicism more generally, play in our town moving forward?"Pentiment is an absolute treasure of a game, albeit not one meant for everyone. If you are interested in realistic relationship dynamics or a nuanced take on history, you will have a great time

_childDocuments_.review: I do feel like we digest art too quickly. The other day I saw a review for Immortality and it said "let this game consume your thoughts for 3 days straight like it did for me". 3 days? An ingenious projects of such caliber only amounts for 3 days? But then again, this is only one of the most ingenious projects that came out last YEAR. There are so many things coming out that deserve our attention and there is simply not enough time to process all of it. 3 days is more than most movies, games or music albums get. Pentiment is also one of the most creative and profoundly impactful things that came out in 2022, which sadly flew under the radar for most people, despite the notoriety of its developers. Due to it being a detective game, it is very hard to discuss it without spoiling it, since even the most fundamental mechanics this game offers are presented as a sort of plot twist. I recommend with all my heart to go in blind and just let this game surprise you. If you are extremely averse to surprises, I can cautiously tell you to expect a masterfully researched historical setting that is also made relevant, even relatable. If you are not a fan of history, this game will make you understand why a lot of people are. The cultural differences recontextualize mundane social interactions in a suprisingly engaging way, while the more-common-than-expected appearance of familiar daily struggles reduces the emotional distance that the centuries usually create. You can also expect a deep dive in into some character archetypes you may have encountered in your life or in other media. The game´s specifics allows to explore them in a much more meaningful way, so look out for how these characters behave and evolve, you may very well use this introspection to make sense of the people in your life as well. But above all you can expect to be entertained. The writing is funny, sad, scary, mysterious, infuriating, thought-provoking; it hits all the beats it tries to hit with mastery of a very clearly talented author. Fight against the tide. Don´t let this game get buried under the tons of others being dropped on top of it every year. Let it occupy your thoughts for more than 3 days - it deserves it.

_childDocuments_.review: I strongly recommend this game to anyone who has interest in medieval artwork, religion, and/or great stories. This is a grounded narrative that spans through generations. Every single choice you make will have a consequence no matter how insignificant you think the choice might seem.Gameplay consists of the same loop you would expect from a point in click adventure. Conversation, choices, investigating, and making sure that you do certain things and have certain dialogues in correct sequence so that you can achieve the result you want. That’s all I can really say without spoiling anything.You will come to love the setting, the characters, the music, and the undeniable charm stemming from the meticulous attention to detail the developers have put into this game.As someone that enjoys all the things mentioned above, I am so happy a game like this was made in 2022, when it seems like developers only want watered down, monetized mainstream games that will rake in millions of dollars. _childDocuments_.review: "Pentiment" Noun. An underlying image in a painting, especially one that has become visible when the top layer of paint has turned transparent with age, providing evidence of revision by the artist. This is a beautiful game about art, history, truth and perspective. This is broadly classified as an "adventure" game but there are no tedious inventory puzzles. Most of the gameplay will involve making dialogue choices that may have unforeseen narrative consequences. If you have a perfectionist's streak, or a desire to always find that "golden path" through a game narrative where you get to save Mary Jane AND the bus full of children, this game will frustrate you. But don't let that frustration stop you from playing! Lean into that feeling and keep playing, ideally without a guide. Follow the story where it leads and draw your own lesson from it. Highly recommended.

_childDocuments_.review: FAIR WARNING: I'm a medieval reenactor, a big history nerd, and I've spent WEEKS of my life reading about the various themes that this game touches upon. I'm very much the intended player, this game is very much scratching an itch for me, and i'm very much in love with it and very biased. But, I'm going to be nitpicky because it's a NICHE game and I want to give it a relevant review.**To sum up:**A wonderful game for a history nerd like myself. If you are interested in history in general, and the Early Modern period in particular, this game might be for you! The attention to detail and history is phenomenal! I can't but salute the effort and love that went into Pentiment. On the other hand, if you don't care about history then it MIGHT be a bit "too much" for you. But who knows ? It might actually push you out of your comfort zone and teach you about this very interesting, very intense period of history. Now, for the more technical part:The game is A LOT of reading. There are no voice overs, only text. That said, they really did a great job (imo) of conveying the background, personality, and social class of all characters. The police changes if you speak to an educated monk or to a farmer. Ink splashes around the words when the characters are shouting. The Printer family have their dialogues PRINTED instead of calligraphed! A very clever way to do without voice acting. And, the accessibility options for texts are unline anything i've seen in a video game before: changing the size, the police, the ligatures, etc. is all supported to make sure more people can comfortably read the game. Now, I don't have any issue reading but for some people, they might want to spend some time looking through the settings before the 2-hours mark in case they need to refund it. , but in some stages of the game there is no music and only ambiance/scribbling noises when people talk, and it's noticeable that something is missing. Graphics: very beautiful and immersive. The whole game is stylized as a medieval/early modern illustrated manuscript or book. Some animations could have used a bit more work (the wool spinning section has a VERY janky bit), but overall everything fits and seems appropriate for the setting of the game. It's a very unique style but if you've spent any amount of time IRL looking at manuscript illustrations especially some Books of Hours, you will really appreciate it.Story: Well, I didn't finish it yet. So far, very promising and historically plausible. As i'm on my first playthrough, I can't say how choices influence the story, but my ♥♥♥♥♥♥ choices have definitely closed off some paths for my story, and definitely opened others. I see a lot of replayability in this game. It reminds me of Disco Elysium and Telltale games, but it's very much its own thing. I definitely did not expect the game to go to the second act and make me live with the consequences of my actions. This game will cause EMOTIONS and FEELINGS. Be warned. : Oh my god this story is wonderfully emotional and really does a good job with its themes. Gameplay is basic but it works: walk around the town, talk to people, find clues. Often, you have choices that will influence how other people react to you and your requests later. Everything is organised around a time cycle: you start in the morning, have to do some tasks, time passes, then you have to eat with someone, time passes, then you have some tasks, again you have to get dinner with another character, and then you have to either sleep or or do some other tasks. Some tasks are dialogues, some are mini games. It's simple but it works, and you're going to wish you had more time in a day to track all your leads!The game autosaves and there is no manual saving in the game. For a multiple-choices/branching storyline game, this is a bold move. And I think it works. It encourages you to live with the consequences of your choices, which is one of the themes of the story. There is no "save scumming", there is no "let me save here and try this dialogue option and if I don't like it i'll reload". History: Now, I'm not a specialist of 16th century bavaria, but everything looks very historical to me, it's certainly convincing! The clothing are nice, the buildings look nice, the way the characters act is very immersive. They definitely did their research and were obviously helped by actual historians to make this. The game is approaching tough topics and does a good job of being tactful and does not indulge in blood/sex/vice like Game of Thrones but keeps a realistic historical approach. I really like that they did not forget to include POC characters, and they did it in a way that makes historical sense, and threw a bit of shade at all the studios who pretend they don't put black people in their games for historical reasons (*cough* mordhau *cough cough* kingdom come deliverance*cough*). I'm not afraid to say this is THE MOST HISTORICALLY ACcURATE GAME I'VE EVER PLAYED. And i play almost every game that calls itself historically accurate. PS: the food looks yummy, I want some swabish ravioli now.
_childDocuments_.name: Pentiment

_childDocuments_.review: It's a magnificent thing, and this story will be lingering in my thoughts for quite some time.Pentiment takes Obsidian's expertise in branching narratives, role-playing, and building evocative worlds, then packages it all up in an exciting and unique way.I was devastated when it was over, and I'm still not over that ending. But now I'm looking forward to playing it all over again, this time with another Andreas.Maybe one who speaks Latin, studied law, and spent his wandering years in Switzerland.There are some bad choices and disastrous consequences I'd like to avoid this time too. That's the beauty of being an artist: you can always scrape the parchment clean and start again.

_childDocuments_.review: Having finished Pentiment I think I now understand my full feelings about the game and... well its complicated. In truth this game is like a 6 or a 7 out of 10 for me but seeing as how there's been so much uncritical praise I think making this a negative review is more appropriate.TLDR: Pentiment is a beautifully illustrated game with a fascinating concept, immersive and enjoyable writing and a wide cast of interesting and nuanced characters. Despite all of this the game has a story that lacks conciseness, a user experience that feels forgotten, and a bigger interest in style than in substance.I'll be short with the praise considering its very easy to find elsewhere. The concept of Pentiment is very intriguing, the idea of a multi-decade long murder mystery is a fascinating concept that pulled me in right away. The writing of many of the characters was quite good and while there were more typos than I expected I was rarely bored by talking to the people of the town even if the discussions weren't pertinent for the mystery at hand. Beyond this, it does truly feel like your actions have meaningful impact on the game, especially by the end. Still I've only played a single playthrough and I'm hesitant to take people's word on this given the amount of games where "choices matter" but this game truly does at least feel like you have a substantial impact by the end. All in all the game does a great job in many places, but I think some critique is in order.I'll start with the smallest things, the bugs. While Pentiment had very few bugs I did notice about half a dozen times where dialogue would repeat or worse, when characters would reference things that were yet to happen yet. This was a small issue, but when it happened it did hurt the immersion of the game.Next is music and sound design. Pentiment really needed more music, what little is in the game only occurs during events or set-pieces but its usually quite powerful. I personally just wish there was something for ambient background music during the rest of the game, as it begins to feel rather barren walking around town without it (and you will be walking around town, a LOT, more on that later). Not only was more music needed but the sound design of the game was very bare-bones, I never truly felt engaged with the sound of the game since so much of it was dull and simple, essentially the bare minimum of what was needed. While this isn't a huge deal I do feel like it pulled me out of the experience and some nice mood music in the background, however faint, really would've helped get me more interested.Now onto the story. As stated above, the story of Pentiment is really quite good, though there are plenty of issues as far as pacing goes and honestly the game really could've used a bit more of an interesting throughline besides the letters. The latter half of the game was much better for me than the first since it dealt a lot more with the mood of the town and generally felt more like a visual novel than a half baked mystery game and I think something more linear like the second half of the game is what the story should've been throughout (which I'll touch on this regarding gameplay). Beyond that, the ending honestly struck me out of nowhere, it felt very rushed and sudden, and while the ending itself wasn't bad, its appearance felt a bit anticlimactic to me.Finally I come to the two things that genuinely made me annoyed with this game and if improved would've made this game much shorter, punchier, and enjoyable, the gameplay and the UI. For the gameplay you'll mostly spend your time running around town spending time with different families, asking questions, and doing activities that progress time and give you more info about whatever lead you're looking into. This is great in theory and those times when you're with the npcs are truly enjoyable but the main issue is backtracking. In a pseudo openworld game like Pentiment you have an entire town and an abby to search for clues. This would be fine if the game pointed you in the direction of all the clues or if there was some way for the player to track what they've looked into, but there's not, the journal feature doesn't actually write down everything you know, and the game is clearly designed for you to explore and find things throughout the map. The problem here is how slow and repetitive it is checking around for things. If you search the map you're in for transition sequences that get old quick, unnecessary walking, and then 99% of the time you won't find anything anyway. This gets even worse when the game changes time or a new event occurs because now there might be new things on the map to find, so you go explore, but then find very little. It just seems like the open world aspect of the game only serves to slow down the progression of the story while boring the player. Its entirely unnecessary. Pentiment would've been a stronger game if it had done away with the openworld element altogether since all it manages to do is frustrate the player and elongate playtime. I easily spent hours in this game just searching around for things and if anyone believes that's not how the game's meant to be played then I'd just refer them to all the readily available secrets that the player is meant to find. I suppose the game just feels very unpolished gameplay wise, the minigames are nice but really just busywork, the openworld is a joke that doesn't need to exist, the UI is fancy but cumbersome and unhelpful, and the town itself could've been much more interesting to the player if the game offered more information about them, family trees, personal notes, etc.In the end this game feels like a passion project that went too far into its concept before thinking about if it would actually be fun to play and while the story makes up for it. If you decide to buy this then just be ready for a slog, at least if you're someone who actually treats the game like an openworld game. My advice would to be just focusing on the leads in your journal, it won't let you see everything and you'll miss a bunch of side options and secrets but you'll save yourself hours of repetitious searching. I only wish I knew before I started.Original Review: This game is really hard for me to pin down because on one hand the writing and style of the game are amazing, but the game itself just feels extremely clunky to play and a bit at odds with itself design-wise. If this game had more quality of life improvements I think I could recommend it but as of now the interactive map is more annoying than interesting, the unnecessary transitions screens get old after an hour, and there really should be more to help the player make sense of the relationships of all the people in town since the cast is quite large and it can get a bit much for some folks to wrap their head around. On another note I also think there should be a difficulty option or optional hint system where the map can show the player certain locations that have something else for them to discover, not even necessarily related to the mystery but just like "oh here there might be an npc you didn't talk to, or you haven't eaten with this family yet, or there's still a puzzle over here" because the journal system doesn't do a great job giving me the whole picture of what I could still discover, only what I have discovered and without something like this I've just been running around like a chicken with its head cut off looking for anything new which mostly leads to the game feeling like a slog even though this is clearly a method of play that is suspected due to the variety of secrets that do exist. I'm still going to keep playing the game since I want to see where it goes and I want to see if these issues start to not matter but I'm not very hopeful.

_childDocuments_.review: One of the very first games I ever played was New Vegas. After a couple hours I knew this was a really special game. As the years were passing and I got to try more games I appreciated the exquisite writing of Obsidian even more.And now I can finally say it, after having played lots of games, mainly RPGs and story-heavy ones, this is one of the best game experiences I've ever had and definitely the most unique one.Everything in this game is perfect. The aesthetic, the design, the music, the writing! Don't get me wrong, it's not a game for everyone, but if you like 16th century Europe, period accurate music and playing a game where your choices have sometimes grave consequences, among many other things, this is the game for you!
_childDocuments_.name: Pentiment

_childDocuments_.review: Blew my mind! Very involved thinking, complete with historic notes and extensive glossary. I was intimidated at first but referencing rich historic data with magnificent illustrations was a journey worth taking. I loved how the layers from pre-pagan to pagan to Christianity is peppered throughout and debated in the game. Customizing character development throughout this journey was fun and sometimes dramatic! Surprises at every turn, too! The music is superb, at times haunting and also timely. A few glitches though -- sometimes dialogue boxes appeared upside down AND backwards, then would flip upward and be from left to right. Just putting that out there for updates in case it was not intentional (did not seem so and would happen randomly with characters). I will be replaying this game the entire way through after really absorbing the experience next few days (took 20 hours this time as I made extra pit stops to explore and deliberately deeply at times or to marvel at the rich scenery and enjoy sounds like the waterfall in the forest or a monk singing in the church). Highly recommend for history lovers and people who like a slower paced game with lots to ponder. I'm not even religious but maybe spiritual. It is a game for mystery lovers, intellectuals as well as those who appreciate sumptuous settings.
_childDocuments_.name: Pentiment

_childDocuments_.review: I probably complete only about 10 percent of all games I start, as I don't have much patience for boredom, sloppiness, poorly crafted worlds, etc. When I finished Pentiment, my mouth was hanging open in appreciation for this love poem to a small village in the medieval Bavarian Holy Roman Empire. The pace of Pentiment is often slow just as village life was slow and routine, but the payoff is more than worth it. I spent 84 hours according to Steam, probably more than many will, but the game is best role-played in small chunks. Pentiment is not for everyone. People who don't like to read much in their games may wish to pass on this one. People who require action combat in their games will be sorely disappointed. People who enjoyed "The Name of the Rose" by Umberto Eco will probably love this game. Pentiment is a video version of a choose your own adventure story. There are some very easy puzzles to solve here and there, but otherwise the game consists of reading dialogue and making choices. And the choices have real consequences - in some cases life or death consequences. A wide variety of subject matter is touched on, including the meaning of faith,. mental illness, the push-pull between societal expectations and one's dreams, the importance of art and literature, heresy, and I could go on and on. But experience it yourself!
_childDocuments_.name: Pentiment

_childDocuments_.review: Prepare for pain. The choices you make matter in this one in unexpected ways. Consequence, action, reaction, flail as you might for an answer, you will inevitably be carried by events. However, don't fool yourself into thinking this is a mystery that you can solve: in two of the three mystery scenarios, you lack the required information to unravel the whole thing and the time to do so- this is the point. You must act with imperfect information and live with the consequences. The game is a wonderful mystery in the style of Night in the Woods, with a wonderfully depicted Illuminated and woodblock artstyle. Few games do as much work to invest in a particular historical moment, and Pentiment goes above and beyond to place the story in a historical moment while not spending its entire run time catching you up on the intricacies of Imperial Law, Botany, the Catholic Catechism. Students of history will be rewarded for knowing what's happening (and punished, hindsight hurts). The writing style is tight in structure, and characters move and change naturalistically with the decades that pass over the story. A few notes: as mentioned earlier, this isn't the sort of game where you can solve the mystery and make it ok in the first act, or even the second. Don't play assuming you can look up a guide and save the innocent and destroy the guilty; one of the points of this story is that truth is a point of view. Additionally, it is not possible to complete every side quest in one play through, and the game is as much about time management as anything else. Finally, with so many leads and interactions, it can be hard to feel that you have exhausted all of your options before you move on to a scene: unless you are compelled, I strongly recommend not hitting every location possible in one playthrough. Simply do your best and don't turn the experience into a chore on top of an emotional one.Strong showing from Obsidian's writing team again with this story; I am eager to see what comes next. 9/10
_childDocuments_.name: Pentiment

_childDocuments_.review: It is very difficult to give a clearly positive or negative opinion of this game. TL;DR:The game is absolutely worth of one playthrough, Act 1 and Act 2 are pure joy, unfortunately Act 3 leaves a bitter taste. To sum up the pros and cons:THE GOOD:- a highly interesting setting and great historical detail,- a unique artistic idea, beautiful and atmospheric graphics,- the overall game atmosphere, the immersion into the story,- the initially fascinating plot with a constant tension and an urge to figure out its secrets (Act 1 and 2),- a very interesting way to present the internal struggles of the main hero.THE BAD:- SPOILER ALERT! - Act 3 feels disconnected and forced, it is a huge step back in every respect. Without major spoilers, it changes almost everything from Acts 1 and 2 to the extent that it discards the very theme of the game: from a tense medieval investigation it turns into some dragged-out smalltown chitchatting. Even worse, the theme of Act 3 is rather boring on its own, except for answering the main clue.- The final explanation provided for the main mystery is completely illogical, unless you consider the completely flawed logic of the main villain (and thus of the developers) as an acceptable explanation for his actions. Also, the explanation on the later all-important decision of our main character is absolutely non-credible, and feels extremely forced. - The characters communicate some ahistorical, 21th century social ideas and the events take some illogical turns to support the idea of social development.
_childDocuments_.name: Pentiment

_childDocuments_.review: This is my absolute favorite game. I've played for over 30 hours and there's still tons of replay value left. The passion, research, and ambition the creators had for this game is clear in every facet. From the medieval art, typography, music, history, story line, references, etc., you experience the changing world of 16th century Europe, particularly the impacts of the printing press and the Protestant Reformation right along with the characters. I want to thank the developers and everyone involved in this game for giving us all the opportunity to experience the magic with you! I hope more publishers take a note from this game's success and fund these passion projects.
_childDocuments_.name: Pentiment

_childDocuments_.review: As a game, it's quite toned-down and grounded in its approach to the (fictional) history it depicts, but it never feels boring or inconsequential. The visual direction really fits with what the game is going for thematically, and looks much better than the small store page screenshots might make you think. The story is engaging and actually allows you to fail in certain ways if you're not paying attention, which is rare for story-driven games. All in all, it's about as good as one would expect from a game director like Josh Sawyer.
_childDocuments_.name: Pentiment

_childDocuments_.review: I'm still not necessarily sold on the gameplay of point and click adventures. The pacing and engagement suffer. But as far as historical fiction goes, I've never seen anything in Pentiment's league. Maybe a Lets Play video would show me everything I'm appreciating here, but I want all games to try this hard to be from a place or from a time. I want to play from more than a solo protagonist's POV. I love to dwell in worlds far beyond what any single narrative warrants. This game gives me that. Along with a headache for its lack of fast travel.
_childDocuments_.name: Pentiment

_childDocuments_.review: Granted, this game is not for those who abhor slow burns, detailed explanations that seem to go nowhere (but they would later on), meandering experiences, lengthy dialogues, intrigue and mystery. The world of Andreas takes a few hours to set up, and by the time I got there, I was invested in the few characters that I have met so far. This is a game for long weekends, rainy days, and quiet contemplation. It does not want you to rush it. It wants you to take in the beauty of the illuminated pages where the story takes place. Don't get this game because of the hype. Get this game because you want to play it.
_childDocuments_.name: Pentiment

_childDocuments_.review: I wasn't sure I'd like it, despite the pedigree of the developers and the unique artyle the base gameplay didn't seem like my cup of tea. But Josh Sawyer has definitely done it. It's not a game for everyone, but it's a grounded game about people with all the heart the developers could muster. It's thought provoking, real, and gorgeous. If you like stories where the stakes are local, and the storytelling is the prime focus, you'll like this game. More of this please!
