_childDocuments_.review: Pentiment takes you back to the early 16th century where you follow a few notable events from the life of the artist - Andreas Maller during his visit in Tassing, a small town in the Upper Bavaria.It surely takes you on a journey and not necessarily a pleasant one at that, one filled with sorrow, pain and some joy. Mostly sorrow though, as the game tries to portray the life of peasants during the time when Christianity was still reigning supreme and was starting to be threatened by Luther and his teachings. And to make matters more intense, it portrays the clash of old pagan beliefs versus Christianity and their similarities.The game is a classic RPG where you are placed into conversation with other characters and are offered multiple choices, some even based on your background or traits and as such, you make choices that might benefit you and alter the lives of the characters surround you. Not all choices play a significant role, but might bring up new conversation subjects if addressed or left ignored.Pentiment is separated in to 3 Acts each noting a serious story altering event and Andreas' slow descent into depression and/or borderline madness.The journey starts off in a tranquil dream sequence where Andreas talks to four of his personality traits (as I see it), after which he awakes in the home of a family of peasants who have agreed to lodging him while he works at the abbey as a scribe and in parallel also works on his masterpiece.As you make your way out of the Gertner household, you get to select your background and traits of which some can affect the outcomes of a few quests, but are mostly tied to specific achievements. During your walk from home to work you make acquaintance with the townsfolk and get a glimpse into their everyday lives before you venture to your place of work - the Scriptorium which is located in the abbey. Conversations can include making statements that the other character might find positive or negative. The game will let you know after you have made the choice however, without straight out telling you if you messed up or not, once the conversation check comes up you will see a tab telling you what you did right or wrong and you will either succeed or fail the conversation check, which can have major or minor impact down the line.The gameplay of Pentiment is very similar to what you would find in point and click adventure games mashed together with traits from visual novels themed around the art style of the time.Every day is separated into multiple sequences during which you can be locked out of doing particular tasks and instead forced into doing specific ones. For example Prime, morning work hours where you are free to explore and engage in conversation with almost everyone. It is also the time for major story events to unfold. During Sext, which is lunch time, the game forces you to find people with whom to have less significant conversions and share a meal with. However you may still explore the world and find objects to interact with. The game is very generous with giving you pointers on what to do and where to go and also includes a glossary of varying subjects that were important during that time.Once at the Abbey, you get to learn about the lives of nuns and monks, and you may also explore the abbey. During work you converse with other scribes as they work on their books or related art. The first day goes by fast and is really only there as a tutorial, it gives you a glimpse of what the gameplay is going to be like.Once the story reaches the first conflict point, Andreas has to help uncover the perpetrator of the presented murder mystery and in doing so help his friend Piero. It is at this point you are given multiple leads to pursue on who might have caused harm to the victim and you're given a time frame in which to solve the mystery. Needless to say, it is your choices on the matter if your investigation will see justice served, or not.Pentiment is a longish game, where it mostly depends on how inquisitive you are, how much you want to learn and how fast you can read. It is a very interesting murder mystery that throws a few curveballs at you at times. My first playthrough took about 25 hours, but if you know exactly what to do and where to go, it can take less than 10.If I were to speak of cons, the game is repetitive and at times feels very sluggish, I would have like to have the option to speed up the walking speed and option to skip cutscenes (for the second playthrough).It is a solid game ad it definitely deserves more praise. I highly recommend it to those of you, who do not mind repetitive gameplay and reading.May you believe in divine Providence.

_childDocuments_.review: I haven't seen such a Boring point & click adventure for a long time. The dialogues are boring, you just want to click through them, the characters are so plain and uninteresting .... the main character - you just don’t empathize with him ... the story is boring to the point of impossibility. _childDocuments_.review: This game is truly a passion project from Obsidian. You can see in all their games that they care a lot about story, but Pentiment is that game no one expected that just blows everything away. I love RPGs and narrative-(and character-)focused games, so this was perfect for me. I'm sure it's not for everyone - some people may find it too slow, or perhaps find the mechanics too simple. But if you love games with good stories it's worth giving this one a shot. There's a lot of depth, a lot of attention to detail, so many little things that add up to create something that's more than the sum of its parts, something spectacular.
_childDocuments_.name: Pentiment

_childDocuments_.review: A great story based game, although you don't really have the ability to change major story beats.  Major events will happen regardless of your choices, but you do have the ability to affect individual character's lives.  Talk to everyone, you'll be able to help some of them make choices that are not tied to the main story but you'll see the effects years later.  Overall a very good game, although it will involve a lot of reading, but I enjoyed it very much.
_childDocuments_.name: Pentiment

_childDocuments_.review: Pentiment — 8.0 ❤️What a treasure it is to have a game like Pentiment in this era, one where it feels like the industry is rocketing towards increasingly massive projects riddled with exploitative monetization. Here’s Pentiment, a beautifully illustrated, captivating, and thrilling masterwork, weaving the melancholic story of a town and its people through 25 years. Only a few qualms here: I wish the resolution of the journal was higher and names were hyperlinked, and I wish my choices impacted the overall story a bit more, but that goes a tad against the narrative. Voice acting would be nice, but the lovingly scripted dialogue makes you understand characters just the same. The scribble sounds, the scratches, the blots of ink to signify anger… it’s perfect. Pentiment is a standout in Obsidian’a repertoire, and one of the best narrative experiences in the medium.
_childDocuments_.name: Pentiment

_childDocuments_.review: I bounced off pentiment the first time I booted it up around a year before my eventual playthrough, making it something like 20 minutes in, getting bored, and coming back to it.On a second attempt, I picked it up and fell in love with it immediately. If you like complex narrative, well written characters, or historical fiction, there is something for you to love here. So little videogame writing is genuinely good, and so little of that is great. This is a pure point and click, visual-novel style adventure game, without much in the way of puzzles or any inventory management. So be advised that you are here for the experience of watching a great story unfold.The next closest thing to Disco Elysium that I've come across. Definitely check this out.
_childDocuments_.name: Pentiment

_childDocuments_.review: Pentiment is three things:1) One of the most beautiful videogames of all time2) Easily one of the best written videogames of all time3) An almost unparalleled labour of loveI loved my experience with Pentiment deeply. The writing had me entertained, both laughing when it was funny and sad when it was upsetting. Not many games can straddle that line with such skill so deftly, and especially not when the subject matter is such well-researched history.No other game has had me hand-wringing over the choices I made. Pentiment is largely a mystery game, with the protagonist Andreas Maler attempting to solve a crime of murder. But the game gives you good reasons for every suspect, and you are forced to act upon what you know despite not having perfect knowledge at any point. Then you must live with your decision, and that alone can be tough.What compelled me the most was seeing the town of Tassing change over time. You see families change and grow over time, suffering both losses and experiencing joys as well. And lastly, if there's anything the game is saying it is that love is the most important part of being human, and that the people of the 16th century were just like us, even if their reality was vastly different to what ours is.I'll be thinking about Pentiment for a long time, and I'll be coming back to it again, of that I am certain.
_childDocuments_.name: Pentiment

_childDocuments_.review: Fantastic story told in a very organic way. No, you won't get to solve everything perfectly, because there simply isn't enough time to be exhaustive. But fear not, you'll have more than enough time to get to know the town, abbey, and all the inhabitants therein and come to develop emotional bonds with them. If you care about narrative and storytelling, I can't recommend this enough (unless perhaps you've yet to play Disco Elysium, maybe do that first if it's more your bag?)
_childDocuments_.name: Pentiment

_childDocuments_.review: Pentiment isn't what I expected, or kinda hoped it would be, but it's an absolute work of art nonetheless.  First thing you need to know: If you're not prepared to interact with a 15-20 hour rendition of early Renaissance Christian wank, this might not be the game for you.  But if you're into 16th century European history at all, I assume your tolerance for that is fairly high, and you're probably good.  xPNow the delight: The art style is beautiful, the writing incisive but subtle, and sometimes to influence a character you really do need to have a solid handle on what they value, personally.  I wholeheartedly enjoyed about 98% of the time I have thus far spent playing the game.  (Which is 17 hours, at the time of this review.  One playthrough, start to finish.)  And it sticks the landing in terms of not doing a total ass-pull with the plot at the end.  It's entirely possible to guess who's pulling threads behind the scenes before the big reveal, and I felt rewarded and vindicated at having done so.On the one hand, the constant autosaves made me a bit anxious about decisions, but on the other, honestly I had more fun just going with my gut than I do on other complicated branched-narrative games where I can save scum every single decision.  The save structure and frequent (mostly in the first two acts) time pressure is really energizing, actually, and I think both were excellent design decisions.  The expectation I had that went mostly unfulfilled: I had the sense, while playing, that I could have had drastically different outcomes (especially in the first two acts) depending on my choices.  Having finished a playthrough and then gone and looked up other people's discussions of various end states, that is not the case.  Still, though, the game does an impressive job of applying a sense of more agency than the necessarily-constrained format of a branched-narrative structure is realistically likely to give.  So all that's to say is, live your first playthrough with abandon and don't tear yourself up over how certain events pan out as you're going along.  The replay value isn't what I'd anticipated, but also, like, a movie ticket is usually what, $16 or more these days?  And this game is $20 (or less on sale) for at least 15 hours of full-throttle entertainment.  But I really did want the option to go balls-to-the-wall pagan heretic.  :P(As a slight addendum, Act 3 felt both less directed and much more railroaded than 1 and 2 to me.  It's kind of weird.  Like, in 1 & 2 there are near-constant, consequential decisions to make about where you spend your time, but 3 doesn't have anything like that pressure, and somewhat paradoxically, because of that, I found myself doing a brute-force search of town locations to get the signal to move on, at least twice.  Whereas, while I'd learned to go stick my nose in nearly every location for interesting side conversations in acts 1 & 2, there were essentially none of those in act 3.  So as much as I liked the actual story going on, the gameplay was significantly less fun than it had been in the previous two acts.  Spent a lot more time running around with a lot less to show for it.)But *anyway*, I deeply enjoyed the game and I'm glad I played it.  It's stylistically and thematically spectacular.  The whole *point* (as I see it) doesn't hit until you look up what the name, Pentiment, means after you actually play it.  And getting that sort of "...oh." moment is kind of my favorite thing in gaming.
_childDocuments_.name: Pentiment

_childDocuments_.review: I know what you're thinking--what could be more uninteresting than historical fiction in Bavaria during the roots of the Reformation?The problem with that prejudice is that may end up preventing you from playing one of the most brilliantly crafted narrative experiences ever created. The passion, attention to detail, and love oozes from every pixel in this game. It is nothing short of perfect.
_childDocuments_.name: Pentiment

_childDocuments_.review: A very unique game, or even better to say experiencece. It starts by immersing the player into medieval Bavaria, captivates with a murder mystery, but at the end it is actually a game about being a human, living among other people, believing what's right and trying to live your life to the best of your ability. Big respect to Obsidian for not chasing another PoE or Fallout: NW (which are amazing games, don't get me wrong) and taking the risk of creating this little, but amazing piece of art.
_childDocuments_.name: Pentiment

_childDocuments_.review: Flawless game for Act 1! Don't expect the game to keep its momentum in Act 2 and 3, however. Act 2 subjects you to the misery and hopelessness of the protagonist without the opportunity to improve the situation of those involved, and act 3 largely abandons the murder mystery in favor of an exercise in reflection and nostalgia that may have better suited the game if it was a much longer experience, but feels out of place in a game this short. Overall, this was a treat, just one that seeks to tell its story at the expense of the player's desires and agency. Realism trumps entertainment for this otherwise excellent narrative game!
_childDocuments_.name: Pentiment

_childDocuments_.review: In summary:  for who like the style and I will heartily recommend it... but not right now because  and the current bugs will likely make it a poor experience for you. Wait for the next patch to see if the problems below are solved.So I will update it if / when the game is updated.Positives:Negatives:Pentiment is a story-focused historical "light" RPG with a good amount of choices and consequences, presented as stylized 2D scrolling areas. The game is not very long: there are 9 chapters in 3 acts and it should take about 15-20 hours, but it is designed to be replayed... to some extent. may not be as gorgeous as 3D games like Kingdom Come: Deliverance (whose story happens 100 years earlier not far from Tassing, incidentally), and there are no spoken dialogues, but it's a very carefully crafted work and it is beautifully presented. In any case, it was a pleasant format for me, even if I'm not used to that type of graphics.To help you, there is a journal, a map, a diary with all the people you encounter, and a glossary. There is still a little running around involved because the game doesn't hold your hand too much, thankfully. You'll spend most of the time in dialogues, trying to solve a series of murders by discussing with people and trying to persuade them to help you. The atmosphere is reminiscent of The Name of the Rose, which was one source of inspiration for the game(*). is simple at first, you mainly play one character named Andreas, an artist illustrator who gets involved in a murder case and tries to resolve it. You get to choose a few background traits and skills that provide options in the dialogues (sometimes they translate into actions which steer the quest events).So there isn't a large choice for your main character, not even his name and main profession, but this allows the game to offer many choices without too much complexity. Some choices are significant, but not to the point of changing the end of the game or the way the main story unfolds - not significantly anyway. But it's well done nevertheless, and some decisions you've made may come back and bite you unexpectedly.I found quite a few bugs in the quests, like some exploration branches that were denied from me even though I was asked to pursue them, or significant dialogue lines in contradiction with what I just did, or NPCs who were where they shouldn't be. For example, I had to gather plants to save someone who was very sick, but the system wouldn't let me and this person died. Other players who had the same problem claimed that sometimes it worked, sometimes not, maybe depending on the timing. Talking of which... for the investigations, unfortunately, so you need to gather as much evidence as you can before you are forced to present your case. In itself, it's not a problem, but this is a bit tricky because the way time passes is not entirely clear: some discussions will make the clock tick, others not. Not everyone is available all the time either, so you have to choose carefully what to do next.At this point I must warn you that there is no real save system. The progression is saved at some points during the game - quite frequently, you can see when it was last saved in the menu but you are not really meant to reload past games, only to continue. Some scenes can take up to 30-40 minutes, which doesn't make it any easier. It is actually possible to reload a  save point but it is well hidden from the player(**) are shown in different fonts, to represent the education level and a few other bits of information. For example, upset people "shout" words written with little splashes of ink all around, or some other words are emphasized by using a different colour. The drawing process is a bit slow, even with the fastest setting (I think that pressing 'E' makes it slightly faster), but there is an option to draw them instantly. But there is no skipping feature and you need to wait a little before continuing the dialogue, so sometimes ... it can a bit tedious or annoying, frankly, like this long scene in an inn where the main character must listen to a song and speak to everyone before the story can continue, and it's only idle chit-chat. It's not too frequent, fortunately.I mostly loved the dialogues though, and how the story unfolds, keeping the mystery hard to find. In fact, some of the murders are not really clarified: Andreas can steer the enquiry to some extent but the outcome is not entirely under his control, and like the Sherlock games, the player isn't even told the truth. There are multiple levels to the whole plot, the main line being revealed near the end, so the game doesn't leave the player entirely in the dark, but just enough to maybe justify 2 or 3 runs. tackles a few very interesting topics. The dominant theme is of course the religion upheaval, and the relationship between land lord, monastery, commons and peasants at that time. The theme of truth, what sacrifices could be justified to preserve it, and how facts are perceived and interpreted by different people is cleverly rendered too. I think that's the type of game that some will like and others will find boring. If you're interested in history, religion, detective games, and if you're fine with the 2D style, you should like this game because it has a rich narrative, a good story, and a fair share of C&C. If 3D graphics, actions or combat are a must, if you need an elaborated class system, freedom of character creation or voice-over dialogues, this may not be for you.(*) The start of the game shows a hint, can you find what it is?(**) Tip regarding saved games: if you choose New Game in the main menu, you actually have the choice between a new game and reloading one of the 8 last save points. I've only seen this after I finished the game. I saw much more saved game files on the disk, so I think it's possible to hack it and retrieve older game points too - to restart from act 2 or 3, for example.

_childDocuments_.review: Before you read, .This was kind of a hard one for me but I can't really recommend this Game nor can I not recommend this Game. For me personally I tend more to not recommend, but I KNOW there are many people out there, that will find a liking in this Game. Hooo boy, where to start?I played this Game on and off over the course of a few weeks (took a big break when I received my new PC, but after I got it, I decided to jump back in) and it took me 27.1hours to complete my first (and I can tell you now, my only) playthrough.When I started playing, I was actually intrigued. I braced myself that the game would probably be slow in the beginning to get everything set up. And yes, it was very slow in the beginning, but it still held my interest. Then it got really intriguing after a while and I wanted to see what's next.Then Act II began (I am not spoiling anything btw. apart from that there are 3 Acts) and it was slow again. In fact so slow, that I began losing interest a bit. It took forever to pick up again and it got to a point, that got me hooked again.Although I have to say that some conclusions weren't that satisfying to me.Then there was Act 3. Man, this was the definition of mundane and super boring. Maybe the Devs/Writers were going for it, but it was just tedious. I wanted the Game to end but it dragged on and on and on...Pure boredom for me. By the time it reached it's conclusion I was kind of satisfied but maybe more so happy that it was over.The ending should've come FAR sooner in my opinion.Some people commend the writing in this Game, well, I can say it had interesting moments and I even learned a little bit, but that the writing gets praised to high heavens?! I can't sign that.It was okay in some parts and it was boring for the most parts.Also the choices matter in the end, but sometimes I would fully exhaust a characters dialogue, then make a choice and 5 minutes after I return with another character to this example character and the character totally forgot that we spoke 5 minutes before as if nothing has happened.And this has happened a few times. So this took me right out sometimes.Something positive maybe: If you just want to chill and read and explore (especially in the beginning and in some parts here and there later in the Game) then this is quite good for that.Just sit back and relax, I needed only to use my mouse and could zone out for a while.Also some people might find the Artstyle intriguing as well.I think that this is a Game where you can't really say that you love or hate it. Even though there are so many things wrong with it and I found it boring for a better part of the Game, I still finished it. And I can see people that are more interested in the medieval times get a kick out of it.But overall it's not for me and since I can't give a thumb that hangs in the middle, it's a thumbs down for me.Ultimately you have to decide for yourself (as always of course) as I can't give my recommendation personally...

_childDocuments_.review: I think I have to sit with this one a little bit! In all I'd call it a very novelistic game. Some of the things that frustrated me about the first half wound up deepening the story for me in the second half, as the conflict became more and more internal. Barring some other nitpicks, in that sense I think the narrative of this game is a huge success, and is at its most effective when it is dealing with smaller stakes.There's a lot that's frustrating about the gameplay, though. The persuasion mechanic remains completely opaque to me (three successes=a failure?) which would be less annoying if the game didn't so often force you into attempting a persuasion attempt. It would also have been nice to have a little more sense about what you're investigating, when you're gathering information. They'll be like "time to investigate a murder: do you want to go for a walk, or try to spin yarn?"This is not a criticism, more of an observation: the most common frustration with mystery games is in communication. You'll be like, "how do I express to the game engine that I suspect character x?" and sometimes you lose the drama of that intrigue in the sheer difficulty of articulation. An impossible problem to fully address in a game with prewritten lines, obviously, but sort of interesting as a fundamental drawback.Anyway, the story is about looking backwards, and trying to fit the past to a narrative, and it works so well in conversation with the player, who is also looking backwards, and trying to fit the past to a narrative.

_childDocuments_.review: Pentiment. The game was great all the way long until Act III. As a player, you can make a lot of decisions. You can make a “huge” impact on the game world. Yes, u can play it differently in another playthrough.  Yes, the lore of the game is interesting, it's interesting to read all the dialogs (until Act III as for me). BUT: sadly, the main scenario is childish, linear, and quite simple. So, “Why negative review?”, until Act III, the same characters as u saw before but 18 years older, and you can catch yourself thinking about why u can now do such things and explore that u couldn't before, after all, the concept of the “Act” still the same – “Find out the traitor, and explore the real history of a town.”. ”Nah, I have already done that before, maybe something new?” — the first question that pops out in my mind. It's okay if you do this as a character from Act I and II, but in Act III you're playing as a different person. Why should I do the same things? In conclusion, the game is great, with good lore, interesting minor characters, their interactions, and some situations you're supposed to be in, but every hour gameplay gets easier, and the plot gets more boring. Also, as a “detective” in game, you can't  charge a suspect that really is an imposter (it's pretty easy to figure out who it is actually).

_childDocuments_.review: Pentiment is one of the best pieces of historical fiction I've encountered in years. There are some period pieces that aim for a historical "feel" without engaging with the material realities, concerns, values, and ideas that people experienced in their time and place. There are others that deal in willful and playful anachronism (often for purposes of comedy or escapism). Pentiment is neither of these. Don't get me wrong, I am fond of willful anachronism, but this is a story that means it when it tells you when and where it takes place and who its characters are. I played Pentiment a lot in the last semester of my M.A., which focused on 16th and 17th century European literature and culture. There were things that came up in the game I knew well and things I didn't. German-language history and literature isn't my expertise—though I once had to read a lot about guild regulations for craftspeople in Nuremberg that I was excited to see reflected in references to what awaits Andreas after Act I! I especially enjoyed the glossary mechanic for this reason, as a terminally-curious former graduate student. But the precise historical elements that first drew me to early modernity as an area of study are the beating heart of the game. Throughout the time period covered by the three acts, and throughout the real-life 1500s and their neighboring centuries, people in Bavaria and elsewhere experienced changes in culture, religion, politics, and technology at a rapid pace that feels familiar to players in the 21st century. They are destabilized and often afraid, but also excited by the potential of a world that can shift so rapidly. Revolution can come knocking at your door any minute, but in the meantime, you still need to do the chores.This is the function of historical fiction at its best. This game tells a story meant to be received in the present through the realities, not just the trappings or tropes, of what we understand to be true about the past. We sympathize with these characters not because the lives they lead or the things they believe are identical to our own, but because we understand what is at stake for them. The characters tell us what they are willing to live, kill, and die for, and why. These don't have to be the same things we live, kill, and die for (though some of them are), but they are recognizable, on a level deeply, conscientiously woven into the story, as reactions to the world by people as rational, scared, kind, cruel, loving, selfish, intelligent, fallible, and complex as anyone playing the game. I value a work that is genuinely interested in telling a story about the past, even—and especially—when it is also a story about the present.

_childDocuments_.review: This game is really good and accessible to anyone. Both the gameplay and the plot is not difficult to understand, basically it's point-and-click Scooby Doo but solo and you piece the evidence together to make one (or four) comprehensible conclusion. There are times where everything clicked in your mind but Andreas, our protagonist, are still clueless. Maybe it's how things were back in the day.I believe the artstyle is what draws people in the first place, and it's doing its job vehemently. The BGMs are very neat. They're not always there, but when they are, you know something is going down. Sound effects are really good, possibly the second best thing after the artstyle. The sound of wind, footsteps, and the "This will be remembered" are all very nice. Sometimes the writing sound can be overbearing but I heard the devs added the option to turn it down so there you go. I don't know much about medieval history and Christianity in middle ages, but having a mystery religion thrown in once in a while is nice.Aside from the douche doctor, the bad things I can say about this game is the lack of voice acting. That and you need to run back and forth around the town to find information every new timeslot, it's very tiring fast. It reminds of me Persona 3 on PS2 but without the battles.Overall this is a nice break from barrages of AAA action shooter games we get these days. I hope Obsidian and other devs can churn out more simpler games with good story like this.

_childDocuments_.review: As a woman who has religious trauma, this was a very healing game for me. To play this game is to be transported into the world of the 1500s when Christianity ruled with an iron fist and to see the remnants of pagan rituals and Roman influences in Europe before they were completely eradicated. You see the community struggle with accepting their Lord and Savior versus the "old ways" and how this affects individuals motivations and actions. It is a well constructed game, well written, and is definitely replayable since there are many decisions you can make that affect NPCs lives. If you were ever loved learning about the reformation and Martin Luther, this game is for you.

_childDocuments_.review: A wonderful game that anyone looking for a strong narrative should consider playing.The core mystery is very compelling and built up in layers, and the conclusion invokes strong emotions. The characters are all relatable human beings, who respond to their situations in believable, often flawed ways. You will come to care for so many of them.The real strength of this game is in the storytelling. The art style for one, captures the look and feel of a late medieval manuscript, which is beautiful to look at and creates a strong identity to play in. The decision to use different fonts for characters of different statuses and vocations is delightfully nerdy and allows for a whole different dimension of characterisation. The gameplay has strong environmental storytelling elements as well - a recurring activity is eating meals with people, which tells the player a lot about the characters' station and prosperity over time.If there is one aspect of the game that could perhaps be better, it might be the pacing. Sometimes it feels like you are proceeding at a glacial pace, other times you are trying to accomplish far too much in far too short a space of time. But it doesn't detract from the overall story. The QA of the dialogue also slips from about the halfway point - I spotted one speech balloon where a character should have been speaking Italian, but was speaking Dutch instead, and the occurrence of actual typos (not the stylistic ones that get 'corrected' as part of the dialogue system) increased.All in all, Pentiment is a well-crafted game with a very compelling narrative and stunning storytelling. The story itself is multi-layered and well constructed, and the characters enjoyable to interact with. If you have an interest in Central European history in the late medieval period (I'm looking at you, Crusader Kings and Europa Universalis players), I think you will thoroughly enjoy this game.

_childDocuments_.review: It took me a year to actually play through this and I'm actually kind of mad at myself for it. A Disco Elysium inspired game made by Obsidian and headed by Josh Sawyer? Sounds like a dream project for me. I only played about an hour back in 2022 and, while I enjoyed it, i got distracted. Cue a year later and a steam deck and suddenly I found myself getting pulled in. It's not all that surprising. The first hour of the game is slow and has you making a lot of choices for your character that you have very little context for. My suggestion is just to dive in with what you think is the most interesting. It's not long before the game kicks into being a murder mystery. All I can really say is that if you don't like reading in games or you really really hate medieval art and it's aesthetics, this isn't the game for you. However, this is one of the most well-wrriten games I've ever played. Not surprising coming from Obsidian. This might be one of the most definitive passion projects I've had the privilege to play. For what it sets out to do and achieve, this game is damn near perfect. The story is involved, the mystery is gripping and the characters are richly defined and complex. Music is stellar despite it bugging out on me periodically, the art is phenomenally rendered and choices feel difficult and carry a weight that helps develop your character. It's spectacular and if you like narrative-driven games, I can't recommend it enough.
_childDocuments_.name: Pentiment

_childDocuments_.review: Unique late-medieval detective adventure, nearly solely focused on conversations and dialogue choices. I adore its aesthetics, historical realism and a well-thought plot (and I very much like the overall outcome). You have the freedom to do the sleuth work as you please and as you choose to roleplay your character and there is no such thing as “one good solution” to the problem. You visit the same place (a monastery and the surrounding village) three times during a 25-year period so you may well observe the impacts of your previous decisions, which is unparalleled.Be aware that to fully appreciate Pentiment, you should know some basics about the classical and medieval history, philosophy and religion, otherwise you might feel overwhelmed.On the minus side, there are so many characters and families that I sometimes found it difficult to remember who is who (especially as they grow and change during the events of the story). Also, some parts in the third chapter feel quite lengthy. But these are very minor complaints; Pentiment is great and on par with modern classics like Disco Elysium or The Forgotten City. (It’s an insta-buy if you like the niche genre of “monastery mysteries” like The Name of the Rose book/movie.)
_childDocuments_.name: Pentiment

_childDocuments_.review: If you've enjoyed other immersive roleplaying games that follow the CRPG tradition but with modern design design sensibilities, such as Disco Elysium, Pentiment will be right up your alley. With it's interesting cast of characters, meticulous historicity that never gets in the the way of the gripping narrative, and sharp and engaging dialogue I cannot recommend Pentiment highly enough. It's clear that for Joshua Sawyer, the director of other acclaimed RPGs you may be familiar with, such as Fallout: New Vegas and Pillars of Eternity I & II, Pentiment was a passion project and a labor of love.

_childDocuments_.review: What a game. "Pentiment" is the folklore game I've always wanted to play. It's the medieval-ish/Renaissance game I've always wanted to play. It's the murder mystery game I've always wanted to play. It scratches so many aesthetic itches that it's hard to know where to begin the praise, but I think I'll start with the deep appreciation of folklore that this game embodies. In essence, this game's message is that the stories we tell matter, and the people who tell them matter as well. The battle between story and storyteller(s) is thick in "Pentiment," and the historical discourse that influenced these positions on stories and how they dispersed is well-researched, cited and able to be referenced immediately in an illustrated glossary, fun to interact with through an easy-to-use UI, and versatile in its artistic rendering. In fact, EVERYTHING you learn about this game is backed up by research that is readily available. "Pentiment" wants players to know that reading is not only essential to their success in the game but also, as emphasized by its diverse cast of characters in different classes, an incredible privilege to be able to accomplish at one's leisure. The characters are beautifully fleshed-out, believable, and diverse in their representations of early modern classes and class warfare. I loved every single one of them and fostered connections with them more than I have compared to other games. The time you spend with people is imperative for not only peace of mind and communal relations, but also communication and cultural knowledge. It's great that something like this can represent that in a video game. Choices matter, and it's harder to accuse someone after sharing a meal with them and speaking with their families. Religious and political discourse/gameplay are also at the core of "Pentiment," and the representation of faith, class, and their conflicts is well thought-out, detailed, and also fun to engage in as a character who themselves embodies a different class and sex (and thus access to opportunities) during gameplay. Secular players might find the many references and thick religious lore a hard slog, but this game demands attention to detail and provides an in-depth (and, again, cited!) look into the world it has beautifully, meticulously recreated. The liberties this game takes with sex, sexuality, and gendered oppression and its politics are also great. I love that both women and men in this game can be proponents of or critics against misogyny, religious persecution, classism, national matters, and more. It makes the game--and the immersion into these characters' lives--more than just a simple point-and-click WASD run. It makes it a real narrative that uplifts the stories and struggles it references while creating a massively successful gamer experience for a contemporary audience.Lovers of folk horror will enjoy this game, as it fits nicely into each of Scovell's Folk Horror Chain's links: Landscape, Isolation, Skewed Morality/Systems of Belief, and quite a few Happenings. I definitely recommend this game for a long rainy day for players who crave stunningly beautiful visuals, immersive storytelling, diverse characters with believable motivations and backgrounds, and good old fashioned HISTORY LESSONS!

_childDocuments_.review: Giving this a tentative recommendation. I like the game but I can't help but think that it's commitment to aesthetic takes away from some of just joy of playing the game. This is a story which I would love to re-play and take different paths, be friendly with different people, follow different leads... but man I really don't want to deal with all the tedium of navigating this village.The first time you move from one area to another and the game zooms out to turn the page of a book it's really cute and fun but when you go from your house to outside your house to the town commons to the church to the meadow to the lower abbey to the abbey to the church to the courtyard and finally into the scriptorium and that animation plays every single time it very quickly gets old. That's a sequence of events that will take place many many times in this game and as much as I enjoyed the world and the story I can't bring myself to deal with it more.on the other hand I never grew tired of watching the creative way that speach bubbles are populated with text and never changed the setting to make them instant because I found those animations to be much more interesting to watch even if they probably wasted more of my time. I think maybe the page turn animation could have stayed for going in and out of buildings but it really is just too prevalent in the game in my opinion.The story itself is fun and intriguing. Early on I wanted to push the RP elements to their limit and see what I could do but it quickly became clear that wasn't the point (and that's fine). I liked solving the murders and making my recommendations as to who was responsible and felt invested in the outcomes of each of these situations. The characters all seem natural and authentic and react generally in natural and authentic way.

_childDocuments_.review: A wonderful game, although it felt a little overhyped for me. People were gushing with praise so I felt I went into it thinking it would be a fabulous epic, rather than a nice little point-and-click narrative package.No one can question that this game oozes with style. The art is honestly the most striking and impressive part of the game. The medieval style that I'm so used to being static and stoic has so much life breathed into it; it allowed me to view the medieval European world in a way that was so new and refreshing. I'm going to happily view manuscripts with a new admiration and vigour. There is no element of the game where its style was forgotten, and that in it's own right makes it a visual triumph of gaming.The game itself is straightforward, with a small and very appreciated allowance for customisation. Not visually, of course, Andreas will look like he always does, but you can construct a background and set of skills that make sense to you and will help you on your journey. There's nothing much I can say for the main mechanics of the game, as they don't do anything too out of the ordinary; you just investigate the town and monastery and make choices. The little minigames scattered throughout the story are lovely! I didn't expect them, and it does make the town a little more endearing.There is a massive cast of characters for such a short game. I was impressed that they all had their own personality quirks, but I did have a bit of trouble remembering who was who, especially when characters grew older. The little reminder you can get when you hover over a person's name did not help specifically for the characters, because a lot of them looked similar (especially the people from the same family). Sure, I could have gone to the tab of people after to remember who they were, but they could have added a little blurb under their character portrait of the quick reminder; having to go to the person tab broke the immersion a little, especially during more tense moments of the story.The story was so intriguing at the beginning and middle, but I felt it fell a little flat at the end. Again, though, I think this is more because it was overhyped to me. People in the reviews expressed it's similarity to Disco Elysium; I felt that Pentiment was more similar to a Telltale game. If I had gone into the game understanding that it would be more like say, The Walking Dead or The Wolf Among Us, rather than the incredible epic that was Disco Elysium, I wouldn't have been so disappointed at the end.I apologise if this review felt flat, because Pentiment really was such an engaging and unique experience! Ultimately, I feel a little upset that the reviews I'd seen and heard misled me, which has soured my experience of an otherwise special game. If you feel intrigued even a little bit by this game, and/or if narrative and mystery are your style, definitely pick it up and give it a try!

_childDocuments_.review: Really enjoyed this game. The gorgeous artwork was a special highlight for me - this combined with the side-scrolling presentation gives it this sort of tapestry-like look which is really neat. _childDocuments_.name: Pentiment

_childDocuments_.review: I got hooked on the plot so much! I loved the characters and exploring their psychology and I think that is the strongest aspect of the game. It felt like I was reading a good book. Not all dialogue is gold but there are some great and even profound bits in there. Some contemporary themes shine through without being on the nose. Gameplay is almost all reading, with very few simple puzzles (quite literally) spread out so you have to be aware of that. Some would probably not even call it gameplay, but the choices and actions definitely have far reaching consequences.The sound aspect is very bare bones with repetitive step sounds and almost no music except for a few key moments. It gives the game a contemplative mood so for me it was not a big deal (the lack of music might even be the best artistic choice). And when the music is seldom there it can be quite haunting and beautiful.On the negative there were a few minor bugs (eg. dialogue looped on itself), sometimes navigating to the stairs was weird and the extra character backstory didn't allow for much role playing as I hoped, because the extra dialogue choices didn't matter quite that much. Overall however it didn't impact my experience greatly, I quickly got invested in the characters I was playing and the demons that haunt them.
