_childDocuments_.review: Pentiment is a slow-paced, narrative-driven murder mystery adventure.If you don't like reading a lot of text, then this is likely not for you.The game's visuals are absolutely beautiful, the influence that illuminated manuscripts had on this game's devlelopment is clearly visible. The audio is overall great. Ambient effects are fitting the locations, with a highlight being the contextual musical parts, and songs performed by certain NPCs, such as .The game's protagonist can select from several different backgrounds and interests, all of which can provide additional options in conversations with NPCs, with some replies having a lasting impact on future conversations. Conversations take place in text windows without speech, with different fonts representing the background of a NPC. While a farmer uses a more casual font, a monk uses Fraktur font. Characters will also frequently use facial expressions to visualize their feelings. The protagonist moves through an 2D environment during different times of the day, which is split into morning, noon, afternoon, evening and night - all of which can be used for different endeavours, such as investigating a clue or having lunch/dinner with NPCs. There is no time limit during a time of the day, allowing for free movement. Investigating clues, however, progresses time and requires the player to plan their investigations accordingly. NPCs can be found in different spots during different times of the day. As an interesting tidbit, the protagonist's movement speed gets slower the later the time of the day is.Set in the fictional Bavarian town of Tassing and Kiersau Abbey, the story follows Andreas Maler during Acts I and II, and Magdalene Druckeryn during Act III. While outwardly a murder mystery during all three Acts, the story presents a plethora of historically accurate information, which can be looked up during dialogue. It also covers controversial topics, such as a romance between a nun and a monk, as well as a homosexual relationship between two monks. By far the most interesting aspect of Maler are his dream sequences, which are a proper reflection of his psyche. While initially cheery and curious during Act I, they paint a drastically different picture of him during Act II, as he  - which explains some of his darker remarks.Developed by a small team of 13 people at Obsidian Entertainment, Pentiment is a labor of love and passion. Its setting and historical accuracy, the easily relatable characters, the gorgeous artwork and ever enveloping narrative make it a true gem. It also offers some replayability, thanks to the different traits and backgrounds available.
_childDocuments_.name: Pentiment

_childDocuments_.review: A masterpiece. I haven't really played anything like it before - a must play if you like these types of games.I'd recommend you don't read much about it before and just start playing. However, I do think it's worth knowing beforehand that the gameplay is you walking around talking to people - almost like playing a book. Just so you don't get any expectations that it's something else and get disappointed.
_childDocuments_.name: Pentiment

_childDocuments_.review: "Choices matter" is a tag that should not be allowed to be chosen by developers.  Everything in this game is railroaded.  And while it is framed as one long story, it is actually a series of smaller stories in the same town.  At the start of each new story, you get choices of backgrounds and traits that affect conversation options and/or clues, but since none of those actually affect the outcome of a story, they are meaningless.  This is an empty game that just takes a really long time, and you are a passenger for all of it.  You don't really solve any of it.  You just go through a lot of tasks for the sake of clicking things and running around, but information is given to you when the game wants you to have it, regardless of your actions.  I would describe this as Telltale-like, where the game constantly tries to convince you your choices matter, while the story unfolds as scripted around you.  So much hope for it, but such a disappointment

_childDocuments_.review: Truly an amazing game! So I want to share my thought with you, some thing I want to play is after finish my first play-though, I had go through the community hub read everyone experience and surprisingly, I have met quite negative opinion about the game, complain like it is not mystery enough, or the mystery is too easy etc. What I want to say is Pentiment is a mystery game, yes, but the beauty of this game does not lies there. Take this game as a story where you are a part of it, live in is as Andreas, the wandering painter and that is when you start the realize the beauty of this game. The world is so nature, and the attention to detail is incredible, from the people, their house, meal, clothes, accessories to their thought and action. When you start to adore the characters, that when your "choice matter" step in. You will feel the depth of your choice as you see the consequences of it, how it affect their wife, children, etc. In my first play-through, I really try to save Piero because I like him, not because I need the story to progress. I kill the stonemason but saw the result of that hurt too. You are never gonna solves the mystery in Chapter 1 and that force you to see and live with the decision you made. One more thing I want to talk about is the time. You are never gonna have enough time to follow all of the leads and that give this game more play again value to explore all the hidden dialogues, all the choices you have not made, etc Overall, I love the game and it will be long until I find another game similar to Pentiment.
_childDocuments_.name: Pentiment

_childDocuments_.review: Excellent game with a rich historical setting, great art style and graphics, engaging and complex characters, and a very satisfying plot.It's more like a book, other than a few minigames the game play is walking, reading, and selecting from dialogue trees, but it's both educational and compelling. Decisions are often difficult because they all have consequences on the characters and town. Some are immediate while others take years, and many have a real impact on future choices in the game's remaining Acts (not simply cosmetic effects).Although after finishing the game I know the overarching plot, I still want to replay it because my character has made a few very wrong choices (Act 1) and I'd like to see how the story and characters after affected if I choose differently.
_childDocuments_.name: Pentiment

_childDocuments_.review: it is a game about themes where some online journalist will start their review by saying "all the great stories are really about storytelling, which is another way of saying they are about regret, and memory, and the passage of time" and if that doesn't sound like the ABSOLUTE worst thing to you, you might not hate this game.it is the kind of game where you really need to go into it blind and be patient and think that those things improve the experience. if you are the kind of person who looks up aspects of a game on the wiki as your go-to move before just trying everything out, you will find this very slow. the story and such makes more sense if you're invested enough to remember who most of the characters are, because if it starts to feel like you're just wandering around aimlessly clicking on everything and everyone to progress it won't be fun - some complaints are that the game is slow paced but it really didn't feel like that to me, i felt like i always (with one exception towards the end where i needed to talk to a character AGAIN who previously was useless, oh well) had plenty of ideas. this isn't a classic point in click where you need to hunt around to solve moon logic puzzles, and (for better or worse) its actually a lot more linear and limited than it feels, but in the end its about the characters and the setting and the "themes," and at least there aren't really many games i could compare it to. also on the theme of the passing of time, i will conclude my review in the spirit of the younger generations, god bless em:you can pet all the dogs and cats 10/10

_childDocuments_.review: This is really disappointing. The save system has ruined the experience for me. This game only allows auto-save feature (no manual saves). I was thoroughly enjoying the game, enchanted by the aesthetics and world...I got about halfway through Act 2, when I accidentally clicked on wrong dialogue option during dinner (vespers) that bothered me because it came off as rude. Of course, being Canadian, I couldn't stomach this lol so i exited to main menu to restart the dinner. I loaded the game back up, only to discover my save file was I guess corrupted and I lost all my progress! I went into "new game" and tried to look up old saves, since it looks like it keeps a certain amount of auto-saves, but the last save I was able to load was only an hour into the game (barely into act 1)! Not a single save file after that?! Bizarre. So I lost almost 10 hours of progress! And I just don't have the motivation to basically restart the entire game and re-watch the same scenes and dialogue all over again. Maybe I'll play it in the future once enough time has passed, but how do I know it won't happen again because of this ridiculous saving mechanic?
_childDocuments_.name: Pentiment

_childDocuments_.review: Terrific game. I think that more than anything, the game becomes more and more moving as you progress. The "feels" creep on you almost unexpected. By the time you finish the game you really care about the characters; their past and their future. Overall the game is very intriguing and captivating, you need to read A LOT, but it feels very rewarding a the end. I highly recommend it.
_childDocuments_.name: Pentiment

_childDocuments_.review: Pentiment is one of the best story-driven games I've ever played. The unique art style attracted me to buy the game, but the intriguing story kept me going forward anticipating what’s next. There are moments that shock me, literally left me jaw-dropped. By the end of the game, I felt a connection with the characters that left me disliking them or empathizing with them.I’m not a big fan of text-heavy games but when you have a perfectly written and engaging story, that is impacted by your own choices, I couldn’t put down the game. There is a Voice Assist option but will not recommend using it.Choices do matter in this game, no matter how big or small they are. For example, you have the choice to encourage a young boy to follow his passion and later, when he is all grown up, you can see how that impacted his life and character.The game's sound design is also top-notch. The crackling of the fire, the squeaking of the wood, the moving grass, or the singing of the birds, all of these background noises create a realistic notion that you are actually there in the room or at that field. I highly recommend playing the game with a headset to enhance the wonderful sound effects and your overall experience.Overall, Pentiment is an exceptional game that will leave a lasting impression on any gamer who plays it. The game's unique art style, engaging storyline, and immersive sound design all come together to create a gaming experience that is truly unforgettable.
_childDocuments_.name: Pentiment

_childDocuments_.review: I cannot recommend this game enough. To say it is a masterpiece would be to undersell it. The fact this game even exists is a wonder.The art-style is exactly that; it is art. I am familiar with the works of art and literature of the era the game is set in, and this game provides beautiful tributes.The writing and story is wonderful. The story of this game captured me from the first few words. I found myself becoming attached to the characters and genuinely trying to find a way to protect them all. When there is a tragedy it hurts. When there is happiness it is joyful. The music only complements this.The game is also thoroughly well researched, and even lists the extensive bibliography in the credits. I enjoyed every second and its authenticity brought me much joy. Especially the inclusion of such wonderful characters as Brother Sebhat and Vacslav, who provide wonderfully authentic insights into the lives and beliefs of people of colour, and the Sisters of the Convent who do much to illuminate and discuss the lives of women.I love this game. 10/10
_childDocuments_.name: Pentiment

_childDocuments_.review: Love the story so much. I didn't know much about the history, culture or religion at that time before playing this game, but this doesn't stop me from appreciating the whole story. I'm so glad to have a look at what the life was like in 16th century Bavaria through this adventure with twists and turns. Definitely amazing!
_childDocuments_.name: Pentiment

_childDocuments_.review: It constantly plays with your expectations, presenting a character to you as a villain only to suddenly reveal something intimate about them that makes you question everything you thought you knew about them (and leaves you wondering if you even care whether they're guilty or not anymore). Definitely my favorite game of 2022.
_childDocuments_.name: Pentiment

_childDocuments_.review: A wonderful game from start to finish. An engaging and narratively rich storybook-rpg with authentic early-mid 16th century art, fashion and music, set against a fascinating cultural backdrop that provides context for the religious themes that are consistent throughout the 15 or so hour playtime. This game is heavy on the narrative, heavy on the walking around the small town to find people to talk to and solving a generational mystery as you go. The story you find yourself involved in is rewarding alone based on the descriptive, colourful language used in the delivery of the conversations between characters - I always felt like I was getting to know a genuine person with fears, aspirations and morals. Further to this, the way the text is presented visually is satisfying - the text will appear in latin, then translate, words appear spelled incorrectly then corrected, and colours and fonts used to portray (what I presume) are accents, intonations and real-time language translation are all accompanied with these warm, deep scratching sounds across parchment. The music is beautiful, this is a game I played with headphones entirely. The setting is so immersive visually, and in its language and story, but the music serves to pulls you in further. Dissonant, morbid string stabs and sustains highlight plot points for example, or the singing of a hymn in an inn with the whole town or the reverb heavy religious singing against strings - it can be pretty striking, and can often feel alien. Obsidian have delivered something special here, and this is of course reflected in the positive reviews. The pedestrian, small-town focussed story and setting is so refreshing - getting engrossed in the deeply rooted religious mechanisms of the 16th century, and the rise of the Artist throughout these times is so lovingly presented in every part of the game. Go in knowing what to expect though, which is a story-heavy, dialogue-heavy, mystery focussed storybook-rpg with big plot points that you as a character are directly involved in shaping.
_childDocuments_.name: Pentiment

_childDocuments_.review: I wanted to love this game, but regrettably it falls flat on its face as you approach the conclusion.The game makes you consider your words carefully as your actions have sometimes long-lasting consequences. I like managing relationships and learning about the personalities and quirks of each character, but towards the end of the game it feels like none of that matters. The final act felt rushed and unfinished, and it plays like a movie since you basically have no agency on what happens.I'll still review this game positively because I enjoyed it, but there was definitely a lot of untapped potential here.
_childDocuments_.name: Pentiment

_childDocuments_.review: While much smaller in scope, Pentiment is right there with Disco Elysium as an achievement of video game storytelling. It brings its own unique flair to the genre with the addition of time. You really see and feel your choices as they impact more and more people over time. This story is engrossing. The characters are complex and relatable. If you are among the lucky to play this game, you will walk away from it completely and utterly fulfilled by a story of your own weaving.
_childDocuments_.name: Pentiment

_childDocuments_.review: I really want to like this game. It has all the earmarks of an immersible point-and-click adventure that involves a reasonably-researched story line. However the pacing is disjointed, the time taken away from the player between stage changes is punitive, and the inexplicable limiting access to certain scenes (i.e. exploration and character interrogation) when I really could use them is frustrating and preventing me from enjoying it.
_childDocuments_.name: Pentiment

_childDocuments_.review: Non stop high-octane action of walking around a quaint little town, talking to its townspeople to figure out a murder mystery, discuss the reformation, literacy, women's lot in life, and the power imbalance between the rich and the poor.This is basically classic literature in point&click form for history nerds. One of the most unique games I've played in the last decade.
_childDocuments_.name: Pentiment

_childDocuments_.review: This game did not grab my attention at first, one of many XGP games that are included all of the sudden without bigger advertising. But after hearing some recommendations from various sources I decided to give it a try. I fell into this rich narrative and beautiful graphical style and sunk into it for hours the very first day. I got through the first two acts, exploring every NPC interaction and visiting every corner of the map. I stopped at that point because I knew that I need to really appreciate this masterpiece and support the creators by making a Steam purchase and adding it to my library. I played the two acts again, with the same excitement as I had earlier, finished the game and knew that it was perfect from the beginning to the very end. Then played the two acts again to get the remaining achievements. The world needs games like that. I need games like that, since it got me invested for many hours, which none of the recent games managed to do.
_childDocuments_.name: Pentiment

_childDocuments_.review: Really interesting historical fiction. There's clearly been a lot of research done here both for the style of the art and text boxes as well as the plot. I was satisfied after 6 hours and finishing act 1. It keeps going into two more acts but it seems to be retreading a lot of ground in those acts so I would have rather it finished strong in one act instead, not that I think most people will mind the larger narrative.
_childDocuments_.name: Pentiment

_childDocuments_.review: Beautiful game with exquisite storytelling. The art concept, the historical placement of the story, the characters, the multitude of theological/philosophical layers that you uncover while playing, they are all memorable.My only gripe is that early on you as a player realize that the choices you make really don't matter in the picture. This is true for all games naturally, but as long as the player cannot peek behind the curtain you can make yourself believe in having influenced the story and the world. Pentinent makes it unfortunately very apparent that this is not the case here.
_childDocuments_.name: Pentiment

_childDocuments_.review: Story-driven Point & click adventure with a great story. Offers a unique experience in a fascinating period in medieval Europe. However, it suffers from a lack of gameplay elements (no inventory and only a few mini-games) and the absence of voice acting, which hurts really bad. Ultimatively, it feels frustrating that the game is railroaded in a way, which makes a "perfect playthough" not possible.
_childDocuments_.name: Pentiment

_childDocuments_.review: A beautiful, well-made, unique game. The story and characters are so engaging, the choices feel like they have weight (still feel a little bad about one of the people I got killed...), the art design and music are amazing. I felt really immersed in the world while playing, and I could probably have played another 12 hours without even noticing.
_childDocuments_.name: Pentiment

_childDocuments_.review: really, really good writing (has a lot of slice of life interspersed throughout the main conflicts, which is both really well executed and fleshes out the personalities of the characters and enhances the overarching plot). Also the game looks really good. To me, a lot of illuminated manuscripts look weird due to the proportions, lack of perspective and color choices. The art style of the game is able to perfectly find a middle ground, where it has the usage of those 3 features (like comics and manga of today), while still also having the look of an illumination. highly recommend.
_childDocuments_.name: Pentiment

_childDocuments_.review: TL;DR: My personal GOTY. A masterpiece combining the best parts of a point & click adventure game with the best parts of a detective investigation game all wrapped in an extremely well-researched historical bow.Pros:Story: The story of this game is probably the best I've ever experienced in recent memory (Some have compared this game to Disco Elysium and, in my opinion in terms of story, Pentiment far outstrips even that high bar). The story has a strong central plot and fantastic characters (Every single Character has a clear motivation, and even when they work against your aims it happens in a way that seems natural even a later twist which in the hands of a less competent writer would fall harshly flat manages too feel justified and you can still empathise with the character).  The decision  is genius and makes this one of the best detective games I've ever played. All of this is without even getting into some of the deeper themes the game explores around Memory, Loss and Historical preservation all of which are handled deftly and in a way that never becomes preachy. Art: Fantastic style defines this game. Every single screen looks beautiful and character designs stand out as being A+. Choices: "Do your choices matter?" I think so. The town of Tassing changes with your actions fairly drastically. Accuracy and Atmosphere: The amount of research put into this game is staggering. It portrays Earl modern life life as complex and correctly identifies how complex and often contradictory various sources of authority were in this period (I particularly was happy to see that Religion and the Church's role in Early modern people's lives were not, as so often happens, stereotyped or ridiculed. The author shows a deep respect for the genuine beliefs of the people of this period something very often missing with games like this but also does not shy away from showing some of the faults in these institutions too). I have never played a game with a recommended reading list but after seeing how much the commitment to historical accuracy added to this game I hope to see more games go this route in the future. Writing: "Wait why is writing down here didn't you already talk about the story?" oh no my friend the writing itself is a character in this game with each "Strata" of the village talking with different writing (The Printers dialogue *Kerplunks* onto the screen all at once, the Peasants speak their dialogue slowly and carefully in rough cursive with frequent misspelling e.t.c.) I loved this feature. Particularly how the writing would occasionally change when we learnt more about the person we were speaking to.Neutral:No voice acting: This didn't bother me too much Gameplay: Small mini games make up the majority of the gameplay. These are all fun and thankfully do not go on too long. More mini games most likely would have crowded the game and the true gameplay here is hunting for clues around Tassing which thankfully never got boring. However I can see how some might be disappointed at the limited amount of actual puzzling.Cons: Saving: You only get one save slot. For a first time playthrough this is fine but it does make one hesitant to go back and play again. Ideally a save slot system could open up after you finish your first playthrough.Conclusion:A fantastic game, my GOTY and easily one of my top ten games of all time.
_childDocuments_.name: Pentiment

_childDocuments_.review: If this game fits your niche, you will love it. Dialogue heavy, thick in history, full of roleplay opportunities, consequence-heavy decisions, and naturally beautiful to look at and listen to. Story refuses to be pinned down to an obvious structure.I'm a Reformed reverend and had a blast with my twenty-or-so hours in Reformation-era Bavaria.
_childDocuments_.name: Pentiment

_childDocuments_.review: --Tassing, Duchy of Bavaria, 1518.. Andreas enters the town--This is an narrative masterpiece, an absolute gem. It makes you care for medieval German history, religion and culture. The developers at Obsidian clearly were very passionate about presenting the philosophical ideas/discussions and history in an enchanting way, and it 100% worked - the characters are fascinating and memorable, drawn in individual style with various fonts for their speeches. The art style and theme overall is amazing. it is very impressive how a relatively short game had such an emotional impact. Although I mentioned that it has historical focus, Pentiment transcends the history aspect and delves into more philosophical themes behind the context. Belief in god, meaning of art, humanity and society are all addressed. I can't recommend this game enough.Also, its refreshing to see no hand holding, its like the game knows you will be curious enough to persist on exploring and figuring things out.
_childDocuments_.name: Pentiment

_childDocuments_.review: Instant classic. Played this game a few years ago and picked it up again on steam due to the sale. I liked it that much. Andreas Maler and his journey through the years will never get old to me. Many things are similar to Disco Elysium. This game needs a complete edition. You know hearing Father Guy getting snippy in the scriptorium would be 10/10.
_childDocuments_.name: Pentiment

_childDocuments_.review: The art is truly tremendous, the portrayal of 16th century Bavaria is exceptional, and the story and characters are compelling enough, but be warned:  It is a You will walk to the left. You will chat with a peasant. You will walk to the right. You will chat with a nun. Rinse and repeat.The mystery and scandals and whatnot are just excuses to envelop yourself in the beautiful portrayal of art and culture and community, but at the end of each act I found myself asking, "Okay, is this when the game starts?" But it does not start. Because this is not a video game.I will still recommend Pentiment, however, because it is still beautiful, despite the fact that it does not use its chosen medium to its full potential.
_childDocuments_.name: Pentiment

_childDocuments_.review: Interesting enough and has a lovely art style, but ultimately not much of an actual game to it. Characters are memorable and intriguing, the setting is relatively historically accurate and nice to explore.In my opinion it's very overrated for what it is, I'd give it a neutral if I could, but given the overwhelming praise I'm going to mark it down.If you expect to be challenged or have to figure things out and have meaningful feedback, you'll be disappointed.
_childDocuments_.name: Pentiment

_childDocuments_.review: Positives:- The story is engaging all throughout the game. There is no real low-point and no boring section.- A lot of effort went into making the dialog special. Not only do your choices impact some interactions, but there are also other details hidden within the dialog. And different fonts for different characters, which sometimes even change, is one of the most brilliant mechanics I've seen yet.- In the German version, the dialog also seems very time appropriate with the family names being gendered, everyone talking in polite form, and the untranslated city names fitting in perfectly.- Art style, music and sounds are all good and work well with the "being an artist" theme.Neutral:- I like to talk to all the people so I can get to know them and see what they are up to, but only if I can decide who to talk to and when. Unfortunately, there are a few times where the story only progresses after talking to everyone, which can take a while.- The concept of the story is only interesting because of the unusual setting. Otherwise, solving a murder mystery or being in a dilemma of aligning with either of two conflicting parties would be rather uninspired.Negatives:- There is a "hint" system for the dialog, which shows more info about people or keywords. The idea is good, but it shows completely wrong or unrelated info way too often. It could mess up your understanding of the dialog a lot.
_childDocuments_.name: Pentiment

_childDocuments_.review: This might just be the most compelling, well-written game since Disco Elysium. I longed for something to fill the void that game left, and I think Pentiment just about delivered it. I'll be perfectly honest: There were times when the game tested my patience, because Pentiment is very dense with detail and is certainly just as interested in portraying the mundanity of these characters' lives as it is in the EXTREMELY INTRIGUING murder mystery. The third act in particular took some time to pick up, but once it does... I am so happy I stuck with it. The ending is a real winner. Rarely does a game move me to such a profound degree. You just don't expect it when you first boot up the game, but this is a true tearjerker, let me tell you. One of my favorite aspects about the game is how it handles time. The *finiteness* of it, and the *passing* of it. You can't experience everything in one playthrough, never know everything, and thus you can never truly trust the incredibly difficult choices you HAVE to make. And the choices have such deep consequences for everything in the lovely town you get to know, and the genius of it is that you return to this town at three different points in time so that you get to see exactly how these choices impact the people living there. And don't get me started on these characters! They're a great cast of lovable and hatable and ambivalent folks. Excellent writing is backed up by great artwork, sparse but effective music and boatloads of interesting, well-researched teachings about life in the 1500's. I learned a lot of stuff, and the game compelled me to learn even more. I LOVED this game, I WHOLEHEARTEDLY recommend it, and now I must search for a way to fill the void again...
_childDocuments_.name: Pentiment

_childDocuments_.review: Playing Pentiment reminded me of reading a book. More precisely an historical fiction novel.You are Andreas Maler, a 16th century artist, who is staying at the fictional town of Tassing, Bavaria, doing work at Kiersau’s abbey as part of your university education. Your time there gets disrupted when a murder occurs and you immediately step in to solve the mystery in order to save a friend, but in doing so you uncover an even greater mystery...Andreas is an Illuminator of Manuscripts; he participates in the creation of all kinds of documents. The game takes place in a time setting where the Gutenberg Printing press is starting to make possible the printing of books and texts in general for everybody, a domain which was previously exclusive to the church and those with the knowledge.This game has a great deal of research an investigation mixed into the narrative. In the end credits, the amount of reference books puts to shame any other game in recent memory. If you have any interest in the time period this is one very special game.That being said, it is important to note, that this game really plays as a book, in more ways than one... Pentiment doesn't have spoken dialogues, only text (And there's lots and lots of dialogues). Each text is written (in a way) like the person who is saying the words is also writing them... Each character will have different styles of text, different forms and colors, and even will make more or less mistakes while writing their own dialogues according to the degree of knowledge they possess. The story is long, with a decent amount of twists and turns, but it does have some slow sections (which set the stage for what it is to come) and so, it demands your attention. You don't have to know everything and remember everything but not everything is on display for you to see. There are in fact, some optional objectives and dialogues which you may miss if you take some main activities that demand time to complete.Even then I would say that the choice to make all dialogues text only could be a very deliberate artistic choice. While it does take more effort to read all text it does create a sense of " being inside your head, in your own created world”. This is why, Pentiment is the closest I've been to reading a book (while playing a game). You read the words, you even see the pictures on the page. But the rest is created by your own imagination. In that sense I would say that even the graphic style for Pentiment is very much in tone with what you could find during that time period, but also of what you could find reading a book....The visuals for Pentiment have some decent amount of animation (specially towards the end sequences) but it mostly remains like a picture you could find in an illustrated book.... that and the fact that there are no voices (mostly) lets you create the character's voices in your head, and maybe even other elements from the story.It will take some time according to each player, but if you stick with the game and keep playing it you may begin to use your imagination (and your visual memory in some strange way) in a way we only do when reading books. That perhaps is the real treasure of this game.All of this of course means nothing without a good story. Pentiment's story doesn't disappoint, it is a good one, it plays like an Umberto Eco's video game adaptation, albeit not a perfect one. There are some slow sections here and there that could've been avoided perhaps or trimmed a little, even if the game clearly doesn't intend to be flashy like a modern fast pace game and play like a slow burn big novel.I liked this game, and even would say it is one in a thousand, very special and very rare and very good at what it does. But it definitely needs some time and dedication (like any good book) and you'll definitely need to be in the right mood to play it.
_childDocuments_.name: Pentiment

_childDocuments_.review: A beautiful, emotional game with rich story.That being said, I have a few gripes with it. I disliked that I could miss conversations because I forgot to run back to the woods for the 8th time and that increased my playtime in the game dramatically. Missing these conversations doesn't affect the outcome of the game but I wanted to get all of the story I could out of the game because I love the writing, the characters and the world they created.The Inability to save hurts the game in my opinion and like most games with branching paths, they all collapse back down to a smaller path that usually changes little in the end. I've made my peace with that in these types of games if a story could branch all over the place it would never get finished. It annoys me to have 3 places to visit and due to time I'm only able to visit 2 in a story game of this type. Replaying the game doesn't necessarily provide too much more to experience. The flavor provided by choosing different backgrounds does provide some more color to the playthrough.This game is a must buy for anyone who likes adventure games, story and medieval settings.
_childDocuments_.name: Pentiment

_childDocuments_.review: if this game looks like something you might be interested in: go for it! I absolutely recommend it! If you take your time to really delve into the game world and get to know all the characters and locations and their history, the game will absolutely reward you.One caveat however: Even though this might look like a detective game, that's not really what the developers were going for. This game is more about choices and character development than solving an actual mystery. So if you're like me and try and find the perfect solution to every problem, you might become a bit frustrated. So my suggestion is: make your choices and then just live with the consequences - as difficult and as heart-wrenching as that may be sometimes. :D
_childDocuments_.name: Pentiment

_childDocuments_.review: How did this game fly under my radar? I'm amazed that I didn't hear about it until now. It's fantastic. I'm having a difficult time deliberating over choices and they have a really interesting impact on the story. It's beautiful, thoughtful, and very well-crafted. I nearly played it all in one sitting.Some people think the pace is too slow. I agree that the third act is where it starts to drag, but I like that the game asks you to really consider what you're doing with the time you have. You get many opportunities to take in the atmosphere. Personally, my only complaint so far is that sometimes I click through too hastily and accidentally select an option because my mouse was hovering over it. The auto-save feature is lovely and makes the stakes higher (I can't just go back to before a bad decision), but it is a bit bothersome when I make unintentional mistakes.Otherwise, this is quickly becoming one of my favorite games I've played. If you like mystery stories, adventure-style exploration, history, and art, I think it's absolutely worth trying.
_childDocuments_.name: Pentiment

_childDocuments_.review: Excellent art direction and design combined with phenomenal writing, interesting characters and a story with strong themes. The game side however is a bit weak, with the gameplay essentially being boiled down to walking around, talking and choosing where to spend your somewhat restricted time, making it more of a visual novel with dialouge options than anything else.I still thoroughly enjoyed it, and it is well recommended.
_childDocuments_.name: Pentiment

_childDocuments_.review: This is a "yes, but" recommendation. The game is strongest when it leans into the history. There are genuinely beautiful sections with period music and paintings, and the costumes and settings are beautiful. It's a lovely period game, with rich attention to detail -- the setting is so much more than surface dressing.But the game itself is a bit tedious -- take away the setting and there's so much running back and forth between the same locations, just to check to see if any of the characters have anything to say. The first three hours this was charming -- the next 11 it started to feel like a lot of padding between beauty, decisions, and story progress. There's a lot of just-OK elements like this -- like the painfully awkward sound design that had this terrible clop clop for footsteps that never stopped for 14 hours of playing.Hopefully, in a future game, they'll focus more on the magical parts of the game. For some reason, there's very spare with the music and the artwork, even those those sequences were reliably fantastic. (They thought we would sit through a flash mini-games but not more singing?!?) Similarly, I loved the glimpse of rooms in far off cities when you write letters to them. Overall, I think I thought about 7 hours of this game was exceptional -- but the 14 total hours I spent overstayed its welcome a bit. (This feels especially long for a choices matter game, which ostensibly wants you to replay it.) I think this view is shared by most players, since only 20% of people have the finishing achievement.
_childDocuments_.name: Pentiment

_childDocuments_.review: One of the best single player experiences I've ever had in gaming. Brilliant and original visual style, great writing, tons of history to learn and be immersed in and a truly interesting take on the detective game genre. I thoroughly enjoyed it and was happy I jumped right in without reviews and the like. So many joyous twists and turns. I read The Name of the Rose at more or less the same time as I played the game and both works are just tremendous for teleporting oneself to the middle ages/Rennaiscance period. Highly recommended!

_childDocuments_.review: One of the best and unique games to kick 2023 off!With the first Act done I can wholeheartedly recommend Pentiment. While being developed by Obsidian is a definite green light, the game itself is carved to be a unique masterpiece in a style like I have not seen in games before. A beautiful amalgamation of art, history, storytelling and impeccable writing with an intriguing mystery to solve and world altering decisions to be made.

_childDocuments_.review: Currently in my second playthrough and I do love this game. Played this first with a friend and then we kidnapped another mutual friend for the second playthrough. The subtle foreshadowing, the different personalities and crimes that need solving are so fun! And MAN does this game come right for the feels in later parts.It has a lot of charme and I love how much thought and heart went into the making of this. The art style is phenomenal, the dialogue is great and your actions and choices do be having consequences! I love the development of Andreas as a character and the way you can see his influences on the abbey and the town even years later. There's also humor in it and the game knows how to play its strengths. It also definitely tempts you to replay, as you won't be able to see everything the game has to offer in a first playthrough.I did encounter some bugs, especially in Act Two, that made a part of the main mission sorta hard to put together but managed fine by googling how to get around it. _childDocuments_.review: This game is awesome. I saw people comparing it to Disco Elysium, so I had to buy the game. However, allow me to make sure your expectations are properly set:This is a playable story where your choices have very minor narrative impacts, unlike DE. I found myself getting frustrated because I set my expectations for it to be "Disco Elysium if you internalize Catholicism for 1,000 years," or whatever. It's not. You're a train on a predetermined track. Your decisions do not matter much at all. There is nothing inherently wrong with this, unless you go in expecting otherwise. Buuuuut... the predetermined track you are on is a lovely ride, and the game has some thoughtful verisimilitude. So yeah 8/10, but not 10/10 like Disco Elysium.

_childDocuments_.review: This game is a must buy for anyone interested in history. The visuals are amazing. The characters are very well written. The main character Andreas is incredibly relatable (I too would ignore the issues in my marriage to go solve murder mysteries).There's no voice acting so that might be a turn-off for some people but I loved it.
_childDocuments_.name: Pentiment

_childDocuments_.review: A brilliant and unique multi-generational murder mystery set in a Bavarian alpine village and monastery of the Holy Roman Empire during the earliest decades of the Protestant Reformation, with visual art directly inspired by period manuscript illuminations and woodblock prints.  I was genuinely moved by the story at several points, and if the setting sparks your curiosity, the in-game glossary and journal provides enough information for a graduate-level seminar on Bavarian Renaissance culture, art, and spiritual practices.  Absolutely not for everyone, but if anything I said sounds even remotely interesting to you, you'd be doing yourself a real disservice to ignore this game.  I bought it on sale, but I absolutely would recommend buying it even at full price.
_childDocuments_.name: Pentiment

_childDocuments_.review: A Masterpiece of Art and History. Pentiment emerges as a video game that is as much a work of art as it is a historical odyssey. The game’s art style is a breathtaking homage to the storybook illustrations of the Late Medieval period, offering a visual feast that is both unique and captivating.As you traverse through the Bavarian countryside, the game feels like a walk through history, akin to strolling through the pages of a book or the halls of a museum. It’s a narrative-driven journey that is rich in detail and steeped in the cultural, social, and political nuances of the era.The minimalist gameplay allows the story to shine, drawing players into a complex and enthralling detective thriller. With every decision and dialogue, you shape the path of Andreas Maler, an artist caught in a web of intrigue, making for a super interesting look into the past.Pentiment is an interactive experience that educates and entertains, leaving a lasting impression with its artistic brilliance and historical depth.
_childDocuments_.name: Pentiment

_childDocuments_.review: A game made specifically for J.E. Swayer, by J.E. Sawyer. And that's what makes it more interesting than a majority of games out there. Fitting for a game about playing as an artist, the passion and artistry shines through. That fact makes it an entirely unique experience and it's why if you're a fan of narratives in games you owe yourself to play it. The fact it was made for one person means there likely won't ever be a game like it, and so it makes it an entirely unique experience worth playing for yourself. I promise if you don't learn something about yourself, you'll most certainly learn a lot about history.
_childDocuments_.name: Pentiment

_childDocuments_.review: Pentiment is a masterpiece of its genre, and yet few in my circles have even heard of it. Anyone who enjoys narrative experiences with a rich environment and complex characters in their games should play it.From the unique art style to historical details that few will pick up on all of, this story is a rich exploration of life in a time and place many of us are exploring for the first time. Pentiment cleverly uses chat bubbles to "trick" a player into a reading-heavy experience. It works. I wanted to soak in every line of dialogue the game had to offer, but the limited number of conversations you're able to have in a day add a real sense of urgency and replay-ability at the same time while fitting neatly within the story. This game has an unbelievable amount of depth to it -- think of movies that have made you excited to go back and watch a second time, now that you know what you know. i'm intentionally being vague about the story itself here, because I don't want to spoil it or paint anyone's impressions of the characters and story. You simply have to experience it for yourself.The only complaint I could think of is that some "meaningful choices" purists may find Pentiment falls short in some ways. I disagree, but can understand how some arrive at that conclusion. Your choices *do* have a considerable effect on the rest of the game, but Obsidian does choose not to tell the player "hey, you were right/wrong about this," which I think makes the story more interesting. Endings with few stark differences may leave some feeling that way, as well, but I am willing to accept that in order to experience the ending Obsidian wanted me to see.A first playthrough of Pentiment seems to run most people around 14-16 hours. I've yet to dive in a second time, but I definitely intend on returning. I got Pentiment on sale, which made this the best bang for my buck on steam in ages. If you love a good story, you should pick this up.
_childDocuments_.name: Pentiment

_childDocuments_.review: I saw this game's trailer and didn't think much of it. It released and I didn't even realize. I saw a video on it and realized I needed this game, and after playing it I can say it's absolutely amazing. As someone who has studied history of this era and is working towards getting a history minor, this game scratches everything a history nerd wants. Not to mention is has an amazing visual style and everything is perfect and  I love it so much. If you like 16th century history and know a bit about it and the Renaissance as a whole, it's probably worth a buy especially if you know languages like Latin or French.
_childDocuments_.name: Pentiment

_childDocuments_.review: Just finished my first playthrough. This is a very interesting game that caught me off guard in many ways. One thing I'd like to say right off the bat is that this is not a mystery game a la Obra Dinn or Case of the Golden Idol which is what I was somewhat expecting. Nor is it particularly heavy on the roleplay aspect, though these mechanics are present to a certain extent. What I think the game is at its core is an immersive historical experience which takes you on a tour of a village in renaissance Bavaria, while informing you about the various institutions, occupations, socioeconomic classes, ethnic minorities, and ideas which existed at the time, all told in a contemporary art-style. What's kind of meta is that the game's themes and story is related to the topic of history and information, and how it is transmitted between generations.This game is probably not for everyone, but if you love learning about history than I cannot recommend it enough. The best way to enjoy this game is not thinking about it as a problem to be solved or game to be won, but a setting to explore. Look around, talk to as many people as you can, drink in the atmosphere, and try to act in a manner that you would if you were actually there. For me, this is an easy 10/10.
_childDocuments_.name: Pentiment

_childDocuments_.review: I am really amazed at how easy it is to get sucked into this game. Its hard to put down, the story is compelling, and you come to care about the characters. I wish there was more control over the direction the characters take, but I'm thinking any choices style game will leave the player wishing for more control and more choices. I also appreciated the Jewish characters and that connection.
_childDocuments_.name: Pentiment

_childDocuments_.review: During my lifetime I've played my fair share of videogames, counting in hundreds, literally. When I'm saying the best game, I don't mean it in some objective sense, taking count of various factors. For me, such game is the one that left the biggest impact. Probably, that goes to Night in the Woods, although my second playthrough 6 years after the first one haven't felt that unparalleled in quality as much as I remembered.Now, I've played Pentiment like 3 months ago, maybe more. But the experience lingers. There is something disturbing about this game. Like the hardships of people are portrayed in such a believable way. Death feels visceral, present. The ongoing murder spree with the sprinkles of magic realism elements create a sense of deep-rooted horror, but in unsettling way rather than scary.The strong impression persists. I oftentimes ponder about the game. But it's not just the excellent story, brilliant dialogue, original artstyle. The best quality for me is how real playing the game feels. A lot of the game is unstated to player. In chapter 2, the game portrays the most authentic depiction of depression I've ever seen in a videogame, yet not once does the game says this verbatim. Other specks of life you notice once you contemplate the game. The crone who wishes to die. Marin, having some strong obvious personal issues you never find more about. The blacksmith, unable to find a wife, decade after decade. Brother Piero, showing genuine paternal care to Andreas, whom Andreas weeps over his beravement. The genius of this game lies in the unspoken. The more closely you observe, the more you see Pentiment as a manifestation of human predicament, a collage of intricacies this experince of life entails. It's so much more than a murder mystery game.If I were to guess a recent game that will reach a cult status down the line, I would vote Pentiment. It's the second time I'm playing this game, and unlike many emotionally strong unique games that had lost some of its spark when I played them for the second time, Pentiment just confirmed my suspicion that it's an outstanding experience that will stand a testament of time.For starters, the games I consider the best are behemoths like Planescape Torment, The Longest Journey, Night in the Woods, Panzer Dragoon Saga, The Last of Us II. I've fallen in love with some of those two decades after their release. Pentiment is on an equal footing in my opinion and it's genius will keep resurfacing in years to come. I'm so glad this game exists.
_childDocuments_.name: Pentiment

_childDocuments_.review: I had lost hope for Obsidian after Outer Worlds. Pillars of Eternity was far too busy with snooping its own writing to be enjoyable for me.  Tyranny was better, but clearly not thought out through enough, and unfinished. Then Outer Worlds happened, and it was to me a miserable game lacking any originality, trying too hard to be both Borderlands and New Vegas. Outgrown (or however it’s called) is a game I’m not interested in at all, so I have no opinion on it, except that it was further indication of Obsidian moving away from what made their work so good to begin with.So, I actually ignored Pentiment altogether, expecting it to be either another overly pretentious graphomanic piece, or another style-over-substance festival of insanity. Add in modern trends of character building and ignoring historical reality and good taste to fit political quotas, and Pentiment looked as grim as it could on arrival.I was pleasantly surprised. Not just pleasantly – by the end I was overjoyed, Pentiment was one of the bright spots on the rather miserable landscape of your humble servant’s “today”.The game is a narrative-centric point-and-click adventure with light roleplaying elements. It allows for some possibilities to influence the flow of the narrative, and for certain nonlinearity in that you cannot perform all possible actions within given timeframe, so you inevitably miss certain bits and pieces that could potentially change your opinion on some characters or events. But the main frame of the story is static, and general events are unavoidable and will happen no matter what the player does.I’d say this game has even less mechanics than Disco Elysium does, and it’s even more compact, and even slower, so one needs to get really into it to properly enjoy, but that’s the nature of games as an art form.Even the “quota” stuff I’ve mentioned earlier is well-woven into the story. There is a black guy in an alpine monastery in 1515. An improbable occurrence, but the way it is presented – not impossible. There are two gay characters, but they act the way gay people of the era would actually act – hide the fact.The game plays well from the customs and ways of the era. it gets a bit to preachy about how hard the woman’s fate at the time was, but never too much to get distracting. Also, the game allows itself a bit too much modern lexicon, I think it’d work better with allowing for more “ye olde englyshe” to get, especially for the characters of more classic upbringing, just like they did with the font system representing levels of education of the characters.But not everything is perfect. There are flaws, some – significant. With the amounts of backtracking you need to perform while investigating the area (which consist of a city, two farms, abbey and a small forest) at least a couple of fast travel points would help tremendously. Their implementation would require some playing with the several events that need to happen on the way from point A to point B, but those could just interrupt the fast travel, for example.The way the game skips time sometimes leads to odd interaction, say some events are discussed after a month has passed as if those’ve occurred yesterday. In some cases, you cannot make some actions despite literally meeting with the characters you need to meet with to achieve those actions because the time system implies you’ve missed the opportunity, while you clearly haven’t.But overall, I’m really impressed and I do hope Obsidian will take note that small projects of this scale can be a good opportunity to realize actual artistic vision instead of trying to follow some modern trends and dip into mediocrity.
_childDocuments_.name: Pentiment

_childDocuments_.review: Great story-based game with exceptional visual and sound design. Really grasping story with solving all the mysteries.However, because it's gameplay kind of only consists of reading and making choices it's not replayable as far as I'm concerned. Maybe it would be better to give the time to lurk through all the storyline than forcing to make really tough decisions what path should be chosen.

_childDocuments_.review: This is just a warning for future buyers that this is not a "choices matter" type of game. If you come into the game with that type of understanding, I am certain you will have a better time with it than I did. I waited two weeks after I finished this game before I wrote this review. "Choices Matter" is false advertisement. This is not a spoiler, but none of your choices really matter in the major arch of the story. Of course, your choices matter in terms of what story line you receive, but there is only one ending for the main character in the game and there is nothing you can do to change that. I was so frustrated in the mid and end game. You can tell that this game was rushed because the mid and end game has far less content and way more explaining than the first third of the game. This game is such a shame because it could have been so much more.
_childDocuments_.name: Pentiment

_childDocuments_.review: Extremely gripping and immersive story with light roleplaying elements.What you see in the trailers should speak for itself. It's a story-heavy game in a historical setting.Most of the gameplay is spent reading as you follow a large cast of characters through their lives.Highly recommended if you've enjoyed games like Disco Elysium or Night in the Woods.
_childDocuments_.name: Pentiment

_childDocuments_.review: I went into this expecting to play as a medieval Sherlock Holmes. That's not quite the case — sure, there is a mystery, but this is a much more story about a place and the people in it rather than a whodunit —, but I quickly forgot those expectations and let the game immerse me in its beautifully illustrated community and show me, through its well realized characters, the impact of happenings over time. It was great.
_childDocuments_.name: Pentiment

_childDocuments_.review: This game is brilliant. It manages to capture a sense of a place that feels so real, and people living within it that feel natural and well written. The game is deep with its themes, and more moving than I expected, it really gets you thinking about a lot of things - but in particular it made me think about the whole concept of history, and our place inside of that.Where does the present end, and where does history start. What is worth holding onto and remembering, and what is better forgotten as you move into the future. Really recommend this as an experience that I think will affect you, and leave you thinking about it afterwards.

_childDocuments_.review: An outstanding story rich game that allows you to grow close to the characters it presents.  It is easy to beat, only requiring you to click and participate in a few mini games, however the game runs much deeper.  You can take as much time or as little to solve puzzles or talk to townsfolk before moving on with the story, however the game will only allow you to find so many clues before moving on and asking you for your decision.

_childDocuments_.review: : Pentiment is a point and click historical fiction game with mystery elements. The visuals are very stylish and impressive. Ultimately though I personally found the game to be too slow, my choices lacked impact, and the core mystery and its reveal disappointing.Heads-up: I do NOT think this is a bad game. I just personally wouldn't recommend it as it's not something that affected me as much as it seems to have affected others. This game is very  similar to  in terms of the vibe, its themes, and its gameplay. I'll be upfront and note that I didn't enjoy Night in the Woods either, but if you are one of the many who loved Night in the Woods, I can guess that you'll probably very much love Pentiment as well.- The character dialogue is pleasant. There are many characters and the conversations feel fine.- The art style is very pleasant. I'm quit impressed with the animation fluidity blending with a pen and ink style of art, hats off to everyone involved with that.- The ideas threading the whole game are worthy of reflection. It's hopefully not a spoiler at this point but as I said before: there's a lot of similarity in theme to Night in the Woods.The solid dialogue and characterization combined with the deeper themes really had me rooting for the residents of Tassing... but perhaps that's where some of the frustration emerges too.Very early on in the game you can feel through its structure that you are merely an observer in this world, even an observer to the character you control Andreas, rather than a player.It can be argued that this ties in with core themes of the game: the inevitability of the passage of the time and the question of which stories should we choose to tell.Personally for me a loss of agency causes me to lose some interest unless I'm really able to enjoy the core story and characters, but unfortunately here I just didn't hve that drive.Similary early on in the game you realize that you aren't going to find the true culprit until the end of the game. The whole reveal and  around it are part of why this whole thing feels intensely deja vu and reminds me of Night in the Woods.This made me lose interest immediate game objectives. I got the sense (and later correctly found out) that there really are no "true" answers for .The way that the final reveal occurs fell flat for me.  We the player do not drive towards this ending, instead we go to a pre-determined location, and then . Ultimately it feels like there were many good candidates, and while the reveal makes sense, it doesn't feel earned.The gameplay is, once again, very similar to Night in the Woods. There are set chunks to the day where you can choose one from a set of activities. The time is set up such that you can't do all of them before a deadline.These activities are like little mini-TV episodes where you usually gain some information to help on your main quest. Sometimes they'll include little mini games for the player to do (Night in the Woods gah! The similarities are everywhere).In between those activities there's still a lot to be done however. By running back and forth through town, depending on what previous flags you've set (by some dialogue), you _may_ or may not have a dialogue scene with a character during your non-event time, when you previously did not. This was somewhat frustrating since it was hard to tell when you'd have more dialogue options for a character after an event, so you end up scanning much of the map to chat with every character and see if new options opened up.And the walking... Your character's pace is not great. I've probably spent a solid 30-40% of my time in Pentiment getting from place to place, waiting for loading screens, and (y'know what, I'll say this counts too) watching my character go to bed in a surprisingly long unskippable cutscene. (This is one of my major gripes with, you guessed it, Night in the Woods as well, although that game is far more egregious when it comes to this).I have it under both likes and dislikes, because well, I like and dislike it. The themes are great. On the other hand the overall mystery is unsatisfying, and while the characters are distinguishable, they still feel somewhat flat. It's hard to say there were any characters I flat out loved...Something that I didn't notice while playing but feels pretty obvious now is that it there isn't much humor in Pentiment. Conversations in Tassing and Kiersau feel mostly about poor harvests, serious conversations about hope for the future, marriage proposals, scandalous relationships... etc., but I don't think I ever laughed out loud and I think that's because for the most part I wasn't meant to.I don't want to wax poetic or over analyze, but I think that humor is very humanizing in games. Life is in fact absurd (as this game very much points out), and for that reason is worthy of laughter. It helps point us towards understanding the oddities, and thus cruxes of what living is about.:Maybe I was setup for disappointment with Pentiment. I had been told that this game was similar to Disco Elysium, a game that I really loved, a game that I think about often, even long after playing it.Even the Pentiment game director noted the comparison was not very accurate:  For those of you who have played Disco Elysium and came here with that in mind, I hope to provide a perspective on Pentium from that point of view.- You only occasionally control your character's dialog rather than always- In Disco Elysium you always have the company of your skills and Kim (for the most part) maintaining a lively rapport or more mature sounding board throughout the game. In Pentiment your character for the most part is in new situations with different people each time, and doesn't spend all that much time reflecting on or reacting to their situation (there are occasional thought bubbles, but they're optional and non-confrontational).- Disco Elysium felt like it had a lot more humor (at least for me)- Disco Elysium is notably longer, 30hrs relative to Pentiment's 15.- Disco Elysium has an inventory system whereas Pentiment does not.- Disco Elysium's city and environment play much more of a character (sometimes literally) as compared to Pentiment.- Disco Elysium's ambience is that of a rundown 1960's-esque seaside town, with sounds of waves, and bars, whereas Pentiment's ambience is simpler (for lack of a better word "flat" like the artstyle, not that the art isn't complex) and more foresty.Overall it had a gameplay loop I found slow and unenjoyable, the dialog didn't fully draw me in, and the core mystery driving the main plot felt pre-ordained and unconnected to my actions.Wow, surprised you made it this far. Honestly this review is partially a way for me to organize my thoughts on Pentiment and help myself lockdown how I felt about the game and why. I do not think it was a bad game, I just don't think it was a game meant for me.Maybe in the coming days I'll think more about Tassing and Kiersau, and if I do I may come back to this review. After all I consider how much you think about a game to be a true testament to its power.

_childDocuments_.review: You'll be amazed by the intricately crafted dialogue and calligraphic expression throughout the entire story. Details such as typos being fixed, font changing on learning more about the speaker, to inc splatters and scratching from a feather to signify volume. All of which makes Pentiment's dialogue one of the most realized mechanics yet to be seen in any story-driven experience.

_childDocuments_.review: This is a very good point and click\mystery solving game. But it’s not the usual “find the pieces, stick them together and go to the next phase. If anything this game reminds me of Pathologic (If you know what I am talking about). The game don’t handholds you, you have a journal which tracks a lot of things but you have to connect the dots and do the detective work without objective pointers. You have to remember what to do, who to talk and there is no crazy item juggling. There is also some kind of “reputation” system which will influence if people will or not trust you when the dices are rolled and the knot pulled.The story spans on a large length of time, you will see characters, choices and consequences evolving during all the game. There is no immediate understanding if you have done all right or you didn’t get anything about what you were supposed to do. The games goes on and you will see what happens.The choices you make for and with you character have a lot of importance and there is a lot of material for another playtrough, just to see everything unfolding with other choices (or doing a better job if you screwed up badly on your first try).The style is peculiar but it’s a far cry from very avant-garde games like A Procession of Chivalry. The miniatures drawing is ok but nothing to scream for. It adds to something that is already well done.

_childDocuments_.review: Very refreshing take on storytelling. It’s an intriguing mystery to unfold where choices really do seem to matter, but in such a way that you’re never quite sure if you could have changed the outcome, which really lends to the time period and overall theme of the narrative. It’s a poignant and well-realized insight into the times and how history can be told through art, what really determines ‘truth,’ how religion both protected and undermined communities, and how peoples across centuries are more connected than they probably realized. Such a great game. I briefly felt there was a slump in the beginning of the second half of the narrative (no spoilers), but that was soon corrected—much to my surprise. Great twists, immersive score, interesting characters…I could go on! 10/10 Superb!
_childDocuments_.name: Pentiment

_childDocuments_.review: It's a brave piece of art that takes unpopular and unusual methods in games' storytelling to shape it into a captivating journey. It's a love for good narrative, uniquely stylised art and academic accuracy in facts that carry you to a different era and make you empathize with the characters. In the end, you feel yourself like the real narrator of Historia Tassiae. A writer only begins a book, a reader finishes it. It'd be even better with more medieval tunes and book examinations which i enjoyed.

_childDocuments_.review: This is going to be a very hard review, describing how much I adore this game without spoilng anything.First, the settings is adoreable. Located in a late-medival town in the 16th century Bavaria and brought to live with an incredible pretty artstyle, the world suck me into it in the first 30 minutes. The characters are non flat and one-dimensional, you want to know more of every character, why they act their way and how they are related to the plot.Second, the story itself, divided into three parts , is with its twist that left me sitting in front of the screen like "OH CMON", but made me feel like I HAVE to know what happens next in our small little town and how things develope.Third, I usually don't want to read a lot of text all the time, but Pentiment made me do it, and I enjoyed it very, very much. Each little piece of dialog is written  rather neatly and presented in small portions, sometimes combined with a bit of game-world interaction.Fourth and final, you can't see everything and have to decide on priorities. While I am usually the completionist when it comes to main story lines, it made me feel my choices had an impact on the world and my experience was rather unique. I know I missed out on some parts, and sometimes had regrets with how I made my desicions. It made me think about my choices sometimes for a long time before committing to any important decision and then delivered.Do I recommend Pentime: Absolutely!Is it for everyone? Maybe not, BUT: GIve it a try.

_childDocuments_.review: I've literally just started but you can tell the amount of work the developers have put into this game and their passion for the 16th century medieval church-isque history. The inner Latin geek in me is so happy. Delightful highlights include listening to sound of scribbling as they talk with their speech bubbles. Music/soundtrack compliments the entire gaming experience.Love how your choices do matter and the way you choose your character's background gets reflected within their interactions with other characters as well as how they solve the mysteries in-game. Such a worthy purchase for this price point. Can't wait to finish the rest of this game!

_childDocuments_.review: Fantastic historical pint & click adventure game. Long text heavy narrative, 20 hours, with none of the typical boring point & click pixel hunting. There's no inventory and the puzzles are self contained. (not many). My favorite Obsidian game since New Vegas and the story is almost as good as KOTOR II. Renaissance era story right around Martin Luther's nailed his theses and the incipient reformation. I REALLY ENJOY how it respects the era these people lived by having the characters believe in religion strongly without being bashful. There is also a technological change underway with the printing press making the monastery scribes obsolete. The monasteries preserved and developed philosophy, art, books, and theology after the fall of the Roman empire. This game touches on all of this.

_childDocuments_.review: I just finished this game. It took me eight hours to completely finish the story. Sometimes I forgot what I had to do so I just ended up running around and talking to everyone until I found the person I actually had to talk to in order to proceed with the story. If you are more focused than I was, I think you could finish it quicker. (also I only got 17 out of 41 achievements just so you know)These are some of the many pros:- beautiful illustration- you can pick the heritage of your character (I dont think it influences the story but it was still a fun feature)- often you will be given multiple options for what you can say in a convo (sometimes it influences how the npcs will treat you, often times it doesnt matter)- even tough there are about 30 npcs you quickly get to know their dynamics and mindset- The soundtracks are complete bangers- I might be wrong but I felt like this game rlly gave me a good look into the 16th century (How the ppl lived, their struggles and the role that christianity played in their daily lives)- I LOVED the minigames, unfortunately there werent many and they didnt take very long or were hard to complete BUT they were still very enjoyable.Cons:- It is a game where you have to walk A LOT, as mentioned before, the map isnt very big, but in the end you walk from person to person and thats basically the game (which isnt super bad but I just wanted to mention it)- The main focus of the game is basically a conflict between the farmers and the church (so if christianity triggers you, this might not be the game for you)- I NEED MORE MINIGAMES!Conclusion:Personally I really enjoyed this game. The main focus is on the story, and even tho I liked how relaxing the game was, towards the end I started skipping the dialogues cause I just wanted to know who the murderer was. I am new to steam and I only have 5 games, but evertime I opened steam I wanted to play pentiment. You dont have to be super focused or remember the controls, so oftentimes I would get something to eat and explore the village of Tassing. If that sounds good to you then I would 100% recommend this game to you.

_childDocuments_.review: Easily the game of 2022 for me and quite unlike anything I've played before. The visual style and music are wonderful and we definitely need more historical games like this.
