_childDocuments_.review: - It's very likely the game's artstyle drew you to it. It's certainly what piqued my interest. I'm happy to report that it does indeed look amazing, with the highly stylized artstyle reflecting the medieval paintings and illuminated manuscripts produced in Bavaria during the 1500s- I was also pleasantly surprised by the game's text boxes, which feels like a weird thing to say. There's all sorts of neat little touches. If you're talking to a monk or nun, their speech bubbles will be written in a old-timey gothic script. If you're talking to a printer, the text will plop down on the bubble with a satisfying "clunk" of an old printing press. The text bubbles of people speaking other languages will autotranslate if you have a skill that helps you speak that language. In all, a really cool approach to dialogue- The music is excellent and similarly of its time. The vocal tracks are especially nice and were a little unexpected- You play as a Flemish artist named Andreas who is living in Bavaria while he works on his masterpiece that will allow him to become a master artist. A mystery erupts suddenly after a local baron visits the town. You'll interview people, play a few minigames and puzzles, and use your best judgement to solve both this mystery and the two others that crop up later in the game- I'm being intentionally vague in describing the plot. The story is extremely compelling and well-written, so I don't want to spoil anything. It's definitely one worth experiencing- The writing is also incredibly good, which helps breathe life into the several townsfolk and tourists you'll encounter. Each character feels unique and interesting. Most of them have pasts and relationships that really flesh them out and make Tassing feel much more lifelike. This level of immersion is really impressive when you take a step back and realize that the screen looks like a painting- It's not all serious, though. The game does have a rich sense of humor. Beyond the occasional situational humor and wry dialogue, you'll also play a few pranks and even be given the chance to headbutt an ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ doctor if you choose the right options- I'm happy that this is an adventure game where narrative choices actually have an impact on the story. Depending on whether or not you piss off the church in the first chapter, the second chapter can have a very different feel to it. Remember that justice was a little more bloody in medieval times, so whomever you implicate as the perpetrators of the various mysteries you solve will face dire consequences- Beyond the typical walking and talking you'd expect in an adventure game, there's not much gameplay. Not that it's necessary in a game like this, but you won't even be managing an inventory- Given the narrative focus and the ability to converse with your own mind when faced with certain dialogue choices, I've seen some reviewers compare the game to Disco Elysium. While there are some superficial similarities and they'll largely appeal to the same audience, you'll be doing Pentiment a disservice if you go into it expecting the same experience. Disco Elysium is such a unique (and in my opinion, better) game that it's not fair judge Pentiment against that sort of masterpiece- I understand that it's difficult (or maybe even impossible) to implement a chapter select in a game where choices matter, but I still really wish there was a chapter select. I want to go back for the achievements I missed. Quick tip for achievement fiends: when it comes time to accuse someone of a crime, be sure to quit to the menu after the achievement pops. You'll be able to make the choice again to collect the other missable ones- Although the game is gorgeous on a larger display, it really shines as a Steam Deck title. It's fully verified and runs perfectly. The frequent autosaves and exploration/narrative focus make it an easy game to pick up and put down whenever you're interested in delving a little deeper into Tassing's mysteries- Depending on how thorough you are on each day of the game's story, you'll wind up with a wide range of completion times. It's probably possible to beat this game in as little as 12 hours if you don't do much exploration, but what's the fun in that? There's a lot of good dialogue to read, history to learn, and subplots to unearth. If you're a fan of narrative-focused games and like your choices to have an actual story impact, this is well worth full price. It's really hard to complain about a game with dollar-per-hour value that spins a tale this good. If you like the art style and enjoy a good mystery, this is easy to recommend

_childDocuments_.review: What a beautiful game. As others have mentioned it is a slower paced story however because of that I gained such a connection with the characters. I really saw their growth through the plot and seeing their conclusions at the end was bittersweet. The art style is what drew me in however I was blown away by the sheer amount of knowledge in this game. I had learned so much by the end of each act and the "pull away" glossary and character identifier was extremely useful. I can see why some people may get bored but if you enjoy long drawn out stories this is a must buy. The history and people of Tassia were so well done. Technically I had no issues besides sometimes getting the characters to go places could be slightly clunky but it barely impacted gameplay. There was only a few segments where I felt like the game was un-intuitive plot wise but besides that I flowed through the story easily. As with other games like Disco Elysium, make sure to not try and "game" the game. Play it as you would in real life and try and get into the characters. Don't min-max since theres no leveling up skills beyond your starting background choices. No matter what you pick you'll experience an amazing story. I actually like that theres no perk system since this helped me from falling into the trap of chasing the perfect character. It took my about 12 hours from start to finish and I tried to get most of the content and didn't rush. I may do a second play though just to see what other plot points I missed on the first run.

_childDocuments_.review: As a fan of narrative games, I was looking forward to Pentiment. And the game exceeded my expectations. Stylish art, beautifully researched storyline (the credits has a full Bibliography!), lots of interesting characters, and a compelling plot. Lots of story-based games claim that "choices matter", but few deliver on this promise like Pentiment. So many choices mattered in ways that I could *never* have predicted-- sometimes the narrative connected choices that were hours of gameplay apart to change the story! Be ready, though-- this is almost a pure narrative game. There are a few very easy puzzles in the game, but the true puzzle is how the narrative threads interlock, and trying to work out how your choices will affect the course of character's lives and the game's story. Remarkable! Bravo!

_childDocuments_.review: (NO SPOILERS)Beautifully stylized, thoughtful and enjoyable role-playing game, in the old-fashioned sense of the word. You won't find skill trees, levels or loot here, but you will find a story with well-written dialogue and choices with real weight. The game doesn't outright tell you whether your choices were right or wrong, good or bad. You just get to live with the consequences and watch as the world keeps on turning. It's one of those games that makes you think about how history is written, by whom and for what reasons. As someone who doesn't play many detective games it took me some time to figure out that I had to use my time wisely as it's limited to specific times of day. You will have to choose carefully who to talk to at noon, supper or evening, and to be thorough with exploration and investigation. Sometimes vital clues may present themselves at the eleventh hour if you make sure to talk to everybody. Sometimes you will curse yourself after having chosen to spend time with the wrong people as you are left with little more than idle gossip when you hoped to discover crucial information. But what's done is done, no save-scumming here. The game offers great replayability as you will no doubt be left wondering how things might have turned out had you made different choices.For history lovers this is a must. Not only is the art style a beautiful homage to the time period the story is set in but there is also a vast glossary of historical terms, places and people, handily embedded within the dialogue in the form of clickable words that act as footnotes. (I especially appreciated the repeated links to people you've met in the game as the cast of character is huge and it can be easy to forget who is who.) You almost feel tricked into learning things as you play, but it never feels like a lecture. The game was clearly made by people with a genuine love of history and I can't help but feel it would be an excellent educational tool, presenting the study of history in a manner that is gripping, immersive and easy to digest.The stylized art also extends to the dialogue which is presented in a variety of medieval fonts, depending on the speaker. These can be a little hard on the eyes but thankfully there are some nice accessibility options that allow you to turn off the stylized fonts or turn text-to-speech.Towards the end I did begin to feel the story stretched a bit long, especially as the "thread-puller" was not particularly hard to guess, but your mileage may vary.All in all, very enjoyable and especially a treat if you're a history fan. If you're not, this game may well turn you into one.
_childDocuments_.name: Pentiment

_childDocuments_.review: This is not a game for everyone and despite the murder mystery trappings it isn't really for fans of those either. At least not the more traditional whodunnit murder mysteries where finding the killer is the main focus. That isn't what Pentiment is about. Much like How The City and the City, Mare of Eastown, and The Name of the Rose are about way more than the murder (or murders) the plots revolve around, Pentiment is about way more than just the murder you become embroiled in. It is about how seemingly throw away actions can ripple throughout small communities, about how no one person can truly shape history, how the pull of socio-economic factors are inescapable even if they are imperceptible at the time, and how the past can never truly be displayed "as it was." The murder is just the jumping off points to explore these themes.Its a game where choices matter but not as much as you think they will, much closer to real life.All in all if you like medieval history, post-modernist literature, and thoughtful murder mysteries this game might be for you and probably be extremely your ♥♥♥♥, but if you aren't into those things it might not be for you.

_childDocuments_.review: I really love Pentiment, but this is not a game I can recommend to everyone. It's mainly driven by it's fantastic narrative, artstyle, characters, and nothing else. Don't expect any challenging gameplay and instead very long stretches of dialogue . Any form of challenge are the occasional speech checks and trying to get enough evidence to prove a person guilty , but there's no fail state. You aren't punished for choosing the wrong person because the game doesn't give you a wrong suspect, and you aren't punished for failing skill checks because the story keeps chugging along smoothly. The knowledge (otherwise builds) you can form your characters around also don't do much and only gives them different smart statements to say. This may sound really negative, but remember I like this game. I like it a lot actually! It has an incredibly beautiful art style with a wide selection of colors, detailing, strokes, and they try to replicate the ancient drawings we see in biblical pictures. Audio designs is really good as well and I like for each character they have different fonts and writing styles, because it shows how that person possibly wrote and their knowledge in English. You get well acquainted with the main cast as the world of Pentiment takes place in a small religious village. The story is the main selling point. Obsidian Entertainment have always had genius writers exploring deep themes and this is another exception. Main theme for Pentiment being, "Should we preserve the past?" Should we keep, maintain, and teach what has come before despite all the bad things that come with it? Hoping that future generations can learn from it and pass their lessons down to the next? Hope that the scriptures and works of artists will be appreciated, and much like said work they too will be remembered. Pentiment is a huge departure from what Obsidian usually makes, RPG with build diversity and complexity, but that doesn't mean straying off to different genres is bad. In fact, they did a really good job a something new. Everything that Pentiment does well helps outweigh the flaws and makes it a true work of art.

_childDocuments_.review: Before I start my review of this game, I want you to know that I have uploaded the final 3 hours of my playthrough on my youtube channel (  ).If you want to watch some uncut gameplay from this game without commentary, I got you covered. So, with that out of the way, let's begin. This game is special, without a doubt. When I saw the trailer for this game during the Xbox E3 showcase last year, I immediately went : " This game is going to be worth my time for the creativity it exuberates alone."It's games like this, that break the monotomy most games fall victim to, you have to keep an eye out for during set showcases, because they usually end up becoming hidden gems. Games that were less popular when they released, but are in the end better than most of the popular ones that released during the same time or after it. This game is an hidden gem. I firmly believe more people should play it. It's one of the more creative video games I played in a long while, and an example of what the team at Obsidian Entertainment is capable off. Let's talk about the art style they used for this game first, the first stroke of creativity the game assaults you with. The entire game plays like a medieval painting, and I love that they made this choice. Not only will this game age extremely well ( again, making this game even more of a gem as time goes on ), but it immerses the player into the game from the moment you start playing it, and it will not let you go until the credits roll. In my entire playthrough, I have not seen any visual bugs. The game runs extremely well, with my laptop getting a solid 165 FPS without fail ( with a Nvidia Geforce RTX 3060 ). Why mention this ? Because the fact that a game releases finished without bugs or issues is a rare thing these days and it deserves my praise every time I encounter one. It reminds me of a time were this was the norm, and not the exception, which as a gamer is a sad thing to think about in this day and age. The story is what you can expect from the talent at Obsidian Entertainment. I'm a writer myself in my spare time, and I like to think I know a thing or two about good writing ( it's the reason why I play games in the first place ), and this game gives you an excellent mystery to solve with a memorable set of characters and excellent dialogue. I especially liked the moments when the story goes inside the mind of the main character. Those moments provide both background information on the main character, as well as some thoughtful conversation with characters living in set character's imagination. Those moments get even better as the story goes on, as the main character's emotional state gets reflected by those imaginary characters living in this city in his head. It was inspiring to experience from a writer's perspective. As for the story itself, I'm not going to spoil it here. I recommend going into this completely blind. As for the setting, the story takes place in 16th century Germany, at the time when Martin Luther started questioning the values of the Catholic Church, and when the effects of the printing press ( one of the most important inventions of all time ) provided a whole group of people, who previously had no access to books, with the knowledge that books can provide, and an incentive to learn how to read thanks to Martin Luther. You play as Andreas Maller, an artist who's in the employ of the local scriptorium, while he finishes his master piece in order to become a master back in the city where he grew up. During his employment for the monks, someone gets murdered at the abby, and a friend / mentor figure of Andreas gets blamed for the murder. It is up to the player to figure out who truly murdered this person, which sets a chain of events in motion of conspiracy and mystery surrounding the abby and the village located next to it. Throughout the story, you get to solve 2 murders, while you live through the stories of the villagers and the monks at the abby, all the while trying to solve the mystery of the Tread-puller, the person responsable for the murders you're trying to solve, and who pulls the strings behind everything that happens in the story. I really liked this story. It provides you with a good mystery, while the story of the village and the abby plays out based on the choices you make, and your conclusions to the murders that took place. The identity of the Tread-puller took me completely by surprise, which is what a good mystery needs, and the twists and turns of the story kept me hooked to this game from start to finish. The only bad thing i can say about the story is that near the end you play as a different main character for a while, and the story grinds to a halt for a moment, becoming quite dull for a few hours, before picking up again with a surprise twist. That's the only bad thing I can say about the story, as the rest of it was excellent and I'm glad I experienced it. The team at Obsidian Entertainment have not disappointed me yet with the stories they tell in their games, and that's an achievement worth mentioning. As for the music, which is a part of game design that people rarely talk about, but is in my eyes a crucial component of games, it is good, with a lot of medieval festive music, a lot of latin/german singing and vocal performances ( which to be honest I'm a little biased to, I love me some good vocals ). All in all, it fits the setting of the game really well and further adds to the immersion ( it's also good to listen to on it's own, the soundtrack is available on Spotify, and I have listened to it several times already ). All in all, I'm really happy how this game turned out. This is definitely one i recommend you buy at full price ( its not even half of the cost of a brand new AAA game ) if you are interested in playing through it. I can already see myself going back and replaying it in a couple of years, just to experience it all over again. Super well done, and congrats to the team at Obsidian Entertainment for releasing this gem of a game. Thank you from the bottom of my heart.

_childDocuments_.review: A point and click adventure game / visual novel with RPG elements (à la Disco Elysium). Your "Choices Matter" in the same way they do in the Telltale Walking Dead games, but you get a lot more of them, some require specific backgrounds and some are playthrough-exclusive if you're a completionist. Well, "exclusive" in the sense that the game has an annoying auto-save system and only one save per playthrough. Normally, I appreciate an ironman mode but in this game it's plain annoying. There are no real bad ends, no ways to die, and all the puzzles are easy enough that that even someone like me (who never finished a proper point'n'click adventure game without reading a guide at least once) could solve them easily. Basically, the save system serves just to arbitrarily increase your playtime, so that you're forced to go through the same dialogues again and again. No fast forward text / skip until new options available. Personally, I went through the first act 3 times, second act 2 times and the third/final act just once. Some backgrounds/traits are significantly more useful than others and you only get minimal opportunities to act in a counter productive manner / consequences for failing checks. I'm mentioning that specifically because that's one of the things Obsidian's Alpha Protocol did right (unpolished as it was), and you could get unique content when you went out of your way to mess things up. I was pleasantly surprised that the game was quite "historically accurate" - compared to my pessimistic expectations. I'm no historian, and I'm sure there are plenty of inaccuracies but by Hollywood standards this is basically a documentary. Sure, they shoehorned in all the possible medieval archetypal characters they could, but nothing that would ruin the suspension of disbelief.TL;DRPlay it twice it's quite nice; on run number three, nothing new you'll see.

_childDocuments_.review: This game hits me in all the right places... I have a degree in Fine Art and Art History coupled with an absolutely passion for the late medieval era so when I meant to start it and just play a few minutes over a cup of coffee this morning, it is no surprise to me that it is now noontime.This game hits one of my favorite moment in history, but especially in the arts - the end of the Medieval era and beginning of the Renaissance period - and it gives me intrigue, rebellion, murder mysteries and coquettish maids bathing in waterfalls.  The visual style of the game is amazing and the art direction is superb and obviously well researched. i find myself loving even the smallest details in the world environment for the references to illuminated manuscripts and early printing. Seeing the tintype used when the print-maker's family speaks, for example, is just perfect and gave me such a smile.It is not for everyone, but those of whom this game was designed in mind for, will absolutely love it.

_childDocuments_.review: To sum it up, I'd say Pentiment is an above average adventure time and I'd recommend it to any adventure games fans. The unique art style feels fresh and is captivating, even though it won't impress you anymore on the latter half of the game. It doesn't help that the whole game takes place in the same town/abbey complex. My main issues with the game were: - Lots of backtracking around the same places, talking to the same people or their relatives about similiar subjects. Due to the nature of the gameplay, it encourages the player to keep doing "full scans from top to bottom" of the town/abbery every day in search of any missing clues that might have appeared overnight. It gets boring really fast.- Most choices you make in the game, backgrounds you chose, etc are mostly there for flavor. You might get this or that character killed but in the end the main plotline is very railroaded. Talk about illusion of choice... - Third and final act felt a bit unnecessary and dragged on for too long. Felt more like a 5 hour epilogue told from a new character's point of view. The story climax, at least in my opinion, also felt a bit underwhelming. What I enjoyed:- Some of the characters are fleshed out and actually interesting to interact with, their personal stories progressing nicely through the decades of the game's timespan. - Somewhat unique artstyle inspired on medieval art, reminds me of those bardcore music videos that were popular on YT recently.- Feels polished. DIdn't experience a single crash or bug during the whole gameplay. Didn't need to fight the UI too.

_childDocuments_.review: It may be somewhat niche, but I believe that to those who find its subjects interesting, Pentiment really is an engrossing tale. It's a narrative adventure game first and foremost, so if you don't like reading through large amounts of dialogue, you probably won't like this. If you don't mind all that though, Pentiment provides a very interesting and often very moving tale discussing a wide range of themes going from art, religion, the nature of history, personal responsibility, the march of progress and our own legacies. However, despite sounding very heavy handed, I was surprised by how the game features countless scenes that have a much more intimate feeling, often showing a tenderness that is rarely seen in a video game, and that I found to often be very moving. Even though you start the game playing as a affluent journeyman artist, a lot of time is spent showing the ritual, habits and hardships of ordinary people. And even though that involves a lot of misery, there are many moments of people finding happiness and satisfaction in small things. Similarly, its focus on the concept of history is discussed both at-large and in the context of the lives of simple individuals. How different people interpret and remember the same event so very differently, what the past means to us as people and how we all try to leave something behind in our short time here on this planet.And interwoven between those themes is a plot-thread that manages to touch on all of those subjects, mostly in a very adept way. In short, if you like narrative-heavy games, I think you owe it to yourself to play this one. I found it both very interesting and genuinely moving.

I am going to assume the last few hours will be as good. Everyone should play this game once. It's worth the money and then some. Maybe one of the best games I've played in several years. BTW as a bonus there is no wokeness, no pronouns, no inserted token characters that have nothing to do with anything. This was just a game the publishers really seemed to get right from start to finish and make believable stories and character development.

_childDocuments_.review: Pentiment is an excellent narrative adventure that takes place in a fictional Bavarian town in the early Renaissance. The setting is well chosen as many things are happening in a — relatively — short timespan. It offers an interesting comment on history and the stories we tell, some of the things told in Pentiment will remain with me for a long time. The characters are expertly written and the world itself is beautifully drawn, it truly feels like you’re leafing through an illuminated book. I also adored the immersive sound design of this game, it blends in but also stands out, at one point I thought one of my neighbours’ chickens had come over for a visit. 🐓 Yet the thing that struck me most is the beautiful and original use of typefaces. The way characters’ speech bubbles are written in different fonts depending on their social class, and how the main character can even misjudge someone, is one of the most unique ways I’ve seen type used in any form of media. Now I am somewhat of a typography buff but I think anyone can appreciate the ingenuity at work here.  If you enjoy a good story in a historical setting then you should give this game a chance. If you love typography then just buy it, you will have the experience of a lifetime. 😉

_childDocuments_.review: This game genuinely made me rethink how I am going to move forward in my life. Every character is a fleshed out human being, and the dialogue is very well written. The people all simultaneously are super relatable to someone now, but also operate within the thought-space of someone in the 16th century, which shows how much research and care went into the game. Andreas and his character arc hit really close to home for me, so I'm a bit biased, but he is honestly one of the most engaging protagonists I've ever played as.As far as negatives go, the navigation can be awkward at times, and the cursor disappears whenever you move and then you have to click around a bit to get it back, which can be annoying. _childDocuments_.review: To put into words my recommendation for pentiment is difficult, but let me try. I think as far as a story goes, it's a perfection and it feels just... right all over it. Everything feels lived in, real, and that means a lot. All three acts follow a very traditional 5 act structure, with the climax happening around the middle, and falling action after that. _childDocuments_.review: Did two playthoughs, and very much liked my experience with this unique historical entirely narrative-focused no-combat/no-puzzle rpg-lite/adventure game. _childDocuments_.review: Excellent, thought-provoking historical detective story with interesting characters, uniquely conveyed dialogue (through different fonts/writing styles, no traditional voice acting), authentic artwork, and immersive soundtrack. There is also surprisingly lot of replay value due to many different endings, side quests, and story/character choices. Strong recommendation.

_childDocuments_.review: A game for true lovers of history. This game never ceased to charm me, with so much love and research carefully put into every corner of this game. The art, story, and characters make for a massive world that unfolds in such a small town. A true appreciation for history as it was, this is one of the only games I can think of that comes with a bibliography (with books and articles that I will certainly be adding to my reading list!). The only game I can think of that even came close to exploring medieval/early renaissance life this much is Kingdom Come: Deliverance and I think this game surpasses that one just in terms of the atmosphere, setting, and research. The mystery aspect is thrilling, with limited time to piece together as much as you can before you're out of time and need to name the guilty party. You'll never have enough time to fully figure out everything, encouraging multiple runs. With minor amounts of character customization that unlocks different paths/dialogue options, it really seems like the devs encourage the player to play through it once or twice.With that said, this is a surprisingly long game. I thought that it was done on 2 or 3 separate occasions but it just KEPT GOING. And that's not a bad thing at all. You certainly get the bang for your buck with this game, even at full price. My first run took about 16 hours and, while I was fairly thorough, I did not exhaust every possibility.  Before I bought this game, I read a couple of reviews saying that the ending was unsatisfying and I couldn't disagree more. I won't say too much to avoid spoilers but I think the ending ties everything up nicely.Overall, an amazing experience. Incredibly sweet and heartfelt, with a true love for history, how history is made, how history is remembered, and how people lived. If you have admiration for medieval history, whether that be great academic interest or a casual enjoyment, I would recommend this game. So much charm and love sprinkled on top of an incredibly robust and sturdy base.
_childDocuments_.name: Pentiment

_childDocuments_.review: I enjoyed my time playing. I cared about the characters, and wanted to learn more about the setting.I enjoyed the way your impactful choices were represented when the time for respective decisions came.I did experience once bug in act 2, and it looks like its been active for a while. I'm unaware if a fan patch exists.I did experience some thoughts that may or may not come up on your play-through.  I think this thing may be pretty common in in whodunit types of stories, though.I would recommend this game to anyone who likes a good story.

_childDocuments_.review: As i'm writing this, I just finished the game and i'm in tears. This review is ecstatic in that sense but I had so many feelings about this game I didn't want to lose track of them by writing this review later. I love Obsidian games no matter the gameplay and I think this is why; they don't scrimp on storytelling and immersion. I became so invested in every single character, every choice I made hurt and I could only rationalize making them as part of the greater good. This world felt so alive and was a beautiful tribute to the deep spirituality and pain of the people it portrayed. I adored the perspective of townsfolk and peasantry, the histories of both are scarce so what Obsidian did for them was an absolute bang-up job. I love how everything was grounded in reality and yet felt like I was constantly teetering between heaven and earth. This was always how I felt when looking at beautiful illuminated manuscripts created by the deeply spiritual and inspired hands of their creators.I loved being able to go into this with a passing knowledge of Medieval, Renaissance, Reformation etc history. I saw the title of Martin's side quest and instantly knew the real-life medieval mystery they had referenced. I loved being able to revisit the crossover of Pagan and Christian traditions, by having the characters explain them from their perspective. I imagine it would be extremely enlightening to someone new to this branch of history as it approached the matter from an "overarching concept" angle rather than throwing random facts out there about different gods and figures. I love how the story did not shy away from the less inspiring realities of peasant life, and I love how compassionately the different factions are treated during a time period as sensitive as the reformation. Few people in this story were truly "good" or "bad", most were simply trying to keep the peace, stay alive, or protect their traditions. This is absolutely a work of art and I hope it endures long after computers become obsolete. Thank you devs,
_childDocuments_.name: Pentiment

_childDocuments_.review: As a History(Especially Medieval History) and a Theology nerd, I loved every second of this game. I am also a big fan of well written interactive stories, so this was a match made in heaven. _childDocuments_.review: I applaud Josh Sawyer and the team for creating such an idiosyncratic game in today's market - it is extremely rare to have any kind of modern media that goes so deep into 16th century Holy Roman Empire history and the sociopolitical structure of serfdom. And the efforts made here are clear to see, from the very unique art style based upon sources such as the Nuremberg Chronicles as well as beautiful fonts and music that harken back to the era. All of those things are fascinating and superlative, including the minutiae of the lore behind the game: remnants of Roman civilization long forgotten, the conflict between the church and the peasantry, etc. However, as a game which ostensibly gives you options to role play as and choose your own character to solve different issues, this aspect is unfortunately is quite flawed. It becomes very clear that many of the backgrounds and traits are not weighed equally or at least made to be interesting - for example, medicine ends up to be really negligible or even negative as a trait in the game compared to others. Worse is that, regardless of any of your choices, you are shoehorned into particular ending in Act 2 and 3. Even if the actions of the character you went with doesn't exhibit any of those traits, your Andreas will end up the same, and that is honestly quite disappointing. I also feel that Act 3 is quite rushed and is the weakest, especially in terms of persuasion mechanic. Worse is that it feels like your Act 3 protagonist has a lot of knowledge that the person isn't supposed to have, but you as the player knows because of you saw what happened in the prior two Acts.  In an Obsidian interview I watched, the team highlighted the potential of deep characterization in such kind of role playing, but also why it is so important to them that the game spans 25 years of history to show how much has changed. But unfortunately, I find that these two goals end up being in conflict with one another, and the team has instead tried to place importance on things which ultimately takes certain choice and empowerment away from the player. Yes, it is good to see how much of the society changes due to the printing press and the Lutheran movement etc., but I'm not sure about the very dictated storyline that we are forced to funnel into, including the "surprise" of Act 3 which just doesn't align with the way I played my character in previous acts at all. As a game that seems to require or encourage multiple playthroughs, the game also makes it very, very tedious to replay the game - from the very slow and repeated animation (those flipping pages in your journal are pretty but are just a waste of time) to unskippable cutscenes (how many of those darm clocks in Act 3 do I need to watch???) to the very awkward navigation around town. Would have been much better if we could just fast travel as otherwise I would need to go through multiple empty screens every time I want to check out something quickly at the convent or at the saw mill, for example. The game also does a poor job of giving you context when you "speak" with someone - for example, talking to Father Thomas can actually raise a few different subject matters. I wanted to talk to him about something, but not about something else - but to my horror it was about what I did NOT want to talk about. True, the game smartly skirts it by making the conversation benign, but I would have preferred if I had a list of topics to choose from, a la Gabriel Knight, for example. This would give me, the player, more control of what is said and what is not said. And let's not get into some of those tedious minigames (cookies)....I may have talked at length about my dissatisfaction of the game, but to be honest its merits are pretty clear when you watch the trailer - its unique time period and subject matter, its gorgeous artstyle and its choice-based gameplay. I just wish that a lot of the issues could have been fixed or foreseen, as it is clear this is a flawed game despite all of its merits. I was left somewhat frustrated when I finished Act 3, due to it robbing me of many choices I have previously made, and the "plot twist" I felt was not super well-earned. Despite my issues with the storytelling here (something I notice in many Obsidian titles as of late, from Pillars 2 to the disappointing The Outer Worlds), I still think the game is very worth playing, though I still am looking for a role-playing game with the same depth and possibilities as Disco Elysium and Roadwarden. All those fancy visuals are great, but give me real role-playing and tangible and impactful choices, please. 7/10

_childDocuments_.review: Pentiment is a fantastic game. If you are like I was and enjoy some Obsidian classics but don't think this one is your style, I'd recommend giving it a chance. This is a rare game that gets better progressively as it goes and has a terrific ending. There are some great emotional moments that even with the 2D art style hit me harder than any game I've played in several years. Honestly. This is possible because the writing is top tier, and the scope of the game allows you to become really invested in the town and its residents. The overall mystery is intriguing and each act masterfully inserts the player character into the events and lives of the townsfolk. I love that the game exists and you can tell it is created by masters of the medium. I only wish more labors of love like this were around. I played the game 100% through on steam deck so can confirm it plays perfectly there and it's a great game for the device.

_childDocuments_.review: An absolutely immaculate mystery drama that is interlaced with so much historical detail and analysis. The game's setting, art design, sound, and characters are extremely fleshed out.The way it tells a story that is directly put into a specific historical narrative is remarkable. The game has completely opened my interest into a whole new world of history, philosophy, art, musical era. I found myself researching Lutheranism, Abbeys, Francis of Assisi, Mysticism, Holy Roman Empire, and that is all thanks to this game.The sound track is wonderful. Beautiful soundscapes of lutes, flutes, and gregorian chants, but also on the contrary ear-splitting sharp dissonance of broken hurdy gurdys.Pentiment is a very human game. It reminds us of our own mortality, family history, class, creed, faith (or lack of), and subterfuge.~~Pentiment is one of the best releases for 2022.~~

_childDocuments_.review: It’s easy to feel that we don’t matter. That our choices don’t matter. Taken individually, our choices are just moments — passing quickly and forgotten just as quickly. Taken over the long term, your choices make up your life. Your effect isn’t weighed on the scale of empires: it’s weighed against your family, your friends, your pets, your neighbours. Your choices have a subtle but important effect on the people with which you live in community.These are the choices that Pentiment presents.Arguably, the farthest-reaching choice you can make involves a few encouraging words to the right person. For you, it’s an incidental aside in a conversation about a wider mystery; for the other person, you changed the course of their life. The effects of your kindness (or lack thereof) resonate throughout the years. It’s not Mass Effect, where the survival of an entire race is placed in your potentially-genocidal hands. Pentiment tells the story of a community, and those who would shape the community with whatever tools they have to hand. Set against those forces: an artist who refuses to stand by in the face of injustice and tragedy, driven by relentless curiosity, and their allies, all of which have their own lives and make their own decisions in their own time.Playing Pentiment is as satisfying as reading a good book. Finishing it… let me put it this way. Most games’ endings want you to look back over the game with a sense of accomplishment, a “You win!” screen. You overcame the challenge.When I finished Pentiment, it pointed me back towards my own life, towards my community, and asked how I want to be remembered.I recommend this game.e: I do have one complaint:

_childDocuments_.review: I surely am not a 16th century Lieutenant Columbo, but I love this game. The art style, the attention to historical detail, the way it pulls you into this small late medieval/early renaissance village and its happenings, how lovingly it describes its population and how you learn much about them by sharing a meal with them (with period accurate fares). There's so much to like and immerse yourself here that I many times forgot I was on the clock to solve a murder and as a result had to (almost) wing it when the time came to solve the "case" - much to the detriment of innocents, I fear. As I said, I am no 16th century Columbo, more like 16th century Inspector Clouseau...What an excellent game and a unique experience. A masterwork, indeed. Two thumbs up!

_childDocuments_.review: Pentiment is an incredibly well-written, well-thought-out, compassionate, erudite (without being pedantic), and loving story told in medieval-style artwork brought to life.  It's amazing and I love it.It's quite an achievement to not only render a particularly remote slice of late medieval life in an appealing and humanizing way (I had always found medieval art from this period to be unappealing and, well, dumb-looking), but also compellingly render complex themes of social relationships, class, and political relationships on the ground during the era.And all this while creating memorable characters you'll come to love and hate, as the case may be.The art is amazing, the animation is surprisingly detailed, the there is so much intricate and delightful attention to detail.This is a genuine, sublime masterpiece, and I don't casually use that word.  I can't recommend it enough.----Special honorable mention 1: They actually artistically showed the direct aftermath of childbirth in vibrant medieval-style art.  Bloodsoaked newborn and all.  Wow.Special honorable mention 2: The end of Act II when fingering the book-cooker was so, so satisfying.  Really unfortunate phrasing, I know, but keeping it cryptic so as not to spoil.  You'll know what I mean when the time comes.  Bring marshmallows!Note on Disco Elysium comparisons: Yes, as has been said, this is on par both quality-wise and empathy-wise with Disco Elysium.  It's not nearly as long or grandiose in sweep, but it sits in the same pantheon.

This story follows the small village of Tassing in Bavaria during the Renaissance Era and is quite lengthy in text, your're essentially going to be reading a moving book with the potentiality of it even being a small history lesson of that time era if you press tab or click on names and words to be given a brief description of what they are (which was helpful since I don't know my stuff). If you like well written interpersonal relationships where characters feel real and with enthralling storytelling having you guessing the whole way through, making dialogue decisions that actually hold weight and will subtly change what people say or do, then this is a game for you. It truly is one of a kind and will hold a place in my memory for a long time to come.

_childDocuments_.review: I loved this game. I do wonder how widely appealing it would be though as it's very history and text heavy which I feel might turn some folks off. I tore through it in 18 hours over about 2.5 days, which should tell you how engrossed I was in it. _childDocuments_.review: The most complimentary description I can give Pentiment is: imagine "Disco Elysium" — which Pentiment director Josh Sawyer said was inspirational to him in a "broad sense" — but with even *fewer* RPG elements, e.g. a game not only lacking combat, but stripped of character stats and even an inventory system. Pentiment is a narrative game that is driven entirely by dialogue, reading (there's no voice acting), and point-and-click movement. Despite the lack of a traditional game loop and features, it completely hooked me, such is the amount of loving detail put into its world-building and writing. I'll admit that I went into this game blind, and bounced hard after the first 15 minutes. I like narrative games, but Pentiment felt a little too basic even for me. I almost refunded the game. But after playing for another 15 minutes, and seeing a couple of beautifully illustrated cutscenes, I was a total convert, and I binged the game for 15 hours over the long weekend. I had no interest in or even awareness of 16th-century Bavaria, yet became totally invested in the seemingly-mundane lives and lifestyles of the town and abbey central to the game's mysteries.It's hard to describe the game's few shortcomings without implicitly spoiling the story's overall scope, but I think virtually all of Pentiment's flaws come down to whether you agree with its creators' philosophy behind their design choices. Even knowing how it ended, I was ready to jump into a new playthrough to see how a different "build" and different choices would impact the town and people for whom Pentiment built in me such a strong attachment. At $20 — $15 during the holiday sale — Pentiment feels like the quriky creation of an obsessed artist, a game so well-crafted but so niche that it ends up causing its developer to go out of business. If you don't hate the idea of a slower-paced game that's 80% reading, I can't imagine you not enjoying Pentiment.

_childDocuments_.review: Short Version:It's a visual novel/story game about a fictional town in Bavaria in the Holy Roman Empire. All of the game's activity centers around dialog, and various choices you make in dialog will affect the outcomes of the store. You will ultimately be solving murder mysteries and uncovering the truth of the town, and you will have to make hard choices about how, who, and what you do about it. If you are into entirely story-driven games about medieval history, this game was made for you.Long version:Gameplay is very simple - you walk around the town and talk to people, and occasionally interact with things. You follow a pretty linear storyline, and are ultimately responsible for solving a murder that happens in the town. You won't have enough time or opportunity to track down every single lead and clue, so you'll have to decide how best to approach the problems. Most of the choices you make revolve around dialog options, and who you choose to spend meal times with. Your actions and choices will have a direct effect on the story and how it plays out, although the overarching plot remains mostly the same (spoiler). There are occasional minigames in various activities, some of which will have a minor effect on the story and dialog depending on how you do (and generate achievements).You won't be able to 100% the game in a single playthrough - there are some choices that will lock out some others, and everyone in the town will have to live with the choices you make.Feeling:This is a game about feeling, really. Immerse yourself in the town, in the people, and the hardness of their lives. They are telling you stories, they are sharing their pain, and understanding their existence lets us draw our own conclusions about today. Thankfully, the game never gets particularly hamfisted about particular moral tale or line of thinking, allowing you to roleplay your character to agree, disagree, or argue with almost every opinion anyone shares in the town.The game is best when you simply roleplay yourself into it, and play the way you would want. The story is compelling and interesting, and the game is short enough that you generally don't get bored. It comes in around 15-20 hours depending on how much time you spend talking to people.It's an incredible historical tale and truly a piece of art in and of itself, and I would love to reward game studios for producing small gems like this that set out to do one thing, do it extremely well, and come away with a satisfying and complete experience. I wish more studios would produce high caliber experiences like this.
_childDocuments_.name: Pentiment

_childDocuments_.review: I came to this game with high expectations after reading some very favorable reviews. Let's make things clear first: this is not a bad product, but it is more of a visual novel than a game. I enjoyed the story and finished all of it, but I will not do so again. The impact of your choices on the world are quite small. I came to play this, because I thought my actions would have more of an influence on the world around me. The only impact seems to be minor alterations to the story and one of the end sequences subtly shows the consequences, but this is only played once and goes by pretty fast, so it can be difficult to understand exactly what is going on. It would have been better if this part would be a part of your save file so you could study it again.The gameplay is pretty basic in the style of point and click adventures, but towards the end of the game it was frustrating how the game forced you to interact with every single character before you could move on. At one point I had enough and just wanted to finish the game as I did not feel that all of these interactions were particularly meaningful. However, I could not and conversations in this games go by rather slowly. The game world is amazing though and clearly a lot of research has been done to portray this world. It comes across as a believable world and it is not difficult to immerse oneself into something with this attention to detail.If you are fine with that the game is linear and you are looking for a great gameworld with a good story go ahead and buy this. But, if you were looking for something that gives you more opportunity to interact with and change what happens in the world around you and with a high level of replayability, I would probably skip on this one. I have mixed feelings about Pentiment, while good, it does not live up to the hype.
_childDocuments_.name: Pentiment

_childDocuments_.review: This game was living poetry. It delves so wonderfully into an extremely well researched 16th century and explores the boom of literacy in Europe, the power of the church, the mysteries of religion and the richness storytelling as always had in all culture. All this is wrapped up in beautiful visuals, compelling characters and a great mystery to sink you teeth into. Take your time and sink deep into Pentiment - I'll be wishing it was my first time playing forever after.

_childDocuments_.name: Pentiment

_childDocuments_.review: It's a fantastic narrative game and a rare gem.Something between a point&click adventure and an RPG.Most of the time, you walk in a familiar environment and talk with people.What is done right:- Presenting history - It's set in early modern Bavaria, in times of Martin Luter, the Peasant War and changes in society, religion, and culture. The game is accessible but doesn't avoid talking about hardcore history. Sometimes it simplifies late medieval/early renaissance reality to popular contemporary taste. And yet, such a large, beautiful and complex game with such fidelity and love for history is a rare bird.- Being a detective - Pentiment is like The Name of the Rose by Umberto Eco. The protagonist talks with witnesses, investigate clues and finds secret passages and occult notes. The time is running out, so it's impossible to explore everything.- Telling the story of a small settlement - The story is set in a small city/village in the Holy Roman Empire and a nearby abbey. Over time you learn the name of each NPC. In 25 years, some people die, and some people grow up. Observing how society changes and what happens to the villagers and monks is the best part of the game.- Visual style - Andreas, the protagonist, is an artisan illustrator. Illuminated manuscripts inspired the visuals.- Writing - The game is very well-written and mature. The writing subtly explains all hardcore late medieval stuff but doesn't dumb it down too much.- Choices and consequences - many minor choices and consequences influence the course of the story. Major ones are also present, but they are not always as significant as I would wish.- Enchanting details - The game is full of tiny bewitching and cute details. Pay attention to little children!Cons:- The mechanics of conducting the investigation may disappoint you because you will not find a satisfactory solution, and the game will sometimes guide you on autopilot.- The game tells you about human meanness and sin, but it's rarely poignant and moving to the bone. More frequently, it's a feel-good story. Sometimes you regret your choices, but simultaneously, you're disappointed that the game didn't allow you to do it right.Overall:Great, full of charm game for patient folks and history lovers.
_childDocuments_.name: Pentiment

_childDocuments_.review: Late Medieval artist, couch-surfer and meal-moocher, Andreas Maler, unwittingly accuses multiple murder suspects across generations and manages to accidentally immortalize his melancholic self into the local history of Tassing.A 'Name of the Rose' style murder mystery with rich historical tones. Excellent artwork, thrilling story and beautiful soundtrack.

_childDocuments_.review: I do not recommend mainly because it definitely tries to push a VERY negative view on the world of middle ages before the Renaissance. Feminism absent but dearly wanted. Martin Luther a background hero who's only issue with the Catholic church were the indulgences (false, he disagrees on many other aspects).Church doctrine bad, monks&priests hypocrisies & greedy & evil - basically the only apparent "good" ones are the ones you do not talk too much to. Let me tell you about some of the characters of the monks and nuns at the monastery without spoiling who is who  : the thief, the one that is "simple", the slut who has an abortion - provided to her by a fellow nun, of course, the gays (yes, two monks), the depressed feminist, the occult enthusiast, the bootlicker, the would-be dictator, the one(s) with big anger issues, the monk-nun couple, the pushover and quite a few that would rather not to be there at all, but they've got no choice. Yeah ... hardly anyone is there because of his devotion to God.Again, without diving into spoilers, the ultimate fate of the monastery and the revelation at the end makes it VERY clear onto the developers views on religion. Let me spoil you this much : it ain't a favorable one.So I would NOT recommend this game for anyone who does not hate, or at least dislikes, the middle ages period and the catholic church.As is the case with a lot of "historical" fiction written these days, it is nothing like a story being told by someone actually living in those times.

_childDocuments_.review: If you enjoy a good story, you will enjoy this game. Full of mystery, history, and emotion. _childDocuments_.name: Pentiment

_childDocuments_.review: I really love this game. But Pentiment is not for everyone.However, the fact that you are reading reviews and are possibly interested, it probably means that you're the audience it's meant for. Pentiment is a narrative adventure, so it's all about the story here. There is a few mini games and puzzles to solve, but if you think this is a point and click game with complex riddles and whatnot you are wrong. Pentiment's gameplay mostly revolves around running from place to place and talking to various characters in town. Pentiment works like a storybook really, with three acts that each have a set number of days. Time is a very important part of Pentiment, as you will want to pursue many leads about the murders, yet will only have time for one or two of them. The day passes every time you go through an important story beat and there are only set number of hours. It is up to you to decide which leads are most promising and how you will use your time. So use it wisely.While this sounds boring on the surface, Pentiment is able to overcome simple gameplay with the power of writing! The story is where it shines in Pentiment, and while the first hour is slow (setting up characters and exposition), it really picks up the pace from there. All the characters in town are lovable (with a few exceptions, of course), and your dialogue between them are meaningful and authentic. What you say to them will affect your relationship with them and possibly affect future conversations. When needing a hand, some discussions will have persuasion checks which will take into account your friendship. So if you happened to piss them off earlier... they might not be willing to help.There are lots of choices and there will be consequences (good and bad) for each of them. If you're a fan of good mysteries I'd say you will really enjoy the story, as the various leads and suspects you will pursue will have you scratching your head. Many times in the game I felt like I truly didn't know who did it and chose who I felt would have less consequences. The gnawing guilt that you may have accused someone innocent is a core part of the game, and it's executed very well. While the third act dragged (more than I think it should've) the story as a whole is stellar and the ending really makes the less amusing third act worth going through.I completed my game in 17 hours, but I believe you could take more or less depending on your playstyle. I believe Pentiment is meant to be played at a slow pace, as the conversations between the characters is what makes it truly meaningful (and believe me, there are LOADS of characters!). If you're willing to sacrifice gameplay and are here just for the story, I think you'll like this.
_childDocuments_.name: Pentiment

_childDocuments_.review: A truly unique experience, which is very rare nowadays.Mechanically its quite simple, like an 90s old school point-and-click-adventure with a few mini games (I was never a big fan of those), but that doesnt matter. Oh and to clarify, it doesnt have the infamous 90s adventure ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ like "search a screen for a hidden two pixel item and combine it in the most illogical way possible".Its visual and audio design is fantastic, its side stories are deeply touching sometimes and its even relevant by teaching you a lot about renaissance/reformation era history but never in a pedantic, schooling way, but subtle, simply via world story telling. Besides its minimalistic gameplay, it features  some mild modern role playing elements like choosing your personal background and on surface level a crime detective story. So far I have them investigated only once and I am unsure if you can even solve them in a "right" way, but whatever clues you follow, it seems interesting.It might be mechanically a bit boring, but it is so unique and charming, its a must for anyone interested in middle ages/early modern era history.
_childDocuments_.name: Pentiment

_childDocuments_.review: Pentiment is difficult to recommend. It features an interesting art style, inspired by illuminated manuscripts, though applied inconsistently, with some characters seemingly lifted from the the vellum and others from a recent cartoon. It is packed with details of life in the early 16th century, and even includes a bibliography in the credits, if players wish to follow up on specific topics. More games should do this. The multi-generational timescale is also interesting.However, it fails both as a mystery and, worse, as a convincing narrative. It's hard to say much about the mystery without spoiling the game, but suffice to say that player choices matter much less than the game leads one to believe. By the end of Act 2, the player knows their choices are almost certainly both incorrect and irrelevant, but the game still forces them to be made, which leads to an unsatisfying, predetermined conclusion. Throughout the game there is a childish insistence that everyone would be happier if they could actualise themselves by choosing their own destiny. Through careful dialogue choices it's possible to more or less stay in character for early 1500s Bavaria, but the game constantly pushes the player to make the "right" choice which is to reject religion and inheritance and choose one's own destiny. The very concept of "following one's dreams" is a much, much later invention, and even now is available only to a few. Art of this time was about craft, not self expression and certainly not recording the world as it was. There are also many typos and incorrect grammar in the third act (“pot shards”).By the end, it's clear that the game is a revisionist fantasy of how things should have been, according to the game's author, rather than how they were. For a more thoughtful approach, try Pillars of the Earth, or the Woman’s Lot DLC for Kingdom Come Deliverance.

_childDocuments_.review: I love this game.Everything from the unique storybook style, to the typography engineered to reflect the different characters' stations and backgrounds, to the nested storylines that unfurl through dialogue and investigation to reflect on themes of history, technology, community, and belief.This is the smartest game I have ever played, and it shows the artistry that can be achieved through the medium.I cannot recommend this game highly enough.

_childDocuments_.name: Pentiment

_childDocuments_.review: 8/10 Very Good.This is basically an art piece for the modern era. A modern take on an adventure game, set during the renaissance in a backwater village, where the religious class faces future upheaval that is coming in the form of reforms.You play as Andreas Maler, an artist who is plying his trade at the local monastery for the time being. He gets pulled into a murder investigation, and away we go. There's no great gameplay mechanics here in terms of investigation, you basically chase up the clues/suspects, and throw up some prayers as you try your best to find some form of evidence against the accused.The issue is, in these days criminal investigations were basically 'he said/she said,' there's no room for legal eagle's, or blood splatter analysis, this is a time period where you say hail Mary and hope for the best.At times, you will feel powerless, such is the nature of the time period.The murder investigations and the story as a whole are quite well written. It is a snapshot of life in the old ages, with some liberties taken (and that's fine), so that we can enjoy a well crafted storyline. The art style is superb, you may see in the screenshots, that dialogue is written like penstrokes, or printed text, and that's because in the intro, it is established that you're writing a book of these events. So, as you write, you stylise the text depending on the person's education or background, so the clergy often write their dialogue in Gothic font.For those with dyslexia or vision issues, there is a prompt to turn these off, so you can get a more cleaner read.Other than this, there's little else to say about the game. You can shape Andreas' choices and backgrounds, which does help with the investigation, having knowledge of languages or logic, can help you solve puzzles in different ways for example, but his overall character remains more or less the same, he is still his own person after all.Really, you come to this game for a story, an investigation into a murder mystery, and the wonderful art, cast and location. It's a wonderful artistic type of game, and to top it all off, at £15 is beyond reasonable, it's almost a steal.So, yes, fully recommended.
_childDocuments_.name: Pentiment

_childDocuments_.review: Art is about showing the truth of life, showing what you see, not hiding anything away. Treat this game as art -- a showing of Art instead of being a work of art. I've imagined how to narrate in an a-phonetic language (means pure writing -- the plan of an idea on Derrida's critique on phonocentrism) back in my day studying linguistics and prowling philosophy at the university. Now this game is exactly what I could have imagined, perhaps even better. Medieval writing fonts and styles are the core of the storytelling, and it offers me perhaps the best reading experience of all visual novels I've come across. Now, I am not planning on giving too much aesthetic ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ pretending to be a Socrates of a sort, but I am honest enough to tell you that it makes me cry out of joy when I did this hermeneutic work: I routed a thread with the concept of art (not the question of 'what is artwork', but 'art is doing what') through the game. I intend not spoil anything here, so this is all I have to say: It is a honest 'just showing', and it faithfully finishes the task. My sincere appreciation, Andreas (or, Obsidian Entertainment.)

_childDocuments_.review: Leave it to Obsidian to create a small game that feels very impactful very quickly. The game auto-saves after every choice you make, and there are lots you don't know you are making which makes this game so much more fun to play through. You can truly try to inhabit the character you are playing as and or pick what you think is the right answer and it may not be revealed until an hour or so later how your choice affects a persuasion check or a critical moment answer. The art style, the music, the writing, the gameplay, it's all very well done and blends so well together. I'm not finished with my first run and currently at 14 total hours, but because of how the game presents choices there are easily a couple more playthroughs for me guaranteed.If you like the older Way of the Samurai games, as well as the time mechanic from the persona series, and want a game with excellent characters that feel completely realized, and want to have a wonderfully fictitious romp through Holy Roman Empire Bavaria, then this game is right up your alley.
_childDocuments_.name: Pentiment

_childDocuments_.review: Andreas (You), is a journeyman/craftsman who has come to the Bavarian town of Tassing towards the end of his WanderJahre. The introduction of Andreas and the game mechanics come in a dream. With the representation of his conscious in 3 man figures along with a fourth being a mediator for Andreas in his dreams. After this dream, the game starts you off by talking with towns folk and giving you decisions that will affect the rest of the game in only the first few minutes. Such as choosing where you originally studied for your WanderJahre, your educational background and even certain personality traits. The game has many interesting characters to interact with and even rival against. The game really makes you feel as if you were back at a tense moment in both German, European and Human History with the game foreshadowing the decline of the abbey system and the rise of Martin Luther and the German Peasants Revolt of 1525. The game developers really took the time to to understand this era of history, how the people interacted and the mix of religious elements that were quite present in many European towns and peasant's lives. The writing that is in Pentiment is fantastic. I always love a dialogue driven game where it both limits you to some degree but gives choices that wouldn't seem out of place with the characters you are interacting with. I even like how you can go deeper into some dialogue choices with your conscious and make an inform decision. I feel that the developers who chose the name of this game really made it almost have a double meaning. Pentiment is a term used in art to describe the presence of underlying layers or changes that have been made to a painting. This term is often used in the context of restoration or conservation, as it refers to the visible evidence of changes that have occurred during the painting process. You are the artist and the setting which you are in is the painting. The RPG elements and the background of Andreas as an artist make it feel that you are both the outsider looking in and main witness of the events of the world around you. I highly recommend people getting this game. If you are interested in mystery, historical presentation, RPG development or even just liking the Early Modern Period of history (like me lol), I definitely would say this is a must buy.
