_childDocuments_.review: I think this game was made for a very specific audience: some combination of history lover, art historian, christian/pagan scholar. I am not this person. I'm also not sure the choices you make really matter - although I do appreciate they don't make it clear that one choice is the "right" choice. Overall, I had to push myself in this game, hoping it would really sink in and I would enjoy it. I didn't. I just wanted to finish the game because I'd spent time in it already. The ending was... ok. Overall, not my cup of tea. And I doubt it will be most people's cup of tea.
_childDocuments_.name: Pentiment

_childDocuments_.review: Pentiment is, first of all, a beautiful game. The art is second-to-none and you could spend hours just staring at some of the paintings. This is probably one of the most lovingly crafted visual experiences in video games. The art and animation are a feast for the eyes, and clearly involved a massive amount of research into medieval art, as evidenced by the extensive reference list in the ens-credits. Indeed, the developers clearly also researched medieval Bavaria in-depth, it shows in that Tassing felt incredibly real.It's also a game in which there's no 'golden path,' no way to bring about any circumstance in which everything is all right. Like Fallout: New Vegas, whatever path you take, whatever choices you make, there will be consequences which are both positive and negative. These consequences are woven through the narrative of the game, and affect each subsequent chapter. But more than this, they affect the characters of the game in meaningful ways, ways which make you think, 'I wonder what would've happened if...' over and over again. It's a game which invites replays more than any I've played.On the surface, Pentiment is a murder-mystery game, but unlike an episode of Poirot, there is no moment in which you gather the suspects together and reveal that you've cracked the case. All you can do is gather evidence to the best of your ability in the time allotted and then make a choice. And then you must live with the consequences of that choice with the nagging doubt in your mind that you might just have got it all wrong. Unsatisfying? Some may feel so, and have said so. But that's just it, the game may be about solving murders *on the surface* but the game is about so much more. It's about guilt, religion, myth, history, mental health, regret and what people will do when they are afraid. The genius of Pentiment is that it reflects real life, because we can all be afraid, we all have regrets, but it's how we choose to carry on which matters. Many games try to be 'realistic' through fancy physics, punishing difficulty, or survival mechanics. But Pentiment does it better, because Pentiment is realistically faithful to the human experience. Pentiment sucks you in to a beautiful, hand-drawn world which allows you to escape the real world so that when it asks big questions about life, faith, and regret, it isn't jarring or immersion-breaking. In some ways Pentiment is almost a space to reflect. A bit like a monastery, really.
_childDocuments_.name: Pentiment

_childDocuments_.review: Immersive. Unique. Fascinating. The first thing that grabbed me was the art - the game feels like stepping into an illuminated manuscript as the past comes to life around you. The next thing to grab me was the deep research that very clearly went into crafting the story. I've never played any game quite like this one, but I have gushed more about this game to family and friends than anything else I've played in years. You need to give this a try.
_childDocuments_.name: Pentiment

_childDocuments_.review: Equal parts delightful and unique, Pentiment elevates itself beyond other games in the interactive fiction genre thanks to a masterful level of artistry in both its writing and design. With its story divided into three, Pentiment's first act places you in the shoes of young journeyman artist Andreas Maler, who takes up residence in the Alpine village of Tassing whilst he completes a commission at the nearby Kiersau Abbey at the height of the Renaissance. However, when a murder rocks the community, Andreas is tasked with uncovering the truth so he might spare the life of his friend, the elderly Brother Piero. Act I is undoubtedly the peak of the game; drawing you in with excellent dialogue, bountiful historical knowledge and deep thematic roots that offer excellent meditations on the nature of art and storytelling. Act II sees Andreas return to Kiersau some years after, where he is once again faced with another murder, and it's hard to not to feel like it's a bit of a rehash, particularly when faced with a noticeable decline in the quality of writing during the middle section of the game as opposed to the beginning. It does choose to focus on more dramatic elements as well as further introspection into Andreas' character, but it also fails to make any particularly insightful commentary through its writing. Thankfully things pick up again in Act III, where you now take on the role of Magdalene, a young woman who works at her father's printing shop in Tassing. When her father is mysteriously attacked, Magdalene is tasked with recounting the history of Tassing and Kiersau in a mural for the town hall, which leads to her uncovering the last few threads of the game's overarching mystery as she learns the truth behind the town and the abbey. While the reveal of the game's antagonist and their motivations felt rather underwhelming, Act III does offer strong thematic commentary on family, duty, consequence and regret that all ties together to make it a largely satisfying conclusion anyway. Altogether the story is well paced and wrought with humour, emotion and sincerity, and although it makes some not-so-subtle strides to remain in line with certain modern-day attitudes, it's undoubtedly an engrossing and masterfully crafted narrative. It's a good job that this is the case, because Pentiment is by and large a whole load of walking about, clicking through dialogue and making choices, nevertheless with the odd little minigame here and there to break up the monotony. You're also placed on a strict timeline to achieve your goals, particularly in the first two acts, and while I can see how it would incentivise replayability, it was also a little frustrating to be forced into choosing some parts of the game at the cost of accessing others. Nevertheless, there's plenty to do and seemingly a number of ways things can play out in the story, not to mention you have a solid degree of control in how Andreas and Magdalene behave thanks to a wide array of dialogue options. Interesting enough, it seems for the most part the "truth" of a lot of what happens in the game rests in the players hands, and although it felt like a strange choice at first, it actually complemented the outcome of the story fairly well. Now, I can't go any further without raising the best aspect of the game - Pentiment is a joy to behold from top to bottom thanks to its absolutely resplendent art direction. The entire experience is framed from start to end as pages in an illuminated manuscript, providing it with an absolutely beautiful hand drawn artstyle with animation that compliments it, and it does so much to elevate the game with its authentic and unique aesthetic. Great audio design also helps bring the game to life, and although I wish it was used more frequently, it employs a fantastic medieval-like soundtrack too. The game is rammed with accessibility features too, best of all being the vast glossary of historical vocabulary you can consult mid-dialogue, helping clear up any confusion whilst also allowing the writers to avoid dumbing down their scripts. In truth, I think a large part of why I enjoyed this game so much is just due to the sheer reverence for art that permeates every aspect of it's development from top to bottom. Art is really what encompasses Pentiment in its entirety; from its design to its thematic elements, every single piece of this game comes together and exudes an unrivalled level of artistic energy that also leaves a wide berth for you to contemplate your own thoughts on its subject matter. As someone who doesn't usually consider this kind of game, I was absolutely blown away even with some minor issues here and there, and if you have any sort of inclination towards art and storytelling I can't recommend it enough.8/10
_childDocuments_.name: Pentiment

_childDocuments_.review: Pentiment is a great experience, worth it at full price. While the main plot is interesting for sure, the story is much more about the people and events surrounding the primary tragedies befalling Tassing's residents. You get to see the effects of all your actions on a much larger time-scale than in most games I've played, given that the story spans 25 years. Even though your character is only somewhat malleable, even after one playthrough I can already imagine how different the events of Act II might be based on what I did in Act I, and similarly for act III based on Act II. Also, Lingua Ignota wrote a song for the game. I remember thinking "Huh, sounds kinda like LI," and now that I googled to confirm that I'm just so happy Kristin is featured in a game which so easily fits the vibe of her incredible music.  I like the idea of representing people's voice through different kinds of old-timey fonts given that the game is not voice-acted, however I only had it on in the beginning as it was just a bit much for my eyes. I suppose if you're a graduate-level student who studies early-modern European literature, you may be fine with it, but I switched on the simplified fonts. If you aren't excited to read modern-sounding dialogue in illuminated script, just check the simplified fonts option. It doesn't kill the immersion for me personally.Numbered scores are tricky as I'm not a regular reviewer, but I go close to a Fantano scale, where 5 is an average game that you could take or leave, and games where the list of cons is larger than the pros don't get a 9 like IGN does it. That said, I would give this game a strong 8. It's far removed from the general chaff of games, worthy of your undivided attention for a couple playthroughs. It's not quite Disco Elysium, my personal GOAT game and easily the best RPG period, but it doesn't need to to be an achievement for Obsidian and their reliable quality.
_childDocuments_.name: Pentiment

_childDocuments_.review: You can read other reviews Video review: There are choices that are quite difficult to make, but what if those choices play such an important role in a narrative that goes hand in hand with our character's personality? Pentiment is much more than a simple click of a mouse button.Andreas Maler, played by the player who will be in charge of deciphering the mysteries that this title will bring to the table, is a traveling artist and a dreamer, advised by imaginary entities during his sleep. Each of them is interpreted by his opinion. Between Saints, Priests and even the philosopher Socrates, opinions differ among them in an attempt to discuss ideas and shape an opinion about the changes that Andreas will be facing, due to the choices he made at a certain point in history. In fact, the adventure begins inside a dream of Andreas, who after waking up learns that court jesters are intractable.The narrative begins with little action, in fact, there are no moments of action at all, but even so, it is a title recommended for anyone looking for a captivating story and accurate historical events. Tassing, is the fictional town in the countryside of the Holy Roman Empire, which serves as a backdrop and which at first glance appears peaceful with modest but super friendly people. Andreas's task until then was to work on his great masterpiece, this being an artist with studies in the field and beyond, but also to enter into the routine of working on the manuscripts of the local abbey. However, he quickly realizes that things are not as peaceful as they appear to be, and suddenly finds himself wrapped in a panoply of mysteries that involve even the death of one of his elements.The history and background of Andreas are completely outlined by the player as he advances in time, being able to choose the areas of study that most interest him and even the types of language that fascinate him the most. These choices will have a direct impact on the story and the possible lines of text available at certain times. My Andreas dabbles in Italian studies and a little Greek, fascinated by books, occult magic, and astronomy. It is important to approach all moments with the greatest possible attention since these can lead to a positive or negative outcome in the activity between characters and with this the possibility of acquiring more knowledge about the subject addressed.Not being a Point and Click in its essence, Pentiment's adventure goes through a narrative divided into 3 acts that involve investigation and the player's attention to places that may go unnoticed. In trying to solve the murder mysteries, it is important to be convinced of the decisions taken, since time weighs on all small actions. The simple act of having lunch with a character implies wasting time that can be used to explore another part of the story in more depth, which ultimately can impact the number of evidence for the outcome of the case. And yes, it's easy to get lost in these small actions because without paying much attention, the next moment, you're already in contact with a character that doesn't add anything to the main point. Everything is very vivid and there is a lot to discover. The map can also help with these momentary distractions since the possibilities are more than many. This is not a Sherlock Holmes where the story has only one ending, Pentiment kinda forces you to pick a culprit with the information that you gathered and subsequently live with it.The direct consequences of the player's choices are what make this experience so impactful. Everything rotates and adapts according to the different branches of choice, and ultimately if you are on the side of the village population or hand in hand with the abbey.Pentiment's graphics pull the graphic aspect of the engravings in a book and make everything quite charming. All its characters and surroundings are quite peculiar and specific to the era, or this one is not set in the year 1518. The menu itself is a book that opens between the map, the different characters, the objectives, and clues. That helps the player not to feel lost about what the next step to take. Another super interesting aspect is the possibility of having specific letter fonts for each character, which although some are a little difficult to decipher, manages to convey the personality of the individual approached since there is no voice acting of any kind. Could it be that if there was voice acting this would be a title that could attract more people? Or, on the other hand, would it throw down any kind of depth that can you can drink from all the reading? Pentiment is a breath of fresh air from the studios of Obsidian Entertainment. Slow at certain points, but pertinent and interesting at just the right points to grab the player even in those moments.
_childDocuments_.name: Pentiment

_childDocuments_.review: The art is gorgeous, the dialogue options hilarious, your choices actually matter a lot and the mystery is very interesting. I loved how religion was portrayed in this game: accurate to the time period. The story has many layers, from the surface murder mystery, all the way to how history echos through the ages and how we are all affected by it. 10/10 would recommend a thousand times to those who like to read and dig into a story.
_childDocuments_.name: Pentiment

_childDocuments_.review: I can highly recommend this if you're a fan of history and narrative-driven games where your choices matter. It's best to go into this game with the least amount of information regarding the story.Pentiment's director, Josh Sawyer, explained that Pentiment comes from 'Pentimento', a change made by an artist while painting. It symbolizes how history, like a painting, can be covered, then rediscovered or forgotten. I initially bought this game because I was intrigued by the concept and art style but it wasn't long before I got hooked on the story of Andreas Maler and the inhabitants of Tassing. It's "Slice of Life" but there's an intriguing mystery at the heart of it.The game oozes with charm and paints a world in change. It's at times contemplative and philosophical without removing itself too much from the everyday life of a peasant in 16th century. It made me think about the people that came before me. I wondered who they were and what their life must have looked like. What they fought for and how, in turn, they thought about the people before them.I appreciated the level of detail found in every little animation, in every piece of dialogue. It doesn't happen very often that Flanders is an actual option for you backstory. It's even more rare to have it reference accurate information, with perfect Dutch.This is an absolute gem. Sit down, relax, pour yourself a good pint of ale and let the story unfold. You won't regret it.
_childDocuments_.name: Pentiment

_childDocuments_.review: I liked it. When I heard about this game it was less than 24 hours from release and was pitched to me as a "if you like disco elysium, you will like this" Then I saw Josh Sawyer's name on the game and to be honest I would have bought any game with his name on it. To start off, it's not disco elysium, it's special, but it isn't disco elysium. If you are interested in history, this game is very rooted in realism and I learned a lot about the time period. There are a lot of choices to make which can have a big influence on the game state, although as far as I can tell the main story beats will remain unchanged. My only qualms with the game are the annoying lack of save/load, I understand why but I feel like that should be the player's choice, mistakes happen and sometimes people click the wrong dialogue, and that the third act is really slow comparative to the rest of the game and I started to get bored. But I was satisfied with the ending and I think it redeems it.
_childDocuments_.name: Pentiment

_childDocuments_.review: Great concept. This is sometimes rewarded, but often only succeeds in feeling like a chore.Overall I'd score this a 4/5, but your enjoyment will depend heavily on your personal interest in the subject matter / setting and level of patience (or lack of).
_childDocuments_.name: Pentiment

_childDocuments_.review: I haven't been this impressed with a point and click "choices matter" game since TellTale's The Walking Dead. Between the art style, the depth of choice, the historical accuracy, the soundtrack, and the story itself, Pentiment is a wild ride from start to finish that I only wish I could experience for the first time again. You may think you're just getting a murder mystery, but in reality Pentiment is about so much more, and the scope of our actions and the consequences we must deal with only become wider. You feel how even small decisions we make can drastically affect history. The choices the game lays before you are genuinely tough at times, and grey area is abundant. At no point in my entire playthrough did I ever once feel like the game gave me a clear-cut "this is objectively right or wrong" decision. The twists and turns of the story are genuinely fascinating, and at no point did I ever feel the game was subverting my expectations for its own sake. The entire adventure is EXTREMELY well designed. The characters feel and act like real people and are easy to recognize and tell apart. Even the title is utter perfection, and references the very nature of the plot. In short, I enjoyed almost literally every minute of this experience. Once or twice I got frustrated because I simply was not sure how to further the story. But the map is small enough that the answer is never particularly far away. The only negative thing I can honestly say is that though the first and second acts are utterly amazing and thrilling, the third act is where some small cracks start to show. A little too much back and forth. Not as many persuasion checks. A few too many cutscenes. An annoying character. A little bit of the illusion of choice. I've heard complaints that it goes on a touch too long, but I never felt that way. I was too busy digging into Tassing's history, intrigued by literally everything I saw, to notice. Cannot recommend this game enough. Nothing is perfect but Pentiment comes about as close as one could hope. I was completely enthralled from start to finish and am already planning a second playthrough. Not bad for $20!
_childDocuments_.name: Pentiment

_childDocuments_.review: Only played this shortly but the game is outstanding so far. Not for everyone but if you like the visuals on the store page and are intrigued by the setting then I recommend to just buy it and try it out.new review after finishing this game: This game is much better than I previously thought. It's not just unique, the story is beautifully written with many plottwists and narratives throughout the game that all connect at the end. Your choices matter too, and the game doesn't hold your hand. The developer doesn't assume you are stupid, and you have to remember certain things and characters on your own. There isn't a "Do X" quest marker at all times and you have to figure out things on your own. Very refreshingThis is basically a piece of art. Only nitpick is that the controls and mechanics are a bit tedious, but this doesn't hurt the games story.
_childDocuments_.name: Pentiment

_childDocuments_.review: Went into it thinking it would be more of a detective style game, but it's more of a visual novel in many ways. There's a sense of mystery, but not a lot of puzzle solving. Much of the game is interacting with other characters and learning to know the fictional town of Tassing and its history - having an interest in renaissance and medieval history helps a lot, but it's all very well written.Throughout the game you have to make a lot of choices which advance time and locks out other options, while having only autosave and one save slot - this means there's replayability, but might frustrate you if you're a frequent save-reload type person. I'm a bit of a reload-type person myself, but found it very rewarding in the end due to how the story is written.Graphics are very good, though I wish they went all the way with the style and worked with distorted scale on the backgrounds like in the old manuscripts. Only a few parts in the game truly look and feel like the style of the time, which feels a bit of a shame when they already nailed the character designs.The biggest downside in the game is the backtracking. Tassing isn't a big town, but you have to run everywhere, and because you only have a few limited choices before advancing time you'll run around like a maniac to find all of them before deciding what to go for. A fast-travel system would've been very helpful.Another issue I had was with the dialogues. Occasionally Andreas will reflect on something in a separate speech bubble, but it will pop up after all the other text and is easily skipped. Things in the dialogues also frequently don't show up in your journal, so some things you just have to keep in memory - quite annoying with notes and books you find and can never read again.All in all it's a very good game, but you need some patience with the slower parts and accept it's more story than puzzle.
_childDocuments_.name: Pentiment

_childDocuments_.review: + Absolutely beautiful illustration style+ Top notch historical accuracy and plenty of information+ Characters with depth, not everything is what it seems+ Tons of dialogue and conversations I could imagine happening- Only autosave, no idea when the saves happen- Unpredictable time management, no clues how long actions will take- The last chapter is significantly more linear and slow paced- Not for perfectionists, you will make mistakes and they are part of the storyA solid B+

_childDocuments_.review: An absolutely gorgeous piece with a quite frankly absurd amount of love and research put into it. It is hard to fault the game's presentation on any merit whatsoever, and it clearly cares about it's setting immensely, and the execution is superb. Pentiment is largely a mid-late medieval murder mystery game, with your freelance artist player character irrationally shoved into the role of detective, as there's no one else better around. The save system, and lack of any realistically reasonable conveyance of the consequences of your decisions can be incredibly frustrating to a certain type of player, a demographic that includes myself. Certain decisions are set up as though they'll have obvious relevance to something you hope to accomplish, only for it to be completely irrelevant, despite being reasonably pertinent from a logical standpoint. At the same time, something that in no way should have any relevance towards a specific outcome may be listed as the most defining factor, despite not lining up with a NPC's decisions, outlook, or motives. What would otherwise be potent bargaining chips are sometimes just left out completely, with the player given no option to even bring up a particularly incriminating piece of evidence. Often I found myself frustrated or outright baffled at the dialogue options presented to me, either not being able to bring up something obvious and useful, or sometimes forcing the player character to willingly reveal, without any in-universe prompting or questioning, something that does nothing but harm your future investigation attempts or sour an NPC's relationship with the player character. It can be disheartening and aggravating to build up to a certain action, of which you have limited amounts, for 45-60 minutes, only for a catch that doesn't really make a lot of sense to show up at the last second and completely shut you down, wasting whole days or sometimes the entire investigation. Understandably for scripting and development reasons, only a limited number of culprits are presented to you at any given stage, with no definite perpetrator. This can be quite unsatisfying, as your specific investigations will never give you enough evidence to reasonably accuse anyone, meaning you choose off of emotion and your character preferences. This isn't necessarily a bad thing, but it does make all the time you've spent slowly backtracking, managing your very limited time, and agonizing over deliberate dialogue choices feel completely pointless. If in the end, you can't actually determine a correct culprit, or even a particularly strong case against a culprit, why run around for 4 fours when you could just sleep for 3 days, and arbitrarily choose the NPC you like the least from the list of culprits? If this doesn't bother you, and you enjoy the very solid world-building, and want to get immersed in the setting and with the characters, then this game's polish, research, and care put into it will make this an excellent purchase. But if deliberate planning can blowing up in your face after an hour due to something small and arbitrary, or slow and methodical walking from conversation and conversation, or the eventual realization that most of your choices really don't matter in any meaningful way, I would give this game a pass. Or at least until it goes on sale. I'm a big proponent of supporting small studios and creatives with good ideas and good execution. I don't like playing this game much at all, but I do like its ideas and execution. So maybe pick it up for five or ten bucks and never install it

_childDocuments_.review: Incredible game, I was completely engrossed until the ending. If you are someone who appreciates exceptionally good storytelling with rich worlds (yes I am aware this is historical which is why I avoided "world building") and memorable characters (I would die for Brother Piero!) the likes of Disco Elysium, Norco, Pillars of the Earth, etc., this game should be an immediate purchase. This comment on its storytelling of course is itself amusing given its themes (you'll see what I mean if you get it). Presentation is incredible with innovations that other point-and-click adventures, especially those with larger casts of characters, should take some inspiration from. Only negatives I'd mention are a few minor bugs (portraits of the wrong villagers in the main reference books) and one slightly less believable character action. A character does something major that I felt wasn't completely earned, though I know there was textual support for it. This may have been because I chose a background that maybe gave the character weaker motivations for said action than the other ones. That being said, other things I thought were issues were beautifully resolved in the end--and I cried, a lot! Anyway, if you're still here reading this, buy this game! If you are someone who doesn't appreciate or care for subtext, and prefers a straight-forward face-value story, then this might not be for you (again this comment is amusing given the game's themes!) though I think the face-reading of the story I personally still find very interesting.

_childDocuments_.review: A point and click adventure game where you can see the love and care being literally scrawled onto the page, Gothic letter by Gothic letter.  The world building is omnipresent because its a world that was and is, and accessibly parceled out to you in a journal you will soon come to call your own. Dive into an anti-smoking gun mystery, where guns abound and the smoke is everywhere. Clinging, coughing, fuming, heralding the coming of an inferno. You will ask yourself: is this right? Am I right? _childDocuments_.name: Pentiment

_childDocuments_.review: Finished Pentiment! Will never be the same thanks for that.Okay in all seriousness I don't think this was the most life changing thing I've experienced - in the way that certain works (mainly books) have literally changed my views on life itself. Possibly because I've already seen Andrei Rublev and if there was ever a piece of media about religion and loss and generations that was going to completely fry your brain, that was it.That being said I really enjoyed Pentiment. Like, first game in years I've finished the entire way enjoyed. It really moved me, and I really was drawn into the story, into playing and learning as much as possible. I certainly did not play this game as fast as I could have, hell I even regret some options I didn't take that I wanted to experience (next time maybe)? I really liked the direction of the story. I liked the way we see Mahler watch everything crumble. I really loved the transition into Act III, all these familiar characters and pieces of information that could only make sense to the player and not to the character of Magdalene. I also loved the sense of living through something that this game had. Terrible things happen. People die. Buildings crumble. It seems like the end of the world and then... it isn't. A new season comes. Babies are born. Children grow up. Humans keep living and living and living even when the world seems on a knife's edge. And I absolutely adore media that portrays this. Really more than I care to admit. I love the story of humanity surviving. Because of choices and because we have to. It's a compulsion in all of us, to survive, and, more importantly, to live.I do think this game would have done better were it set a little earlier? I do think that Tassing does not ultimately feel like part of the 16th century, though some of this is of course aesthetic. The style is more medieval than Renaissance to me, and though I do appreciate and understand why Tassing should feel out of time and like a backwater - I mean like, it is and that is a clear theme in the story - I still think a little earlier might have been better? But of course you're constrained by historical events and when the Reformation started so I get it. Maybe I'm just too big of a fan of the 14th and 15th centuries in terms of art. My loves forever and always. Overall I really did like Pentiment though and would give it like... 4.5/5 stars. Again, really rare I complete a video game so in my book this is like Hall of Fame level video game stuff. Shoutout to Obsidian. I may not leave the historical realm for Disco Elysium, but I do love what you did here.

_childDocuments_.review: My law degree did nothing but piss people off, just like in real life.In all seriousness, if you are at all a fan of any or all of Early Modern Bavarian History, art, theology, frogges, Disco Elysium, and choices with consequences that hit you like a bullet from a flintlock blunderbuss, play this game.

_childDocuments_.review: Pentiment is a murder mystery story/adventure game that scratches all sorts of itches for my medieval historian's heart. While not without its flaws, it's clear how much love and thought has gone into the dialogue and characterization of the world of this game. Portraying three periods at the start, middle, and late periods in the Reformation, painter Andreas Maeler navigates a changing town in Bavaria. Also murder. A couple of murders.Pentiment's visual design is immersive, detailed, and well bolstered by some stellar writing that gives your decisions within the narrative just a modest level of heft. This is, ultimately, a story lifted from Agatha Christie where there "is" a murderer, and your ability to change those facts are limited. But if you're willing to go along for the ride there are few other games like it.Pentiment pauses at times to ponder revolutions, religious conversions, faith, relics, the saints, the layered nature of history, marriage, and half a hundred other topics in ways that are inclusive and thoughtful. Often, I found myself questioning what was right, and not just in a video gamey morality sense, but in a truly hard angled provocation.All that said, it's worth noting that the "game" parts of Pentiment are on the weaker end. Once you get past the stellar art design (the whole game appears as a book), the little minigames and other elements just don't work as solidly as Disco Elysium's total dedication to adventure and deduction, to give one recent example. But that's a minor flaw. If you're playing this, it's for the story, and that delivers in spades. Well worth the journey a pilgrim should take.

_childDocuments_.review: For those who enjoy narrative-heavy and "choices matter" games, Pentiment is wonderful. The atmosphere, the art style, the writing, everything were engaging to me. I may not be someone who's interested in 16th century European history, but I still greatly enjoyed it! _childDocuments_.name: Pentiment

_childDocuments_.review: I want to start this by clearing something up I've been seeing too much in these early reviews:  is  Obsidian's take on  (shout-out to the guy who said it was medieval , even though I wouldn't say this is half as difficult or mind-bending).  is Obsidian's take on Ubisoft's . You will not be decking out your detective in the finest gear, min-maxing your favorite traits for the funny dialogue options, and asking strangers if they are (in fact) a member of the homosexual underground. You will be walking from conversation to conversation in a wonderfully realized moving historical artwork, occasionally seeing a special dialogue option but mostly clicking around, wandering through familiar paths in the terrain or choosing between various naturalized (but still deeply referential and historical) dialogue bubbles. You could call it a visual novel with some added religious and historical pizzazz. I would call it a nerd game, but the kind of nerd game for nerds  (and little time for things as complex as level-up screens and deep, engaging combat loops, or long-winded real-time strategy). This game has a bibliography. You will be able to tell. It's also full of lovely little details (like the little errors in the wonderfully specific dialogue boxes that let me go "Oh, I remember the wild days of Middle English too!"). It's a deep dive into the ancient winding world of religion and politics, a less player-oriented Obsidian tale with a lot to give if you can bear a game that speaks a lot more than it moves.In short, this one's for the boys (the boys being all the people with degrees in history and literature).
_childDocuments_.name: Pentiment

_childDocuments_.review: I'm writing this review since I fear this game won't see the success it deserves and really want to urge those on the fence to give it a try.Obsidian are the best writers in the business, and Pentiment, for me, is their finest work. While I went in expecting a breezy and light historical murder mystery, what I got was a profound, moving experience. Funny and poignant in equal terms, I think the developers need to be commended for crafting not just a totally believable and immersive setting, full of memorable characters, but also a mystery which kept me guessing until the very end. All this while maintaining total commitment to the historical setting. I'm not ashamed to say the story had me tearing up at times. Unforgettable.In terms of gameplay, this is sort of a "light" CRPG. Certain facts chosen about your character's background impact how you interact with the various characters in the game world. Dialogue here is really the primary mechanic, as well as choosing how you spend your limited time. The loop is kept interesting throughout the feedback provided to the player. The world responds to your choices and the plot moves forward accordingly.  Your Andreas will likely be a different man from mine, and his choices will differ as well. The art and sound direction tie it all together very nicely. The visuals are totally charming, and the animations, though limited, are really good at showing subtle details. This elevated many scenes for me. I really urge people to give this a try. It's easily the best thing I've played all year, probably my favourite game since Disco Elysium. Unmissable for anyone who likes strong stories in games or unique settings. It's perfect as they come.
_childDocuments_.name: Pentiment

_childDocuments_.review: The game is good. The story was wonderful. I only wish that there was some kind of option to let you know who were the people who actually wanted to have a conversation, instead of needing to run around checking every single person. And, like i said, I think a bit more stream lining would have had me enjoy it more. But who knows? Maybe this is a moment where if I did have it the way I think I would have liked it, I wouldnt actually have liked it. Idk. Im not a game designer.

_childDocuments_.review: It's like Weird Medieval Guys on Twitter, but a game! Text-based and unfair, yeah, but with a sophisticated story and some sad food for thought. _childDocuments_.name: Pentiment

_childDocuments_.review: Incredibly beautiful game; the art direction is gorgeous, even if (like me) Catholic Marginalia isn't your favorite aesthetic and Gregorian chants don't set your world on fire, you are made to feel every inch of it in a way that (coupled with the ludicrously well-researched historicity) grounds you firmly within the narrative and made me feel thoroughly invested in nearly every role-playing decision the game puts in front of you.The writing is what you'd expect of Obsidian, which is to say: excellent. Authentically funny when its trying to be, deeply moving during its big emotional beats, and manages to invest enough personality into its characters that I never forgot who anyone was or what their relationship to the town was.It's slow, that can't be denied. Even the pacing of the cinematic animations seems deliberately drawn out, and though the map is helpful you'll probably find yourself running around a lot, which doesn't feel great. That said, they do an admirable job of filling the walk-around portions with flavorful character interactions, which is helpful in a mystery story.That mystery is probably going to be the biggest bone of contention for people who are already on-board with a Walk-N-Talk. It's tactically vague with its verdicts, and you're left feeling like there's more going on than you necessarily have a shot at uncovering, at least in a first playthrough. Personally, I kinda like that, since historical mysteries rarely have super concise conclusions, and it doesn't lead to any fail-states you feel like you should have been able to enjoy.Definitely not for everyone, but as a fan of Disco Elysium and Hell On Earth, I loved almost every single second of this one. Highly recommended.

_childDocuments_.review: Here is the selling point for me:you will usually have three-five responses available, but you can only pick one of them. Picking a response often locks you out of all other responses. This is game-changing because it makes you critically think about how other characters will respond and how you are impacting the story and ending. In this game, what you don't say is just as important (if not more) as what you do say.If you love Holy Roman Empire history (especially around the 15/1600s), this will be your jam.But even if you don't, the humanity present in these people shows how similar these people, and indeed people throughout history, are to us today. With murder mysteries, juicy hot goss, and religious oppression, there are plenty of themes, ideas, and philosophies to dive into and explore in this stunningly hand-drawn world. One of the best point and clicks out there.

_childDocuments_.review: I was captivated from beginning to end. A true passion project through and through. You can tell the love that went into making this, the careful attention to detail and the precision with which everything was written. Pentiment is a beautiful game which deftly demonstrates the uniqueness of video games as a vehicle for compelling story telling, even education, without ever feeling heavy-handed or contrived. I loved every second of this game, and find myself with a hole left in me after finishing it. It was a refreshing splash of vibrant originality, and such an unequivocal labor of love that feels almost anachronistic in this day and age. I only hope that this game was enough of a financial success for Obsidian to encourage them to continue to break the mold like this in the future. Games like this deserve to exist, and I want to believe in a future and a world where we reward those with the fortitude to create unique and potentially polarizing new things.

_childDocuments_.review: Pentiment is hard to review - especially without spoiling. It's not at all what I expected based on the trailer. Primarily, it's a text-heavy game about a fictional town in Germany, its inhabitants, a visiting Artist and the events they participate in that shape the town's history. It takes place across multiple time periods in the early 1500s, which makes it interesting to see how things change. The characters are believable, the town feels alive, and I think it does an excellent job of exploring the history of the time. I am glad that I experienced it, but it definitely falls into "game as an art form" rather than "enjoyable game". 3/5 for me, 4/5 if you like reading. Finished in 13 hours- It feels like a unique idea for a game. It's not one I particularly enjoyed, but it is unique- The artwork is beautiful- Although it’s not voice acted, when each character speaks they have different handwriting depending on their status or education. The commoners have handwritten dialogue, monks have gothic lettering etc- Character animations and expressions are good. Although they're relatively small and hand-drawn, you can see believable expressions on faces- As the dialogue is written out, the characters sometimes make mistakes, then erase letters and correct them after finishing a sentence- Time passes when you take actions that would take a few hours (like sitting down with a group of people to chat) and it usually warns you in advance. Normal conversations don’t make time pass- It does a fantastic job of exploring early Renaissance history, relationships between the abbey and the town, social classes, commoner life and many other issues of that time period- Although I didn't like it, the game does do a good job of making you feel unsure of your decisions. In acts 1 and 2 you are required to name a suspect for a murder. You're not given enough time to make a good decision, but you're forced to name someone anyway- Although I think the hand-writing and spelling mistakes are a nice idea, considering how much of the game is reading and how short people's sentences are, I quickly found them a barrier to the reading and switched to instant display of dialogue- Actually moving your character is clunky. There's an acceleration on it so you start moving very slowly and speed up (well, speed up to "leisurely"). It makes precise movement or changing directions frequently annoying- The gameplay consists of about 70% reading, 30% walking from one end of town to the other. The primary loop is to wander around talking to people until you've talked to everyone, then the story progresses- None of the choices you make actually change anything- There's no music, and almost no sound effects - the game is frequently silent- You don't get enough time to investigate all leads for the murders - and in my case, not enough time to even finish investigating ONE lead, which means (as Yahtzee said) "you end up just pinning the murder on whoever you investigated the most"- The game is unclear about how time works. I went to eat with people hoping to uncover information, but really it’s a mechanic to advance time and get to know people- I failed every single “convince this person” dialogue challenge- It’s often unclear what you’re meant to do next. There is a journal, but it often doesn’t give you an objective, so you just wander around talking to everyone- You cannot solve the murders - there is no correct answer. I was kind of under the impression this would be a murder mystery game, but it's more like "We're telling a story, and you're going to listen"- At the end of the game where everything is explained, there were some extremely confusing explanations for what was going on (which I won't go in to in detail, but I felt unsatisfied about several things)
_childDocuments_.name: Pentiment

_childDocuments_.review: I probably shouldn't have binged this game mercilessly in the two days since it's release. Do I regret it? No. After finishing the game what struck me most was how much it lived up to it's name. We are left viewing history and folklore like a hastily covered up painting, where pagan myths are covered up and adopted into Roman myths which are adopted into the christian faith, where the disenfranchised and outsiders are forgotten under the weight of history. This game lives up to the promises of gaming as an art form, it could not have been made as anything else. The more I write this, the more pretentious it sounds so I am going to stop now.Any downsides? Some may find it tedious, particularly after a certain section of the game. I don't know if it has much replayability. And while it is probably the most polished obsidian game I've ever played it is not without it's bugs. Finally while it is intelligent, the constant stream of tragedy harms it's emotional impact.Overall if you have an interest in history, or art, or literature, or just off-kilter games this is a must play. I honestly think that this game and it's approach to history will be studied and praised for a very long time.John

_childDocuments_.review: This game is difficult to assess — on one hand, it offers a considerable amount of choice, and goes to great lengths to make it feel like your decisions have impact. It also gives you freedom to think through the investigation yourself, even if it does mean that you end up solving the big mystery in Act 1, and have to wait until the end for the characters in the game to figure it out, as I did... The game also explores potent and complex themes, with believable characters — however, going into detail here would not be feasible, and would spoil the main draw of the game for prospective players, so I shall restrain myself.At the same time, the gameplay itself can be a drag — it is pretty much just reading, and the prose is not particularly interesting, largely due to the fact that most all text is dialogue. The pacing also suffers in the third act, as you are not really investigating anything anymore, and it becomes more of a checklist for you to fill out whilst the game shows off how much impact the decisions in the first two acts had... the third act is the longest in the game.I have already mentioned my main gripe with the plot, but I feel that it bears repeating: I quickly figured out that there was a major suspect whom the game would not let me accuse, and as the game kept going, the evidence just kept piling up and the characters would not acknowledge it until the big reveal at the end. It was kind of infuriating.Overall, I like this video game — the graphics are good, the freedom of choice and the genuine detective work serve it well, and it does discuss many interesting things outside of the main murder mystery. It also has no combat, which saves it from being absolutely awful to play; A fate which befell Tyranny, the other Obsidian RPG I have played.

_childDocuments_.review: Pentiment is essentially a video game version of The Name of the Rose. If that sounds as exciting to you as it did to me, then I 100% guarantee that you will love this game. Take that book and add in lovingly crafted artwork and a branching narrative with RPG character building elements, and you've got Pentiment. This game probably has an extremely niche appeal. A very historically accurate, narrative-focused, RPG, murder mystery? Who would play that? Me. As soon as I saw the announcement for this game, I immediately felt that it had been made specifically to appeal to me and other people with similar interests (i.e. huge history nerds who also like role playing narratives). Its probably not for everyone, but for the people who will find it appealing, its an amazing experience. Its almost kind of a misnomer to call it an "RPG" in the modern sense of the term, because there's no combat. The RPG elements, like the whole rest of of the game, are entirely dialogue/narrative focused.  You are playing a pre-made character, technically, but you still have the agency to control how he behaves, as well as his backstory, etc. I would say that its a role playing experience in the purest sense of the term: you're role playing a person who doesn't have fantastic, superhuman abilities, who can only do things that a normal person could, and who will face realistic consequences appropriate to the historical setting of the game. If you're the kind of person who, when playing an RPG, always tries to talk your way out of every situation, and attempts to take the time to find every bit of information available before making a decision, you will appreciate this approach. Its one of the best games I've played in years.

_childDocuments_.review: Pentiment isn't a game. It's a masterpiece. I started playing Pentiment early on a frigid Christmas Eve with the intention of playing it for a couple of hours and became so engrossed I played it for 11 hours straight. I could not bring myself to stop. It's now daylight outside.Everything from the presentation, artwork, story, characters, dialogue, and the soundtrack are so polished, so honed to narrative perfection, that you forget you're playing a game. Instead it feels like you're taking part in an interactive stage play / murder mystery co-written by Umberto Eco and Henrik Ibsen.Graphically the game is gorgeous and told through lush, beautifully animated scenes inspired by the artwork in medieval illuminated manuscripts. However, unlike Terry Gilliam's cutouts in , Pentiment's characters are given high quality animations that avoids feeling 'cartoony'. Character design in particular is excellent, telegraphing information about characters at a glance, yet despite no spoken dialogue in the game they emote their feelings naturally. By the end of the game you will find yourself caring for a lot of Pentiment's characters.Pentiment's story is about solving a murder but at its heart is a deeply human story about the clash between past and present, progress and tradition, faith and science, power and politics, and uncomfortable truths and necessary lies. Throughout the game you'll be tasked to navigate all these things and more as you explore the game's mystery. While there are tons of games out there that claim 'choices matter' more often than not I find these choices superficial or simply offer up slightly different outcomes. Pentiment avoids this trap. At the start of the game you are given a handful of choices for your character's background which, given the opportunity, leads to different dialogue as the story develops. What feels different this time is that the dialogue choices feel weighty and your outcomes will vary greatly depending on what you chose; an artist with a medical background or botanical background will see the world differently than one who went with a theological or legal background.It also does this without abstract stats or skill boxes; it all comes down to your initial choices and how you interact with characters. My only quibble (besides a lack of fast travel) is, despite earning a character's respect through saying the right things, pivotal dialogues can still fail because of a dice roll, even when the roll was weighed heavily in my favor. This, combined with the fact there is no way to create a checkpoint (the game continuously autosaves), it means these failures are permanent until your next playthrough. This can lead to some frustration even if it heightens the consequences of your actions.Nevertheless, after eleven hours I'm still not done with the story. I *think* I may be in the final act, I'm not sure, and even then I haven't even scratched the surface of the mystery. Pentiment is the type of game that requires multiple playthroughs in order to see everything it has to offer. I'm already looking forward to my second playthrough.So should you get Pentiment? Yes. Pentiment has something for everyone.If you have an interest in late medieval / early Renaissance history or art history get Pentiment; even if you don't, Pentiment gives you easy to understand info blurbs that you can bring up mid-dialogue.If you love a good mystery or love losing yourself in a good book Pentiment is for you.If you like morally complex stories that avoid simple black-and-white characters then Pentiment is for you. Every character has their agenda but none of them are purely good or evil but driven by internally consistent motivations.Pentiment is a triumph of narrative and artistic design and, despite his already-lofty resume, Josh Sawyer's magnum opus.Now if you'll excuse me... I need to get some sleep.

_childDocuments_.review: God (forgive my momentary blasphemy), this game is something else.It's just incredible.The art is so beautiful, the music is incredible and the characters and the story is just so human.Almost every choice you make matters, and when you make some of the most important ones you might not be aware just how important that one choice was until much later on.This game is one of a kind.If you love a mystery, it's for you.If you love slice of life, it's for you.If you love history, it's for you.If you love drama, it's for you.And if you just love a damn good game, then by God, it's for you.

_childDocuments_.review: Very good, but I'd rather this be a visual novel or animation than a game. Being a game it has to justify the medium, and Pentiment does not do that very well. Most of the things "game"-y felt like arbitrary filler rather than contribute to the concept. Pentiment is a murder mystery and as such the player may or may not interact with all sources of evidence to come to any sound conclusion - but this too this hardly works in the game's favor as all it achieves is poor pacing.The writing in Pentiment is REALLY good. It is probably one of the strongest literary pieces I've seen expressed outside books, being up there with games like Disco Elysium. It is also rather pretentious, as most literary work is - but not to jarring degrees. Occasionally the game will expose you to rather disconnected historical tangents just to "impress" (especially the first dialogue scene with the Baron is quite painful), but most of the time it flows rather naturally. I would say the game is most enjoyable for those at least vaguely familiar with the late roman empire as it will frequently refer to prominent historic events. Characters are believable and act naturally, as opposed to caricatural and quirky. The role of the protagonist is a bit bland (another historical novel with a journeyman artist in the lead) but allows for a good medium to express "intended" dialogue through. The game clearly expects a more progressive mind to take the center stage here as a juxtaposition, which will most likely succeed considering I don't think anyone born in the early 16th century would play this game. You don't agree, but you want to understand.Worth playing if you're in the mood to read a book. As a game Pentiment achieves rather poor, at times even obnoxious pacing.More reviews at .
_childDocuments_.name: Pentiment

_childDocuments_.review: This roleplaying, point-and-click, investigation game in a historical setting (early age of reformation in the Bavarian alps) is an absolute work of art.The main storyline is filled with endings that are merely beginnings, as well as abrupt endings when you thought you were holding the right piece of the puzzle. Characters are incredibly well written, whether they are primary or background ones (a word of advice: maybe skip this if all you ever want to incarnate is Mr Nice Guy). Historical setting is fairly unique in videogames. Minigames are satisfying.That said, there are a few blemishes that are worth mentioning:- the menus are evidently console-oriented, which is somewhat problematic because there is a lot of interesting text to read in various journal sections, but navigating with arrows and page loads everywhere is vastly inferior to what you would expect from a PC experience- there are a few inconsistencies with character interactions due to the large number of branches the story can take (the tax quest ended up broken for me)- I should have said *almost all* minigames are satisfying - the card game one is actually awful- French translation was excellent for two chapters, but the third chapter was glaringly inferior. Multiple issues with gender or plural agreements, a few literally-translated expressions, enough to break the immersion. Reverted to English for my second playthrough, despite the medieval technicalities.
_childDocuments_.name: Pentiment

_childDocuments_.review: Pentiment is such an excellent game with gorgeous, thoroughly researched art and historical details. I can hardly put into words how much I love this game.The characters are written excellently and thoughtfully. Almost every choice matters, and you can play several times over and still have plenty of avenues left to explore.I thoroughly recommend it for anyone with an interest in medieval history, particularly that which pertains to religion, art, literacy and publishing. However, if you're looking for a detective/murder mystery game that will test your wits as I was when I first bought it, be warned - you will never find out for certain if your deductions are correct.

_childDocuments_.review: The newest game by Obsidian's genius game designer Josh Sawyer, Pentiment bears the hallmark of his style yet presents one of his most original work to date. Everything about the game is incredibly unique, from the art style to the setting and gameplay. I've rarely played something that felt so real in the depiction of the characters and Pentiment allows you to explore the time and events that happen in the game as if it were a real place, and you were there to live through them. Pentiment deals with themes such as truth, faith, and loss, in an clever and elegant way. Overall it's a brilliant game with a great atmosphere and a unique premise.

_childDocuments_.review: In my opinion thus game is a true masterpiece!  A very engaging story right from the start with characters that make you really feel for them and understand their point of view ... about how things were back then. It is very educating and gives a lot of insight about the life of this era and how people lived and thought. No decision ever felt easy to make. For some I even felt remorse.I decided to play it in my native language, which is German, since the game is set in Bavaria it just made sense to me and the dialogs and texts are extremely well written.Since time is a factor and one won't get to explore everything but has to decide what storyline to investigate further, it has very high replay potential.I can't wait to play the game again to take the paths I didn't choose the first time.

_childDocuments_.review: So, while it's not long, this game does require a little bit of patience - to be honest, my one complaint is that, if I opened and the autosave had been at a point before when I had exited, trying to get through dialogue I'd done before could be a mite tedious.
