_childDocuments_.review: Originally released by Giant Sparrow and Santa Monica Studio in 2012 for the Playstation 3, The Unfinished Swan saw a PC  release in September 2020. The story follows the adventure of Monroe, an orphan who discovered a mysterious little door which led him to a world of imagination. The gameplay involves exploration with evolving game mechanics as the narrative progresses. Intentionally the mechanics remain fairly simple for the entirety of the game favoring enough innovation to be exciting, but not so complex to distract from the narrative. Similarly we see very early versions of the camera adjustment later featured in the Giant Sparrow release What Remains of Edith Finch. The art direction is minimalist, the narration done by Juli Pari is very well done and features Terry Gilliam as the King which I thought was a nice surprise. I began The Unfinished Swan originally looking for more answers from the game What Remains of Edith Finch. After finishing both games I can definitely say that each game stands on their own entirely, and the cameo of the young king as an easter egg in What Remains of Edith finch is just that, an easter egg. Originally I left this game a bit disappointed since I was hoping to earn a new perspective of Edith Finch but after spending some time with both I have come out with a new appreciation of The Unfinished Swan. Before moving on to spoilers for the story of The Unfinished Swan I will leave a short rating of the main elements.Gameplay 5/10Graphics 7/10Story 7/10Sound Design 8/10Voice Acting 9/10The Unfinished Swan blurs the line between the adventure and walking simulator genres. At many points the exploration feels open and I think that Giant Sparrow have done an excellent job with the level design. There are lots of examples of attention to detail, as well as clever subconscious player motivation. However while many of the interactions of The Unfinished Swan feel fluid, providing a natural extension of the main ink throwing mechanic, there are too many examples of poor implementation to give The Unfinished Swan a passing grade. Most notably the vine growing mechanic felt slow compared to the rest of the game resulting in lots of waiting, and I think that the forest section of the game could have used a bit of work. Similarly the nursery felt like it had lots of untapped potential which could have been explored in it's own chapter entirely. The balloon finding secrets could have been streamlined, awarded to the player automatically. It's current implementation is clunky; most confusingly of all a majority of useful features are gated behind finding all of the balloons. As always I'd like to give a few thoughts on the themes of The Unfinished Swan. I think the storybook narration fit the aesthetic feeling like a fantastic unofficial Shel Silverstein story in the process. While I feel that What Remains of Edith Finch and The Unfinished Swan may have originally had more through-lines towards the beginning of Edith Finch's development, I think both games stand separate now.

_childDocuments_.review: The Unfinished Swan is an absolute delight of a puzzle game that everyone should play, not just puzzle fans. The game has a beautiful minimalist design which combines wonderfully with the tightly design puzzles that never ask too much of the player but are still satisfying to work out. The balloon collecting side-game (which in any other game would be an annoying element) is an invitation to branch out from the straight forward path and explore every nook and cranny of the surprising intricate maps. If I have any complaint about this game, is that the tone of the game is a little unsettling at the very start. Despite the childbook story opening, one can't help but wonder if they've accidentally walked into a horror game as they slowly explore a desolate, silent landscape. Once you realize that the exploration is meant to invoke curious wonder and not dread, the game became extremely fun to play.

_childDocuments_.review: This could have a been a vaguely interesting, short conceptual demo. Instead, we got an exceptionally boring and pretentious high-budget console exclusive with a celebrity voice actor. I've waited so long for this to come to PC, because I loved Giant Sparrow's , but this game is just objectively bad.The game is very short, and yet within that limited time span nothing of interest happens. The levels are simple. The "puzzles" (I am being very generous calling them that) are at once trivial and tedious. The game is famous for its visual concepts, which are creative in themselves, but the minimalistic graphics do not do justice to the ideas. And that's it. There's nothing else to the game.I often enjoy "walking simulators" even when there is no significant gameplay. However, here there are just ... concepts. Well, there is a story that tries very hard to be delightful, but is instead disjointed, nonsensical, and inconclusive. Terry Gilliam's excellent voice acting (used sparingly) is the only thing that keeps the thin narrative from being downright annoying.Skip this.

_childDocuments_.review: The Unfinished Swan a pretty good game that can be finished in around two and a half hours, which for me is the perfect time that it should last. The story is divided into four chapters with each one having its own different mechanics for gameplay, so if you're worried about being blind the whole game and having to throw around paint for its entire duration you're good. There was one mechanic in the second chapter that involved growing plants that did overstay its welcome but besides that the new mechanics that were introduced were enjoyable. Don't come into this game expecting a story like the one in What Remains of Edith Finch. The Unfinished Swan's is a much more simple one that plays out like a children's storybook with you exploring the world of a painting as a child who has travelled into it. I feel inclined to mention the chances that you might get motion sickness if you play The Unfinished Swan so be wary if you're prone to it, and especially don't go for the "Minimalist" achievement because I, as a person who isn't afflicted with motion sickness got dizzy after a while.Overall, besides a small amount of flaws, The Unfinished Swan is a fairly solid game. The only advice I'd give though, is to not go into it expecting another Edith Finch as this is a completely different game, so you might come out disappointed. Besides that and the motion sickness issue, I still wholeheartedly recommend The Unfinished Swan because it's relaxing, story-based, and perfect for drinking hot cocoa while wrapped in a blanket at 11PM.

_childDocuments_.review: This is a FANTASTIC game!  And yet, it almost doesn't feel like a game.  Its interface could not be simpler, and its style is just beautiful and takes you to a place that's peaceful (thank you, soundtrack which I almost never otherwise pay attention to), and gameplay that lets you explore but never punishes you.  There is no way to make a mistake, or lose...it just might take you a little longer to get from A to B...and therein lies the fun!I am recommending this game to everyone I know and I hope to be gifting it to family and friends. If you want a game that's relaxing and yet rewarding, that does things differently and in a genius way, THIS is your game!I simply can't say enough good things about it. _childDocuments_.name: The Unfinished Swan

_childDocuments_.review: This is probably the first time I write a review after not even finishing the first gaming session (though I expect it to be possible to finish the game in one go).This is truly brilliant! I've played plenty of interesting puzzle/adventure games and I can tell from the first glance this one is going to be in my top favorites, even if it won't get much better than a few first levels. The mechanics feel fresh, which is surprising after seeing as I thought so many. I'm not going to spoil any of that, just as I didn't want to learn too much about this game and just jumped in instead. The game not only looks interesting and very artistic, it makes you feel like a part of the creation of this beauty by utilizing game mechanics. It's really up to you (to a point) how some parts of this world would look. Don't expect design or painting in the usual sense, but more of a "final touch" that you can make to the masterpiece. But it's not just that. The story telling is so beautiful too! I like all about it: the story itself, which immediately presents you with drama, adventure (escapism, if you please) a place to interpret the story your way and in a form of a really good old fairy tale. The voice acting and sound quality is so great it really brings me back to childhood.But enough of words, see it yourself! Highly recommended!
_childDocuments_.name: The Unfinished Swan

_childDocuments_.review: The Unfinished Swan is a videogame about exploring the unknown. The player assumes the role of a young boy chasing after a swan who has wandered off into a surreal, unfinished kingdom. The game begins in a completely white space where players can throw paint to splatter their surroundings and reveal the world around them.

As the leader, your choices will shape Sordland's destiny. Gripping Story : Traverse a 900K-word branching political saga packed with deep and layered conversations. Choices with Impact : Make critical decisions on security, economy, welfare, and diplomacy. Your values will be tested beyond the confines of your office. Your Legacy : Drive Sordland towards one of 9 unique major endings and more than 25 sub-endings. What will your legacy be? Grand Cast : Engage with a diverse cast of more than 50 characters, each with unique personalities and ideologies. Duty vs. Personal Values : Witness how your presidential decisions influence the country but also your family and relationships. Stay Informed : Keep tabs on the state of affairs through country or interactable city tokens, policies, situations, news and reports. See the impact and result of your actions. Discover the Suzerain Universe : Read about newly introduced nations, codex articles about history, and feel the pulse of the world events. Emerging from the vestiges of a traditionalist regime and wrestling with a challenging transition to economic liberalization amidst a recession, the populace of Sordland craves democratic reform. Economic uncertainty casts a long shadow as the political landscape transmutes, with rival superpowers casting keen, watchful eyes on the unfolding scene. Stepping into this maelstrom, you, as President Rayne, must forge effective policies alongside your Cabinet and influential figures. Balance the precarious scales of politics by retaining loyal allies, gauging your values against political necessities, and steeling yourself against potential adversaries. Remember, each character in this narrative carries unique ambitions, fueling the complexity of the political landscape. As the drama unfolds, the delicate equilibrium between your duty to the nation and commitments to your family will be put to the test - a balancing act that challenges the essence of leadership. Can you hold the reins of presidency successfully while being a good parent? Best of luck, President Rayne - Sordland awaits your leadership.

_childDocuments_.review: Great game. It's political in nature, but I find it very balanced. For instance, excess expenditure can cause both inflation and a death spiral that aggravates even more the economical crises. Policies outcomes are somewhat logical and consistent with real life. For instance, to approach the west block, one needs to apply democratic and free-market reforms. What makes this game really special are the dialogs and schemes behind the policies to make it possible to implement them. I can TRY to be anything in this game: warmongering dictator, liberal reformist, etc.Anyway, first run, try to go blind. Don’t let any guide or post spoil the fun. This game is about the first journey, not the destination.
_childDocuments_.name: Suzerain

_childDocuments_.review: UPDATE: After replaying thru the game it has become obvious that none of your choices matter. This is simply a death simulator. All of my choices were different on this run and yet it ended the same. My country was destroyed, and I was murdered. There is no good ending from what I can tell and I've wasted far too much time on this title. New score: 4/10 One of the most immersive and thought-provoking titles I have played in years. The depth and scope of your choices throughout the narrative will draw out every emotion one can experience when placed into a position of power. Sadly, I failed my people. My nation fell and I was remembered only as a centrist who spent his entire tenure as President, rolling over to appease whichever side of the political spectrum wanted something from my administration. I cannot stress enough just how good this game is. I am immediately playing it again, this time, from my personal political standpoint to see where I end up.  10/10
_childDocuments_.name: Suzerain

_childDocuments_.review: I thoroughly enjoyed this game. I approached it as an RPG and had a very firm view of the type of leader I wanted to be. I was able to inhabit this character making tough choices for the future of my people. This immersion is accomplished by interacting with your cabinet - a diverse set of characters, each with their own agenda and ideas of how you should run the country, and how they feel their ministry should behave. You will not be able to please everyone. You will have to make weighty decisions about the trajectory of your country - at times this took me off of my planned trajectory. Where will you spend your government's money? Will you use it to increase internal security at the expense of opportunities for foreign investment? Will you use it on beefing up your armed forces to protect against foreign invasion, or will you use it on welfare for your people? You will not be able to please everyone. Periodically, the game will throw crises your way, and you will have to decide how your government will react. Other nations in the region beat the drums of war, and try to enlist your support. Members of your cabinet will be smeared with scandal. Militant partisans will fight in the streets. All decisions pull resources and time away from your plans for the country. I would be remiss if I did not mention the fact that you will make decision on how to interact with the presidential family. In keeping with role I decided to play, I decided to play a grade A jerk to my family. I was especially hard on my son, as both Teddy Roosevelt and Stalin reportedly were to their sons, pushing him to be as strong and disciplined as I. You have choices  to make on the micro scale as well as the national scale. All in all, a fun immersive game. My ending sucked, but I can't say I felt cheated. I stand by every decision I made. Ultimately, I know I did what was right for Sordland.
_childDocuments_.name: Suzerain

_childDocuments_.review: I was doubtful I would enjoy Suzerain coming from Paradox's large grand-strategy games as I was accustomed to the freedom they provide. However, I'm glad to say I was wrong as I was able to appreciate its mechanics and story. The writing in this game is brilliant because all characters feel authentic including the protagonist despite him being able to be played as many different combinations of morals and ideologies. I appreciate how every choice has logical benefits and consequences which build upon each other to give the player an experience similar to watching a great political thriller.
_childDocuments_.name: Suzerain

_childDocuments_.review: Man, I really didn't want to like this game as much as I did.This game is kind of a Central/Eastern Europe simulator. Analogues of both the major capitalist and communist powers of the early Cold War appear. The practical political questions that face you mirror those facing small powers during the early Cold War. You can choose to focus on healthcare, infrastructure, the economy, law enforcement, or military spending, but given your limited resources, each choice has drawbacks and successes, such as they are, come dear. Just as the early Cold War saw small states forced into the umbrella alliances of NATO or the Warsaw Pact, in Suzerain, you can choose to align yourself with capitalist or communist mutual security treaty organizations. Each choice will both enhance and restrict your options diplomatically.  The game does a fine job of slowly ramping up tensions overseas and each foreign policy decision feels like it has real stakes: do I recognize this island as a possession of a neighbor and gain an alliance? Do I stand by and watch as crimes against humanity are committed, and win favorable trade terms? Domestically, you face an embittered ethnic minority and a tradition of political violence that threatens to erupt into full blown civil war. Your constitution is creaky and the people generally demand reform. Even within your own party, those loyal to your nation's controversial former leader, Soll, and those eager to see Sordland break free from his shadow, squabble. The intraparty tensions have real consequences for your own agenda. Will you cut a deal with the Old Guard, or establish a new police force to root them out? Will you ally with the reformers and risk emboldening the opposition, or will you close ranks with the Old Guard and embrace Sollism? Even the class divisions of Sordland can be exploited. You can choose to cut a dirty deal with the Oligarchs, earning their support for your efforts, or you can try and break their power forever as a champion of the people; each choice brings unexpected consequences. Your own family and friends form a huge part of the game's content. Your wife's desire to see the liberalization of Sordland and legitimization of the rights of women might prove an asset- or an embarrassment. Your son's choice to join the military or attend university is more political than it would appear at first glance. Even your chauffeur has opinions and demands you have to consider and balance. One thing I want to highlight about this game that I think is exceptionally rare:  Characters have consistent motivations and qualities that inform their decisions and how they react to your own choices. Human frailties and flaws are telegraphed early on; sometimes these frailties lead to bad ends. The dialogue has a few moments of well-chosen humor (although I don't know if I'll ever be able to forgive the Toto reference), but generally the serious tone of the game is maintained throughout. This gives real gravity to every text option you click. I'll never forget the tense meeting with a Supreme Court justice as I sought to earn her support for reforming the Constitution. Depending on how I handled it, she might secure the votes I needed to win. It was a delicate balancing act and I chewed through my fingernails wondering how far I could push her before risking losing her. Ultimately... well, you should find out for yourself. The game excels in these moments. It's because of the writing. It's exceptional and believable.Overall, I am delighted with this game. P.S. While I normally deplore the bloated DLC-heavy state of game design nowadays, I want nothing more than to have one, or god willing, two more terms as the Sordish president. I like this game so much I'd pay full price for a "sequel" depicting Sordish society in the mid-to-late Cold War.
_childDocuments_.name: Suzerain

_childDocuments_.review: I found the game quite interesting, having to think each decision that I make (especially since the game does not allow you to save, you can't reload to change something you have done). There is always a tension in the air, with a suggestion that if you make too many mistakes you will go down. I would say this is not a game to be played hastily, rather it was design for the player to think about everything he is doing in order to succeed.
_childDocuments_.name: Suzerain

_childDocuments_.name: Suzerain

_childDocuments_.review: As someone with an interest in politics and the process of decision making of political leaders, I think this game does a good job of representing that. It forces you into tough choices and lets you role play the main political ideologies well. I think the story is also very well done. There are moments in the game that are very gripping. I especially recommend this game if you have an interest in political history, maybe you watch alternate history videos on you-tube or something.
_childDocuments_.name: Suzerain

_childDocuments_.review: If you ever wanted a choose-your-own adventure as president of a middle-income, non-aligned country during an alternate Cold War, this is the game for you! I failed to turn round the economy or make durable constitutional changes - but did at least eke out some improvements to education and women's rights, avoided getting invaded and wasn't too corrupt or repressive! Centrism is hard, but there's always another run...
_childDocuments_.name: Suzerain

_childDocuments_.review: If you're interested in stuff such as politics, economics or international relations, this is the game for youThe game does a solid job of simulating like you're at the helm of a country: From having to navigate constant information and events/situations, to engaging with different stakeholders/entities in your country, such as big business and ethnic minorities, and even engaging with your closer staff/Cabinet members and the legislature and judiciary (including differences in opinions and values)
_childDocuments_.name: Suzerain

_childDocuments_.review: One of the best narrative games I've ever played. Every choice is agonisingly multifaceted and consequential. Compared to something like Democracy, the human nature of individuals lends itself to better understanding how politics plays out in the real world. I'd highly recommend this to anyone interested in politics regardless of affiliation. Or just those interested in narrative, choice-and-consequence-based games who don't mind the generally more serious and sometimes depressing tone of this game.
_childDocuments_.name: Suzerain

_childDocuments_.review: This is a good game. Lovely music, the writing is great as well. Definitely a commentary on Turkish Coup history as well. But there is a bias towards a certain take on the history and that definitely is felt through out the game. Soll feels like an analogue to Kenan Evren but they are again picking at Ataturk as well indicating some uber-ethostate or blind personality cult narrative which is one isn't correct, two is in bad taste when the guy spent his entire life to implement a multiparty democracy regardless of ethnic background. There isn't enough perspective to include how much religious cults were threatening democracy and how more American-liberal (PFJP) crowd worked to install them into the bureaucracy. The communist-conservative divide is very simplified in this narrative. More so again USP (analogue to CHP) didn't install the 10% barrier to make sure they were the ruling party, it was there to keep the islamists out essentially not "Bluish" people. I am just disappointed that with so much love given to the production narrative falls so short as a commentary on the history, it feels more like an European history student reading about Turkish history to write the plot about oppression vs freedom and less like actual Turkish speaking people conveying a context in a clever way. Otherwise it is a very successful production, if you acknowledge the clear bias and philosophical faults.
_childDocuments_.name: Suzerain

_childDocuments_.review: This game gave me a new perspective on politics. It made me feel like I was truly a president of a fragile country. You have to think about what to reform (if to reform at all), the best way to reform it and who to trust and team up. The choices are truly meaningful and have big consequences.For the real-like political world and choice magnitude i give this game 10/10
_childDocuments_.name: Suzerain

_childDocuments_.review: A game that I describe as a country simulator mixed with visual novel and while I haven't played any visual novels before, I must say that this has surpassed any of my expectations. As the well told story and multiple characters with different political agendas immersed me to the story.While the game might be a bit complex in the beginning and the lack of “clarity” when making some of the decisions and their consequences. The 45(ish) hours I played (with the Kingdom of Rizia DLC) went by like a breeze and I would have kept playing it in one go if I didn't have to sleep and go to work. Furthermore, as it was my first playthrough and both the base game and the dlc might have ended somewhat prematurely, I will have lots of content to comb through. With this sad I highly recommend this game to anyone thinking of buying it!
_childDocuments_.name: Suzerain

_childDocuments_.review: Great game! It is nearly perfect in its immersion, but there is one thing I heavily noticed: Its heavy-handed approach to Feminism. It goes so far as to completely disrupt the logic of the game world.The beginning status quo of the game indicates a strongly paternalistic society in which women are not allowed to study what they want, in which they earn less for the same work in the same position and in which they don't get to have careers at all.But your starting cabinet is distributed evenly with regards to sex. And there are many female leaders of oligarchic / capitalistic structures who would be very rich and influential in everything. At the same time, we are always reminded that women are oppressed in this game and lack rights and representation. This is where the quota-based writing approaches its limits. It hinders any meaningful change within the game by basically making up an issue which has already been solved. There are many female leaders to interact with here who were in that position for more than 10 years and more. Many trailblazers and "first female to ..." are seen here which would be impossible in the state which the game describes. This completely breaks the immersion. They inhabit strong positions of power while the game pretends otherwise. It would have been far more impactful to really showcase such a society with the player being able to tangibly change things, by, for example, appointing a woman to the cabinet and doing these first steps.Apart from that I can wholly recommend the game for everyone who would like to try their approach to survive an everchanging political landscape with many, many conflicts which point back to our times and our recent global history. Great game!
_childDocuments_.name: Suzerain

_childDocuments_.review: Suzerain is a lot of fun if you are interested in playing a political visual novel, and enjoy reading lots of rich text. I come back to this every year or so to enjoy again. It's very 'choose your own adventure' but the decisions you make do tend to bite you in the backside later. Game play wise, it is just clicking and reading. But it is definitely one of the richest, gripping clicking and reading games out there.Very heavy into it's narrative and the how the world and it's characters react to your decisions. One of the highlights is seeing how a policy or deal you made unfolds as you progress through a play-through. Your decisions can be anything from populism to the extreme, but a lot of the big decisions you make, in my opinion swing to the far left or right. Other characters will call you out for taking an extreme stance at points (quite rightly at times), even if you considered it to be somewhat moderate so read your choices carefully, and consider the wider implications of the actions you take. At the end of a playthrough, you will be rewarded with a screen that shows you where your government falls on the political compass.Very rewarding and enjoyable experience, haven't played the DLC as of yet but the game is worth your time and money at full price.
_childDocuments_.name: Suzerain

_childDocuments_.review: I would recommend this game to any Paradox enthusiast, fan of the Democracy series or indeed any other strategy game. Beautiful graphical style and excellent writing make this already excellent set of mechanics into a masterpiece.This was genuinely one of the most thought provoking and enjoyable experiences I've had all year. 10 hours of ceaseless and unforgiving gameplay highlight this masterclass in political, economic and diplomatic game design.Guiding your nation out of its troubled past into whatever bright future you can percieve, through the troubled waters of a well designed (and fictional) 1950s cold war setting, there is little doubt this has been one of the best games released in the genre all year.
_childDocuments_.name: Suzerain

_childDocuments_.review: So I failed to secure reelection. This is despite fixing the economy, strengthening the military, quashing internal paramilitaries, improving healthcare and to some extent education (although removing creationism from the curriculum ended up pissing off a lot of people), and resisting foreign aggression. Nonetheless I conclude my first play through of Suzerain thoroughly glad that I played it. I would love to see a sequel or some DLC involving a second term, even though I never got one, but there's always next time. A'Morgna wes core!
_childDocuments_.name: Suzerain

_childDocuments_.review: Brilliant and fun game that puts you in the seat of power in the fictional nation of Suzerain.  You take part in politics, drive economic strategy, uncover intrigues, and plan spending on projects.  10/10, and I only got it because it was part of a bundle... turns out to have been a very lucky break for me, would have hated to have missed this!
_childDocuments_.name: Suzerain

_childDocuments_.review: Suzerain is a text based adventure about the president of a young, struggling republic. The stereotype of a political game is that they are vehicles for poorly disguised propaganda, so I'm glad this one actually manages to represent the subject matter in a mature and fairly realistic manner. Particularly the fact that, just like in real life, it's impossible to please everyone.The story is also generally well written and it can change a whole lot depending on the player's choices, although I think some events may be semi-random. Apart from that, there's not much else about the gameplay as it's a text adventure after all, the player is limited to picking dialogue choices and ticking boxes every once in a while.On the topic of limitations, one would think a game with so many possible story paths would have a lot of replay value, but sadly I believe this isn't the case because of the mandatory ironman mode. I think that's fine and a completely valid design choice for the first playthrough, but it's annoying to be made to repeat the entire first chapters every time. It doesn't help that some actions have dumb consequences, such as a tax on imported sumptuary goods instantly shrinking the economy of a developing nation by 20% or how refusing to ban a violent organization doesn't have any negative repercussions for public order. Overall, Suzerain has my full endorsement for the first playthrough, but I'm somewhat disappointed by the lackluster replay experience.
_childDocuments_.name: Suzerain

_childDocuments_.review: A very kino politically-themed CYOA in a world sadly bereft of them. The depth, nuance and complexity of the writing and world building on display here is well worth the price of admission. The game is very Hidden Agendasq in that your decisions are almost all purely reactive: President Rayne seldom gets to do anything on his own initiative. I would recommend this game to anyone with even a passing interest in the genre provided they take the (reasonable) perspective that this is in fact a CYOA and not a government management simulator. My main gripes:*Your relationship with your wife (and family in general for that matter) is really simplistic: If you're a (based) authoritarian there's no real conflict since you can just pass her agenda with ease and she'll love you for it. Your relationship with Petr is similarly simplistic. *You cannot align with a mixed economy from the very start for some reason despite it being a completely viable path. Your advisors discourage you from pursuing this development strategy. *You cannot skip ministry briefings on repeat playthroughs. This is incredibly tedious.*You can only allocate budgets to the ministries once in the entire game: there's no putting things on the backburner until your economy improves and the fact that there are only three funding pips means that being able to alter the budget later would be completely imbalanced. This, along with several other economic and legal decisions feels extremely artificial. *The radical newspaper is far too diffuse in its opinions. Ideally there would be a communist/socilaist newspaper and a liberal/demsoc one instead of this bizzaro mishmash where the paper praises communists while crying about .The ending slides are pretty underwhelming. Ideally there would be either a Hidden Agendasq encyclopedia that gives various perspectives on your rule or more fleshed out slides.
_childDocuments_.name: Suzerain

_childDocuments_.review: I'm going to be honest. This game is one of the best games I have ever played. It is a game where every choice matters, from in office, to your own family. With over 350k words in this story, the ways you can play this game is endless. Each of it's endings shocks you to the very core and it changes your stance on politics. Politics is where you are lied to and forced to make difficult decisions where someone will be mad with each choice. Suzerain IS Politics. This game has taught me so much about how the real world works and I think the point of this game is to change how you think on how the world works. No such thing is just White or Black. It's all gray. Every choice you take has a good and a bad. Every Ideology has a good and bad. Communism is neither good or bad. It's grey. Capitalism is neither good or bad. It's grey. Reformism is neither good or bad. It's grey. Authoritarianism is neither good or bad. It's grey. This game is a MUST PLAY if you are up for a challenge. My only complaint is that not enough people know it. -MJ
_childDocuments_.name: Suzerain

_childDocuments_.review: I've played this game through now 4 times and loved it even more every time. An entirely unique game without equal. Every story-line evokes real emotion and you can't help but become fully invested in your story, the variations of which are nearly unlimited, I don't know another game that possess this level of replayability, especially at this price, you just can't beat it. I should note that for anyone concerned about it, this game relies entirely on you reading and understanding what is being presented to you with careful thought. Not that this is a bad thing to my mind, but some bad reviews or negative comments in the discussion page strike me to be from people that maybe don't like games that are quite this 'wordy'? Which is totally fine, we all have our tastes. So far, every ending I have experienced (I will not spoil anything) has left me feeling a multitude of emotions (shock, happiness, immense surprise to name but a few), far more than any novel I have read. The twists and turns the writers have managed to implement into this game are just incredible, and they should be immensely proud of their skill to achieve what they have with this game.Writing aside, the game is easy to actually 'play'. Menus are easy and simple to navigate, as is the readability of text on screen. While the graphics are certainly not the main focus, they are easy on the eye and colour choices are not too extravagant or distracting, which all helps with the visibility of the text (of which there is of course a considerable amount being a story driven game).In all, I highly recommend this game to anyone who enjoys an extremely well written story, understands or has an interest in basic Geo-politics
_childDocuments_.name: Suzerain

_childDocuments_.review: overall, this seems to be a good game, but due to several disabilities i struggle to read for extended periods of time, and this game doest have any read-aloud options, and my usual text reader doesnt work with it. of course, this is very much a me problem, and if you're able to play games which rely almost entirely on long passages of text, i suspect you'll have a great time with it :)that being said, i also had some issues with the UI, which might be unclear delibertaly to be more realistic, it makes it hard to play as a strategy game, and makes it feel un-interactive, and at times drawling. simple progress bars, or a more clear techincal intro, or the economic growth bar showing a full history insted of momentary growth or decline would help.i want to see how my actions impact the world without having to sift through paragraphs or seek it out, and without a simple way to see it, the game ends up feeling quite stale.
_childDocuments_.name: Suzerain

_childDocuments_.review: I don't really like that I have to click through the same conversations to replay the game. Sure you'd get new conversations eventually with different decisions but I'd have to slow down my clicking through the scenes I've already been through if I don't want to accidentally skip the new ones. Plus you won't see the results of the new playthough until 8 hours after starting the new game. It's just tedious clicking through. I like Democracy 3 better as it's just a top down political simulator that I can tinker with and see the results immediately. No faffing about with the same endless dialogue.
_childDocuments_.name: Suzerain

_childDocuments_.review: The game is like an multiple choice exam. You have options, but only one of them is correct. It is very boring when you realise this as the intrigue of the game disappears and the characters around you delivers simple good/bad job depending on how your choice aligns with their predetermined values. You may find that they lack diplomacy and perspective in their reasonings as it is impossible to change their mind no matter the argument you give. Would have bee nice to see what the impacts of my choices would have been before chosing as it feels like you can only really play the game once you have already finished it (more like The Life and Suffering of Sir Brante).5/10
_childDocuments_.name: Suzerain

_childDocuments_.review: You can commit war crimes as a ruthless authoritarian, be a corrupt robber baron, or even try to build a socialist utopia. Heck, you can even get assassinated! Text heavy, but pretty fun political simulator. *Bangs shoe on your desk* Buy this game comrade! Together we'll build a world where no one wants for a copy of Suzerain! The dawn will come!
_childDocuments_.name: Suzerain

_childDocuments_.review: I hope you like reading because the writing in this game is incredibly dense. The writer's succeed however, with world building that is expansive and deep and characters acting true to life. I am already looking forward to my next play through.If you consider yourself a political nerd, pick this game up. Especially if you're the type that watches House of Cards and reads The Economist in between playing rounds of Twilight Struggle.
_childDocuments_.name: Suzerain

_childDocuments_.review: This game is a gem. It's over 90% text based so it's not for everyone. But it is immersive as can be. The well written complex characters and conversations, backed with superb music and sound effects really pull you into leading this country and you feel connected with everything that happens in it. If you are looking for a complex, story driven politics simulation with some of dem feels.. This is the game for you!
_childDocuments_.name: Suzerain

_childDocuments_.review: Great political simulator with nuanced choices that result in powerful outcomes. Be the President of a small, struggling and corrupt State and give it the outcome that you fight for. Almost every decision- personally, politically and culturally is remembered by the characters around you and informs their choices. Capitalist or Communist, Elitist, or person of the People, you will have to struggle against a recession internal and external threats. Leave office in shame, with honour, a pocket full of cash or destitute- it will be your Legacy that is remembered. A new morning has come!
_childDocuments_.name: Suzerain

_childDocuments_.review: First playthrough, I successfully:-Drove Sordland into a great depression-Collapsed the value of the Sordish Ren-Had half of my cabinet resign on me. -Bolstered military, education, police, and health spending to levels never before seen-Empowered Sordish feminists-Collaborated with media moguls and was found out-Was betrayed by the Judicial System-Was the first Sordish president to be impeached, convicted, and sentenced to life in prison-But I sent my son to a nice collage, at leastOverall, a fantastic game, and I  make all of these mistakes again. This cannot be prevented.
_childDocuments_.name: Suzerain

_childDocuments_.review: I am amazed games like this are not commonplace in current gaming scene. There are a lot of third worlders playing games and this is the very fun simulator of our daily struggle. Apart from younger audiences, everyone can play and have fun in Suzerain. Game is not too long or too short. Just like real life, you are going to fail very very hard. And you will like it. Such is the life in a Banana Republic.

_childDocuments_.review: Very dialogue heavy game but that's to be expected considering its basically a visual novel. However I find it very intriguing. It really does a good job at putting you in the shoes of a president. Especially one in a very very fragile and annoying political environment. It actually gets you stressed. You have to learn what sides to appease and which ones to keep hating you. All of them have their benefits and negatives, there will be no making everyone happy. Solid game for sure. I'm yet to complete my first run, but will soon enough. As other reviews say, if you're into games that have a lot to do with politics and managing your resources. Give it a shot.

_childDocuments_.review: Has the appearance of great depth at first, but is largely based around pre-scripted events. Some of the more complex and interesting game paths, such as constitutional reform, can lock out extremely late in the game for very silly reasons (ordering a salad, not thinking several thousand words earlier to hold back one personal wealth). The only real way to play without guides is to hammer your head fruitlessly through the same unbelievably long dialogue sequences to work out how the designers WANT various events to turn out, and then doing them again...and again...and again. Play through it once, enjoy crashing out and leave it there.

_childDocuments_.review: Probably one of the best Political Simulators I have ever played, you have tons of possibilities, whether to reform to constitution to a more democratic one, to reform it in order to strengthen your authority, or you can work with the Old Guards to protect it, and this game runs great on low/medium performance machines, the graphics can also easily be adjusted to ensure maximum performance, however, I also have some problems with it such as the constant Ironman mode, quick repetitiveness, and the core gameplay relying on trial and error, I'm not saying that these are specifically bad things, but they can get super annoying sometimes, overall, I give this game a solid 8/10.

_childDocuments_.review: Well, what a great game! I enjoyed every part of it and wished it never see an end. It was a great journey. If you are looking for a sandbox experience with politics, this is not a game for you. But if you are looking for a politics game with a pretty decent narrative, this is just the game for you! And by the way, I must admit as a Turkish citizen that, the main narrative of the game was pretty similar to those of Turkish one. If you liked the story behind the game, maybe you should take a look at Turkish history and politics!
_childDocuments_.name: Suzerain

_childDocuments_.review: There isn't really any game quite like this. Embodying a high level political figure where your decisions actually matter and you get to interact with characters one on one? This game is a gem I recommend to everyone with any interest in political games of any kind. I wouldn't recommend more than one playthrough once in a while as it's a bit too heavy for constant replaying.

_childDocuments_.review: First off, this review is a "I recommend it, but I wanted more." It is also long, but I hope you will read the entirety. I clocked in a solid and relatively non-stop 11.5 hours, but I wanted at least twenty. Mild spoilers will be listed at the very end of this review that talk about this. This time decision is completely unrelated to the price, as it is well worth this amount, I simply wanted to play more.Suzerain has you take the role of a newly-elected leader of a not quite mediterranean/balkan/baltic/who knows country. All you need to know is that there is the not-United States, the not-USSR, and you border many countries of differing opinion about you, your country, and there are questions of all political flavors and even ethnic issues. It is an *extremely* well developed simulator, with the simulation understanding my decisions and giving me feedback that was not meter-involved besides a bar showing "economy". Your advisers give you advice, cannot be trusted completely but are not out necessarily to backstab you in comical or immersion-breaking fashion like many other games. There is also not a hard-coded ridiculous "it was me all along!" reveal of one of your cabinet members, every single one of them seems human to the extent that I was feeling certain feelings for characters that were quite literally a static image and text. This is without a doubt the best political game I have EVER played, and without a doubt the most realistic one I have ever seen. In my playthrough I chose to embrace capitalism and the west, as well as support these goals, which for many games would mean that the Republic of Lespia, the westophiles and capitalists of the regions, would be my best friends. However, in Suzerain, probably because of a previous deal with the Republic of Wehlen thec leader of Lespia was not a fan of me, for spoilerish reasons. He demanded too much, deals broke down, and I refused. The fact that Suzerain has one event influence another, yet still allows something to happen, blew me away. Usually Visual Novel and Political type games like this are extremely railroaded, with true choices masked around dozens of ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ ones that are easy to identify, but not so with Suzerain. Every decision felt like it mattered, and even though I "won" I regretted many decisions I made along the way, like a real leader, but stood by my decisions. This is a masterful game about tough decisions for a fledgling country that will have you love every minute. A Morgna Her Coren!*Spoiler Parts Below*-  Very Mild spoilers about one of the potential game ends (wow theres a way to win), and the aftermath.There are elections in the game, which should be obvious, and your game "ends" if you win your re-election. As I was clicking through and reading the dialogue presented talking about my re-election, I thought to myself, "man, I really hate early access games. They would have stopped the game right here and I would have to wait a half year to play more."And then the game ended. This is my only gripe. I wanted more. I wanted to keep going and fulfill the promises of my first term. I wanted to shepherd my people through the hinted at war/dispute between two powers you'll see about. I also wanted to see if the nation that most threatened mine would be crazy enough to pull the trigger, since I had massively reformed the army with brand new equipment and an unnamed higher power had completely reformed and modernized our air force. In fact, I could see the issues being linked, since the two powers butting heads could very easily drag me into their struggle, which could drag said unnamed higher power into the conflict. If the developers manage to read this, then first thank you for this masterpiece. And second, give me more.

_childDocuments_.review: In a word: obsessive. A game you start playing and then look at your watch and realise you've been playing for 3 hours non-stop. Not just a "one more turn" game, but one that is incredibly compelling as all your choices are taken into account. You take over the presidency of Sordland, a politically and economically troubled, socialist republic - it's future now in your hands. Will it be dictatorship, democracy, planned economy, crony capitalism or your best effort in between? The game allows you to pick your path.The basic nature of the game is that of a Choose Your Own Adventure, but with so much detail on its characters, history and geography. The quality of the writing is high, yet there are inklings that the creators were leaning more towards liberalism than conservatism and you don't get to argue much in favour of how things may have been better pre-revolution. My one criticism is that the game doesn't have much nostalgia for the old times. The second President of Sordland is the political figure that most conservatives rally behind - a corrupt, tyrannical monster. I hope the upcoming Kingdom DLC goes some way to allowing greater freedom in this respect (I'd love to play as a monarch in a modern setting). Still, it would have been nice to have been able to invite the old monarchy back from exile, if only to be able to serve as private citizens - and show conservatives could be something other than racists in one group, and scheming backstabbers in the other.I recommend you act precisely as you want to during your first playthrough - don't try to game the system, don't read guides or spoilers, and don't feel too upset about how the game reacts to your choices. I fled the country after my first playthrough - but I left with some satisfaction that my family were safe, and still loyal to me - and that I had laid the groundwork for future success. I wanted to go for a "perfect" run for my second playthrough, which I have just completed. Sordland has emerged as one of the biggest economies in the world, the envy of its neighbours. I am now waiting for Update 2.0 before I give this a third playthrough - where I intend to run an authoritarian regime and set myself up as a dictator for life. I can't wait.
_childDocuments_.name: Suzerain

_childDocuments_.review: If you love politics and history then you need to play this game. I bought it and was hooked. It shouldn't be as fun as it is. The visuals are pleasing but remain the same through out the game. It is largely a text based Politics RPG, it has no right to be this good. But the writing, the characters, the plots and twists and consequences of your actions make it one of the best political simulators on the market.
_childDocuments_.name: Suzerain

_childDocuments_.review: I wanted to like this game very much, yet the tedious conversations that have little to no impact on your relationships combined with the puzzling responses from the NPCs, and, frankly, weird responses that don't match the situation are deeply frustrating. Coupled with the general lack of depth, the result is a game that is rather wearisome to play. Resource management - such as it is - functions at the macro-level and isn't particularly interesting because once you've made a decision, you're unable to make any further adjustments. The political component lacks nuance and the NPCs behave like caricatures. There's no ability to truly adapt to changing circumstances and the game moves inexorably forward in what is essentially an unenjoyable choose-your-own-adventure. If you're looking for something thoughtful, enjoyable, and nuanced with a high degree of replayability, this is not the game for you.
_childDocuments_.name: Suzerain

_childDocuments_.review: Very much recommend this. Now, just so people don't go in expecting the wrong thing. This isn't a game like Democracy where you got full control of what to launch and where. Better compare it with a Choose Your Own Adventure story, with a whole load of detail. The mood is best compared with the game Hidden Agenda.  It doesn't shy from reminding you that there is a price to pay for doing some right things, but it's not too grimdark, and it shows you the consequences of your action, good AND bad.  And it doesn't do it in dry numbers, but in newspaper stories and reports, bite sized bits that tell you how you're affecting the lives of people.It's way more personal than most nationsim games as well. Your president is a character in the world, with a wife and kids, and those things affect you as well. I found myself caring about all those folks.Bit of a content warning though, depending on how the game goes, it might contain a suicide. Nothing graphic, but it is discussed.
_childDocuments_.name: Suzerain

_childDocuments_.review: VERY good political simulator. Amazing lore, story, and characters. Decisions you make *heavily* impact you later down the line, and since you can't save, you have to deal with the unforeseen consequences of your decisions. The game also offers a ton of replay ability, as one playthrough you can be a full-on communist revolutionary reforming the constitution, and the next you can be an ultra-capitalist declaring a state of emergency and undermining basic human rights. The sheer amount of options is insane, and this game is fantastic.I demand a second term.
_childDocuments_.name: Suzerain

_childDocuments_.review: Yeah really great story telling, good dialogue, branching narrative. Very hopeful this inspires other games in the genre. Finished the game as a centre-left democrat and will most likely explore some of the other potentialities. The dynamism of the advisers' responses and their debates in meetings really placed you in the story and set up the feeling of meaningful choices. More please
_childDocuments_.name: Suzerain

_childDocuments_.review: I'm not entirely sure how realistic this game is but it certainly -feels- realistic in how it challenges you to navigate the political sphere. There are no clear cut paths to victory if you can call any ending a victory as you juggle the many demands of factions within your nation.Gameplay: It's one of those games where you click through dialogue options to progress the story in a direction you'd like it to go. You're expected to read the in-game Newspaper alongside various dossiers to get a good understanding of the world around you. Doing so will allow you to make better/informed decisions when it comes to dealing with faction interests.I wish the game had a better method of showing you the potential effect of some dialogue options because sometimes the text responses aren't as clear what the intent behind it is and then next thing you know you've pissed off religious sector.Overall, it's an entertaining game with enough twists and turns in the story that it will suck hours out of your life if you enjoy reading and exploring the politics of running a country. It showcases why no one is truly all powerful. No king rules alone and you have to keep your supporters happy if you intend to stay in power... Which is easier said than done when you're trying to juggle the fact that there are other countries in the world that are bigger/badder than you are and willing to mess with you for their own needs/interests.One thing I wish the game allowed you to do more of is break the mold and gain more influence to mess with  other countries more. But then it'd likely be a different type of game.
_childDocuments_.name: Suzerain

_childDocuments_.review: The game relies heavily on text o deliver it's narrative while obscuring what your decisions actually mean. A politically centrist approach is discouraged. There is very little good choices in the game with most choices causing you to lose something either support, money or the economic/social power. Lots of negative reinforcement here. If the game actually was more transparent about your decisions instead of obscuring them to make the game more narrative focused it would be more playable. Right now it feels like make choice get bad result, reload make choice get bad result. Down the road bad result hits you again.  repeat ad nosium.Weird decisions like not having saves in 10+ hour single player game (Checkpoint system is lacking), lack of information and the not being able to backtrack choices really hurt this game. The game is also very dark and after a while wears on you. The strange thing is that it feels like outcomes are outside of the player control. Again with the lack of transparency on choices. If I had a clearer Idea of what did what I wouldn't feel so sour on the game. Feedback is important. You can make tough games as long as the player can see what they are doing wrong. Forcing the player to use guides outside the game to play your political sim where only right wing or left wing extremist choices are the only valid ones is a hard not recommend for me and for the most part I like political game. At the very least the game doesn't force a specific ideology down your throat. Dialogue is well written and since the game is 99% text dialogue that is important. The last 1% of gameplay is overhead map navigation...rivitting. As it stands though it feels more like a choose your own adventure or visual novel (without CGs) that you play once. Even with the extra choices I can see the long winded dialogues getting very boring if you were trying to go for achievements or be a completionist.
_childDocuments_.name: Suzerain

_childDocuments_.review: 4/5Really liked it at first. Enjoyed the choices and seeing how they affected your country. But eventually I hit a point where the economy was great and support was high and then overnight, the economy busted and there were protests. For no reason at all. I kept trying to understand what happened and then I realize the game has certain story lines that it wants to hit and that's why it happened. Completely ruined the immersion and my sense that my choices mattered. I clicked around un-enthusiastically for awhile after that and now I don't really want to finish it. Sad to see the illusion fall apart before my eyes.
_childDocuments_.name: Suzerain

_childDocuments_.review: Overall, this is a great game, with rich story and a very strong RPG element with decisions that actually affect the story in many ways. The only area that has considerable flaws is the gameplay, due to the lack of guidance.Great plot with many events very similar to past or current events, giving a very interesting background story behind them. The story and the choices and how they affect your game are more than decent. At some points, the game is not very clear on the effect of your decisions. There are moments where you might feel like pressuring your opponents or potential allies a bit more to get the best deal (whatever the circumstance), but instead it is taken as an outright rejection of the offer with no possible room to go back to the offer.This where the game could improve MASSIVELY. Although it does offer you a codex for information, there is no tutorial or "tour" of the UI or even a vague explanation of how your actions might affect the outcome of your presidency. You're thrown in the game blindly and that is, I believe, the biggest flaw of the game.Despite the many endings, I doubt many would attempt to play the game more than once due to the lengthy dialogues that are repeated, which is to be expected since this is a story that does change based on your decisions but certain parts will remain the same.
_childDocuments_.name: Suzerain

_childDocuments_.review: This is an amazing little VN. The game does a good job portraying people and politics in a realistic manner. If you've played Hidden Agenda, you'll recognize the fidelity to history, although this game portrays a fictional Middle Eastern (Turkey?) country and not a Latin America one. Bravo to the devs, I hope to see more from you!
_childDocuments_.name: Suzerain

_childDocuments_.review: Political RPG in a made-up world, but with very real politics. You can write your own story for the president you play but also for the country and other characters too.The thing is, whatever you do, a lot of people will not like it. If you do it too much, they'll protest you. And all of your choices could lead to half of your cabinet betraying you. Especially Serge, don't trust that guy.And at the end of the day you're left with the urge to play the game again but try somethings differently.The most amusing thing this game achieved for me is how it got me to care about the story and characters so much that i cheered when i achieved something against all odds, but also cried at heartfelt or sad parts. Which is ordinary for most games but this is a text-based political rpg.

_childDocuments_.review: Let's get this out of the way right now. Suzerain really isn't a strategy game. It's a Choose Your Own Adventure political game. When viewed in that context the game succeeds quite well. If judged as a strategy game, well....it doesn't succeed at all.So what is it? Suzerain is a mostly text based game where you run a made up country in a made up area of the world. You have both internal and external challenges as you try to deal with the geopolitics of the 1950s. So you're going to have to deal with the ramifications of past political turmoil, major economic challenges, deciding between capitalism, communism or trying to find that ever-elusive middle path. You'll make choices and the game will spell out the next part of the story, whether that is a fight with your wife because you wouldn't let her speak at an event or accepting an underhanded deal to control the media.These tales are well written and often throw in some twists (mostly to your detriment) as these tales are spun. There are local headlines to read and trying to keep up with everything can be quite the challenge. So yeah, there's a LOT of reading in this game but I welcome it because the prose is pretty good. And the game doesn't shy away from tackling some tough 1950s issues like women in the workforce or the teaching of evolution.Given the difficult subject matter and the numerous failures of other games to create an exciting political game, I really give Suzerain high marks for their efforts here.You make your decisions and you deal with the ramifications of those decisions. And that's good. Here's why it doesn't succeed as a strategy game - the game has essentially hard-coded in the "correct" or "incorrect" decisions. They're not particularly obvious either and because the player doesn't know what choices will be presented to them, they're not able to really plan much of a long term strategy. As a player, if you refuse to go online to look up the best choices, you're always flying blind. You'll never know if you get to pull that particular "lever" again and the game will do what it wants.Example: I invested deeply in the country's infrastructure at the "wrong time" (due to pre-scripted events) and I was punished heavily for it. I managed to dig the country out of debt and the unemployment rate and inflation rates dropped. That's good, right? Except about a year later unemployment had risen again and inflation was out of control. I made absolutely no choices regarding the economy between the time things were going in the right direction and the Great Depression started. That's not a strategy game in any way, shape or form. That's just someone telling a story. A strategy game wouldn't have pre-scripted events that would automatically make my choice a "bad" one and would provide me the levers to fix what was going sideways. Are there logical decisions you can make to help set the correct path? Of course. But there are logical decisions you can make that derails your efforts and it's not really possible to separate one from another. Again, that's not a strategy game. It's a puzzle game.If Suzerain succeeds well on one front while failing miserably on another, where does that leave the buyer? Well, it comes down to this - was it fun? And yeah, I had a pretty decent time failing. There are different paths, different choices I could make. Not to try to succeed but to see how things played out. That's why it gets a thumbs' up from me. I'm invested in the story even if the results of my decisions seem more than a little arbitrary. Recommend: Buy on Sale

_childDocuments_.review: The perfect presidential simulator. Every decision you make feels impactful and difficult since you'll always be angering one faction or another. It's basically impossible to do exactly what you want and be successful so you need to make compromises that make it feel like an accurate depiction of real world politics.The lore and world building are really well done. Clearly grounded in reality but different enough to make you interested in learning more about this world. Would highly recommend this game if you enjoy political simulators and want to try your hand at being president.
_childDocuments_.name: Suzerain

_childDocuments_.review: This game is a beautifully written story that lets you choose how a politician leads his party and country forward. The world is detailed with historical backgrounds that immerse you within this believable world as you make difficult choices in your first term. If you like to read and are interested in games where you can choose your path, then I'd suggest you push the "BUY ME NAO!" button in your Steam. It's absolutely one of the best Steam games in my library.
_childDocuments_.name: Suzerain

_childDocuments_.review: A phenomenal game! I've been a strategy gamer for the longest time so I'm used to playing games that have extended UIs, lots of graphs, etc.. Initially I was feeling that this game was lacking such things but I soon got captivated with the story and I realized that I had everything that I needed when actually talking to advisers, they are the gate keepers of their own data, kind of how it would be in real life!If I could give the team one pointers: It's hard to remember and keep track of numbers (unemployment, number of military personnel), it would be nice if advisers could issue memos that you can keep track of and look up in the UI.I look forward to more work from this studio either in the form of an expansion to this game, or another game that has the same mechanics but a different setting: different time era, playing as a region or colony seeking independence. If I could make a recommendation to the team, please check out the book "The Island at the Center of the World" by Russell Shorto. Its the story of how before New York, the colony of new Amsterdam was struggling to make money, create more autonomous institutions, dealing with local neighbors, and dealing with geopolitics.Congrats on the amazing game!
_childDocuments_.name: Suzerain

_childDocuments_.review: Interesting game with a wonderful storyline and deep interactivity. Honestly, I can play this for hours due to the different paths you can take and how they affect the game's world/story. However, it crashes every single time on the same mission. Verifying game files has not fixed the issue. Leaving a bad review until this is addressed and solved.
_childDocuments_.name: Suzerain

_childDocuments_.review: Suzerain is a great game about a political struggle of an upstart president in a country filled with strife. It was great fun on my conservative democrat run and I can't wait to try different approaches to the various problems that plague Sordland. The characters in the game are very nuanced and both understanding them and then exploiting this knowledge is great fun. I wish the team the very best, I hope they will bring us more amazing stories and experiences!
_childDocuments_.name: Suzerain

_childDocuments_.review: This is a flawed game, a slow choose your own adventure which encourages replayability but forces you go through the same screens over and over. And yet, as a policy sci major, I can't stop thinking about this game. The characters, the choices I made, and how things might have turned out differently (even if I'm still pissed about how the game decided I failed). The developers have tried, very very hard, to create a modern game Game of Thrones style intrigue and it shows. For those with a political bent there's not alot like it. Even now I wish I could go back in time and bring this game up during my college years to see what folks would think of it.
_childDocuments_.name: Suzerain

_childDocuments_.review: I was very optimistic towards this game given its glowing reviews and my love of choose-your-own-adventure games.  Unfortunately, the writing is inconsistent and largely dull, the characters are uninteresting, and the "choice" system is terrible.  Most of the "choices" you make (dialog options) do not matter in the slightest; often, these are variations on the same response or wildly different statements that go largely ignored.  As a result, it is often difficult to tell when the game is actually asking you to make a choice.  Sometimes, all the dialog options in a conversation are ignored and the only choice that matters is the last one (when an advisor asks what stance you'd like to take) while other times, seemingly probing dialog options very early in a conversation will lock you into a stance you didn't want to take.I really wanted to like this game and was hoping it would scratch that choose-your-own-adventure game itch, but ultimately, I couldn't bring myself to keep reading/playing.
_childDocuments_.name: Suzerain

_childDocuments_.review: A digital-novel on a political genre. I say its a pretty good game. Not many like this in the market (for-now) and i enjoy almost every aspect of it. - Visual, not much. its not a visual novel more of a digital novel.- story wise, Player driven story with lovable the characters, story does genuinely impact playthrough although somewhat forced linear from here and there (like one of the character relation doesn't really chance despite your best effort). It still an absolute blast tho. - Amazing music, an ear-worm from time to time.8.5/10 would absolutely recommended.
_childDocuments_.name: Suzerain

_childDocuments_.review: This is a great game. In a lot of ways, it's also probably the longest Political Compass Test you will ever take, but just saying that is a massive disservice to just how good a game it is. The story you play through is one of the most engaging and entertaining I have played in a long while. It's simple enough to play, but quite deep and I feel like the choices you make do mostly matter. It's also really hard and some of the decisions and compromises you have to make can be a real struggle.I think more games like this can only be a good thing and would recommend you give it a go if you can, especially if Political sims are of interest to you. The fictional setting of Sordland is really interesting but you can also see real world parallels within it. I feel like there is a fair amount of replayability too. A sleeper hit for me, looking forward to other games by the devs.
_childDocuments_.name: Suzerain

_childDocuments_.review: Where to begin? This is, in all honesty, one of the best games I have ever played. It is a political simulator rpg that masterfully grasps the functioning of a presidency, a country and a world. Where other political simulators are often limited in their scope, Suzerain succeeds in highlighting every factor that matters. The press their reactions, the backroom politics, the international ramifications of a certain decision, ... - it's all there.Every decision - no matter how small - has an impact and shapes the game environment around you. I have found this game to be a true blast to play, and it has become one of my favourite games of all time. There's no doubt that I'll be replaying many times to try out different paths, as there are so many to choose from. I'd like to really commend Torpor games for this masterpiece, and I wouldn't mind seeing some more additions or similar games to this being released: it's a very refreshing experience.To all those who generally like political sims, decision- and strategy-based games: pick this game up. It's truly worth it. If you don't, you might be disappointed, though I'd still reccomend simply trying it out: you never know! 10/10, will play again.

_childDocuments_.review: Okay so I'm going to give this game a thumbs up. I personally am super irritated with the game and will most likely never come back to it again (reasons are below) but I can't deny that the game is pretty good at giving me what I wanted when I purchased it. And hell...it did keep me occupied for a couple of weeks.1. There are like 8 endings. Only 2 of them positive. So there is an 80% chance that you will get a bad ending. Not cool...not fun..2. The game is super complicated. I don't know much about politics and had to struggle for a long time to figure out what was what. I mean its already complicated enough that this is a fictitious world with fictitious stuff so why make it more complicated by getting super in-depth about politics? Just make it a bit more simple in this fictional world.3. The game isn't really that long. I have 20 hours on my play time over 2 weeks. But that includes 4 play-throughs. Which means that each play-through is like 5 hours. So if you are hoping for more, then sorry but thats just how it is.4. The game talks a lot about choices and how they matter. They don't really. I did everything right to make my economy great and then boom, random chance and ruined everything. So my choices didn't matter. When I made a choice and it said it would do this one thing and everyone is congratulating me about how awesome this thing is only for it to show zero boost to anything in my government...it means my choices didn't matter.5. The game is just stacked against you in almost every way. By the end when it was time for my re-election I had so many pros to spread to my people. Built hospitals, lowered taxes, increased jobs, improved economy, improved the constitution the list goes on. I had like over a dozen huge accomplishments. The game even says "you had a square that could fit a million people in it and it was packed. Your advisors say its most likely the largest gathering of supporters in history. PLUS THE FINAL RE-ELECTION SPEECH WAS TELEVISED and I STILL LOST??? The game gave me literally every freaking clue and hint that I was going to win re-election and then didn't. Then I supported the new president and was kicked out of politics. It was my best run yet and that STILL HAPPENED??? In other words proof that this game is unfairly stacked against you and you'll never see a ♥♥♥♥ ending coming.So why did I give it a thumbs up? Because it took me on a journey. And as irritating, unfair and stacked against you as it is...the game did do one thing right. It did a great job of making me feel like a president. Too bad they stuck me in literally the worst country and worst position in the world.Next time can I get a game like this that is maybe a bit easier? Maybe not AS STACKED against you as this one was? Maybe a futuristic version or a medieval version more like this?Should you buy it? I'm not sure. If you want to play as a president of a super poor, racist country and fight against a system meant to defeat you at every turn as you try to fix it...then sure give the game a try. But you'll be frustrated and angry pretty much the whole time you're playing it. Is THAT worth you're money? It's up to you.
_childDocuments_.name: Suzerain

_childDocuments_.review: This isn't a game for everyone. No matter what you do, the story will always leave you unsatisfied. Everything you do has a downside, so forget about doing everything right.This story offers so many more possible outcomes than I could have ever imagined: Wanna reform the country? -go ahead. Change the education system? -sure. Commit a genocide? -if you really want to.. The only thing I really didn't like is how the game rarely gives you enough information to base your decisions on. So it just becomes a guessing game for which option works better. However, if you want to get some insight on why governments never seem to do the right thing or what your political belief is, this game is just for you. I was actually surprised by how few of these different opinions were represented in a biased way.
