_childDocuments_.review: Sincerely, knowing that on the official Discord account there was a counting of positive rewiev, I was tempted to do some lil' trolling and publish a negative one and give Letanomics dude an aneurysm, but I simply can't. Truth is, this game is what I craved for years. Suzerain really has the ability to capture you in its world while being able to feel important in it.Every choice I made, from what place you are born to your first term ends had as tangible, great impact as small, interreletional one. Small pieces of dialogue reflect every subtle decision you made along your journey throught your precidency, making it lifeful and real.Next thing, the characters. They are the main element of your journey. While on the outside governance seems more numbers and actions, on the inside there's the real part of it: relations, alliances, compromise and a silver tongue are necessary to fulfill the objective to have an efficient cabinet. Sometimes is really too efficient, unreal in a certain sense, and the possibility of a reshuffle, while surely tedious to implement for the necessity of new characters and the respective dialogues, could be nice.at the end, you will realise that every character, excluding only a few of them, is a piece of ♥♥♥♥ on his own. They will be just corrupt, or powerhungry, or maybe being actually good but acting in very, very wrong ways. You will conflit with them, and you might be tempted to oppose them simply on spite, but remember: they aren't just people, they represent a group more vast that you might think, the voters.obviously, not only the home front, but even external affairs need your intervention. During the game you will have the possibility to meet the leader of various countries, making decision that will resonate in History. In a world consumed by the strife of the gargantuan political presences of Arcasia and United Contana and their respective ideologies, would you pick a side or decide to remain neutral, isolating yourself or paving the path for your country to be more than a piece in the great chessboard of Merkopa?Good Ol' Ideologies, the things that drive the world, the people and their leaders (most of the timef or this ones). the game offers you the possibility to pave your own path, be as a reedemed nationalist or a die-hard communist. as I said before, remember the people you govern: your path will influence their opinion of you based on a consistent historical viewpoint of Sordland (the country's name). being able to balance everything will be crucial to gain the favour of your fellow politicians and citizens. some choices are more difficult than others, but it will be your job to figure out something. Fortunatelly, the game offers an extensive and detailed codex about the main characters, countries and historical events: using it is highly suggested.Last but not least. achievments. it feels strange to read it, they aren't the main part of the game, so why in this review?I want to say that I was deeply impressed by how easy it was for me to get achievment, even some rare ones, by simply playing the way I wanted to. In most of the games they are just some crazy s**t, a challenge that require specific, unnatural choices in a gameplay sense, but in this case I was able to get a lot of them. these choice is very courageus and the most correct that I ever seen. Achievments, in substance, became a way to track your choices, leaving an indefinitly lasting mark. Sometimes, I look at some of my ones, being able to remember why I receive it, what I did and how much was that playthrough exciting. That's something that everygame should strive for.I absolutely DON'T recommend this game to everyone. Only a small fraction of all the gamers would like this tipe of game, which sometimes seem difficult even for me for its wall of unskippable text: but if you are a part of it, You will love it. I consider it another courageous choice by Torpor Games, not every developer house have this specific, yet surely passion-oriented playerbase.Good game!

_childDocuments_.review: Having completed my first playthrough, I believe I'm ready to review.Suzerain is very much like a 'Choose Your Own Adventure' novel. Except that it's about x20 more complex.You play as the leader of a small country. In what appears to be a fictionalized version of north-eastern Europe.The entire game is based around making decisions. However, that's pretty much all you do. It's like if you took away all of the gameplay from 'Fallout: New Vegas' but left only the dialog choice sequences. That might sound bad, but it's actually quite enjoyable.This is a game for people that have a deep understanding of politics, or people that want to. There are a number of factions. Nationalists, conservatives, socialists, communists, oligarchs, and an ethnic minority hellbent on terrorism. It's not as simple as picking a side, however. As you'll need multi-partisan support to accomplish anything.The number of branching paths is staggering. With every decision having a ripple effect.For instance, I made some deals with the democrats to get a bill passed. However, this angered the conservatives. 18 months later, and the most conservative member of my cabinet resigns. That character then went on to challenge me in the primaries. And I was defeated!I would like to give more examples, but I can't. It would ruin the game. Because the only thing you do is read, make decisions, and deal with the results.I have only two significant complaints about the game.First, there's actually a little  story. It took me around 15 hours to complete the game for the first time. (It'll probably take you a lot less time. I read slower than most people.) As such, I'm reluctant to continue my second playthrough. It may be months (or even years) before I'm ready to go again.This is compounded by allowing only one save file. Which auto-saves. I want to see the results of alternative actions, but not if it's going to take 15 hours to get through.Second, the game's writers have a clear bias. The democratic socialists are presented as people just trying to make the world a better place. They are compassionate and honest. The conservative nationalists are resistant to any changes at all. They are paranoid, racist, fearful, angry, hate-filled, xenophobic, religious, traitorous, and irrational.If that seems a bit one-sided? That's because it is. That said, it's a fictional version of real life. So, I feel like I can let it slide.This is a game for people that listen to talk radio, read a lot of world news, are politically active, vote, or care about the future. You also gotta love the slow burn. It's definitely not for everyone.{SPOILER!}Result screen for my first playthrough:

_childDocuments_.review: Suzerain has solid writing that gives an authentic view into how complex and messy modern republican democracies are and how you must push your agenda while doing a political balancing act to actually stay in power. There is also a planned extension where you play as a monarchy, which will add an extra dimension to the game.The game is an RPG with a central narrative and different endings determined by certain choices during the story. It's not a grand strategy sandbox where you can freely choose to rule as a Dictator or communist leader and choose your own fate from there. Imagine Democracy 4 dynamics with a sprinkle of Disco Elysium world building, and a small splash of Tropico. If you're in the mood for a political visual novel with decent replay value, give it a try.In terms of specific complaints of the game (Minor spoilers ahead):-Be aware decision-making and the consequences are more scripted than it appears on the surface, in order to fit the narrative. Also there's a lot of dialogue to skip through when replaying. Remember, it's more of a visual novel than a sandbox.-It needs more romance options. Politicians can be scandalous and you should be able to romance at least one other person besides your wife, then have it become a scandal with consequences. You can accept blackmail, successfully cover it up, or have it leak to the public and be shamed, etc. The game is basically set up for a good scandal, but devs decided another character does the cheating, not you. Your task is to do damage control instead.-I find it odd the conservative faction are against privatization during a recession. Typically, wanting state control/big government is something the nationalists would want but not necessarily conservatives. The conservatives prioritizing fundamentalism over fiscal conservatism and not being flexible about it is just odd, but understandable somewhat given the world building (Sollism).

_childDocuments_.review: My first time to play the game resulted me being ousted in office thru a coup by the military lead by my defense minister. He's a traitor, if you can fire him early in the game better do it.What I dont understand is that the economy was doing so well, it was almost full bar minus 1 but after pressing the "Continue" button and few dialogs in between, the economy suddenly tanked to 2 bars. My other concern is that there is really mo means for the government to have a positive balance or at least to earn extra money. For the entire game I was running in debt with the lowest being -9 and the highest would be -3 or -4. I have privatized the construction company and the mining group and waited for the said big amount of cash that the government would gain when the shares enter the market, it did not happen. There was no surge of government funds.I like the concept of the game but it seems that there is a strict storyline here and the predictability is obvious. Based on the comments left by other players, it either results to you being assassinated or being ousted in a coup. It will not proceed you being re-elected for another term. The chapters in the game is limited for you to proceed so dont expect this game to be unlimited time. Whatever choices you make it will still end up to those two results stated above. _childDocuments_.review: This game is right on the intersection of my interests, as a political simulation RPG / visual novel. _childDocuments_.review: Suzerain is an underrated gem. How is it nobody is talking about this game, I myself came upon it when searching steam and was immediatly struck by its description and screenshots.Suzerain is all about your choices, you take the role of a newly elected president on a country that is facing tough times, people want to move on from its dark past but some members of the assembly and government want the country old values to remain. It is a clever war of attrition that you battle throughout the entire game, trying to please everyone whilst making changes.The game is very hard to get a good ending, at least it felt like it on my first run, I completly botched everything during the last part of my term and had to go into exile or risk prison just because I tried to stand up to the Old Guard.The storytelling and replay value of this game is beyond amazing and you are doing yourself a disservice for not trying it out. _childDocuments_.review: Suzerain is actually a really good game, whether it is a first play through or numerous plays to see each ideological pathways. It is very immersive and shows a brutal, realistic depiction of a leader thrown in a political arena of backroom deals and intrigue. You would have to make gut wrenching sacrifices in decisions to not do what's right but to do what is necessary to achieve goals.HOWEVER,I cannot fathom the lack of saving features, and I would like to stress as a person with wants and needs, I cannot restart an hour and thirty minutes worth of game play each time I forget one step to be successful. _childDocuments_.review: Suzerain. What can I say about this game other than that it is fantastic? This game has got to be one of, if not the best political strategy/sim games that I have played. Suzerain allows you to lead the Republic of Sordland (a nation in the middle of an economic crisis) under the Rayne administration in whatever way that you would like. Do you want to transform your country into a totalitarian Oceania-esque police state? Maybe you'd like to see your nation transformed from an authoritarian democracy into a worker's republic and align yourselves with the communists? Or perhaps you'd even like to make Sordland a neo-liberal stronghold and an economic superpower? In Suzerain, you can do just that! It is also presented in a believable way, with in-depth things like discussions of policy with your ministers, to managing foreign relations and considering other countries views on your domestic policies. The thing is, though, that you are not free from the consequences of your decisions and ambitions. Yes, you can transform Sordland into a socialist utopia, but do so carefully, as you could easily upset the conservative wing of your party and the general staff, risking a coup. Not only that, but all of your decisions on economics have significant and heavy impacts; you will notice if your policies are successfully implemented or have failed.The lore and story of this game is amazing, too, with histories of the various continents and countries all written out, to even something as seemingly small as the histories of individual companies and corporations. Pair this with a well-told story and memorable characters (like, all of them), all with complete backstories, and you have a believable and extremely immersive world that will involve you almost instantly; you'll feel like you are living in East Merkopa.I should also mention that the soundtrack for this game is lovely, and really adds to the relief and tension of some portions of the game.However, something that I have noticed with Suzerain is that some concepts are left rather vague, like the passage of time and the economy. Timespans between turns can range from a day or two up to months. This can make it rather hard to understand where you are in your presidential term. As well, the economic health of your country is simplified to a bar graph of projected economic growth or shrinkage, but you do not get precise values for important economic factors like unemployment, inflation, and GDP from this, and you only learn these at specific meetings with your minister of economy- it isn't readily accessible information apart from that. These don't impact the overall quality of the game too much, though, and are just things I've noticed to keep in mind.In the end, if you haven't played Suzerain before, go ahead and pick it up, even if you aren't a very big fan of text-based games! It is just amazing, and definitely worth the asking price considering the quality!

_childDocuments_.review: Just finished first play through. I would say more, but I'll focus on my main item. It's short. (At the time of writing I finished in just under 9 hours without rushing.) I hesitatingly gave this game a thumb's up because I have a hard time justifying paying $15 for less than 15 hours of gameplay. A dollar an hour is usually the threshold for me. This is both a criticism and a compliment. I enjoyed it quite a bit, so much so that I was really interested in continuing playing after being reelected, but that didn't happen because it's a one-term game. To me this is a fatal error for this game, but that's just me. Part of the joy of playing a political sim or management is seeing how your actions actually play out. I feel this game is too short to actually do that much justice. I'll update this after another play through to comment on replayability. A charismatic leader, with millions supporting him - at the end of the day, supporters don't count for Sordish cash. Retiring to his Villa, becoming a fine winemaker, supporting his wife from the sidelines.. always carrying the burden of defeat upon his shoulders. Though he isolated Rumburg, supported Merkopian democracy, he never succeeded with Sordland - which he took with him to his grave.God, this is an amazing game. It's like a story game with political ramifications. Buy it. Give it your MONEY.

_childDocuments_.review: Really deep and engaging narrative with plenty of choices to shape the outcome in multiple ways. I prefer nonlinear games, where I can decide to do what I want when I want, which this type of narrative-fueled game doesn't typically allow for - but every choice in Suzerain has long lasting impact in the game that requires you to approach each interaction with the long-term consequences in mind. As far as political games go, the evolving narrative format feels more realistic as it forces you to deal with the immediate circumstances as they come instead of punting on critical issues to pursue your preferred pet projects. Unsure about replayability yet though. There are clearly different outcomes but hope to see an expansion one day that allows you to carry out another term if you make it to that point.

_childDocuments_.review: Don't read antyting about story, dialogue options etc. before playing for the first time. _childDocuments_.review: Suzerain is an incredible game about Cold War politics. You play as the newly-elected President of a country struggling to emerge from under the shadow of a military dictatorship, poised halfway between the capitalist west and communist east, standing on the precipice of an economic depression, with potential enemies and friends on all sides, and no clear mandate from the people other than "fix it".What makes Suzerain so great is that it's concerned not just with what your policy decisions are but what your relationships are to all the other power players in the government. You might have a brilliant plan for pulling your economy out of the recession, but can you get everyone else on board? Can you reform away the constitutional relics of the dictatorship without getting yourself deposed like the last guy? Every character in the game has a detailed history, as do you, and that history matters as much as your choices in the present when it comes time to convince or threaten them onto your side.Furthermore, despite its depth, the game is short enough to engage in multiple playthroughs to try different approaches, and the game will reward you by unraveling new secrets and playing out new confrontations in completely different situations each time. You get a lot of game for your money!

_childDocuments_.review: Suzerain is, overall, a good game, even if it is not without serious flaws.First of all, it must be recognized that this game is original, both in its concept and in its universe.I would like to see more games with this concept : not a political/strategy/management simulation game where you manage everything in an abstract way, but rather where you directly incarnate the leader on a daily basis, with his personal problems, power relations that are embodied by personal relationships, etc., and which therefore has aspects which are very typical of a "visual novel."This kind of game is very rare: I only know of "Long Live the Queen" and "Yes, Your Grace" which are close to it, with a very different approach than Suzerain, RPG-oriented for the first, and very simple strategy for the second. Suzerain is trying to be a realistic political simulation, with difficult relations with the different political forces in the country, with the National Assembly, an economic recession that must be faced, etc.In terms of general quality, I would say that Suzerain is a better game than "Yes, Your Grace," but not as good a game as "Long Live the Queen," although this is still a very relative assessment given that these games have different approaches.The universe of the game is also very interesting, reminding me to some extent of Disco Elysium.It's a totally alternative world to ours, but also very close to what it might have been in the 1950s/1960s, with a cold war pitting a capitalist bloc against a socialist bloc, in a region quite similar to our Middle East. The player becomes president of a country that seems to be more or less an alternative Syria. It is not, however, a copy-paste of our world, since the socialist bloc still seems less authoritarian than ours (the equivalent of the USSR looks like the one that might have existed if it had not been led by Stalin but by Lenin, and the larger socialist neighboring country is more inclined to promote self-rule, resembling communist Yugoslavia in some ways), and the region still has some important differences with the Middle East. In short, it is quite interesting to be president of a country in this universe.This game is a lot of fun. But although it has a concept and a universe that I like very much, I must also admit that it also has some serious flaws.A list of the flaws :1/ If the narrative structure of the game gives the player many possibilities (+++), which is excellent, it still leads to some inconsistencies (--), even if I'm hopeful that patches will correct them. 2/ The characters lack charisma. (It's a point on which "Long Live the Queen" surpasses Suzerain by far.)I didn't get attached to any of the characters in the game, except maybe the protagonist’s wife, and to a certain extent his son (his very young daughter, on the other hand, appears to be totally transparent, which contrasts very negatively with the character of Cedani in Yes, Your Grace, who has a similar but very interesting profile).But for the rest, the player essentially spends their time with boring politicians and bosses, which is, in the end, quite realistic, but not really exciting. The person who is supposed to be our best friend is really annoying, the ministers are only characterized by their political positions (which are far too different to belong to the same government, giving the impression of a sort of national unity government ranging from ultra-nationalists to free-market maniacs to socialists…), etc. Finally, only the other Heads of State have an interesting personality.3/ Some of the biases regarding the consequences of your policies are questionable. In itself this is not necessarily a problem. It is necessary to stand a position and it would have been impossible to satisfy everyone. While some biases seem desirable (for example, gender equality is good!), others, especially those concerning the economy, seem really strange. I will explain the problems I have with the game’s economy in detail in the spoiler section.4/ Oh, and I almost forgot: you can't manually save! You only have checkpoints and can only load the last one! It's a deliberate choice from the developpers to deepen realism, but it's really a poor choice. It lowers the replayability a lot, and we're old enough to know how to have fun, seriously !In conclusion, I would say that this game is worth buying because it remains a very nice political simulation, but keep in mind that you will not necessarily agree with all its biases and flaws.

_childDocuments_.review: I like this game, the developers make a great job but I have to say No because the game needs major improvements. 1. Dialogues are pretty cumbersome. On the second or third run, it gets ridiculously annoying to get through these dialogues over again. I assume, developers didn’t want players to enjoy exploring different scenarios; from which I conclude this is the game is to play two-three times which brings to other conclusion that the price should be $5 tops 2. Dialogues are full of meaningless response choices. It’s basically white noise that doesn’t affect the outcome. I understand, developers wanted to create a special game atmosphere but providing with three or four greeting responses at the beginning of every dialog (that doesn’t affect anything) is too much. Or the driver character that doesn’t affect anything but waste time. I’d suggest a straight-to-the-point dialogues option or something like that.3. At some point it gets pretty boring reading long dialogues. I’d suggest liming choices to a few where you actually can make meaningful choices. I’d also extend the game story and the complexity with different outcomes. Like similar to other text based games, such as "Crisis in the Kremlin". I’d also mark choices with the corresponding colors. For example, red – confrontation/demand/threat, gray – neutrality/consideration/information/deception, green – agreement/reasoning/compromise, etc4. There is no way to save the game. Only one autosave file. Why? It’s frustrating to read forums where people ask what folders/files they have to copy on their computers to go back a few steps. Forced Iron-man is unnecessary. Copying save files every time before next steps is inconvenient, people won't play this game for long. If devs want make this game a successful product and create dlcs they need to ensure that it's engaging and comfortable to play5. Undeveloped dashboard. You can’t actually see the main indicators like inflation, GDP, unemployment, etc. It’s buried in exhausting two or three dialogues during the game. There is no way you can see how your choices actually affect the economy, political processes, main political powers, support of the parliament, business-public-army-police opinion, etc. Every choice is tied to dialogues that you have to wait to pop-up. Newspapers alone are not helpful.6. 99% of dialogues are linear. It doesn’t matter what choices you made before and how they affected the game, the same/all dialogues will pop-up as scheduled. So, no random events/dialogues tied with previously made decisions.7. There are no advisories/notes/recommendations/consequences on choices or how to improve certain things (see “country overview” dashboard). You have to guess or read forums. So, for example, how the heck to improve “Lorren Rust Belt”? Ah, hello, any suggestions? Like build the road and keep surplus or something. Same for the main indicators (see 5.)8. Including Notepad for notes is a desperate attempt to help players to keep track of this mess. 9. I’d not even suggest, but it would be nice to have some kind of simple dubbed (with actual sound like in "This is the Police" game) animation/pictures for main events like speeches or key-dialogues. This would bring another level of interaction to the game.I hope the developers can improve this game.

_childDocuments_.review: This game is a rich, deep, velvety, textured visual novel. It got sold to me as a strategy game, which, I think, is correct, but does make it look, and seem, like more of a 4X or Grand Strategy game than it is. It's not that - not by a long shot, but it definitely scratches the same itches for me, you feel like you're managing a country by managing personalities, and playing with a delicate balance of political threads. The stories it tells are comprehensive, and the Codex is wonderful. Come to this game with patience, and come to it with the intention of allowing it to absorb you. Read the codexes, click all the blue names during your conversations, immerse yourself in the lands, allow yourself to learn the characters around you and care about them in turn. I'm not /far/ into this game, but I eagerly await all it has to reveal to me. Based on the testimonies of many others, it's going to be a lot.

_childDocuments_.review: Having just finished a run through the game, which took nine hours! _childDocuments_.review: It’s an interesting game that gives a firsthand look at how complicated it is to run a country, especially one this broken. At first, I was delighted with the decision making and chess style politics, but the ending is usually the same and straight out ridiculous. Unless you’re completely militaristic and kissing up to your bald general, you’re going to get coup by the military. I fixed the economy, kept us out of war, made strong alliances and improved my citizens’ way of life, all for what? I expected this result if I was a dictator and filled my pockets with money, but you shouldn’t get such a horrible ending for improving the nation and giving the people what they truly need. Everything is already stacked against you without the trash ending being so common. It doesn’t help that skipping the dialogue isn’t an option, good luck going back and spending 50+ hours just to choose a different ending.

_childDocuments_.review: Suzerain is an amazingly engaging political simulation game with a high degree of replayability. Choices do matter and there are a lot of different outcomes based on those choices. The lore of the world is pretty well designed, clearly drawing on early Cold War geopolitics and certain countries are rather clearly stand ins for real world countries. However the focus on Sordland, the country you are President of, creates a deep and engaging world with its own history. The game lets you play as anything from a Democratic Capitalist to a Military Authoritarian, to a Nationalizing Communist and pretty much anything else on the political spectrum (the game shows you where your character ends up on the political spectrum compared with other characters in the game after each play through). Other characters are also on the political spectrum and this influences their goals and agendas. Put simply I recommend this game to anyone with an interest in geopolitics.

It's another type of game, one that feels more like the day-to-day business of a ruling politician with the ability to change without actively changing the grids of your nation. Instead, you are talking to ministers and so on. Suzerain was worth the purchase and I am looking forward to play it again.

_childDocuments_.review: I greatly enjoyed this visual novel/government simulator. The story is intriguing and the writing is well-done. The world-building is excellent and there are in-depth pages on each character, organization, and government system. Choices do matter and manifest in consequences that ripple throughout the entire game (many not seen until much, much later).Where this game falls flat is replayability. Unlike other reviewers, I would argue that this game definitely warrants multiple playthroughs. I have done two (at the time of writing this review) and will likely do one more to try decisions on the opposite end of the political and economic spectrums. A massive failing of this game is to not have discrete save files where one can pick up and replay at points in the campaign on one's choosing. I really wish I could go back to certain points in the campaign and choose an alternate path without having to replay from the beginning. There are multiple game-ending choices, resulting in bad endings, that can really deflate the feeling of a playthrough. For gamers without a lot of spare time, the lack of a save system really makes this game a hard one to recommend without this caveat.

_childDocuments_.review: Edit: my original review below followed a memorable but fairly punishing first play through, and at the time time I thought I was done with the game. That memory though kept burning bright... turns out I couldn't walk away from it and with the help of some reddit research figured out a better strategy for a second run through. The bottom line is, this game is fantastic, and its commitment to its unique setting is absolutely beguiling. With the new 2.0 update out sounding like it smooths over some of the rough edges that chafed on me first time through, I have absolutely no hesitation in demanding that you buy this immediately, or face the execution squad in the morning (which is probably how your first play through will end anyway).Original review: The thing to appreciate about this game is that its really not interested in being winnable. That's not to say that you can't fumble over the finish line with a positive outcome for your character and/or country, but just that if you do it with be due to a large dose of blind luck. In that sense it can be a deeply ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ frustrating play. You find yourself at times making sensible, well considered decisions and simply not getting the expected results, and not having any real sense of why. That is largely though a result of Suzerain prioritising role playing over dopamine-hit game mechanics. And it does that incredibly well: despite and because of the above it is brilliant. Its not without flaws - in places the information it does give you doesn't seem internally coherent, or carries consequences that are not communicated until too late, even allowing for the constraints of the game world - but most of the discomfort I got from playing this felt like it came from its absolute commitment to giving a sense of how brutally challenging it must be to try to lead a minor nation in difficult circumstances, whilst looming super powers try to push you around their chessboard of geopolitical rivalries. On that, Mission Accomplished. I can't deny that I wouldn't have enjoyed my play through more if it had made more concessions to being a game, and with it more of a sense of player agency over events, but judged on its on merits its pretty unforgettable.
_childDocuments_.name: Suzerain

_childDocuments_.review: Take one half Crusader Kings and one half Disco Elysium. This game is full of tense political machinations and decisions that will follow you for your entire presidency. No victory is easy or comes without a cost, and it does a great job of showing just how your choices impact Sordland. Just an incredible game. Anyone who likes political thrillers like House of Cards or Argo absolutely must play it.
_childDocuments_.name: Suzerain

_childDocuments_.review: I really like this game. The choices feel meaningful and thought provoking, and there are so many opportunities to really role-play. Ultimately, I messed up my presidency pretty badly, but I still felt satisfied with the things I've accomplished, and loved getting to act in character and see the  consequences of my decisions.Be aware that this game is not strictly a political sim. It's more of a visual novel and RPG with sim elements. I wish there were more games in this style!
_childDocuments_.name: Suzerain

_childDocuments_.review: I really want to recommend this game, because it really tries and it does some things really well.But in the end I wouldn’t recommend it.The game tries to be a very realistic simulation, and a text based life and politics simulation. And to some degree it does that very well. The problem with the game is there’s no real way of getting feedback on your decisions. On my first play through I spend a long time, as most people would, trying to build support for certain government reforms. The game and the actors in it told me we would pass these reforms, everyone I talked to said they would support them, compromises were made and everything was looking great. Then the day of the vote comes and the No, but failure. Now that’s disappointing, but the problem for me is that I have no idea why the vote failed. Everything the game was telling me was saying otherwise. So maybe the NPCs were lying to me?In a way this realism is interesting, and maybe what some are after, but for me it makes for frustrating gameplay. I have no feedback on my decisions, and I have no idea what went wrong or when. Furthermore there is a forced autosave after every important event, so you can not go back and try things another way.The only way to try again is to, well, replay the last 12h. I don’t really feel motivated to do that.I generally like hard games, but for me I need to understand WHY I failed at something. Otherwise it becomes a frustrating trial and error, and combine that with no save system and you’re looking at either rolling with the punches and guessing at what you could do different on the next play through, or giving up.So on the whole, interesting game, but quite frustrating.

_childDocuments_.review: A masterpiece of a game. Suzerain helped me understand how the political system works, how diplomacy has its flaws, and explored the philosophies of capitalism and communism so well. I wasn't able to be the best president but I pushed for human rights which was good enough. Certainly not going to get into politics thanks to this game. But damn, I was in for a ride. _childDocuments_.name: Suzerain

_childDocuments_.review: Got this game recommended and at first it does look like an exciting political simulation. Unfortunately the dialogues are very long winded and it's a LOT of reading. The world building is great with all the detail, but I very much prefer a more condensed experience. I enjoyed playing it for 2 hours, but I'm going to request a refund, because I don't see myself playing this for much longer. While I'm curious how the story will unfold, this is just too much on the reading and not enough on the strategic decision making side. TL;DR: This is unfortunately more a visual novel than a strategy game.I wish I could give a neutral review, as this is certainly an entertaining game IF that genre is your taste.

_childDocuments_.review: This is such a hard game to recommend. The story is rich and engrossing, but there is so little information to help guide your decision making. You think you are turning the economy around only to find out the growth graph is meaningless. It points practically straight up for dozen turns in a row, you still end up in a depression. You make a series of decisions and there is no feedback on what those decisions influenced. Very confusing interactive novel, but still a great story.

_childDocuments_.review: This is THE BEST political game to date. The amount of detail that has gone into this game is astonishing. Every single decision you make will influence your country's success or decline. Hours upon hours worth of quality story telling and decision making. There are a multitude of complex issues that need resolving. Such as stimulating your economy to dealing with difficult foreign policy. If you are a fan of political games, this is a MUST HAVE.
_childDocuments_.name: Suzerain

_childDocuments_.review: Though I found myself wanting to reload previous saves to change choices, I'm glad the game didn't let me. The politics of Sordland, a country on the brink of recession was a challenge to manage with many make or break decisions. You rule how you want, wanting to reform this collapsing republic into a country of democracy or communism. You can open the country up to a great open future or solidify your hold on it and secure your rule.Either way, the game is very in depth, with bills going through National Assemblies, political climates, corruption, war, or even impeachment. All these things can be avoided or run into depending on how you decide to run your country.
_childDocuments_.name: Suzerain

_childDocuments_.review: I love this game, it's one of the best political sims I've played.  I want a sequel.  A friend gave me this game and I cannot praise it highly enough.  I love the setting, the hair styles, and the attention to details.  i love the music of the game--this is rare for me. Another great feature is the consequences of your choices--in this game your choices DO have SIGNIFICANT consequences.  Even something simple can have major implications down the line.  Sometimes I get tired of games that pretend to offer you choices but don't in reality. This is NOT one of those games.  In a very real sense you set your own fate.I love the wit of some of the dialog choices.  You can be snarky, kind, or downright rude.  You can choose to do something you object to, or not do something you object to.    The consequences of your choices make sense.It does have a "permanent save" feature--there is no load option outside of the main menu.There are enough branching paths that there is a TON of replay value--you cannot possibly get all of the achievements on one playthrough.  That being said, an option here to skip dialogue you've already seen would be very useful.9/10(I don't care for some of the language choices--this deducts 1 point.  If there was an option to remove the swearing/foul language that ever so often crops up, that would be nice.)
_childDocuments_.name: Suzerain

_childDocuments_.review: It's a really cool concept and pretty well executed as well. Also I really got into the story at first. However I feel as though you are set up to fail and in the end that just ruined it for me. You can no doubt min-max your way through the game by failing a few times first and knowing all the events and triggers. But that ruins the whole point of a story based game to me.I think the developers idea is that you are supposed to side with one of the few ideological groups in the game and not actually exercise your own judgement at all. Either you're capitalist, commie or a facist but oddly enough not a centrist as most decisions are without any nuance to them. So best way to play seems to be to pick one of the factions and go all in on them. And I'm sure you'll win...I'll give an example of lack of nuance: You can either choose to limit migration or leave it unregulated. It's a black and white decision that will piss off one of your two neighbors regardless of which way you go. Why can't I just regulate it on one border and leave the other one open? The leadup to that decision even said 'it's a nuanced decision' and then I'm given a binary option. A more options would even make sense in the story context as one border has some Taliban like terrorists on it and other has some actual civilized people.. FML.One other weird situation I had was when I asked my Gestapo to assassinate someone. Only for them to somehow poison the persons dog instead. My chief came back and literally said "The dog drank the poison instead." Like what in the name of..?! Did you pour it into the dogs water bowl and expect the assassination target to get down on all fours and lap it up from there? I can't even..So high marks for concept and technical implementation. But at its ultimate goal of being an actually fun game / engaging story I feel it falls short of. As such not really recommended.
_childDocuments_.name: Suzerain

_childDocuments_.review: One of the greatest games I have played in recent years, though it is not without flaws. Especially the purely reactive, linearly sequenced decision making can be frustrating and even confusing at times. That aside, I felt really involved in the story and was always anxious to see how my decisions would turn out. I would love to see more games of this kind in the future.
_childDocuments_.name: Suzerain

_childDocuments_.review: This game is an amazing look into how politics in developing countries work and the many levels of difficulty in trying to implement positive change even with the best of intentions. The story and events are amazing and every decision is tense and haunting. Amazing game by an amazing studio that still continues to support it with free updates.
_childDocuments_.name: Suzerain

_childDocuments_.review: Suzerain is a phenomenal game. I haven’t seen anything like this ever, it swept me off my feet. I couldn’t recommend it more.The first time I saw Suzerain I thought It was some kind of political sim, or just a plain old grand strategy game. But to my surprise it was part of the “choose your own adventure” genre and the only gameplay was making decisions in text form. Nevertheless I was instantly hooked on. The game has an ingame codex about everything of interest, it works more or less like the dialogue system in Morrowind. In the first 10 or so hours I did nothing else but to read most of the codex. The attention to detail on everything was breathtaking. It had detailed histories of most of countries, it explained the alternate ideologies and even had information on every single company of interest, not to mention all the expansive biographies of relevant, and not so relevant characters to the main story. But that in itself is not the thing they did the best, as they say the devil is in the details – they made it in parallel to our reality. Meaning you can contemplate on real issues, their ramifications and ultimately discover your own personal views on the various matters. The more I read, the more I questioned everything I knew and believed. If that was not enough to immerse myself in the world of Suzerain I was met with a diverse cast of characters. Which ranged from an alcoholic best friend to a power hungry judiciary. As the storyline is concerned it was nothing short of perfect. It had high intensity drama, as well unexpected plot twists and most surprisingly quite a lot of real life references. I was so enthralled at some parts that I felt like it was real, to be frank I even shed a couple of tears. The game is extraordinary but not without flaws. The one thing that enraged me is that the decision making can feel static at some moments. I am specifically talking about taking some dialogue option which seemingly doesn’t have an impact to the story, but to the contrary it has. This can be an issue as it dictates relationships and further events, but I don’t think it’s something that can’t be fixed.This game is a must for everyone who has the time to play through it. Its price is adequate, for it has about 26 unique endings which gives it a lot of replayability value, but for the sake of saving money I will recommend waiting for Suzerain to be on sale. But at the end of the day it's not only a game, but also a medium for understanding the real problems of the day. Not only does it address real issues but makes YOU make the real hard hitting decisions. Will you be different, as you think you’ll be or will you understand that this is a thankless job.
_childDocuments_.name: Suzerain

_childDocuments_.review: Pros: * Great is really impressive, depth and storytelling sometimes is over the roof.Cons: * Speed of animation is painful (especially when replaying game) and no auto-skip of dialogues that you already saw (on consecutive runs) * Unfortunately it has quite a big flaw, not enough feedback. You signed trade deals, you invest into infrastructure, you got reports that all is improving at pace. Suddenly there is unrest everywhere and your adviser that 6 months ago told you that unemployment dropped from 16 to 12, says that currently it stands at 24%. I have no idea what happened and why but nothing could be done. Game is based around meeting that are scheduled by NPC's so you are only allowed to passively watch everything fall apart. * At times you can make accidental decision (like accepting bribe) only because you went to some meeting and game didn't allow you to refuse an offer. This spoils quite a bit of immersion. * Some characters just disappear in the late game * Typical issue for game branching narrative: inconsistencies, dialog lines that not follow your earlier decisions, or choices that have no outcome whatsoever * Lack of epilogue fallout style is a big letdown * As with many games (especially those with branching storylines), early to mid game is superb, top-notched, mid to late game has increasing number of errors, mistakes and becomes shallow

_childDocuments_.review: I thought that i was getting into a political sim game to dip my toes into a calm relaxed shallow pool, not get shoved into a submersible dropped into the middle of the ocean and imploded upon. This game has you not only has you lead a nation that is beyond scuffed nation but also has you playing a life simulation as well. Its a given that being a president will have you making tough calls but actions and decisions with your own family affect those around you. Decisions, Decisions, Decision: the ability to shape internal policy and international policy is immense. Each choice you get has immediate consequences but what you as a player can only hope to avoid the unintentional consequences that can quite literally be a major hurdle to over come in the future. This world is dynamic and individual conversations can have impact full consequences. You will have to do your best to "shape" the future you want for Sorland, and hope you get it to where you want it to be with out pissing off everyone and their mom along the way.My only gripes is that I got impeached and the trial doesn't give you any representation and to defend youself with out making a spectical in court. I was undewhelmed at the outcome of that playthough. Aslo I wish i had some further depth to control of the country, rather than viewing it as a spectator in the president's seat.quick note, the game only allows 1 save file at a time. its good to keep you in a game but you can't hop out of a game to change your play style. But now i can try the power trip of being a ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ Grammar and writing have never been my strong suit, thank you for reading
_childDocuments_.name: Suzerain

_childDocuments_.review: Did you study political science? Then oh boy do I have the game for you. Suzerain's dialogue trees are a masterclass in how to write impactful relational dialogue in video games. Every single sentence you click feels like it has the weight to change all of the dozens of character's opinions of you, and each of them are very well written. The tense political discussions around dinner with individuals you NEED to sway to support you are just incredible. Suzerain rewards you for listening, paying attention, and being socially competent. That's a rarity in video games.
_childDocuments_.name: Suzerain

_childDocuments_.review: Suzerain is not a strategy game, but you'll manage a country. It's not a simu, but you'll end up having to decide major investments and chose an excluding path that will get you celebrated as a hero or direct to jail. It's not (only) a textual RPG, but you'll be playing the president of a country trying to enter the modern era, and also manage your relations with your family.Get ready to read a lot, a whooole lot of very well written stories, interlaced with lots of very well written wikis.And this is the main point : the world Suzerain takes place in is the main character of the game, and it absolutely rocks. Discover a 1950's alternative earth, with complex political issues, racial tensions, economical challenges, betrayal, suspicion, fake smiles and crooked diplomacy, greed, communication wars, ancestral feuds and game changing alliances, war, conspiracies and so on. The whole political part feels really solid, and lets you decide how you handle it : you're in charge of the fate of Sordland, and you can make a paradise from it, or give Sordlanders and the world the nuclear hell you think they deserve, it's up to you. Chose a political path, lie, cheat, stay true, betray or get betrayed, jump into the free market mutation or stick to planned economy, charm the Assembly or the oligarchs, please the generals or get a secret police, ban unions or sign treaties, launch infrastructure modernization or close borders, start a war, build peace, whatever, but don't forget : you're not alone coveting power.The whole game is pretty much linear, but the choices you make really make every run unique, and it's a good 50 hours or more run.If you feel like being president, enjoy challenges, political shenanigans, or just a very well written textual adventure, do not hesitate longer : Suzerain feels like playing a modern era Crusader Kings without the boring strategical map troop movements. Stick to the stories behind the curtains of power and leave the rest. The only blades in the game are the one you're gonna stab in your friends' and allies' back, or the ones they're gonna stick into yours. The whole feeling is pretty casual in the mechanical aspects of the game, but the story goes deep into the subject, and lets you go through a rollercoaster of emotions, which I think is the point of a good narrative medium.If you're bored with political games being too kind, not complex enough or afraid to face the harsh realities of the modern world, you're gonna enjoy Suzerain. A lot. And play it again, to see if a worse solution to a problem is not even funnier to play. It's not your usual strategic simulator and a system you will understand then dominate. It's more like riding a donkey on steroids with a bee nest sticked to its tail : enjoy the ride while it lasts, but in the end, you're gonna fall. And if you ever compare the before/after pics of presidents, you get why Torpor games did a tremendous job.Welcome the Dark Soulest Roguelike Political Simulator ever. Have fun. Be nasty. Your opponents are gonna be worse.

_childDocuments_.review: Absolute masterpiece of a game! just finished the Sordland story pack and the devs did a great job in making it, every decision i made had me thinking, my family in this game, the love for monica my adorable deana and amazing son franc truly what made me love this game.The politics side of the game is great as well! it certainly felt unique to make political decisions, especially the ones that supported my people.The whole game was a bundle of joy and i will reccommend it to anyone who enjoys these types of games. i will be supporting the devs and eventually buy the Rizia DLC to not only enjoy the story, but also commend and support there passion in the game. and i would certainly be thrilled if they launched more DLC's or a possible sequel of the main story cause i am dying to see President Rayne again.Overall i would give the game a 9/10! a very respectable and deserving rating!
_childDocuments_.name: Suzerain

_childDocuments_.review: 8 hours for a single play through and i'm already planning a few more to see how much difference the choices make.But the game itself is beautiful for what it is, I got everything i hoped for after playing the demo.Always being on the brink of collapse and having to allocate the non-existing budget to try and save something, every decision felt heavy and always kept me wondering if I did the right thing.Sadly i'm not as good of a writer as the game creators, so the review is lackluster, but to sum up, be sure to try it out if you're not afraid of reading, a lot, and like the idea of managing a country and internal politics.For sure my top 5 game this year. so far I've:Still have plans for additional runs.There are some minor issues with flavor texts/comments triggering without you completing required actions but probably the main issue for me personally is the lack of a "skip text you already saw" setting which would increase the replay speed a ten fold, as despite a lot of branching possibilities the main issues and the main story path is the same.
_childDocuments_.name: Suzerain

_childDocuments_.review: Nails the whole depicting-a-system-through-an-individual's-interaction-with-said-system thing that Papers Please did so well, though Suzerain does it through incredibly well-written text and a relaxing-yet-oddly-anxious soundtrack that reminds me, more than anything, of Gran Turismo 4 on the PS2. Despite the clear mid-century cold war era set dressing, there's a lot of delightfully anachronistic inclusions here, with references ranging from contemporary British newspapers to 80s pop music. The same goes for the kinds of political decisions you get to make; as Kennedy-and-Khrushchev-esque as they might appear, one can't help but find Thatcher and Blair once one looks past the cordon sanitaires and starts dealing with the privatisation slider. There's enough variety to keep you engaged through subsequent runthroughs; though the lack of a faster way to get through dialogue does make certain reoccurring sections a bit of a slog to get through. Would recommend this to any poli-sci major who thinks that lobbying for a hypothetical state budget sounds like a great way to spend a leisurely afternoon.
_childDocuments_.name: Suzerain

_childDocuments_.review: Thumbs up with some reservations.  First there is the save issue which others have highlighted, also some of the dialogue is downright sophomoric.  However, the richly detailed environment with ethnic tensions, border issues, economic choices and human rights issues makes this an appealing game, even if as noted by others, the story arc seems to have some built in blind spots and biases.

The writing is pretty good and I felt some excellent "Designated Survivor" vibes.The game has a lot of replayability. However it needs the option to skip already known dialogue, and instead present a summary and available choices. Still, if you are interested in politics and political top-level decision making Souzerain is a must-buy.

_childDocuments_.review: The painstaking nature of a making a decision in this game is perhaps one of the most exciting and mentally draining experiences I've had in a game before. While you have brief victories, every financial, social, and political sacrifice comes at a cost often veiled by the complexities of bureaucracy. I cannot recommend this game enough. The depth of choices available will allow for a multitude of different campaigns during the course of exploring this storytelling gem hidden beneath the hoards of new releases this time of year. Buy it now! The price is far below the level of intricacy and story the developers and (especially the) writers have forged. Bravo to all involved! Now join in the wonder, everyone!
_childDocuments_.name: Suzerain

_childDocuments_.review: This game is fantastic. I find that the most significant problem with political games is that it's very difficult to form an attachment to a fake country you're leading without the right world-building, characters and atmosphere. I found this game to be great at all three. I just finished my first play through and I'll admit I was happy with some of the progress I had made, and regretted others. If I had one criticism, it'd be that you're often given choices at the leisure of the game. If you want to make a decision to increase military spending after fixing the economy, it can't be done. So the first budget allocation is essentially your path for the rest of the game. That being said, I loved the choices, and I felt that I was able to move the country in the path I choose. And ultimately paid the price for it. Which is what a good politics simulation is all about.
_childDocuments_.name: Suzerain

_childDocuments_.review: Having just finished the game, I have to say it is the best political game I've played. The depth of information about the different institutions, individuals, and states is incredible. The game really illustrates how difficult it is to stay pure in politics. Even though I tried my best to revolutionize and reform the country I failed miserably (got impeached and died in jail) due to unscrupulous backroom deals that later caught up with me (and which I didn't conceal too well). Either way the game is extremely well made and I definitely recommend

But with the recent patch it didn't just become more consistent but also more thrilling and engaging.One problem with the recent patch though; In my story line my Vice President committed suicide after I forced him to resign due to his big scandal but later on in the game during the Party Congress he was there alive and well supporting me to be the party's nominee.If I didn't encounter that problem I'd give it a 9/10 but because if it I'd give it a 8/10.

_childDocuments_.review: One of the best games I played in a while. Given the setting and CYOA mechanics it was surprisngly engaging and kept me glued to my sit for two days straight.I tried to play fair, but in politics, as we all know, it doesn't really work. _childDocuments_.name: Suzerain

_childDocuments_.review: I'll start off saying this is one of the best political games I've ever played. There's a ton of world building and lore that's easily accessible by the wikipedia style codex that gives you backstory on not only the characters, but the terminology, nations and even historical events that have taken place in game. The choices are tough and will really make you consider what you want to do going forward in the game and experimenting with choices can yield surprising ( I never realized eating a salad could make or break me) results. Lastly the story is really compelling and quickly sucks you in to the world. You will really come to love and hate some of these people and in some cases they will make you question your own beliefs and what you're willing to do to achieve your goals.While this may not be CKIII  or Power & Revolution in terms of micromanagement, if you're looking for a game that will make you truly feel like the leader of a country with the weight of the world on your shoulders, this is it.
_childDocuments_.name: Suzerain

_childDocuments_.review: The only good political single player campaign game out there. A lot of free choice but not too much to be able to compare the game to one of those chaotic sandbox games. This game combines the political aspect perfectly with just enough realism to create realistic politics in an alternative world.This game is definatly worth buying, it has a lot of potentional. I would recommend to buy it for 10 euro or less tho, paying more for this game is also a bit too much compared to what you get.
_childDocuments_.name: Suzerain

_childDocuments_.review: I really enjoyed this game's narratives. Every choice has a consequence, every action has a reaction. Sometimes what you doing what you think is right will come back to bite you later, and I really like that. It makes you think about what you're doing and how it affects everyone and everything around you.
_childDocuments_.name: Suzerain

_childDocuments_.review: Suzerain is a text-based adventure that sees you leading a fictional, failing Eastern European country a few decades after a civil war. You are faced with difficult situations in which you must make tough choices about how to lead the country. It's interesting, but I can't recommend it at full price for two reasons.First, the game has little practical replayability in my opinion. The game does not let you reload an earlier save, so if you want to change anything you have to play the whole game again from the beginning, and a playthrough takes about 10 hours, unless you just skip all the text (which defeats the purpose). Even skipping through the text it takes over 4 hours to try for a new ending. That's too long. While I appreciate the ironman gameplay, I think it should be optional, at least after the first playthrough, so that people who want to experiment with alternate endings don't have to spend such a long time going through the same stuff repeatedly.Second, the game bundles decisions together in a way that annoys me. For example, there is the question of whether you want to reform the education system. I was playing as a Sordish traditionalist who was making reforms to improve the country without losing its core values. The existing, traditional education system has two facets: 1) it teaches students patriotism - to love their country, to want to serve it, and to revere its founders as great men, and 2) it guides boys and girls down different paths, where girls are generally prohibited from taking advanced math or science classes and are always funneled into homemaking (unless their parents can afford a private education). The minister of education wants to abolish both of these facets. There is no way to say "let's improve girls' education, but keep the patriotism". If you want to improve girls' education, you must also abolish the patriotism. Let me choose!For another example, a big issue in the game is women's rights. Men are legally allowed to beat their wives. Women's primary place in society is the raising of children. Etc. The minister of education - plus your own wife - want to push through a women's rights bill, but some of their proposed policies are destructive, and, if the game was implemented realistically, would foster poverty and homelessness among many poorer Sords (including poorer women), while primarily benefiting well-off women who already have many opportunities. Others would harm families and set the country on a path towards long-term demographic implosion. But there's no way to pick and choose. You can't say "let's protect women from domestic violence and give talented girls equal access to education but not try to push all women into the workplace". It's all or nothing. Either you pass policies that would ruin the nation, or you support men beating their wives. C'mon! Let me choose!Overall, I enjoyed my first playthrough and I want to try again making a different decision or two, but I can't justify spending so many hours to try the game a second time.
_childDocuments_.name: Suzerain

_childDocuments_.review: This game is well thought out and designed.  The authors clearly know their history.  The story is realistic and conveys the sense that you really are the individual at the head of this country.  While it is largely a chose your own adventure, it has nice layers to it that makes the story feel alive and dynamic.  The writing does an excellent job of making your decisions feel like part of the story.
_childDocuments_.name: Suzerain

_childDocuments_.review: Remarkable game. Unlike most politics simulations I've played, this one does not give you the metrics associated with your decisions ; you have to try and discern which trigger led to which result later in the game, but apart from economic decisions, which are calculable, the game won't give you exact or immediate information about them, just like in real life.This makes the game appear unforgiving at first, which it is if your goal is to achieve a perfect presidential term ; but then again, achieving a perfect first term is extremely hard in real life too. The game makes sense when you approach it as a simulation of writing a page of history. In the end it does not matter so much if you "win". You can have a run that's extremely difficult, in which you end up assassinated or imprisoned, but which result is a turning point in the history of your fictional country.One must not be afraid to start over multiple times to explore all the options or find out how to achieve the desired reforms or results, and to not be helped by the game while doing so, in order to appreciate it.All I can say is that I truly hope to see more installments of this format, either as a sequel or in a different setting.
_childDocuments_.name: Suzerain

_childDocuments_.review: It's very rare that a game will come along now that so exceeds expectations that I actually bother to review it. Suzerain is just such a game: a brilliant cross between choose-your-own-adventure and the political compass questionnaire. It is deeply replayable, and completely engrossing: I clocked up over 40 hours over about a week and half of playing it (and I work full-time). The writing is really good and it's clearly been put together by people with a lot of knowledge and interest in 20th century history and politics (though the game itself is set in a fictional location). Shame they aren't releasing any expansions but it stands alone as a great achievement. My only small gripe is that it only has one auto save for your whole playthrough so if you make a mistake or want to see what happens if you make one decision differently you have to go all the way back to the beginning. I think they should compromise on having it autosave at the start of each turn or chapter. Otherwise perfect.
_childDocuments_.name: Suzerain

_childDocuments_.review: I thought the writing and dialog choices in this game were very well thought out.  It was very difficult in certain chapters to see a way forward.  I think this game provides a real window into how difficult it must be to thrive in politics.  Playing this game is as close as I want to get to pulling the strings of power.

_childDocuments_.review: "Children will die because of this decision.  How does this administration sleep at night?"A great question posed by the Sordish newspaper "Radical".  The truth is, by this point late in my first term as President of Sordland, my long-term predecessor Tarquin Soll has appeared in my dreams.  Or should I say nightmares?  I'm not really sure.  But it a testament to the strength of the political world-building in  that Soll has infiltrated my subconscious, something that Dostoevsky achieved with  but few if any video games have.It also speaks to why [i/]Suzerain[/i] is my new favorite political simulator.  Most that I have achieved are high-level economic simulators that let you set essentially whatever policy you want, and see how it affects things at a statistical level.   (and presumably its sequel) is in this category, and is immensely unsatisfying, especially given its title.   does a little better by leaning into the "trends and forces" theory of history and making it so you generally have to bend to the demands of the populace or face unrest, but the trends pretty much move in one direction during its time period.   has multiple political parties and lobbying to pass legislation, but the situation remains high-level.  In , however, you are confronted both with the human impacts of your policies, as well as the impact of Sordland's legistlative body, the Grand National Assembly, and the Sordish Supreme Court.  Think Chief Justice Hawker is going to approve everything you do?  I wouldn't be so sure!The newspaper system is a thing of genius, as given the different viewpoints they advocate, it's almost impossible to satisfy all of their audiences at once.  And that points at what makes the game so compelling in general - you aren't going to make everyone happy.  Did George H.W. Bush make everyone happy?  Did Bill Clinton?  No.  Neither will you.  Your advisors will disagree.  Some of your policy choices will backfire.  The economy will fail to revive, or you will fall into a debt trap, or you might wind up angering your next-door neighbors in Rumburg, or perhaps all three.  And it's not just national policy, you've got a family to tend to - or ignore - at home, too.Which leads to the next point - the character building is on point.  In a remarkably short period of time considering how large the cast of characters is, the game builds the characters into people you know and care about.  You'll be amazed by some of their actions, reacting as you might to gossip about one of your old friends, and likely come to favor and grudgingly put up with others - and the ones that you favor and begrudge may be different than mine.I recommend playing your first playthrough as you would if you really were made president - favor your policies, make compromises, or don't - and see how it goes.  I've enjoyed a great high point driving on the newly-opened H-3 Highway from Lachavalen to Arvory, and a great low point... well, it's more like a  of moderate low points from a policy level, and one major disappointment in another character that I won't spoil for you.  I thought I'd be doing pretty well by Year 4 of my presidency, and instead I can point to some policy improvements that ought to pay off over the long term, a lot of things that haven't panned out so well, and a likely upcoming election loss if I can't find a rabbit to pull out of a hat somewhere.  Perhaps by trying to make everyone at least moderately happy, I've instead made everyone unhappy.Which leads to a final point - it's difficult.  So many games make it easy to fix things and make things so they seem to be going well, and  prefers to take the approach of "reality is difficult, and a game about it should be too".  It's a weighty game, despite occasional moments of levity.  If you want to govern a utopia, go play .  By playing  , you'll instead have some understanding of why Jimmy Carter said he couldn't have handled the stresses of being President at age 80.  You'll understand why all but the most stratospheric of presidents have a mixed legacy.  And you'll likely both want to become more civically engaged, and really not want to have the stresses and responsibilities of the highest offices at the same time.Highly recommended to anyone who enjoys reading and discussing public policy or politics.

_childDocuments_.review: Read more of my short essays on video games at Suzerain is a text-based role-playing game where you play as President Anton Rayne leading the fictional country of Sordland in a political drama driven by conversations with your cabinet members and other significant people. The decisions you make will determine the future of Sordland and of its people, how will you lead?Suzerain is a narrative-driven game. Playing the game involves reading a lot of dialog, news articles, biographies of people and more. All of this text serves to immerse you in the political world of Sordland. Using its writing, Suzerain does everything it can to convince you that the people of Sordland are as real as you are.It worked for me. I love games that make me feel something, those games are the ones I end up writing about. There were moments in Suzerain where I felt the same stress that President Rayne would have felt if he was a living breathing person. There's a difference between reality and fantasy, but the fantasy Suzerain delivers is powerful enough to convince you otherwise.The decisions you make have weight to them because the game does a good job of immersing you in its world and because there's no undo button. The game saves your progress whenever you make a choice and forces you to live with the consequences. You sign off on a draft for a revised constitution without knowing all the ramifications, reporters ask you questions you don't have good answers to and, sometimes, you make mistakes and you have to live with it.Suzerain, like most video games, is inherently political. But unlike most other games, it allows you to participate directly in the political world of the game giving you room to think about and come up with answers for all sorts of interesting political questions. That's what makes Suzerain special and a game worth playing.It's hard to discuss a narrative-driven game without talking about the narrative in some detail. This is what I'll be doing next. If anything I've said about Suzerain sounds interesting to you then please stop reading and play the game yourself.In my playthrough, I was, or at least tried to be, a man of the people. I reduced military funding and improved universal healthcare and education. I helped give women a voice, I championed workers' rights and I reduced the power of my own party to give minorities seats in parliament.Buuuuuuuuuuuuuuuut…When you become the president, Sordland is about to fall into a depression. During my time in office, I wasn't able to bring meaningful economic change to the country. My focus on healthcare and education was a long-term investment in people that wasn't likely to pay off during my presidency.By operating the military with reduced funding, Sordland was at risk of possible invasion from Rumburg, our imperialist neighbors. To protect Sordland, I became allies with United Contana (a stand-in for the USSR) through a military alliance. United Contana was trying to stop the spread of capitalism at all costs and along the way committed a few too many atrocities for my taste. But, we needed protection and they could provide that.Throughout my term, I needed to have the people support my actions because I expected the Oligarchs (business moguls who controlled more than they should) and the Old Guard (loyalists to the dictator for life who stepped down a few years earlier) to do everything in their power to tear me down and stop me from enacting change. When Marcel Koronti, the soon to be CEO of the company controlling most of the media of Sordland, came to me with a deal, I accepted. I would need to do something for his benefit later down the line but, in the meantime, he would ensure that the media was championing my cause and that any controversies within government would be covered "fairly".I did a lot of good for the people as the president but I had to make difficult choices along the way. Despite the Oligarchs revealing my shady dealings with Mr. Koronti to the public, the people felt that the good I did for all of us outweighed the questionable decisions I made and they elected me for a second term. Although, who knows how much an influence my control over the media had on the election itself. Who's to say?That's how my playthrough ended. I gave you a brief look into a few of the decisions I made during my reign. Each one felt impactful and gave me a sense of what it might feel like to be a president. A lot of video games are power fantasies, there aren't many games out there that make you feel the crushing expectations of your people weighing you down with every step you take.Suzerain achieves a lot with a little. I'm always looking for games that push the boundaries of what video games can do and Suzerain surprised me with an experience that surpassed my expectations. I'm still trying to understand how a text-driven video game could provoke such a strong emotional and physical response from me. I hope I've convinced you to take a look at Suzerain, you're unlikely to be disappointed. Now, if you'll excuse me, I have to finish writing my manifesto.
