_childDocuments_.review: I have played through the game twice, and I can recommend it to anyone interested in an engaging political strategy game. The price point is currently perfect for this game right now, as it is basically the cost of going out to the movies. Suzerain is very well thought out, the story thread is believable, and I found most of the political mechanics work as they would in a hypothetical nation of the 1950s. There is a smaller, personal story line that follows your domestic life, which adds a bit of unexpected depth to your President. The game mechanics are simple, and nicely designed, making it more visually stimulating than some past games about political strategy.Now, a couple of caveats. No matter what your politics are, this game is biased toward a neo-liberal ideology. For those who do not know what that is, it is basically a belief in very basic democracy reliant on corporate "donations" to fund political parties, with nearly unregulated free market capitalism, no public health care, few social services, and only cursory investment in public education. In an economic crisis, they would recommend austerity.I have heard of people winning as a communist leader, but it sounds like it was a very particular kind of path they had to take. A balanced game politically would have several win paths that could be taken, be it full-on fascism, capitalist democracy, social democracy, or full-on communism. I would also add here that it seems highly biased toward militarism, as there is an immediate threat of incursion upon starting the game. If you choose not to fund the military enough, you may very likely lose.The budget in this game is broken. In real governments, when the economy is booming the government actually takes in more revenue through higher income taxes, through more trade, and production - especially in countries that have some nationalized industry. As it stands now, the only way the budget is affected is if you pass legislation that costs or will merit you budget points, and getting a +1 or +2 is exceedingly rare. This seems like the developer wanted to make the game "more challenging", but it just forces you to run the country in debt constantly. This is an annoyance, and I think there should be some effect on the budget if you have the economy either maxed out, or in a shambles. I had a fully maxed out economy, but my budget was at -8 for a while, which had people complaining that we were in a debt crisis. How was that a crisis? We were in debt to ourselves. It just made no sense, and as I said, where was all of my wonderful revenue from my hot economy to ease the debt?One final critique: The player is very beholden to the story. You tend to be a very passive and reactive entity in the game as president. There are times when you are given decisions to make, but they are still "given". Maybe this is unfair, but in a second version, some consideration to this fact might be given. How can the player be the main actor in the game play? Even though there are a few problems with Suzerain, it is still a strong game, and is fun to play.  It is pretty complex, and I appreciate the thought that went into it. The developers did  some amazing work threading all of these paths together into a cohesive game.

_childDocuments_.review: Never had ever been emotionally invested in a game. The music fits so well with the narrative.There are so many choices that you can led your country into, ranging from a pure libertarian capitalism to a complete communist dictator. During my first playthrough, I was a very moderate centrist. Our economy was booming and people were enjoying their good healthcare, education, and women's rights. I was on my way to a second term. However, unfortunately, I didn't take my country's military spending very seriously and I paid for it... There was a coup and they threw me into jail.This game really makes you think on your toes. Every thing your character says and does literally makes the biggest differences. You have to be very strategic about how you spend the government's budget. Not only that, if you don't read through the game's lore to understand the history of the world and who people are, you won't get the outcome you wanted. There is an incredible amount of world building in this game.Something that is interesting about the game is that it gives you alternative viewpoints. Your cabinet will always voice their opinions about one choice or another. Ultimately it is up to you to decide what is best for your country.

_childDocuments_.review: This is a really wonderful political sim with great world-building and characters.  It's choose your own adventure style, which comes with some annoyances....namely often two choice will really seem the same but are actually completely difference in effect, or two choices that look different are actually the same.  Or all the choices you get seem to ignore another, very obvious possibility.  Also sometimes the reactions you have available are completely inappropriate to the situation...like getting a choice to be ragingly irrational or completely apathetic.  Some of the events that get triggered by your decisions are pretty silly...like one of my ministers resigned saying something like this: "Yes, you literally saved millions of lives and you pushed all my policy ambitions...but you made a mildly shady backroom deal once so I'm tendering my resignation right before the election."But there are not many games that do what this game is trying to do as well as it does, and I am finding it addictive.

_childDocuments_.review: Suzerain is very, very good at what it wants to do: inviting its players into a high-stakes, richly detailed, fictional universe loosely based on the Cold War. You, as the player, have been elected president at the worst time possible. Sordland's constitution is imbalanced, its economy broken after past presidents seesawed between communist and capitalist systems, and its people divided between rich and poor, nationalist and Bludish (an oppressed ethnic group), secular and Dastnurist.Here is what makes Suzerain such an enticing game: You must make sacrifices. You cannot fix everything. You must choose what you care about and what you don't. But the better you understand the lore and world and mechanics of Suzerain, the better choices you can make. You can sacrifice less and push for more gains. That's what brought me back to Suzerain over and over again, leading me to eventually craft runs where I could achieve everything I wanted in exchange for some short-term or relatively small sacrifices. The Torpor devs reward understanding and replayability, and I really appreciate that.In my first run, I decided that—no matter what happened in the game—I was going to do three things: (1) reform the constitution, (2) end the economic recession, and (3) reconcile the Sordish and Bludish peoples. The leader of the conservative wing of my political party frightened me into making only minor reforms to the Constitution (though I was still able to pass the Constitution in the Assembly and Court). My economic investments were too diffuse to end the recession and actually made it worse. The weight of this particular failure felt appalling. Unemployment, inflation, and government debt soared, and my economic minister Simon's distress only made me feel worse. I did, however, manage to reconcile the Sordish and Bludish, vetoing every racist bill against them and speaking up for them whenever I could.If you enjoy reading or like strategy games, Suzerain should be right up your alley.

_childDocuments_.review: I write this with the with the caveat that I enjoyed the first 16 hours or so, spent playing (over several days) but the shine fell away with more play.To really succeed I'd have to strike a ballet pose beneath an elephant's anus and juggle chainsaws. Either that or go full out neo-liberal serf-state and let the oligarchs run the joint.This game should be called "Stand here while we throw jagged objects at you, but don't forget to smile!"UPDATE:After more play, a few things crawled under my skin:-- You have no agency. This is a game of multiple-choice Jenga and you cannot initiate anything at all.-- You have more birds waiting to take a dump on your head than you have towelettes.-- The only game mode available, being ironman mode, is unforgiving. If you want to try out different approaches (most approaches will fail) you have to endure the the tedium of restarting over and over and over and over.In light of this, I opted for the only agency that I actually did have. I uninstalled and will now move on to other things.

_childDocuments_.review: One of the best entries I have seen into the underexplored genre of narrative/strategy hybrid games.The presentation is excellent, the characters are likeable, the world is interesting and generally believable, the arc of the game is logical and the choices feel consequential.There were only a few instances where dialogue seemed to forget past decisions, and they were largely inconsequential. As that's always a major difficulty with games of this sort, I think that's quite good. I should note that your experience with games of this sort is heavily dependent on your individual playthrough. I have only completed one playthrough, so while for me the game worked very well, I can't say how well the game adapts to different choices.That all being said, I do have some concerns about the flow of certain events, such as , and the . It also feels, at least in my playthrough, that the . In general the last chapter of the game felt a bit weaker than the earlier parts.Additionally, there were a few instances that may have been bugs, as the budget seemed to change without explanation a few times and it was never clear exactly how the economic situation bar was supposed to work.Even with those issues, it's an excellent game. I look forward to another playthrough, and I'd be very interested to see the developers explore the concept further in another game.
_childDocuments_.name: Suzerain

_childDocuments_.review: Excellent game. Apart from being entertaining, it really makes you think about a lot of things (basically, making choices in complicated situations where each option has advantages and disadvantages). This genre (narrative RPG about politics) deserves so much more games and attention from developers in general.What is true is that your choices take time to take effect. The game is quite slow. But that's actually how politics really works. So, I don't think that's a bad point.At the end, you could be frustrated not to be able to go further, as if you had just finished a book and wanted to read the sequel, but this sequel didn't exist. This is proof that the game is very well written.

I haven't played any game like it and I had to weight out my decision option, which i did not expect from this game. I do feel saddened about the ending and wish for more choices for different endings and not just a coup. It breaks my heart to see all my progressive reforms and policies just go down the drain by one person. What happened to my allies and the people? Why did they not speak out against the military? Why did they just go in their merry way and forget about the person that gave them so much to rot in jail? All in all, i would give this game an 8/10.

Stats like in the final page would be amazing for example, just a suggestion. Anyway, wonderful game!
_childDocuments_.name: Suzerain

_childDocuments_.review: Suzerain is handsdown the best political drama ever portrayed in a game. Taking heavy inspiration from the Cold War politics of our own world, while still putting a unique and captivating twist on its own setting, the game focuses around the life of a turbulent country's president, as they(you) navigate their way through a web of interesting political dilemmas. What separates this game from the rest that attempt this kind of story, is that Suzerain takes a much more human approach to politics. Rather than being a faceless entity that controls a nation, only looking at perfect statistics and percentage sliders, you roleplay as a living person with their own unique background and worldviews.I can honestly say this is one of my favourite games of all time, and would recommend it to everyone who comes across it.
_childDocuments_.name: Suzerain

_childDocuments_.review: Seriously this game is incredible. It's not for everyone though. It helps to be politically active and somewhat knowledgeable in politics, though it's not required. The game plays like a choose your own adventure book, quite literally. Everything is text based, but it really allows the information to sink in and is impactful since it uses your imagination to fill in the imagery of how things are playing out. I felt very much like I was in Sordland making these decisions, and every decision felt like there was a large impact. Also the game is much longer than I expected.Every choice that you make will likely have an unintended consequence, it's up to you to manage what consequences can come up. Quickly I was able to start thinking of all of the difference things that might happen, and even though this helped with a lot of decisions to minimize the risk, the game was still able to throw me some serious curve balls that made me question my own real life morals and ethics.Some hints that I can give you is to read the newspapers and all of the reports that come up in the cities. Some of them will provide good strategic information when going into meetings, or just in general a good idea of what's happening around the country and where things are headed. Also there's a notepad in the game, use it to remember certain criteria or patters. For instance when your advisers tell you a leader has certain demands that they won't give up, write that down so you know where the line is. There's also a potential spot in your play through where you may need to remember a certain pattern of decisions for a ceremony, this helps with that as well..though I just took a screenshot of the sequence.SPOILERS BELOW!Here's a synopsis of how my story went...- While in the military I disobeyed direct command to allow refuges through- Supported the our party until it became less about the people and more about nationalism- Won presidency even after creating a division in the party- Brought unity after tragic events at the beginning of my presidency. This took a long time, but treating people with respect regardless of who they are or if you or your supporters agree with them goes a long way- Kept borders open to allow refugees from mass casualties happening in Wehlen- Funded a long term project to develop an ailing region of the country rather than a mega project that would help out the already large and productive cities. Though the construction partner I chose ended up delaying it through a significant portion of my Presidency- Never took a bribe- Enacted and rejected laws on the basis of principle and merit rather than nationalism, sexism, and religion- Passed constitutional reform which strengthened the legislature, and removed excess power from the Supreme Court and the Presidency (for the long term good of Sordland!) while never needing to threaten or bribe anyone for votes (I didn't take any bribes and I wasn't going to bribe anyone else). Also opened the door for more parties to be eligible for the assembly and presidency (if I remember correctly)- Invested and became co-owner of a football team- Diplomatically fought back military advances from Rumburg while only needing to retaliate once to show strength.- Built alliances with Agland and Lispia for economic prosperity and for military assistance to try and prevent an invasion by Rumburg- Launched another infrastructure project for agriculture, mainly for trade to increase economic output (this was a hedge since the other project was delayed)- Passed reforms for women's rights- Increased education access to the rural areas of the country- Kicked polio's ass- Fired a secretary (though I was sure the story was going to go a very different way [Those of you who have played, Petr and Lucean were acting pretty weird...])- Condemned the mass casualties in Wehlen, and the military aggression from Rumberg in front of the AN- One of my advisers whom didn't see eye to eye with me challenged me for the the party nomination for the next election cycle. My amazing speech dazzled the party so she lost.- Ended up losing the election to an ally from another party who offered to join forces earlier in the game and I declined out of uneasiness to fully trust him, all while his party was only able to run due to my constitutional reforms (aint that a kick in the nuts, for Sordland!)- Left politics. Supported my wife in leading more women reforms, was overshadowed by her, then became manager of the football team I co-owned, lead them to victory after victory. Four years after the last election the ally who beat me in the election offered me Vice President in the next term. I graciously accepted which resulted in him losing (another kick in the nuts). Rekindled with my son, and lived happily ever after as a wealthy man with my family.I may have missed some things, this game has a lot of stuff that it throws at you, so it's difficult to remember it all.What's odd is I recovered the economy, won the nomination even while implementing vast reforms that lessened their power and generally increased happiness throughout the country and I still lost the election and was not liked enough to sink an election with me as VP. So I'm not sure there's an ending where you actually win reelection.
_childDocuments_.name: Suzerain

_childDocuments_.review: Let me start by saying that I played the demo earlier this year and loved it. Even going in with very high expectations I was still impressed. The shear amount of detail and world building within the game is incredible, and the alternate world cold war setting proved to be quite the backdrop for the story.I would honestly recommend this game to anyone with any sort interest in politics, but don't expect much in terms of action; the game is essentially a highly detailed political visual novel. _childDocuments_.review: Suzerain is a narrative political game that is a failure as a game, as politics, and, most damningly of all, as a narrative. Major characters act implausibly, most egregiously the wife: we are expected to believe that, in an analogue of 1950s Turkey, the President's wife—who married him knowing he was a conservative nationalist—would suddenly divorce him because he wouldn't introduce gender equality laws so radical they would be controversial in the Middle East even now. Similar can be said of the judiciary, who are supposedly Sollists (the game's authoritarian faction) but act towards a loyally hard-line Sollist President the same as they would to a Communist. These unrealistic follies constantly pull you out of the immersion necessary to sustain the illusion and the enjoyment. This is made worse by the stupid and irritating war at the end of the game. Even if you support the military and gain allies, the game still auto-resolves the war against you. This is done as an abrupt cut-scene ex machina, again yanking you out of immersion in a horribly jarring manner. Ask your Defence Minister what you did wrong, and he will just reply that you were in the wrong place at the wrong time: there was nothing to be done. I cannot express strongly enough what a terrible narrative experience this is as a player. It is as if the writers have no care for the player experience whatsoever. There is some minor pleasure to be had in the day-to-day game-play and the interesting background lore, but even there both elements are hobbled by frequent grammatical errors introduced into the English text by the dev team's non-English speakers which, yet again, pull you out of the immersion that is necessary in a narrative game more than any other genre. Like so many other writers who turn their hand to gaming, Torpor Games needed to remember that a game is not the same as a novel. Perhaps in a novel this nihilist story of the inevitability of failure might be interesting to read, but in a game the player's agency needs to be respected, and abrupt unhappy endings are not a pleasant experience. This is especially true given the arrogant decision not to provide a save game functionality. As a result, I cannot recommend this game to anyone, no matter the price. Avoid.
_childDocuments_.name: Suzerain

_childDocuments_.review: As someone who has a passable portion of knowledge in political science ( ͡° ͜ʖ ͡°), I appreciate the attention to detail the devs have put into making this game feels true to life. It would be awesome if animated cutscenes were added in some parts of the game so we could see a visual presentation of the state of play from every decision we make. All in all, it's the best text-based political RPG I've ever played!

_childDocuments_.name: Suzerain

_childDocuments_.review: Brilliant. Not more I could say but here I goSuzerian is a blend of political sim strategy and visual novel - weird but works wonders in execution!You play as Anton Rayne, newly elected 4th President of Sordland, who you can play in whatever way you want, be that die-hard communist, capitalist, moderate, facist, nationalist etc. Decide budgets, invest in major projects, make laws and decide the livelihoods of millions... all while keeping the peace and ensuring the republic doesn't fall to nefarious forces.Suzerian is surprisingly nuanced take in the realm of all things government and politics, with no ideology specifcally promoted or condemned, rather allowing the player to form their own opinions on current conditions in the game world. In fact this is likely the intent of the writers: to show how people with varying views come to them as a result of the conditions around them.I believe this game is a masterpiece of writing and political commentary of the 21st century (even though it's set in a faux 20th century cold war obviously shaped by real world history).As I said before, this game blends political strat-sim with visual novel, however this game *should* be treated as a visual novel, as all gameplay is derived through long, novel-like text through narration and dialogue; if long bouts of text and reading don't appeal to you, then reconsider this game. Major decisions such as singing or vetoing bills, budget allocation, international diplomacy and law & order are actually scattered through the game's ten chapters or *turns*.What surprised me the most about Suzerian is both the length of the game and the replay value. This game is *long* although this is due to plenty of good story-telling making up an enormous overarching narrative through the game, with plenty of substantial content making up playtime; padding is far and few between through playthroughs. Indeed, different decisions and roleplaying directions can ***actually*** have real changes and consequences to the development of the story. Decisions you make in chapter 1 could bite you in the end... well you *are* the president.This game deserves so much more praise and attention as it deserves it for a beautifully crafted story, allowing for meaningful choices that *DO* make a difference (unlike superficial telltale games) and such dedicated world-building that almost makes you forget that Sordland is a fictional country.GET THIS GAME!

_childDocuments_.review: The rapid switch from naive idealism going into office to panicked realpolitik as you're trying to just keep things together is amazing. Everybody has an agenda, and it's not necessarily aligned with yours. Mostly, this is a game of figuring out who's going to support what you're trying to do and who's going to oppose it, and how you can work with the cards you're dealt to turn out with a majority.Or at least, that's how my game played. I tried to legitimately make the country a better place, while respecting democracy, fighting corruption, and working with my enemies rather than suppressing them. Ultimately, I got a 'good' ending, but I did have to do some things (or maybe, just allow some things to happen) to get what I wanted. It was so easy to forget what I'd done, until that interview towards the end started dredging up my past decisions...If you've got the patience and are going to try and meaningfully engage with the themes and setting of the story, you'll enjoy this. But be warned, there's no real 'gameplay' to be had here beyond simple budget balancing. Think of it as a visual novel, and you'll be fine.

_childDocuments_.review: This is a fantastic, choose your own story political narrative.It's got great writing, storyline, difficult choices and a good balance between need to know info and exposition dumps.Lead your country through a turbulent period of history, become capitalist, communist, neutral. Become a dictator, true socialist, democratic leader. _childDocuments_.review: Few games have captured my imagination quite like 'Suzerain.' I simply cannot express how much i love this game enough. _childDocuments_.review: I don't think I've ever left a review on Steam before. Suzerain is unlike any other game I've played. Its story is rich and engrossing. I found myself hooked to every line and scenario in ways I typically experience in novels I love. The choices are sometimes clear-cut, but more often than not it is brutally challenging to pick a path or discern the best option. Every action has consequences, and those consequences certainly are not always apparent. There are wide-spread ripple effects that can impact your run in ways you may not have considered.The characters, world, and scenarios are thoroughly fleshed-out. You can (and I did) spend hours reading through the codex entries. The game intrinsically rewards you for doing so, too, as the added context from the codex can greatly increase your ability to make informed decisions. I am excited to try more runs of this game. At some point it is less about winning or losing (though maybe I'm biased, happening to "win" on my first run-through), but about exploring this world and the wide range of options it holds within.I have only a few constructive criticisms:* I would have loved a zoomed-out map view where I could see the entire region without scrolling.* A read-only view of the world for context would have additionally been neat* There were a few typos (I think I counted four total that I noticed) in some of the dialogue. Understandable given the immense amount of writing in the game, in hindsight I wish I'd taken note of them.* There were times, especially when voting on bills or programs, where I felt I didn't have the ability to discuss with advisers beforehand for context and strategy.* I wold love if the end-screen detailed the most important journal bullet-points of the runThese points pale in comparison to how engaging and fun this game is though. Absolutely worth the $15, you will get more out of this in time and enjoyment than from many modern $60 AAA games.
_childDocuments_.name: Suzerain

_childDocuments_.review: I must say I even though I have purchased many games over the years, I don't usually write reviews. I'd rather play the games and let people make their own mind about them. There are many very well written reviews out there detailing what sets this great game apart from others of this genre: the realistic and life-like challenges, the compelling story, the wonderful art style and the amazing universe that Torpor Games created for us. I won't repeat what has already been said. But... ever since I was a young teenager I've been looking for a game like this. One that puts you in the shoes of a self-made man that history puts in charge of a country where everything still needed to be done, at a time in history where people still held to their ideals and looked at the future with shining hope in their eyes. What the developpers understood and tried to relay here is that being  a "suzerain", isn't so much about speadsheets and technicals, although the game does a pretty good job at abstracting those. It's about the story of the people put on and behind the proverbial throne (sadly this is "early cold war" era, no women rulers yet, although you can bring change in that direction, should you  wish to). The strengh of this game lies in it's execution: that life story is not only credible but emotional as well. I would like to say thank you. For making a game that 20 year old me dreamed about played. Everyone who's ever dreamed about changing the world at some point in their life would appreciate the effort that's been delivered here. Thank you,

_childDocuments_.review: I have done a few play throughs so far and I love it , be it with a but.. following descriptions of a play through might contain some spoilers - but they are necessary for you to understand what you are getting yourself into...First time I didn't really know what I was doing, and just went with the flow. Introduced free market economics, boy, the big corporations loved me. It came with a price though, small businesses hates my guts because I hiked up their tax rates.. I introduced some nice big projects which benefitted the country for sure. Also drastically improved the health and education for everyone. However, due to external and internal threads, I let the old guard talk me into calling out a state of emergency , great , we finally gonna get the bastards threatening the state. (ok, the promised constitutional reforms had to be put on hold, but hey, the country's existence is at stake here!) If only it wasn't a ploy by the old guard - first chance they saw they tried to impeach me! ( I only followed their advice, now they are punishing me for it? oh yeah, I might have taken some tiny little bribes but all for the country , didn't make me richer) - bottom line, got impeached  and arrested by the military when they launched a coup. Hey, all I ever did was in the interest of the country, ungrateful bunch!Then another run I stood my ground - fixed the economy , pushed through institutional reforms (with majority of votes even from the supreme court.. due to intensive lobbying and compromising) , tried to be fair to all communities , tried to stay as centrist as possible. Everyone was happy , got a lot of support from everyone, no more riots going around (ok, the sollists and traditionalists weren't happy as they thought I had gone off too far from the party lines..) - so I was doing great (or so I thought) and I was very sure of my second term. But then Rumberg started stirring things up, and in order to be ready to defend our beautiful country I aligned with the ATO , which most of the newspapers agreed was a necessary step. But somehow those damn sollists/traditionalists though otherwise and accused me of giving the country away. Before I knew it, the economy hit rock bottom (don't ask my how, pretty sure I was sabotaged - that's a minus in the game - you have no real insights) and that nasty woman of a minister stabbed me in the back, ran for party leader, won the majority of the votes! I tried setting up my own party, but nobody wanted me anymore - Such ungrateful ******, after all I had done for the country. I made the country great! So I finally retired to that cute little winery I had purchased , made loads of money while my wife was suddenly getting high up the ladder in the political world - we became the most influential couple ever. Made up with our estranged son, and lived up to a ripe old age.. Something good came of it after all!And with above tales of how fun a play through can be, follows the but.. It feels that whatever choice you make, in the end the game always set you up for failure - only if you follow the party lines will you succeed and for that you have to put aside all of your values. It doesn't matter that you actually succeed in unifying most of the country, creating a fair and democratic  constitution, create a better healthcare and education system, lift women out of their second tier status, are respected by the majority of the citizens - in the end all that matters seems to be that the ones in your party only want to continue their ways and that you keep on going with the unfair rules (no matter your promises to the voters, the ruling party knows best after all...) All in all, I have been enjoying this game a lot, and it is interesting for sure - just know that your idealist views and good intentions might land you in hot water while playing this game.

_childDocuments_.review: Suzerain, really sets up a realistic and tangible world to explore politics and geopolitics through a personal lens. The mechanics it uses for me was easy to get into while having depth. They did a great job with the codex and having the clickable links in the text to allow easy access. I highly recommend this game if you have an interest in politics, geopolitics, history, or player driven narrative story.
_childDocuments_.name: Suzerain

_childDocuments_.review: Imagine the Paradox grand strategy game Victoria 2/3, but as a choose your own adventure book instead. The game is sufficiently long and detailed enough that your policy choices have logical consequences (at least for the paths I chose), and you feel like each action has an opposite reaction. Stick to your ideals, but don't forget that no man rules alone.Text is cheap nowadays with AI, and I would love for the developers of this game to take their financial success and roll it into a Suzerain 2, as the world building so far has been rich and deep. This game, but twice as long and twice as in-depth, would be a cult classic along the lines of Disco Elysium. I might recommend we move the timeline forward to the early 1990s, and put you into control of the first democratically elected president of the Russia equivalent country after the collapse of the comintern pact. You can then try to reforge the pact, pursue the free market, reinstate the monarchy of old, ect.Not many games have so much potential, but this is one of them.

_childDocuments_.review: TLDR: I think the game is interesting but did not have a lot of playing it. For me, the game had a strong start with slowly falling flat in the second half, as did the general gameloop. Decisions felt unimpactful at times. Review:I played through the game and although I think it is interesting as concept, which I appreciate, I did not have a lot of fun playing it (to be fair, I had a chuckle here and there, especialy with "I bless the Raynes down in Anrica). I played through the game just to see the story and the big ending event, which was very dissapointing to me. As a positive, I think the game can be intriguing at times and if you pay enough attention, it lets you connect dots to anticipate certain events happening down the line. Other times, foreshadowing of some events overstayed their welcome and felt unrealistic, as I do not think a president would ignore these obvious signs for 3+ years. Another positive I think is that the game has a really strong start. On the other hand, the more the game progressed, the more flat it felt, for me. Some characters I tried to interact with them positively throught the game and it did not matter at all, since a lot of them ended up not liking me.Things I did not like in my playthrough was the "blindness" you have on upcoming events. They are mentioned in reports and conversations and you are allowed to make your own notes, but yeah. Wish there was more game to it? I would appreciate the game telling me - these are the policies currently being worked and this is the amount of budget it will cost to implement them. I could have tracked this by myself for sure, but really did not find it exciting enough to make notes after work on which policy will probably eat my budget.Also the game loop was fun at the start, but by the end of the game asking everyone about their opions three times and then clicking "I am ready to make a decision" started to get repetetive.Other thing I did not enjoy was the fact that sometimes my decisions felt unimpactful. There are three main areas where I felt this the most:I feel like this game would be best enjoyed (at least the first playthrough) by playing heavily into either the extremely ATO narrative or into the UCP narrative.

_childDocuments_.review: its fun and innovative story telling with great characters drives this gamethe decisions you make seem complex and nuanced, but fall flat on simulating their actual consequences its a game about politics so unintended effects are the core of decision making and interesting story telling, but it quickly gets exhausting to have everything implode because you tried to compromise, which causes triggers for multiple bad events that compound each othermy advice for your first run: Pick a role in the prologue and stick to it, the more ideologically charged the better as this will protect you from exposing yourself to too many threats the game throws at you at once.

_childDocuments_.review: Suzerain is an incredible game full of complexity. It creates an environment where political ideologies, organizations, social movements, characters and companies coexist, and the player must decide who to support and favor. The wide range of personal choices allows you to shape the nation to your own style and experiment with different ideologies. In addition, the plot goes beyond politics, including the personal story of the protagonist with his family and friends, which adds layers of immersion and humanity to the narrative.The only downside is the lack of translation into other languages ​​(such as Portuguese), which limits the experience for those who do not have an advanced knowledge of English. Despite this, I was able to enjoy the story using the camera of the Google Translate app on my phone and the translation of screenshots through the Google Translate website. Even with this obstacle, it was worth the effort to immerse myself in this unique and complex world that Suzerain offers.

_childDocuments_.review: Suzerain has a great premise and a captivating story. That said, the games presentation (and marketing) contradict the game play experience. Make no mistake, Suzerain is little more than a novel with limited RPG elements and a frustrating strategy game interface.Suzerain  a strategy game and neither is it a political simulation. There is essentially one story, one plot you are following. There is no variation. Every time you play it, you're faced with the same series of events, the same faces, the same actors, the same political situations, and despite radically different attempts, the majority of your choices will land you in the same spot. Suzerain taunts the player with a veneer of choice.Your choices in Suzerain have very little impact on what actually happens. The majority of major events are boiled down into a few main outcomes, and depending on certain choices made before the game starts, you will almost inevitably find yourself there.In regards to the writing, the story initially drew me in, but upon additional playthroughs (something which encouraged by multiple different paths and over 80 Steam achievements). The fictional world of the game is neither charming or interesting. The nations, regions, and people are charactures of real ones, but the charactures are grating and at times offensive — if its meant to be satire, it's not good satire. The overwhelming number of characters hamfisted into the story (combined with their obnoxious names) leaves you utterly confused as to who is doing what, where, and why. Don't get me started on how you also have to learn not fictional region names, but also numerous fictional city names. Constantly zooming in and out of the map from the dialogue screen is physically sickening.This leads me an irking issue with the game in general. The lore of the game and core mechanics seem to have been written by someone who is both heavily biased and largely ignorant (or just didn't care). You can't challenge a free market economy. It's obnoxious. Your advisors, those around, everyone urges you to constantly pursue capitalism. The game has already decided the outcome of your choices. If you choose one route, it will not allow you to succeed. Keep in mind, I say this as a staunch capitalist. If I'm given a choice, allow that choice to be viable.Which leads to one of the biggest gripes with the game: choice. In a game which gives the facade of agency, most of your choices have no impact. You will choose to click many options. The game assaults you with a nauseating amount of choices. Do you say "let's begin" or do you say, "Welcome, everyone. Thank you for joining us." This choice or some variation of it make up the majority of the interactions you will have in this game.Again, remember, the developer wants you to *play this multiple times*.The indicators in the top left of the screen are next to useless. And, honestly, most of your decisions which affect the indicators too. Even if you're doing amazing with the economy, it will reflect in the red until suddenly, the economy is great and everyone loves you. Have you ushered in peace and stability by focusing funding on the military and police? You will still see repeated dialogues and confrontations about how there is "No Stability or order in Sordland." The consequences from decisions are often unclear or irrelevant to the actual decision. Often times, your decisions have no discernible affect in the outcome. The number of significant events which just cease to ever be mentioned again or have any impact on reality.I want to like this game. If you had asked me after my first play through, I'd have told you I loved it. But multiple play throughs later and I can't recommend this game. For a text-based game it's not acceptable to offer just support for one language. Having your game translated in at least a few languages greatly boosts sales and is really not impossible to finance even for smaller studios. Secondly I wish the game would support Steam remote play but that's probably not on the priority list. Another problem about accessibility is the lack of responsiveness from the gameplay itself. It's pretty hard to plan ahead when you have a hard time finding out how your decisions affected the country. There is a country overview and there are newspapers and reports but it's not easy to see the difference between what is fluff and what is a key result of your policies. Or take the budget for example. It's very hard to find out what budget you could spend if you have no idea how much money you will make back over the future. It would be much better if there are funds added to your budget each turn so you could plan. On the top of that the economic development will jump up and down immensely for no obvious reason. _childDocuments_.review: The best game I've played in a while - hands down. Work, life busyness and changing interests mean I don't play videogames anymore however this game changed that. Sinking a good amount of time (32+ hours) over the past week after work, I can heartily recommended this text-based choose-your-own-adventure game to anyone interested in strategy, resource management, politics (duh!), corporate decision-making, and roleplaying and immersion. This game sits at a unique intersection between all these things and does it with no competition. I'm immersed, submerged in rivalling political advice and suspicions of intrigue, and my girlfriend jokes I'm addicted. I also co-govern the country with her when she comes round. Suzerain rewards sound decision-making and attention to detail. It doesn't spoon feed you - you remember a detail from an hour ago? A suspicious gap on a potential political hire's resume? Factor them in your decisions and avert disaster. Good outcomes from your choices are seriously satisfying, and bad decisions leave you winded - it’s that well-designed. I have never felt so much suspense playing a videogame (or while watching a movie or reading a book) ever. I held my breath up to an important vote that could make or break my administration, I wondered if I had done enough, and... I'll stop it there. The story is well-crafted and well-written. Final comment: I work in the public sector, I like politics, and I like strategy. With that in mind, I seriously recommend this choice, Mr President.

_childDocuments_.review: Here's a truth about the world: Everyone has their own ideas on how things should run, and when you're in charge of a nation, that's going to cause headaches and rob you of sleep.Enter Suzerain, a game about precisely that. In short, Suzerain is a political sim/visual novel. Instead of giving you a country to do with as you will, you will follow a relatively linear plot, but with a lot of freedom to steer it. As Anton Rayne, newly elected president of Sordland, you couldn't have wished for a messier start. After a couple decades of coups, civil war, and stagnation that culminated in a catastrophic recession and societal collapse, you've got your work cut out for you. No matter what you promised to get elected, whether reform, or to uphold the legacy of the past leaders, you will need to contend with people who wouldn't like anything more than your head served on a single platter, and that's before you face the fact that the nation is in shambles, a lot of problems need fixing, and you don't have the resources to tackle them all.The characters you meet all have personalities, ideals, dreams, and agendas (though some are more fleshed out than others). Understanding them is crucial to winning their support, or at least getting them not to oppose you directly. Sordland is a troubled nation in an unstable region of the world, the world itself is locked in a Cold War-esque era of ideological tension that's threatening to turn hot. Guiding a nation to reform or to reclaiming some sort of a past glory in such an environment is no easy task as vultures circle. The game doesn't shy away from difficult topics and does a brilliant job in relaying a second truth about the world: People have reasons for their ideas and agendas, and those reasons are rarely as simple as "Oh, they're just naive/misguided/bigoted fools". This, especially in today's world, is going to make the game extremely niche, and not only because of its very specific genre mix, and I do need to congratulate the developers for making something this daring. You will be forced into decisions. Some of them will be easy, some of them will not. How easy or hard they are will depend on what kind of President Rayne you want to play, but nothing is free, no good deed goes unpunished, and no ideal exists in a vacuum.Want to get of a corrupt Chief Justice? You may want to pass legislation that allows you or the Assembly to remove judges from service, but what kind of precedent does it set, and is that the right way if your problem is limited to that one judge who puts personal gain above duty? Maybe you recognize the fact that the office of President holds too much power, and wish to address that for the good of the nation, but how does that help if your own proposal, if it passes, can get you booted before you manage to accomplish any significant constitutional reform because some vengeful rival decided to use it against you and then install someone unscrupulous?Suzerain does well to realistically simulate the politics of the real world - as in, even if you don't opt for campaigns based on guile and deception, but value honesty and transparency instead, it's still going to be a tangled mess, and you will not accomplish anything with just ideals and charisma, because, in the end, no man rules alone, and Anton Rayne is no exception. Every decision you make will affect the nation, and the region. Sometimes even something as innocuous as phrasing your proposals may make someone support or oppose you. Or what you order for lunch when meeting them. Do not take power lightly, for it is not a toy. Suzerain may not appeal to a wide public. It's slow, it deals with topics that people can be uncomfortable with, and it really pushes the message hard, that the world is complicated, people are complicated, that sometimes doing something good will involve a painful concession somewhere else, but you'll still be expected to figure it out and deliver on what you promised to deliver, no matter how bad your hand may be.So, good luck, Mr. President. You will have a hard time. Your choices will have consequences. And you will question if you're doing the right thing, even if it looked brilliant on paper.And, with the 2.0 update, you'll have even more content, lore, character development, and headaches. Give it a whirl, it's worth it!

_childDocuments_.review: I've never written a steam review before but my excellent experience with Suzerain has prompted me to sing the praises of a game that I've thoroughly enjoyed. Suzerain is a nuanced and engaging political and economic simulator set in a fictional vaguely eastern European nation called Sordland in the 1950s. You play Anton Rayne, the newly elected 4th President of a troubled country facing several seemingly insurmountable challenges: a deep recession, a flawed and fractured political landscape, and looming international crises. On its own these challenges make for interesting player choices. Do you privatize certain industries to bring market forces to your country or do you maintain state control in order to prevent people from being exploited by businesses? Its all up to you. But are you ready to accept the consequences? Your decisions will impact the lives of many and not always for the better.In the political arena, your nation must come to terms with the complicated legacy of its living, but retired, larger-than-life founder, who casts a long shadow over your Sordland's constitution, your presidency, and fellow countrymen. However, not all struggles you face will be a result of his decisions for Sordland's customs and ideas around ethnicity, nationality, gender, and ideology are deeper and more pervasive.To top it off, you must balance your personal relationships with all the important figures in Sordland. From business people, to prominent elected leaders, and members of your own cabinet, you will make choices that inspire, disappoint, and frustrate many who you will need to rely on to fix your country. Meanwhile at home you struggle to balance the needs of your family with the demands of your job as president.While all the above pieces are enough on its own to make a worthwhile experience the thing that elevates Suzerain above other similar strategy and simulator titles for me is the writing. Torpor Games have been able to create deep nuanced characters, each with their own motives and realistic reactions to the world and your choices. Some are petty, others professional. Negotiating with someone to ideological, another leader might be more compromising. For President Anton Rayne, the player character, the writing is particularly strong and flows in a way that makes the path you walk realistic while keeping the characterization strong. Is Anton good at hiding his worries and frustrations? Does he value his principles above making a material difference for his country? Does he believe that his compromises are worth it. Is he a power hungry raging misogynist? You are given a wide range of ways to respond to the world and your own choices that forge an interesting and believable character. The dialogue is witty, the world filled with deep lore, and the humor of the game shines through when you need a chuckle. Multiple times during my playthroughs I found myself in shock, disturbed, humored, saddened, and deeply touched. To me, the writing matches any decent novel and has impacted me in a similar way.If I had one personal frustration with the game which was the save feature. Torpor clearly want your decisions to matter so after almost any choice your save updates to make you live with the consequences. As a design choice it works well and works to resist your impulse to save scum and simply enjoy the result of your decisions, good or bad. This feature is probably one of the best in the game but after one or two playthroughs I found myself wishing to experiment to see what different choices in the dialogue would do. However, the autosave feature does, in my view, limit that kind of experimentation as you might have to restart a save or create multiple save files in order to conveniently accomplish this. Nevertheless, the auto save feature does help make the game what it is and is better for it. However, maybe Torpor's future titles could explore a chapter save feature, but my gripe here is minor and did not severely impact my enjoyment of this excellent game.I am certainly looking forward to whatever is next in the world that Suzerain has created. It has become one of my favorite games this year and I've recommended it to many of my friends who also have found enjoyment in the story, characters, and choices that Suzerain offers. Suzerain is clearly a labor of love and that dedication shines through. In an era where many studios cannot seem to write compelling stories Suzerain stands above. For anyone who is a fan of strategy games, rich stories, choose your own adventures, and simple gameplay. Suzerain might just be for you.A Morgna wes core. Vectern sis da!

_childDocuments_.review: For disclosure, this product was received for free for testing purposes prior to game release. Also, my favorite thing in this game has got to be the music! It's well done, timed quite well, and it'll certainly set the atmosphere for ya.Suzerain is an interesting political simulator that, as many will tell you, works in a choose your own adventure way. The numerous decisions give you the ability to apply your own thoughts and feelings on the world around you and the decisions to be made. Who needs that bailout money more? Businesses or people? Perhaps neither? Should you even bother with that mega-infrastructure project? It does seem quite expensive! Maybe all these protesters should be declared enemies of the state? Or perhaps they just need to see you in person or on national TV? All these choices and much more are possible in Suzerain!You are the President Anton Rayne of Sordland in 1954 and you have just begun your first term, congratulations! The economy is in a recession due to the 1951 crash of your predecessor, the Northern neighbor Rumburg has been becoming increasingly expansionist, two ideological superpowers both want to draw Sordland into their sphere due to its critical resources and location, there is growing social unrest due to ideological differences in Sordland and several minority populations, and finally you have your group of ministers who each have their own ideas on what should be done to solve the problems that plague the fledgling Republic. Some don't agree with each other and you're stuck with them!How you lead will quite literally save or break the country in one of the most high tension moments in its history. Can you save the Republic from the hounds of dictatorship and fix its broken Constitution? Can you stop the recession from the crash of 1951 and bring back a booming economy? Will Sordland stand strong alone, find allies, join one of the two ideological superpowers, or be crushed under the boots of superior invaders? Will you be a good father to your family or will you be abusive? Will Serge become your friend? Will your Sordland survive or will she be reduced to ashes in the wake your failures Mr. President?Only you can figure that out by leading Anton Rayne through his first term as President of Sordland! Come take the oath and be inaugurated during the most trying time in Sordland's history!A morgna wes core, vectern sis da!(A morning will come, victory is close!)
_childDocuments_.name: Suzerain

_childDocuments_.review: Tagged as a political simulation, it's actually a visual novel.It's very well-made. Good world-building, believable plotlines, decent writing, few spelling mistakes, agreeable visuals and music. It also manages to treat all political decisions as justifiable and reasonable from certain points of view, and as far as I've gotten into it has not done any overt ideological moralizing. But it's still just a visual novel, and I hate visual novels. They occupy a disgusting wet patch between games and books that gives me nothing but disappointment. The writing is good, so I'd like to read how the story goes on, but that's not possible because it's not a story but a bunch of scripted events. I'd want to play a simulation game, but it's not that either.This wouldn't have happened if nobody had mis-tagged it as a sim, but here we are.
_childDocuments_.name: Suzerain

_childDocuments_.review: Very simply, there is another review around that states "I did what I would have done and it worked out." I am here to say, I did what I would have done and  and during the next playthrough I . On the third try, . Lastly, I know from accidental spoilers that you can , etc., etc., etc...The fact that my game was different than the other review, and from the other games I had played, is what you're looking for in a good review for Suzerain. The game is intricate, enjoyable, and replayable. You definitely feel like the leader of a struggling nation. Your allies feel like allies, your enemies feel like enemies, and both can become the other as you understand (and exploit) their desires and weaknesses to help you secure a future for your country. The creator put a lot of thought into the personalities and paths you can discover, and you can easily get at least 4-5 solid playthroughs before even considering the Rizia DLC. The price is worth it. You should buy it. That said, there are two flaws in the game:1) The map is beautiful, and the icons are nice, but it doesn't really change in the way that a usual map-based grand strategy game does. If you're into beautiful maps, you'll love it. Just don't expect to paint it. The game is beyond that simple objective anyway.2) The entire game is dialogue-driven. You can make the dialogue go faster by clicking through the narrative, but be careful not to accidentally click a confirmed response by your character, because there is no going back. For this, you need to engage with much of the same dialogue during subsequent playthroughs, and so replayability suffers a bit. However, I think it would hurt the game to offer simple, dialogue-skipping options such as (Stay Sollist) or (Push Reforms) or (Be Moderate). The feeling of being an actual person among actual people is unique, and I'm personally okay with this singular issue with replayability.

_childDocuments_.review: This is another one of those games where I would click on "Neutral" if I could. In the end I have decided that I don't want to recommend this game, despite having had a unique experience playing it.Like many others have already pointed out, this is not a simulation, but rather more of a choose-your-own-outcome type of novel. The experience as I have said is very unique, in that you can really live through the things you have to deal with as a head of state. Unfortunately, I have found the system to be too simplistic, especially in terms of managing the budget. You are never given the rundown of exact figures about the income and spending, so it is hard to gauge if the current balance is acceptable at any given point.The game revolves around a series of choices, and there are plenty of them, but there are a number of issues with this.The game keeps track of your most meaningful decisions, and it feels good to look at the records of your actions accumulate, but the problem is that once you hit the ending, the game does not recap your achievements, and it ends up feeling very hollow. The game roughly feels like a 1950s cold war era, and the atmosphere is set up to feel very gloomy, which is not necessarily a bad thing, but it all really piles up on top of you emotionally when you are trying so hard to make the right decisions and things constantly go wrong.I found a few of the characters to be charming, but as a whole, they all feel a bit forced, as by the end you realise that every single one of them ends up having some sort of a problem. It all gets a bit predictable. The state of the country of Sordland at the beginning also is incredibly abysmal, so much so that you wonder how the hell the country managed to exist so far without more drastic upheavals. At a developer's standpoint, I see that the intention was to create a situation where the player is forced to prioritise between all the different problems, but it really hurts immersion when the problems are so numerous that the country might as well be called a failed state right from the get-go. (Perhaps the problem is that I am applying 21st century standards and values on what is supposed to be a roughly 1950s country - but hang on, aren't we all doing that right now as players? We are all living in 2020 after all, not in the 1950s.)I have sat through 23 hours of this game, engrossed in the narrative of it all despite getting more and more exhausted, but at the end, all I got was a bad ending and no acknowledgement of what kind of country I was shaping Sordland to become, no acknowledgement of all those numerous thoughtful decisions. A save/load feature would have helped, and I think I get what the devs were trying to do in not including such a system, but alas, I don't think I can sit through another 23 hours of depression just to try and get a somewhat more satisfying version of the brief ending that I had gotten, especially when I cannot even obtain the help of a save/load system to ascertain that I will indeed succeed in doing that. Where's my reward?

_childDocuments_.review: Take this review with a grain of salt. If you enjoy text-based simulators that makes you feel immersed in its world, this game might be for you! This is more for me to vent and explain my exasperation with this game.As I am writing this, I am still gripped with the feeling that I should love this game. The text-based decisions and storytelling, a cast of characters that often feel fleshed out with clear motivations, and the atmosphere of the world building (one that mirrors the cold war atmosphere of our world) has at times made me feel as though I am in the shoes President Rayne as he attempts to pull Sordland from the brink of crisis. Yet at the same time, every attempt at the main campaign (successful or not) has left me frustrated and wishing I hadn't bothered. This game is walls of text leading to political/social/economic/interpersonal decisions that have major implications with little to no feedback as to how those decisions will affect your play through. The only indicator of economic growth? A single line on the top bar that either goes up or down. I had my economic minister tell me all the great things my economic plan had wrought and that we were making strides to tackling the recession. In the next breath he tells me that Sordland has entered a depression cycle due to "The Debt Crisis" and we have failed to address the people's economic concerns. Following this conversation, the economic bar graph shows a super green upwards trajectory despite the depression. What frustrates me more, you cannot find a solid explanation or consistent reasoning for when events like this trigger. I can only assume that My VP tells me we are going to sweep the elections with a 20% gain for the party despite lowering the threshold to 3% for new parties! We are headed for re-election! The result: I lose the election as the USP comes in third...The next turn. After navigating a diplomatic mission spanning the entire campaign to avoid going to war. And spending money on all ministries except for military to address welfare and corruptions concerns. There were no indications that I had suddenly lost this support at any point.2.0 added additional content for Bergia, leads to a greater story line regarding the Bluds. However, This game PUNISHES you for not knowing the sequence of events ahead of time. You are forced to use guides in order to get an optimal outcome, and even then the guides are not fool-proof. There is a lack of consistency on top of the lack of transparency as to which events or bills or decisions affect the big picture. It gets especially frustrating when you have go back through the text trees every time you restart.This could be because I am just not patient enough for the game, or that I am obstinate in my play style, however I can't help but feel baffled by how this game is structured. What's more, 3.0 came with the release of the Kingdom of Rizia DLC that looks intriguing on its own with unique mechanics and I was initially excited to transfer my Rayne campaign over after purchasing. I am glad I decided to wait until I played this game again to remind me what I did not enjoy about it the first few times around.Also, Despite all the additions to the game after 2.0, Kind of a let down, and even moreso when you consider there is a more in-depth war mechanic in the Rizia DLCRegardless, I encourage you to look at what others think. Many others enjoy this game, so I must be missing something!

_childDocuments_.review: One of the best games I've ever played in my life. It is a visual novel. A choose your own adventure game about political power in a richly defined and immersive universe. This game takes a lot of reading. The main way you play the game is through reading through dialogue with your ministers, reading status reports from around the country and ratifying legislation. There is even an extensive codex filled with background information about every nation, person, corporation, branch of government etc. This is a very nerdy game. You will get the most out of it if you take your time and get to know the world that you shall be playing in and, most importantly, the country that you shall be leading.

_childDocuments_.review: I bought this game after it was sitting on my wishlist for about a year because the description seemed interesting and I was bored. What I got was possibly my favorite game I've ever played, and certainly one of the most artfully crafted games since This War of Mine. Bravo!Edit:After completing the game for the first time, I must say that Suzerain is a masterpiece of a narrative game. It has brought me to tears over and over by the incredible depictions of love, duty and humanity. I'm not sure I would play it through a second time, only because I feel like I ran the country exactly aligned with my values and achieved a successful ending, but as far as quality of gameplay, strength of narrative and lasting emotional and intellectual impact, that one playthrough would have been worth the $60 of a major studio game with hundreds of hours of gameplay and replayability. 10/10. 5 stars. The atmosphere is great and it forces you to make difficult decisions that have a true impact on the game. Very reminiscent of 1984 and other Orwellian stories. I also enjoyed the story around your private situation, which gives it an extra layer that you don't immediately think about when you think politics.There is a lot of reading involved, but I didn't mind that because the it's written well. _childDocuments_.review: Suzerain is a text based game that revolves around becoming the president of a country and leading the path of said country over a presidential term. This is a great game for people who find political intrigue and management to be interesting and appealing. When I first fired up this game, I was afraid that the minimalist presentation would turn me off. That said, the longer I played this game, the more sucked into the plot line I became.After checking out some of the discussion threads on this game, It seems that many of the events and organizations in this game are analogues for some real world counterparts. The thing I found the most interesting is how the interpretations of things can vary based on where you are from in the world. I'm sure there is something much of this was based on but many of the scenarios and factions can really fit into whatever world view you are looking at it from. I hope that more games of this type come from this developer. This is a unique game and I would love to see it expanded on a bit in another title or a sequel.

_childDocuments_.review: This game is currently in the Humble Choice for April 2022, this is part of my coverage of the bundle. If you are interested in the game and it's before May 3rd, 2022, consider picking up the game as part of the current monthly bundle.A visual novel mixed with a country simulator. Suzerain takes a bit to start. The first half-hour has you playing the backstory of your character in a visual novel style while making choices to define your character. Do you stand against tyranny or avoid conflict? Do you want to become a lawyer, economist, or history professor? Each of these helps define your character.Then one day you become president and the real game begins. You’re in charge of a vast country and now need to bring the country out of the current recession, fulfill promises made to the populace, and navigate the waters of the presidency. This is done through a lot of visual novel style discussions complete with the player asking questions, and choosing different answers depending on the situation. These answers should likely change the course of the country or the game, but I didn’t have enough time to see this. There are nine different endings and even more sub endings so it’s very likely what you do will matter throughout the game. Pick this up if you like the idea of a visual novel that’s focused on running a country, rather than trying to date random waifus. It’s a unique take and the writing is well done, but it’s also a lot of writing. It is an interesting concept though and I’m curious as to how far it will take the story. If you enjoyed this review or want to know what I think of other games in the bundle, check out the full review on or subscribe to my Youtube channel:

_childDocuments_.review: Suzerain is truly an immersive political "visual novel". Although the world is fictional, it has many connections to our world and as result it is very believable and immersive. Set during a "cold war" between capitalist West and communist East, the game places you in the shoes of Anton Rayne, newly elected president of Sordland. You will be presented with various choices during your term ranging from how to deal with deep recession to how to respond to multiple differing internal and external threats preparing to take advantage of the weakened Sordland. You must be vary of many factions and persons trying to influence your decisions. Do not however underestimate your opposition, as they are ready to end your presidential term prematurely given the chance if you force them no other choice.There are many ways to play the game. You can basically choose yourself what kind of a character Anton Rayne is depending on the choices and answers you make. You can be right-wing or left-wing, authoritarian or libertarian, progressive or conservative, corrupt or idealistic and anything between. I felt that choices I made truly mattered and changed how the game progressed, as there are so many different ways to react to and solve those problems. I have only played one game so far, but I can confirm that that path worked well and felt very immersive all the way from the beginning to the very end.I consider this probably to be my favourite political simulation game of all time. Only con would be the length as I managed to get through the game in ten and a half hours, but as they say, quality over quantity. I am very eager to one day try a different path for Rayne and Sordland.I will end this review with a lengthy summary of my game for those of you who might find it interesting. There will be spoilers.*Spoilers*In my playthrough Anton Rayne took as his utmost goal to continue free market reforms of the last president as a means to lead Sordland out of the deep recession that was forcing this once fine nation to a path of certain new civil war. Investment programs, privatization initiatives and free trade deals are examples of the measures taken to revitalize the economy. Rayne was not a puppet to the local oligarchs however, as along with the market reforms he also adopted many pro-employee programs to help them during these difficult times. Minimum wage laws and relief coupon bills were passed through the Great Assembly with the support of the president, even though the mighty corporations were against these reforms. As a result, after his four-year term the economy of Sordland had recovered. GDP almost had almost doubled, and unemployment dropped by staggering circa 12 percent.Second goal of Rayne administration, probably at least as important for the stability of Sordland, was to reform the old constitution. It had made republic of Sordland to something of a presidential dictatorship. With skillful diplomacy the Rayne administration managed to pass the constitutional reforms both in the legislative Great Assembly and in the upper Court. Sordland was on the path of democracy. New constitution included reforms like lowered election threshold, clear division of power and curtailed presidential powers. It was not perfect, as compromises had to be made, but result was acceptable by all standards.During his term Rayne also managed to lead Sordland to join the alliance of western capitalist democracies, ATO (equivalent to our NATO), raised living standards of all citizens, showed diplomatic excellency avoiding conflicts abroad and helped the dire situation of women and Bludish minorities in Sordland. His personal life felt the stress of the presidency too, but in the end his family always stayed by his side. As his term came to an end, Rayne had yet again managed to get his divided party to unite for his reelection by defeating his nationalist conservative opponent within the party. Rayne had finally gained the upper hand, or at least so he thought, only to lose it all in the upcoming elections. The people of Sordland had decided, that they wanted even more liberal reforms in the future. Major opposition party had won the elections for the first time in the history of Sordland. Although a loss and a vote of non-confidence for his party and rulership, Anton Rayne felt relief for the first time in all of these years of turbulence. Finally, the Morning had come for Sordland and her people.

_childDocuments_.review: The best political game I've come across. It somehow feels like a tabletop RPG. Very addictive, intriguing, and well-made. _childDocuments_.name: Suzerain

_childDocuments_.review: It's a great visual novel with many endings, it encourages replayability with the many outcomes and special dialogues but it really feels like a chore for each consecutive replay just because you have to go through the same starting dialogues in the first hour. Developers please, add a fast forward conversation or save point so we can skip the intro and starting turns to find the different endings. It'll make the experience for us more enjoyable. _childDocuments_.review: Suzerain has many hidden mechanics and is extremely unforgiving. This is Murphy's Law the gaming simulator. Some people will enjoy the long and complex narratives, I found them interesting the first couple of times. _childDocuments_.review: Really interesting stories and lots of cool decision making! It definitely makes the game replayable with all the potential pathways and choices. And the decisions you are faced with are most of the time not easy to decisions to make, and you're forced to make some serious trade-offs.
