_childDocuments_.review: EXCELLENT GAME, BUT STILL TOO BUGGY TO RECOMMEND.This game is unique because it puts you in the role of running a tumultuous developing country. The branching choices are also highly nuanced—there is no "right" or "wrong" thing to do because no matter what option you pick, you will alienate large parts of your country. Suzerain is so good at capturing the stress of being president that I now have tremendous compassion for leaders worldwide. Heck, during my first term in virtual office, the economy tanked, and riots broke out in the streets. If there's one thing this game does, it shows you that you're not as good at solving global problems as you think.Having said that, I can only recommend the game once the branching storyline bugs are fixed. Although these are rare, just one bug destroys the entire experience—you're going to spend hours worrying about making the right decision, and the story veers off in a nonsensical direction. For example, I increased the health budget and spent considerable money on it. The health minister told me we beat the pandemic thanks to the funding, and there's nothing to worry about. The next thing I knew, he resigned from the cabinet and told me we couldn't beat the pandemic due to lack of funding. Huh? Other players have also reported similar inconsistencies, such as aligning with one nation and later finding out that the game aligned them with the opposite nation. Or send someone to prison only for that person to appear in public later.As I said, these bugs are rare, but in a game where even the most minor decision can have disastrous ripple effects, it ruins the experience. The developers have acknowledged these bugs and are closing them one by one with every patch and update, but if you want to purchase this game, wait for a while until a final version comes out that fixes everything.I should have done that myself.
_childDocuments_.name: Suzerain

_childDocuments_.review: This game was a sleeper hit for me. I bought this when it came out and almost three years later I still play and think about it. Torpor Games really knows how to get the player invested in their characters as well as develop choice mechanics that have significant impact on the game world. I cannot recommend this game enough.
_childDocuments_.name: Suzerain

_childDocuments_.review: This is the game that I have been craving for many years now. The story and mechanics of the game are very compelling and the many different paths that you can take has provided a lot of replayability. I can only hope that we will either see another 4 years of Mr. Raynes or at least an indirect sequel to this very promising game.
_childDocuments_.name: Suzerain

_childDocuments_.review: This is an amazing narrative driven political journey that puts you in the position of being 4th president of Sordland, Anton Rayne, a new leader to a country with a turmoil filled past that has left long lasting impacts on the culture and state of the nation. You must save the country from a recession, address the concerns of a lingering military threat from the nation of Rumburg, deal with the Oligarchs whom dominate the private sector, enact or oppose democratic reforms, determine the budgetary priorities of your administration, deal with scandals, and make constant hard decisions that will ultimately decide the future of the Sordland. This narrative does all it can to draw you into the story behind Sordland, the current climate of the world geopolitically and most importantly the life of Anton Rayne whom you play in this story. Your decisions shape Sordland, will you enact Democratic Reforms, will you make the Soll Dictatorship look like a walk in the park, or will you succumb to the many temptations by Oligarchs and attractive women looking to take advantage of your presidency for their own agendas. What will you do? I will tell you what I did, I bought this game and highly recommend it. It is one of, if not the best political sim available. The game is an absolute masterpiece when it comes to making hard decisions in which you feel the impact of every decision,  in addition to creating a realistic political narrative with amazing world building to back it up. It would be a mistake to let this gem slip by without even giving it a try. And this narrative presents enough choices to give you the ability to replay this and see dramatically different results for both your character's ending and the impact of your decisions on the world. I know I certainly plan on replaying the story to see what different routes I can bring Sordland down. Hopefully you will too!(P.S. I have been following this game for quite a long time and I can say for a fact I was not disappointed and the team who worked on this did an amazing job and deserve all the love and support they get for this massive achievement)
_childDocuments_.name: Suzerain

_childDocuments_.review: Without power, you can't make change.I loved this little game.  I found myself furiously reading line after line of text, thinking about the various political interests and constituencies that would either love or hate the directions I took  (and/or the way I communicated them), determining whether I needed to reach out for new political allies or protect my flank and shore up my base, and, most thrillingly, occasionally finding myself compromising on my own ideals (the way a great game will) to generate more power with which I could then pursue the policies I felt strongly about.I'm a political science grad and an attorney, and this game is very good on two levels.  First, it scores points for realism, in the sense that you're immediately confronted with the fact that you cannot get everything you want without angering damn near everybody.  You can't get rights and equality without prosperity, you can't get prosperity without security, and you can't get security without power. Therefore, power = rights?  This is heady political stuff.  And so I found myself trying to garner more and more power and partnering with very questionable political players at the risk of being considered a tyrant in order to enact the reform and humanitarian policies I set out to achieve.  The plight of being a leader forced to make compromise (with others and with yourself) is what this game brings to dazzling light.Second, it's a fun game to play.  I found the adaptive nature of the game and the cause-effect to be intuitive and sensible (even though the political realities could be frustrating).  The ambient music is nice, and the level of detail is perfect - unlike Mass Effect or Skyrim that have tomes upon tomes of background literature, the people who wrote the memos got the  that the reading is manageable and not so overwhelming that you skip it entirely.The only critique I will give is length of the game.  Admittedly, the game summary says it's about "your first term," and I missed that before playing - I was fairly disappointed when the game ended after being reelected (yay!  hint: be a centrist).  I realize that the game can't be a repository for decades of subsequent political developments, personalities, events, and consequences, but at the same  terms of additional gameplay, we're only talking about more text bubbles and map updates, right?  Doesn't seem too much to ask for another term, so that you can gun for reelection AND have another go at governing.  I digress, as I plan on going back as a nationalist dictator with a penchant for violence.  Also, is it possible to get into an extra-marital affair?  Let's find out.-Scooter

_childDocuments_.review: A neat little visual novel about a fictional country and your efforts to bring it into the latter period of the 20th century. It's worth checking out. Here are some thoughts I have about it.With the 2.0 update, the budget implications of nationalization/privatization have become a bit more normal. Nationalizing a major conglomerate only costs 1 budget because the profitability of the company is now sorta taken into account. On the other side, privatizing frees up budget the government would have been spending on maintaining those services as well as giving a little bit from the businesses buying shares/stake/whatever.The conservative faction is for economic planning and against communism. The liberal faction is for workers' rights and against communism. There's a lot of political incoherence going on in general.Some of your ministers that you apparently appointed will be against your stated campaign goals to the point of active sabotage. Others will simply resign at the end of your first term (the end of the game).International events are predicated on the deficit/surplus of one country in order to discourage the player from spending too much money early on. This makes sense as a game mechanic, but can be frustrating to new players.For some reason the local communist party either hasn't read or hasn't internalized Draft Theses on National and Colonial Questions by the Lenin equivalent and therefore isn't trying to unite with the oppressed minority unless they really have to depending on the electoral percentage requirements.There are 3 major political "routes": Democrat (reform the constitution for greater assembly power), Dictator (reform the constitution for greater presidential power in a country with an already very powerful presidency), and Autocrat (work with existing political establishment to maintain the constitution). Both of the routes where the constitution is changed play very similarly. All 3 routes have mostly the same events happen regardless of which route you're on.

_childDocuments_.review: The 25 hours you see on my playtime as of this review are all over the last three days.This is a politics simulation game, presented mostly through text.  There will be lots of reading, and if you want my advice (the only game advice I'll give here, promise) read as much as you can in the in-game encyclopedia before you even make your first decision.  You will roleplay as the new president of a young, troubled republic set in a thinly fictionalized central/eastern Europe.  It will be up to you to make decisions about budget, policy, foreign relations, and even your family life.Is the game good?  The writing is good.  The political situation is both challenging and, imo, believable.  Making good decisions comes down to ideology, pragmatism, and good ol' fashioned interpersonal maneuvering.  In other words, politics.  In other words, leadership.To say it's good would be an understatement.  I was glued to this game.  I cared about the characters, I cared about the imaginary nation of Sordland.  I picked it up during the Winter Sale for six bucks, and that's a criminally low price for a diamond of this luster.10/10  A New Morning Dawns; Victory Is Near; Sordland Forever

_childDocuments_.review: This should be quite an interesting experience between a political sim and a choose your own adventure game. But it’s really not. You can do a perfect job and suddenly without any explanation something tanks in the passing of chapters. I’ve once reached full economy growth going on a full economy state (capitalism, free market and so) but at the start of chapter 4 everything tanks without any explanation. In the same game I calmed all the internal problems (with the most troublesome racial group and the farmers) but suddenly there is unrest everywhere and when you try to understand who is provoking it the games answers on “don’t know, someone is pissed”. This is not even remotely fun, the game is rigged to be one way or you lose, is worse than a choose your own adventure, it’s basically a railroaded experience triggered to fail if you don’t play as the devs wanted.After three playtroughs and after seeing some guides, cause i really wanted answers, is pretty clear that every nationalist, capitalist, liberalist or generally on the right side is a game over, winning by nationalism or supporting a free western market is basically impossibile without a guide, meanwhile if you join the not-soviet or go for full communist choices the streets are paved.This is horrifying agenda, the game punishes you on doing all the right things just cause the devs wanted you to follow only one way, theirs.Avoid it at every cost, if you want a political sim there is better, if you want a cyoa game, there is better.

_childDocuments_.review: Finally a political game that forces you to confront your personal ethical and ideological values with the limitations of the real world. Suzerain is essentially a visual novel political simulator as you try to reform a stagnating and crumbling society while beset by numerous threats both external and internal (some very close indeed!). I enjoyed learning about the things I thought to be important but I could actually compromise on. I learned of values I normally took for granted stringently upheld. I have a deeper appreciation of the difficulty it is to try and run a government and guide a society. I wish certain aspects are a bit more clear in terms of the result but I suppose today's leaders would wish for the level of clarity in this game but otherwise I think its a beautifully made story.Highly recommend if you're interested in civic, history, political science and what it means to be the citizen with responsibility.P.S. Screw you Rumsberg.

_childDocuments_.review: This game gets so many things right and even perfect that its almost impossible to not recommend this game.I will start off by saying its NOT a Political Management game like the Democracy series. This is a linear story whose outcome you massively influence. Imagine a text based Tell Tale game but your decisions actually makes a difference. The first thing you will notice is the extremely detailed lore of the fictional country. Every historical event, landmark, politician, city, political party is extremely detailed and contains lots of information. Take any politician  you will get to know so much about them, their background, their actions, their motivations that you can connect to them and understand why a particular person is the way that they are. You are pulled into this fictional world where every person has a story, every country has a history, every political party has a motive and you feel like a real person making real decisions. I cannot stress how well this is done in this game. Bravo!Secondly, This is not just a game where you manage some budget slider and click a few check boxes. This is a extremely deep simulation where you are given a situation, like which major infrastructure project to invest, whether to take a bribe, be capitalistic or socialist, be traditional or reformer, which country to ally with and a myriad of other choices that directly effect both short term and long term outcomes. I finished the game and went to see the achievements and realised there could have been dozens of other outcomes. This makes replaying the game at least a few times worth itThe political structure is extremely detailed and realistic. You can implement changes to the political structure and see how it actually works and effects your country like Amending constitution, removing the president's power to veto, separate The judiciary with legislation etc. If you love politics and its structure, this is a treatThere are no vague choices. Every choice is distinct and leads to different outcome. Almost no two option for a situation was the same or would have led to similar outcomes. Makes it easy for you to make decisions because you know what it would lead to and how varied it would be. This game pushes you to take a distinctive stance and gives you all the background and motivation to not just be a Centrist, something that's very difficult to implement since being a centrist is always easy. You will always have a sense of what you want to do and what stance to take and your hesitation will come from the political ramifications of those choices, not from the feeling of "Eh, both sounds equally good"There are some issues in the game though. Flow of time is very difficult to comprehend. There is a rudimentary turn based system but time also flows during the turn. Its difficult to grasp how much time has passed between two actions. So sometimes an action you take will show its fruit 1 turn later while some will show right away.The budgeting system is extremely simple consisting whole numbers. You spend somewhere, you get a -1 to that number and you get an income, you get a +1. Its a linear game so this is expected, but I really wish there was more freedom. I cannot change the budget of something unless the story wants me to, or abolish a law right away. The story progresses linearly and you only can make changes in that flow. That's what the game is, but I just wish there was more freedomThis game has been a treat for a political nerd like me. I was pulled into a believe able political struggle of a fictional country and I enjoyed every second of it. I highly recommend this game to anyone who has any slight interest in Politics
_childDocuments_.name: Suzerain

_childDocuments_.review: An absolutely captivating game that I just happened to buy on sale and wish I  had discovered earlier. An absolute gift to those interested in the blending of politics, ideology, strategics, consequential relationships, geopolitics, quality writing and decision making games. Bought and played on the 2.0 update onwards.I could not put this one down, even after my first disastrous run cut short by the ramifications of my rash decisions. Immediately followed up by a second equally captivating playthrough and many more to come I am sure.You will need to read a lot (this will be a dealbreaker for some), and you should invest time in game to learn the hand crafted world with the in game codex and map, but you will be rewarded with an immersive and compelling story, driven by changing set of events depending upon your choices. UI is simple and intuitive, map and characters have good art style and font is nice and readable throughout the game. (important since mostly text driven). I experienced no performance issues in 25 hours over multiple long sessions. I will be buying the DLC and have high hopes for the continued quality of the game with the addition of another playable country. My ONLY selfish wish is that we got to play out a second term, to see our past efforts in motion and new challenges to face, though I do recognise the gargantuan effort that would be required to push forward a story with already so many consequential decisions made and multitudes of alternate paths. Thanks Torpor games, it's a 10/10 in my book. Also EU4 comet sense reference 11/10

_childDocuments_.review: I remember reading someone say how this game perfectly captures the political landscape into game form, where it is all about the people around you. Your advisers is what enables you to do everything in the game, they make your will come true. It makes for the most true to life political game there is, one focused on the people and the journey they go though.
_childDocuments_.name: Suzerain

_childDocuments_.review: Suzerain is probably one of the more enjoyable political simulations that I've ever experienced. It is very different to the other games in the field such as Democracy and is far more story oriented. At times I felt as though I was very involved as President Rayne and making the decisions that would take Sordland forward but it is not without flaws. The writing is quite hokey at times with a clear SJW bent which does feel contrived given the mountain of other problems facing the country. Furthermore it does feel that your choices are binary in places and it's as simple as A or B. However there are some decisions that may have you second guessing and the consequences of your actions are not necessarily immediately clear. The codex of characters, organisations and regions is really well done and helps to immerse you in the story more, and the feeling of a world is something really missing from other games in the genre.Pros+ Immersive world+ Good soundtrack+ The weight in decision making+ ReplayabilityCons- The writing falls off a bit and at times feels forced- Abrupt and unsatisfying ending (there are multiple endings)Overall I can confidently recommend Suzerain for political nerds such as myself. If you like political sims with story this is for you. It's more akin to a visual novel than a sim but it is highly enjoyable while it lasts.
_childDocuments_.name: Suzerain

_childDocuments_.review: The choices that you can make in this game are often dense and crowded in mystery, meaning you never know what the actual decision of your decision will be unless they spell it out. Essentially, this is the narrative version of those 90's point and click puzzle games that gave you zero clues and expected you to stumble in the dark until you somehow figured out the random combination of things to click
_childDocuments_.name: Suzerain

_childDocuments_.review: Absolutely stellar writing and worldbuilding. Being a politician is difficult. Despite my best intentions, I have had playthroughs where I plunged my country into a deep economic and political crisis, after which I was convicted by a military tribunal. I have had others where I died trying to protect my family after losing a war I had initiated myself, riding the high of hubris and overzealous advisers. On other hands, I have presided over booming economies and happy, healthy and educated citizens. It sure brought a smile to my face.A Morgna wes core!

_childDocuments_.review: Suzerain is the ultimate CYOA Political Sim, and it was really a lot of fun. At first the game is overwhelming with everything going on, all the people and countries that are important; but the game does a good job introducing the characters and gameplay in the first chapter. I wish some of the choices were more explicitly clear on what your response was choosing, because I definitely contradicted my policies without realizing it. Also, there appears to be a bug after starting a new game and customizing the character, everything is inaccessible (menu, conversation, etc), forcing a restart of the game. I mistook this for the game being unplayable at first occurrence, but I liked the prologue so much that I reinstalled and was able to play fine after that. But on my second playthrough I experienced the same bug. After closing the game and opening again, no issues. Anyways, back to the game, you really feel the consequences or benefits of your decisions throughout the entire game. From the policies you campaign on in the beginning, to every bill that crosses your desk, to what department needs funding; everything ends up mattering. I really, really enjoyed the storyline and all the vastly different directions you can take the president. I ended up as a Centrist on my first game. I thought I would play this through once and be done, but there were so many regrets I had; I just had to start playing again. First playthrough took ~25 hours reading through all the text (massive amounts). I am certainly skimming through quicker on the second round. Definitely recommend to anyone interested in political sims, CYOA, and who like reading!8.5/10

_childDocuments_.review: Congratulations to Torpor on the release!It's fantastic to see that the project displayed at GIC in 2019 has come to fruition. I was greatly excited to get the game and its living up to all of my expectations! I can't recommend the game enough, even to players who usually pass by text games without giving them much thought.Suzerain really makes you feel invested in the running of Sordland, trying to keep your family safe and whole and your ideals intact. The game creates the atmosphere of tension and scarcity brilliantly and the Codex contains all the vital information so you do not need to memorize every detail of your acquaintances' lives. The writing is clear and logical, while really creating the illusion of an existing country with its culture and history. Moreover, the political processes presented in the game faithfully mirror their real-life counterparts.Cannot recommend the game enough and once again, congratulations to Torpor on this huge succes!

_childDocuments_.review: I haven't finished my first playthrough yet, but I feel I've seen enough to get a feel for the game. This isn't necessarily a bad game, but it is more of an interactive novel rather than a true political sim. I plan to finish at least my current save, but with a much different understanding of what the game is trying to be. *Edit below.If you're looking for for something akin to the Democracy franchise, this is very much not that. The game is set along a narrative (with a story about the president's personal life that I find fairly boring) where various politicians approach you to negotiate legislation. You really don't have any choices to make outside of the narrative. There are no charts or graphs to study prior to making your decisions. You're given only a few short intel briefs and a couple of comments from the appropriate cabinet member before you are required to make major promises and decisions. And you often receive new information about how various factions will react immediately after making your choice. If you are expecting to make a lot of impactful decisions and see results relatively soon thereafter, this is not the game for you.The game map is mostly aesthetic. You move around to different cities to address issues and reports around the map, but there are no real game mechanics that use the map or any of the UI outside of the narrative part of the game. Unfortunately, the narrative part of the game itself is a bit of a slog. Most issues require paragraphs-long interactions with your advisors before making a promise or drafting a bill, but most of the important information could be conveyed in about a quarter of the time. The meat of this game is really the lore, which is decently in-depth. Has clear real-world influences with enough variation to make it interesting, but, again, doesn't really affect the gameplay much. Politicians all have ideological and political alignments, but they are pretty blatant about what they want and there isn't much opportunity to play them against each other. Again, there's no way to interact with any characters outside of the narrative, so who you talk to, about what, and when are pretty forced upon you. Beside that though, you're constantly forced to make decisions with little nuance, being encouraged to follow you campaign promises and/or side with different factions, but these often conflict with choices you made much earlier in the game (even from the prologue) before you had context for the actual issues presented.I picked this up on sale hoping I finally found a decent political sim, but it really is just a choose your own adventure with a political backdrop, at which point I'd honestly just rather play Disco Elysium again.Edit: I've restarted this game 4 or 5 times now, and really feel as though I'm not seeing what the other reviewers are seeing. There is a frustrating lack of ability to deal with you inner circle (especially that annoying VP of yours), and the pacing of you decisions and diplomacy options feel really off. The order in which you deal with issues and meetings is always the same, and the dialog for the main events rarely changes regardless of your choices. There are plenty of paths and new pieces of info to uncover, but every new revelation makes it feel like your past playthroughs were completely useless. Your choices definitely matter, but mostly because a single wrong dialog option will send an entire party against you and because of the shoehorned autosave feature. If you're looking for a political drama narrative and don't really care where the story takes you, you will probably enjoy this game, at least on the first playthrough. If you want to make informed decisions and shape a burgeoning mid-century country in your image, this is not it.

_childDocuments_.review: Suzerain is an excellent game, showcasing the political turmoils of a country in transition. It shows you how complicated politics can be, how staying true to your morals and ideals in such an environment can destroy you, or that compromise with an enemy may be the only way to improve your country. The developers have deftly woven a whole world, with intricate and interconnecting lore that makes the Suzerainverse feel like a real, living world, with each new issue cascading from some earlier historical event. Truly up there with some of the best worldbuilding in video games. Highly recommended, and hopefully Torpor will be able to continue this exploring this universe in the future. They've certainly made me a fan who follow them wherever.

_childDocuments_.review: I find this to be a fantastic game in the way it manages to create engagement and stakes behind almost every decision. There are some minor improvement points. The game's economics - though technically simplistic - are troublesome as it takes time to understand how much "points" you might have to spend and roughly what can cost points and what cannot. The story is also deterministic as far as I can understand; taking the same actions in 2 different games will yield the same results. With the number of choices available this still leaves room for replayability, but you might end up having to replay the early chapters because you fail to understand the scope of the budget. However, in my opinion the game more than makes up for this with its engaging characters and how every decision is a conversation which someone will react to. So many situations that feel tense just because a decision might turn out to have a big impact (politically, personally or economically).

_childDocuments_.review: I do like this game but after some time it becomes painfully obvious that the endings are very poorly designed. Despite all the freedom the player is given throughout a playthrough, not adhering to specific conditions results in always getting certain bad endings. Rather than having endings that fit the player's choices, the player ends up forced to change choices in order to get specific endings (or, rather, not get them).Despite the wide breadth of things that the player can undertake, the nature of the game funneling you into certain endings if you actually do some of the things severely limits your choices in the end. "Mistakes" made early on - and I use the word "mistake" very liberally here - result in failstates showing up hours later.Not only does this idiotic design go against the rest of the game, it's made a million times worse with the whole "one auto-save only" thing and how one playthrough typically takes at least 6 hours. It's not uncommon to play for 2-3 hours only to realise that the game is screwing you over with one of its nonsensical failstates yet again, meaning that your current playthrough is worthless.The endings themselves are also severely lacking. Follow-ups on what happens to individual characters and factions would have gone a very long way.It's a real pity because there is a huge amount of potential here, and the game does feel like something magical on your first playthrough, but the bad ending system and barebones endings just ruin the entire experience. Once the magic wears off and the veil comes down, it becomes very clear that the game just does not respect your time, and that most of what you do doesn't actually matter.Extremely disappointing.

_childDocuments_.review: Wow what a hidden gem, heard about this after Rob Zacny  from Waypoint Radio recommended it. My favorite part of the game is the interpersonal relationships that you develop and how each character has their own agenda, people will lie to you, steal from you, take advantage of you, just like real life! And it's up to you to parse out who is telling telling the truth and who has interests other than their own in mind. There's multiple different endings.. but ... they don't all happen at the end ;)  The game can go multiple different ways, and there's some pretty wild outcomes. _childDocuments_.review: This Was an experience. While i have only had 2 playthroughs both were extremely memorable. This is the potential of video games. To tell stories with the player feeling like their changing the outcome, for better or for worse. Let me tell you the story of my first playthroughWarning SPOILERSI was President Rayne. Elected on a campaign to improve the healthcare, change the constitution and bring liberty to all. A hard line reformer. For the infrastructure project i promoted a grand highway, Improving the roads for the north instead of  a railyard in the center only for the richest to use. When it came to a budget, i drove the country into debt. Spending on everything in hopes itll bring the economy up to pay for it. Healthcare and education were state owned, not privitized. When it came to policy, i went hard with reform. Supporting my wife on freedom of women, rejecting any bill that would hinder the rights of anyone. And when it came time to reform the constitution, i went all in. Changing almost everything, Making the system far more fair and democratic. Democratic, I was labeled a democrat. Refusing to budge with the conservitives on the issue and gaining the support of the left i was confident we could win. we lost by 1 vote. Soll. Reforms crushed as the economy went down. My frivilous spending had a negative effect on the economy, along with the taxes i imposed to try and fix the debt. we tried to fix it with more projects but it wasnt enough. Rumberg was knocking on our door and we made allies with Agnolia, Our long time trade partner. When war came our military was as advacned as we could get. A Volunteer army of 200k. Against rumbers Million soldiers. We fought hard, attempting to encircle them and be on the offensive. But we failed. As i sat in my office a handgun in hand, listening to rumberg soldiers storm the palace, i had accepted my failure. A soldier stormed in, young, much like i was when i was conscripted. I fired. The poor boy dropped dead but his squadmates didnt let me readjust my aim. By the time i was on the floor, bleeding out Knowing for all my failure i would at least not go down a coward.

_childDocuments_.review: The game has both great components and poor sections. Hopefully the following will help you determine if it's for you. The first playthrough is a tour de force of tense decisionmaking, the decline from idealism into cold practicality, and dealing with the shortcomings of others. When it's over, it's not always clear what decisions led to the ending, It's a solid 6-8 hour experience, and if I wrote the review then, or if you only want that one playthrough, I'd recommend it.The following playthroughs are the problem. The text-heavy gameplay means either re-reading the same text once again (there's really less variety than it first appears) or just mashing the space bar until a choice pops up or you see new text. This glacially slow gameplay loop combined with an ironman style seve system means that the number of different endings is immaterial unless you're interested in reading the same story again and again with a handful of changes. I've played this through two and a quarter times, and I won't return.If you're in for one playthrough, I really strongly recommend it. I played until the sun came up that first run. The graphics are fitting, the sound is reaonable, and the decisions feel like real decisions. It's a solid story, and it's great that first playthrough. If you're willing to just spam space, manually back up your saves every turn, or just min-max ruthlessly or follow a guide, you'll know better than me if you want it.If you want a pure governance sim with replayability, it's probably too opaque and slow.Again, if you're keen on getting one amazing playthrough, treat this like a recommend, but I don't see this as replayable, and the ends are simply frustrating. A game with multiple endings, mostly hidden metrics and mechanics, and a slow game tempo, combined with ironman saves, is simply not something I can recommend.

What are my goals? Do I keep my promises? How do I approach conflict? How much do I crave power? Who do I choose to stand beside when times get rough? I feel more human somehow for playing through this. But I don't think I can play it again. I got a good ending (2nd term), my head hurts, and I was on edge the entire time. _childDocuments_.review: TL;DRThis game's dialogues are too long and frequent. The game is not dynamic. I got exhausted by skipping dialogues at some point.----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------You may say, that this game is atmospheric, immersive, versatile in terms of choices.But what I have felt playing this game is not only that feeling of being a part of this really interesting post-war-times-inspired story, I have also felt very bored by some of the trivial dialogues. I expected decision making. What I got was more story-telling focused rather than strategy-focused.Of course, I believe that picking different choices will lead to different outcomes (although some of them are really obvious, one or two really caught me off guard), but I can't play this game like it was something that had all my attention. It feels like a Netflix series themed alike "House of Cards" with some elements of economy and choices. The dialogues are written really nicely, it feels like the characters are talking to you, you can feel the different personalities and points of view. I hope that all the players that are fond of this concept will enjoy and experience the game as it deserves.Overall, this game is decent in my personal opinion. I find the dialogue mechanics too time-demanding for long game sessions.Though speaking objectively, this game is awesome in terms of style and atmosphere.

_childDocuments_.review: Suzerain is a game almost a visual novel in which we play the role of Anton Rayne, who has just been elected president of Sordland, a country modeled on post-Atatürk's Turkey. Sordland is in a difficult situation. He is threatened by, among others, a polio epidemic, war with Rumburg, the Blud rebellion and economic recession. The interior of the country itself is not prepared for sudden changes either. There are fascists in parliament, Soll's conservative influence still remains in the hearts of many politicians. Oligarchs control the country economically, and propaganda education destroys subsequent generations. Put in this situation, Rayne can decide to become a reformer, a sollist, a dictator, a commie, a capitalist, a nationalist, or whatever his heart desires. But he will never be able to fulfill all his goals, because despite becoming president, it turns out that his control over the country is far from perfect. Anton will often have to wonder what is more important: democracy or security, workers' rights or the state's economy, rapid reforms or influence and re-election, and finally politics or his own family.Apart from the great lore and characters, this is the first game since Beholder 1 that presented me with really difficult choices with far-reaching consequences. There are so many choices and they influence each other so much that even though the game does not contain random elements, you often never know exactly what to expect, almost as if you were playing a roguelike. I highly recommend it to anyone as long as they're able to withstand reading a lot of text.

_childDocuments_.review: Hey folks. This game is a real gem. The development team just released a huge content/quality of life update more than a year after its release for free, along with a huge discount so yeah, now's the best time to pick it up and experience it.This is a strategy game with maps and politics, sure. But don't come in expecting a Hearts of Iron-like. For me, this was a wonderful and engaging novel that had me glued to my seat. You are a newly elected leader of a troubled country in a unique time in its history. The soundtrack is enthralling, the writing and characters are fantastic, and the situations/decisions are hugely suspenseful.A very unique aspect about this game is in how it frames the different pathways of political ideology you can choose for your country. The typical left/right divide you may think of in contemporary Western politics is in many ways turned on its head here. This isn't just a cheap reversal of political leanings, the issues facing this country are steeped in real political history. The spectrum of "conservative" to "progressive" is unique to the country's individual geography and history. Fascinating game with engaging and suspenseful writing that may very well help you to better process and rationalize the politics of today from a different perspective.

_childDocuments_.review: Very engaging and enjoyable game. More of a visual novel or choose-your-own-adventure game than a typical political management/simulation game. Choices and decisions have real consequences and have a real sense of weight to them. _childDocuments_.review: ===You should read this b4 buying===Unfortunately there is a character limit, so I can't flesh out my points as well as they deserve to be. Oh well. There are two main problems, the story problem, and the game mechanics problem. =====Story=====The second half of your play through, about 6 hours in, you become a wet rag, and stop doing anything. It's like your character gets a lobotomy and just sits there. Then someone takes you over, coup, invasion, superpower, whatever. Everyone seems to be experiencing this problem, no matter the play style. The threat, whatever it is, is hinted at well in advance, but the game never gives you any options to do anything about it. You gotta understand, the whole game is scripted like those "Walking Dead" comic-book looking games. You basically just choose from responses. You can't do anything that isn't a pre-written event, offered to you at a specific time. Like, idk, missions. The game presents you missions, you go do them. The choice is in how, chosen from among the pre-written responses. So if the game never specifically offers you a way to solve a problem, it CAN NOT be solved. You will run into this. No matter your choices, you will not succeed. I am curious whether this was intended, or just the result of the dev team not being able to tighten up the exponentially branching possibilities. I can totally forgive the later, but it's got to be fixed. pronto dude.====Mechanics====What I cannot forgive is the entire other half of the game. The Economic system. It is absolutely abysmal. Literally retarded.I originally wrote a longer review, so I'll just post whatever fits from the economic part here now. Feel free to read until you get bored. TLDR: don't waste your time! Go outside! Pet a dog!Alright here's what fit:"It's really tempting to get into some economic theory here, and I feel like the game is literally designed to encourage that conversation because you are designing an economy in the Cold War...but I'm not going to. I'm not going to say that National Debt is a ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ issue. I'm not going to say that historically recessions and depressions have been created, not stumbled into because of 'UnEmPlOyMeNt'. I'm not going to say that economic development comes from actual work, not capital....there, I didn't say any of those things ;)I'm just going to talk about the things we can all agree on. The basic math. First of all, there is no budget, and it isn't accounted for periodically. You use these things called Budget Points (ok sure), you have so many when you start from the decisions of the last administration (yeah), and you allocate them to projects you like (great). Problem is, there is no financial cycle. You see, the world runs on schedules. Periodically, Governments replenish their BUDGETS. Even if you treat a Government like a household (don't!), there's income and expenditures. Money comes in, and it goes out. Every year you get more money, and then you spend it. Very simple.The game doesn't do that. Budget Points don't get replenished every year! You NEVER get a Budget Renewal! These budget points...they can be allocated for a 6-month-long construction project, and you will continue to have a suppressed budget total for 4 years! It's infrastructure! It costs a lot to build, but once it's built it basically just sits there, making you money!Imagine you leave college, you've got 40k in the bank (somehow...) and you move to a new city to start a new job. You should buy a car, so you can get to work. You are making 80k a year at your new job. Good for you. So you buy a real nice 40k car, and then someone tells you, "ok, we'll take that 40k in your bank, and another 40k every single year until the end of time. You make 40k now. Same job, but only 40k, permanently.". It's like, what? No, I continue to make 80k a year, and make a one time payment of 40k. When I get paid again at the end of the year, and for all the years to come, I still get 80k!Not in this game!There are a number of choices that heavily factor in on your playthrough here. Because of this dumbass decision, for instance: you can send checks to 'the people' to alleviate their suffering when you get elected. Stimulus checks. [-1 Budget]. So...are we just doing that permanently now? Did we just implement UBI? 'Cause you are NEVER getting that Budget Point back. When the new year comes...the money doesn't get replenished. So that must mean every Sordish citizen is getting a phat check every month, continuously, for the whole 4 year term, right? Ok. So why does the game tell me people are starving in the streets (yeah, just casually thrown in some report is that 'people are dying of starvation'...like, how is that not a bigger thing?) if I'm literally sending them food money every month? Why do my farmers complain to me that their industry and regions are failing because they can't sell all their crops? Am I not giving starving people money? Will starving people not usually buy ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ food if they are starving to death and have money?! It's a simple government subsidy to the farm industry (except hungry people are actually getting food....imagine lol).Why is unemployment a 'serious' issue if everyone is on UBI? Unemployment didn't go up when I sent the checks out, so apparently no one quit their jobs, so apparently we are producing the same amount of goods/services....so...why are these problems still around? Alternatively, where did my money go!?You build a highway, and that money is taken from your total cap. So, does it cost as much to maintain the highway every year after it's built as it does to build it in the first place? Cause that's ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ nutz. You fund the construction off 'hundreds of schools and hospitals' across the country, and your budget is permanently decreased. Does it cost as much to staff these places as it took to build the giant buildings?!  You increase the budget of the police to bring national stability to rioting streets...so what now there's just hundreds of SWAT guys with riot shields walking around everywhere? Is that just how we roll now? Cause they stopped protesting like, 2 years ago.....You see what I'm getting at?Here's another very simple thing that got totally screwed up: You can increase taxes on luxuries by like, 10%, from 25 up to 35%. [+1 Budget Point]. Ok,  You can make enough money from that, immediately, that you can fund a huge construction company to build a national highway [-1 Budget Point] that goes half-way across the flipping country? HOW MANY ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ LUXURIES ARE THEY BUYING HERE?!? That's a LOT of money, apparently, from a very small, niche tax. We're talking tens of millions of dollars. So, is the luxury market in the country on the scale of hundreds of million of dollars? My GOVERNMENT'S BUDGET never went above 2 Budget Points, but the luxury market is the equivalent of 10 Budget Points? ARE YOU TELLING ME PEOPLE ARE SPENDING MORE ON CAVIAR AND YACHTS THAN MY ENTIRE GOVERNMENT IS SPENDING on the ENTIRE ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ COUNTRY?!?!Scale aside, the basic accounting skills are still absent. Is it a one-time thing, or a permanent revenue increase? Cause I didn't change the law back after 6 months....so this is a new revenue stream, right?....(You might argue that people stopped buying luxuries when the prices spiked, so I got a little money in the short term, and them killed the industry, but that makes no sense. The price spike is immediate and pronounced, so would be the response. You don't go buy an overpriced diamond bracelet for your gold-digger, see the 10% increase and say, "Gee golly, that's too expensive!...tomorrow. But today it's fine.") So I should be getting a brand new shiny budget point every year, right? So four times over my term?BTW why wasn't this an option at the start of my term? Why am I only being given the option in the last 5 yards of my Superbowl game?Look, this is really important. This game is ABOUT managing a co-"

_childDocuments_.review: A genuinely enjoyable political storytelling game. It is very irksome that there is such unrealistic politics at times. You can choose to so left or right, traditionalist or reformist at the start and the game will only work out if you stick to your guns and ONLY go along with your pre-conceived ideology, as opposed to taking every situation at face value and solving it the best way possible. _childDocuments_.review: Anyone interested politics around the world will find many parallels in Suzerain's universe to ours, but it's different enough to make the discovery enjoyable. _childDocuments_.review: Fixed the economyImproved healthcare, prevented a pandemic, gave free eye testsReformed the constitutionPrevented warImproved conditions for womenImproved conditions for minoritiesLost the election to the Freedom and Justice Party AND the Nationalists...I was devastated by the resultsA great political RPG. Very astutely written. Plenty of weighty and difficult choices. I can see why some players may want the game to be more transparent about the consequences of choices, and political popularity, etc., but that's kind of the point; you're living the consequences of your choices before you can be totally sure what they are. Still, ploughing nine hours into becoming Anton Rayne and being relatively satisfied with the results, then to not just lose the election narrowly but tank completely, was pretty annoying. I get that the difficulty is kind of the point (and, honestly, I can see why people would want to vote for reformist Rayne but not his ass-backward USP), but give a president a break here. The sudden turn of falling well short of reelection felt a bit like hitting a brick wall. I can see where some choices could have been made differently to improve the outcome, but not for things to go that badly with no huge alarm bells beforehand. But maybe again that's the point. I look forward to playing through again to find out!

_childDocuments_.review: I don't review games often, but when I do I absolutely LOVE that game. Suzerain is no exception. My first play session was eight hours strait of "just one more turn". But what makes the game so satisfying for me isn't just the great writing, world building, and game art. If the game was just these previous points it would be a light novel. It's not. The core of this game's quality is the choices you the player make as President. Choices are weighty and frequent. I warn you, if you are a political idealist unwilling to compromise you may have a rough road ahead and find yourself disappointed.

_childDocuments_.review: This is honestly the first time I've felt truly compelled to write up a review of a steam-purchased game (so forgive me if I'm not exhaustive or professional in my review) but I have to say that, coming to the end of playing Suzerain, I was left stumbled by the conclusion of the story. This is a good indicator of a quality, story-driven experience. The characterisation and emulations of the periods social, cultural and political issues were very well done in terms of parody that didn't come off as hackneyed or excessive. Ultimately it did make me truly invested in the characters and the situations and interactions that occurred.For a game at around £10 in cost, the value for money is excellent, and the quality for that low cost is quite staggering. The only things I truly noticed as bug bears of mine were some spelling errors and phrasing issues (if the team is not native English speaking then I still find it commendable the level of accuracy they managed).If I had to push myself to be critical, however, there is a degree of lack of variety to the interactions and input the player can have besides the implementation of policy and different dialogue outcomes. This is the Police - another excellent game in this genre - seems to have, by comparison, much more variety of scenarios and emergent game-play situations crop up, both due to narrative and the game-play loop. Suzerain seems to reference major happenings via reports that due come across some-what bland after a while.Overall, however, the 15 hours I spent with Suzerain was very enjoyable. Considering the foundation, it would be nice to see the game expanded, or perhaps warrant a sequel? Regardless, I can safely recommend this game for purchase to anyone interested in the political strategy game or in a faux-Cold War-era Eastern Europe-like scenario that throws together all the greatest hits in terms of that turmoled-filled era's history.

_childDocuments_.review: An original text-oriented strategy game, with a plot that both emphacize your actions and is very well written in itself. First and foremost, it is important to keep in mind that Suzerain is not a game that intends you to outright win in the first place, you will need several attempts. Without purchasing DLC, I'd achieved a succesfull run in almost fourty hours playing.On the details now, I've found that the way to improve the economy in the game is very one-sided, highlighting deregulation and orthodox economics over wellfare and heterodox economics. Today's economics are witnessing health and education sectors as factors of competition between countries, calling them "human capital". Having skilled and healthy workforce - and therefore having the equipement alongside it - can be seen as an economic advantage over other countries. In the game, improving education or healthcare has no impact on the economic situation. It highlights the fact that your country needs short-term solution as opposed to long-term ones. But as such, there is no real incentiveness to boost health or education despite their role in the economy.Furthermore, economy in the game is built around a classical economics perspective, meaning that offer carry the economic growth over demand. I've got some issues with that statement during my campaign. When playing as Sordsland, you have the possibility to sign the Worker's Right act early in the campaign. The bills describes itself as a way of improving workers condition and wages, in return for a negative economic impact throughout the country.The issue I had was this negative economic impact triggered by this bill. It can be explained by the fact that higher wages can hold employment back, increase production cost of businesses, and encourage them to look abroad for development rather than in your country.However, it is possible to look the other way around. Increase wages for the workforce means a better transfer of wealth. More income for the general population means more customer's demand. More demand means higher prices, which in return increase production, thus increase GDP. This is particulary true for country with little to no reliance on international trade - which is the situation of Sordsland early in the campaign.I do not condemn classical economics. There is no best way to handle economics, the best way really depends of the situation. I was just disappointed to see that was no room in the game for a demand over offer economic doctrine, like keynesianism. At some stage, I really wished the game had a more balanced approach. Anyway, the game creators never intended to promote anything, it's always interesting to see how economics are perceived today.Overral, the game is good !
_childDocuments_.name: Suzerain

_childDocuments_.review: The game that finally scratched my itch for a political simulator. It's a narrative choose your own adventure kind of game, but I found the choices and their outcomes compelling and enjoyed turning Sordland into a communist state, an seeing the different challenges and problems that emerge, even if I got overthrown by a military coup in the end.
_childDocuments_.name: Suzerain

_childDocuments_.review: As a devoted fan of political simulators  text-based/visual-novel style games, I had my eye on this for some time before it released. I can honestly say that it far surpassed any of my expectations. It was extremely engaging and I often found myself forgetting that the world that Sordland inhabits exists only within the game itself.Playing through the story felt like watching a prestige television drama, and I often found myself emotionally exhausted after playing through major story events. The characters (including the man you control) were believably human and each had realistic strengths, flaws, goals, and ideals. If you, like me, strive to reform the government and resist the machinations of the "old guard," you will often find yourself frustrated by setbacks—unmotivated or unwilling politicians, reactionary elements in Sordland, even internal and external threats from Sordland's neighboring countries. Of course, this makes it so much more rewarding when you manage to succeed.This is not to say that that is the only way to play the game. Though I have no experience doing so, you can increase Sordland's national defenses and become isolationist, ramp up the military and become a warmonger, or devote yourself to working closely with allies resembling either the United States or the USSR at the height of the Cold War.The visuals are simple but crisp (the game map is represented by an actual political map) and the soundtrack is amazing: intense at the right moments, relaxed when it needs to be. With the recent overhaul, the UI has become even more informative and intuitive while retaining everything that originally drew me to it. The mechanics are also simple to learn, allowing the focus of the game to remain on the story.Overall, my only regret after playing this game is that I will never again be able to experience it for the first time. Luckily, the Rizia DLC will be releasing soon! I  recommend this game, especially if you share my interests; 10/10 is not enough.
_childDocuments_.name: Suzerain

_childDocuments_.review: Few games have made me as invested in the story and characters as they developed than this, where I've had to balance between my country, my family and various groups and factions, depicting a cynically realistic expression of politics. I've done 3 full playthroughs, and I greatly enjoyed them, trying to lead as I personally would. I don't see myself going much deeper into alternate endings; it starts to feel very slow and at times frustrating when one ambiguous decision can block off an entire path. If you enjoy going for many different endings, it's worth reading guides as it can be difficult and frustrating without fully understanding the cryptic game mechanics.

_childDocuments_.review: I'm stealing this entire review word-for-word from Hexaboo, because they have said everything I wanted to say and with more skill with words. "Suzerain is a fairly good and fun game, but I don't think its current rating on Steam (93%) accurately reflects its quality, for the shallow experience the game delivers past a certain point, so here's a fat thumbs-down.The basic premise is excellent, the game uses dialogue choices to guide you through your life prior to your election, and beautifully throws you into a quasi-realistic world of the 1950's, to lead a country with a detailed geography, and people with extensive bios, opinions and allegiances. There is so much to explore in addition to the story, and the story itself captivates you with difficult choices interspersed with all the boring appearances, functions, and official dinner parties that you have to live through for that authentic head-of-state experience. The game does not let up, and you will easily spend the next 10 hours aching to see what the next decision brings, what the newspapers write about you, and whether the economy finally gets back on track.But once you go beyond just the story and the basic world building, you can really feel the game was made by a bunch of first-world libby millennials who don't know better, and clearly had no intention of changing that. The whole 1950's world of the game is an incredibly hammy projection of the modern mainstream in politics and economics, like having a whole party of neoliberals, second biggest in the parliament no less, even though their economic policies were a very marginal academic idea post-WWII, and never got to any power until the 80's. Sure they're everywhere now, but what the game dismisses as 'old, outdated Sollism' was the very successful and burgeoning capitalist mainstream in the first world that made rich boomers rich boomers. The social liberalism of the liberal bourgeois party in the game is also fairly anachronistic: they wouldn't give a crap about any downtrodden or minorities, certainly not in the 1950's.The policies that make you a dang commie in the game are the typical watered-down and anachronistic 21-century third-way social-democrat ideas like 'let's not privatise schools, pretty please!' or 'let's choose the state-owned enterprise over privatised ones to build stuff just this once, despite obvious government failure, obviously!' The phrase about 'guaranteed minimum income' as this bold socialist thing in the end really reveals the lack of research in creating the universe of the game (it's neither bold, nor socialist, nor period-appropriate).There was no attempt to break out of the usual moulds, and give the player a good deal of freedom to weave their own credible story, and offer them an exciting slice of almost-real history. That all in addition that there is no player agency in a pure game-mechanics sense. You are the head of what looks like a reactive branch of the government, rather than the executive. I know there are limitations in terms of what you can have in an interactive-novel game like this, but having virtually no influence on the composition of your cabinet, and no active control setting policies in the country really ruin the idea of you being at the top of executive power.All in all, don't expect any kind of management gameplay in Suzerain (Democracy is a decent, if limited, option for that). It is an interactive novel, and will deliver enough good story for one playthrough. However, the game is way too shallow and repetitive, and doesn't offer enough player decisions and agency amid all the text fluff for any replay value."

_childDocuments_.review: Probably the best political sim out there. Allows you to tread your own path - you can be a hardline socialist, an ardent capitalist or follow a pragmatic mixed economy path. You can propose wholesale reforms to the Constitution (including providing rights to the minority), follow a gradual reformist approach by democratising your government and emancipating women, or strengthen your party's grip on power.Similarly, for foreign policy you can follow an interventionist path or an isolationist one; you can opt to join the western bloc, the eastern bloc, or maintain an equal distance from both. You can enter into beneficial trade deals with other nations by granting them concessions. The best part is that your decisions will have positive and negative effects down the line - your decision to enter into a deal with a country will preclude a deal with its rival; your lack of support for your wife - and women's rights more broadly - will negatively effect your relationship with your wife; your lack of respect for the nation's founder will lead to your reforms being blocked by the conservative wing of your party; too much internal disturbance would lead to a coup.The DLC only serves to make the experience even better.Overall a solid 9/10 game.

_childDocuments_.review: This game delivered what it promised. A great political simulator. It completely immerses you to the world of politics, how great and how dirty that world could be. You actually take moment to think about the consequences of your actions, being it consequences to you, your friends, your family, your people and of course your political career. It demonstrates very well that world of politics is. This game truly sets the standard of what a good political simulation should be and i hope there is a day where this is considered mid, not because its bad but because games like Suzerain have raised the standard to such great heights that in face of those great political simulators of the future, this masterpiece is considered mid

_childDocuments_.review: **There is a key component if you will like Suzerain. If you enjoy reading or if you don't.** Without question if you're somebody who has a low attention span or doesn't enjoy reading, even when the context is intellectually stimulating and shaped by your own decisions **IF YOU DO NOT ENJOY READING** you will not enjoy Suzerain. **IF YOU ENJOY READING** and engrossing narratives that have almost endless possibilities and consequences with the task of being thrust into the president of a country with a unique approach of love and care put into their game. The game is not voiced acted instead filled with branching text and dialogue, with numerous options and paths. Suzerain rewards those who pay attention to the narrative and punishes those who don't use critical-thinking when coming to a decision.   - this is done though in such a way that you're not sure as the player if you resolved each conflict the correct way, and finding that out in the future is what makes Suzerain such a compelling unique journey.The game is a agonizing balance of push and pull and decision making. Who should you trust? Should you make allies? What are your policies? Do you have religious ideals? What is  the focus of your administration? That will be up to you, and Suzerain does allow you to do that - I rarely felt constricted in what I hoped would be a option in my choices related to decision making, I often regretted the way I resolved some conflicts due to the unforeseen consequences and outcomes, but that is something I'm eager to tackle in another play-through of the game, that I can confirm changes drastically depending on the paths you take as President. I'm currently nearing 20 hours and haven't completed an initial run yet. It is a VERY challenging game if you're somebody who must have the game play out like a perfectionist - but I stress to not look anything up online, and live by your decisions as that is a major strength in this game - and makes the replayability all the more fun, as I am very eager to play another run of the game that will be DRASTICALLY different than my first thanks to the freedom of Suzerain. Like I noted, if you enjoy reading, choose your own adventure games/books, and complex narratives and politics and potential scandals, all wrapped up in your own quest for world domination or peace or whatever other direction you might take as a world leader then Suzerain Is the game for you.I often pondered if I wished to purchase the game, and was concerned about the occasional negative review. Some mentioning bad translation. The translation of the game is perfectly fine and in 20 hours I noticed only one poor translation as follows:  "are you ok?" Was replaced with "are you fine?" I stress there is little to no other translation mishaps and anyone saying otherwise is being beyond critical as that is the most minor of details to complain about and somebody who already was put off by this genre. Give the game a try if you can, as you will enjoy it if you identify with my above points. If you've been on the fence about buying it I highly suggest to go ahead as the price more than justified the return with hours of gameplay and replayability, and if it is ever discounted on sale there is even more reason for you to purchase and give it a try. Suzerain, a game I should have tried a long time ago as I enjoy it very much and look forward to continuing to play, and play again multiple times after my initial completion. I applaud the developers as I enjoy this genre very much and hope to play other games like this. I regret not trying it sooner. 10/10 from me. (YOU MUST LIKE READING AND THIS TYPE OF GENRE HOWEVER!)
