_childDocuments_.review: I'm a US congressional staffer and I have never played anything like Suzerain. It's a masterpiece. For one, this game made me significantly more thankful to live in the United States. For all of our problems, bribing politicians is not the cost of doing business and our neighbors are not say, warmongering monarchies. Differences with the American political system aside, there is no game on the market that captures political decision making so well. In essence, a great bulk of governing is being in a room with many different people giving differing opinions and having to make sense of why people are saying the things that they are.  That is also in essence, the core gameplay loop of Suzerain and thanks to excellent writing and characters, it succeeds in making this an engaging yet authentic experience. My only major complaint is the way legislation was handled. Bills from the assembly being sent to my desk often seemed to be presented at random and there was no discussions with any of my advisers prior to deciding whether to veto them. Considering the large impacts many of these bills have on the country, this was a surprising oversight in an otherwise excellent experience. Despite that flaw, as someone who participates in the political process on a daily basis, this game is the real deal. I bought the game on a lark so I know little about the background of the developers but a huge congrats to the team on a job well done.
_childDocuments_.name: Suzerain

_childDocuments_.review: An interesting game, very well structured, generally engaging, truly political. Set in a fictional yet familiar world, this is clearly intended to be a 1950s central bloc country simluation/roleplaying game. For the most part, it plays that tune very well - and the world is convincing and easy to get sucked into. One major criticism arose from my first playthrough: There are two topics which this 2020 development team clearly misrepresented about a country such as this in the 1950s. Attitudes to gender roles and female leaders in general are simply unrealistic. This topic plays heavily into the game in ways that are too inflexible to truly capture the past. Consider it a re-imagining or censored version of the past. The other topic which is glossed over in the same way, predictably, is immigration. Ethnic strife is still, to this very day, perceived very differently in the centre-east than the west - and international attitudes towards this area didn't form in the way the game presents it until the early 2000s.It's a shame that inevitably some historical revisionism seeps into games like this - but I suppose it is literally a fake historical world anyway. The game remains very enjoyable, and a true credit to its developers.
_childDocuments_.name: Suzerain

_childDocuments_.review: This game is honestly such a hidden gem and incredibly unique - you will struggle to find any game that scratches quite the same itch. That being said a fictional political simulator RPG is not for everyone.The story is great and the intricate web of decisions and outcomes makes for many thrilling play-throughs. Having completed the game 4-5 times and had several other attempts go south I can say I am still experiencing new twists and different options even now. It's the perfect game to come back to every six months for a little weekend escape.You will grow to love and hate many of the characters, from Serge the friendly driver to Mr. Tusk the evil billionaire oligarch. Half the joy of the game is in finding all of the different interactions with these characters - it's quite fun to go from cozying up to a character in one play-through to "mysteriously disappearing" them in another.Seriously, try the game. It's clearly a labor of love from the studio and one that is STILL getting updates years after launch.A Morgna wes core, vectern sis da! Glory to Sordland!
_childDocuments_.name: Suzerain

_childDocuments_.review: When I became President of Sordland, I was an idealistic reformer determined to solve the tough problems I faced, who would not bow to corruption. The economy was in recession, my party was divided, the constitution was broken, extremist groups threatened internal peace, and our aggressive neighbor's next target seemed to be us. I had some successes, too. A cautious free market policy saw the economy slowly recover, trade increased with our neighbors, and a diplomatic foreign policy averted war when we joined an alliance. At home, the constitution was reformed for a better democracy after a tough fight, women's rights saw a breakthrough, and I acknowledged minority grievances.It then all went wrong. A debt crisis broke out and the economy plunged into a huge depression. We lost control and every day I read new reports of protests and fighting between different groups. I threw my best friend to the wolves for a major scandal who then killed himself, then my driver friend died saving my life. My party would be crushed at the next election and I had decided to retire when worse came. The military overthrew me in a coup and I went to jail, not the first president to be crushed by Sordland's broken system, but not the last after my failure.My second try, I pursued similar policies but won re-election in a landslide. The economy was booming and we had joined an alliance with the West. Women's rights were secured, a new constitution was passed with 90% of the vote and the minority Blud group came peacefully into the wider community with new rights. I had a loving family and the country as a whole was pursuing the Sordan Dream thanks to my leadership. Some would say I had certain financial irregularities, that I was too close to oligarchs, that I bribed opponents. That I may have averted the Rumsberg danger, but at the cost of tying us to a greater danger of a cold war that could go hot at any second. They claim that I neglected healthcare, education, workers rights. Some say that the strange affair where my VP chose to resign was hushed up. My vaunted anti-corruption campaign may have taken down one minister, but many more in the shadows were left free from justice. But you shouldn't listen to the critics. Just look at the totally free press- they all freely chose to sing my praises. After all, everything I've done has been for the greater good. Right?Suzerain is a good game and a pleasant surprise. Most strategy games have the player as some detached observer who can pursue the rational course, but here you're stuck in the middle of a lovingly detailed country that reminds me of 1950s era Turkey (and some other countries too, this is their own unique creation), a much more realistic version of politics than usually given. But there is also downsides to this approach compared to say Paradox. While the political situation makes everything from a nationalist dictator to a Communist dictator plausible and everything in between, close to the same things will keep on happening. With no save slots and lots of not needed small dialogues, I ended up skimming through my 2nd run. I wouldn't count on replaying the game too many times. There is a certain fog of war, which makes sense, but some of the economy and security matters are rather opaque- I'm still annoyed by the way my debt crisis broke out. Bills should have a little discussion before choosing to sign, as it makes no sense that I don't know anything about the political consequences until after I decide. Despite these complaints, I still enjoyed the game.
_childDocuments_.name: Suzerain

_childDocuments_.review: Very fun little game, took surprisingly longer to finish than anticipated, circa 15 hours, which could be much longer if you wanted to take your time reading through the individual reports, news-articles, an archive entries.The world's fun, the nods towards the real life equivalents likewise, even if cheesy at times. I'd say the Devs did a good-enough job to make all sides (ideologies, forms of government, individual characters...) look more morally grey rather than picking sides in most* scenarios. This is a very good thing for a game like suzerain. Allowing ideological wiggle-room whilst still allowing a narrative to unfold in an alternative universe. The characters and their writing aren't best-seller material, but for a contemporary dialogue-box based game, it's way above average.This game is a great experience, but it's not as great of a "game". I feel like many of its systems could be better explained... but it isn't a one sided argument. On one hand, being thrown into presidency, naked and unprepared makes the adventure more captivating from the start. Your character will be confused and swarmed with advisers, foes, allies, and endless issues. And you navigate the entire game-space through conversations layered over a map and a (wiki-like) archive panel for reference to help your disorientation. On the other hand... unless you're already familiar with basic economic & political terminology, I can imagine you'll be utterly lost and forcibly educated on the matters by experiencing crisis first hand. Especially since the exact functioning of the government budget isn't quite well explained... What your HUD tells you will sometimes feel like the complete opposite of what your economic adviser tells you. Your progress is non-existent unless that one explanatory conversation happens. And sometimes you'll be stuck waiting for the repercussions of your actions for hours on end, as this game is not a simulation, in which you could open a tab and see if your new policy aggravated or pleased the voters. But more of a structured choice-based narrative experience. Make of this what you will all I'm saying is do not expect Democracy 4. I've thoroughly enjoyed my time with the game, and I can see myself replaying it in the near future to see how far on the political spectrum I can push the nation of Sorlandia.
_childDocuments_.name: Suzerain

_childDocuments_.review: I was quite pleased with how this game turned out, after having anticipated it eagerly for some time. As a political simulator it understands the importance of telling a narrative. The game's idea of letting you be the presiden does not just amount to giving you a bunch of buttons and sliders to control everything from the tax rate to the cost of health care. Instead it situates you in a larger historical context (in an alternate history) where all the issues that come before you are the results of a multitude of forces both within your nation and without that shape the politics of the day. And these issues that you make decisions over have consequences in turn, shaping the present and future reality of your presidency and country. The gameplay is inextricably tied together with the narrative, where the events that unfold affect what gameplay choices you are presented with and what choices you make impact what will happen next in the story.In short the game is a story-driven simulator game with heavy emphasis on choice & consequence. The kind of game we could use more of, in my opinion. The political vision the game presents tries to cast a very wide net, giving you glimpses and interactions with a large number of topics and issues (which history nerds will recognize from many different places), and more often than not letting you as the player express sympathy or opposition to them. Quite a fun game to play, if you accept that the game revolves around a lot of text, and that you must live with your mistakes as there are no reloads.
_childDocuments_.name: Suzerain

_childDocuments_.review: Many thanks to Torpor Games for making this amazing game. Despite its many shortcomings, it is still, by far, one of the best political simulation games.However, I would like to address the issue of language support. Being a visual novel type of game, supporting only English is a very big challenge for many non-native English speakers, especially considering the huge amount of text in the game.I am from China. There are a lot of people in China who have provided Chinese localisation for this game for free. However, due to the specificity of the game, there are still parts of the Chineseisation that are incomplete as well as using translation software (e.g. deepl, chatgpt, etc.). This makes it difficult to experience this excellent game, but there are still many players in China who love this game.We hope that the production team will bring us an official Chinese version and expand the game's content in subsequent releases, two countries are still too little for us!!!! And hopefully some of the unreasonable game mechanics can be changed!At last, thank you Torpor Games for all your work! We hope to see more of your work!Translated by deepl.
_childDocuments_.name: Suzerain

_childDocuments_.review: It's a well written world and story. I got immersed and quite invested. I haven't played a game before where you're the leader of a country and that means you're a physical entity in the world, signing papers and holding meetings, as opposed to an omniscient overseer, who somehow magically controls every component of their country. Anyone with an interest in history or politics should consider it.You'll have to persuade (or bribe) people to get reforms pushed. Most people aren't on your side. You will make hard choices. You cannot afford to do everything, or even most of the things you want to do. The game benefits from there being multiple paths to take. There's many endings, and so far I've found two. .Complaint: The game's systems, especially the economic system, are horrendously opaque. On your first playthrough, you won't know how much you should spend or save, because it doesn't tell you how many spending decisions there will be in the future or whether you gain more budget over time (you don't - debt happened). You won't be told regularly enough how things are going. You won't know whether you're on track to meet your goals or not. Advisors will not tell you of the implications of your decisions (which is called advising), only insist you make them. You can think you're doing well the whole game (everyone loves you, growing economy, peace on the streets) and then have everyone decide they'd like you to resign anyway, and also the economy explodes. God forbid the game give you enough information to plan ahead or make good decisions. Even so, play the game blind, at least for your first run. It's a story game first and foremost. Play as if you're the president and make the decisions you'd make in his shoes. You can look up guides for specific runs/endings afterwards. If you want to do well (spoilers): .If you're looking for a game that's actually about simulating a country/economy, let this one pass you by. It should be thought of as a multiple-endings story about politics rather than a real country-running game. If that interests you, grab Suzerain and dive in.

With *little* alternatives given and internal crisis' growing the suspension of several rights to accelerate the process was needed. Ended the game impeached by nationalist judges for violating the constitution and accepting a few oligarch bribes.Economy looked great, even through my prison cell window.8.9 / 10 --Honestly the experience was great, if handling the seemingly minute yet ultimately important details of state in dire need of change is your thing. The characters also grew on me rather quickly - finding yourself actually wanting to help the people you're stuck with as the player (especially with little to gain in return) indicates good story/plot to me.My only con, the value of replay-ability.The auto-save will trigger after every meeting/conversation which means completionists or those simply wanting to try a different route will have restart completely for different runs which honestly seems to be a rather huge oversight for veterans like Topor Games.

_childDocuments_.name: Suzerain

_childDocuments_.review: A very fun narrative game with great writing. _childDocuments_.name: Suzerain

_childDocuments_.review: There are a lot of things this game could improve upon, but for what it was - it was an incredibly gripping playthrough and I was very sad when it came to an end because I wanted to keep playing forever. The positives: - World building. You become incredibly invested in what happens. - Realism. You can't make everyone happy but you can navigate their disapproval the best you can.- Introspection. Do you sacrifice your in game economy for your real life morals or do you do something bad to be able to hopefully do more good down the line with your increased funding? The negatives: - Lack of saves. When you make a mistake or if you experience unexpected consequences out of no where, you just wasted 5+ hours of your life because you can't go back to an earlier save or roll back a decision. In some games it makes sense, but for a game where very little will change on your replay ....... I have no desire to sit and read through everything again to try to find a new ending. - Questionable logistics of certain events. For the game to constantly say you've done an amazing job and you've fixed the economy and managed to improve the lives of all of your citizens and increase Sordland's international standing, and then let you lose your bid for reelection felt ... off? It left me wondering how you could actually win the reelection when it didn't inform me of mistakes I made to fail. Overall: amazing game, worth every second spent on it, but would massively benefit from a guide, more meters to gauge your citizens' approval, party approval, etc, so you know what you need to work on, and a better save system.
_childDocuments_.name: Suzerain

_childDocuments_.review: Suzerain is a narrative-driven political game where you (attempt) to lead a nation in the '50s while doing your best to avoid pitfalls like a military coups, a belligerent neighbour, the tug of war between the superpowers of the east and west, and internal elements who disagree with your direction.The setting is a fictional version of Europe, with the various nations being a pastiche of real-world countries, some more directly paralleling real life than others. For example, the superpowers of United Contana and Arcasia are pretty obviously the U.S. and Soviet Russia. My knowledge of history around this time is spotty at best, so I can't really comment on that aspect much.I would describe the game-play basically like the "sim" games in the visual novel genre, with you making dialog decisions through various events. The decisions you make can influence the direction of your country or your reputation amongst the various figures involved in your government. You are also afforded the opportunity to make decisions on investment projects and laws that directly affect how the country is run. Some people will be more or less willing to co-operate with you based on your type of governance.The focus is definitely on story here, rather than managing the statistics of your country. The statistics like economy, public order, budget, etc. serve to determine what events you may encounter and how you are able to approach them. That's not to say the game is devoid of freedom, there's actually a decent amount of branching paths, some differing in larger ways than others (do you want to be a dictator?) and various endings. This is not a micro-management, sim-style game, though, nor is it something like grand strategy game.I like the writing, though there are some instances of odd phrasing and spelling mistakes. I presume that's due to not being written by native English speakers, since Suzerain was developed by a team in Germany. Being somewhat based on the real world, I didn't expect to be intrigued by the setting but I found myself enjoying reading through the codex entries. I'd love it if the histories of these fictional countries and figures was expanded upon a bit.It's not a long game, but the branching paths and multiple endings means it lends it some replay value. In my case, three back-to-back playthroughs. Since it's a story based game, you probably will end up skipping a lot of the same dialog on subsequent plays, but there are also a wealth of newspaper articles and small event popups that reflect the decisions you make if you go down a different path.
_childDocuments_.name: Suzerain

_childDocuments_.review: An incredibly solid story-driven game, where choices have cascading effects long after you make them. It's legitimately tense, with paranoia and uncertainty surrounding every decision. In comparison to high strategy games such as Hearts of Iron or Civilization, this is a much more personal story about a man's rise to power, and his ultimate success or failure at leading a country. I highly recommend this to anyone looking for a roleplaying/strategy game with solid characters, impactful choices, or just a different type of game that you haven't seen before.
_childDocuments_.name: Suzerain

_childDocuments_.review: A modern day Hidden AgendaThis game is very similar to the 1988 game Hidden Agenda and that's a compliment considering the legacy of that game.Suzerain is interesting as it has an immersive story line, and full interactive map with a decked out codex.I get the frustrations that some people might have but this isn't like Democracy 4 or Lawgivers where it's simply a simulation. Suzerain is more comparable to games such as For the People and Lapse: A Forgotten Future where the story line is the main focus while the mechanics are just an added bonus.Do I recommend this game? Yes! The replay value is pretty large and I hope they expand the game in the near future.

_childDocuments_.review: Suzerain is an unrecognized gem flying under the radar.  In this game, you play as a backward country that has slid into recession.  It is your job as the newly elected President to save it from getting worse.  In this game, your choices matter.  Will you play as a socialist tyrant, keeping your citizens under your thumb, rejecting the will of the people, or will you play as a Democratic reformist, bringing freedoms to all but having to deal with the wrath of our political allies?  This game has real replayability.  In my playthrough, I was a good guy who took no bribes and tried to bring the country into the modern age with diplomacy and trade deals.  I can’t wait to go back and play a bad guy who takes all the bribes.  This game is mostly narrative, with tons of text to read.  If you hate reading, this game is not for you.  It has a huge cast of people.  It is hard to keep track of who everyone is at first, however, the game does a great job of dealing with this with a sidebar codex. You simply click on a name and it brings up a little dossier on them.  Cons of this game are that it is text based.  Because it is choice based, you are limited in your actions.  Sometimes the choice I wanted was not available.  If I wanted to replace a cabinet member, I couldn’t just click on my cabinet and fire someone.  However, these are minor issues.  This game was way longer than I thought it would be.  I clocked about 12 hours for an entire playthrough.  Because of it’s replayability and its enjoyable nature, I would say this is a must buy for anyone who enjoys this genre of game.

Pretty realistic, if you ask me. I will try to Make Sordland Great Again in another timeline and get rid of the old guard. A'Morgna wes core - Vectern sis da!!

_childDocuments_.review: Suzerain is an education in politics that many people need these days.Suzerain is a political text-based crisis-management simulator set in a fictional region, of a fictional world which closely resembles our own during the early Cold War era. For fans of text-heavy CRPGs such as Disco Elysium, text adventures in general, and politically-minded folk. It caters to everyone (ideologically-speaking) in a the-things-you-want-to-achieve-are-mostly-impossible-and-the-world-is-a-frick kinda way. Like seriously: don't complain about the game because your ideology didn't work out as a form of government. Literally nothing works out well here. Politics is a freaking nightmare, and this game will teach you that.It's honestly a lot of fun seeing how many of your personal values you are willing to sacrifice to achieve your political goals. The story and characters are generally well written (occasional typos and grammatical errors), distinct and interesting. You will quickly learn what each and every character is about. The fictional world with its history and various powers inhabiting it are both deep, and easy to learn about (thanks to the encyclopedia) on the fly.The game gets points for:+Being surprisingly easy to get into. This is NOT Crusader Kings or Hearts of Iron. Whilst the game frequently feels overwhelming, it is never the gameplay or UI which causes the stress. The writing and decision-making is where the tension is effectively built.+Proper budget and personal wealth systems which affects how you can play the game and your outcomes.+Presentation/art style is nice.+Soundtrack fits the mood perfectly. Extra points for that X-Files piano ditty.+Great writing overall. Characters are distinct and well-written, and all are potential enemies/allies in the political game you choose to play.+Realistic politics presented without bias. You will come to understand why everybody sucks, and why idealism is political suicide.+World-building (this is set in an entirely fictional world, albeit one very analogous to ours)+Replayability. So far I've only played as myself, but I can't wait to roleplay in subsequent playthroughs. I am fully anticipating a filthy corrupt capitalist playthrough, as well as trying to create maximum chaos as some sort of crypto-anarchist.+The possibilities are honestly crazy. For example, I agreed to give an oligarch's company a government contract for a bribe (which I then demanded he double, and he subsequently did). I then handed the contract to the state corporation, and ignored the oligarch at a dinner party the night after. When the oligarch finally came to my office, crying about how I screwed him over, I nationalised his entire business empire for lulz and threatened him with prison. I then later donated the bribe to a improving gender equality in Sordland, and allowed the oligarchs to continue exist purely to manage the privatised prison industrial complex. You see, in glorious Sordland criminals are subjected to the brutality of capitalism in private prisons. I like to think I'm teaching the lumpen a lesson here. And therein lies the beauty of this game.As for complaints, so far I have none. There are the occasional grammatical slip and typo in the writing, but considering the scale of this game, that is very easily forgiven. This is a modern classic.

_childDocuments_.review: When I bought Suzerain, I was expecting the sort of IF that I can complete in a couple of hours. I have been pleasantly surprised by a game of far greater depth and breadth than I anticipated. The possibilities covered by the game, from civil war to creating your own political party, the fact that the multi-party system leads to interesting intersections and deviations of alliances based on the topic... even the map that functions as the game screen provides a level of verisimilitude beyond other games covering this topic. I have not yet finished, but I find myself hoping that this is the sort of game that gives me a "where are they now" of the dozens of characters you interact with, because there is just enough characterization in the text and static portraits to make them feel like more than plot devices. As with most IF of this ilk, there are still moments where the logic that produces the text is a little too obvious, such as when a character runs down the list of their opinions on the things you've done in their area of interest, and how they feel about them. But they are few enough that I almost never felt myself being pulled out of the narrative. In the genre of political, choices-matter IF games, this is the best I've played.

_childDocuments_.review: Fun decision-making strategy game. As someone who plays a lot of strategy games, this one was nicely done. A lot of reading, and honestly a decent amount of the choices just seem like flavor text, but the game really can go in very different directions depending on how you handle the big decisions, which is nice. I got this in a bundle and I'm not sure I would have picked it out on my own, or been happy about paying full price for it, as it is kind of a short campaign and once I played it through a couple times I pretty much lost interest, but it was an interesting game to play with refreshingly difficult choices and I'm glad I took the time out of my life to give it a shot. I don't really see myself coming back to it; games like Tropico are more my jam if I want to play a dictator, but this was a nice change of pace from my usual.
_childDocuments_.name: Suzerain

_childDocuments_.review: An excellent choose-your-own-adventure political novel about leading your minor power country through turbulent times. The writing is well crafted, and aside from a few anachronistic terms that have been created in the recent past (personal stimulus checks, the deep state), you could easily be fooled that you're looking at a 1960s snapshot. Make no mistake though, just because it's a choose-your-own-adventure doesn't mean that it's easy to make it through. Your actions and dialogues have consequences, many of which can take a long time to be felt. Characters have personality and agendas, which can and do conflict with whatever you decide to do. You need to not only read the text, but also catch subtext and read between the lines if you wish to be anything close to successful. Your economic decisions also take time to fully develop, and can have especially nasty surprises. Do not think that the only effect of your policies is what is written on the page, or you will run into trouble.My personal favorite character is Lileas Graf, as though I disagree with her on ideologically, I can still find common ground with and sympathize with her a lot in other areas, even with a communist Rayne. She is no strawman Sollist (conservative, roughly speaking), and I respect her for that, even though she tends to be my antagonist.The game's slow burn pace does hurt it in subsequent playthroughs, as it takes awhile to go through the opening stages again, and the rude economic surprises are not nearly so welcome when you're trying to go through alternate endings and have to slog through hours of work to test something new. Your budget in particular is hugely influential, and a screwup here WILL turn your run into a slow motion crash no matter what. From what I can tell it is nearly impossible to make it through Rayne's term blind without a deficit, unless you purposefully keep a huge surplus or read a guide. The trial and error it would take to unravel the economic game on your own would take hours, so if you want the best endings possible, either grab a guide or prepare to trial things for a looong time. Still, if you like reading a book's worth of material on Cold War politics, you should definitely pick up this game and give it a run or two. There are entire aspects of the plot that go untouched in certain routes, so you definitely get additional content out of trying another path. As to the plot itself, I'll say this: Everyone has an ideal that they want to make reality, Everyone. How much are you willing to bend in order to make real change? And what happens if you compromise without an agenda of your own? Well, good luck Mr. Rayne. You'll need it. A morgna wes core, Vectern sis da!

_childDocuments_.review: I have honestly fallen in love with this game. i couldn't stop playing once i started. the characters, the narrative, the setting all beyond fantastic! i had choices that seemed natural to me and ones that made me stand up, think, and get a drink while thinking about them. i managed to get reelected my first playthrough but during the end i felt i would surely lose, this game took me on a roller coaster and i enjoyed the whole ride!

_childDocuments_.review: The demo set me up with high expectations.  The full game delivered on those expectations really well.I agonized over a number of decisions, applied my real-world understanding of politics and diplomacy, and got to the end of chapter 5, only to discover that I had chosen to trust someone that I shouldn't have trusted.  As a result, I got a bad ending.  On reflection, I shouldn't have trusted that person: the clues I needed had been there the whole time.The decision to lock players into Ironman mode is a little frustrating, because I would love to roll back the game one turn (the full game takes 5 turns, that include many decisions each) and play from there.I was a little surprised at how well my policies worked, reducing unemployment by 80% was a miracle felt a little heavy-handed (although I worked hard at it). I'm mildly curious about how my economic choices could have been different, and the difference that would have made.  I'm also a little curious about whether going with a different personality would have changed things much; but I agonized so heavily over my decisions that I'm not sure I want to play again.Overall, this game is a tremendous achievement, that reminds us all that politics is made out of people, and that the conversations you have with people are important.

_childDocuments_.name: Suzerain

_childDocuments_.review: The game is great, but don't buy it until they add some sort of save system. The lore is interesting, the complexity is phenomenal, and I think it is a fantastic example of a political simulator.That being said, the forced Ironman aspect of the game severely diminishes the replayability of Suzerain. The game loves its writing, rightfully so, but I get sick of dealing with dialogue that does not have many options over, and over and over again. Given the fact that there are 3 main paths to go (Constitutional Democratic Reformer, Autocratic Putinist-Erdoganist Constitutionalism, and State of Emergency enthusiast), and the fact that the margin of error is soooooooooooooooo small, that one small dialogue choice results in failure (i hate salad), there is nothing but pure frustration after 4 hours of slogging through monotonous lore and background. And guess what? You're stuck with that failed result, because the game told you that you were going to win just to lose and give no explanation. I get it, the game is a political sim, and politics is a tense, merciless world. But I'm playing a video game. I just want to PLAY THE GAME. I get so mad at this game, BECAUSE I love it. I  to see what happens. I  to get all of the achievements. I  to explore all of my options, even the ones where I fail. But if i want to do anything, I have to slog through an hour of dialogue that I've already read and I already know.I've seen some comparisons to Dark Souls-style difficulty, but I disagree because in Dark Souls, YOU DON'T HAVE TO RESTART THE GAME BECAUSE YOU ACCIDENTALLY ROLLED OF A CLIFF AT THE LAST BOSS.The Life and Suffering of Sir Brante did it best: the option for ironman, and save points every chapter.

_childDocuments_.review: This an amazingly immersive game with lot of politics, relationships and presents the real struggle and inability of fixing problems in a country as its leader. It has great characters which you get to interact with across the entire game which makes you truly care or despise them. Thanks to the atmosphere every time you have to talk and make a decision holds so much wait. I fell in love with this game, finishing my first playthrough in the three days I owned it. However it isn't perfect. For one dealing with the economy and people in the game is much too vague on the whole and doesn't properly represent your choices. I made trade deals and built railways and agriculture yet the economy just sat there and I only made money off of random tax laws. I changed the constitution and helped people from all sides and yet by late game only one group in the entire country supported me. The biggest complaint of all is something that happens with alot of game like this, FINAL TURN FAVOURITISM.  By that I mean every single decision you made is completely undone by one or two in the late game. Perhaps it depends on what path you go down but this happened to me and I HATED it. It felt like my 15 hours of leading this country, learning these characters and making these tough calls were undone by no fault of my own. And yes I am very sour about this cause I was grinning my ass of throughout this entire game and I was in near tears by the end. The variety of choices in the game is staggering and I highly recommend it for the writing, choices, world building and atmosphere alone. Those points I just made against it probably only apply to certain paths, I guess I'll have to find out when I replay it.  A Morgna wes core. Vectern sis da!

_childDocuments_.review: Suzerain, While i AM giving this a positive review, fair warning you will get BORED reading the Large amount of text over the course of the game. With that said, what does Suzerain have to offer? Well its a Political story where your choices have consequences. You play as Antan Rayne, the newly elected president of Sordland and YOU decided what kind of President you want to be and how you deal with your nation's problems. According to steam my first full playthough has taken me 12 hours, so their is plenty to see and do over the course of the game. But as i said, your going to be reading seemingly ENDLESS text and picking responses to other characters, it will get a bit boring after a while.More importantly as i said above, YOUR CHOICES HAVE CONSEQUENCES! Many Bills will come and decisions will come across your Desk as President of Sordland and you decide weather to VETO them or SIGN them. You also have a National Budget and Personal Wealth to think about, if you go into national dept (which will ruin the nations economy) or have no money on hand some options will not be available to you.Their are plenty of endings here depending on your choices, so i do recommend giving it a shot if you like this kind of game.

_childDocuments_.review: As a student of history and an enthusiast in politic I really love the setting of the game. The country you'll have to run has several problems and crises that cover many topics you would have to deal with when running a country. I didn't expect to survive my first playthrough but apparently I did because there're many approaches to deal with certain problems. If you pay attention to your surroundings and your cabinet you'll know what you have to do. You have an experienced and hard working cabinet but like anywhere in the world they have their own agenda and ideology.Though some of the crises the game introduces are not as big of a scale as others but I think they include them with enough importance to not just "be there" and any "small" problems can be a big problem if you don't deal with it efficiently.It felt so good when you tackeld down the crisis or when you pass the vote on the constitution which you have to work for half of your term, when your economic decisions bore fruits or knowing the outcome of the war after series of decisions.The game let you approach with many way and many ideologies, you can either put your ideology to test as realistically as possible or go all the way. Making decisions and live with consequences. The political compass at the end of the game will tell you what you are throughout your term.There are many possible endings and plotlines to go through. _childDocuments_.review: My biggest issue with the game is that there seems to be a huge disconnect between the decisions you make and the events that unfold.After struggling to revive the economy because of the lack of information provided as to the effects policies would have or the overall state of the economy (represented by a single line), I managed to turn things around. These were the economic results of my term:- Inflation: 2% (down from 10%)- Debt: 310 billion SR (down from 427 billion SR)- Unemployment: 5% (down from 16%)- GDP: 513 billion SR (up from 310 billion SR)I simultaneously enacted policies that gave more rights to workers and increased wages, while investing heavily on education, leading to improved standards of living. I fought against the oppression of minorities and brokered a peace deal with my warmongering neighbor, avoiding a war.Despite all this there were widespread riots which sprung out of nowhere calling for my resignation, I lost my party's primary elections and finally suffered a military coup.

_childDocuments_.review: This was a good game. For approximately 80%. But the end dissapointed me so much that I just can't give it thumb up.I dislike games that demand you to lose again, again and again untill finally the stars align (or you use walkthrough) and you finally do something you should be able to do on your first walkthrough - not fail. Unfortunately, this is exactly that type of game. Even worse there are literally no "legal" ways (as far as I know) to change something or go back few steps. The game has 1, an ONLY ONE, save file which gets replaced on every checkpoint. Why? What was the reason behind it? To make the game "hardcore"? Well, congratulations, you did it I guess. But would it be so horrible to make it an optional feature (like Crusader Kings 3 with it's optional "Iron Mode", for example)? The reason because it's such a problem for me is this: I've spent 14 hours according to Steam to finish the game I was having fun, honestly despite the game problems (I'll get to them later) untill the end where you  and that destroyed me. My country was prospering, well-fare, military, law and justice, economy, everything was excellent, but I lost and got the bad ending. I cannot change anything, cannot fix anything, I just lost the game and 14 hours because I didn't perfectly follow a guide. . So yeah, as much as I liked most of the game the ending ruined everything for me.Good.-Interesting although not new concept.-Visual design is nice, especially liked portraits.-Visual character customisation, not much, but still nice.-Freedom in choices.-A pointless, but still nice roleplay. Hypothetical example: you meet with your minister, you can say "Hello", nod your head to him or shake his hand. All three choices don't give you anything, they just advance the dialogue, but, at least for me, they allow to "get into role" of my character so to speak. Developers easily could've removed these micro-choices without losing anything, but they still decided to add them and that's nice.-Hyperlinks in game text and glossary. That was very helpful.-Game actually makes you think and shows very realistically (compared to other games) how politics work.-Low price.Bad.-Too difficult without any ability for "casual" playing.-Game expects replayability, but doesn't give any tools for that.-No tutorial, at all.-In order to get good outcomes from events it's not enough to just don't make obviously bad choices, you have to either strictly follow a guide or restart the game a lot of times. I honestly doubt that many people will get "good" ending on their first try without outside help. And dependind on how late in the game you'll ♥♥♥♥ up it's more than 10 hours of replaying.-Sometimes the game restricts you too much and choices are arbitrary. For example you can improve the army and have to choose which branch: land, air or naval. Why the hell can't I improve all of them? I have enough funds. Improve equipment or hire more people? Why not both?! Made the wrong choice? -I felt the family and personal life of MC wasn't developed enough.-Music is forgetable and I personally found it slightly annoying, so I quickly decied to mute it and turned on mine.The game has potential and if there will ever be a second part I hope that it will be better.

_childDocuments_.review: I've done about 3 playthroughs so far. One as a nationalist dictator (basically Franco/Mussolini), one as a Communist autocrat (basically Lenin/Stalin) and one as a moderate capitalist reformer (closest to my real views).This game is very fun! I love the writing. I like how every decision has weight and consequence, especially if you try for the Dictator route, since one mistake when negotiating with politicians or planning your reforms can ruin your entire run and force you to start over. All the real-world parallels (e.g. ATO and Arcasia being NATO and the USA) are easy enough to understand while still being unique in a way that adds to the depth of the Suzerain world's story. The world-building is superb with your own nation (Sordland) and all your neighbours having unique national histories, beliefs, structures, and approaches to political matters. The characters you meet in the game are also very well-written and have distinct agendas and personalities, making them all believeable individuals as if they were real politicians. Some of them appear to be nods to historic personalities and if you know your history, it'll be very easy for you to connect the dots and figure out who's being parodied. Some of them you will grow to dislike (screw you Tarquin Soll you meddling dinosaur), some you will use and abuse, and some you will come to adore (Sure thing Serge, I'll pay for your kids to go to university you wonderful man)  I also enjoyed the realism in how if you push too far in any direction without appropriate measures and safeguards, you'll either get ousted in a coup, betrayed by your ministers, impeached by the Supreme Court (Damn you Hawker!), or lose the second term election. You can also get assassinated or killed in a war, but no spoilers! So in truth, unless you're going for the absolutist dictator approach where it's a case of "screw everyone except me", you have to make deals, compromises, and maybe take/offer a bribe or two. It's a brilliant allegory and reminds me of the saying: "politics is the art of compromise." The big thing at the start is fixing your economy, then trying to pass constitutional reforms if you want to be a pro-democracy reformist or a dictator in the making. Otherwise, you can try to stop the reforms if you want to maintain the status quo (hail Soll) From there, many other things can potentially unfold including a refugee crisis, genocide, trade deals, diplomatic posturing, and even a war can break out in the late game if you don't handle a certain situation smartly (or if you want the war and deliberately push for it!) Hell, you even have family life to contend with: a son, a daughter, and a wife you may not always see eye-to-eye to...The game has many branching paths that you can go down, depending on your character's ideology, past actions, recent decisions, and so forth. These mean each run will be different if you don't pick the same choices every single time, so the game provides a lot of variety for you to explore, depending on what kind of President you want Anton Rayne to be. I've played 3 runs and I'm nowhere near bored of Suzerain and I imagine I'll keep playing for a long time just to explore all the possibilities. Do you like political games with a lot of machavellian scheming, meticulous planning, and tenacity spanning? Then this is a game for you.A morgna wes coreVectern sis da!

_childDocuments_.review: I am updating my review based on multiple play throughs.I wish there were more games like this, but this is the only one I've ever found. This is not a "Graphic" game. Be prepared to read - the writing is exceptional. at first, you will be confused by the names because they are all approximations of the real world. Deridia or Rumsburg won't mean much to you at first. The game features a full wiki of places, concepts, names, etc and it is very useful.You take the role of a world leader that you customize (somewhat) and much like Crusader Kings, you have advisors and policies you set to govern your country. It has branching storylines that can take you in very different directions. I've been deposed, arrested, beheaded, even with the best intentions for my people as their leader in this game. You can align yourself with socialism, capitalism,  nationalism, religion, etc.The game has lots of hidden events that you may not even realize exist unless you happen to to make one decision differently and then the entire thing shifts down a totally different path.You also have to balance your family life. I've had my family be supportive, but with their own agenda and if they feel they are not being listened to, they will react accordingly. You have to be really patient with this game, and you also have to be willing to fully read the information in the events.There are some flaws in this gem:1. The "Continue" button MOVES as you read text, and sometimes I have accidentally clicked a dialogue option that I wouldn't have chosen because the "Continue"  button moved slightly as the text displayed.2. The game is fairly brutal. It is simple to learn, but especially in the Rizia campaign - there is a negative spiral where you lose authority as the people become unhappy, and since you lose authority you lose the ability to make them happy with reforms, so you continue to lose authority.  Additionally, there is a punishing fee to store energy, so if you ever become energy dependent, you will lose -3 treasury per turn just storing energy, (Rather than lowering prices, so your energy is costing you money, not making you money)I am not sure if the developers care or read the forums, but I have posted about this in the hopes they will balance it.3. It's not a "Sandbox". there is no way you can get "Re-elected". I mean, I guess you can, but the main/original game ends after your first term and the epilogue tells you what happens after. There are basically around five chapters of a story arc of the game and that's it. I wish it was more of a sandbox with a little RNG,  and someway to keep playing towards a particular goal, but nope. You can enact about two mega projects and then your time is over.So, replay value is very low. I tried running as myself (what I would do), I tried running as a fascist/trying to get rich. I tried running as a religious conservative, and a socialist who cared only about improving his people's lives. Never did I feel like I could actually succeed except as  fascist. Rizia I could never succeed, it feels less balanced.So while I do appreciate this game for what it is - and I give it a thumb's up, I do want to warn you that you will probably not play more than 3-4 times. I do not know if the devs intend to allow a steam work shop so people can make their own campaigns, but that's the only thing that would make this replayable to me now. I've done all the runs I want to do until the next story pack comes out.

_childDocuments_.review: ***Spoiler Alert*** Is this the Kobayashi Maru?  I enjoyed this game, but it is unwinnable.  I've played it through a couple times and no matter the decisions you make, you'll lose.  So, this game feels more like a playable book vs. an actual video game/political simulator.  There are some dynamic changes to the story depending on your choices.  But you'll always end up at war with Rumburg and lose.  No matter how much you fund or update the military.  For that reason, it's not a game I can recommend.  Because your decisions really have no effect.  I think they should revise the framework of the game to make it more realistic and dependent on player's choice. _childDocuments_.review: This is my new favorite political sim. The fictional setting of a non-aligned nation in the early Cold War period is extremely detailed, paralleling real events of the period in depth. The history and domestic issues of Sordland are filled with nuance and ambiguity that makes evaluating decisions difficult. It provides a glimpse at many of the different facets of being an elected leader from egotism to family strife to complete desperation and paranoia, and decisions made usually come with unexpected consequences that shift the entire plan repeatedly throughout your Presidency. A definite buy.

_childDocuments_.review: If I had to describe the game, it's like a political choose your own adventure book set in a fictional cold war. The number of ending and branching paths are almost limitless, after two playthroughs I felt like I only scratched the surface of the possibilitiesHowever I have some minor criticism with the game. These include minor spoilers, but shouldn't turn you away from buying the game, but are simply critique based on my limited experience.

I've just finished my first playthrough, and I'm already contemplating replaying this game multiple times to get all the endings. Seriously good value for money. _childDocuments_.name: Suzerain

_childDocuments_.review: Suzerain is a very complex, intriguing political simulator with a wealth of different outcomes and player choice. 9/10 for me.The biggest thing I want to commend the devs for is their fair and pragmatic approach to the different political philosophies that exist in the game's lore as well as their real life counterparts. As a very politically involved person, I am always interested in finding a political sim that actually offers some levels of broad political depth and intelligence, and not just "freedom and liberty vs tyrannical 'radicals'" liberal slop. Suzerain offers that intelligent depth in its politics, and I am most pleased to finally play a politically oriented game that does not portray socialist governments as cartoonish prison cities with egotistical dictators. Do you have a radical plan for Sordland? Awesome! you could definitely achieve your goals, but you have to play it smart. This game takes place over the course of a single 4 year term. Know your limits, how to spend, who to ally with, and how to compromise. Whether you aim to bring the next socialist revolution, maintain the status quo, or go full gamer mode on women and  minorities (if you're some kind of psychopath), there is most likely a path for you. highly recommend for anyone that likes visual novel/style games and politics.
_childDocuments_.name: Suzerain

_childDocuments_.review: For someone from an ex soviet country, this game very much allowed me to experience building your nation from the rubble. Very engaging and authentic parties, business interests and factions that remind me of my own history. I did feel like a politician, who had to make choices that he didn't want to make. I had goals and I compromised my own morals to reach them. I love that this game makes me do that. It does peter out in the end, especially if you don't fully commit to a particular archetype and the ending especially feels abrupt, lacking nuance that the game very much has otherwise. A lot of the plot points remain unsolved here and it makes me angry that the story was wrapped up such, but days later I can't stop thinking about my experience. I guess you can say the journey made it worth it.
_childDocuments_.name: Suzerain

_childDocuments_.review: I am not what you would call a "reader", in fact the last book I read that wasn't some kind of technical manual, was probably a graphic novel with lots of pretty pictures. If you can adjust to the slow pace of the game (a clear nod to the grind of politics), then this game is 100% worth picking up. It is a straightforward visual novel with many choices on how to run the government, who to take sides with and work with, and even balancing things like family and scandals. There are lots of key moments that will have you worried, and for me many of the choices I had to make made me push my keyboard away, cross my arms and really heavily consider. If managing a government and visual novels are your thing definitely pick this up!
_childDocuments_.name: Suzerain

_childDocuments_.review: Yeah, its kind of a choose your own adventure. Could do with a LITTLE more customization of your character (ability to play as a woman perhaps) but there's a million ways for the story to go. Its fun, maybe even unforgiving. You can edit the saves if you wanna cheat lol and its not a nickel and dime pay to win type game. Give it a shot
_childDocuments_.name: Suzerain

_childDocuments_.review: One of the first major political strategy games I've ever played. I'm not that far in yet, but I am thoroughly engaged. As a fan of House of Cards, it is interesting to have the opportunity to make such large-sale decisions that determine how well a country fares in game-form. This game features decisions that require you to take full inventory of your integrity, conscientiousness and regard for human rights. Are you willing to risk freedom for enhanced security? How far are you willing to go for economic growth, even to the expense of violating human rights? Are you a man FOR the people or "The Man" serving corporate interests? I would recommend it - just be prepared to do a lot of reading as it is text-based. This game stimulates a lot of critical thought about our current political climate and foreign relations as well. Enjoy! Lead Sordland into greatness!
_childDocuments_.name: Suzerain

_childDocuments_.review: A great game, probably my favourite game I played in the past few years. (not exaggerating) Exactly the sort of game I wanted someone to make. In fact I wanted it so badly that I actually wrote a design document for a game like this to make one myself, only lacking the time to actually start development, my attempt at a CYOA political/cold war/visual novel-like game like this one would be nowhere near as good. I am amazed at how similar my design ended up being to this game lol. (Player being the leader of a country post-revolution, trying to fix the economy/reform into either a democracy/authoritarianism/communism etc)The game has great characters - some of which you will love, others you will hate. Has many different endings & branching paths.Although my major gripe with this game is how short it is. My first play-through took me around 7 hours, though I am a quick reader. (ignore the steam game time - I played the game offline). This game is good for multiple play-throughs but another issue is that you don't get many tools for skipping text you already read & see the decisions you've already tried like in most modern visual-novels though this game is not a visual novel it could adapt some of the ideas of the genre, although in all fairness such a system showing the player branching paths & already read text could detract from the game immersion in a way. A lot of the fun in this game is trying to achieve what you set out to achieve.
_childDocuments_.name: Suzerain

_childDocuments_.review: Suzerain is a well written visual novel with some "chose your own adventure" options added.Due to the fact that the game have these options, it's a game thats worth playing through more than once.It fun to read how making 1 seemingly small change can down the road make a huge difference in the outcome of things.In my oppinion, there is however one small problem. But this is just me nitpicking.Most of the game is switching between looking at the country map, or reading text.and I would have personally liked if perhaps some of the decisions would subtally be shown on the map.For instance, there map shows a drawn border between the different countries.depending on the relation between the countries, the color of the drawn border could slightly shift darker or lighter.Or perhaps when you decide to start a "mega project" it will show up as more than 'just' a progress bar under the city.
_childDocuments_.name: Suzerain

_childDocuments_.review: It's a difficult game at times, as the choice you make really do leave an impact on how the story and narrative will unfold as you get later on into a play-through. There's also a steep curve in terms of knowing what decisions to make, and how they will affect your administration, depending on your administrations political leanings. What I especially appreciate about this game, is that unlike many other Diplomacy / Politically charged games available on STEAM, this one doesn't punish you for unfairly for having inherent conservative ideals when you play, if you play according to said ideals. It reacts in a fair and balanced manner, which is refreshing.Overall, it's the best of this sort of game I've played thus far, and I'm hopeful for an eventual successor.
_childDocuments_.name: Suzerain

_childDocuments_.review: This is a truly great game where you play as the fourth President of Sordland, Anton Rayne. Your country sits in the middle of the world, Merkopa, with the tension flaring between the communist east and capitalist west. Both the communists and capitalists wish to influence Sordland and have it join their respective military alliances. Both are prepared to offer aid or sanctions to get their way. But your country faces more problems than just a cold war. To your north lies the Kingdom of Rumberg, a country hellbent on the destruction of Sordland and subjugation of your citizens. Will you be able to avoid going to war? Will you rely on the international community to protect Sordland? Or will you face this threat head-on?Beyond international relations and threats Sordland, and by extension you, faces many domestic issues. After twenty years of authoritarian rule under Tarquin Soll and a brief and tumultuous presidency under the capitalist Edward Alphonso your country has entered a terrible recession. Your economy is in shambles and thanks to Soll your country's political scene is undemocratic and isolated. With an election threshold of 10% and with a supreme court that can block any and all constitutional amendments there is a need for change, or not. It is up to you what direction the country must go. Ultimately it is up to you as Anton Rayne how Sordland approaches this time in its history and whether or not Sordland survives. Just remember these words: A Morgna Ves Core! Vectern Sis Da! Good luck, Mr. President.
_childDocuments_.name: Suzerain

_childDocuments_.review: This is a well-developed political text-based rpg. If you like games where you are the decision maker and your decisions count, this could be a good choice for you. There are consequences for each choice (good, bad, and in between), and those decisions affect not only immediate outcomes but also middle- and long-term outcomes. Some customization of character occurs that is both cosmetic and story-affecting, which adds to the immersion. Worth the buy.
_childDocuments_.name: Suzerain

_childDocuments_.review: Fantastic political choice based game. Really enjoyed the story and character development. Lucian is the GOAT. Started riots, went to war, had a Great Depression, betrayed the people, betrayed foreigners, supported foreigners, accepted bribes then nationalized said business --- obviously you shouldn't give me any modicum of power.Waiting for Suzerain 2 --- I want my second term and world domination ;)
_childDocuments_.name: Suzerain

_childDocuments_.review: Where to start? Suzerain is a text-based adventure asking you to tackle questions and manage concerns the way a President ought to. There are few easy choices in Suzerain and even the most innocuous clicks may spell doom for Sordland or your career. To start, I would say one of the games strengths is also its weakness. It's length and ability to make you feel as weary as a real President means that replaying the game for different endings reproduces that same feeling every time. Perhaps that is part of the experience but I can certainly see that sequential replays are not going to be easy with this game. However, if that is not a deal breaker and you are willing to try you hand at real politik, I have found few works as capable as Suzerain.
_childDocuments_.name: Suzerain

_childDocuments_.review: I do wish it was more to this, as you only serve the first term, and don't go much beyond regional politics.But, it wasn't a bad game, it just needs a dialogue skip button for after you beat it in case you don't want to go through 8 turns worth of dialogue just to see how one choice might have changed your fate.I will say this though, the war phase was lacking, it was just a few hidden variables based on your choices that decided its outcome. The war phase is hardly a phase, since it's just a single turn that details if you made the right choices through the game which aligned with the tactical choices you advised your general on.There was no back and forth, build up, or tactical choices once the war started, it was simply hit continue to find out if you pass or fail. The war should have lasted a few turns, with negotiations, espionage, assassination attempts, or something and you should have been able to make budget or otherwise choices during that time to change the outcome of the war even if you made good or bad choices leading up to it.
_childDocuments_.name: Suzerain

_childDocuments_.review: As President Rayne, lead Sordland into ruin or repair during your first term in this text-based role-playing game. Navigate a political drama driven by conversations with your cabinet members and other significant figures. Beware or embrace corruption; shirk or uphold ideals. How will you lead?
_childDocuments_.name: Suzerain

name: Monster Truck Championship
detailed_description: A true Monster Truck simulation! From Las Vegas to Orlando, go head-to-head against experienced drivers in drag races and freestyle competitions! But before you can pull off doughnuts, wheelies and bicycles, you must first tune your truck to perfection. These machines are spectacular and impressive yet highly technical to drive. The game faithfully reproduces all the unique demands of mastering these powerful trucks, including independent front and rear wheel management, mass transfer anticipation in bends, and predicting bounces after jumps.   But what's performance without style? Customise your Monster Truck to reflect your style and show it off to your 7 opponents in online mode. 16 different Monster Trucks Over 50 customisable elements 25 arenas 3 different leagues

_childDocuments_.review: All monster truck fans should get this game.Anyone who grew up playing Monster Truck Madness should get a kick out of this game. People who liked Monster Jam Steel Titans but wanted more of a real feel and less arcade, will get a kick out of this game. Racing fans looking for something challenging and new will dig this.On easy and medium the game is fun for all ages and challenging at times, higher than medium and the game gets very realistic and hard. The trucks actually feel like you're driving a massive vehicle. First person view makes that more apparent. Stunts are far harder to manage than in other monster truck games, just adds to the feeling of driving a massive truck. The sounds of the truck slamming around are perfect.Truck customization is very Wreckfest for anyone who has played that game. There are bodies, liveries, sticker packs and colors to choose from and mix and match. It's not full out customization like Forza, but it has enough stuff and options to keep things fun and interesting.Career mode is cool because you actually manage a team and finances. Your team members all have +/- perks which can include larger payouts, better truck stats, lower repair costs and so on...makes the team aspect worth paying attention to. There's also sponsor challenges to win parts and upgrades. I def think anyone who wanted more from the last Monster Jam will find that in this game.
_childDocuments_.name: Monster Truck Championship

_childDocuments_.review: I'm a depressed 28-year-old dude who's lost a lot of interest in most aspects of life, including even video games, unfortunately. I just can't get into long, complex strategy games or RPGs anymore. I don't have the mental energy to do it. I just don't care.Nowadays I'd rather fire up something simpler that gives me quick bursts of joy. Like racing games. Anything that just lets me hop into a cool car or truck, and makes me feel like I'm really driving it. It appeals to my inner 5-year-old and revives some of the excitement about cars I had when I was a kid. I don't even care what kind of car it is, I just want to drive it. "CAR GO VROOM", basically.I'd forgotten that Monster Truck Championship was coming out until I suddenly got a Steam notification for it. I haven't played a monster truck game for a long time, probably not since Monster Truck Madness for the N64. I remember enjoying that game when I was a kid, and I also remember years ago when real monster trucks would be exhibited at the stadium in my town, running ads on TV every day (although sadly I never actually attended one of the events).I pulled the trigger on this game, and man... I'm so glad I did. This game has basically made my week (maybe even my month?). It's probably the funnest driving game I've played in a long time - no, one of the funnest games I've played in general, driving-related or not. Without going into a ton of detail, I'll try to explain all of the things I like about it:What else do I say here? The game has pretty good graphics, it runs well, and it seems to be mostly bug-free. The career mode has some legitimate team management and vehicle upgrade options too. You can hire team members who give you various bonuses, sign on with sponsors who give you money for completing objectives, and then use that money to slowly upgrade the parts in your truck. Not to mention you can change your truck's cosmetics and put some pretty wicked designs on it.Keep in mind that once you set a difficulty level, you can't change it without resetting your career progress. So if you're an experienced racer, I recommend starting out with Hard AI for a bit of a challenge. Otherwise, if you don't want to be challenged too much, then Medium AI is fine.If you like offroad racing games, or you're into "light" driving simulations, or even if you just like racing games in general, then this one's a no-brainer. It's just a damn fun game overall. I can't really think of a better way to spend a lazy afternoon, or evening, or any time of day, appealing to your inner childlike love for giant trucks and doing backflips with them. I'm a simple person sometimes and this game is a very pure form of joy.
_childDocuments_.name: Monster Truck Championship

_childDocuments_.review: What a shame. I was hoping this game would be better than Rainbow Studio's Steel Titans Monster Jam games, but this is just poor. The big killer is its physics. This game is a 'simulation' in everything but its physics. The monster trucks slide around like they are driving on ice. The suspension is not bouncy at all and just will be stiff and soft at the same time. The trucks float around like they have reduced gravity. I tried different tuning settings yet nothing could fix the total jankiness of these physics. Its such a shame because it completely ruins the rest of the game which is quite good. Its cool to choose different sponsors, manage team members and customize your monster truck. Yet, the actual gameplay is just so weak. For $40, spend your money somewhere else...
_childDocuments_.name: Monster Truck Championship

Monster Jam Steel Titians Is the OFFICIAL Monster Jam game and Its fun...but this Is a sim and It nails It! The Physics In this game are even better than Steel Titans!! Now Its not perfect but when you get on 2 wheels on the rear you cant go In reverse and back out of It...Its like the truck doesnt have rear wheel drive so gotta reset. Other thing Is when you break the truck doesnt settle down either so kinda gotta wheel It and hope It lands lol. THE SOOOOUUNNNDDDD...holy cow Is It GREAT! The engine sounds are dead on! Idle Is a little off but man It sounds like pure alcohol burning 1400hp! havent even done Career yet Just basic freestyle getting use to the feel of the truck and  I LOVE IT!!! _childDocuments_.review: Nowhere Near A SimulatorI have been a fan of monster trucks my whole life. I follow the sport religiously, and have attended dozens of events, so I'm pretty familiar with it. I purchased this game not at all expecting it to be a simulator, but rather an arcade style game, and while I think there is a good game to be had here, I think it needs to be tuned before it gets there.By far my biggest gripe is with the physics. The trucks don't feel like they have any weight to them, and everywhere you go it's like you're on ice. This makes cornering absolutely obnoxious as the trucks constantly want to spin out, but what's more frustrating is you're powerless to stop it. Once it decides its gonna spin out, it does it, regardless of your input. Once it starts, even if you hold the accelerator all the way down, the truck still slows down and engine rpms go down, as if you're letting off. Realistically, you should be able to power out of SOME of those situations, but the game won't let you. Powersliding doesn't even exist in this game, I should be able to pitch the truck sideways and drift around corners if I want to, but the game just doesn't allow it. It's as if engine rpm and acceleration are tied to your speed somehow, you can't break the tires loose like you could in real life. That needs to be addressed.Rollovers are also a problem, they are very stiff and jagged. I have watched monster trucks roll over I don't know how many times, both on television and in real life. It's a very fluid motion. The rollovers in the game are almost as if there are stages to them, I think this is to make it easier to perform saves and various other maneuvers that can arise from the truck being on two wheels. That would be great if the truck would respond the way it's supposed to. Really, every time the truck does anything in the game whatever input I do does not produce the result I would expect it to. So for example, in a rollover, if I want to save the truck and bring it back on four wheels, it doesn't seem to matter if I steer into it, steer out of it, accelerate, let off, or any combination of those, the truck just kind of does what it wants. And once you're upside down, there really isn't anything you can do to drive out of it. Once you go past a certain point, the tires just stop gripping and you're resigned to watch the truck come to a stop on it's roof.One thing that I think contributes to a lot of these problems is the way the game handles the transmission and shifting. In the game, the trucks have a four-speed transmission with a clutch (there are options for other transmissions in the garage, they may have more gears idk). You can set the transmission to automatic in the settings, but all that means is the game shifts through the gears for you. This is entirely unrealistic, monster trucks do not use manual transmissions, they are all automatic. A few still use a 3 speed such as a Turbo 400, but the vast majority use a two-speed powerglide. Changing that detail alone would make the handling make a lot more sense. Also, as it is, the automatic gear-shifting is a bit slow which is frustrating when you spin out and need to quickly back up to continue.There are numerous flaws with the truck models themselves. Steering rams and tie rods aren't animated, lower four-link bars (referred to as swing arms in game) are not triangulated but rather parallel, which mans the tires clip into them when steering. You won't really be able to see it unless you're upside down. I feel like the devs modeled the trucks off of pictures and videos without really understanding what a lot of the parts are and what they do. Also, idk if it was just in the shop, but while I was browsing the customization I noticed that my truck didn't have a seat in it.Now for some things that I DID like. Customization looks pretty neat. They didn't license any real trucks so everything is fictional. There are a bunch of different bodies to choose from, from more simplistic pick-up designs to more radical unrealistic models. You can further customize them by choosing different colors, patterns, and stickers. You can also customize performance by unlocking better engines etc, however there are no pros and cons to using different combinations of parts. Each component you unlock is just a straight upgrade over the last one.I like what they're going for with the career mode, and the added touch of securing sponsors is a fun extra. I think there is a good game here, but to be completely honest I'm just too annoyed at the physics to really give it a good playthrough. I realize that as a hardcore enthusiast I am not really the target audience for this, however I should be because the game is marketing itself as a simulator even though it clearly is not.For now I will be marking this as not recommended and requesting a refund, but I will keep an aye on the development and if the developers address the problems I have, I may pick it back up and give it another try in the future.
