Boil and stir. Add the base: water, oil, or… something else. Congrats on your first potion! Was it easy to learn? Now try mastering it! Experiment and invent new recipes Carefully plan your route via the Alchemy Map to combine different effects. Be mindful of common sense: you won’t find a market for a poisonous healing potion… right? Or would you? Sell potions Every day customers will come to your store looking for solutions to their problems. You will face consequences depending on what you decide to sell them. Attract guilds, befriend notable figures (or feud with them), gain riches and influence - and one day, you may even decide the fate of the whole town. Buy ingredients or grow your own Every alchemist needs ingredients. You can buy them from traveling merchants: it can be pricey, but successful haggling may save you some coin. Or you can just grow your own! Get creative with customizing Want to give a special appearance to your best potions? Go ahead! Change bottle shape, label type, icon, and colors. You can even give it a custom name and label description. Carefully arrange your unique potions to showcase them on your shop’s shelves and tables… or carelessly throw them around - we’re not gonna tell you what to do, just have fun!
short_description: Potion Craft is an alchemist simulator where you physically interact with your tools and ingredients to brew potions. You're in full control of the whole shop: invent new recipes, attract customers and experiment to your heart's content. Just remember: the whole town is counting on you.

_childDocuments_.review: I completed this game during the Early Access period and again after its official release.The game is quite enjoyable and relaxing. You will assist many eccentric customers in finding the perfect potion to suit their needs.As you progress, you will encounter some customers who become increasingly particular about their requirements, so you will have to continuously improve your recipes.The endgame (around chapter IX-X) can become grindy and painfully tedious. The developers have already confirmed that they will make improvements (you can check them out in their Discord),  but for now, it makes no sense to complete these chapters as they are too monotonous and dull. Although I love this game, in my opinion, this is currently the main issue.
_childDocuments_.name: Potion Craft: Alchemist Simulator

_childDocuments_.review: A super chill game.  For some reason, the sounds made when crushing ingredients in the mortar are really satisfying.  Music is catchy and relaxing.  The subtle humor is cute.  The game does have tutorials and helpful hints, but definitely doesn't hold your hand.  Wasted a bit of money and ingredients trying to figure out how to use the minerals that can teleport your marker past bone walls, but I'm also not super clever, ymmv.
_childDocuments_.name: Potion Craft: Alchemist Simulator

_childDocuments_.review: [edited review]I'm changing my review from a not recommended to recommended a year later. since the release, i saw potion craft regularly getting updated and patched and recently decided to check back in to see what has changed. did all the updates make a noticable difference? the answer is a very clear yes. wow, they really put in the effort to improve upon their foundation. i'm not even salty that i had to restart from the beginning again because it seems like they made some core changes as well. a lot of what i was annoyed by early on has been fixed and evolved. making money is much easier now with more haggle options, ingredients are more varied and less difficult to come by, the characters feel more alive, the shop takes on a personality of their own depending on the customers you chose to serve, more meaningful progression with the room at the bottom, .. really, i'd have to think hard to find something to complain about at this point now. also love that they added steam achievements <3 i guess imma go get me some carpal tunnel still with how much i still use the mortar but it finally feels like it's worth doing so - even at full price. if you enjoy brewing potions and alchemy, i'd say this game implemented the concept the best :) nothing else i've played has come close so far. i hope they will continue to pour so much love into this project as they have in the past year, i'll be around. [old review below]it's okay, but wouldn't reccomend it at the price this game is sold currently. the fact that it's still EA is very noticable. i got bored / stuck after like four hours because people keep asking for the same kind of potion i haven't discovered yet. so i was like, sure. guess imma just go explore the map only to waste a load of ingredients on finding nothing at all for a few days, ending up with a situation where not only can i not brew the potions i already know, because i spent all my ingredients trying to find the ones i don't have yet, i now can't explore anymore either, because what's left is the top section of the map and the game kinda refuses to give me anything but ingredients going down and righti think this would be so easily fixed if we could choose not to open the store some days. since i'm forced to answer to every customer before i go to sleep, i feel obligated to do what they ask instead of find new potions since otherwise my reputation is just gonna suffer endlessly cuz i have to decline everyone or let the garden be a more valuable assetanyways, i hope the game will continue to improve and if you're still reading, i'd reccomend you check back on this game at a later date, or at least wait until it's on sale to try

_childDocuments_.review: It's just a wonderful chill time, perfect to put on and unwind with for 10-15 minutes. The way potion making works is an intriguing notion. _childDocuments_.review: There's something rather zen about this game.  It's weird, because technically it's just a job simulator: wake up, do work, handle retail, and then go back to sleep. _childDocuments_.review: The first 4~8 hours game is fun and interesting. The late game is pure tedium and achievement hunting this game was insanely painful. Trying to get Popularity Level 15 is just not fun because at that point in the game you have every recipe for every potion saved and its just clicking through menus. The customers with requirements for potions only make it worse because you lose double the popularity you gain on average by turning them away. So it's just a complete slog. Another annoyance I ran into was through bad RNG I was constantly short on many of the gems that make the high tier potions possible (mostly frost sapphires). My final big late game annoyance was remaking previous alchemy machine salts is just SO ANNOYING. I would have dropped the game if I didn't add a mod that allows you to save the alchemy machine recipes. I understand it's a feature that's intended to be added, but its not in the game now so I can complain about it.   Hopefully future updates eventually arrive and change my opinion.  TLDR; Early Game Good, Mid-Game Good, Late Game Atrociously Boring

_childDocuments_.review: Really interesting and has a ton of potential. I love the game. Hopefully they expand on the shop side to make it a more important part of the game. _childDocuments_.review: This recommendation is based on simply what we have right now, I'll be happy to change my recommendation once the game has been updated upon. If you want to support the devs to continue making the game, that's great!Just for context, I fully completed the demo that has been available up until this EA release. Potion Craft has a lot of great mechanics and style points going for it, but I don't think they have updated or changed enough stuff since I played the free demo to justify paying for it at this moment. The game feels like it's progression just isn't there. The economy is very strange and unbalanced in the beginning of the game. Everyone seems to want the highest quality potions at all times for even trivial needs, but the amount they're willing to pay for them is almost always less than what it took to make it. After making it 4 chapters into the alchemy challenges and leveling up to around 15 I didn't really feel like I was better at alchemy, just some background numbers like how much the potions were selling for were shifting slightly more in my favor. It still took a bunch of ingredients to make those tier 3 or multi effect potions that everyone wanted, and you rarely have all the ingredients you need for an optimal brewing that doesn't require 100's of gold in ingredients.I also honestly just do not like the haggling system as it is. I find it pretty repetitive and feel like I am forced to do it with every customer to get close to the appropriate price I should be selling a potion for. I feel that if it were dialogue based instead of this clicky minigame I would be more inclined to take interest in the customers, my reputation, and read what they were telling me rather than parse through their initial text to just see what they need. It is also worth mentioning that while the music in the game is not bad, it becomes very repetitive as there is no variation, so I eventually just turned it off. I'm sorry if I'm sounding harsh, I really do like this game and find it very charming. Like I said before, I find the art style, mechanics of grinding potions, and maneuvering the potion map to be very fun and relaxing. I hope with a few updates to the economy of ingredients, gold, and skill progression I can change this review and recommend that others buy it.

_childDocuments_.review: This is the first good alchemy simulator. Whilst other games have tried to simulate alchemy, they've done so without a specific aesthetic and a clear vision. Unlike the alternatives, Potion Craft doesn't have you running around in a 3D world haphazardly chucking whole ingredients into a cauldron. It offers a rich, complex, open-ended crafting system and a beautiful medieval aesthetic. There are countless ways to brew each potion, and the game rewards you for taking the time to experiment and find more efficient recipes. The economy also feels fair. A smart alchemist can end up with a huge surplus of coins and ingredients, whilst more haphazard play can lead you to deplete your supplies and be forced to turn down your customers. Reviews that complain of the game being punishing, or too difficult, or running out of ingredients, just haven't approached their alchemy thoughtfully enough.

_childDocuments_.review: Potion Craft has been able to create a really interesting mechanic of crating potions that was challenging, but also fun and interesting! This takes something that would normally be a mini-game within a larger game, and puts it front and centre. The potion making turns into a puzzle and a little journey that you take the potion on in order to make it! But it also makes sure it doesn't wear out its welcome by giving the player ways to save past potion recipes and automatically generate past ones they have made! This makes it fun to try to make the perfect recipe, so the repeated creation of potions never gets bland!As well as boasting a strong potion making mechanic, Potion Craft also has quite an enjoyable game outside that. There is a nice way to get ingredients, with a relaxing little garden to pick herbs and flowers from, as well as traders you can haggle with. You can also use alchemy to get new ingredients for potions! You run a potion shop where customers will give you hints as to what potion they want instead of outright telling you and you have to figure out the right one. Most of the time it is pretty obvious, but sometimes I just had to guess. Interestingly, some customers will accept different potions and pay more or less depending on how well it fits their situation. You can also get a reputation for giving evildoers potions vs giving regular people potions!If the gameplay wasn't enough, Potion Craft also has really a really art style, atmospheric music, and really nice feeling controls! The way that you can manually grind, stir and drag ingredients and potions is so satisfying! You can also customise potion recipes and potion appearances! I was surprised that I was able to get 34 hours out of this game, the way it looked, it seemed it would be quite short. If you can ignore the high price, considering it's an indie game, it's quite a fun game to get addicted to for a couple days.

_childDocuments_.review: Certainly a game that can be enjoyable if you're into the concept of alchemy - being able to work as a shopkeeper and haggle with your customers can also be amusing, though that's if you can increase your sales price through haggling.This is one of few games I play that actually works better with a tablet of some sort rather than the mouse due to the way the game mechanics work - that said, there's no need to go out and obtain a tablet of your own just for this game (i just happen to have a pair of tablets from before due to my other gaming and educational experiences)While there are always issues with every game you play, there are some hints and pitfalls a potential player should keep in mind;- effects on completed potions can *not* be changed when using said potion as a starting point for another, you can only add ingredients to reach the second or third (up to fifth) desirable effect.- in light of the above mentioned point, it's better to save your desired potion prior to heating thus completing it.  This will allow you to use the "continue brewing" option while permitting changing the original effect's level (assuming you saved the recipe when it reached tier 3 status, downgrading from here is just diluting with the proper fluid), depending on the customer's requirements, before continuing to the final product if there was a requirement of extra effects.The reason for suggesting saving incomplete recipes that have reached your desired tier is simply to avoid having to create potions from scratch, especially if you need to make something that only required a few extra ingredients and steps to reach... using a completed potion as a base would mean you are stuck with whatever potion you used and chances are you wouldn't even be able to make the desired potion that originally started from a completed potion - result? you have to start from square one having just wasted all the materials to create both the original base and the unusable final product... an expensive mistake if you're running low on the ingredients you used.Also, by using an incomplete potion recipe as a base, you can skip the extra work required to reach the incomplete base due to the marker being moved instantaneously from the centre to the previously marked point, ie if the potion you need to create was a long way from the centre, an incomplete potion would save you a lot of time & effort depending on the distance (incomplete potion A requires 10 mins to reach, while completed potion B requires 20 mins to reach, or use A to reduce the production time to just 10 mins with less effort required in total)

_childDocuments_.review: Game has a nice aesthetic and vibe, but once you realise what this game actually is, the 'fantasy' of brewing potions is obliterated and what's left behind is a fairly uninteresting mini-game that you'd likely see as an afterthought in a full-fledged RPG.Basically, the way this game functions is that customers request potions with specific criteria, with a little bit of personal interpretation to figure out what they want most. For example, they could request a healing potion, a frost resistance potion, poisons, etc. There's also an alignment system, but it doesn't seem to alter gameplay in any real way, just what potions you're crafting and what flavour of NPCs you talk to.The problem is that crafting any potion is no different to any other. To craft a potion, you're given a map, and the ingredients you use determine your course on the map. What this means is that you're not crafting potions in a way you might cook or produce something in real life, but rather you're rolling along a flat space in directions determined by whatever ingredient you're using. It's not a potion crafting game, it's a map-navigation game.I'm not a game developer so I can't tell you what a truly immersive potion crafting game should look like, but Potion Craft loses any immersion/fantasy when you progress into more complex stages and you're randomly throwing mountains of ingredients into the cauldron to explore an uninteresting map interface to discover new potion qualities. This is what I mean when I say crafting one potion is identical to crafting any other - you're simply using ingredients to draw out a path to whatever quality you're looking for.Another let down is that potions for me, as an RPG addict, are synonymous with usability. They're made to be used! But the game blue-balls you with a total inability to use anything you craft. I feel like there could be a whole extra half of the game attached to this that requires you to use potions to find and acquire ingredients. They've teased the ability to use growth potions to increase the yield of your garden (which is the only source of ingredients aside from merchants), but you can't use healing potions, because you don't have a use for them, you can't use charm potions to barter with NPCs or Merchants, you can't do ANYTHING with them, whereas to me it seems like you could multiply game options with the use of potions. Again, this is why I say there's no difference in crafting potions, because you can't use any and the method of crafting isn't unique. Once you have a number of recipes recorded, then there's even less gameplay/decision making involved. It's like working as a cashier, but also not being allowed to shop at the store you work at. You don't care what the customers buy, because you have no interaction with the products you're selling.

_childDocuments_.review: Update:I gave this game a second look after PirateSoftware streamed a Let's play. The addition alone of the element compass was a massive quality of life improvement, and it was much easier to get back into the game than it would have otherwise been. The progression is now solid, if a little grindy - you have to keep making the same special reagents over and over out of lesser potions, but it's actually quite good fun once you get past the annoyance of running out of ingredients all the time.I've changed my review to a recommend - it's now a proper full game with somewhere to go once you learn the basic mechanics. My only gripe is that they should TELL people that the "swirlies" are harmless and you can travel over them. I spent ages trying to edge around these things when i started playing. :/Previous review for context:The potential for a good game is there, but it just hasn't been realised yet. I love the art style, and the basic mechanics are interesting, but there's no story and no depth. There's also no goal or endgame - you just either increase the counters for money and ingredients, or you don't, and there's no purpose for doing either. Right now it's worth a couple of hours of fiddling about before you resort to internet lists of recipes, but not much more.Hopefully in time the devs will flesh it out, and justify the recommendation I would love to give it.

_childDocuments_.review: It's fun and relaxing. One of the better 'job' games out there. The gameplay loop of mixing potions and selling them in your shop feels satisfying and the game is pretty easy once you've got the basics down. That being said, writing this review at the end of 2021, there is very little endgame or goals to work towards. Sure, there is a list of objectives, but all it does is reward you with some xp to level up faster. While the rewards are nice(?) they provide very little incentive and ultimately have next to no effect on the actual gameplay. There's a lot missing in terms of this system and a lot of others, but hey, little wonder - it's in early access for a reason.Nearly a year in the developers appear to be building the skeleton of the game, we just need to wait for the actual meat to arrive.To sum up, if you're looking to kick back after a long day, mix some potions and not worry about your session length(it's great for short bursts as there literally nothing that locks you in) then I would very much recommend it. If you're looking for something more involved, wishlist it and see how it gets along.

_childDocuments_.review: While I had fun at first, the tedium quickly rears its ugly head as you reach the later milestones.Potion Craft is a fun game in concept: Exploring alchemy map, finding new potions, using very different ingredients to get similar results. At first as you're exploring and mixing potions, you're having decents amounts of fun as most potions takes 3-5 ingredients if you're optimizing, 6-9 if you're using bad ingredients. However, as the game progresses, you'll have potions so far on the base map that it takes literally 10+ ingredients just to get there, and sometimes even special ingredients to let you go through danger zones on the map.Then you have the alchemy machine, which at first seem deceptively easy, until it requires you to make compounds of 3-4-5 potions in specific concentration just to make ONE product. Then, you either need to use that product to enhance your alchemy, or to continue your main game objective: Philosopher's stone. Note that once it's used, it's gone.In the later levels, that means having to do every difficult recipes with compounds twice over to both get the tool to improve potion making AND to advance the objective. This, for a lack of better term, is incredibly tedious and IMO is absolute padding on the game's meager features.Though, one of the worst part IMO is the RNG of ingredients. You might have several thousands gold in the bank, bartering and trading like a pro; but it won't matter because you have an RNG supply of ingredients you can't really control. Your garden is RNG every morning, and the sellers are RNG and usually comes once every two days if you're lucky. This means that saving recipes is almost pointless as you'll eventually run out of a key ingredient and have to make your own sad way back to the potion you want to make. Then you can save spare recipes, but then you're using ingredients you might need for more potions. GAH!This game would be much better if you could just outright buy the ingredients you need at a steep price instead of RNGing it all.In final, I'm between recommending this game on a deep sale or skipping it. I just think the game gets very tedious early on.

_childDocuments_.review: There's a serious risk of becoming addicted to this game. The gameplay loop is extremely simple: gather ingredients, make potions, sell them, gain more money for more ingredients and more potions. Despite its simplicity, the game manages to keep you entertained by gradually presenting you with more and more complex requests for potions, adding objectives each chapter that guide you into making the right potions at the right time, to the end goal of creating your magnum opus: the Philosopher's Stone. At least, that's the game's official objective. If you're like me however, the game will quickly devolve into an accountant simulator. You will start calculating the price to brew each potion by summing the price of the ingredients, you will haggle like your life depends on it and you will only buy ingredients when they're on discount, all of this with the final goal of maximizing your profits. You will also quickly realize that some potions are more profitable than others. With some of them you will hardly make your money back or even lose money, it's up to you whether or not to satisfy your clients' orders or lose reputation in pursuit of that sweet sweet positive cash flow. If you're like me, you will organize your recipes maniacally, you will make spreadsheets with ingredient prices and brewing cost calculators, you will lose sleep over the best way to brew a potion, using both expensive and cheap ingredients in order to achieve balance and use them all in equal measure. You certainly don't want to accumulate ingredients just to end up never using them, do you? That's a waste of money. If you're like me, you WILL use the annotation function on each and every potion recipe, annotating the brewing cost, the selling price and the selling price after haggling. You WILL keep a ledger containing the costs of crafted items and you WILL calculate the price of each and every grain of the salts you use to make potions. For some reason sun salts are much more convenient to use than moon salts, i'll have to look into why that is. If you're better than me, you will quickly realize all of this is not healthy, it's true that there are no wrong ways of having fun with a game, but the game cannot become a second job. You need to scale back, cut down the hours you play or even uninstall it. It's not good for you to keep playing. Uninstall it. I beg of you. My every waking hour has been consumed by the potion game. I eat and think about potions, shower and think about potions, do chores and think about potions. I sleep and dream about potions. Potions. Prices. Sell. Buy. Must increase my profits. I have to. I have to make a better spreadsheet. I need to organize my recipes in decreasing order of profit. The recipe book must be appealing to the eyes. It's a must. I shall optimize every single aspect of this game or my life will never be complete. "Potion seller, i only want your strongest potions". Well guess what, peasant, my strongest potions aren't fit for you. They aren't fit for anybody. The potion you want is not profitable to make. It requires too much moon salts. I will not sell you my strongest potion for my strongest potion is not profitable. You will get the weak potion. You will like it and i will squeeze every last gold coin you have by save scumming my way through the haggling minigame. I am a god of time and commit no mistakes. Never. If i do, i alter reality and load a previous save game. I cannot waste money, i cannot waste ingredients. I. Must. Profit.But the game has also flaws. First of all, it's extremely resource heavy. Why is that? There's no reasonable explanation why this game consumes so much ram and GPU resources. Secondly, there's some stutters here and there. It would be fine expect for when you're haggling and a random stutters makes you lose money. That is annoying.There's also some quality of life improvements that would be much appreciated. Like automatically sorting the recipe book, allowing us to better place recipes by disabling the snap mechanic and so on. Small things but that would really make a difference in optimizing and streamlining my potion making routine in order to maximize the gold i make every single day.Finally, we need shelves. I want to stock my store to the brim with potions and there's not enough space on the counter, i want shelves, give them to me. Please send help.

_childDocuments_.review: Relaxing background music and graphics is one of the most important features in an indie game. Alchemy system is quite different in comparison to other games with similar systems. Mixing herbs, shrooms or ores doesn't give you a speecific mixture. Instead, there is a giant map with a cauldron in the middle, each herb moves your ''Potion symbol'' in a specific direction. There you need to take it to the designated point to create a potion.Map has lots of ''Experience bubles'' you can randomly throw herbs just to collect those bubles. It does not effect you final potion if you placed it right into a designated point. Herbs are limited, use them wisely or else you will have none at the end of the day. Herbs are obtainable from alchemy shop garden or mecrhants that will passby once a day. Prices for their merchendises are always changing. Try to buy most useful and cheap ones. Herbs spawning totally randomly at the garden. Later in the game you will need lots of gold, approx 1600 to buy an alchemy machine. This will create new ways to make potions. Until that relax and sell potions, don't waste too much money.

_childDocuments_.review: Nice puzzle/management game with unique graphics and mechanics, unlike any other alchemy simulation. The graphics is stylized on illuminations in old manuscripts. The potion-brewing mechanics is absolutely brilliant, giving many opportunities to experiment with various combinations of ingredients and actions. Basically, you have a big board with various active zones and spots. Adding ingredients moves you vial in various directions and you must operate it so as to it lands in one of the potion-creating spots. You may collect ingredients from your garden, sell created potions, fulfill orders for client, buy items from wandering merchants, upgrade your alchemy shop to gain more alchemy options, and complete tasks in your alchemist diary. Definitely one of the most original games in its genre.

_childDocuments_.review: The core concept and gameplay is pretty decent, but does get repetitive after a while. Though I'm sure this could be resolved with more content.Speaking of that, the game seems to feature an extensive roadmap for future content. However, so far it seems none of said features have been added. (Please do correct me if I'm wrong on this, but I couldn't find anything nor have noticed any updates)I had a quick look through the official Discord server, and it seems the developer's last messages are from back in January (3 in early February), with fairly few other messages regarding development (this year). There also hasn't really been any communication regarding future updates, beyond the developer replying to a question about when the next version will be out with "when it's done" (back in early January). Instead, recent announcements have been regarding sales.The most recent bit of concrete information I could find on the official Discord server is a reply back in November 2021 that says the following:"The main problem with the updates, that it takes time to make. We are working on a lot of new stuff, but our team is not very big (5 people), and we spent a lot of time making hotfixes after the release. We are currently working on new update, but it's pretty big for us, and we can't divide it to 2-3 small updates, that's why it will take time to implement."It's entirely possible the upcoming update is just that big, but considering the lack of communication and actual visible progress, I'd recommend to steer clear of the game until the developers (hopefully) give the game a couple more updates and show the game has not been abandoned.UPDATE 25/03/2022:It seems the developers have released an update teaser regarding the haggling system just now. This definitely is an improvement, but it remains to be seen if this is a short term response to some of the other reviews and users that raised the same concerns. I will update this review when the update actually releases.

_childDocuments_.review: Looked interesting at first, but gets boring and repetitive after about 5 hours and just annoying by 10 or so hours.Not to be pedantic, but the 'alchemy' of this 'potion craft simulation' makes zero sense. Not like "I don't get this" but as in, "this is stupid."Most of the customers are basically criminals that either want to kill someone, or escape justice, but I'm fine with that.Magic tree giving you herbs once a day. Sure, why not.But to craft a potion you use ANY AND OR ALL available herbs and mushrooms and leaves etc  to explore the maps to get to the "craft me now" spot.And if you want or need a level 2 or 3 potions, or a combo potion, it's even more tedious and wasteful as you are chucking stuff into the pot to go in circles just to a few pixels away from the same point. Madness!Then you 'save' the "recipe".Then another customer wants it, but you are out of 1 or more of the many herbs you used, so you can't make it, so you skip (taking a reputation penalty), or you delete the saved 'potion' and find a next set of ingredients to get you to the spot  (any will do).The chemistry version would be "As long as you are at your desk, it's fine. Blocks of lithium, concentrated hydrochloric acid, sure, toss it in the pot with the rest, what can go wrong?"It's just too annoying.What I think it should have been was to explore to find the missing pages of the alchemy book to unlock them, then experiment to see what works. Instead anything and everything dropped into the cauldron works, just so long as the winding route around the (hard to read) map gets to the 'finish potion' stage.One to miss.(Reviewed as at v0.50)

_childDocuments_.review: 100% Yeeeeeeeee to brewing potions, and you're also doing alchemy recipes for your clients! :D It also teaches you to become more patient, not just a mixture of creative and painstakingly precise with the potion's journey on the map. It forces you to evolve your mind and train your thoughts with your book. Feedback?------- Though I wish there were a few ways to mark each essential recipe (for what alchemy machine-based recipes require), the same way for ingredients you may/would need later shortly would also be appreciated. Game Developers, I'd suggest you consider including a mechanism or an organization tab where the game lets you have pages be separated for empty blank ones and filled/written recipe pages to have a less complicated time navigating around through the book by either cursor or arrows/letter buttons to use perhaps? :)It makes sense to have a lot of backups (a lot of blank papers/either wholly or partially polished recipes for various purposes (tiers of strength, order of ingredients inside those 5 icons, and availability of your ingredients)!There's a need to make it easier to keep track of it (too many recipe pages or blank pages can become overwhelming for people who might need help organizing or keeping track of something; keep that in mind!).I'd also love to see more spicing up (puns intended) herbs/plants and possibly even a few new expansions or lands to explore outside your backyard instead of constantly staying inside your home/store and relying on other merchants to do the work.I also wish there was a way to clarify vague requests, just enough to understand what clients are asking you. I did have a bit of a hard time understanding what a few clients were asking me, and unfortunately, I annoyed a few of those clients over it. Some requests were vague, and sometimes, the other half used euphemisms (making it trickier).The last suggestion is to include a flexible tiny shortcut option to the journey pathing between the start and end (of a potion) of every interaction between an ingredient and another ingredient. It'd make the alchemy brewing feel less long to go through using a mouse.

_childDocuments_.review: TL;DR - The gameplay is solid and the art direction is amazing, but the moment to moment gameplay has little variation and there is no meaningful progression after map exploration. Updates are very slow (on the scale of years, not months). Expect  less than 10 hours of gameplay, 20 if you push it. Fills the niche of a calm, relaxing, vibey game, but ultimately feels like unfulfilled potential to me. --------------------------------------------------So, had I written this when I first purchased this game in early access, around 2 years ago, I would have been singing this games praises. However, in the time since, we have only really had 1 meaningful update. The "1.0 release" didn't really add much after that. Since then, they have committed to the "garden update". This is baffling to me, since the garden is so minimal and far from the core gameplay, calling it a tertiary system feels generous. After a year, the garden update has still not released. Given this track record, I recommend you go into this expecting that the game never receives a single update.So, is the current content in the game worth the price? Well, the game is very well made for what it currently is. The gameplay revolves around adding different alchemical ingredients to your potion to build a path through a potion map towards your desired effect. There is a lot of satisfaction from exploring different combinations of ingredients. Discovering new potions, refining old recipes, all good stuff. Add on to this the economic challenge of maintaining a stock of ingredients without running out of money, and you have a compelling gameplay loop.However, where the game really shines is the aesthetic. The sound effects and visuals are spectacular. The sound effects of the mortar and pestle are top quality: grinding weeds, mashing mushrooms, crunching gems, it is pure bliss. The art is beautiful, I love the faded yellow background and how it sets off all the colours. And the music, oh, it is just pure vibes. This just elevates the elegant gameplay to an obscene level.Where the game suffers is longevity. Since you can only explore the map once, the game gives you the alchemy machine to extend the gameplay. Each alchemy recipe requires a list of highly specialised potions which are supposed to be challenging to make. However, as the potions got more and more complex, I ended up finding them quite tedious. It was the same thing as making the regular potions, just with more steps. And for all this, the rewards are salts that are never economical to use due to how many herbs they require to make. Yay.Moreover, once you figure out how to make money efficiently, the act of exploring itself begins to feel tedious. Who cares if you burn a million herbs revealing the map, you're rich. Optimising potions doesn't matter either, since you can afford the extra 50% material cost. I guess this means you can use salts without worrying about the cost, but you can't save salt recipes like potion recipes. Instead, you need to save the constituent potions and combine them in alchemy machine, every time. This can result in just flicking through menus for up to 2-3 minutes for the higher salts, once again, just feeling tedious.Beyond that, all the tertiary systems are lackluster. The garden is essentially a pity mechanic to stop you from running out of herbs completely. The haggling system is a glorified quicktime event that gives you free money. The merchant quests are just regular potion requests. The karma system is entirely superficial and just changes your customers from villagers and knights to murderers and warlocks. I suppose the karma system is kinda neat, but again, not much change in gameplay.The thing that hurts the most is, I can see the devs vision for this game, and it's beautiful. More than 2 maps, each with their own mechanical twist. Different ingredient types with their own quirks and niches. A variety of alchemical recipes serving as milestones to mark your mastery of the system. Character questlines and charming stories from a creative cast of NPCs. A customizable shop you can add your own personal flair to. And it's just probably too much for this dev team to handle. I'm sure the war in Ukraine impacted this dev team, as I'm pretty sure they have at least some people from Russia, and for that, they have my sympathy. However, this sluggish pace of updates started way before that, all the way back in Early Access. There are so many features were promised then that just never made it to full release, and they are nowhere in sight. I doubt we'll ever see many of them.If I could give this game a mixed recommendation, I would. Because I really do like it. The fact I got 70 hours out of it is amazing. But a lot of that was just replaying the same content over and over, sustaining myself purely off the chill vibes. And the vibes are great, don't get me wrong, but if you're on the fence, probably skip this one.

_childDocuments_.review: One of my favorite gotos for relaxing gameplay. The design of the alchemy is very clever. The way the maps, ingredients, and simple set of three tools make you feel amazingly clever. The game doesn't really have an intended path to follow, so a lot of the amazing potions you make, you need to figure out how to do. You'll find yourself muttering like the stereotypical alchemist, gently prodding your cauldron, hoping you haven't overstirred. You'll drop the wrong ingredient in and facepalm, then try and figure out how to fix your mistake through clever play.I know some people complain that there's not enough game here, but for me that isn't the case at all. The crafting game here provides many dozens of hours of interesting and unique mixing. There are plenty of challenges to apply yourself to, if you feel like it.The game just feels good to play, too. It looks nice and the UX is well done, so that actions feel snappy and yet fluid. There was a lot of care put into the interactions here.If I had to lodge a complaint, it would actually be lack of difficulty. Yes, in the first 10-20 hours or so of gameplay, you'll be plenty challenged figuring out the mechanics and trying to figure out what your customers want. But after that, the difficulty rapidly loses steam, if you play well. You will realize that you can simply PAY your way out of problems. I mean, you don't have to do this -- you can find challenges for yourself, the game gives you plenty of tools and options to brew interesting potions. But having ascended to the top, I find myself wishing there was some way to spend my money on something besides ingredients...Anyway, it really is a great game, a classic in my library.

_childDocuments_.review: I like cozy and relaxing sim games with cute art styles and this seemed to fit the bill. Unfortunately the game gets grindy and unappealing very quickly. What I thought would be a few slight ramps in difficulty or complexity or even a new level of crafting just turned into more of the same thing except annoying. There are positives here, I really enjoyed the first three to four hours and was going through parts of the game and customer requests quickly enough. The art style and music are also nice, the character's designs are cute and the references to other media is adorable. Unfortunately having a unique art style and soft fantasy tunes didn't keep me for long after I got to very unappealing section of the game. You just run out of ingredients for things constantly and if you want to experiment to make new things or see the map you end up out of luck because you just don't have access to certain things due to RNG and vendors. There are a lot of great concepts here but they just don't work together or it was easier to overlook them than spend the time dealing with it. It left me with no real reason to return to the game as the loop itself isn't interesting and there isn't really a story here. That and the promise of more content which still hasn't been mentioned is odd. Its not for me at all.

_childDocuments_.review: Potion Craft: Alchemist Simulator as its name suggests is a potion crafting game where you manage your own shop, buying and selling the potions that you brew. Playing it so far, I am loving every aspect of it including the gameplay, visuals and music which all fit well together. In this game and in your shop, you have various rooms including a garden where your ingredients grow daily, the kitchen where you brew the potions, the basement with exciting gadgets, and the front shop where you greet the customers in the town. The main sections are the kitchen and the front shop. In the kitchen, you have various tools to brew your potion including the cauldron, bellow, and mortar. By mixing and matching the ingredients and how you use the tools, you can brew various potions for the specific need of the customers. In the front shop, you are greeted by various people who tell a little story, and from that you find which potion they require. It is quite fun to read what they did or what happened for them to arrive here. Furthermore, there is a neat, little haggling option system where a minigame comes when selling your potion. Here you can either slightly raise the price of what you sell or lower the price of what you buy depending on how it goes. All in all, the gameplay portion is very entertaining as there are a lot of combinations to discover with the potion making.The visual aesthetics is very pleasing with the olden medieval look of the game, the texture and designs of everything, and the colours used. There are numerous amounts of ingredients and potions, all with their unique design which keeps the game more alive. Though the game already does this by the endless mix and matching, and discovery of the potion world. There is also an “Alchemist’s Path” chapters section where tasks are set out, which earns points going towards unlocking the next section which there are several of. The graphics also goes very well with the music that is played which is some charming and relaxing medieval like instrumental.The UI is friendly and simple to use with various section for things such as the potion making, ingredients and recipe portions. Controls are straightforward to use with mainly using your mouse to navigate through the game.The price of the game is well suited and fair to offer, with the game having great aesthetics and fun gameplay. Overall, it is a solid game and worth checking out if you want an entertaining potion making game or a nice simulation. I do recommend it since it has been very enjoyable so far and I’m looking forward to seeing what gets added and expanded in the future.

_childDocuments_.review: Potion Craft... what a game.The first few hours were the most fun, unlocking so many new things to do, and exploring all the recipes. After a while I started doing the same thing over and over, just different combinations of potions. At first it looked like I would never finish those potions, but combine Potion Craft with chatting to friends or waiting for someone, and time passes like nothing. Sometimes I found it a bit unclear what the customers wanted, but there are enough guides out there that will help you out.Towards the Endgame, I started reading the first 3 words of a request and already knew what they wanted. It's also really interesting, that they made so many different requests, depending on whether you got good reputation or a really bad one. I find it a bit sad, that once you got everything of the main story finished, there is nothing else to do. You can keep earning money into to the hundreds of thousands, but you can't really do anything with it. It would've been really cool if you could customise your shop or upgrade/customise the garden. Also you can't do anything with the 25+ leftover levels you gained.A little tip; Make sure to sort your Recipe Book and don't put every single recipe you find in there. Once you got it all sorted you can really start making money like hell.Overall I found the game was really fun, and I can recommend it to everyone as a good past-timer.

_childDocuments_.review: Well, put some more time into this game and unfortunately I have to change my initial reaction/review.This game is a bit of an interesting experience.  On the one hand it almost feels like a puzzle game with some random elements, but on the other like an almost unfinished management game of the tycoon variety.  It obviously isn't complete and what is there feels more like a teaser and less of a full game at this point - which is perfectly fine being Early Access, but after a longer play session it feels like too much is missing.+  A casual game that can be played with the mouse alone+  Relaxing play with no killing or conflict+  Haven't encountered any bugs or crashes yet-  The gains from leveling up feel very minimal (especially the map one)-  RNG controls your fate in regards to what ingredients/vendors you get-  Can feel like a mobile game or too simplistic-  Unfinished (obviously) with unimplimented UI elements-  The 'alchemy' map is static - meaning basically no replay value-  There are huge portions of the map that contain no effects+-  The  looping song is appropriate to the setting, but is nothing special*  More music variety*  Balance out the RNG a bit*  Perhaps have a procedurally generated mapThe biggest reason I changed my recommendation for now is the simple fact that with a static map, full of large areas that contain no potion effects and a level-up feature that seems to do very little, everything becomes a grind.  Then on top of the grind you have what appears to be either bad RNG or a deliberate change in the frequency that certain vendors visit you - leaving you basically stuck trying to grind out the map with less than ideal ingredients.With it being unfinished and in its current state, you can enjoy a few hours of play before you start to see the limitations.  If you  enjoy this type of game you'll play for even longer with no problem, but again, you'll probably start to wonder about all of the missing elements and how development will progress.  Hopefully all of this gets ironed out by release, but I've bought the game so am all-in at this point.If you're on the fence, never played a game in this genre, or don't enjoy casual games - hold off for now and check it out a bit later.
_childDocuments_.name: Potion Craft: Alchemist Simulator

_childDocuments_.review: In short, this game is fun and I spent my morning playing it, but it really needs more content. I expected way more control over what happens in your shop because I mean, the description literally says, "You're in full control of the whole shop." Which is a lie.Let me tell you why:You have zero control over which herbs you collect because you aren't growing your own, you are simply harvesting whatever you find in your garden and buy from whatever vendor happens to stop by. You can't mix and match different herbs to create your own which the description also states. You can only create what the game allows you to, which isn't experimenting at all. You can choose from different potion abilities to create your own. Example: "poison/acid." However, that isn't really experimenting, it's more just combining a few things that your customers aren't even asking for. The lack of experimental potions is disappointing because that's one of the reasons I bought the game. To wrap up the review, I feel like the game was only fun because it's basically alchemist themed "Dealer's Life" which I played before on my phone. So, is it fun? Yeah, you'll get a few hours of game play but it gets annoying and you'll soon realize there's a lot about the game that needs revamped. Is it worth the price? No. I got it on a sale and paid $11 for it, and I still feel a bit gypped.I wish there was a "meh" recommendation, but I'm giving it a thumbs up just because I was able to burn 3 hours playing.

_childDocuments_.review: This game and concept is amazing, don't get me wrong, but it's not worth it to spend that amount of money on an extremely good crafting system and art and... nothing else.It lacks so much, and I'm not just talking about how plot and lore are completely missing.The beginning is as good as the endgame is bad.Once you unlocked all potions you have to go around the map again and again and again to craft the same effects in different combinations and it's boring as hell.And now all I have left is to reach popularity 15. I'm at 14 and it's making me hate the whole game SO MUCH. I have dozens of copies of the same potion and keep giving them away, I don't even buy ingredients anymore. Well, it took me 3 hours to go from popularity 13 to 14, and I'm using all the right techniques.Lastly, it's seriously addicting, I still can't stop playing and I'm not saying this in a good way. I wish I could but I can't.

_childDocuments_.review: Before 0.5 Beta, I would have recommended you wait on this game. As of right now, this game has enough content that I definitely say you could buy this game as an early access game, and as a game that has a somewhat unique niche, it is well worth it.This game has a gorgeous aesthetic. It kind of shares the same idea of Don't Starve or Darkest Dungeon where it has an obvious thematic art style, and very specifically sticks to it throughout the game, and even leverages it in some cases.It is also the epitome of lay back and just relax while not thinking too hard. It doesn't punish you too much; even if you mess up really badly and lose all your herbs you can just go to sleep and get some herbs from your garden the next day. You might lose some reputation and popularity, but that'll build back up again no problem.The whole concept of using herbs to explore a hidden map to find different potion effects is my favorite part of this game. A customer comes and asks you for something and you think "There's a potion that does that?" so you just pick a direction and explore that area and find something new.The UI in this game is also top notch. The recipe book's tabs can be moved around so you can group them however you want, and you have to purchase new pages (I like this a lot!) The game can be played solely with a mouse, which is nice, and all of the elements are intuitive.This game is the best games of its kind that I have played. The design space is still open, and I can't wait to see what else the development team has in store for the rest of early access and beyond its release.

_childDocuments_.review: Potion Craft takes place in a magical fantasy land where a single-salary income can support a two-story household, a garden, and a pastime activity on top. During the day you do customer service for the local townsfolk in order to fund research into the alchemy field; in between jobs you tend to your garden, as well as trade ingredients with the local vendors - both of which you must do proactively if you wish to meet the demands of your customers.The gameplay loop consists of attending to the queue in front of your shop while doing various chores to maintain your stock of plants and minerals. Your objective is to sift through the rambling and smalltalk to figure out what the customer wants, devising an elegant solution to a problem that may or may not have been within your field of expertise to begin with. If this is not the most accurate depiction of customer service out there, I don't know what is.Jokes aside, figuring out what each customer wants breathes life into the game by giving each a distinct personality, making you feel like you're actually talking to them. Going out back to make a unique item for them ends up being an incredibly satisfying experience, mostly due to the clever implementation of the potion-making system, as well as the UI that helps do so more intuitively - both of which I will go on to describe now.First, a base solution for the potion is chosen - the map which the player will chart a path through to get to any one desired effect. These effects have a predetermined location, however the map is initially shrouded in fog-of-war, and obstacles block your path - so discovering where the effects are and getting to them, play a big part in making a potion. The marker must travel to the effect and sit on top of it to be applied to that brew.Getting to these effects is done by adding ingredients to the solution. The ingredients are categorized based on the direction they take you in, and the pinwheel UI can help limit the choice to any one direction. Hovering over an ingredient shows you the path it allows you to travel even before adding it to the mixture. Ingredients are also colored based on their element, and are categorized by type - herbs, shrooms, and minerals.The idea is to chart a path towards an effect in the most optimal way possible, without hitting obstacles, without wasting materials, and with as much precision as you can. This is because potion strength varies based on how accurate you were in your assessment of the potion marker trajectory. If you were able to fit the potion snugly within the effect's confines, you will make the potion strong, netting you extra pay and reputation with your customer-base.Part of what makes potion-crafting feel so natural is the act of physically manipulating the tools you have at your disposal. It is possible to add raw ingredients to the concoction, however, if you want to extend the path an ingredient will go, you have to grind it to a fine paste with the mortar and pestle first. You can also add more base solution with the teeming ladle, in order to move the marker closer to the center of the map at no cost.To make a chosen effect stick, you fan the flame under the cauldron with the bellows, and you mix the concoction inside the cauldron with a mixing spoon to move the marker along its designated path. I do wish there were more tools to manipulate ingredients, perhaps a chopping board or a grater? However the act of physically moving tools to reach your intended goal is what made the gameplay loop so immersive and involved to me.You can save the potion recipe with all its ingredients in your recipe book, personalized bookmarks and everything. I do wish the customers asked for (or at least appreciated) the effort put into customizing each bottle and writing its labeling, as if you were a pharmacist directing patients on how and when to use medicine. However, that part of potion-making remains optional, despite the personalized label icons and bottle shapes. Saving recipes is done to prevent tedium and repetition during consecutive play, though you may save a recipe before having an optimal ingredient, forcing you to redo it. Or, you may run out of a saved ingredient completely, having to chart a new path altogether. Still, I appreciate the amount of customization and freedom you are given with the recipe book and the recipes in it, it's certainly a nice optional feature in the game.The vendor encounters inside the customer queue are what enables you to purchase new ingredients, and are the main source of new ones in the game. The garden eventually becomes unable to support customer demand, and cannot grow the large variety of plants needed for full recipe optimization. This is something the devs intend to address with an update, however the implementation of this garden remains lacking as of writing this review.One vendor in particular is the source of new recipe book pages, and, more importantly - blueprints for alchemy station parts. If I had to voice a complaint about the game, it'd be that alchemy is made extremely repetitive in the later parts of it - with each rock requiring a combination of multiple specialized potions, and each subsequent rock requiring its predecessor, one you already use to craft the alternative powdered recipe.If you don't save the recipes for each potion, you quickly find yourself repeating hours of work just to get to the last progression point you've reached. This is because making rocks is the real goal of the game - with the last rock created the game can be considered complete. I also wish there were more uses for these rocks; as it stands, there is one alternative recipe for each rock aiding in potion-crafting, and that’s about it.Another complaint I'd like to voice is the way the reputation system interacts with your customers during the day. You see, the more people you help, the more customers you receive per day - which actually doesn't matter, since the passage of time has no bearing on your resources or character. However, customer demands are split into good and bad asks, and helping each customer nets you either virtue or infamy, never both.If you have lots of virtue, you attract customers with good intentions - those that ask for health, courage, growth and improvement - and vice versa - with infamy, those looking to hurt, sow fear, steal, or manipulate. I can appreciate the variety of asks put on offer here, but helping all people will eventually only attract one type, and you may end up in a situation where you only help good or bad-intent customers, without the variety the earlygame offers.Before I wrap up, I want to mention how much I appreciate the game's presentation, namely its use of vibrant colors and whimsical depictions of plants and stars. It's very endearing, and gives the game this fairy tale look that's been done extremely well on the artist's part. The sound played as you pick up each ingredient and grind it to a paste, then throw it into the cauldron, is also very calming and soothing for this type of game, almost ASMR-tier.To me, Potion Craft is the ideal busywork title, including just the right amount of interactivity I'd have wanted to see from my simulator. Each task has an involved process of steps: evaluate the board, select the right ingredients, grind them to the right degree, throw them into the cauldron, mix everything and bottle it, then finally serve it to yet another satisfied customer.There's a real sense of progression with each saved recipe, each earned sack of coins, each spread rumor about the little shop you've opened to advance humanity's knowledge of the occult. It is also open-ended, meaning there’s room for the devs to add more content after the final rock has been created. I genuinely have high hopes for this game, that it will continue to improve and be built upon with each new consequent update.

_childDocuments_.review: Very unique take on a potion-crafting system, and an enjoyable gameplay loop. It's an especially nice game if you're achievement/goal oriented, and if you're a fan of figuring out efficient setups.Potion crafting is basically a puzzle of moving across a big map to specific points, the challenge being that each individually ingredient moves you across the map differently. To make specific potions, you need to reach specific points that determine an effect. That coupled with the "experience point" bubbles to grab as you go, and the general challenge of both acquiring ingredients and making good use of the ones you manage to get ahold of keep things interesting as you try to build up your ingredient supply to go for the costly, over-arching crafts that make up the bigger-picture progression. All the while, you're running a shop to sell potions to folks, requiring that you make quality potions to sell at prices that let you buy out the said ingredients you need.A way to summarize the gameplay loop is you start a day, grab some free ingredients from your garden, sell to some folks and buy out what you can from merchants. Once you feel you've got a good supply (Or are waiting for certain progression upgrades to show up in said merchants), you start experimenting with exploring the potion map to find more potion effects and marking down shortcuts, or getting to work on making those complex potions you need for advanced recipes.Really unique system to see and experience, even if you don't feel like sticking to the end of the game. Highly recommend checking it out.

_childDocuments_.review: The game loop and progression system is tiring more than interesting. I have a love/hate relationship with the Potion Map (the main challenge mechanic of the game) as it is simultaneously fun and infuriatingly tedious.Rewards for milestones are rather insignificant in my opinion as well. The shoppe barely evolves, the herb garden doesn't change all that much. Really just the item count and variability, which is just enough to make you want to, but not always, attempt to explore a new part of the potion map. The map is very unforgiving with how you can create paths and explore. More often then not, I feel like my efforts were wasted in exploration as i never felt rewarded for my time. The new potion i learned was weighed down with the sheer number of ingredients i wasted just trying to find it. And now i gotta do it again to make a legit recipe for it.A possible progression improvement could be instilled on map navigation and traversal with a learning/logic branch on the leveling tree. Your alchemist could make ingredient group inferences to help you streamline/strengthen your path to new or stronger recipes. "This ingredient goes into fire > it will also go into explosions > will it also go into light creation? This ingredient goes into healing > will it help me make a better growth potion too?" A way to improve the "fast travel" mechanic as it were. This seams more streamlined then the hundreds of ingredients i have to constantly scroll through. I played my 9 hours over a weekend, and i think that might be it for a while. I may return later, but i've had my fill as of right now.

_childDocuments_.review: Potion Craft: Alchemist Simulator is a refreshingly inventive game that transforms the process of potion-making into an art form. With its medieval-inspired, hand-drawn art style, the game invites players into a beautifully crafted world where alchemy feels as mystical and intriguing as you’d imagine. The visuals are a perfect match for the theme—earthy, detailed, and with a sense of warmth that makes the whole experience feel inviting.One of the game’s strongest points is its originality. Instead of simply mixing ingredients in a traditional inventory, Potion Craft uses a creative system where players grind, stir, and even adjust the heat of their potions, all within a delightful crafting interface. Each action you take affects the potion’s outcome, requiring experimentation and a bit of intuition, which makes every successful potion feel like a personal achievement. The creativity extends to customers' unique requests, encouraging players to experiment with new combinations and potion effects.The game’s balance between relaxation and challenge is another highlight. On one hand, it’s soothing to grind ingredients, explore the alchemy map, and create potions at your own pace. But on the other, the intricate recipes and demanding customer requests can be genuinely challenging—and even a little frustrating! This balance adds depth to the gameplay, keeping it from becoming repetitive while still providing moments of zen.Overall, Potion Craft: Alchemist Simulator is a wonderfully creative, visually charming, and engaging game. It’s ideal for anyone who loves experimenting and enjoys games with a mix of relaxation and challenge. Whether you’re looking for a calm, meditative experience or a brain-teasing puzzle, Potion Craft has something for you. Highly recommended!

In my opinion, the tutorial drops a lot of information on you all at once and it was very hard for me to remember exactly what everything was for and how the alchemy map works (i still don't even entirely  understand..). When I got more customers, I started becoming confused on what the customers were even asking for sometimes. This lead to me experimenting with a bunch of ingredients, only to end up wasting them all and having to turn the customer away. I was unsure how to make a fire potion in this game, so i googled a guide on how to make it. I know this is not the Dev's fault but most guides for this game don't give clear and exact instructions on how to craft potions, so once again I've tried 78 different ways to make a potion and ended up wasting all of my ingredients in the process. Not to mention haggling in my opinion is one of the most confusing messes I've ever seen in a game. I really like this game and I love the concept and gameplay, I just wish maybe customers could give more obvious hints to what they're looking for sometimes. And I wish The tutorial would walk you through everything a bit more thoroughly. Overall, I want to like this game way more. I think it could be great with these improvements.

Please please, for the love of all that holy, allow us to at least request specific ingredients from the Herb/Mushroom Seller for next time....2. Spending one day a week to go buy/procure select ingredients would be godsend.3. Make it clearer we need to remake the reagents a dozen times.4. Some way to upgrade the Enchanted Garden5. There's a "Shop" which implies you can upgrade the Cauldron, Spoon, Ladle, etc; but no one sells these?--------------------------For new players; here are some tips:1. _childDocuments_.review: I'd just like to preface by saying that this game is by no means bad - in fact, it is quite good. The artstyle is very pleasing, the sound design is crisp, and the UI is very clean and manageable. For the hour I played, I enjoyed it quite a bit. While Potion Craft is therapeutic, I couldn't help but feel as though it got rather boring quickly. Personally, I wish the actual "alchemy" process was more involved, instead of just clicking and dragging, being that it is the main gameplay loop. There is a little too much breathing room for a process that should feel far more honed. As much as I appreciate that you are given time to explore and experiment with different potions, the experimenting process is somewhat dulled by the fact that you can see clearly what exactly will and wont work ahead of time, rather than actually discovering that the potion is useless, volatile, or any other undesirable characteristic. I do wish there was a lot more visual feedback for tinkering with potions, and I'm of the belief that it could use some heavy improvements or even a complete redesign. My final complaint for the game is that while graphically it's sound, there is too little color for a game about alchemy, where in real life, the color of a chemical is largely important. The amount of tan/light brown that is plastered everywhere is disconnecting and makes the game feel somewhat gloomy and spiritless.All in all, the game seems promising, but I would not recommend it in it's current state for anybody looking to sink more than a couple hours into it. Hopefully the developers are willing and able to give it the attention it needs to properly fill the niche alchemy/potion making genre.

You waste all of your ingredients, you may not be able to brew the requested potions from customers, buying new ingredients is expensive, and the developer hasn't added any content updates in well over a year, despite them being mentioned in the game.

_childDocuments_.review: Grab your vials, alembic and crucible because you're in for a treat with this little wonder!Do you remember when gaming was fun? Do you recall when games bore challenges and rewards? Do you reminisce the days of high school chemistry? Then I welcome you traveller, to Potion Craft: Alchemist Simulator.Step into the literal parchment of this story... you, a lowly beginner alchemist plant your roots in the local town to become the next Master of concoctions! Starting off humbly with a garden of mystical ingredients and little knowledge of the paths ahead, you must discover ways to brew potions as efficiently and creatively as possible.This 'puzzle' game will have you hooked for hours.To support your newly opened Alchemist's shop, you must spend your days picking and buying ingredients and utilising them to make specific potions for the various customers that enter. Do a good job and they pay well... But are you good and kind? Or slightly cunning and a teeny bit eeeeevil?When you create potions you can choose a righteous path to support the town and the various denizens that populate its winding alleys by selling them for a good reason. Or you can choose to support the wicked, and fuel their desires to wreak havoc on the local population. Either way, your decisions matter and will dictate how your reputation can attract certain customers.Haggling for the best deal? Great for the coffers, but hindering on the reviews. It'll take you longer to build a positive reputation if you keep bleeding their purses dry! But with shiny coin comes more ingredients, special crystals and alchemical equipment to advance further into the world of potion crafting.If I were you... I would transmute the very essence of your bank balance into Potion Craft and set yourself on a gorgeously crafted journey, hooked by a repetitive but stunningly designed soundtrack that will have you humming in your sleep. Seriously though... how have they created a looping soundtrack that you can't get sick of?!Genuinely relax, enjoy the game, and find the best way to create your potions and remember fellow alchemist... with practice, comes mastery.

_childDocuments_.review: It took me 27.7 hours and over 170 in-game days to get all the achievements. Although my popularity level was high, I felt like the chance of getting pricey ingredients was still pretty high. Additionally, I think the penalty of failing the haggling is too much. I was screwed if I missed twice or thrice. What's more, the difficulties of 5-star and 4-star haggling is significantly higher than that of the 3-star, and they give only a 5% discount. I think they're not worth the risk at all.The clients' requests are sometimes weird. Many players, including me, do not get the needs of the clients in some cases. And some requests do not make any sense, such us "I want only a weak potion." when it comes to protection against lighting and fire.Overall, I think this is a good game. _childDocuments_.review: I find this game to have a unique take on crafting mechanics. So many games have crafting systems (I know that in this game it is technically brewing but shhh) there is one and precisely one way to craft something; one set of ingredients, put into one interface, that normally does the whole crafting process with a single click. This game lets you create, for example, a potion of healing by combining any number of ingredients as long as their total effect lands you in the zone of restoring mana. The game smartly limits your access to ingredients so that you need to forge the same potion but with different ingredients in a different order. This mechanic is the unique mechanic that all the other mechanics and loops of the game revolve around: the experimentation with your ingredients to turn a profit. The haggling and dialogue systems are simplistic but serviceable. There's an entire system of the game that seems like it'll take a lot of time and money to unlock which might be the sign of late-game content.

_childDocuments_.review: I used to recommend this game but am changing my review.In the Demo and Early Access we were promised many features that have still as of "release" not made their way into the game. They still say these features are coming but it has been 9 months since the last major update and all we have seen is dev logs. If the game were in a "finished" state I'd be fine with this but even in their most recent dev log they stated that the current system used for level ups is a "place holder" for what they really wanted. That means we are still playing Early Access and this whole experience has felt like promises were made but not kept.This is a chill and novel experience but gets stale quickly. The endgame is mostly devoid of meaningful content and requires an absurd amount of grinding to complete the "Alchemist's Path" (the main progression system in the game) to the point where 1% of the players who own the game have actually completed it (and really, completing it is not hard; it will just take a shift's worth of clicking "sell" to get there).In the last update (almost a year ago now) we saw a new potion base added (something that had been promised in the Demo and EA) which gives you a new map to explore. Sounds great! The catch: it is significantly smaller than the first map and pretty much only serves to give you a tool to use back on the main map. There weren't even potions on that map that you couldn't find on the original map; just the same potions (not even ALL the same potions) with a shorter distance to get to them (and a different rotation angle that you have to reach to make a "tier 3" potion). What is the point then? This seemed like a pretty gift filled with air; just another way to spend time doing the same thing with very little to show for the effort.I really was enamored by this game initially but with how much was promised and the fact that 1.0 came and went without the majority of these promises being met means to me that the dev team might just get tired of working on this and move on and there is no accountability for them to follow through on the things this game originally told us would be in here.I hope to come back and change this review again down the line but until then I will say that "release" felt like a cash-grab/lie and hope that this team delivers on the promises made to the people who invested in them the first week of EA.
