_childDocuments_.review: I love supporting certain games in early access that I can see have active development, and plans to take flight into a 1.0 version. This seemed like one of those games to me because I bought this earlier on in its development before we had the steam achievements, and whenever there was a giant label below the main room that said something like “we will implement this feature soon,” or something. And they did. Which I love this because even something as simple as this shows follow through. These smaller observations out of the way, let’s see about reviewing Potion Craft.✅ - I bought this game in early access because it's an interesting concept before I saw dozens of games that released that were related to potion making. (Here I'm not looking at release dates necessarily, but for me this seemed like an original idea and a distinct simulator game). Over the course of the early access and release, there have been noticeable quality of game improvements that have been excellent. (For example, the haggle mechanic. You used to have to hit the skill checks and then inevitably -- hopefully if you got the max amount -- you would have to hit a final skill check on the left or right. This isn't the case anymore. When you've maxed out, you've maxed out. I think this is a great improvement and doesn't force you to have to try and manage hitting a bunch of skill checks to hopefully get near the max.)This is one simple observation that I’m making regarding the game that is a quality of life improvement, but the collective of all the changes that have been made about this game are important. It’s what makes the game better in general. ✅ -- despite the varying, sharp shades of brown that color the entirety of the game, and that might normally seem as an eye sore, the art style is distinct. Not to mention that there are plenty of other colors with the patrons, the UI in the potion making screen, the greenery, etc. But there is a shade of sepia over almost everything. Despite all this, I like how it is. There are some hints of realism while maintaining a somewhat cartoonish style of the patrons visiting the potion shop that you have. This is a noticeable positive for me. ✅ to what I would imagine Medieval times would be. I don't know if the music is actually accurate, but again, the point is not to be accurate to what exactly Medieval times was, it’s more just “does this seem pretty original and interesting,” and it seems original to me. It becomes more of a background feature, too, after a while, and I am inclined to turn it down because it loops, but it is enjoyable nonetheless. ➖  -- This is mostly an observation of the game as this is mostly stating the game in general, and it doesn't have to be a lot of things. Really the thing here is that whenever you buy this game, you are buying a game where you craft potions. This is the primary thing you are doing. This isn't a game like  where you are able to get gear that you later sell in a shop and buy upgrades and such. No. You are making potions, you are selling potions, you are upgrading your workstation. That is mostly it. I enjoy this, though. For $15? Absolutely.❌ - I can't quite place this idea, but whenever I play the first game that a developer publishes (not makes, mind you. I realize game developers make a lot of games before they publish their first game, etc.) I feel as though it happens that the game catches this distinct quality of "Okay, let's make this thing, get it out there, so that we can understand how this works as far as developing, marketing, patching, listening to feedback, etc. goes, and then we'll either make a new game that we actually want to make (For this I think of "An Airport for Alines Currently Run by Dogs" being published first by Strange Scaffold and then they make "Space Warlord Organ Trading SImulator")  or improve upon this existing product  (like Hopoo games and the Risk of Rain series.)" I know that's not succinct, but I'm hoping someone understands that thought. More importantly, here, the game does one thing -- make potions. I get how this could be frustrating to some, but whenever the core gameplay mechanic is presented to you almost instantly, and there's an expectation of this very particular gameplay loop netting you hundreds of hours of gameplay, maybe a readjustment of expectations is necessary. Whenever there’s a game out there that shows gradual improvement over time, is a game that is the first game a developer publishes, continues to support development after the game is released actively, and is a decent game, I want to give it credit where it is due. With original artwork, original music, a core gameplay mechanic that seems to have enough polish to function well, and much more, I can absolutely recommend this game for people who want a game that doesn’t try to do too much, and you just want to make some potions for people.Strong 6 to a light 7 out of 10. ✅✅✅➖➖

_childDocuments_.review: Stylistically beautiful, mechanically interesting. Potion Craft provides a solid foundation in mechanics but falls short in a few aspects that lead me to not recommend this game in its current state. Map exploration is one of the core mechanics that let players discover new potions, refine existing ones to higher quality, and collect experience orbs to level alchemy. While it encourages players to experiment, the limited daily resources is a serious hindrance that punishes inefficient use of ingredients and mistakes like excessive stirring, grinding, and diluting.Finite resources also cause needless tedium where you feel obligated to haggle each customer as to "not leave money on the table". Especially as the ramp up in demand for the highest quality potion comes quickly after a few days, expectations for optimal resource management creates a level of unnecessary stress.Limited potion recipes detracts from the feeling of progression as it fails to strike a balance between the cost and quality of life. Buying new tabs to prevent the need to reproduce high quality potions creates a strain on your money that could otherwise be used on ingredients that are already sorely needed for exploration and experience.As it is early access, there are features that have yet to be added that may alleviate some of these issues. However in it's current state, the game needs to decide whether to lean into being a punishing resource management focus or a relaxing sandbox take. Potion Craft definitely has the potential to rectify these problems with some simple balance changes and more generous exploration mechanics, and I hope to see them addressed in future patches.

_childDocuments_.review: This game is currently (Early Oct 2021) in early access, but here's what I have to say about the game as it is right now:First off - what's currently here is really, really good. The gameplay captures the "part science, part art form, part guesswork" vibe that all fantasy alchemy should aspire to incredibly well, and the tactile interactions of crushing up ingredients and brewing potions is completely knocked out of the park. Everything looks and feels really great. It's very clear that the developers wanted to get the "feel" right before diving into the "big picture" features like progression and such, and their work has definitely paid off, because it really is just a pleasure to interact with the game even in its current state.Here's the Early Access asterisk to this review: This game definitely feels like an early access game in a lot of ways. There are several buttons plainly labelled "this feature isn't available yet", a handful of mechanics (eg Reputation) have no real impact at the moment, and there isn't a lot of weight to the currently-available progression. The missing planned features means that the main thing you get right now is the "core gameplay loop" of making simple potions to satisfy customers every day and unlocking a small handful of advanced recipes to tinker with. This is very enjoyable on its own, but it gets a little repetitive without an impactful progression system to build toward. You definitely get the sense that a lot of the vision for the game hasn't been completely realized just yet, but the fact that the core of it is *so* good just makes me really excited to see what's coming. Overall, I do really like what's here, and I can absolutely see the amazing potential this game has going forward. I'm glad I bought it! I think anyone who just likes the idea of being a fantasy alchemist brewing up potions will have a lot of fun with it even as it is right now. Definitely worth picking up or keeping an eye on.You can get an overview of planned features in-game by clicking on "About Early Access" in the menu, and I'm really, really looking forward to all of it - especially stuff like having more control over gardening and growing ingredients.

_childDocuments_.review: Potion Craft is, by far, the best crafting system I have ever seen in any game. It genuinely feels like you are crafting. It is exceedingly clever. Because of the way the system is set up, things like "more powerful potions require more ingredients" emerge naturally, rather than being arbitrarily required. The crafting in Potion Craft is a delight.And I wish I could recommend Potion Craft, but I can't. I can't, because the morality system in Potion Craft is awful to the point of distraction.Technically, it is a "reputation" system, and later in development it is meant to dynamically affect the customer base of your store. That, by itself, is not a terrible idea. What is terrible about this system is its implementation.There are no specific effects that are "bad" in this morality system. Rather, it is the people you sell to who are good or bad. A village woman wants deadly deadly poison? That's "good." Someone in rough looking clothes wants poison? That's bad. Selling potions to cops is always "good." And the cops ("guards") in the game ask for some seriously horrific ♥♥♥♥. Sell acid to a thief? Extremely bad. Sell fire potion to a guard so he can burn the homes of his enemies, the actual stated purpose for this in the game? Good. Sell battle rage potion to guards? Good.Potion Craft has an enormous authoritarian streak that makes playing at length extremely uncomfortable. A huge chunk of the sales you are expected to make in this otherwise lighthearted game are to guards whose openly stated purpose is to brutalize and murder people, committing various war crimes along the way.It should be rewritten, because it's awful as it stands.ACAB

_childDocuments_.review: Pretty fun alchemy shop game. Basically you bounce between a mini-game of adding herbs to explore a map of various effects, organize your recipes and another mini-game to haggle for potentially more or less sale prices. There is a moral compass duality going on where you sell to people doing something "bad" or "good" and you will get more customers like that, but otherwise there are no other effects on the game nor narrative to follow.One con to this game is the chapters and content seem well paced until the very end, where there remains only 1-2 more objectives and they take hours of grinding (repeated activity without anymore exploration or creativity necessary). It seems like it would have been a better decision to end it earlier or otherwise include additional content to make this section more enjoyable. I also would say if you like this type of game to check out Strange Horticulture--it is more fleshed out and less of a mini-game/more of a story.

_childDocuments_.review: I bought this game in early access, and game is fun, or at least is for the first few hours when you're learning everything. However the grind is real, it's REALLY real. Trying to get all of the achievements for this game was genuinely a painful affair. I mean that literally, as the amount of potions you make and the amount of ingredient grinding and stirring can lead to some mouse hand fatigue. There is very little guidance throughout the game, and lots of time saving features are completely hidden, I only discovered them nearly two dozen hours in the game.You spend A LOT of time just doing repetitive movements. Heating up the cauldron speeds up your potion's travel time across the map, but also activates the teleportation whirlpools so you're better off with the glacial default travel speed. The game also never tells you that right clicking your completed potions and ingredients automatically adds them to the customer scale and mortar & pestle respectively. Later in the game when you have dozens and dozens of ingredients with hundreds of quantities of them, not having any sort of user friendly read function besides hovering your mouse over them is incredibly time consuming and irritating.There are a few typos in the customer requests as well, while not debilitating, it does take you out of the life sim the game markets itself as. In general you're just grinding for RPG elements that just add a % increase to what you had already in the game. With the exception of your first alchemy machine project, the entire game can really be boiled down to only a handful of very repetitive actions. If you play this game for 2, maybe 3 hours, you've already experienced everything it has to offer- just with slight deviations.After you finish your first Nigredo, Albedo, Citrinitas, Rubedo, and finally your Philosopher's Stone, you realize that they're really just further ingredients to make the various alchemy salts. However, you only really need moon salt, so you just make 5, maybe 6 of those and you don't have to bother making Sun Salt, Life Salt, or Philosopher's Salt. As you only need one type of these to rotate your potions to the correct angle, and Philosopher's Salt comes so late into the game that you should have hundreds of any ingredient you require to make any potion you'd wish.Adding onto that, the very last alchemy machine potions are just effects separated by one side of the map to the other. I understand that this is a simple system, but it's just time-padding plain and simple. This game could have been very nuanced with a lot of complex customization features. You could have combined potions to make potion tiers above 5, or utilized your alchemy machine ingredients into super expensive panaceas that could net you the thousands you need to get your alchemy stashes stocked up and ready for the final projects. I also have to imagine that the 10,000+ ingredients really fit into your tiny medieval alchemy shack, and that you're not some time traveling Bezos slave peddling Amazon snake oils to medieval peasants. Overall, There's a very fun essence and art style to this game, someone poured their heart and soul into the art style and it does feel thematically accurate. I just feel like it's half baked and a time sink without the level of depth that it first appears to. I hope that it has some updates, but from reading the other reviews, I believe this game was really released before it was totally finished and just labelled as such to move onto a different project. Buy it on sale, I bought it when it was $10 in early access, I'm sure it will dip this Christmas and you can spend 40 hours playing this instead of hugging your family or something.

_childDocuments_.review: This game is so simple in its design and thus surprisingly addictive in the same way Game Dev Tycoon got me hooked. I have started over a few times because there is replay-ability. You can focus on being good or evil by choosing which customers to help and which to turn away and depending on who comes to you, the majority of the potions they want are different. Furthermore, you can craft various potions in an endless variety of ways and save the recipes. Customers will sometimes give you a challenge to make them a potion with only so many ingredients or using a certain type, which increases the strategy and puzzle-solving. I usually hate puzzle games, but this one is really fun because of how open-ended the solutions are. It is fun to find a way to make someone's request work; it feels like an accomplishment. I also like that you have to figure out what potion would meet the customer's needs. The balance and progression are just right. You can also design your potion bottles and the label art to be unique to each potion and/or each time you play, making your potions feel more like your own, personal creation. I recommend going onto Nexus and downloading some mods that improve the game even more, like the mods that help you organize your recipe book and the ones that add more ingredients. But even without mods, this game is incredibly fun!

_childDocuments_.review: Everyone dreams of being an alchemist at some point in their lives, and with Potion Craft, you can finally live out those dreams. Developed by niceplay games, your job is to run your own alchemy business by brewing unique potions. Using the dirty flowers and disgusting mushrooms you find in your garden out back, without rinsing them, you must make different combinations to achieve different types of potions to help each customer out in a specific situation they present. Haggle with customers, buy new machines, and grow your business to be the best there ever was. With a multitude of ways to customize each potion, gorgeous artstyle, and physics-based interactions, this game is one of the better early access games I have played in recent times.

_childDocuments_.review: Games like this could aspire to be even more than they are, as it stands, it is a pretty simple gameplay loop. Your job is to find the most efficient recipes, save them, and keep stock for special orders, you buy bulk ingredients (I would), then sell for profit. _childDocuments_.review: This game is worth playing, but don't expect to play it very long until they expand on the gameplay loop. It is about experiencing what a nice crafting system could be. What would essentially be a simple side-minigame in another MMORPG, has been purified to it's concentrated form and expanded into a full game in here. Unfortunately, for now I find the game "finished" at around mid-game. Everything later than that seems like a more tedious repetition of the the exact same routines. I feel it lacks on a story-wise and the puzzle-wise front. Nevertheless, developers are constantly working on it and posting devlogs, so we will see how it goes. IIRC I bought it on sale, and for that I am grateful -- the game earned for itself. If I had bought it at it's regular price, however, I could have been underwhelmed and disappointed. This game works as a prototype or art form, but to be a fully-fledged, 100% completable casual title it needs some serious core gameloop improvements. Nonetheless, I am happy that I experienced this piece, thus I recommend trying it out... but at the same time -- maybe wait for a sale, or for some major patch first.Pros:- Unique and simple mechanics which are fun to play and mesh well together- Beautiful art and meticulously crafted details shine brightly in this game- Calm and serene atmosphere without any pressure of time and without inducing a fear of missing out- Mechanics are generally intuitive, assigning one of 8 attributes corresponding to the ingredient gives this game another layer of depth- UI and UX are very good, it is just a pleasure to interact with this gameA room for improvement:- For a game that you most probably spend long time playing during one session, the diversity and amount of music is very lacking. At times it even makes me dizzy listening to the same music on a loop, which forces me to either close the game or mute it. For example dwarf fortress has 18 or so, minecraft has 2(3?) albums while this game, for now, has only 2 very similar tracks.- It has (a bad type of) grind at times, and from what I have heard and experienced already, the it's even more severe mid-to-late game. Several repetitive in-game days often pass by without much progress and doing essentially the same thing over and over, crafting the same potions but varying the ingredients from time to time, only to wait for a specific merchant to bring you a new part for the alchemical or none of the ingredients you lack the most. I Definitely didn't reach end-game. Maybe I tapped onto the front doors of the mid-game, but for now it gets quite repetitive. I have not unlocked the new alchemical map -- I got tired of doing the same thing over and over.- It feels claustrophobic at times as well. Seeing the fields outside the windows makes you want to go outside and explore the world. Seeing the bedroom makes you want to interact with it, but it's essentially a whole screen added for the sake of one and only interaction - the bed to skip a day.- There is a purely cosmetic mechanic of the reputation that has no real gameplay impact, but it has a yet untapped potential.- There are several places where you can progress, but they feel a bit disconnected. The Alchemist's path feels a to be of little importance and not very impactful. I Breezed though 4 pages (almost half of the book) in one (6h?) sitting almost without noticing it. Talents are a bit weirdly distributed in time: you can reach level 28 and learn >50% of all the talent levels in the first sitting. I guess final levels are the hardest to get, but if not, You may be wondering layer "what now?". I see they have plans for new talents so I'm looking for that and maybe some more improvements on that system.- Haggling is something that you almost always want to do, so there should maybe be some balancing on that matter. - Performance: for a game that moves around a bunch of sprites, it has a surprisingly high impact on the my machine. From the simplicity of the machanics and graphics I assumed this game could be played on a toaster. but it felt a bit sluggish at times and ventilators start working considerably louder. I also don't understand the very long load time, somehow? It uses 2.2 GB when in background (on Linux Proton), 85 vt-threads and 20% processing power of a 6 core processor? How?- There seems to be a lot of content (look at all those potion stickers!), but it's quite inaccessible due to the grind. I find maps to be a bit too big, the trips of potions too long and the lack of different starting points tedious. Maybe if there was some way to move the potions larger distances it would be better. For example some kind of pressure mechanic - when brewing under pressure, the whole map would shrink (or the ingredient path would expand) allowing for travelling bigger distances quicker?- Alchemical machine is underwhelming. After using it you are left with "...was that it?"My ideas for growth:- It would be nice if the potions crafted in the game had some more uses. A good example is the upcoming feature of the wild growth potion for plants. Crafting a potion of fire or a potion of cold is essentially the same thing but using different ingredients. It would be nice seeing some real impact those things have on the world around us. Libido/love potion could affect bees which would in turn pollinate flowers, or increase a chance of random plants growing. A Potion of strength could be used to break a broken door for the inaccessible part of the house (or the city, read below). A slowness potion could be used to increase the accuracy of using tools, while a speed potion would amplify the effects of paths or something- If the alchemical machine was more interactive, it could give another dimension to the game. Twisting corks to mix potions in right proportions, pouring out the sludge or sediment from vials, heating and keeping mixtures at good temperature for a certain amount of time, adjusting angles of tubes, lighting up flames and adjusting their height and strength, connecting the tubes, releasing or increasing the pressure and whatnot are some of the examples I would think about adding if I were a part of the team. Maybe instead of buying whole sets of alchemical machines we would buy flasks and components which we would later combine and place on our own? Managing space and using available tools?- There is an untapped potential of discovering the world's lore while progressing through the game and feeling like a part of the a living universe. Merchants could bring books or tell tales. We could buy paintings of distant lands or explanations of the origin of plants etc.- There is a place for a story about the mystery of the alchemical cottage and it's previous owner, which we would progressively unravel. Rooms we could unlock, repairs we could make, notes and bits of knowledge from him etc.- It would be very nice to see some more locations. A city or a village, a cave, a forest, a tavern, a castle and whatnot could be added. Different shops in the city to make use of the earned money and use the potions to interact with NPCs in there. See them walk around and do their things. Haggle for tools with villagers, use strength potion to break the doors of a closed abandoned shop, use potion of nightvision to access a cave, Combine it with the reputation mechanic to make some locations more accessible or restricted than others, for example bad reputation would prevent you from interacting with rightful shop owners but would in turn give you access to the backalley and black market, where you could buy some exclusive forbidden items. With good reputation you could buy certified exclusive goods from good merchants etc.Ultimately this game is constantly growing, and planned features will probably resolve some of the issues mentioned above, so I'm only looking forward to it! The above critique doesn't impact my positive reception of this game, and I still highly recommend playing it.

_childDocuments_.review: This game is so much fun. It does not have time limits that would stress you out or any threat of losing your shop. As far as I know, there isn't even a game over. It's a puzzle game where you're tasked with making potions for people, and have to find different ways to make potions using the herbs, mushrooms, and crystals available to you. Once you get enough of a particular item, or you find a way to reliably make a potion, you can save it for later in a handy "Recipe Book". From there, you can automatically make that potion without going through the trouble of actually brewing it. It just consumes those resources and makes that kind and quality of potion that you saved. You can hand craft everything, or try to make more efficient potions, and sometimes people will come in and ask for specialty ones or mixed potions, The demos show how it works pretty well, and I recommend anyone who is interested to buy it now while it's at a lower price in case it gets more expensive. (Also there is a cameo from a certain "Hunter" who asks for potions and bombs to handle ghouls and ghosts, trolls and the like. He's a fan of women and dice. Later i think he gets into cards, but in his early career, it was definitely dice.)

_childDocuments_.review: A very good game for the price, relaxing but weirdly engaging at the same time.I started to feel that "Zen" level of concentration that comes from other activities like playing an instrument, working with tools... or practicing an actual trade, which is what I felt like I'd learned by the time I finished playing. The game recreates that realistic vibe through the physical experience of using your lab instruments. You can stir rapidly or slowly, but with the movement of the mouse and the animation onscreen it's easy to forget that you're not actually stirring. You can pulverize ingredients methodically or even violently with your mortar and pestle, but again, the translation of mouse movement into onscreen action gives a sensation like you're actually working in your own laboratory.Things start out simply enough, and the mechanical underpinnings of the game stay pretty much the same, but challenge and complexity continue as you progress through the game. This comes from a few different factors. Initially, there's a scarcity of effective ingredients to work with. As you progress further, your toolbox gets bigger but your objectives on the alchemy map get more and more difficult to reach. And as all of those pieces finally fall into place, the game generates new novelty through the sometimes-exacting specifications put forward by your customers - combinations of effects, including/excluding certain ingredients, limiting the number/type you can use, etc.By the time I got to the VERY end of the game and picked up the last couple of achievements, I kinda just wanted it to be done with... But, then again, there are so many games in my library that I never 100% finish because I feel like it's not worth attaining for the level of effort involved. This was within reach, so I went for it, and I certainly enjoyed all of the hours I put into the game short of maybe the last 2-3 that I did just for the sake of being a completionist. Maybe there's some room for improvement in the gameplay loop all the way toward the end of the game? Either way, I'm not too concerned.Maybe my only other complaint is that Potion Craft has ONE single music track on a perpetual loop - listening to a 2-minute loop for 30 hours can be tough to manage in large doses. But they've mentioned that that's something they're already working on, so by the time you pick up the game and get to the 10-hour mark maybe your head won't be ready to explode and you won't need to take a day to cool off.Overall, I enjoyed my time with the game, and I plan to revisit it once they add some of the new features they've hinted at. But that's not to say that Potion Craft doesn't already feel complete in its current state. It was fun, it will be the next time I pick it up, and I feel perfectly fine recommending it at the full price listed.On a side note... If you like dark humor, feel free to start catering to some of the more questionable people who visit your establishment and asking you to do questionable things. I got a good laugh out of some of the ridiculous explanations customers gave me for a bunch of their potion requests.

_childDocuments_.review: I have played this game for around 40 hours, from the beta launch to version 1.0 . This game has a lot to offer, both in gameplay and visuals, but is a little bit rough around the edges in a few ways that over time become more grind than actual engaging gameplay. The core mechanic in Potion Craft is, as the title would suggest, crafting potions. You use ingredients that lead you in different directions on the alchemy map in order to discover and create potions with new effects. The other portions of the game are spent selling the potions you've learned to make, improving new recipes, and seeking out ingredients both familiar and new to you.Recently, the game moved into version 1.0. I feel that 1.0 may not have been advertised entirely accurately, as I myself thought a lot more content would be coming to the game. I was both excited and disappointed by the content that was added in version 1.0 after launching it for the first time. There are some places where the game feels fresh and exciting, and some where it's the same, excruciatingly similar slog to the beta.Here's the good, the bad, and the ugly of it all:+This game has a really calm and relaxing atmosphere+It will challenge you, but has an obvious endgame where you have a recipe for every potion and every part of greater recipes+It feels gratifying for one of the visiting merchants to ask you for a potion to help them find you more ingredients+Getting over the hump of not having enough ingredients gives some real satisfaction for an hour or two+The new haggling system mixes things up and makes you consider whether a tiny health potion is worth haggling for, whether because of the skill it takes, or the time it takes.+For what it offers, I feel that this game is fairly priced. It doesn't feel like the developers are trying to squeeze money out of anybody, and you simply get exactly what you pay for. Much better than paying $15 for an indie game that can be completed in an hour.-Hearing the same music over and over again gets a little grating after a while. Sure, you could mute it and play your own or watch a video on the side, but I feel that doing so really takes away from the atmosphere of the game.-Merchants feel as though they need more depth, though this has been improved on slightly already. I think it would add a lot to the game to have more ways to interact with them, even something as simple as showing off your salts or created stones to the sorcerer in exchange for some advice.-Not being able to save large recipes that use a dozen different potions is a large obstacle. Though it's not the end of the world to click through the recipe book and cook up one of each potion in order to craft something, doing it once for each tier of stone gets tiring quickly.--People often ask for things that seem entirely impossible. For example, a potion effect in the corner of the map that clearly needs more than one ingredient, they will ask to be made with only one ingredient. Even worse is that these stipulations are often required in order to make the sale at all, forcing you to turn a customer away and lose reputation.--The last three or so hours of 100% completing this game are a complete slog. Beyond having every possible recipe written down, there is really no end-game content beyond grinding out the last stones and achievements. There is nothing to keep you on your toes besides occasionally whipping up a weaker version of a potion you already have a recipe for.--The new haggling system often feels unresponsive in that sometimes the hits feel completely off, or I have to click the mouse twice in order to get it to register. --Once you've completed every achievement, or even just completed everything the game has to offer, there's no fanfare, nor any point in playing for even five minutes longer. I don't think that the gameplay loop is exciting enough to warrant further play, as it's just repeating the same three actions over, and over, and over again.Overall, I think this is a really nifty little game that will sometimes challenge you to think outside of the box. What it feels like it needs above all else is some more work done to pad out the content that does exist in order to create a gratifying endgame and achievement hunt.

_childDocuments_.review: 29.1h (100% achievement, finished the game) No (the game might be grindy depending on your playstyle). Yes (1 achievement). No. is a management game that combines potion-making and shop management. You will craft potions based on customer demands and sell them. The potion-making mechanic allows you to be creative, whether it's to make a potion based on the available ingredients or find a way to make the same potion with fewer costs for more profit.- A lot of potion varieties to craft- Freedom in creating the potions however you like- The end game can be problematic to some people; potion-making becomes exhausting to do while shop management becomes repetitive- Buyable ingredients rely too much on RNG early gameIntel Core i5-9300H 2.40GHz, 8GB RAM, NVIDIA GeForce GTX 1650 did a good job to depict the medieval setting. The brown color is used as the majority of the game's visuals, with characters and objects that look like drawing from the same era. The relaxing music that accompanies it also helps to promote the medieval theme, making it feel as if you are there.The only "story" that you'll get from the game is the cutscene when you start a new game. The rest of the dialogues will be coming from your customers to tell you what potion they want to buy.The game title describes the gameplay perfectly. You are a potion maker in the medieval era, and it's your job to make potions based on your customer's demands. However, they won't say which potions they would like to buy right away; instead, they will tell you about their issue, and you need to suggest which potion they should buy by presenting it in front of them. Some requests have more than one solution, and although some are easy to figure out, others can be vaguer, making it hard to understand what they really want.Customers differ based on your reputation. Serving good people will increase your reputation and attract more good people while serving the bad ones will decrease it and attract more bad people. Both sides of customers have different sets of requests: good people will ask for something that can help them do their daily jobs, and bad people will tend to look for ways to kill others. To be honest, I found the bad customers' requests to be more straightforward, although sometimes I appreciate it more than the more obscure requests from the good customers."All roads lead to Rome" is the perfect idiom for potion-making in . It is done in a map-like interface where you need to move a flask to the flask symbol(s) on the map. Each symbol will give a different effect, with a higher quality if you manage to bring the flask closer to the symbol. Ingredients are used to move the flask - each ingredient has a different pathway, and you need to decide which ingredient to use based on your stock and strategy. You can get more profit if you manage to make a potion with fewer and/or cheaper ingredients, although those adjustments aren't mandatory.Ingredients are limited, especially in the early game. Random ingredients might spawn in your garden every day, but it's usually not enough. You need to purchase more from the NPCs that are coming to your shop every day to fulfill your needs. However, their selection is randomized. It's easy to overuse a certain ingredient early game, making you unable to make a potion from the recipe that you have saved. It takes time to make a potion and redoing it for some potions every few in-game days just because you run out of ingredients is exhausting.Speaking of exhausting, the same can also be said in the end game. Although the game is fun, the last 10h feels more like a chore. You are forced to make a potion with effects that are located very far from the map, ruining the experience. It was fun to make a perfect potion for each type, but having to spend your time making a potion with multiple effects that can take a very long time to finish is not. It's easy to get burned out from making each potion because of it.I finished the game in 28.4h and continued playing for one achievement for 0.7h. The game isn't hard to finish - it takes some time to get used to the potion-making mechanic, but it only takes endurance to finish it once you know what to do. Yes, the game is overstaying its welcome. It becomes a chore to finish once you have finished making all of the potion types. I lost motivation in continuing because I felt that should be everything that the game has to offer, but it forced me to continue playing by giving tasks to mix potions with different effects that can take a long time to finish as a finale. It took hours to get them all after a lot of complaining.Serving the customers becomes some sort of relief later on, but it also turns out to be repetitive. You need to listen to what they want, make a potion with a single click, sell it to them, and repeat it all over again. Some customers might ask for a custom request, but with the potion-making being exhausting as it is, I find it easier to either give them what I have or reject them, even if I had to take a hit in popularity that affect the number of incoming customers. Having too many recipes is a nightmare since there is no paging option. My experience with  is a bit mixed. I thought the game would be like  at first, but it ends up focusing more on the potion-making rather than the shop mechanic. Although I enjoyed the game at the beginning, the end game ends up as a chore, ruining my experience. The game becomes manageable once I tried to play it in short bursts, although the exhaustion is still there. I could recommend buying it because I enjoyed 90% of the game, but please keep in mind that the last stretch of the game won't be as pleasant. I would even suggest stopping playing the game altogether after it reaches that point unless you care about the achievement or still enjoyed the game - there won't be an ending or anything waiting for you after you finished everything.

_childDocuments_.review: So I was really expecting to like this one and bought it as soon at 1.0 hit, thinking it was really my sort of game. Unfortunately, it really fell flat for me.The potion-making core gameplay (95% of the game with a bit of ancilliary stuff which is basically working out which potions you need) is a simplistic maze game where you move through a repetitive and slow process. Unlike many of these high-concept, high-theme indie games, this process never changes or develops, rather you just have to go further into the maze later in the game. Once you have played for ten minutes you have seen everything this game has to offer.This would be fine if the core gameplay was really fun but it isn't. It's kind of intriguing at first and I like the abstraction of representing chemistry with a maze but ultimately it's just a very basic maze game where you have to go through three steps (always the same three steps) to move anywhere.I put up with this for a while (14 hours in fact), hoping that the game would develop some new twist on the formula or significantly speed up the exponentially-increasing grind to reach the next level. It did not, and it's a shame.Pros:Theming is great - looks and sounds fantasticConcept of alchemy expressed as a maze input game is interestingDependent on tastes:I really think this would be better if you could buy ingredients at any time - when you end up with loads of money but no ingredients that let you move in a certain direction it's very frustrating.Cons:Repetitive beyond all beliefGrindy, with the later recipes requiring a total repeat of ALL earlier onesSome of the requests can be annoyingly vague: 'I want a potion to stop my fruit from going rotten.' Is that a rejuvenation potion? A growth potion? A necromancy potion? An ice potion? I honestly never figured it out.The save recipe shortcut doesn't really work as is for any but the most basic potions (the ones you need the shortcut for the least) because you will use so many ingredients you inevitably won't have the same ones next time - again, something that being able to buy ingredients on the fly would help with.

_childDocuments_.review: this game is trying so hard to be a good game. i wanted to love it SO badly. i honestly think the design is gorgeous, the concept is sound, and the writing is clever. the sound design is nice. it manages to feel rather immersive at times, too.however, what makes the game suffer is thus: the mechanics of brewing the potions are SO unforgiving. you are barely given any guidance apart from the very brief tutorial (meaning i had to google most solutions when i got stuck). they don't explain what half of the tools do (ex. i had to google what the ladle did, as it isn't included in the tutorial). but most of all, there simply aren't enough ingredients available in a given day to allow for practically any mistakes. especially as the potions get more complicated, the first time you attempt to brew something is often a nail-biting experience of hoping to god you won't fail, because if you do?, you waste absolutely everything you just put into the cauldron. _childDocuments_.review: Potion Craft: Alchemist Simulator is a 20-30+ hour relaxing medieval sim with in which you craft and invent a multitude of potions, dabble in chemistry, and slowly work toward making your Magnum Opus, the Philosophers Stone. Running your day-to-day life is peaceful, there are no time constraints, no micromanagement, and the day ends when you want it to. Taking care of the shop is pretty simple, customers come in, ask if you have or can make something, and depending on what you give them to solve their issue, you get reputation points that affect what kind of customers that show up. As expected, having a negative reputation gives you creepy necromancers, murderous assassins, and terrible people in general, while a positive reputation will give you normal working citizens looking for something to help their backyard garden grow, nobles looking for some amusement, town guards, and other friendly wizards. Actual potion making is pretty fun, interacting with your tools to grind down your ingredients, stir and heat up your cauldron, inventing, discovering, and bottling something useful. Eventually, you will have a plethora of book tabs and saved recipes in your notebook, something for any situation. With book tabs, you can automatically make any potion you’ve made before, provided you have the exact same ingredients you used in the initial making of said potion. You have two Alchemy Maps, in which your potion is either water or oil based, which changes how and what can be made, and as you gain experience, you get points to put into useful traits and learning skills. To overall highlight my positive experience, despite coming out of early access and hitting the market with a positive impact, there are still frequent updates with a major one coming out in the near future. At the time of this review it hasn’t been released yet, but a garden expansion + more interaction with it has been planned, new talents and skills to pick up, more ingredients and salts to create, shop customization, more merchants and customer variations, more maps and even more potions. The developers are also a frequent sight in the community itself, showing off the development processes and running art festivals. The community, while I’ve only lurked, is very positive and I hope to see more of the above in the future.

_childDocuments_.review: I really want to love this game, and I unfortunately did not return it on the hopes that it would become something I could enjoy but even after the major update, I still kinda hate it. My issues with the game won't be everyone's issues. One, I hate the haggle feature. I'm an older gamer who, let's be real, never had great reflexes in the first place. I don't want to do timed things. Period. Even the stirring feature is irritating to me because if I accidentally move my mouse too far, I can mess up a potion level. So the haggling is next level. On the easy level, it's fine (though not enjoyable to me), but on harder levels it's just too anxiety inducing for what should be a chill game. My other, bigger, main issue with the game is that it seems to punish exploration and experimentation, even as it requires it for progression. It's so easy to lose massive quantities of ingredients on wild goose chases, to accidentally "die" and reset back to center, to think you figured out the combo for a potion only to have it be something else and then not have the ingredients left to make the one you needed. Some of the whirlpools spit you out at seemingly useless or weird positions. Every time I try to play around and have fun with exploring the map, I just end up extremely frustrated, broke, and ingredient-less. The game is also very repetitive, as mentioned in other negative reviews. I don't always mind this in games, I love to grind, but the lack of a truly rewarding mechanic and the difficulty creating new potions makes the tedium...well...tedious. I love the artwork, and I love the premise, but sadly the execution of this leaves me wishing I could get my money back.

_childDocuments_.review: Very fun game, cool concept, cute visuals, and fun to play. I enjoyed it enough to 100% it, but while the beginning is fun, past mid game it gets extremely tedious. I would give this a middle thumb rating if I could, because while the beginning is indeed fun, the mid to end game is frustrating. You will have plenty of recipes for certain potions, so that you don't have to spend minutes making the exact same potion over and over, but they only work if you have the ingredients for the recipe, which you have absolutely no control over, as your enchanted tree, which gives you ingredients every day, is completely random on which ones you get, and the merchants that sell you ingredients, also completely random! Meaning that you may have to simply delete one of your recipes because you haven't been given a certain ingredient in weeks. There is also an alchemy machine, which you use to make the ingredients for the philosopher's stone, very cool concept, until you get into it, you have to make a ridiculous amount of super specific potions that only work for making the stones, which in of itself takes quite a while. But, because these potions are super specific, they require a lot of ingredients, which goes back to my previous point. On top of that, you have to hand insert all the potions you made, as there is no recipe to instantly make the gemstones. At one point, I had to make a salt to help make the potions I needed, I had to go through cooking things up in the alchemy machine... 15 times!! It took like 10 minutes just to finish making the salts.Finally, the final achievement, in which you have to get to level 15 alchemy level, took me 5 hours of extra playtime, just giving potions to new customers, and taking reputation hits when people would come in for legitimately impossible orders.TL;DRI am conflicted on whether to give this a thumbs up or down, I like the game, but it gets stale pretty damn fast. This is all coming from somebody who loves to 100% games, if you are a casual player who will pick this up, play until you feel fulfilled and leave, I highly recommend it. But the 100% grind is so mind numbing and tedious that I had to push myself to make it all the way

_childDocuments_.review: This is a great little puzzle game with a simple and satisfying mechanic for creating potions. Add ingredients whole or grind them for a different effect, carefully consider how finely you want to grind an ingredient to nudge your path this way or that, and then stir and dilute until you reach a perfect mix. Finally, boil the cauldron to lock in your potion effect. The potion map's hazard zones force careful use of rare ingredients, or you can brute-force your way through with larger numbers of cheap and common herbs. There are no timers to pressure you so feel free to take your time pondering whether to add Hairy Banana or Red Mushrooms, or plotting a route through several effects for a special health restorative sleep potion.

That's pretty much my only gripe at this point. I'd love to see more ingredients, customers, random events, a more robust skill tree, conversations, quests, shop management, customization. I've only gotten up to void salts, but after getting fairly far in the game I feel like there should be some more variety in ways you can craft potions other than having enough money to throw ingredients at problems. Maybe life salts (and whatever's after that) spices things up more? Though I do feel like something should be available sooner. I have minor complaints about the reputation and morality system, but it appears very early in implementation so I won't get into that.Anyway, enough rambling. Great game.

_childDocuments_.review: I do think this is a fun game, clearly I enjoyed it enough given I've 100%'d it. However this game is very grindy if you want to 100% it. I've played this game since beta too. The early game is very fun as you have all the exploration you could want however it is held down by the struggle to get enough ingredients. I think the mid game is best I greatly enjoy the oil map exploration and the flexibility you have with more ingredients and money. Also I loved creating prefect recipes and customising the potions. The late game struggles though. One of my fav parts of interacting with customers is the little story bit you get, the fisherman the brewer the merchants telling you about their lives. In the end game you've run out of things like this and regular customer interactions feel like a slog cus it's all the same stuff you've heard before. I do like the additional requirements they add though. The alchemy machine stuff is fun but after sun salt it gets very grindy and loses it appeal. Plus finishing chapter X and Philosopher's salt are very underwhelming. You get 5000 Philosopher's salt with an effect that's just sort of fine. By the point in the game it's not very helpful and you've probably gotten very good at understanding and using the potion brewing mechanics like whirlpools and adding more base making the salt not that helpful. Plus the reward for finishing Chapter X is exp points which you definitely don't need seeing as you will have maxed out all your skills by the time you do Chapter X. It would have been nice to having something actually useful. A garden upgrade or whatever. Also the fact the save recipe function for salts and rocks isn't working is annoying cus you have to do it manually. I don't think I will boot this game up again after this cus there's nothing left to do. I feel like this game would benefit from the NPC's being just a bit more interesting. The fellow alchemist becomes useless pretty quick once you don't need paper anymore, I feel like it can't be that hard for him to congratulate you on academical progress. Overall, fun game with a super cute art style but grindy.

_childDocuments_.review: Seems simple but is surprisingly addictive. There's a lot more going on than just making and selling potions. You can spend time perfecting a recipe to use a wide range of ingredients in their most efficient usage, rather than just one ingredient that you soon run out of. You can sell potions to dubious customers when you need coin, and reject their business when you need reputation. You can experiment to gain experience and unlock new effects or better paths for more difficult potions. Top it all off with some lovely music, sound effects, and pleasant art style and you have yourself a winner. My only criticism is that I want more, and I consider that a win.

_childDocuments_.review: I like it. It's chill. There's a real sense of exploration as you discover new potion effects in a fairly unique system: On a 2D board, you add ingredients to go in a direction on the board. (These ingredients never go straight.) The stronger you stir, the farther you go. The closer you land to the potion effect, the higher quality the potion will be. The result is a game of exploring the unknown and dexterous crafting. Pretty neat.The game allows you to save recipes (which aren't just the ingredients but also how you used them) so you won't have to mortar & pestle every single potion.

_childDocuments_.review: TL;DR: Potion Craft is reminiscent of classic flash games you used to play in the computer lab at school. If you enjoyed games similar to the Papa's Pizzeria games, you'll enjoy this as well. Main issue is the popularity system, but is easily ignored because of other features.PROS:- Fun and heavily repeatable core gameplay loop.- Tons of different ingredients mean tons of different options when solving each brew.- Main quest goals (almost) all very engaging.- Alchemy Machine Feature leads to very fun thinking processes.- Early patrons have a ton of flavor.- All travelling merchants are fun to interact with.- Relaxing yet engaging gameplay.- Haggling lets you ensure people can't put their kids through college.CONS:- Gold seems arbitrary at times but then super important at others. I'm not quite sure how to describe this one.- Popularity system feels grindy and is the leading cause of slow quest progression.- Reputation system not well explained (Early Access).- Patron and merchant dialogue eventually runs out and repeats basic lines (Early Access).Summary: Potion Craft is a great fusion of strategy and puzzle elements that creates a very enjoyable experience. The main potion brewing mechanic is robust and with around 4 hours into the game I'm not certain how many potions I'm missing, I just know it's more than 5. The thought process of wanting perfect potions as cheap as possible leads to really engaging gameplay even though it just consists of moving your mouse and clicking. The main questline comes in the form of the Alchemists' Path and seems to be quite long, as I am only on section 4 of 7. Popularity is the main thing holding me back, as the measly +2 or +3 per potion is a drop in the bucket when 100 or so is needed to increase the level enough to progress the quest line. Ingredients have a great sense of scarcity, and a common yet fun issue is running out of a certain ingredient which leads to new and inventive solutions for everyday brewing. I've very much enjoyed my experience with the game so far, and am excited to see where this game goes.As of patch 0.4.2, I give this game a 7.5/10. Purchase if it seems interesting, I assure you it will be.

_childDocuments_.review: Disappointing. So much potential, but just hasn't hit the mark (yet). I am still hopeful that the devs are continuing to work on this game and plan to release the promised (and hopefully more) changes, but until then, I have uninstalled it and don't plan on playing again. I WANT to enjoy this game, it's a great concept, but it just isn't "ready"...let me explain...As a neurodiverse person, the sounds and feels of the game (with the exclusion of bargaining) are extremely satisfying - especially the mortar and pestle. The game is beautiful, is enjoyable, but misses the marks on mechanics (specifically relating to brewing potions, storing them in the recipe book, the bargaining, and access to materials). For that reason, it's a no from me...for now. If any major updates come, I will write an updated review, otherwise, I personally think this game was not ready for publishing.

_childDocuments_.review: Initially, the game is charming and fun. It has a short tutorial and then kicks you out the nest to fly on your own, where learning how to create numerous potions in a variety of ways is the main source of fun. Unfortunately, the game loses it's charm after awhile and just feels like a big ol' grind. After playing for 10+ hrs, I learned that everything about the game stays practically the same except for the maps you can create potions on. Sure, you get asked to make harder potions and there's the machine in the basement, but other than that, it's the same old same old. I wish there was a bigger sense of progress; the garden expanding, gaining an assistant to take care of customers, etc. But there isn't.I like the game, but the grind makes me unmotivated to finish it - hence, why I don't recommend it.

_childDocuments_.review: I really want to recommend this one, but I can't in its current state. I bought this game two(ish) years ago in early access. The basic gameplay loop is satisfying, the artstyle cute, but at the time it felt like 50% complete . In the two years since, the devs have:With the 1.0 release and the 1.1 QoL release, this game now feels...about 55% complete. The basic gameplay loop is still there, but that is all there is. There is no story outside of the needlessly grindy 'quest' towards forging various salts (far too expensive for what they do and never necessary for actually doing things) culminating towards forging the Philosopher's Stone (insanely grindy, during my two 15 hour playthroughs I gave up well before coming close to getting the stone).The devs have been promising all of these features in development and just fail to deliver. I would love to see this game get the attention it deserves, and if the devs actually implement what they've promised I will easily recommend it. But I have my doubts.

_childDocuments_.review: It's a nice game to pass the time and it is definitely worth the price.+ Fun game+ Great art style+ Cool mechanics+ Diversity in client's requests- Gets boring over time- Repetitive after some time- No clear objective (basically you just grind potions to complete the chapters)It took me 33 hours to complete 100% of the game, including all achievements. It was really fun in the beginning and it was nice to discover all the parts of the map and all the new effects I could make, but after some time it just gets too repetitive and you start to do things "automatically" without thinking too much about it. The game doesn't have an end, so even after you complete everything, you can keep playing and doing the same thing over and over again. There isn't a linear story so, in the end, there isn't an end.In summary, I do recommend the game if you want to pass the time for some hours. The first 20 hours were really fun up until I got the last stone and started to grind the achievements. It is really worth the price.

_childDocuments_.review: Early access review: This game definitely has potential (potiontial?)! The early access version doesn't have all the features yet. The UI shows a shop upgrade button and several other unlockable features that will be available in the full game. This game needs some work to make the potion crafting more enjoyable. Right now, it's a frustrating grind--ingredients are too expensive, the garden doesn't give you enough basics to work with, the map is absolutely huge and you don't have enough information to make good decisions. However, I do love the concept that, like a real alchemist, you have to experiment and waste ingredients to figure out what works in the beginning, getting more and more efficient as you learn. Even after spending a lot of skill points to unlock higher earnings on potions and increasing my haggling skill, patrons just do not pay enough to turn much profit, hence the grind. I have been tempted to look for recipes online, but I'd like to learn on my own since that is really the magic of the game. I am eagerly awaiting the full release to see how the new features will change the experience and if the economics are better balanced.

_childDocuments_.review: I did not think I would like this very much, as I tend to like story games, but here I am, sweating the tiny degrees as I add water, wondering which way the foggy parasol mortar and pestle treatment moves the upper cap path, zooming past the boneyards on high-speed-stir, mapping the swirlies so that I can teleport  to save on ingredients. It's a little like cooking, and people stop in to tell you what they are up to as you help them (and occasionally haggle). I also like the music, so it's pretty relaxing. The little guide lines are really useful in lining up for a max strength potion. Warning: "big experience book" is FOUR books in a single clump, not five. Do not despair! You'll find some up in the NE area, got to wriggle through a passage in a bone wall to get there, though - fiddly, but that will show you new useful effects up there as well! From other players, all of the 4-book clumps are outside the first ring of bone walls, so you have to look for the gaps to complete Chapter 4.

_childDocuments_.review: The basic gameplay of combining ingredients to make different potions is really clever and solid. I had a lot of fun exploring the potion effects "map" and optimizing potions and coming up with alternate recipes. The UI was generally quite good, with nice touches and quality of life. I got a good 24 hour of play before I didn't want to do it any more, which is pretty good.If the macro game were better, then I'd play it even more. As it is, the macro game asks you to make a bunch weird potions that are otherwise unusable, which was fine for a bit but ran thin for me. The other thing the macro game wants me to do is keep serving up the usual potions for the locals far far far beyond the point where I need the money any more.If the macro game was better designed and changed and evolved more over time, I could see playing this for far longer. As it is, the game is still worth it.

_childDocuments_.review: Its a fun game for a couple hours and then the repetition kinda gets to you. I cant experiment with so little ingredients per day, can't skip to the next day without seeing all the customers first either. merchant prices are too expensive and I can't turn much of a profit. There should be some sort of "foraging" option where I can visit enchanted garden locations and pick ingredients that replenish on a timer rather than day-by-day. It would also be nice to see merchants anytime for normally priced merch and then they come to you with discounted merch but I can understand if that messes up the balance of the game. So far, if I want to make money for the day, then I'm making health potions, poison, etc and using all my base ingredients. I'm on level 13 and im already kind of anxious to try doing anything more with my ingredients because I dont want to waste them all and not have enough for the customers. Leveling up alchemical ability only makes more "exp books" show up on the map and not anything else. I feel there's a lot of potential there for more potent brews (like a larger bottle icon or let me make strong brews and not have to perfectly center the icons), or better abilities like to forage more ingredients per plant in the garden, or even propagate the garden with a particular ingredient and then using quick grow or bountiful harvest potions to enhance them or to make certain plants grow or even crystals grow. Through exploring the brewmap, what if there was an option to unlock travel to different biomes with enchanted gardens in them that I can travel to? Like If I go all the way down on the map, I can unlock a cavescape with crystals, going all the way in the poison direction is a mushroom rich swamp, all the way left is a desert, and to the right is a forest etc.

_childDocuments_.review: A good friend of mine purchased this game for me.Potion Craft is an incredibly chill, conflictless (so far) game revolving around you, an alchemist and potion salesman, brewing up concoctions for the local peasantry and warriors for everyday use, from healing potions to rodent poisons and other miscellaneous brews. The game involves learning how to most efficiently use herbs and fungi grown and bought with correct use of the mortar and pestle as well as experimenting with your ingredients to find cheaper, easier ways to brew potions that previously required a lot of effort material-wise. The game, while in early access, has very clearly defined methods to playing that are very easy to catch onto, and feel satisfying to execute in normal gameplay. Perfect game to wind down with after a long day.Not too complex, yet innovative enough to warrant buying. It's cheap and fun!

_childDocuments_.review: Before you buy, PLEASE watch a video of the gameplay because I don't think I would have bought if I'd known how the gameplay loop works. (It's not bad, it's just personally not for me.)I really wanted to like this game - I was drawn to the simulated act of picking plants, grinding them, adding them to my cauldron, and selling potions to customers. But I noticed a sharp drop off in the Steam achievements, with about 50% of players completing chapter 1 of 10 and 1% of players actually finishing the game. I imagine that most people drop off because unfortunately, a lot of the game is a repetitive grind. Pretty much my biggest problem with it is that it feels. so. repetitive.The game started out great, beautiful artwork and fun mechanics. I enjoyed exploring the map. But then I learned that exploring the map consumed materials rapidly, especially as I traveled further from my starting point - which, by the way, is the same no matter what. You always start at the same point in the map, and by mid-game, you have traveled over the same areas over and over again. It was fun to fulfill requests at first, but then they became repetitive too. Unlocking alchemy seemed promising and I was hopeful as I created the first materials (Nigredo), until it turns out that it just requires the same gameplay but with even more grinding. Now I don't mind grinding when I think the effort is worth it, but this game didn't offer enough "newness" to keep me engaged.Another problem I have is with inventory. I never have enough of a particular plant, which is alright - that's what vendors are for! Except you have no guarantee that any particular vendor will be available when you need them. Which is still alright as long as they appear often enough - except most of the time the herbalist or mushroom guy aren't carrying what I need! My garden will not stop giving me more of a plant that I already have 100+ of, but yields like 3 of another plant that I have 0 of. Lack of control over inventory (being unable to grow or buy what I need even when I have the gold) contributed a lot to my frustration.Overall, this is a game for some people who enjoy the gameplay loop, and I still think the early game is fantastic. It just didn't have much to offer me past the first few hours.

_childDocuments_.review: It's got a ways to go but I am so here for this! It's a cute indie game with a lovely art style, a great tutorial to walk you through everything which is far harder to come by in many games. It's fun, interactive and I am looking forward to the progress of the game as it is developed. Right now, there is limited content or at least it appears that way given what I've played but do not let this detour you from giving this game a shot, they post updates quite frequently and keep their audience apprised of where the game is headed. It's a nice gem for casual gamers.

_childDocuments_.review: Really can't wait for the full version! This is perhaps my favorite casual game. _childDocuments_.review: The idea is not bad, but the actual game play gets boring fast.Selling potions and haggling about prices isn't really interesting. _childDocuments_.name: Potion Craft: Alchemist Simulator

_childDocuments_.review: This is very much a strategy game with a puzzle element. And if that is what you are looking for then I do recommend this one to you. I enjoyed this a lot.It has big potential and that is basically the best thing you can say about an early access game.Game play right now:- You create potions by setting out a path on a map. Each plant allows only a fixed path. So you need to combine plants, decide how much of the path you want to take and how much to dilute to get to the potion markers on the map. The better you hit the mark, the better quality potion you create.- You need to decide which potion recipes you save for later- Sell the people the right potion and try haggling for the price- Decide which plants/items to buy- Harvest the plants from the garden each day- buy an alchemy machine and craft higher level itemsPro+ relaxing+ resource management+ strategy+ art style+ exploration, experimentationCons- just one music track right now- hardly any sound effects right now- needs further development since its early access

_childDocuments_.review: This game is really relaxing, and the game-play logic is so much fun! The controls do get sticky sometimes, but closing and reopening has never failed me yet. Highly recommended!
_childDocuments_.name: Potion Craft: Alchemist Simulator

_childDocuments_.review: A lovely fun game, relaxing to play and overall not too difficult to finish. Creating recipes and managing your recipe book is satisfying and trying to use as few ingredients as possible creates a sense of problem solving that makes progression fun. It gets a bit tedious at the end with the more advanced creations but would still say 10/10 would experience again.
_childDocuments_.name: Potion Craft: Alchemist Simulator

_childDocuments_.review: Cute graphics, decent UI, very original and clever approach to alchemy mechanics, so many loving little details. As of the time I've played it, Potion Craft is an early access game with the major mechanics settled. The major mechanics are very playable for a good 5-6 hours while you figure them out (and longer, if you are slow at learning things like me). Beyond that point, I feel like the game is going to benefit enormously from ongoing development - maybe more of a story, more goals, etc. So it doesn't yet feel complete in that there is nowhere to "go," really, but the mechanics themselves are such fun that the game feels worth the price of admission.I personally am very fond of repetitive games that I can play to keep my hands busy while I watch TV, and I can see this game being one I frequently pop into while Star Trek is on the other monitor, even if the developer does nothing else from here. I like it a LOT.

_childDocuments_.review: I'm sort of in the middle ground with this game. While it is mostly cool, and the minigames are great and addictive, i feel that it is a little unbalanced right now. I'm in my ~20th day and there's no way i can make the amount of money needed to buy the stuff in the basement. My popularity level is stuck at 3, and i can't make the necessary potions to gain another level. The materials are never enough, and customers always ask for the hardest potions on the east side of the map, and i feel like there aren't enough materials to go there, most of them go west, or up and down. Besides, the path they follow is way too weird and random, so it's hard to create a simple potion to reach the furthest places. The garden falls short as time advances, since potions require more and more materials, and the things you get on your garden aren't as many as needed. I have to buy everything from the merchants, and each time i do that, half of my money is gone. Then, when i sell the potions, i can't make enough to cover the amount spended, so i'm losing money most of the time.Of course, this being an early access, it will change sooner or later, so i think this could be an amazing game some day. The minigame its cool, and i love the interaction with all the tools, the short conversations with the characters, and the art and music are fantastic, so i believe it is definitely worth it.Edit: After a couple of hours of playing, i've changed my mind, it's stressful as hell. Its supposed to be a relaxing little game but i had to ragequit after the fifth customer asking me for the same potion i can't make because i don't have enough blue flowers that are the only material that goes to the right of the map. I hate it, i'll wait until its more balanced.

_childDocuments_.review: It's fun at first but after a while gets kinda boring and tedious, there's really not that much to do and the customers and sales people are so repetitive it's painful they all want the same potions for the same things "I need to climb a tower but I don't know how, do you have a potion for that?" Yes of course I have a potion for that! Everyone who's come in here is climbing that damn tower! I've made 50 levitation potions today already so yes here you go! _childDocuments_.review: I'm surprised this game has so many positive reviews. I lasted about 3 hrs of gameplay. The mechanics of having to grind the herbs and stir the pot quickly becomes tedious, especially once you've discovered all of the nearby spells and are trying to travel further on the map. Spending a lot of ingredients and time to travel only to have the potion fail is a frustrating feeling.I kept playing for a bit to see if they would add a feature that automated the grinding and stirring, but it doesn't look like that happens. I think the game would greatly improve if it recognized doing those slow manual actions is novel in the beginning, but needs to be automated as the player advances.I achieved developing the first crystal, and when I saw the recipe for the second crystal my reaction was "nope, no way," haha. It would take way too much time. If I saw this as more of an idle game where I was multitasking (listening to a podcast while I played, i.e.) and slowly working through the goals, perhaps I wouldn't mind so much?The whirlpools while discovering potions are a cool idea, but rarely seem to help out with travel - they don't go far and usually send me back the way I came... awesome..However, the game does have great aesthetic and graphics, it is a neat idea, and it is satisfying problem solving and achieving a lvl 3 potion. It seems the developers are still actively working on this game, hopefully there will be updates for the better.

_childDocuments_.review: It has a very nice art style and the devs promised a lot of things, namely garden 2.0 and talents 2.0, both of which would've helped a very shallow experience. Since then there has been little news to the game other than them adding it to several bundles with other indie games.There is little to no story, unique encounters with NPCs run out very quickly, gameplay is great for repetitive hand strain, and ultimately, a shameful amount of content for 20 USD. And it's a slow, repetitive minigame.Perhaps it could get better in the future with some more ways to manipulate the brewing process and whatnot, but it just didn't do anything for me at present.
