_childDocuments_.review: Rewarding medieval potion crafting game.  It take a while to get how to play but once you get the hang of it you can make progress fairly quickly.  You have to move around an alchemy 'map' by adding ingredients to a cauldron.  Each ingredient has its own path on the map so you build paths by combining the ingredients.  The 'effects' such as healing, poison etc are hidden around the map and when your path reaches them, you can add that effect to the potion.  Later one you make potions with multiple effects.  Experience points are also scattered around the map as book icons and many of the ingredients have paths designed just for gathering these icons.There is a haggling system but I never got into it.  Merchants will appear from time to time and offer you ingredients or equipment.  If you run out of certain type of ingredients you can get stuck having to wait for a merchant to have what you need.  There is a 'garden' next to your workshop that gives you a few basic ingredients each in-game day, but it isn't enough to sustain completely.  After you make a fair bit of money you can buy large amounts of ingredients, but the ones you need might not be available in the needed quantities.  I always run out of ingredients that move up and right.  There are plenty of ingredients that move down and to the left.  I really liked the visual style of this game and enjoyed playing about 20 hours so far.  It started to feel grindy in the second half of that, but all games of this type feature grinding to some extent.  It is quite rewarding to brew a perfect potion, as they strength of the potion is determined by how precisely the potion marker matches the marker on the alchemy map.  If you get it centred perfectly you can make a tier 3 potion.  It takes a bit of patience to get them exact.The later part of the game shifts from selling potions to fixing your alchemy machine and assembling more complicated recipes with multiple potions, and multiple effects in each potion.  I stopped at this point as I got tired of waiting for the merchants to offer enough ingredients of the right kinds.  I may come back to finish it sometime.  There are seven in-game chapters, and I finished 5 plus some of the 6th in 20 hours.  There are no steam achievements, just chapter breaks in the game.Overall I would highly recommend this to anyone who likes the idea of alchemy, herbs, folk medicine or medieval themes.  It's nice to play a medieval themed game that isn't centered around warfare or the succession of royalty.  It has a relaxed pastoral feel with a beautiful wood-carved style.
_childDocuments_.name: Potion Craft: Alchemist Simulator

_childDocuments_.review: In this game you craft potions with ingredients to sell to customers. But your crafting is like a chessboard, and your ingredients your chess pieces - each with their own unique movement style. You need to experiment and work out how to reach a location/potion effect in the most optimised way to be cost efficient, but also your potion strength is controlled by how accurately you line your potion up with the effect. If you enjoy gathering resources, crafting, and finding satisfying solutions, then this will be a relaxing game for you to sink some hours into.

_childDocuments_.review: Potion Craft shows excellent promise as a shop management game, with a unique medieval inspired art style and sandbox crafting systems that places emphasis on player ingenuity. The gameplay loop consists of harvesting ingredients from your garden, crafting and selling potions to your customers, buying supplies from traders and experimenting to perfect and create new potion recipes. This is all done in a solid physics engine where potion bottles clatter and flip when you toss them and minerals give a satisfying crunch and crumble under your mortar and pestle.In it's current early access state, the game runs well and I personally didn't notice anything broken, though some users have reported running into bugs, and has about 10 hours of progression content followed by an endless grind. The developers also have an extensive roadmap of content they want to include in the final game, which will add further depth and replayability.If the game looks like something you would enjoy, you probably will.

_childDocuments_.review: Potion Craft has more depth in its few screens than most AAA games made. It's also more enjoyable than most games for how simple it is and easy to start. Tutorial won't take more than 5-10 minutes and it gives you more than enough information. If more good content gets added as the developers progress through early access this could become a masterpiece in no time.

_childDocuments_.review: There is no reason for this game to be as addictive as it is.  The concept is simple, there's goals but no real story (other than the one I developed in my head as I played), and there are no clever puzzles to solve or monsters to fight.  And yet, I love this game.   There is something satisfying about crafting custom recipes and figuring out the pathway to find new ones.  I enjoyed figuring out how to get where I needed to go using ingredients I had on hand and there are moments of surprising tension as a potion nears an explosion point but can be saved with a delicate hand.  This is not a game like any other and fits nicely into a gentle, almost meditative space in a gamer's library.  Don't dismiss the seemingly simple premise of this game.  You'll find time flies by once you start.

_childDocuments_.review: Despite the general lack of instructions regarding certain things like what whirlpools do and just exactly how those crafting machines work, this game is basically a crafting exploratory game. Explore the map to find unknown potions, figure out how to make those potions with the least amount of ingredients, how to make the highest grade or combined potions and satisfy customers who sometimes make special requests.Once beyond the main menu, instructions are generally pictorial which can be a bit puzzling. However, a large part of this game is all about exploring and experimenting. All the herbs, mushrooms and crystals have a designated path so being creative in path building to the target is a necessary requirement.Most strategy is involved with the customers and making money. Though money is not the main focus, it is needed for alchemy machine upgrades, ingredients (herbs, mushrooms, crystals, and especially the much needed potion recipe paper) that need to be purchased. There several merchants that stop by on a regular basis (one merchant per day) who offer specific items. Which items, when, and how much is purchased is all part of the overall game strategy. It is possible to haggle with both merchants and customers (which is explained in-game) but can be difficult for those with slow reflexes. Haggling is not required expect for one chapter list requirement.   There are ten chapters total, each with a list of requirements to complete. Any requirement from any chapter once completed is recorded. This can be accessed at any time so progress can be tracked. Achievements are game play based and most, if not all, can be achieved while playing. The two reputation achievements are the only ones that need special attention and most likely some grinding.  Throughout the game play there are progress points earned which can be used to increase money received from customers, increase the rate of map clearance, increase number of level point books and haggling ability.Highly recommended for crafting buffs especially since there is no grinding needed for progress, only creative thinking. Plenty of crafting to do, lots of exploring needed and enough strategy to keep busy and not be bored. Easy enough for all with focused requirements for progress. Worth the price.

_childDocuments_.review: Bought this game in October of 2021, and had some fun, especially in the beginning. Towards the end, everything became kind of repetitive, so i quit playing, hoping for some sort of update that would add more depth to the gameplay. Since then, there have been roughly a dozen or so of announcements from the devs, 3 of which talked about/announced new features (save states, a new haggle minigame, and an autohold feature). To be fair, there was an event and new textures, but i don't really care about that. All 3 of these "updates" seem very minor, something that could have been done in a week, not 2-3 months each.Anyway, my point is that the communication & progress from the devs has been staggeringly bad, epetially considering how popular the game is- steadDB estimates the game has sold at least 200k copies, which should be more than enough to pay for a couple of full-time developers. Yet we've seen seen almost nothing in terms of progress. Did they just take the money and run?Don't buy this game. You'll have fun for a few hours, then get bored and decide to wait for more features to get released- which, for now, seems like it'll never happen.

_childDocuments_.review: Not a bad game, just lackluster for me. Maybe worth the price if you really like what you see.It's a decent game to relax, but not much reason to play it after a while. The upgrade/progression feels weak and meaningless, and there's no difficulty to challenge you.What you see in the gameplay video is all there is. There's no extra feature, nothing that would feel supergood later on.Also the potion requests are very limited in what they accept, there's not much room for creativity. Sometimes you're even penalized for adding an extra effect which would seem helpful.Again, not a bad game, looks really good, sounds and music are decent, and I've had no technical issues.But I see no reason to recommend it to anyone. There are more intricate games to just chill and relax with, as far as I'm concerned.

_childDocuments_.review: This game simulates the life of a novice alchemist trying to pave his way to fame and glory discovery after discovery. Just like in real life, it requires dedication and perseverance, which do not always go hand in hand with casual game philosophy. The system of moving along the alchemy map will entice you to experiment for a few hours in search of the ultimate formula, but an uninspired endgame relying on grinding might turn away even the most ambitious alchemists. If you're looking for an original sandbox puzzler and aren't afraid of repetitive gameplay, it's definitely an interesting game

_childDocuments_.review: WOW, I am so disappointed in this game. As a fan of dorky little sim games, I had been looking forward to this one for a while. I waited for a sale (bless you Steam, or I would have lost even more money on this game) and only paid $8.99 for this but it still feels like an L. I'm not entirely sure what the developers of this game were thinking... You have this wonderful idea for a potion crafting and selling game and, instead of focusing completely on the actual crafting part of potions, you tied "crafting" (I use the term loosely here) to a map and exploring said map? And TRUST ME, I hear you when you say "Well wait, crafting but based on map exploration sounds kind of neat!"; I was with you there buddy, trust me, but let me try to explain through a VERY long winded review. Buckle in.Now let me nip this in the bud right quick: the map is just that, a map. A paper map. A pirate's map. X marks the spot and all. It's cute and it fits with the style of the game, but you yourself do not explore it, and all movement on this map is tied completely to the loose term of "crafting" I'll be using throughout this review. You put your ingredients into the cauldron, be it crushed or not, and then stir to make the potion bottle move across the map. That's the gameplay loop. There are also whirlpools you can choose to move with (they will move you a small distance away) and skeletons/bones(?) on the map that will basically instantly kill you. The crafting happens when you find a bottle on the map and "craft" your potion in that spot. It does not matter the ingredients you put in it to get you there, so long as you got there.This itself is baffling to me. You created a crafting game where the gameplay loop is move around a map? And perhaps I could see /some/ merit in it if you had to use specific ingredients to even craft the potion when you got to it on the map, maybe? But you don't even need to do that, just any old ingredient that will get you from point A to point B will do. And then there's the stuff on the map. Jeez bro, what is with this? Was the map too easy to navigate so the devs had to quickly slap some stuff ontop of it that would diversify the experience and drag out the runtime? Navigating the map already takes ample resources to get from A to B; any you'd like, yes, but ample of them. They all have designated move patters associated with them - one item always goes to the left in a silly squiggly way, while another item will always go right in a silly squiggly way and so on - so you already need to use your resources sparingly and in an optimal pattern to get where you need to go on the completely fogged/hidden map. That's well and fine, and could be a fun way to do things: use an item associated with "wind" that goes in the direction of potions all associated with wind and discover new "wind"esk potions. But... then they slapped these skeletons or bones or whatever the ♥♥♥♥ they are onto the map and... they just fail your potion almost instantly whenever your giant potion bottle even slightly touches it? And so what that does is it fails your potion and sends you all the way back to the starting point of the map. All your resources used and all your time wasted. And sure, there's a dilute option that moves your potion a little bit, but all it does is move it back to the start point, so in most situations it isn't helping you. If anything, why not make the dilute move you slightly away from the closest skeleton or fail state or whatever it is? It makes the map extremely hard to navigate because, remember, we only have a few set navigation patters to choose from. It also makes it so, when I need to go around a skeleton, I have to use ingredients that I feel would NEVER be in the potion I am attempting to craft (aka so it will move me in a completely different direction on the map). The whole thing feels counter intuitive and, if that weren't bad enough, they throw more at you on this map! Remember the whirlpools I mentioned earlier? (It's okay if you don't, it's been a minute.) Well they have this neat little ability where they can teleport you to another part of the map nearby. Love that! Makes navigating those skeletons a lot easier right? They're probably designed in a way to help the player, as a mechanic, go in the right direction with less resources. WRONG. It's like I said, the map was designed to be counter intuitive. The whirlpools almost always made me feel like a fool for using them. On the perfect path to a potion and want to see where this'll take you? Assuming it'll be closer to the potion? IDIOT xD! BEGONE INTO THE SKELETON PILE! ..... Like... why? Thanks for the gut punch niceplay. :\ Speaking of counter intuitive, what's with that tutorial? I'm sorry but LOL what the actual ♥♥♥♥ was that tutorial? You teach the player what a mortar and pestle does and then don't teach us about: the whirlpools, the skeletons, the diluting, the auto-craft feature, the reputation system, haggling, the gifting mechanic, whatever was in the basement idk I refuse to play more to find out, etc. And listen, that's not to say that I didn't appreciate them telling me that crushing the ingredients makes them more potent, but you had a whole text box for what I just said in 7 words and then no tutorial for that entire list I just typed up. Why? You already built the UI for the tutorial boxes and everything, all you had to do was type like 10 more things. I'm about to do a whole lot more typing than those tutorials would have taken and I'm doing it for free just to ♥♥♥♥ atop your game so like... I think it would have been worth your while.Meanwhile, the real tutorial of the game is given to you via the quest log. Read what to do, do it, book crosses it out, you get progress toward a perk. It works, but it's just so poorly delivered. The perks are very bland by the way. No idea why that's even in the game. Pressure to have it like other game do? Idk it's boring and useless.It's like... I want to give this game more credit cause I love the art, music, overall concept, good chunk of the writing, and some of the smaller concepts within the game but.. it's just so hidden by a bunch of annoyances that I can't excuse. For example: Love having a reputation system, but not only did it take me at least an hour to even realize it was there (because again, no tutorial, never pointed it out) once I did finally figure out it was there and how to make it go up or down I not only didn't understand what the point to having a better reputation was but I didn't understand what was making some sales increase my reputation while some decreased it. For example: I had a pretty bad reputation by the time I noticed it was a thing. I fulfilled all requests that came in and chalked up all the extremely bad requests as just quirky writing and moved on, but found out that wasn't the case and started trying to improve my score and reject people with negative requests. I thought the game might be less black and white about things and I fulfilled some requests that I told myself were "morally grey" and should be allowed. The game did not agree. Okay, that's fine. I will only give the most goodest and neutralest of patrons my beautiful potions. "NAY!" said the game, very loudly into my reputation meter, "-6 YOU FIEND!" The ♥♥♥♥?! The dude had an almost identical request to one that gave me a positive score like 3 customers ago. I don't get it. I just don't.idk I'm running out of characters and at the end of the day, it's just a game that disappointed me. I just don't want someone that was expecting what I was expecting to waste their money and be sad afterwards. This was 1 of 4 purchases I gave myself for the Steam Winter Sale and I feel a bit cheated with all these lame, overused systems in a potentially cool game. Don't get it if you liked my review, get Recettear or We. The Revolution. If you hated the review uh... why you still here? Go play the thing.That's it. Bye.

_childDocuments_.review: Where to start.On the surface I expected Potion Craft to be simplistic - more of an ASMR satisfaction simulator rather than an actually independent gaming experience. Boy was I wrong.Potion Craft has such awesome depth in the best way possible: it's subtle. It gives you a meagre 2-5 minute tutorial to learn the basics and the rest is on you - but the game is intuitive such that this never feels like it wasn't enough. What's more, you find yourself constantly finding more things out ON YOUR OWN. This sense of satisfaction paired with the innate completionism of coming up with a new potion is an epic feedback loop that'll have you saying 'just one more potion' a few thousand times.And note that this is EARLY ACCESS. In it's current form - incomplete and missing some major expansion features - I still think it's well worth the price as an independent game. If it didn't receive a single update from here on out (which I damn hope it doesn't, given the potential) I still think it'd be well worth the 15-20 buck pricetag.Do yourself a favour and support this game.

_childDocuments_.review: it is a fine game, but its not what i expectedi thought of a game where you need to think logically to create potions, but that didnt seem to be the case. the main aspect of this game is the alchemy map. using an ingredient to make a potion creates a path on this map, wich you can direct to the desired effect, while avoiding static skulls wich will fail your potion.as such, the game doesnt really feel like its about making potions, its more about exploration and pathfinding. and this is fun for a few hours, but gets boring after a while, especially because there are 4 cheap ingredients in this game that can be used to make all of the potions, with other ingredients very rarely coming into play. after you get a hold of the mechanics and have every potion in your recipe book the game wants you to make legendary subtances wich needs you to create new paths on the alchemy map from areas you have already explored. _childDocuments_.review: The core gameplay consists of you using ingredients to move a potion flask across the alchemy map to effect symbols to add these effects to a potion, then finishing and selling it.Pro- very clean, have not experienced any bugs yet and everything runs smoothly even on my mediocre laptop- gameplay is exactly what you expect: Craft potions, sell them, unlock new effects, save recipes, buy ingredients- you get your money's worth for sure, I'm at 13hours played and I think I'll get to 20 before reaching endgame- Day counter makes speedruns possible -> increased replayability- Most importantly, the core gameplay - the crafting mechanism with the different ingredients, the mortar-kettle-ladle-bellows combination and their interactions with the alchemy map (which itself has certain effects as well) are unique and funCon- Early access means many features that one would like are still in development (in my case, I'm very much looking forward to the store upgrades)- Gets a bit repetitive after a while- Being unable to target-grow ingredients means you have to wait for specific traders to show up and sell them if you need much of one, this can be frustrating if your stored recipes depend on ingredients you're short on- No steam cloud saves (yet?)

_childDocuments_.review: I was NOT expecting this game to be so immersive. Whoever came up with the potion-making mechanic is a GENIUS. It preserves the excitement of discovery while also giving you just the right amount of direction to make you feel like you're actually progressing based on logic rather than luck or brute force. I love when games allow you to discover them authentically, without the need for background research (googling feels like cheating to me); this makes the learning experience--which is, and should be, an important part of this game--feel immersive and exciting. This game falls right in that sweet spot, like Return to the Obra Dinn and Hollow Knight (and unlike Minecraft, which I still love, but the Minecraft learning experience is significantly more community-based rather than integrated into the game itself). However, after 5h of play, the game does leave me with two questions:(1) What is the role of Reputation?  Popularity is well-specified, but I'm not certain what Reputation does. I think having a better reputation improves the prices merchants offer you, but I'm not sure yet. I think it could be cool to have different "alignments" as an alchemist where seedier merchants will give you better prices if your reputation is worse. It is also incredibly easy to lose reputation points (you gain rep points 2-3 at a time, but the max I've lost off a single sale is 30), which makes sense, but just be aware. (2) Are the "book points" you earn from completing parts of the Alchemist's Path the same as the experience points you get from picking up books while making potions? This is probably a stupid question that will be answered with more play. I think both of these questions will be answered as I accumulate more playtime, but I look forward to the release of the manual in the full version. It could also be cool to be able to buy or brew different fertilizers for the enchanted garden that encourage different kinds of plants to grow. 5/5 stars. I absolutely love this game--can't wait for the full version!!

_childDocuments_.review: Wishlist this. Get it later when there is more content, as a lot of the joy comes from discovery. It's got a lot going for it, but the late-game content just isn't there yet. It's really exciting in the discovery phase when you are first starting out, but it quickly becomes a chore, in my opinion. I think when there are more potion bases added and the customers requests are more varied, then the game will be better. Also, the alchemy experience could use some fine tuning. If you need to, you can brew any recipe using the same four ingredients. However, you'll quickly run out of those if you do. Getting ingredients is currently pretty random, so you never know if you're going to run out of ingredients and need to brew a new recipe. There's a charm to that, but I found it tedious after awhile.You can record recipes in a book, but the book quickly becomes cluttered with bookmarks as you add more pages to it. I hope that the developers improve the UI experience of this part. I also wish it was easier to work from old recipes. By the end of the available content I was so tired of needing to brew new recipes for the alchemy machine that I only kept going because I just had to see what was waiting after I completed it all.For now, nothing.

_childDocuments_.review: Awesome idea ! Really good game design. I think this has a lot of potential. (Nigredo) And when you finally craft it, seemingly nothing happens. And I can't seem to use Nigredo for anything. So there is no motivation to use the machine for further research. _childDocuments_.review: Preface: I really want to like this game but as of now, the development seems to be dead.I bought the game when it became available in Early Access in September 2021 and I have to give props to the devs for the concept and aesthetic of the game.This is a very soothing game, perfect for unwinding during short breaks.Sadly, the game is pretty barebones as of now, which means that after a few hours you will have seen/done everything the game has to offer. This is fine by itself for the pricetag but it does leave a bitter aftertaste because it could be so much more.Sadly, the devs have stopped posting any kind of gameplay updates after the Early Access release and have only produced behind the scenes concept art and ideas on their social media channels.This is such a shame really, because the game got nominated for the Steam Awards, which shows that the game has potential down the road.TL;DR: Feel free to grab this if it's on sale but be aware that there might not be any further updates.

_childDocuments_.review: This game used to be wonderful, honestly, it's still great. Problems with the game arise when the dev team adds new content. Their development philosophy is "chill instead of min/maxing" – when they say this it means “Progression doesn’t matter, and things will be just as difficult and tedious in the end game as they are early game.” This is easy to see when looking at ingredients. Simple recipes used to be easy to make and, there was a method to the madness. Now anything you want to do is costly and time consuming. You can’t just save up money and resources then mess around and discover things. If you wanted to play a game that gives a good sense of progression (Doesn’t make you do tedious things constantly / Allows you to experiment and have a good time) you won’t find that once they leave early access.

_childDocuments_.review: It's a fun, relaxing game with not overly complicated mechanics that you can just zone out to. Even though I couldn't complete everything, I don't regret my time with this in the least.

_childDocuments_.review: The core game mechanics are solid and provide a satisfying and relaxing experience, particularly in crafting potions. Also we can all appreciating the fantastic artwork! Also, the developer may have hurt the game's reception by releasing it and then announcing soon to be added features.What I really want is something different to happen. New spoon so I can make potions a little easier! But then some other complication to arise. I know about the rocks but that's not exactly what I mean. Or it would be great if I was building up to something. It kinda feels like I'm waiting around so the merchant will sell me parts for the basement so I can check off the achievements. The achievement book is kind of a boring substitute to make players explore the potion map. The point is just selling the same poison and health potions to people over and over isn't cutting it for me.Overall, while Potion Craft offers a satisfying experience, there is still room for improvement. I can't stress enough how unique the main potion mechanic is and how much it pains me to not recommend it. This is a light no. Obviously a lot of people like the game, this one isn't for me.

_childDocuments_.review: Key points at a glance -✅ Gorgeous artwork✅ Nice music and sounds✅ Neat crafting mechanics❌ Gets highly repetitive very quickly❌ Core gameplay loop just isn't that funThe game is upfront about what it is and the screenshots and trailer accurately depict gameplay. Sadly, even for a casual game it feels incredibly shallow. There just isn't enough fun to be had.There are a bunch of interesting mechanics in the game (for the first couple of times, at least) all portrayed with the most beautiful art. However, once you've mixed a few potions, gathered herbs, sold some of your remedies and retired to bed to start a new day you've seen a lot of what the game has to offer.Ultimately, there's nothing fundamentally wrong with the crafting. The game just needs more interesting and fun gameplay around it because that's where I find it lacking. It's a simple and very pretty looking game so if that's enough to keep you happy then go for it, otherwise I cannot recommend the game.

_childDocuments_.review: A very cozy and relaxing game, played it a ton during closed beta and open playtests, that's why the low total hours (so far)Pros:- Great artsyle- Incredibly satisfying potion crafting (every steps of it)- Multiple ways of approaching the same goal- Cool long term goals to work on while you attend your shopBefore I meantion the cons, you have to keep in mind there is tons of features that can be seen in the "about full version" menu option, so obviously the game is a bit barebones feature wise. That being said, I will address the cons of the game that don't appear on the full version feature listCons:- After a 'certain point', the game turns repetitive. Its just a lack of pre-written content, probably will be more on release- Haggling. There is little gain from not using haggling, but it's completely offset by the enormous benefits of haggling, making it a necessary mini-game with little consequence, and not a real choice- Imbalanced ingredients: There are just not an even amount of ingredients for every direction, making certain herbs incredibly valuable and some totally useless, This is a con because there are more or less equal demand of potions from every direction, but this can cause shortages of some ingredients very quicklyOverall great game, but you gotta wait till they add everything. For the time being, a good 8/10

_childDocuments_.review: It's a good game, for a few hours.For now, the game is too empty to be really enjoyable. At first, the game is exciting, you learn to make potions, discover new potions by exploring the map, new paths to move through the map... But at the 3-4 hour mark, you get to a point where you are just making the same potions for the same clients all over again.And then alchemy comes, i consider it could be a refreshing and fun mechanic, but for now it has huge design flaws. The first recipes you make are pretty simple and easy, the same potions you made before, but with interesting and different combinations, the problem comes with later recipes.The late game recipes are obtained in the point where you have already done everything else, and don't offer anything new to the game. Each recipe can take about 11 potions, each one of them increasingly harder to make, taking up to four hours to make all the recipes. It really feels like WORKING to progress, as you are still doing the same thing you have been doing since the beginning, but without anything new, and a much higher difficulty (difficulty here meaning more tedious work and more time consuming). Gameplay really needs something new at midgame, get another way to make potions different from moving on a map, other way to process ingredients, but not the same over and over.And the potions you make at the alchemy table doesn't work for anything else, are potions designed just to be hard to make (or easy, depending on the difficulty). They could be potions that you could save for certain clients, for example:1.- The guy that wants to have creative dreams wants a  or a , a 3+2 combination of the two is more valuable, if the alchemy table asked you for that potion, you could save it for that client.2.- The guy that wants to bypass or fly from an enemy needs a  or a , same thing before, the progress could help your gameplay insted of making it tedious.To end, i must say this bad rating is temporary, i enjoyed the game, but i got really burned out at the end. It was way too early to release the game, i want to see what it ends up becoming. It looks ASTONISHING tho, the art and the way you interact with everything is unique, but it feels like they had put too much time on the artistic part, and very little on the game design and gameplay part.

_childDocuments_.review: This is a great game, it should be used as an example of how to make games in many areas: Gameplay mechanics design, art direction, execution...The game is about making potions. Potions can have different effects based on the ingredients and exact recipe (obviously). There are many ways to obtain the same effect with different ingredients. Effects can be higher quality if you are particularly precise with the steps. You can save recipes you like so that you don't have to do steps manually every time, but the game limits the number of slots you have (you buy more slots as you make money).Of course, there is a variety of ingredients and not all of them are good for every type of potion. You can get ingredients from different sources, but not all sources are equal. For instance mushroom man only sells mushrooms (not always the same ones), and you have to wait for him to show up. This means you have to tailor your recipes to available ingredients, and you have to maintain a selection of ingredients to cover different types of potions customer might ask for. I think this is a pretty fun aspect of the game. Ingredient scarcity gives you some pressure to think about efficiency, but also it's usually pretty easy to find ingredients if you really need it, so it's not a source of much stress.The coolest thing by far is *how* the potions are brewed. It's not just a checklist of add this much of this, that much of that... There's a map, and every potion effect is a location on it. Every ingredient moves you in a certain predefined way. So it's about figuring out which sequence of ingredients will get you close enough, and also is something you can repeat multiple times with the ingredients you have. But there are various tools in the game that can modify the path of an ingredient, and there's a huge number of ingredients as well as multiple alternate maps, so you really get to explore a huge space of possible ways to make potions. The map is not revealed at the beginning, so there's an exploration aspect as well.I think this map idea is brilliant. In real world chemical research there's a lot of efforts to summarize the essential properties of millions of possible chemical compounds, and then use that to automatically discover new reactions. One of the solutions to this, which I find really neat, is to calculate the similarity of all compounds (using the full list of their many chemical characteristics) and use machine learning and/or some fancy statistics to map this to 2D or 3D space so that similar things end up close together. Human brains are very good at comprehending physical space, but not good at comprehending tables of numbers, so this is a great way of leveraging that innate ability to make it easy for you to navigate a non-spatial thing (chemistry). This game is basically a gamified version of this approach. They've gotten the details right so it feels smooth, and it's very immersive to imagine yourself as a medieval alchemist who doesn't really know these modern statistical approaches, but is arriving at them intuitively through trial and error.It's worth saying that the interface of this game, graphics, music etc. are really beautiful. They're all very polished and animations work smoothly. The controls are pretty good with a gamepad - the only issue is that you can't give a custom name to your recipes without a keyboard. The game is basically "find the recipe" (aka combinatorics, if you like math), but with the 2D map abstraction I described. You find the recipe over and over. This would suck if the UI wasn't slick, and in this game it's really slick. It doesn't really get old.I found that it's a fun game to play with someone as well, taking turns every hour or so. You can play at a slower pace and have a conversation as you play, whether about the game or something unrelated. Most of your brainpower goes to planning and thinking, not fiddling with controls, so the person watching can meaningfully participate. A lot of winning tactics are circumstantial and subjective, so it's not a case of you figure out the solution and there's nothing more to discuss. You can always go back to old recipes or strategies and re-examine them.Incidentally, pacing is another great aspect of this game. In most things you do, you can choose whether you want to do it with high stakes and more intensity, or lower stakes and more laid back. For example the haggling minigame is about reaction time. If you don't have fast reactions, or maybe you do but don't feel like making the effort that day, you can just choose the smaller haggle margin and get a slower minigame. If you're trying to make some amount of money, it takes you a bit longer, but it's not like the game becomes so slow that it's boring. Or you can go hard with higher stakes and advance faster. This isn't done by going to the game settings and fiddling with a "difficulty" slider - it's all part of the game to keep adjusting what intensity you want for each bit.I'd recommend using a good gamepad for this. Something you do a lot is "grind" and "stir". Both are done by actually moving your cursor in a circle. I started with a cheap knock off Xbox controller (and also a knock off PS4 controller), and circling with the stick was not very pleasant (still playable). This was one of two games (other one was Sekiro) that convinced to fork over $60 for a real PS4 controller. It was a huge improvement because the coating and spring on the real PS4 analog stick is much higher quality and feels much more ergonomic. I never played with the mouse much - it seems playable, but I get shoulder pain from too much mousing so for me a gamepad is mandatory.I feel like the game is pretty much perfect for what it is - a puzzle game with an original mechanic that is explored pretty in depth. Because the interface, graphics, audio, controls and other "minor" technical aspects are well done, the game feels very smooth and brewing potions for hours is relaxing rather than tedious. It's one of those games that you don't really care about completing, you just want to keep going back to the meditative experience. There is however a generous amount of progression when you want it - the game doesn't force you to progress if you feel like just staying at one level for a while.I just wish they added voiceovers :)

_childDocuments_.review: Potion Craft , to me, is a game where the novelty wears off quickly. I put approx. 22 hours of time into the game but eventually dropped it because of how tedious it became. I wish I could like the game more as the art style and concept is wonderful, but the game feels forgotten about now. The Beginning (1-5 hours): You spend time familiarizing yourself with the ingredients, and recipes, & the customer requests. Everything is new and sparkly and you have so much fun! Learning the in's and out of potion making is a great process. This is the space where you have so much hope and feel like you'll be obsessed with this for weeks. Although, at the end of hour 2 you've muted the music and put something else on. Listening to one track on repeat is too much. The Middle (6-15): Things are starting to slow down, you unlock harder and harder recipes, it's getting monotonous but with recipes you learn how to make things more efficient and less time consuming. 'Haggling' with merchants is a chore, but there are still some interesting and new ingredients out there. You hope you can unlock the tool upgrades soon. Middle Pt.2? (16+ hrs): You get tired of everything at this point. You are no longer reading the requests, just keywords, you angrily given them what they want and move on. You are praying for merchants to show up so you can finally get more  ingredients that you can't grow yourself (90% of them). Rapidly you are developing carpal tunnel in your hand and you realize there are no upgrades for your equipment at all. It was never put in the game. The objective of the game became too tedious and complex to manage and eventually you give up. If you are still really interested in this game I would suggest waiting for a sale. In it's current state it feels closer to 5-10USD, not 20.

_childDocuments_.review: You’re a novice alchemist and you have finally found somewhere to settle down after travelling around. You have found an old abandoned house which seemed to have had an alchemist live there prior to your arrival. It’s got a garden ideal for growing herbs and other ingredients, along with alchemy equipment in the basement. It’s been a while since anyone has lived there and the alchemy equipment is in need of being fixed up but after some hard work, you’ll have your very own Potion Shop up and running. For now, though while the alchemy equipment is out of use, you have your trusty Cauldron, Mortar and Pestle, Bellows and Water Ladle. Using these basic tools will allow you to make your potions, you have a couple ingredients to begin with. You can just put the ingredients straight into the cauldron; however, you’ll get better mileage out of your ingredients if you crush them in your mortar and pestle. You will get twice the benefits out of crushing your ingredients than if you just dropped them straight into your cauldron. Using the Water Ladle will allow you to add water to your potions, it will move your potion bottle back towards the centre of the potion map where you started.  To make potions you will have to put the ingredients into the cauldron. This will then lay a dotted line with an “X” this way and that on the potion map, the map is almost completely covered in a Fog of War. As you potion bottle moves around the map it will reveal more of the map along with open books and potion bottles with a Question Mark on them. You will need to add ingredients until laying a path to one of the bottles with a question mark on it. Stirring the cauldron will move your bottle along the dotted line laid down by your ingredients. Next you will use the bellows to heat the potion up in the cauldron after a few blows of the bellows a puff of smoke will appear from the cauldron. This is to let you know that the potion is completed, revealing what the mystery potion is. Finishing the potion will have it put into your inventory allowing you to sell it to a customer.  You can create a mixture of potions so instead of finishing a potion upon reaching a potion you can carry on to another potion bottle. This allows you to mix two or more types of potions into one potion, such as you could have a health potion mixed one that restores mana. You can save a recipe in your book of potions, although you only have enough space for five potions. You can use these saved potions to create them with a push of a button should a customer want one. This will save you from having to add ingredients and is handy for those potions of more complexity. On the map you will move over some books, collecting these will unlock Talents which you can use towards four categories. The categories are Alchemy Map (Visibility Radius), Alchemical Practice, Trading and Haggling. They have levels ranging from six to ten levels depending on the category and they cost from one to three Talents to unlock. In your little place you’ll find the front area is your shop, here every day customers will come and tell you their problems and you’ll have to get the right potion for them. If you offer them the wrong potion twice then they’ll leave your shop not very happy. However, if you give them what they want then they’ll be as happy as Larry. The happier customers the more your popularity will grow. While you can sell your wares for a price you can also try to haggle for a better price, this will also go for passing merchants which will visit you in hoping that you buy some of their ingredients. You will find items and mushrooms which you may not have access to, which can lead to need potions. The backroom is where you’ll prepare all your potions, out back is your garden, here you’ll have some herbs, mushrooms etcetera grow each day. You can collect these items and use them to prepare potions for your customer's needs. In the basement is your Alchemy Machine however, it’s seen better days and is currently unusable. You can repair the machine if you find a merchant selling the parts you need to bring it back to its former glory days. The final room in your place is the upstairs attic, here is where you sleep at night after a hard day's work. Once you have done everything you can in a day going to bed will reset the day, allow need ingredients to grow and be ready to make more potions for the customers knocking at your door. You’re not going to be able to keep everyone happy, there are going to be plenty of people who you’re unable to sort a potion out for. This could be because you don’t have the required ingredients or knowledge of the potion a customer wants. You will have to uncover the potion map as much as possible revealing all the potions. However, scattered around the potion map in between the potions and the books are piles of Skulls. You don’t want to have your bottle move over these skulls as your potion bottle will empty the longer time you spend moving over them. If you empty your potion bottle crossing the skulls then the potion will fail and you’ll have lost all the ingredients you had in your cauldron. There are goals to complete as you progress, these goals can be found in you’re the Alchemist’s Path book. Currently there are Seven Chapters with varying amount goals to complete. Completing all goals in a chapter will open the next chapter and you will also gain a reward of some sort upon completing a chapter.  The game is still in Early Access currently so there will be some problems along the way, news things being added to the game and even possibly some things removed. So, bear in mind that it is in Early Access and things can change. There’s more to come in future updates with new potions, maps, upgrading your garden and more. The game is easy to play and learn, it will take some grinding to fill the coffers, uncover some of the potions, fix the alchemy machine and you will upset some folks by not fulfilling their requirements but your reputation will grow as will your shop. The game is a little bit copy paste what you did the day before for the upcoming day so far. I haven’t been able to get the alchemy machine up and running yet, I’m a bit short of the old pennies when the merchants come a calling. In the settings there’s option for Window Mode (Borderless or Windowed), Limit and Show FPS, Language (English, German, French, Polish, Chinese, Korean and Russian). Positives  + Nice artwork + Easy and relaxing to play + Active developers Negatives  - Repetitive - No achievements - No cards currently Become the latest buzz around town, with folks from near and far visiting your shop for potions to cure ailments, poisons to rid vermin or even a potion to make paint glow in the dark in Potion Craft. 6/10

_childDocuments_.review: This is a cute little game. The concept is simple - use your resources at hand to make potions to solve the townsfolk's needs. The mechanism an interesting one - your ingredients plot out a course on a map, and you can grind them to their full course or limit their effect. One by one you add them, to reach a desired effect. The closer you get to the point on the map, the stronger the potion. If you make the perfect potion, you can save the recipe for the next townsfolk who needs it. If you don't have the right ingredients on hand for the next time, you can try plotting another course using different ingredients.  It really does feel like you're a master at your craft, grinding just so, stirring just so, diluting just so, knowing which plants can be used as a substitute when you don't have what you need.To be honest, most of the goals in the game are self motivated. Personally, my primary motivation is creating the most economical recipes. There are mechanism to level up, and there are goals, but most of them you meet during the course of play by customer requests. It seems like the developers are working on more features, which I look forward to.Overall, this is a fun little casual game, especially for those of us with a perfectionist streak. If you were hoping for more from Pottermore's potions game, this game will scratch that itch.

_childDocuments_.review: I am very excited to see its full release! I have completed all current goals (as of 6/20/2022) within 30 hours. With the addition of many more ingredients, bases, costumers, and goals, I could see this game surpassing 100 hours with ease. It is obvious this game was made with great attention to detail, as there are many little features that never fail to make me smile like, for example, the turning of pages in books, the grinding of ingredients, the dialog with the costumers, and much more. I recommend this game for anyone who likes to take things at their own pace and immerse themselves in a fantasy world. In its current state, I wish there was more ingredients that take you Northeast, as there is one (maybe two, depending on if you count the red mushroom) that takes you that direction. Of course, this is already in the plans to be fixed (as I have seen in the dev logs). More crystals would also be wonderful. A skill tree would be preferable to what we have now, as there is no way to make it your own. With only 4 categories for your skill points to go into, it feels very limited. I would also like something to do with the extra skill points after you bought everything you could, like maybe a way to trade them for cash (maybe the value could fluctuate each day?) or perhaps a way to trade them directly for rare ingredients or other things like that. A way to separate regular ingredients from the crystals would be nice, as i found myself having to dig through every ingredient to find the crystal I needed. Branching off of that, there needs to be a better way to sort the ingredients, as sorting them with the element button does not have consistent sorting, and it doesn't feel... well, sorted. Maybe have a small separating bar between each category instead of one continuous list, but do not make it too large of a space, as that will create a chunky ingredients list.Of course most of these comments are a bit nit-picky, but these are little things I would improve on if it was me developing (but I am not, I am not skilled like you!). TLDR, beautiful game with great potential. Recommended for single players that do not wish for pressure or time limits. Great game to relax to and listen to music/podcasts/etc. Thank you for this wonderful game, devs!

_childDocuments_.review: This is one of those games that you enjoy right up until you get familiar with it. Then you realize it's never going to change and the mechanics are not actually fun. It's an interesting enough concept that doesn't reward you for progressing.To start, everything is random. You have absolutely no control, no way of adjusting for what you have learned.Some examples:You have a garden behind your shop. If you were an actual alchemist you would plant stuff in your garden as needed. But here, a random selection of plants spawns in your garden each morning. There's no connection between what spawns and what you've used. So you end up not being able to make recipes because you are missing a key ingredient. And you can't just run to the local grocer and buy stuff either.Speaking of buying stuff- there are vendors who come in selling crystals and tools. But they appear randomly and their inventory is random as well. So you might go through the whole day rejecting customers only to have a vendor show up at the end of the day with the crystal you needed to make recipes earlier. Or the vendor might show up first thing in the morning with nothing you need. You can't just run into town at the end of the day and get what you want from local shops.The recipe "map" is actually a pretty neat mechanic. But it could be improved. It's nice that different plants take you in different directions. It's just clunky that the amount of stirring and grinding is what controls how far you go. You can't really plan a recipe to any great degree, which an alchemist should be able to do. Make it so that the weight of the ingredient matters, dried or fresh, make it something you can design ahead of time. As is, you grind and stir one ingredient, then add another, then a another, etc. until you get where you want to be.Speaking of design, the game punishes you for experimenting. The only way to explore the map is to make recipes. Fair enough, that's what you would do. But with the ingredients being so difficult to acquire, you don't want to waste them playing around.Interactions with customers are often vague. They'll tell you, "I need something to help with X" and it's up to you to figure out what might do that. The recipes aren't always clear as to what they do. And the ingredients are irrelevant since you can use multiple recipes to get the same potion.  And very often you'll get a customer offer you a bonus for using more ingredients. Not only is it silly to imagine a customer caring how many ingredients are in their potion, I'm not wasting scarce ingredients for an extra coin.Eventually, you get to the point where you can only make a couple recipes because you don't have the ingredients you need to make more complex potions. So every day is the same, you make a basic healing potion for a couple customers, send a few more home empty-handed, maybe buy something from a vendor, then go to bed so you can do it all again.

_childDocuments_.review: In Potion Craft you play as an alchemist setting up shop. Customers begin to arrive with a range of different needs and you have to brew something to match their requests. Despite the simplicity of the concept, Potion Craft does well to make the experience engaging and fun. Harvesting and selecting ingredients, crushing them, stirring the cauldron, discovering new effects, placing potions on the scales, haggling etc. means you're involved in every step of the way and the game never becomes boring.The dialogue of the customers is varied enough so as to not get repetitive and the progression system ("The Alchemist's Path") provides a good balance between being challenging and flowing with natural discovery of the game's mechanics. The game offers a high degree of customisation, allowing you to give unique names, symbols, labels and bottle shapes to all of your creations which is a nice touch. Recipes can also be saved and quickly brewed using a recipe book, which is ideal for when you don't feel like manually brewing a potion (although I usually find myself doing so anyways because I enjoy it).Potion Craft's style is incredible. The music, sound effects, dialogue, and visuals all do an excellent job at creating a magical and old-timey atmosphere. The world of Potion Craft has a real charm and charisma to it - it's easy to get lost there.I also have to mention the tactility of the game; the experience of Potion Craft feels very hands-on. The herbs in the mortar and pestle provide just the right amount of resistance and the potion bottles have a certain weight to them that feels very realistic. It's clear that the game has been crafted with huge attention to detail.The game runs smoothly and I've never encountered any bugs.Despite being an early access game, Potion Craft provides a satisfying experience with a decent amount of content. Almost twenty hours in, I'm still discovering new recipes! With that being said, the game is lacking some features (such as shop upgrades and alternative potion bases) which will likely come in a future update. I'm usually wary about buying early access games but I've been really impressed with what Potion Craft has to offer so far and am excited to see where it goes upon full-release.

_childDocuments_.review: Lovely game, very unique, with gorgeous visuals. I absolutely adore the vibe of the game, which is very relaxing and cozy in a certain way, and appreciate the simplicity. _childDocuments_.review: (all the chapters or main objectives) / achievements:   30hr +   from 10hr onwards   1500+   1400+---------------------------------The main goals in game are to create legendary substances and their respective "consumables".There are 5 Tiers of legendary substances and each need all the preceding tier ingredients to make, and you will need to make 2 substances of each tiers to complete the objectives.i.e. You have just made a Tier 4 substance, and your next objectives will be making a Tier 4 consumable plus a Tier 5 substance.So you will need to use your Tier 4 substance + 12 potions to make the Tier 4 consumable,and another Tier 4 substance as an ingredient (making it from Tier 1 to Tier 4 again), + another 12 potions to make a Tier 5 substance. This situation happens in every tiers throughout the game, from Tier 1 to 5.You will be serving 1400+ customers, so you may not want to brew the potions from map every time.And for the ingredient potions of legendary recipes, many of them requires you to travel back and forth the map, corners to corners, or 5 different spots on map.So you will not want to do them twice for any recipes, but save the path of recipes so you can one click it when you need to make them again if needed.The game becomes a resource management issue, you just need to replenish the ingredients, buying all the discounted goods from merchants everytime, and one click the recipes to serve customers until reaching the final reputation required.For the reputation system, there are no endings for the good or evil side, no stories or hidden missions to complete, just different types of customers you will encounter.Consumable are so tedious to make, and you may not want to use them on fulfilling the customer additional needs, but just saving them to make legendary recipes. Therefore making the consumables are merely just objectives to complete the game.

_childDocuments_.review: It's a cute and chill game, but the gameplay gets very repetitive after a couple of hours. Every day you go to your garden and click the plants there, which takes about five seconds. Then you serve that day's customers, most of which consist of clicking a saved potion in your book. If a seller comes by you might buy some ingredients.You might optimize some recipes or try to find a new one, which is basically a little puzzle: add ingredients to your cauldron and stir, which moves the marker over the map. Each ingredient moves it along a different path, so you try to find the combination that gets you to the effect marker most efficiently.Some effects may be more difficult to reach than others, and sometimes a customer will ask you to use a specific ingredient, but that's pretty much it. There's an advanced alchemy machine, but so far that felt like a lot of effort for little reward.If you want a calming puzzle game to burn a couple of hours I would still definitely recommend this. The graphics are charming,  the concept is great, and the gameplay is novel and well-excecuted, if a bit samey after a while.

_childDocuments_.review: Let me preface this by saying while I was given a free copy, I played the demo well beforehand and knew that this was going to be a day one purchase for me provided the price point was not outrageous (I was pleasantly surprised to see it was quite reasonable). Anyway, on to my thoughts:Potion Craft is an incredibly unique and relaxing potion creating/selling simulation game. The potion creation method and exploration allows for a multitude of ingredient options (some more efficient than others) to create and eventually sell your concoctions. The characters, situations, and moral dilemmas from the various encounters keep the overall lighthearted gameplay interesting.The artstyle and music is quaint, the audio effects (although sparse) are satisfying, and the UI is simple but fit the setting well.While there are many other features and content that could be added and some aspects could be nitpicked, I am very excited to see what comes of the early access phase but don’t let that label fool you, it is a perfectly competent and entertaining game as is.I recommend giving Potion Craft a try; I had personally never played anything like it previously and I’m glad I was able to have the experience.

_childDocuments_.review: Charming and engaging game play loop of making and selling potions to make enough money to buy ingredients and gear to experiment with new potions. The mechanics really made me feel like a medieval alchemist, experimenting is fun, failures frustrating and successes rewarding both mechanically and emotionally.  Obviously the rest isn't there yet, but developers, if you're reading this, you HAVE TO make the vendors more accessible. Whatever RNG formula that decides when they show up would spread them out so far sometimes as to be down right game breaking. If the dwarf doesn't show up for 20 days that's fine, he just sells 'shortcuts', but if the wizard or herbalist don't show up for 20 days the game is in a total stale mate. Maybe make a 'go to town' option, or put a shorter cap on the spread like if they haven't shown up in 5 days they pop in guaranteed?Other than that I'm looking forward to future content. There's a morality gauge that doesn't do anything yet, maybe make some potions stronger/weaker or easier/harder to craft based on morality? I'd love to see a story element added via recurring characters like the herbalist and the brewer and the fisherman etc. And upgrades for the shop and especially the garden. I wish it kept track of how much I was spending to make potions, the profit margin was always just a guess, so a ledger element would be cool. Also the music is great but a bit thin, it gets repetitive quick.Final verdict: Cute and fun mini-game that in it's current state didn't really feel worth the sticker price but shows a lot of potential. Maybe buy, for sure follow.

_childDocuments_.review: A lot of unexplained (and luck-based) mechanics that require you to explore at great cost to yourself. For example, there is a portal on the map that I assumed takes you to a random location on the map. However most of the time it teleports you very close to where the portal is, basically wasting the resources spent getting to said portal. A lot of resources are also required to explore around the map as each resource only moves you a little bit, and new potion traits are very far from each other.Considering that so many resources are required to make and discover new potions, the game doesn't make it easy for you to get these resources. There is only a limited number you can gather from your garden each day (and even then, it's random as to what is available to gather). Merchants who sell resources also offer them at a rather hefty price, and it is up to luck as to which merchants appear (if they even appear at all). Considering that potions often sell for peanuts, it is difficult to sustainably obtain resources to be able to reliably explore the potion map.There also doesn't seem to be an overarching storyline to this game which makes gameplay feel pointless and repetitive after a while — all you're doing is trying to achieve the potion-brewing related goals the game has for you.Cool concept but execution is lacking, and gameplay becomes boring and frustrating after a while.

_childDocuments_.review: Potion Craft is a great relaxing game.  As many have said, it can get a bit grindy and boring when you hit a lull in progression.  Some of the negative comments have been about the lack of specific resources available for harvest/purchase when needed.  I think the reason for that discouragement is the misconception about the game's genre.  At it's heart, Potion Craft is a puzzle game more than anything else.  Figuring out how to reach specific potion effects without the ideal ingredients is part of the fun early in the game.  Later in the game, you may have better ingredients, but not the ones you have used in saved recipes.  That forces you to revisit some of the easier potions to try for better efficiency.  This game is definitely not for everybody, but I think it's definitely worth a look for people who like puzzle games.  I wholeheartedly agree that it needs some more exploration and maybe more world interactivity.  Upcoming updates with Talents 2.0 and Garden 2.0 look perfect for that.  I'd love to see some actual adventuring to gather ingredients, meet customers that become regulars, etc.  That might taint the allure of this game's simple relaxation, however.Look up some videos on gameplay before you buy, but don't go too deep.  The exploration and discovery is a good chunk of the fun!

_childDocuments_.review: Potion Craft is a game where you play as an aspiring alchemist who runs a shop in a medieval town. You have to mix ingredients, brew potions, haggle with customers, and manage your finances. Sounds fun, right? Well, not so much when you have to deal with the most annoying and demanding customers ever. They want potions for everything: love, health, beauty, strength, invisibility, you name it. And they’re never satisfied with the price or the quality. They’ll complain, bargain, threaten, and even try to rob you. And don’t get me started on the ingredients. You have to gather them from the forest, the swamp, the mountains, and other dangerous places. You have to dodge traps, monsters, bandits, and angry villagers. You have to spend hours grinding them, boiling them, stirring them, and hoping they don’t explode in your face. And you have to do all this while keeping track of your recipes, your inventory, your reputation, and your competitors. It’s exhausting!Potion Craft is a game that will test your patience, your creativity, and your sanity. It’s also a game that will make you laugh, cry, and rage quit. It’s a game that will make you feel like a real alchemist, for better or for worse. Would recommend to anyone who likes a challenge, repetitive gameplay, and a good sense of humor.
_childDocuments_.name: Potion Craft: Alchemist Simulator

_childDocuments_.review: An inventive, involved, yet still fairly intuitive crafting system allows for wonderful variety in how you make your potions - which is good, because the ingredients you have available might vary from one day to the other. _childDocuments_.review: I can't recommend the game in its current state, maybe that will change after the devs add in the content they spoke about in their December 16th announcement.The core concept and potion-making mechanic are pretty cool...for the first few game days at least. You have a good amount of ingredients and only a few customers, leaving you the ability to navigate the alchemy map. But if you use too many, and the garden/merchant RNG are not with you, you won't be able to make the potions the customers want - losing you money, reputation, and sometimes karma. There were multiple days where I never got enough ingredients to go in one direction, usually the one containing customer requests. This also makes you hesitate on expanding the alchemy map, as you might need those ingredients tomorrow. I think the garden should not be random, you should know what you're going to have. Later, add the option to add/change ingredients. Relying on travelling merchants for ingredients is ok, but I wish you were able to buy from an herbalist shop or something.I might give it another try once the new features are added, but I've got no desire to keep playing it currently.

_childDocuments_.review: Potion Craft has a nice idea at its heart, of a geeky potion-crafting and -selling simulation. Its art is endearingly old-fashioned, and the central conceit of the alchemy map is original and interesting. Also a shout-out to the pleasant and helpful community.But then the game spoils it all by adding a twitch clicker game at its heart in the essential haggling mini-game. You have to do this in order to make enough money, but if you're not an FPS twitch fiend—if, god forbid, you're just an older gamer looking for a nice relaxing potion-making game—you're going to crash and burn, losing all your money.This haggling mechanic, so central to the game, fatally undermines everything else the game is trying to achieve. There isn't even a mod on Nexus to guarantee haggling success—I know, I looked, because I really wanted to be able to rescue the game. As such, with deep regret I cannot recommend Potion Craft to anyone who isn't a whiz at manic twitch clicker games.

_childDocuments_.review: I really like this game. I has a very unique concept I've never seen before. The fact that you choose your ingredients to navigate on the map and reach different potions is astonishing! You can save recipes but in case you don't have the ingredients for it, you can just do the same potions using other ingredients you have at hand that you wouldn't normally use. _childDocuments_.review: Very fun and relaxing game.Outside of the unique visual style, the biggest strength of the game is how tactile it feels. _childDocuments_.review: This non-recommendation is to inform the developers that I don't think some of their ideas for increased difficulty are realistic or fair to the player. Adding conditions like "I only want a potion with 1 type of ingredient" is not just unrealistic, it's unfathomable that anyone other than a mage or alchemist would come with such a request, and realistically, they probably wouldn't make such an utterly ludicrous stipulation either. The requests to avoid or include a specific ingredient are much more realistic and understandable. Any limits on the number of ingredients are just silly. How is a bloody peasant supposed to KNOW what's in the love potion you just offered them? How are they supposed to KNOW you didn't just give them a health potion? The game uses some direct logic that defies the reality that most of your customers wouldn't be able to discern the effects of your potion until they actually take it.And the hits to reputation are silly as well. If I refuse service to some idiot who comes in and DEMANDS a potion with only 1 ingredient AND multiple effects and refuses anything that doesn't meet those IMPOSSIBLE criteria, why should I get penalized for telling that customer to go somewhere else? And at higher rep levels, the hits should be LESS, not more. Because your reputation is STRONGER, the complaints of a single person should mean LESS. Here's the simple logic, as your reputation increases, more of the populace will have been your customers and also had good experiences, thus the effect of a dissatisfied customer's complaint will be dismissed by the greater balance of good experiences. This effect would naturally increase as your reputation level increases and customers beyond your town also carry word further.It might make more sense if these complications were tempered against your trading skill, which at this point doesn't help you much except to acquire gold a bit faster. It would also make some sense that you could haggle a customer down on their requirements, like instead of 1 ingredient, you could haggle for 2, or 3 depending on your skill.And why is everyone demanding poopshroom when it hasn't even been offered for sale and I've literally never even acquired it? Why are customers demanding impossible criteria that my only option is to refuse? Just for more artificial difficulty?

For me the game has not crashed or lagged once, again lending to my sense of relaxation.Not as much love:Like others, the music can get a bit monotonous although its fitting for the game experience. Would love to see more variety. I'd like the 'option' of having the a different color scheme to the game; I DO think the current scheme may lend itself to the calming effect it has on me so not totally sure about this. Limited interactions with patrons. I'm not sure if there are more plans for this.I'd love to see an option of a way to trade/share/interact with fellow game players somehow. I think that would be an interesting concept.I've not spent a ton of time with the game yet so I know there is more than what I've experienced, but bottom line is that this game is addicting, relaxing, well thought out, and worth every penny (and more) of what I've spent.

_childDocuments_.review: If this game was a potion, I'd say that it has a very well-developed base, with many innovative properties ripe for expanding upon, has a pleasant smell and an appealing texture. But the rest of the potion was made by taking that wonderful base and pouring water. More, more, more water. More water. Endless deluge of the clear liquid, enough to fill the entire cauldron, flood the lab floor, and ruin your downstairs neighbour's ceiling. In the end, the aquatic ordeal leaves the potion completely devoid of anything it could've been, and you end up pouring it down the drain.It starts out . There isn't much of a plot, you're just a young alchemist who stumbled upon an abandoned workshop (biggest wish fulfillment of 2023) and decided to reopen it. People ask you for potions, so that's what you get them. The brewing system is ingenious: adding ingredients moves your "potion marker" on the effects map, and in order to get a particular effect, you have to reach its designated point, and heat the potion up to a boil.At first, the map is pure joy to explore. You're constantly finding new effects, collecting experience books, finding out how the map itself works, and unlocking milestones that make you move forward in the "Path of the Alchemist", which unlocks new NPCs, new ingredients, new merchants.But then... you slowly start noticing the unmistakable flavour of . Everybody wants a healing potion. Sure, I can brew you a healing potion. Oh, what's this? I'm out of a critical ingredient! But I can replace it with something else that "moves right", I'll just save both recipes so I won't have to do it again. Oh, but in order to get more exotic effects you have to move further into the map. And it's just so slow. So many ingredients just so you can explore the map. The same path, over and over again. Take the ingredient, smash it into pulp, put it in the cauldron, repeat. And again. And again.Note that many actions are achieved by the "pumping power of the mouse" so to speak. So to crush an object in the mortar, you literally have to crush it by holding it with the mouse cursor. Same for stirring, same for pouring water, same for using the bellows. Not only this becomes extremely tedious later on, it also makes crafting tier 3 potions an exercise in ridiculous mouse precision (it's not about the recipe, it's about making the potion marker be  in the right place. Hint: doing it is not fun).Eventually, a new option shows up: you get an alchemy machine that's supposed to be able to craft legendary recipes. Wow, a gameplay change! Exciting! Until it turns out that those recipes still need lots of "normal" potions to be made, and often these potions require a weird combination of properties that will have you make your potion take a very long trip across the alchemy map...And that's what this really boils down to. Everything is just so shallow and tedious. There is a reputation system, but it's pretty much a bare minimum. There is some dialogue with unique NPCs (including a discount Geraldo del Riviero), but it's quite rare, and incredibly short. There is a barter system with a nice dressing of difficulty levels and topics of conversation, but in practice it's just a QTE, and not a fun one.Like I said: there's a solid base, but it ends up drowning in an industrial amount of water. There's more to complain about, such as the annoying way the game provides you with ingredients (they're working on this part at least), but I think I've said enough.To wrap things up - some statistics. This is a game with 17k reviews at the time of writing, indicating a very successful, well-known indie game. And yet, the achievements paint a quite rapid dropoff rate. Some 50% of players have completed the first chapter, only 25% completed the third, 11% the fifth (I gave up right before that)... and only 0.9% have beaten chapter 10, the final one. Part of it is probably because a lot of people are drawn in by the unique art style without considering what kind of game it is, but I think a lot of people simply find the game gets very boring very fast. That's what happened to me at least, and I have an inkling I wasn't the only one.
