_childDocuments_.review: I've enjoyed my time with this game. It has a fun, unique art style, I just love the concept of running a potion shop, exploring the potion map to find new types is fun at first, and learning about new mechanics like crystals and void salt early on. That's my main issue with the game: all the evolutions of then game are early on. At first the gameplay is fun because it's a new system, and the fact that the game iterates on it early by giving you new plants for different traversal, things like moon salt that change up your strategy, learning how to effectively use water and whirlpools, new goals by having a bunch of routes to go for new potions as well as the alchemy machine giving more interesting goals than new customers, the shopkeepers asking for more complicated potions to improve their shops. However, you get through a lot of the truly new stuff decently early on, and you start to realize how repetetive a lot of the game is. There's a lot of plants but they barely differ in mechanical use. just different directions. The skill tree has very little depth and is really just linear upgrades in 3 categories. Having a low reputation  makes it so you find more dubious customers, but that really doesn't change the game much. New alchemy machine creations require different combinations of effects, but obtaining each effect is pretty much the same. Haggling is decently fun, but it functions the exact same way as a simple timing minigame every single time. You get into a pattern of waking up, picking your garden, buying as much as you can from shops and selling to customers what you can, seeing if you can make any new alchemy machine progress, going to sleep, and repeating. Picking your garden takes 3 seconds, and the npcs aren't particularly interesting. You start to get a lot of repeating requests down to the reason they need it, and it feels rare to find one you have to think about or that has multiple options. It's frustrating to make a potion that should help, but the customer doesn't see it. For example, I had a customer wanting to burn a place down. Of course what they really wanted was a fire potion, but I had an explosive potion on me that should work just about as well realistically, but they would only accept fire. The game just becomes so monotonous eventually where now I just play for like an hour every few months.TL;DR: It's a cute concept for a game that starts pretty strong, but becomes monotonous very quickly

_childDocuments_.review: It's a calming game, and I really enjoyed making crazy concoctions to develop potions.  When your potion map visibility improves, you can see the hint of a new potion in the distance.  The journey to get there involves destroying precious resources (if you're less than competent like me) and a mad insane dash, but when you reach it it's beautiful.  I really feel like a crazy scientist with a brand new crazy "invention."But then there's the "job" part of the game, where you have to remake the same old potions over and over again.  Resource management becomes very important then, and it can get very tedious having to figure out when customers speak in riddles.  A guy who wanted to not be tired won't accept dexterity or swiftness potions, but strength ones instead.  Sure, he came in with a big sword and shield...  But surely a dexterity potion would help him with endurance!It also seems like the devs have promised a lot of features and updates that just haven't appeared yet.  Granted the game was released less than a year ago so they aren't *too* negligent, I still remember waiting for seven years for Kentucky Route Zero to finish, but it's not that good of a look when a dev promises a lot and doesn't deliver for a while.  Lots of games have stopped updating over the years, makes an end user nervous when another game they kind of like might have the same fate.All in all, wait for a sale.  It's a fun experience but the "you're a crazy chemist making new potions and tossing resources into the void to do it" and "you're a pharmacist who has to make medicinal potions or rat poison for people while maintaining your stock of ingredients to do it" parts of the game are in direct conflict.  I want to feel more like a mad scientist, not like some burnt out pharmacist who's about to demand that customers just state what potion they want lol

_childDocuments_.review: ETA after a year and a half:No meaningful updates since launch. For months and months on end, they kept promising new shiny things while not actually delivering any new content. At 1.0 "release" the game still wasn't actually finished, which can be proven by how many additional (and crucial) features they promised right after the "release"... Or by how many existing features are visibly broken even as of now, with e.g. buttons and UI sections that literally don't do anything, but still made it to "release". This would be tolerable if it was left in this state for a month or two. Not 18.And look, this is not some programming rocket science. It's a cute grindy 2D game with simple mechanics. All the foundations are already there. So how the ♥♥♥♥ do you manage to not finish something this simple for so long, with the absurd amount of cash you already have? Five people should be able to finish off all the promised features in three months. And I'm a dev by trade, I'm not just making this up.At this point I consider this game a scam, a half-baked cash grab that was only "released" because they wanted an additional cash influx after their EA money proved insufficient for finishing production. And see, it worked. They already got incredibly rich off this game. So they don't even have a material reason to actually finish it at this point.Right now I don't expect anything good from this team, and personally, I'll surely never buy anything from them ever again. If you still want to spend your money on Potion Craft, well, I can only say I'm sorry you got successfully lied to.-----Original review:A very pretty and very gripping, but ultimately boring grind. A super nice experience on the surface, but as of 1.0 release, it seriously lacks content.- No plot or story of any kind. NPCs are absurdly dull. Despite the "reputation" system being in place, there's no story-driven decision-making in giving specific kinds of potions to specific people (which was so well done this year in "Strange Horticulture").- No variety. Only two maps are not enough. The sequence of all tasks is exactly the same after ~10h. The "soundtrack" is one single repetitive piece looped over and over (!!!). There's no equipment upgrades or variations. Why can't I switch my "wooden spoon" with some "golden spoon" that would work differently?- No challenge. After ~15h you're rolling in money and ingredients and can do literally whatever you want. The customers with very particular demands are still fun, because they give you fun puzzles to solve (and all of them seem solvable so far, which is a huge plus). But to *get the fun customers to come* you need to grind through hundreds of boring ones. I'd love some "hard mode" that only gives you the most demanding customers and is actually punishing in some interesting way if you don't manage to serve them (e.g. limits your potion-making abilities). Also there's no achievements for those fun challenges, even though they would be perfect for that.I'm happy to wait a year or two to see if this gets any meaningful updates, but for now I can't really recommend it over many better games.

_childDocuments_.review: A very good game for the price, relaxing but weirdly engaging at the same time.I started to feel that "Zen" level of concentration that comes from other activities like playing an instrument, working with tools... or practicing an actual trade, which is what I felt like I'd learned by the time I finished playing. The game recreates that realistic vibe through the physical experience of using your lab instruments. You can stir rapidly or slowly, but with the movement of the mouse and the animation onscreen it's easy to forget that you're not actually stirring. You can pulverize ingredients methodically or even violently with your mortar and pestle, but again, the translation of mouse movement into onscreen action gives a sensation like you're actually working in your own laboratory.Things start out simply enough, and the mechanical underpinnings of the game stay pretty much the same, but challenge and complexity continue as you progress through the game. This comes from a few different factors. Initially, there's a scarcity of effective ingredients to work with. As you progress further, your toolbox gets bigger but your objectives on the alchemy map get more and more difficult to reach. And as all of those pieces finally fall into place, the game generates new novelty through the sometimes-exacting specifications put forward by your customers - combinations of effects, including/excluding certain ingredients, limiting the number/type you can use, etc.By the time I got to the VERY end of the game and picked up the last couple of achievements, I kinda just wanted it to be done with... But, then again, there are so many games in my library that I never 100% finish because I feel like it's not worth attaining for the level of effort involved. This was within reach, so I went for it, and I certainly enjoyed all of the hours I put into the game short of maybe the last 2-3 that I did just for the sake of being a completionist. Maybe there's some room for improvement in the gameplay loop all the way toward the end of the game? Either way, I'm not too concerned.Maybe my only other complaint is that Potion Craft has ONE single music track on a perpetual loop - listening to a 2-minute loop for 30 hours can be tough to manage in large doses. But they've mentioned that that's something they're already working on, so by the time you pick up the game and get to the 10-hour mark maybe your head won't be ready to explode and you won't need to take a day to cool off.Overall, I enjoyed my time with the game, and I plan to revisit it once they add some of the new features they've hinted at. But that's not to say that Potion Craft doesn't already feel complete in its current state. It was fun, it will be the next time I pick it up, and I feel perfectly fine recommending it at the full price listed.On a side note... If you like dark humor, feel free to start catering to some of the more questionable people who visit your establishment and asking you to do questionable things. I got a good laugh out of some of the ridiculous explanations customers gave me for a bunch of their potion requests.

_childDocuments_.review: tldr: Game feels incomplete, doesn't feel like it lives up to advertising, gets boring the more advance it gets, and is very light colored which sometimes puts a strain on my eyes. I have mixed feelings on this game. I had fun for a while and have some friends that love it. But this game isn't finished and you can tell. First, there are some requests in the game that you just actually cannot fulfill. Sometimes customers come to me with special requests and I cannot do it based on what the request is and where the potions location is on a map. It is not the end of the world and would not turn me away, it is very rare, but I feel like that could have used a little more QA. Next, there are features shown in the game that you just can't use. For example one tab advertises to upgrade your shop tools. I was so confused as I could not figure out how to upgrade anything. Well I looked it up online and people were saying that it is an incomplete feature. Then when using the alchemy equipment I tried to save the recipe as that option is there but I noticed I could not select it. I again looked this up online and again it was noted that this was another uncompleted feature. Lastly there are the maps. Some potions are much harder to make on certain maps. They eat up a lot of ingredients and personally I don't feel like it makes sense to try and make them for customers when looking at potion selling cost vs. ingredient cost. I only make those potions when I have to because I am trying to make one of the key items I need to meet game requirements. There has been talk for a while of a third map that would definitely add to the game and make certain potions more practical. However I see many threads discussing that this has been coming for over a year with no updates. As it stands the two maps do not feel like enough, and I feel like this leads into the game feeling more repetitive and incomplete as the game progresses to more advance potions. The third map point leads into my other complaint - I also find some of the advertising misleading. To advertise you can grow your own ingredients doesn't make much sense to me. Sure, there are ingredients growing in your yard. However you have no control over what grows and don't interact with growing ingredients besides clicking to pick the daily randomly generated plants. The haggling system also isn't that extensive or interesting in my opinion. Just some quick clicks of a button if you need more cash. To call this a sandbox game is also a pretty big stretch. Also the whole "Sell your potions to the townsfolk while role-playing as a noble artisan, a greedy weasel, an occult dark master, or whomever else you may wish to be!" comment feels like a stretch too. This would literally just be you role-playing that is not a feature of the game. Sure if you sell to sketchy people your rep goes down or up. That does not align with the advertisement. I really wanted to love this game. I had fun for a while and if this type of game interest you I would for sure buy it on sale. It just doesn't feel worth it to finish the quests in game when it gets so repetitive and when you can see where it is lacking. Some of those "upcoming" features they advertise really felt like they should have been in the game upon release. There are areas you can see/click that just aren't completed. If they ever add those updates I'd happily come back and play more. But for now I just feel like I've reached a part where I get it and there isn't many more interesting things to be done. It does have a lot of potential and I'd be excited to try again with updates in place. Also one final note - I did recommend it to a friend that bought it because I thought she would like it a lot more than me. She ended up having to return it due to having a hard time reading the light colored map. I agree it can make my eyes sore after a while. I wish they had a different more visible color scheme option even if it breaks from the aesthetic.

_childDocuments_.review: A great game on the surface, I had a good time delving into the atmosphere of the game and the interesting system for discovering new potions.The issue I have with this game is how quickly the alchemy minigame begins to take up the majority of your gameplay time. This would be fine if the minigame was more engaging. Unfortunately you eventually realise it's really just a matter of moving in a certain direction on a map. Putting an ingredient just allows you to move in a certain direction, that's it. There's no sense of combining specific ingredients, they all just move you in a certain direction, so the uniqueness of each ingredient feels a bit lessened. Then you also hit the issue of having to make incredibly convoluted "potions" to reach far away spots on the map. That's where to me it's no longer a game about alchemy and more of a game about moving through tight spaces with clunky controls. That minigame is pretty cool in concept, but it quickly lost its charm. I would have liked less focus on travelling through the map and more focus on using specific ingredients to get certain effects.  There's a lot of things that could have been done with the minigame itself too, like having more than one kind of obstacle, letting you go through certain areas if you have certain kinds of ingredients for instance. Or at least making it easier to reach the more complex potions. Or just less focus on spending a ton of playtime on that minigame and more focus placed on interacting with npcs or building your lab in various ways.I also just have no interest in going for the philosopher's stone. Doing this game of cautiously going around the whole map just to make a specific potion that is a fraction of what you need for one step of the game's completion feels like pointless tedium to add more play time to the game. They got everything right, except their core gameplay. Please understand I'm here to play a game about alchemy, not spend hours slowly moving around on a map. I wanted to love this game but I don't think I would ever go back to it after a few hours of playtime. But hey, at least it was a fun time while the charm lasted. Despite my complaints, I would say it is worth the price since it's such a unique experience.

_childDocuments_.review: So far this game does not have good longevity. It doesn't take long (16-ish hours of gameplay really) to get to a point where all that's left to do is complete all the potions needed for the philosopher's stone and that process is so long and so boring and there's nothing to do alongside it to take away the tedium. Although the beginning of this game is fun, I can't recommend it to anyone who is budgeting for games because you can't get many hours out of this one at all, not in the state it's in now. I still haven't gotten the philosopher's stone made, but I'm very close and it's hard to push myself forwards on the goal when it's the exact same action over and over and over of making the potion bottle move around to specific points and nothing else. _childDocuments_.review: The art is nice, the gameplay mechanic is fun at first.At the start, money is a problem. You barely make enough to get by, having to rely on your garden for ingredients. As you level up, potions sell for more, and money becomes pretty easy to come by.But towards the end, it gets hugely tedious. I'm at 9/10 chapters done but can't bring myself to put in 5-6 more hours to get the final chapter done. Literally nothing new is being added, it's just the same old stuff, making very complicated potions for the legendary recipes, selling the same old boring potions to the same old boring customers. Same thing every day.Honestly, for what the game is, cutting down the length to complete would be fine. Otherwise it needs more mechanics to stay interesting through completion.Mechanics such as tilted bottles and warp stones could be explained more (i.e. at all). Feels like it's still in early access despite the 1.0 release.

_childDocuments_.review: I started playing this game during Early Access, and while I have enjoyed it (enough to play for 73 hours). I feel as though it is not updated enough to combat the repetitiveness of the game play. The last major update was in December of 2022 and it is now 8 months later. I love seeing the dev logs on what they are currently working on, but having no timeline on when those updates would be implemented causes me to lose interest quite completely. There are many times I forget that this game is even in my steam library because there are barely any updates. The game itself is nice but not amazing. It has a good and unique art style, and they have added more unique challenges, but the availability of magic pages for your recipe book allow you to easily save the recipes for any of those challenges so they no longer require any work. In fact, when I originally started playing, I had the recipes saved for every potion (weak, regular, strong, and the unique ones for the stones and salts); it caused the game to just be series of repetitive clicks (practically a money making simulator). The last major update had quite nice improvements on haggling, and customer base. They also added merchants asking for potions to bring more materials. They added a new potion base, new ingredients, and did a lot of maintenance on the reputation system. I enjoyed the updates, but for as long as the updates took to implement, I was underwhelmed and disappointed. The next major update looks promising, but with no real deadline in place for when that update will come out, I am not optimistic that the game will illicit any different emotions than the last update. I would personally prefer much smaller, more frequent updates over one massive and disappointing update once a year.
_childDocuments_.name: Potion Craft: Alchemist Simulator

_childDocuments_.review: The premise is fun, and definitely original, but after years of development, I played months after its release in early access, and here we are now, more than a year after its release, and almost nothing has really changed, the game is identical. The haggle system is as boring as it was day 1. The map is the same as day 1, the ingredient list is the same as day 1. The game is just... the same. I don't really know what the devs are doing, to be honest, nothing seems to have been added during this whole time.

_childDocuments_.review: There should be a more specific way of evaluating games on Steam than just YES/NO.So, in general I can say I enjoyed the game. Preparing the ingredients, exploring the alchemy map, mixing them in the cauldron felt very relaxing... for some time. After that it felt more dull and tiresome and then I found myself considering rejecting requests from customers because I just didn't want to spend several minutes doing the same thing over and over and over again. I wish there was maybe a better kitchen mortar allowing faster preparation of ingredients.The lategame is simply a painful grind. After you create the philosopher's stone and all the salts you only need to reach very high reputation level to finish the last chapter. That requires you to spend several dozens of in game days. Advancing from the 14th reputation level to 15th requires 1250 reputation points while typically one can gain about 45-50 per day. At the moment of creating all the substances you are most likely around 11th level of reputation. That means, if you want to complete the game, you will have to spend almost a hundred of in-game days doing the same thing every day, when all other stuff is done around day 40 and fun from playing evaporated by day 20. You still gain experience and skill points, but there's nothing more to spend them on, so brewing potions feels pretty pointless except for grinding the reputation.Designers probably did not have an idea to create more challenges at this stage of the game.I miss content. I miss challenges. I miss promised alcohol base for the potions. This game doesn't feel as if it is done.If you just want a fantasy kitchen simulator to relax, the game is for you. If you are that kind of person who wants to have the game completion badge, you can try it, but probably there are games that are more satisfying and richer in content.
_childDocuments_.name: Potion Craft: Alchemist Simulator

_childDocuments_.review: This is the kind of game that has potential but, quickly looses it's luster. You just explore a map that is your typical "undiscovered area" RPG map except you need ingredients to explore. The ingredients take you in various directions depending on the ingredient, you're aiming for what looks like a potion on the map, then you hit the fire and BOOM effect added.I didn't have to learn anything about the properties of the ingredients I just throw whatever in the pot that takes me right, left, up or down. This could have probably been a cool free browser based game at one point, this day and age it fails to excite me.I asked for a refund.
_childDocuments_.name: Potion Craft: Alchemist Simulator

_childDocuments_.review: This game first appealed to me as the perfect game for introverts. Who wouldn't want to pick herbs and make potions all day? I really enjoy the crafting portion of this game. I love the picking and grinding and general potion making. I'm excited to play further and experiment with the alchemy machine. The thing I DON'T love, however, is the customer interaction. Don't get me wrong, I think the characters are generally delightful, and I love the subtle pop-culture references (looking at you, witcher character). But this small portion of the game triggers the trauma of retail. I get very frustrated when a customer asks for a potion, and I don't have the ingredients. I hate that I have to take a hit in reputation by turning them away because it's impossible for me to brew the potion they want. I understand that this is somewhat resource management, but I can't hoard my ingredients for personal experiments and serve customers at the same time. The haggling is stressful for me, like the impossible fishing on a certain farming game. My only solution to avoid this stress is to never haggle. Ever. Despite all this, I will still recommend the game. The art, music, and sounds are very peaceful and cozy. I find it very relaxing and enjoyable... just not the interacting with humans part...
_childDocuments_.name: Potion Craft: Alchemist Simulator

_childDocuments_.review: This game has some engaging elements, it's a fun concept, but it doesn't really seem to go anywhere with that. The worst thing is that as more dialogue was added it seems to have gotten more confusing to new players. I had recommended this game to people in the past, but from the time I recommended it to the time they played it, the game changed in some subtle but significant ways where it asks players to make a leap in logic and that leap is multi-directional so they might end up all over the map and still not find what they where looking for. In some ways that is fun when the game does it well because it helps you explore segments of the map and be adventurous, in others it feels like it's wasting your game resources and real-life time. And when you are reminded of the fact you are playing a game and spending a portion of your life on it and you just want to make it to the fun part... weeell that's not a good thing. On top of that, this game has made a lot of promises and I have seen others mention this as well. Where its been a long time and they keep promoting and collaborating with other games while never really adding those features. I think a lot of people feel wronged by this and it's understandable. So while you can have a bit of fun with this game it is hard to recommend it as it might be frustrating and you might be buying it thinking that you want to see all the flashy new things they say they will add and because it seems as if they are actively working on it. But as it has been years, it's hard to believe in that. And the full game release is barely different than its early access version.

_childDocuments_.review: This game is great and I understand that it's still in early access and there's very much a possibility things will be fixed, but there are few issues I have with the game so far. The tutorial was unfortunately lacking. Maybe I missed some information, but I had no idea adding water to the potion would help me not die from hitting the bones during the crafting phase. I learned it from a YouTube video. My other main complaint is the lack of journal/recipe space. I am not able to save very many recipes and instead I have to write them down on my own notebooks. It's a minor thing but still incredibly frustrating. I should be able to save all my potions as I do them in order to keep the game actually running smoothly. When it comes to buying the new set for the basement, it's a bit frustrating try to save up enough to buy it when I have to constantly buy new pages, crystals, and herbs for when I run out. It wouldn't be that big of an issue if I wasn't constantly struggling to make the potions needs for the customers. It's a bit frustrating handling the customers. It's hard to find new potions without possibly wasting a ton of herbs and supplies. I understand you can get more from the garden after a new day, but in order to move on to the next day, you have to help the customers or just flat out deny them and ruin your chances of advancing through the game. Other than that this game is great. It's a fun experience and quickly becomes addicting. I hope to see a few more changes as time goes on. The game is still fully playable with the listed complaints, it's just frustrating at times. I'd definitely highly recommend this game.

_childDocuments_.review: TLDR;A fun game which contains more then I thought it would. relaxing and challenging at the same time.9/10 for me. (ignore my playtime, I played offline for about 30 hours or so).The detailed review:You make potions and sell them to adventurers, townfolks, good and evil people for different purposes.The game contains several mechanics and inner games, complementing each other, which you need to progress in, in order to finish the game (potion discoveries, potion creations, selling to people which has haggle mechanics which I liked and is quite challenging at high levels, and alchemy machine creation and operation which gets very complex at high levels).The way it works is you have a potion "discovery" map, the different potion locations are hidden from you, and the map is full of obstacles which you cant not see until you encounter them.You navigate this map by brewing different plant and mineral ingredients into your cauldron, anywhere from 1 to infinite amount of ingredients, each one moves your location on the map based on a specific path unique to that ingredient, and you can take part of the path or all of it, and also use water the center yourself a bit in relation to your origin point.Overall it allows for pinpoint exploration on a fairly large map that is not so easy to navigate with all the thorny obstacles.You discover potion formulas on the map over time as you progress in discovering it and then you can make that specific potion you discovered and sell it.There are maybe 30 potions or so, each unique, and you can create mixed effect potions, with 2 or more effects combined.The customers come to your shop every day looking to buy potions to solve their problems. some are for good purposes and some are for evil ones, and you can decide to sell or not to sell, which affects your overall alignment as good or evil and which progressively affects the types pf future customers who show up at your shop.At the same time there is a morale mechanics at work, which is part of your advancement in the game, based on how many potions you've discovered and sold, whether or not you've haggled for prices, your advancement with the alchemy machine and what you create with it, and this affects how many customers per day you get, which allows you to sell more potions and make more money.You get the ingredients daily from your garden which grows them, which at first is all that you have, but as time passes, sellers start to appear and sell you ingredients, and you rely more and more on them, and you need to prioritize what to buy and try to haggle with them for better prices.might sound a bit complicated, but its really quite easy when you get into it.The game requires patience for potion discoveries, some strategy for potion creation and sale and some very quick reflexes for the advanced haggling mechanics,I've played it for about 30 hours, and i'm not done, I estimate im about 60-70% away from full completion, and i paid 9.99 for the game on sale, so I got a about 50 hours worth of playtime for 10 euro (about the same in Dollars) which is a good and fair price.Recommended.Hope this helps someone make up their mind (:

_childDocuments_.review:
Potion Craft is an alchemist simulator where you physically interact with your tools and ingredients to brew potions. You're in full control of the whole shop: invent new recipes, attract customers and experiment to your heart's content. Just remember: the whole town is counting on you. 

Every day customers will come to your store looking for solutions to their problems. You will face consequences depending on what you decide to sell them. Attract guilds, befriend notable figures (or feud with them), gain riches and influence - and one day, you may even decide the fate of the whole town.

name: YesterMorrow
detailed_description: What is YesterMorrow? YesterMorrow is a single-player time travelling 2D platformer, mixing action sequences with puzzle elements, all wrapped up in an engaging story about our young hero, Yui, who must save her family and to change the fate of a world that has been plunged into endless night. This can only be done by journeying into the past and repairing the mysterious Clocktower controlling the cycle of time. Setting Her world - destroyed. Her family - kidnapped. Join our heroine Yui in a desperate attempt to save everything she loved. Learn how to use Everlight, embark on a journey through four islands (Forest, Desert, Ice and Clockwork island) and use time travel to overcome obstacles and access hidden locations. Free your family from the clutches of Shadows! Find out what really happened to the Sun and whether it can be reversed. Features Learn how to wield Everlight, unlock six special abilities and use them to cleanse your world from Shadows. Explore a vast world of YesterMorrow spanning four different islands (Forest, Desert, Ice, Clockwork). Encounter dozens of creatures and defeat challenging bosses. Use the environment to your advantage and solve puzzles in different ways. Traverse the world in two different timelines. Enjoy the serene calmness of the past and battle your way through the corrupted world of the future. Discover the rich lore as you interact with the world and its inhabitants. And don’t forget to pet all animals! Locate hidden areas and collect power-ups and lore entries. Supported using public funding by Slovak Arts Council

_childDocuments_.review: Gorgeous pixel-art, but... that's about all i can say about that game. Story starts simple and doesn't really grab attention too much, platforming feels really floaty and not enjoyable, physics on moving blocks and puzzles feels way off, cutscenes are slow and non-skippable... Didn't finish, because puzzle-platforming started to feel like a chore. That's a no from me.
_childDocuments_.name: YesterMorrow

_childDocuments_.review: Is this game a masterpiece? Yes, sir, I would agree to that question. It's a cute platformer made in Slovakia that requires fast reflexes, but offers a fair level design and very tight controls to overcome any challenge... after some training. You play a young girl named Yui that tries to save her village from a terrible fate of endless night. Years after the invasion by the Shadows who now corrupt their world, she finds a way to travel back and forth in time, which might give her a chance to save the future. Platforming, killing enemies, learning special abilities, finding secret rooms, petting cute animals just waiting to be caressed... all the usual stuff, including some really great bosses. Apart from that, there is a lot to see, some puzzles (involving time travel) to solve, people to talk to and did I mention... cute animals to pet. Ultrawidescreen is not supported, a controller recommended. Saving is possible at save points spread throughout the levels. The game feels very polished, but it really lacks cloud saves. Fantastic action platformer with an emphasis on platforming. Run, jump, and roll to save your family (and world).
_childDocuments_.name: YesterMorrow

_childDocuments_.review: "YesterMorrow" is a decent platformer. This game is a great pick if you're into platformers.

_childDocuments_.review: Pixel art is great, everything else feels slightly unfinished and early access.-Movement and physics just feel slightly clunky-Dialogue and cutscenes are unskippable, slower than they need to be, and pretty uninteresting.-The music loops very awkwardly and doesn't always feel like it fits the game, the OST is also incredibly short which would explain that a bit. Pretty sure in 1 hour I only heard the same 3 tracks loop.-Certain sound effects are either completely missing or extremely quiet, the whole mix of the game is a bit weird.-Level design feels unecessarily large, filled with mostly nothing or straight paths and basic jumping-Enemy's feel like they are placed very randomly and collision feels strange.-Game direction is completely missing sometimes, no idea where to go or what to do, easy to get lost.I gave it an hour and felt like I had enough. Pretty early on I felt like something was off with the game and after an hour it didn't seem to improve, so I'm gonna say pass on this one.

_childDocuments_.review: An amazing platformer with beautiful pixel art. The gameplay is smooth and feels great. My ONLY two complaints of this game is lack of keybind settings (can be fixed with steam overlay) and NOT BEING ABLE TO SKIP THE CUTSCENES OR AT LEAST THE DIALOGUE OF IT! The cutscenes are painfully slow. Past that cutscene complaint, this game is solid.
_childDocuments_.name: YesterMorrow

_childDocuments_.review: Actually really nice game. Less combat more puzzle, speed/timing and precision focused with growing difficulty of the levels. I wish there would be some kind of hints/names of the portals or marker on map where you are, because levels are huge and you can get lost pretty easy. There is also no option to "teleport/travel" to location you want, so you have to remember every level. Controls on PC can be frustrating sometimes, there is no option to change the keybindings, also I got troubles to throw the bomb up, w+arrow up, wasnt throwing up very often. Do not listen to bad reviews with only 1-1,5 hours playtime. The game starts be more challenging after 2-3 hours.Overall nice game, would play it again for sure.
_childDocuments_.name: YesterMorrow

_childDocuments_.review: Great puzzle platformer with beautiful pixelart style, good story (simple but good)It would be good if cutscenes could be skipped. After playing demo not that long ago it was somehow irritating.Its hard to find spots where its possible to talk with npcs.While I played there were some bugs, probably will be better with some updates (stuck at worm boss where it froze after being defeated, next 4 times one of traps didn't worked, only after 5 tries it worked as supposed to)
_childDocuments_.name: YesterMorrow

_childDocuments_.review: This game had potential to be a decent platformer however there's 2 things that breaks this game:- Plenty of bugs. Leading to softlocks because of how the save system works, because the whole game is one persistent world more or less. So if you get to a savepoint and do something and die then anything prior to said death gets saved regardless and does not reset which can lead to plenty of softlocks.The first boss can lead to a softlock, I saw it slowly happen because you have 2 ways to kill it, but one of said options just bugged out and went away. But I quickly understood what would happen if it continued further so I just quickly killed it with the last option available. The second one which ended my run is when you get to the hub island which leads to everywhere else. The moment you save on said island and then teleport and happen to quit afterwards leads to a permanent softlock because the teleport items you use get stuck on the other side which you can no longer collect/visit because the save takes you back to the main hub.This could have been avoided by just having said items be a permanent addition, but I guess they tried to be fancy where it didn't matter and only made things worse.It's also running on some unstable Unity version and being abandonware more or less doesn't help either. - Floaty platforming mechanics, from rubberbanding to snapshotting due to said floaty mechanics. This does not belong in a game like this.It's like this game had zero QA which really shows on the 2nd boss and everything else I just mentioned.Avoid!
_childDocuments_.name: YesterMorrow

_childDocuments_.review: This game is ok but not great. I'm on the borderline of a thumbs up or down, but the complaints feel significant and there's no shortage of Metroidvanias that do better.Pros:* Generally does all the Metroidvania stuff competently. Controls are ok, and while the powers aren't super unique they at least have their own spin on it.* Generally good platforming challenges.* The optional challenge rooms are clearly labeled as such.* It uses the dual-worlds gimmick well.* Not much backtracking (so far). Generally always clear where you should go next.Neutral:* Pacing is a bit slow, but that's because it's going for a more cinematic feel.* The story's nothing special, but they did put some effort into the setting and included a bunch of lore bits.Cons:* Combat... is weird? Your attacks don't kill most enemies, they just force dark spirits out of possessed enemies. The freed animals are just as aggressive and don't even change their attack pattern, and the freed spirit is itself sometimes quite dangerous (mostly because your first attack is awkward to hit them with). So there's not much point to attacking. And in the Past (aka half the game) the enemies aren't even possessed. Enemy design isn't very great anyways.* In some places it has a bit of a problem with things that can hurt you looking similar to the scenery. Also, the dark barriers that block your path in many places are only partly destroyed when you attack them once; they leave a little bit at the top and bottom which still hurts unless you attack them again. It's hard to see, unintuitive, and even when you remember it just slows things down.* As far as I can tell, there's no proper map. The "map pieces" just give you lore dumps. No map in a Metroidvania is a big problem, and kills any desire for completionism. At many times I had vague if any idea where I was relative to places I'd been before, though it was still clear where to go to advance. In any case it's very linear and your path only occasionally loops back on itself.

name: Hohokum
detailed_description: Take on the role of a curious flying kite-like being and travel to colorful, curious worlds waiting to be discovered. Interact with characters and environments to uncover secrets or simply roam at your own pace and be amused at the surprises that unfold. While there are goals and activities, at its heart, Hohokum is a playground - a place to wander about and get lost in. - An Expansive and Playful Universe with loads of eclectic characters and toys to interact with, like a gigantic playground. - Stylized Gameplay Encounters – From diving with sea creatures to soaring with kites, each world has custom goals, activities, interactions and secrets to uncover -- no two places look the same! - Captivating Original Artwork – Brought to life from the imaginative artist Richard Hogg, the world of Hohokum is surreal, youthful, and full of color and fun. - Entrancing Original Soundtrack – Hohokum features music from various talented artists in collaboration with Ghostly International Records.

_childDocuments_.review: A delightfully cheerful game about music and color. It’s simply fun to snake around and figure out how the many unique worlds work. The order in which you can explore each world is pretty open-ended. It’s nice to simply wander around without a ‘level select’ screen in the way as well as being able to move on and keep exploring when you come across one of the game’s trickier puzzles.Since the game is committed to minimizing direct communication for the sake of maximizing its wordless cuteness, it can be a bit difficult to know what exactly you’re supposed to do. Spending a few minutes cluelessly dithering around and feeling a tad dumb takes away from the playful atmosphere of it all. Although, I wouldn't be surprised if I'm just really good at missing Hohokum's cues. Either way, more time spent dithering meant more time enjoying the soundtrack, so I can’t really complain.
_childDocuments_.name: Hohokum

_childDocuments_.review: The glowing review I wrote still stands but as I have played more I have run into some bugs that mar the experience a bit. Sometimes animations replay several times in a glitched manner which left me sitting there confused wondering what was going on. In one instance, in the hat level, animations did not progress leaving me softlocked and unable to finish the level, exiting and returning erased my progress for that zone. Fix the bugs and I will edit my review.In Hohokum you take control of the "Long Mover", a multicolored worm-like creature that looks suspiciously like a sperm, and wander around a set of beautifully illustrated interactive worlds. I first saw this game at a friends house and I was intrigued by how strange and colorful it was, I sat there for an hour or two and zoned out to the little dioramas I stumbled into. Later I bought the game for myself and had a blast completing it. I bought this as soon as I saw that it was on Steam and I hope to see it get steam deck functionality soon as well.While not entirely obvious, The story of Hohokum is  You slip through portals to travel to different levels and sometimes there are little interactive transitional zones as well. Each level has its own "theme" and/or story (For Example:  and ) and as you interact with things you find a worm friend hiding in each level. The main objective of this game is to find all of the other worm guys but it really is a game like Flower, Abzu, Journey, etc. where its great to just zone out and enjoy all the pretty colors. There is also a side objective where can you open these eye things scattered in each of the levels by touching them. The levels are connected in these branching paths like a tree so if you ever get lost just look up a guide and you can find your way around that way.The music in this game is great as well, its very relaxing and fun.All-in-all Hohokum is a unique little zen-game that you can just put on and zone out to some pretty colors and funky landscapes. I recommend you check it out if you are into that kind of stuff.
_childDocuments_.name: Hohokum

_childDocuments_.review: -- UPDATE -- Ok, so I gave it another go, and I think I mostly get it now. You're a snek and you travel to different places. If you solve whatever puzzle is in a place, you unlock a new snek bud that hangs out in the Home area around its little portal. However, I still don't love it...some of the puzzles are kinda fun, others I never would've figured out in a million bajillion years without a guide. Achievements are even more obtuse than the puzzles. Navigating between different areas was a complete mystery until I finally looked up a map. Overall, I was usually too frustrated to enjoy the intended "chill" atmosphere, so I'm gonna go ahead and stop trying to love this game. :/--- ORIGINAL REVIEW ---I...don't get it :( I want to get it. It's colorful verging on hypnotic, and there's lots of areas to explore. Little dudes jump on your rainbow snek and ride around making silly noises. I really, really wanna love it!!!But ultimately I was quite lost on what I was supposed to do. It's a virtually text-less game, and it seems like you're supposed to discover the puzzles organically by just wandering around. While I like that in theory, it somehow wasn't intuitive to my brain. After a half hour or so of aimless wandering, I'd kinda had my fill of just enjoying the pretty colors, and a hint to get me started would've been really helpful.I also ran across a number of bugs that really affected game play, and they appeared very reliably no matter how many times I left and came back to an area or restarted the game. And because the game is so hands-off and quirky, it took me quite a while to realize when it was actually broken versus just a puzzle I didn't understand.Overall, it's very pretty and would probably be amazing when you're high, but I just had too much trouble with it to give it a thumbs up :/

_childDocuments_.review: Playful puzzling-adventure romp in an enigmatic, colourful world awaiting your explorations. I absolutely LOVED this!!It's a 'cult classic'(?) from the Play Station era, apparently. Fairly recently ported to PC.It's vibrant and childlike (not childish!) and fun and favours exploration and experimentation and an open mind.But may have rather a high threshold for new players going in blind - I saw it described as 'maybe too obtuse for its own good'! And, yeah, I can see that ;-)Not difficult in the gameplay as such, no QTE or platforming or arcade or shooting or anything like that. Pleasant and wholesome and do-it-at-your-own-tempo and VERY nice-looking. But yeah - can be bewildering:  am I,  is going on here,  is the purpose or goal of this whatever it is... The game Steam forum is pleasant and helpful (and there's recently a completionist guide on the game forum, too, for the 100%-ers out there). For myself, I was very happy that a web search turned up an old 'paper guide' from 10 yrs ago when it was PS-only. Especially happy for its basic tree diagram of the structure of the world connections, which was such a help in getting my head around it enough to actually manage to get INTO the game and understand where I was. (I'm working on a 'newbie Guide' for the game, based on my experiences and bewilderments with it, but it's my first Guide ever, so may take a bit of time still to get there...Setting it in writing here, will hopefully push me along ;-)).It's great fun, and I love games that reward pattern recognition and open-ended exploration. And cheerful. Music is lovely,  and fits the various worlds.Plays fine on mouse :-). Despite game saying controller recommended. Or you can play on KB if prefer (and keys are rebindable). Be warned that there is NO MANUAL SAVE, and AUTOSAVES ONLY on LEVEL COMPLETION. After completing a level ('world') it will be reachable in a short-cut through a sort of level select mechanism that you will have to figure out for yourself. Or you can go back to anywhere 'the long way round' at any time (this will make more sense to you once you're in the game)TIP: There can be a tendency to softlocking in a couple of the 'side-room dead-ends' in the DOT world, but a quit-and-restart will get you back into the game. May be smth to keep in mind in that level/world, though, so that you do your explorations BEFORE starting in on the puzzles or achievements. As it won't autosave your progress if softlocked but you'll be back to level start.I'm not an achievement hunter at all, but got 8 of the 12. Most are attained through exploration and trying things out, but a few require some speed and accuracy, and one is a classic speed-run. Which is why I didn't manage those.
_childDocuments_.name: Hohokum

_childDocuments_.review: A very goofy but fun game for what it is, travelling the multiverse as a weird sperm/kite/worm creature. Fun but chill music plays as you explore many worlds and this soundtrack just adds to the game's atmosphere and unique aesthetic.Nearly every world has it's own unique puzzles/challenges for you to discover and solve, the world's that don't are connecting worlds that house other portals but even then the backgrounds they have are trippy af and relaxing to stare at.The game is kinda short but for the small price-tag, it's more than what I expected!
_childDocuments_.name: Hohokum

_childDocuments_.review: I think the game is designed to be open-ended, even though there is a way to "complete" the game.  For example, there doesn't exactly seem to be instructions, and you kind of learn how to play the game as you go along.However, the visual design is striking (and, at the same time, peaceful).  So, even if you don't make formal progress zooming along in a colorful world with interesting sounds and rumble feedback is a unique experience!In terms of being goal-oriented, I am not sure if I would recommend emphasizing completion.  For example, I think it would have been very hard for me to "complete" the game without additional assistance.  However, at the same time, I think my first playthrough would have been shorter if I didn't have a goal, and I am not sure when I would have curiosity again to explore the game.So, with that being said, to try and balance looking up details with understanding what is needed to accomplish tasks, you can "complete" the game by .  This is accomplished by completing .  If you look up more details, then that ruins some of the surprise.  However, I found certain "required" tasks otherwise hard to determine and/or complete.  For example, they are not all immediately obvious (at least to me), they are arguably not necessarily the most fun (but some certainly are), and they certainly don't represent everything that you can do in the game.However, I hope this helps you with deciding what you would like your experience with the game to be like.
_childDocuments_.name: Hohokum

_childDocuments_.review: (Is this game for you?) If you play games for completion or expect significant gameplay depth, then you won't get much out of this. If you want a short and sweet audiovisual experience where you can relax, it's perfect for you!Gameplay: 8/10May seem aimless at first glance, but this game is all about exploration and discovery, and it's very fun to find everything these worlds have to offerVisuals: 10/10Incredibly vibrant and stunning 2D environments with tons of artistic varietySound: 9/10Stellar music and pleasant sound design, headphones recommendedStory: 8/10Oozes charm and childlike wonder despite not using a single wordValue: 9/10Will only take about 4-5 hours if you know what you're doing, but if you play it completely blind and just immerse yourself in the discovery it has the potential to last several hours longer. Decent amount of replay value as the game is nonlinear and every playthrough will be a bit different.Subjective score: 44/50 (Right up my alley!)TOTAL SCORE: 88/100 (Highly recommended!)

_childDocuments_.review: At first the surreal atmosphere looks awesome, however the game play quickly makes Hohokum very boring.The only things to do are find all the portholes, open all the eyes, complete the optional missions some maps have ( which reset if you leave ), and acquire all the achievements. Eyes can be hidden behind objects, and some are invisible.  I've spent way too much time in individual maps going back-and-forth, in a search pattern from one side to the other, attempting to find all the eyes. This game play mechanic sucks all the fun of exploring the worlds, and instead creates a boring & repetitive experience.
_childDocuments_.name: Hohokum

_childDocuments_.review: While I appreciate  ambitious commitment to redefining what a game can be, I rather liked how they were made already because this is a "game" that so deeply lacks purpose, vision or a clearly defined goal. You spend hours coasting around as a celestial worm that draws coloured squares, organises weddings or saves swimmers from the trip to the pool. I just don't get it. If someone asked me what this game is about, I couldn't tell them. Over 2 hours of play didn't bring me closer to understanding it, just more frustrated that I didn't. So I quit. It's colourful nonsense, perfect for a toddler maybe.
_childDocuments_.name: Hohokum

_childDocuments_.review: This game is gorgeous and the music is cute.  The puzzles are fun and satisfying, but there's a lack of direction for what you're doing.  This is definitely an intentional decision to encourage exploring and experimenting, but it does get frustrating occasionally.  Definitely worth pushing though though!
_childDocuments_.name: Hohokum

_childDocuments_.review: Hohokum is a game developed by Honeyslug and Richard Hogg and published by Annapurna InteractiveThe game offers some nice graphics and a really beautiful aesthetic, it is pleasant all the sameThe game does suffer with it being incredibly short and not offering much in terms of gameplay and more of a short, touching story. For me personally, it didn't bug me at all but if you're expecting a really deep, intricate game with some clever gameplay mechanics and such, Hohokum isn't the game for you.Hohokum overall, however, is a short, beautiful game to play, it is a good interactive adventure game to play in short bursts!
_childDocuments_.name: Hohokum

_childDocuments_.review: Like the description says, it's a playground more than a game, so if you are a goal-oriented player you may find it frustrating. Reminds me of games by Vectorpark though he hasn't put anything out for a while. I love the music, the playful interactions and the joyful feeling of flying around in some areas, and if I get frustrated I remind myself that the puzzles and nonlinear structure are just an excuse to hang out in the world and listen to the pretty sounds.I've been playing on a laptop with just a mouse and keyboard. I think it will be more fun when I plug in a controller (as the game tells you when you start up) but I haven't had any major tech issues.

_childDocuments_.review: I get that this is an old PS3 Port (originally this game released in 2014), but dang, this title is criminally underrated!!It should be known that this comes from the exact same publishers that put out Flower and Journey (also once former PS3 exclusives): Santa Monica Studio and Annapurna Interactive. name: The Jackbox Party Pack 7
detailed_description: Five new incredible party games to bring the fun! 1. The say-anything threequel Quiplash 3 (3-8 players). Get big laughs answering the quirkiest prompts. 2. The collaborative chaos game The Devils and the Details (3-8 players). Can you survive the daily torture of human life? 3. The drawing fighting game Champ’d Up (3-8 players) . Can you take down the heavy favorite? 4. The on-the-spot speech game Talking Points (3-8 players). Just keep talking whether it makes sense or not. 5. The pop culture guessing game Blather 'Round (2-6 players). It’s a good fun time experience. Play using phones, tablets or computers. No extra controllers needed! NOTE: The Jackbox Party Pack 7 is in English only. NOTE: The game is local multiplayer but can be enjoyed over streams with remote players. How to Play Remotely Players use any web-enabled device (like a smartphone or tablet) to join the game and play along. When playing with remote players, you can use a video conferencing tool like Zoom, Steam Broadcast, Google Hangouts, Discord, and more to connect with others! Just share your screen while on a call and make sure you look for prompts to share audio.

_childDocuments_.review: This is a great pack with a unique assortment of games. All of them work over the web, which is a big plus.- Quiplash 3: It's good ol' quiplash. Can't go wrong with this one. The prompts are good, and there are custom packs if you get bored of the defaults. The last lash is always the same- every player gives 3 answers to a prompt. I'm not a huge fan of this, but meh. It's quiplash.- The Devils and the Details: This is my favorite, simply because of the chaos it creates. Players yelling at each other to finish collaborative tasks, scolding the selfish players, and freaking out when there is an emergency. It can get a little old, but the wide variety of "scenarios" keeps it fresh enough.- Champ’d Up: Head-to-head drawing game. Pretty fun even if you suck at drawing. Playing multiple games in a row allows for comedic callbacks, since the game lets you "tag in" drawings from previous games. It gets pretty silly.- Talking Points: This is a close second favorite. Players have to bulls**t their way through a wacky presentation. It's fun to make up something as fast as possible on the spot. Lots of improv is involved. I wish there were more images to choose from- when images repeat it gets a little less funny. The custom mode is pretty fun if you have creative players. The scoring system kinda sucks.- Blather 'Round: This is the one I have played the least, but it's interesting. It's not as funny as the other games, but it's still very entertaining to try to deduce what the word is. It's like charades with words. Seems to have good replayability. Overall, awesome pack that is well worth the asking price. Plays great over Discord or IRL :)
_childDocuments_.name: The Jackbox Party Pack 7

_childDocuments_.review: This is the first Jackbox Party Pack in which our group felt all 7 games were "winners".Quiplash 3 - The "Thrip Lash" is, finally, the perfect structure for the final round of quiplash.The Devils and the Details - Mechanically has the potential to get the most repetitive, but you'll be having too much fun shouting at your friends to drive you to the dentist to care.Champ'd Up - A drawing competition where only one player knows the prompt. The game shines in it's last round, however, when you get a random prompt and have to pick one of your previous drawings to fight for it. This gets very special with repeat plays, as the game keeps your entire roster of drawings around as long as you select "same players".Blather 'Round - "It's a Spicy Box Place". "Taco Bell!" "HOW DID YOU GUESS THAT?"Talking Points - A classic improv game. Give a speech, with no idea what your next slide is going to show. Creates some truly special moments when the assistant selecting pictures and the presenter psychially align. Also you can mash upvotes and downvotes, which is very satisfying.
_childDocuments_.name: The Jackbox Party Pack 7

Party pack 7 has the same feeling as party pack 5, not in the bad way. there was so much more effort in this pack, brand new ideas, cool concepts, and the classic Quiplash.QUIPLASH 3:amazing. just, perfect. i LOVE the new style, i LOVE the new music. also the extra funny prompts. but that's it. i was expecting just a little more but i'm content. the brand new settings caught me off-guard though. i will say this, this game somewhat looks incomplete, there are bugs, errors, i had to task manager once. but hopefully its fixed in the futureDEVILS AND THE DETAILS:just like quiplash 3. amazing. nothing much to say about to say about this one. i will enjoy this with family, by a lot. it's just a good game! honestly my second favorite. _childDocuments_.review: As always, Jackbox brings hours of laughter to my group of friends.Favorite game: Champ'd Up.The drawing tools are expanded from those of previous entries, such as Drawful, allowing for more creativity and freedom in drawing. The fun really kicks in when you draw the challenger, using only your opponent's drawing as a reference point. I definitely recommend using the extended timer so you don't feel as rushed to get your drawing right.Least favorite: The Devils and the Details.This game just doesn't flow well for my group of friends, but I still recommend trying it for yourself. It doesn't have the same format as most other Jackbox Party Pack games (Prompt, respond, vote), and is much more continuous and at times hectic. While there is a bit of competition, it's mostly a cooperative game. While this could definitely be a big drawing point for some people, it wasn't very fun for us.The brain game: Blather Round.This game is essentially word charades. You choose one of three things (person, place, etc.) and have to vaguely describe it by filling in the blanks of a sentence using a list of terms the game provides. As the round continues, you can form more clues in the same manner while other players try to figure out what you're describing. Lots of fun, and if you're like us you'll end up playing it multiple times in a row and forgetting to try out the other games.The chill game: Talking Points.A much less competitive game, but that's not a bad thing. You take turns giving presentations on material you've never seen before, and while you're briefing each slide, another player is creating the next slide. Forces you to think on your feet, and even for a group of people who all hate giving presentations, we had a lot of fun.Ol' Reliable: Quiplash 3.If you liked the previous Quiplash entries, you'll like this one. The only real changes are the ability to choose your avatar, and the new final round: Thrip Lash. In Thrip Lash, you give a three-step response to the prompt, with each step being revealed one at a time. We found that some of the prompts in Thrip Lash were weak, but overall it's a solid addition. You also have the ability to create your own prompts in the menu.

_childDocuments_.review: Easily the best Jackbox in years. Quiplash 3 continues the high quality of that game, even if little has changed aside from the final round. Champ'd Up is possibly a contender along side Drawful for best drawing game. Blather Round came completely out of left field and is one of the most popular Jackbox games among my friend circle now.Now for the less glowing critique.  I personally really like Talking Points, but it seems to be massively unpopular among those who I have played with, and I understand why.  It requires a performative personality and a sense of improvisation that isn't for the shyer folks in your group, and may end up with some people feeling left out.  Also, the scoring criteria isn't super clear and seems to be heavily weighted towards those who go later.I have not had much experience with the Devil and the Details yet and while it seems fun, it is almost impossible to play virtually as it is too hard to coordinate in a video chat when all voices end up drowning each other out.  In person, I can see it being a fun collaborative affair, but COVID has unfortunately put the kibosh on that.Champ'd Up and Blather Round alone make this the best Jackbox since #3 and the one probably most in the spirit of the original games in terms of accessibility and straight of fun.  Time will tell if the two games I mentioned as weaker will be more viable once in person gatherings are a thing once more, but regarless the pack gets a strong recommendation.

_childDocuments_.review: The Jackbox Party Pack 7 comes with some good games, it is not my favorite though.Quiplash 3Always a classic. Always fun. In Quiplash you come up with the best punchline. There are no noteworthy changes except the art style.Devils in the DetailsOne of the few co-op Jackbox games, but with a twist: there is still a first place. For me, doing chores virtually is even worse than in real life. On the plus side is that you do not have waiting times.Champ’d UpThis game can be really, really funny. You draw multiple characters and give them names to win in certain categories. Later, you use the same characters to win other categories, which can lead to hilarious combinations. Talking PointsThis Party Pack does not only have a game where you do chores, it also has a game where you do PowerPoint presentations like you are back in 7th grade. Do not get me wrong, it can be hysterically funny. Just make sure that everybody in your group feels comfortable giving a speech. Otherwise, it can get awkward.Blather ‘RoundI got this Party Pack only for this. It is like a trivia game, where one person chooses computer-generated hints. It can be a magical moment, when you already gave up because the hints you could give were not so good, but then somebody guesses correctly at the last second.Keep in mind that you play with one smartphone / tablet or web browser per person. If you want to play with your friends online, you can use Steam Remote Play or Discord. It is still fun.

_childDocuments_.review: The Jackbox Party Pack 7 is one of the best Party Packs that has come out recently with 5 different new and unique games that are great for parties and streams. Since this is 5 games in one I will review each one individually.If you have played any previous Jackbox games you probably know what Quiplash is. In it every player gets prompts with fill in the blanks that you try to create the funniest answers you can. And then everyone votes on which answer they thought was more clever or funny and then the person with the most points at the end of the game wins. This version of Quiplash has some unique rounds to spice things up along with obviously an abundance of new prompts. Also you can make your own questions in the game if you want and whats really cool is you can actually play other players custom made questions in a featured content tab so that is awesome. And the artsyle is this really cool looking claymation vibe and so overall this is probably going to be a lot of players favorite game in the pack.In this every single person is on a team of devils trying to do everyday human chores to fit in. So the gameplay consists of there being a huge list of chores on everyone's phones and when you do them there are small and simple minigames you must complete to get points for the family. This game overall has a very interesting and unique premise but my problem with it is all the chores you are doing kind of feel like actual chores. I think if the minigames had been a little more fun almost like little Warioware games this could have been incredibly fun but every single task you do consists of you doing the most mundane things ever like looking through a phone book for a specific phone number to type in so it kind of makes the game fall flat a little in my opinion.This is stupid fun and honestly one of my favorite drawing based Jackbox games ever. In it each player draws and names a champion to fight others and then gets to create another champion to fight another players champion. Then the rounds start and each person votes on who they think would win in a fight and in the later rounds you can tag in your other fighters which is awesome.And one really cool feature about this game is if you continue playing with the same players across multiple games when it comes time to tag in some of your other fighters you can actually use your fighters from previous games which is super cool. Also the music in this game is way better than it has any right to be.This is one of the games that you kind of need to have the right group of people to play because it’s less of a competition and more just a fun little experience. In it each player will give speeches kind of like Ted Talks to the other players and when its your turn to give the ted talk another person acts as your assistant by choosing what the words you have to read are and what pictures accompany your power point.Everyone can like or dislike your speech at any time and that is what determines how many points you get but overall you should just be playing this game to give hilarious speeches to your friends or family and it is pretty fun when you get a group of people to really commit to this game.This is kind of like a game of charades almost. In it each player chooses a word from a list of 3 and it could be a person, a place, or a thing and when it’s their turn they try to form sentences with a very limited amount of words to give the other players hints. The entire time the other players are trying to guess the word and sometimes the person who is giving the hints can even include the previous guesses in their hints. So say someone said the hulk but the real word was a different super hero the person giving hints could make a sentence saying “it’s very similar to the hulk”.And if someone guesses the correct word then they along with the person giving the hints gets points and if they used any other words from other player's guesses they get points as well.And so overall this one is really fun because I haven’t really played a charades like game in a Jackbox Party Pack and so it is a very fun and unique experience.And so overall I absolutely loved this party pack. I loved 4 out of the 5 games and the one I didn’t like I didn’t hate I just wasn't a super fan of. If you are a fan of previous Jackbox Party Packs you will definitely enjoy this one!

_childDocuments_.review: Another year, another Jackbox Party Pack. My friends and I are huge fans of this series and return to it numerous times throughout the year. Usually, with each new Party Pack, you get maybe three good games and two bad ones, so I was interested in seeing if the latest would keep up that trend.Quiplash 3 was a good bit of fun. It’s by no means the strongest game in the pack, but it takes the already solid Quiplash formula and delivers the best version yet. You basically answer a series of prompts with what you think is the funniest and best-fitting answer and those answers go up against others in a series of rounds until you get to the multi-answer finale and all the points are tallied up. It’s pretty simple really, but the Jackbox team has done a great job with all the creative prompts, the visuals and music, and just the overall presentation.This is something you’ll see extend to the other games in the pack as well, they’ve really upped the visual side of things this time around. Regardless, Quiplash 3 is a solid first game for the pack and one my friends and I will be returning to.The Devils and the Details is easily one of, if not the most, chaotic games I have ever played in any of the Jackbox games. It plays very differently from the rest of the pack, being a co-op survival game of sorts where you each play as a member of a family trying to complete certain tasks before the end of each day. However, each family member has a personal score and it can be increased by completing selfish tasks that harm the rest of the family. This creates this cool dynamic where you’re both trying to help out the rest of the group while also trying to stay above the rest.The actual tasks are divided into individual and group tasks – with the latter being where the chaos comes into play. They oftentimes require you to instruct another player, but when you have seven or so people playing at once, it quickly becomes a mess of players shouting instructions at others and trying to get everything done by the time limit. It can get very loud, but that’s the point of the game and I quite enjoyed the change of pace compared to the other games’ comedy-centric focus. It may not get the laughs, but it will definitely get the communication going in a chaotic fun sort of way.Champ’d Up ended up being my favorite game of the pack. Every pack has a drawing game, and Champ’d Up not only expands on the drawing tools offered in the previous packs through colors choices and an undo button, but pits drawings against each other in a very cool way. You’re basically tasked with drawing something against another drawing without knowing the category that the two are competing in – only the original drawer knows the category. This can create some very cool matchups and the worse your drawing skill, the funnier it becomes.This was one of the two games in the pack where my group literally couldn’t breath because we were laughing so hard at some of the drawings, and the way the game facilitates these matchups just makes it all that much better. Jackbox always seems to knock it out of the park with the drawing games and Champ’d Up is no exception.Talking Points is the game that had the most laughs from my group. And not just regular laughs, but the kind where you find yourself wheezing. It’s a presentation-style game where you have one player presenting on a topic they know nothing about and another player feeding the first player new text and picture slides for their slideshow. As the presenter does not know what slide is coming up next, there is a ton of adlibbing involved, but that’s what really makes the game shine. You gotta somehow link together all of these unrelated images and lines and it can lead to some pretty funny moments.For example, I pitched my presenter an image of a squirrel, then sausages, and then house keys, and he managed to weave it together into this werewolf narrative that had the rest of the group dying. It’s definitely the simplest game in the pack in terms of its design, but it’s got some top-tier execution and provides a solid foundation for a simple, yet fun party game – the type you can just bust out with any group and get to playing.Blather 'Round is without a doubt the weakest game in the pack. It’s not outright bad, but it definitely doesn’t click like the rest of the games do. It’s basically a trivia game played using word charades. You get a word and have to convey it through a limited set of other words and player guesses as they come in. What my group found was that a lot of the prompts are simply too hard, even the ones marked as “easy”. For example, I would get something like Bikini Bottom, which you would think would be at least somewhat easy to pitch, but the clues are so abstract that half of my group was guessing oceans and lakes and such and the other half was guessing coastal cities.Of course, just like the other games in the pack, this is all going to depend on the group you play with. Blather 'Round is just the type of game that is better played among those that like trivia games (and this is coming from someone that does).The Jackbox Party Pack 7 is yet another solid addition to the series, definitely one of the better ones. It’s got some really good highlights – most notably Champ’d Up and Talking Points – but some other fun additions as well – Quiplash 3 and The Devils and the Details. The only one that didn’t quite stick was Blather ‘Round, but even then, it’s not outright bad like the usual bad game included in past Party Packs. If anything, this might be the most well-rounded pack yet.Follow my  for more reviews + videos!
