_childDocuments_.review: While my review for this game as a whole is going to be negative, I'm saying that I would recommend it at the end of the day because it's a popular party game set, and despite my thoughts on how it's designed, it does have a lot of general appeal.With that in mind though, I just don't really care for a lot of Jackbox games. I'm an artist and I like doing the drawing ones, but besides from that a lot of the games, especially the ones that have some type of competitive goal, don't really feel like they're well-balanced to give people a fair chance to win, especially if they didn't do well early on.This isn't as big of a deal in the games with a more standardized system of who did the best, but especially in the more subjective games like Talking Points, Quiplash and Champ'd Up (as well as several from other packs that I won't be talking about because they aren't part of this specific product), it feels like the act of actually *winning* the game is based on so many factors entirely outside your control that it may as well be luck-based. For example, the two big factors in the Talking Points system are the engagement and the final awards at the end. The engagement system doesn't really work well because it relies entirely on people remembering to engage on their device, and if someone forgets to do that, it can tank your score regardless of how well you did. The awards system isn't much better since there's no guarantee that people will use it to actually reward people who did well- most of the time in my experience they just give it a funny name and hand it to a person for le epic troll. Because of this, the actual main part of the game has very little affect on the final results, because the systems used to measure how well you did are both inconsistent and subjective, based on factors that you as a player cannot control, making victory feel hollow and defeat feel unfair.For this game specifically, I'd recommend just having it so that the players rank all the speeches from best to worst in the end instead. That way the factors of who wins feel like they actually relate to the speeches themselves, rather than just the trophies in the end and who spammed the clicker when.Champd Up is also an issue for some similar reasons. How it works is that one person draws a character who is the "Champion of X" and another person draws what they think could beat that character in a fight without knowing the title. While there is an underdog bonus to compensate the second person, usually the first person ends up winning because the second person's drawing doesn't fit the theme- something they couldn't do anything about because they didn't know what it was. So, the first round just feels entirely based on whether or not the second person got lucky and drew something that fit the theme AND worked well against the first drawing. The second round feels a bit more interesting, with a secret second category thats revealed after the first voting where you can swap your character out for another, but usually the end result just winds up being the same as the first vote and that person wins out. Because of the way these are designed, it feels like most of the actual decision of who wins is based mostly on getting lucky with prompt compatibility, and it ends with the same issues as Talking Points.Quiplash is a bit better in this regard, because it doesn't feel like it's necessarily luck based- but the entire game's premise is based on "who's the most funny" where comedy is basically inherently subjective, so there's not really any way to do well there either and the end result also feels out of your hands.I haven't really played a lot of Blather Round, so I'll skip that and move onto Devil in the Details. Devil in the Details is a very controversial addition to Jackbox- people either love it or they hate it, and at least for me personally I hate it. The entire premise is really interesting and seems fun, with the players being a cast of demons living mortal life on the surface while trying to fulfill a quota of goals set by their overlords down below- it seems like a really fun idea for a high-stakes team cooperation game, but then you get to the individual competition part. Here, they advertise that family members can take on selfish tasks in order to get a lot of individual points while slightly hurting the team score, and whoever has the highest individual score wins the individual division. This seems fine and dandy, though it makes the game a lot more toxic, but then you realize that a lot of the selfish tasks require you to spend a lot of time doing them, and that stopping someone from doing a selfish task takes much less time by comparison- so if someone just so happens to get to you doing a selfish task early on, you fail it and get behind on points. Since stopping someone from doing a selfish task takes so little time, and it's also openly advertised that you're doing one to everyone else in the game, you have a very high chance of being entirely out of the running if you get stopped from doing selfish tasks- not helped by the fact that stopping someone from doing a selfish task gets you points, so I'm just kind of left wondering why anyone would go for selfish tasks in the first place, and makes me personally feel betrayed by the game encouraging you to do them on several occasions. It's genuinely frustrating and I don't like it.Overall, the games in Jackbox feel very poorly designed in ways that punish people for trying to win them, and that issue can deter anyone who has any interest in the competitive element, because the game makes it not really *feel* like a competitive game with a level of skill involved despite its insistence on making the games competitive. If you play these party games with winning in mind, you are not going to have fun, and unless you're someone who genuinely believes they can put any care about the end result of the competition at the door, you're going to feel burnt out by it very quickly.

_childDocuments_.review: tl;dr: Solid pack with only one total dud, worth it for sure and also a good starting pack with a lot of variety.Quiplash 3: Take Quiplash 2, remove the absolute mess that was The Last Lash, replace it with a much more entertaining final round, and make using safety quips actual sort of viable. Great game and a good start to the pack.The Devils and the Details: The dud. It's basically just Among Us tasks for 15 minutes with the tiniest bit of social deduction (which just boils down to "check the main screen to see if someone is doing a selfish task occasionally"). Try it once just to see the jokes, then move on.Champ'd Up: Drawing game with a cool twist of "first person gets the prompt, second person only gets the name and drawing of what the other person made". Not super dependent on drawing skills and has given a lot of good laughs to me and my friends.Talking Points: Give a presentation based on a user generated prompt. _childDocuments_.review: Quick overview over every game before I give my overall take on the pack itself:Quiplash 3 is, in my opinion, the best Quiplash that has been released as of July 2024. The biggest problem with the first two games (including the original and XL as one) is the final round: both games reveal all jokes at once, which hinders the presentation and makes the jokes less funny. This edition fixes that problem, and since Quiplash is a proven formula and popular party game already, its inclusion makes the pack a safe buy if you do not already have a pack with a Quiplash installment.Champ'd Up is among the best drawing games that Jackbox has released. It is somewhat similar to Tee K.O. in design, but is slightly different in concept, designing "champions" of certain categories rather than designing T-shirts. I won't go much further into it, but as someone that is not good at drawing whatsoever, I have had TONS of fun with this one and it may be my personal favorite Jackbox game period.Devils and the Details is an interesting game with a much different approach than anything Jackbox has done in the past, perhaps aside from Push the Button. I have heard everything from very positive to very negative opinions on the game. Personally, I'm somewhere in the middle, but have enjoyed playing it. It is definitely worth a few tries.Talking Points is among the best presentation games in the Jackbox series. While many are not comfortable with standing up in front of people, if you have a group of friends that know each other well or are willing to have an audience, this game will give some of the best and funniest memories in the whole series.Blather 'Round is very solid. It may take some time to understand for some players, but I find the game to be very underappreciated. Most of the other games in this party pack are very high-energy (which makes sense, because it is called a "party pack"). While that is not a criticism of those games, Blather 'Round is not a game that takes a lot of energy or effort and instead has a lot more of a general appeal. It is similar to Charades or Heads Up! in a sense, and although it isn't a "wild party" vibe, it is a very welcome addition in this pack.Possibly the best pack purely by value. None of these games feel like misses to me, and chances are, most people will REALLY like at least 3 out of the 5 games in this pack: it has a Quiplash adaptation, potentially the best of two kinds of games (drawing in Champ'd Up and presentation with Talking Points), an interesting idea in Devils and the Details, and a nice wind-down game in Blather 'Round.If you are a series veteran, I strongly recommend adding this to your collection solely for Talking Points and Champ'd Up. If you are new to the series, I think that this is one of the best packs to begin with (that and Party Pack 3, which is also critically acclaimed).

_childDocuments_.review: Hilarious installment that is worth it for just one game alone. I really like the Jackbox series. Just as Knowledge is Power, it is a party game with lots of fun, silly animations and a high replay value. Unlike Knowledge is Power however, Jackbox is a little bit more versatile. Instead of being bound to your PlayStation and your smartphone, you can now use your phone or your pc/laptop to connect to jackbox.tv, and play. The connection and overall stability of the game is also a lot better.There are many Party Packs for the Jackbox games. Each pack offers a set of minigames that you can complete with your company of friends or family. Most of them revolve around choosing the funniest answer, predict who might have answered a certain question in a certain way, or, in general, just who made the most ridiculous drawing. Throughout the mini games, players score points, the player with the most points wins. Easy and simple. Of all the Jackbox Party Packs, the seventh installment came as a very pleasant surprise. However, this is only because of one masterpiece of a minigame. To start off, you got Quiplash, a game in which you describe a word or situation with three words. These are then displayed beneath each other and two players fight for the most lolz and get the points.After this, you got Blather ‘Round, a pop culture guessing game. You just guess answers and try to guess which player might be right. Simple, a little boring but fun enough. Another very disappoint game is Talking Points. You get a series of pictures and need to comment on it. A little lazy in my opinion. Then you got The Devils and the Details, a game in which you need to do chores as fast as possible to earn points. Personally, I thought this one was a little chaotic, too complicated and overall, not that much fun.When reading this, one could question why I would even play or recommend this game, but then came Champ’d Up, the best game in this whole pack. In this game, you draw your own unique hero, name it, and let it battle against another player. You win the fight by receives the most upvotes from other players. This process repeats until a winner remains. The animations and art style of The Jackbox Party Pack 7 is colorful, jolly and silly. My biggest compliment here, is that all animations and slides within the games, are really fast, keeping the pace of the game at a very healthy levels.The silly sounds, the jolly music in the background, enhances the experience and lets you have a good time with the game. With the right company, I can get aches in my stomach from laughing and I think that The Jackbox Party Packs are the best party games out there by far.The Jackbox Party Pack 7 was great, but only because of one game. Champ’d Up was hilarious and I would startup this Pack any time to play it again.Definitely recommend this one.

_childDocuments_.review: (Edited after playing Blather 'Round)For context, I've played most (but not all) games from packs 3, 4, 5, 6, 7, 8, 9, and 10 as well as a little Drawful 2 and Fibbage XL with friends and family. I don't have all of those games on my Steam account, though. Anyways, time to review this pack. Keep in mind that this is all just my opinion.Champ'd Up - 9/10I've never been a super big fan of T.K.O. I think I'm in the minority there, though. Champ'd Up, however, in my opinion, is a big improvement (since my packs 4 and 6 reviews, I've played pack 10 and I honestly still like Champ'd Up more than both T.K.O. installations). It's creative and has well-thought-out mechanics. My main complaints with T.K.O. are that its pacing is a bit poor and it falls apart if you metagame. Champ'd Up not only solves both of those problems, but it adds new mechanics and ideas. Swapping out champions is smart, and the whole underdog idea is clever and funny. This might honestly take the cake for my favorite drawing game.Blather 'Round - 8/10Solid game. It's a very simple concept but it's well executed. There's a lot of fun strategy here, like giving the speaker words to use as hints instead of them being guesses, if that makes sense. It's a very simple and easy to learn game from my experience, but the more I play the more I enjoy it. Some prompts can be very difficult depending on your group and who knows about them, which weighs down this game a bit, but I still think it's a fun and engaging game.Devils and the Details- 6/10I think my opinion of this game has changed a lot from when I first played to now. At first, I really liked it, but the more I play, the more my opinion of it sours. I think the mechanics are cool and nice ideas in theory, but in practice, most of them are useless. Selfish tasks, for example, are really creative, but almost never worth it. They're too easy to cancel, and it's basically free points for the player who stops you. Of course, this is just from my experience, so take that with a grain of salt. The team tasks often don't give enough points to justify them, too, from my experience. It's alright as a game, and works well in both small and big groups, but the more I play, the more I feel like most of the cool and interesting mechanics don't mean much in practice.Quiplash 3 - 8/10I can't speak to the quality of any Quiplash games before 2, but I think this is an improvement for sure. Quiplash 2's main weakness is the final round. It isn't bad, per se, but it feels like it could be better in my opinion. Quiplash 3's addition of Thriplash as the final round is good and well executed, keeping the humor of earlier rounds and ending the game well. As for the visual changes, I personally like the animation style. It's nice, and the addition of motion sickness mode is cool, too. It still has the problems that all Quiplash games have in that it requires a lot of wit and humor, so if you aren't playing with funny people, it's really hard to be humorous. It takes a lot of effort to be funny here, at times. When it's funny, it's hilarious, though, but some people (including myself) struggle with coming up with funny things on the spot. It's a Jackbox classic, and the 3rd installation doesn't disapoint.Talking Points - 8/10This game is simple, but well-executed. It's funny and has a lot of room for creativity. It encourages spontaneity and doesn't require as much wit as Quiplash while still being hilarious. It's a great game and very well made. It is definitely an improvement over Patently Stupid. It's better than Junktopia, too, despite Junktopia being in pack 9. However, the voting system is what holds it back for me. In groups where no one metagames, it works fine, but if you're playing strategically, then it sort of falls apart. That's a minor complaint, of course, and most groups will do just fine with this. Overall, it's a nice game, though.Again, keep in mind that this is just my opinion and if you disagree, that's perfectly fine. Everyone has a right to enjoy or not enjoy certain games. Hopefully this review is helpful.

_childDocuments_.review: The Jackbox Party Pack 7 is the laugh-inducing lifeline your gatherings have been waiting for. It's a virtual circus of comedy, an assortment of mini-games that'll make your game nights unforgettable with side-splitting humor."Quiplash 3" is the game where your quick wit takes the stage. You'll craft the funniest responses to quirky prompts, and your friends will judge your comedic prowess. It's like stand-up comedy where the audience is the star, and it's a barrel of laughs."The Devils and the Details" puts your group in the shoes of a suburban family of devils. You'll be juggling chores and trying to maintain a low-key demon lifestyle, all while dealing with the absurdity of everyday life. It's like The Sims on a caffeine high, and the hilarity is endless."Champ'd Up" is the game of absurd artistry. You'll create larger-than-life champions and pit them against each other in epic battles. It's like a comic book convention where your imagination runs wild, and the results will have you giggling uncontrollably."Talking Points" is all about making up speeches on the spot, and you'll be given the most bizarre slides to accompany your oratory. It's like a PowerPoint presentation gone hilariously wrong, and you'll be amazed at your friends' public speaking skills—or lack thereof."Blather 'Round" is the ultimate guessing game where you'll be using limited words to describe elaborate phrases. It's like charades for wordsmiths, and you'll find out just how bizarre your explanations can get.As with previous packs, all you need is a smartphone or tablet to join the fun, making it inclusive for everyone. It's the ultimate level playing field where everyone can be a stand-up comedian, a suburban demon, an artist, an impromptu speaker, and a word wizard.The Jackbox Party Pack 7 will reveal just how creative and zany your friends can be, which can be both entertaining and a bit unnerving. You'll question your friendships, laugh till it hurts, and wonder if you've stumbled upon a group of comedic geniuses.So, if you're ready for a night of rapid-fire humor, domestic demon chaos, artistic battles, spontaneous speeches, and language riddles, The Jackbox Party Pack 7 is your ticket to comedic euphoria. Gather your crew, embrace the absurd, and get ready for an unforgettable evening of pure digital hilarity.

_childDocuments_.review: tl;dr: The games in The Jackbox Party Pack 7 are really good, and I highly recommend picking this up as your first Jackbox Party Pack.The Jackbox Party Pack 7 is a great pack of party games, and I have thoughts with each game. is my favorite game in this entire pack. A presentation game where you have to present impromptu, while another player assigns you text and image slides. Usually I don't vibe well with presenting in public, but I oddly find myself having fun presenting in this game. Especially considering how really in this game points don't really matter, what matters in this game is making the most insane, funny, and sometimes absurd presentations. Though I will say, it does bug me that this game does have a scoring system, and at the end you are asked to give out awards, which could heavily affect a player's score (such as if one player made an outstanding presentation, but never received any awards). There's also the Free Play mode, and I'm not sure if this was entirely done as an afterthought, none of the charm present in the original game is here, especially jarring without any music at all. Despite this, I really like Talking Points, and it is a go-to game if you getting Pack 7. is also a good time as well. It has taken me months to get warmed to this game, and as of now I do prefer this over my classic-favorite Quiplash 2. The art style, visual presentation, the final round Thrip-Lash where you get to put out three separate responses. Heck, most of the time we played this game, we never really listed three items and used it to add suspense to each response. I'd say Thrip-Lash is a better final round than whatever Quiplash 2 pulled out, but I feel that XL had a better final round overall. While Quiplash 3 is the same game as the other two before, I think it stands out just enough to be a great game to play. is a surprise to behold. You and up to five other players play a game of charades, only that you have to enter fill-in-the-blank statements and everyone has to guess what that prompt is. People say this is the weakest entry (more on that later), but I like Blather 'Round actually. The fun is that each guess will always have a text-to-speech voice replying, and what the presenter types out can be funny as heck. For instance, we had several users (me included) spamming the word "bread" to another player, tho in all fairness, it was supposedly to get things moving along as we were playing a modded Blather 'Round and wanted to get the custom prompts. Then there's the fact that there were instances where I immediately typed the answer in just seconds in and it just made for a very enjoyable experience. Besides that tho, you really need a group of people willing to comb their way into guessing each topic as quick as possible. Because if they aren't guessing well or the presenter creates vague responses, no one will be able to have fun. But I do like Blather 'Round. is a fun concept for a Jackbox game. You do the basic household tasks to get your devilish family working in a human society, but you can also unleash devilish tasks that if taken, you earn your own selfish points but also raise a bar that if raised too much will cause a family emergency. There's also challenge tasks that also give a lot of points, tho it's necessary to nab them as quickly as possible in order not to miss out on scoring points. This game is enjoyable to play, but I prefer (for the most part) to play Jackbox games on a browser, and I had issues completing tasks as a result because my browser cannot easily drag or rotate something that a phone could easily do. For instance, anything related to swiping or rotating is hands down the more annoying thing to do, but it gets used to once you figure out what to do. I do enjoy chaos too, with everyone talking over each other, tho it can be difficult for many and I'm sure that it is impossible to do teamwork tasks if everyone is unable to hear each other. Especially if they're muted. This game is really fun, I love the sitcom aspect and that theme song (nobody skips the intro please), but I think it's a game that asks more for what it's doing. But it's good for what it's worth.Honestly the game lineup here has been fantastic and outstanding...except for one. I'm not listing it for mental health sake, but just so you know, if I'm feeling a bit stressed or pressured to make something funny that fits a prompt and as a way to counter someone else, I'm not having fun, and I would love to not play a game that does this to me ever again. I can enjoy the Quiplash series because I know what I'm typing, but not with this one game. So besides this minor hiccup, I'd say this Pack is outstanding and if you want to host a Jackbox game night, please consider buying The Jackbox Party Pack 7.

After a round, people start typing in dirty words. Talking Points - just an insane business presentation where someone picks the images and you read or pick out the words. _childDocuments_.review: The Jackbox Party Pack 7 has to be one of the greatest and one of the most fun party packs in my opinion. Quiplash 2 was a pretty average sequel to the original Quiplash. However, I always feel like the sequel had lacked something special about it despite it always being fun to play with friends. Quiplash 3 had made Quiplash so much more fun and so unique about it such as the clay like style and the new 3rd round that had made it more enjoyable compared to all 8 answers being in one round that made it feel not enjoyable. This new round had made it feel more fun and in general a great game. Definitely the best Quiplash and one of the games that you should play with your friends as you can make a bunch of funny prompts to laugh at with everyone else.The Devils And The Details: A very unique concept for a game but I have some mixed feelings on this game. The point of this game is to present to other people including an assistant who chooses images to present in front of your friends. This game is such a funny and wild experience to play and it is honestly one of my favorite games to play as you can get a lot of laughs out of it. This is recommended to anyone who is either into improv or just willing to display a funny presentation and make your friends laugh. Talking Points: Freeplay is a very messy mode for this game and seems really rushed and unfinished but its so funny how you can just add whatever you want. In general though, this game is one of the best games for this party pack.Blather 'Round: The final game of this party pack. This game is basically charades. I do think this is a very underrated game and I think its decent. Although the prompts you get is a bit hard to guess and describing the thing itself has limitations, it can be fun to play if you are just chilling with your friends as it isn't too crazy of a game. I think one of the silly things about this game is the text to speech and how it can completely interrupts the host from talking. If you just want to play something that is calm and fun, then this game is for you.To conclude, this party pack has to be an excellent pack to play with your friends and laugh together. Although there are some nitpicks I do have on some games, its still a blast and is a great experience for everyone.

_childDocuments_.review: If you have the money, and love Jackbox, please buy this pack, behind (unpopular) Party Pack 8, this is the one I always find myself and my friends going to.QUIPLASH 3: As somebody who always hates it when party packs reuses old games, I LOVE QUIPLASH 3, the art style is 100% my favorite of the current 3 quiplashes.  But besides the artwork, usually jackbox will reuse there old games and change everything that made them fun to make them look like a "new game".  What I like about this is that it doesn't change to much, while the changes that were made make the game more fun, the thriplash addition was defo necessary and causes for more laughs!THE DEVILS AND THE DETAILS: By far my favorite game in this pack! This game has "episodes" you can play, and there are a ton, making the replayable of this game insane, where you can play this more than once and have a totally different experience.   Besides that, the sheer chaos it causes makes this something me and my friends go back to all the time.TALKING POINTS:  So much fun! The amount of BS that you have to make up ON THE SPOT can cause for so many laughs and actually makes me involved with what is going on.  I will say if you want to play jackbox with random strangers, for this pack this would be the game you should play.  The laughs come from what you say on the spot, in Quiplash and Champ'd up, its usually only fun with friends making jokes at each otherCHAMP'D UP: I'm never a fan of jackbox drawing games, I wont lie, and this is no exception.  For somebody who usually hates drawing games, this ranks 3rd out of all of them for me (behind Tee K.O and Drawful Animate) I have two major issues with this game which makes it not my favorite in this pack unlike other people.  1. I think this game is a little bit to much like Tee K.O, where you name and make character that "battles" against another where whoever gets the most votes wins, and personally I think Tee K.O. does this better.  2.  I hate how in the second round you can switch fighters in the middle of it after you can tell you are losing.  I've had multiple experiences where I am winning in the second round then a fighter gets switched out for something like a pe**s and it wins automatically even though its not on theme.  I think this game is overrated, HOWEVER, like I said I am not a drawing game person, so I would say when you buy this pack this is a game you should try, however, I don't think this is a game worth spending the $30 on solely to play that game alone.BLATHER ROUND:  Everybody universally agrees that this is the worst game in the pack, and its not even that bad which should tell you how good this pack is.  I think its a fun game, and a good concept, it makes up for the fact there is no trivia game in this pack for us trivia lovers like myself.  I just think when you play Blather Round, don't go in expecting as many laughs as you would get from the previous 4, sometimes the way words are formed can cause some laughs, however its just simply not as funny as the other 4, however I would say behind the Devil and the Details this is the 2nd most challenging game to win.CONCLUSION: I think this is a great pack, the only people I would say not to buy this are people who play jackbox for solely the trivia because you will get none of that here.  This is the pack you would 100% get the most laughs from with friends, even strangers, if you have the money, and want to buy a pack, I would recommend buying this oneRANKING OF GAMES:1. Devil and the Details2. Quiplash 33. Talking Points4. Champ'd Up5. Blather Round

_childDocuments_.review: A Party Pack full of Jackbox Goodness.Jackbox Party Pack 7 is the 7th entry in the Jackbox Party Pack series and currently at the time of this review is the one I've used the most during game sessions. Featuring 5 unique party games this easily has to be one of the best packs you could get as your first pack and with it being so recent you have a ton of polish and production valve given within each game that's it's just a enjoyable experience.The first game is Quiplash 3. The third entry in the very popular Quiplash series, where quirky prompts get responded by whatever you think is funny, crude, or both! This game has become the best game to warm up especially with a group who aren't familiar with Jackbox as it's simple to pick up and generally very fun. The major difference between the previous entry mainly boils down to new prompts, a very distinct claymation art style, and a new final round. Overall another great Quiplash entry.Next up is Devils and the Details, which is sort of a hybrid mix of both management and Wario Ware. Here all the players are in a family of Devils and have to complete human tasks together while at the same time competing to get the most points with the help of devilish tasks. I feel this game is best with larger groups as you have have a handful of people working together while someone else is secretly breaking the rules and then someone notices and calls them out. It's quite chaotic and might be confusing at first but the payoff is spectaular. Huge props to the sitcom theming, theme song, and character designs.Up next is the obligatory drawing game Champ'd Up! This game is quite similar to other head 2 head drawing games but with brawl-esque theme, having you design champions for a category. The catch is that your challengers get no context for your prompt and simply have to go off of their competitor, making the standoff being quite wild and hilarious. I personally love this game as it has caused the creation of a few designs I would later go and recycle for my own art. Overall, a fantastic drawing game and another game I often bring up to play.Now here comes Talking Points. This game is the embodiment of fears of presenting a presentation with absolutely no prep. As this game has you make a presentation with a randomly choosen prompt while a partner creates the slides from random images and it's up to you to make a convincing enough presentation. It's honestly a pretty good concept only if everyone's on the same page and willing to actually present cause I could see a lot of shy people not being too fond of this game. At least the trophy mechanic is quite entertaining.Lastly, there's Blather Round. While it's a simple guessing game, the use of making jargon/broken english sentences to make the people guess what your prompt is along with a TTS voice is just very fun. This game does have a lower player limit than the others I would agree on that as even with 4 players it's still a lot of fun trying to guess through the broken nonsense of words. Also love the theming and narrator for this game.Overall, Jackbox Party Pack 7 is a phenomenal bundle of games with each game having some sort of merit and appeal. I mean if Talking Points in my opinion is your worst of the of the bunch you've made a damn well Party Pack. Easily some of my favorites are in this pack and there's Quiplash 3 so it's very good starting place for those looking to get into the Party Pack Series.

_childDocuments_.review: For those of you not familiar with Jackbox, it's a fantastic set of games (that's streamable!) that are played using your phone or any browser capable device to drive what are essentially Gameshows. Of all the Jackbox Packs, the 7th is one of the strongest ones:- Quiplash and its sequels are always fun. The carnivalesque tune and swirling claymation vortex will haunt your dreams. It's competitive response where players face off 1v1 to give the best (read: worst) response to a prompt. Ending on a Thriplash (a 3-response prompt) makes for a fun an discrete ending.- Champ'd up is the drawing version of Superflight where you draw the Champion of X. Here we discovered that the Champion of THE PURGE is clearly "A GIRLSCOUT DEATH CULT"- Talking Points is an improv game where you hold a Ted Talk... and someone else drives your slides. Best served with alcohol, nothing like breaking your fear of public speaking but giving a completely improvised nonsense talk to your friends.- Blather Round is verbal charades meets Mad Libs. You're given a "thing" and you have to describe it prompt with fill in the blanks and pool of words. Phrases like "He is the Soft Big not Nice", "So much burning!" are used to describe pop culture and everyday objects. Gotta use your thinkin' meats to put yourself in the presenters brain, and try to see their angle as well as assess the clues.I'd say a a little pricey for $30 but I've more than gotten my moneys worth. 7 is definitely worth full price. No brainer at a discount.

_childDocuments_.review: Planes: Fire & Rescue (also known as Planes 2) is a 2014 American 3D computer-animated comedy-adventure film produced by Disneytoon Studios and released by Walt Disney Pictures.[4] It is a sequel to the 2013 film Planes, a spin-off of Pixar's Cars franchise. Dane Cook, Stacy Keach, Brad Garrett, Teri Hatcher, Danny Mann, and Cedric the Entertainer reprised their roles of the voices of Dusty Crophopper, Skipper, Chug, Dottie, Sparky, and Leadbottom, respectively. New cast members included Hal Holbrook, Julie Bowen, Ed Harris, Regina King, Wes Studi, Patrick Warburton, and Dale Dye. In this film, Dusty Crophopper is assigned to become a wildland firefighting plane, after he learns that his engine's gearbox is damaged.Planes: Fire & Rescue premiered at the El Capitan Theatre in Los Angeles on July 15, 2014 and was theatrically released on July 18, 2014 in the Disney Digital 3D and RealD 3D formats. The film received mixed reviews from critics, with many calling it an improvement over the predecesssor, and grossed $147 million worldwide on a $50 million budget.[2]Since winning the Wings Around the Globe race, Dusty Crophopper had a successful career as a racer. Unfortunately, his engine's gearbox becomes damaged because Dusty routinely operates the engine beyond its design limits. With that particular model of gearbox now out of production and none available anywhere, Dusty's mechanic Dottie fits a warning light to his control panel to ensure that he doesn't damage his gearbox any further.No longer able to race and faced with the possibility of returning to his old job as a crop-duster, Dusty goes on a defiant flight and tests his limits. In doing so, Dusty exceeds his limits and makes a forced landing at Propwash Junction airport, causing a fire. The residents put out the fire with some difficulty, but the accident leads government inspector Ryker to condemn the airport for inadequate firefighting personnel. Aggrieved at his carelessness, Dusty offers to undergo training to be certified as a firefighter to meet the necessary regulations to reopen the airport.To that end, Dusty travels to Piston Peak National Park, where he meets a fire and rescue crew under the command of a helicopter named Blade Ranger. The leader of an efficient unit, Blade is initially unimpressed by the small newcomer and Dusty's training proves to be a difficult challenge.Maru, the team's mechanic, replaces Dusty's original undercarriage with two pontoons fitted with retractable undercarriage wheels for his new role as a single engine air tanker firefighter. During training, Dusty learns that Blade was formerly an actor who played a police helicopter on the TV series CHoPs. Later, Dusty is devastated by a call from his friends at Propwash Junction, telling him that all attempts at finding a replacement gearbox have failed, and his racing career is officially over.Lightning in a thunderstorm over a forest near Piston Peak starts several spot fires which unite into a serious forest fire. The team fights it and seems to have extinguished it; but later, during the grand reopening of the park's lodge, visiting VIPs fly too low and create air eddies that blow embers about. This creates a larger fire, forcing the need to evacuate the lodge.A depressed Dusty's education in the midst of the large fire falters, much to Blade's frustration. Things come to a head when Dusty makes a forced landing in a river while trying to reload his tanks against orders and is swept through the rapids with Blade trying to extract him. Eventually, the pair make it to land, and Dusty confesses his physical disability. Blade advises Dusty not to give up. They shelter in an abandoned mine while the fire passes. The situation is complicated because Blade was gravely burned from protecting Dusty in the fire and is grounded for repairs. While Blade is recovering, Dusty learns from Maru that Blade's co-star Nick Lopez from CHoPs was killed during a stunt gone wrong on set that Blade was helpless to stop. Afterwards, he decided to become a firefighter to save lives for real.When the wildfire threatens the lodge, the national park's superintendent Cad Spinner selfishly diverts the entire water supply to the roof sprinklers to prevent the lodge from burning. This prevents the firefighters from making fire retardant for their firefighting duties. With only their pre-existing tank loads, the firefighters manage to help the evacuees escape the fire.Dusty is alerted that two elderly campers named Harvey and Winnie that he met earlier are trapped on a burning bridge deep in the fire zone. He races to the scene and pushes his engine to the maximum to climb vertically up a waterfall to refill his water tanks to drop water to save the campers, as the only other surface water nearby is the river in Augerin Canyon, too shallow, twisty, and rocky for him to scoop from. Simultaneously, Blade shows up and assists Harvey and Winnie by hooking up Winnie, preventing her from falling. Dusty successfully drops water and extinguishes the bridge fire, allowing the campers to escape just before the bridge collapses; but his gearbox fails completely, his engine stalls, and he crashes.Unconscious, Dusty is airlifted back to base where he wakes up five days later to find that park ranger Jammer is now in charge of the park, to much delight. Maru tells him that not only has his structure been fully repaired but he has built a superior, custom-refurbished gearbox for his engine that allows Dusty full performance once again. Impressed at Dusty's skill and heroism, Blade certifies him as a firefighter. Propwash Junction is reopened with Dusty assuming his duty as a firefighter, celebrated with an aerial show with his new colleagues from Piston Peak.During the mid-credits scene, the audience learns Cad Spinner has been demoted and reassigned to park ranger duty in Death Valley National Park.

Partially because the narrator reads out everything you write and we're immature buffoons at heart. Regardless, it's one we always make time to play. The only problem is it's limited to 6 people and it should really allow for 8-10. You'll quickly run out spots when playing with other couples.Champ'd Up is good but Tee-KO from another Jackbox game is more fun. We haven't tried it since the latest update -- I think they added some new features. There wasn't really enough to do and making terrible T-shirts is more entertaining in our group*Update* Devils in the Details - this one is very fun, it is tricky to play virtually because you have to talk over each other. Very chaotic and fun. The minigames feel much like the super simple Among Us style puzzles with required interaction between players. It's a weird game and we had a great time shouting over each other. Talking Points - we had a good time with this one but it has some flaws. _childDocuments_.review: The Jackbox Party Pack 7 is a pretty great pack and also came out at a time when pretty much everyone was stuck in a bad year but this pack definitely redeemed a lot of things and helped with the stay-at-home atmosphere of the time. This is also the pack I recommend people to start off with to get a feel for Jackbox along with Party Pack 3.Quiplash 3 of course expands Quiplash even further and is always a great time. Definitely one of my go-tos although I would've preferred more variety with the Final Round but it's still a solid addition to the series.Blather Round is another one of my go-tos even though I definitely have gotten too good at it. XD Would definitely be down for more Blather Round content for that reason. It's basically charades but in the form of constructing sentences for people to guess a variety of things. Definitely a quick one to do with people.Champ'd Up is one of my favorite drawing games and in many respects, I do actually prefer it over Tee K.O. which I do find a bit too involved at times but this a sharply-paced version of it where drawings face other to see what fits the prompt best and it is a lot of fun.The Devils and the Details is a co-op game in the vein of games like Overcooked matching that level of chaos but with a humorous family of devils theme that satirizes sitcoms. And players can also be selfish to try to get more points.Talking Points is a great presentation game that does make it mandatory for people to either be in the same room to vocally present or on VC. It's definitely a gem that makes fun of TED talks and is best with the right group of people. I have been in a couple games of it where only the streamer presents for everyone but imo, that misses the point entirely and is not nearly as fun. I'd rather just vote for people on their own merits when they are presenting themselves instead.So overall, this whole pack is a winner and honestly a great one to start with if you are new to Jackbox.

_childDocuments_.review: I've only played 3 Party Packs so far but this one is by far the most fun. Quiplash 3:Its Quiplash. Its always fun. The shouting match is always frantic and fun, and trying to come out on top is always a challenge. Shouting match games aren't always fun but the context this one gives is engaging. _childDocuments_.review: Quiplash 3 is more of the silly say-anything fill-in-the-blank favorite, with the "Thriplash" at the end replacing the previous system of everyone receiving the same prompt. I have a blast every time I play this.The Devils and the Details is a cooperative game where you are attempting to complete tasks while speaking over eachother to make sure enough gets done to hit a point total in the end. I did not like this game as much as some of the other co-op Jackbox games like Bomb Corp.Champed Up is similar to Tee KO, but I don't find it as fun as the latter.Talking Points is a great game if your friend group loves improv. You are given a topic to present on by your peers and another person controls what pictures are placed on your slides. It has tons of silly stock-photo-esque things to choose from.Blather Round is one of the most fun games in the pack, perhaps tied with Quiplash. It's sort of like a game of Password or Pictionary with pop-culture items, but the clue-giver is given a limited pre-determined set of words to get the idea across.All around, this is a fun pack that you are guaranteed to get hours of enjoyment out of.
_childDocuments_.name: The Jackbox Party Pack 7

_childDocuments_.review: Best one in the series so far. Newcomer Blather Round is a lot of fun, and kinda feels like playing 20 Questions, if the questions were terrible and unhelpful. You're given a code word that you have to describe using very vague clues, and you can use other players' guesses in future clues to help narrow them in.Devils in the Details is a fun little game where your players will form a family of devils just trying to get basic chores done to blend in, but you can also try to get away with selfish tasks to raise your individual score.Quiplash is fun as always, and though Talking Points feels a little flat with certain groups it's not bad. Biggest complaint is the lack of any trivia-esque games like Fibbage or the Murder Trivia series. Not the biggest dealbreaker but it is a little annoying to have to open up a separate game for anything in that genre.Overall, really good option if you've gotten any mileage at all out of the older games.

_childDocuments_.review: Like every other Jackbox pack I've played, this one is packed with fun, and I haven't even played all the games yet! Blather 'Round is my group's current favorite. Having the words for your clues in a list you have to choose from is not only challenging, it's great when you pick the perfect clue. Talking Points is a great concept, but a bit hit-or-miss; you need the right group and the right vibe for improv. Many people aren't comfortable making stuff up off the top of their heads. But when it works, it's amazing. Quiplash 3 is a classic; seeing the answers everyone comes up with is great, whether your group tends towards the raunchy, or the family-friendly, it's sometimes quite surprising which answers garner the most votes! The Devils and the Details is a great little minigame adventure, with the same awesome artwork of Monster Seeking Monster, but with more approachable gameplay. We haven't played Champ'd Up!, because we tend away from drawing games, but I'm sure it's just as good as the rest. Overall, a great pack. Get a group together and play.

_childDocuments_.review: Jackbox Party Pack 7 is perhaps one of my favorite Jackbox games to date due to one game included, Talking Points. Short review, this offers a lot of variety though it may be some people's favorite Party Pack. Quick review of each game:Talking Points: This is THE GAME of this release. This game will either slay your guests or kill the mood. Basically it's improv power points but believe me when I say it's more fun than it sounds. While Quiplash may bring reliable chuckles with witty answers, if your friends are on point it's like short bursts of stand up comedy. With my D&D group we were in stitches during the entire thing. It can be awkward when you decide to play with your in-laws on a Zoom call and their neighbor you haven't met jumped in to play though. Party matters.Quiplash 3: Quiplash, you know it by now. I think I may prefer Quiplash 2 to be honest, but Quiplash is a reliable staple of any party night.The Devil and the Details: This is your cooperative/competitive game. Kinda like Warioware but you need to talk with people at times so it leads to a cacophony of orders and requests. It's a good type of chaos though.Champ'd Up: Drawing game, didn't get to this one. Will update if I end up playing it.Blather' Round: Gonna be my chap of the pack. It's a guessing game where you're given something to describe with limited ways to describe it. Players then type in their answers. If you want trivia and puzzles sure, but honestly I started putting in joke answers just so the game's Speak & Spell to read it out loud to make people laugh.
_childDocuments_.name: The Jackbox Party Pack 7

_childDocuments_.review: Jackbox has a lot of great games throughout the many versions, and I believe that this one has the most good games.  The return of Quiplash is what made me buy this game in the first place, and I wasn't sure that the other games were gonna be any good. Let's just say I was wrong about that.The Party Pack 7 games are great. Along with the aforementioned Quiplash, games like Talking Points and Champ'd Up are so much fun playing with your friends, making strange speeches and drawing weird imagery. And while I personally am not a big fan of The Devils and the Details or Blather 'Round, I still enjoy playing them every once in a while. This game is of course meant to be played in person, but playing it over an app like Discord still works great. The art and graphics are much better than previous games as everything looks polished and well made, which is one of the best upgrades from previous titles.The only things I would do to improve this game would be to add Mad Verse City to this game, probably my favorite Jackbox game ever, but that will likely never happen. Overall, this game is really fun for parties and rainy afternoons alike, creating some of the funniest moments that video games can make.

_childDocuments_.review: What's better than a Jackbox game? Five of them!In this unique collection of online party games, players can compete against each other like never before. Featuring instant classics like Blather Round and Champ'd Up, the seventh installment in Jackbox's long-running series of packs brings a whole lot of laughs.
_childDocuments_.name: The Jackbox Party Pack 7

_childDocuments_.review: Jackbox delivers again on its seventh party pack. If the purpose of the games included is to create unique, hilarious scenarios, it succeeds. Through smart use of the smartphone, this product "shatters" the ice by helping each player feel like an important part of the group activity (the game).My group liked Quiplash and Champ'd Up the most, but I think the others still add value to the bundle. Each of the party games are innovative in their own ways. For example, Talking Points has a really interesting points system and The Devils and the Details does a great job of creating hilarious teamwork scenarios. Each game is different from the others, which is a good thing because their different play styles suit varying personalities and social scenarios. - Using Zoom's screen share feature is an easy way to set up online multiplayer. Line up participants' video feeds on the top edge of the screen, and modify the volume until they say it's at a good level. Then, you're ready to go. My group's favorite. Players submit answers to prompts which are put up against another answer. The rest of the players give points to the answer they find the best. EMOJIS WORK!Requires effort. Players work together in a family to complete tasks like clean the kitchen or drive to the orthodontist. Co-operative tasks require communication, and having to talk over other players creates chaos. For example, a task undertaken by two family members is to drive to the hardware store. One player holds the map but not the wheel, and the other player holds the wheel but can't see the map.Only game that involves drawing. In the first round you're given a championship title like "worst roommate". Players draw and name a figure that fits this description. In the second round you are shown a player's drawing from round 1 but not the name of the title. The figures clash in the third round and players decide which drawing should win the title.Players first think up ridiculous speech titles. Then, players take turns giving speeches that are controlled by their "assistant", another player. The assistant chooses which images go up on the board from a few options given to them. This game has a very innovative voting system.My group's least favorite. Unfortunately, compared to the high energy, creative game play of the other inclusions Blather 'Round felt lackluster. A player gets a person, place, object, or idea and has to put together sentences with vocabulary provided by the game. As other players guess, they have the opportunity to use guesses given in their sentences. Most of the fun in this came from typing weird stuff and having the computer read it out.

_childDocuments_.review: Beginning with its first release all the way back in 2014, Jackbox Games ditched the quirky gameshow aesthetic of You Don’t Know Jack and leaned into a more varied batch of party games for groups to enjoy with The Jackbox Party Pack.  The yearly drop of odd drawing challenges, snappy social endeavors, and occasional spatterings of Cookie Masterson have been solid for the most part, but Party Pack 6 was a series low that concerned me that Jackbox Games may have finally been running out of gas after being so consistent for 6 years.  But I’ll go ahead and break the ice here: I’m sorry for doubting you Jackbox Games.  I love 7.  Give me more of this every year.  Now let me explain:A familiar face starts us off.  The blueprint remains the same as players will answer two questions with either the most relevant or funniest remark they can think of and will face off against another player with the other contestants and audience voting on the best answer between two players.  A “threes”-based final round remains the only real change, but Quiplash has been consistent since its debut in 2015.  I will Quiplash is the lowest in the pack, but know this is a pretty high bar once we get to the others.Players take on the roles of a devilish family looking to meld into the daily routines of human life, while also trying to be the “bestest devil” by completing the most mundane tasks in a white picket fence suburbia game show.  Players will have to work together to complete challenge tasks (main tasks to help coordinate big events like getting ready for Prom or making a Folk-Rock family band) to finish the week’s checklist, but smaller tasks (like doing taxes, feeding the murderous cat played by the audience, or making breakfast) will help increase individual score as well as fill the Family Meter for the day.  Selfish tasks can net players more points at the expense of not helping the family, but too much selfishness can run a family emergency that hurts everyone.This game is a logistical nightmare as most tasks require a helping hand that players will need to communicate with each other to complete, but a majority of the time other players will be trying to do the same thing while the odd man out may be out being selfish which people can intervene if they aren’t already preoccupied.  With so much talking over one another and shenanigans happening off-center while also making sure you’re the best family you can be if only for a split second to check the list is chaos at its finest.  You’ll be mentally exhausted keeping up with everything, but the outcome of winning feels fantastic.  Devils and the Details usually feels good for one round before moving on for a breather, but it’s a dang hoot.Your obligatory drawing game is actually a banger this year.  I’m notoriously bad at Jackbox’s drawing games, so they don’t usually peak my interest because I don’t have the capabilities to even remotely play them well, even if the joke is to have terrible pictures.  But Champ’d Up gives each player a “champion” of something: has-beens, maxin' and relaxin', Florida.  Once your champion is made you’ll be given another player's champion, but not told what the drawing is the champion of.  Here you’ll create your “underdog” to hopefully sway the audience when the two drawings go against each other in penciled combat.Winning rounds in my groups has all revolved on the punchline instead of the consistency, and the extracurricular arguments and comments absolutely sell the feel of an underground fist fight between 2D amalgamations.  Add even more shenanigans with the later round Tag Teams and Champ’d Up stands tall as Jackbox’s best drawing game, and that was an opinion of multiple people I’ve played with, not just my janky-drawing self.A mental nightmare for introverts, but an absolute goldmine for the word-vomiters.  Talking Points is structured as a PowerPoint presentation for your friends and your only knowledge going in is the opening slide.  Players create three random, weird-as-can-be-thought ad-libs for others to choose for their talking point.  You have control of how fast your slides go, but a randomly assigned partner has the task of picking your transition slides as well as your picture slides.  You as the speaker need to keep your audience engaged as they see each slide for the first time, just like yourself.  The more engagement, the longer the talk, the better score, and your assistant receives an extra half of your total as a thank you bonus for not throwing you to the wolves.Trying to talk your way through situations can lead to some absolutely gut busters, especially watching someone explain how a clown with a balloon in front of an abandoned gas station coincides with how you escaped from a prison of flesh (a real task I had!).  The replayability of this game is near limitless and even people straight bombing has produced some of the best scores.  Talking Points is definitely my Game of the Pack here and one I’m always down for.Stir together a combo of Charades and Taboo with an unnecessarily funny text-to-speech module and you’ve got a recipe of success.  Players pick a word or phrase and instead of explaining it with your voice, you must use a bevy of descriptions to explain the word or phrase without actually saying it.Blather is the easiest to pick up and play and I feel this game will have the most longevity of the Pack as the game feels better with a smaller audience.  Having played this with a full 6 and a smaller 4, I like the smaller intimate parties as your choices play more to the audience and answers don’t get slapped correct immediately nearly as much.  There’s something enjoyable about racking your brain and really chewing on clues to eventually get the correct answer that’s worth the other times you feel like an idiot.  This game is easy to pop on for 30 minutes and enjoy it, much like Earwax does in Party Pack 2 or Guesspionage from Party Pack 3.I could not be happier seeing Jackbox Games back in prime fighting form with a masterfully composed set of games to enjoy with your friends, and I have renewed confidence in what future tidbits the team can make going forward.  Here’s to next year!

The trivia games are great fun.This is one of my favorite additions to the series so far, but one of the games...It's something to do with a household of demons or something like that? _childDocuments_.name: The Jackbox Party Pack 7

_childDocuments_.review: Best Party Pack since Party Pack 3.I love Jackbox games, and I own them all, but honestly, I felt that they had a dip in quality after Jackbox Party Pack 4. I feel like this revived the series. every game on here is extremely fun, rather than just having one or two good games.Since there's a bunch of games in this one, I'll go game by gameQuiplash 3: I mean it's quiplash. What's not to like about this game? The formula of ask a question, funny answer party games will always be fun, regardless of how innovative the game is, and while it may not be the most innovative game, it's certainly fun.9/10The Devil's in the Details: This one is a really fun game to play locally, which is a bit unfortunate given that the world is exploding right now, but if you can get a group together, it's a really fun task based game where you help each other out in this Co-op competitive game. Yelling at your family members and telling them to stop being selfish, then immediately doing a selfish thing is very fun. That being said, a lot of the tasks are a bit simple and the gameplay is a bit repetitive over time.8/10Champ'd Up: This is the kingpin of this pack. This is just better T-KO. All of the negative qualities of T-KO (Your good designs meaning nothing if they go up first, The length of time T-KO takes, the difficulty of complete open-ended creativity, random ways the tie-breakers were broken) were solved and became strengths. You don't have to beat every other player, but you just have to beat another player, and the "underdog" who doesn't know what the competition is, wins in the case of a tie. The game is shortened because you don't have tons of time to design a character, but you still have a good amount of time. There's also not dialogue in between every choice made, you just make the character and name it. In addition, one person gets the category the fighter is fighting in, and then the other person just gets the competition, and not the category. This doesn't give any advantage to one player, and makes it so it's not just open ended, try to be funny.TL;DR - This is one of the best Jackbox games they've made by improving upon one of the other best Jackbox games.10/10Talking Points - Ever been in a class where someone else made the entire presentation, and you were assigned to present it? Well this game somehow made that awkward and difficult situation into a hilarious game. Honestly, the most fun role to play in this is the assistant, just controlling what the next slides will say, and just compounding on the comedy the speaker is making.9/10Blather 'Round - This is the hardest game Jackbox has ever made. Trying to describe something with the extremely limited choices you have makes for basically a word version of charades, that works. It's vv difficult, but vv fun. It's hard to describe it without playing it, which I definitely recommend.8/10

_childDocuments_.review: What an amazing set of innovations for Jackbox!Several of the games adds customization for yourself, such as changing your character in quiplash, or your pointer in Talking Points.Quiplash 3 is one AMAZING build-up.  Not only is it more of the same amazing game, but it allows you to create your own set of prompts to publish, and discover.  Furthermore, the old concept of "Last Lash" is abandoned (thankfully) and replaced with thriplash... which is far better and more fun than "Last Lash"  Also, the character counter is a welcome addition.The Devil and the Details is also a really good game! An among us-esque minigame simulator that throws you into the chaos of working together with friends, and sabotaging the family.  It really is quite somethingChamp'd up is also kinda neat! Not for the theming, but for the drawing technologies added upon compared to the other games.  The undo button, the marker that doesnt overwrite the pencil, genius.  I would love to see this template reused in any future drawing games, or even retroactively added to some of the other games in other packs like drawful.Talking Points is pure GENIUS.  I only wished it was longer, but I still enjoy this a lot.  The idea of spouting some random junk improv is totally genius.  Improv acting classes everywhere have just gone out of businessBlather 'Round........ pass.  It's not fun.  There's no creativity at all, or any chaos, nothing fun.  It's like trivia, but more ambiguous, and it has you more angry at the game than yourself for not getting a question right.  Not cool man.
_childDocuments_.name: The Jackbox Party Pack 7

_childDocuments_.review: All five games are great, we all think. The only drawback is the tendency for Blather 'Round to suddenly quit in the middle of a game. We haven't been able to play a complete game of Blather in some weeks now. OTOH we are normally playing on Saturday evenings, when the load on the Jackbox servers is presumably very high.
_childDocuments_.name: The Jackbox Party Pack 7

_childDocuments_.review: I know that Jackbox Packs can be hit or miss, but I think this is the best one they made. Quiplash is still as fun as always, and it feels more refreshing with the new Final Round and artstyle. The Devils and the Details might be my new favorite Jackbox game. It's a Co-Op/Vs. type game that involves you doing simple tasks to basically survive human life, and the themeing and chaos makes this amazing. Champ'd Up is a really good drawing/voting game, kinda simular to Tee K.O, but the wildness of it makes it a great game, and a good replayable one too! Talking Points gave me the most laughs I've had in a while. Giving speeches with no prep time is super oddly enjoyable, and the shock factor ties it all together nicely. Blather 'Round falls kinda short compared to the other 4, but it's still a fun, kinda relaxing experence where answers fly and descriptions are vague. Overall, this might seem a bit high for most, but this is a 9.2/10 game for me. If the pacing for some of these games were upped a bit, and Blather 'Round was a bit more enjoyable, then it would be almost a perfect 10. If you need to relax from COVID, or just wanna have a good time, you can't go wrong at all with the Jackbox Party Pack 7. Also as a side note for the entire series I love that these games go on sale a bit, and once you own a Jackbox game, the rest are ~20% off! Sweet!
_childDocuments_.name: The Jackbox Party Pack 7

_childDocuments_.review: I can't really find anything bad to say about this pack. This is the first pack where every single game has been good or great.Quiplash is as good as ever, and though it doesn't feel all too different from previous outings, it still remains rock solid.Talking points is a laugh riot as we attempted to improv some sort of speech or pitch to the goofy stock image style slides our friends presented us with.Champ'd up is one of the best, (and quickest) drawing games they've created yet.Devils and the Details is a great co-op addition to the pack (a rare thing) that has us shouting at the trouble-makers while laughing at the ludicrous prompts.My favorite game is blather round. Trying to get across a point using limited references really scratches and itch I didn't know needed scratching.If you have friends, buy this game. If you don't have friends, make some so that you can enjoy this game, and then buy this game.
_childDocuments_.name: The Jackbox Party Pack 7

_childDocuments_.review: Welcome to the parade! Here's the festivities:Quiplash 3: Has a claymation style and a new final round where you have to guess 3 blank answers to a question. More of the same as previous Lashes.Blather 'Round: Players have to guess what your'e describing to them but you do a terrible job having them figure it out.Talking Points: How to make a non-coherent TED Talk with "help" from your assistant. This one is a personal favorite!Champ'd Up: Draw your best fighter....literally.Still need to play the Devil's In The Details. Will update when I get to it.Overall: A decent collection for this year. _childDocuments_.name: The Jackbox Party Pack 7

_childDocuments_.review: Each game has it's own charm and works well with 3+ players with only Blather Round being 2+ players.Talking points was the only have my group of friends had trouble getting into, but we still had a few laughs. If you have a talkative group who likes improv then you'll enjoy this one.Quiplash is what you expect but with some amazing claymation visuals and fun music. The ability to customize the promots makes it even more perfect for inside jokes to be incorporated into the gameplay.Blather Round is great. I've played this with 2 people and a full room and had so much fun with it every single time. The only complaint would be I wish there were options to add more than 2 rounds when there are fewer people.I've always had a fun time with drawing games in all Jackbox games and Champ'd Up is no different. Even the non-artistic people in my group were cracking up seeing their drawings go head to head against other players drawings.The Devil's in the Details is fun and engaging, but does take a while to get into it and used to the gameplay. _childDocuments_.name: The Jackbox Party Pack 7

_childDocuments_.review: Probably the highest-quality package of all of the Party Packs since the 4th one.  All of the games provided stand out in their own unique and fun ways:-Quiplash 3 is the usual Quiplash experience, which is always a good time.  Player-made prompts are pretty fun too!  The only thing is that having a single "final-round" game, Thrip-lash, is kinda strange.  Having all of the round types from Quiplash 2 would be nice.-Devil in the Details is really unique for a Jackbox game, but it's super fun and really well executed.  It's a really fun balance of having to talk over your friends to achieve all of the group's goals, while also staying back long enough to earn enough points for yourself to win the overall game.-Champ'd Up is the "art" game of the pack, but the premise is probably my favorite of all of those so far.  It's a simple premise that provides an incredible range of creativity and choice for each player, which some of the art games in the past don't always achieve.  The production values go above and beyond here as well, and they make drawing much more intens than it should be.-Talking Points is a ton of fun, encouraging snap-judgements in order to make your presentation shine.  I've had a ton of fun with this one, especially when me and the person running my slides can find some great synergy together.  I'd almost like to say this has helped me with giving presentations in college, but I also remember screaming about spaghetti at one point so maybe not?-Blather 'Round is a really clever spin on games like Catchphrase.  It's pretty simple, but the little additions like using player guesses for reference add a ton to the experience.Overall this pack is a ton of fun, and far and away the best value of any pack so far.  If you can only buy one Party Pack, make it this one.
_childDocuments_.name: The Jackbox Party Pack 7

_childDocuments_.review: Some of the best work from Jackbox. Quiplash 3 has a new final game that is much more satisfying than the previous versions. Also, Blather 'Round and Champ'd Up are refreshing versions of the trivia and draw game varieties we come to love from jackbox. That being said, every new party has a dud and for me, that dud is The Devils and the Details. It's simply too long and too convoluted to make for an enjoyable Jackbox game. Also, I've forgotten one of the most innovative game in this new pack: Talking Points. Lovers of Patently Stupid will be at home in this presentation-style improv game where the points don't seem to matter and the main goal is truly to just have fun with it. 8/10.

_childDocuments_.review: Excellent addition to the Jackbox lineup. You've got Quiplash which is always fun, Champ'd Up which is a hilarious drawing game that is bound to get lots of entertainment, even if none of your friends can draw well. Blather 'Round is probably what I end up playing the most, as you can play it at 2 players and it is quite fun with just that amount of players. Talking Points also ends up being pretty fun, even though it can get quite random with the prompts and images. It has become my favorite game of the bunchThe Devils in the Details is the only game I'm not really a fan of. It requires players to work together to perform simple tasks on their phone.

_childDocuments_.review: This one is one of my favorite packs, maybe even the best one. The games:- Quiplash 3: Still my overall favorite game, easy to pick up with lots of comedic potential. The new third round is interesting, but not neccessarily an improvement - but a refreshing alternative. Making your own themed matches or play the ones from other people online is also very interesting. 5/5- The Devils and the Details: By far the most boring game of the pack, if not of the entire series. The tasks are boring, the itneractions are meaningless, the goal of the game is also whatever. Maybe you like it as a team-building excercise, but it really stinks otherwise. 0/5- Champ’d Up: At least on par with my favorite drawing game T-K.O., if not better due to newer functions. The audience has meaningful interactions and the quips help a lot to avoid a spontaneous lack of ideas. 5/5- Talking Points: Basically powerpoint karaoke, somewhat similar to Patently Stupid, but different enough. Requires a little more time and attention by the players, but can reward them with a lot of fun. Points are quite arbitrary here, but whatev. 4/5- Blather 'Round: An interesting take on word guessing games like charades or Taboo. Easier to pick up than the other games in the pack aside of Quiplash and the pre-selectable sentences and voiced guesses by the players generate enough engagement by all sides for a few amusing rounds 4/5

_childDocuments_.review: This has to be the best Jackbox yet. There wasn't a single mini-game on here that I wouldn't try again. Please see below for my take on each mini-game.Quiplash 3: Standard Jackbox game, if you liked the other quiplashes, you'll like this.The Devils and the Details: My least favorite game in the pack. You have to collaborate with your friends to complete tasks, and work to accomplish a main goal, such as building a tree house. Tasks are given in the form of prompts that require multiple players to read things from their phone, and also single player tasks that you use gestures on your phone to accomplish. Players could also do tasks that were worth more points, but would sabotage progress. Overall, it never really felt like any single person was winning in this game, and if you tried to win by doing the higher point sabotage tasks, you'd still lose because the main task wouldn't get completed. Replay value seems good, as there is a decent selection of main tasks you can choose to have your party play. This was a decently fun game, and other groups may get more enjoyment from it than we did. Not one I'd play every time, but certainly not one I'd try once never play again.Champ’d Up: The group I play with usually HATES the drawing games, but we all enjoyed Champ’d Up very much. The premise is, each person gets a different prompt for a champion that they have to draw. Let's say you get "Champion of the USA"; you'd draw something that corresponds to that prompt. Next, on your phone you see a champion someone drew, and you have to draw a champion based on what you think their prompt was. After everyone is done drawing, the champions fight and you vote on who best fits the prompt (or however the people you play with like to vote). After that round is a couple more drawing rounds, and then a tag team round where you select from your fighters to fit a random prompt. The concept of the game felt very unique and fresh, and having the prompts really helped everyone's creativity to come up with unique champs.Talking Points: My favorite game out of the pack. It starts out by everyone getting a complete the sentence prompt, and then everyone gets assigned a completed prompt that they have to do a presentation on. The kicker is: someone else chooses the pictures that show up during your presentation. We had a lot of laughs about what pictures were chosen during each slideshow, and it was hilarious watching everyone come up with ridiculous ways to relate the pictures to their topic. I'm not sure how large the variety of pictures is, so that could affect the replayability of this game, much like it did with the later rounds of "Survive the Internet" from Jackbox 4.Blather 'Round: A guessing game, kind of like charades, where you pick a word that players have to guess. After you select your main word, you then have to complete sentences (usually resulting in broken caveman english) by selecting 1 or 2 words from a list that shows up on your phone. Players keep typing their guess, and hopefully things get narrowed down enough by your hints that somebody guesses the correct word. This game wasn't as comedic as other Jackbox mini-games, but still created the right amount of chaos that you expect and love about the Jackbox Party Packs

_childDocuments_.review: Here's a quick review for all the games here:Quiplash 3: It's Quiplash. Of course it's great. The Thrip Lash that makes you give three answers per prompt is a cool twist and has lead to some fun moments in my streams.Devils and the Details: Depending on who you play with this is either fun or insufferable. My recommendation is to play this with people you know instead of randos in your stream chat that way you can communicate effectively.Champ'd Up: The drawing game of the pack. If you played Bracketeering in PP4, it's that but with pictures. Talking Points: As soon as this was revealed I knew this would be the hidden gem of the pack. You and a randomly selected assistant have to improv an entire TED talk and if it wasn't for Quiplash, it would be the best game in this pack. We have yet to have a game that didn't make us laugh. Hoepfully Jackbox gives us a sequel to this.Blather 'Round: The weakest game in the pack in my opinion but it's still fun. My biggest problem is that there's nothing stopping the presenter from simply giving the answer so there's a bit of an honor system that has to be had with this.TLDRQuiplash 3 and Talking Points tie for best gameChamp'd Up is alrightDevils and the Details is love it or hate itBlather 'Round is weaksauce

_childDocuments_.review: Probably my favorite Party Pack for playing with friends. Quiplash 3, while the final round is a little worse, is the best visual in the series. Devil in the Details gets more fun as you play it which came as a shock to me because I'm not the biggest fan of some of the previous collaborative games from other Party Packs. Champ'd Up is TKO 2.0. If you are a fan of the drawing games this definitely goes up there as one of the best. Talking points is by far my favorite game in this Pack. Especially with friends. I love having to improv a speech not knowing what will show up. It's a mini game straight out of "Impractical Jokers". Blather Round is one of those short but sweet games and is perfect for just a casual round. I don't think there is a single minigame that I really hate in this pack. If you primarily play this game with friends, this is the perfect Pack for you.
