_childDocuments_.review: It's without a doubt that, in recent years, the once iconic and highly-respected mainstream series of Pokémon has gradually gotten worse over time as it's gameplay has been simplified in ways that appeals to a more broader audience without offering much for it's more seasoned and mature gamers, coupled with the sharp increase in a lack of quality assurance and the masses of bugs and glitches that have turned the series from a pioneer in the video game industry into just another 'has-been' title that's mainly played by casual gamers or those who primarily play what's 'popular' to play as it were.Given the desire to go back to Pokémon's roots then, it's no surprise that we eventually came to a point where a serious effort was made into actually replicating those fond experiences that Pokémon used to bring back when it was strictly a 2D game from it's origins on the ancient Game Boy all the way to a not-so-old Nintendo DS, hence the eventual release of what I would consider to be quite the ingenious inspiration in the form of Coromon, a game that was in the works since as far back as 2014 having taken approximately 8 years to fully release.Since no doubt immediate parallels will be drawn between this indie and the big franchise it is taking obvious inspiration from, before delving into the gameplay itself (since some of it's gameplay mechanics will be very similar to Pokémon whilst others are surprisingly different) it is best to showcase first what this game does similarly to it's famous counterpart followed by what it does differently to detach itself from Pokémon to form it's own unique identity.Starting off with the similarities, obviously monster collection is still a big part of this game as, alongside the natural aim of being the most powerful of them all for some players, the main focus of this game as a 'Duelist Researcher' is to capture and discover all 122 species of Coromon as well as face off against an evil force that gradually becomes more significant to the core story as the game progresses.Adding onto that is the important of type match-ups against various Coromon you fight in the game, as ignoring this in favour of using those you like and any moves that are 'cool' to use will likely result in some serious struggling in certain parts of the game depending on which Coromon you mainly use, hence the focus of diversifying your team as it's a key theme to the overall plot of the game alongside other expected aspects of the Pokémon games. (A 'hub' to heal your Coromon as well as to engage in online battles, stores to sell you various useful items, talking to NPCs for general chit-chat alongside the occasional useful items given away, either for free or when you complete a favour they ask for you to do etc)Now for what Coromon does differently, one of the things that stood out to me immediately was that, although Coromon has fewer types than in it's aforementioned counterpart with Coromon only having 7 types as opposed to even the 1st generation of Pokémon having a considerably larger pool of 15, this game diversifies the usual type gameplay by adding a further 6 that are exclusively tied to moves that Coromon can use, with each of the 7 types of Coromon (noting that each Coromon will only have a primary element as opposed to Pokémon's main and secondary types) having their own strengths and weaknesses against the 13 different types of moves which results in a strange alteration in type-match ups that is surprisingly welcoming for both simplifying the process for casual gamers whilst also introducing a new way of keeping track of types for more experienced players when keeping in mind the extra types for attacking moves.Another key difference is how the story plays out where the main narrative is concerned, seeing how each Pokemon game has largely followed the same plot of becoming the 'best trainer' of said region by means of defeating each of the 8 gym leaders in a set order followed by facing off against the Elite Four before a final face-off against the leading champion to end the game on, as Coromon does not have any 'gym leaders' of the sorts to fight against, rather this game's primary goal is to reunite each of the six Titans in an attempt to fend off this game's evil foes who, to keep it light on spoilers, are bringing forth a new 'element' of sorts that seeks to dominate all the others and become the only essence on the planet Valua.This funnily enough ties into the game in it's gameplay so to speak, which is a good point to touch upon as, although if you know Pokémon well enough this section may come off as redundant, Coromon's main gameplay cycle revolves around using the monsters you have captured and raised to fight off other wild or trained Coromon, either to battle them for XP/gold or to catch them with this game's version of those Pokéballs, that being 'spinners' that vary in quality and effectiveness depending on the situation at hand, as each level gained will increase a Coromon's stats as well as potentially evolving it into a stronger form with bigger boosts to said stats.Much of this and more is what made Pokémon an incredibly fun RPG for many players, both new to the genre and veterans, to come back to time and time again to enjoy for wildly different reasons but all, more or less, enjoying the simple to learn but VERY hard to master gameplay that was as deep and difficult as you wanted it to be.Such is what Coromon truly leans into as, rather than have the one set difficulty like most Pokémon games save for Black & White 2, Coromon truly allows it's players to customize just HOW hard the game can be as it can be as simple as having every battle heal any damaged Coromon to full and shops being at half-price on it's easiest difficulty to  the complete opposite whereby any Coromon that faint are permanently lost to the wild and are only able to catch ONE Coromon per area among other strict rules, all of that and more to offer something for every kind of player here!Speaking of which, another popular feature seen in Pokémon games is the incredibly rare 'shiny' versions that many a dedicated Pokémon player will spend MANY hours finding for just a chance of finding one, as Coromon brings about this feature in a somewhat unique way, having not just uncommon 'potent' versions at around a 1 in 35 chance or so of appearing but also the true bona fide 'Perfect' Coromon that have even more visually distinct colours than their Potent counterparts, approximately a 1 in 3,500 chance of appearing.Something to note though is how this ties into Coromon's other levelling system of 'Potential', a somewhat slower meter that, once filled, will allow the player to allocate 3 points at a time to any of their Coromon's specific stats, with those with a higher potential ('Potent' Coromon having at least a level of 17 Potent whilst 'Perfect' ones have the maximum of 21 Potent) having a higher statbase than their weaker counterparts which, although not quite enough to make a huge difference, still does have an impact where competitive gameplay is concerned, so no doubt it has it's drawbacks too where this game's online battles are concerned!And indeed, with how multiplayer has progressed over the decades, Coromon does come equipped with it's own online system that allows you to engage with other players to fight them with your own carefully-built team, albeit I had some difficulty with finding people to fight against at the time of this review, suggesting that the online scene isn't as active these days sadly.In conclusion, Coromon is a Pokémon-inspired game that pays homage to it's main source of influence in the best ways possible by taking what works so well and carefully putting it's own spin and alterations to keep the gameplay fresh so engaging for both newer and more experienced players and I would wholeheartedly recommend this to anyone who is looking for a new Pokémon-inspired game that lives up to it's name!

_childDocuments_.review: Basically Pokemon for PC, only much, MUCH better, Here is why you should go with this version over the tried and true classic: 1: The obvious plus side is it is on PC, which means a decent screen size, which is great for those of us older folk and just those with less than stellar vision or who just get migraines trying to make out images on a 3 inch screen any real length of time. 2: A much smarter story line. The story line is much more intelligent and well thought out. Coromon also has some tongue-in-cheek humor moments that is while still family friendly is aimed at a slightly older crowd. 3: you don't permanently loos skills. You can choose between battles which skills you want your Coromon to have, so unlike Pokemon when you gain more than 4 skills you have to start choosing which to kiss goodbye to forever (or pay an large amount or use a rare/hard to find item to regain a skill if you decide it was the better choice) , in Coromon you never lose those skills and can interchange as needed when not in a battle. 4: Customizable characters. Finally! You have the ability to change up your appearance, from skin color to outfit to glasses to the hat you are wearing. none of the 1 of two options nonsense here. You can finally have a character that doesn't embarrass you with how they are dressed wandering around.Also for the female model, none of that feet splayed far apart while keeping the knees together nonsense pose either. you stand and walk like a normal human.  Hurrah for equality that Pokemon is still struggling to understand in the year 2024. Now to be fully honest: Normally I don't care -scantily clad maiden warriors are a dime a dozen after all in many games- but with Pokemon it is so glaringly obviously meant to make them look incompetent and less than intelligent, it is aggravating not to mention that it is also pointed at young female gamers, many of which are struggling with their body image and sense of worth enough already. So, I am calling Pokemon out for it, yes. 5: finally one that may just be my own taste but I like the music in Coromon better. While the battle music is fairly similar, the background music to me is far less grating on the nerves when you have to listen to it for any real length of time. true you can always mute the music, but having something that doesn't drive you to do that in the first place is always a plus in my book. Summary: In short, this is Pokemon with all the major requests the fan base has made of the years and never got, and all those complaints never addressed finally someone listened to and resolved. I will take this game over Pokemon or Palworld any day.

_childDocuments_.review: Oh boy, Coromon was definitely an experienceEDIT: They fixed perfects, no longer is it rng to turn a 20<21, so ignore that nitpick plus flappy swurmy is changed to a different swurmy game that's much easier to complete hazaaaFirst off beautifully stunning game, gorgeous pixel art, very very polished graphics, of all Monster Collecting games this one has to be the most polished yet, not only that but it runs extremely smooth and doesn't require much to run...But that's where the good endsWhile this is a beautiful game overtime I noticed some small nitpicks or issues that begin to pile up over time, first off the difficulty, for the first and second titan they're an actual challenge, but the moment you hit the third and above things start rolling over, it seems like titans just aren't caught up to speed at all when it comes to the players party, sure they have an ability that gives them an "edge" but the edge doesn't really help at all, as you can just simply "over-level" to win which is a huge disappointment, I was hoping titans would at least be on-par with the players team but they aren't they have set levels so if you got free time you can essentially just over-level one mon and bam there you go challenge eliminatedNext up is monster designs, which some are pretty cool! I like quite a few of them but some have this awkward tendency to just.."Get bigger" and that's it which is disappointing, especially since some again become really cool! So it just sucks that some mons get dumbed down while others get a cool make-overNext upx2 is the story, bland, basic, I did not care for it whatsoever, I barely remember anyone outside of my mother lmao, you don't need a good story to have a good game, the corrupted mons were cool but we didn't even get to fight the villains who created them in the first place, wasted opportunityAnd finally the nitpicks and small issues that begin to pile up, such as lack of coverage for mons, weird unneeded side quests to push the player off the main story for...Whatever reason? Flappy swurmy's entire existence being shoved in the main story, 1/25 perfect chance in the lab forcing people to save scum, not being able to re-battle tamers for cash, the fact that you're forced to do small meaningless tasks like walk around for 1000 steps just to change your mon's spinner, the lack of mon families-44 is a large number I'll admit but it just feels like half of the game yeets everything back at you the second half so you barely run into any new actual monsters, the general lack of post-game outside of completing your "dex" and doing PVP there really isn't anything you can do which is disappointingNow I LOVE Coromon, if you are willing to let these slide and wait awhile I'm sure they'll come up with new content, fixes and the sort, the game's been delayed for 2 or so years now, so I believe they do deserve recognition and praise

_childDocuments_.review: Hi, I'm a casual monster taming gamer!Coromon is incredible! The sprite work is so pretty and animations are so smooth! The lovely environments and illustrated battle settings are so wonderful! I'm so impressed with the attention to detail all-around! Really great art direction in my opinion!Coromon offers character customization and cosmetics throughout your journey! So if you're big on customization (like I am), you'll really love that!Coromon also features 114 monsters to collect, including two additional 'shiny' variants of said Coromon called Potent and Perfect Coromon. Potent being the 'Uncommon' shiny and Perfect being the rare shiny. I really liked this because it really motivates the idea of collecting monsters in a fun way that offers more shiny variants, especially for more casual players who don't enjoy long grinding for the rare shinies. I really like how engaging the story in Coromon is with the player. Instead of your player being mute, your character actually converses with the Story NPCs, making it feel way more natural and fun. I really enjoyed this as it felt more like I was there VS playing a character. I really love the emotes that appear when conversing (that they also use for battle moves)! It makes it much more interesting to engage with NPCs both in story and in side quests. Side Quests are also awesome to see in a monster collecting game. I love it so much as I enjoy completing side quests before continuing story and the side quests just add onto that so well. It's not overwhelming either, it's just the right amount of quests to complete alongside story progression. I don't want to give too much away, as Coromon has and is so much more than what I expressed here. If you love monster collecting games, you will absolutely fall in love with this one.

_childDocuments_.review: This is a really solid creature collector game, similar to Pokemon. None of the Coromon feel particularly weak. There are some nice QoL changes like how you can level up Coromon that aren't in battles to allow you to grind one quickly. You can try new moves you unlock and quickly switch it out if you don't like it. Sometimes you'll fight multiple Coromon but the game will scale them down several levels so they don't feel overpowered. There's a lot of small but welcome changes from what you'd be used to in Pokemon.A big difference within the story is that instead of collecting badges by defeating gym leaders, you fight legendary Coromon. These are Coromon you cannot catch. They have about 10x the health similar leveled Coromon have but their attacks will be just the same. Most of them have some kind of gimmick as well that typically triggers when you get them to half HP to throw you off. If you have trouble, just abuse items on the stronger Coromon against that type legendary or grind. Don't worry, there's also XP boosters to grind faster.The world has some beautiful pixel art. A lot of the Coromon have some cool designs and the attack animations on the stronger attacks are really fun to watch too. If you're looking for a Pokemon-like game but don't have a Nintendo system, this is definitely for you. Even if you have a Nintendo system, I still think this is worth your time. _childDocuments_.review: I really don't have anything bad to say about Coromon, it's a decent game in itself and if you like monster collector games you will (most likely) like Coromon. The new system of being able to change your monster's "skins" on the potency system based on which ones you've collected so far is ingenious and I have nothing but praise for the idea. The game is pretty customizable both in character/monster appearances and team- there isn't really any WRONG ways to play the game. I'm always a fan of combat systems that break the mold of Pokelites, and Coromon's stamina system is appropriately punchy and easy to both pick up and enjoy. The OST is, while not bad, fairly lackluster. I don't remember any of the tracks after playing them nor did I find the majority of them to be particularly impactful. The Sound Design is... fine, but similarly nothing stands out. It's a good, decent game that is very worth the price you pay for it. Theft Mode is my favorite additional game mode of all time and it's what elevated this game to one of my favorites in the niche. There is nothing funnier than catching someone's monster and then releasing it in front of them.All in All, 8/10, Good game. Solid Game. A little forgettable among the heavy hitters in the genre coming out- said as someone who really likes this game. If you like monster tamers you WILL (probably) like Coromon.

_childDocuments_.review: Would I recommend Coromon to a Pokemon fan that is looking for a more in-depth Pokemon?  No.  But is Coromon an adequate clone?  Yes.  Coromon is basically the original Pokemon from Pokemon Red and Blue, with some improvements.  The basics of gameplay remain the same, certain Coromon types have advantages and weaknesses against other types; while Coromon has simplified the Pokemon types and added some new ones, if you're familiar with Pokemon types, you're largely familiar with Coromon types.  Beyond that, Coromon adds a "Stamina Point" system, basically powerful attacks eat up Stamina Points at a higher rate, and you can inflict status effects that will damage stamina points, such hazy or poison; this replaces the limited uses of the Pokemon system.  Al of the advancements in Cormon are solid changes, but none of them fix the central problem, nor the central lack of my interest, in Pokemon/Coromon combat. That said, there are some very helpful diffuculty settings in Coromon.  If you want to make things easier for your kids, you can.  If you want to make it so you can catch other trainer's Coromon, you can!  My biggest complaint is that none of this livens up the central combat sytem, nor the central premise of the game, namely collecting all of the Coromon.  So...here's my recommendation, if you want a game that is truly trying to do something new with the genre, try Cassette Beasts; it's a way more adult, way more interesting monster collection game.  If you just want Pokemon on PC, or Pokemon with a slightly different coat of paint, then Coromon is for you.

_childDocuments_.review: As someone who is a hard Pokemon fan I cannot recommend Coromon enough. You can cancel evolutions and get bonus' to the mons traits! There are Commons, Potents, and Perfect Coromon - a shiny system that not only has two variants but also actually has effects to the stats! There is even a Potency Increase machine that allows you to basically semi-shiny your Mons if they're high enough on that stat! You can change moves WHENEVER YOU WANT. They still allow for HM like things with Skill Flashes, but if you scroll to the bottom of your Coromons available moves it just shows you all the kind that are available! The game comes with essentially Nuzlocke difficulty settings and customizable difficulty that can be altered as people need! On top of all those pro's it's witty, it has side missions, the 'potency hunting' feels rewarding even as a grind, I  recognize the story where I'm used to the latest stories of Pokemon dragging and being somewhat slag. Overall I have the highest praise for this game. I'm currently 22 hours in and I'm just about to reach the second 'boss', I've been streaming this game and enjoying it a ton. Even for full price I'd recommend this game, but I suppose that depends on your money situation so look forward to a minor sale if you're on the fence! _childDocuments_.review: Another day, another Pokémon carbon-copy... but hey, it only makes sense when Nintendo refuses to let their favorite cash-cow out of sight. The demand for a PC-version is there, and SOMEBODY'S gonna fill it! So with that in mind, how does this one stack up? It's not the worst one I've played, honestly, and it captures the aesthetic of the older Pokémon-games well, along with providing a slightly more mature, if also rather nonsensical, story. So far so good.Thing is, this game has the same problem that a lot of these attempts to duplicate the Pokémon formula do - it's SHALLOW. Wherever the gameplay of Pokémon hasn't been copied directly, it's been simplified, dumbed down or otherwise made less interesting. Fewer types, fewer interactions, no type immunities, no dual-types, status-moves don't take types into consideration (sand-type takes less damage from electricity but can still be paralyzed just fine), no breeding or egg-moves, no natures...Now, credit where credit is due. They've added a neat system of 'Potential', which gives each critter two potential level of 'shininess' that doesn't just provide a palette-swap but also makes them stronger. Depending on the Potential of the 'mon, it'll gain extra stat-points as it levels up - with high-potential critters getting them faster and thus winding up with more of them by the time they hit the level-cap. These points can then be distributed as you please... which the perceptive might notice is just a simplified, more openly-displayed version of Pokémon's IV/EV system.Honestly, I was very close to giving this one a thumbs-up - yes, everything's been dumbed down compared to the real Pokémon-games, removing the underlying level of complexity that made those games a treat for adults as well as children, but that seems to happen with EVERY BLOODY GAME of this kind, so hey. However, a bigger flaw became apparent as I kept playing, and then confirmed by skimming the wiki: There is no end-game to speak of. Most of the available 'Coromon' reach their final evolution in their late 30's, early 40's at most - with the few that take longer being rather unimpressive and not worth the hassle. There are no Dragonite/Tyranitar/Salamence type 'Pseudo-Legendaries' that stand out noticeably over the rest of the cast in terms of strength, just like there are no actual Legendaries, no Mythicals... by the time you've finished the first dungeon, you'll have a team of level 30-something creatures who've reached their last evolution, and there's basically no reason to ever trade them in for anything else - especially since you can freely swap between every ability they've learned AND your entire stock of TM's whenever you like. Combined with the fact that the game only has 106 catchable 'mons, and it kind of feels like playing a Gen1 Pokémon-game where the last third of the Pokédex has been amputated. You even get to meet some awesome 'Legendary' types - the Titans - but they're purely boss-fights, and cannot be caught or obtained by any means.EDIT: Turns out, right at the end of the game, you DO get a chance to catch something the game CALLS 'Legendary Rarity' Coromon... but they're nothing more than slightly souped-up palette-swaps of mons you've been able to catch since the very start, so my point stands.So, yeah - can't recommend. It's got its moments, certainly, and for a Pokémon rip-off it's decent value for the money... but if you've ever played the real thing, you'll be hard pressed not to notice how many ways it comes up short.

_childDocuments_.review: EDIT: now that I beat the game, I regret to say that the ending is very underwhelming and anticlimactic. (I highly recommend Liquid Crystal, Glazed, and Gaia versions if you're interested.) It got me interested in checking out more legal, totally original Pokemon-esque games, and out of the few I've played, I like Coromon the most. It improves on some of the more finicky aspects of its forebears (you can choose move sets & EVs, change difficulty settings, status effects are more fair, and completing the "Pokedex" is far more equitable), while also making the world just as fun to explore. Some mechanics unique to this game are fun, too, like different sprays that can make Coromon easier to catch or increase the rarity; character customization; boss fights; a plot that has clearer and more dire implications; and its own sort of side-quests. Personally, I like the fact that the graphics resemble Mother 3 or Stardew Valley over the more traditional GBA era Pokemon graphics you might otherwise expect. However, the higher quality battle graphics can be kind of ugly and jarring, but that's just a nitpick. Overall a very fun experience!

_childDocuments_.review: Gamefreak, take notes! THIS is how you make a monster collector game! Coromon is undoubtedly one of the best games I have ever played, easily overshadowing all recent Pokemon games. It brings back the nostalgic feeling of when I first played Pokemon almost two decades ago, while also bringing actual challenge back to the genre. Coromon is one of many Pokemon clones that I have tried, but this one really gets almost everything right. I'm going to highlight some of the pros and cons I thought about while playing, as well as give a few suggestions for improvements in either an update or a (hopeful) sequel. Pros:- Incredibly customizable. From battles to catching to item management and more, you can really customize just about anything you want in this game, allowing you to make it as friendly or challenging as you like. I personally played through the game on the normal settings, not changing anything, to see how balanced the game felt as intended by the devs, and I have to say I think they did a pretty good job. Fights were tough, but not impossible. Strategy is very important, and while I did grind a tiny bit for levels, it was only to equalize my party to the enemies, and I never came close to feeling overpowered. - Tons of Quality of Life improvements. I say improvements as a comparison to Pokemon. There are SO many helpful QoL changes from Pokemon here that for some reason a multi-billion dollar company cannot be bothered to implement, but this game pretty much has everything you could ever want in it as far as ease of access and accessibility goes. Don't like your Coromon's trait? Change it! Don't love your current moves? Switch them around! Your Coromon died but got enough xp to evolve? It will evolve anyways! This game seriously does just about everything right. I cannot even begin to list everything here.- Reasonably interesting storyline. The story in this game certainly won't win any awards for incredible writing or plot twists, but it definitely did an effective job at keeping me engaged and interested. Certainly more interesting than the stories of 90% of other games I play. - Bopping Music. The music bops. - Not just a clone. I mentioned this is a Pokemon clone, and while yes, it is, it's also very much more. From the different Coromon types and matchups, to completely original designs and ideas, to a new Stamina system in battles, Coromon definitely differentiates itself from the competition. What I really liked was the balance it found between Pokemon-clone and unique game. It felt familiar enough to hop right in and play it similar to how I would a Pokemon game, but different enough that it was fun to learn the new mechanics and adjust my usual strategies accordingly.- Plenty of cool Coromon to catch! There are over 100 Coromon, each interesting and unique, and many with special traits or skills unique to them as well. I absolutely intend to play the game several more times, using different Coromon and strategies.- Some good puzzles and non-battle gameplay. There are some fun puzzles throughout the game like switches for doors, moving around walls, switching up cart paths, etc. that are not too tasking on the brain but still require a bit of thought and can be satisfying to solve.Cons:- My only major con for this game is the "mini-games" it forces upon you. Not to be confused with the puzzles, these reflex-based, timing-based abominations are incredibly aggravating. Specifically the spirit one. Unlike the puzzles, they do not require any complex thinking to figure out, and simply require you to act fast, which is not particularly easy due to the one other con I will mention, poor controls. These mini-games end up feeling incredibly tedious as you attempt them over and over again just so that you can continue with the actual game. There should REALLY be an option to skip them. With how customizable everything else in the game is, I'm almost surprised there isn't. - Not the greatest controls. This isn't a huge deal. Outside of the abysmal mini-games mentioned above, the awkward controls aren't really a big hindrance or issue, but they could definitely be improved. I think the game would play much better on a controller. That being said, they could be much worse, and being able to use either keyboard, mouse, or both is a nice touch.- Sudden ending. The story was cool but ended kind of abruptly. I would have liked a little more wrap-up on what exactly happened after you beat the final boss.Suggestions:- Show stat increase value on level up. I love that the game always shows you the stat improvements whenever a Coromon levels up, but it only shows the original value and the new value, not the actual number it's being increased by. This is obviously an incredibly small issue, but it would be nice to just see the numbers at a glance instead of having to go through each stat doing quick math to see what the value change is.- Unique Final boss music. The music in this game rocks, so I was pretty disappointed there was no unique final boss theme.- Balance the Dark Magic Coromon a bit if possible. I'm no expert on game balance, but the Dark Magic Coromon being resistant to literally everything is pretty annoying. Kind of defeats the purpose of type matchups and requires you to just try and brute force your way through. Maybe make them resistant to what they would normally be neutral to, and neutral to what they would normally be weak to?- Healing around events. Something Pokemon did that I liked was to heal your squad up before a big fight, or at least give you a chance to heal yourself before starting a fight. Some of the events in this game come out of nowhere and through you into battle and your squad might be already mostly dead and in no condition for a boss fight. Giving the player a chance to heal before starting these fights would be pretty nice I think.Verdict: 9/10 - An absolute blast of a game, only marred by its unskippable reflex-based mini-games. Why spend $60 on a company that doesn't care about its playerbase when you could pay 1/3 of that for an amazing game like this?

_childDocuments_.review: ★★★★☆For anyone who enjoyed the classic Pokémon games, Coromon delivers an enhanced and improved experience. The mechanics are familiar yet refined, bringing in new features while staying true to the old-school formula. It’s the perfect game for relaxing on the couch with a Steam Deck! ★★☆☆☆The storyline is decent but lacks a strong conclusion. It’s long enough to keep you playing but doesn’t stand out or feel particularly fulfilling in the end. ★★★☆☆The visuals are lovely, capturing the nostalgic pixel art style. While some monster designs could use a bit more flair, the skins are a nice touch and add variety. However, it lacks the kick of something fresh and innovative. ★★★☆☆The weather effects and environment-based puzzles bring a fun, nostalgic feel. The shiny system, though a classic feature from Pokémon, has a new twist here that makes it interesting. However, it’s still missing a fully immersive experience. ★★★★☆Playing on the Steam Deck while relaxing on the couch, especially during downtime, was a blast. Multiplayer battles with friends added a lot of fun, and farming skins, shinies, and milestones kept me engaged. Overall, a great experience for the 40 hours invested.Coromon is a fun, nostalgic trip for fans of classic monster-taming games, with some well-thought-out improvements. While it doesn’t revolutionize the genre, it offers a solid experience perfect for handheld play and casual enjoyment.

_childDocuments_.review: Coromon is a Monster Taming RPG with great design, lots of love put into it, and adorable creatures to capture. The game manages to make you feel like you are an 8-year-old rediscovering this on your Gameboy for the first time and before you ask, it is not a bootleg pokémon.Coromon is a refreshing take on the monster taming genre with the help of an easy system, adorable creatures to discover, excellent battles, and old-school 2D sprites that are making me feel nostalgic for when these games first appeared.First things first, there is finally a story to follow in such a game! While the bar really isn’t high and the story is quite hit or miss, this just proves anyone can actually input a storyline no matter how basic to these games.You are a young researcher for Lux Solis, an organization dedicated to the study of Coromons. Very quickly, your hero abilities kick in and despite being completely inexperienced you are tasked with quite literally a titanic task and set out to explore the Velua region.Gameplay-wise, Coromon offers a lot of replayability with various levels of difficulty that you can fully customize as you wish including some permadeath features. These customization named Nuzlocke allow the Coromon experience to be an on-demand thing adapted and customized by the player. On top of that, online PvP battles are available including a ranked mode, which can honestly be really fun.  You will get to catch Coromons with a fidget spinner and get to level them up through battles, in the wild, or against other tamers. Each Coromon comes in various forms, standard, potent and perfect, each affecting the stats and potential of the creature. The most perfectionist of us will know exactly what to do with that information should they want the best possible team.Sadly, while you can breeze through dungeons quite easily, you will encounter some boss fights that will be quite challenging and will require you to do some grinding due to them being absolutely overpowered. Graphically speaking, the design is simple and yet really well done. The use of 2D sprites in such a modern context is aesthetically pleasing and at no point did I feel like it took away from the game. As mentioned earlier, it is a good mix of modernism added into a game that will not fail at making you nostalgic.Furthermore, the level design is really good. The zones are extremely fun to explore, and quite different from one another. The puzzles and side quests offered are at times interesting, but can also quickly turn into a chore should you be lost in a dark cavern with an absurdly high amount of encounters. Coromon introduces some variety with environments that have an impact on how you navigate the map, like a desert burning your feet unless you find shade in time for instance. These mechanics, while unique to Coromon are sadly at times quite painful and add really little to the game.Finally, let’s address the  in the room, Coromon doesn’t hide from taking huge inspiration from Pokémon you can find a lot of references to it throughout your adventure. Though, Coromon stands out in the fact that it is a project made by fans for the fans, it is definitely a labor of love, made by developers that are proactive and taking the pulse of their community (a quick look at their Discord will show you that it is the case). It is definitely neither a bootleg of Pokémon or a cashgrab. If you are interested in the monster tamer genre, Coromon brings an interesting and refreshing take on it while making it feel both different and familiar enough.

_childDocuments_.review: This game is amazing - great artstyle, great evolution lines, good QoL changes that current pokemon still hasn't learned to implement - puzzles are fun and actually make you use your brain (I know, such a difficult concept for some of you).  The level up mechanic in Coromon where you can put stats where you want is a great change - no longer are you only limited to getting an increase in specific stats when you level up.   When you unlock "potential" you can put points wherever you want.  Want a special attacker that decimates everything it touches but as a result is a glass cannon?  Want to dump all the points into sp def and def to make a tank?  Go ahead, you are not limited - obviously some Coromon will do better than others, but the idea is you are not limited, you can do whatever you want, including respec your coromon if you don't like what you've done so far. I have seen people complaining and saying they are not going to buy because there is no speed up mechanic.  I say to you, good riddance.  We don't need people who just speed their way through the entire game to get their quick dopamine release then post on the forum or a review about how bad the game is because they fast forwarded their way through the entire game.  If you like Pokemon but dislike what it has become over the last 10 years, you will love Coromon.

_childDocuments_.review: TL; DR: A really, really fun monster taming JRPG. A familiar experience to classic pokemon with it's own flare that changes how you look at battles.The good: .The art in this game is amazing. The overworld looks clean and simple while still being vibrant. The coromon sprites are amazing with great designs (props to them for listening to the feedback of megalobyte during the demo days). .The battles are really fun. While it uses an SP/MP system like other monster taming jrpgs, it's far more plentiful about how much it gives you when recovering. This gives the battles a fun structure where a coromon can continually be in battle and still do something meaningful while at the same time still ebig somewhat restricted..The bosses offer a nice challenge, for the most part you can expect to have a decent chunk of your team be knocked out(even if they are easy enough to beat on your first time around). They also have fun abilities that help to seperate them all and prevent them from just being big creature with big stats.The bad: .Technical issues. While I believe it is fully fixed now, release day was full of clashes. This seems to have sorted itself out after that day as it has never crashed again for me after that day and there was a patch later that has fixed it. One continual issue i've had is that the game is that sometimes it would turn black and it would then come back just fine but now it continually switched between me using the gamepad and keyboard. .Movepools. While coromon have stats that match their designs great, the same can't be said for some of the movepools. Sometimes there will be mixed attackers that will only ever get good support in one of their attacks. Somethimes there will be pychical/special attackers that have movepools completely focused on the other type of attack..While a much smaller issue, the main vilains of this game rarely appear, making it feel like they're almost non existant during the story. And the mixed:.The potential system. It's a fantastic way to have your own version of shinies while changing the effectivness of each coromon in a similar way to EVs but it's not casual friendly. You can make it through the game just fine without any perfects but even if you're just going for potent team members they can take an annoying amount of time to hunt, often stopping the game in it's tracks ust to find one.Bonus stuff I can't really comment on:.Online, it's really nice for them to go out of their way to include an online mode, I've never used it though so I can't actually comment on how good it is sadly.

_childDocuments_.review: As a game clearly inspired by Pokemon, I'll start off with the positive differences.The SP system can be tedious at times, but the variety from being affected by certain attacks and statuses, as well as overcharging, keeps the battles entertaining.Your party earns experience even after fainting. Such a small change from Pokemon, but I would say it's objectively better than having to lose out on experience, especially since it saves me from an annoyance Pokemon has stuck with for decades.The Potential system is just so much easier than the cluster of IVs and EVs Pokemon have. Having a second experience bar to allocate points, or save them for later and use them at ANY time, is convenient."Shinies" being objectively better than other Coromon. With Pokemon, the alternate color palettes are completely useless, other than bragging rights. With Coromon, I was always excited when I encountered a generally more pleasing color palette and the "Potent" popped up, acting as a double incentive to add it to my party.The animated sprites. Pokemon Black/White had so much charm, and the animations were so impressive that they completely overshadow the 3D models used in current Pokemon games. After seeing the trailer for Coromon, I was immediately swayed by the animated sprites into purchasing it. Newer Pokemon games lack the ability to charm me, but most individual Coromon sprites are simply fun to look at, and make the adventure more enjoyable.The individual route music, while not particularly memorable, is pleasant enough.The different battle music is all catchy, with a unique matching feeling for when you're in a cave or against a Titan.The negative aspects of this game are also intertwined with some of the positive aspects.The way it's designed.Certain story events introduce unique Coromon, but you are not allowed to catch them. There is NO reason given. When trying to use an item to catch the Coromon, the game will simply state "You aren't allowed to do that here." After the first Titan fight, you immediately encounter a different type of Coromon which somehow resists every type. If you try to catch it, you will again be given the message "You aren't allowed to do that here." This ingrained the idea in my mind "I'm not allowed to catch these, so I shouldn't even try", but they did receive an entry in the Dex, so it can be reasonably assumed the player should treat them as unique boss fights to overcome rather than add them to your party. Much later on in the game, you encounter more of the mystery type, but for some reason you are now allowed to catch them. There is no reason given. It is simply poorly designed.To completely bar you from even attempting to catch is, at first, just a disappointment. The Titans are understandably stronger than any single party member you could add to your team, but having to use your entire team's strengths with statuses, debuffs, and a bit of luck end up making the Titan battles surprisingly enjoyable.The Dex entries have a pathetically small amount of information about the Coromon. Considering the main character is specifically part of an organization of SCIENTISTS, it was almost offensive to read an entry on something I had newly encountered but the only information available was "the two dog heads fight over who the goodest boy is."By far, the biggest disappointment is the writing. Everything is so generic, based on a generic fantasy plot. I was initially intrigued at the change of the main character having a prominent speaking role, in addition to being part of an actual scientific organization, could have potentially lead to interesting plot developments. That intrigue was replaced with annoyance as I realized the main character has no personality whatsoever apart from being a goody two-shoes hero. The most personality encountered is inspecting different items and having a random pun ready. Instead of having character personalities be shown through dialogue, they are instead shown through emojis. Emojis pop up over a character's head after they say something. This makes sense for Coromon, since they can't talk, but it seems like more of a crutch when it's used alongside human dialogue.The main antagonist group sometimes speaks in backwards sentences. When you read them backwards, they are generic bad guy phrases. I don't know why; a potentially interesting alien invasion coupled with having to slow down to read normal sentences does not make them compelling whatsoever and only serves as a nuisance when forced to turn what should be a normal sentence into a chore.The story ends on such a flat note. A simple boss battle that tries to seem more important than it actually is. It does make a decent attempt by having all the previous boss fights contribute and giving small, but important, buffs throughout. Unfortunately, I never felt as though they mattered. The final boss doesn't do anything drastically different from previous ones. There isn't even a different soundtrack for it. Afterwards, the main character is sleeping in bed and visited by an NPC that goes "wow wasn't that a fun adventure? wait til next time, we're going to SPACE!" It felt like slap in the face after such a lackluster ending.Overall, I enjoyed Coromon. But I cannot recommend it. The main reason I purchased Coromon is because I had lost interest in Pokemon over the years, but the animated sprites of Coromon were so charming and reminded me of Black/White, games that had an actual interesting plot which is nowhere to be found in Coromon. I would only recommend this to people like me who are bored with the lifeless 3D models Pokemon use nowadays.

_childDocuments_.review: Fantastic game. Launch-day hotfixes seem to have fixed every technical problem I've come across - had one crash before the hotfix, but the game's autosave function put me right back where I was anyway. Also, I've heard people talk about a launcher, but I haven't seen it. Seems like if there was a secondary launcher it was patched out almost instantly.Getting past the technical, yes, it is very similar to Pokemon, but there are some vital differences. The most important, in my opinion, is potency. Shiny-hunting in Pokemon is a headache, but Coromon's equivalent to "shinies" (Potent and Perfect Coromon) are much more rewarding to go after. There are basically two XP tracks, one that gives your Coromon an across-the-board boost when it levels up and one that lets you distribute points to make more deliberate builds. Potent and Perfect Coromon advance along the second track more quickly, making them easier to customize and more powerful on the whole.There are other differences from Pokemon, too. There are fewer types, and you can view type advantages during fights, making the actual combat a bit less daunting while putting more focus on party composition. It makes it both more accessible and more rewarding to put together a team that really works.Coromon is also hard. Not Shin Megami Tensei hard or anything, but I lose party members pretty consistently in trainer battles. If you're a nuzlocke enthusiast, you'll have a field day with this one, especially since it actually includes a nuzlocke mode. I've never done a nuzlocke run myself, but I know they're very popular with creature collector fans, so it's a nice gesture to include a mode that enforces nuzlocke rules.Overall, Coromon is a refinement of the creature collector. It's not "just" Pokemon, but it's also not entirely different. It's complex but also approachable, blending the best of Pokemon with new, clever elements that set it apart and make it its own beast entirely. Can't wait to see competitive play, nuzlockes, speedruns, etc.

_childDocuments_.review: 60.4h (78/80 achievements, finished the game) No. Yes (~64 achievement). Yes (~1 achievement). is a monster-taming game, similar to . It offers 124 monsters to collect, separated into 8 types.- Fast-paced gameplay- Customizable difficulty- Easier rate to catch "shiny" monsters- Grindy endgame content- Slow saving timeIntel Core i5-9300H 2.40GHz, 8GB RAM, NVIDIA GeForce GTX 1650 was displayed in top-down, pixelated visuals. Despite having simple-looking characters, the monsters look more varied, ranging from cute to cool. Combat is also displayed from a different angle than  games, giving a unique take on the visuals.The story is straightforward. It tries to follow the same route as  games where there is an antagonist group that is trying to do bad things, except that rather than focusing the story on you becoming a Pokémon master, 's story revolves around stopping the group from doing anything worse. The dialogues are lengthy, but you won't miss anything if you don't follow them.  is played just like : you choose a starter monster and use it to go on your journey. The difference is that you'll get a second monster after you choose your starter, and instead of gyms, you'll have Titans. There are 7 Titans based on each type that are spread around the world. Going to each location will be done on foot, triggering battles whenever you step on grasses outdoors or anywhere you walk indoors. Trainers will also be placed around the areas to test your strength and give you exp.Despite the similarities, some things make  different. The potential system is one example. Each monster has a potential value, separating them into normal, potent, and perfect. Monsters with higher potential will benefit from extra stat points and be distinguishable from their different color. It's similar to shiny, except that it will also have a stat boost. Finding potent monsters is easy. I found 10+ potent monsters in the wild without even doing anything. You also can increase the rate by using other items, which also work for perfects. This makes it easier to hunt for them, and the game really accommodates this by providing a different encyclopedia entry for normal, potent, and perfect monsters.Puzzles are also in the game. It is available in most areas, which are mostly related to the story. I didn't have any difficulties in finishing them, although it served as a good breather from the monster hunting. However, some of these require you to walk slowly, which can give you issues if you speed up the game speed too much.What I liked about this game is that you can speed up almost everything. You can speed up the text, battle animations, and even the game speed. The game is quite slow at 1x speed so this is a blessing. Again,  uses the same combat system as , albeit with different typings. Each monster is categorized into one of the eight available types, although other types that are exclusive to skills exist. To be honest, I had a hard time remembering the weaknesses and resistance, especially the non-standard ones since I couldn't map them in my head.You can only choose up to 4 skills to bring to battle, but you can change which skill to use whenever you are not in battle. This is very useful whenever you want to set up a strategy, especially for monsters that have a lot of typing coverage. Playing the game at a low level will also require more strategy on your end, which will make you swap the skills based on the enemy that you are about to face. The game itself is easy to beat if you are over-leveled, though, and you might be doing that without realizing it if you explore each area thoroughly.Aside from catching all normal, potent, and perfect monsters, there is a single content that will open after you beat the game: Battle Dome. It's like Battle Frontier where you have to beat an endless amount of enemies. To be honest, I hate these kinds of modes. However, I still found the content to be easy, provided that you have a team with decent type coverage. It'll get boring if you try to get everything that the place has to offer though since you need to repeat the whole thing several times in each difficulty - my mind went numb from doing it.I finished the game in 30.3h. I then tried to catch every monster for an achievement, which got me into ~40h mark. The rest of my playtime was spent in the Battle Dome to get all 3 stars from getting enough winning streaks from all modes.The game offers 4 preset difficulties with a customized one. I finished the game in the hardest difficulty and didn't find it too difficult as long as you are over-leveled, which I did without realizing it. The only issue I had is the hardest difficulty that is similar to , meaning that 1) you can only catch the first monster that you find and 2) your monster will leave the party if it faints. Both that and all other content (including Battle Dome) can be mitigated by save scumming. Despite having a lot of similarities with ,  still manages to stand up as its own game. I liked how you can speed up everything, and how each area is not too long to clear - it just makes it so addicting. I couldn't stop from exploring new areas and kept on wanting more. Moreover, the game seems to encourage you to catch them all by introducing items that can increase its encounters and different encyclopedia entries for normal, potent, and perfect monsters. The end game might be a grind and there might be not much room for competitive players, but it's still there if you want it. If you like monster-taming games, you can't go wrong with this one.

_childDocuments_.review: This game was my first experience with a monster taming game that isn't Pokemon, and it was just alright. For context, my favorite Pokemon game generation was 4. I think overall, there are some good mechanical and QOL improvements made here over Pokemon, but nothing groundbreaking and I found nothing that would make me want to replay this game over and over like I did Platinum & SoulSilver (and Red & Emerald, for that matter). I liked the puzzles (they are mostly movement puzzles/mazes). I liked that you can change traits (inherent abilities) and upgrade Potential (stat ceiling). I liked that HM equivalents are used by the player character, not locked to monsters and taking up a move spot. The environments were relatively varied and interesting. I liked the music overall (the synth-laden battle theme is a standout). The plot is original, although this does not necessarily mean it was a great story (basically it's a cautionary tale about the environment, but includes aliens and it's *their* environment that's been destroyed). Lastly, I liked that there was a reason to try to catch better versions of the same monsters beyond a cosmetic difference. On to dislikes: the names/appearances of monsters in this genre of games are very important IMO and even Pokemon does not nail this (especially after Gen. 4, thus my earlier comment). This game suffers from uninspired monster names (Mudma, Squidma, Arcta, Skuldra) and the corny name issue Pokemon exhibits throughout its history (Cubzero, Bittybolt, Acie/Deecie, Chonktoad). I didn't like how there were only 7 types (Fire, Ice, Water, Electric, Normal, Ghost and SAND) and no dual monsters were dual type. I especially didn't like that there are several more TYPES of moves that are not represented in monster typing (Poison, Foul, Heavy, Magic, Air, and CUT) when several of those could have easily been represented and many monsters were begging to have that typing but didn't. Overall, the type interactions made sense but were oversimplified due to the limited monster types. Water type is overvalued (especially in the early game), as it is the only type to be 2x effective against 2 actual monster types and 0.5 affected by those types (Fire and SAND). I'm stylizing SAND and CUT in caps because they deserve to be highlighted for being so dumb (how much of a leap would it have been to make it Earth type?). Ice type somehow resists the most types, so it wants to be defensive, but most ice types don't seem tailored to this role. You can't feed a monster a berry outside of battle. You can bake that berry into a cake and feed that cake to a monster, but this is not advertised or made clear at any point. You have to read a book in-game or stumble upon the "oven" you carry with you to find this out, but also why force the player to do this extra step? Frivolity. The player character is a "battle researcher", but it's never explained why this is a job in this universe, or what the ordinary battle researcher does (aside from stand in various fields and caves throughout the game to generate XP and money for you, the player character). You are, of course, the chosen one, so your role/goals are special and only you can save the world, but if the world didn't need saving, it kind of seems like your job would be to make animals fight each other basically so you can watch them do so. This makes for an even flimsier and less defensible idea than that in Pokemon, where battle is basically a sport. Finally, the most objectionable 3 aspects of the game are the move similarity (to Pokemon moves), the catering to "hardcore" players, and the low monster species count. I can count on 1 hand the moves in this game that are not a 1-to-1 copy of a move in Pokemon (to the point of copying damage and accuracy values). I was immediately turned off by this because if I wanted to play Pokemon, I'd play Pokemon. I want to see some originality in the fights, not just set entry hazard, increase stats, use high damage move, repeat. This was done, I believe, in service of the second issue - catering to "hardcore" players. This is immediately apparent when the game asks you "do you want to play this in Nuzlock mode?" right at the beginning. There are also sorts of unnecessary difficulty modifiers and ways to mix up the vanilla experience, and it seems resources were put towards these zany tryhard game mode modifiers instead of the base game, to its detriment. Release these later, or as mods for those who want this. Lastly, there are technically 114 monsters, but 8 of those are "evil" versions of others, so there are functionally 106 unique monsters designed for this game. That makes for an average of 15 monsters per type, which isn't so bad until you consider that almost every evolutionary line consists of 3 monsters. So there are basically 5 monsters per type, and if I had known that from the outside, I probably wouldn't have purchased this game. The aesthetics were there, and some improvements were made upon the familiar formula, but I think it is an overly simplistic, dev wish fulfillment rip-off of the games that defined many childhoods.
_childDocuments_.name: Coromon

_childDocuments_.review: I grew up in the 90's and the only Pokemon games I've ever really played were Gen1 and Gen2. I've always had an interest in playing a modern Pokemon game in my adulthood but modern Pokemon is way too large and complex for me to both get into and relate to the experiences I had with Pokemon while growing up. Coromon did an incredible job of taking me back to the OG Pokemon days but with the conveniences and QOL improvements of modern game design. The only negatives I would say are that the story's writing is abysmal and some of the Coromon are kinda lackluster but the same could be said about the original Pokemon (probably modern Pokemon too idk). Overall this is a great game and I highly recommend it if you want a SIMPLE yet highly enjoyable Mon-style game.
_childDocuments_.name: Coromon

_childDocuments_.review: It's a pretty good pokemon-adjacent game.Some nice quality of life features: HM move-equivalents are attached to the trainer, not the monsters (so you always have access, no need for HM slaves). You get the ability to teleport between towns quite early on. There are fruits you can grow in various locations on the map, but there's a drone that will both retrieve and re-plant them for you. You can access coromon storage from anywhere after you get a certain item. Relatively cheap to change the Trait of a coromon to any other Trait its species could have. The Exp Share type item(s) are acquired pretty early, and they don't reduce the experience gained by the coromon that actually battled. Some interesting wrinkles on the formula: all coromon are single-type, and some types *only* exist as moves, with no coromon of that type. Titans, the gym leader-equivalent, are (mostly) a single super-massive opponent rather than a team (combined with the fact that they're all single-type, the main effect is that it's a little easier to plan for each).The IV-equivalent, Potential, is easily visible (especially after you get a certain item relatively early game). Rather than IVs going directly to stats, it's a second experience bar. Every time it fills you get 3 points you get to distribute however you want, which is nice (and there's a way to reassign them for a cost). Shinies are based on Potential - higher potential forms have different colors. There's a Daily Achievements feature that's trying to encourage you to log in every day, which I find a little annoying for this kind of game, but honestly you can ignore it entirely and your progress in the game will still be perfectly fine.Competitive has some nice balancing features: level and Potential are set the same for all coromon in PvP, low-accuracy moves are all set to 100% accuracy with an adjustment to their power based on their original accuracy, moves with a % chance of inflicting a status effect instead become "every other" or "every third" or so on depending on the original %. I'm not super into PvP but what little I've played with it, I've liked so far.Overall it's good! Honestly you probably knew if you wanted this or not based on my very first sentence up there, but I hope this helps.
_childDocuments_.name: Coromon

_childDocuments_.review: This is basically "We have Pokemon at home" but instead of disappointment you are happy for the reminder and don't feel the immediate urge to spend 60$ on the newest Pokemon game and instead go home to play the built in nuzlocke challenges.I will say not every player will like it and its not some grand innovation in monster collector games but somehow it got me to sit and level a coromon to level 99 (almost did this two more) and spend several more hours shiny hunting. So they did something right to keep me play this long on what should have been a much shorter adventure.Also Pokemon should take not of the Nuzlock features for those who want a challenge and the game speed options. For someone who's attention span is shot the speed options made playing through battles so much better instead of having to bear through the slow motions of turn based battle.Alright devs I finished your game I am ready for my space adventure sequel and my perfect Eclyptor plush. I wanna see space themed coromons. Galaxy wolf, star dragons and a whole space themed typing would be fun to see.But I do request that you avoid the irritating platforming puzzles. Push puzzles, ice skating and lever pulling are enough.
_childDocuments_.name: Coromon

_childDocuments_.review: I've had a really hard time to decide whether to recommend this game or not. Ultimately I had fun playing the game, and with over 100 hours of gameplay, it'd be a shame if I hadn't.The problem I have with this game, is that it really fails to stand out and be its own thing. It's clear the game is trying to be similar to pokemon and that's fine. But the developers should really have spent some time to come up with some more unique aspects that it's doing better than pokemon.The combat mechanics are pretty much the exact same as pokemon - rock-paper-scissor turnbased. The graphics look nice, but the design of the monsters leave a lot to be desired. The storyline is child-friendly and nothing to write home about.There are some more things I feel the game should have dropped and went in its own direction instead of just doing a more boring version of what pokemon is doing:- Instead of pokeballs you have spinners. they are exactly like pokeballs but their design is, well meh- You get to chose between 3 coromon at the start, each one of their own type and probably the worst one that comes to mind:- Throughout the game you learn to remove obstacles, surf on water and other things, but instead of it being your monsters that learn those abilities, it's some kind of sci-fi hoverboard that teach you to cool technology like surfing or fishing. I mean sure, that's different from pokemon, but instead of it being your monsters that interact with your environment, it's now some sci-fi aspect that is completely disconnecting your monsters from the game when it doesn't come down to fighting, making your coromon feel like little more than trained warriors.Do you think you'll feel a close connection to the first coromon you caught? Well, too bad cause it probably wasn't a perfect coromon. If you want the BEST team, you need to scratch all your weak coromon and spend hours grinding for the perfect coromon that has cool colors.TL;DRUltimately I had fun playing nostalgic game, but I find it hard to imagine why I would ever recommend this game over what it's trying to mimic. I haven't touched a pokemon for 10 years, but if someone told me they really wanted to play a child-friendly game where they catch and train monsters, I would still tell them that the older and bigger franchise has coromon beaten.

_childDocuments_.review: [EDIT] I decided to change the rating to positve, given that my opinion was more of a neutral one, and also due to the fact that the game is still being improved with new patches coming on monthly basis. Initial opinion follows:The first impression was very positive: nice looking graphic, great music, and some basic ideas taken from *MON series. Unfortunately the further you are in, the more of a slog the game becomes. Exploration becoms boring as most of the things you find are cakes (no fun equipment for our pupils similar to *MON series). Story is lacking any meaning or memorable characters that would get you hooked in. Dungeons are tedious and unnecessarily long - which I think even developers noticed by introducing checkpoint system. My last big complaint would be menus - UI in general - and controls. The menus are clunky, for example accessing Save option from the menu requires 6 button presses. I prefer to play games on a gamepad but the game was definetly designed for touchscreen in mind, as some of the tooltips are not accessible through gamepad controls but are accessible instead if you click them with a mouse (therefore simulating a touch event), not mentioning that big Cross button that can close the menu in the upper corner.

_childDocuments_.review: Recommended for you to buy if you like pokemon games. _childDocuments_.name: Coromon

_childDocuments_.review: Edit: Saves are uploaded to the cloud on the developer's side. Transferred over to another PC just fine.Literally just pokemon on PC but with various QOL additions and some slightly deeper RPG elements. If you like that, go ahead and grab it. If you don't and wanted something different out of an RPG that isn't just Pokemon again, well look elsewhere. You've got a lot of detailed pixel art and a ton of poke- I mean coromon to mess around with. There's genuine effort here and it wears its inspiration on its sleeve. Whether or not that's a good idea to just copy a game formula that itself has copied itself for almost 30 years, well that's another debate. At least it's not locked to a Nintendo platform or an emulator to play it. You can play it right here on Steam or even mobile. Mobile version I believe has microtransactions, so far I haven't seen any for the Steam version.Otherwise I'm curious how they'll handle cross play (if they do) between the PC and mobile versions in addition to future content. TemTem is advertised a pokemon MMO on Steam but this is more of a single player experience so I wonder if this is going to be a one and done kind of thing or if there will be expansions/dlc to keep players coming back. I haven't had any launcher issues that were purported by other players, in-fact I don't think my saves are going to any sort of cloud despite showing icons for it every time I save. No Steam cloud either and I can't seem to find my save folder to back it up. A bit frustrating for a game that might have hundreds of hours of progress put into a single save file... One crash so far, game has an autosave so thank god for that but you should save whenever you can.We have a curator page if you're interested in checking out more titles:Thanks for reading.
_childDocuments_.name: Coromon

_childDocuments_.review: I'm pretty well into the game now and have been loving it. I'm a long time Pokemon fan (gen wunner) who has become a bit disenchanted with the current crop of games, but this game scratches that itch!I love the difficulty options and built-in Nuzlocke options, so you can really tune your play-through regardless of your experience level. The "dungeons" and Titan fights also have a really great feel difficulty-wise. Difficulty is something Pokemon tends to fail at, so it's nice to have a monster taming game that feels challenging enough to make the whole experience worthwhile.I love the Potency system! Great job taking the obnoxious EV/IV system from Pokemon and turning it into something I actually enjoy engaging with. I also like that the "shininess" of a Mon is tied to it. I've played competitively with Pokemon, but still felt that the whole system of tuning and re-stating was a convoluted mess. The soft-reset and hard-reset options are great!I have a few gripes though that I hope the Devs may take a pass at when they can. I really like to sort my Mon's skills manually, so the fact I can't do that seems like a really odd decision or oversight. Even R/B/Y let you do that.Another issue is that the Coromon PC is pretty bare bones and it would be nice to see that get some of the features in the newer Pokemon games (box organization, move, tag/marking). Overall though, I'm very pleased and look forward to more updates and hopefully expansions. I'd also love to see some of the "Skill only" types become fully fledged types. It seems like it's hinted at in game, so that is nice at least.
_childDocuments_.name: Coromon

_childDocuments_.review: Coromon. It plays like your classic pokemon game which is good for players that are looking for something like. The monsters and pixel art are really good. The side-quests adds a bit of activity and life and that's nice.There's a lot of convenient features such as being able to change a Coromon's trait, the moves they learn are permanent so you just need to pick and choose the 4 you want to use. Change your characters appearance or your coromon's spinners and so on.Now for the bad. The story/game is very short and roster is even smaller than pokemon's base game with some duplicate mons in the form of the dark magic typing that can't even be used competitively. So if you take those out you are at about 106 mons and you'll encounter the entire evolutionary line without even needing to evolve to discover them through your gameplay which kills the magic of discovering coromon through evolution alone.End game is also non-existent. The ending of coromon feels like a rush job and tells that the game was released in a incomplete state.Another issue I have is having a coromons stats gated through their shiny forms which still feels very grindy for me despite the conveniences that were put in place. But if you don't mind these issues then go ahead and buy the game.

_childDocuments_.review:
Coromon is a modern monster taming game with retro pixelart. Coromon brings an immersive storyline, strategic turn-based combat and challenging puzzles to a classic genre.

Use powerful moves to take down your opponent's Squad. Use your skills to poison, stun or damage your opponent with an arsenal of available skills.

In the region of Velua where Humans and Coromon live in harmony, a shady organization is on the verge of releasing a dark power upon the world. Will they succeed in their evil plans, or can they still be stopped?

Step into the role of a young hero joining the technologically advanced organisation of Lux Solis. Gather your favorite Coromon to create a powerful squad. Together with your Coromon, you'll have to train, fight and puzzle your way through an adventure-filled world!
