_childDocuments_.review: Tries to be one part platformer and one part Souls-like but didn't manage to create satisfying gameplay of either of these genres for me.Primarily, this game is a platformer and it controls well with a fun dash move and an eventually learned double jump that helps stabilize your character + give you more opportunities to do long ranged and tricky maneuvers. But the game rarely offers interesting platforming sequences and is full of slow, tedious platforms that mosey their way over death pits where you don't have many ways of showing off your skills, and what's worse is the game loves dotting platforming obstacles with unnecessary floating enemies that add discordant shockwave attacks nudging you into its awkward combat which mostly involves dashing into something's face, getting in 1-2 attacks, and dashing away, and HOPING you don't fall into any one of the millions of death pits enemies are contractually obligated to float over (This also applies to half the bosses in the game for some reason too, and it never stops feeling clunky to me even though I didn't find the combat to be difficult.)I think the game doesn't do a great job monopolizing on its own ideas or bringing things to a greater potential. A good example of this is in an early dungeon, you activate these slow moving statues to get them to stand on buttons needed to progress. This is an idea taken right out of Zelda: Wind Waker (where the game mirrors a lot of its visual design from) but the problem is this mechanic never gets any interesting use. The button that needs to be pressed by the statue is always only a few feet away and there's just... no obstacle? No puzzle? I don't understand the reason for even including this in the game, it never gets more complicated, and no I'm not boiling it down or oversimplifying it, they really are: Move statue 5 feet to the left. That's it. And I feel lots of obstacles in this game feel like this: A concept that's not utilized well at all almost as if you're completing the opening chamber from Portal over and over again where the game is just explaining the concept of putting blocks on buttons to you.But on the reverse end, the only real hint of challenge the game offers comes from mostly optional obstacle course rooms entered via shrines littered around the world. These can be a nice change of pace simply due to being focused platforming sections (which the rest of the game is ironically lacking in) but they're either far too easy or brutally punishing in a very un-fun way (and there's no in between) And by punishing, I mean in that way of making things fake-hard where no individual obstacle is a challenge but you have to do 10 or so simple/medium obstacles in a row and if you mess up even one, you go all the way to the start again. It's lazy and frustrating and a shame that this is the only time the game even attempts being challenging. And what's worse is the first platforming shrine you encounter HAS checkpoint platforms in it, but they never use these again for reasons I simply don't know. it's as if they forgot they even existed when this could've made later "difficult" shrines actually fair and perhaps even fun. Oriane's Saw was the most notable offender to me.Blue Fire has a major padding issue in its second half. The game attempts to double up on itself where the final chapters of content almost all require you to do a tremendous amount of backtracking throughout effectively the entire game. One chapter you're tasked with finding four gate entrances that stem from old content areas that you likely came across before, but couldn't interact with because you didn't have a late game MacGuffin. And another chapter has you return to almost every major area in the game and collect scattered orbs that simply make you replay the level cause they're not placed in interesting or hidden locations for the most part, they're almost all on the main pathways that you already traversed the first time you entered the area. Imagine if the second half of a Mario game had you return to World 1-1 and simply play the level again but you HAD to collect all the coins, and then multiply this for about half the rest of the game. It's just not fun. I wouldn't be complaining about this if it was something you could've done the first time you entered any of these zones, in fact, that would've added some zest to the kind of bland straightforward sections and possibly even give the game a less linear nature, which could improve its overall flow and replayability.And when you complete these backtracking chapters, the game launches into its final boss. This surprised me since the game is mostly a platformer, I was hoping for a large difficult finale feeling platforming dungeon before the climactic boss fight and felt pretty disappointed since I felt like I hardly did anything new in the last couple hours of gameplay and the game was becoming a bit of a boss rush in its final hours, sadly highlighting its wonky combat even more.The final boss IS fantastic though. The visuals, music, and attack designs are astonishing and the game ends on a high note for sure. I'm glad this boss didn't float over a death pit the whole time lol. I wish the rest of the combat could've been this fun and well-designed... I'd unfortunately go as far as saying it was the only boss fight I enjoyed.Blue Fire's visuals are sensational and I think this is where most of this game's praise is garnered from. The main character is cute and cool with tons of instantly lovable cosmetics and emotes to collect and all the environments could've been lifted directly from Wind Waker with a colder tone. I was immediately impressed from the title screen alone. Unfortunately the gameplay constantly feels like it's in an unfinished Alpha stage, as if they planned out the game but didn't really finish it or polish it up.And despite how long this review already is, I'm glossing over several things throughout the game I also felt were not well-handled, such as its broken (and kind of pointless feeling) economy, long distance between and awkward placement of NPCs you can sell items to, dialogue boxes that have its text blend into the brighter parts of the environments, an abundance of boring fetch/backtracking sidequests, annoying level traversal before you get double jump, an underwhelming plot with a rather abrupt ending, an inability to warp between zones until the late game furthering the padding problem, ALL the weapons in the game are identical in gameplay making me wonder why you don't just get permanent damage increases instead...With better level, obstacle, and world design, this game could've been pretty great, but as it stands, almost every element of the game beyond its visuals and the feel of controlling the main character are lacking in quality.
_childDocuments_.name: Blue Fire

_childDocuments_.review: This game is an absolute masterpiece in many ways!The noticeable inspirations seem to be Hollow Knight, A Hat in Time and Wind Waker, but they combined it all in such a masterful way! They took it and absolutely OWNED it!Music? Gorgeous! Movement? Fantastic! Exploration? Rewarding! World? Memorable!However, with many amazing things often come some things that are lacking.There is no map - In many games I wouldn't even notice, but a game that is so critical with backtracking due to new skills and items you earn along the way should have a way to pinpoint locations you have been to. Maybe doors you have forgotten to open or elevators that haven't been used.Ores - I like the system a lot where there is 1 major currency used for many different things. You seen it in Dark Souls, Hollow Knight and Nioh for example. The part where it bothers me is the crystal ores they have. It works in a similar way to Dark Souls' compact Souls you can find around the world and get from bosses. There is just 1 major flaw with this. There is only 1 person you can sell these to. At the start of the game this wasn't that much of a problem, but later on there are places where you can buy stuff, which of course is no where near the Wizard that buys them. If only there was a way to pop them like the Souls in DS this wouldn't be as much of an issue, but the walking back and forth does wear thin.Combat - Combat is very simple, which to me isn't the problem. In many games I just use 1 attack anyhow. What I want to bring up however is that not all hits connect like they should and that hits have such a push back on some enemies you can't even combo them if you wanted to. This over time started to really pull my nerves, especially with airborne enemies above pits for example.Overall I do really recommend this game. It is challenging and beautiful!The devs have already been really amazing with terminating most bugs from what I heard from community members and I totally believe they will get rid of the one I shared here as well!I'll be continuing the game soon and will edit the review if needed, but these are my thoughts so far.I hope you have a nice day! :)Edit: I removed the part about the bugs as it seems they patched it.Today I completed the full game and I must say that my opinion has stayed the same over this time period!The game is absolutely beautiful and memorable in all the good ways, but when it drops the ball it drops it pretty hard for me. Luckily it doesn't happen too much.Should you try out the game? FOR SURE! Especially if you are a fan of Wind Waker, A Hat in Time and Hollow Knight!

_childDocuments_.review: Honestly, the art style looked charming and the game play looked like it could've been a decent action, 3D-Platformer. _childDocuments_.review: I thoroughly enjoyed Blue Fire, it has a lot to like. As far as gameplay goes, the combat has great aerial movement and the platforming is challenging enough to feel accomplished when you make it through levels. The artwork is aesthetically pleasing and the characters are quirky and fun to interact with. I would love to see what else the developers can come up with, I think more interactive combat - more enemies would improve the game. Additionally, larger dungeons and more challenging puzzles would be great.Even though I wish the game had more to offer, it is $20 so I think it was worth it for the amount of content and fun I had. I think it's evident Blue Fire does rely heavily on concepts from Zelda and Hollow Knight, but it does so successfully so not a huge problem for me, again, hoping to see how they take things in their own direction. I'm excited to see what Robi Studios will develop next.Shoutout to Iron Pineapple for the recommendation!

_childDocuments_.review: Visually, a nice cute game. Mechanically it's rage inducing. The controls, especially camera can only be described as sub-optimal, like you can't have 100% control of your character's movements at any moment . Also the game is terrible at depth perception, you just can't tell how far anything is and whether you can make a jump for it or not. You can feel that especially in the challenges where the platforming is gradually getting ridiculous. I'm gonna finish the game still, but so far the experience is miserable.
_childDocuments_.name: Blue Fire

_childDocuments_.review: I'm not a fan of the review I'm about to write because I feel like this game hits a lot of marks for me, but in other regards it comes so short it hurts.(Quick edit: I did complete the game 100% before writing the review)I'd describe this game as "It's really good, but..." As in, I LIKE what the game offers, but there's something about it that frustrates me.For example, the platforming is fun and brutal, BUT sometimes it's not clear how you're supposed to get somewhere and it's not clear what walls you can run on or what platforms you can stand on. The combat is really fast and flashy, BUT enemy hitboxes (especially melee enemies) don't make any sense, and there isn't enough enemy variety to make me use most of my kit. The level design is pretty good and allows for exploration in places I'm not explicitly told to go, BUT a lot of the way the game progresses you is by showing you a random cutscene that only then tells you you should go interact with these things you've been finding.I could go on about more things that are good, but fall short, but that's not a fun review to read or even a very helpful one, so I'll sing the games praises that it does deserve.The overall atmosphere and aesthetic was rad. I super enjoyed the goofy characters as well as some of the more serious ones. You definitely don't get too attached to any of them seeing as you never interact with them more than a couple times, but none of the dialogue was offensive, and some of it gave me a good chuckle. The music is fine enough. It's mostly there to create atmosphere, but I'm a huge fan of dark souls, so it did what it needed to do for me. The areas all had nice colors and were decorated enough that it wasn't super confusing where I was.Ultimately, I did enjoy the game, but it's hard for me to recommend something like this. Platformer games and Souls-like games are up my alley, and I have a lot of patience for them, but I really had to force myself to finish Blue Fire.  While I did have a mostly positive experience with the game, I don't think I can recommend it to anyone.

_childDocuments_.name: Blue Fire

_childDocuments_.review: Yet another iffy recommendation.You can tell the creators have a good understanding of the basics. Level design is fun, lore is decent, and the controls are tight.It feels rather unpolished, though. Just a lot of little things that you'll notice that more experienced game devs would have ironed out by now.Like, for instance, when you jump, there is a particle effect that looks like it's meant to be a trail behind the player. Instead, however, it spawns in all at once in a vertical column. This means that when you jump, a pillar of particles appear above your head. Worse, if you just tap jump, and thus don't reach the height of your jump, your character's head won't even reach these particles.It makes jumping look more like you're being beamed up by aliens who lose interest partway through. It's not a big deal, but it shows that someone somewhere didn't know how to make these particles emit from beneath the player as they moved upwards.Another small one I noticed were on these plus-shaped rotating platforms during a void challenge. When you stand on them without input, your character slowly slides across the surface as it moves under them. It's minute, and so not a big deal, but it's again a sign of sloppiness.All these small things don't bog down gameplay, but it makes the game feel more like a college project more than a finished product from a serious development studio.Also, to those drawn to the game for the Soul-Like tag, that is a straight up lie. The game is not anything like Souls. It's incredibly easy, for one. Seriously, none of the bosses are harder then you might expect from a Zelda game.As for atmosphere, it's much closer to Hollow Knight then Souls, in that while trying to be dark and atmospheric, it's in fact fairly light-hearted with colorful characters and a sprinkling of comedy here and there.It's a fun game, just probably reserved for discount purchases only.
_childDocuments_.name: Blue Fire

_childDocuments_.review: Blue Fire takes me back to 3D platformers I played when I was little. It's hard as nails, but sometimes that's just a part of a game. There's one disclaimer I will make though: it's rough around the edges.I think only time will tell just how good this game can get. Right now it needs some TLC on the dev side, but they know that and I'm confident they know what needs to be done. A community around Blue Fire has already sprung up and they want the best for this little adventure.When it comes down to it, we've got a charming game with loads of untapped potential just waiting to come out. Keep Blue Fire on your radar if you can't decide on getting it just yet.

_childDocuments_.review: This game is basically dark souls by way of a hat in time and it's pretty dang neat. The atmosphere isn't exactly amazing and it's all got a cutesy style to it that kind of cuts out any bleakness but honestly I prefer that, and the environments themselves are pretty fun to explore too. There's definitely some minor issues - the camera can be a bit unwieldly during the platforming challenges, combat never really feels -great- (good luck using your air attack consistently without the attack range upgrade, lol), and it has some weird ideas about progression - an early game cash gate and at least one main quest requiring optional upgrades to complete (also - I didn't even -find- the spin attack until post-game, despite how big of a deal it's made out to be it's just... sitting in a secret area where you'll likely miss it). The game abandons dungeons entirely in favor of collectathon-esque sidequests halfway through, which... okay, weird. But like... I can have my gripes but overall I had a good time. It's not too hard, surprisingly - I died in two places, one midgame boss and the DLC boss - though maybe the recent balance patch had something to do with that since I remember dying when I played the demo a while back? I dunno. The devs have continued to update the game and even added in an entire postgame area as free DLC with some of the more creative platforming challenges in the game which is really lovely to see. It's all around just a pretty fun time despite its roughness in a few places.
_childDocuments_.name: Blue Fire

_childDocuments_.review: Excellent, one of the best games I've played in a long time. Dark souls meets Zelda with metriodvania aspects. The game is not as unforgiving as Dark souls but still has that challenging combat. Having the movement mechanics from metroidvania style games like double jump, dash, and wall jumps in a 3D space is brilliant, fun, and really brings the parkour of the game to a new level. Even when I was struggling to do some of the more challenging parkour failing again and again I was still having fun. I always felt like I was in control, every death felt fair. Every time I died I knew what I did wrong, not once did I feel like I got screwed over by the game. There are very few games I 100%, but I enjoyed every second of it. 10/10 A must play.
_childDocuments_.name: Blue Fire

_childDocuments_.review: Blue Fire looks like a very promising hybrid between 3D Zelda and Hollow Knight, but sadly the game has too many flaws for me to enjoy:- The combat is very underwhelming. Mindless button mashing is often more effective than timing or tactics.- The game only has a handful of save points. Quitting or dying means you have to replay a significant portion of the game.- The platforming can be very frustrating, especially when you have to jump to platforms you can't see (arounds corners, behind a wall etc).- There's NO map. If you find a new key or ability, you'll have to search every area again for a locked door or a new path you can access, which is very annoying without a map.- Shopkeepers are spread throughout the game world, and are hard to find without a map. Warping is only possible in the second half of the game, and only between the sparse save points.- There's way too much needless backtracking. For example, to access some of the later bosses in the game, you need to find new paths or dozens of hidden orbs in sections that you've already played. The latter actually made me quit the game: to reach some of the orbs, you need abilities that are well hidden in other area's. This game requires you to search the entire game world over and over again, without a map and with only a few save/warp points. With over 500 games in my backlog, this felt like a huge waste of time to me. Meh.

_childDocuments_.review: This isn't a "this game is terrible" thumbs down review, but sadly I don't think it's really worth playing. There's the core of a good game here, as it's basically a 3D Zelda with an extra focus on platforming. But there are so many minor annoyances in the controls that the game feels really unsatisfying to play.The main one is the auto-lock system, which is a bit too overzealous. Anything destructible (crates, enemies, etc.) in a pretty wide radius gets auto-locked onto when you attack. This will have you zipping around all over the place when you really don't want to outside of combat.The ledge latch feature also feels very unsatisfying. Definitely functional, and makes jumps forgiving, but the way ti snaps to the ledge and jerks your camera around feels very bad to play.This is the kind of game that will make me think about playing other games from the publisher if they have a more refined and polished game later, but this particular offering? Pass.

_childDocuments_.review: My top indie game of the past year.Blue Fire is a wonderful little mix of every Zelda game with a touch of Souls for flavor. The game's visual design is reminiscent of Wind Waker, down to the individual dead rats and gems. The main currency is gained by breaking jars and pots and other world items of the sort, while others are gained through completing challenges and defeating enemies. The game has 2 types of powerups; permanent abilities gained through story progression, and spirits which have their own special slots and can be swapped at save points.The story is vague and your goals are usually spelled out, it's a very direct game. There is no missable content, then entirety of the game can be completed without worry of skipping anything, all game features are available without need of Internet access.The game offered both Normal and Hard difficulty modes upon first starting, Expert mode became available after completing my Normal mode playthrough. Expert mode is permadeath, so you'd better be prepared for this one!The majority of the trials (pocket dimension challenges similar in style to BOTW shrines) were pretty easy to do, but a couple got downright mean. They were optional, so no harm done there.Here are my times for total completion:Normal base game, around 8 hours.Normal DLC, around 1.5 hours.Hard base game, in progress.Hard DLC, TBD.Expert base game, heck naw.Expert DLC, also heck naw.

_childDocuments_.review: I have no reservations about full-heartedly recommending this wonderful game, except for the caveat that the combat, while adequate, is far from a major draw, and the void puzzles, regardless of difficulty setting, can be some real head-bashers—as in, they're so hard they'll feel like bashing your head repeatedly against the wall. But for the most part, the latter caveat applies to a select few of the total puzzles, and they are, technically, optional. Also, I can't help but admit that, while tough, they are never exactly "unfair," and gitting good will carry you far.The world as a whole is full of personality, approximating a kind of N64 Zelda-meets-Dark Souls. The story is a mere pretext for the action, and is therefore rather thin, but many adorable characters and an overall charming aesthetic more than make up for any lack of context. The star of the game is its platforming, and it absolutely shines in that department. Jumping, double jumping, charged high-jumping, wall-climbing—and all with nice, tight controls and good responsiveness. Good audio and a great soundtrack are icing on the cake.

_childDocuments_.review: 15h 22m (based on the in-game clock, 100% achievement, finished the main game + Void of Sorrows DLC) No. Yes (11 achievements). No. is a 3D platformer game with action-adventure elements in it. You will have to explore some areas, clear closed-off platformer sections, and defeat bosses. It also tries to incorporate some Metroidvania elements, introducing power-ups that allow you to access new areas and possibly secret items.- Challenging and unique platformer sections- Power-ups to make the platformer sections easier- Widely explorable areas that hide secrets and easter eggs- Enemies can disrupt the platforming sections- Combat relies too much on platforming controls- Dashing to flying enemies tend to not workIntel Core i5-9300H 2.40GHz, 8GB RAM, NVIDIA GeForce GTX 1650 characters use simplistic models with cell shading techniques. Characters only have glowing eyes as their facial features, with a black body that makes them look like shadows. On the other hand, backgrounds look more realistic with their textures and shadows. Despite the style difference, they look good together, especially since the camera tends to be placed far from the character.I couldn't seem to find anything about the story. The game has a lot of world-building, though. Most dialogues tell about how everything came to be, and the threat that looms over the place. However, it doesn't tell more than that.  You can only make assumptions - there isn't even an ending after you beat the final boss.'s main focus lies in exploration. You will use your platforming skills to explore the areas and finish some quests. These quests are usually in the form of finishing a dungeon and beating the main boss, which again, involves your platforming skills. You can only do basic skills at the beginning, but more techniques like double jump and dash will be available as you progress.What makes  unique from other games is how it does its exploration. You can take the more direct path to exit the area and progress with your quest, but doing a full sweep on each area will net you more items. Some areas will also be inaccessible until you get the right power-up. Most items tend to be useless, though. The only thing that you need to watch out for is the existence of s, a closed-off platformer section that can give you an extra heart if you manage to complete it. Entering a  will teleport you to a closed-off platformer stage that you need to traverse to reach the exit. It's not as easy as it sounds, though - some areas might require several tries to finish due to their difficulty. Luckily, checkpoints are scattered between the areas. It still won't make it easy to beat, especially since some checkpoints are still placed far from each other, but it makes most s manageable. I don't even think I could beat them without dying once.Some s require you to have a certain power-up, but it never tells you that you need it to proceed. It also works the other way around, though. Completing s will be easier once you get more power-ups, which can be easily done as long as you explore everything. To be honest, the  is my favorite part of the game. The power-ups feel like a great excuse to test out your platforming skills and the  seems to take on the challenge by providing worthy stages that you can try. You will have to try the levels over and over again until either your muscle memory hits or you get lucky, and although I kept on saying I hated it, I ended up saying that I loved it once I finished it. I want more.Sadly, the combat feels like an afterthought. I don't like how enemies can stagger you when you get hit, but they can't be staggered in return. Their attack also persists for several seconds after their attacking animation is over. Moreover, they have a lot of HP and attack quickly, making it hard to dodge with a dash. You can always use a shield to deflect the attack, but I found that the shield takes too much mana - you can only recover it from attacking the enemy, but trying to kill an enemy without taking damage with the shield will net you less mana than you had before the fight. Besides, it's faster to just spam the attack button to beat them.The most annoying thing about enemies is how they tend to ruin the platforming sections. Flying enemies will be placed between some platforms and you need to kill them if you don't want to die from falling because they hit you while you jump. There is still a chance that you might fall if you don't manage to land properly after you attacked them, though. This causes an issue in one of the areas where you need to climb a very high tower. A single fall will mean that you need to redo the climb. Bosses feel similar. They might have different attack patterns, but I found half of them to be vulnerable to attack in mid-air. This forces you to fight at that height, which can be hard to execute if you don't have all the extra power-ups that can make you stay in the air longer. Dodging boss attacks also can be problematic, especially if your extra power-ups are in cooldown. I found myself dying from falling more often than I thought in the boss fights.Luckily, bosses can be cheesed. Although potions can take a long time to take effect, you will find yourself killing the enemies before you ran out of potions. I only died ~3 times in the main game, and 2 of them happened because I forgot to use my potions. The DLC boss is different, though. They feel unfair with their HP - I had to change my power-up loadout to the one that gives extra damage before I could beat them.The in-game clock says that I finished the main game in 11h 27m. The DLC content is only accessible post-game, and I finished everything in 15h 22m. There are 2 difficulty modes that you can choose at the beginning, and the regular mode, the one that I chose, felt right for me. It wasn't hard to beat but it still manages to give me some challenges, especially the s.The game manages to balance the exploration and  sections perfectly. To be honest, I was overwhelmed by the number of s in the DLC - I was almost burned out from all the annoying platforming, but the exploration sections in the main game helped to give me some time before I could tackle another one. Moreover, I like how each  looks unique and still manages to test my platforming skills with its difficulty.If you buy  for its action-adventure content, don't. It might have combat, but that's not where the game truly shines. You want to get  for its exploration and platforming sections - the s. It's all about navigating the terrain, overcoming obstacles, and testing your platforming skills.

_childDocuments_.review: This game has an amateurish design, but polished finish, feel to it -- everything is very straightforward, with regards to combat, platforming, even the art style is a shallow cover for the same-old, same-old for every platform brawler I can think of.This game has a feel to it, like a resurrection of the PSP-era "Death, Jr." franchise -- the art style is similar, and the gameplay feels simplistic, in the same manner.  A lot of early 3D platformers had a similar feeling, and they are utterly uninspiring today (TBH most of them were bad then, as well).It's a simple 3D platformer with very simple fighting mechanics, and take my review with a grain of salt -- I got tired of it after about 30 minutes, because I just couldn't find anything original, or otherwise appealing, about it.  The controls were pretty responsive, but the level design is such that I got myself stuck, unable to even kill myself, in some places in the first dungeon, just trying to platform from one broken staircase to another.  No charm, "modern" indie game art style (i.e. bland, cartoony, but in a depressing way), no elegance in the dance of combat, and the platforming was simple and occasionally broken -- although I suspect this part, at least, gets better (the first "void" level had some sparks of platforming interest).  Combat moves involve attacks + uncontrolled motion on the part of the player character, which sometimes cause you to fall off the narrow platforms you fight on, to your death, while locked to an opponent, unable to perceive your immediate surroundings accurately.  Since some odd lava blobs are littered randomly around the environment (in the early level, at least), and tiny blobs enter each combat with a larger foe, the combat is really more about avoiding the environment while staying locked on to the main enemy, and jumping in and out to attack without falling to your death, than it is about dealing with the actual challenge of the opponent.  As such, it's not fun, it's just a relief to be done with, so you can get back to platforming.If you're looking for even remotely good brawling, combined with platforming, avoid this one.  If simple platforming is all you care about, and the occasional "environmental don't-fall combat" sounds fun to you... I guess?Not recommended.

_childDocuments_.review: I don't often write reviews, but for some reason I felt compelled to here.  I've played Blue Fire for 11 hours as of writing this and have only experienced 1 crash (after an early death in the sewers). Obviously most people here have not been so fortunate, but I can only base my review of the game on my own experience with it. The visuals and music are great, and the combat and platforming flow nicely. The complaints about the money being too tight seem over exaggerated; just sell all of your gems to the library guy in Stoneheart and you'll be able to afford basically everything with minimal grinding (2X Money spirit helps too). Overall, it's a fun and challenging game for platformer fans like myself :)I'll update this review if the game becomes an unstable mess at any point towards the end.UPDATE: I took a break from this game for a few weeks because the fire boss kept kicking my ass, and there now seems to be a ~35% chance that the game will crash upon entering the fire boss room (it did not do this before), which is particularly frustrating because I still keep dying. I won't be playing any more until this is fixed. [Updated March 7th]UPDATE 2: Finally revisited this game a couple months later, and wouldn't you know it, it doesn't crash anymore. I don't know when they updated the game because the latest patch notes I could find were from February (which is also part of why it took me so long to pick this game back up), but at least it was fixed. I ended up finishing the remainder of the game in one sitting, it really is that good. [Updated May 9th]UPDATE 3: I'm updating this for the 2021 Steam Awards task. I guess the new content looks cool? I haven't played it yet lol.

_childDocuments_.review: I enjoyed this game immensely, I experienced crashes like some of the other reviews are saying, but it wasn't enough to make me stop playing or softlock me out of the game. I did have some problems with the spirits spawning after I died, so I lost a lot of ore. But overall the game was fun! The platforming felt good, the art style was nice, the later boss fights were challenging, and the spirits made finding them feel worth while. The only problems I would say I had with this game was the lack of any direction when completing quests, I felt that I had to wander around a lot until I ran into something that I could now access this time. A map, or a little guide on where you should go for the quests in the quest log would be a massive improvement. I also think that the ore that you obtain out of chests should have a note that says "can be sold" I stock-piled it because I thought it might be needed for an upgrade system later on. The story felt kind of non existent though, I had no idea why I was doing anything, all I knew was that I had to kill some shadows.The strategy guide that the dev's released was very nicely put together, however I wish I knew it existed before I got stuck on the final boss for an hour. Overall I enjoyed it, however with the rough edges I believe that there just needs to be a bit more polish in this game and then it will be something great! 7/10

Literally trial and error to figure out where the path leads through invisible walls, requiring a jump through unknown obstacles. Every failure is a half minute climb back up, mostly waiting for a damn slow elevator.TL;DR Tedium and frustration combined. Boring, unrewarding, yet broken enough to make you angry.And plenty of other issues. Ledge grabs often fail, wallruns trigger when they shouldnt.Combat is clunky mess. Way too easy by default, yet horribly clunky to offset that. Shield/parry has an unreliable delay, enemy attack hitboxes are way off, and some can just stunlock and kill the player once caught, without any chance of escaping.Targeting an enemy or object turns the simple, short and horizontal dash into a long distance teleport almost, but does it unreliably. Sometimes the normal dash is executed even when locked, sometimes it drops the player close to the enemy, but still just out of attack range. Otherwise, the mechanic is exploitable to bypass certain platforming sections.Backtracking, backtracking. No actual gain, no worth, no challenge. Just remember stuff to get back later when you have the ability to actually reach it. Then you get a pat on the back, and something mostly useless.Killing a normal enemy is sometimes more fun than a boss... Why am I playing it? Well, I don't. Not anymore. Halfway through, no thanks, enough for me. Got plenty of other (better) games.This game might worth its price, but not the time spent on it.

_childDocuments_.review: It's pretty much Hollow Knight 3D. If that speaks to you, just get it already. If you're that scared ya won't like it, just get it with a discount. It's a ton of fun and the developers don't mind at all. You've some extra "shrines" ala Breath of the Wild that give you more health. Some of those can be incredible difficult (potentially sadastic), but the movement makes it a ton of fun. The difficult spike is kinda everywhere, but I expect nothing less from a somewhat Metroidvania game.I didn't really bother much with the story, not always in the mood to read a ton. The characters are all very great, I wish that they weren't only useful for 1 quest and that's it, but hey!Looking forward for more!

_childDocuments_.review: Hi internet-stranger!As you can see I have played this game for 14-ish hours, I did everything it asked me to do, I got all the  achievements there are to get and now I sit here, contemplating how to talk about Blue Fire.I will keep this short and simple:Blue Fire...... starts off as Zelda, then turns into a "open world exploration game" without any sense of directing you towards your goals.... is crammed full of instanced jump-and-run skillchecks, that will make your eyes bleed.... has cheap,  cheap difficulty spikes caused entirely by the fact that enemies start out as pushovers, then suddenly stunlock you to death while dealing incredible amounts of damage.... forgets how it wants to be played and rushes you towards an ending once you get to the half-way mark.... only lasts 10-ish hours depending on how dedicated you are to finding everything in this game.... assumes your Galactic Alphabet is very polished, otherwise you are faced with boss monologues which you won't be able to read.... has the same 2 enemy types for the entirety of the game, one being a floating turret, which will kill you, whenever a new rendition appears on the screen.Blue Fire...... may possess the most responsive and natural feeling controls I ever experienced in a 3D Platformer.... also has some really challenging and fun instanced jump-and-run skillchecks (which makes the horrible ones feel worse, tbh).... has really cute character design.... offered me 14 hours of not-being-bored.... will be 100% completed achievementwise from just finishing the main storyline and all sidequests, which are conveniently placed around said main storyline.Blue Fire is a really nice game, it's fun to play, it's responsive, it's a great platformer and has a rather charming look to it.Sadly it has major flaws in the way it is build, it feels rushed, like half of the game hasn't been made and instead you are sent out to do some stupid exploration quest in order to fight bosses that seemed to have belonged into proper dungeons instead.Over and over again you will find yourself biting the dust because of ridiculously stupid reasons, like enemies hitlocking you, stunning you over pits or bosses insisting they have to float over a vet of lava, so you can only fight them in the air, then you slip, get hit by the boss, are hit by the lava and upon respawn you respawn in a void-zone causing even more damage. 1-2-3, dead player!The game is frustrating as hell, despite all the fun you have inbetween, which, all in all, makes Blue Fire even more frustrating and a real disappointment.This could have been a dark and gritty Zelda-like, with an amazing story, fun dungeons and platforming and instead... it's kind of a mess.

_childDocuments_.review: Blue Fire is an interesting start. That is the first thing that comes to mind when I think about how I feel about this game. My overall feeling with it once I finished it was contentment, with a feeling of slightly missed opportunity that was filled in by how solid other aspects of the game are.Graphics are simple, soundtrack is good, yadda yadda yadda. You already know the deal.What stands out here is the gameplay. Metroidvania platformers are extremely fun. This is one of those and therefore is extremely fun. Using a limited moveset to get around the map, only to use your expanded moveset later to breeze through it is a defining moment of this game.Combat is alright. Parrying, Arial bounces, dodge. It is all here. The thing is though, you are platforming through the combat it creates this satisfying dodge and weave play style that is very nimble and unique. It is extraordinarily easy though. I played on hard, and the combat was pitiful in most cases. That is not what you are here for though, you are here for the platforming.The platforming in this game is so good that it holds everything else in the game up. While the other aspects may be ok or lacking, the platforming is a proper challenge that will test your patience and willpower. By no means of the word is it undoable or the hardest, but it is a fun challenge. Especially with the DLC this game has.My major complaint with the game is the badge system. It is kinda just tacked on. Sometimes they're borderline useless (Damaging dodge anyone?). Other times they are game breakingly good. The double double jump and double dash in specific. Those trivialize some of the void challenges. They do give way to some fun skips, but they feel like a last second addition that doesn't mesh with the rest of the game most of the time.Voids are the peak of this game. Most if not all are extremely fun bite sized platforming challenges. I love these so much, and they felt so rewarding to playthrough. They made a whole DLC dedicated to challenging voids, and it is 100% the most fun you will have with the game. Sadly, there are no achievements or even a sign that it is there, so I almost missed it. Just make sure you play it. It is extremely fun.Blue Fire is overall a great game. While some aspects are lacking, none are bad, and the platforming more than makes up for any short comings. 8.5/10

_childDocuments_.review: Just completed all content in the game and I can safely say it was one of my favorite experiences of the year. If you like 3D platformers at all and dont mind a slight challenge this game is for you. I was blow away by the quality and quantity of the content for the price. I saw in another review that someone compared this game to Dark Souls. This is completely inaccurate. For one thing combat is not this games focus. Moreover It shares practically nothing in common with the game play of souls other than an interconnected world which is also a key trait in many other games and most obviously The Zelda Series which is really what this game is structured most like. This games elevator pitch is really "what if Zelda was the 3D platformer?" It has a connected world and several dungeons that are built upon the lock and key game design of Oot era Dungeons. Wherin you often unlock a traversal tool to help complete the dungeon and then open the world to reach the next challenge. The twist is the main challenge of all the overworld and dungeons is platforming. I would describe the tool kit to be Mega Man Zeros abilities but in 3D. The Dash mechanic works very similarly to Mega Man X  where you utilize the dash to boost forward momentum to gain more control and reach farther areas. This game offers many places to use its ever expanding platformer tool kit in optional shrine like platforming gauntlets. They are heavily incentivized as the offer health upgrades. The exploration of the game is extremely open ended and fulfilling, exploring often leads to even better platforming tools to find even more secrets.

_childDocuments_.review: Amazing first effort for the developers, but not without its issues.  I had a mostly great time 100%ing this game.For major issues, the combat sticks out as the easy target.  To put it bluntly it is not good, but it feels like the devs know it isnt good.  That doesnt make it okay, but I think the devs designed around its flaws pretty well.  Your basic swing comes with a dash forward making controlling it pretty awkward.  Ground fights turn into these weird skating matches with you dashing around the enemy or zooming to a different target.  It doesnt help that enemy variety is lacking all around, both in moves and types.  The dashing makes platforming awkward too, but I dont think this one is actually a fault, just something you have to get used to. Anyways, since grounded combat kinda sucks the devs focused on aerial combat for most of the major fights, which is much more reliable. This means its greatest issue isnt really that big of a deal in retrospect, even if in the moment it can be annoying.  As for the much better side of the game, the platforming, I dont have a ton of complaints.  Some platforming sections were a little rough and as always in these kinds of games making your way through the world in the beginning is a little painful, but by the end, you are insanely mobile.  I was pretty impressed with what the game would let me do with a full mobility build in terms of skipping sections or tackling them my own way.  You have so many options of what you can do mid air that its actually a little hard to keep track of.  But I very much enjoyed mapping out the exact string of jumps and dashes needed as I pushed forward through a tough level.  Doubly so when scouting a level and saying "no way I can make this jump from here" then proceeding to do it.  Something I found neat that I would like to see in other games or expanded on in future titles by Robi Studios is useful emotes.  They basically act as a collectable in this game, as each one will unlock a chest for you nearby.  Right now you just stand on a plate with the picture of an emote, but it would be cool if NPC's could react to you doing different emotes.  Just as an example, doing a threatening emote to a shop keeper could produce different results.  If the shopkeep is a coward maybe he will lower his prices to appease you, but a brave one would raise them in defiance.  When the emote seller told me emotes would be useful my mind raced with ideas, and even though what Blue Fire delivered on was a little middling, I think an expanded system could be really cool. One last note.  Its pretty obvious that this game wears its influences on its sleeve.  This in and of itself is not a bad thing, though if done poorly it can be.  I think this game teeters close to that line, but doesnt cross it.  Yes, it has Hollow Knights charm system, Zelda/Dark Souls' exploration, and 3D Mario/A Hat in Time's movement systems (hell one of the emotes is even a direct reference to hat kid), but I think they mesh together well enough to become something unique.  Nothing exists in a vacuum anyways, and if those are the games you're pulling inspiration from, then I think its no surprise that the game ended up being as good as it is, even if a little rough around the edges.

_childDocuments_.review: I see people referring to this game as a cross between Hollow Knight and Zelda, and while that's fair, I have to say that playing it gave me feelings of Super Mario Galaxy - the movement controls are excellent.  As a 3D platformer, this is an extremely fantastic game.  The world does feel a bit small yet empty, though that is mostly mitigated by the time you get to the first town.  I do have a few grips:-Primarily that the game is too short.  I still got a good 11 hours out of it and just started the DLC, so saying it's "too short" is really a matter of wanting more.-The combat needed a little more polish.  This is a tad nitpicky, as the combat isn't BAD by any means, it just felt like it was missing something - it's about one step above a hack and slash.  This is most evident when facing the bosses, as they all felt a little underwhelming, but there also isn't much variety in the enemies - of which there are 4 types in the entire game (5 if I'm being generous), which I could categorize as leeches, fighters (possibly splitting off another category from this one called 'sewer monsters'), 'Floating Heads', and Shooting Heads.  Some shoot ice, or fire, or lasers, but that's basically it.  I guess technically there are giant worm monsters in one area too, but they pretty much just attack from a distance and hide if you get too close.-On occasion (three separate times I can recall off the top of my head) the camera just kind of...doesn't really do you any favors.  It happened to me consistently in one specific spot of the last Void challenge, which...made things more annoying than they needed to be.-The endgame feels rushed - there's arguably two to four "dungeons" in the game.  The first two are clear cut, with ability items and bosses at the end, then you might count the Steam House and maybe even the tower in the Abandoned Path (personally, I'd say the former is and the latter isn't).  But there's six bosses - the first two, the Shadow Lords, and the final boss.  It works out this way because two of the three Shadow Lords (depending on if the Steam House is a dungeon, otherwise it would be all three) are behind other barriers besides dungeons.  That said, it still feels much better done than "that area" in the first Dark Souls game - not really an 'incomplete' sort of rush.  It's still very serviceable.-Related to the above, a lot of abilities are obtained AFTER this endgame section begins, which just feels like a missed opportunity to expand the world a little bit more after you get some upgrades.  Again, this would be better if the game was a little longer, and the world a little bigger.These are relatively minor gripes.  I still enjoyed the game very much.  It's got good graphics that honestly remind me of OG Wind Waker, the movement is tight and controlled in a way that...I don't know I've EVER seen in a 3D indie title.  Play it for yourself, the game's a solid 8/10, and I look forward to seeing what this developer does next.EDIT:  Regarding my criticisms of the boss fights, I'm going to make a VERY big exception to the DLC boss.  Although it follows much of the same patterns as the other bosses, they are more fleshed out and a lot more fun and challenging.  Easily the best fight of the game.

_childDocuments_.review: This game looked a lot more appealing in the trailer. It's not a bad game, honestly, but there's better things out there.I went with normal mode because it's, "For new players," and didn't expect it to be so easy. I only died once, and it was to the final boss. Up to that point, I hadn't been paying attention to my health at all because whatever damage you take can be mitigated by a healing-on-kill spirit. Nothing did enough damage or ever really stood in my way. Half way through I just started avoiding enemies because I wouldn't gain anything by killing them. Needless to say, the combat isn't by any means challenging and neither are the bosses. The first boss is a joke. It's a plant that shoots a wave around itself that does so little damage you can tank the entire boss without healing yourself. The rest are a bit more creative, but none stand out as especially fun or challenging. The platforming is the highlight of the game. Some of the void missions feel like a joke, but the four and five star ones are especially challenging. The main challenge is really just angling the camera into just the right spot so that you can actually gage the distance between you and the wall, diamonds, spikes, and blades.There's nothing about this game that is punishing or there to make you suffer. It's cute, simple, and kinda boring.As for the lore, there's barely even one. Nothing deep or complex by any means.If you don't like dying, and you want to play a relaxing platformer, Blue Fire is the game for you.Maybe it's more of a thrill on hard mode, but there's nothing about my experience that makes me want to play it again. _childDocuments_.review: This is a very solid 3D platformer with strong inspirations from Legend of Zelda's storytelling, worldbuilding and gameplay mechanics. The gameplay consists of a mixture of platforming using various abilities acquired over the course of the game, such as dashing, double-jumping, a vertical boost (spin attack), wallrunning, etc, which starts very basic, but becomes fairly demanding over time and gave me a feeling that proper technique building was necessary to get through it all, as well as a Zelda-style lock-on combat. The combat has a strong emphasis on vertical movement and use of the lock-on directed dash, which gives it a very mobile feel. The more you move, the less you are hit. And indeed, while there is a shield and a ranged attack (which, incidentally, are the only real use of the mana bar present in-game), these are practically unnecessary if you manage to play your spacing with the enemies right.In addition, hitting enemies while mid air keeps you up in the air, which results in extremely satisfying air combat. This is particularly fun in the late boss battles (of which there are 6 in total).The difficulty curve is moderately steep. Enemies hit much harder with subsequent areas, but with some practice and confidence they are no particular obstacle. Similarly, boss battles are no big challenge compared to some of the platforming sections.The most difficult of those are formed by the voids, which are mini-platforming environments where wallrun distance is extended and extra objects like sawblades etc. are introduced. These are optional, but highly recommended.The benefit for doing these is collecting void souls, which allow you to craft additional spirit slots. Additionally, upon completion, they grant a permanent health boost of 1. As there are 16 voids, the potential maximum health is immense.Spirits are passive buffs collected via challenges and side quests and applied at savepoints. These can range from negligible (damage upon dashing into enemy) over useful(increase damage while in air) to completely game-breaking (double dash/triple jump).Since the maximum spirit slots seem to be around 9 or 10, the benefit of these buffs is positively riveting. They allow for such a boost in mobility that playing with them changes the game entirely, if not trivialising it.The game provides a number of side quests, which all remain in the territory of fetch quests. Their rewards are usually similarly stimulating.There are 6-7 areas in the game, and while my initial playthrough took 29 hours, a more conservative estimate by a competent platformer would probably put the game length at 6-10 hours.Overall, what the game lacks most is content. A lot of the game's mechanics are made obsolete by proper technique management and spirits, making the experience feel like there was much more intended to be done with all of these tools.While the tools given are manifold and precise, there is a distinct lack of need for most of them (e.g. the running ring).However, the game must be praised for its art direction and sense of fun. There are small conveniences littered everywhere that show the developers care about making a non-obnoxious gaming experience.E.g. the ability to catch ladders mid-air and jump them up fast, the consolidation of money into chunks by an NPC so they aren't lost upon death...Finally, the obtainable tunics for the main character and the emotes are plain adorable. The latter also serve a rudimentary purpose in the form of collecting them and using them in specific places to obtain collectibles. Those collectibles are themselves useless, but one of them at least was very much worth it.Overall, this game is very competently made and deserves a lot of praise. It needs more content but is otherwise polished, fun and challenging. Too many people are sleeping on this.

_childDocuments_.review: This is pretty much two games stapled together. The main game is a beautiful platforming-lite adventure with some optional movement additions, with only two forced upgrades: wall-riding, and the eventual double-jump. You start with a single jump and a dash/air dash, and with this you can brute force a lot of puzzles that seem to need the full double jump.  And then there's the precision-heavy "bonus" void challenges. They're not necessary but they give you extra health. Except the "increased jump height" spirit. Several platforming challenges are based around the default jump height and are impossible with the higher jump. In addition to completing the challenge, there's 30 collectables per challenge, get 60 and you get an extra spirit slot to give you even better movement bonuses. My favorite example is there's a really tall area, if you schmove your way to the top of it with only the double jump, it gives you a triple jump plus there's some bells you can hit for fun.It's a game of two systems, combat and platforming, and while you need to be okay at both, you only need to be good at one.

_childDocuments_.review: Nice game with simple graphics but a fitting art style.  Gameplay is basically Hollow Knight + Zelda.  Places to explore with new skills and tons of treasure chests all over.  Controls feel a little loose and the player character feels like it's drifting along the floor rather than running.  Double jump literally slows your momentum for the animation and having to charge up a spin attack to gain some altitude while jumping means that the movement isn't always very fluid.  Combined with overly dark areas and small platforms means you'll be overshooting jumps often until you get used to it.  Nothing amazing about this game but definitely worth it on sale.

_childDocuments_.review: SOME AMOUNT OF SPOILERSgame starts out fantastic, honestly top tier. super curious about everything, really wondering about where things are where every path goes, the customs and characters are interesting. Overall fell its a 6.5-7.5 out of 10 and think that score is justified. A lot of great things in the game, think it loses points for various aspects but overall game is enjoyable and i dragged two mates into buying and playing it as well and they feel the same about it as i do which is its worth playing, there are some small elements to dislike but ultimately its worth the time put in.great stand out thingsin the first half its really challenging the parkour/platforming is wonderful and challenging and skill testing, really enjoyed figuring out how far i could go in a leap and tying together certain abilities. The power up rate felt appropriate (until later) and everything felt rewarding as you got throughart style is great, main character is wonderful little design. fighting is cool, though i disliked the timing overall, i think the shield is too slow by like 5-10 frames and everytime i did it to parry it felt really really early which took me forever to get used to but in the end just went with dashing instead cause it was annoyingly out of sync for me.. a negative comment about combat (mild spoiler) they dont do enough to tell you what you can and can't do so for example dashing then hitting then dashing infinitely until the creature is dead and having attacks refresh your dash and jump was something i didnt find out to way later in the game. im not saying i need an instruction manual but something like a string of enemies placed in a way leading up to a platform in a way testing me to push that boundary would have been nice because it is absolutely a key skill and if you dont learn it then certain parts of the game become really hard to manage as you wont WANT to attack mid air enemies for fear of falling having not learned the skill. happened to both my mates as well and we're all avid gamers, really feels odd not teaching that skill more.void challenges are fun!some critiques;story is wibbly wobbly after the midpoint and bit thin. At the outset the story seems dark and deep and really something to stick your teeth into. after the midpoint it gets a little dimmed and pulled back in on itself and then lots of things just feel shallow as a result. think a little bit of time spreading the story out on the latter half or putting in things to make the story seem deeper without ways to explore wouldve been nice. I think the power up system breaks the game and actively works against it. At the outset the power ups in the game for the most part are not necessary to complete the game, you can beat the final boss without any spirits though tougher they arent really necessary. The platforming elements never get tougher than either running through the fire area with the afar enemies pressing you to be mobile and tactile in movement or the tower in the abandoned path when you have single jump and wall climb available. beat those things were wonderful experiences to me playing because they were actively challenging and engaging and i was really enjoying on a deep level the challenge they presented at playtime. Later in the game (and small concession i didnt get spin jump until an hour before the boss fight) the spirits you get are so powerful platforming wise they absolutely trivialise the platforming elements of the game and that to me makes them work against what I enjoyed about the game. I really REALLY wished for another abandoned path tower challenge later in the game after getting all the power ups and spirits because it would've been so challenging to have to engage max distance jump affects, small platform timings for getting a spin charge set up right like that wouldve been so cool. but with all the spirits and no more really complicated pieces it just made all the previous things so childish by comparison it was actively un-enjoyable. (is this game supposed to be tough and thus rewarding for getting from A to B or not like?)on a similar note, not having a map is a bit a of a d**k move. like i can understand some direction being taken for not having maps but i also think you can stuff that idea out the window, this place is plenty complicated to have to remember everything about it including little things like where tf a certain temple is when you want to look for something. just give a map out or even a map stone of some kind thats only available in certain places so its not omnipresent if you like and give it out much later in the game so you still get all that exploration. For example getting the four jar fetch quest thing was cool, and is "just about" the limit i'd accept of not needing a map but there were many times when even after doing the whole game I felt lost and just needed a pointer. think its tough to be so broad and not have SOMETHING to help maintain direction guidance in the latter half of the gamethe weapons were a little disappointing that the most powerful weapons you can get are ones you buy. that feels super unrewarding. thanks i guess for like letting me spend money and now get the most powerful weapons....? wheres the rewarding feeling in that? weapon designs super cool, thematic's are awesome, just really question the powerful ones being a price point and not an achievement of some kind. yuck. robes were cool, was not clear they dont provide a benefit (if they DO provide a benefit and im incorrect than i guess thats a self explaining critique right there haha!) they were pretty though and i liked them. another critique, whats with all the random weird a$$ items you get? rotten apple? dead rat? an old boot? what am i doing with these? Also an ancient text/scroll i think was there somewhere and i dont recall using that at all and ive 100% so i dont think i missed anything??music and ambience was great! another point in favor there, always felt i played better listening than having music on. end boss fight was a little disappointing, there is a mechanic forced into the fight that if you're not aware of won't trigger and if you miss it the fight is impossible with it (almost impossible it MAY actually be possible without triggering it but i certainly couldn't do it)would've liked more fights like the fire boss, that was super exciting and I had so much fin doing it. that was a real challenge of both fighting knowledge and platforming knowledge. the ice one felt pale in comparison and the green one was pretty good honestly but the fire one was just da bomb, it was so good. i talked about it for AGES afterwards.I dont remember the ice one and that was only 2 or 3 hours ago. I have some other small nitpicks, like I climbed that tower and when i got there nothing happened, proceeded to do some other stuff then roamed the WORLD looking for what to do next and nobody i talked to was helpful (like right here a quest pointer or world pointer or somebody to talk to would have been so great) so i climbed the tower again and BAM got a cutscene, that miffed me right off that i was able to get there previously and there was no reason to believe i should go up there again afterwards. those are pretty much all of my critiques, the game overall honestly is fun. i wouldnt pay more than 15-20 quid for it. like 15 quid or less in a sale is a steal and so worth the time you can get out of it. there are some great platforming at the start of it and throughout most of it. i think the platforming was really well thought out and designed and thats at the heart of the game till the end. I even bought a second copy for my mate to play is how much i like this game so take my critiques with the knowledge that i DO really like the game i just think there are some things they couldve gotten better. would definitely visit other titles by this developer as a result

_childDocuments_.review: If I could sum up this game in one word, it would be "disappointing". So why do I suggest playing it? Because it's still a pretty good game. The problem is it is so close to being a great game. The game has everything going for it, interesting story, unique character design, great maneuvering mechanics, etc. But it seems to stumble at the finish line in every department. The story just kind of ends, the characters are dull and (in some cases) broken, and those great maneuvering mechanics stand in stark contrast to the terrible battling mechanics. There are little bugs everywhere, like rocks you can just walk through, or hit timings that don't match the animations. I still had fun playing it, but had they let it bake a little longer, I think this could have been a great game.

_childDocuments_.review: This game is definitely fun if you are looking for a platformer in the vain of Hollow Knight, with puzzle and dungeon elements from Zelda thrown in. The variety of moves you have is also very nice, as you have up to two mid-air jumps (with the spin attack from the sewers), in addition to 1-2 dashes depending on your spirits; However, this is where my issues arise. your traversal options are fairly limited if you don't shop or explore, since upgrades for more dashes, higher spin attacks, or longer wall-runs are held by vendors or behind exploration. Combat is also fairly simple, not due to your access to attacks, but due to the lack of enemy variety later in the game, as you'll most often see enemies from the first level re-textured with more health and damage later in the game; Though, you will occasionally find the unique enemy here and there to add variety. Aside from these gripes with the game and its mechanics, this game has solid mechanics which flow well together; though it must be said that there are a few rough edges at the current time with enemies and level design.

_childDocuments_.review: Blue Fire is a strange mix up of Zelda in tone, Dark Souls in mechanics, and Journey in appearance...with LOTS of platforming. A strange combination, sure, but one that works in practice.Blue Fire starts off with very little exposition of the world you're dropped into, and while it does manage to explain some of the setting and lore, much is left to your imagination. This might bother some, but the mystery and intrigue behind the world kept me just interested enough to get through the story being told. All in all the story is quite a simple and straightforward one, with some optional humorous and melancholic sidequests peppered throughout.Mechanically, Blue Fire is truly a platformer at heart. Your bread-and-butter arsenal of jumps, dashes and wall runs will carry you through most of this game's challenges. Both level design and combat are designed around platforming, with much of the obstacles in both relying on your ability to successfully navigate the environment to progress. In combat, much of the challenge relies on dodging attacks, as most enemies are quickly vanquished (as are you)! You will be darting in and out of attack ranges to deal damage in almost all situations and this is only complicated by enemies' area of effect attacks which pose additional obstacles to stop your approach. Other enemies will float over dangerous terrain, requiring you to jump towards them and hit them in the air while ensuring you've left a jump or dash to return safely to the ground. At the very least, combat was always demanding, and at worst it became predicable as enemies types and strategies began repeating.With so much demand on precision, it was great that the controls were up to par. There's a lot of finesse to master in Blue Fire and learning the slight difference between a short hop and long jump, or a short vs long dash is an important skill in many of the demanding (but optional) "void trials". These are short to long platforming sections that will really test your abilities. There are multiple of varying difficulties which, when completed, give you an additional heart as well as containing a currency in them that allows you to purchase additional "spirit slots" (which grant you place abilities which amplify your combat, platforming or other benefits). These trials varied from entertaining to downright frustrating as some are very, very long and dying places you at the start, instead placing checkpoints throughout to ensure you didn't need to complete the easier, rote beginning. Thankfully the rest of the game outside these trials is relatively easy. There is a dark souls-esque feature that drops your accumulated experience at the place of your death, which you can then retrieve if you manage to return there the next life, but this was honestly never a problem for me, as most deaths relating to platforming placed the lingering soul at the start of the platforming section rather than on the isolated platform I was trying to reach. Combat as well is rather simple with one button required to attack, a useless ranged fireball (more useful to interrupt opponent's attack), and a shield which counters with good timing (not terribly useful as most combat is aerial). Most platforming required in the main game is rather tame, especially compared to what is present in the void trials.At the end of Blue Fire I was left quite pleased with my 15hr experience. Most of my memories of the game come from the quirky characters you might find in a Zelda game, the lovely (if simple) aesthetics similar to Journey, and the feeling of power I gradually gained by the end of the game with the various weapons, abilities and skills I unlocked. There's plenty to love here and the game never outstayed it's welcome; on the contrary I wished it was a dungeon or two longer! Besides, what other game lets you dress up as a dual wielding banana who can break out to techno music whenever you want?

_childDocuments_.review: This game is pretty good, I had lots of fun dashing towards the enemies and attack them while in the air, it reminds me the time when I didn't have a gaming PC but instead I only had a PlayStation 2 and I would play games like Vexx, Jak 2 and 3. The game has elements borrowed from dark souls which I'm ok with, I'm not a big fan of dark souls because is a bit overrated and Dark souls game-play copies the monster hunter game-play. The bosses are pretty fun too.The only downside to this game, it sort of lacks Enemy variety because it uses the same enemies and monster npc but with different animations, skins and faster attacks. In the game you get to use a bubble shield which you can't upgrade or make the shield do special abilities and same thing with the range attack it barely does any damage to the enemies.Overall I give this game a 8 out 10. _childDocuments_.review: This is a 3d platformer that takes elements from Legend of Zelda and Dark Souls. Now imagine that it takes the jump and plattforming aspect of dark souls instead of LOZ. The jumping feels wrong. The Dash is controlled by how long you hold the button which is interesting considering the duration is between 0.1s and 0.3s, leading to you over/undershooting a lot. Combined with the camera which is completely player controlled, this leads to moments where you put the camera in top down only to jump against the wall because it was too high to grab.Oh speaking of grabbing, the game allows you to grab ledges to climb up, except when it doesn't and you fall to your death/the last point the game deems checkpoint worthy. Sometimes this is the very start of the level.Considering how frustrating the jumping is and how poorly the checkpoints are set you can only imagine how fun it is when combined with timed levers, you know the ones that already sucked in a good game like LOZ.I fought my way to the first dungeon to get my first progress item which gave me the ability to wall jump and run (with a limited stamina bar). But wall jumping does not automatically jump straight away from the wall, instead it uses the stick to determine if you want to jump 37° away into the next abyss (to not respawn on the last solid ground/before the ledge but a ladder you have to climb before you can try again). Oh and sometimes the wall grabbing works and other times you just fall along the wall (or the grabbing works but not high enough leading you to jumping too low to grab a ledge).Ok i though i will endure, but guess what, you know the time gated levers i mentioned earlier ? Combine them with this wall grab mechanic and absolute unintuitive level design and i decided i don't want to waste any more time, although i usally like LOZ-inspired games.I won't mention the combat which is barebones at best: you have a attack a parry where the timing is weird and the dash and most of the time attack attack dash is enough.The game needs some improvements before i would call it playable:-better checkpoints for jump and run areas (don't spawn me back at the very beginning because i couldn't grab the ledge caused by the camera) -stop with the timed levers, nobody likes them-maybe don't let items drop into the water, you know the water where you will get to the last respawn if you touch it.-improve the plattforming and rework some areas that are poorly builtSo all in all i would not recommend the game although there are some (although not original) features. If you are masochistic and want a plattformer that feels more like a tech demo, be my guest.

_childDocuments_.review: (Got through Humble Bundle)(Plays great on Steam Deck)(9.5/10)If you're a fan of platforming games and are looking for a challenging adventure, then this game might be perfect for you. It combines elements from two popular games, Zelda: Breath of the Wild and Dark Souls, and adds a unique platforming twist to it.The game features challenging voids that provide a refreshing break from the normal pace of the game, and the rewards for completing them are satisfying. The graphics are impressive and fit perfectly with the game's style.Combat can be tricky to get used to, but once you've mastered it, you'll feel like a powerful warrior. Although the game isn't extremely difficult, there are some areas where you might need to consult Google for help.The game features a linear dungeon crawling style that requires you to utilize every part of the map. The developers have clearly put a lot of passion and effort into this game, and you'll be rewarded for exploring areas that you might not have thought possible.Overall, this is a great game that will keep you engaged for hours. The game offers plenty of challenges and rewards, and it took me about 19.1 hours to achieve 100% completion. I highly recommend this game to anyone who enjoys platformers and dungeon crawlers.
