_childDocuments_.review: Blue Fire starts with you waking up alone in a container filled with water, not knowing where you are or how you got there. Ok I know what your thinking and yes this sounds very much like the start of Breath of the Wild and... uh... well... I got nothing but moving on...Other then basic tooltips for movement and other controls, the game doesn't outright tell you where to go, which is great because immediately Blue Fire is already setting a precedent that if you want to make progress, the only way to do so reliably is to simply adapt and explore.On the topic of adapting, the first thing I noticed when hoping into Blue Fire is just how good it feels to move in this game. Running, Jumping and Dashing is incredibly fast yet precise all at the same time. This flows equally well into combat situations, which Blue Fire is certainly not shy to introduce you to.Shortly after your first battle experience appears a chest, where you'll find your first permanent upgrade. A shield. Its a simple feature and doesn't come into play much in the rest of the game but it does sets the stage for the rest of your adventure. In just the first 5 or so minutes of the game, Blue Fire has told you that exploration and discovery for the most part is up to you, and that at least for now, your character is incomplete.For those of you who’ve played anything close to resembling a Metroidvania... Alarm bells have already started ringing and you're likely already expecting that there may be sections made inaccessible until you've progressed a bit farther into the game. Within the first 5 or so minutes of gameplay, Blue Fire has already introduced you to the concept of dungeon keys and surprise encounters... and 5 minutes later, Blue Fire introduces the idea of quest, side quest, and a glimpse to the grand narrative of the entire story. All without direct explanations or immersion breaking tooltips. Its a small thing and not really something you'll notice unless you actively look for it... or unless something so directly pointed towards the player is said that it completely ruins any sense of immersion you may have gathered at that point....[/code]Combat takes... a bit of a back step in favor of movement here. Sure it can feel REALLY good at times to hit the perfect parry before delivering swift justice...but that high only last for so long when your fighting the same 3 or 4 recolored enemies over and over again. Not to mention that enemies... Don't really do a lot of damage. Now before we continue with this line of thought... please do take this with a grain of salt as I have committed the unforgivable crime of selecting the... Normal difficulty... So... Just keep that in mind.Very early on, it gets to the point where enemy damage output simply can’t keep up with how much health I have to tank with. This makes combat encounters feel very mundane to say the least. I thought I could fix it by just raising my difficulty but it turns out that once you start the game, there's no changing that...The healing ability. Now having a healing ability on its own is certainly not a bad thing for a game like this to ship with. Dark souls famously has the Estus Flask and no one complains about that so why is Blue Fire any different? Well healing Items like this aren't usually meant to serve as a reset to combat. The Estus Flask will typically works as a walk back for maybe 2 or 3 mistakes before your back where you started. Blue Fire doesn’t work that way... for most of the game, your healing ability i enough to carry you all the way through a dungeon and to the next shrine or previous shrine if you have to backtrack...The times where difficulty does spike up feel random and misplaced compared to the rest of the game. Add the fact that you really dont have to fight the enemies past a certain point as the currency rewarded for defeating them is used only as a way to buy a limited supply of mana upgrades. Once you’ve upgraded that mana bar completely, theres no other reason to even engage with these guys unless your forced to.[/code]I ran into 2 boss battles that I thought were genuinely entertaining. As far as all the other bosses? Well...Throughout the entire game, there's an emphasis put on movement, exploration, and discovery. When ever you find a new permanent upgrade, the game either puts you in a situation where it'd be beneficial to use it or had given you the upgrade after leaving an area where you wish you had it. Yet when it comes to most boss fights... non of that stuff matters.Kind a like now is a perfect time to round out this video.Whilst playing the game there were so many moments where it felt like Robi Studios really wanted me to sit down, take a breath, and ground myself in the experience I was in... Yea that's right... This whole game is a huge vibe check...The whole is greater then the sum of its parts and for that reason, If you’re even a little bit interested in what Blue Fire has to offer then I’d say Its definitely worth picking it up.

_childDocuments_.review: I first heard about this game after seeing one of Iron Pineapple's videos about soulslike games, but I don't think this could be further from that definition. Aside from the death mechanic where you lose your money and recover them where you died, Blue Fire is a game that mixes elements from platforming games (it reminded me a lot of A Hat in Time, which is high praise from me) and Legend of Zelda-like dungeon exploration (there's a lot of other similarities like small quests, the structure of certain places you visit and the appearance of the main character, which looks like a mix between young Link from OoT and the Knight from Hollow Knight). The platforming is its strongest point, with exploration that demands you mix your moves in the most optimal way, extra missions with progressively higher difficulty called Voids (self-contained maps that put your platforming skills to the test and reward you with extra health points and containing currency to expand your spirit slots, basically passive powerups for attack, platforming, defense and whatnot which you obtain via quests or exploration) and a very, very well done soundtrack (ranging from moody and melancholy to upbeat and mysterious depending on where you are). The recent update also added a lot more content, which I was fortunate enough to play given that I only received the game two days ago and absolutely stormed through it to completion and full achievement hunt. Combat isn't really very demanding, until you hit the midway point in the game. Then you need to pay attention. Some bosses will be very challenging, especially the last one.Definite recommend for me if you're into Zelda or story driven platform games. I really hope the devs add more content because I'd love to have an excuse to dive back into this beautifully crafted world they created.

_childDocuments_.review: Noticeably lacks in polish, but it's fun for its money. Some might find the lack of checkpoints frustrating, however this is more of a platformer, you'll rarely ever be forced to fight. And there are only a few Void trials that could get on your nerves if you insist on doing them as soon as you can.The combat is very, very simple. The shield, its parry and the magic attack you'll never need, thanks to both your dash and double jump refreshing whenever you hit an enemy mid-air. They don't seem to scale in any way either, so it's mostly mashing the attack button and staying airborne while dodging away whenever an enemy attacks.Platforming is decently fun, but feels like it's restricting itself. You get most upgrades for it at about 25% into the game, but it never makes it complex nor gives you a whole bunch of freedom with it. You make the jumps you were meant to make. Voids are sort of an exception for this, because they (well, actually only a couple) demand something of you, and if you fail you have to restart it from the beginning.There are a whole bunch of collectibles, but they're either 1) useless, 2) quest items, 3) ore for sale or 4) robes that have no gameplay effect. You also find spirits sometimes, which are basically Hollow Knight's charms, but there aren't that many of them. They do have a pretty significant effect on your character, but mostly the movement based ones. They're what makes it fun, I'd say.Bosses are a highlight as far as combat goes, but they aren't very complex either. Closest comparison would be Zelda. The game could've benefited from way simpler combat that didn't feel like you have to spam attacks.Still, pretty good for its price. And you'll probably enjoy it a lot more if you don't feel the need to be a completionist and leave the voids you have trouble with for later. I got 22/22 achievements, and one of the worst parts of the game is probably the UI. Especially when you're trying to quickly go through shops.

_childDocuments_.review: Very well executed adventure/platform game.Main focus of the game is on its platforming, broken up into metroidvania style progression arcs in which you collect more movement technology and progress though the game.The world is beautifully presented with a soothing soundtrack and the route gives you plenty of agency to backtrack to previous areas to pick up secrets and flex on your new abilities.Controls are responsive and tight, which is really critical for the precision platforming needed, particularly in the challenging void sections.The free DLC adds 16 more platforming levels and another boss all of which are dedicated hardcore endgame content which pushes all the mechanics in the game to the limit. Well worth a look, even if you arent a fan of the genre

_childDocuments_.review: just play hollow knight. blue fire seems to want to desperately be hollow knight but 3d, but it's just not on that level lol. idk i'd rather play hollow knight than blue fire. hollow knight's more fun in literally every way.in terms of actual review though:The game is inconceivably difficult to navigate. you won't make any progress unless you bash your skull through a wall, because there is no map, and also backtracking is literally a requirement to progress the plot and get to some of the later bosses.platforming challenges can be needlessly unforgiving. the first dungeon has a challenge where you're timed, and if you screw up and fall you have to start over, but you're new to the game so you literally don't have the expertise the game wants and expects you to have, so you're kinda screwed and you have to do it over and over and over and over again until you finally manage to get through it.It does this again just before the second dungeon, but worse because its a giant tower, not a 2-minute task, and you'll get knocked out of the air numerous times by poorly placed enemies that you can't kill because you're out of mana and there's no way to reach them with your swords, and also they freeze you midair so you can't reorient yourself in time to keep from losing massive massive chunks of progress unless you're extremely lucky.There's a void challenge where the hitboxes of the obstacles are too big, it makes trying to get through it feel like scratching my nails on a chalkboard. It doesn't feel like I'm the one screwing up, it feels like the game just hates me in particular for daring trying to complete the stupid thing.Progression is a gigantic drag, I enjoyed it at first but after walking through the world 50 times for an hour or two because I couldn't figure out where the hell the next town was really soured that. You can't have mapless navigation, confusing structures, AND hidden entrances to plot-relevant locations. Actually, scratch that, your plot-relevant locations shouldn't be hidden to begin with, I had to look up how to get to firefall river and I only barely figured out where to find the ice forest areas.It's also sometimes extremely unclear what I need to do to get further in the game. I have no idea how I got as far as I did in the first place, aside from just wandering around and collecting stuff. For a good chunk of my experience I thought the game was JUST stoneheart, the forest boss, the sewers, and whatever the first area is. I was not excited when i was told about the ice area, I was solely "oh there's more places? okay where" and then spent 30 minutes trying to figure out where it was.The combat is boring and a bit unintuitive. Fights aren't fun. Don't buy blue fire hoping for combat, it's just not a combat-centric game, it's a platformer with a sprinkling of badly-designed enemies.Enemies don't receive any kind of knockback, they can still attack even as they're taking damage, meanwhile you, the player, can be knocked back several in-game feet or whatever and you'll have to run back up to it to try n hit it again.Flying enemies are a massive pain and often the only way I can easily reach them is magic, which rarely ever does enough damage to take them out in a reasonable amount of time. Some of them can be reached with your swords, but they might hit you before you get up there and knock you away or, uh, off the stupid ice tower.The bosses' attack patterns have no regard for how the player character is designed; I don't think it's possible to beat the first two hitless, because it's impossible to jump all of their attacks due to how the jumps are timed.Overall it's just not that good a game, which is kind of a shame. The lore is kind of neat, the platforming can be really fun and it's rewarding, but the bad experiences and the terrible balancing really stick out. You can only fail so many times before you want to do something you know you won't fail miserably at and have to start over.You can only deal with so many Paths of Pain before it loses meaning.

_childDocuments_.review: Blue Fire~~~~~~~~ROBI Studios just brought in another of their excellent 3D Action-platformers, Blue Fire. An excellent mix of well-crafted gameplay with amazing audio and visuals. A dark fantasy filled with hack and slash combat and platformer elements with a strong push to explore the game's beautifully crafted world. Initial reaction to the game? A fun hack and slash platformer with stunning visuals, which also comes with a strong storyline. But it’s not all sunshine and sunflowers, Blue Fire also comes with it’s a fair share of issues which we will get to in a bit.Plot: Penumbra is a far-away, desolate kingdom, engulfed in darkness and ravaged by the dark forces.  Penumbra once was a peaceful and prosperous land but now it’s in the grasp of malevolent forces. Just when all hope of light fades, a hero awakens in a laboratory. He finds nothing but death, destruction, and darkness upon breaking free from his comatose slumber. Now our young hero must investigate these dark forces and save the kingdom of Penumbra from their grasp. Gameplay: Right from the get-go Blue Fire pushes players to explore and investigate the world that surrounds our main protagonist. At first, nothing is certain and there are very few clues given in the form of item interactions as to where the story is heading. But as you explore further into the game, you will be greeted with more pieces of the story through the NPCs. And as you explore you will encounter handy stepping stones that will give you more insight into all the neat features of the game. The base movement machines are simple and effective, with WASD to move and the mouse to move the camera. So far so good, but where the game starts to confuse me a bit is with its jump machines. Many people seem to be okay with it ,but tbh I am not a big fan. To perform some simple jumps all you have to do is face the right direction and hit W and jump at the very edge; simple enough. For longer gaps, it’s the same process; just hit Dash with the ALT key. I actually changed main to CNTL Left for convenience, which also works well but I failed quite a few times due to lag/game freeze midair. My main issue is with the difficult jumps, that felt quite unpredictable and difficult indeed with these controls. Even when performing jumps from static object to another static object I failed a lot!! Why? I have no clue. One moment it’s all seamless, and the next I’m constantly failing.  This is mainly due to the lags/freezes that I was facing, which is cool by me as every game faces issues, but these random unpredictable jump fails are weird and kinda hard to explain. Jump machines are really important when it comes to Platformers, so I think these issues should be resolved asap. The good thing is that the difficulty level goes down as you begin to upgrade your main protagonist, boosting his stats. It was mainly getting more jump airtime that helped a lot for a noob like me. Combat: In simple words, I absolutely loved it! Simple left mouse click combat system, which works really well with Blue Fire’s simplistic movement and jump machines. The game also features a decent target locking system, which works really well and surprisingly adds a fun flavor to the game; it’s hard to explain that a basic target locking system makes things more interesting, but it just does. You also get to use abilities (which for the most part work well), and power by collecting mana and being in the fight. Felt a bit underpowered and taxing. The enemy types and bosses you will encounter on your journey are pretty well designed, and they playout really well, with each having their own unique thing, and every time you encounter something new it totally throws you off-guard. The enemy types and the bosses are not too difficult to beat but they can certainly pack a punch if you’re not ready. Blue Fire also does a great job of involving the environment around you, and its platformer elements are put to good use. World design: At some places it’s dark and grim with an appropriate light gradient, and on the others it’s well-lit but appropriately tuned out which fits the game's theme nicely. Other than the Lava and the manner in which the main protagonist interacts with it, I loved every single bit of the game’s world design and detailing. Very well thought out throughout the game. Music and sound effects: Awesome background music selection that goes really well with the theme of the game. Gave my playthrough a great flavor. The same goes for the sound effects, which are very well-designed and thought out (apart from the sound it makes when you interact with the lava; that one is pretty annoying). Positives: + Great Storyline + Good number of quests and side quests + Fun combat system + Void Challenges + Great visuals + Great background music and sound effects + Well thought-out platformer elements + Encourages exploration Negatives: - Quite a few lags/game freezes while jumping- Not a big fan of the jump machine- Certain sound effects could use a retouch - Abnormal loading times - The game often froze while loading A great hack and slash platformer with an incredible storyline and enjoyable combat system.  7/10Key provided by the developer/publisher for review purposes. Any opinions expressed are entirely my own!

_childDocuments_.review: Blue Fire is a great game beneath obnoxious faults. Jumping and dashing feel precise and easy to control. Gaining more platforming abilities leads to exploration in a way reminiscent of classic Metroidvanias. Combat has a hit-and-run like fluidity to it. BUT, and it's a big but, there are flaws ridden throughout that frustrate the moment to moment gameplay. The most noted issue is a lack of checkpoints within the Void platform challenges. Any challenge above a three star rating, you can expect to be extremely lengthy, and one mistake sends you back all of the way to the beginning. You can be 99% of the way through a challenge, having collected every orb within, and one error means back to the beginning, and these challenges are no joke. I like the challenge. I appreciate what the developers are demanding of players, but these challenges are ruined by a lack of proper checkpoint systems. Then there are various other small issues that need to be addressed. In the open world, while exploring, falling sets your character back on platforms you're not sure of, and there is no time to readjust to the reset. That means, if you jumped away from a platform near a ranged enemy and fall, you are sent right back to that platform with the enemy mid-charge on their ranged attack. This has led to deaths that feel frustrating as I cannot do anything to prepare for the reset before getting hit again. The game does not stop you from selling more Ores than you have room for in your wallet. Without realizing the wallet limit of 2,999 initially, I sold easily 10,000 worth of Ores, losing 7,000 of the value in the process. I could not reset this mistake because of the auto save system. Lastly, I have had numerous bugs and crashes throughout my four hours with then game so far. Even with the auto save feature, you are sent back to the last shrine rested at, meaning I have spent 10 minutes of progress lost multiple times. One major bug I had made my character hurt himself in confusion every time I swung my swords. I was simply trying to hit a lever and my character ended up beating himself to death. This has been a lot of complaints, but I genuinely have had so much fun with the game when not dealing with the aforementioned issues. I am really invested in the moment to moment platforming, branching exploration, and appealing aesthetics (the music is great, varied instruments with a flair of Austin Wintory). This has a classic Zelda vibe with heavy-handed influences in Dark Souls and Hollow Knight, all in a good way. I really think the Devs have something great here, they just need to go back and address these issues that frustrate their otherwise great game. With that in mind, this game sadly sits at around a 6/10 for me right now. I do plan on finishing this game because I find it fun, however I will not be attempting to complete all of the side quests and challenges like I normally would want to do with a game such as this. If the Devs can go back and correct the design frustrations I have and patch up the game to rid it of bugs and crashes, this game could easily jump up to and 8/10 or 9/10. As of now, buy this game if you are craving a challenging 3d Hollow Knight. $20 is not too much for that. Otherwise, wait and see if the Devs make updates to the game over the next few months.

_childDocuments_.review: A true love letter to the Legend of Zelda, Dark Souls and Hollow Knight, which are some of my personal favorites! It has been great so far, but the game keeps crashing half of the time I enter into a new area. Hopefully the devs can work that problem out so I can continue to explore the mysterious world they created!EDIT: The game only crashed 2 more times through the completion of the game after that, thanks to the devs for working so hard on this! The game was truly a delight and cannot wait to see what they have coming down the pipes next! Definitely recommend this game to anyone who appreciates LoZ or adventure games in general.
_childDocuments_.name: Blue Fire

_childDocuments_.review: The problem with this being a precision platformer is that there's not a lot of precision to it. You stumble around trying challenges and you don't know whether you've got the skills to tackle them. Some stuff you succeed at feels like you lucked out or found an exploit. And when you get your double-height triple jump, double dash, extended wall run and the extra high spin, it feels like you can just fly around all of the challenges and your only fault was struggling with stuff earlier, rather than knowing where to find the tools to cheese it.Combat is barely there and feels useless. The only thing you get out of fighting enemies are an item that lets you upgrade the magic remote damage spell. The damage that does compared to the melee option is so low, it's really not worth even bothering. Fighting mechanics are very rudimentary and the trailer really does mislead you into thinking it's a substantial element of the game.The world starts out by building expectations, but fizzles out into generic filler pretending to be lore.The only "souls-like" thing about this game is dropping you coins if you die (which is not even a common thing to happen) and having to go back to get them. It's ok, because you actually have a cap on how many you can carry. They're very easy to farm and you don't need them for much anyway.
_childDocuments_.name: Blue Fire

_childDocuments_.review: Although it takes some initial getting used to, there is a solid handcrafted experience here that feels mostly well designed, especially in the character's moveset. From the dashes to double jumps to spin attacks, it all flows nicely and the various tunics give some awesome touches to the overall look. The only gripes I have with the game are when I came to some of the later void challenges. Once I had obtained all the charms and abilities, they were either cheeseable or not too hard to get through, but trying to do them the normal route is incredibly frustrating. Not only is the timing precise on many of them, but there is a lot of jank involved especially with both wall sliding and moving platforms. It's not atrocious, but it really starts to stand out when you reach the end of a challenge and die to something like that. The addition of checkpoints would drastically help this I think. Overall, a solid game regardless and there's a lot of charm to be had.
_childDocuments_.name: Blue Fire

_childDocuments_.review: I've entirely completed this game with the exception of one void that I couldn't beat. Now that I'm putting this down, I have a lot to say about this game.tl;dr:Blue Fire has the potential to be one of the best games I've found on steam but inhibits that potential with bizarre game design and poor game direction. However, I will still recommend this to anyone.The strongest thing that this game has going for it is how it feels and looks.  There was passion in the art here. It was very obvious a lot of hard work went into making the aesthetics of Blue Fire look phenomenal and successfully did so. There was so much detail in every raindrop and the synergy it had with the surrounding environments and textures was perfect. Another, strength is the platforming and the control mechanisms that make it work.I'm not going to consider this a spoiler because of it being introduced almost immediately when you start the game but the voids are what I looked forward to during my playtime. Gauntlets and platforming challenges scattered throughout the levels create such a strong contrast between these mini-levels and the actual environments that are necessary towards progression. They're hard, they're original and they will challenge your patience. Controlling my character and getting to know it's limits was hard to get used to and was the cause of some frustration at the start. I learned that any mistake I made was entirely my fault. I've read a lot of reviews criticizing the platforming mechanics and although they're different and sensitive, its something to master. I feel like it was designed that way as well. Looking at a platform  the size of a penny across a huge gap then being able to maneuver your way to it, landing directly in the middle, just as you planned it. There isn't much room for mistakes and forces you to learn and perfect every stroke.The story felt like watching a folk singer at a small town bar it was so boring and unoriginal. It was predictable. It was dull. The dialogue had me spamming A through every encounter because I knew there wasn't a single word that would've been remotely interesting. Listening to the quest-essential blabber of NPC's would've made you thought this was created by beta phase AI. Everything about the lore and the story fell by the wayside in my mind, making my experience feel heartless.Another glaring issue was the progression design and its back tracking. I mean like, yeah, hollow knight is a clear inspiration that successfully bounces off of while still being somewhat original. But the metroidvania style backtracking made no sense and led to nothing but disappointment. You'll go through six really small biomes/levels. Then you'll look at your journal and think to yourself "Oh, I'm only 22% completed wowee!" Then you'll get a quest to go collect 20 orbs back in the beginning three levels, bored to death and hoping it opens up some exciting new biome or quest. And then it opens an exciting new door, dripping with potential, relieving your anxiety that there isn't anything new to explore. The door opens, it's a boss fight. You exit the arena and receive another quest involving backtracking through the same ♥♥♥♥ for some meaningless and boring reason.This game disappoints. A small yet hard to ignore flaw is it's heavy reliance on cosmetic cloaks and emotes. It's a single player game and you'll spend two hours collecting a random object for an npc and your only reward is a pink cloak. Emotes serve the purpose of uncovering hidden chest. But after just finishing the game with every quest completed, I look at my inventory with all the random loot I got from emoting and they are literally useless. Can't sell them. No more quests to serve possible purpose. I have three dead rats and a bowl of rice just for my viewing enjoyment I guess.HOWEVER.I've spent twenty-three hours playing this game, thinking about how something so structurally beautiful and satisfying can no longer be squandered by the annoying and seemingly lazy poor choices. My answer?An update.A huge update.An update that will turn this game around, onto the road leading to be one of the greats."But ewan, you just made me decide not to buy this with everything you wrote above!"Well, continue reading chap.This game deserves downloads. This game deserves players and most of it all, it deserves appreciation. But not right now.What this game doesn't deserve is to be seen as a failure and cast away to the pit of failed passion projects. I really hope the devs read these reviews because all this needs is an update. A fix. In my perfect world, an massive overhaul of the bland and disappointing aspects will come to make this game the beautiful ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ masterpiece I know it can be.Enough of my tangent, this game is fun. And if I were you, buy it. Play through the entirety of it. Gain a great knowledge of how the devs excelled at such a project and where they failed miserably.Because one day,one daythere will be an update.And all this ♥♥♥♥ will be fixed. Opening up the door for a new contender for the spot of favourite game of 2021.Get it.

_childDocuments_.review: Genuinely fun but I could not ignore many things that bugged me, for instance, the many many similarities to hollow knight, such as the almost charm-like system, the mentions of the void, even the swinging of the duel blades matches similarity to the knights nail. I'm not saying stuff wasn't original, like I'm a big fan of the main characters design but that could be recipe for a lawsuit. Secondly there are many glitches and problems with the flow of the character such as there no being any downtime between getting attacked by a creature, it leaves you in a stun and lets every enemy nearby pummel you. Also I'm not 100% sure but in the first area in the room with the boxes you have to climb up to unlock the door for I'm pretty sure I took falling damage? Which shouldn't be something to worry about in a literal platformer. And take into account I only have 31 minutes on the game so far and I'm seeing this all already. This isn't made to harass the game developers because this game genuinely looks nice but you need to fix this stuff if you want an indie game like this off the ground.

_childDocuments_.review: its pretty good! It's like a weird hybrid of Legend of Zelda and hollow knight. The marketing made it seem like a Dark Souls platformer which in some spots it is but for the most part it's actually a really great adventure game.The bosses weren't too difficult and nothing really to write home about except for the last one which was actually pretty fun! the combat is fine for a platformer game not overly complicated.the challenge stages that you do for heart containers are Dope and a great change up from adventureingthey are really well done and i have no complaintsthe character moves really fluently which i like he can jump like four times!the sound design and music are great!i would say my favorite place is the tower in the abandoned path it's really fun to traverse.now for some criticisms..... the first two bosses of the game were lame As It Gets! we are talking literally almost no effort you can tell most of the boss budget went to the last four bosses. the shield is so worthless that i actually forgot about it during gameplay and apparently you can parry things but the enemies in this game are so easily conquered i don't see a point literally almost every enemy can be thwarted by jumping and hitting them on top of the head repeatedly by doing this technique you can actually avoid all of their attacks... but i really don't mind that because more complicated Fighting would have ruined this game.the main character is like way too edgy looking for this game...he looks like the emo kid that no one takes seriously and everything about his looks contradicts The Game and how he plays in the game because in the game i actually like him and he's kind of adorable with all the little outfits you can get for him....if there were different masks that you could get that possibly could fix it!And the ending was lame as hell and i felt amazingly unfulfilled After playing such a great game!but in the end i can't recommend this enough it's a really fun timeit's very nostalgic for me to play it! _childDocuments_.review: This was a good compact souls-like platformer. Overall not too challenging, though the Voids can get difficult. I also had difficulty with depth perception at times with the platforming challenges, but I guess that's part of the fun! Overall enjoyable.

_childDocuments_.review: Every review of Blue Fire begins with a comparison to give a general idea for the feel of game, Zelda comes up alot alongside Dark Souls (but what isn't compared to Dark Souls these days?). However I'd compare it mostly to Hollow Knight if only in terms of general vibe.Its not Hollow Knight though, obviously its 3D, but its more that every element of the game comes across as lesser. The world is smaller and less interesting, the controls more limited, the platforming slightly floaty, the enemies less varied. Its by no means a bad game but its put itself into a position where its compared to some of the best games out there and thats a problem.So ignore the comparisons if you go in expecting a Zelda x Dark Souls or a 3D Hollow knight you'll be disappointed, instead know that you'll be getting a competent action platformer somewhat flawed but good enough that the majority of players will enjoy it.

_childDocuments_.review: While the story isn't particularly mindblowing or interesting, the side quests and dialogue of characters is well made. The biggest draw in this game for me is the execution of the platforming and the feel of free form to it - the game may feel slow at first, but the more you explore, and the more moves you unlock, the traversal becomes extremely fun. The customization and unlocks really feel worth the explaration on a similar level to how Hollow Knight's upgrades felt.The challenge platformer levels feels challenging and the amount of solutions and skips you can incorporate in them based on the skills you have picked, can make it a different experience each time.Now on the other side, the things that don't work well in this game is combat... While the enemy attacks are well telegraphed anything aside from the bosses feel clunky to fight - the hitboxes on some enemies and especially flying enemies are the bane of enjoyment in this game. Parry will be your best friend for the most part.The last thing that I feel iffy about this game is the camera work, because of how small the character is and how high he jumps, the camera tends to drift a lot in different directions and it's definetly not helping during some advanced air movement that you need to pull off in this game.
_childDocuments_.name: Blue Fire

_childDocuments_.review: Blue Fire does well in several areas, such as level design, platforming challenges, soundtrack, movement, controls, and visual design. However, there are a lot of confusing design choices that I think keep it mediocre:- The money system becomes irrelevant because every level has large collectible packets of money that respawn every time you reload the level. - You are quickly introduced to temples of the gods reminiscent of Legend of Zelda, and each gives you a movement ability - but the game suddenly abandons this concept after throwing two at you in quick succession.- The difficult platforming segments required to increase your max health are very fun, up until the game throws a series of upgrades at you that you can equip to completely break these platforming segments by giving you additional jumps and dashes.- You can guarantee you'll revisit each area up to three times, as the game waits until the very end to let you activate certain objectives you've passed by several times already. - The game advises you to try mixing up your combo, but there's nothing to mix it up with - you have one attack combo and one ranged ability that you can't really weave into the combo.- Finally, the story is completely dry - every piece of lore you receive sounds the same (X number of gods, Y number of champions, etc), the ending is totally unfulfilling, and the plot never advances past "You are a special boy, go beat the big bad and save the world".Overall - not a bad game, but I think your time would be better spent playing or replaying the games that inspired it, like Wind Waker, Hollow Knight, and Hat in Time.

It's taken all of the worst aspects of N64 games and very few of the quality of life improvements that have been added to games since.

_childDocuments_.review: Blue Fire is Hollow Knight meets Wind Waker meets Hat In Time, but only half as much polish and a fifth of the content of any of those three. The first two dungeons are perhaps the best zelda dungeons I've ever seen outside the zelda series. Unfortunately they're literally the entire game. After a series of nearly linear hallways, you go through two dungeons and then the game hands you three hour long fetch quests requiring you to just barely retrace your steps through rooms you've already been to and then the game just ends. There is a core platformer here that is really, really good, but unfortunately the combat and bosses form the vast majority of the content and the combat is sub par at best. There are a long string of side quests that are simply not worth your time, given that they only hand out cosmetic rewards, and most of the level design outside of the two feature length temples is substandard to broken, featuring gimmicky jumps, downright abysmal camera angles, and more than a metric ton of softlock locations that you can simply fall into from a higher location and be utterly incable of escaping.The Game flat out promised me that there would be 5 Temples in it, numerous times, from numerous NPCs as you play through the game. To find out that there's only 2 (and a half) is a gigantic slap in the face. The three final bosses of the three final fetch quests aren't even New. they're reskinned versions of each other because the devs ran out of either time, money, or care.If You're starving for a new Ocarina-Like, Blue Fire provides. But I recommend it with two caveats. First is get it on sale, its only about 9 hours long but only about two to three of those hours is any good, and second is that you can go ahead and quit the game after beating the Water Temple / Uthas Temple, because every point after that is unfinished, threadbare, and quite simply not worth your time. It just drags on and on until the game ends.

_childDocuments_.review: I can't even finish the game because it keeps crashing at the same place over and over on the elevator. The further you get through the game, the more frequent the crashes. The developers shouldn't have released a game this broken. This feels like a Cyberpunk situation. They were probably hoping to release it now and patch it later.Besides the crashes, the game is a lot of fun so far. The combat and platforming is a lot of fun and challenging. I really like the customization such as weapons, tunics, souls, etc. This games doesn't tell you where to go which adds more to the challenge of the game.

_childDocuments_.review: This game RUUUUUUUULES!!!!!EDIT: now that I have beaten the game (just got through with the final boss, nothing after and not every quest), I will write an actual review of what I thought:THIS GAME RUUUUUUUUUUUUUUUUUULES!!!!!!!!!!!!!Blue Fire is a great example of a 3D platformer that really understands movement in ways that put it up there with classics of its genre. if you are even a small fan of games about jumping and moving around, I recommend you buy this as soon as you can, for you will not regret it. The level design in Blue Fire is so well done that everything you can and can't do is very clear. There are many ways of getting to where you want and need to go, and those ways will come to you very naturally just out of how the play feel works. This game understands platforming.I must also give praise to how the act of collecting things and the sword combat are also a good mix with the movement and level design. Everything in this game surrounds movement, from jumping from one place to the other, to defeating a powerful god (?)I will say though, I personally did feel a lot of other aspects of the game were really not as strong, thus making some of the game feel... weak? That feels mean to say, but it is how I felt playing. The story, premise, world building, characters, etc. all made me feel... like I didn't have much good reason to care, aside from a few exceptions (who doesn't find the elevator guy at least amusing?). Though none of this felt much intrusive.The real problem of this is the bosses, which do get a little bit in the way of my fun. I admit that they are all just as much platforming-oriented as the levels themselves, but their huge heath bars and telegraphed attacks don't do a super good job at making you feel like you're in a fight, and I wish the more difficult jumps and all were more integrated into the fights. Fortunately, none of the boss fights ever get super in the way of playing this good game.What I liked the most were definitely the optional "void" platforming challenges. Those tests of button-pressing skill are my favorite parts of any game with confidence in its movement mechanics, and the confidence in Blue Fire's is extremely deserved. I beat all the void challenges before the final boss, finding the portal to each one very naturally when exploring; none of the things I really wanted to find in the world map were ever difficult to find, and I love that about this game.I hold much excitement in my heart to see what else this game and this team have in store for me, because Blue Fire is genuinely some of the most fun I've had with the jumps and the wall runs of video games in a long time.

_childDocuments_.review: The videos I saw looked fun, but if you're interested in a platformer with tight, consistent controls, this aint it. Between the weird fish eye lense feeling and the variable dash AND jump length, it feels like trying to park a boat sometimes. When you swing your sword, you move toward the target, and for a really long time surrounding the action you can't use your shield, so it definitely doesn't reward the fast paced style of play of many other slasher games.I haven't played a lot of this game, sure, but I was looking forward to it being fun and I find myself anxious to put it down after less than an hour. So no, I don't have the full story on how things progress or if they get better, but I'm a customer like some others might be considering, and this is a real, valid experience I had before putting the game down. _childDocuments_.review: I found this to be a decent enjoyable game. Before I played this game I was expecting it to be a sort of 3D Hollow Knight, mainly based on the similar aesthetic. While it does borrow some ideas from Soulslikes, the gameplay is quite a bit more similar to Zelda with a heavy emphasis on 3D platforming.The platforming in the game is pretty good. You start off with a basic jump and air dash movement but can unlock items that grant you wall running and double jump for example, that improve your movement and allows you to explore previously unreachable areas. What I liked about this game is that it reminded me of 90's 3D platformers in the way that you could sometimes cheese your way to reach some platforms and areas you shouldn't be able to reach till later. Basically that freedom to utilise the movement in creative ways. The best example of this is with the Void levels which are optional platforming challenge levels scattered throughout the game. While there is a "correct" way to do them you can also cheese your way through some of the more difficult parts by clever use of the movement abilities. The early void levels are trivially easy but I did quite enjoy some of the more challenging ones you can find later in the game.I quite enjoyed the design of the different areas in the game as they're all designed around getting you to use the full range of your movement particularly if you want to dig out some hidden chests and items. It's worth taking time to explore and trying to get to the more out of reach areas to see what you can find.This games biggest weakness is the combat. Although this game takes a few ideas from Soulslikes, it is definitely not reflected in the combat. It is quite simplistic and offers little challenge. You can gain additional health slots and health recovery slots quite easily, to the point where even the late game bosses are trivial. The only boss that gave me difficulty was the final boss, and that was more down to not understanding the mechanics of the fight initially rather than the difficulty. So overall while I found it to be a pretty good game, Id recommend it more as a decent 3D platformer . If you want a more challenging game with excellent combat and boss fights you won't find it here.

_childDocuments_.review: Having 130%ed the game, I'd say it's safe to say this is a masterpiece and a personal favorite. It's not that often you see this good of a progression system and such good movement, all from a platformer that also has some of the best OSTs I've heard in a game.  However, the game suffered from some stutters, sometimes leaving me with up to "20fps" according to the counter, which would go back to normal, only for them to drop again. It's surely a "my PC problem", but it's still worth pointing out, since it ruined a big part of the experience for me. Also the camera could be unfair on some challenges, which I'm not a fan of, giving you unfair deaths (it's very rare though). Overall, very good game, definetely recommended.

_childDocuments_.review: Before I start the review proper, I find the comparisons to Zelda and Hollow knight somewhat misplaced, but not in a negative way.But first, what is Blue Fire in the first place if it's not that? Blue Fire is a swift action-platformer with a high emphasis on mobility. Most of your challenges are not related to fighting enemies, more on that later, but navigating the platforms and navigation puzzles the game throws at you. The biggest source of these challenges are the 'Voids', semi-optional challenges based around pure platforming you can complete for extra maximum health. Rather than killing you, falling off the platforms or touching a hazard will just reset you to the last checkpoint with no damage taken, so you usually can't get a game over in one of these locations either, allowing you to try as often and as long as you like.Now feels like a good time why I don't think the comparisons to Zelda and Hollow Knight aren't entirely fair to the game. Zelda is a game about finding many tools and using the right tool for the right job, and Hollow Knight is a vast Metroidvania with a huge amount of exploration. In Blue Fire, what you unlock are for the most part mobility tools. After unlocks you have access to a dash, double jump, wall running and a whirlwind attack that acts as a tertiary jump you only get access to by deliberately charging it up beforehand. In addition to that the game is also very linear with very little backtracking, weapons you find only increase your numerical damage without offering new utility and the things you need to do for progression when backtracking are very signposted. The aforementioned whirlwind attack is actually one of the most fun tools in the game. You're supposed to obtain it after unlocking the double jump, but with some clever wallrunning you can actually use it much earlier, acting as a means to navigate platforms in a much more creative and fun way and accessing locations that are supposed to be out of reach at that time.In truth, the way the game builds itself around mobility and platforming reminds me a lot more of a faster-paced A Hat in Time with advanced airdashing and some speedrunners are probably having a field day with that fact. Unfortunately, like A Hat in Time, combat is very lackluster and bland, but AHiT deliberately avoided combat where appropriate and built its bosses primarily around platforming. Blue Fire feels very confident and its combat, and unfortunately there just isn't enough meant on those bones to really dig into for that. Bosses are extremely formulaic and all feel more or less the same to fight. You have a parry mechanic (using a shield that drains a separate resource you fill by dealing damage), but it feels greatly underutilized. There is one enemy in that game that you defeat by parrying their projectile, which will send it back at the attacker, but this mechanic isn't used by any other boss or ranged enemy so it feels like a real missed opportunity.Having gotten all that negativity out of the way, the platforming in this game is excellent. The developers have hidden all kinds of silly knick-knacks in strange out-of-reach places in the main game and the Voids are really fun to learn and navigate. If you aren't particular interested about the combat part of most 3D platformers I definitely recommend sticking to the regular difficulty, all the increases do is make enemies deal more damage and add some extra tedium by removing some checkpoints. It's nothing that adds to the challenge in a interesting or organic way and the game shines by the far the brightest during its platforming challenges, of particular note the optional free DLC content that unlocks automatically after beating the final boss, giving you access to 16 new challenging Voids.But if you can stomach a serviceable if rather mediocre combat system you are rewarded with an extremely fun 3D platformer that will not disappoint on its movement mechanics.If I had to give the game a numeric score, I'd probably give it an 8 or 8.5. A well-crafted world for platforming with extremely fun movement, held back by largely uninteresting combat and monotonous enemy design.

_childDocuments_.review: Pros:-Nice souls-like world and cute artstyle-Action combat and parry system are decent overallCons:-Camera can't be pulled back and is very wonky while platforming, which also throws off depth perception when its needed-No checkpoints during the platforming challenges making for some classic-levels of difficulty that can be off-putting to some and not even worth trying after many attempts-Difficulty cannot be changed once selected-Lacks a much needed map for a metroidvania that has many tucked in paths that have to be explored, some of the required backtracking can be unnecessarily tedious without it.-Lacks warp points for the above reasonsThe game just became unfun to play after a few hours. The gameplay and level design feel like a mashup between Souls, Zelda and Mario games without much cohesive synergy that makes it stale and somewhat boring to play after a while. Its a cheap pickup when its on sale, however I would not recommend this game at full price and would have refunded if I could.

_childDocuments_.review: The first half is great but it runs out of steam super quickly. Only 2 dungeons in and the game is completely out of interesting content. No new abilities, only 2 new areas, nearly-identical NPC's, and 3 underwhelming boss fights + the final boss as well. Imagine a metroidvania where you have every ability only halfway through, and how dull that would be. This game does exactly that lol.For the second half of the game you end up backtracking through very long-winded sections to get to 2 different sets of interactive objects, which you have almost-certainly already found your first time through them. Only now you can finally interact with them because of totally pointless mechanical gatekeeping. One set of these interactables is just 4 orb things that make a bunch of collectibles appear, that you have to then go grab. (Like those bits in Skyward Sword except even more tedious cause there's no gameplay twist). And the other set is 4 switches hidden behind load zones with absolutely 0 indication that that's where they are. (Tons of load zones throughout the game will also just have locked gates behind them. Why not just have the gate block off the load zone itself???? It's such a waste of time.) Both of these sets allow you to access a very basic boss fight. Then there's a 3rd one that is accessed after getting through the 2 new areas, but I would assume it's just as underwhelming as the others. I cannot be bothered to finish this game, it is just too tedious.As good as those dungeons in the first half of the game are, the bosses in both of them are nearly identical. They only have 1 attack, and it's the same one between them. Combat is definitely not a strong point for this game, but with the boring boss fights, and super unreliable air combat, it ends up being a detriment to the gameplay rather than something simple enough to be inoffensive.Anyway, the pacing overall in the first half is great. New characters to meet, with cool stuff to buy from them, a bunch of sidequests that you'll pick up, and the Zelda-like structure with the dungeons and gaining new abilities is super well done. The second half of the game however, you will have nothing left to spend your currency on, besides like 1 special case where you get an overpriced item that lets you run a bit faster. Every NPC is just the same model with like 1 different piece of clothing on it, and the final 2 areas you gain access to feel way too sprawling and spread out, with much sloppier platforming compared to everything encountered prior. The game suddenly feels so much more empty and I would theorize that basically what happened is that this latter part of the game is simply unfinished. Cobbled together a lot more sparingly than the first half of the game was. It's genuinely baffling how lifeless everything suddenly feels once you reach that point. Almost like playing an unfinished beta or something.I cannot in good faith recommend this game just for it's better first half. You'll only get like 3 hours of fun stuff, followed by 5 of endless tedium and mundanity. It's just simply not worth it. The potential is absolutely here for something incredible, but it completely flops on execution. Like, REALLY flops.

_childDocuments_.review: Slight warning i dont think this is a game for everyone, you have to already like 3d platformers and be used to not having a mini map. (Played on steel update)This game does a lot of interesting things, but falls flat by the finishline.  I would like to see what this studios next game is now that they found some success and can finish their vision.Good:-Platforming feels pretty good for an indie 3d platformer, completed all the voids which are probably the best part of the game and only found 2 to be blatently unfun(even then was able to skip about 75% of lucas climb with some tricks). Bringing us to our 2nd point.- there are no real invisible walls, and most terrain, even sloped is pathable.  If you see a place you can likely get to it with some tricks.- Endgame movement feels really clean and almost busted with how fast you get around.The mediocre-Lore/story; kind of interesting that everything takes place in an enormous castle reminded me of metroid fusion, there are some weird boss dialogues that are in a language you dont get to understand which feels bad since i dont want to look at a wiki to know the story. - No map.  While some compare this game to darksouls it feels more like OoT with mario controls, this means that a map would be extremely helpful in some of the dungeons- Only 2 real dungeons in the first half of the game, this is where the game feels unfinished, i expect that the 3 shadow lords were going to have dungeons that got scrapped due to time or budget (this feels especially obvious in Beiras shrine).  In addition to this your character pretty much has all their abilities by hour 3-4 which seems like their could have been more things to add to a zelda style experience- This game wants to be dark souls but doesnt really commit meaing you lose money if you die and you have an estus equivalent but not the actual difficulty or bosses that the "genre" is known for.  Personally these felt extremely underbaked with the estus never improving in potency and improving in quantity 3 times in bursts rather than spacing your 8 upgrades throughout the game- the voids are both your health and utility upgrades, i didnt mind this since i liked platforming, but if you didnt or werent good at it the game probably will deadlock for you- Combat, this was OK for me playing on recommended difficulty.  I thought the game was probably too easy due to the shield being able to instantly block all damage the second you see the enemies movement.  Like other people said most of the enemies look like reskins even if they have a few different moves.  Honestly it would have been better to have less guy in armor foes and add in some beasts or larger monsters to reinforce the sense of scaleTHE BAD- The bosses, which in normal zelda esque games are a fun puzzle are excruciatingly boring, while they have some cool designs and lore the 3 lords of shadow are essentially just strafe til the invuln phase breaks then dash in for a combo or two.  The final boss was decent but unchallenging due to the fact that you can just plummet off the arena to avoid damage.-The spirit vessal, this is pretty blatant and boring padding.  You are forced to revist old areas and collect 60 glowy orbs to progress with the storyline.  If youre going to make a collectathon section use the areas that are fun to move around in(the voids) instead of a filter over an area that has already been explored, or at the very least let us use all our cool movement options and make it a timetrial where you know where the next orb will be and go fast.-Tunics/swords: Again this feels really unfinished, i can almost see that they wanted a majoras mask thing where different tunics could give you different abilities, for example at one point you can buy a disguise of an enemy guard but nowhere do you need to disguise yourself.  The swords as well feel like they may have had extra mechanics but are just very slight damage increases and extremely minor cosmetic changes.  You may as well have just had a unique resource like in hollowknight you could turn in for damage increases while progressing through the game.-Money/ore/shade orbs:  Why is the optimal way to get stronger to run in and out of the town gathering large ore orbs from reloading the area. Why even have a mana system if the only offensive tool is terrible and why make enemies worthless for progression in anything that isnt mana.  At the very least there should have been a way to trade shadeorbs in for ore, not that you ever really run out of money since in the very first town you can double your ore drops.In conclusion this game shows a lot of promise but really could have used a cleanup pass on development.  Still if you like platforming in an oversized world I would still recommend this.Probably a buy it on sale game and run through it in a weekend never looking back

_childDocuments_.review: Love the art style, the music, even 70% of the movement ideas. But the character is so floaty, using an Xbox Controller for reference. There is a camera setting rotation speed but nothing for movement sensitivity. And on a scale of 1-10 it's somewhere around 18-19. Every little flick shoves you about 3ft in a direction you don't want to be. There's no movement deadzone, there is camera deadzone, and even with camera sensitivity cranked to max, the camera is still pretty slow to adjust. Normally there is some room for error to overcome some of this. But there isn't here, and I want to like this game.There are challenges you can find that so far give me only more hearts. And one of those, I can speed to the last 2 "souls" then all of a sudden I can't make a jump 3 ft in front of my character, almost like gravity got cranked up or the "grab ledge" mechanic suddenly switched off. Character just falls. Period. After about 12 attempts on one basic jump, mind you there are a few pinpoint dash jumps you have to hit to get there in the first place, it's rather annoying. I'm not done with the game but it quickly went from, "Wow, this is an awesome title!" to "Wow, they really failed on the precise movement huh?"At this point I can not recommend this title to anyone.Update: Essentially tripled my time. Got to the first "temple", think the game mentioned 4 total. 30% of players have the achievement for getting to the first temple. And I feel like it's because of the "sewer" before it. It's an absolute pixel perfect jumping nightmare. The check pointing in this is so weird. Fall on one side of the room (Even if it's towards the exit) and boom. Back to the starting platform 25 jumps away. Fall on the other side? Pop back up on a ledge 15 jumps from the exit. And when I said pixel perfect, I meant it. There's a narrow band, just as wide as your characters feet to walk on on each pipe. Even if they are narrow or wide pipes. Too much one way or the other, down and back to 15/25 jumps away. As stated before, the game expects you to be precise but gives you the handling skills of someone floating in space using a fire extinguisher to move. The floatiness of the controls is insanely high. And the sad thing is, I want to see more. The combat, the evironment, the music, sound effects, art style. It's all on point. And it's brought down by the movement.

_childDocuments_.review: Game starts out slow but after 5 hours I've unlocked warp and am on the hunt for the remaining 3 temples, 3 mini bosses, and a corrupted queen.It's a connected world like OG Dark Souls, but the game is closer to Prince of Persia: Warrior Within/Reboot. There are basic combat encounters on tricky platforms or in tight corridors, usually one enemy at a time or one strong with one to two weaker enemies.The hardest parts of the game relate to platforming and momentum. You little dude is a bit too floaty, and casts a small shadow which makes launching into jumps a bit of an art. The moves themselves are great, with the usual stuff from platformers complemented by a few neat touches; wall running is free from sticky routes which means you can (while wall running) run along at full speed, come to a halt and slide down, or change direction and go back the way you came; jumping off a wall can be followed by a dash toward it which allows you to climb a little.If there is a complicated sequence of moves you can imagine, I've found it in this game. It's generally difficult in a way most traversal focused adventures won't attempt. For instance, a nice secret I found early on had me dash into a series of vertical wall jumps with another dash at the top to reach a fairly narrow ledge.As for story, it's probably what you want from an action adventure, and where the Zelda and Dark Souls influences are felt most. The world is on the brink, and you could in theory sort it out for everyone by killing off a whole bunch of bosses. Naturally, you're the chosen one, wear a light tunic, and are about 40% the height and 20% the weight of every NPC you meet. You travel the world, saving the gods from corruption overrunning their temples, and dealing with characters from various factions of unclear allegiances. So, not exactly A* work, but like the combat, the story and world building gets the job done allowing the true strength, the traversal, to take centre stage.In other words, it's good.

_childDocuments_.review: This game is fun like gas station nachos or like a hot dog at a sport event. It isn't the highest quality game but its very satisfying. I am playing through the game right now I am guessing closer to the half way mark based on the reviews and video ive seen of the game. I just can't recommend this one. I find myself constantly enjoying the game and then the janky platforming and controls shakes me back out of it. The platforming which is honestly the largest chunk of what make up the game is fun but the controls don't work as they should because this game requires some pretty quick thinking and fast reflexes and moments and the controls can't keep up. example. wall running/jumping works like this. you run at a wall jumping at it your character grabs and slides either forward or backward if you stay still you might think your character would slide directly down NOPE, you slide either forward or backward, and when you jump away from the wall instead of jumping diagnol toward the direction you jump you jump directly away from the wall... The biggest pull of this game is pin point platforming goodness and it delivers sometimes but with the janky controls it just sours my experience with every moment that I should think "yeah I messed up" clearly is more of a design flaw by the devs. The game makes a lot of strange choices and could really use some quality of life improvements with controls and menus but the over all experience is solid. I got the game on a pretty good sale meaning I didn't pay anywhere near full price... I am glad I didn't I'd of wanted a refund quickly... but since I didn't pay full price I don't mind just enjoying what I payed for finishing it and moving on. The reviews ive seen have been gearing toward the positive and I can see why. But if you were expecting a platforming adventure with tight controls and tight combat its not here. the combat is bouncy and floaty and the platforming is janky. But if you come in lowering your expectations and want a fun little game to just turn your brain off to play it. if not find something else.One last little shout out the music here is amazing like seriously Ive turned most of the sound effects off and just left the music running on high with my speakers, its beautiful.

_childDocuments_.review: Edit: While the below points are all still true, it has now been 2 months and this game still can't run on my PC. The fire boss fight still causes an unreal engine crash every time in different spots each time. I have messaged the developers, created support threads on steam and sent in many, many support tickets. They are unable to fix it. There is no excuse at this point unfortunately, not even for a small indie developer. I'm sorry. I can't recommend supporting this game, although I can't deny it's an incredible one. My PC has an RTX 2060 Super, a Ryzen 5 3600 CPU and 16 GB of RAM. That is to say, it's fairly powerful. I experienced about three dozen unprompted crashes to the desktop throughout my 15 hours with Blue Fire, ending in a particularly egregious one. During the fight with the boss of the Fire Temple, ten times in a row, Blue Fire crashed with no warning, leaving me with a message that Unreal Engine 4 had stopped working for an unknown reason. I uninstalled and reinstalled the game, verified the system files, updated my drivers, and continued to experience the same CTD. The boss fight is bugged, and I am unable to continue or finish Blue Fire as it currently stands. I sincerely hope this is addressed in a patch soon, as this game is too good to miss out on. But in a soulslike game where every bit of lost progress is a brutal step backward, issues like this are impossible to look past.Overall, I am extremely impressed with Blue Fire; it walks the line between Zelda, Dark Souls, and Hollow Knight so finely that it truly finds its own identity. If not for the consistent crashes, I'd recommend this game to absolutely anyone who enjoys any of the aforementioned titles in a heartbeat. As it is, I'd advise readers to wait for a patch. Blue Fire is unbelievably fun, engaging, gorgeous and just the right level of difficulty. Your hands will turn blood-red and sweat will drip from your brow as you try to stay alive for just a second longer. With the success of the immersive sim open-world style of Breath of the Wild, fans of the traditional 3D Legend of Zelda games are unlikely to see another one in the next decade. Blue Fire feels to me like a genuine new Zelda title, and that's perhaps the best praise I could ever give it.

_childDocuments_.review: I really wanted to like this, but it feels unfinished. First off, what I liked:+ The movement is generally quite fun and you get to perform some impressive maneuvers near the end.+ The Void sections, which are focused platforming rooms disconnected from the general game world, are really great+ The game is not afraid of asking the player to use the whole moveset in challenging ways+ The artstyle is pretty good and the game seems impressively well-optimisedNow for the unfortunate properties:- The world design is lacking, which is a critical point in an action-adventure game. The game has a strikingly unique setting on paper with the whole game taking place inside a giant floating castle. But you only get to even see the outside world and part of the exterior in like two small rooms. The places inside the castle feel disjointed and not very evocative of the larger setting (volcanic caves?), which is a huge dissapointment and missed opportunity. Seeing how cool the castle design is in the menu screen made me want to go there. The individual areas also don't have a very good sense of place, which isn't helped by the game not having a map at all, making the world layout difficult to imagine as a whole. Furthermore, they're more or less laid out in a straight line with two large interconnecting rooms that don't feel very organic.- There are parts in the game world where the platforming gets frustrating and punishing (the graveyard tower is a good example), which could easily have been mitigated if the overworld made use of the shortcut system that is already implemented very well in the voids. Often, it is not very clear where you will respawn after falling, and sometimes it is right next to an ememy that will repeatedly blast you over the edge again.- The story seems as promising as the setting at first. You are seemingly an experiment made of equal goodness and corruption to be able to withstand the evil, and you see many earlier attempts at making you disposed in huge piles, bluntly explained as "corpses". Then the game never elaborates at all. You also get the story of a god betraying their pantheon seemingly as a setup for the main villain, thus leading to the corruption, but that is also just forgotten. There is barely any cutscenes or narration after the (pretty terrible) final boss. You just see it die, there is a vague explosion and the credits roll.- There are points where the game world does not seem fit for the movement at all. Some platforms were more tiny than the movement feels precise enough to deal with. And while wall running is fun, the same mechanic is used for Mario 64-style vertical wall jumping without distinction, which doesn't work at all.- The music gets kind of annoying and forgetable, as is the npc's going for a kind of Zelda-quirky that it does not nail at all, but that's a matter of taste. There is a great game in here, the parts where I had fun were excellent after all. But sadly, for me the sum ended up being less than the parts. I hope the developers learn from their experiences, because I am very sold on a great adventure-platforming game in a unique setting with this kind of movement.

_childDocuments_.review: This game is aspiring to be a Legend of ZeldaxHollow Knight game and does a decently good job of mimicking a lot of those elements, but overall it doesn't feel cohesive.  It looks very nice, but is lacking greatly in many aspects in terms of game design.  Here are my (many) issues, which evenutally led to me quitting the game, in no particular order:- The movement doesn't feel right, you have a decently high top speed when running and you essentially hit that speed instantly when starting to move, this leads to minor movements for platforming being very difficult.- The world feels empty, there aren't many details in each of the areas and a lot of places are just mostly open space- In order to move out of the first major area, i had to collect 2400 of the currency in the game, which was very annoying because i was picking up currency every chance I saw, and I still had to go back through the level grinding for the last 600 or so. In my opinion, early game should NEVER be gated by currency pickup.- It doesn't make any sense (and can be very frustrating) when entire towns are platforming challenges.  - You drop your soul EXACTLY where you die, with the exception of boss rooms, so if you die by falling off a platform into water far below your platform, when you respawn you have to take intentional damage to jump to retrieve it rather and void out, rather than it appearing on the nearest solid ground.- The wall run ability doesn't work on all walls (which isn't explained, it makes no sense and it really feels like there is no rhyme or reason to which walls you can run on and which you can't). Your stamina use during a wall climb is also different between the overworld and in void challenges, which doesn't make sense.- Combat early game is pretty trivial, flying enemies can be killed with 2 or three energy blasts from a distance (you can shoot around 8 before running out of mana, and there really aren't many flying enemies)  and most ground enemies can't hit you if you are above them, so you can just spam aerial attacks and never have to worry about getting hit- This is a small, but incredibly frustrating issue: barriers that are immediately on the other side of a loading zone.  there are a decent number of places that you clearly come back to later with a key or something, but you have to go through a loading zone to find out.  I don't want to sit through a loading screen to take 2 steps to find out i just have to turn around and go through the loading zone again- Some of the void challenges suffer from global cycles mixing with variable timed platforming.  The point of a global cycle with platforms and things is for a player to be able to sit back, figure out the pattern, and execute the movements they need to get through the challenge. There were some challenges that I faced where a platform starts moving through an area with global cycles when you step on it. This is not an issue on its own, but when you can't see the parts of the global cycle until after you get on the platform and move partially through the area, the point of global cycles is immediately negated and it makes the platforming basically impossible unless you get lucky and happened to start the process at the right time by accident.- The bosses i did end up fighting didn't pose any challenge at all, and seemed pointless overall.  The only reason i had to take 2 tries to fight the second boss was because he glitched and wouldn't pop out of the ground once i killed all the enemies he spawned in the second phase, so i had to kill myself to reset the fight.  They don't utilize any of the skills you pick up in their dungeons so they feel like just variations of the same fight... run up and hit the boss, run away to not get hit back, there is no variety.- This is just being nit-picky but was incredibly frustrating for me when platforming: the dash has a variable length depending on how long you hold the button, which feels really awkward.  holding a button to jump higher makes sense, but with a dash ability, it just doesn't feel right.- NPC's are REALLY boring, none of them feel unique and i found myself just skipping talking to people if they didn't sell me anything, I quickly stopped caring about the plot because everyone just said the same things over and over again, with no new information- I also don't understand why interact and shield have to be bound to the same button, i found myself on many occasions shielding briefly instead of grabbing a ladder, talking to a person, opening a chest, etc.There are a few other issue that i didn't mention because at this point I am already beating a dead horse. Honestly i don't even think all of these things would need to be addressed for me to want to pick it up again, the big issue is that all of these problems compound onto each other at the same time and annoyed me to the point that i didn't want to pick it up anymore. If even a few of these things were fixed, i would be willing to try it again, but until then I don't really think it is worth my time.

_childDocuments_.review: Blue Fire is a 3D adventure platformer first and foremost.Pro: - Looks cool and atmospheric- Music is okay- Sound effects and special effects are alright- Exploration is rewarding- Freeform puzzle solving, platforming sections in open areas are funCon:- No map or quest markers in large 3 dimensional areas with multiple exits and hidden sections. If you're playing this blind, you'll waste lots of time running around searching for the right exit or items that you need to progress.- It's a platformer with the 3D camera of Dark Souls, meaning you are effectively blind in narrow corridors where there are obstacles everywhere- Combat is pretty much irrelevant. Enemies are pushovers, movesets are heavily limitedConclusion:If you don't like platformers, you won't like Blue Fire. If you do like platformers, Blue Fire is going to make you feel like 3D platformers were a mistake. Having to deal with the camera getting stuck and randomly turning or not turning on its own is miserable, especially since the more difficult the platforming sections require precision jumping in narrow spaces. On top of that, you don't even know where to go half the time, so it all feels like you're just wasting your time.It starts out fun with platforming in open spaces and few enemies, but after about three hours in, things turn sour.
