_childDocuments_.review: I am only an hour in. That's it. So in a lot of ways. I have no idea what I am talking about and this "review" should be completely ignored. Having said that...I have been at my computer all day and wasn't totally pumped at the idea of opening up a game that would require more mental focus, but my a$$ has a mind of its own and wasn't going anywhere. So I opened up Norco. I remember noting about 30 minutes in that I was enjoying myself. And here is why... It is well written and does not use a lot of words to convey the story. I like that. This is a bad analogy, but imagine you are reading a book in point form, but the points are written really well and you don't feel like you are missing out on the story. The story is progressing at a good pace.So an hour in, I have a monkey as a friend because I won a staring contest against him. I have a robot friend driving me around on a motorcycle. I have punched an a$$hole - not literally. I might have offended Jesus. I changed the script of a Hollywood movie and... you have to pet the cat. That alone was worth the price of admission. Pet the cat. Good times.In the opinion of a small round purple fruit - it moves at a good pace, story is really well written, it has moments of solid humour. Need I say more.
_childDocuments_.name: NORCO

_childDocuments_.review: I've only just begun maybe about an hour in. Pacing feels nice, not overwhelming although get into reading mode. Enjoying the visuals, narrative, location, fun creative world building with potential to become more challenging the further I go. So far it feels like my choices have held a lot of weight, which feels good! And I don't feel like I'm going to get soft locked or pulverized for missing a small detail, always a +I'd recommend it!
_childDocuments_.name: NORCO

_childDocuments_.review: I absolutely loved this until the ending, which disappointingly left a lot unresolved and unanswered. On balance I still enjoyed it though and would recommend it. I played the demo of this around 2017 (it was completely different) and don't remember much except enjoying it. I'm also from the South and hadn't gone home in a long time and had a lot of other weird parallels with the main character here, so that also colored my playthrough some. The best part of Norco is the high weirdness all co-existing in a single real place. There's a lot of wild stuff going on, but people still have to use the toilet, go out for groceries, and pay the bills. The wild apocalyptic biblical predictions, cyberpunk dystopian eco terrorist body horror, and goofy humor all roll one into the other, blending into something unique and, somehow, plausibly human. The devs have released a kind of lore pack that addresses some of my issues with the ending. An info dump isn't as satisfying as an in-universe explanation but it's something. See it here:
_childDocuments_.name: NORCO

_childDocuments_.review: Norco is a point and click that tackles abstract themes about Religion, family and guilt in an even more abstract manner. While being as vague as possible, Norco still delivers a narrative which is tight and keeps you clicking as you uncover layers upon layers of mysteries. A lot of text is like poetry, and sure seems inspired by religious texts. If you enjoy such darker mature themes, you would also enjoy NORCO.
_childDocuments_.name: NORCO

_childDocuments_.review: Reading some of the reviews here, I feel like I was playing an entirely different game to everyone here.I went into this game with really high hopes, looking forward to an interesting point and click experience (one of my favourite genres!) - but I got very sick of the writing very quickly. I didn't connect with any of the characters, the worldbuilding was boring. Halfway through the game I was really bored and started skipping through dialogue because I didn't care, and the last 20% I was just trying to check the game off. I should have stopped playing earlier really.There's also a bizarre inclusion of a combat mechanic that really makes the world feel extremely fake. One of the first events you come to is some big guy who's a bit of a ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ and says you can't go into a shop so you just beat the snot out of him. Then shortly after you're trying to break into a facility to retrieve a cardboard box of gubbins that you don't know the contents of, because it was stolen from you. You have to do this by beating up two robots with rifles, who shoot you repeatedly but it's fine I guess? You can just lose the fight where you get shot like 5 times and there's no penalty, which just makes the world feel like there's absolutely no stakesMaybe there's some hidden meaning that I just didn't 'get' that makes this game a beautiful piece of art, but I guess I got too bored to get anything out of it. Really couldn't recommend it at all. If you want something along these lines, the Bithell Circular games are enjoyable text adventures (Subsurface Circular and Quarantine Circular), or Disco Elysium is a fantastic pick, but if you're reading a review for NORCO, you probably already know about it.
_childDocuments_.name: NORCO

_childDocuments_.review: I wanted to complete this game fully before giving an honest review. As someone who lived in Southern Louisiana for the first two decades of their life and moved away out west for work, I didn't want to give this game a great review on just nostalgia and an ache for a past life. So I finished the game and I can still solidly give this masterpiece a 10/10. I'm not going to give away plot points as I want everyone to experience this game on their own. The story is rich and inventive with sci-fi and gothic elements that make the moody atmosphere pop. The writing is beautiful as well, as I found myself getting lost in the visual descriptions as you often study your own thoughts in the game. I don't think I can describe how beautiful and creepy the pixel art can be in this game. This game is by no means a horror game but I did jump a couple of time due to one particular character. "Eerie" and "unsettling" are the best words I can use for this game in some instances and its freaking great. The game felt fresh with all of its little surprises.My one complaint? I wish it was longer, but I know the developers worked hard on this beauty.  I loved this game. I may play it again one day to relive the days of riding down Airline Highway and the Bonnet Carre spillway.
_childDocuments_.name: NORCO

_childDocuments_.review: Not really a game for me. I am a huge fan of point and click adventure games, but this really didn't do much for me. The story was not that interesting, and all the way through it tried to be a lot more "artsy" than I liked I guess... The puzzles were trivial, but that would have been ok if I had fallen more in love with the story. All in all it was more of an interactive story than an actual adventure game.
_childDocuments_.name: NORCO

_childDocuments_.review: Fantastic game, with incredible sense of place and atmosphere. Memorable and haunting characters. Doesn't spoon feed you the plot. The puzzles aren't especially complex (and it can spoon feed you the answers sometimes) but it's really about exploration and the journey rather than puzzle solving. Lived up to my high expectations.
_childDocuments_.name: NORCO

_childDocuments_.review: I felt like I was part of it all, wandering through every last stretch of the wretched, deteriorating land in Norco, and, having found myself now a stranger to where I was supposed to call home, I was haunted at once by a peculiar sense of nostalgia for a past I never had, and an ever-intensifying curiosity about my own detachment. Truly an experience. The writing is fairly strong: poetic, enigmatic, and, at times, fresh as morning dew.
_childDocuments_.name: NORCO

_childDocuments_.review: Apparently, an absolutely insane 6-hour-long point & click adventure game.Graphics are utterly gorgeous, the music is absolutely wonderful. The story is certainly unique and engaging, but Christ is it nuts. Gameplay is simple and relatively on-rails, with some light-medium puzzles and a few minigames to space it all out. Humor is modern and irreverent, and so is the social commentary. The characters are very colorful with wacky, vibrant personas, in a kind of delusional Louisiana at the end-times. I don't really know what to make of this, it's certainly a very polished game, it's certainly a very good game, and for better or worse it's also a really bizarre one.
_childDocuments_.name: NORCO

_childDocuments_.review: Never heard of it, but took a chance and grabbed it during a Steam sale - because it looked interesting. What an awesome find. For me - in most game categories - story is everything, and NORCO did not disappoint. It had;' - classic mystery elements that pulled you forward - appropriate puzzles (challenging, but didn't slow down the story) - family relationships, warmly and honestly realized (both hopeful and sad) - some interesting - and also twisted - characters - well written interactions (albeit sometime obtuse) - lots of humor and funny references - sci-fi tones, including a cool robot - a toy monkey (should have had more screen time) - a very "special" catI have 400+ games, so I intended to occasionally jump in and out of this one. Once I started, I binged for 12 hours over a weekend and finished. I had to know how things would play out. I was not disappointed. Plus, the "Point and Click" style  meant I never had to put down my beer.
_childDocuments_.name: NORCO

_childDocuments_.review: Life was never easy for you so you left home and decided to explore what the world had to offer, but then your mom died and you decided it was about time to come home just to check on your brother, Blake. When you arrive home you find that something is definitely not right, and your brother is nowhere to be found. There are whispers that your mother’s death, caused by cancer, wasn’t as straight-forward as it first appeared, and that there’s some sort of dark underbelly that is trying to pull you into its depths.In the game, NORCO, you will be playing the role of Kay, the estranged daughter. The only thing that is slightly normal is the robot, Million, a robot that your mother rescued and used as her assistant in whatever strange investigation she was conducting at the end of her life. You will visit different locations all over the city, and a couple outside of the city. In most of these areas you’ll get to interact with the locals and discover how strange and mysterious things have become in your hometown. The game is primarily driven through your dialogue choices, and you will notice that highlighted text in the game will be of the utmost importance, so when you see some, make yourself a note. I can honestly say that it definitely helped keep the game moving when those highlighted text items were part of a solution to a puzzle that stood in my way. You will be retracing your mom’s last days, as well as trying to figure out whatever happened to your mom. If you are not a gamer into doomsday savior vibes, this is probably not for you, but without giving too much away, I wanted to just state that this game has DOOMSDAY VIBES all over the place. There’s a ton of different characters, some you want to strangle, some you feel sorry for, there’s even a couple that you wonder how they are still alive, but overall the characters all have their own personalities, and that helps the gamer get further immersed into the story. The one thing that really made me scratch my head, throughout the game, was the very strange battle mechanic(s). It felt like the developer thought the game needed a bit more spice, or knew that the game needed some battles to the death (which for the record NONE of my characters EVER came close to dying). You may have noticed that I put that ‘s’ in parentheses when I said battle mechanic, and that’s because there were a couple disjointed ones slapped together. Now that being said, and the fact is that this game is very puzzle heavy, the mechanics are puzzles in themselves, so I guess that was the developers approach.This is definitely a game that is not going to be for everyone, but there’s something to it that kept me playing from start to finish. From my understanding there is more than one ending to the game, but once I completed the game for the first time, even though I felt there HAD to be a better ending than the one I had, I did not go back and try again.
_childDocuments_.name: NORCO

_childDocuments_.review: What a beautiful game. I wouldn't spend too much time trying to explain, but I think if you are a point and click fan, or enjoy graphic novels this one is for you. Beautiful visuals, deep writing, amazing music, a variety of different gameplay sequences, intriguing story, morbid jokes, and so much more. Completed it in 6 hours. Highly recommend this experience.
_childDocuments_.name: NORCO

_childDocuments_.review: Poetry, in words, in images, in world conjured and story told. It's a beautifully written game, evocative in its surreal and meditative aesthetic. It went in directions I did not expect, delving into the esoteric. Thematically, it's in the lineage of Disco Elysium and Night in The Woods as concerned with the intersection of past with present, and futures once imagined, lost and stolen. This is a work of American hauntology.The artwork is beautifully rendered via detailed pixel art. I have never been to Lousiana and New Orleans and I found myself throughly immersed within Norco's depiction of this region. Given the developer's having been raised in the town of Norco, there's a clear personal connection and intimacy that comes across, a sense of place, of belonging and displacement. These are not mutually exclusive. There's a tension throughout. There's a social function in this. Much of the town and region's history is interspersed throughout the game, and the company, Shell, plays a key role, loosely disguised as "Shield." History here is not static. The past exists in the present, running through it like a livewire, shaping and reshaping it. The writing's good enough to pull this off, with poise, poignance and profundity.The writing's also pretty funny at times. While some things don't land as well as others, but one moment in particular had me laughing my ass off. I'm also impressed by the quality of the characters. Some great exchanges between them.If I have any critiques, it's that the combat is basically just a placeholder, but it functioned well enough to lend excitement to the moments where it was deployed.
_childDocuments_.name: NORCO

_childDocuments_.review: I don't really have anything substantial to add to the polygon or uppercut crit reviews, or indeed to any of the steam reviews - I think the Disco Elysium comparisons are reasonable, although I do also think that Disco Elysium was almost boundlessly optimistic while Norco is melancholic to the point of being depressing, despite daft jokes and quirky characters. The art and music are stunning, and the writing is gripping. There's also minimal-to-zero 'moon logic' and pixel hunting, making it quite easy to blitz through to the somewhat abrupt ending in about four hours.But perhaps the most resonant thing that I took away from Norco was the string of wikipedia pages I opened to try and get to grips with what i'd experienced in the game, as well as the IRL Norco, LA, where the developer grew up. "Norco, Louisiana". "Fenceline community". "Shell plant explosion in Norco, Louisiana". "Cancer alley". "Toxics Release inventory". "Sacrifice zone". "Locally unwanted land use". "Transport divide".Things are bad, man, and this game won't help you feel like they're getting much better. Give it a go when you're feeling just a bit too happy.
_childDocuments_.name: NORCO

_childDocuments_.review: 我只能无情揣测为这是一个不敢讲但恐怕以作者的理解也有点讲不清的控诉。 前期有点魔幻现实主义，又有点美国众神的味道。能投影到美国的现实，是个无尽的不可解的既知结局但还想听听别人如何讲述的虚无故事。I can only ruthlessly surmise that this is an indictment which dare not speak but which, I am afraid, in the author's understanding, is somewhat ambiguous.garretts（ditch men） is  just like rednecks, powerful but can only engage in some abstract activities, completely against the erosion of capital.Even if there were prophets (martyrs) pointing to where their "moon" was（with her hand）, but these stupid, unarmed minds would only stare at the hand, make a statue of her, and paper it, this activity even became an opportunity for some people to stomp on their own kind for a moment's survival, sadly.Capital even welcomes such a "rocket launch", and they dress up for the event, even if they do not understand its dangers.This is the most novel of the numerous parties of capital, but it is also the most regrettable entrance before the silence of Red Neck.Let your prophets flee to the imaginary kingdom of heaven, and religion is the triumph of avoiding reality.Such an America is only dark, only dying.A little bit of magic realism, a little bit of American gods.The reality that can be projected onto America is an endless, unsolvable story of nothingness with known endings but still wanting to hear how others tell it.
_childDocuments_.name: NORCO

_childDocuments_.review: one of those games where you are immediately sucked in by the art and atmosphere. a surrealist neo-noir story set against the backdrop of a crumbling cyber gothic version of southern louisiana. very well written storyline with memorable characters and even a funny moments that made me genuinely laugh. the only other time I had this much investment into the story of a game in a similar genre was Kentucky Route Zero, even though that game dragged on spots (albeit one of the best game soundtracks I've ever heard). visual novel / point-and-click adventure type games are very hit and miss for me, but this is one of those experiences where every element of the game all bounce off of each other and create this really potent and memorable experience.
_childDocuments_.name: NORCO

_childDocuments_.review: If Disco Elysium is a meditation on lost futures and the value of self destruction, Norco answers with an indictment that we might be inhabiting the end times and should hold on regardless. Every scene and character portrait is a painstaking work of art that works along with the dreamy soundtrack to draw you into the gorgeous, hazy bible belt setting. The point and click gameplay is straightforward (and at times a little overbearing with handholding), with small minigame sections to mix things up somewhat, but rewards interacting with the world and the people in it to uncover another small truth about it. I don't think I've come across anything that quite captures the sense of melancholy and unease that dominates the current moment in the 20s.
_childDocuments_.name: NORCO

_childDocuments_.review: I want to write a really long, detailed review about this one day coming from the same parish Norco itself is in, but I'll save that for the next time I play through it. Even though I'm not much of a writer and it'll probably be a mess. I felt like this game perfectly captured things I've never been able to properly express. There were parts of it that had me sobbing, I felt so seen in understood in a way it was like ripping a nightmare from my brain and putting it on screen in a video game. But that's not to say only people from southeast Louisiana can find something of value in this, I think absolutely anyone can play this and find things that they connect to and relate to.It's a wonderful work of art and I am so glad it was made.
_childDocuments_.name: NORCO

_childDocuments_.review: I expected a bit more from Norco because it was kinda trending and while I liked the dreary setting and atmosphere, it also felt like stuff was just happening and then the game was over.  Maybe that was the point or maybe I'm big dumb... could be both.  Hard to say.For a point and click adventure, I never had to look up how to solve any of the puzzles and that's a big plus for me (because it makes me feel smart).I liked the aesthetic.Giving it the Thumbs Up because it's still an interesting ride and the price is right.-e- Also, pretty easy to get 100% achievements if you care about that sort of thing.
_childDocuments_.name: NORCO

_childDocuments_.review: I would highly recommend this game to any point-and-click adventure fans! It is something to check out even for those that simply enjoy nice storytelling, well-written characters, and atmospheric games. This game oozes style and atmosphere!It is a techno noir game, that reminded me of Blade Runner, a mystery bigger than life in the style of the Da Vinci Code and a kind of autobiography and reflection on a real town in the United States called Norco. I would even dare to say that Norco is a character on its own.Part of the game is a typical old adventure-style game, part is like a visual novel, and part is like a textual adventure.Pixel art graphic style is suitable and only elevates the game to a higher level. For music and sound, I also only have high praise. The soundtrack is simply as haunting as it is beautiful. All those things just enrich the game.Puzzles in the game are quite well balanced and not obscure at all. For me, game mechanics are hit or miss most of the time. Some mechanics are put in the game just to consume the time as I see it. Mind Map, though nothing new in games, is superbly done and enjoyable. Maybe my favorite mechanic. I liked most puzzles, even though they are easy to figure out and they are generally nothing that special. I'd say solving the puzzles just follows the flow. The game isn't too long and it doesn't overstay its welcome.Story-wise, there are a lot of different topics, but they are masterfully interwoven. There are also quite a lot of moments that, even though the game is mostly serious, had me laughing. Those little moments are best experienced by finding them on your own. A combination of serious topics, with masterfully added quirks and humor, is top-notch!The game has multiple endings and some of the choices do matter. I'd say its creators are big fans of old point-and-click games like, for example, Monkey Island, and I believe some of the puzzles in the game are inspired by it.Don't let this game slip under your radar, especially if you are a fan of the genre.My only problem with the game is that most puzzles are just too simple, but even with that issue, Norco is one of the most enjoyable old-school adventure games in recent times.9/10
_childDocuments_.name: NORCO

_childDocuments_.review: I first played Norco on Xbox gamepass and was left so astounded by it, that I had to buy it on Steam (plus the artbook and soundtrack too). After playing it again, I am certain to say that it is my favourite videogame narrative. The writing is superb, poetic, relatable, mysterious, humorous, it's perfect. The setting and story have so many layers that link together seamlessly. The pixel art is the best I've ever seen. The music fits the tone of the visuals beyond perfectly. Norco is without a doubt one of my favourite interactive artworks.
_childDocuments_.name: NORCO

_childDocuments_.review: Norco has a charming artstyle and it is very intriguing once you first start the game out. However all that quickly wears out since the game's story is rather pointless, with very poorly written character dialogue and very out of place mechanics. While the game does a good job of immersing you into the world from the start without overexplaining too much, I just found zero reason to care about the it. The characters are all either very bland or they all talk like they are from 2014-5 forums and image boards. BRUH BRUH BRUH. The game does offer some very significant choices they are very few and far between, it's, for the most part, linear without any good puzzles to spice things up. It throws a  couple new mechanics here and there trying to keep up variety but they all fall short. The RPG fights are laughable and the boat sections are tedious. The story as a whole also suffers from a pacing issue, while it was short it felt like it dragged on because it offered no intrigue. For a point and click there just isn't enough interactivity with the environment (while good at the start, this gets a lot worse about halfway through the game), and Kay, being the blank  slate that she is offers no interesting descriptions or thoughts about anything around her. There's even a "mind map" that lets you keep track of characters and everything that has been happening yet there's no flavor. We are supposed to be in a mind of a character and it's basically just a game wiki. There's just nothing interesting there and it all felt like a big waste of time. Neither the journey or the ending felt fulfilling in any way. I love good point and click adventures but this just isn't it. I'm sorry.
_childDocuments_.name: NORCO

_childDocuments_.review: Highly recommended to everyone, but ESPECIALLY if you're from South Louisiana. There is a universality in what it's presenting that will strike true regardless of where you're from: about Home, about industrial sickness, about online, about dysfunction.  But it cannot be overstated how much NORCO is Norco is New Orleans is Louisiana. Within the towering flamestacks and twinkling lights draped in sci-fi spectacle is a living, breathing place that this game captures in such a raw, poignant way that I'm not even sure how to begin to articulate. It feels exactly like the many sleepless nights spent at my grandparents' in the suffocating heat, watching car headlights blink over the overpass from the window, trying not to think about the roaches skulking on the walls.Quite a few published reviews focus mostly on the sci-fi elements. I don't want to downplay them, because they are an integral and well-executed part of the whole package. But to me, the reason I'm never going to forget this game is because of its setting and characters taken straight off of the cushions of my family's couch. Short and beautiful. Worth it for the pixel art alone. Great soundtrack. Compelling story. You're missing out by skipping this one.
_childDocuments_.name: NORCO

_childDocuments_.review: I disagree with the comments that were disappointed in the second and third acts of the game! If anything I thought the very beginning was a bit slower but once I was hooked, I was hooked. Loved the artwork and various gameplay styles incorporated into the overall point and click game. Very absorbing, would recommend :)
_childDocuments_.name: NORCO

_childDocuments_.review: God called you and you said that sounds ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ crazy dude. The system, the petrol, the smoke and the water and the people. Transformation. Blood and broken lines of family, how could it be any other way? From the heavens to the gutter, the gutter to the swamp. These people are poor, dirty, drunk, laughing. So have you been. An astonishing work.
_childDocuments_.name: NORCO

_childDocuments_.review: A southern gothic science fiction adventure game taking place as the protagonist Kay returns to her hometown in a post Civil War US amid worldwide catastrophes in order to find her brother after your mothers death from cancer. New Orleans is an industrial dystopia overseen by the Shield Chemical corporation (a stand in for Shell Oil that is in the real life area) and as you explore more you learn about a mysterious client your mother was working for and the different people that had taken an interest in her. The lead occasionally shifts to the recent past where you play as Kay's mother. Norco has little focus on traditional adventure puzzle solving where you mostly find and combine items and instead will often give you multiple ways to handle a problem, minor turn based QTE and memory based combat, text adventure scenes, driving a boat in a swamp set in an alligator hand puppet's poetry. While Disco Elysium and Kentucky Route Zero dabbled in some similar themes and dealt with stranger and magical elements of an otherwise often serious and more realistic setting, Norco goes further into the strange and leaves with much less concretely answered.Well written characters and story filled with corporate conspiracies, ghost, scamming tech companies selling false hope, cryptids, humor, cults, broken family ties, and sudden violent twists with strong world building, a melancholic dreamlike atmosphere, and some of the best artwork in the genre (or industry in general). The mind-map mechanic is utilized well to fill in character details as you learn more about people and examine your thoughts on them or on the information you have learned, also giving a clearer picture of their face over time.Screenshots:
_childDocuments_.name: NORCO

_childDocuments_.review: Norco is an old-school adventure game, taking place in an alternative futuristic/supernatural Norco, Louisiana.Pros:+ Mysterious setting, outstanding world-building, refreshing and diverse characters+ Very intriguing, unique and vibrant yet despairing story, which touches many themes+ Beautiful and colorful pixelated artstyle & subdued electro music, which blend exquisitely together, elevating the experience+ All of the above woven through splendid narrative techniques and direction+ Runs well on low-end computersCons:- "Puzzles" are too easy to understand and follow, making the game unchallengingDo I recommend this game: Yes, absolutely!
_childDocuments_.name: NORCO

_childDocuments_.review: Such an amazing narrative! Southern Gothic is a genre I've never dabbled with, but this game gave me such a wonderful first experience with its aesthetics. I've never thought of the American South this way — it is indeed a suture of industrial capitalism (the olden days of plantation and the newer ages of oil) and evangelical faith (of multiracial origins). And they both rely on the myth of a New World (although in their own narrative, they'd call it *the* New World). The artworks and the music  (including the SEs) did an exceptional job setting the atmosphere. I enjoyed every single second of this game!
_childDocuments_.name: NORCO

_childDocuments_.review: I don't even know what to say about Norco, so I'll try to keep it brief and ask you to watch RagnarRox's take on the game on YouTube.This is a profoundly American story, yet it felt extremely relatable from the start (I've lived my whole life in Buenos Aires, ARG). There are a lot of topics that don't particularly affect me in my personal life (religion, homesickness, estranged family, etc.), but it all still connected on a very visceral level; the storytelling prowess of the Geography of Robots team cannot be overstated. It has some of the most beautiful and creative pixel art I've ever seen, but I feel that the music is what made me fall in love with its aesthetic vision; both are unique and wonderful. The gameplay mechanics were simple and intuitive, and you'll always have elements to guide you in case you get stuck or somehow can't advance.The game is probably not for everyone (its narrative style definitely adventures into some nice and weird places), so I would recommend trying the demo first in case you're not too confident about it; I think it's a very faithful representation of the rest of the game. I noticed several accessibility options in the menu, but didn't feel the need to use any of them, so I don't know how effective they are.Lots of love for the GoR crew and everyone who made this work possible... And Crouton, obviously.
_childDocuments_.name: NORCO

_childDocuments_.review: Overall I tried to lower my expectations when it came to Norco, but when I got to play it, it pulled me right in and I have enjoyed every minute of it. It will tell stories about loss, terminal illnesses, religion, hope, and penetrating sadness with a will to come over it. The presentation is what caught my eyes, the writing and all the details made me played it through 3 times. I would suggest this game to anyone who is mature enough to handle it. Give this game a chance, you won’t regret it!
_childDocuments_.name: NORCO

_childDocuments_.review: This game is an absolute masterpiece and probably my GOTY 2022. If you have any interest in amazing writing in a cyberpunk-ish setting in the style of Neuromancer this is for you. The graphics are done in really great pixel-art.Gameplaywise it's a point and click adventure game with some minigames added in between, but the main focus is lots and lots of text.
_childDocuments_.name: NORCO

_childDocuments_.review: I don't know what this aesthetic is called but I love it. For me this was a truly unique experience. The aesthetic is nothing like I have seen before, the characters are fun, the story is told in a really cool way and it has robots. It's niche and maybe not for everyone, but if it's up your alley, you will love it.
_childDocuments_.name: NORCO

_childDocuments_.review: An oil soaked fever dream which unfolds in a distorted and dystopic future Louisiana. Dense worldbuilding, beautiful pixel art and an understated but evocative soundtrack combine to render a palpably decaying world occupied by: a mall-dwelling cult of micro-influencers, a rogue security robot, and hand-to-mouth gig economy workers carrying out bizarre clandestine tasks in service of a mysterious (and vaguely sinister) phone app.The best point and click games transcend the limitations of the genre because of truly excellent writing and this has that in abundance. Strongly recommended if you're in the mood to soak up some melancholic near-future sci-fi, which occupies a strange metaphysical void somewhere between the work of David Lynch and Charlie Brooker. Despite the dystopic atmosphere, it's also genuinely funny at times, successfully tapping in to the same vein of wry satirical humour as it's influences.It's not going to blow you away with any gameplay innovations, but it's well worth playing through for it's immersive atmosphere and memorable storytelling.“Black as midnight on a moonless night.” - Agent Cooper (Twin Peaks)
_childDocuments_.name: NORCO

_childDocuments_.review: Best game of 2022 so far for me, and I don't say that lightly. Finished in about 7 and a half hours. but it has a surprising amount of replayability in it--alternate endings, alternate dialogue branches. Details of the story change based on choices you make in the game, and the consequences are delightful and feel impactful. Something as seemingly meaningless where Kay was in a wild party might end up carrying a detail that gets referenced all the way to the end of the game,  The writing honestly makes me jealous as a wannabe creator for just how good it is. Recommend you play with a Louisiana native just to see how many references they catch in the gameplay!

_childDocuments_.review: How did this get made, much less published? Point-and-click adventure game combining Southern Gothic, cyberpunk, magical realism, and post-[insert socioeconomic concept here]? Yeah, that screams Mainstream Investment Opportunity.Yet, it did get made, and it’s amazing. Lots of comparisons are made to A Night in the Woods and Kentucky Route Zero. They’re valid.  NORCO and the Pennsyltucky Games both combine the struggles and insecurities of the post-American Empire working classes with obscure academic concepts. Whereas A Night in the Woods goes for a cartoonish ironic metaphor and Kentucky Route Zero spins a mystical, aching sadness, NORCO is aggressively psychedelic, hardnosed, and nihilistic.This is not the most punk thing I’ve ever played, but it’s the most accessible punk thing I’ve seen in the interactive space, and that accessibility draws you in for a pretty wild ride. It starts with a future fried hyperlocal take on New Orleans, with its rotting infrastructure and twin income streams of petroleum and gullible tourists. There are tiny stabs at the city’s popular kitsch – vampire novels, voodoo shops, ghost tours, and questionable street food. But these are footnotes compared to the obsession with environmental damage, climate change, hurricanes, flooding, and institutional collapse that underline life in The Big Uneasy these days. The scene is so thoroughly soaked in a hard boiled tincture of Eric Brockovich-meets-Neuromancer verisimilitude and wry humor that the post-humanism, cryptozoology, and psychedelic mysticism come crashing into the frame with surprisingly dramatic force.Is it perfect? Nah! For all its deeply perceptive powers, NORCO fails to invest the player in the main character or the McGuffin of her tepid affection, her brother. The endings – while gorgeously nihilistic – hold little emotional weight as a result. NORCO, literally, loses the plot by the third act. The “Well, that happened” cliché can just be slapped on the experience as neatly as a packing tape on a gaping wound. This feels like the result of trying to cram a large novel’s worth of concepts and characters into a running time the size of a short miniseries. On a mechanical level, NORCO is less impressive. The minigames feel tacked on, formulaic, and immersion breaking – existing solely to avoid the “walking simulator” label. The ending areas suffer extensively from asset reuse, robbing them of uniqueness. But the game rewards those curious enough to try illogical item combinations, poke around in dialogue trees, or click into obscure areas of the map. Like the real New Orleans, there’s a lot to find in the darker corners of NORCO.

_childDocuments_.review: In the bayous of Norco, Louisiana, ghosts linger. Not the types in horror movies that jump up in your face, screaming unabatedly, nor the ones you see on strange found footage that you proceed to show all your friends. These ghosts are vestiges of the past, remnants of a bygone time. A time that won’t come back. Having grown up in Norco, Kay is no stranger to its peculiar inhabitants and rural landscapes. But one day, she’s had enough. She packs her backpack, leaves the only place she’s ever known, and heads for the road. This is how she spends the next five years: aimlessly travelling from state to state, not really achieving anything, her existence reduced to a shadow. But then, her mom dies of sickness. Overcome with a feeling of regret, Kay travels back to her hometown — to Norco. But home is not as imagined. Slowly but steadily, a power conglomerate is taking over the local towns, and the Norco she knew is getting overshadowed by their capitalist ideals and futuristic machinery. Her house, too, is in shambles, the messy kitchen and living room serving as gateways into the past, a trip down memory lane, if you will. Kay describes these events with a certain apathy, like they belong to a different person; the person who vanished when she ran away. Her ghost. Like one character says, she’s a  Plenty of games have tackled the homecoming trope, but none do it quite like Norco. Typically, this return to a former life concerns itself mostly with what has already happened, the details the protagonist already knows about but we don’t. The home Kay returns to, however, is different. It has changed, molded into a gruesome shape by family dramas, disease and perhaps even occult occurrences. And this is only the beginning. Slowly, the strange circumstances around Kay’s family and the happenings in Norco are revealed, and a mystery shapes. Carried forward by sharp, concise writing, Norco shifts into something much different and far stranger, a dazzling piece that maintains a fine balance between uncanny and mundane.  The story is told not only from the perspective of Kay, but also a character in the past. Often, a premise is introduced in the past and then further explored in the present, merging these two viewpoints and making the transitions between them almost seamless. As such, you never feel like an interesting part of the plot gets paused, delayed even, by something else. It’s rather clever. The gameplay also varies, with cascades of different ideas and concepts colliding. An encounter with guards in cutting-edge armor sees the game shift into a turn-based showdown reminiscent of a JRPG, with each round having you either attack with a character or heal them to prepare for the next turn. Then, you attend a puppet show about a hunter travelling the swamps, and you’re transported into a top-down view of the area, able to control the direction of the boat and make a few discoveries along the way. And in perhaps the smartest segment, you undergo a reading of your memory and must decide which recollections to keep and which to forget. Few of these segments are innovative, but together, they lend Norco an ever-bending and unpredictable nature. What’s so impressive about this story is the way it manages to wrap everything up by the end. A seemingly random encounter early on turns out to be related to a major plot point, and every element of surrealism, no matter how weird, carries a deeper meaning. These aspects don’t feel like they were randomly thrown at a board like dart pieces, but rather like intentional decisions made by the storytellers. I was so engaged that I even started taking notes, attempting to grasp the deeper reaches of the symbolism.  The game carries in its juxtaposition of rural America and the supernatural a likeness to the magical Kentucky Route Zero. Just like the ragtag cast travelling the dreamlike roads of Kentucky, the characters of Norco face uncertainties in life. They’re driving down blurry motorways in a car fueled by doubt, suppressed by the changes occurring around them. Some try to fight it by searching for purpose, while others give in to the hopelessness. It puts things into perspective. In a world ruled by the rich and the fortunate, can we — us normal individuals — even hope to change anything? At the entrance to the oil refinery that towers into the skyline, a sign says, “for a greener future.” Feels awfully familiar, doesn’t it? The truth is, as pretentious as it may sound, we live in the world  of Norco. The small get suppressed by the large, faceless corporations control our daily life and opinions through bureaucratic algorithms and overwhelming technology. Bleak when you think about it, isn’t it?And yet, we cling on to life, try to give it meaning. One of the fascinating groups in Norco is a collective of religious zealots all going by the name of Garrett. They wish to transcend this earthly prison, to build a spaceship and reach for the stars. It’s a grand project, one likely to succumb under its own ambition, yet it has a symbolical power. In our own world, too, there are people trying to escape from mundanity. But then again, we all start out reaching for the stars; most of us just give up on that dream. Theoretically, this game is set in the future. People have stopped using traditional ways of measuring time, there’s an android with what seems like real emotions, and even the local gas station, which lies on an empty parking lot in the middle of nowhere, is managed by an automaton. Yet I would often forget that this is purely speculative fiction. It sure doesn’t feel far from our own world, both in its depiction of towering corporations, but also in the technology that, when you think about it, is not too unachievable. That’s an achievement.   This is what Norco means to me. It’s a reflection on the world we live in, a subtle critique of the way conglomerates crush and oppress the small, but also a story about the people we meet along our individual journeys and the things we leave behind. With heavy symbolism and wacky yet ultimately human characters, it’s an extraordinary work of magical realism, and it achieves this with a rare brevity, every line of dialogue flowing into the next, not a single word wasted.To present your ideas is one thing. To do so through delicate hints and the circumstances of your story? That’s art.

_childDocuments_.review: I bought this game after playing it non stop sleeping for the night in-between on PC Gamepass.While I don't come from the area this game takes a lot of its inspiration of, it all felt familiar and identifiable to me. In spite of its melding of cyberpunk aesthetics to its overall background, the game is very much a reflection of what a "normal" life would be these days. Its a very personal tale not just of the central characters but also of the area itself. I wanted to know more of why certain characters became who they are as well as what led to this place becoming what it was. Its writing, artwork, and soundtrack help get all this across and really highlights why interactive media such as video games can have its advantage over purely literary works. Would I feel like books could match the same level of detail? A good author could definitely do so but would my attention be held long enough to do so? I guess i don't have personal confidence in myself these days.Mechanically it's very much a point and click adventure game, though I greatly appreciate its puzzles not being obtuse and are overall very easy to follow. One aspect of the game you could argue doesn't fit in with the rest but I appreciate its inclusion if only for its variety.I also want to give special mention to its artbook included in the special edition of the game. It not only includes the game's beautiful pixel art but reference photography, sketches, newspaper clippings, and narrative information about the game as well as interviews from some of its staff. Absolutely worth looking through after beating the game and part of me is hoping a print version would be released down the road (as well as some poster size prints for some of its artwork so i can throw them up on my wall while giving more of my $ to the developers)It's easily have joined my collection with the likes of Disco Elysium and Va11-Hall-A of games that transport me into a place in time that felt like I've been there this whole time. Play this game

_childDocuments_.review: Norco is, for lack of a better word, a very weird game. I bought it after I saw a YouTube video talking about the game and I really don't regret buying it: It's an experience I don't think I ever really had with a game before, and even though there are things in the game that didn't really resonate with me, it's going to be an experience I'll remember for a long time.Norco is a point-and-click-game, but one that follows a very fleshed-out story with a broad cast of characters living in a corporate town that is poisoned and deeply marked by the oil refining complex that slowly takes over town and buys out everyone else. The game is a mix of detective mystery, finding items and using them in the right spot, solving riddles, and incredibly creative and experimental game controls. For the most part of Norco, you talk to characters and slowly unravel the mystery of your missing brother, your dead mother, the company that rules your town, a weird cult, and a weird supernatural neural network. Norco is actually a real place in Louisiana, just that the company destroying it in real life is Shell Oil and not Shield Refinement and I really recommend just looking up stuff about the actual town, because it's real-life paralells are quite interesting to look at.The game deals with quite a lot of heavy themes, but has a way of wrapping them in layers of humor and metaphor, that I at first (in all honesty) found a bit off-putting, but later started to warm up to. I think the game was at its best when it was cryptic and dark and poetic, starkly contrasted with comedic moments that made the emotional scenes even better. When I just had finished the game, my impression was that some plot points just didn't fit the story and were out of place, and while I later came to understand that a lot of these beats had a grander meaning later, the game at first still left a rather sour taste in my mouth, as I found the ending way too absurd.What I think I loved most about the game were the absoluetly beautifully written prose texts, story beats, and the game's willingness to occassionally be evry dark and somber. The characters are all very loveable and very distinguishable in how they are written and what I really enjoyed was how no character in this game was only likeable or only unlikable - I think every character had both sympathetic sides and unsympathetic ones and that was really great to experience, because they all felt very human and very grounded, with real troubles and worries, but also with ideals and hopes. I found the story generally really engaging, even though I think initially wasn't prepared for how absurd the game would get at times, because I at first expected this to be a more grounded story I was a bit thrown off when the focus at the end kind of shifted away from the themes I personally found the most resonant to me and really embraced the absurdity of the story coming to a close in a very bizzare way, that takes some interpretation to be understood. Regardless of the story, Norco both had plot points where I was stunned in awe at the scene and the descriptions and at other times had moments where I was laughing my ass off because a scene was so bizarre and entertaining.Norco is a game that often introduces a random mechanic out of the blue and forces you to react, and I really enjoyed that part of the game - Norce didn't just feel like a standard point-and-click game with a narrative on top of it, but like the game developers really thought about how to make each part of the game stand out mechanically, and it works really really well, especially since almost every single one of the game's bizarre mechanics is used again in the last stretch of the game, creating a great finale.There are some really cool moments where you feel really smart for having figured something out - a lot of the passcode riddles in the game are really creative without feeling contrived and at one point, recording something in one act will help you when you're almost at the end of the game and these moments just feel great! But I felt like the game was holding my hand like 80% of the time - important stuff people say always gets highlighted in green and that makes it less fun if you actually had the thought yourself - ESPECIALLY if then a companion repeats the hint another two times, just in case you forgot, and I know that some players need that, but I felt like 50% of the time, riddles were a bit too on the nose. There were very few moments in the game however that I found contrived or illogical, which is almost never the case in point-and-click games and I really liked how logically coherent the game was. There were 2-3 points where I was a bit confused because a thing was either very meta (I don't want to spoil what it is, but near the end of the game you do something really unethical for literally no reason and someone screws up and in turn does something that helps you. But there is NO reason why you would, as a character choose to do that very unethical thing in the first place) or a thing wasn't really logical (at some point you have to use an item to find something hidden, but there is no reason why you would think to use that item in that situation), but those were really the only moments I felt a bit at loss.The music and art of the game were really great and even though I usually am not the type to like pixel art styles, the compositions and imagery often really impressed me. The setting and world are beautifully done, and I had a lot of fun exploring the locations in Norco.Generally I would say, I totally recommend the game if you like experimental, cryptic, mysterious games and are open for plots that are a bit more absurd, too. This game really isn't like Disco Elysium at all, but if you liked Disco Elysium, I think you might enjoy this game too! Also - if you played a lot of old school point-and-click adventure games, I think this game will make you feel really melancholic, but without the game being clunky and incomprehensible. For the price it's being sold for, I think it's totally reasonable to buy Norco!

_childDocuments_.review: I came across this game during a frenzy for pixel art games, not knowing what to expect. While it has the most stunning pixel art, its real strength is definitely the narrative. From the moment I started playing Norco, it felt nostalgic, with a sense of familiarity and emotion. After my first playthrough, I found myself getting teary-eyed whenever I thought about the game. It stayed with me in the most unexpected way, like a homesickness for a place I've never been to. During my second playthrough, I realized the combat system kinda sucks, but I guess that's why there's an automated combat option. The game is also quite short, but I don't see this as a negative given its long-lasting effect on me.

_childDocuments_.review: NORCO is totally my type of text-heavy game. The writing throughout is top-notch. The pixel graphics are stunning. The way they capture light in those graphics, whether the flicker of refinery flames or the warmth of a sunset, is just beautiful. Plus, pixel images don’t have large amount of details, so there’s no distracting players’ attention from the text. Perfect balance between immersive storytelling and gorgeous visuals.Some complain that too much info in dialogues and items are unnecessary to push the story line - just boring extra work. But I just love discovering them and piecing together the vibe of that unique place and time in NORCO.

_childDocuments_.review: What did I just play.I was worried the lack of animation and a lot of text would bore me, but nope. It's one of the best games I've played, topped only by Disco Elysium, and Lion's Song also comes to mind.The developers have a lot of fun with the incredible art, crafty zoom ins, and minimal movement. As the game progresses, the art is just getting more and more insane. I love it. Gorgeous.The music and sound is so pleasant and moody, and the first second you play in your room feels like everything is a bad dream, the day is beautiful and full of hope. Hahaha. Ha.The arcade fight was cute. I felt I had something to do and was fitting for the game. Easy.But the story and the world are something else. It starts casual. It proceeds to become less and less normal, both weird and realistic. There is a cat you pet that foretells stuff, but you just don't believe it.The way the real world mixes with increasingly futuristic and ludicrous themes is so well written and out there, I can only be jealous of the creativity displayed. I want a developer commentary mode, which is a documentary probably to cover everything in the game.Masterpiece indeed. I don't know why this game isn't more popular. It should!
_childDocuments_.name: NORCO

_childDocuments_.review: I may replay this game, which is unusual for me. Interesting vision of a near future; pessimistic, but nihilistically optimistic and vaguely reactionary. It doesn't bluntly intellectualize much; It instead uses allegory and myth, the supernatural, surreal and day-to-day, supported by a mostly plausible setting, to bring its world to life. This is what makes it so compelling: the marriage of believable and fantastic. It's a short novel that doesn't feel dated, and there's plenty of patterns and mystery to sink your analytical side into. The music was probably the weakest point. Puzzles were fine and fun; combat easy. More days of fuel pirates and cults lie ahead.
_childDocuments_.name: NORCO

_childDocuments_.review: An engaging story that carried me in a feeling of sci-fi surrealism and unexpected twists.I loved how Norco manages to transmit the characters personalities so well, without actual recorded voice - excellent writing.The pixel Art is wonderful and together with the music and sfx were very successful in portraing the many different environments and moods.The simple yet challenging systems used for the mini-games, get extra credits for being implemented in an adventure point & click - it's refreshing and brings an extra layer of dynamics with that action component.How all of the above fits around a story that bridges history and fiction, reality and prophecy, religion and technology, was  masterful.A work of Art, special and unique, Norco is the result of a lot of good choices.

_childDocuments_.review: This game is a absolute 10/10 for me. I laughed, I teared up, I got chills over my entire body...man, it really pulls you into the world so effectively. The music is perfect, probably some of my favorite game music, and the sound design is excellent too. I did not expect the art style to be as visually appealing as it ended up being - it does so much with so little. _childDocuments_.review: Well, it's definitely a weird game. I don't even know what to say about it.I don't agree with people saying it's similar to Disco Elysium, or that if you love DE you'll love this. DE is probably my favorite game ever and I don't find them similar at all, it's just alot of text in both. However the writing in Disco Elysium is god-like, it's like an impossible standard to compare to. There is nothing like it.The writing in Norco was a bit difficult to follow, I found myself having to read the same thing over and over. It's often too abstract. At times I was like come on say what you want, say it with your chest!Gameplay-wise, I didn't like that you don't see your character, you kinda just click through different locations, like it's almost just static images with a little bit of animation that you interact with. I've never been a fan of games like these. (I know there's probably a word for these sorry, english is not my first language.) I don't know why, but I really really like seeing the character that I'm playing, and being able to move them around and see them interact with the world. Otherwise I sometimes feel like I'm just sitting there clicking through images, I just can't get fully into it.However, despite all this, Norco managed to suck me into the story and I did enjoy my time playing. I don't think it's something I'd want to play through again, but I do recommend giving it a go if you like weird story games (with lots of reading). It's definitely memorable.This game reminded me of Loom for some reason.

_childDocuments_.review: NORCO is a game that captures multiple tones successfully while other projects in games, television and film, struggle with just one. I went into this game apprehensively, as I'm truly not the biggest fan of point and click games, but as the story, enveloped in themes of existentialism, class, and religion, unveiled its true self the further I got in, I found myself lost in the journey of Kay and her many party-mates. Though this game definitely isn't for everyone, I truly believe it to be a perfectly crafted Southern-Gothic tale with healthy doses of science fiction, eldritch mysticism, and absurdist hilarity.I hope Geography of Robots continues this formula down the road as this one has become one of my all-time favorites.A narrative experience unlike anything I've played before.10/10

_childDocuments_.review: I savored this game and wish it lasted 4 hours longer. The graphics, the ambience, the sharp wit. I will be looping back for achievements.-Too many near-future *-punk narratives go out of their way to utterly debase all humanity. I'm tired of my nose being smothered into the muck of melodramatic robo tropes. Been there, done that. The suburban swamp world of NORCO, with its multi-generational cast and the uncanny familiarity of indigenous techno-Catholicism, glows with heart and soul, even when all the chips are down. Call it NORCOZY. -This is a weird reference but if you're a fan of “iceberg memes” or "rabbit holes" you'll probably like this story? Can't say much without spoilers...-All the chill vibes of retro point-and-click adventures without it being a tiresome pixel hunt. Enough difficulty to make you feel like you're unraveling a mystery worth unraveling - not just auditing a game script-My one critique is I did feel rushed in the final act. I still have questions...A slice of Americana for dessert, with a bittersweet aftertaste
