_childDocuments_.review: Norco is a good game with a horrible story. There is:stunning sights with gorgeous pixel artfantastic point and click gameplay with systems that keep the player from being lost, beautiful but also funny writing that doesn't censor its often very inappropriate humorect. ect. It's simply a good point and click adventure!The problem lies with the story. Upon playing the free first act, you should discover 4 deeper themes this game aims to inspect in its (by then) expertly set up story: However, the plot is indicisive about which way to head in. While playing, it feels like you are untangling many different storylines that promise to be involved with one another - while the game is really just stalling -, until the very last chapter, where the game picks (in my opinion) the most uninteresting theme and bends everything towards an inconclusive and nonsensical end. Even the central mistery of the game, , is not related to two thirds of the story. This clearly is a more personal game for Geography of Robots, nonsensical or not- but the story is just disappointing. Even if you try to "untangle the authors personal ties to the real Norco in Lousiana", it will still be devoid of sensical meaning. Maybe that is the underlying conflict this game seeks to portray, but I felt this made the entire story fall flat. TLDR:The many facets of the story, which lead to a wonderful gameplay experience, end up being nothing more than loose ends on a story that struggles to find its deeper themes.
_childDocuments_.name: NORCO

_childDocuments_.review: I am sorry to give this a 'thumb down', as it is obvious that a lot of thought and creativity has gone into this game. Norco is a mix of American Gothic and, perhaps, magical realism, with a bit of cyberpunk thrown in. There are some interesting characters and places to be discovered. As much as I can judge this, having lived in the Deep South but not in Louisiana, these are well chosen. Two features of the game ended up disappointing me. In terms of gameplay, there is not much here for an adventure, in my view. Norco's classic adventure puzzles are for the most part too easy and transparent. At the same time, there is quite a number of action sequences and challenges that require quick reactions; these feel out of place, poorly done, and, at least for me, not enjoyable at all. Then there is the way the game's plot is constructed. Norco's particular brand of magical realism (or perhaps surrealism?) comes with an 'anything goes' kind of storytelling, which makes major plot points quite frequently seem arbitrary and random. For this reason, the game did not manage to hold my attention.There is clearly much to like here, and other players will perhaps be more forgiving than me. Still, neither Norco's gameplay nor its story managed to convince me in the end.
_childDocuments_.name: NORCO

_childDocuments_.review: NORCO is a great, short adventure game with very particular and interesting tone and style. The story is interesting and at times was quite surprising to me. The characters are decently written and the key figures are memorable and interesting. At times the game can be *very* funny, but the overall tone is often more serious and filled with a certain sense of enui and "lostness", but this is well done and not overdone. Note that there is a, in my opinion, unfitting and poorly executed combat system, but since a past update these can be skipped (rather, automatically be done). This is not a big minus, because combat is very rare and not important to the game as a whole at all. Play the demo, see if the graphics and tone of the game vibe with you. If they do, you can expect a nice story spiraling towards an endpoint that you probably would not have anticipated going into this game.
_childDocuments_.name: NORCO

_childDocuments_.review: Norco is a point-and-click adventure game developed by Geography of Robots. Set in the futuristic titular town of Norco, Louisiana, it sees you in the role of Kay, who has returned home after years of wandering throughout the US following the death of her mother. When she gets home, she is greeted by the family's AI robot, Millions, to be told that her brother Blake has gone missing. Kay resolves to pick up the pieces that remain of her childhood home and ventures out into her hometown to track down her brother. This is fairly well-worn ground for a story, find your brother, salvage your home. But then Norco goes and tosses you headfirst into a densely layered magical realist sci-fi tale with religious cults, oil companies, conspiracy theories, Aliens, sentient AIs, and space rockets. Make no mistake, this is a Sci-fi game to its core. But one which goes so deep into the genre that it reinvents its tropes even as it fulfils them. Alongside the usual themes of climate change, industrial capitalism, and slavery, Norco uses the traditional sci-fi trappings to delve into intensely human themes such as loss, familial strife, poverty, and regret. The town of Norco is a hollow, soulless place. An area that has been bled dry by the surrounding oil company, Shield, to the point that whatever hasn't been stripped to the bone for a profit has sunk into the industrial swampland that dominates the landscape. It's also, as you'll find when you start exploring, populated by a load of complete weirdos. After all, who else chooses to stay in a town where the land and air are toxic and anything of any worth is immediately taken? And it's here, in this assembly of nutcases that Norco calls a population, that the game world comes to life. Norco has easily one of the most well-fleshed-out casts I've seen in a long time. Every single character has a backstory that makes them seem real and that drives their, at times childish, actions. There's the robot Millions who showed up with your mother one day and won't speak of its past, there's an eco-terrorist called Lucky who you're never quite sure if he has a cause he's fighting for or if he just likes blowing ♥♥♥♥ up. The local PI constantly talks of how well he's doing and how he's one of the few remaining good guys, but his office is so run down that the toilet is next to his desk, and won't tell you about a break-in at your house until you buy him a round and some fries. One of my favourites is a local called Keith who's setting up a boxing-themed news website called "Keith's corner" in what is one of the most hilariously wrongheaded endeavours in gaming history because, you see, Keith is a complete idiot. He's a gloriously stupid character and that's what makes him real. He doesn't have any insight or even anything interesting to say, he just wants to say something to make it seem like he's got a handle on things, when in fact, he's just as clueless as everyone else. That, in a nutshell, is how Norco manages to sell the more fantastical elements of the story. It presents them straight up as matter-of-factly as it can. The characters react to these as though they were mundane, almost trivial things to consider. So when the guy you've been helping on a job-share app finds out that the app is run from a warehouse by a giant eagle with alien machinery for entrails, reacts to this news by shrugging his shoulders and saying "I see a lot of weird stuff on this app" it doesn't break immersion, it reinforces it, because this guy has other ♥♥♥♥ to deal with and needs the money to keeps the lights on and his family fed. This is a result of the short-termism that poverty inflicts on people. That's why no one seems to want to leave Norco even though it's poison. They're all just trying to make it to tomorrow. I also need to point out that the writing is second to none. I'm serious, this may be the best-written game for years. It may even be better than Disco Elysium or Kentucky Route Zero. It's definitely on par with both of those classics. The story is split into two main branches, Kay's search for her brother and Catherine's, Kay's mother, final moments before her death. Telling the story in this two-pronged manner helps keeps everything fresh and always presents you with new backgrounds and interactions. The descriptive text is almost poetic in places and the dialogue is written as authentically as possible given that the writer is actually from the area depicted in the game and it contains some of the funniest scenes I've read in ages. It's a testament to how good the writing and setting is of Norco that it has taken me this long to mention the stunning pixel art. I've been constantly amazed by pixel art in recent years and this is no different. The scenes of complete poverty and desolation are so detailed and perfectly capture the despair that hangs over this town like a thick fog. Each scene brilliantly conveys the brooding atmosphere put forward in the writing and some of the more surreal scenes are striking in their beauty and detail. On top of all this, the soundtrack is excellent. Truly excellent. So good I wound up buying it. In conclusion, will you like Norco? I do think you will. I think it's easily one of the games of the year. Norco is an intelligent, evocative story of a ♥♥♥♥♥♥ world and its inhabitants. It tackles themes head-on that are rarely even touched upon in gaming. That's not just in terms of its portrayal of a community buckling under capitalism, but also in its compassionate, thoughtful portraits of people on the margins. That, even in the most desolate places, there's always hope and the warmth of human connection to help us find meaning in our lives. As the game itself puts with one of the best lines ever: "Even the synthetic has its time and place"
_childDocuments_.name: NORCO

_childDocuments_.review: I loved this game, played through it in almost one sitting when I bought it and I can't wait to play more of it. Elegant storytelling and easy to grok mechanics made this a gripping experience I struggled to put down for even a moment, fixed to the edge of my seat with every story beat. All in all it delivers all it promised and more with its marketing, and you can feel the elements of southern gothic literature pervasive throughout the story complementing its futuristic setting, and in true gothic fashion giving you just enough of what's beneath the surface to hang yourself with.
_childDocuments_.name: NORCO

_childDocuments_.review: Quality writing, engaging story, and most of all an unmistakable amount of love and care that went into this game. The sheer amount of specific details and quirks that are displayed in every single backdrop and line of dialogue is astounding and fully immerses you in the world of this Southern Louisiana town. This game feels like both a love letter as well as a candid portrayal of a town that's past its prime. Add in the extremely personal familial aspect and this game is guaranteed to tug at your heartstrings. Definitely planning on playing it again and would highly recommend it to anyone who enjoys story-rich or point & click adventures
_childDocuments_.name: NORCO

_childDocuments_.review: This is definitely not the type of game I usually play, but I've been following Geography of Robots on Twitter for some time now because of the amazing pixel art. So when I saw that this game had finally been released I had to give it a try, and I really liked it. The atmosphere is wonderful, the art itself is just as incredible as any other piece of theirs I've seen, and the soundtrack is sooo good. Great writing and an interesting story, too! Would definitely recommend if you're into point & click games, and if you don't mind a lot of text. But like I said, games like these aren't usually my type and I still really enjoyed it. :)
_childDocuments_.name: NORCO

_childDocuments_.review: The story is strange and you have to do a lot of reading, but if you up to that, this game will be a wonderful experience. It looks good, sounds good and the story is interesting.For me this game is so much I wish for a game to be. Funny, melancholic, mystical, beautiful, ...I think I wasn't bored for one second, despite its rather slow pacing.
_childDocuments_.name: NORCO

_childDocuments_.review: SPOILER FREEIt's a magnificent game. Stunning visuals, good sound design. intuitive game design and over all incredible writing with a powerful message. Now, that's a lot of adjectives, but this is the not-too-long list of if this game is for you:     - Do you like the idea of a Louisiana-Bayou-Southern Gothic setting? Try NORCO! (Same answer if the Resident Evil game you liked most was RE7, based on setting alone.)     - Are visuals something that you value a lot in a game? Especially in an artistic way? Try NORCO!     - Do you want a story that's meaningful on a personal level, while also relating to bigger and deeper issues in the current world that we live in (with an anti-corporation sentiment on top)? Try NORCO!     - Do you like vaguely poetic and definitely beautiful writing that makes you reflect about it even if you're not playing? Try NORCO!     - Do you want a relatively short game you can play in a few days or a really invested evening and night? Try NORCO!     - Do you like explorations of Americana*? Try NORCO! *For many of these points, if you don't like them it's probably not a game you'll be interested in, but this question is optional. Yes, the game feels deeply US centric to me (in a very emotional way, not necessarily patriotic), but as someone who's never stepped foot into the United States I quite enjoyed it. It's more of an added bonus, I think. I wouldn't recommend it if you have trouble with taking things genuinely: while this game can be funny, it's better if you engage with the topics and the core emotional dystopia right away and get personally involved. Also, there's relatively not that much room for personal choice, as the story is lineal, so mind that.
_childDocuments_.name: NORCO

_childDocuments_.review: A visual novel set in a strange alternate Louisiana. The characters and dialogue feel persistently gross, but the background scenery is gorgeous. Some choices matter; some choices don't; you won't know which is which. It's Southern Gothic mixing with Gothic-Punk, full of corporate espionage, eco-terrorism, religious cults, family drama, cyberpunk quandaries, betrayals, and unsolved mysteries. Don't expect closure. Don't expect answers. Just buckle up and enjoy the ride.
_childDocuments_.name: NORCO

_childDocuments_.review: Best point-and-click adventure I've played in recent years. Really solid and immersive game. Fully recommended!Shout-out to the text settings panel where you can pick your preferred font, colour, size and speed for the text, which is something so obvious yet so ignored by most of the text-based games out there and I'll never understand why...
_childDocuments_.name: NORCO

_childDocuments_.review: This game is very dear to me. It presents plainly the often contradictory balance we must strike in our lives between industry, the land, familial ties, and just straight up surviving. Nobody comes out clean, but we're lucky to make it through with a few laughs and a few bumps on our heads.I'm from Luling, a community across the river from the actual site of this game. This area, the River Parishes of Southeast Louisiana, very rarely gets any accurate depictions in media. The closest -- at least visually -- is the first season of HBO's True Detective, much of which was shot in Norco, LA, but its setting is more inland. Growing up here, though, nothing is as painfully accurate a depiction of growing up in "Cancer Alley" as you'll find in this game.A lead developer on the game, Yuts, has been my friend for a while. We didn't grow up together, but our lives took similar paths. Watching this game grow from early sidescrolling efforts in JavaScript to a final game with multiple talents involved has been an unparalleled joy. For the first time in any media, I saw myself and my lived experience depicted.The amount of research that went into this game by such a small team is astonishing. Echoes of real world locations and events are depicted, distorted through a dark lens and placed into this timeline to weave an unforgettable narrative. Nearly everything in this game has an actual world counterpart, even if they're partially obfuscated by a warped technological veneer. For a local, this feels like one big Easter Egg (like, Flannelass is straight up an actual well-loved member of the New Orleans DIY music scene), but NORCO never comes off as an in-joke. Broader themes of exploitation of land and human life in the name advancement of industry are clear and should be witnessed. Incels and edgelords from the internet exist everywhere, and the cult of personality surrounding their figureheads is examined here. This game is of its time, but it could be set any time in the past or next 20 years.NORCO is never hateful or accusatory in its tone. It asks no direct questions, and it asks no more of the audience beyond their attention. It's wildly funny at times, especially so if you care to note the distinct identity of residents of the River Parishes. There is no overbearing narrator; everything presented is from afar, like a dream you can't slow down. Encircling the reality of industry and its massive impact on life without explicit condemnation is a feat ... especially since the narrative is primarily grounded in a reunion of the Madère family.Selfish as it may be, this truly feels like a video game that was made just for me. Often I feel that there are too many video games, that as the medium grows and becomes more accessible, we've seen a glut of garbage (クソゲー) and naked attempts to cash in. Games that are trying to "say something" can be limited by the conventions of the medium, expertise of the writers, or external pressure for accessibility. In my view, NORCO doesn't suffer from this: the celebration of Southeast Louisiana as a painful place of beauty that is forced to coexist with industry, that maybe you need to escape from but which you're inextricably tied to is done with a clear voice and I feel it in my bones.God bless the Madères, and God bless Norco.
_childDocuments_.name: NORCO

_childDocuments_.review: This is exactly what Backbone wanted to become, initially disguised as a classic detective story, at some point turning into something completely radical, but stumbled precisely at the moment of this transition. Here the classic "homecoming" is transformed into some insane mix of Southern Gothic;  dystopianism and Terry Gilliam's distorted absurd images;  political manifestos, none of which are shoved down your throat by the creators; crazy mumbling in your head, as if you are preparing to remove the corpse from the tree in Revachol, but again you will be too lazy to do it. Describing the plot in detail in this case is a useless task, because it is precisely in the ability to convey even the strangest things to the player as accurately and beautifully as possible, the unique way of arranging the plot into a single monolith, that the unbearable charm of this thing lies.The game does not seek to make you comfortable, but this is what immerses you in some strange state of southern relaxation. That relaxation that begins somewhere in a jazz bar with a glass of bourbon, and ends in a mangrove with alligators wandering nearby. Even the genre of the game constantly seems to elude you in the fog of deceptive swamps, whether it's an adventure quest with puzzles, or a visual novel with a non-linear narrative, or something else. And it works. Surprisingly, it really works. Perhaps the point is the attention with which the creators approached the development of both the story and the characters. Every minute you understand that the authors are incredibly fond of the strange universe of their game, investing in its creation the most valuable of themselves, striving to polish even the smallest details that many players will not even get to during the game. And it is precisely this quality that most of all unites this game with Disco Elysium, and not obvious markers, even if the magnitude here is not millions of words.NORCO brings a lot of discoveries, but the most important of them are extremely interesting new creators, whose name must be remembered. Geography of Robots team - my respect to you personally for the excellent work. It's like a breath of fresh air, giving hope that the adventure genre is far from saying its last word and is able to evolve. Bravo.
_childDocuments_.name: NORCO

_childDocuments_.review: Good game. The story is a little confusing in the first hour but as the game progresses you get the hang what's going on. The art and the soundtrack is fantastic. The story blends sci-fi and religion, it's worth checking out if you're into narrative games involving a lot of reading, it almost feels like reading a sci-fi novel. Voice overs would be great but they're not there at the time of writing this review.
_childDocuments_.name: NORCO

_childDocuments_.review: If a cinematic point-and-click tech-noir adventure with lots of birds and a sublime score featuring sludge masters Thou is something you would enjoy, welcome to NORCO.NORCO is a debut point-and-click adventure game developed by Geography of Robots and published by Raw Fury (Kathy Rain, Whispers of a Machine). The game follows Kay returning to her hometown of Norco, Louisiana, to check on her younger brother after the death of their mother. The town is an industrial hub and a shadow of an oil refinery that works 24/7, providing the region with jobs but also with pollution and property issues in a near future of environmental and economic downfall.The game introduces several interesting design choices. The main heroine and her brother have smiley faces instead of regular faces in photos and on character icons, while all other characters appear normal. That makes the story a bit more personal, I guess. Another notable thing is the absence of proper voiceovers; they are substituted by artificial ones that only convey the character's voice but not what the character says. Some barking and laughing NPCs were especially amusing! Humor in the game is dark, awkward, and often self-depreciated. For instance, the showgoer's "hotdog adventure" is hilarious, but only if you are willing to listen through the whole thing by requesting the showgoer to continue with the chagrin. Also, renaming Shell to Shield with the slogan "A Greener World Awaits" is pretty comical.Going through the game was compelling because its mood and atmosphere corresponded with my mindset; the experience might be much different for those who maintain a positive outlook. The only thing that I did not like were religious connotations, even if twisted enough to call them blasphemy.NORCO is bird-heavy. You get all kinds of birds in different manners as they shape both the story and the setting. From a casual mention of little wrens nesting nearby to a gruesome scene of a gigantic bald eagle, and from prolific bird calls to epic Mardi Gras bird costumes, Geography of Robots clearly intended to feature birds as much as possible. One way or another, the game also mentions ducks, crows, egrets, pelicans, cardinals, and more.What is your favorite bird-related scene or idea here? Let me know in the comments. I will tell you mine as well.As NORCO is rooted in Louisiana's cultural and industrial landscape, it's only natural to hear the local sludge band Thou in a mix with otherwise somber ambient music by Gewgawly I.Sometimes epic, sometimes jazzy, but always mournful, synthetic tunes with occasional instrumentation shape the principal soundscape. Distorted drone/doom songs by Thou give the necessary heaviness to the most dramatic moments, and the abundance of natural sounds in appropriate areas like swamps contribute immensely to the whole thing.In my taste, the game's audial side is a masterpiece in itself.Even if depressive and tense, NORCO is an outstanding story-driven adventure set in the grim future that will surely grab the attention of those who appreciate its overlapping themes.One warning, though: if you miss your mom or experience difficulties in relations with your older kids, the game might be a bit too heavy on those matters. Tread it lightly!
_childDocuments_.name: NORCO

_childDocuments_.review: NORCO, by developer/artist collective/terrifically named Geography of Robots, is a bitter sweet Southern Gothic psychodrama about family, capitalism, religion and everything in between. It’s an absolutely masterful use of the point and click format to explore a multifaceted narrative, with a presentation that perfectly recreates the razor thin line between dream, nightmare and reality.
_childDocuments_.name: NORCO

_childDocuments_.review: NORCO has a personal story fitted well within an interesting world, but as a game it is lacking. After playing four hours of NORCO, I have trouble getting back into it. The clicking back and forth between scenes to find a piece of dialogue or object I need to move on became too tedious.Though I respect the developers effort into story, art and sound, I want to help potential buyers make a right choice. If you, like me, want an active participation in understandable game mechanics, this game is not for you. If you want to immerse yourself in a dystopian New Orleans future and are willing to put in a lot of reading and effort to understand the point of the more poetic parts, NORCO is for you. I don't recommend this game to the general public, but have to mention that the ambience was so perfect that I left a scene open as white noise while reading a book.
_childDocuments_.name: NORCO

_childDocuments_.review: This is a very tentative review with the hope this game can only get better. I have finished the game after 4 hours and have achieved two endings. I'm happy to come back in a few months to play it again after some some minor QoL adjustments, i.e. fixing dodgy click spots, no ability to scroll text, important text highlights before you know things are important and no option to turn them off. The story is a very tantalising offering giving explanations, while consistent often don't have to make sense. If you are a fan of neo-noir style films such as Blade Runner, Donnie Darko or Under the Silver Lake you will get a kick out of this. I still feel like I am missing big chunks of the tale but as I said I am happy to come back.Only major gripe is when it comes to combat or puzzles the game grinds to a halt to shove them in your face. it feels a little disjointed and took me out of it. But hey, small passing issue in an otherwise good game.If you've read all this check out the Demo at least, you'll work out pretty quick if you'll like it or not. Whats to lose?

I finished the game in one sitting and was absolutely enamored with the world, story, the atmosphere, the characters, all of it. Do yourself a favor and give the game a shot.Also, LeBlanc is the greatest character of all time bruh.
_childDocuments_.name: NORCO

_childDocuments_.review: The first game that I like in this genre, which before that I it found completely boring, was Disco Elysium. _childDocuments_.name: NORCO

_childDocuments_.review: NORCO is an incredible fever dream of a story. It's tangible, relatable, aching, and compelling; and mutates into a bizarre fantasy. Other reviewers (Hatchet) have done a better job at explaining the shortcomings of the weird (and disappointing) second half. I got a lot of closure from the lore docs in ditch-whit-1, on geographyofrobots's itch.io page, and from episode 112 of the podcast 'Gaming in the Wild' which covers an interview with Geo of Robots.I still enjoyed it, and spent about 7 hours on it (offline, so it doesn't show my time)
_childDocuments_.name: NORCO

_childDocuments_.review: Beautiful art and deep, beautiful narrative design - sometimes I don't know where the plot is heading towards, with its well-blended sci-fi and religious (Christian) elements. The kind of game that leaves you with a "Wow, what?!"Reminds me heavily of Kentucky Route Zero (with more cults and disturbing imagery in a good way) - if you like KRZ then there's a high chance of you enjoying NORCO too.
_childDocuments_.name: NORCO

_childDocuments_.review: Really fascinating game. Beautiful pixel art. Instantly absorbing worldbuilding. Great moody music reinforcing the game's narrative themes and honestly has me looking at vinyl editions of the soundtrack--THOU! Straightforward and simple puzzles; definitely leans more toward a narrative game than a puzzle game. The story was engrossing but I do feel like it lost some steam in the last act for me; though the game as a whole fits a 7-8 hour playthrough perfectly and it doesn't overstay it's welcome. You can tell a lot of heart and thought went into this. I'm thankful for creators out there making this kind of beautiful weirdness.
_childDocuments_.name: NORCO

_childDocuments_.review: a truly stellar and singular game. the vibe is herculean, brah. memorable writing throughout with meticulous attention to character and voice. though norco never cannibalizes its influences, fans of philip k ♥♥♥♥, twin peaks, true detective, space/police/hero's quest, will find shades of each dancing in the periphery of this modernist paean to home. BUY BUY BUY
_childDocuments_.name: NORCO

_childDocuments_.review: Listen, I could sit here and write a 10,000 word essay detailing how I truly feel about this game: its plot, mechanics, graphics, etc. But I'm just going to summarize it all by saying this: It's weird.Go into it blind, and be prepared for the weirdness. Also, be prepared to read a lot. This is a text-based point and click.It's not the best game that I've ever played in this sort of avant-garde, surrealist "what in the heck even is this?" abstract and obtuse niche genre, but it was still... well, it was really something.Months later, and it still lives rent free in my mind.
_childDocuments_.name: NORCO

_childDocuments_.review: I really wanted to like this game. I'm from around New Orleans, and so rarely do I see mostly-authentic representations of this place. I like text-based games and weird philosophical ♥♥♥♥, so it seemed like it'd be right up my alley. But Norco was sadly underwhelming. I played it from start-to-finish in two sittings, doing a mostly-completionist playthrough. The plot is barely coherent and the ending(s) are disappointing. I'm not opposed to convoluted narratives in games; for example, I'm a huge fan of Kentucky Route Zero, which has similar vibes to Norco as they both stem from the Southern Gothic genre. But Norco's narrative goes beyond convoluted to inexplicable, and not in a good way. Leaves you unsatisfied, and it's hard to glean any deeper meaning even after reflecting on it. It does have some redeeming moments. The artwork can be good, and they nailed the regional character-- it looks just like the Greater New Orleans area. There are some events and dialogue that are quite provoking. However, these redeeming elements still don't make it worth playing. Probably not worth your time or your money.
_childDocuments_.name: NORCO

_childDocuments_.review: A really weird game that reminded me of Kentucky Route Zero. This tells the sad story of a decaying town and its inhabitants; people who are lonely, lost and desperate. There's plenty of symbolism and parallels to our own reality to go around. Really cool music, too, that goes well with the bizarre tone of the game.
_childDocuments_.name: NORCO

_childDocuments_.review: This is a game that I went into with great anticipation. To the game's credit, many of its elements are wonderful. The star of the show is the worldbuilding. NORCO's setting is deeply thought out and lived in. It feels like a real place that one would want to explore. Within the first act of the game, you do explore, and it's here the game shines; the people you meet, the areas you visit, the sounds and music, all engaging. As the story builds, it seems to be weaving a tale that straddles the line between thrilling and emotionally resonant. However.As the game approaches the end, this balance is completely thrown out the window. The people we met vanish, plotlines left either unfulfilled or resolved in a lazy and unfulfilling way. Where we could have an emotional climax we are given a silly and tonally off action climax. While I know the developers avoided this influence, I can't help but think of how Kentucky Route Zero rounded off its story. It, too, was a jarring shift, but one that over time built towards bittersweet resolution, one that allowed us to say goodbye we spent all this time meeting. I think NORCO wants to be A Game of Some Importance, that has Something To Say About Life, in the vein of the aformentioned KRZ, or Disco Elysium, touchstones you see mentioned in other reviews here. Whereas those were games by writers, this feels like a story by game developers, shackled to the idea and tropes of the classic Adventure Game.Having played through to the ending, it threw the earlier parts I really did love into a new light. Characters I thought would end up important were left by the wayside. Mechanics I thought were for throwaway gags ended up being vital parts of the game. To put it bluntly, it infuriated me. There was such promise here, to be thrown away by such a unfufilling ending. I wish I could recommend this game. There's so much love and care in most of its corners. To its credit, I'm only so infuriated by it because it did make me feel things. It was never boring. But, like the rushed ending of the Game of Thrones series, the lack of impact of the ending made me rethink the worth of the rest of the story. I'm sorry.
_childDocuments_.name: NORCO

_childDocuments_.review: Norco is a game I've been looking forward to for nearly a year, so I jumped on it ASAP on release date. First, a few things that are perfect without compromise: the art, while pixel based, is still gorgeous, capturing an amazing sense of melancholy right away. The sound design and music is just as incredible; they work together to form what I can only describe as some EXTRA thick vibes, of rot, and loneliness, and disrepair. The story is also just as interesting, at least in Acts 1 and 2, and honestly most of Act 3. Characters like Million and Superduck had me interested, immediately, and chomping at the bit to learn more. Really my only criticism has to do with closure on both the story, and many characters. It ended rather abrupt, leaving me with a lot of loose ends and questions. It wasn't bad enough for me to regret playing, but the ending did leave something to be desired.All in all, play Norco. It has a lot to say, and you should listen to it.

While the setting isn't particularly the main focus, it is insane to see how much this game gets right about southeast Louisiana, specifically around New Orleans. I saw the snowball stand I went to as a kid in Norco and a store where I live currently in this game and that means a lot to me. The way the setting is tied in to the story, characters and everything else at hand just felt right. _childDocuments_.review: and now onto the short review//intro//Welcome back comrades, this is MF Kraven & you are watching less than 10 mins reviews. The Youtube series where I take a look at games i think seem cool & give my thoughts on them in less than 10 mins.Today I take a look at Norco. Norco is a text based point & click adventure game set in a dystopian Louisiana. Visit your childhood home full of trauma to bury your recently deceased mother, but upon arrival fall into the surreal story of your small refinery town that awaits you. But can a point & click game in this day hold up to gaming juggernauts or is it not worth getting? Lets find out//Graphics, Sound & Artstyle//Described on their steam page as a Southern Gothic point & click doesn't truly do this game justice. See, Norco has a pseudo nightmare aesthetic that drew me in. I come from a small suburb in Los Angeles where the factories were prominent & the scenery haunts me to this day. To say it is surreal is an understatement, it's filled with scenes that seem oddly familiar.... in a nutshell the ambiance of Norco elevate the artstyle of this game to almost recommend it to you guys based on it alone.//Gameplay//As aforementioned Norco is a Point & Click adventure game, expect to read a lot. There are a few instances of "mini games" or it's condensed fighting mechanic that offers very little other than a remember a pattern, timed clicks and two short boat "adventures".Well half of the genre of point & click relies heavily on the story and while it starts off very innocuous it quickly turns sardonic, religious undertones accompanying strafed relationships in a family- it makes for a story that actually- hit very close to home... Your brother Blake has gone missing in the aftermath of your mother's death. In the hopes of finding him, you must follow a fugitive security android through the refineries, strip malls, and drainage ditches of suburban New Orleans. What comes in the journey to finding him, you'll never guess.//Price// 14.99 USD//How many hours estimated//I finished the story in about 5 hours. And while it does feel tempting to go back and 100% it.. I think one go around on the story is enough for me. I'll elaborate further in my Final Thoughts.//Is it Playable on Steamdeck?//While it is playable on SteamDeck, the combat and minigames are far more tedious on it than on PC. Plus without Steam Cloud- I had started my adventure on SD originally but when i tried it out on my laptop, none of the save data was there. Luckily for me, I was only 20 mins into my adventure so I just opted to play it completely through on my laptop.//Final Thoughts//*deep sigh*Wow what a story, Norco is undoubtedly a tour de force. The story hit way too close to home, no pun intended. I also fled my family home and traveled across the country seeking a new home, my sibling is also a very coddled person with the same kind of tendencies as Kay's brother, my mother also terminally ill... i have a strained relationship with. My childhood home is a mausoleum of nightmares.... but why am I opening up about all this? Simply said, Norco did a number on me. Clicking through Kay's home seeing the unfolded laundry, pills on the counter, overall just unfinished business of her mother gave me a grim look into my future.The journey to finding your brother spirals almost immediately into the whimsy and over-complicated. See the narrative structure is approached in an artistic manner, you have a mind map that can catalogue basically all the information you need from each character you meet or setting you remember. Its divided into three acts however you are switched between the main character Kay and her terminally ill mother. You see the world in two very abstract perspectives and while I can appreciate the effort- the parts with the mother, I could not wait to get em over with. This is where my subjective opinion will drag this a bit, all the characters feel real, they feel gritty, I'm truly disgusted by some of them. The way they talk with such dissonance, malcontent and disrespect... I found myself needing to take brief pauses and realizing I may need to speak to a therapist- I joke but I cant praise the writers of this story for conveying people in ways I've dealt with first hand.But going back to the plot, it's something I can't truly talk about without actually spoiling anything and in my opinion it's a story that should be at least experienced once. There are a few funny interactions here and there and ill say this with no context. Hot Dogs. Santa. Garret. It's a beautiful game with a haunting cyberpunk esque story. There's corporate espionage, terrorism, murder, drugs, & a hillbilly getting his ass kicked.I recommend Norco 100% to anyone who wants to indulge your brain in a little bit of literature. Maybe it can even take some fringe FPS players down a notch... it's a nuanced story for admittedly pretentious people. Still- I say buy it Now.

_childDocuments_.review: Norco is a dystopic sci-fi adventure game about a nomadic drifter named Kay who comes home after her mother passes to find her missing brother. Taking place in an overindustrialized part of swampside New Orleans, Norco's thematic ties to capitalism, oppression, connection, and loss flourish within a gorgeously bleak color palette of pixel art and a script that should be recognized as one of the medium's best.Norco mainly plays out like a standard point-and-click adventure game. Much of the 6-ish hour runtime is spent hopping between locations, talking to the quirky characters, and finding items and information to move forward. These elements are standard fare and the game mostly swings on the easy side in terms of logic and item usage. There are no out-of-pocket inventory combinations and most instances of a puzzle can be solved with a few seconds of backtracking. I was only stuck at one moment of the game, where the mindmap didn't say there were new options to explore. Speaking of, Kay is able to source her thoughts and progress into the mysteries of Norco with a detective-board-like mindmap. It's not very complex, but it was nice to browse when I came back to the game between sessions or wanted a quick summary after long conversations. Apart from the main plot, Norco has a knack for detail in its literature. Many of its best moments are the descriptions of the world, a land pulled apart by division of inequality and rebellion. The lore here is so rich that the game is most enticing when you can fully sink into the bats*** insanity of it all. There is also a light combat element, which I actually enjoyed. Using basic JRPG mechanics, you perform attacks with the characters in your active party by timing moves, akin to Paper Mario. It was a welcome addition that I actually wish was a little more frequent and had a broader purpose.As I mentioned, the world is unbelievably realized in Norco. Each of the environments is a dark, twisted pixel masterpiece, and the character design and the grimy nature of the aesthetic connects you to Kay's home and her struggles. Norco isn't afraid to push boundaries, and several moments flip the traditional genre style and add in new ideas to the presentation that are clever and surprising. The relationship of the player to their audiovisual experience is played with in subtle, intelligent, and sometimes off-putting ways, but all to serve the story brilliantly. Special mention must go to the music, which is a blend of electronic hellscapes and funky tunes that capture the energy of a land seeped in culture on the precipice of insurmountable change. Many of these tracks I will surely be listening to in the coming weeks.What I wasn't expecting most from Norco was its acceptance of choice. Right from the opening, you can choose elements of Kay's backstory, and you can continue to make foundational choices throughout your playtime. Dialogue doesn't just run you through every option, so conversations feel weighty and real, and several achievements and interactions have binary choices that have alternate options. I'm usually not a fan of having an amorphous approach to character like this, but Norco still manages to contain the setting and tone despite what options you choose for Kay and her family.Norco is going to be one of 2022's best titles. In a year where more than ever, understanding the value of family, our homes, and the growing dissent in corporations, the internet, and humanity at large is at its critical mass, the game handles its lofty perceptions of reality and dials it in for a crafted, enjoyable experience you should not miss.

_childDocuments_.review: If I could give NORCO a neutral rating rather than yes/no recommendation then I would. Normally I would start my reviews with  a synopsis of the story and what you do in the game but I can't do that for NORCO. It's a narrative-driven game but even if I spoiled the story, the spoilers wouldn't make sense without context because the story is so crazy and out there. Even with context it barely makes sense. Instead, I'll provide a summary as best I can.NORCO is a point and click narrative heavy game set in a fictional, possibly futuristic southern US. There are religious, specifically Christian, themes and symbology that run through the story, though it's not overbearing and doesn't dwell on it. It's very hard to review a narrative heavy game while avoiding talking about the story too much but suffice to say this game is largely about reading! Most of the gameplay is reading the story then selecting an option or clicking the right thing on screen, apart from some brief and VERY light turn-based combat that is so infrequent and basic that it's not really worth discussing in more detail.I'm a huge fan of narrative heavy games and I don't mind doing a lot of reading at all. For reference, Disco Elysium is one of my all-time favourite games. I actually picked NORCO up because it looked to be along the same lines, but NORCO doesn't come close to the greatness of Disco Elysium. It's not a bad game but it's quite short and it feels like it just kind of ends. The worldbuilding is lacklustre and so many characters' motivations go unexplained. Events happen but the game rarely tells you . What NORCO has is good but I found myself wanting more and the depth that I was hoping for just wasn't there.
_childDocuments_.name: NORCO

_childDocuments_.review: This game is a narrative masterpiece. It's artwork that's decided to use the video game medium as a way to tell a story and a beautiful world.As many people are saying, NORCO isn't a game for everybody. It's primarily point and click, with simple, straightforward puzzles, a point-and-click mode of navigation, and little mini-games for battles and certain travel sequences. I shy away from calling it a game, really - it feels more like an interactive visual novel, than anything else. But there's so much beauty in that.I am a sucker for rich storylines and a pixel art style, and NORCO delivers on both fronts. The art is GORGEOUS. It's like if old paintings were pixilated. Huge praise to the artists and art directors that came together to create such a visual masterpiece. As I made my way around the map, I found myself engrossed in the world. I often came back to different scenes just to marvel at the way the colors and lines blended together and immerse myself in the artwork, which mixes cyberpunk and antique art in both a literal and visual way. I think it takes incredible talent to be able to do something like this.The story is a poignant exploration of nature versus nurture, of technology versus natural forces, of religion and corporate interests and how they corrupt humans and ecosystems alike. The story, without going into much detail, concerns a young woman, Kay, who returns to her hometown of Louisiana in search for her brother after the death of their mother. She finds herself embroiled in various conflicts, whether it be the aftermath of a neo-Christian cult that has sprung up in Norco, the devastation that the oil industry wreaks upon the swamps and bayous of Louisiana, or the strained relationships between Kay and her family members. Alongside this, the player also assumes the viewpoint of Kay's mother in the weeks before her death and her own adventures prior to Kay's return.NORCO is confusing. There is no real resolution to its plot. Many questions are brought up only to be left unanswered. Many loose ends are left behind by the end. More than just a linear plot, NORCO shines because of how it explores various themes and allows its players to draw their own conclusions on topics that may be too complex to resolve with a single stance. I think that's what I love about it, honestly. It's more speculative than anything. If a beautiful pixel art style, thought-provoking storyline, and fantastic cyberpunk Southern Gothic setting are all things that you're into, I highly recommend NORCO, it's one of the most beautiful games of its genre that I've played thus far, and it's left me thinking and feeling things I can't describe.

_childDocuments_.review: Grim and mody visual novel (or slight puzzler). The strong parts clearly are the atmosphere and the writing style. Note there is an expert mode which might render the game actually a game. I missed it, but I would encourage you to give it a try - it's really off-putting easy otherwise.What I'm not sure about is the narration. 1) For me, many of the humorous/playful/cheerful parts didn't really blend with the dark, gritty scenery displayed elsewhere (e.g. the ). Imo in such a gloomy scenery the only humor which doesn't conflict is sarcasm/cynism. 2) I didn't really get the story yet (I'll do some more research on that), so this point might be improper. But my first impression is that the story couldn't decide where it's some kind of fairy-tale, where it's a grim and realistic journey and where it's just a delusion of yours (example: ). Of course, it all could be "just in your head", but you make progress by dealing with such unrealistic events, so it's hard to take them all as just imagined. Or it's really just a fairy-tale where lots of wierd and unrealistic stuff helps you to breeze through dire situations, but then again, that would conflict with the whole build-up of this place, or at least it wouldn't be my cup of tea.Anyway, recommend! Despite all, it's a beautiful, haunting game with an unconventional and interesting story! Maybe it's a bit to convoluted/confusing, but you have to judge that on your own.
_childDocuments_.name: NORCO

_childDocuments_.review: I very rarely binge any games, but NORCO made the cut. It could have done without the quicktime event-ish fights, but I didn't mind them. The depth and length were pretty Goldilocks level fit for me (a bit less than nine hours to complete) although I do understand why some feel that the game is intentionally padded with filler to stretch the playtime. Despite the surreal setting and story, the internal logic and puzzles are congruent, which make it a relatively easy solve. With the built-in gameplay aids I doubt anybody would ever get stuck, while allowing everyone to take only as much advantage of them as they feel comfortable with.Characters and locations feel thin at times, even if everything is woven together nicely, but I enjoyed the trippyness and the mystery of the whole so much more that it didn't bother me in the slightest. Being able to just move forward with clear enough pointers allowed me to focus on the text, putting the pieces together, and trying to guess where the story would take me next. 4/5, would probably play through again, even if just for the missed achievements.

_childDocuments_.review: Ultimately yes, it's worth it, but despite having several moving (poetically and literally) sequences in the game that ooze mood and emotion, the ending itself is *. And I'm like, seriously? That's what you're gonna give us? The story technically answers all its questions and technically wraps up all lose ends, but it's just bizarrely unsatisfying. Imagine if Lord of the Rings Return of the King (the book) ended with "And Frodo tossed the ring into Mordor, which killed Sauron, so everyone was happy and went home" and . That's how the ending to this otherwise really interesting and mysterious game feels.

_childDocuments_.review: I have completed the game in 3 sessions, mostly being utterly sucked by the fascinating story. This is a near-perfect game, for me a strong 9,5/10. Wonderful pixelart graphics. Tremendous music that you will be listening to long after finishing the game. Two years have passed and I am still listening to synthwave tracks by Gewgawly I and heavy Thou tracks. You get a crazy, gothic and cyberpunk tragic story with well-written characters and interesting locations. The game is mostly slow-paced, focused on narratives, but it fastens up when needed. The only problem I see is an  uneven pacing in the second half of the game that made me bored in few moments. But really, this is such a minor flaw that is not worth mentioning. If you are into narrative adventure games with a lot of reading - just be kind for yourself and play Norco. If you like mysteries, play Norco. If you like Greek tragedies, play Norco. If you are a cyberpunk freak - play Norco. If you love space cats - also play Norco.

_childDocuments_.review: An exceptional game, a must play for fans of story-rich adventures. The dystopian suburban setting is eerily reminiscent the deindustrialized exurbs of today. Themes ranging from automation to abandonment to ecological collapse are dealt with thoughtfully and are woven expertly into an enthralling narrative that is paced well and avoids genre tropes and pitfalls. The characters are fully developed and the relationships among them are realistic and complex. It's easy to get invested in the characters and you'll find yourself raging with them against the despair of powerlessness in the face of monolithic corporate power. Amidst all the anger an elusive motif of justice haunts the story and drives the player forward. An excellent soundtrack combined with striking artwork and compelling writing create a weighty atmosphere that at times can feel almost suffocating. Norco is an excellent game whose narrative maturity is a breath of fresh air; it proves that games can not only be art but vehicles for truly excellent storytelling.

_childDocuments_.name: NORCO

_childDocuments_.review: Great atmosphere, world state, soundtrack and overall vibe.I had hopes for the Mind Map system to be an extra layer of puzzles and conclusions (akin to recent Sherlock Holmes games) or different interpretations to the events of the story. As it is, Mind Map system only reviews the story elements, which is great too, but I feel the game could have used a bit more difficulty in terms of the puzzles.But then again, the story had me few times laughing manically to the madness of the world, tearing up to the stories of the characters and left me speechless at the end.Highly recommended.
_childDocuments_.name: NORCO

_childDocuments_.review: the music, visuals, and atmosphere are top notch - the vibes are all there and i'd recommend solely based on that fact.however, through a more critical lens, the game definitely does feel indie at times with some of the gameplay mechanics which are pretty barebones and rough around the edges, although it's still more than most other point-and-click games have.the writing is decent; it definitely favours a more abstract, surrealist tone to forgo much of the actual explaining that they might have to do otherwise and because of that the plot itself becomes somewhat muddled, especially towards the end. or maybe i'm just spoiled by disco elysium, which, at least with regards to themes and writing, shares some similarities with norco.feeling a strong 7 to a light 8 on this one
_childDocuments_.name: NORCO

_childDocuments_.review: The gameplay is your typical pont-and click adventure, with items to find, places to visit and decisions to make. There are a couple of turn-based battles. It's the only element of the game I would define simply "average", because the rest is very good.The game mainly revolves around text descriptions and conversations and both are very, VERY well written. For the most part they are not verbose, which usually is a difficult balance to strike. To enjoy the game you still have to like reading, though. I do, but it's not for everyone.The pixel art and the music are well executed and always appropriate for the storytelling, but the best element of the game is the story itself. I'm not going to spoil anything, let's just say that it revolves around a big oil company and a group of fanatics. It's pretty crazy and emotional at the same time.8/10
_childDocuments_.name: NORCO

_childDocuments_.review: I don't write reviews for games on Steam. This will be my only one, because it deserves to be written about. NORCO is a game, that despite being a point and click, has changed me. I have never played a game before that has left me with such a strong feeling of being haunted. Literally, when I finished the game this feeling of unease followed me around like a ghost for days afterward. The game left me in deep thought for weeks. As an avid reader, the narration is immaculate. The story is so layered it's impossible to understand the depth of it all with just one play through. Playing it a second time is equally as enthralling, trying to pick up the missing pieces. The love that the entire team has for Louisiana can be seen and felt through the attention to detail in every sense of the word all through the entire game.Every character, all of whom feel are destined to face some sort of tragic, ill-fated doom, garner moments of empathy from the player. It's all tragic with grimy moments of dark humor.The attention to detail in the pixel backgrounds, rich in color, are animated in such a way that gives this game a nice touch. The music is haunting, becoming more and more distorted and sinister as you progress through the game. There's nothing I can say bad about this game.I could go on and on, but I will end by saying if it's a game that deserves to be bought and played it's this one. Amazing.
_childDocuments_.name: NORCO

_childDocuments_.review: Short and Sweet. Not much in the way of actual gameplay. There is no real challenge to the game. All the game's mechanics work towards building the atmosphere of the game and telling more of the story. Having just played Disco Elysium I feel a bit disappointed that the game railroads you through most of the actual mystery. Most of the answers and solutions to any problems in the game are given to you outright or surrounded by signposting.  I would have definitely enjoyed a game that challenged me to put the pieces of the puzzle together myself and given me different outcomes based on the work I put into uncovering the story. That being said. This game is awesome and through the art, writing, and music, paints a vibrant tragic world that is fun to get immersed in and explore the characters that inhabit it. The game oozes style and while it may lack in overall challenge or gameplay the absence of said mechanics does help you get right to the heart of the story allowing you to take it all in at once. Would definitely recommend to anyone looking  to explore a unique setting with compelling characters but who might not want the added challenge of more strenuous or complex game play.
_childDocuments_.name: NORCO

_childDocuments_.review: A post apocalyptic sci-fi mystery set in a small town rural south Louisiana swamp! What’s not to love? This is the best point and click game that I have every played. The writing is superb. The setting and general mood of the game is right up my alley. The characters are unique and quirky and dreary. The story keeps you guessing and never drags for a second. This high concept sci-fi stuff sometimes can be a drag but this is not the case here. I recommend everyone gives this one a shot even if “reading” games aren’t usually your cup of tea. You may find yourself pleasantly surprised.
_childDocuments_.name: NORCO

_childDocuments_.review: NORCO is a compellingly written, lovingly researched, surreal point and click adventure game about Louisiana, which makes the people and feel of the place practically tangible. My only complaint is that it suffers from some shrinking of scope in its third act, as interactable elements grow scarcer and text dominates instead of the beautiful visuals. However, it's one of the most compelling story games I've played in years, and the imagery and poetry is iconic and distinctive and earns it its place as one of the best games of all time.
_childDocuments_.name: NORCO

_childDocuments_.review: This is the best game that's been released this year in terms of writing, in my opinion. Fantastic surrealist play on Louisiana. If you liked Kentucky Route Zero or Disco Elysium, you'll love this. The gameplay is mostly driven by narrative. There are a bunch of "secrets" that might not be possible on your first run, however. I can only hope there are more games like this in our dystopian future.

_childDocuments_.review: I absolutely adore the art style and story of the game. It is very depressing but also witty and the characters and the dialogues with them are masterfully done. Something else is the sound design. Since the game has no voice acting, only rumbling, the sound of the environment had to be believable and it really is. It captures the atmospehere of the area around New Orleans and it is accompanied by great soundtrack. I played demo of the first act, then I bought the full game and the progress save is possible to be used. That's why the short play time showng.Very big thumbs up and reccomendation. :)
_childDocuments_.name: NORCO

_childDocuments_.review: This game walks a tightrope of whimsy, melancholy, humour and complete wank and pulls it off for the most part. Some nice gameplay sequences break up the point and click monotony and the pixel art is incredibly well done. The writing is good for the most part although admittedly it does disappear up its own arse a few times over the journey. At around 6 hours Norco doesn't outstay its welcome and I found the end to be oddly moving.
_childDocuments_.name: NORCO

_childDocuments_.review: A supremely weird point and click mystery that really rules. I have so few notes, it feels like a game that is exactly what it wanted to be. It really kept me interested in all the moving parts the whole way through. Absolutely a must-play if you want to work on unique world building. I think the ending I got was a smidge sudden, but overall, what a hell of a ride.
_childDocuments_.name: NORCO

_childDocuments_.review: This is a game from people who understands what a good game supposed to be. Art is never lazy to provide you visual details, music never your carbon-copy cyberpunk synth preset but anything which greatly dive into NORCO's unique setting. And most importantly, this is a different setting and it doesn't try to be something like 'other games'.  Even though, the whole game seems to be pretty basic, it's filled with small details which makes me appreciate and express my huge respect to the developers of this game.Speaking of other games, I've noticed that the dialogue system is inspired from disco elysium and the mind map system inspired from Pathalogic 2. Which is VERY good because those two were the most innovative decisions within 4-5 years. This is a game from people actually understand how to make a game - with amazing vision and creativity.If you like adventure games like gemini rue, technobabylon, promordia, disco elysium and pathalogic, this is a must play game for you.
_childDocuments_.name: NORCO

_childDocuments_.review: Norco is an excellent latterday point and click adventure set in a deeply intriguing soft-cyberpunk Louisiana brought to life through a host of fascinating characters and simple yet evocative game design. The core of the experience is the narrative, which aspires to explore lofty themes concerning the relationship between identity, spirituality, and class and their roles in our technologically alienated society. To this end, I think it achieves admirably. Its magical realist bent and prose that interweaves apathy and wistfulness into its dreamy tone definitely reminds me of Kentucky Route Zero, and in many ways it examines a similar cultural cross-section, but Norco definitely has its own messages to impart and its own vibe to convey. The plot is strong, if slightly thin towards its climax, but the game has more than enough to offer in its densest parts to make up for it. Highly recommended.
_childDocuments_.name: NORCO

_childDocuments_.review: NORCO is an effective sci-fi dystopia because it is set hardly a generation in the future, with characters dealing with only slightly exaggerated versions of the problems and technological promises of today. The ubiquitous self-checkouts leave people angry and unemployed, false prophets lead wayward incels into a Mars-bound death cult, nature melds with AI to produce nightmarish amalgams that spy and feed information to shadowy organizations - all without ever feeling overwhelmingly bleak. The story is interesting and engaging, but relies heavily on Christian imagery and themes, which may not appeal to some.Beautiful pixel art, soundtrack, and writing, too.
_childDocuments_.name: NORCO

_childDocuments_.review: southern gothic story steeped in christian mythology thru the gameplay of a japanese adventure game. basicly an excuse to talk to louisiana weirdos and go thru this little ode to an area that will be lost thru time and climate change. a nice mix of overly dramatic conversations/prose about what it means to live in the dying gasps of an area intermixed with 30 paragraph stories about guys their toilet experiences.
_childDocuments_.name: NORCO

_childDocuments_.review: It's deliciously absurd. Reminds me a bit of Kentucky Route Zero, but with some nice silliness, secrets and more interactivity. Finding secret dialogue and extra items feels amazing and the characters are so good.Don't play it if you don't like puzzles or you feel stories need to "make sense". It's not a "lol so random" or "it's just symbolism bro" narrative but you do have to accept some weird lore and just go along with it.
_childDocuments_.name: NORCO

_childDocuments_.review: Very much my thing, this felt like the southern gothic lovechild of Kentucky Route Zero and Disco Elysium. I love when games try dare to try weird and out there things without fear of alienating the audience. A mix of visual novel and point and click gameplay elements, its real hook is its writing and visuals. It boasts some of the most moving and evocative writing I’ve read in a videogame probably since playing Disco Elysium last year. It’s hard to wrap my head around how a team gets to write and actually design such an experience. It’s also comprised of beautifully crafted pixel art. There’s a particular frame that instantly became my new desktop wallpaper. And the music, what a surprise. Just a terrific moody score that goes so hard.There’s just so much depth and thematic nuance here, enough to think about for a long time after playing. It oozes creativity and artistry, and a certain kind of weird earnestness and sincerity.
_childDocuments_.name: NORCO

_childDocuments_.review: I think this game belongs at least adjacent to Disco Elysium in a conversation about excellence in video game writing. A beautiful, horrifying, funny, and deeply poetic game which somehow manages to be acutely a game about the present and the now, despite containing androids, mutants, and visions from God. Feels like a dirge in video game form, and it uses the video game part well, using the interactive medium to make you feel, more than anything else, like a person in a family, a person with history, a person who has come home.If I had to criticize anything, there is a combat system which feels not ancillary per se, it adds a bit of spice to the otherwise-straight-adventure-game gameplay, but it's definitely not interesting. Some of the puzzle design also features a smidge of pixel-hunting and a smidge of moon-logic, but nothing too terrible on either front.Genuinely something special, play this immediately.
_childDocuments_.name: NORCO

_childDocuments_.review: The story in this game is extremely enthralling.  Lately when I play a story game, I find myself accelerating to the end.  However with NORCO, the setting and story grabbed and held my attention all the way until the end.It’s intriguing and very well done, so much so that I’d elevate it to (what I would consider) art.  There’s too much time wasting slop being pumped out these days, it’s nice to see creative people putting their skills to work and gaining recognition.We need more quality over quantity, especially in the VN genre.

_childDocuments_.review: NORCO is a fantastic point & click adventure that ties a personal tragedy to a very specific region in Louisiana. The game explores a bunch of themes over its three acts, including capitalism and its effects on the environment, religion, (blind) faith, generational conflict, gentrification, internet edge lord subculture and so much more. The written dialogue between characters felt realistic, never too dramatic, and most importantly, made me care and root for or against them.The core gameplay is simple, there are a few combat parts sprinkled throughout that are nothing more than trivial, the puzzle solving ranges from finding the right location to progress the plot to using gadgets on your in-game phone. There was only really one time where I hit a wall and got lost but that was because I didn't pay attention to a specific line of dialogue, thankfully you almost always have a sidekick with you that recaps your current objective and gives you hints on what to do.The beautiful pixel art landscapes are accompanied by an evocative synth soundtrack and the ambient sound effects did a fantastic job of getting me immersed in this weird world.If there was one aspect I would criticise NORCO for, it's that the game wraps up at an exhilarating pace. There is what you could call a "point of no return" that didn't become apparent for me after I crossed it. What followed in the last 45 minutes, some reviews I've read might say it's rushed, I can see the intention behind it. Just know that when the credits of this game are rolling, you will still have unanswered questions. But does it invalidate the experience we had? Do we need the answers?Overall, you're in for a fascinating story set in not-so-distant alternate reality swamplands. I know comparisons to Kentucky Route Zero are easy; both games explore the history and cultures of a troubled region in America. But what separates the two is that KRZ had a scope far bigger than its main cast, it paid homage to various forms of folklore and art and served as a vessel for all kinds of ways to tell stories.NORCO focuses more on a very personal and tragic story of a family in disarray and takes as much time as it needs to explore its characters and their connections to the titular town and the area of Greater New Orleans. Yes, both games grew from a recent genre of local narrative games, but I would describe NORCO as the realer sibling of KRZ, even despite how surreal some parts of its plot felt.It's a great game, a great story, and the devs are very cool. I think that about sums it up.
_childDocuments_.name: NORCO

_childDocuments_.review: An engrossing, cerebral sci-fi point-and-click adventure game set in rural Louisiana.  The game starts off in the small town of Norco, Louisiana as you take on the role of Kay, a runaway who is returning home upon the news of her mother's death.  As you learn more about Norco, its residents and their collective history, the game morphs into a different playing experience altogether and becomes something truly special in the process.The game's strengths lie in its atmosphere, set piece design and honest depiction of Southeast Louisiana and its residents.  It's clear that the developers have a connection with New Orleans and its adjacent rural communities, and it shows in the idiosyncrasies of the game's NPCs and accurate recreation of some of the game's locations.I'd recommend this game for fans of minimalist, atmospheric, story-driven games.  The payoff is rewarding.
_childDocuments_.name: NORCO

_childDocuments_.review: The introduction part may let you think, you will just walk through a strange world - but as soon as the intro is over, you are full in a story, which asks for action (light), puzzle solving skills and mystery ! The story is partly sad,  people, you meet are crazy, hopeless, weird but others are by your side and help you with your task to find out, what had happened here in this town.  Good thrilling story with excellent art style and music.  Highly recommended!
_childDocuments_.name: NORCO

_childDocuments_.review: At first I wasn't sure if I should buy Norco but after completing it I can say I really enjoyed this game.Yes, there's no voice acting and you have to read a lot but it really didn't bother me as I quickly realised that the developers put a lot of heart into Norco.The story is interesting and has a lot of facets, it touches topics like sience fiction, family drama and social criticism in a very believable way.But it also has a funny, humorous side so it keeps a good balance storywise.The game mechanics are good old point and click with some nice additions.You can use maps for faster travel, there´s a fighting mechanic and other more or less unique things in this game.The player also has freedom of choice and can actively forge the story right from the very beginning.Be it in conversations or deciding to progress in a violent or stealthy way within the storyline and choosing different endings.I also have to praise the visual stile of Norco, despite being a pixel art style of game (or maybe because of it)  it really looks nice and has a lot of interesting visual ideas.If you´re a fan of old school style point and click games with a good story and great visuals - go and get Norco.
_childDocuments_.name: NORCO

_childDocuments_.review: What an experience. I don't presently have the brain power to write the kind of review I would want to for this game, but I wanted to capture some thoughts while the experience is very fresh in my mind.If you are even remotely a fan of Southern Gothic, you'll enjoy this game. I honestly cannot say that the story or setting remind me of anything else I've ever read, which is refreshing. There is, of course, a heavy dash of magical realism that is handled masterfully. Even if you have no idea what on earth is happening, it's still very coherent. Watching things fall into place at the end, where even the most minute detail of the game was suddenly very important and relevant, was a real treat. I had to put the game down for two months because of moving and my work schedule, but I was able to recall much of what had happened in the previous two acts as I picked up at the start of Act 3. The vibes were immaculate, the music was amazing, and the story was engaging. Is it the best point-and-click game I've played? No, but it is the best one I've played in a while.

_childDocuments_.review: Norco seems to have found the perfect balance between powerful narrative and unique click-and-point style game play. I haven't really played something with this style of combat and puzzles. Going into the game, I knew the visuals were going to be beautiful, but the soundtrack has been something that really caught me off guard and has blown me away. _childDocuments_.review: Alright, screw this, I have better things to do with my life than click through this pretentiousness.Today is the second time I have attempted to play through Norco after a bug deleted my previous cloud save, and it's the second time I have bounced off. It's a shame because the setting sounds unique and interesting - a 20 minutes into the future crustpunk Southern gothic jam fest... And it is that, kinda, except the dialog is boring, the characters are flat and the locations are disappointingly dull. Everything is described in these long-winded, meandering snippets of pseudo-poetry that make you feel like you're reading a collage of English Lit essays instead of playing a point and click adventure game.I wasted 20 hours of my life plodding through similarly tedious prose in Disco Elysium, and that game never had any payoff, the characters were as vile at the end as they were at the beginning, and all I got out of it was pretentiousness points that aren't worth anything if you don't hang out in the kinds of circles where people listen to cassette tapes and stroke their chins and talk about antiestablishmentarianism or something. If that sounds like you and your friends group, you might appreciate Norco. If you're a fan of point and click adventures, there are way better ones out there. If you're an indie gamer who liked Kentucky Route Zero, eh, this is not that. I know this sort of stuff appeals to a certain demographic, but it is not me. Buyer beware.
