_childDocuments_.review: I have just finished and immensely enjoyed playing the closest thing to an interactive (and very playable) novel...and I mean that in the most complimentary way I can express this point.  By this I don't mean that the game is typical Interactive Fiction.  Norco looks gorgeous with its unsettling and dark pixel graphics; the music is brooding, understated, and unsettling; its UI is intuitive, using a shadowgate-style corner in the bottom right along with a helpful world map (yet it stays minimalistic, as you are meant to feel as if you are looking through the eyes of the enigmatic and unseen protagonist); the gameplay is varied during the times you are not in adventuring mode, with a trippy combat system, a cellphone UI, and a boat navigation system; the atmosphere is familiar--it takes place in a world we recognize by its American cities, and yet there is always lurking...just underneath...the tinge of the unfamiliar--be it supernatural, alien, psychadelic, or just an uncanny yet unmistakable sense that something is always amiss.  You are meant to always be off-balance no matter which of the game's 2 timelines you are currently playing through.  But make no mistake, this amazing game uses all of its considerable assets to frame the most important parts in this game in expert fashion.  First, we have Norco's environment.  Norco, located in southern Louisiana is already by itself a unique place that this game almost treats as a character in itself.  The mysterious amalgamation of the supernatural, of magic, and of the religious are a natural part that comes with Louisiana's rich history.  Along with that, the enigmatic dialogue, vague suggestions of some unknowable mythos too deep to truly understand, and the existance of impossible beings make you question what is real and what is not.  It also helps enhance the constant sense of paranoia as conflicting stories have you guessing who is your friend and who, perhaps, might be using you for their unknown and yet nefarious ends... and guessing what those ends may even be.  Yet in the midst of all this fantasy, we have a sense of the familiar as well.  We have a home, a cell phone, cryptocurrency...and from the very start, even though we start so far away from Norco, we inexplicably find our way back home.  There is a sense of an unending cycle that is more powerful than your will...that while you may change things from day to day, in the end, the cycle will inevitably repeat itself forever.  Your face (which is not shown) is immaterial...irrelevant...only a trivial curiosity compared to the scale of the issues you wrestle with in this story.  I am aware that this explanation I have written all seems so nebulous as I explain it, but that is where the writing and the dialogue in this game truly shine.  Locals talk like locals and act like they are unique, but familiar identities in this strange land.  And somehow, while local yourself, it is you that is the stranger.  The dialogue (of which there is quite a bit) is all expertly written.  The prose is professional and arrests your attention and grips you firmly.  It is the impotus that keeps you searching and thinking and wondering and attempting to make sense of it all as hard as everything may be to grasp.  However, a VERY helpful tool in this game comes in the form of the mind map in the top left of the screen.  It displays a visual representation of your interactions and how they intertwine as a web, but by clicking each item in the web, you get a very helpful summary of the protagonist's current understanding of the events which have occurred up to the point where you have played.  All of these factors: the beautiful pixel graphics, the music, the ease of movement, the story, the dialogue, the writing, they all come together to create a work that is greater than the sum of its parts.  I have deliberately minimized an explanation of the story and characters, as I feel it is not necessary to get into that in order to know if this is a game you will appreciate.  Also...the most fun I had in this game was in reading through the story while knowing nothing ahead of time and attempting to wrestle with this tale that is so complex and irregular and severe, and mysterious, while in a way also being strangely familiar.  I will summarize: if you don't mind, or even enjoy reading, you will find an incredible adventure that is well worth your time.  If you are not a fan of clicking through text and would rather shootaman, this game isn't for you..but then again if you are reading this far, chances are this is not the type of person you are.10/10  if you read this far, dont think. just buy. thank me later

_childDocuments_.review: Even amidst the adventure game renaissance that we've all been so fortunate to live through lately, "NORCO" stands out as one of the best and most original of the pack: a mash-up of sci-fi, surrealism, and suburban Louisiana slice-of-life. Your mileage may vary regarding how many off-the-wall story elements you can take, but it never succumbs to annoying "lol-random" irony or pretentious self-importance. It even manages to be genuinely funny at just the right times! And as one of those people who easily loses track of even a "normal" game's plot, I was able to follow along throughout the end.I only wish I'd realized up-front that the game comes with an "Expert" mode that you can toggle on the settings menu. Although it's definitely an adventure game and not a visual novel, "NORCO" signposts its puzzle solutions quite heavily, especially if you're playing the default (non-expert) mode. Some folks may appreciate this level of hand-holding, especially if you dig the modern emphasis of point-and-clicks towards story over puzzles; but I preferred to turn off the more obvious in-game hints. Even on expert mode, I wouldn't describe "NORCO" as a difficult game, though it has enough puzzles and non-linear exploration to solidly qualify as a classic adventure.A quick word to the action-averse: "NORCO" contains about a half-dozen arcade fight sequences. In typical adventure game fashion, these are quite awkward to play, but they are also nearly impossible to lose. If this sounds like a giant turn-off, be advised that you can disable these sequences on the settings menu.A special shout-out must be made to the incredible pixel art of this game. "NORCO" features dozens of landscapes and street scenes of New Orleans and its run-down, industrial environs, all of which manage to be both moody and loving at the same time. If they ever make a sequel to that wonderful "Art of Point and Click Adventures" coffee table book that came out a few years ago, I'm sure "NORCO" will be prominently included. I only wish the end of the game had included a final piece of art instead of just a wall of text, but this feels like a needlessly petty complaint to make of such an overall incredible experience.Hats off to the "NORCO" team for one of the most unique, engrossing, and even moving adventure games of the modern era.
_childDocuments_.name: NORCO

_childDocuments_.review: Early GOTY-contender on the strength of the writing alone.Reading into the history of Norco is like being presented with a disturbingly clarified mindmap of American wounds that remain gaping to this day; slavery, murder, corporate indifference, economic collapse, widening inequality, and reactionary politics. Set in the same district, NORCO is a confronting video game; a confident, biographical and bewildering point-and-click narrative experience that feels more like something you inhale rather than play, with an effective cocktail of magical realism, societal heartbreak, and bummer coolness.From the opening act of the game, it feels appropriate to draw direct comparisons to other luminaries of the ‘video games for wonks’ genre, such as Disco Elysium and Kentucky Route Zero, as you wade deeper and deeper into NORCO’s magical realist miasma of inter-familial trauma, vicious class critique, and gorgeous, kaleidoscopic renderings of a constant Louisiana pre-dawn half-light.The game knows when and how to puncture its darkest moments and depictions with some of the most incisive and word-perfect jokes, relieving it from simply being a slog of desperation. In one moment, a character in a bar can be plied for more information about the whereabouts of your brother, provided you do something to quench his thirst. By the time the conversation is over, your contact is three pints deep, hoeing into some ridiculous ‘loaded fries’ on your dime.

_childDocuments_.review: “NORCO” is a game that I thought I’d really like as it is some kind of a mix of an adventure/point-and-click game and a visual novel, two genres I am quite into. I tried the demo and enjoyed it wholeheartedly. Strangely, the longer I played “NORCO” the less I enjoyed it. But let’s begin with the good:-The soundtrack is great. No spectacular songs, just some very good atmospheric synthietracks. Never repetitive or annoying.-The story is intense and overall well told but a bit longwinded.-The gameplay is an interesting mix of different game styles.-Hardly any tiring backtracking.Well, here comes the bad:-About halfway through the game I started to lose interest in the plot as I got tired of reading through those aforementioned longwinded texts. As I stated before I like visual novels, so I am used to reading large quantities of text. I usually enjoy it.-I did not care very much for the pixelated art as it feels forced. What I mean is, the art looks as if some really good and mysteriously dark artwork has been brutalised into pixels. At the start of the game it was tolerable, but somewhere in act 2 I started to wish the devs had chosen a different style.-I think the storytelling really suffers from the jumps back in time when you play as the protagonist’s deceased mother. The first time this happened I got significantly less involved in the story.-There are some extremely annoying mini-games in “NORCO”. Clicking fast on circles, remembering sequencers of symbols and the worst of all: navigating a boat through labyrinthian swamps with incredibly clunky controls. Those mini games are not really difficult, they are simply extremely tedious. So much so, that after 7,7 hours of gameplay, being stuck in swamp somewhere in act 3 I decided to give up. I simply don’t care anymore how the story ends.
_childDocuments_.name: NORCO

_childDocuments_.review: NORCO is a pretentious but lovable little gem. Pixel art, appropriately minimalist ambient music, very well-written dialogues, and a hauntingly melancholic bayou-meets-Blade Runner atmosphere. The ending was downright cretinously incredulous, but, overall, it's very enjoyable for enthusiasts like me who love story-rich, must-read-thousands-of-lines gameplay. Also, the UI is really excellent and makes playing with a controller and reading a breeze.
_childDocuments_.name: NORCO

_childDocuments_.review: This isn’t your typical point and click adventure. There is hardly any inventory puzzles or any inventory management at all. Not once did I have to combine an item, and throughout the whole game I think I only used a handful of objects. It was a nice change actually not having any silly puzzles involving inventory items, it made the adventure seem a lot more realistic and engaging.Instead, progression is hampered geographically mostly, with locations being unlocked by talking to different characters who reveal destinations which can get added to the map, or by examining objects for clues. There are still plenty of puzzle elements but they’re very logical which makes it so much more fun to solve. I usually get stuck in these types of games and when I look up the solution I always grimace because the solution is stupid or unrealistic.I didn’t get stuck in Norco and I think that is because the puzzles were intuitive and plausible, but at the same time quite imaginative. There are a few interesting gadgets to use in some puzzles and some clever mini games that tie well into the story. I think it hits the right difficulty level between keeping you challenged and engaged without leaving you frustrated and wandering around aimlessly not knowing what to do. The story and character interaction are the main draw of this game and the puzzles entertain but they don’t bog you down and break up the flow of the story. They just add an extra layer of interaction and immersion. Currently, there is no diary or notepad entry system so you will need to take notes on paper in certain situations.I have never been much of a fan of visual novels, nor much of a reader of books. I tend to lack the patience or discipline to read too much text. There is an awful lot of reading in Norco, but it is so well written that I honestly didn’t even think twice about it, and actually thoroughly enjoyed the experience. If you’re visually impaired then the text size, font, and delivery speed can be changed in the settings to hopefully cater for most needs.The dialogue is presented at the left or right of the screen rather than at the bottom. It took me a while to get used to it and I found that I was missing a lot of the visual treats on offer because I couldn’t read the text and view the graphics at the same time with the way it was displayed.I enjoyed playing the different characters, teaming up with them and discussing the case as we progressed. It gave a feeling of comradeship and teamwork and bonded me closer to that character. The mind map feature was original and acted as a useful reference for story arcs and relationship reminders, and it felt quite rewarding unlocking a new node on the map.Norco looked and sounded gorgeous with some beautiful and imaginative locales and a nostalgic sounding synth soundtrack that’s both relaxing and atmospheric.I would have liked more than three save slots, especially with all the achievements, and it would have been useful to include time stamps.The town of Norco has various locales you can visit which you can travel by foot using fast travel or travel by car to places located on your map. Travelling by car costs money but it is worth noting that you will never run out of money as it gets topped up as you get overdrawn. Talking to characters and observing the scene are your main avenues of investigation, Pressing the space bar highlights all things of interest and will reveal either a , a  or an . Selecting the magnifying glass will examine objects or people giving a brief description, possibly revealing a clue or adding a location to your map, the speech bubble initializes a conversation with the character, and an ear symbol means you can listen in to a conversation.You play as Kay mostly and different characters join your party throughout the game who you can interact with and ask their advice in certain situations. A green circle appears next to their face indicating they have important information to share or you can interact with them at any time. You also play as you mother, Catherine, in events leading up to her death.Through conversations, observations, or examinations you might uncover information that is added to the mind map. The mind map is a web of connections which slowly evolves and builds as you play, uncovering truths between characters and revealing events that have a bearing on the story.There are some imaginative puzzle and mini games. You have a mobile phone which has a few different gadgets that is used in certain puzzles, like a voice recorder, and virtual reality. The mini games were really fun and absorbed into the story excellently.There are some rudimentary combat scenes involving QTE and memory sequencing. A decreasing circle intersects another circle when you have to click your mouse to score a hit and you have to remember up to five flashing boxes in sequence and repeat them to kill enemies. It’s very simple and I never died once in battle.

_childDocuments_.review: Endless streams of dialogue and descriptive text with almost no dialogue trees are what characterises this visual novel, masked as an adventure game.I loved reading in Kentucky Route Zero and Disco Elysium. Here it's more like reading a book, and not the best one at that. Some ideas are straight out stolen from Kentucky Route Zero, like a dialogue tree about memories of yours, that change through player interactivity. But KRZ used this in a masterful fashion with many choices, which in turn shape the story, here it's rather lackluster with one or two choices. It's used once (maybe twice) and then never again.Four times I encountered this: You walk down a corridor and then get the 'choice' to walk further down and see what is there or walk back. Progressing forward doesn't change anything else, so why pretent like there is interactivity while you as a player are only supposed to read on.The more interesting dialogue is like in old adventure classics, you have several topics and just click on every option to get some information. But those games had something else - puzzles, there are hardly any here. The few puzzle mechanics introduced (of which one or two were pretty good) are hardly used at all and to very little effect. There are some rather boring exploration sequenecs in between that are like taken out of Kentucky Route Zero, just without hardly anything for you to discover.In the XII Games / Wadjeteye game Resonance there was this great idea to use impressions or memories like inventory items. In Disco Elysium you had thoughts you could use to mess around with your stats. Here you have a mind map. But that only serves the purpose to remind you what the plot actually is. This plot is somewhat ok, but mostly also just borrowed from here and there. The graphics and the setting I really enjoyed, but in the end I was pretty bored and angry at this game, that brings nothing new to the table and also can hardly be called a game at all.If you want an adventure game, better go buy Dropsy or any Wadjeteye realease.

_childDocuments_.review: One of the hardest parts about writing reviews is talking about your experience with a game – without spoiling that experience for any potential players. And I experienced a lot in ’s  alternate reality Louisiana that I would like to talk about – but unfortunately can’t.  offers a lot of surprises related to its mysteries, so even broadly talking about how much I enjoyed a certain puzzle mechanic for example would ruin the fun for new players. And with a playthrough only lasting between 3.5-5h, even the smallest bit of information might be crucial.So instead, I’ll only be able to broadly talk about what I enjoyed in  so much – and why I would recommend to it to everyone who appreciates a narrative-driven game that is light on actual gameplay, even for a point & click adventure.The best thing about  is, without doubt, its world and characters. It only took a few minutes of playing and I was fully immersed, drawn into the game.  immediately sets itself apart from other dystopia-depicting games by choosing South Louisiana as its setting – and keeping the technical advances of its world on the smaller side. While I love a good sci-fi dystopia, sticking with a more “realistic” future makes the game even more haunting.With dozens of mysteries to offer, you’ll quickly want to see what answers the world of  has to offer. With a literal “mind-map” keeping track of the protagonists’ thoughts from the beginning, which is being expanded upon learning new information, I was quickly invested in unravelling the web of ’s secrets. And there sure were plenty of things I was wondering about, be it the protagonist, some of the characters & their history or the world itself.But not only was  drawing me in with its mysteries, it was the world building itself that really made play through the game in one go. Strange places and even stranger inhabitants made me want to see just what’s next around the corner. Thankfully,  carves out its own identity in the big market of games depicting dystopias by focussing more on the unique aspects of its South Louisiana setting. While common elements of modern dystopia stories are still there, I never felt like they were taking frontstage in a way that made me go “haven’t I seen this before?”.Instead, I was pleasantly surprised by how wonderfully weird  can be at times – one scene especially made me burst out in laughter because it was just that unexpected. Others kept me on the edge of my seat because I just could not predict where things might end up. In the case of gameplay though, thankfully, I was always able to predict what to do next. Point & click adventures have the tendency to keep a player stuck when it’s too unclear what to do next – but  evades this problem by always offering a help function that doesn’t break your immersion: If you’re moving around with a party of multiple characters, for example, you can ask them what might be next. I personally think this is a great way to offer help but still not remind you that you’re just playing a point & click adventure game in the end.That said, I wouldn’t mind if the puzzles were a bit harder to solve. While there are some great & unique ways to solve problems in this game, most of them are also very obvious and don’t require you to take a pause to think. One could argue that this makes the story flow better, as you spend more time reading dialogues than thinking about how to solve a riddle, but then again,  IS a point & click adventure and not “just” a visual novel. Still, this is an extremely subjective topic and I’d definitely rather breeze through a game thanks to easier puzzles than being stuck with too hard ones. Treat  as a point & click adventure with a focus on narrative instead of gameplay and you got it right.While we’re back to talking the narrative, I want to use this opportunity to speak about the characters of . As I mentioned earlier, you can expect a lot of strange personalities – however, they’re also more than just that, more than being strange for the heck of it. Dialogues are the primary literary device in , which explores a lot of topics, from setting-typical ones like the consequences of capitalism to more niche ones, like internet culture & influencers. Thankfully, the dialogues in  are really well-written, so they never come off as forced or unnatural for the characters.As for the story itself, well, as other reviews have already said: The final act of  can be somewhat divisive. Some plot threads or characters are tied up more hurriedly than I wanted them to be while others feel like they haven’t really been wrapped up at all. Without doubt, it can be said that the final act of  moves at a different pace than what came before. If that’s a good thing or bad thing, if lingering questions are a sign of quality or not, that’s something quite subjective.Personally speaking, I think I would’ve preferred a different final act. In fact, I’m still not completely sure what to make of it. It’s highly possible my feelings about it are going to change over the next few games but as I finished – and hours later, as I’m writing this review – I feel more taken aback by the final act than getting a wrap-up as great as the events leading up to it. I would’ve also preferred it if it leaned less into the  side of things than it did.However, and this is the more important part, I’d still recommend playing  regardless. It’s just such a unique game, from its setting & world to some if its puzzles, that it would be a shame if it didn’t get more recognition. Sure, due to its chosen genre and setting, it’s not exactly a game for everyone. But if my and/or other reviews make this game sound interesting enough for you, please, give the game – or its free demo – a try! It’s been too long since I’ve played through such a refreshingly unique dystopian story, that even a weak(er) final act shouldn’t stop you from seeing what  is about.

_childDocuments_.review: NORCO is a point&click adventure game where you interact with the world and characters by clicking them. There are a few combat areas where you're required to memorize patterns and reproduce them or respond to simple quick-time events. They are rather easy and offer little challenge if you use the right type of character.Compared to other genres where you, the protagonist are the strongest member of the team, here it felt like your partners were.Exploration is done by interacting with the world by clicking and speaking with characters. Exploration is done across the city of NORCO from both Kay's perspective but as well, her mother, Catherine. I normally don't dive into point-and-click adventure games and my biggest problem was the fact that I've had to read quite a bit through dialogues. I'm not the type that enjoys doing it and games usually fell off for me without a narrator/voiceover that helps my ADHD brain to keep focused. I found myself often moving away from my PC doing something else than actually staying hooked and exploring the game willingly, hence why I spend so much time with the game.That shouldn't stop you from trying the game out if you're into adventure games, just be warned that if you're not into these types of games it might not feel as fun. The main thing that attracted me to this game was the visuals. They look like the old-school type of point&click adventure games back in the 90s with a very surreal and interesting touch.Despite its simplicity and art direction as a pixel art, the game tells a lot through the minimalistic look. One of the most interesting parts from this game was the sound effects and music. I think they are done pretty well to keep somewhat an intriguing feeling at times and not feel annoying at all despite it's repetition.I really wish it had a voice-over for those who love to listen to stories than to read them as I am very sure I would have paid more attention to random dialogues and gotten more immersed in the main plot.  The story is a rather strange and fascinating one. You play as Kay, a girl who lost her mother to cancer and returns back home to find that things have taken an unexpected turn. Your brother, Blake is missing and you partner up with some of the strangest characters, yet fascinating individuals in a quest to find your brother and uncover the secrets behind your mother's death and the city you once called home.I found the writing to be well thought out, where characters held somewhat of a good background despite not requiring to know them for a long time. The game can get rather strange at times in what events occur, so be prepared for "WTF?" moments as well as humor sprinkled here and there. The game can be completed in possibly an hour to a maximum 6. It depends on how quickly you wish to go through the plot, how fast of a reader you are, and how much you want to engross yourself in the world. My time spent is partially to repeating from the very beginning a second playthrough to get 100% and as well being away from keyboard.Difficulty wise it's not something I found hard at all. Combat is rather straight forward and people with experience with turn-based strategy might find it extremely easy. The game guides you well enough and it's not difficult to keep track of where you are and where you need to be if you communicate with your companions and other NPCs you meet in the world. NORCO can be a hit or miss for people, depending on how you view and how familiar and how much you like the point&click adventure genre. For some, the game might bring nostalgia and the plot might be considered a Masterpiece, while for others might be an interesting and strange story that forever will confuse you with its plot. I personally feel in the second category, but that might be just me. Please do take my personal opinion of the game rather objectively and consider trying the game out despite me liking it or not as much.

_childDocuments_.review: I waited a long time for this to come out, so when it was finally released I bought it right away. There's always a chance of being disappointed when that happens, so I'm glad to say that wasn't a concern for me at all.NORCO is a point and click adventure game and the way it proceeds feels like it has a lot in common with the old 90's hypertext novels that fell out of fashion. A parallel evolution of the visual novel, it feels like the team learned from mistakes of the past where the puzzles you deal with make complete sense and you're rarely, if ever, scouring the screen for a single pixel that you need to click on to proceed. Combat feels a little tacked on from time to time but is relevant to both the narrative and the overall vibe, so it's never onerous (and the game provides an option to automate it if you feel the need to do so).As far as the theme - NORCO is a southern gothic cyberpunk manifesto. The very definition of high tech and low life where the marginalized and impoverished people of NORCO live under the shadow of a corporate oil behemoth that's poisoning the land and water while even stranger things happen where they can't be easily seen. This is totally unlike games along the lines of Cyberpunk 2077 or Deus Ex where you're a sort of superhero-esque combat figure - you're a drifter who came home to her ♥♥♥♥♥♥ town after her mom dies to help tie up loose ends. You deal with the people around town you grew up with, slowly realizing you don't know what you even look like - and apparently others can see that, too.There are mysteries you don't even know are mysteries when you start playing, mysteries you're never even told you're trying to solve, nested carefully like matryoshka inside each other where you're never sure if you've made it to the last doll. NORCO is a little light on gameplay if you're looking for tight action and a fast pace. But thematically, it's beautiful. The audio is terrific, it's not a farce but it does possess a wry and pointed sense of humor despite the bleak environment, and it's a fantastic example that cyberpunk - perhaps something of a zombie genre, now - still has flashes of life left in it if people care to look for it. Highly recommend.

_childDocuments_.review: just an incredibly well-written, atmospheric, experimental, and brutal point & click adventure.not brutal in terms of difficulty with mechanics, but more challenging in terms of its writing and what it has to say. if that sounds pretentious, it's because games rarely have challenging narratives (which I don't have a problem with regarding individual games, but I'd love more games that provide as much food for thought as NORCO does). I'll clarify what I mean, exactly, and will try to be broad and avoid spoilerish chicanery. this game grapples a lot with severing ties with blood relatives--namely parents. are we obligated to forgive our parents if they traumatize us or treat us awful? why can people who were treated TERRIBLY by their parents still feel some ethereal connection to them? it's a very rough topic that speaks to me as someone who has mutually disowned both of my parents. they mean nothing to me, but this has all been relatively recent to me (been about 3 years since I last spoke to either) and I don't even know if either of them is alive still. to be honest with you, I don't really care, they were terrible and violent and cruel and vindictive--and if reading that makes you a little uncomfortable, you now know what to expect from NORCO. it is painfully honest.edit: I find it genuinely, deeply disturbing that someone "found this review funny". nothing I said here was even darkly humorous, and it was 100% earnest. edgelords gonna edgelords, I guess.edit 2: edgelords when they see some stranger discussing how a piece of art spoke to their experiences with parental trauma and then saying that finding this funny is emotionally unintelligent and disturbing: "wow, wouldn't I be so cool and so funny if I said this was funny"

_childDocuments_.review: And once again, we walk into the tricky bed of thorns of 'games as art.''Norco' would likely be classified as an adventure game above anything else, but the puzzles are infrequent and generally of low difficulty.  The combat is simplistic and a bit awkward, but it's so rare it hardly matters.  Occasional deviations into different gameplay modes, like driving a boat, can be safely rated as 'serviceable.'  So it's up to the writing, characters, and production to carry the day.  And my goodness, do they ever.Personally, I'd classify this game as a visual novel.  It's those elements that are going to hook you in if you're going to be hooked at all.  'Norco' is a story of delightful contradictions, celebrating both the beautiful and the grotesque; the sacred and the profane.  The setting is... cyberpunk lite, let's call it?  Think 'Blade Runner' shot through the prism of Southern Gothic, where rogues and tramps huddle together for dear life.  Everything in the game seems to be rapidly decaying, from the people to the land itself.  I wasn't surprised at all to find out that the project began as a documentary about the devastation of Hurricane Katrina to Louisiana, given the game's grim tone and focus on environmental destruction.  And as the land falls apart or is shattered by heavy industry, what about the people who live there?  In 'Norco,' they suffer quietly, go mad, look for God, join a cult, or, in the case of our protagonist, they run like hell until circumstances call them back to whatever home they may have left.So, let's get the obvious comparison point out of the way - 'Disco Elysium,' the 800-pound gorilla of modern games-as-art.  The developers don't cite it as an influence, but there's no denying that 'Disco' has made the waters much safer for games like this to swim in.  There are some strong points of similarity between the two games - long strings of gorgeous purple prose, finding beauty in urban decay, a tangible Marxist influence, and so forth.  I can't flat-out say that 'if you liked one, you'll like the other,' as 'Norco' never hits the heights of dark hilarity that 'Disco' does.  (Granted, how many games have?)  But 'Norco' is bleaker by design, where even the "good" ending is pretty macabre.  'Disco' offers the faint hope of redemption and a better world; 'Norco' is basically an hourglass draining out.  Also, a shout-out to 'Kentucky Route Zero' is probably in order here, too, although again there is no stated influence.  This just seems to be a genre of game that is taking shape organically via modern economic circumstance.I'm not going to touch on the story much - it would basically just be spoilers.  Fair warning, though; if you've recently lost a parent or have a sibling you can't quite connect with, this game will hit especially hard.  I literally called my parents after finishing this game the first time to remind them that I loved them.  This world of ours is designed to isolate us; this game shows the consequences.  One of my favorite moments is when a character in poor health tells one of your allies that the best thing he could do for him would be to simply visit more often.  It was perfectly bittersweet.Production-wise, the pixel art is fantastic, full of detail and style.  Nothing hits me quite like gorgeously-depicted ugliness.  One of my favorite little touches is when a character will occasionally emerge from the shadows, but slowly, so it's not so much a jump scare as just... unsettling.  The music holds up its end, too, haunting and eerie exactly when it needs to be.  Everything is very somber, like you're at the wake of human civilization.So should you buy this game?  You kind of already know the answer, don't you?  I mean, it's unlikely you landed here by accident while looking for the hot new looter shooter.  If you want to travel across Louisiana with a rogue's gallery of characters and tons of beautiful florid prose, hop on board.  (There's a free demo available if you're still on the fence.)  I like shooting zombies as much as the next person, but I'm grateful that more and more games like this are emerging, which take the medium into deeper waters and stay with us long after the credits roll.  Escapist fare is fine, and maybe even essential, but perhaps, like the protagonist of this game, we escape too often and for too long, averting our eyes from an admittedly frightening reality that needs to be dealt with.  I pray we're not at 'Norco' yet.  Maybe we are.  In either case, make sure to reach out to everyone that's important to you, and seek out and embrace the remaining beauty in our world.  It can all disappear so quickly.Highest recommendation.

_childDocuments_.review: Every iteration of , from the game’s initial demo to the release of the first act, has clarified its weird, haunting voice that little bit more. That’s an obvious enough observation, but it was a voice that promised more than most. And as each iteration expanded the art’s dimensions, that voice’s potential was amplified. Still, I was uncertain of its reach. Now  has arrived, having deliriously flung open its doors, and my first trip down the rabbit hole is over.Thinking about it some hours later, I’m pretty sure it’s one of the best games ever made – or at least a fresh direction of travel for the medium.When her mother succumbs to a persistent cancer, Kay returns to her hometown of Norco, Louisiana, after an exile’s journey across a collapsed America. Beneath a molten sky abused by smokestacks, the family home is empty except for an android whose face sparkles like stars in a pool. Kay’s brother should be there but he’s vanished, leaving bad vibes in his wake. With some prompting from the android, Kay sets off in search of him, exploring shadows old and new as an arcane mystery quickly devours what’s left of her life.American greats like McCarthy and DeLillo and even Dos Passos percolate in  mystic dystopia, but the language is its own. As a piece of eco-criticism,  is a revelation, crafting a world we both know and do not know. Possibly the last world we’ll ever know if we can’t take apart the dead-end capitalist perdition we’ve all but committed to. , with exceptional clarity and imagination, demands nothing less to avert an apocalypse that connects every one of us.But for the developers, that apocalypse has a personal nexus. Sat on the Mississippi River just west of New Orleans, the Norco of the game is a strange and sinister dreamscape, textured with history and biography. Like a reflection on a beloved memory of home. Only that memory has been contaminated, phosphorescent light blinking on sallow water. Stretched into its own future, memories like these are up for grabs and committed to servers, taking the last piece of home.When I went looking for Norco in the present, I was struck by the hotspots on Google Maps: they were almost all oil companies, as if that passed for an identity. Somewhere in the ley lines connecting this unforgiving industry, the tragedy is very real in a place that’s only ever been owned, cultivated and drilled. The accumulating tragedies become something like a scream in the game, channelled into a statement about the singular tragedy of the failed American system. And as I write that, I want to reach for  –  is that damn good.As a point and click narrative adventure,  is just as exploratory. There are items to gather and people to speak with, but the genre’s hallmarks are kept to a minimum. Instead,  is a layering of experiences, always mindful of perspective – whether that’s Kay’s or her mother Catherine’s, who share the narrative. Perspective informs what players .In one sequence, you’re slinking through a rainy night at the behest of Superduck, a horrifying artificial intelligence that operates like a self-aware Craigslist. Superduck’s mission spins into infiltrating a motley crew of gross white dorks, who have shacked up in a local mall. To gain entry you need to utilise their leader’s mobile app to find digital signposts across town. It’s weird as heck, but also completely believable, and it’s the framework for your back-and-forth between locations and characters.The action unfolds organically, opening nooks and crannies in Kay and Catherine’s respective nights that find the profound nestled in the mundane. Small scenes that indulge anecdote and myth, deepening the flawed, broken, and messy humanity splattered over Norco. Small scenes that don’t ever lapse into whimsy; each one inserts a fresh layer, building towards catharsis. You rarely run into such snapshots in games, making them all the more special here.Creatively, it’s not easy producing something fundamentally about Now – and  really is about Now, in case there’s any question. It’s a problem that pops up in far too much literary fiction – reflexive observations on the present that lack authenticity. But there’s nothing reflexive about . Its understanding of digital languages, and their impact on self and our internal and external landscapes, is behind all the amazing pixel art, the dreamy, eclectic music, and every perfect bit of prose.The game just sort of  what matters , which is what the best science fiction does, right? The water is rising, the institutions of government fraying, and the collective madness building, yet still we retreat into the loveless inhumanity of corporate systems. Even their own creators can’t escape them in , in one of the game’s many quietly devastating moments.Which is all just to say  is a vital piece of videogame art that absolutely everyone should play immediately. Its dreamscapes shift beneath us, bending towards the quasi-religious until you want to cling tight to the few hands left in reach. Because as unrelentingly bleak as it can be,  is still holding out for a better world than the one it sees dead ahead.

_childDocuments_.review: Lots of interesting ideas that ultimately don't fit together very well. It's nice to see a game set in Louisiana, and it captures a lot of aspects of that region well, but the sci-fi elements feel half-baked conceptually, the motivations of the characters—villains especially—are a bit cartoony and incoherent. Overall, the worldbuilding just needed to either be more realist, or more surrealist, and the middle point that it chooses just feels a bit cheap and lacking in detail. However, it does have some fun puzzles and characters, hinting towards what the same team would be capable of with more resources and discipline. If the game had an even more broadly simulated and nonlinear world with more choice and consequence, as well as more realistically explained sci-fi elements or no sci-fi elements at all, I'd probably be raving about it, rather than being disappointed but nonetheless intrigued by what could have been. Still, there's nothing else like it on the market, so recommended on those grounds alone.
_childDocuments_.name: NORCO

_childDocuments_.review: Imagine a point and click adventure on the Amiga 500, but the graphics do some things that wouldn't have been possible back then.Interface like Deja Vu. An excellent soundtrack.Very good writing with the story being a mix of religious themes, coming home and family conflicts and a thriller told from 2 perspectives.This really gripped me and I had to finish it day 1, I just couldn't stop.For me it's a strong 9.
_childDocuments_.name: NORCO

_childDocuments_.review: NORCO is a short, point and click adventure game.The story is a highlight, managing to capture horror and heartbreak both mundane and fantastic. However, due to its brevity, characters are largely flat and the story overall lacks emotional depth. Though the setting itself is very distinctive with its mix of industry, poverty, and mysticism. The pixel art is gorgeous and at times psychedelic and the game overall has very strong visuals. On a similar note, sound design is also excellent, strongly emphasizing the identity and mood of each location visited in the game. Gameplay is overly simple and easy. Whether its the point-and-click segments that dominate the game's runtime or the rare mini-game based combat encounter, it's almost impossible to lose or get lost.Overall, a solid thumbs-up from me.
_childDocuments_.name: NORCO

_childDocuments_.review: I bought the game based off the stunning screenshots alone and didn’t really have much expectations. The best parts of Norco are definitely the visuals and the setting. The writing is also a standout for sure, it can be somber and emotional one moment, then sharply funny the next (poor hot dog guy). Game-play wise it was quite simple and there weren't really much puzzles like you expect from a normal point and click game. The only thing that marred the experience for me was the ending. It felt like a rushed fever dream that didn't really mean much.That being said, I still highly enjoyed my time with the game and would highly recommend it.
_childDocuments_.name: NORCO

_childDocuments_.review: Norco is a fresh breath of personal and weird storytelling in a market saturated with open worlds full of chores to do. Norco is not a distraction, it is a story about where we are and how it is awful. It is your friend commiserating with you in the midst of a global pandemic as you stare into the twin barrels of capitalism and climate catastrophe, nodding and saying, "Yeah, maybe we don't make it. Want another beer?"I have never been to Norco or Louisiana, but I suspect anyone who grew up in a suburb or a small town will be able to commiserate with the prose and people of this game. There is one moment in particular, in Act 1, where you're standing in the street and you can hear a dog barking. The sound echoes off the asphalt in a way I heard so many times growing up. It's a sound of summer, of wandering outside 'cause there was nothing else to do, of feeling alone and anxious and wanting to just run away, to find yourself, to find anything other than the mess you are stuck in. Norco's story and presentation will stay with me for a very long time.
_childDocuments_.name: NORCO

_childDocuments_.review: UAHGUHUGHUAHGUHGH GOODcoming back to this, 15 days later: I haven't stopped thinking about Norco. i don't think a video game's story has stuck with me for so long, and has left me with so many questions that I'm delighted to not know the answer to. Norco has the perfect amount of threads that are satisfied, that still leave lingering questions...sure, I know what happened when this character did this thing, but *why*? And that's a good thing, because in life, you don't always get all the answers and motivations. From a single perspective, Kay, you can't know everything, and Norco balances it perfectly. With stellar music, writing that is both melancholic and thought-provoking with bursts of absurdity and humor, and an amazing aesthetic art style, this game is my 2022 game of the year!
_childDocuments_.name: NORCO

_childDocuments_.review: Man this game is a trip. I didn't know anything going into it and I gotta say I was not a disappointed. The biggest draw is honestly the pixel art. It is incredible, there are some truly stunning images that come up over the course of the game. The story is super interesting as well. It definitely feels like it walks a thin line between playing it super serious and being somewhat goofy, but it rarely stumbles on it. Themes that come up throughout seems poignant, and unraveling exactly what is going on with your family is fascinating enough to want to finish the game all in one sitting (which I did). This was definitely a sleeper hit for me, I thoroughly enjoyed it.EDIT: Play this game. I still think about it constantly, there's so many incredible scenes, so much incredible artwork. The more time passes the more it works its way up my ranking. Genuinely a modern classic.
_childDocuments_.name: NORCO

_childDocuments_.review: It's not a very long or challenging game, but the pixel art is gorgeous, the writing/story engaging, the general vibe somewhere between Jeff VanderMeer and bayou gothic, and a decent soundtrack to top it off. It's the kind of game I want to replay right after finishing, knowing the plot's secrets, to see all the hints and foreshadowing I missed on my first run.The only two minor issues I have with the game are 1. the record dialogue function is finicky and tends to disappear as I tried to click it, and 2. having a trigger warning at the start that weighs blasphemy on the same scale as suicide (seriously that's a little ♥♥♥♥♥♥).
_childDocuments_.name: NORCO

_childDocuments_.review: I'm recommending this because it's a damn damn good game, but I swear to god playing this was a mistake.It was devastatingly depressing, exhaustingly chunky, and ... a lot. It was super well written and the characters were really fleshed out, but I think I may be worse off for having played it.In short, 10/10 don't recommend.
_childDocuments_.name: NORCO

_childDocuments_.review: The first time in a long while I've really loved a game. It's more of an immersive graphic novel. Very well written and enjoyable to read. The art design, music, sound, pixel art, is all really well done, but the story is where it's at. Very immersive and enjoyable world to vibe out in. I really recommend digging into the story and the characters as much as possible. It's not a game for everyone, but if you're looking for a relaxing late night vibe of a game, this is it. Point-and-Clicks have a mindfulness quality built into the genre. The music and story-telling really ad to the immersive quality of this game. I love using the optional CRT monitor emulation mode, but I'm an oldie. It helps me remember how immersive point and clicks felt to me at the time. I do plan on replaying without CRT to really appreciate the pixel art. You can tell this is a game created with a lot of love. It has a quality that AAA titles will never be able to emulate. It's something people want more of IMO. Games created with this much love and attention are rare. It's nostalgia, existential, sci-fi, history, future, cool-characters and... there's just a lot lot to appreciate about it.Apart from the story and the vibe (which is what I'm here for),. the gameplay is simple but it's not a cakewalk. There are larger riddles you must solve, and challenging mini games. You are casually solving a mystery, which is a lot of fun to uncover. It doesn't ever feel repetitive. The mini games always result in something surprising and/or the game itself is unique in some way. There are generally a lot of ways to get hints if you are stuck on any particular puzzle (i.e. talking to other characters). If you're someone who just wants to progress a story as fast as possible to beat a game, this isn't a game for you. You've got to know going in that this game is a total vibe game. You've got to want to read and immerse yourself in it. Take your time with it. The creators did such a good job making a detailed story and setting. The text is so well written, concise, and fun to read, but the game does allow you to take it as deep as you'd like, allowing you to discover characters and stories deeper if you want (you do want) . Anyway I'm rambling but this game is great and I suspect I'll replay it a lot into the future to get the most out of it.
_childDocuments_.name: NORCO

_childDocuments_.review: My mom called me today from my childhood home in the Biloxi area, roughly an hour east from nola on the gulf coast, and she told me about her depression, isolation, inability to cope with family being gone or passed. An hour later, I finished Norco. This game is an artistic achievement in atmosphere and allegory for any audience, but being from the area (especially after having fled it in adulthood) makes it personal. Beyond recognizing the I-10 overpass and Metairie and the early-imprinted memory of watching your mother pull up carpet after a flood (Georges, for me), there's a desperate melancholy that comes with knowing your home is being slowly but surely washed away. The experience of going home to visit, seeing the changes that sculpt and disfigure your past, the new developments and the abandoned businesses both, is made physical. A corner of your consciousness set fluttering free to swallow the land. You can bet I sobbed like a baby walking with Kay through that house as the waters claimed it, seeing it as mine in my mind's eye, recounting my memories alongside hers.It's not a long game, not a huge investment of time or energy. It's forgiving for people on a trackpad and it's honest with the choices it gives you, and their consequences. It's dark without reveling in its darkness, sincere in its love of people and place, and as enjoyable as it is gut-wrenching. If you happen to be from the area, whether you're a Blake or a Kay, so much the better. I'm going to call my mom back.
_childDocuments_.name: NORCO

_childDocuments_.review: If this game piqued your interest, but you're on the fence, I would say dive in.  The game plays like a good book reads.  The characters are real, interesting, and distinct.  The plot is wild in the best way.  The world is so interesting to explore.  I haven't been pulled into a game like this in a long time.
_childDocuments_.name: NORCO

_childDocuments_.review: I've followed the development of Norco for approximately two years and am very proud of what it's become. This is an extremely ambitious project for such a small team and is clearly inspired by intimate and personal life experiences. The grounded descriptions of mundane memories -cockroaches in a microwave, the smell of a grandfather's old pick-up, the bayou and the poverty- contrast strongly with what I can best describe as post-left esoterica: bitterly ironic collapse mysticism, poetic descriptions of intelligence networks and industrial infrastructure, and pockets of flavor text that seem deliberately written in the style of analysts like Deleuze and publications like Tiqqun. Not to mention the blend of paranormal and technological horror.At no point was I sure where the story was headed, and the ending was fittingly surreal and tense. My only complaints are that it left a lot of questions unanswered, which was unsatisfying in a few places; and that Lucky was rewritten from being an insurrectionist android to an elderly oil pirate, but he's still a very rad character.What else? The art is fantastic- this much I expected from everything I'd seen of Geo's work beforehand. The music and atmosphere are at no point bad and contribute well to a tense and heavy atmosphere. The gameplay is largely inoffensive but doesn't shine, either. The writing -the one thing of which I wasn't sure what to expect- turned out to be exceptional, thoughtful but concise enough that it never felt like I was just reading walls of text, poetic and clever and always just a little bit detached and mournful.Norco is absolutely worth the price, you should really find out how good it is for yourself.
_childDocuments_.name: NORCO

_childDocuments_.review: Absoloutely wild ride that manages to mix fascinating historical details about Louisiana with great sci-fi social commentary and a mix of extremely entertaining, memorable characters. The game can be rather bleak and unnerving at times, but it manages to mix that really well with a particularly sardonic sense of humor. My only criticism is that I wish there was more - certain elements could have been more fleshed out, like Thomas St-Claire or Pawpaw's bizarre origins, but it's a minor nitpick.
_childDocuments_.name: NORCO

_childDocuments_.review: I loved every minute of this game. The visuals alone are breathtakingly beautiful, but the writing is what really drew me in and kept me hooked. I found myself pausing at multiple points throughout just to take in the details and admire the gorgeous pixel art as well as the music and sound design. So many moments really stuck with me, but the song that plays in Dimes outside of Duck’s house is one I lingered on for an especially long time. The ambient sounds of birds and traffic added so much texture to the experience and left me feeling homesick.This game would be impressive regardless, but knowing it was made by such a small handful of artists is remarkable. Norco strikes the perfect balance of being deeply sad, hauntingly surreal, and surprisingly humorous. It’s apparent how much care and attention to detail was poured into this piece of art. As a native Louisianan, I am so grateful for this. While I don’t think someone has to be from or have even visited south Louisiana to enjoy or appreciate the game, I do think having a deep understanding of and relationship to the area makes the experience of the game that much more meaningful. This is the first time I’ve seen my home accurately reflected in all its nuance and am left with feelings of nostalgia, heartbreak, and pride, rather than embarrassment and frustration. Highly recommend this game.
_childDocuments_.name: NORCO

_childDocuments_.review: If William Gibson were from Louisiana, NORCO is probably the kind of thing he would have written. A strong blend of family drama fueled decision making with corporate over-extension crashing into local superstitions that may or may not turn out to be true, and all presented in a powerful and dreamlike way to keep you wondering if what you're experiencing is real or an illusion brought on by digital psychosis or chemicals or your own mind rebelling.NORCO utilizes a slick first person point and click interface for you as Kay to figure out what has happened since you mother's death. Navigate between rooms and locations, interact, join forces and fight with a wide cast of weirdos and freaks, hunt for clues and map the relationships between them in your mind.Beautiful game. If you've read any reviews you've spoiled too much already. If the trailer or free demo didn't intrigue you enough then I'm not going to convince you.
_childDocuments_.name: NORCO

_childDocuments_.review: A reasonably well-made narrative experience. It does nothing special. Doesn't excel in any aspect. It tries to tell a mindblowing kind of story that might amaze some people who's never seen similar one. But if you have, it's all just meh because the presentation is simply mediocre.Another part of the draw might be the American rural culture, specifically that of South Louisiana. But as a non-American, I simply don't feel it.In conclusion, I can see someone enjoying this. But to me, coming here seeking good writing, good art, or deep characters to know, I came away disappointed.(The playing hours is inflated due to me leaving the game open at all time. Not indicative of actual game length.)
_childDocuments_.name: NORCO

_childDocuments_.review: Wow, just wow! The tags are really very accurate, and if you're into more than two of those, you should deffo try it out! This game is one of a few I've really enjoyed this year. It really, really is very well-written, and it's literally what I've been looking for in games for the past several months. I was looking for something dystopian, noir, ver atmospheric, and I hit the jackpot. AMAZING arts, beautifully fitting soundtrack. A "little" but of mystery, religious conspiracy. Combat, while not frequent, is also very easy.It's not an expensive game. You lose just a few bucks but can potentially fall in love with AMAZING NARRATIVE.
_childDocuments_.name: NORCO

_childDocuments_.review: Since it's coming up, let's talk about my game of the year. Norco was an early contender when I played it at the beginning on 2022 and it has kept its spot rightfully. I love how down to earth this game is even by cyberpunk standards and I love its music and I love its silly plot and the little vignettes you get into this New Orleans community. It's special in a way I can't describe. Play it if you like point and clicks. Play it regardless. It's that good.
_childDocuments_.name: NORCO

_childDocuments_.review: A well-crafted narrative, brilliant writing, and gorgeous visuals. Norco, at a base level, is a story about grief while you try to find your brother. It shows it's more than that, though, almost immediately. The interactions you have with characters, the descriptions of the landscapes and objects around you, are humid with meaning. They're brief, yet manage to portray real weight. Through these subversively simple little sentences, a spectacle of themes is unveiled, each tying in to the Southern Gothic visuals. We pick up on past environmental destruction, and future annihilation; we see the cages of poverty and drug addiction; we see a search for meaning through technological advancement and religious delusion. We see how time and space are as entrenched in us as mud and grass in Louisiana bayous. It's utterly cliche, but a game like this, especially in this style, does not come along frequently. This is a meditative experience, and it's not one you should miss out on.
_childDocuments_.name: NORCO

_childDocuments_.review: Well made, looks good and a lot of effort is put into the artwork. But it sort of feels......."rushed"?  Don't know. It constantly made me feel there was supposed to be more in the story but there really wasn't. Just feels unsatisfying. Like it want's to be very important or deep, but it really is a bit shallow. That, or the story just doesn't make sense to me.Doesn't make me feel like coming back to get all achievements.Buy on a sale I guess.  I'll give it a thumbs up, but not a recommendation.
_childDocuments_.name: NORCO

_childDocuments_.review: A short but worthwhile story. If you're a fan of Disco Elysium and Citizen Sleeper and enjoy the likes of Jeff Vandermeer, this may be a game for you. A little bit of environmental sci-fi intrigue, corpo bashing,  supernatural weirdness, and silly dialogue options to cut the tension.Overall, I really liked the story and interactive mechanics. Largely a visual novel with a couple of mini-games sprinkled in, none of which are particularly difficult. Content warnings for substance abuse, religious iconography, and an unavoidable (non-graphic) depiction of suicide
_childDocuments_.name: NORCO

_childDocuments_.review: If you're wondering whether to buy it, yes, absolutely do to try it out if it looks decently interesting to you. To me, it's a masterpiece of atmosphere, writing, game design, and art. It has impressive worldbuilding, a luring backstory, artwork to mesmerize, and a soundtrack to lock you in... and then there's that ♥♥♥♥♥ Rosie, who I'm guessing to be the digital manifestation of one of the dev's early childhood trauma likely permanently imprinted by what I'm sure is a lovely aunt named Rosie. There's no other way someone can come up with something like Rosie without some serious issues that need to be addressed sooner rather than later. Go see a therapist because I'll need a reference for a good one - I got second-hand trauma from that experience.
_childDocuments_.name: NORCO

_childDocuments_.review: What a good, weird game!It starts slow and almost mundane but chooses unexpected directions to go from there.The game masterfully conveys a sense of place through writing, art, and music. You don't have a character who can freely explore — instead, you switch between different screens-locations. And yet, you feel like you are there. It all comes together into an open-ended experience. Not all questions are answered, and not all mysteries are resolved. You are encouraged to interpret your thoughts and feelings, and maybe dig some more if you wish.It's great.
_childDocuments_.name: NORCO

_childDocuments_.review: A point and click game with not only a very good writing and well-made art style, but also has decent puzzles and turn-based combat that is enough to add flavor to the game. The creator(s) definitely have a complex love/hate relationship with real life Norco. Which should be a relatable feeling to many people.  It is best if you play it knowing nothing about it.
_childDocuments_.name: NORCO

_childDocuments_.review: I have no idea what genre I'd describe this as, to start with. There's elements of point & click in here, the occasional simple turn-based fight (though never very difficult, it feels more like an expression of mood and maybe a little tongue-in-cheek parody of such things than a real attempt at making combat a part of the experience), there's a few choices you can make...it feels quite varied, but never incoherent or scattershot. The story and world is very intriguing so far, there's a lot of melancholy here, a lot of rot everywhere you turn, and despair at the way Norco's world is going. I was first turned on to this game when looking for recommendations of things that are like Disco Elysium, and in terms of the narrative and how it's delivered, the tone and state of the world, there are similarities...but I also would never want to do this game the disservice of calling it a copycat or trying to imply it's not very much its own thing. I think if you liked Disco Elysium, you'd probably like this, I know I do. I also think it's different enough from that game that if you go in expecting something that uses even a vaguely similar framework for delivering its gameplay and story, you'll be quite surprised and taken aback.It's a little tricky to summarise Norco, but I can confidently say that I love the depth and style of the writing, and I enjoy the way it blends different gameplay and presentational styles to create its own unique voice. Like I said before, there's a lot of melancholy in everything from the writing to the art style, but it is also quite funny at points and it doesn't shy away from revelling in the odd bit of surrealism/whackiness. It's a game where you alternate between playing as a grieving, estranged daughter and her cancer-stricken mother, but it's also a game where you can pet a cat so well that it rockets through the ceiling out of excitement, or pressure a man into telling you the thrilling story of how he broke into a limo so he could relieve his diarrhoea, and it moves between these very different tones with a skillfulness that makes it all feel perfectly consistent.If that sounds good, then you should absolutely give it a go.
_childDocuments_.name: NORCO

_childDocuments_.review: I was recommended Norco after Disco Elysium, and like Disco Elysium the writing and story are phenomenal. On top of that, the pixel art and soundtrack are pretty dang good too. Norco takes place in Norco Louisiana, which is apparently a real place. It's a small town with an interesting atmosphere after a large oil corporation moved in next door. You'll go about investigating fanatic cults, the oil business, research facilities, what secrets they're keeping from everyone, and how your late mother was wrapped up in all of it.
_childDocuments_.name: NORCO

_childDocuments_.review: I enjoyed this game very much. It is very atmospheric and lovely to just play. It is a point and click style game, lots of reading and minor puzzles to solve. It is also fairly funny. Would recommend to someone who enjoys point and click games. If you do not, then this probably is not for you, although it may be one of the best of those kinds of games I have ever played.

_childDocuments_.review: Fantastic dialog, world building, art-style and a generous helping of toilet humour. Story might be a bit too abstract (or is it?) your never quite sure what is real. _childDocuments_.review: Hits a little close to home. A reminder that some things run deeper. Norco is surreal - it blends the real and imaginary. _childDocuments_.name: NORCO

_childDocuments_.review: Set in a technologically advanced near future, Norco is a hauntingly beautiful pixel art depiction of Norco, Louisiana; a town run through by the oil industry, robotics, and mother nature. And while I did like a lot of the humor and general craziness of the game, it's ultimately the somber moments that really stand out, offering some of the best bits of writing in any game this year.I do think the game probably could have used some reworking to better drive home its themes and ideas, but I also kinda don't care. Because those few sobering moments of inevitability will always stand out to me. And whenever I think about Norco, I will see those oil refineries burning a hole through the night sky. I will hear those synths and horns crying out for a better day that won't come. And I will immediately be brought back. And to me, that's more important than worrying about all the details.
_childDocuments_.name: NORCO

_childDocuments_.review: Fully immersed since I've started playing. I've been attentively going through every bit of text since the writing, accompanied by the ethereal and inebriating soundtrack, really work together in pulling you into this carefully crafted industrialized dystopia. Will keep playing to see what other surprises are waiting for me down the road. Highly recommend.
_childDocuments_.name: NORCO

_childDocuments_.review: This game is so clearly a labor of love and vivid proof of the artistic merit of the medium. Granted I almost can't imagine a a story more perfectly tailored to my particular tastes, but it is an absolute treat from beginning to end. This is my first time reviewing a game ever, and my first point-and-click adventure, and I could truly not recommend it more. Everything from the pixel art, to the music, to the writing is fantastic. What a fantastically beautiful examination of American industrial decay, erosion of family, ennui and emptiness blended with an almost X-Files degree of weirdness. My girlfriend insisted I play this after I got it for her originally and I will be exhaustively insisting to everyone I know to play it for months. I am thrilled such a thing can exist, hats off to such a small dev team for creating such an amazing piece of interactive media. Do yourself a favor and play it.
_childDocuments_.name: NORCO

_childDocuments_.review: Never thought that a pixel art point-and-click game would manage to capture such rich atmosphere. NORCO isn't just about atmosphere, it's a beautiful looking game rich in story and characters, it is funny, smart, a little eerie, somewhat sad but above all, entertaining. I can confidently say that throughout my ten hour playthrough there was never a dull moment. That alone deserves applause.
_childDocuments_.name: NORCO

_childDocuments_.review: Eloquent, humorous yet poignant writing tells an engrossing tale that is brought to life by wonderfully immersive pixel art and sound design. Yutsi/Geography of Robots faithfully captures the mysteries (and truths) of growing up in the deep south, and touches on themes that, despite being science-fiction, felt totally relatable. NORCO easily holds a place among the best point-and-click adventure games I've ever played (and I've been playing them since the early Sierra/Lucas Arts days).

_childDocuments_.review: Please play this game. I'll probably update my review later, but. Wow, oh wow, oh wow, oh WOW! It's just fantastic. It is the perfect combination of thoughtful and engaging storytelling. NORCO is why video games exist. The game is captivating, clever, and mind-bending. NORCO is the reason you got a PC. To play a video game. Not some throwaway benchmark game that’ll be replaced by next year’s throwaway benchmark game. No. You play NORCO because you want to see just how ♥♥♥♥♥♥’ good video games have gotten. Well buddy, they’ve gotten ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ good.

_childDocuments_.review: Great writing, very unique story and characters. You can see the graphics for yourself, I think they're pretty good for the style they're going for. The choices you have to make during the game seem to really matter, and will create quite different experiences, so replayability should be good. I've only completed the first act, though, so it is a bit early to say what route I'm heading down on my first play. Only thing I know is that I'm very curious to see where it's all going.
_childDocuments_.name: NORCO

_childDocuments_.review: I keep thinking about this game. I love this game. I love the unashamedly poetic writing that manages to avoid pretension, I love the idea of a slice of life in a magical realist post-cyberpunk deep south -- in fact that might very well be the best setting for a game ever. I love how effortlessly it manages to root itself in reality and society.Be aware that the demo is not fully representative of the whole experience, the full story is a wilder ride than the first act lets on, which is not necessarily a bad thing. It's its own thing, a unique game which deals with mundane and current topics in a way I haven't seen often in video games, and while I've read reviews that state that it will never be as impactful as KRZ, in my particular case I disagree. Yes, its conclusion feels like there wasn't ultimately much to say, but it does so in a way that feels so true to life that I still can't stop thinking about it.
_childDocuments_.name: NORCO

_childDocuments_.review: NORCO is a fantastic game, I wish there was a button to recommend 1000 times.Being from West Monroe, Louisiana I can both attest and deeply relate to the depictions of refineries and entire communities centering around these industrial complexes. These things are not pretty, and to see this sentiment echoed in media, specifically pertaining to Louisiana, is reassuring and comforting. Alongside this potent and accurate representation of the land being depicted, the story is heady, riddled with religious symbolism, and honestly psychedelic at points. The narrative is dramatic and intense, bringing me to tears at several different points with its heartbreaking honesty surrounding the dynamic between the protagonist Kay and her family, and filling me with frustration in reference to industry's impact on surrounding communities. I found the mind map to be a really good tool for recounting details of the narrative, and enjoyed seeing it develop as I uncovered more about the characters and locations in NORCO.Aside from the gripping story told throughout NORCO, the art and mechanics keep the game alive and constantly reinforce the sense of discomfort and regret provided by the narrative. There were several moments where my jaw dropped at the sheer beauty of the scenes, namely the depictions of the bayous and refinery stacks littered throughout the game (oh man @ that introductory train cinematic). The puzzles were fun and thoughtful, and the use of the cellphone as a critical gameplay mechanic was fun and fit well with the narrative. I know I've picked up my phone to make money on DoorDash- it makes complete sense that Catherine would seek money on QuackJob if times were hard. I also enjoyed the boat driving sequences, and found them to be very visually striking as well. The combat feels great, and the major encounters of the game are both humor-riddled and engaging (drone priest rules, baby). Utilizing sweet monkey to do battle was a really fun way to introduce combat mechanics as well, his gaze is powerful. Another important factor of NORCO is just how funny it can be at times. The game strikes a remarkable balance between heavy subjects and lightheartedness, and keeps the player pushing through the occasional emotionally difficult material. Detective LeBlanc is genuinely hilarious- I wish I had his level of confidence.I could write a book on everything I liked from this game, and I can't encourage a purchase of NORCO enough. Personally haven't been this moved by a piece of media in a long time. If you're looking for a game with a thoughtful story, beautiful art, great thematic music and sound, and engaging mechanics, this is the one.LeBlanc for president
