_childDocuments_.review: Such an amazing experience. Maybe the only point and click adventure game I've not only enjoyed, but was utterly addicted to from beginning to end. I’ve never been so satisfied with such a short game. The setting is this wonderfully unique take on cyberpunk mixed with Southern American lore. Every single screen is filled with beautifully hand-crafted pixel art, dripping with atmosphere and hypnotic animations; every single area in Norco would make for an amazing desktop background or poster. The writing is sharp from beginning to end and there wasn't a moment in my eight-hour+ playthrough where I wasn't engaged or that I was filled in entirely on what was going on; there were always several mysteries hooking me at once, character's whose motivations I was unsure of and several clever twists that kept me hooked on Norco up until the finale. In Norco, you play as two characters in two timelines - Catherine, a sort of eccentric ex-researcher who’s resorting to a new form of employment via a mysterious corporate phone-app in a desperate bid to secure money for her children before she dies from cancer. Then there's Kay, Catherine's daughter who bailed on the family in pursuit of her own life and is returning home after her mother's death to explore the mystery surrounding her death with the help of her mother’s old droid, Million. Kay is more of a player surrogate and while her story is incredibly interesting, she's far less expressive in my opinion then her mother, Catherine, who really steals the show due to feeling more like a fleshed out character with real struggles you can fully empathize with. Other characters you meet along the way are equally interesting, from a cult of disorganized adolescents who call themselves "Garretts”, a reoccurring character who thinks Catherine is the descendant of Christ named Pawpaw, it would be wrong of me to spoil to many of the details but they're all great and their often ambiguous motives add to the ever growing mystery. It explores several different themes and tones throughout the story, somehow balancing edgy humor, surrealism, religious themes, and just being down right real and depressing sometimes.There was even one segment that was on the brink of horror with one moment that gave me an incredibly good  scare, I never knew what to expect with Norco and that felt wonderful. The setting itself of course steals a lot of the show both from the presentation and the writing. Being based in and inspired by areas from Southern Louisiana, but taking place in a warped dystopian nightmare version of it where corporations rule through a network that's supposedly connected to a “living brain”, there is just tons of backstory and lore fleshing out this very real world. The game does a wonderful job of keeping a lot of the plot points and lore together through a mind palace like mechanic in the game where you can track story beats, characters, and revisit it to work out new plot threads that could help you advance in the case. Though I do feel that this mechanic could have ultimately served more of a purpose, as it’s ultimately there to simply expand on information. There are also several mini games mixed throughout to sprinkle some variety on what you'll be doing throughout the game and these were all well done. Fighting for example occurs several times with each character having their own little mini game during battle. There are a decent number of puzzles and they're all pretty easy to figure out, with important information usually being highlighted. Though the devs thoughtfully included an expert mode you can check on so key info isn’t highlighted, though I doubt it would make it any harder. The really good news is in this point click game there is ZERO-pixel hunting, with the game usually emphasizing you find information. This means that the entirety of the game is spent focusing on Norco's excellent story and exploring its breathtaking locales. Overall, if you couldn’t already tell, I thought this game was amazing from beginning to end and I think you should BUY IT! I rarely think shorter games are worth the experience but this is 6-8 hours of pure bliss depending on your reading time and how much you explore. I really hope we get a definitive version with some of the cut content the dev has mentioned or even a sequel – I NEED more of this world and this writing.

_childDocuments_.review: Ah yes, NORCO is one of those games which one has no qualms about recommending. Something of a detective mystery interactive visual novel with unique characters and a fantastic setting straight out of a modern weird fiction short story.It is simple, succinct and well made. The art direction is depressingly pleasing, the vibe is mysterious, cosmic and dreary. It pulls at some deep emotion which is not quite nostalgia or melancholy but something in between. Well written with a nice soothing soundtrack, I am assuming a few secrets and more than one ending. There is nothing in here I would like to complain about apart from the need for more combat sequences perhaps which were fun button prompts, or  short memory games.One play through took me around 6 hours and for me it was worth it at full price since it is pretty beautifully made with love, it is clear that a lot of effort has been put into it. In short, a visual treat, get it for the story, the art, the writing and the unforgettable interactions.

_childDocuments_.review: NORCO is a short point-and-click "mystery" game. Isn't worth getting imo, but see for yourself:=Solid conversation/text system=Has a very cool mechanic of piecing together a "mind map" of every person, thing, and piece of info the protagonist knows so far. Well established; snappy; and the story sometimes plays with your expectations of it.=There is TONS of unexpected comedy. All the dialogue is played straight, but the people you encounter and the things you have to do for some achievements are gold.=The story, even at its highs, is not the most engaging. It'll please you in some cases, and might interest you with its themes about the bleak future and the nature of religion, but other times, it just kinda falls apart. Lots of awkward dialogue throughout, plus a weird choice to incorporate internet slang into the vocabulary of the future.=Has some borrowed RPG elements like a changing party of characters and some turn based-fights, although the latter is practically nonexistant (you even have the option to automate it).=Because the story is so short, the narration and dialogue are very GM-like. Lots of pushy "you  care for  character because of  reason!" Especially getting started in Act 1.=There is no real mystery to actively solve with the puzzle pieces you are given, nor will most of the dialogue choices affect the story; you just sort of passively experience the story and then  it starts to come together.=Some bugs surrounding the conditions to get certain achievements + the saving system being not very polished = a somewhat annoying trip for achievement hunters.=The catherine sections in Act 2 were so unnecessarily finicky.

_childDocuments_.review: I hear a lot of people compare Disco Elysium and NORCO and I see where they're coming from but it is more that the prose can be very evocative or surreal that I believe their comparisons are based on. If you're looking for something akin to Disco Elysium it's not exactly this but it's still good! I put about eight hours in (probably 7 if you rushed your way through it) and I enjoyed them. I'm, personally, from the Mid-South US so there were some references to places that I recognized or have been myself although this is a different timeline than our own. There's an intriguing premise that develops and some opening questions about your past (as well as a later sequence involving 'versioning' at the beginning of the second act that likely impacts the game in a way I will need to go through again to truly figure out) that serve as a way to just let you have a bit of say in how Kay feels about their childhood and parents before it lets you loose. The narrative is fairly consistent with the occasional absurd easter-eggs you can act on that people will continue to remark on and the music has a good feel to it (in addition to the ambient sound design). I also genuinely appreciate any game that allows you to use a key (spacebar, here) and see all the interactive elements rather than having to run your cursor over every pixel. Also worth mentioning is that I never ran into a cheap 'gotcha' death trap or anything. Interacting with things in my environment, exploring never got me punished.There are some things that people who are sensitive toward religious themes (Not sure if Louisiana is technically Bible Belt or not but it's right next to it if not but Christianity is very present) might be unsettled by but they're part of setting and story. There is a warning up front about people sensitive to suicide or depictions thereof but I can say it's pretty brief and nothing you see in any detail and it's clear it's not done for shock value given story elements and plot threads. it is tied to so if you're only sensitive to graphic depiction or morbid attention to it then you are likely fine (I can't speak to how sensitive you are to it, just offer my observations). A particular I feel worth mentioning: They offer multiple (four, I believe) fonts and three degrees of scaling as well as coloration to customize to your preferred taste or readability. Especially worth mentioning is the OpenDyslexic font that allows for easier reading for some of those who deal with dyslexia which I thought was really, really cool to see the devs take the time to do. I don't have it myself but it's just really cool that they went and added that little bit of accessibility for a text-heavy game. Another element people might be conflating with Disco Elysium is the MindMap. Do not expect to have conversations with yourself about your actions. The MindMap occasionally offered a bit of extra detail but it seemed more like it was there to remind you of story elements or possibly let you pick a few details about your memories or thoughts related to particular things. It certainly has a purpose but it is not the 'thought cabinet' you would expect in a comparison to Disco Elysium. I know I have mentioned that title a lot but it's simply because the biggest draw was the mention of the title being so frequent but the early discourse around the game and descriptions of the set-up and what the devs were aiming for is what got me to buy it.I'll stop myself from going into nauseating detail and just say that I enjoyed my time with it, I didn't have any bugs and there is absolutely no 'try this inventory item on everything you see' kind of puzzles and you don't carry a backpack full of inventory items.  I recommend the game to people who are into surreal and/or darker themes and while I feel the ending left me rail-roaded that might be because of choices I made (but I am unsure if you can progress to the end without them) but it's a story and enjoyable. It's got a really good atmosphere and I'm honestly looking forward to seeing what more these devs put out in the coming future. I'm planning on jumping back into this for another playthrough soon to see how much the story changes with different choices me.Buy it! There's a free demo of act one, even, give it a shot.

_childDocuments_.review: I don't know where to start with a NORCO review, so I'll try my best to recall my feelings rather than telling you about the stellar writing, the brilliant usage of the medium and how it bent the limits of the many genres it masticates and spits right in your face whenever you least expect it.I could talk about the way it exposes that old americana and bayou culture and folklore, how it leaves the decadent great gatsby illusion dissected on the table for you to poke, remove and escape from it. All of that without disrespecting it, instead coming from a place surely too close to home. It loves itself as much as it hates the fact that it exists at all, because its lungs are filled with smoke and its house is flooding over and over again. You can't keep the waters away.By the end, I was left both heartbroken and hopeful, in tears for a world so unlike mine, yet the same at the end. For a family that isn't mine, but could have been. I was reflected in the murky waters of the complicated feelings, questionable relationships and the continuous search for meaning. Was some of it true? Does it have to be? Strangers tagged along for the greater good, or simply for the sake of it, or simply because they, too, needed to know what lays beyond. People I trusted became my very own Brutus, and people that antagonized me became instrumental for my final act of magic.My escape, whether alone or accompanied by the results of a successful mission, left me empty. That's not bad. It's left me with space to fill with whatever I want to, with the opportunity to fill it with the memories I cherish the most, and with the decisions I'll have to take from now own.NORCO tells you the ending before it makes you go through it, making it seem more like a suggestion, a possibility, because even then, you can change a couple of things and tell it that it was wrong. Or maybe it could be right. It doesn't truly matter. And yet, it does.It was a great story, an even greater game that invited me to involve myself and think out of the box, that made me laugh and despair in equal measures. It got to me. I fell for its tricks, and my life feels much richer because of it.for more reviews of games that are cute or creepy, or both, find me on my curator page:

_childDocuments_.review: I wouldn't say I play to many point and click adventure and visual novel but every now and then one of these game does catch my interest and it happen to be Norco. Narrative:Norco is a visually beautiful pixel art southern gothic sci-fi point and click game that I am seriously considering to be Game of The Year for me personally. From the well written narrative that has many humorous moment as well and much darker depressing story that left me feeling sad,depress and honestly just gave this haunted feeling of dread at time; had me captivated from beginning to end. There also many WTF moment that just caught me completely off guard. There is no voice acting in this game which could be seen as a negative but the game is so well written and the use of many natural phrase and dialogue make this game very easy to digest and understand. There is complexity to the writing but it not going to stop you from understanding the core story depicted.Music:The music is good, from electronic to jazz, it not overpowering and give off a very atmospheric and moody feel which set the tone for the game. Visual:Visually stunning pixel art style that has many fluid animated moment such as scene of driving the motorcycle down the highway to watching the bird fly off into the distances. It good, nothing more to say about this. lot of the game location are detailed very well.Gameplay:Point and Click Adventure game for the most part which include travelling to different location, interacting with people and object, multiple dialogue choice that has minor affect on the story.  There also a few QTE moment for some event as well as these short puzzle game which I found to be some of the weaker part of the game for me.Final Thought:Overall it a really good game with a few minor negative that I believe are just not worth mentioning. It a rather short experience with three act that should take about 7-8 hours to complete so hopefully if anyone does pick it up, it doesn't end up in the backlog for to long.. I totally recommend if your fan of game like Disco Elysium, Kentucky Route Zero and even if this is your first time playing a point and click adventuring , it still a game I definitely recommend for first timer of the genre.

_childDocuments_.review: It's difficult to encapsulate NORCO as an experience in a short, spoiler-free review. However, I can fully recommend this game to anyone looking for something truly unique and inspired, with an excellent story, beautiful art, and atmosphere.A large part of what I think makes this game so captivating is how it contains bits of normalcy interspersed with sci-fi and surreal elements which is expressed in both its environments and its themes. It remains relatable on a human level while also being completely alien in other aspects. A perfect balance of the benign and the surreal. What is, on one hand, a very interesting depiction of life in an alternate New Orleans and a very personal story, also manages to be something incredibly unusual and captivating. NORCO paints a desolate and at times, very oppressive picture of the future. Moments of warmth are few and far between. However there are some great bits of comedy here and there, which all seems to land pretty well- the game can definitely be very funny.I believe the pixel art speaks for itself in just how well-crafted it is. Each environment has a distinct atmosphere that absolutely adds to the experience. It very much immerses you in it's moody southern landscapes.Most of the gameplay is what you might expect from a point-and-click adventure game. Mostly dialogue with some puzzles here and there- none of which are too difficult but are satisfying to complete and progress. It does take a unique approach with some mechanics and puzzles though, which keeps things feeling fresh and interesting.This game is a thought-provoking experience unlike any other that is undoubtedly worth the time and money. If you're considering it, just buy it and jump in. You won't regret it.
_childDocuments_.name: NORCO

_childDocuments_.review: Poetic, impressionistic, bleak, funny, and intensely absorbing, this is the most engaging adventure game I can think of in years.  Don't let any of the descriptors I mentioned scare you off- Norco is accessible and fun. The stunning graphics bury deep into your psyche's nebulous nostalgia zone, so much that you will find yourself deeply missing Norco, Louisiana when the game is done. Highly recommended.

_childDocuments_.review: Just when I thought Elden Ring would be my game of the year no contest Norco swoops in and knocks me off my feet. _childDocuments_.review: I don't get what everyone finds in this game. Disco Elysium left a huge Disco Elysium-shaped hole in my heart that I try to fill sometimes, Norco was often recommended as a similar experience so I tried it. The game starts promising - setting, graphics, narrative all feels nice, and then it just all falls apart.First of all, the plot is irrelevant to the setting. With minor adjustments to characters and MacGuffin, the story could happen in any other place, which really takes away from the surreal atmosphere authors try to build. This together with short storyline of the game never allows you to feel the world around; despite all the interesting ideas behind it, the setting always acts like decorations, not a place. You wish you could explore it more but the game gives you a set tour so you feel like the in-game characters complaining that it was supposed to be fun only to hear in reply that it was fun for the authors to write it.Characters are underexplored. You never really get the obsession of everyone else with MacGuffin especially when the main characters are decidedly not that interested in it so it’s hard to relate with their motivations. Your actions lack effect on both in-game or from meta level. It is okay for Point & Click games to be linear but at least some of the things you do should force reaction from other characters but the game pretty much tells you that whatever you do doesn't matter. This culminates in the ending where, for example, the choice you make about your brother, who is the supposed focus of much of the story, is barely acknowledged.Gameplay is pretty boring, combat is lackluster and the game would do much better if it was removed altogether and replaced with narrative choices. Some puzzles feel like they were created only to pad out the already short gameplay time. Generally, it feels that the game would work better if it played to it storytelling strengths rather than try to fit to gameplay clichés.Overall, the game leaves you wanting for more, for a deeper experience, for a more meaningful social commentary rather than allusions it prefers to make, for a sense of closure in the end. To quote Macbeth, it may not be a tale told by an idiot, but it is full of sound and fury, signifying nothing.

_childDocuments_.review: The art is really cool. The music is very solid. The vibe is strong, and the world draws you in at first. But the writing is really not good. I like that they're trying, but it just isn't interesting. I finished Act 1 & 2, but I'm too bored to finish Act 3. I'm happy it's getting all this praise, and I hope the devs hire a couple more experienced writers for their next game.
_childDocuments_.name: NORCO

_childDocuments_.review: I was initially a bit worried that this would be one of those games that leaned too heavily on the visual novel side of things - with gorgeous graphics but minimal gameplay and overtly complicated writing - a subgenre I'm not that fond of.However, those fears were unfounded. NORCO is actually in many ways more of a traditional first person point and click adventure with puzzles and some minor rpg/action elements, a mix that might sound odd, but works really well with the games story. And the story is definitely unique: equal parts southern gothic and cyberpunk, this tale of broken families and religious fanaticism in a polluted capitalist dystopia is convoluted, but totally engrossing. A big reason the story works is the meticulous production values: The graphics are some of the best pixel art I've seen, the music(by doom metal band Thou) is both ominious and dreamlike, and makes the exploration of desolate malls, underpasses and ghost bayous feel like a perfectly realised world. NORCO is by no means a game for everybody, but it is totally one of a kind, and a must-play for adventure gamers who likes their retro cyberpunk/sci-fi point and clicks with a healthy dose of refreshing twists.
_childDocuments_.name: NORCO

_childDocuments_.review: this review is hard to write, because i barely have words to describe what norco is and how it feels. this is one of those games that absolutely destroys the concept of games not being art. it's a game that reveres its influences and setting, but not by putting them on a pedestal - it displays all the gritty glory, the dark and the light, all at once, and manages to be faithful and cohesive. it's a game that is both distant and personal - weird and unfamiliar, but in a way that draws you in, makes you feel at home, even while you're surrounded by things that make no sense to you. it is truly a masterpiece and i can't recommend it enough to people who like to really feel things when they play games.
_childDocuments_.name: NORCO

_childDocuments_.review: I was looking for an adventure point and click game, but what I got is probably best described as narrated experience. Gameplay is there mainly to drive the story and presents no challenge. Norco isn't about solving tough puzzles, it's about following the narrative and reminiscing about your own life. Visual style is nice (and great at places), music is OK, plot is present, but it seems a little bit out of focus, as if multiple themes and ideas were tied together in a dream-like sequence, which never really gets to a satisfying resolution (at least the way I got through the game in approximately 8 hours). The best parts of the game IMO are: unique atmosphere, beautiful narration and opportunity to reflect on Norco's many themes, which include but are mot limited to: strained family relations, memory and regret, cancer, environmentalism. P.S. yes, it kind of reminds me of Disco Elysium, but Norco is very much its own thing
_childDocuments_.name: NORCO

_childDocuments_.review: At first you think it's a neat sci-fi pixel art game, and then it goes places. The giant, malformed bird-monster offering you gig work seemed like it would be the weirdest thing at first. Towards the end, the game throws a lot of imagery at you that I honestly don't feel I had the grounding to contextualize, not in terms of plot, I think I knew what was going on, but in references that would be an honest spoiler to reproduce here. Definitely a case for quality over quantity, if you think hours spent in-game is the best measurement.
_childDocuments_.name: NORCO

_childDocuments_.review: I got this game on steam for a second play through while I was away from my ps4 and a year later Norco hit just as hard as it did the first time. Beautiful art populates this game's entire runtime, soundtrack is super emotional and atmospheric and the writing is so exceptional that Norco is the first game that's ever made me weep. A lot of the characters are incredibly funny and for me a lot of the story elements feel very fresh. Do not go into this game expecting much gameplay, it's a story first and foremost. Go in as blind as possible. Masterpiece. I love this game so much.
_childDocuments_.name: NORCO

_childDocuments_.review: NORCO is so good, it made me pause my Elden Ring playthrough lolIf you love story – driven games, PLEASE give this one a chance! It tells a very engrossing story that starts out pretty familiar, but by the midpoint takes some unexpected turns going places I didn’t expect it to go. It’s so hard to put down, because the writing makes the game flow seamlessly, from start to finish. Whoever WROTE this game, give this person a raise or something, because the writing is so smooth and natural. It’s poetic without sounding pretentious. Idk how else to describe it, but it just feels right. Overall, the tone of the game is rather dark and bleak, but there are moments of humor and real comradery, which balance it out. Funny situations happen quite often actually and unexpected friendships form from time to time. Somehow looking back at the game I could recall a lot more hilarious interactions than sad ones, so maybe it isn’t as hopeless after all :)I also love that this is a Point & Click adventure that you could actually finish without looking for a guide. You always know what to do and where to go and it’s such a relief after playing Full Throttle and Monkey Island lol. Hey, maybe I’m just too dumb for those games, but NORCO is actually FINISHABLE without pulling your hair out after sitting for hours on one puzzle. I know this review is all over the place, but this is my first one, so that’s that. I really wanted to write it, because this game is SO GOOD and I just wanted to share my feelings! If you are a fan of strong writing, please try it, you won't be disappointed.

_childDocuments_.review: Norco is a dystopian visual novel located in the not too distant future that is mainly driven by dialogue. What is at its core an interesting and complex story about the fate of a dysfunctional family is dragged down by questionable game design choices, missing voice over, and very inconsistent pacing.You return home to South Louisiana after your mother died. Your brother is nowhere to be found. Is his disappearance connected with the research your mother conducted before her death?The majority of your playtime (in my case about 6-7 hrs) will be spend reading dialogue, there is no voice over. Occasionally, you have a choice how you want to approach a topic with one of the characters you meet, which can lead to changes in how characters react to you, but as far as I can tell, there are less than a handful of occasions where your decision changes the outcome.In addition to the dialogue, you also fill in a mindmap, where you collect tidbits of information about the people you meet, and the places you visit. It is gamified a bit in that you can frequently put your own spin on your recovered or newly added memories, for example, you can decide if you regret leaving your brother behind, or don't care that he was devastated by you leaving. Initially, I thought there'd be a wrong and right answer, and you had to put together clues to answer correctly, but what was I thinking? That would've been actually fun, and we can't have that. Instead, your answer is never brought up again.Occasionally, you play from a different perspective in the past, which helped fleshing out the story, but gameplay-wise it didn't add anything new.Each location of the story is a mostly static screen. There are a few interactive spots to discover that for the most part just add some flavor. There are only a handful of puzzles in the game, which are mainly fetch quests at their core, but they fit into the story, are creative, and add to the mystery, so it is a bit of a shame that there isn't more of that. You "move" from screen to screen by clicking on one of a few boxes in the corner of your screen, with each box symbolizing a new room or place that is accessible to you from your current location. To see the descriptions, you have to hover your mouse over the boxes. This makes it difficult to get a mental map of your location, and it is easy to overlook a possible direction or place that is only available from one screen. You'll likely have to circle through all available screens at least a couple of times to make sure you found everything. There is a map of the whole area which allows you to quicktravel seamlessly between these locations, which is much better because it is an actual geographical map, so you know at first glance where you have and haven't been. There's one "exploration"-minigame that's even revisited on a second occasion where you move by dragging yourself over a map with the mouse which is god-awful. I have no idea what the intention was, because it adds literally nothing to the game. It's clunky, slow, and annoying. I almost forgot, probably because it is the most superfluous and forgettable part of the gameplay: There's combat in form of a minigame that checks your ability to click on stuff quickly.I just checked, there is an option in the settings that auto-resolves combat, which keeps the game accessible for people who otherwise wouldn't be able to play. Thumbs up for that!I'm not the biggest fan of purely narrative-driven games, and Narco is a case in point for me. Narco is partly the story of a dysfunctional family, and partly a detective story, and both storylines are interwoven. Elements of it are a bit over the top, at other points it tries too hard to be edgy, and it can't really decide if it wants to be taken seriously or not. But all in all, it is not a bad story! I did want to find out what happened.But the pacing is all over the place, at times it slows down to a crawl, and there is at least one story arc that you could remove without losing anything. The actual gameplay very rarely adds anything to the story, and both the combat and the "exploration"-minigame are such a jarring contrast to the rest of the gameplay, it completely ended any immersion for me.Finally, the game would have benefitted greatly from some voice over. I don't mind reading, I'm one of those boring people who have reading as a hobby, even, but by the end of this game I was sick of reading dialogue. What was, according to the story, the action-filled finale of the game still had me read through multiple overlong dialogue trees. All in all I was almost glad that the game was over.

_childDocuments_.review: Steam recommended me this game because I played Disco Elysium, and I have seen people make ample comparisons between the two. I suspect this is because both games primarily take the format of reading long stretches of writing & selecting dialogue responses, because that's where I felt the similarities ended. NORCO is uniquely American in the themes and ideas it asks the player to confront, opening by making the player evaluate what balance they believe should be struck between what they owe themselves and what they owe their communities (to, I would imagine, the tune of a largely individual-oriented answer). It then spends the rest of the game asking if it's wrong for that balance to stay the same when you find out your community is dying.Don't let the backwoods setting mislead you - NORCO is asking players to confront questions that even Silicon Valley wunderkinds are staring down the barrel of every day. I admittedly missed the big-picture applicability of it until a character in the game described themselves as an "internet of internets." That was the moment it hit me: NORCO has so seamlessly and lovingly blended some of our most pressing contemporary ideas (the all-encompassing sprawl of surveillance capitalism, the death throes of the environment under traditional capitalist endeavors, the seeding of a certain type of neo-fascism into American communities and the inability of most to fully articulate it, class war) into its setting that I hadn't been able to recognize them on first pass. This is a part of the country that I didn't grow up anywhere near, and I had to shift my framing of these issues, which I am more familiar with, to be able to see them as the residents of NORCO are seeing them - which, as NORCO shows us, is often as a monster breathing down their dying necks.Steeped in a culture than encourages ruthless self-sufficiency, NORCO makes us ask how far these things have to go to become our problem, even when the problems that are solely ours are building up by the minute, and how we justify the answer being too damn long. This game isn't long or fancy, but it has deeply stuck in my head since I first started getting into the meat of its story. This game is worth playing, and worth re-playing after that.

_childDocuments_.review: This is the kind of indie sleeper I enjoy greatly.  I was googling something else about Norco (the city) and happened to stumble on something that indicated the game dev worked for years and learned how to do pixel art just to get this game realized.  The odd art style lends to the story.     Although it's heavy on dialogue, it's not overly so and the pieces add to the game as you work through the mystery to solve what happened.  This game is a slow burn best enjoyed as a snack.  Don't burn through it in one sitting.  Play in short stints.  Google in between and learn about the real city of Norco that this game is based on; it's eerie that real life has some parallels.  This game has a new take on its approach to point and clicks, and it's worth unveiling it slowly.

_childDocuments_.review: Imagine a life as child, you're morbidly obsessed with a demonic city, illuminated in the night by flaming skyscrapers, dressed in black smoke clouds. It floats on the horizon, across a swamp of cypress tree husks hinting to the natural glory of a landscape ravaged by man in a different chapter. You on look in horror, fascinated, something pulls you there, but it's hell on earth. You now know is a refinery. People work there, live there, and die there, as it poisons and provides.Then someone makes a beautiful, soulful game capturing everything that speaks to you about this place. It's such an incredibly sincere and thoughtful homage to the trauma of living in marginalized spaces like Norco, Louisiana, and it runs much deeper than "big industry" moving in and changing things. Every screen is worthy of living in a frame on a wall, the music will drag you in and envelope you in this tragic world, the narrative will make you cry.
_childDocuments_.name: NORCO

_childDocuments_.review: A spectacular story, rich in sense of place and atmosphere, told with supreme confidence.A game whose story is as interesting as the finest novels, but with the extra stuff a videogame can add sitting richly atop it.A game that picks from genres as it sees fit in totally appropriate amounts - not too point-n-clicky, not too text-adventury, truly just a goldilocks balance.This game has some serious topics at heart, but it somehow manages to be this divine balance of seriousness about them. In that sense, it feels like a game of our time but not a game intent on making you suffer under the weight of issues in our time. Norco is way more subtle than that, and that's what I mean by its confidence. Climate disasters hover in the background without it being shoved in your face, a large corporation controls the happenings of our world, and we are far past the point of being able to question whether the systems that govern us are truly fair, but there's no voice of the author interjecting to tell you it's smart or brilliant for doing so in ways that I think can affect even the most well-respected pieces of media in our time. And in that sense there's a hope in it - that lack of obsession with doom pornography really offers space for Norco to find joy in our/its world.It's interesting that so many people are mentioning Kentucky Route Zero; this feels more like a game about the South from a true voice of the South; it's less neurotically self-considered than KR0 and much more comfortable sitting in the setting naturally. The more you play Kentucky Route Zero the more you realize it's a toybox of its creators' passions, as much art object as story, whereas Norco feels decidedly focused on the story it's telling. And in that sense I think they're quite far away as games.All in all, a serious work of art and a delightful game. The way the story is told in interweaving narratives is also masterfully executed, the pace is perfect - what else to say without sounding overly effusive? The main character is a tiny bit underdeveloped, there could be more there, but the world is so interesting you probably won't think about that much.
_childDocuments_.name: NORCO

_childDocuments_.review: An excellently written game overflowing with striking visuals and beautifully surreal audio. The entire mood of NORCO is one that will linger long after you’ve finished the game, like waking from a bizarre dream that you can’t shake. This is a feeling that I chase and so rarely find in games or other media. NORCO requires your attention but that is not difficult to provide. I felt captivated throughout my entire playthrough. I encourage anyone who plays to take their time. Explore everything. Read the books on the shelves. Watch some TV. It all adds up to make this game what it is. Many of the characters are flawed yet endearing, and relatable in their own ways. Even the more ridiculous ones. (We all have a little Garrett inside of us.)

_childDocuments_.review: NORCO is bizarre and beautiful. I was actually taken aback at how its final sequences shook me, almost to the point of tears. I have such a weakness for stories about families and the distance we put between ourselves and family for all sorts of reasons, intentionally or not. The game’s layering of religion on top of that core conflict, swinging wildly from its maximally absurd and blasphemous grotesque representation to a light touch with how the more grounded characters treat it, made it all hit a little harder for me.Don’t have it in me to unpack those themes or the other heavy topics the game tackles that are very much about that specific space in New Orleans, but they certainly made me feel some type of way! The off-beat humor also certainly made it all go down a little smoother, which its disarming presence reminds me why I was also so taken by Disco Elysium.It also deserves a lot of praise for its music. The synth soundtrack is brooding, melancholic, sinister, and at times surprisingly chipper, setting the mood perfectly for every scene. It does so much to elevate the storytelling, and I hope more people appreciate it as being just as important as the striking pixel art and excellent writing.
_childDocuments_.name: NORCO

_childDocuments_.review: There are certain books and movies that might hold a certain amount of niche indie appeal for the general public but then tend to be pretty well known in whatever specific region they're set in. For example, Cormac McCarthy's novel Suttree might be fairly well regarded by people who know about the author's less popular works, but if you ever go to Knoxville Tennessee it's much more widely known and talked about, specifically because they have a connection to it because of the geographical location in which it's set.Videogames are a medium that doesn't really lend itslef to that in the same way, in my opinion. There's a few games that have New York, Southern California, or even New Orleans as their settings, and yet those games never really take on any special meaning for the people who live in those places, at least not as far as I'm aware.Norco might be the first game that actually manages to hold a specific regional appeal for the place in which it's set. Nothing else like this has ever really been made in the videogame space that focuses so specifically on a particular place and the weird realities that make up that place. As someone who has spent his whole life on the Gulf Coast, this feels very special to me, but I do worry that this game might be too niche, and too regional to ever have any broader appeal.Norco is a traditional point-and-click adventure game with some mild turn based combat, set in a dystopian cyberpunk version of Southern Louisiana.Gameplay is exactly what you'd expect from such a venture. It mostly involves interacting with the environment through clicking, some mild puzzle solving, and a lot of dialogue. There are some (very easy) combat sections mixed in depending on the choices you make which are turn based RPG combat/quicktime events.The main draw of the game is of course, the setting and the story, all complimented beautifully by the exquisite pixel art.Since the setting is the main thing I'm focusing on I just want to say that I think it's very special to see a game come out like this that highlights this particular region of America because I've looked for sci-fi interpretations of Southern Louisiana and the Gulf Coast before and I gotta say they're almost nonexistent. Most of the time if New Orleans or this area gets mentioned in science fiction at all it's usually just as a half-assed warning about global warming and they'll say the whole region is underwater. But there's so much about this particular part of the world that is unique and fascinating that makes it perfect for interpretation in the context of sci-fi but this is the first property I think I've ever seen that attempts to do that.Norco is a real place in Southern Louisiana. West of New Orleans and dominated solely by oil refineries and factories. Industrialization, it's effects on the environment, and the parasitic relationship it has with the people who are harmed by it, but also rely on it for money and community, that's a perfect theme to be explored by the cyberpunk genre, and Norco is a perfect place to set such a story. In addition, the game shows us the region's similarly parasitic relationship with religion, politics, and hints at a much wider world where all of the current problems America has been facing have been magnified tenfold.I absolutely love this game and it's story but I do worry that many gamers won't be able to connect with it since it ties itself so specifically into the nature of this one particular region.The pixelart beautifully renders all of this as well, like I said. I'm always a sucker for good pixel art. Especially when it gives you scenic swampy vistas that you can just sit and stare at for a while to absorb the ambience.The game makes a big deal about it's soundtrack but I wasn't as impressed by it. Although it's good none of the songs in particular really stood out to me, except for maybe the overworld theme, called 'Parish.'Overall I would definitely recommend this game to anyone who wants to give a forward thinking cyberpunk storyline a shot, and is comfortable with it being light on gameplay, and having obscure references. But although I heartily recommend it, I do worry that the game will end up only having a certain kind of niche, regional appeal to the people who are familiar with the setting it takes place in, the same way only other obscure pieces of media have done so in the past.
_childDocuments_.name: NORCO

_childDocuments_.review: Norco deserves all the praise I can give it and more besides. From a long tradition of adventure games comes something that builds upon it and still feels so unbelievably, shockingly new? It's singular. I can't begin to explain it to you without taking away from its wonder. I can't tell you what part of it coheres most in my mind, because they're all fighting each other for the top spot. I'll be thinking about Norco for probably the rest of my life.

_childDocuments_.review: Rating: ★★★★★"Norco" is a mesmerizing journey into a dystopian world unlike any other, blending captivating storytelling with innovative gameplay features to create an experience that is both immersive and thought-provoking. From the moment you step foot into its hauntingly beautiful landscape, you're drawn into a narrative that is as dark as it is compelling.Set in a near-future version of the Gulf Coast, "Norco" presents a world ravaged by environmental collapse and corporate greed. The landscape is a haunting mix of neon-lit cities and decaying industrial ruins, each corner hiding secrets waiting to be uncovered. The attention to detail in crafting this dystopian setting is breathtaking, with every pixel dripping with atmosphere and history.What sets "Norco" apart is its innovative gameplay features. Rather than relying on traditional mechanics, the game encourages exploration and experimentation, allowing players to uncover the story at their own pace. From hacking into corporate databases to scavenging for resources in the wastelands, every action feels meaningful and impactful.The narrative itself is a masterpiece of storytelling, weaving together themes of identity, power, and resistance in a way that is both poignant and thought-provoking. As you delve deeper into the world of "Norco," you'll encounter a cast of characters who are as complex and flawed as the world they inhabit, each with their own motivations and agendas.Visually, "Norco" is a work of art. The pixel art style is both retro and modern, with its vibrant colors and intricate details bringing the world to life in stunning detail. The soundtrack further enhances the atmosphere, with its haunting melodies and pulsating rhythms perfectly complementing the game's dystopian setting.In conclusion, "Norco" is a triumph of storytelling and game design, offering players a truly immersive and unforgettable experience. Its dystopian setting, innovative gameplay features, and captivating narrative combine to create a game that is both engaging and thought-provoking. If you're a fan of dystopian fiction or innovative indie games, "Norco" is not to be missed.

_childDocuments_.review: I found out about this game because of the OST with Thou. When i saw the themes and setting of the game, i immediately bought it. It is like playing a story about my life living in Houston near Sheild refinery there. It's obvious the creators grew up in a similar petrochemical hellscape. The writing is spot on, funny and evocative. I will update my review when i finish the game.
_childDocuments_.name: NORCO

_childDocuments_.review: I would 100% recommend playing Norco. GORGEOUS pixel art, cool music, great writing, fun mechanics and interesting and compelling world building. It never goes where you expect it to, in a good way. It made me laugh out loud, confused me, amused me and made me cry (like actual tears streaming down my face sobbing kind of crying, although I have to admit parts of the story hit really close to home). Tons of little easter eggs and secrets too, which I love. It's not for everyone, if you are not a fan of point and click, story-rich and/or text heavy games this is probably not the game for you, and it does overdo it a little bit at times , but I have never played anything like this and it was an instant favourite. Finished it in one 6 hours sitting because I could not stop playing... do yourself a favour and play this.
_childDocuments_.name: NORCO

_childDocuments_.review: NORCO is a stunning work of art. I'm sitting in my home in South Louisiana, seeing the drainage ditches outside and then it reflected back on the pixel art on my screen. NORCO feels like a conversation with a familiar face. This game touches on topics like disaster capitalism, community exploitation and extraction to approaching religious zealotry with a sense of earnestness. The gameplay is simple and effective, storyline enrapturing and bizarre. I enjoyed the subplots getting different phone cases to the achievements you can get. I encourage anyone to get this game and I'm excited to play through it again.
_childDocuments_.name: NORCO

_childDocuments_.review: I loved the immersion in the religious southern gothic / sci-fi setting that Norco proposes. One of the best game I played this year.A well written story that was thought-provoking, I enjoyed reading every bits of text that the game was willing to throw at me.The story comes with one of the best pixel art I ever saw, and the OST is also absolutely stunning. I found myself in awe several times just by looking at the scene while being rocked by the mesmerizing ambient tracks. Feeling melancholy, yet a strange calmness.Playing this game also gave me the opportunity to learn about Norco IRL, and knowing what I know now makes me see the game and some of the themes it adresses in a different light.I already was interested by this area, but playing Norco strangely made me long for the Bayou. I'm thankful for this wonderful journey.Oh and there is a random dude with a Eyehategod tattoo, so that's pretty cool.
_childDocuments_.name: NORCO

_childDocuments_.review: Weird. Intriguing. Technically impressive. An interesting indie adventure game with some unique twists.+ Art style is great; game looks really nice for pixel art+ Story keeps you engaged+ Some interesting unique gameplay elements like a light combat system and a "mind-map" where you can review stuff you've learned and sometimes come up with new insights+ Decent ending that wraps up the primary plot- Most of the ancillary story threads do not get resolved at the end of the game. I hate that!- Puzzles are way too easy. Actually most of them barely qualify as puzzles- (eg, "hey you need to pay for that!", so you *use* your bank card on the checkout scanner- not exactly rocket science).- On the short side. I felt like the story was just picking up steam when the game ends.- The protagonist that you play as has very little backstory herself; the game lets you fill in a little but you learn a lot about everyone else in town. Its a little hard to sympathize with a character who you know almost nothing about.
_childDocuments_.name: NORCO

_childDocuments_.review: This game made me relate to things I pretty much don't have anything in common with.Every backgrond is a work of art, the soundtrack mesmerizing, the world feels melancholic, yet cozy and nostalgic.All of the main characters (and a few side ones!) are made memorable by how bizarre or surreal they are.The story itself is one of the best works of sci-fi I got the pleasure to experience in a while.
_childDocuments_.name: NORCO

_childDocuments_.review: This game is intense. It has elements of Hotline Miami, David Lynch movies. The writing is immersive, characters express a lot in the way they speak. The game is often scary. It's not difficult, which didn't make me enjoy it less. I play these kinds of games like a data-miner. I never do what I'm supposed to do, I always leave that for last while exploring every other possible avenue first. And I've found that the game doesn't give you much space to maneuver, but what it does give you is handled with care. I would have finished this in one sitting if it wasn't for the fact that I literally passed out while trying to play through the night. My head propped up against my pillow, with the laptop on a tray, screen aimed at my face. I slept until morning, listening to the background music in Duck's library. This soaked me with the atmosphere of the game. It's so intense, it ended up feeling suffocating. I kept playing because I wanted to get out of this dark tunnel. You keep going deeper into the mystery, you find answers everywhere yet somehow everything becomes less clear. Also, I love how the Quack currency crashed in value by over 100% in a few days time. Nice little detail. I wonder how many people noticed that. There seem to be a few branching paths, nothing major, but I haven't checked. At one point I had to choose between different drugs. At least, it seemed like I had a choice, but my lack of money chose for me. The music is great in this game. And the dialogue noises are really cool. The customization options for the fonts are great. The CRT filter gave me a headache, but it's there if you want it. It's kind of interesting. The people you meet, the whole narrative. It's the story of the world we inherited from boomers. Who grew up in a world where everyone knows everyone, because they haven't left their town. Where I grew up there was a massive brewery, and a sugar factory. So you had the wheat and sugarbeet farmers, the people who worked at the brewery and the factory. It often smelled like yeast or the boiled beets, depending on which way the wind blew. And the people don't really change. At some point in their life they get stuck on repeat, and then they ferment and become stale. They talk about the same things over and over. It's charming in a way. The characters in this game really reminded me of that. All of them obsessed with something, mostly the past.
_childDocuments_.name: NORCO

_childDocuments_.review: This is one of my favorite games of all time. My time living in South Louisiana was the best time of my life and this game does an incredible job of capturing both the essence of the culture and the socioeconomic and political issues the people there currently face.As far as the gameplay, the puzzles are not prohibitively difficult. My only complaint is that I wish they had used voice actors speaking for real to fully immerse me in the game instead of gibberish babbling so I wouldn't have to read if I don't want to.
_childDocuments_.name: NORCO

_childDocuments_.review: I have mixed feelings about Norco.I got the impression from artworks and trailers that it would be a sort psychedelic dystopian Sci-Fi adventure game with a lot of very unique and multi-faceted gameplay elements. While it has indeed a bit of all that, most of the game is more of a classic point-n-click game revolving around a well written but rather mundane story about you trying to find your brother.Not a bad game per se but one that won’t resonate with everybody. Do not expect a ground breaking genre defying experience.
_childDocuments_.name: NORCO

_childDocuments_.review: NORCO is a game like few others, it's hard to make an area feel so rich with culture like it does. I struggle to put into words the concept I'm describing, but NORCO pulls off whatever this vague idea is in strides. When you play you're instantly immersed, you aren't where you live in the real world, you're part of this community, learning the secrets and quirks of those who live there.I recommend NORCO thoroughly and I can't even describe why fully, it's just a game that has that FEEL to it.
_childDocuments_.name: NORCO

_childDocuments_.review: (I've never written a review on Steam before, but felt compelled to do so for Norco - as even if it only encourages one more person to play it, I would be happy with that!)Norco is a hard game to summarise. To describe it as a point and click adventure would seem to do it a gross disservice, but if you're really looking to force it into a box I guess it would be that?! However, the ambition of the storyline is breathtaking, the characters are genuine and memorable, the dialogue is frequently hilarious, disturbing or both, the artwork is incredibly beautiful even when representing hideous environments, and the mechanics that carry the whole thing along are novel, smoothly integrated and most importantly fun.Discussing too much of the story would spoil the best aspects of the game, but broadly speaking it is about an alternate near future Louisiana community coming to terms with the fallout of the petrochemical industry, both physically and emotionally. Each of the characters, as well as the earth itself, is scarred or displaced by generations of abuse and are grappling - collectively or individually - to understand and transcend this legacy. However, if that sounds too high-brow for you it also features one of the greatest toilet humour sequences I've ever encountered, and has motorbike riding androids... and also a minigame where you can agitate a cat to the extent it blasts into orbit.All in all I cannot recommend Norco highly enough as an experience. I was dubious as to whether the mechanics would be interesting enough to carry me through the storyline, and in the end I'm incredibly thankful that they were because I found the whole experience uniquely thought provoking; profoundly disturbing and beautiful in equal measure. (Afterwards if you are interested, there is a lot of fascinating writing about the colonial history of the parishes of Louisiana and the surrounding Gulf of Mexico, and their direct lineage to the petrochemical corridor and its socio-economic effects; I would seriously recommend checking them out for some greater contextual insight. However this is not at all mandatory to play the game and fall in love with it!)

_childDocuments_.review: It starts strongly, but at least one more act is needed to fully wrap up the story (it ends way sooner than expected), leaving us quite underwhelmed with 3 so-so endings and plenty of underdeveloped characters. _childDocuments_.review: Oh, NORCO. My shoes are still caked in swamp mud and my hair smells like cigarettes after playing this game. _childDocuments_.review: norco was entirely not about what i imagined it would be about, but i was so glad to be surprised. the text style and language reminded me a lot of disco elysium. i enjoyed the mind map mechanic to keep track of the developments you learn. the characters and story were compelling and excellent, i also enjoyed the art style a great deal and found the switchbacks between characters really interesting! my one wish (not even a criticism) is that i wish you had explored the relationship between two characters a little more from one side rather than the other, as it didn't feel as well thought-out. you can clearly tell the care that went into making this game, and the sporadic spots of humor and secrets/alt pathways you can find if you hunt enough feel worthy of your time. i can't say that i've played many games like this and doubt i will find similar titles, but that's completely fine, it was an amazing and unique experience that i will for sure recommend to anyone looking for a great few hours spent on a carefully crafted point and click story game!

_childDocuments_.review: I've started playing "Norco" and after 1 hour and 45 minutes I reached Act Two.So what is this game about? It plays in some futuristic version of Louisiana, USA, where several floods have changed the world and now an oil refinery named Shield pretty much owns and runs everything. You play as Kay, a young woman who once left her hometown to look for luck at the west coast, only to return home at the news of her mother's death. Your brother, Blake, has always stayed home but now you can't find him. Luckily there's this robotic version of a butler/personal assistant (who reminds me a bit of "Guardians of the Galaxy"'s Nebula, only less grumpy) who helps you look for him.  During your explorations you unlock elements in a mindmap, which works as some kind of notebook to keep track of important information. There's some hints to your mom finding something weird in a lake, but she succumbed to cancer before having a chance to share her findings.  At the end of Act One you get a flashback to two weeks earlier where you suddenly play as Catherine, Kat's mom.If you like reading fiction like me, this is a game for you. It plays like reading a book. There's lots of text, but it's well-written text, it's a story that pays attention to detail. There's not a single generic description of hotspots in this game; everything earns its own paragraph.The game isn't voiced, so you'll have to do your own reading. There are some weird gameplay elements (like QTE's, a version of Simon Says, and having to navigate a little boat through a swamp during one very strange puppet show) but luckily they are far and between. I haven't encountered any puzzles to speak of, other than going to a store to buy a spark plug to fix a motorbike, and finding a stranger to go buy a hotdog from a vendor in exchange for information.Most of the gameplay centers on how you react when talking to other people, but I haven't seen any special consequences following those discussions.4,5 hours into "Norco", I'm still in Act Two, and the game has taken me places I never expected.There were actual battle sequences I had to go through! Man, I haven't done that since my Final Fantasy days so I took a lot of damage, and luckily I had no need of phoenix downs.So for a moment there the game felt a bit like those first person RPG's where you search through a dungeon looking for treasure and fighting monsters. There was this puzzle where you have to move drones through different security sections so you can pass through unseen. Other than that I'm just following the flow, talking to people, and seeing where things lead. I feel like I don't have much handle on the plot and am just tagging along for the ride, with no idea how it's going to end.I finished "Norco" in about 8,5 hours. And boy, did this game keep surprising me! Suppose they ever make an adventure game of season 3 of "Twin Peaks", then it would definitely have the look and feel of this game.Lots of stuff happened, I'm not going to elaborate on them, but finally there were some cool gameplay elements added to what is otherwise a very much narrative driven game. I got a recording app on my phone which I had to use to manipulate NPC's, and it was quite interesting to hunt after the correct voice samples. I had to steer a boat all across Lake Ponchartrain, with an added puzzle element to unlock more of the map but which was actually way too easy but still, it was fun to actually have something more interactive to do in this game.There were some more fight sequences, and then the finale came. Not going to elaborate on that either, except I loaded a saved game to get a second ending which was just as bad, and then I loaded an even earlier saved game to finally get the good ending. I like how you really had to pay attention to the details to realise what to do to get that good ending, because I didn't realise it the first time and it's very easy to move on without having done it at all.I don't think I understand everything that went on in this game. Like I said, "Twin Peaks" season 3. But I'm glad I played this game, which was very different from the games I usually play. I'm glad the demo intrigued me enough; it was all the text that won me over, combined with the gritty visuals.
_childDocuments_.name: NORCO

_childDocuments_.review: Played the game on GOG, Purchased on Steam for review because the top comment was bothering me so dang much. This is one of my favorite games of 2022, if not THE top contender.NORCO is an absolutely stunning foray into tiny industrial city misery. It is personal, intimate, and not afraid to showcase the absurdist heights of despair. To claim that the game eschews all its themes about family, loss, exploitation and so forth past act 1 is just *blatantly false*. It is an outright refusal to engage with the text & imagery on its own terms. This is an adventure game that proves point-&-click is not dead, and that it doesn't have to resort to uninspired, extensively backtrack based, random-option-roulette puzzles. The design of its UI is simple, interactive, and immaculate. One of the gameplay features is that of an in-character mind map, where you can question certain portions of the world unfolding around you and watch how the intricate web of events and people comes together. The pixel vistas can be gorgeous, immersive, and sometimes deeply unsettling. (Maybe even all the 3 things at once!) I love the TV filter.NORCO It is ALSO a southern gothic filled with magical realism elements; YES, THIS IS A *WEIRD* GAME. That's exactly why it rules! This is an entire school of literature, specially literature about complex, difficult to grasp feelings. More to the point; NORCO is explicitly telling a story about the insanity of late-stage capitalism (REALLY late stage, as the game is set in some near robot-bearing future,) and how that sense of invasive aimlessness and endless exploitation can sometimes feel just like a farce, even more so if you're among the poor. How people of all ages react to a sinking economy and dying earth in the most ridiculous, outlandish ways: conspiracies, cults, apocalyptic religions, aliens, crypto schemes, SpaceX, "That Da Vinci code sh*t."And that leads me to my next point of praise: this game is really funny. Don't get me wrong, we are broadly dealing with a lot of heavy subjects here (The protagonist's mother has just died from cancer, her brother is missing, the oil refinery looms unkillable and all consuming above the skyline) but NORCO understands that Real Human People have awkward and stupid interactions as one of our main paths to communication - and that it's not a bug, but a feature of our species. The people in this game have memorable faces, distinctive speech patterns, riveting dialogue and a LOT of heart. 'Atmospheric' doesn't make a dent in it for me. The humor adds depth to the very real structural decay that surrounds their region, and it hit home Hard for me. These are some of the people I know.I'm reminded of my favorite short story collections, where real events are extrapolated through a narrative voice that balloons the minutia of day to day life into wildly strange encounters with the unknown.The writing is almost effortlessly entertaining. A good bulk of the game is just dialogue, and it never feels like a chore, because our rotating cast of comedians and tragedians keeps each moment alive and counting. The game has 3 acts and a few story-progression minigames sprinkled in the middle for fun's sake. The combat can be turned off as you wish. The pacing in NORCO is tight even as you play in two different timeframes- first as Kay, then as her late mother, alternating between the two to build a larger version of the truth- and in many ways I feel as though the experience hasn't left me after reaching the end.I want to play this game again and see what little intricacies I might have missed the first time around. I also want more people to play this game, desperately; maybe they'll have the same bugs my brain does and have as much of a good time as I did.If you wanted to try NORCO, please do. I can't wait to see what the developers will come up with in the future.
_childDocuments_.name: NORCO

_childDocuments_.review: Norco has a lot of weird, sometimes goofy, characters and abstract moments. Yet it combines those with a serious story in a cohesive manner. Gameplay-wise it's a point-and-click adventure, which sees you interacting with items, environments and people in order to find out more about the story, about certain characters or to solve puzzles. The weakest part of the game to me was the combat: a series of basic QTE's, though it did not hamper the overall enjoyment at all. The visuals are amazing and they definitely punctuate some of the more impactful moments in the game, while also bringing all of the strange characters to life. Sound-wise there was a good amount of ambient noise, though no spoken dialogue, as the voices were portrayed by indistinct warbling sounds. The music was beautiful, melancholic and it fit the mood of the scene(s). This is a great game if you enjoy a story that makes you think. That makes you want to explore and find out more about everything going on.

_childDocuments_.review: Nice game, which combines some uncanny psychedelic motives, retro style and ton of gloom and dismay (I'm guessing, drawn from the Louisiana "vibes"). The gameplay is fairly simple, so for the old-school gamers it will be a walk in the park. But beware of some nasty bugs. I got stuck in Act 3 and was able to continue only with a fortunate help of the tech support. Suggestion to the developers: next time don't opt for cheap QA in India and add more polishing to the game before release.
_childDocuments_.name: NORCO

_childDocuments_.review: It's weird, dark, sad, and funny, but it also felt really earnest and compassionate. Even toward people the game ridicules. Some real-life people really are caricatures of themselves, and the ones in Norco felt like authentic, outrageous caricatures I have met. Their inclusion felt like it was done in a spirit of familiar, teasing camaraderie, not like an attack or sneer.One of my favorite things is when a piece of media makes me feel like I'm a part of a big, eclectic, intricate, ridiculous global-cultural-temporal tapestry. Norco is an absolutely beautiful experience all the way through.
_childDocuments_.name: NORCO

_childDocuments_.review: modern cosmic horror. i had the pleasure of visiting new orleans for a week once, and while i was there all i could think about was the disconnect between the sort of spirituality being advertised to tourists and the possibility of another world beneath all the cracks in the pavement. i wrote down these journals in the style of a lovecraftian protagonist. it was fun! so you can imagine my delight at seeing a game that is not only set in the bayou, but also knows how to construct and make rich a version of it that crosses over into cyberpunk, magical realism, dark comedy, and horror. i've been playing this game off and on for months, and sometimes i'd boot it up for just 30 minutes, read some dialogue, get absolutely lost in the synth soundtrack, and find myself doing something else entirely. i don't want to detract from how visually rich and colorful the art style is, but it really felt like i read a book. specifically, it captures that feeling of a book you can't put down. i'm not generally one to play point-and-clicks with a lot of text, at least until recently. highly recommended for people who want to play call of cthulu in a setting where half of the NPCs call you (female protagonist) "bruh"
_childDocuments_.name: NORCO

_childDocuments_.review: there is no way i can coherently express how much i adore this game - maybe my cosplay of the protagonist and all of my fanart will do it justice? not sure. just can't put into words how much this game resonated with me. beautiful pixel art. wonderful prose and worldbuilding. surreal, at some points humorous and at other points heart-wrenching. i keep finding myself thinking about it long after i've finished playing it, it's a story clearly written with a lot of love and care.
_childDocuments_.name: NORCO

_childDocuments_.review: It's a P&C story of a city full of personal tragedies you can only get a glimpse of as you pass through. A mystery, a depressing cyber-gothic mystery in the bayou, a tale of people trying to live while lives collapse.The plot and characters are incredibly engaging.The P&C aspects not only work on their own, but tie in quite well with the narrative.The art does the same, to incredible effect.  Visuals with the power of the Gatsby eyes or the Blade Runner flames, throughout the entire game.I wholeheartedly recommend this game with the one caveat that you do not want to blaze through it.  Take your time and let each act sit.
_childDocuments_.name: NORCO

_childDocuments_.review: Christ, what an amazing  game. A must-buy for folks who liked Disco Elysium or Inscryption (unless you only liked the deck-building aspect of the second). The graphics are beautiful. The combat is simple-- plus fun. And the story? God, amazing. It reminds me of Faulkner more than it does normal, ♥♥♥♥♥♥ video game writing. There is so much good content here.
_childDocuments_.name: NORCO

_childDocuments_.review: This game knocked my socks off and made me cry all in one sitting. The art, story, and characters are at the same time deeply grounded in the emotional realities of SE Louisiana and transcendent in the scope of their imagination such that when a friend asked me to not spoil the plot of the game for her I realized that I probably couldn't if I tried. If anyone is reading these reviews and wondering, "okay we get it, so the game nails Louisiana. But how's the cyberpunk?" I want to make it clear as someone who's not from the area but lived there for several years, that the Present in Louisiana, especially in places that white supremacy and capitalism have left behind, like Cancer Alley/Death Alley, Angola prison, or Isle de Jean Charles, is more cyberpunk than many of the futures I've seen imagined for other games. Norco is genius in the ways it's made that clear in this game.This was a 10/10 for me! But I'll admit it's probably not for everyone, especially if you don't want to read much or like to play games that are difficult. I think the most difficult part of this game is working through your own feelings at the end.
_childDocuments_.name: NORCO

_childDocuments_.review: NORCO is a truly excellent and highly intriguing point and click game with a surprisingly expansive story after what originally appears to be a simple premise. You primarily play the role of Kay who is returning home for the first time in years after her mother's recent passing and then discovering her brother has gone missing. The narrative then unfolds into a delightfully complex tale of sci-fi mystery and conspiracy. It's certainly one of the most powerful stories I have seen in this genre. The writing is superb, the pixel art looks fantastic and the overall atmosphere is really well crafted. There's also a few interactive elements with combat and moving around the map which adds a nice extra layer to the gameplay. Thankfully you aren't too bogged down in puzzles and pixel-perfect searching like in some similar titles. Sadly there are a couple of frustrating sections in the second half and some users may also find the narrative leaning too far towards crazy within its complexity as the game wears on. The story does make some pretty big shifts but I think most people will be fascinated and hooked especially if you are familiar with point and click games of this nature. Overall, NORCO is a brilliant 6-8 hour experience that will keep you engaged right to the very end. It's also an absolute steal in the sale and you can even play the whole of Act 1 in the free demo!
_childDocuments_.name: NORCO

_childDocuments_.review: Norco is a strong contender for best narrative game of 2022, even outside the point & click genre. This is not limited to the story, but everything from the writing, to visuals, and gameplay feels cohesive and satisfying.There are some cyberpunk themes on the periphery, but the mix of real world issues, religion, and technology sets it apart from the more common neon-soaked games which target that genre. It creates a strong mythology of its own, both from the geography of the surrounding landscape and culture, and from a well developed antagonistic future. It does not use sci-fi as a crutch or a short-hand, but creates its own vision of the future built on a past.The usage of pixel art does not hamper the visuals. The style creates images that are mundane, nostalgic, horrifying, alien, or surreal.The game is exactly the sort of thing I love Sci-fi for. It shows a familiar yet strange culture with a lived-in richness. It does not always let you comfortably explore, but shows the change in a world falling apart as something else creeps in...

_childDocuments_.review: +While I wouldn't say I'm a known fan of the Southern Gothic genre, and the fringes of world building are muddled (i.e what year is it exactly? What wars are going on?) I do feel that the world building is  cohesive enough to keep me engaged. I did get a few chills as I remembered the summer bible camps I was forced to attend in my teens, of how the surrounding wetlands really felt like alien landscapes that could swallow any and everything.+Mechanically it does a few neat things that won't surprise people who play modern point and clicks, but they're executed well and never overstay their welcome.+The soundtrack is pretty good; it's reminiscent of FTL's atmospheric, almost detached sci-fi with a dash of doom metal. It really captures of the creeping dread of traveling the bayou as you watch sun set into night.=I agree with negative reviews saying the back-end of the game takes a drastic turn in terms of story - though I feel it's less of a writing issue and more that you can really feel where the devs ran out of time and/or money. I don't necessarily think the game would've been better as 10 hour game vs 7~, but I do feel more side content would've fleshed out key characters or better stitched together certain story beats.-I did run into some minor bugs - lingering character portraits, a couple audio glitches and the game soft-locked once, but nothing a reload of a save or just carrying on couldn't fix.The game definitely has it's faults and there are story elements that may feel dated sooner than you'd think, bu it's post-modern genre blending makes it a stand out experience.

_childDocuments_.review: This really resonated with me.I read a lot and play a lot of story driven games, it is something that I take into great account. I can forgive a lot of things if it doesn't get in the way of the story. Norco balances so many things and manages to make them interweave seamlessly.The amount of lore, worldbuilding, characters, and concepts the developers can cram into this 8-10 hour runtime is astonishing. The pixel art and the sound design pair very well together, the characters all have their own texture and feel very unique. It waltzes that character v characterization line all the time and still manages to make everyone feel like they have depth. You feel sympathetic for monsters and empathy for characters you barely get to engage with. Finally, these different strings and notes all create this haunting story of New Orleans as it is sloughing off it's primitive path and being born again in the brackish waters of the future.
