_childDocuments_.review: A quirky point-and-click adventure game set in dystopian Louisiana. It's like a combination of the LucasArts games Full Throttle and Beneath a Steel Sky, but with a Faulknerian twist. The game is more cinematic than challenging; there's no hunting for the right pixel to click on, no using ten different items on a thing to see what works, nothing like that. In fact I found the game to be a little *too* easy -- the areas you can explore are small, you never have more than 2 items in your inventory, and your companions and so-called "mind map" are always on standby to tell you *exactly* what you need to do next in order to advance. However the game does contain several mini-game sections that were a refreshing challenge compared to the easy point-and-click main game. The story is completely on-rails; I can only recall three instances where there's more than one way to complete an objective, and even then the "choice" is not about making a moral decision or anything like that, it's just two different ways to accomplish a task and whichever one you happened to try first is the one you go with. If you want your adventure game to present you with moral dilemmas and meaningful choices with far-reaching consequences, Norco might not be the game for you, because it contains nothing like that.The pixel art is gorgeous, and the prose is incredible. And often hilarious -- there were quite a few parts that had me laughing out loud. The story itself is kind of silly, but not every game needs to be a self-serious commentary on societal problems with heroes and villains and epic choices that decide the future of the world. Sometimes a game can just be about poor people in a polluted swamp trying to earn some money so they can pay for their next meal. And the result is still beautiful.
_childDocuments_.name: NORCO

_childDocuments_.review: A fantastic pixel-art dystopian adventure game set in a narrative world that is kind of a cross between True Detective and Blade Runner.  I haven't had a game hit me so hard on so many levels in quite a while.  They art, humor, writing and music are all incredible and come from a very unique voice.  Can not recommend enough.

_childDocuments_.review: - Interestingly stylized pixel art that oscillates between scenes of dystopian cyberpunk decay and oddly beautiful--but often creepy--psychedelic scenes- The music is fantastic. The credits song is a banger and worth sticking around for- This game pulls off "weird" well. The narrative is cohesive and complete, just strange- There's imagery and subject matter that some may find disturbing, but those facets of the game lend themselves well to plot's themes. I wouldn't call it tasteful, but it is consistent with the game's world- Like other well-crafted adventure game worlds, the setting feels like another character. You're often given the opportunity to look at the skyline during important moments, and it's worth doing- Despite the dour themes investigating the various catastrophic results of unfettered capitalism, the game is full of humor. If you explore enough, you'll find extended gross-out gags, darkly funny situations, and some incredibly absurd scenes- It's a story-focused point-and-click adventure game. You can imagine the gameplay- The story is a lot to process, so I'm not itching to jump back in anytime soon. Wouldn't mind getting the remaining achievements someday, though- Ran perfectly, no bugs. Won't tax your hardware too badly- Should only take 5-7 hours to beat- . It's a great story. If you're into adventure games, this is one of the best of the year so far

_childDocuments_.review: NORCO is a captivating adventure game with a disconsolate world. It feeds you a relatable setting and includes a quirky cast of characters. The main protagonist, Kay, is a faceless person that can be entirely different from you, or the same depending on the choices that you make.The gameplay mechanics are designed as an efficient pipeline for immersion: simple and intuitive. NORCO is a point-and-click that leans on simple dialogue trees. The dialogue is effective at keeping your attention and absorbing you into the world, which is precisely what it should serve to do. And yet, despite its simplicity, NORCO has moments of brilliance wherein the beautiful prose stops you from mindlessly scrolling and makes you think about a deeper meaning.What immediately struck me about NORCO is the 90's nostalgia that is reminiscent of other games from my childhood, namely Might & Magic IV: Clouds of Xeen and Might & Magic V: Darkside of Xeen. I can vividly recall the real MT-32 tracks of Xeen within the instrumental soundtrack. It often has a funky, upbeat, and at times melancholy surrealism that compliments the dark, dystopian atmosphere in a near future New Orleans. Each area of the game has a fitting theme with elements of jazz or front-and-center punk distortion. I'm also convinced that Might & Magic and its RPG derivatives played a role in inspiring the party system, in which characters situationally join your group on the sidebar and add their own flare to the mystery, offering you helpful and funny dialogue.Rather than shoehorn an attempt at the profound right in your face (as a modern AAA title would), NORCO presents you with the world as an abject reality: You are a passing traveler with a hand in the direction of your own fate. NORCO's combination of simplicity, prose, and nostalgia render it as a game well worth playing — and one I would recommend to gamers and non-gamers alike.-Ssschah
_childDocuments_.name: NORCO

_childDocuments_.review: NORCO is what can be called a game with a soul, I haven't come across a similar experience yet:The visuals are stunning pixel arts, the story is intricate, captivating and immersive; plus the music is just enthralling one of the best I've heard in games so far. Purchasing the special edition with the OST and the art is totally worth it imo.The whole game focuses on various themes such as Hauntology, Christianity and paradoxes inherent to a dystopian industrial future. The tone is dark yet humorous, not Manichean and manages to keep a subtle balance that makes each character lovable in their own way. If you're into late Mark Fisher's works and Philipp.K ♥♥♥♥'s Valis trilogy, this game will without a doubt be an experience worth your time! Highly recommended

_childDocuments_.review: "...There is something antagonistic about returning home to the American suburbs: the vast swaths of copy-pasted homes; of meticulously manicured lawns; of fences and stone demarcating delineated spaces; of dogs barking in furious animosity when strayed too near. Everyone here is a little king or queen of their empty fiefdom, solitary in their halls and wondering why: when they’ve walled everyone off, an empty loneliness is all that seeps in with the draft.There is a certain melancholy of coming back to a place you thought you left behind. _childDocuments_.review: I am of two minds here (not a spoiler or maybe):the game does an amazing job with having its own style - the music alone is like, very very plus good - and doing the great sci-fi-ish thing of having a world you gets revealed as the story goes on without hitting you over the head with it too much (I'm looking at you, theatrical release of Blade Runner with inner monologue). considering how small the team is, the overall design of the game and atmosphere and etc feels very fleshed out, especially for what it is - a retro throwback to umm POV-based point and clicks (think "Deja Vu" which I played on the NES back in like 1885 or whenever), but with a lot more self awareness in the storytelling - even in minor details such as representing the main character with a shaky neon smiley face.but at the same time, its not for everyone. Point and click games are usually billed as mysteries, and atmospherically (and in the story, I guess) this is a mystery, but the gameplay itself is much more along the lines of an interactive novel or "walking simulator." There aren't a lot of choices, and the puzzles are either bascially handed to you or simply consist of "I need a rock, I will have to go back to the location where I saw a rock" None of that bothered me so much, and most newer retro point and clicks tend to lean this way to avoid the dangerous excesses of the 90s (I'm looking at your Day of the Tentacle, though I will always love you) where puzzles could not be solved by anyone in touch with reality and any rational person today would give up and look it up online. This is all fine.What was a bit more ambivalent for me:a lot of different mechanisms show up in the game both for gameplay and for story purposes. The Mindmap gets a lot of praise, for example, but the other stuff ranges from the obvious (picking up stuff to go into your inventory) to a bit more complex (having a smartphone with some different apps, or combat). These things all make sense as implemented and work well within the story and gameplay, but they are all used VERY sparingly. You pick up items and carry them around, but they definitely go out of their way to avoid the 90s logic here (e.g. I pick up a random piece of dried bread in a bakery in Act One because the game lets me, and in Act Four I use it to pick a lock somehow.) Everything you need to do is given to when you need it, and not much creatively is required. The more complex mechanics, such as involving the phone, seem like they could be used a lot more but instead kind of just fade out: they worked for the story and experience, but in the end a lot of it felt to me like I had gone through a narrative tutorial where I was learning how to play the game, only to have these things never come up again and spend most of the following act simply moving through rooms and reading text. The game felt very short because of this (also it took me less than 5 hours total) but at the same time more.. maybe not immersive so much as .. deliberate. There aren't a lot of answers here, but the path leading up to them (which stops short) is very careful to make you consider where you are going (even if you dont get there)So I liked the game as an experience, its clear the devs were interested more in telling an impressionistic story or painting a portrait or some kind of abstract thing like that rather than making a "game" in the old fashioned "kill the turtle men!" way, so, again, not for everyone, but I would be very excited to see what they did next.8/10 you get to pet the cat (but you shouldn't)

_childDocuments_.review: It offered me a good amount of confusion and not for a moment I felt the game wasn’t artsy enough or interesting. It’s bold, experimental, interesting. The constant flux of new backgrounds, characters, story threads, small gameplay systems, worldbuilding, and some shocking moments changing the formula kept the game fresh. A Visual Novel that feels like a true adventure game, with fancy visuals, explorable areas, and very smooth “puzzles” that offer no actual challenge, but help with pacing out the moment-by-moment experience.At the same time, something about the game hasn't resonated with me on an emotional level. It’s a “me” problem. I saw the game praised for its anticapitalist, post industrial themes - and because of my interests, those topics are now getting a bit stale for me, no matter their value. I didn’t enjoy the humor, aside from Pawpaw, but it’s definitely crafty. I already had my share of searching for stories about leaving your home and having another look at your difficult family relationships, and this time they just bounced off of me. I didn’t enjoy the religious themes. I didn’t feel so captured by the wetlands as I was playing Kentucky Route Zero, but KRZ had the advantage of being the first game that sold them to me presented in a similar fashion…I think I just played through a masterpiece, but it occurred at the wrong time in my life. Maybe five years ago it would inspire me like no other game, but right now, I can only appreciate it on an intellectual level. And the small shard of intellect I have left tells me I should return to NORCO in 2028, and in the meantime say - if it feels like you’re a part of the target audience for this game, you can trust that it’s as good as people say.

_childDocuments_.review: Extremely enjoyable. NORCO could be best described as a mix of point and click adventure in an RPG set up, where you investigate the strange things that happened around your mom's death and brother's disappearance. There's fun mix ups in what you're doing, including a simple and quick battle system with a focus on little microgames, exploring a swamp via overhead angle, and puzzles revolving around making use of a smartphone. The writing is very strong, going from complex and resonate prose to top tier sh*tposts where a cult member will go on a tangent about bong hits or you can listen to a guy you tricked into eating old hot dogs earlier describe what happened after when he couldn't find a bathroom.It also just looks beautiful from start to end, with lovingly crafted sprite art on every screen, and some really out there imagery alongside the attempts to capture the reality of the actual real oil town of Norco, LA. Good, resonate music, lots of text options for accessibility needs, and a solid seven hour length with some added replay value to mess around with choices and get achievements you missed. Highly recommended.
_childDocuments_.name: NORCO

_childDocuments_.review: Few games offer up a sense of place like NORCO does, and fewer still are able to make that sense of place so familiar. These people all live in my town, until they don’t. In NORCO the line between reality and absurdity is blurred so often that you begin to question if the line has ever really been there. Of course it hasn’t. NORCO doesn’t offer us a glimpse at a horrible future, like all great science fiction it just rephrases and recontextualizes what is already here. And NORCO is nothing if not great sci-fi.
_childDocuments_.name: NORCO

_childDocuments_.review: Pros:-Interesting story. Stays interesting until the end.-Solid characters.-Fun dialogues and scenes.-While I wouldn't call it's soundtrack a masterpiece, it works really well with the game's setting and themes.-Despite mainly being a point & click game, it introduces a couple of gameplay systems here and there that serve as a breath of fresh air.Cons:-The game can feel a little bit too artistic/abstract for me at times. This is 100% a personal thing, I just tend to prefer a less "abstract" narrative. It's not a problem anyway, in other games like Kentucky Route Zero, it's abstract narrative completely disconnected me from it's story. In Norco, it just got mea little bit  lost in a couple of dialogues, and I just had to re-read some stuff.-It frequently uses modern slang. Words like "memes", "influencer", "brah", "bruh" and the like pop up in most dialogues. I guess this is a personal thing too, I'm just not used to read this kind of language in games (and I don't really find it appealing), so it kind of made me roll my eyes a little bit whenever a character said one of those words.Veredict:-Really fun and interesting experience. A little bit too artsy at times, it's still an amazing game that I would recommend anyone used to playing narrative games.

_childDocuments_.review: I don't ever really feel compelled to write a review for a game, but this is an exception.  Please follow the reviews and know that if you take the time to read and follow the story, it is a great ride.  Around 5 hours for me to finish the game at the price of going to a movie. _childDocuments_.review: I'm recommending this game primarily for my appreciation of the art and sound, since both are awesome. I think where I have issues with this game is the story. The story doesn't really know what it wants to be. It starts off great, and sets an emotional somber tone. You feel like this is going to be a deep moving experience. But then, soon the story flips upside down to where it just gets so far out there, you kind of lose interest, and aren't sure how you even ended up there. I don't know if that is some intentional twist they wanted to achieve, but if so it kind of misses the mark. If they had included some interesting puzzles that were a little more in-depth and more interactions in general (along the lines of Maniac Mansion) I think the game would be great despite the lackluster story. For this price though, it's a pretty interesting experience.

_childDocuments_.review: I purposefully waited a couple of months before writing this review because I wanted to see if any parts of NORCO would stay with me. And I am glad to report that my appreciation of the game has actually increased with time. Although I feel like it is basically impossible to write a review of this game without coming across a little pretentious, here is my attempt;NORCO is essentially a Faulkner book wrapped in a really depressing (in a good way) futuristic setting. It's the classic southern tale where the world seems both stuck in a distant glorious past and also moving steadily towards an unsure future. The art style is the main selling point. Yes, it is pixel art, but not all pixel arts are created equally. NORCO's visuals made me feel nostalgic for a nonexistent past, you know the feeling. This is definitely one of the best uses of pixel art in gaming. There is not a lot in terms of gameplay, but still, there are some really cool moments with engaging game mechanics like a section where you get to traverse a lake. If you can vibe with it (especially with all the southern gothic thing) 10/10 chill experience.

_childDocuments_.review: I was born in Baton Rouge. My dad and his side are from New Orleans, and I remember trips on the weekends. Of course, everything changed with Katrina. Family spread, drifting apart. Playing this game was a reminder of what I loathe and love about Louisiana, or home. I relate so hard to the protagonist Kay. The meandering web of Southern religion justifying the absurd, the lost of family members to cancer, the tangle of family relationships with lies sprinkled in. To me, this game hit hard. I think I cried twice. It was a beautifully crafted game, and I felt giggles of approval of the inside jokes *wink wink* Mr Bart, Esplanade Mall, pointing out bald eagle nests on I-10 (to name a few)But not only was it beautiful, it left me feeling melancholy. I can't be sad because I already know about Cancer Alley, I already know that our world is being held up by a barely functioning swamp, and I know that oil rigs and companies couldn't give a crap about the environment and what they burn down. I loved this game. I didn't want it to end, because then I wouldn't have this version to turn to. I don't think I'll view another sunset from Crescent City Park or The Fly without thinking about y'all. I could go on and on...Obviously I have a lot of feelings about this game. So I'll just leave it with: buy this game, it's wonderful.

_childDocuments_.review: Norco feels like a game tailored for me. Geography of Robots made a smart choice by extracting the 90's adventure game pixel art design while leaving the tedious and unintuitive puzzle design.This game is all about the narrative. Between the dystopian cyberpunk politics and southern gothic tendencies, there's a lot of world building and characters to chew on.The combat is nothing special, but it was never supposed to be the focus. I do wonder about a version of this game that has no combat whatsoever, but it doesn't affect the overall impression. Can't wait to see what else this studio makes next.

_childDocuments_.review: Came into this game because I was looking to scratch that Disco Elysium itch, and this game came up more than anything.But boy, was it something else.I can see why this game is being compared to DE: both fall into that "serious game" niche where, through powerful storytelling, you come out with new ways of looking at the world around you rather than just being like "haha cool that was fun". And to be very fair, if you liked DE, you will probably enjoy this game too, and vice versa.But where as DE deals with ideologies, NORCO is much more grounded in how landscape is lived and transforms those who live within it. It is the critical geography to DE's political philosophy. It is much smaller in scale-- both literally (in terms of game size) and narratively (for its themes and overall story)-- but not necessarily for the worse. Sure, you could argue that in the end, NORCO is every bit as anti-capitalist as DE, perhaps even more so, but while playing it you get the sense that all those talks of big ideologies fade away in the face of the bayou, the refinery, the streets, and the sheer  of it all. And the grandest ironies of them all is that even those who tries to escape the confinement of such materiality ends up being mortally confronted with its brutal, unmistakable reality.So at the end of the day, even though I've just spent this whole review comparing this game to DE, NORCO is its own beast, and all the better for it.
_childDocuments_.name: NORCO

_childDocuments_.review: I would heartily recommend this game. Point-and-click adventure games are not really my thing, but this one kept me wanting to see it through. That in itself means that it was really good.The writing in this game is truly excellent. The atmosphere built up through the art design, the sound design, and the general rhythm of the game are also really good. It was really quite engrossing at times, and as such I had no trouble finishing this game across the space of 4-5 days. The story was interesting, and the characters seem deeply human. The game hasn't convinced me that I should now dive into a ton of other point-and-click adventure games, but I think that if you are like me and don't ever engage with these games, NORCO is a good candidate to pick as a way to dip your toe into the genre.

_childDocuments_.review: True Detective like mystical P&C adventure? Oh my how excited I was to see it and first two acts lived up to my expectations so much! Even with some dull "What-what was I supposed to do to progress?" stuff Narco still hold me tight in it's grip with solid dialogue, intriguing world building and some plot-twists.And... Act 3 just feels like hasted ending. All the plot hooks somehow got solved off screen, the pacing becomes so fast you don't realize the game has already ended. Personally, I think they cut of 2-3 more acts in between. I just wish this hasn't ruined it for me as a whole experience.But this South USA industial theme is strong and worth checking out even just once.

_childDocuments_.review: This game left a hole in me that I haven't been able to fill. I'm itching for more games like this but none match up. NORCO skyrocketed to my favorite games when I first played it, as so many elements hit very hard, and very close to home for me. _childDocuments_.review: NORCO has a bunch of unique ideas, but I felt like they failed to follow through on some of the most compelling facets of their story. I still found it to be overall an enjoyable and thought-provoking game, if a bit disappointing in some ways. If you're into unusual, story-driven, word-heavy games, it's probably worth picking up. But if this genre isn't normally your cup of tea then you might want to pass on it.
_childDocuments_.name: NORCO

_childDocuments_.review: NORCO is this type of game that you like or dislike. It doesn't grow on you. It is offering something plain and simple : you just have to be the right target for it. At first glance, we can tag this game as a story-based point'n'click. The gameplay is not taken only from those genres. It takes a bit of everything to deliver many aspects through mini-games. The gamer is thrown into this universe made of pieces cyberpunk/voodoo/religious subjects. This is what makes it so good : it plays perfectly on several sides to avoid redundancy.This is also part of why I really enjoyed NORCO. Mostly, the game doesn't take you by the hand. It doesn't have to as the puzzles are really easy. You have to discover what you want. You have to be a bit invested to really appreciate the story. By the way, its unfolding is at the perfect pace until you get drag into it for good. For sure, the end seems kinda rushed as there are still some loose ends. We own to imagine what we want ! The universe is strong, I am sure it would have been longer if the team really wanted to develop it.To sum up, NORCO is, for me, a good cocktail of gameplays & universes delivered with the right amount, at the right time. The demo sets the tone for an hour of your time which will help you making sure it is a fit for your gaming style.

_childDocuments_.review: NORCO garnered my interest initially due to its setting of a sci-fi magical realist Louisiana ravaged by capitalism and the unquenchable greed of oil companies. It reminded me of two of my favorite games, Kentucky Route Zero and Disco Elysium, which have become common comparisons to NORCO. NORCO definitely initially feels like it’s trying to follow in the footsteps of those games and their mix of fantastical elements and grounded themes pertaining to our current world, and initially it does a real quality job as the world is an enthralling and resonant one. The game’s graphics and aesthetic are beautiful in their own beaten down, grungy way, and bring the setting to life. The prose is also mostly of similar quality to KRZ and Disco and be quite evocative and got me into the game pretty well. The puzzles are fine; there’s not a lot of them, but they fit with what you’re doing in the narrative so they’re not moon logic-y. The game also has a combat system where you have to match symbols or time your clicks right. Combat in a point and click adventure game usually ain’t the best idea but it’s mostly alright.Unfortunately the game gets more and more nonsensical as it goes along; it loses the thematic strength and character writing it had started off with and the whole final conflict just feels so far removed from the initial one of the protag’s mom investigating the oil company’s shady dealings. Both KRZ and Disco had surreal endings too, but they still reinforced and were grounded in the real world themes both games had been building the whole time and tied into the arcs of the main cast wonderfully. NORCO’s ending feels like the devs just ran out of time and ideas. The ending just also throws a bunch of the combat encounters at you in quick succession too which also makes think it was rushed.  It is actually frustrating because I feel the game was close to being great, they just really needed a second pass on the third act.Overall NORCO is still a quality adventure game worth your time but I really can’t help but feel its “The Kentucky Route Zero we have at home” as it were and it could have been more.

_childDocuments_.review: Norco is 2022's Night In the Woods/Kentucky Route Zero/Umurangi Generation, and one of the first of a new generation that replace clunky text boxes/speech bubbles with a Disco Elysium-style text scroll. Though not as snappy as Disco Elysium, it can be quite funny, such as infiltrating the all-too-believable tiktok influencer cult that's taken over the local mall or a lot of the incidental writing from people trying to live normal lives in an increasingly bizarre world. _childDocuments_.review: I found myself being somewhat overwhelmed by the narrative, largely because there is so much going on in terms of world-building, not to say that it didn't have many good moments, but for me, some of the side objectives were more enjoyable than the actual plot. The game is very artistic in the way it approaches the narrative structure, you could potentially see it as heavy-handed in some aspects, but my criticism of it is largely subjective, and I can see that a lot of work went into making it. I often found myself confused by the details - constantly trying to find some solid ground from which I could attempt to analyze it. I think the writing in this game is generally really good, the problem for me was that sometimes I didn't care for the characters, or maybe the game didn't give me enough of a reason to care. Now I wouldn't say that story does not take itself seriously (well okay maybe aside from those 3 side achievements), but at the same time, there are moments where it undermines its own efforts to be something suspenseful. What I find very interesting is that for a game that should in theory have a lot of tension, it completely ignores it and just chills all the way to the end - I mean, maybe you could interpret it as an artistic choice, that is how I choose to see it, but it has an unusually relaxing atmosphere all things considered.The length of the game really depends on how much you are willing to read, I would say it's closer to 7 hours, but if you skip a lot you will only get 4 to 5. There are all kinds of creative gameplay elements, even a very underdeveloped combat system, but it's still a narrative game, keep in mind that it has a lot of text walls. So the combat system does not have much of a presence, there are only a few fights in the game so it's not even remotely relevant, and while the characters do have some unique attacks (not sure why because they are completely unbalanced), you will generally complete the fights on a first try anyway. The world has decent support for optional achievements, and as I mentioned earlier some of the best dialogue is in those side quests, I had some genuine laughs listening to the limo story and the conversation between Paw and Santa. There are some detective-like elements where you have to connect the thoughts to progress, although the game mostly holds your hand and helps you with the color-coding. It had some moon logic with the puzzles, sometimes I found myself backtracking and clicking everything, but overall, the puzzles were creative and I will take that over something generic - you can also click on the characters and they may point you in the right direction. I thought the exits were a bit confusing, I initially thought all connected areas would have exits on the screen, but sometimes the map itself has the exit which is a bit odd.(+) So the game has a lot going on with world-building and various narrative surprises. I would acknowledge that it has good writing, but personally, I was a bit overwhelmed. There were still moments that I enjoyed, and I will disagree that the ending was not interesting. Among the alternating chapters, I enjoyed Catherine's playthrough a lot more because she was a character, and not just an avatar.(+) The world has various optional objectives, some really funny interactions as well, I would highly recommend doing as much as you can. Good achievement support.  (+) Overall pretty enjoyable artwork and music, lots of locations to visit, good amount of content, and some creative puzzles. (?) I don't really have any objective criticism for the game, it was just a bit too much for me with all of the artistic ideas, on a personal level I don't fully appreciate having random things smashed together without a clear purpose. For example, you gave characters different attacks, one is like 3 times better than the other, and you only have what, some 6ish fights? The second swimming minigame was a bit odd, compared to the rest of the game you didn't put as much effort into its visuals. One thing I think could have been better, I would often return to characters to see if they had something new to say, but you kept many old locations without giving them much to do. So for example I would record ***** ***** ***** from Santa, and I am thinking to myself, surely everyone will comment on these, surely the devs were thinking this far ahead. Just small world-building reactions, not having as many of them made the world feel, smaller.Honestly, very subjective review, it's a very artistic game and it really depends if you appreciate what it does. My interest in the story kept going up and down, I thought the tone in the game was flatlining a lot, even during the moments of suspense and danger. It seems like an intentional choice to make this game very chill, so in that sense, maybe I am just biased, I just think it should have made me worry for the characters more than it did.

_childDocuments_.review: NORCO has a lot of good things going for it. I absolutely loved the beginning of the game, the captivating Southern Gothic vibe, beautiful artwork, captivating characters, an interesting mindmap mechanic, and the fascinating mystery of the protagonist's missing brother.Not only was the presentation stunning, but the themes were absolutely hitting too. NORCO seemed like it was about to really delve into a deep discussion of the socioeconomic consequences of industrial spoliation, automation, and class conflict in this interesting dystopic sci-fi setting around a real-world Louisiana oil town that its creator has a deep personal connection to.However, about halfway through the game, NORCO inexplicably  and almost everyone that you met and everything that you did in the 1st act becomes irrelevant. The change is sudden, and everything interesting that the story's been building up to is dropped. I powered through until the 3rd act, hoping that this was just a slump, that  but the story only dragged from there. That was roughly the point where I gave up and just used a walkthrough to see the conclusion, which was  It's a such a shame because the game could've potentially been so cool, a fusion between Southern Gothic and Sci-Fi is an objectively rad one, and hybrid genres like Weird West and Crime Fantasy have produced great works like Iron Council or Disco Elysium. However, these works are great not because of how they bend convention or shirk common tropes or have excellent world-building, but because they use their odd setting as a vehicle to discuss interesting and poignant themes. NORCO fails to connect its setting and its interesting genre subversions to what it has to say about the world.It's such a shame because you can sense the complex mix of disgust, love, familiarity, resignation, hate, and love that the creator feels for southern Louisiana. You can tell that they have a lot they want to say about it, and for a moment they almost manage to. I wouldn't have written such a long review if the game didn't make me feel *something*. But ultimately the games doesn't manage to cohesively weave everything together and very little of the themes are followed through on. In the end, you're left with the distinct impression that there are two games: an absolutely exceptional first half that hints at real greatness, and an absolutely bewildering second half that squanders that potential. And because of that, I can't really recommend NORCO.

_childDocuments_.review: : I have been interested in this game for a long time now before a publisher was even announced for it. I also played the Act 1 demo, so I kinda knew what I was getting myself into. Also, I'm originally from Greater New Orleans, the very setting of the game, so I definitely had a personal investment in enjoying the game.Okay now the pros and cons.✔ The setting is quite accurate to the real-life Greater New Orleans, with just enough changes to really make it its own setting that stands apart from anything else of its kind.✔ The pixel art is on point, with varying styles and complexity which convey each area and function the art has. From the simpler areas of Norco proper, to the vast panorama of New Orleans, the art has its place.✔ The music is in the same vein, ranging from eerie atmospheric pieces, to thumping, intense sequences.✔ The writing is absolutely top notch here. The writers clearly had experience in the Greater New Orleans area with the more local flair and vernacular, but also don't flood the writing with it. It's still understandable to players not from there. Also the juxtaposition between this informal tone with more sweeping, grandiose prose, sometimes in the same scene, really shows the mystique of the setting and the characters within it.✔ The game eases you into the different mechanics you'll run into during later parts of the game, so nothing feels like it just suddenly happens and throws you out of the immersion.✔ The "mind map" is a wonderful mechanic which helps you keep track of the relationships between characters and story elements, updating them as relevant info is mentioned during the game.✔ The puzzles are engaging but not obtuse, allowing the player to enjoy the a-ha moments of figuring it out without too much of the head banging against the wall of trying to figure it out in the first place.✔ The game is dense, has lots of content, but doesn't overstay its welcome. In my first playthrough on stream, it took me just south of 10 hours to complete. Not bad for a $15.00 purchase!✔ The game offers several font choices, since it's heavily text-based. You have some serifs and sans serifs, but most notably it has OpenDyslexie as a choice. OpenDyslexie is a font specifically designed to mitigate most, if not all, of the difficulties which arise when someone with dyslexia is trying to read text. Its inclusion surprised me and it's what I used for my streaming of the game to ensure that as many viewers would enjoy the experience.❌ There are moments which may trigger seizures in people with epilepsy. There is a warning when you start the game, but there is no way to turn that off.❌ Navigation through locations with multiple rooms or areas can be a little clunky at times. Sometimes there are areas you can click on the scene which move you to another area. Other times, you can only navigate to another area through the minimap on the lower right of the screen.❌ You can't scroll up on the text bar, which does me no favors whenever I forget important details when reading through the otherwise excellent writing. When I get to a point where I have to make a decision based on what I read several paragraphs ago, I can't go back and reference that information.❌ The pacing feels off during the later parts of the game. It feels like there were some loose ends that should have been tied up, but perhaps time constraints got in the way and they had to resolve the main plot points.I'd definitely recommend this game to anyone who:• is a fan of the point-and-click adventure genre;• enjoys stories where the mundane and fantastic stand side by side;• loves games with strong writing;• and/or want a fresh take on a near-future, dystopic, slow-moving catastrophe-in-progress setting.The game has its fair share of faults, but for a first outing from developer Geography of Robots, and against all of the bigger things it did right, I think this is a must buy!

_childDocuments_.review: I’m not sure if Norco quite succeeds as an adventure game, but it fascinates me.Much has been said about Norco’s foremost influence, Kentucky Route Zero. These are, after all, both games about ghostly fugitives of the “American Limbo”, whose characters drift through the vast, empty spaces of a dreamy and mythologised American South. But while I consider KR0 to be a perfect example of the genre of magical realism, because it treads carefully between the mundane and magical worlds without falling into either — its mystery or magic, as critic Franz Roh put it, is of a kind that never intrudes upon the real world but rather “hides and palpitates behind it.”Norco, instead, swiftly departs from its beginning wonderful ambiguity into realms of pure sci-fi or psychosis in its final act. As a literalisation of religious and familial or petro trauma, I can get on board with this, it’s like the moment when the mind just breaks and floods; but it’s a intrusion that seems so abrupt and so incongruous with the meditative pacing that came before. There's also a bizarre combat gauntlet in the final stretch — not sure why, because video games, I guess?This game is also a frightening example of petrofiction, and the monopoly of the city's oil refinery, Shield, on the natural landscape and the lives of its residents, feels monstrous. Shield burns whatever will burn, and the fires spread. In protagonist Kay’s dreams these monolithic industrial structures become cathedrals, places of worship; the worship of Oil and its refined products, its shining cities. I would love to see more games explore petroculture.And for fans of the Southern Gothic, there's a lot to dig into; the Christ-haunted landscapes of Flannery O'Connor or Cormac McCarthy are realised in the cinematic style of True Detective. The pixel art is marvellously evocative of not just a state but a state of mind.Ultimately, I think I like Norco as a set of disparate evocative ideas more than as a game itself. For me it never coalesced into a thematic or emotional whole the way KR0 did. I’m not sure Norco had one thing it was trying to say, or a grand thesis statement, but perhaps it doesn’t need to. Sometimes it’s enough to be like Kay or Conway, just passing through.

_childDocuments_.review: I got this game over a year ago when it first came out. I played it a little back then, but for some reason it took me until now to actually do a full playthrough. I regret waiting so long because this game is amazing. It really blew me away multiple times. It's like an amalgamation of all my favorite things; Blade Runner, Kentucky Route Zero, and Disco Elysium rolled into a stylish point and click adventure game with great writing, great atmosphere, great worldbuilding, and great characters. It had some genuinely funny sections to balance out the surrealist creepy overtones and the noir tragedy undertones. One scene in the final act actually had me tearing up a little. The endings are a little obscure and mostly ambiguous, but I like to think that the one I got leaves a little bit of hope for Kay (who is probably one of my favorite characters in all of gaming). I really loved this game from start to finish, probably one of my all time favorites. Definitely check it out if you're interested in the cyberpunk and/or surrealist genres, or if you just want a game with a very well-written story.

_childDocuments_.review: I haven't yet played it through, but NORCO is a tour-de-force of storytelling, graphic imagination, pixel art, regional history, left critique, and environmental science fictions. The gameplay is smooth, the puzzles are well-designed, the soundscape is impeccable, and the art is stunning - the use of light and texture belongs in a museum.It's a work of political art that is also deeply local and deeply rooted in a real place with a real history and real wounds. _childDocuments_.review: This is one of those games where when I load it up, I just sit for a moment to take in the title screen. It's just one of those games that's immersive from the start and where everything comes together -- graphics, attention to detail, atmosphere, plot, writing, characters, soundtrack, and gameplay. The mind map that helps you keep track of the characters and plot points is incredibly useful, too, and I wish more adventure games had it.I'm no Louisiana native, but the depiction of the setting feels authentic, and I like that it weaves real-world locations and events into its narrative -- Norco is a labour of love by locals, and it shows. It's suspenseful, it's funny, it's gritty, it has so many unexpected twists and turns, and it is endlessly creepy. And the ending. Oh my god, the ending.If you want a game that has a wonderful story and also offers an introduction to the rugged life in a Louisiana refinery town, with a dystopian/futuristic twist, buy this game. If you want something to compare it to, it reminds me partly of Night in the Woods, but also the horror game Last Door, but trust me, it's its own thing. This is the most creative game I've played in years.Edit: oh, and it's one of those games where everything fits together. Things you expect to just be throwaway references to set the mood end up being tied into the plot.Also, I love how there's optional things you can do throughout the game to influence the story, if you're clever enough to think about them.

_childDocuments_.review: I'm really on the fence about this game. It's extremely short (see my playtime) and absurdly easy (save for the occasionally finicky combat mechanics). It handholds you so hard that it's kind of patronizing, and more or less tells you the answer to every puzzle. I think it would have been more appropriate with an optional hint system for those who got stuck, instead of constantly having characters outright tell you what you need and where to go. When you never get to think for yourself, you stop feeling like a person with agency and start feeling like an errand boy whose path is padded with constant, unnecessary roadblocks.The story was intriguing and the pixel art was beautiful, but the ending was wrapped up so suddenly and with so many loose ends that I was left scratching my head. I managed to get a "hidden" ending, so I would have expected something even more, but it honestly just felt unfinished. So much of the game built up the idea of returning home to the place where you grew up, being a lost youth, and the emotions between you and your family, but the ending abandoned any kind of resolution to this in favor of talking about an occult mystery. And it doesn't even conclude the mystery, it just ends on a cliffhanger at the climax. I don't think it was worth the money to me.Now, I love Disco Elysium and really liked Kentucky Route Zero, but this game almost feels like a more cliche, trope-filled version of either. It wasn't godawful, but it was certainly noticeable if you've played those other games. The writing itself was decent once the story got going, but at the start it was definitely a bit pretentious. It initially had kind of a "I just found out what a thesaurus is" flowery quality to it, which is ironic considering the game is about working class people.

_childDocuments_.review: Very good and intriguing game.The gameplay follows a point-and-click style with some enhancements. There is some combat that involves choosing who to fight, each requiring a different type of memory game to see how successful an attack is, this adds some very light turn-based elements, it isn’t used very much at all so it works well here. There are also some segments that involve navigating a boat around, these are less enjoyable but minimal and break up the text well. The point-and-click aspects are done with hotspots that can be clicked in order to get information as well as using an inventory to have objects interact with the world. There is also a light party system that adds some light RPG elements to the game. All the little bits come together to make a pretty effective and engaging point-and-click-style game.The story is the most important part of all of this, the premise is that the player is Kay a girl who left home and has been busy for a while, she comes back following the passing of her mother to find that her brother has also gone missing. Throughout the story, great mysteries will be presented and unraveled as themes of familial trauma are dealt with. The story also deals with the impact of Capitalism on the town and the disastrous climate change it helps bring about. A refinery owns most of the town and area and lackluster safety has caused it to flood many times, people are without jobs and get replaced with machines. Another theme follows AI and its effects and how it can be dangerous. There is also a rather bizarre theme about the elusiveness of cults for young tech individuals that believe everything can be solved with space exploration and get wrapped into things they don’t fully grasp. It features cryptocurrency to help illustrate this point. Southern folklore also plays a role as crazy stories about local legends are told and explored. Characters are given many dimensions and their own flaws and motivations that make sense for them. There are also some comedic moments in the game to break up the bleak and dystopian nature of most of the rest of the game. All of these elements come together to tell a beautiful story with exceptional writing.Despite being pixel graphics each piece has a lot to say. The warmer summer-like colors invoke an almost hellish heat as this Louisana town with a refinery would exist. The pieces have great detail and convey intent incredibly well. It features both realistic depictions and strange creations of Sci-Fi.The soundtrack is very nicely done. A more subtle sound but it works well with what’s presented. Each piece feels somewhat distinct and fitting to the locations they’re found.Norco is an incredible game, it has some amazing writing that tells a fascinating and deep story.
_childDocuments_.name: NORCO

_childDocuments_.review: Trying to describe NORCO to your friends is like it's "basically Present Day Louisiana, except you have a C3PO sidekick" and "post apocalyptic louisiana, but the apocalypse is just like 3 more years of the current trajectory of what's going on" and "cyber punk southern gothic eco terrorist core" and "really ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ sad but really ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ good." This game made me ache for the people of Louisiana, and furiously heartbroken all over again about the struggles that permeate the area. It's a story that ignites frustration and rage in me when I thought my heart had been almost completely scarred over. My mom has cancer right now, and I played this game between weekends of commuting back to my hometown to help her. The guilt, fatigue, feigned and real apathy, obligation, grief, and rage that returning to your hometown under those conditions is captured .... truthfully. Despite (or due to?) the unrelenting bleakness of the setting and story, the game was so cathartic. I felt emotional the entire playthrough and I am still thinking about it weeks later.Also I just want to say mechanically, my favorite thing about this game is the mind map. It really felt like I was remembering things about my hometown and making connections. It was really cool. ok thank you for making this game bye!

_childDocuments_.review: Norco is a character narrative that never shows its character. It is a somber societal reflection on the vast American limbo that we find ourselves in today. On paper, we are at such a fast paced and eventful point in human history. Norco explores the role that most of us play in this eventful era, the role of sitting back and watching. Set in Norco, Louisiana, a suburb west of New Orleans, the southern industrial swamplands bleed through every inch of the game. Corporate overexpansion controls every walk of life in this small town, just like it does in every town today. Finding the moments of beauty in this horror is something necessary. Norco manages to reflect this very real, horrifying reality while still being able to feel comforting and providing life-changing, potent moments of existential meaning for us nihilists. Masterful writing, imaginative and unique worldbuilding, breathtaking art direction, and an unspeakably beautiful story.10/10

_childDocuments_.review: Absolutely loved this game. Bought it on release primarily due to the fact one of my favorite bands, Thou, did some music for it, with no other expectations. Immediately drawn into the nostalgia of games I grew up playing like Snatcher but with some clear Disco Elysium influences - namely future surrealism and a text system that instantly felt familiar. As far as point and clicks go this is about as easy as it gets. The game pretty much holds your hand from A to B with the exception of the very light RPG elements that occasionally come up. I played this on a Steam Deck which made the battle minigames incredibly hard until my dumbass remembered that the Steam Deck is touch screen at which point the game resumed being a walk in the park.Utter weirdness and originality oozing from this thing while it somehow still manages to be somewhat affecting with a story about grief, trauma, and loss (and a Juggalo sidekick that really put this over the top.) Loved every minute.

_childDocuments_.review: In this game, I tricked a guy into eating rotten hot dogs. I run into the same guy later, where he retells a VERY long story of him getting food poisoning. He can’t find a bathroom, so he sneaks into a rented prom limo, takes a s**t inside, gets locked in and driven around, and eventually ends with him running from the cops. Also, you can buy drugs from Santa. Brilliant stuff.I enjoyed Norco because it plays opposite to most point-and-click games. Namely, 1) the puzzles/problems have straight forward solutions and 2) the UI has loads of quality-of-life aspects that make playing quick and easy. This lets you enjoy the main attraction: the unique characters, crazy situations, and dialogue.In reference to point (2) above: you can back out of any dialogue instantly. You fast travel without any animations. Pixel graphics means no load time. Party members nudge you in the right direction. Really helps with the pacing.Unfortunately, the actual plot makes no sense. It asks a lot of mysterious questions, but never provides satisfying answers. It’s still enjoyable because it works like an absurdist comedy. Nothing makes sense, but who cares when you can talk to sentient birds, infiltrate a teenage cult, and gift dismembered heads?

_childDocuments_.review: Ok, so I finished the game and got what I assume to be the good ending (having looked on Youtube for the alternatives) and I've got to say that the game really didn't stick the landing (pun intended for those who have played until the end). This is one of those experiences where people will believe the story to be deep when in actual fact it's just a confusing jumble of information that doesn't tie together.If you're the kind of person who loves Twin Peaks because it doesn't make any sense, thus allowing you to assign meaning where there isn't any then this game is definitely for you.If, on the other hand, you want plot threads to come together in satisfying conclusions and mysteries to have revealing payoffs then avoid this frustrating mess. Columbo this ain't.There are cool ideas at play and I really wanted to play through the game to see where everything was going but, in the end, I'm just left disappointed I wasted my time. So many of the strange and bizarre choices which were made by the development team have zero explanation and that just leaves me with no goodwill towards the game.Ultimately, there are better point-n-clicks out there with far more to say and which are more worthy of your time.As for the overwhelmingly positive scores on Steam? Well, I'd challenge any one of the people who posted one to give me a conclusive and meaningful reason (drawn from information in the actual game) as to why Kay and her brother don't have f%$king faces???

_childDocuments_.review: Incredible. Aesthetically innovative in the way that you can only do if you're telling an authentic story about a region that you know deeply well. You won't find any fetishized plantation homes, appropriated voodoo culture, or romaticized mardi gras aesthetics in Norco. Instead, you'll find religious-trauma-informed surrealism, oil-refinery-dystopian cyberpunk, and hurricane-flooded horror. The mystery is quite compelling, and the mind-map mechanic is such a perfect way to track your findings through this surreal point-and-click adventure. Play if you wish that Night in the Woods leaned harder into the horror elements, if you're aching for media to tell a real story about Louisiana, or if you're a fan of point-and-click adventure or narrative-heavy games in general.

The characters are shallow, barely sketched out, and flat. The story is not so much a woven completion as it is a few scraggly threads that end frayed and disintegrating. This is clearly a passion-project of someone who wants to capture the vibe of an area they very much care about, but in the format of an adventure game that passion fails to translate.
