_childDocuments_.review: Norco. Another standard-bearer of the last ten years of video game renaissance, which reproduces a winning formula now widespread: evocative 2000's graphics, often not instantly appealing, paired with elements of a somewhat forgotten genre reduced to its primary essence, combined with authorial writing (we've seen this blueprint in Disco Elysium, Signalis, even Golden Idol), here taking the form of a goth cyberpunk adventure in rural America.The project began over 10 years ago with a series of sketches in the actual locations of Norco, Louisiana, a town born out of a Shell refinery, of which the developer, then in his twenties, is a native. From those powerful landscapes sprung the idea for a video game.It is said that the a good cyberpunk work is not about the technology but using it as a metaphor for current phenomena and issues, and here Norco is second to none: it includes references from environmentalism to neoliberalism to the pipelines of the alt-right, evangelical preachers, and crypto-millionaires, plus a stateless protagonist with elderly and sick parents with whom our generation can easily identify.The game's formula is that of the visual novel, with a substantial amount of text that characterizes the game world in an almost poetic manner, with clear references to Disco Elysium, even in the interface itself and the attention to typography. This genre is married to the modernized and simplified skeleton of a point-and-click investigative adventure, of which Norco captures more than anything else the flavor, avoiding the typical difficulty and inaccessibility.While I very much appreciate the inclusion of a Pathologic-like "mental map", which in the end feels even a bit superfluous, maybe in a testament to its usefulness, these are not exactly my favorite genres, as i find it a bit difficult to maintain the necessary concentration, but Norco's unique atmosphere and its attention to every detail did not make me regret undertaking this journey.4/5
_childDocuments_.name: NORCO

_childDocuments_.review: Genuinely one of the most impactful and incredible games I have ever played. I find myself thinking about it pretty often even though I only played through it once. The story is insanely rich and well thought out, I've really never seen anything else like it. I was so absorbed in the plot and invested in the characters and what would happen to them. I played it pretty much in one sitting because I needed to piece everything together and figure out what was going on SO bad. It integrates a lot of different play styles to keep things interesting, and the art is amazing. I can't recommend this game enough if you are a fan of story rich point and clicks.
_childDocuments_.name: NORCO

_childDocuments_.review: This game is awesome.  Spooky, beautiful, future, sci-fi, decay, surreal... the story and all of its details were totally engrossing.  The writing is at times poignant, and at other times hilarious.  It harkens back to games like the first Gabriel Knight (also set in the New Orleans area).  The only thing missing is voice actors, but the developer did a good job of coming up with a vocal facsimile.  It's basically point-and-click adventure, in the 90's style, but without the random object collecting.After playing through I have so many questions.  So many thoughts provoked.
_childDocuments_.name: NORCO

_childDocuments_.review: NORCO is visually beautiful, conceptually dense, and tremendously well-written. More importantly, it has something very few video games do: a narrative voice unburdened by the tropes of the medium that is nonetheless extremely well served by its form. The experience is somewhere between a point-and-click adventure, hypertext fiction, and political-psycho-spiritual manifesto. It's deeply strange and sad, but hopeful enough not to leave you completely grated by the harrowing events of the story. I see the comparisons to Hunter Thompson, KR0, and other well-known examples of hallucinatory road fiction, but this is in a genre and class of its own, particularly with regards to its depictions of terminal capitalism and the complexities of family, place, and belonging. There's also an abundance of hilarious and astute nods to crusty/anarcho-punk/crimethinc aesthetics and subculture, if you came up through those scenes. Even if none of NORCO's specific references resonate, the visual, sonic, and emotional landscapes are irresistibly compelling.I barely ever write reviews, but I can't recommend this enough. For me, it delivers above and beyond all expectation, and I'm genuinely grateful to see something this far off the beaten path of video game narrative supported in finding a wider audience. I hope it sticks with you as profoundly as it's sticking with me.
_childDocuments_.name: NORCO

_childDocuments_.review: I came for the visual, ambience, story rich point and click and I stayed all until the end as I loved it.I used a guide to get all achievements which are possible in one play-through (just need couple of save to go back to just  before a choice as there are only couple of mutually exclusive achievements).Very much enjoyed the game and will recommend to any fan (or anyone) of point'n'click who are looking for a story rather than puzzle focus as there is no real puzzle/object to combine.
_childDocuments_.name: NORCO

_childDocuments_.review: I love Louisiana, I love cyberpunky near future settings, i enjoy text heavy games with good writing, and I enjoy bizarre ♥♥♥♥ so this game was right up my alley. I knew nothing going into it and all I can say is wow, what a trip. In some ways this game was very grounded and depressing and in other ways the game was hilarious and unbelievably weird. I love it. I find that it took away a lot of the frustrating aspects of classic adventure games while keeping the same general framework. The puzzles for the most part are not very obtuse and there was only one that I felt wasn't very clear at the midpoint. There isn't really any pixel hunting, and there's tons of fun hidden content that can be found throughout this game.
_childDocuments_.name: NORCO

_childDocuments_.review: The credits rolled while letting me astonished by the ending and revelations of the game. What did I just experienced ? It is quite cryptic, but it also gives you hints to understand the world imagined by the authors. I think it is quite difficult to review this game, it is quite unique and better experienced by yourself.As some people said it is really bizarre and haunting, it makes you want to discover more of the lore. It never overstays its welcome and you always want more. More weird characters, more doomed places, more mysterious elements. I needed an intriguing story heavy game and this game delivered quite well ! The art is as you can see in the store page: beautiful. The OST you ask ? Same, it really suits the atmosphere. The storytelling ? Very well written, you feel like you are meeting people from Louisiana, even though I never went there myself, but it feels on point ! Gameplay ? There are some cool mechanics that make the game a bit more exciting (though it remains a point'n'click experience).It took me around 9 hours to go through the game, I don't know if I will try to 100%, but it was a top notch experience.If you are on the fence whether to get it or not and enjoy mysteries and narrative games, don't hesitate anymore and go get it ! I would say it is really worth its price.
_childDocuments_.name: NORCO

_childDocuments_.review: +loads of varied and inventive puzzle mechanics (day of the tentacle style point-and-click, rhythm action, riddles)+compelling story (sad, funny, sadfunny)+beautiful in sound and vision-no real opportunity to get lost, as NPCs are _constantly_ _repeatedly_ telling you what it is you're meant to be doing in a way that can get a little irritating
_childDocuments_.name: NORCO

_childDocuments_.review: I won a staring contest with a cat and it made it launch itself like a rocket, 10/10.What I have learned though is that the setting in this game is not far from reality. Norco is a real place, with a real refinery, run by a real evil corporation (Shell IRL, Shield in the game) running their business on an old plantation land and pumping cancer causing chemicals into an impoverished community that can't leave and is constantly in legal battles with them. Even Apple Street is a real place in Norco.
_childDocuments_.name: NORCO

_childDocuments_.review: Amazing writing, very far removed from anything else I've ever played/read. If you're someone who is drawn to strange unique things definitely check this out.It is definitely heavy on narrative, gameplay is somewhat light, but honestly even if that doesn't sound appealing to you, you should check it out anyway if the strange story is at all interesting to you.
_childDocuments_.name: NORCO

_childDocuments_.review: Stunning.  I have an ever decreasing attention span, and I often feel guilty about the way I flit from show to game to book.  I blame myself for my own failings in being able to focus.  Then sometimes along comes a piece of art that arrests even my attention.  At the end of Norco, I couldn't speak.  I could scarcely breathe, so rapt was my attention.  The soundtrack is excellent, the visuals are excellent (and I'm someone who does not automatically think pixel art = beautiful), and the writing is very good all the up to often truly sublime.  It took my 7 hours.  This game deserves at least that much of your attention.
_childDocuments_.name: NORCO

_childDocuments_.review: One of the most beautiful and emotionally gripping games I've ever played. Just goes to show you don't need AAA graphics or an ensemble cast of voice actors to construct a weird, yet wonderful story. All of the characters feel so alive. The soundtrack alone is so hauntingly good. You won't spend a long time playing this game, even in one go, but it will stay with you for a very long time. Take your time, read the dialogue, explore the world. You won't regret your purchase.
_childDocuments_.name: NORCO

_childDocuments_.review: This game is a beautiful meditation on faith, environment, and community. I played it all the way through on gamepass before deciding I wanted to own it.Though an adventure game, you probably wont have many instances of being lost, or confused on where to go. The transcendent pixel art and droning music are a perfect accompaniment to the dry, honest, sardonic, hopeful prose. You may know these characters, have felt them over your shoulder. Met their gaze and averted yours. I would like to see more from the team at Geography of Robots but hope they pursue whatever they want.I loathe to make comparisons , but I would recommend this game if you enjoyed such games as :Disco Elysium, Kentucky Route Zero, or Umurangi Generation.
_childDocuments_.name: NORCO

_childDocuments_.review: Fantastic game. Great pixel art and mood. Blends mysticism and cyberpunk, as well as commentary on our current world, also several hilarious things to find. Some similarity to Kentucky Route Zero, the Wadjet Eye games, if you liked those. Will probably play again. Mostly point and click, a few quick time events. I played it in one sitting and will probably play it again for the vibe.
_childDocuments_.name: NORCO

_childDocuments_.review: I thought I'd enjoy Norco as a fan of point and click adventure games, as well as narrative-heavy games. Unfortunately the further the game went along, the more it lost me and left me wanting to get to the end so I could move on with my life. The writing just seemed flimsy to me and every part of the world felt utterly forgettable. Same could be said for the puzzles and game systems, if you skip this game you won't be missing anything.
_childDocuments_.name: NORCO

_childDocuments_.review: This is an extremely cool, evocative, idiosyncratic point and click linear adventure game set in an at least somewhat fantasized version of Norco, LA. It has a dreamlike quality without being too fantastical. The dialogue conveys a depth of emotion and quirky humor. The pixelated graphics perfectly tie everything together. The only negative is the "fighting" elements that the game contains are not really interesting or difficult, to the point where I question why they were even included. But you can get through them quickly enough and everything else about the game is amazing, assuming you like this style of game.
_childDocuments_.name: NORCO

_childDocuments_.review: NORCO is a pretentious arthouse game where you play between a daughter and a mom who have to solve a mystery that really goes nowhere and is a game about why you shouldn't let hobo's into you life.In the SCARY HYPER FUTURE of Louisiana instead of gambling, jazz bands, people arguing over LSU, over priced drinks and terrible city planning, you instead now have a CYBERPUNK-light future where instead everyone enjoys arthouse puppet shows and having the most absurdly non-human dialog on the planet. Honestly, the problem with NORCO is the story sucks. It's boring, it has probably the worst conclusion I have ever seen in writing where it gives it up every single interesting plot point to instead whimper and die in the most laughable endings you could ever imagine. The puzzles in the game? Not bad. You don't need a guide or anything and they don't feel too tedious, but it's really just a writing problem. The author, a man I can only assume who wears a beret and makes Stephen King look like the brevity king makes this feel like such a slog - But unlike other authors, he has a million interesting openings and then says "AW SCREW IT! IT's TOO HARD TO TIE THIS UP!" and instead Poochy has to return to his home planet.NORCO also has an identity crisis. Does it want to be comedy? Family drama? A horror? A morality tale about capitalism gone wrong via SHADOWRUN style cyberpunk-isms? What about a goofy story about ghost swaps and a noir style hammy detective? Oh, that's not enough? Why not add also in some three stooges style slapstick and fart jokes. Well, it tries to do all of it and fails miserably. This isn't worth buying or playing. It's pretty much a uninteresting hipster game where 99% of the cash you get to these guys will go to overpriced coffee and cloves.
_childDocuments_.name: NORCO

_childDocuments_.review: Very impressive game and wonderful story. Love the visual style and the music is flawless! Everything has a great style here! Loved the characters and dialogue options, and many of them had me laughing out loud. People who say that this is "the next Kentucky Route Zero" however, are completely wrong as there is very little that they have in common other than that both are interactive narratives. If any criticism, I'd say that the ending I got was very VERY unsatisfactory. Mostly because I felt that it didn't really end at all, and just plain & simply "STOPPED." But that just means that I'll play through it again and see about one of the other endings! Love the game, and a high recommendation for adventure game fans.
_childDocuments_.name: NORCO

_childDocuments_.review: A really wonderful piece of storytelling :) You can find creativity in unexpected places! The developer has mentioned their work in GIS - which, on the surface, sounds about like the least inspiring thing imaginable. But that would be wrong. There is such a precision about the layout of this game - a lot of thought went into why environments are the way they are, and how those environments affect us. It certainly helps that the developer grew up in these very environments - but NORCO really makes it feel like you're the one who grew up here. And in a point-and-click adventure, that's already a lot!You can feel that same respect in every character, and in every bleak development. The art and music hold up their end, but my favorite part was just how human everybody feels. You can really lose yourself just listening to people talk. I appreciated this dedication to telling, for the most part, a very contained story, allowing for layers on layers of dialogue.There are a ton of instances where it would've been so easy to throw in some repeated line of dialogue and leave it at that. You have to convince a character, for example, to split off from a cultish religious group - you have to go and record other members explicitly defying their faith. You learn that the group is generally anti-technology, and you recorded one kid talking about being on his phone all the time!In the game, though, you do learn that the cult recruits people on a message board. So, I half-expected this character  to get outraged, and half-expected an autogenerated 'That doesn't convince me' you would get from any other line of random dialogue. But the developers actually thought of that! They have a special line for that bit of dialogue! There are so many instances like this where you really feel like you're having a real conversation, and I just love that!Apart from the little things though, it's just a very interesting meditation on identity in the modern day. We find identity, now, in increasingly niche and bizarre places - the game makes the point that in all of its strangeness, the world is still grounded in the same institutions as always. If I have one criticism, I thought the ending was a little too grand. The sheer bleakness isn't the problem - I think that fits pretty well with the game. It's that NORCO, to me, felt like a very personal story about being caught up in things out of your control. There's a little dissonance there, I think, where we are small and malleable, but our protagonist is... ultimately not that.But overall, I loved it. Even if I would call the game pessimistic, there's definitely this thematic out routed in empathy - and, without spoiling anything, how you understand that will impact the game. All in all, it's a wonderfully thought-out story with very human characters that convey a lot of emotion.Also, I really love Million :)
_childDocuments_.name: NORCO

_childDocuments_.review: The good- Artistic aesthetics with gorgeous pixel graphics and nice chromatic palette. Sometimes it looks like a vintage graphic novel.- Well designed, immersive dystopian world with lots of details and post apocalyptic elements. It has solid, surreal, kind of depressing atmosphere. So unique.- Good writing. Descriptions are great, the stories that you read feel alive and the dialogues are always interesting. It has some strong poetic moments too.- Awesome characters with unique appearance and vivid personalities. Some of them are completely crazy and it's hard to forget them afterwards.- It has some interesting, refreshing mechanics for the point and click genre. Having companions and talking to them is great. The mind map with all these thoughts, nodes and lines connecting them is interesting too.- Nice lore. The town has history, characters with rich backgrounds and there is a small small network of human relationships going on.- Cool storytelling with flashbacks, and secrets that gets revealed to you gradually making it even more interesting. The actual story is a little bit over the top for my taste though.- Great music that enhances the dystopian atmosphere.- Inside all this darkness and mystery it has some moments with pretty inspiring sense of humor.- Good design that guides effectively your glaze to the interactive objects inside each screen eliminating pixel hunting. There is a reveal button that helps too.The bad- Despite having some refreshing mechanics its puzzles are pretty straight forward, unchallenging and lack imagination. Also, it tends to guide the player too much making the game easy and linear. You're doing many things mechanically without much though.- The story has great beginning building a mystery that promises rational explanations. Yet, after its middle point it gets over the top with things that look random and excessive like it desperately wants to impress the player. The endings are abrupt and leave many questions unanswered.- The RPG style, turn based battles are shallow and don't fit the point and click style of the game. Even more there is no need for a big final boss battle.- There are only few interactions with objects per screen. Some more comments on scattered things would make it feel more alive and immersive.- Voice over would have made it much more atmospheric, replacing these annoying mumbling sounds.
_childDocuments_.name: NORCO

_childDocuments_.review: I don't know what this is. It's an amazing game, but at the same time, it feels like an LSD trip on salvia. Lots of references to Christianity, very well done but creepy sound design, story which I am not sure how to make sense of.Buy it, play it. Wouldn't call it game of the year, but certainly worth the money.
_childDocuments_.name: NORCO

_childDocuments_.review: Southern Gothic, Cosmic Horror, Magical Realism: All of these mix alongside ambitious writing and a beautiful art style to weave a fable that reflects our current times.I struggle to define NORCO any further. It is both more and less than a game. It is an experience. I can not say with any certainty that you will have the same favorable opinion as me about this game. But I think that, like with any good piece of art, even invoking a more negative response than mine will leave you with something important.Buy it. Play it. You will not be worse off for your time spent, and it will be impactful either way.
_childDocuments_.name: NORCO

_childDocuments_.review: NORCO is a point and click adventure game. The character Kay comes back home after her mother's passing. This leads her into a story of finding out more about the mysterious network and how her bloodline might be significant. It's an interesting storyline. It also has robots so win! The game does have a lot of text and immersive descriptions in them. I personally  like games like this but I know not everybody wants to read a giant text wall all the  time. There are several humorous characters, as well as some heavier serious themes. There are cats, and not to spoil anything, but one of them has a unique "power". The mapping system is a different one I haven't experienced yet. It actually displays the different direct locations on the map in which you can click. I actually found it incredibly useful compared to most mapping systems. I have no sense of direction so in games like this it's often difficult for me to tell where I have/have not been. This made it super convenient to figure that part out. The puzzles in the game were moderate difficulty. I was able to solve all of them without getting additional help from the internets. I hate puzzles that are over-the-top and with solutions that make no sense. That wasn't the case here. I would say everything could be solved if the texts were well-read. Overall, a lot of positives. Story rich, moderate puzzles, cats, robots, and a nice mapping system. Downside to some people may be the large walls of texts. That depends entirely on preference. Would recommend if you like those aspects of a game.
_childDocuments_.name: NORCO

_childDocuments_.review: Weird. So weird. The best kind of weird. And it gets more weird as it goes on, too. Basically the game feels like True Detective  Season 1 if Rust had schizophrenia. A bonkers mix of cyberpunk, depressed futurism, rusting oil rigs and swamp fever dream. There are a few images toward the end that I'll never get out of my head. Wish we had more games like it.
_childDocuments_.name: NORCO

_childDocuments_.review: "You got a pecan for a brain." Almost unrivaled as an evocation of setting. As an NO native nothing quite matches the intimate specificity that NORCO touches on, especially in a medium that rarely delves deeper than French Quarter caricature. Married with a brilliant thematic structure and devastating mood; the real Norco region is a cruelly perfect setting for sprawling petro-dystopia.
_childDocuments_.name: NORCO

_childDocuments_.review: Starts out strong but veeres into a senseless stoner fantasy pretty quickly. All the pseudo-philisophical trappings are just a front for what is basically a text-heavy linear game with QTE combat and nothing of import to say. The only thing it has going for it is the setting and art direction. Not sure what everybody was gushing about. They must've played only the first 15 minutes. Very disappointed, bruh.
_childDocuments_.name: NORCO

_childDocuments_.review: Norco absolutely rules. One of the best written games I have ever played, feauturing a gorgeously realized and mesmerizing setting so confident in every step that you can't help but be sucked into the fever dream it is presenting. I stopped playing the demo after 10 minutes because I knew immediately that this would be amazing and I am glad I was right.
_childDocuments_.name: NORCO

_childDocuments_.review: Well... It was an unique experience for sure. With a good visuals. I enjoyed every bit of it (almost, since it has some ♥♥♥♥♥♥ mini games). But overall it was a good experience and I loved it. But I still believe it has a big gaps on the story itself. I can write tons of questions regarding to story. I'm afraid devs think story was a self explanatory however it wasn't at all. Maybe I was the one missing things but, I couldn't find any article or review which is explaining anything more than I know. If I'm playing a story driven, narrative game I want to know what is story about.In short good experience, mesmerizing visuals, with a lack of lore.
_childDocuments_.name: NORCO

_childDocuments_.review: As haunting and seedy as it is twisted and darkly amusing, NORCO is quite simply one of the most impressively conceived and written point-and-click adventure games I've ever played. Its plotting can be dense and intentionally obtuse, but its gameplay design is very smart overall, featuring a superb array of dialogue and lore to chase through exploration, as well as a series of puzzles that engage the mind without descending into moonlogic.This is the kind of game that may demand a couple of playthroughs to fully grasp its storytelling, but enthusiasts of point-and-click adventure games will nonetheless find this to be one deranged hidden gem. Just watch how many times you pet the cat. Mistakes were made.
_childDocuments_.name: NORCO

_childDocuments_.review: NORCO is a strange, surrealist point and click with an weird ass story, good humor, fantastic pixel art, and great atmosphere. I love its depressing, futuristic take on New Orleans and its suburbs and was captivated by the increasingly surreal events NORCO presents. The puzzles are also fun and many small choices causing certain outcomes make me interested in a second playthrough-- not because they affect the story much, but because of the fun new characters and scenes I might unlock. It's also paced well at 6hrs. Well worth the asking price.
_childDocuments_.name: NORCO

_childDocuments_.review: Despite all the critical acclaim and hype, the game disappointed for me. It isn't entirely bad, there are worse games but it just seemed to be a bunch of random things mashed together in the end. If you want your games to make sense throughout and have a satisfactory conclusion this isnt't it. It's basically a 4-5 hr long acid trip in the form of a game.
_childDocuments_.name: NORCO

_childDocuments_.review: This game is so good! It's like True Detective S1 meets Blade Runner with a little bit of David Lynch. It's pretty text-heavy for a point-and-click game but it really fleshes out the setting and characters. It's funny, creepy, and weird. Play the demo if you're unsure about it - that's what got me hooked, and you can continue your progress if you end up buying it!
_childDocuments_.name: NORCO

_childDocuments_.review: Yo, my beautiful bastards,Get ready to dive into the sweaty armpit of America, where the spooky magic of the bayou meets the crusty, rusted-out wreckage of industrial hell. I’m talking about the hauntingly badass game, Norco.From the second you fire it up, Norco drags you into a Louisiana that’s like... weirdly real, but also trippy as hell. It nails that Southern Gothic vibe like no other—environmental decay, broke-ass economies, and folks who just won’t quit. It’s all woven together in a story thicker than swamp mud.You play as a character grinding through a world that’s basically Louisiana with its guts hanging out. All that real-world mess—pollution, corporate greed, and people just trying to survive—isn’t just some background scenery. It’s baked into the bones of the game. You feel it in every step of the journey, like the game’s calling out the BS we see in real life, and it’s doing it in a way that hits you in the gut.And let’s talk visuals—pixel art that straight-up slaps. Every soggy swamp, busted-up refinery, and rundown shack feels like it’s alive. The sound? Oh man, the sound wraps you in this sweaty Southern blanket of cicadas and far-off storms, dragging you even deeper into this twisted beauty of a world.The people you meet? All kinds of wild. Some are beat down by life, but damn if they’re not fighting. Others? Well, let’s just say there’s some spooky stuff going on under the surface. The whole cast brings a storytelling punch that you don’t see in many games. It's all depth, no filler.And because I’m a freak like that, I hit up the devs for more juice. Turns out there’s a goldmine of extra lore and backstory you can dig into if you’re feeling obsessed—like me. Trust me, once you start, you’re gonna wanna know everything.Norco ain’t just here for a good time; it’s here to make you think. It’s like a neon sign flashing “wake the hell up” while still keeping you hooked with a killer story. It’s rare, it’s raw, and it’s brilliant.To wrap it up: Norco is a masterclass in storytelling and atmosphere. It’ll take you down a swampy, metaphorical river you didn’t even know you needed to cross. If you like your games with some brains behind the beauty, this one’s calling your name.Stay magnificent, my beautiful bastards.Key Points:Your ever-classy commentator,The Magnificent Bastard
_childDocuments_.name: NORCO

_childDocuments_.review: NORCO is a graphic novel game that tells a fascinating story in a unique and creative way. I think it has excellent ideas and moments of brilliance, but it falls short in polishing them which was a bit frustrating to me, but let's get into it.First of all, NORCO has an engaging and well-written story that keeps the player engaged throughout. The game's narrative unfolds in a nonlinear fashion, which adds to its overall appeal. Additionally, some parts of the story are just brilliantly written, such as the Showgoer's tale, which is a standout moment in the game.The MindMap is a great example and they should have exploited it more in my opinion. This feature ties together various elements of the game's story, making it easier for the player to understand and follow the narrative. Furthermore, I think this game displays a great sense of humor. In terms of characters, NORCO has some well-written ones (such as Leblanc and Catherine) However, the game has a weakness in this area too. Some characters who felt they were gonna be crucial to the story were not developed at all. Characters like Blake, Laura, Duck, and PawPaw left me feeling unsatisfied and wanting more of them.Aesthetically, it is a success. I love this weird, decayed industrial world and the game manages to be unsettling, sad and even funny at times despite being an interactive Novel. Unfortunately, NORCO has some shortcomings that detract from the overall experience. One of the most significant cons is that the game's story feels unfinished and incomplete. The player is left with many unanswered questions, which can be frustrating. Additionally, some parts of the gameplay, such as the fights are not engaging enough and can become tedious.In summary, NORCO is a game with a unique approach to storytelling that is sure to appeal to fans of the graphic novel genre. While the game has many strengths, it also has several weaknesses that keep it from achieving its full potential. I would still recommend it because it felt pretty unique and had a lot of great ideas. You just have to play it knowing that not everything will be explained.
_childDocuments_.name: NORCO

_childDocuments_.review: When I was young, I wrote a lot of very bad songs that I thought were very deep and meaningful and serious. Mostly they were just shoddy assemblies of genre cliches and tropes. That's the vibe I get from this game. My problem isn't with the concept, to be sure. I really enjoyed Kentucky Route Zero, for instance, a game that Norco desperately wants to be. But this just ain't it. This doesn't feel real or substantial or earned. It feels like a costume being tried on, or a fake accent, or an awkward poem scribbled on the outside of a math notebook. I've read a lot about the "great writing" in Norco and I'm at a loss to understand what I'm missing. What I experienced ultimately has the styling and energy of a Thought Catalog essay, or a bad personal zine written by a teenager in the 1990's.I guess I appreciate the aspirations at work here, but I don't think any of it lands. Obviously, the story and the writing are intended to be the stars of the show, but they're creaking under the weight of pretension. All of the text feels cloying and pandery and a little too eager to be Very Meaningful in a way that the author doesn't seem capable of achieving. And the Crass sticker in the character's childhood bedroom made me groan out loud. Skip this.
_childDocuments_.name: NORCO

_childDocuments_.review: This game has some gorgeous writing and visuals, but the ending has left me at a loss. Think if the original Neon Genesis Evangelion was a thriller set in rural Louisiana.The ending just kinda peters out, leaving too many threads unresolved, too many characters dropped without a completed arc, and no catharsis. I feel like the game was just one last, load-bearing scene away from a 10/10, auto-recommend, but instead it sorta leaves you hanging.I'm still recommending this game, because a lot of its ideas and mechanics are incredible and ones I hope to see in future narrative games. Not to mention the incredible pieces of pixel art that made me legit disappointed whenever I only got to spend a few seconds with a cutscene background (might buy the artbook just for that). I also loved the incorporation of rural working class culture, touching on topics of climate collapse, labor exploitation, and late-stage capitalism.Despite my gripes, it's a beautiful experience, and I want to leave this with a huge thank you to the devs for sharing this weird and wonderful little fever dream.

_childDocuments_.review: NORCO is a pretty solid visual novel in the style of old console VNs like SNATCHER or The Silver Case, where there are semi-point and click segments in addition to the walls of text. I've gotten I think a little more than halfway through the game and haven't gotten to any points where I felt outright bored, though there were a few parts that I felt kinda dragged a little. I think my one complaint about this game is that the UI isn't always the best. There's a part halfway through the game or so where you get a voice recorder that you use by clicking a tiny red button underneath text in a dialog window. The problem is that left-clicking is also the "advance the text and/or close the dialog window" button, and a couple of times I wound up accidentally clicking out of dialog that I wanted to read because I saw something that I wanted to record. Actually, there is a second thing. The game is ostensibly a cyberpunk story along the lines of SNATCHER or Policenauts, but it doesn't feel like one for the vast majority of the plot. The setting for the most part is present-day Louisiana, and apart from a couple of things (namely humanoid robots and AIs) it doesn't really feel cyberpunk in the way that the old Kojima VNs did. It also doesn't necessarily get its setting across or do worldbuilding as well as a game like Disco Elysium - NORCO takes place in what is effectively a low grade post-apocalypse, but unless you're reading a bunch of optional material you'd have no idea this is the case. I almost feel like it would have benefitted by taking some inspiration from Policenauts - namely the Saturn version - and having a glossary or something you can access to sort of explain things along better than it does.Even with the writing issues, NORCO is still a solid VN and I'd absolutely recommend it.

_childDocuments_.review: Kentucky Route Zero by way of Monkey Island, with a dash of Disco Elysium.---EDIT: Having completed the game, I feel the need to provide a counterpoint to some other reviews which expressed dissatisfaction with the Third Act of the game. While subjective personal experience is certainly important, especially for a game as abstract and interpretive as NORCO, it's also just that -- subjective. I loved the final act of the game. It genuinely brought me to tears. It also made me call my mom.NORCO's greatest strength is its utterly unique Industrial Surrealist / Southern Gothic atmosphere, held together by evocative pixel art, gripping prose, moody soundtrack, and singularly melancholic worldbuilding. NORCO's First Act feels magical in part because you're experiencing all these elements for the first time, and the world is still being constructed around you such that you genuinely don't know what to expect next.From this perspective, it's understandable to feel like the Second and/or Third acts are disappointing, because at some point NORCO becomes more than an abstract tone poem and instead consolidates its setting and characters into a discrete plot. Compared to the infinitude of possible stories that could have branched out after Act One, it's easy to see how some people may find the specific story told to be disappointing compared to What Could Have Been. However, I don't think it's fair to take this as a mark against NORCO -- if anything, it's a testament to the creators that the world they've created is so vibrant and resonant that the specific story they tell seems to pale in comparison.Kentucky Route Zero manages this dynamic in part by remaining abstracted above any singular plot or character arc. Every Act and Intermission feels like an isolated vignette; there's an ensemble cast of perspective characters and no clear protagonist; the ostensible 'goal' of the game (to travel the Zero to deliver a package) falls by the wayside almost immediately and is practically a MacGuffin, a contrivance to motivate the player's continued engagement with KRZ's world. This isn't a complaint about KRZ, which is a phenomenal piece of work that I pretty clearly love, but as an experience it's definitely more "art" than "game".By comparison, NORCO is a much more "traditional" adventure game: you (mostly) play as a single perspective character throughout, the mechanics and presentation of the game remain fairly consistent, and there are fairly clear goals and antagonists (though you have a bit of freedom to decide what matters to your character, which may influence which forces you perceive as antagonistic). The game lays down a lot of cards in Act One and doesn't pick all of them up by the finale, but on the whole I was satisfied with the story it told. The characters and events that set the game's plot into motion are interwoven somewhat densely, and if you're not paying attention throughout it's more likely you'll come away feeling like some plot threads were left hanging. Once again, though, the aesthetic is the star of the show here. If you like the *feel* of NORCO, the plot is really just an excuse to keep hanging around its world.Judging by the liner notes (yes, this is the kind of the game that has liner notes), a lot of disparate people contributed to this game, but it only came together because of the vision and labor of a comparatively small number of people. Frankly, it's a miracle it exists at all, and you should buy it to help ensure there will be more games like it in the future.

_childDocuments_.review: Beautifully written and scored with visuals to match. The game is hilarious and very moving. The developers have woven a world of AI, cybernetics, the occult, sleazy P.I.s, hobo prophets, alligators, cryptids, cats with jet thrusters in they ♥♥♥♥♥♥ asses and a very cute monkey, draped in a veil of southern gothic against a backdrop of the very real ways in which the Shell corporation has destroyed, and is continuing to destroy, lives and communities in coastal Louisiana. Being poor is a ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ death sentence and Norco makes clear a large factor contributing to that reality. But none of this takes away from a deeply felt family saga; the sci-fi and the occult and the magic-realism, that's all just the trappings of this game. Norco doesn't simply say that capital has gouged our world, destroyed our community and killed our loved ones; it expresses how that feels. There is an undeniable atmosphere to this game's tapestry, its thick and vivid, a sense of longing, aching loss and tiredness. In the end its the little things you remember, the minutiae, small things you wish you could've said, pauses you wish you had acted on, trivial moments which in hindsight you wish you could stretch out for a millennia. And how it feels to lose them, and how it feels to live in the shadow of what took them from you, to have to breath it in every day, as it blots out the sun.

_childDocuments_.review: Mad. Just mad.Incredible art style, and really well written - reads like a mixture of True Detective's Rust Cohle's internal thoughts, Disco Elysium, and Stanislaw Lem.Devs crafted this lovingly. _childDocuments_.review: Beyond its poetry and entrancing pixel-scapes, Norco has a powerful, magical pull that I have felt from the other side (of the planet). I saw so much of myself in its people and I saw so many parallels between Norco, Louisiana and my own hometown. There is universality in places like these - towns ruined by corporate greed, corruption and natural disaster.  After ruin and tragedy, there is poverty, homelessness, gentrification, catastrofitti, hopelessness, list goes on, but there is also people trying to cope and to fight. Norco gets this more than right and this aspect is something I've related to the most. Though it's seemingly sombre and bleak, it's full of heart. Through everything you experience playing this game, you can feel the love the developers have put in it. It's really intimate.There's an odd sense of comfort behind everything Norco tackles and shows, behind the fact that a story like this can exist and be so magical. I'm hoping we'll see more of stories like this in the future. I hope my town will get a similar treatment one day. I'm thankful to have learned about a place like Norco through this game. I'm thankful to have met the wonderful people behind this landmark piece of art. And I'm so excited to see what's next for Geography of Robots.

_childDocuments_.review: As others have mentioned, it's a game that desperately wants to be the next Kentucky Route Zero, yet it doesn't understand what made that game so powerful. Norco's biggest flaw, as with many fantasies and SCFY stories, is it's a well-developed world without characters (It's one of the reasons those genres are so hard). Instead of letting the story happen naturally and showing growth, it just tells you what happens and what to make of certain aspects of the world and narrative. There isn't the ambiguity and the multilayered depth of KRZ, and exposition and overly explanatory dialogue trees lack the focus of KRZ's innovative approach to players making the script as they go, rather than choices matter twine based design.Its got some great industrial backgrounds, but some interiors are severely lacking, and it has a habit of shoving obvious symbolism in your face to imply its depth. I'm honestly bewildered by the reviews. I was expecting another point-and-click masterpiece and ended up rather disappointed. It's far from bad just don't expect anything revolutionary beyond an interesting concept. I liked features like the mind map, which helps to organically put together narrative information and the mystery of Norco, and I think with another game or writer, the dev could make something great. I don't know, the writing has a very first draft feel and definitely had the potential to be excellent with some more time. Check out Backbone or KRZ if you want some better diselpunkish noir mystery point and clicks.

_childDocuments_.review: I'm not from the American South so I can't personally relate to the setting as much as some folks, but Norco's writing and atmosphere are very good. The pixel art and look is decidedly low tech but provide a unique experience, and the character portraits are very expressive. Gameplay wise, Norco is a simplistic adventure game with simple verbs, item use, and companions that deliver some hints. There are battles but the tactics are very simple, and they're usually a bump in the road more than anything. Buy this game if you like dystopian, surreal narrative games with a heavy helping of social commentary. My only complaint is that the way things wrap up felt abrupt, even as Norco doesn't outstay its welcome. The narrative is more about a creating a feeling than trying to explain itself clearly. Compared to a game like Disco Elysium the characters and plot feel cryptic. On the other hand, Kentucky Route Zero (which I enjoyed for different reasons) is much more highbrow and abstract.  A final note: The soundtrack is very good. I don't think I'd listen to it outside the context of the game, but it sets the tone perfectly.

_childDocuments_.review: Visually lush and tonally evocative, Norco fails to stick the landing in ways that undermine the rest of the game retroactively. That is, the *plot* of the game resolves well enough — you figure out what happened and why by the end — but the emotional arc is muted almost to the point of nonexistence. There's no epiphany or catharsis, no moment when the disorientation and alienation of the game's terse, poetical style and worldbuilding suddenly coheres into something meaningful or moving. The recent genre touchpoints are Disco Elysium and Kentucky Route Zero, but both of those games were *deeply* invested in the emotional realities of their protagonists, even if the presentation was fractured, elusive, and allegorical. Norco establishes some potent tensions between family, place, and legacy, and then doesn't actually *do* anything with that setup.It's a game well worth playing — the presentation and moment to moment writing are both phenomenal — but it never becomes more than the sum of its parts, unfortunately.

_childDocuments_.review: I will not forget this game's story for as long as I live.Kay's search for her brother through Norco, Louisiana, employs magical realism, mystery and noir elements, environmental and religious themes that keep you intrigued throughout the game's entire runtime.  The game's plot elements are explained masterfully by the time the credits roll, but its broader themes are left to your interpretation.  I've read the other reviews, and they all say "this game means *insert message here*.  And there are so many interpretations. I think most of them are totally correct, this game just says a lot, about a lot, and it's all packaged in this deeply personal mystery. There are so many striking interactions in this game, and it feels like it warrants genuine critical analysis to properly interpret what all the characters/factions represent.  It's like reading an American literary classic but with really sick pictures.This game is steeped in Americana.  From the descriptions of the roads, cities and swamps, to the vividly drawn subcultures of people, the world feels believable, even despite its sci-fi and ambiguously magical elements.  The way the game always keeps one foot firmly in reality, allows you to connect deeply with its characters.  The believable backbone is what this entire story hinges on.  If this world didn't feel so acutely like our own, the stranger turns of the plot would feel like regular sci-fi/fantasy.  Instead, we feel ourselves embroiled in a conspiracy, learning things that we feel we shouldn't, a mystery that somehow confirms the worst of our modern day existential struggles, while offering us small but hopeful avenues to a better future.I think this game is a masterpiece, it's so ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ good.  Bruh.

_childDocuments_.review: Come for the vengeful alligator spirits and shopping mall cultists, stay for the gorgeous pixel art and brilliant writing!NORCO is a point-and-click adventure game set in the cursed bayous and oil refineries that lie outside of New Orleans. Kay returns to her hometown Norco after the death of her mother and disappearance of her brother—throughout the game you switch between Kay's perspective and her mother Catherine's. It's not wrong to describe it as a dystopian sci-fi story, but I think that it might be more appropriate to describe it as a haunted and magical realist parallel universe. It's a game that is both deeply gloomy and funny. It has a strong sense of place, developed largely through the lovingly rendered pixel art environment, but also through the top-notch writing and sound design. The characters and environments you interact with generally feel grounded and real, until the game confronts you with well-crafted moments of rupture and subversion. The game is worth playing for the story alone, but the design of the environment makes it an experience to savor.The game mechanics primarily unfold through dialogue and interacting with items in the environment, although there is also a pretty nifty "mind map" in which you can refresh your memory or further ponder narrative events as they unfold. The only quibble I had with this game was with a few of the mini-games—specifically the boating and QTE-style combat encounters. I found this part of the game experience to be frustrating and it felt like a prolonged distraction from the story and writing elements that drew me in. Part of this is that I was playing the game with a set-up that wasn't particularly well optimized for fine mouse control, so it's possible that these would be less frustrating with a decent mouse. Also, to the developer's credit, I never got a game over in these mini-games (despite feeling like I was close to one every single time).

_childDocuments_.review: I'd recommend this game if you are a Disco Elysium fan who wants a little more of that vibe. Both games have very similar themes, narration, and art direction.I felt overall underwhelmed by what the game seemed to promise; the scope of the story was all at once too grand and not grand enough, and the conclusion ultimately felt unsatisfactory. There were perhaps too many bizarre and absurd elements in the world to make it believable or cohesive, and the half made attempts at social commentary and odd humor didn't aid in that. its fine for what it is, but I can't help but feel that this developer is capable of greater things.

_childDocuments_.review: NORCO is a Southern Gothic point & click narrative adventure that immerses the player in the sinking suburbs and verdant industrial swamps of a distorted South Louisiana. Your brother Blake has gone missing in the aftermath of your mother's death. In the hopes of finding him, you must follow a fugitive security android through the refineries, strip malls, and drainage ditches of suburban New Orleans.

name: Detroit: Become Human
detailed_description: Detroit: Become Human , the award-winning video game production from Quantic Dream , is finally available on Steam! Featuring world-renowned actors including Jesse Williams (Grey’s Anatomy), Clancy Brown (Carnivale), Lance Henriksen (Aliens), Bryan Dechart (True Blood) and Valorie Curry (Twilight). WHAT MAKES US HUMAN? Detroit 2038. Technology has evolved to a point where human like androids are everywhere. They speak, move and behave like human beings, but they are only machines serving humans. Play three distinct androids and see a world at the brink of chaos – perhaps our future - through their eyes. Your very decisions will dramatically alter how the game’s intense, branching narrative plays out. You will face moral dilemmas and decide who lives or dies. With thousands of choices and dozens of possible endings, how will you affect the future of Detroit and humanity’s destiny? PLAY YOUR PART IN A GRIPPING NARRATIVE Enter a world where moral dilemmas and difficult decisions can turn android slaves into world-changing revolutionaries. Discover what it means to be human from the perspective of an outsider – and see the world through the eyes of a machine. THEIR LIVES, YOUR CHOICES Shape an ambitious branching narrative, where your decisions not only determine the fate of the three main characters, but that of the entire city of Detroit. How you control Kara, Connor and Markus can mean life or death – and if one of them pays the ultimate price, the story still continues… COUNTLESS PATHS, COUNTLESS ENDINGS Every decision you make, no matter how minute, affects the outcome of the story. No playthrough will be exactly the same: replay again and again to discover a totally different conclusion. FULLY OPTIMIZED FOR PC Detroit: Become Human is brought to PC with stunning graphics, 4K resolution, 60 fps framerate and full integration of both mouse/keyboard and gamepad controls for the most complete Detroit: Become Human experience to date.

Every choice you make affects the outcome of the game, with one of the most intricately branching narratives ever created.

_childDocuments_.review: Superior to Fahrenheit and Heavy Rain in every way. The game is carried by amazing cast and I absolutely loved different gameplay sequences that cater to the context and the sorry. Clues gathering, action sequences branching simulation and social engineering are the best out of all Quantic Dream roster. Kamski is back right after resigning from Blume in Watch Dogs 2, which is also a great thing, to see the return of this character. One single jumpscare in the game, and it sucked.With the good out of the way, something needs to be said about the way the plot is written.The game is ridden with superfluous plot twists, contrived events and comedically obtuse bad characters that all exist just to advance the plot. Numerous times, with Todd, Zlatko, sometimes Alice, they are wearing their mind on their sleeve and they go on to express audibly how frustrated they are with this world, and they all deliberately go out to claim that there is no escape, that they themselves are to blame, that everything is done beyond repair. And it made me angry many times, that I as Kara, am not capable of soothing of any of their rants just for the sake of the characters developing into something that will drive the plot, and I'm sitting there with an answer to every single one of their questions, and boiling, how deliberately stupid and uncontrolled they are.Why did Todd and Zlatko not just buy an android that would have a function of a psychologist?Why Carl's son also happen to be at the cemetery at the same moment as Marcus?Why did a police man come to Rose and Adam house exactly the moment when Rose was out?Why did somebody make a noise upstairs knowing that a policeman was on the ground floor? This one, made me scream at the top of my lungs like "GUYS CAN YOU STFU REAL QUICK IN THERE?"Why did Alice ask "What will happen of their family and their baby" at the end? They're supposed to be humans, nothing really endangers them, they'll just go back home...

_childDocuments_.review: Like any story driven game I've played before, I don't load this game for the game-play, as the story and the way it's presented carries the game for me.- quick-time events a large part of game play and at times feels repetitive.- long, unskipable / unquitable shader loading on first launch of game that you are not warned about prior.+ story that while initially somewhat predictable, becomes more immersive and in depth as you progress.+ interesting and engaging flowchart system, showing mission/level progression with options to see what others chose/did.Easy recommend for those who like story-focused games.

_childDocuments_.review: I love the story. _childDocuments_.review: Absolutely the greatest and most in depth game I have ever played. I knew most of the scenes from when I watched people play through the game and it still has blown me out of the water. This game is the one game that I can sincerely say that there are little to literal no complaints as far as game play and menu display goes.The face that there are so many unique choices that can determine your outcome is plain amazing, I do in fact know that there are story game that may be like this but this game takes those similar and just run away with it making even the earliest choices that you make determine how not only the character thinks but also how the game will steer you towards the choices. One of the things that unexpectedly blew me away was the menu. The android in the menu not only interacts with you but also gives you something to think about and will progress with its thinking throughout your gameplay. The only downside I do have with this game is the fact that most big choices that you have to make have one word descriptions that make it hard to decipher which is best for your play through. And the only other complaint that I have is that at some scenes there isn't a way to skip a cutscene making your fun "what if's" just a bit annoying. Other than that I am absolutley blown away with this game and it will be among one of the greatest games I've played.

_childDocuments_.review: This game is amazing. It is the Magnum Opus of the story driven games. I almost don't have a single bad thing to say. Story is amazing, acting is phenomenal, game play is interesting and fun. It took me 17 hours to beat it but it felt like a lot longer, A LOT! There is a ton of re-playability with this game too. I plan on doing another play through soon. I usually go way more in depth with my reviews but I really don't have to here. If you like story driven games this one is A MUST BUY! 10/10, 5 Stars, Two Thumbs Up, Certified Fresh, all that stuff! The only thing I did have an issue with was the fact that some of the button time segments are really hard on the advanced controls mode and the exact combo you are supposed to do can sometimes be very confusing on the PC. Like, the instruction they are displaying is not easy to interpret. Kind of annoying when you are being strangled or shot at or something. Otherwise I loved it. Give it a try, you won't be disappointed.

_childDocuments_.review: I can see the high reviews for how beautifully cinematic this game is. Absolutely stunning. The story line is fairly rich and well written, even with a lot of cliche buddy cop stuff. The voice acting is some of the best in a game and the audio in general is great.Now to what makes it an UNPLAYABLE MESSThe lack of camera is the worst I have ever seen in a game. Especially when most things are timed and you spend half the time trying to turn and look at what you want to see. It's unacceptable. I really enjoy the use of the left stick for actions but it is not worth the loss of basic camera functions. It feels like they tried so ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ hard to make every movement in the game so cinematic that they locked the camera to not show bad angles. Seriously. The the lack of dedicated buttons is an also unplayable feature. I enjoy telltale type games where it is story driven and the actions are small and not as time driven. In Detroit the fact that I shoot a gun with A half the time and B the other half, B is sometimes block and sometimes hit in melee, it leaves you just waiting for a stupid button to pop up instead of actually giving you the ability to anticipate through dedicated buttons. Next is the way many scenes are just completely cut off being able to walk between a bush and a person in areas where you should have the room. It's like the hit boxes for people are square and to large. I thoroughly enjoyed some parts of the game and it is stunning to look at. Otherwise it is just a frustrating mess to actually play. It feels like the developers tried to hit the line between an action FPS and a movie with controls like TWD series and they failed in both respects, IMO. I promise if the game was not so beautifully rendered no one would give it a good review. It is worth tolerating the bad gameplay for the story and visuals if you can buy it at a discount.

_childDocuments_.review: Attempted to play the game, which appeared to have potential - but the game just has too many issues.1.  Takes way too long for initial installation and setup.  After installation,  it should take seconds to start a game.   Half an hour for "shader compilation" is ridiculous.2.  The game is very unstable, and appears to have fairly high end requirements, including very specific graphic cards, which my 4 year old system doesn't have.3.   The interface is extremely clunky, and appears to be a shoddy port from an iphone style game.  If you're going to have a pc game, it needs to play like a pc game.4.    There doesn't appear to be any way to save progress in a scenario and resume from that point.  That is an absolute requirement for any adventure style game imo.

_childDocuments_.review: when a game say 'your choices matter' i always take that with a huge grain of salt but this i'm glad I didn't OD on sodium because they probably raised the bar for these types of games.  Yes the game is on a track to an end but you can easily get derailed and perma death some of your characters if you aren't careful.    While it does have some that "The Walking Dead" story mechanics, the game thankfully has more to offer than "Kenny will remember that" bs.   There was a choice I made from the very start that affected an ending and I'm still blown away that it even remembered  Even after getting 100% of the achievements there is still a lot of story content I have yet to unlock.    The story is really good and the bromance between Connor and Hank is absolutely hilarious.  Visually the game looks amazing, so amazing in fact that it might not run on your machine.   Now I haven't experienced any of the issues people have brought up in the forums so download the demo and if you can run it on your machine, you can feel safe that it might work for the full game.

_childDocuments_.review: Great game, and better than Heavy Rain which for it's time was revolutionary.The story is incredible, if there's any complaints its that the action sequences can be a bit too unforgiving, i.e. you complete 10 out of 12 actions successfully but the two actions you miss may get you or someone killed. I would definitely buy Quantic Dream's next game based on my recent playthroughs of DBH.

_childDocuments_.review: The graphics were nice but some places were somehow empty and missed a lot of details. I had the same issue with "Beyond Two Souls". The first levels were really good with lot of details but then it just went down. But in Detroit Become Human it was still way better then in Beyond Two Souls. They did a lot of work with the faces. I liked it a lot.The controls are easy, just as you expect them to be in any 3rd person game. You move around, you analyze stuff and investigate. The investigation reminded me of the Sherlock Holmes games. It was quite interesting. But unluckely there were not as many scenes for analyzing stuff as I wanted to be. Quickevents are nice (played it on easy), so I had only to press A and B. Sometimes the quick events were ♥♥♥♥♥♥ up since you had to repeatedly press A and at the end B.There is a kind of slow mo feature which you can use to get interesting points shown in your surroundings. This is mostly used if you have to make fast decisions during gameplay. Reminds me of the pip-boy aiming in Fallout if you press "Q". The game does not stop, it just slows down hardcore.I played it on easy and it felt like that ... easy. Not comparable to Darkes Dungeon where the developers seemed to misinterprete the definition of "easy". I think it would be more interesting if more characters would have died.The game was quite good regarding the cringe level. Way better than Beyond Two Souls. What was really strange: the survey. I messed up during the answers ... but you have no possibilty to change your answers anymore. Really?I have to say that the storytelling is well done. The decisions fell good and it looks like they somehow change the outcome. The way it was shown and told: I liked. The idea itself is nothing new. Machines which develop consciousness. I don't believe in this ♥♥♥♥, so I played the cop "evil" and the trashbot was the "good" one. I also liked that it was not that easy to increase relationships between the characters. I totally ♥♥♥♥♥♥ up between robo-cop and human-cop. But it played well for my story, so I kept it. But what I really didn't like was this ♥♥♥♥ here:  ... this was the worst part and for me it ruined a lot ... I was about to let them all die.In the end I sang a song and everything was fine. Except .Also the main face in the start menu was disappointed by me and let her "go". I think, I did a good job hating the machines.Bye

_childDocuments_.review: Let us be realistic, the fact that the technology is advanced enough to create androids look like human does not mean all of them have to be exactly like human. They can be much smaller, much bigger,  they can have more than 2 arms or no arm. There are so many possibilities. But there is little creativity or imagination in Detroit, the androids have to be EXACTLY like human, even the androids do the road construction use shovels! I guess CYBERLIFE's next business plans would be replacing all the cars with androids carrying people around, and replacing all the washing machines with androids hand washing your underwear. Not surprisingly, the robotic birds and bear in the story have no intelligence, not to mention all the  autonomous cars and drones. Having the drone to utter something like "I am alive" when Marcus broke it can make a powerful scene, but that did not happen in Detroit, must violates some sacred laws of the universe, besides inconvenient  to copy and paste what happened in the concentration camps and during segregation era for the story. I have to say I am disappointed with this game, android is such a great topic and many amazing stories have been created, but Detroit sacrificed all that potential for a shallow moral lecture.

_childDocuments_.review: Rating: ▰▰▰▰▰▰▰▰▰▱ Absolutely phenomenal game, even on a second playthrough. “Detroit: Become Human” is one of the  few games that take the  phrase seriously . This game has many branches to a chapter and many possible routes, most of which  on future outcomes/decisions. Meanwhile Telltale and many other choices matter stories just ask you what fruit you'd prefer, apples or oranges, and give you apples regardless of the choice.Story-wise, there are many paths and endings you can take, most of which are generally pretty interesting to watch. You will follow 3 main characters: . Connor's and Markus' stories are always interesting to play. As Connor, you play as a detective trying to solve murder cases and find clues to the cause of deviants. While as Markus, you play as the leader of androids and work towards  for androids. Both of these characters have such a captivating story and the many different outcomes you can take are really interesting to see. The same unfortunately can't be said for Kara's story. In her story, you play as a mother figure looking after a child, her story has a heavy emphasis on the importance of family. While Kara's story has its moments, it's still  compared to Connor and Markus' stories, some even find her story to be a chore to play. As previously mentioned, this game has an incredible amount of branches and paths to take. The focal point of this game is the choices you make, and how they impact your story. In some cases, things you do in one character's playthrough . This game is also quite unforgiving, aside from Connor, if you mess up and your character dies early, , the story continues with or without that character. And although Connor is pretty much immortal, there are still consequences for dying too many times as him and/or failing his investigations. And if you go down a path you don't like, that's the path you have to follow through with. Either that or restart from an early save point and retry everything again. The sheer amount of paths and choices in “Detroit: Become Human” naturally gives it an incredible amount of replay value, making sure you really get your money's worth.The gameplay consists of mostly walking from one point and another, talking to characters, scanning and solving puzzles, and QTEs. It plays more of like an interactive movie rather than a game, despite that, I would still encourage you to play this game instead of watching a playthrough on YouTube as it is still a much better experience. This game is also accompanied by , with . The game also has a convincing crowd AI, giving life to the bustling city of Detroit and adds to the immersion as you walk along the streets.To top it all off, “Detroit: Becomes Human” has an impeccable OST, the music in Connor's parts are , being able to immediately set the mood and give off this badass vibe to it every time. Each character's themes also fit really well, Connor, as mentioned, has a cool badass theme. Markus' theme has a heroic and somber feel. Kara's theme sounds gentle and soft. All themes reflecting the stories and experiences the characters will go through. The overall background OSTs are also fitting and nice to listen to. - “Detroit: Become Human” is a really immersive story-rich game that follows 3 characters, Connor, Markus, and Kara, all of which have many important choices that affect future outcomes. It's a game that delivers a great story with interactive gameplay, beautiful graphics, and has an amazing score peppered over it. A definite must play.

_childDocuments_.review: TL;DR Definitely a 9/10 gameThe first thing you notice in this game - Just how amazing this game looks!Even though the game originally came out in 2018, it still is one of the best looking games out there.Maybe it got some graphics upgrade when it was released for PS5 or on PC.But the animations look crazy good. Especially face animations.Now playing the game itself, is like watching an amazingly well done sci-fi show.From the first few missions, when you first start to discover the characters and stories - you're just drawn-in, and can't wait to discover where the story goes next.What makes it so great, is beyond being a Sci-fi story, it's also one that is alarmingly close to our reality (especially in 2023, with the advances in AI in recent years and even months).Similar to shows like Incorporated, Handmaid's tale or Upload - you feel that the world in the game/show, could easily be our world in a few years.It all just feels so seamlessly real... The game-style is similar to Quantic Dream's previous games, and similar to Telltale games - a choice matters game.At every step of the way you choose how the characters will react - and the story progresses accordingly.At the end of each level, you're shown the choices you took, the choices you didn't take, and even percentage of people who made the same choices. Like in a Telltale game.What's especially good point in Detroit Become Human - is you can easily replay each part of the chapter you finished, and discover other paths and where they lead. And can choose to change your choices accordingly, or keep them as you chose.It's a really great option, if you're a completionist, or just want to check other options before you continue.The game apparently also remains as popular as it was 3 years ago, when it first entered Steam.In most games you would see huge numbers of reviews in the first 1-2 months after release.And then drop significantly, and keep reducing over time (with jumps in case of deep discounts or freebies).But Detroit Become Human has strong consistent reviews almost every month for the past 3 years. On part with the month it was released.Which shows how good of a game it really is.Unfortunately, as much as I would like it to be - the game is not perfect.And has some negative sides as well.There are occasional crashes. Although very rare, and the frequent auto-saves/checkpoints make sure you don't miss much.But there is also an issue with the story.The story starts amazingly well. The pacing, the backstory, the dialogs - all work.And it ends pretty good as well. Not as amazing as the beginning. But still, pretty good.But at some point, towards the second half of the game, the story just becomes too drawn out.Out get the feeling the writers wanted the game to last X hours instead of Y (which is less), so they started filling it with fluff.Story arcs that don't progress the plot.Prolonged cutscenes where nothing happens.Action sequences that have you click on buttons at correct time frames - but don't add anything to the story.And that's a real shame - as it ruins a near perfect game.Developers should know - sometimes less is more.It's better to have a short game, with perfect pacing.Than a longer game (with more bang-for-your-buck) that just become boring.

It’s about living with the consequences, good or bad. That’s where the game shines: it forces you to reflect on what freedom, morality, and humanity really mean. Each character shows a different side of what it means to want more out of life. The story isn’t perfect, but that’s what makes it feel so real. Life isn’t perfect either.If you’ve ever wanted a game to challenge you emotionally and philosophically, this is it. Just don’t overthink it—go in blind, make your choices, and see where the story takes you.It’s more than a game. It’s an experience!!11/10

_childDocuments_.review: If machines became intelligent and with reasoning similar to humans, what would separate them from us? Isaac Asimov already addressed the topic in “I, Robot” with the three Laws of Robotics, Philip K. D1ck got into the subject in “Do Androids Dream of Electric Sheep?” (and spawned the movie Blade Runner), HBO addressed this in its retelling of "Westworld" and even "Ghost in the Shell" touches on the subject from a different point of view. Now, Quantic Dream's David Cage ventures into the topic with The game by  is practically a successor to  in terms of gameplay and choices, impressing in multiple aspects, whether in the well-tangled story, in the jaw-dropping graphics or the option of going back and redoing everything differently, shaping a narrative that is extremely flexible to the player's actions.In Detroit: Become Human, we follow the story of three different androids in the year 2038. Connor is a hunter of deviants, androids who are becoming aware and acting differently than expected, and who becomes partner with a police officer who hates machines; Kara is an android responsible for taking care of Alice, a girl who was abused by her drugged father; and finally we have Markus, the leader of the rebel machines insurgency.During the narrative of more than 15 hours, Quantic Dream takes us on a journey filled with memorable and dramatic moments that make us connect with the characters. Really connect. As far as the protagonists are concerned, they all have a spectacular story in different aspects. Kara shows a human and more maternal side, Connor is calculating and completely moldable to the player's actions and Marcus is full of morality doubts that affect us during the progression.I felt driven to protect Alice with Kara, to give the androids a voice and justice with Markus, and at the same time hunt them down with Connor, finding out along the way what to think about it all. Gradually, each one's story spreads out like a network and connects, creating something bigger that joins global events.One of the downsides that  and even  had was the slow pace at first.  does have character introduction chapters, but they are interesting and insert the player into the futuristic context of 2038 or help contextualize the protagonists' relationship with humans.You'll have at most one or two short chapters before the plot takes off for good, and from there, you won't have any dull moments or uninteresting bits. Despite having about 15 hours into the campaign, Detroit doesn't lose momentum at any time. When there are slower sessions, they are interspersed with more hectic sessions by another protagonist.It's no secret that David Cage increasingly aims to create adventures that take into account the choices made by the player to shape a more organic plot. Heavy Rain had that purpose, but it hit it a little shallower than it promised (the end was most important, not the journey). Detroit: Become Human doesn't achieve this unreachable goal of near-infinite paths, but it's a giant leap from its predecessor (we won't consider Beyond here because the footprint was different). is not a short game, which was one of the biggest concerns. It will take you around 15-20 hours to complete it, 20-25 hours to platinum it, and a much longer count to see everything it has to offer. The replay factor is very high, the decisions really impact the plot, the immersion is great and the graphics are one of the best of the generation. Of course, the plot is not the most amazing there is, but the characters and the city are very well constructed and the performances are convincing, impressive and moving.No, the game is not revolutionary and yes, it can fit the nickname of “film games”. But the narrative content found here is of the highest quality. In the end, the game is indeed made for a niche, but that doesn't reduce the genius elements employed. In this dish made, the only seasoning that is missing is a more evolved gameplay that comes out of the shadow of  but the lack of it is far from spoiling the exotic flavor.Interactive dramas are not for everyone. What ends up differentiating the game is its huge amount of choices that impact the narrative, ensuring a very large replay. In the end, the summary of the opera is the following: if you like  and games of the genre,  is the best there is and will certainly leave your mark on the generation and wall of quality works by ☉ Cohesive and very well done story that addresses a very interesting topic☉ First class presentation with very detailed background and amazing analogies☉ The characters are excellent and it really takes us in a plot capable of creating bonds☉ Decisions really matter and can change or bring new content to your experience☉ Some chapters are so varied that they are scary☉ Relatively long campaign for a single player game with very high replay factor☉ First-rate acting and great voice acting☉ One of the best looks the PlayStation 4 has had to date (and now on PCs)☉ Completely dubbed in PT-BR☉ Gameplay still follows the  formula and doesn't innovate (and the movement controls are still painful)☉ There are small plot holes and “magic solutions” in the plot☉ Some chapters can be quite linear☉ There is certainly a predetermined path with little room for error in the plot (could be more random and risky)
