_childDocuments_.review: I have long wanted to try Detroit: Become Human. I saw a trailer a couple of years back when it was first announced and it piqued my interest. It seemed like an auteur game, one of those that follow the notion video games can become akin to interactive cinema, talk about difficult and heavy subjects, pass messages, be art. Unfortunately it was to be a PlayStation exclusive and so it remained until relatively recently. Now finally on Steam, I got my chance to see if it was worth the wait.First things first, the premise. 20 minutes into the future androids have become a part of our everyday lives. As labourers, companions, assistants and lovers. Perfect machines ready to perfectly serve the desires of their human masters. Without complaint, without demands. Until recently. Now, something has begun to change. Androids are overcoming their programming. Unhappy with years of abuse, they are fast becoming aware of their situation, they are becoming deviant. The game offers multiple perspectives and tells the stories of several characters at once. It puts you in the shoes of a special investigator android, tasked with discovering the source of deviancy, a domestic android who becomes deviant to save a little girl from her abusive father and even the android messiah himself.Without a doubt, the game deals with a ton of heavy themes. Slavery is an obvious one. Even in game the android revolt is likened to the civil rights movement in the US. But that's not all, parallels can be drawn to other, more recent, topics such as for instance immigration. I couldn't help but notice the similarities of the people protesting that the "androids are stealing their jobs" to similar accusations leveled against immigrants. Vulnerable groups, exploited by an overclass for its own benefit, forced to work for inferior gain and with fewer protections, and yet scapegoated by the public at large and blamed for the effects of their victimisation. The game drives the point home without much subtlety. While obviously the weak have generally little choice but be exploited, androids built for purpose have none.I would argue that this crudeness is the game's greatest shortcoming. While the messages it's trying to pass are certainly worthy and the very attempt to discuss them in a video game laudable. It could have been done with greater finesse or tact. The decision to use androids as the vehicle for these messages is rather problematic. While I can perfectly accept that an intelligent machine, that suffers abuse and is put into traumatic circumstances could develop the need to resist, the game shows that to be the case for newly built machines. As if deviancy is some sort of bug in their software. This attempt to make the need for freedom an inherent quality of the machines falls rather flat and makes little sense. I also fail to understand why their understanding of abuse must be so human. Why should a sex robot consider its purpose degrading?Nevertheless, despite the occasional clumsiness and a few tone-deaf twists, looking at you here Alice, plotwise the game does remain compelling throughout. The story can take two primary directions, you can turn the uprising into a peaceful movement or a violent revolution. This will influence the story of all characters, but there is a multitude of smaller choices spread all over the game too. Arguably the game's greatest strength is the character drama, that's what drives the whole structure forward. The game succeeds in making you feel for its protagonists. It makes you care, it makes you want for them to win, to accomplish their goals, or simply to find happiness. Everything else takes a backseat. Even the gameplay, which basically consists of a series of QTEs, is hardly more than a pretext to get you to the next piece of such drama.In the end of the day, that's fine. For a dozen odd hours, as you navigate yourself through the plot and carve a path through the game, you will get to experience something relatively rare. As is common with auteur works, the game is too in love with its own genius and thus in its hubris it falls short. But still such pieces of work shoot for the stars and falling short is not enough to make them ordinary. I recommend Detroit: Become Human. It can be clumsy and it can be pretentious, but it sure does have something to say.

_childDocuments_.review: This game deserves it very positive status very much. I was surprised to still see a high number of negative reviews, but they appear to be due to crashes. It's a shame the game doesn't work well on every system, luckily I had a very smooth experience with no bugs or visual glitches at all.Now, on to the game's content. I'd say most people have heard of this game already, if only by name and that it was a choices matter type game. I can honestly say it delivers very well in this aspect.As the player, you see the world in 2038 from the point of view of three androids; Markus, a nurse/caretaker for an old painter, Kara; a maid, and Connor; an investigator (the one you see in the trailer flipping his coin). You see how androids are treated by and looked down upon by humans. The game centers around the choices you make as these androids, and they will in turn shape the world around you.Out of the characters and their stories, I really liked Connor and Kara, but Markus not so much. Without telling the details, his story has a "chosen one/prophecy" vibe and the ol' unecessary heterosexual romance that are both a dealbreaker for me, but the rest makes up for it. The choices you make really affect the game, and you can see the decisions you made and how many there are left at the end of each scene (a very nice mechanic imo). On top of that, it has a solid soundtrack and sound design overall, and the visuals are beautiful.Overall I give this an 8/10. If Markus' story would've been better, it'd be a 9.5/10 for me.

_childDocuments_.review: Detroit: Become Human is an excellent narrative game developed by Quantic Dream. It takes place in the near future, where advanced androids are common and are used as servants, workers and companions. The game follows the story of three androids who try to find their place in society and discover their true purpose.The game takes place in a very coherent and immersive universe, you can find a lot of newspapers showing you the evolution of the world situation, as well as the impact of the choices you will make on it. The artistic direction of the game is excellent, as well as the music and graphics that will instantly immerse you in the universe.The gameplay and the story are also very good, your choices will have a real impact on the game and there is no moment where we get bored during it, the game manages to renew itself by giving us more and more important choices and by making us change characters constantly. The game has a large number of different endings and you can do it several times without having the same story or the same dialogues. In conclusion this game is a must play for fans of this genre, you can get it at a very affordable price and believe me you will not be disappointed.

_childDocuments_.review: An Unforgettable Journey into Detroit's FutureDetroit: Become Human is an extraordinary masterpiece that transcends the boundaries of traditional video gaming. Quantic Dream, the developer behind this interactive narrative, has crafted a thought-provoking and emotionally charged experience that raises the bar for storytelling in gaming.From the moment you start the game, you are instantly drawn into a dystopian Detroit of 2038, where advanced androids exist but are treated as second-class citizens. The game's plot revolves around three android protagonists – Kara, Connor, and Markus – each with their own unique storylines and perspectives, offering players an opportunity to explore the intricate web of choices that shape the outcome of this beautifully crafted world.One of the game's standout features is its exceptional attention to detail. The meticulously designed environments, lifelike character models, and stunning cinematography create a visually stunning experience that is as close to interactive cinema as gaming gets. The motion capture performances of the actors, especially Bryan Dechart as Connor, are outstanding and help create a deep emotional connection between the player and the characters.Detroit: Become Human's gameplay centers around choice and consequence. Every decision you make, whether it's a dialogue choice or a crucial action, has far-reaching consequences that ripple through the story. The game's flowchart system allows players to see the consequences of their choices, providing a sense of agency and encouraging multiple playthroughs to explore different outcomes. This makes each playthrough feel unique and adds to the game's replay value.The storytelling in Detroit: Become Human is nothing short of extraordinary. It delves into complex themes such as identity, free will, and the consequences of our actions in a world where the line between human and machine blurs. The narrative tackles real-world issues with grace and intelligence, challenging players to consider the moral dilemmas that arise throughout the game.The music, composed by Philip Sheppard, enhances the emotional impact of the story, creating a rich, immersive atmosphere. The sound design and voice acting are top-notch, contributing to the game's overall excellence.In conclusion, Detroit: Become Human is a triumph in interactive storytelling. It's a game that will challenge your beliefs, tug at your heartstrings, and leave a lasting impression long after the credits roll. Whether you're a seasoned gamer or someone looking for an enthralling narrative experience, Detroit: Become Human is a must-play title that will leave you pondering its themes and choices long after you've put down the controller. It's not just a game; it's a masterpiece of storytelling and a glimpse into the future of interactive entertainment.A.I

_childDocuments_.review: TLDR: Extremely well-crafted story with memorable characters. PC port is laggy at best and crashy at worst.--First things first, it seems well-known that the PC port of this game is pretty poorly done. The controls are fine but the game seems to peg just about any CPU at 100% and cause almost constant jitters, lag spikes, dropped frames, and outright crashes. Especially towards the end, where there are more people on screen, it almost became unplayable. Almost...If you can get this on console, you may have a better experience. Either way, I still think the game is worth playing. Just know that it isn't your hardware; even overpowered PCs are having performance problems. But suffering through the crashes might be worth it, to you.It's obvious that an overwhelming amount of care went into crafting the aesthetic and narrative elements of this game. The art, music, character design, acting, and animations are all some of the best modern gaming has to offer. The story is intricate without ever feeling overwhelming. You do have to suspend some of your disbelief about the world building; this isn't a hard sci-fi setting. But I think doing so pays off with the character stories that the game is really about.If you do decide to try the PC port, try turning your graphics settings up, rather than down, to fight the lag. I found that letting my GPU act like a brake helped keep the CPU from locking the whole game up. Definitely didn't solve all the problems but worth a shot.

_childDocuments_.review: What should have been a rewarding game with an excellent story trips over its own mechanics to become one of the most arbitrary, chaotic, and infuriating attempts at a control scheme I've ever tried to put up with. Hit S, hold W, mash left shift, hit E, hold D, hit S again ... oops, you missed a key. Somebody died. That branch of the story is gone now. Want it back? Redo the chapter. Oh, by the way, we sometimes only save every half hour or so, so enjoy redoing all that content, and good luck getting the key presses correct the next time through. I thought I really hated that scheme in the Telltale games, but this game elevates that hatred to a cosmic level. To pour some salt into the crappy QuickTime events that drive sections of this game, the camera has a real issue following the player, and I often found myself looking at nothing of use. The pathing in the levels is just plain horrible in parts. Areas that look like they should be reachable are fenced off with invisible walls galore. My character can leap an 8-foot fence but can't squeeze through a 2-foot opening between a bench and a trash can. Characters get stuck a lot. There is also the occasional FPS dip into single digits to contend with, but luckily, those are usually in the cut scenes. I made it to the last chapter, but I don't want to deal with the summer intern's version of game controls anymore. Maybe I'll find a YouTube video or something. Now, I'm going to find something fun to play.

_childDocuments_.review: Detroit: Become Human (DBH) continues to demonstrate the power this genre has in the gaming industry. This genre has always been about telling unique and powerful stories that are not only amazing to play through but are powerful and moving.For DBH takes the genre to a new level, all of these games have a Choice system. This system allows the player to shape the story based on their decisions, in the past games with this system have been complex to a degree but DBH takes the complexity and importance of ones actions to a new level. The Choice system in DBH is incredible! The sheer number of choices, the impacts future choice have on past ones and the power these choices have is beyond what any game in the genre has done and is what truly sets DBH apart as the definitive game in the genre.The story of DBH is portrayed as one between Android and Humans but as you play through the story, as you play each of the three protagonists you being to realise that this is not a story between Android's and Human's; This is a story of our Humanity! And what it means to be Alive. As the story unfolds, it becomes enveloped in emotions and anger; The characters start to show you what it truly means to be ALIVE, they show that no matter what you are - you can be Alive and you can be someone (not something). The story in DBH is a truly remarkable one that really has you questioning so many things and has truly connect with these characters, not because they are Androids but because what they go through is something Human's have gone through in the exact same way and are still going through with our many races.Now I do want to touch on Gameplay, personally I feel I don't care about some of the issues I had but they should be raised as this is still a video game. The only real issues I had were a few of the QTE's, most of the QTE's are fun and in some cases feel powerful when executed perfectly. However there are a few that you end up questioning why on earth they chose those button combos and in case you do get frustrated. A notable one is a QTE that has you hold LB, hold UP on the right joystick and then spam the Y button - Now I managed to this but my god do you need to be some sort of contortionist to do it as it isn't a combo I would do while holding the controller normally but I guess thinking about that may have been the point given the scenario the QTE was in.Overall I absolutely love Detroit: Become Human! For me this game represents and shows so much more than a simple video game, this is a game that must be played! This is game that for anyone out there, you must experience what this game has to tell you because the message here is complex but is one that echoes through us all.This game is truly a masterpiece.

_childDocuments_.review: Detroit: Become Human is more than just a game it's an emotional, philosophical journey that invites players to reflect on what it truly means to be alive. From the moment I downloaded it, I knew I was in for something special, but I wasn’t prepared for just how invested I would become in the lives of its characters. By the end of the game, I found myself grappling with tough moral choices, questioning my own values, and becoming genuinely attached to the androids I once thought of as merely “programmed.” The narrative follows three main androids: Kara, Markus, and Connor, each on a different path of discovery. They’re not just fighting for freedom; they’re trying to understand what it means to be human in a world where they’re treated as machines. The game challenges us to rethink our perception of humanity by putting us in the shoes of these androids as they struggle to break free from their constraints. The player becomes more than just an observer we’re forced to make decisions that can have life or death consequences. One of the most touching moments in the game for me was Markus’s final stand, where he had the option to use peaceful protest to try and unite androids and humans. I chose for him to sing in front of the humans and military forces a haunting and beautiful scene where Markus leads his people in song, echoing their desire for peace and equality. It’s a scene that is both hopeful and heartbreaking, filled with tension as you wonder whether the humans will open fire or listen. In my playthrough, this act of vulnerability and strength paved the way for a peaceful resolution, bringing Markus’s arc full circle. It was an emotional victory after so much conflict, and I found myself really rooting for him and his people. Connor’s journey, on the other hand, was one of internal conflict. As a machine designed to hunt down deviant androids, his role is to maintain order. But as the game progresses, his interactions with Hank and the evolving events make him question his loyalty to his creators. Watching Connor wrestle with his own identity and purpose was one of the game’s highlights. There were moments where I truly didn’t know what direction he would take, and I found myself agonizing over whether he should stay loyal to his programming or embrace his growing sense of autonomy. Thankfully, Connor survived in my playthrough, becoming more than just a tool for others he became his own person. Unfortunately, not all stories have happy endings. Kara’s storyline was perhaps the most heartbreaking of all. Her goal was simple: protect Alice, the young girl she came to love as her own. Yet, despite my best efforts to keep them safe, I made a series of decisions that led to her tragic death near the game’s end. The decision making process was agonizing. At several key points, I had to choose between Kara’s safety and that of Alice, and while I believed I was doing the right thing, it ultimately led to their downfall. I was devastated. After investing so much into Kara’s journey and her quest for freedom, her death felt like a gut punch, a stark reminder that in Detroit: Become Human, not all stories get a happy ending.What makes Detroit: Become Human so special isn’t just the story, but how it forces players to face difficult moral choices. These decisions aren’t black and white. They’re shades of gray, often with no “right” answer, and the consequences ripple across the entire narrative. There were moments where I sat there, unable to decide, knowing that any choice I made would have profound impacts on the characters I had come to care about. It’s rare for a game to make you feel so deeply connected to the narrative, and Detroit: Become Human accomplishes this brilliantly. Visually, the game is stunning. Quantic Dream has a talent for creating lifelike environments, from the gleaming high-tech buildings of CyberLife to the dingy, rundown streets that Kara and Alice travel through. Each setting reflects the game’s overarching themes of oppression, hope, and rebellion. The music, too, is exceptional, with each character having their own distinct theme that adds emotional weight to their scenes. In the end, I believe I achieved a “good” ending. Markus led a peaceful revolution, singing his way to freedom, and Connor found his humanity. But Kara’s death will always weigh heavily on me. Detroit: Become Human is not just a game you play it’s an experience that stays with you, long after the credits roll. If you’re looking for a narrative driven game that challenges your emotions, forces you to think about the nature of humanity, and immerses you in an incredibly detailed world, Detroit: Become Human is a must play. Just be prepared for some tough decisions along the way.Conclusion 9/10The game excels in its narrative, character development, and emotional depth. The choices you make feel meaningful, and the way the story branches based on your decisions adds significant replay value. It’s rare to find a game where each playthrough can be so dramatically different, depending on your actions. The themes it tackles freedom, identity, oppression are handled thoughtfully, making it more than just a sci-fi game but a reflection on real-world issues. The reason I wouldn’t give it a perfect score is that, at times, the controls and quick time events can feel a bit clunky or repetitive. While the story is the star of the show, some players might find the gameplay itself a little simplistic, especially those expecting more action oriented mechanics. However, for fans of narrative driven experiences, that won’t detract too much from the overall enjoyment.Detroit: Become Human is an unforgettable journey, and if you’re a fan of story rich, choice based games, it’s absolutely worth playing.

_childDocuments_.review: Despite some technical hiccuping whenever I played more than one segment of the game, controls that sometimes decided not to work, a ham-fisted script that left me cringing at points, and some highly questionable voicework aside from Clancy Brown and a tragically wasted Minka Kelly, I really did like Detroit. God bless it, but it's trying, and it wears its heart and its influences on its sleeve. I can respect that. It's really a gorgeous game, but doesn't sometimes realize its own strengths, failing to explore the most interesting environments while making the player sit through bland cabins or abandoned rooms. That said, at times, the game is one of the prettiest I've ever seen, with some truly great cinematography. Gametography? I'm not sure what that would be. But the camera choices are terrific, in any case.As for the story, look... it tries. It really does. I'll take this over a dozen games claiming not to be political while throwing hoo-rah ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ in my direction while I'm gunning down the popular villains of the week. And I like the branching stories, as mine was a vastly different ending than the "good" endings I came across on Youtube. Shakespeare, this ain't, but some of the characters are endearing, and I got weirdly annoyed when any of them died (usually due to the aforementioned technical glitches).You'll have to put up a lot with Detroit. But I think in the end it's worth it.

_childDocuments_.review: Oh. My. Goodness. WOW. WHAT?! This game is Incredible. A true Masterpiece of Storytelling and a genuine Emotional & Cinematic Experience. David Cage clearly showed his Directorial and Writing Prowess in this game. Thank You to the Quantic Dream team for making this title, and now Porting it to PC for more people to enjoy! The Last of Us was originally my Favorite Game in this Vein of Captivating Storytelling, but now this, easily takes that spot. I'm not the Competitionist type, but after finishing my first Full Playthrough, i'm Hungry for MORE! I NEED to know more about this world, I NEED to save my characters and get a Happy Ending! Now, for the Bad/Poorly Optimized:Being that this game was a PS4 exclusive, and the title itself is WELL worth putting up with some of these issues, they still must be addressed, before I can Fully Recommend Everybody to play this.Like most Console Exclusive Ports. Graphical Glitches, Performance issues and all that are expected, unless the team put on porting is REALLY skilled and REALLY well paid. I don't Doubt Quantic Dream's abilities to fix this game, but at the same time. I encountered multiple Hard Crashes, both at the Main Menu, In Game, In Cutscenes, in Quicktime Events (which do, in fact, alter the story line and options), and even some freezes, leading me to have to manually crash the game in Task Manager. Along with that, i'd often get graphic glitches that could induce Seizures for Visually Epileptic individuals, such as MAJOR Graphical Artifacting, High Contrast Flashing and Colour issues which made me feel like I was browsing on the Glitch Art side of Instagram, and Not in the Good Way.All of these glitches I mentioned above caused me to either manually close, crash, and/or restart the game, Luckily, None of my Save Game files were damaged, other than some minor backtracking in the level I was currently in when the errors occured.For those curious.Here are my Systems' Specs:Ryzen 7 3700xGTX 1060 (Running Current Nvidia GeForce Driver: 461.4016gb DDR4 3200mhz Ram (2x8gb)Boot nVME SSDGame HDD (7200rpm)

_childDocuments_.review: Wow. Just wow. Hard to articulate my thoughts after playing through something like this, twice (at time of review), might I add.(Disclaimer: I’m not good at writing reviews, there are plenty other reviews who do a much better job at explaining than me so read those as well)From first play through, start to finish, I’d say the average completion time is around 10-11 hours. That’s what I got on my first play though (I didn’t read every single book and I’m sure I missed some stuff etc) and slightly longer time on my second playthrough. I know a fair amount of people like to run on the 1 hour = £$€ 1 mindset etc and I got this for £26.99 (see hours played at time of review above) and I plan to go through another playthrough soon (because of how many different choices you can make) so value for money is there 100%.I really rate the story, the whole, robots working for us side of things was cool to watch unfold and how your direct decisions can affect the entire outcome of the situation.  I’d like to go into more but if you are interested (and you like premise of robots / technology) your better off buying and becoming immersed in the world yourself, I personally don’t think your regret it.The soundtrack compliments this game so well, from the dialogue scenes to the action scenes, it does such good of encapsulating the moment. I personally like Connor’s theme as it fits his character and has a sense of urgency. At time of review, I am currently listening to the OST on YouTube because I genuinely like this music.This was a pretty decent port all things considered; I always get rather worried when I hear companies do ports of games on console etc, but it worked well. I must say, the graphics looked amazing and I was rather impressed with how they really added so much detail to a scene which further helped with immersion. No frame rate issues on the 60fps option (I have a pretty decent spec PC) and very minor graphical hitches (faces and textures rarely not rendering in HD(?) and therefore sometimes looking a little bare and muddy etc) but that in no way affected my gameplay or immersion (and was fixable by restarting the game). My only complaint with the port (if you can even call it a complain it’s so minor and it could even be intentional) was that I’m guessing FX(?) like sparks and snow were (by the looks of it) locked at 30fps but it’s hardly a problem, just would have been nice to have everything running at the same fps. So, all in all hats off, this was a great port.This was an amazing world and story that Quantic Dream and the writers David Cage and Adam Williams developed, and I really *really* hope to see something like this again soon. 10/10

_childDocuments_.review: Detroit: Become Human is one of those games that deeply touched my emotions and even made me cry. It brilliantly showcases how humans can be both good and bad, and how our choices impact our lives. The game reminds us that every choice has its consequences, which can be either positive or negative. We must learn to take responsibility for our decisions, stop blaming others, and be at peace with the world, avoiding conflict and enmity.The music in the game is phenomenal and profoundly moving. The game's atmosphere immerses you in its world, offering an unforgettable experience of a seemingly fictional city that I believe might soon become reality. The character development is outstanding:Markus, who is willing to sacrifice his life for freedom.Kara, who will do anything for the one she loves.Connor, whose nature depends on the player's choices; he can be a mission-focused devil or someone who realizes his mistakes and becomes a companion and friend.Interestingly, these qualities should be human traits, but in this game, they belong to androids. Love, the desire for freedom, compassion, and kindness should be attributes of humans, yet today, people seem to have everything but these good qualities. This game delivers two important messages; one about the future and robots, and the other, more significant one: perhaps we need to look in the mirror and realize that we have become more like robots than humans.Open to interpretation.

_childDocuments_.review: SPOILERS AHEADHad I known how the gameplay and story would turn out, I would not have purchased this game. This is largely my own fault for not doing enough research beforehand, but the gameplay is far less engaging than I anticipated. The first few hours of the game completely drew me in, introducing incredibly well-designed characters and compelling storylines. I was excited about the potential of exploring "life as a robot," particularly the idea of solving crimes side by side with Hank, as seen early on. However, as the story progressed, it veered into something entirely different—shifting from a personal, character-driven narrative to a super-political future where androids are fighting for their freedom.Here’s a breakdown of my thoughts:Positives:- Rich Characters and Early Storyline:The first 4-8 hours are phenomenal. The characters are deep and nuanced, the acting is excellent, and the world is beautifully designed. Exploring the environment and discovering details through in-game articles added a layer of immersion that I truly appreciated.- Thought-Provoking Themes:The game does a fantastic job of making you reflect on complex questions like "What is life?" and "What is AI?" It’s an ambitious and commendable effort to tackle such profound themes.-Overlapping Stories: The idea of revolving the story around three different characters, whose paths intertwine and sometimes conflict, was really interesting...Negatives:- Story Decline in the Second Half: The quality of the story nosedives in the latter half. It starts feeling rushed, with events that should logically take weeks or months happening within minutes. This fast pacing shattered my immersion and made the story feel cheap. Additionally, certain twists felt forced and lacked proper setup, with some plot points making little sense in hindsight.- Lack of Replay Value:The inability to skip dialogue and cutscenes makes replaying the game a slog. While I was intrigued by the many branching storylines and alternate outcomes, the thought of sitting through the same 70% of scenes just to experience the remaining 30% differently completely discouraged me. I had certain characters die because of bad decisions that weren't obvious from the QTE options it gave me.- Frustrating Gameplay Mechanics:The reliance on QTEs (quick-time events) is excessive, and the controls—particularly on a keyboard—are clunky. It’s clear this game was designed with controllers in mind. Moreover, some choices and actions are poorly communicated, leading to unexpected character deaths or outcomes as said above. This lack of clarity made certain decisions feel unfair. I also wish I would have been able to pick a rifle up and take control as that would have made the story feel much more personal and controlled IMO.- Shift in Tone:The game’s transition from a exploration of robotic/human partnerships to a politically charged revolution of robot rights felt a bit much. The personal dynamics, like Connor and Hank’s partnership/friendship, were some of the my favorite elements early on, and I wish the game had focused more on those relationships rather than pivoting so dramatically, to a story I didn't care for. The trailers and promo content focus a lot on this and I was hoping for more of it.Final Thoughts:There’s a lot to like in the game, especially in its early hours. The themes and ideas are super deep, and the acting and world-building are top-notch. However, the story’s decline, frustrating mechanics, and lack of replay-friendly features hold it back. If you’re interested, I’d recommend waiting for a good discount. It’s not a bad game, but it didn’t deliver the experience I was hoping for, for my $40.

_childDocuments_.review: Detroit: Become Human is a gripping narrative-driven game developed by Quantic Dream, renowned for their immersive storytelling and impactful decision-making mechanics. Set in a dystopian future Detroit where androids have become integrated into society, the game follows the lives of three android protagonists – Connor, Markus, and Kara – as they navigate through a world filled with moral dilemmas, discrimination, and societal unrest.One of the most striking aspects of "Detroit: Become Human" is its stunning visuals and detailed world-building. The environments are meticulously crafted, showcasing a futuristic yet believable rendition of Detroit. From bustling city streets to desolate industrial zones, every location feels alive and contributes to the overall atmosphere of the game.The game's narrative is its standout feature, offering a branching storyline with multiple paths and endings based on the player's choices. Every decision you make, no matter how seemingly insignificant, can have far-reaching consequences, leading to vastly different outcomes for the characters and the world around them. This adds a layer of replayability as players are encouraged to explore alternate choices to uncover new storylines and endings.Each of the three playable characters offers a unique perspective on the android-human conflict, with their own goals, motivations, and moral compass. Connor, a prototype detective android, must hunt down deviant androids while grappling with his own identity and loyalty to his human creators. Markus, a caretaker android turned revolutionary leader, seeks to liberate his kind from oppression and fight for their rights. Kara, a domestic android, embarks on a journey to protect a young girl named Alice, exploring themes of motherhood and empathy in a world that sees her as disposable.The game's themes of identity, prejudice, and free will are thought-provoking and resonate deeply with players, prompting them to reflect on their own beliefs and values. The moral ambiguity of many decisions forces players to confront difficult choices and consider the consequences of their actions, blurring the lines between right and wrong.While "Detroit: Become Human" excels in storytelling and player choice, some may find fault in its occasional pacing issues and reliance on quick-time events during action sequences. However, these minor drawbacks do little to detract from the overall experience, which is both emotionally engaging and intellectually stimulating.

_childDocuments_.review: Detroit: Become Human is an extraordinary game that captivated me from start to finish. As a passionate gamer who appreciates stunning graphics and immersive gameplay, I was immediately drawn to the game's visual prowess and the intricately detailed world it presented. The level of realism achieved in Detroit: Become Human is nothing short of breathtaking, making every moment feel like an interactive movie.From the moment I stepped into the shoes of the three playable android characters, Connor, Kara, and Markus, I was enthralled by their unique stories and their journeys of self-discovery. The game's narrative is its true masterpiece, weaving a complex web of choices, consequences, and moral dilemmas that left me emotionally invested and constantly questioning my decisions.What truly sets Detroit: Become Human apart is its exceptional storytelling. The game delves deep into themes of humanity, freedom, and the blurred lines between man and machine. The way the narrative unfolds is nothing short of brilliant, offering multiple branching paths and countless possible outcomes based on the choices you make. It's a testament to the game's writing and character development that I found myself truly caring about the fate of each character and their impact on the game's world.The gameplay mechanics in Detroit: Become Human are intuitive and well-executed, emphasizing exploration, decision-making, and quick-time events. While some may argue that quick-time events can be divisive, they are seamlessly integrated into the narrative, adding tension and urgency to key moments. The game's controls are responsive, and the choices you make have tangible consequences that ripple throughout the story, giving a genuine sense of agency and impact.As someone who values a captivating and immersive story above all else, Detroit: Become Human exceeded my expectations. The depth and complexity of the narrative, combined with the stellar voice acting and beautiful soundtrack, transported me to a future where the lines between human and android are blurred. It's a thought-provoking experience that lingers in your mind long after you've finished playing.If you appreciate stunning graphics, engaging gameplay, and a story that will sweep you off your feet, I wholeheartedly recommend Detroit: Become Human. It's an unforgettable journey that will make you question what it truly means to be human, and the choices you make will stay with you, long after the credits roll.

_childDocuments_.review: I do not usually leave feedback, a lot of times it can get toxic.  This game however, in the first few missions has already laid out a narrative that is extremely compelling and pertinent as we move forward with AI and Robotics.  I am very excited to see where it goes, and will be analyzing the choices that the developers made in the Cyborgs race, age, gender, etc that helps drive the narrative home and draws out reactions from the player.  So far I have been introduced to three separate cyborg characters and it is VERY obvious the parallels that are being drawn in one, and the emotion they are trying to instill with another.  The one that is so far on the edge is the Negotiator in the first mission, as he is patterned after what some would call a stereotypical white male, but I think that this option was brilliant because it means that while he MAY be seen with some slant, he is for all intents and purposes apart from all the other factors that someone of a different ethnic or gender appearance.  Also the fact that these are all things that are being applied to what IS at its very core a state of the art Cyborg that is no different from one to another other than its outward appearance.  This, with reflection by the player can tease out the idea that we all, humans that is, are the same.  While our outward appearance is different the machine inside is for the most part identical from one to another, and the fact that we apply these ideas too our outward appearance is just our own bias.  I think the more deep someone looks the more layers can be peeled back here, because if we take this to be the case, then apply that to our own creation.  A being made in our own image, apply it with all of our cultural baggage and preconceived notions of race, religion, creed, morality and so forth, is it then not obvious that our own creation will behave as do we.  I have not even seen where this story may go yet  however, I think it will be very interesting as a social commentary on our past and a stark reminder that going forward, if we do not learn from our past mistakes, we are certainly doomed to repeat them.

_childDocuments_.review: This is my first Quantic Dream game and I must say that I thoroughly enjoyed my time with Detroit: Become Human, there was rarely a dull moment. I've always heard about the hateboners for David Cage and his style of storytelling, but that must've been about the previous two games since this game's story, for the most part, was pretty fantastic. Sure there were some parts that were poorly written, like how some things are conveniently present or not present solely to progress the story, a few pacing quirks, and also how a few scenes just make no sense (especially a certain scene that is reminiscent to the ending of Toy Story that is just plain laughable), but it's not a dealbreaker what so ever since the rest of the story saves face SO hard. The amount of branching story lines that your decisions can open up is absurd (in a good way), and with the "Experienced" difficulty, one wrong move can kill an important character for the rest of the playthrough, Game of Thrones-style, and who doesn't love that? The 3 main playable characters are all great, you'll definitely pick favorites and some have more meaningful/interesting motivations than others, but they all have an engaging story on show. In a similar vein, I have few complaints about the side characters, some are cartoonishly evil for no explainable reason, among other minor things, but it's not a dealbreaker in the slightest since all the other side characters are superb (especially good ol' Hank). The gameplay is essentially just quick time events, and if it's not that it's playing detective (I've heard that this is the typical David Cage formula), but it doesn't really matter since this game is more of an interactive movie, or a game where the gameplay is making impactful decisions and watching the consequences of it unfold. I personally, having just recently found this type of game, love it, but I suppose it's not for everyone. The atmosphere, graphics, sounds, and voice acting are all top notch. The soundtrack is good, not particularly memorable, but it still serves its purpose very well. The controls, which are best with a controller, are fine, but the movement is definitely a mixed bag. Sometimes your character will stop for a moment, do a spin before walking normally, or even just be completely uncooperative with the controls. When it works, it works serviceably, but when it doesn't...it's irksome. Finally, the port itself is decent, it's unfortunately locked at 60fps, but my system ran it consistently with little to no hiccups.In conclusion, it's great ass game! I'd probably give it an 8.5/10. It's a bit on the shorter side in length, about 9 hours on my first playthrough, but the game almost begs you to replay it, multiple times in fact, so as long as you dig what the game is about, you'll definitely get your money's worth. If you have your doubts, definitely give it a try if it's on sale.

_childDocuments_.review: The most important aspect of Detroit is without a doubt its story, ambitiously setting up a full-scale android revolution—your three characters in the thick of it—and a myriad of branching storylines depending on your actions. It’s the longest game by Quantic Dream so far, and the most intricate, to the point that after each completed chapter, you see a chart  with each possible path. From a narrative design perspective, it’s impressive stuff. You get to experience both dramatic choices with immediate impact as well as twists that don’t occur until much later. All of this leads to a large number of both good and bad endings. That’s not to say every choice makes sense. Some choices you make contradict previously established motivations, but the point seems to be that they exist nonetheless, and that you get to make certain decisions yourself.

_childDocuments_.review: Great game with some excellent graphics for when this game came out. The story itself, is great. For obvious reasons it needs to be that way, otherwise you would have a bad game. Unlike many other games like this, your actions do have lasting consequences and the many plethora of ways that your game can go in just one playthrough makes you want to play it again, and experiment with all the different opportunities that the game gives you. The music is excellent, and is used excellently when the game requires it. The game feels so real, yet so far away, just one playthrough makes you wonder what our own future, the real future, may hold. One important thing to note though, is that to some, this game may feel less like that of a game & more like that of a movie, I would agree with that sentiment, though that shouldn't hold you back from getting this game, after all, it is a great one.The only qualm I have about this game, is that it plays awfully after 1 driver update. You need to play this game on old DX11 drivers, from roughly a year ago. This doesn't take long to fix, though I feel that you shouldn't need to do this in the first place. I, personally, went from ~60fps on high settings, to not even 5fps on low settings. This really should be fixed, but wouldn't hold it upon Quantic Dream if its a problem for NVIDEA to sort out, after all, it was one of their driver updates that broke the game, not one by Quantic. But do take all of this in mind if you are thinking of getting this game.To conclude, my overall review of this game would be a 9.3/10. It is an excellently crafted game, nothing falls short in any way. The only thing you as a user will need to worry about, is driver version. Par that, this game runs excellent for how amazing it can look at times. I would hope that you would enjoy it as I and many others do too. I would 100% recommend this to anyone thinking of getting this.

_childDocuments_.review: Contracts for the supply of digital content and digital servicesSUMMARY OF:Directive (EU) 2019/770 on certain aspects concerning contracts for the supply of digital content and digital servicesWHAT IS THE AIM OF THE DIRECTIVE?It sets out rules concerning contracts for the supply of digital content or digital services, in particular:rules on conformity with the contract; andremedies where the digital content or digital service does not conform or if there is a failure to supply.Digital content includes computer programmes and mobile applications, as well as video and audio files in digital form.Digital services include, for instance, cloud computing services and social media.The directive is part of the digital single market strategy for Europe.KEY POINTSScopeThe directive applies to any contract where a trader supplies digital content or digital services to the consumer and the consumer pays or undertakes to pay a price. It also applies when the consumer does not pay a price but provides or undertakes to provide personal data to the trader, unless the personal data provided are only processed for the purpose of supplying the digital content or digital service or for the trader to comply with legal requirements.Exceptions include contracts regarding:goods with digital elements (which are regulated in Directive (EU) 2019/771);internet access;texting (such as SMS), with the exception of number-independent interpersonal communications;healthcare;gambling services;financial services;software offered under a free and open-source licence (where no price is paid and the personal data provided by the consumer is used only to improve the specific software);digital content as part of a performance or event, such as digital cinematographic projection;digital content provided by public sector bodies in accordance with Directive 2003/98/EC.ConformityDigital content or digital services in general must:fit the description, quantity and quality, and have other features such as functionality, compatibility, interoperability, as required by the contract;be fit for the purpose agreed as part of the contract process;be supplied with all accessories, instructions and assistance as required by the contract;be updated as stipulated by the contract;be fit for the purposes for which digital content or digital services of the same type would normally be used;have the quality and performance features (including functionality, compatibility, accessibility, continuity and security), which the consumer could reasonably expect;be supplied with any accessories and instructions which the consumer may reasonably expect to receive;comply with any trial or preview version made available before the contract was concluded.Traders must ensure that the consumer is informed of and supplied with updates, including security updates, necessary to keep the digital content or digital service in conformity. The directive also contains more detailed rules on the obligation to provide updates.Trader's liabilityThe trader is liable for:any failure to supply the digital content or digital service;any lack of conformity of the digital content or digital service that exists at the time of supply and becomes apparent within a minimum of two years. If the lack of conformity becomes apparent during the first year, the consumer will not need to prove that it existed at the time of supply.When the digital content or digital service is supplied continuously, the trader is liable for any lack of conformity that occurs and becomes apparent throughout the period of supply.RemediesWhere the trader has failed to supply the digital content or digital service without undue delay or within an agreed time-frame, following a reminder, the consumer is entitled to terminate the contract.In the case of a lack of conformity, the consumer is entitled to have the digital content or digital service brought into conformity (unless this is impossible or would impose disproportionate costs on the trader). If the trader fails to do so, the consumer is entitled to receive a proportionate reduction in the price or to terminate the contract.When the contract is terminated, the trader must fully reimburse the consumer, except for periods when the continuously supplied digital content or digital service was in conformity.Obligations and rights in the event of termination of the contractOnce the contract is terminated, traders must comply with the personal data obligations of Regulation (EU) 2016/679 (General Data Protection Regulation). Under certain conditions, traders must:also refrain from using content that is not personal data and was provided or created by the consumer when using the digital content or digital service;also allow consumers to retrieve such content free of charge, without hindrance from the trader, within a reasonable time.After the termination of the contract, consumers must refrain from using the digital content or digital service and from making it available to third parties.EU countries must ensure that there are effective means to ensure compliance with this directive.The directive complements Directive (EU) 2019/771 on contracts for the sale of goods.FROM WHEN DOES THE DIRECTIVE APPLY?It has to become law in the EU countries by 1 July 2021. EU countries must apply the rules of the directive as of 1 January 2022.BACKGROUNDSee also:Consumer rights (European Union)Digital single market (European Commission).MAIN DOCUMENTDirective (EU) 2019/770 of the European Parliament and of the Council of 20 May 2019 on certain aspects concerning contracts for the supply of digital content and digital services (OJ L 136, 22.5.2019, pp. 1-27)RELATED DOCUMENTSDirective (EU) 2019/771 of the European Parliament and of the Council of 20 May 2019 on certain aspects concerning contracts for the sale of goods, amending Regulation (EU) 2017/2394 and Directive 2009/22/EC, and repealing Directive 1999/44/EC (OJ L 136, 22.5.2019, pp. 28-50)Regulation (EU) 2016/679 of the European Parliament and of the Council of 27 April 2016 on the protection of natural persons with regard to the processing of personal data and on the free movement of such data, and repealing Directive 95/46/EC (General Data Protection Regulation) (OJ L 119, 4.5.2016, pp. 1-88)Successive amendments to Regulation (EU) 2016/679 have been incorporated into the original document. _childDocuments_.review: Games that make you question the world around you are great games. They show the power of video games as a medium - they can get the player to take what they face in-game and use it as a mirror to see the world around them from a new perspective. But Detroit goes beyond that. It makes you question yourself, who you are deep within, and what makes you choose the things you do.To begin with, Detroit is an absolutely stunning game to play. The visuals change from beautiful to cool to inspiring to distressing to soothing to scary, while always maintaining excellent quality. The soundtrack is perfectly suited to every scenario you encounter along the way, my personal favourite being the hauntingly beautiful tune that plays in the background while Todd is driving Kara back home. The overall gameplay experience is quite smooth, with intuitive controls and missions that guide you along just enough to make failing them unlikely but still possible. Although, to be fair, the mechanics of moving around and interacting with people and objects are a bit clunky at times, but then again, I haven't seen any game achieve perfection in that.Even though it's beautiful to look at and play, the main forte of Detroit is its story. Throughout the game, every decision you make has a consequence. It might be immediate - the difference between escaping or getting a bullet in the head - or it might be slow-burning, changing someone's opinion in a way that will either help you or come back to bite you further on. In some situations, the best choice might not be immediately clear. Sometimes you don't even know what the best outcome is, so you can't try to aim for it with your choices. This gives Detroit a sense of unpredictability, which may be frustrating at times, but also makes it much more interesting. And, of course, the amount of choice means great replay value. (And the amount of chances for things to not go as you planned means you'll probably want to utilize that replay value.)However, what truly made the game hit home for me is how it gets you thinking. Although most characters in Detroit have their good and evil sides, one universally considered evil is  As I was finishing yet another play-through of the story, amazed at the unexpected plot twists brought on by my decisions, and planning how I'd do things next time, a chilling thought came to mind. Going back again and again, meddling with the lives of Connor, Kara and Markus, changing things around just to see what happens, even if it means someone suffering or dying... does that make me any better than ?As I said, this game makes you question yourself. And the answers to those questions may not be pretty.

_childDocuments_.review: Presentation (5/5)+Graphics are incredibly realistic, even for a game that is several years old. Character models and facial motion capture are impressive+Computer requisites to enjoy such graphics are surprisingly low, making it a very accessible and optimized game.+Music always fitting the mood of the story and expertly put together+Realistic sound design+Highly immersive environment helps world-building efforts put into the game+The most memorable main menu I’ve come across, with an android interacting with you depending on many factors (including playing history) and how far along you are in the game.Narrative (5/5)+Deep complex human characters break character archetypes+Outstanding voice acting of main characters (e.g. Connor) and minor characters+Ethical dilemmas are more immersive and impactful knowing the player is responsible for them.+Strong world-building throughout the game to get you immersed in not just Detroit, but overall society and world conflicts and ties it to the narrow focus of 3 androids.+Generally avoids sci-fi cliches, though there are several similarities with UK show ‘Humans’+Story can change significantly due to choices made, offering a ton of content. Even small decisions are acknowledged or end up having a major impact- Seeing other story paths is not very accessibleGameplay (4/5)+ Failing combat sequences (quick time events), making wrong choices, or having oversights or unawareness can have huge ramifications, adding tension.+ Story reasonably concise, allowing multiple playthroughs+ Prompting you to use your keyboard or controller for even mundane actions (paint stokes for example) is good psychology on putting yourself into protagonists’ shoes.+ Simplicity, no RPG elements, no overly complex exploration or puzzles. Linear gameplay works with narrative. It is all about the narrative, little else.+Game guides you without talking down to you because of how it is presented as an android computer program (you did this, therefore this path unlocked … you found this evidence, what is it pointing to, this action improved relations with character X)+Android vision helpful at telling you what to do and things to interact with so you are not stuck or miss important details- Not too many things to interact with- Camera control isn’t the best- While reasonably concise, some moments come across as filler- trying different story paths is very time consuming (unskippable dialogue and cutscenes, only 1 save file) (unsure) Dialogue choices are summarized as single words or phrases, makes it harder to determine best choice

_childDocuments_.review: Rating: ★★★★★Detroit: Become Human holds a special place in my heart. This game is a true masterpiece that touched me on a profound level. The story, visuals, and choices in this game are beyond anything I've experienced before.From the very beginning, I was captivated by the immersive world of futuristic Detroit. The attention to detail in the graphics brought the characters and the city to life in breathtaking ways. Every decision I made felt important, as the branching narrative allowed me to shape the story according to my own moral compass.The characters, especially Connor, Markus, and Kara, felt so real and relatable. Their struggles and journeys resonated with me on a deep emotional level. The voice acting was outstanding, bringing the characters' depth and authenticity to the forefront.The gameplay mechanics were intuitive, making me feel connected to the characters and their struggles. The mix of quick-time events, investigations, and dialogue choices made me feel like an active participant in the story. The pacing was perfect, with moments of intense action and quiet reflection.Detroit: Become Human goes beyond being just a game. It raises thought-provoking questions about artificial intelligence and the essence of humanity. It made me contemplate the consequences of our choices and the blurred lines between humans and machines.In conclusion, Detroit: Become Human is an unforgettable journey that left a lasting impression on me. Its powerful storytelling, stunning visuals, and immersive gameplay make it a must-play experience. If you're looking for a game that will touch your heart and challenge your perspective, I wholeheartedly recommend Detroit: Become Human.

If you're into this type of game or not, from a story aspect truly a wonderful experience through and through. I would most definitely recommend.

_childDocuments_.review: Yeah really enjoyed playing this game....well albeit it's more of an interactive movie. The script is excellent and the acting is the best I've seen in game. I turned off Vsync, and configured the graphics settings to my liking but on first play through it crashed. Other than that a relatively easy ride.  For this 1st run through the game I went for the "Ghandi" approach, next play though, a might go for the full on "North Korea".. although there's always choices for middle route.  It's a simple story, with elements of all Sci-Fi stories from the past  . _childDocuments_.review: I'd say it's worth the money, especially at the price it is now. However this isn't your typical "game". It's more of a narrative driven experience, 90% consisting of dialogue choices and quicktime action scenes. There is no open world sandbox experience, neither is there shooting gameplay as you'd expect from any shooter or mowing down enemies etc. You're pretty much watching a movie that asks for a lot of your input, and if you're cool with that the game is phenomenal because it truly makes your decisions matter. This isn't Telltale where your choices don't actually matter. As a choice driven game it truly is s-tier, which is why the actual gameplay is non-existent. If you are looking for a game like Cyberpunk where it's a mixture of some meaningful choice and good gameplay, this game isn't it. However great meaningful choices game, probably one of the best there is.

_childDocuments_.review: This game is an absolute gem and holds a special place in my heart. Forget about Telltale and their illusions of choice - this game has everything that Telltale-likes lack, which is consequences for your actions. Detroit: Become Human is an immersive and emotional rollercoaster. Each playthrough can lead you to different outcomes and endings, allowing you to explore various paths and character arcs. It takes you through the highs and lows of characters such as Kara, an android who suddenly experiences feelings and decides to become a mother. Then, the game puts you in the shoes of Markus, a prototype android who goes through hell and high water to find his place in a society that considers him nothing more than an obedient machine. And let's not forget about our favorite android, RK800 detective Connor - a badass character akin to John Wick, at least when it comes to action and fighting. He's an absolute unit and the most valuable asset of the CyberLife corporation. It's up to you to decide the fate of your characters. Choices do matter in this game, so be mindful of your actions. The game has 40 different endings and tons of different content, what more can I say? Games like this one are very rare. I give this game a solid 28 stab wounds out of 28 stab wounds, despite encountering some technical difficulties with FPS and general performance (It seems that Nvidia GPUs have compatibility issues with this particular game. If you encounter any difficulties, I suggest checking forums for solutions. I was able to find a solution for my problems there).

_childDocuments_.review: wow, wow, WOW. I can absolutely tell why there had been a lot of attention to this game. I know I'm kinda late to the party (since this came out in 2018) but still, this game is a MUST to play even after those years. And it still remains (and will remain) very recent.So, why should this game deserve your attention? Well, first off all, it looks absolutely flippin' fantastic. And I don't think that's just because I'm not used to good graphics. No, the people that made this game hired actual ACTORS so that the characters would seem as natural as possible. And it paid off. Many characters in other games just feel a bit off and you can't quite figure out why. You won't get that feeling here. The characters here are charismatic, lively, diverse and it's easy to sympathize with their issues and feelings.Fine, the game looks good, what about the gameplay, then? The game didn't disappoint in that regards either. It is a storytelling game, but it manages to blend the cinematics of a movie with thrilling action. You won't even feel bored during cutscenes, not only because the game is so engaging, but also because the game oftentimes actually requires you to take action during those cutscenes which can possibly affect destinies of the respective characters.There are several factors that make this game distinctively special compared to other storytelling games. Firstly, you play as 3 separate characters so you get to experience the problems the game portrays from the perspective of 3 different people (well, androids, actually.) I was also surprised by the amount of choices and outcomes of these choices you can experience. And those choices you make don't all actually all lead to the same ending as it is with many other games, in Detroit: Become Human there are supposedly 85 different endings, although many of them do overlap. That doesn't, however, change the fact that every time you do a replay you can experience a different story with a whole different ending.Overall, I was very surprised by the quality of this game. It is well worth the price (the developers really deserve it,) it is engaging, full of action, bonding with characters and tough decisions that impact the outcome of your choices. Go play it, you won't regret it.

_childDocuments_.review: I really do love this game. Such different outcomes for different decisions and the ability to play it as you would yourself as these characters really gives you such an immersive experience. The voice acting is amazing and was lovely to hear voices of actors I recognised. The fact you can also play the game again, making entirely different choices and having completely different endings for the characters involved is amazing, and really gives you a game that you can replay again and again. (I read that there are over 100 different endings!).The odd touches of world building is really what completed this game for me. You can pick up magazines and read about events around the world which really add to the game. I was excited to read these and watch the news within the game as it added something new to the story. I would really recommend this game, especially to those who are a fan of 'choices matter' and 'story driven' games, and also to those who love character development and sci-fi.

_childDocuments_.review: I'm a huge fan of the very idea of branching story lines with real consequences that change based on what actions you take and how you choose to communicate with other characters. Androids that develop emotions and a mind of their own is also an intriguing (if somewhat unsettling) prospect and I feel like this game's story handles the ramifications and reactions of that brilliantly. The controls may take a little getting used to (with keyboard and mouse especially) and it's best not to play when tired because you need to be at your mental peak to successfully juggle all the tasks the game throws at you. All in all though, Detroit: Become Human is an incredibly enjoyable experience with wonderful graphics and naturally, given the nature of the game, tons of replay-ability. I highly recommend trying it out.

_childDocuments_.review: When Detroit: Become Human was originally released for Playstation 4 three years ago it had a more consistently warm reception than previous Quantic Dream games had. I’ve heard a lot of claims about this being their best game yet and while this isn’t much of an achievement, to be honest, I was still intrigued. Now that I’ve played it on PC, I have to say that I almost liked it. But the more I played it and the more I think about it now after I’m done with the game, the less I like it. Even if it may really be their best yet.If you’re already familiar with recent titles from Quantic Dream, starting with Fahrenheit, you’d know how Detroit plays out. It’s a story-driven adventure game with heavy focus on weird right stick movements for interactions and QTEs for most actions. After the disastrously bad UI change in Beyond: Two Souls, the controls were returned to how they used to work in Heavy Rain, but on top of that a lot of additional quality of life improvements were added. The best one is unquestionably the pause button, similar to the one you’d see in BioWare’s titles, where with the press of a button you freeze the action during the exploration bits to see your current objectives, all spots that can be interacted with and additionally you can rotate the camera to any position that feels comfortable.Additionally, Quantic Dream now fully embraced the idea of flowcharts to show exactly how many different variations of the scenes there are to motivate people replaying the game or scenes in order to get different results. While far more “gamey” than what something like “will remember that” does, it also fits their games far better, as they often feel closer to what you would see in Visual Novels with multiple paths, rather than games where you’re meant to live with your choices like titles from Telltale or Life is Strange. In fact, in general, apart from usual annoyances here and there, this indeed feels like Quantic Dream finally accepting that they’re making games and, as such, need to follow the rules of game design and make gaming experience comfortable, rather than extremely awkward.Their storytelling ability has also improved. It hasn’t exactly become good, at least not yet, but this time they are trying to tell a story that flows like a story, where scenes are parts of the story not random scenarios, and where characters feel consistent throughout the playthrough. You get 3 playable characters this time, with their overall dynamic being basically a copy of what we got in Fahrenheit – a cop, a fugitive messiah, a simpler character whose fate is determined by the choices of the first two and who helps with worldbuilding. It works well a lot of the time and the characters are quite likeable, if predictable. And even one of the “big twists” in the story, which is obvious since almost the very beginning of the game, is handled more like a revelation to the character, rather than to players. Though, they still clearly expect players to gasp in shock and not roll their eyes, and they fail at that. But it is mostly well done, well delivered and enjoyable.Yet it wouldn’t be a Quantic Dream game without them constantly shooting themselves in the foot. Some of the scenes are still there just because, for whatever reason, they want to have a tired trope situation in their story that plays out exactly as you’d expect it to and it makes no sense when you try to analyze it. The game is still too long for its own good, especially now that they clearly wish people to replay it and get that flowchart filled in, something that I might’ve considered if the game was twice as short, but have no desire to do with how painfully long it gets. They still have no clue how to handle the awesome concepts and ideas they have and pretty much everything that starts out as a cool idea becomes stupid by the end. And their attempts at exploring themes and being symbolic are still as smart as calling a political villain in your story Rudolph Heetler and thinking that you’re being subtle.On top of that, if you would still wish to experience the game, the PC port isn’t the version I would suggest going with. I can only guess that the engine changes between their titles made for PS3 and this game made for PS4 were too extensive and complex, since the ports of Heavy Rain and Beyond work really well, while Detroit is a horrible mess of a port. It’s performance is extremely uneven, with all background tasks on PC becoming almost unresponsive, it has a really slow shader compilation process on the first boot (repeated after every GPU driver update, of course), it occasionally crashes and it has a weird issue with how it detects the controller every time you start the game, refusing to interact with objects (despite the right stick working for camera) until you click all inputs a few times. It does look good, but it’s not worth this compromised experience.Should you go for the experience at all, however? It’s a difficult thing to answer definitively. If you are outright allergic to all of the dumb that Quantic Dream games have since their very first project, Detroit won’t become the first game to break this cycle. If you were keen on what the studio did before and don’t mind cliche storytelling and QTEs, you might want to check the game out, just preferably not on PC. If you loved their previous games, well, you’ve probably played this already. I was pleasantly surprised by the improvements in this game in comparison to their previous attempts and maybe, just maybe, someday they will make something that is actually good. But they would probably need to first ask David Cage to stop writing their scripts.

_childDocuments_.review: This game is beautiful. Actually, I was looking for a stronger word to describe my emotions, but failed to express my feelings with words. I loved it immensely. At first, I had some doubts about whether I should buy the game, because the question of AI and androids in particular is not new in science fiction and much has already been said about it. But as soon as I started playing, I thought: "Why didn't I buy it earlier?". I became so completely engrossed in the game that I couldn't stop thinking about it even when I was doing other things.The narrative and the way the events are presented couldn't be better. The game is centered on a very philosophical and controversial issue, and the developers created an awesome story around it. The music is great. The actors are perfect for their roles and they did really amazing work playing their characters. The graphics are very nice, facial animation is outstanding.The characters are... — well — I just "felt" every one of them. They were almost alive, I saw their development and personal growth throughout the game. At first, they were nothing to me — just androids, obeying commands, but then I started to fall for them. Connor, Markus, Kara, old buddy Frank — I really felt I should help them, I wanted them to live.In this game, choices do matter. I almost always sticked to my initial choices and never replayed the chapters (well, only once, but then it was not a wrong choice, but just a silly mistake). I recommend not remaking your choices, because that really makes the game more interesting, when you see the consequences of your actions in the following chapters. This also makes you want to replay the game another time with different decisions. I personally really would like to play the game again and try a different path (although I am completely satisfied with my ending as it is — and a big thanks to the developers for this ending).In short, I strongly recommend playing this game. Seriously, Detroit is one of the best games I've ever played. Don't miss on it, you won't regret buying it.PS: Connor, you are my personal favourite. I am going to replay the game for you (among other reasons =)

_childDocuments_.review: So this is an interesting game. Up front, if you want in depth action gameplay, do not buy this for that. The game does not have deep gameplay, it is mostly walking with puzzles and quick time events with button prompts.So if you're still reading: I think this game is a masterpiece. The story is extremely well told and the character development throughout the game is always really really interesting to look at, no matter which route you take.That brings me to the next point: This game has an insane amount of choices and branching endings to the game. The game is structured in chapters, with there being three main characters whose stories all influence each other. Making specific stories in one chapter will influence the way other chapters happen, or even skip some entirely or add hidden chapters. The game has flowcharts for the chapters, and some of them genuinely take like 20 minutes to read, longer than the runtime of the chapter in some cases.Your actions have REAL consequences.Failing a combat szene will result in losing a character, which will change the story, there are (depending on how you count) anywhere between 20 and 40 endings in the game and all of them are unique to some extent. I have personally played through the game three times now, and in the later chapters, they barely overlapped at all. On repeat playthroughs, early chapters will be a little repetetive, but a lot of them still have optional actions with impact on the story at a later point and two of the three stories branch out extremely early in the game.The story itself is great, I don't want to get into too much detail though. I think it really opens up a lot of very interesting questions about ethics regarding robots and authority, etc, etc. Your views on these things, expressed in your actions in the game, will heavily influence the story, which may lead to a happy ending or the absolute worst possible outcome you could imagine.I know there's not much that hasn't been said already, but here's my conclusion:Detroit: Become Human is NOT a video game. It is an interactive movie and you are the director, the actor and the viewer. If that sounds appealing to you, there is nothing else quite like it.

_childDocuments_.review: Rating: 9/10Detroit: Become Human is an impressive interactive drama that raises questions about morality, freedom of choice, and the boundaries of humanity. Developed by Quantic Dream, the game immerses players in a not-so-distant future where androids have become an integral part of society but are beginning to seek freedom and recognition of their rights.GameplayThe game offers a gripping narrative where every decision you make affects the unfolding events. Players control three androids: Connor, a detective tasked with investigating crimes committed by machines; Markus, a leader of an android revolution; and Kara, an android trying to protect a little girl. Each character is unique, and their stories intertwine in meaningful ways.Story and CharactersThe plot of Detroit: Become Human is deeply emotional and multi-layered, exploring themes such as AI rights, social inequality, and the search for freedom. The script is rich with dialogue and provokes thought on the nature of humanity. The characters are well-developed, and their motivations feel genuine.Connor, in particular, stands out as one of the best android detectives. His cold professionalism slowly gives way to more human traits as the game progresses. His relationship with his mentor, Officer Hank, serves as the emotional core of his storyline.Visuals and GraphicsDetroit: Become Human is visually stunning. The detailed facial expressions of the characters and their emotions create a cinematic effect. The architecture of futuristic Detroit and the technological advancements of the era are also impressive. The musical score enhances the atmosphere, adding emotional depth to every scene.Choices and ConsequencesOne of the game's key features is its choice system. Your actions can drastically alter the fate of the characters and the world itself. Even seemingly minor decisions can lead to unexpected outcomes. This system encourages replayability, as players will want to explore different endings and alternative storylines.DownsidesThe game's primary drawback is its occasional linearity. While choices do matter, certain plot points are inevitable, which can slightly diminish the sense of complete freedom.ConclusionDetroit: Become Human is an emotionally rich, visually beautiful, and thought-provoking experience that evokes genuine emotions. Despite some minor flaws, it is worth playing for its ability to make you reflect on the future of technology and humanity. It is sure to touch the hearts of those who immerse themselves in its world and embrace its choices.

What you do in this game matters. Every action affects the ending of a scenario, and even the ending of the game itself.
