_childDocuments_.review: Objective rating for pure gameplay, plot, and FPS mechanics: 8/10Subjective rating for dumb oldschool FPS + WH40k fans: 10/10In brief, this game slaps. There's a campaign with mostly well scripted events, interesting objectives, vibrant locations, secret areas, and diverse enemies. Then there's a mission board in the hub where you can take quick bounty missions to grind for gear and credits. They're pretty homogeneous and reuse the same maps for the type of missions, but you unlock the S tier missions pretty quick and get big credit bonuses when you need em.Pros:- Pretty game, runs pretty well at 90% resolution with my upper medium rig- Guns are great representations of all classic WH40k and handle really well.- Weapon customization has a lot of options to fit your playstyle. Stripped down Fallout 4- Lore is lore. It's great and immersive and you really feel like you're in a hivecity- You jump, double jump, dash in air, wallrun, walljump, and just fly around shootin', melee takedownin' hoes- Xray vision, melee 'berzerk' mode, shock, electroblast, crush, autoaim, slow-mo, etc- Dog- Dog Augs- Pet dog- Progression through game feels fluid and hasn't gotten stale (at 8 hours)- Loot is plentiful and has a vast variety of statsUgly:- EDIT: Default pistol is now able to be swapped out! Great work! - Gun customization has some issues. Each gun is the same base gun (there is a large variety tho!) with different mods on it. However, if you get two of the same kind of guns and unequip a mod (say a long barrel), it doesn't keep the mod, so you have to re-buy that same mod for a different gun. Trinkets and damage mods are able to be swapped between guns, but it would be nice to strip guns for parts.- Inventory UI needs an overhaul. No shift/alt/etc click equip, no hovering over equipped gear for stats, no stat comparison unless you begin to equip an item and you have to specifically click on the slot to equip it. Small quality of life issues but take a look at WH40k Inquisitor in comparison.- Dog is busted. Terrible AI, dies pretty quick, only useful for summoning to see enemies outlined through walls. Which is super cool!! But that's sort of similar to the augur vision ability. Some better dog AI would definitely be cool. Personally, I'm not a fan of having companions in FPS games so it doesn't bother me at all, but if you compare it to other titles with friendly friends at your side, it does fall short.- EDIT: They fixed this glitch very quickly!  Great work devs. - Inventory is a bit limited. Would like to see some more slots for certain gear and weapons. Game autosells loot you don't pick up after a mission, which is kinda rad, but the low slots for certain items means you can't hold onto a variety of gear and have to make the decision immediately whether you want to use X or Y. For an FPS that kinda saves you a headache but I'm a Lootaholic so I like to have a bit more options.Game rocks. Go buy it. It's worth. A little rough around the edges, but it's a solid dumb shooter and a GREAT WH40k lore game.

_childDocuments_.review: I've cut off somebody else's thumbs and grafted them to this stick, which I've attached to a lever.  I can just pull this handle here, and... THUMBS UP!  and keep on typing.  That's a high tech solution, I tell you what.So you could be playing this game instead of reading it, so let me give you a quick paragraph to send you on your way:  Doom and Metro 2033 drank too much and fell into Sunset Overdrive's closet.  Nine months later, they named the baby "Hired Gun".You run around at high speed like a cracked-out lunatic, jumping off walls and firing wildly at dudes while people talk in outrageous cockney accents.  I guess there's a plot?  There's people who have a chronic lead shortage and it's your mission to remedy that imbalance.  You can get healed by being aggressive, so it's to your advantage to go utterly crackhappy on fools.  You don't need to skulk about or take cover or whatever, you jump off walls and generously share lead, that's what you do.The game just looks gorgeous, frankly.  Mmm.  It's rusty and claustrophobic and weirdly industrial and looks pretty much like the seedy underbelly of the basement of a giant, planet-spanning city should.  It oozes character, and I'm enthralled.  You're even encouraged to explore as they hide various goodies hither and yon, and with all your movement skills the game is as vertical as it is horizontal.But in the interests of being honest, the melee animations are kind of a mixed bag.  A few look off.  A lot are really bewildering.  I mean, yes, you're frantically trying to kill somebody who isn't cooperating, but it's really hard to parse the action.  I'll be the first to admit that hasty melee ambushes are going to feel very confused and off-center, but it's a bit personally bewildering and I don't like it.  A few others have complained of bugs, but I have not had that experience, it's been remarkably polished for me (melee animations aside).But in the end, I'm glad I bought this game, and I'm likely to stream or record it when I go back to it.  I'm quite stoked and I wish I had less work to deal with so I could play this longer.  If you liked E.Y.E. Divine Cybermancy, this isn't it.  But you know how atmospheric that game was, so you don't have to take my word for it:  this is too.  Two (of somebody else's) thumbs up.  On a lever.

_childDocuments_.review: There's just no doubt in my mind anymore. Games Workshop don't like video games and don't like people playing video games. As in all of the Warhammer and Warhammer 40k franchise games since the early 2000s, the only people who seem to be even remotely interested in providing some sort of quality are the artists. I'm going to start by saying I don't know nor do I care if the developers had little time, lots of crunches, impossible demands. It's not my problem and should never be my problem. You should get this game if:- You like infinite enemies spawning immediately on top of you, behind you, in front of you, all within 3 feet of you. - You like game breaking bugs on every level, including the main hub. - You like auto aim grapnel (which you cannot change) which prevents you from using it for its intended purpose to reach tricky platforms. - You like wasting your money. So I'll start by saying there was a lot of potential in this game, but it was completely squandered to the point where I cannot imagine myself completing it in its current state. Let's start with the main draw to this game - progression. This game has no progression. There will be no point in this game where all the money you spend on your bionics, dog, weapons and items will seem worth it. Why? Because the Mastiff's only use is to see enemies highlighted, its attack is ridiculous, takes too long and more often than not, enemies ignore it completely. The bionics? They give you new abilities, that barely work, even upgraded, are too short, and cooldown for too long (even with the fastest cooldowns) all this while you are under constant attack. The game tells you to complete side missions if the main missions are too hard, but the side missions are MUCH harder than the main missions for the simple reasons that enemies spawn infinitely in them. You think you cleared a room only for enemies to respawn in it the second you set foot outside, shoot you from behind as you're stuck in a corridor under fire from the next room and kill you. In one of the FIRST SIDE MISSIONS I've killed over 100 enemies before I could even get half of my objectives. The items they dropped were mostly ammo, sometimes grenades, rarely refractors. So I didn't even get anything out of it and my kill style was C, even though I utilized takedowns, wall runs, grapnels and slides constantly. Guess when you kill 100 enemies you just can't look cool enough to pull it off. Any enemy in the game has better shields than you. No matter how much you upgrade your refractor, the lowest scumbag in the weakest gang will always have a stronger refractor than yours and no matter how much you upgrade it, a single shotgun blast from the weakest enemy will always take it down. I'm good at shooter games, been playing them since the 90s, almost always on the hardest difficulty. Completed both the new dooms on ultra nightmare even. So that's about progression. Enemies are boring. They just are. Other than the occasional special enemy all enemies in the game in all factions are exactly the same. (At least from what I got to so far, so take this with a grain of salt). The combat is far too quick guns do too much damage (both yours and the enemies') and since sniping isn't an option in this game (due to enemies spawning on top of you no matter where you are with the exception of extreme platforms occasionally) doing so usually gets you killed. The enemy AI is garbage, they run at you and shoot and sometimes throw grenades. No group tactics, no utilizing strengths of individual enemies such as shield units to go ahead while others form lines of fire, no using the environment. Why even bother? The original FEAR had much better AI and that's over a decade old already. Takedowns take too long (even though the animations are very quick they're just way too long forming sometimes 3-5 actions in one animation) which allows enemies to instantly get to you and blast you as soon as you come out of it (because giving you invincibility for long enough after you come out so you can get out of the gangrape didn't occur to the devs) so using them often to get kill style is a pain in the ass. Your mastiff's AI is so bad that he won't attack an enemy right in front of him because he's standing on an elevation of one inch. Most of the time, it doesn't even do anything, just standing wherever you leave it and barking, often causing me to get confused when I think other mastiffs attack me. This game should have been about the environments, and in the levels it is, except there's no interactivity, no time to absorb the atmosphere and the levels are extremely contained into arenas and corridors with little to no actual exploration (no looking up and seeing a chest on a ledge is not exploration). They present you with this insanely interesting world and then just give you the middle finger by making your hub about as big as Commander Shephard's bedroom on the Normandy. The tutorials and informations are basic and don't cover half of the aspects you'd want them to. Now let's discuss bugs.This game had no QA and if you tell me otherwise I'll call you a liar. Nothing is polished. The bullets don't even align with their visual effects. Enemies will run into a wall for an hour because they can't path their way around a door. Stims will respawn you over a pit causing you to fall out of the game and be forced to quit. Grapnel hook sometimes auto aims at nothing even when you're aiming right at a platform (especially if that platform requires you to jump off of a railing into a death pit so you can get a shot at it, which makes some levels piss me off.) My only question is why do game devs don't have pride in their work anymore, what drives someone to release a game that could be the hit of 2021 as the ♥♥♥♥ of 2021? Force your executives to play the games through on hard difficulty so they actually have to experience the game. Feels like there was little to no passion put into this game gameplay wise and it's a damn shame. I hope future updates will fix this into something better. ♥♥♥♥ Games Workshop. ♥♥♥♥ their money laundering figurine scheme. ♥♥♥♥ their inability to understand that good video games can make them a lot of money and the Warhammer and Warhammer 40k franchises are the kind that BEG for a good video game. And ♥♥♥♥ whoever released this game without QAing it.

_childDocuments_.review: It's buggy in places. The story is confusing. The dialogue is bad. But you won't care about any of that, because it's immersive and it's fun. The environments are huge and beautifully rendered; I've never seen ANY game capture the grim, industrial-gothic darkness of Warhammer 40k as well as this. The levels are varied, taking you to a variety of Underhive locations that really establish the world through visual storytelling. There are tons of hidden details that establish the feel of the setting, and it's really cool to stumble across each of them. Character designs are equally fantastic, both enemies and NPCs in the hub zone, and add to the amazing visual worldbuilding. Gameplay is straightforward but fun. Warhammer 40k games have often focused on having players be the big, slow, tough Space Marines, but Hired Gun is all about mobility and frantic action. It definitely owes a debt to the new Doom games, but in a good way. This soundtrack is also a BOP, helping set the tone of the world. It's different from what we've heard in 40k games before, but in a way that really fits the different setting and protagonist. I really hope the game gets enough support to expand with DLC so that we can see new enemies and new environments, two places that this team REALLY seems to shine.

_childDocuments_.review: Necromunda: Hired Gun is a fast paced solo shooter that has amazing stage design, fluid movement and fun combat and is a great homage to the 40K (Necromunda) setting, though is a little rough around the edges and could have used some more polish to really make it shine. If you like fast paced combat, execution finishers or the 40K setting I recommend picking it up if you can get it on sale.As a fan of the 40K setting (and the Kal Jericho books), the story fits right in with that series. Set on the hive world of Necromunda (a massive city where billions live, separated into different strata layers) you play as a bounty hunter, taking on missions to earn your keep and survive. After accepting a bounty on the Silver Talon, the mission goes awry almost immediately and ends up with your team dead, you nearly being terminated and only surviving because of Kal’s timely intervention. Working with Kal and rebuilt with a range of new cybernetic limbs and parts, you hunt down leads on where the Silver Talon has fled to, while you are hunted by those who want both Kal and what’s been installed inside your head. I thought the story was good, and seemed like a good epilogue to the book series.Movement and combat are the focus of the game, as you slide, grapple and wall-run around the spectacular environments, killing as you go. Staying still will get you killed fairly quickly, continuously moving is what the game is all about, and the game fully supports you in this as you can wallrun and kill with abandon. You have a grapple to get to out of reach areas quickly, can slide fairly long distances at speed, or can sneak (but this would be the most under unitised ability in the game). The environments are well designed for this, offering multiple approaches with loot chests hidden in difficult places that encourage exploration. Combat is ultra fast paced and the game does a great job of making it interesting by having a fairly decent amount of enemies to fight, and plenty of weapon options, and “powers” to use. The game has light RPG elements, as you purchase upgrades to both yourself and your dog, which can do standard things like giving you more HP, shields, or energy, or unlocking other powers and better rewards. In a somewhat nod and wink to the table top games close combat is completely overpowered and with plenty glory kill animations, HP recovery and a fairly generous invulnerability windows that can mean when upgraded you can conga line from one enemy to the next with pure impunity. Some of the other powers just disintegrate enemies. You can call your dog, who will happily maul everything in the game (including the genestealers!) and acts as a great distraction magnet.There are a large selection of weapons from the 40K setting, and they perform as their background suggests they should. Bolters make enemies explode when shot and sound great, lasgun’s can take limbs off when overcharged, stubbers actually feel powerful and shotguns do stupid amounts of damage. Grav guns fire black holes, and plasma guns obliterate enemies. The smaller guns (like pistols) are actually useful, and each weapon can be significantly modified (it’s not just boosting stats). You can take 6 into a mission (from 4 categories), but actually keep a selection of around 20 or so you can choose from.You fight enemies from a few of the major gangs found in Necromunda, (Goliaths who generally favour the big guns and close combat, the female only Eschers and the tech heavy Orlocks). Each have multiple different types of troops, with their psykers (magic casters) being different, and Ogryns having both ranged and melee versions. There are Ambots, which act like giant robotic weapon platforms, and a genestealer cult to take on. While the enemy AI isn’t anything to gush about- most enemies rush towards you in an effort to blown apart or group together making group kills easier, the genestealers are stupidly fast, strike from weird places and they absolutely destroy you in combat before you know what has hit you. There are plenty of boss battles throughout the game, and these are surprisingly difficult. The bosses are absolutely bullet sponges, and are constantly receiving reinforcements and force you to use the terrain and all your powers.All that said, there are some issues which reduced the fun. I had significant crashes to desktop until I re-installed the unreal engine redistributable that comes packaged with the game. If playing with a keyboard and mouse forget trying to use keys for any shortcuts, and use the mouse wheel instead to select your powers. The game doesn’t point out that its nearly pauses when you do this, so it’s much quicker when trying to use powers. I found in some instances when wall running the guns refuse to fire when aiming down past a certain angle.The stages are wonderfully designed and really capture the of the setting. From fighting through derelict cities, wastes, sewers, a power station, spaceships, a moving train, chapels and foundries it is quite unique and a lot of care seems to have been put into how the environment looks. That said, this game pushed my old 1080 to the max, and I had quite visible screen tearing issues when playing at ultra settings. Dropping the visual quality down to high resolved this. The game won’t win any awards for character models, but there’s enough variety to keep things interesting (and to be honest you are usually moving too fast to really pay attention). The animations and vocals from the doc don’t seem to be in sync, with the animations playing once, before the vocals kick in and the options menu appears.The games soundtrack features plenty of heavy metal, which amps up in combat before quieting back down in between firefights. This suits the fast paced gun battles. A stand out mission for atmospheric music would be where you encounter the Genestealer cult. As soon as you enter the area the music changes, and it actually makes it feel quite eerie as you are looking at what appears to be a massacre. You get the nod that something coming up (with tons of ammo laying around), and then nothing, and then when you think you are safe you start screaming as you are attacked from random places. The vocals were a bit of a letdown with each gang seeming to only have 1 voice actor and repeating the same lines for every enemy, though the NPC’s, Kal and the hired gun were serviceable.Easy to get 100% achievements, with only a few requiring some work to be put into them.For more reviews please visit

_childDocuments_.review: Plenty of features you would expect from a looter shooter are not present:- adjusting your loadout during a mission- inspecting your inventory, like, at all- having a key that swaps between two weapons (traditionally mapped to Q)- bosses and mob types that require vastly different tactics and weaponsThe game quickly devolves into a sloppy, hectic mess. Bullet-sponge enemies, mobs spawning behind you, dark silhouettes on dark backgrounds, annoying screen effects, whatever your shooter heart despises.In the end, I found myself mowing down enemies willy-nilly, not even caring what they are or what they can do. Every once in a while you must use one of two skills that destroy magic armor (good luck if they're on cooldown), and for enemies that have shields, you use the grappling hook. Beware: If your back is not making constant love to a wall, enemies *will* spawn behind you. If you run out into the open to engage enemies head-on, you *will* get shot at from various angles by enemies from miles away. You can regain health by killing them, but unless you significantly upgrade that particular skill, you'll survive barely, paycheck to paycheck. Enemies hit like a truck, and they all have assault rifles, so there's no dynamically dodging projectiles, just frantic dodging to up the imaginary "dodge percentage" and get hit less.The game lifts about half of its ideas from Doom 2016 and Eternal wholecloth, in both function and design. Unfortunately, the devs aren't quite capable of reproducing all of them flawlessly, and many they straight-up misunderstand. Here's one for you: What was so great about the glory kills in Doom? They're quick. Well, down here in Necromunda, they take, literally, up to 5 seconds, and even then, most of the time I can't tell what in the Emperor's name even happened.Did I mention that you're actually controlling a third-person character in first-person? You know what I'm talking about. That awkward feeling that something's off, the slight delay before every move, the camera jolting back and forth after every input.Graphics are stuck in 2013, but the art direction is so stellar that you won't care. Voice acting is good, audio mixing has some issues at times. Music is pretty forgettable, but far from bad.I'm truly sorry to say that it's just not fun enough to keep playing. I love the 40k IP, I love shooters, and all I see with this game is squandered potential. You might get a kick out of it, but don't expect a smooth gameplay loop. This one's jank all the way through.

_childDocuments_.review: A decent old school feeling fps at least compared to most fps games that come out these days. Pretty fun game you can double jump and grapple hook and you can upgrade your character with different abilities and things which is pretty cool. You can also find a lot of new weapons and items around the levels which you can equip and modify and stuff. You can also buy weapons if you need to. The main story is quite short unfortunately if you are half decent at fps games you can probably get through it in 6-8 hours depending on the difficulty setting. The game does have a lot of side missions though which you can do to earn more money to purchase things which is neat. You can also replay previous weapons to find hidden chests to get some better loot if you want so there's a little bit of replay value there. You even get a pet dog that you can upgrade and its pretty useful when there's a lot of enemies after you. The graphics are quite good and I like the aesthetic they are trying to go for although sometimes it is a bit difficult to see things. The game runs okay, could be better, I did have to lock the framerate to 80 to get more stable framerates and there are still some framedrops here and there which is a shame. The game in general does feel very unpolished, like there are quite a few bugs like one bad one I encountered was when looking through ironsights the crosshair was super off center which was pretty bad and there was another bug where an elevator stopped working for whatever reason but aside from that I didn't have too many problems. I didn't really like the female voice actor for the main character but otherwise the voice acting was pretty decent. Cutscenes were a bit scuffed though, definitely could have used a bit of work. Overall its an interesting fps, could have used a bit more polish but mechanically it works pretty well, would have preferred a longer campaign but other than that its not too bad. 7/10

_childDocuments_.review: Necromunda: Hired Gun is a fast-paced FPS, taking place in the Necromunda planet, within the Warhammer 40K universe. It's a bit rough around the edges, but all in all, it's a pretty fun and old school game.Despite being a pretty straightforward game (there's no open world, no infiltration, you're just supposed to run and jump around with all guns blazing), it lets you handle situations in a whole lot of different ways. There's a good amount of guns and powers, you can wall run, use a grappling hook, double jump, or jump-dodge-jump again, use a bullet time, an aim bot, etc.Once you start getting good at it, it's pretty satisfying to run around at a crazy speed, dodge a million bullets, blow up half a dozen guys in an instant, will doing some pretty neat parkour.But, let it be known that the game is still slightly bugged. While strafing and jumping around like a moron, I found myself stuck in a rock or in a wall more than once. Some jumping mobs end up falling off the map (which can prevent you from getting any further when it's a boss). Other than that, my main beef was the execution animations: they are, truth be told, quite bad, and would have looked bad back in 2010. And I wish the dog/mastif was more important. It was heavily advertised as a selling point of the game, and it ends up as a slightly disappointing companion you can summon every few minutes.Lastly, I'm not really familiar with Necromunda, and the game won't help you get acquainted with this sub-universe. The plot makes no sense and the game makes no effort to explain its setting to the player.

_childDocuments_.review: I'm putting this review as a "Yes", but it's mostly because Steam doesn't have a "Neutral" option and I'm a positive type of guy. But really it's a "maybe".To be simple, it's a StreumOn game, through and through. Which means a lot of good stuff in some aspects, and a lot of jank and lack of polish in some others. If you've ever played E.Y.E Divine Cybermancy, you know exactly what I'm talking about there.I'll fully admit I wasn't entirely convinced in my first 2 to 3 hours of playtime, it may also not help that I'm not the biggest War40k connaisseur. But the more I play, and the more I'm starting to get upgrades and getting the hang of them, the more fun I'm having with.Let's start with the jank.There are some mechanics that are... uniquely implemented and kind of poorly explained, notably the inventory and loot system. Basically, despite some looter shooter aspects, you're not allowed to keep more than a handful of guns in each category, and if you find a weapon in-mission, you're allowed to equip ONE, without knowing its stats. Whetever you keep it or not is decided at the very end of the mission - take what you want, sell the rest. See that small grid on the right of the loot screen? Yeah, that's your entire inventory. It's not THAT bad, but it does take some getting used to and you need to be aware of that.There are also some faux-RPG elements, like armor, items and archeotechs... But basically, there's only one type of armor that I've seen so far, one type of lucky charm, and the equippable items all have basically the same function, buff one of your stats up. It's weirdly "elaborate" for what little there is in terms of variety on that front.And then, gameplay wise, some animations are janky as all hell, most notably the Takedown ones. It serves at a simili-Glory Kill system à la DooM 2016/Eternal, but with some misunderstanding of what makes them work in that game. Here it's slower and jankier, and you can basically walk up to a dude a shank a ♥♥♥♥♥ whenever you want, unless it has a refractor shield. And you'll be bound to do that a lot, considering it's one of your primo ways to regen health.The plot... exists. It's serviceable. The voice acting is also serviceable, but there was an issue with the audio mixing. It may be fixed now.You can do some basic mercenary missions in the same maps than the main campaign, with an objective. It's basically there if you need money or just want more combat, but the spawn rate of enemies can get completely out of hand.And the Mastiff mechanic is also a tad buggy at the moment. Sometimes it works fine, sometimes your dog just won't do ♥♥♥♥.On a more personal note, there's no animation cancel for the guns. You know in some games, when you can switch to another weapon as the new mag is loaded? Yeah, that doesn't exist here. You either wait for the entire animation, or cancel it entirely, even as visually the new magazine is loaded in. It still trips me up more than I'd like.There's also a distinct lack of melee weapons and combat, you have one Augmetic that makes you go super fast with a massive knife. It's powerful and quite useful because of other mechanics, but... that's it. In an universe where chainswords are a thing, tis a bit of a bummer (well, okay, to be fair, a Hired Gun may not have easy access to that kind of tech).On the other hand tho...The game is fun.The combat is actually quite good, in good part to the weapon's feedback. Every gun feels powerful, sounds powerful, and will leave some nasty marks on the basic goons you'll face all the time. One shot to the head with a Stub gun will be enough to make the head go somewhere else. A sawed-off shotty point-blank shot? The entire body will be purée'd. It's satisfying.The mobility is pushed quite far, you can wallrun, wall jump, dash, slide, double jump - and you're even rewarded with a dodge bonus for doing so. It's not Titanfall level, but it's not that far.You have a lot of Augmetics, all with powerful effects like slow down time for anyone but you, pull out a big knife and run around like a madman, have a temporary aimbot... And all of those are on separate cooldowns. Yes, it gets as ridiculous and awesome as it sounds.As for the weapons and visuals... It's 40k through and through. The scale is absolutely massive, and the universe has a lot of details put into it. I was a bit giddy when I got my hands on a Bolter or a Stub Cannon - talk about a Bigger Iron !And even the Mastiff gets some love from me as well despite its janky state... At some point, I just see him maul a random hiveganger, I'm finishing mine, and I just see him bring me the leg of the poor sod he killed. What a good boy !So yeah. The more I play it, the more the game is winning me over, despite its flaws.Just know what you're getting yourself into, and you should have a good time once you can get past the jank.Either that, or wait for patches.

_childDocuments_.review: No, sorry, another swing and a miss by the same ship of fools who created Space Hulk: Deathwing. It just doesn't work well enough to be fully satisfying especially when rightfully compared to DOOM: Eternal, which may have been a bit over the top but at least worked. Execution animations get old after just a few of them and the animations themselves don't seem that well executed. It's frustratingly difficult (not to mention grind-heavy) to the point of being nearly unplayable as a single player game on anything above Easy mode, the side missions are much harder than the actual campaign missions you're trying to grind up currency for the upgrades to attempt, and most environments in the game look even worse than Space Hulk: Deathwing. It's just a very low-grade experience in every category identifiable, and all it does is bring to mind better, but still not perfect games like Destiny 2 and DOOM: Eternal. If you've already played either/both, you may be better off just passing this one by until it's at least half price. It is fast-paced and violent, as advertised, but neither thing really qualifies it in any way as a good game.Forget about the dog; it's an advertising gimmick. Basically a navigational tool (to light up enemies and objectives) and fully upgraded he's still less useful than a weak Palico in Monster Hunter. Not very useful in any situation with more than one weak enemy engaged.

_childDocuments_.review: I'm enjoying the game so far, i finished the first two levels and two side missions. _childDocuments_.review: People who expected anything but a typical fun but janky Streum On Studio game are fools and deserve the disappointment.Honestly a very fun game that is eerily similar in parts to Streum On Studio's first (and best) videogame E.Y.E: Divine Cybermancy. The game overall just oozes atmosphere and drives home the fact that Streum On are a bunch of Warhammer nerds who deeply care about the franchise. The good:Visual presentation: Absolutely stellar. The whole game is incredible eye candy filled with an insane attention to detail according to the gritty feel of Necromunda, same as it was in their previous title Space Hulk Deathwing. Where as Space Hulk Deathwing had more diverse areas, Necromunda's areas are all in all a mix of rundown industrial wastes. Given that, the team still did amazing job with what they had in terms of terrains.Gameplay/Gunplay: Very fun. Your character is extremely agile and able to traverse all sorts obstacles with a mix of wallrunning, grapling hook, or just his sheer speed. Gunplay, as is the staple of Streum On's games is top notch and tight, all the guns have a very satisfying feeling to them, enhanced by the very visceral gore of dying enemies. The gun selection is very decent for such a title, from Warhammer's regulars like bolters and heavy bolters, to some more gritty options, like the extremely oversized Stub Cannon. Another personally great part of the gun selection is their scale, while the regular revolvers and autoguns are more reasonably scaled, guns like the aforementioned heavy bolters and stub cannons are comically oversized, as it should be in a Warhammer game (this fact leads to hilarious confusions by the members of steam discussions, who are confused that heavy bolter takes up half the screen even with maximum FOV). The gameplay is further enhanced by buyable and upgradable abilities, which while not as wacky as in E.Y.E still have fun stuff like bullet time, autoguided laser projectiles, and a literal aimbot. Sound/Music: Great soundtrack by the composer of E.Y.E Divine Cybermancy Olivier Zuccaro perfectly sets the atmosphere for all the parts of the game, be it a huge battle or exploring a deeper parts of the hiveworld. I am personally not one for listening to soundtracks while playing videogames, however I made an exception for Necromunda, and it did not disappoint. The sound overall is well done, especially when it comes to the weapons (answer for the great question of whether the videogame bolter sounds good is a resounding yes in this case). Length: For a 40$/€ game (29 in my case with launch sale + greenmangaming sale), the 10,5 hours that it took me to get through the main campaign + around 3 optional missions is more than adequate for me.Price: As already stated, thankfully Streum On Studio don't try to act like triple A developers and the price reflects that. From my experience I would say that even the full price of 40$/€ is adequate.The bad, ugly and janky:The gameplay jank: New players who might not be acquainted with Streum On's previous titles, might be put back by certain elements that they like to put into their games. Namely stuff like random critical strikes regardless of headshots, optional missions being just a simple objectives (kill 10 beefy enemies, defend point etc.) on the maps that you have already went through in the campaign, or respawning enemies. I'm thankful to say that respawning enemies happen only in the optional missions and not in the story missions. However the combination of two makes optional objectives not really that engaging, or fun to grind repeatedly. Thankfully the only reason to even play the optional missions is to earn some extra credits for buying upgrades or upgrading weapons, so if you're not into that sort of thing, you can easily skip them, the game should be completable without them. As a last thing I would like to mention the grappling hook. While a nice addition, it works only when it feels like it. When it does feel like working, it will most likely not grapple you to the exact place where you were aiming at. Feels like some kind of countermeasure so that people won't use it where they shouldn't and get out of bounds. Also the weird HP regen system: you get 3 medkits for a mission, and 3 respawns (if you buy them before the missions that is). After that the only way of regenerating health is first getting damaged, and then for a certain amount of time you heal from the damage you inflict (kinda sorta lifeleech). The issue arises when you get as low as 3 HP, where every single hit kills you, and therefore you have no way of getting health back, other than dying and respawning.The difficulty jank: Every enemy you encounter has an aim equivalent to a typical 12 year old Fortnite gamer on 60+ mg of adderall. When they lock onto you, they'll just rip you to shreads with absolute pinpoint accuracy. In several points where you have to fight several enemies at once it gets kind of silly. The only types of attacks you have a chance of dodging are slow moving projectiles like rockets, or hammer dudes jumping on you. The only way to combat these god gamers disguised as hive world inhabitants is to either hope that the weird HP regen is able to keep you alive, or to start glory killing them (and boy.. will we get to the glory kills). The difficulty selection tells you that the higher difficulty will grant you more rewards, but I haven't really noticed a difference (in loot, I have noticed the huge difference in number of loading times I had to sit through after getting my face violated on hard difficulty). Therefore I see no reason to play anything but normal difficulty, or even easy, if for whatever reason you want to just finish the game for the story. But about that one..The story jank: It's pretty meh. You won't get any epic Warhammer sagas here, more of a run of the middle hive war gang war stuff. The animation jank: The biggest glaring visual issue in the game are some of the animations. For enemies it mostly applies for the big guys like Ogryns. Sometimes their animation while running onto you just bugs out and they appear to be angelically floating/almost T-posing towards you. The biggest animation issues come from the glory kills. While glory kills were a nice addition, they are flat out broken, gameplay and animation wise. You can glory kill an enemy from any HP level, the only thing that stops you from doing so is their Refractor Field (aka. armor/shield). When you do so, you are put into a state of complete invincibility. Yes, that means that you can just straight up glory kill whole squads of enemies, even the ones with Refractor Field if you get a certain upgrade, without any repercussions. Animation wise, while there are about 3 different glory kill animations that look decent, most often then not they just don't connect with the enemy, and you end up stabbing the air. Also, when you are in a process of glory killing, any sort of knockback (biggest offenders being hammer dudes) will knock you away insane distances, but only in the glory kill animation, so when you finish the kill, you'll get instantly teleported back to the corpse. Very disorienting.The inventory jank (look, i just like writing the word jank ok): There is no inventory. Yea, I'm not kidding. Yea, I don't get it either. The only pseudo inventory you get is in the hub world, where the only way of even accessing it, is talking to a weapon's merchant. So when you get a new weapon in a missions, you can either bank it to the aetherial inventory (for selling or keeping at the end), or equip it straight up. But for some reason, into missions you can only go with 2 main weapons (bolters, grenade launchers, what have you) and 2 pistols. I really do not understand what they were thinking with this.So all in all, a very fun, but janky (told you) game. Don't let the length of cons dissuade you, I fully recommend it.

_childDocuments_.review: There are only two reasons you’d be reading this. Either you’re my steam friend and this review is up on your activity feed (if so keep scrolling) or you’re a hungry Warhammer 40k FPS fan checking out if this morsel of 40k FPS action is worth your time and money. Either way, I feel bad for you.40K Fans know good 40k FPS experiences are few and far between. Seeing as there are only like five 40k FPS games and some of them are multiplayer focused. Even so, I would only recommend Necromunda Hired Gun to the most diehard 40k fans for its sale price. For the average FPS enjoyer, you’re not going to get a memorable or high-quality experience out of this game. It’s trashy fun, and it has its good aspects, but since I want others to take my recommendations seriously, I do not recommend this game. I wish I could rate a game “neutral.”First, the good.Necromuda hired gun tries. It does. It just doesn’t do a great job. Its level design, environment detail, and environmental story telling are good. A part of what kept me going was seeing where I would go next, and some of the environments I thought were legitimately high quality.  The lower hive of Necromuda is rich in lore and detail, and the developers made the most of it. I think this aspect made me decide to keep playing. I didn’t ask for a refund because I truly enjoyed the opening few missions.The weapon selection and gunplay is good as well. Plasma weapons, lasguns, bolters, etc, feel good and are fun to use in combat. The plasma pistol was especially fun to use and see your enemies get melted to pieces from it.That’s pretty much it for the good stuff. Environments and gunplay are important yes, but don’t outweigh the other considerations. But for a diehard 40k fan, this might be enough for you! And if so, I’d recommend it on sale.Now, the bad. No matter my subjective opinions of the game, an objective fact is that the game crashes a ton. During my playthrough, it crashed at least 5 times. Its frustrating for sure. You lose your progress, lose your immersion, and lose your steam. And its not like this is a long game. If I play a game for 40 hours and it crashed 5 times, that’s one thing, but an 8–10-hour game crashing that much is not a good look.The story is also bad. I mean this is 40k. We’re not expecting 500 IQ story lines with subtle complexities. But the story in Necromunda Hired Gun is told poorly and the game is not even designed to be a story focused experience. In between missions, you get a handful of dialogue lines from NPCs that push the story along, but you always return to the “select missions menu” and can play any mission out of order. Its more of a retro “Mission select” but with story elements. But, they could have done a better job with the story elements, especially having 40k lore handed to you.The combat, to be brutally honest, gets old. Enemy AI is bad. They do not take cover, they do not use tactics, they do not present meaningful gameplay challenges to the player besides having big guns and big health pools. Aside from environmental aspects, much of the combat looks the same from level to level. Spam your movement abilities and use every gun until they are all out of ammunition.Also, some gameplay elements serve to annoy the player and draw out the gameplay time. There are several missions where you must collect little power core things and take them to a power station to get something running. This means wandering around an environment looking for objects. Lame.A part of me feels bad for giving this one a negative review. Its not horrible. I finished it and didn’t regret my purchase or time spent playing. It’s just not good either. 40K fans looking for a high quality “doom-like” shooter might want to try Boltgun, which I would recommend.

_childDocuments_.review: This game is currently in the Humble Choice for July 2022, this is part of my coverage of the bundle. If you are interested in the game and it's before August 2nd, 2022, consider picking up the game as part of the current monthly bundle.Necromunda: Hired Gun is based on a Game Workshop game called Necromunda, in the Warhammer 40k universe.  You’re on a mechanized planet, and the locations here do not disappoint, whether it’s the furnace locations during the first level, or an epic train that passes in the second, there’s a huge sense of scale and discovery here, that’s impressive. It’s too bad the rest of the game just doesn’t work as well as the levels and locations.  There’s a particularly bad character model that I’ll try to show here of a big brute, but it was a bad enough model that it made me start realizing it’s more visual trickery and filters that made the other enemies acceptable, at least I think so.  The gunplay in the first hour is average at best, and there are some weird control choices, such as combining the use, melee, and reload all on a single button, which is awkward for the melee takedowns. Then again some moments reminded me of Ghostrunner for the wall-running that’s rather good, and a few moments were visceral like Doom Eternal, but a weaker form of both if I’m honest.Pick this up if you love First Person shooters, I liked the environments here and would love to see more, but this is a Games Workshop game that tends to have a decent amount of Jank.  As always when it comes to these types of games, I recommend people check out Mandelore’s reviews if they want a more in-depth look at the game, which ultimately is positive though it does mention a lack of polish at launch.   Though one last point, there’s a dog you can summon by squeaking a toy and letting him go after enemies. _childDocuments_.review: I had a fun 12 hours with it. As always, Streumon's visual presentation is fantastic, but expect bugs from anything they make.Their *core* gameplay is incredibly solid. Lifesteal augmetic that only activates when damage is taken forces you to stay fighting in order to keep your health up. You hide in cover only in order to wait for that power to come back, so you can run back in, take damage to activate it and refill your health bar. It's brilliant... I didn't think you could do that to encourage the very DOOM 2016/Eternal-like brawling gameplay, with hitscan enemies. Mixing in powers to quickly destroy the shields of tankier elites makes the combat flow incredibly well.There is a lot of negativity coming up now, but it's mostly talking about wasted potential in a single aspect of the game, rather than real problems the game has. It's a single, super minor issue I take seriously, and it doesn't change that the game is fine (albeit short).Firstly, to finish off the previous train of thought: when your opponent is plinking at you from far away, you use your movement to get to them. Obviously a double jump and grapple is going to be welcome to close the distance (or create distance) quickly, but you're immediately introduced to wallrunning and wall hopping, while 90% of the game is not built with it in mind. There's an entire augmetics tree for improving dodge chance while wallrunning/hopping but there's basically nowhere you can practically do that in the game. But my single most major issue with the game is weapon variety. I've always held the belief that EYE had some of the best guns in gaming, and I've been following Streumon because I believe they can make a roster that can top it. This is not that roster. I'm going to review every weapon in the game, starting with guns that are good, and ending with guns that are bad. This really should just be in the Steam Guides, but I felt it was important to illustrate what's happening here.Pretty standard automatic weapons. Shoots fast, good at close to midrange. Pretty good bread and butter weapons, combine with the slowmo and aimbot powers.For the heavy weapons, don't use the precision mechanics. The heavy bolter's special shield barrel makes it basically unusable outside of aimbot, both because of the accuracy/stability loss and because of visual clutter.For the plasma weapons, don't use the condensed cells. Gaining a bit of extra damage per shot is not worth losing 27 shots per reload. With the exception of the Plasma weapons, which fire projectiles, these are all the exact same weapons, with slight variations in magazine capacity, fire rate, and damage. You're gonna want 2 or 3 of these in your loadout, because none of the other pistols are good, and they're the best, most reliable ways to deal damage, working very well on their own, and making empowering abilities like slowmo and aimbot even more empowering. You mod most of them the exact same way, too - Max out damage and armour penetration first, accuracy and stability next, and every sacrifice to handling is worth it because you never need to aim down sights with these. Streumon included 3 good semi-autos, though!Pinpoint accurate, perfectly stable, and a lot of damage to boot. Pretty good precision weapon. Death machine when combined with the slowmo and aimbot powers. Kills Ogryns in one charged shot to the head!Remember, these things are tiny flashlights to things like  and  This is what they do to It's like a slow, homing missile that only has an explosive payload when it kills something. Hurts to get hit by the projectile. Hurts the victim's friends even more when the projectile explodes. Good for fighting faraway crowds, and sometimes agile enemies. Don't combine with slowmo, the projectiles aren't hitscan, don't inherit the speed you get, and are already very slow.Use the high explosive rounds for a very big area of effect that does good damage. Good for clearing crowds at around midrange, or if you're feeling lucky, use it at close range to activate your lifesteal augmetic.You use the stubber pistol in random execution animations and to open chests. You will always have a base level stubber that can't be replaced because of these. I'm pretty sure the full auto counterparts actually do more damage per shot than these. I wouldn't go out of my way to use these unless, I dunno, I felt like setting up a turbo fire macro. Long Las but bad. Has recoil, low capacity, slow firing, and like 2 points of extra damage over an uncharged las shot. a shotgun modded for full damage can only imagine to perfectly land all pellets on an ambot or ogryn in your face (an unwise position to be in) and still does less damage than a single bolter shot. they murdered my precious depezedore so bad i'm in tearsStreumon are usually pretty good at bringing interesting weapons into their games. I personally believe that EYE has my favourite weapon roster of all time, and despite its flaws, I think Deathwing has a good weapon roster too. It's unfortunate that this game only has, like, three entire  guns, and it's one of the main reasons that I would never say that this game is "EYE 2." It's a shame, because the rest of the guns have potential, if only they were better tuned. And if some of them... didn't exist?And it's not like a lack of variety hurts the flow of the game too much. Your guns are still very powerful, but they're taking a bit of a backseat. You're more focused on movement and using powers strategically this time around, rather than just using 4 different, uniquely powerful guns (though I think both would have been nice haha ;-;).Overall, I think it's a good game. I don't think it's Streumon's best game, but they worked hard on this, and this is clearly what they wanted to end up doing.

_childDocuments_.review: Got this in the July Humble Choice bundle, and I am loving it! It's the most fun I've had in a single-player FPS in a long time - it's dark and gritty, difficult in places, and the story is forgettable, but the gunplay and skills are so satisfying to unleash that I don't care why I am murder-machining my way through the game. Plus it's Warhammer, and Warhammer is badass.I think it's the structure of the gameplay that has me enjoying it so much. There are main missions to complete, of course, but after the 2nd one is done side missions open up. These offer ways to earn more money with which to upgrade my skills and abilities, which in turn make completing main missions just that much easier. They're awesome, too, because they're quick and fun, the rewards are good, and they've allowed me to unlock things like greater rewards for completing side missions and improvements to my abilities.And using abilities is very important in this game, because having decent FPS skills alone has not been enough to keep me alive. The improvements in my combat abilities are tangible, too, and it's really nice to go from struggling to take down certain foes (♥♥♥♥ those ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ with energy shields) to being able to chew through them after disabling their shields with an upgraded Haywire Pulse. Being able to slow down time for longer has likewise proved incredibly helpful.The guns themselves are also satisfying to use, largely due to excellent sound design and damage upgrade variations that offer decent spectacle (fire damage on a fast-firing shotgun looks SO cool!), and Hired Gun encourages using them as much as possible. For example, it takes a leaf from DOOM's book by giving you a skill that lets you heal by shooting enemies in a small time window after taking damage, so you're incentivised to keep moving and shooting as much as possible. Traversal is pretty sweet as well, with wall-running, sliding, double jumps and dodges to make getting around the huge environments a lot of fun.I am also only playing now, with the game patched and stable like it apparently wasn't at launch, so I'm seeing it at its best. After playing for 12 hours or so, I can definitely say that if you've been thinking about getting it but you've been on the fence, you should totally grab it. At the time of writing it's on sale, so it's a great time to dive in.I am only on the 4th story mission as of this review (I've been farming cash for upgrades via the side missions), so maybe it gets worse in the future, but for now I am very happy with my purchase. I'm enjoying myself so much, in fact, that I am considering grabbing other Warhammer titles that I've had my eye on (Underhive Wars in particular), in the hope that they have also been improved by patches in the time since release.

_childDocuments_.review: I got this on sale, so take that into consideration: it's worth around $20, $25, no more than that.Necromunda is... OK. The game itself wasn't too buggy once it got started up, but the startup is extremely unstable--for some reason starting up the game would immediately cause my computer to go into a BSOD and the only workaround was to stay tabbed on something else until the opening intro started playing. Visuals are fine. I'm not an aficionado for graphics and I had them set to medium for most of the playthrough, nothing stuck out as particularly ugly or unsightly (at least, unless it was deliberately meant to be as part of the visual style).I'm not too familiar with W40k but I know enough to realise Necromunda diverges from the usual tone of crazy Commissars and Space Marines. I'd say the store pages' art and videos do a great job of exhibiting Necromunda's specific take on the W40k franchise.Voice acting is okay. The female player character voice actress does a better job than the male one, and I think that's because the male player character voice actor was pushing his voice too far out of its natural range to make himself sound gravelly. Nobody's taking home any awards here, but there's no lines that stick out as "I-need-someone-to-go-to-bleak-falls-barrow-to-fetch-something-for-me" or "English voiceover dub" levels of awful. That said, the dialogue ends up feeling a bit shallow since all of the conversations the player interacts with are strictly 1-to-1 conversations between the player and one character at a time.The story is flat. It's mainly a thin framework used to get the player between action segments and the story ends pretty abruptly and unceremoniously.The gameplay itself isn't everyone's cup of tea, but it was a fresh change of pace from what I'm used to. Technically the player can get healing items, but the main way to recover from damage is to get melee kills in this game, so there's a lot of emphasis on close quarters and mobility--the structure of how character progression works reminds me a lot of the Far Cry franchise, but the actual gameplay reminds me more of Warframe: speed, aggression, and special abilities are most important. The game doesn't take the time to tell you this, but it's important to always bring a couple of weapons specifically with high armor penetration+radiation damage. There's an armored enemy called an "ambot" which becomes fairly common in the later sections of the game and they take forever to kill without weapons that are specifically modified with them in mind.Enemy variety is shallow. Said simply, there's several "factions" in the game but they're all essentially reskins. There's one type of big monster enemy (I'm not saying what just for spoilers' sake) that appears for a single mission then never shows up again and never gets mentioned again.The mastiff companion is also quite useful as-advertised, though the mastiff's appearance changes permanently and irreversibly when you have it upgraded, so be aware that upgrading the mastiff's skull past step 2 will turn it into some horrific nightmare-thing, admittedly appropriate for W40k's tone.The best I can say for this game is at least I don't feel ripped off for the $25 price tag. Necromunda is not everyone's cup of tea. Parts of it are clearly underpolished and it's clear that the developers wanted to do more with the game and the setting, but shoved it out the front door before really putting the elbow-grease into finishing it properly.Is the game stressful due to the occasional clunkiness and unstable programming? Yes.Am I going to put 300+ hours into it as tends to be my average for games I really enjoy? No, I'm pretty sure I won't.Was it also memorable, visually interesting, and kinda fun? ...Yeah, despite everything, I guess it was.The gameplay tries to come up with its own thing instead of just copy/pasting the gameplay from somewhere else, and it's at least not a total mess. The best way to avoid disappointment is to avoid expecting too much (and avoid overpaying).

_childDocuments_.review: This being Warhammer, it is simply bonkers; The aesthetics/story/content of the game is overblown, cheesy, gritty, dumb and it is an absolute joy to blast through hordes of enemies. I was surpised by the variety of enemies. The game is not too challenging and looks absolutly stunning despite this the game is fast and runs well. The environments are huge and it is possible to discover many alternative routes to the mission aim. This is also one downside of the game as it is not always clear what the aim is and where the player needs to go. Even though the game has up until level 3 a very managable difficulty, enemies always know where you are once spotted and almost always have perfect shots. The AI on the other hand is not always ideal as enemies can get stuck on terrain and then do not move and fire anymore. This happened to the first ambull and various ogrin in my game.There are probably better games of this genre, but everyone who likes the Warhammer 40K/Necromunda universe and tolerates fast-paced shooters should give this a go.

_childDocuments_.review: Your tolerance for jank will determine how much enjoyment you get out of this. It's definitely a budget game, feels like Rage 2 made with a tenth of the budget. Absolutely has  a lot of ugly animations to it and some bullet sponge enemies, but if you can get past that its a satisfying fast paced shooter with some neat powers and a lot of jank. _childDocuments_.review: Just finished the campaign after two days of playing (14hrs) and whilst I can't say this is my dream game, I would certainly recommend it to 40k enthusiasts. The recent history of 40k games have been appalling, so in that light this game is a really solid step in the right direction!Game play is fun, very much inspired by Doom's frantic run -wall run- and gun, with less hordes and enemy variety. There are plenty of side missions to stretch out the brief campaign, augmetic and weapon upgrades are handled nicely. But the weapon options feature several classes that soon become obsolete, leaving you with 5 - 6 solid weapons (boltguns are sick in all formats). Yes there are little glitches and the graphics can be a little janky at times, but the environments and character models are all stunningly reproduced. The voice audio also needs drastically raising and general sounds effects could use some tweaks / fixes as others have statedThat said, Devs please make some FLC or DLC to give a bit more replayability! The story wasn't really that enthralling given we didn't get any solid backstory on our protagonist or any emotional connection, so I would just focus on exploring more of necromunda, perhaps even seeing some of the upper hive! Fix the plasma guns and gravguns, I feel they really don't hit nearly as hard as the bolt gun or grenade launcher. Also it really bugged me being forced to carry that level one autogun, please let us trade it for higher level equivelants!I'm really looking forward to a sequel or perhaps another 40k game in a different setting (Armageddon would be pretty sweet). Thanks Devs! <3

_childDocuments_.review: If you're looking for something close to Doom 2016 without the 'weapon/enemy restrictions' of Doom Eternal, Necromunda: Hired Gun is a good "B Budget" choice. I'll go in greater detail here in just a moment, but for those who want the quick version: The game runs and works really well, especially for a fast paced FPS, but be prepared to forgive the poor animation quality. If you're in it for the gameplay itself, it's a great power-fantasy parkour shooter with enough challenge in it to keep things interesting.Okay, long version. And we'll start with the main negative that you will notice as soon as you hit "Open This Rust-Damn Door!"The Janky AnimationsY-yeah >>; I have no excuses here. They definitely look off and it takes a while to see past them. Takedowns are something you will be doing a lot of if you want to go for 100% Achievements (since they are near crucial  to increase your Style Kill rank at the end of a level). They're choreographed well, and I can see what the animators wanted to do, however they really do lack a lot of impact and rely on 'camera shakes' to fill in the gaps... Which doesn't really work. Granted, these animations do not hinder the gameplay specifically, but you will be disappointed if you expect "Glory Kill" levels of detail and impact here. You're invincible while doing them, and they do give you a little bit of health while getting rid of an enemy (or at the very least their shields).Menus are kind of a mess, but you get used to them. Some things were kinda dumb, like having 3 slots for 'pistols' and three slots for: Basics (assault rifles, shotguns), Heavy (Miniguns), and Specials (Plasmaguns, Grenade Launchers, Sniper Rifles). A little weird, but I found just having the three basic guns were enough for all my needs/encounters. Especially with the amount of powers you get.Finally, A personal one...The Dog AugmentationIf you're a fan of WH40k, you know what you're getting into: Hardcore Cybernetics and Skull Decor. I honestly really liked the add-in of the dog (Mastiff) in the game, let alone using it as a 'power' of sorts. However, you are pushed a little to upgrade it; afterall you want your companion to be useful to you and not just get immediately killed once summoned (not permanently in the slightest, don't worry). Annnnd the way to upgrade it is through Augmentation...You can see where this is going.At first, I started with the Body so I could summon it faster or something, and that altered the looks of the dog itself; as expected. It just got some plates along his back, and I thought "Oh, that's not so bad. Let's try paws next, give it a bit more armor on the legs-" NOPE! If you choose the paw option, you Amputate Your Dog's ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ Legs, then replace them with bionic ones.I'm not a WH40K fan, but I should have expected this >>; However, I didn't, and there's no way to "go back". So the reason why this is a bit of a 'negative' thing for me is that I'm a bit torn with having my dog being Useful to me while looking... Unpleasant (in a matter of opinion, of course. Especially the damn head "options"). Or, you can have it look good (love that Hellhound skin) and be a rather unreliable 'power'. If they could just allow players to customize the Mastiff's looks (aside from like two main-skin choices that are 60% replaced by any Augmentation upgrade) this entire section could be waved off. But really, it just left me feeling guilty through the rest of the game....Really. That was about it for negatives. The story's kinda meh, might be better if you're a fan of the franchise but it didn't connect with me. However, nothing offensive here, no strong feelings about it one way or another.Positives! This'll be alot longer of a section because it has a lot of good points here:-Gunplay: I played with M&K and after some adjusting I got it to where I felt really comfortable with the aiming. There is a lot of movement in the game, but often enough using movement abilities will increase your aim assist (especially with wallrunning). Weapons themselves felt good, honestly. They had a decent variety and could be customized quite well to your own play style. Don't want to ADS while moving around? Build your weapons with a focus on accuracy. Want to turn your Sawed-Off Shotgun into a 'Sniper Rifle'? Go for it. And this was something I honestly really praise about the game: it didn't really need to balance the weapons too hard because you're the one doing the balancing. One gun can probably get you through a mission, sure, but it probably won't be easy, let alone entertaining. Have fun with what you're getting. If it doesn't play the way you want, spend some coin and get some parts to change it to fit your style/purpose. Say, if an enemy is giving you a hard time, build a gun focused on taking that bugger down. Its really cheap to buy parts (save for ONE part) and everything's unlocked once you have that gun.-Parkour: This was implemented really well in N:HG. In the beginning you have a Dash, Wallrun, and Slide. After the first mission you get Double Jumps, and after the second you get a grapple hook. Doing any of these will give you a passive Dodge bonus on top of actually being hard to hit (as well as the aim assist mentioned earlier). As expected with games like this, you are constantly moving around at relatively high speeds with plenty of places to use these abilities. In theory, it may sound a little off, but in practice I found it was a lot more fun. To the point where N:HG nearly ruins a lot of other games for me after getting so used to the mobility and speed >>; Mix that with...-Powers: This is a Power-Fantasy game, and your character- though a bit squishy, gets an entire arsenal to play with. Apart from your mentioned Mastiff, you can slow down time for better aiming while keeping yourself at the same speed. You have auto-target that can give even the weapons with the most ridiculous spread have pin-point accuracy for a short time. You have teleportation/laser explosion thing(?) as well as a long ranged version that can auto-target up to 6 people within range. They all have decently long cooldowns, but once you get them unlocked you have them all on you at all times. They are made to be used, and they are fun to use, honestly. And that's kind of the point of them: They're Fun.-Level Layout: As mentioned before; this is a Warhammer game. And it's... Let's just say that the theme is quite 'creative' in general. I honestly think the art direction of the levels themselves are quite good, but how the layout makes use of your powers and abilities is quite outstanding. A few places were hard to navigate, but I never really found myself lost or frustrated attempting to get somewhere/figure something out. There's lots of little hidden credits, ammo, and shield refills if you go looking for them, but none of which are really needed. If you are going for a high rank though; you want to search for hidden chests (your Augur Array ability can help you seek these out). Going for the "A+ Student" Achievement will slow the game down quite a bit due to needing to find most of these chests in a level (not all required) but that's about it.Overall, I highly recommend the game if it sounds fun to you. I barely encountered any bugs (grappled myself into a wall once, but that was it. The game has a slight checkpoint system, so I barely lost any time) and if you can get around the stiff animations, you'll have a good time. I'd give it an 8/10. If they could fix up those negative two points I had, I'd probably push it up to a 9. A tad expensive, but I definitely had my fun with it. It's currently this month's Humble Bundle, and N:HG alone would be worth the price there

_childDocuments_.review: Another in the long line of warhammer games that are better then the average warhammer game but subpar when compared to basically anything else. It's like if doom eternal took itself more seriously, but then made the gameplay and music worse. The best thing about it are the visuals and ill admit they are incredible, but that doesnt make up for the short comings.Enemies with absurdly high health totals are essentially a constant issue. The enemies are inhumanly accurate, making fun strategies like wall sliding and dashing behind them essentially worthless. The take down animations are cool for about the first mission, and then you realize just how long you spend stuck in cutscenes of you doing the same "super cool" take downs. The mastif is a fun addition, but sadly they are very buggy and often get stuck on geometry or flat out refuse to attack enemies within sniffing distance. Overall a solidly underwhelming experience that i could not be asked to see to completion. If you want a good 40k game go play mechanicus, if you want a good shooter go play any of the dozens of exceptional ones.

_childDocuments_.review: There are some very cool set pieces in what I played of this game and it's got a great visual style but it's ultimately let down by fairly mediocre gameplay and a customization system that throws you into the deep-end without doing much to keep you from drowning in options.The parkour system is OK but feels clumsy compared to games with similar controls like Titanfall 2. In one instance, I got "stuck" on a pillar where I was just doing a loop, wall running in a big circle trying desperately to find my bearings. In another instance, I wall ran along the side of a platform instead of grabbing it - I ultimately ran off to my death that time and lost some credits as a result. Cool...A couple other issues that ultimately led me to uninstall and write this review:* The B-missions / side missions are just kind of combat arenas made up of parts of existing levels and are filled with pretty annoying enemies. They're shooting you with some pretty high-damage weapons, higher damage than anything I've seen in the campaign. Toward the end, most of the enemies what felt like too many shots to kill and a good half of them came out with body-height shields.* The hissing noise that the chests make is way too close to the hissing sounds in the environmental music, so much so that it impossible for me to tell if I was near a chest or just at a point in the music that *sounded* like a chest. Hidden chests are fun but the audio confusion made me stop searching for them which is a huge bummer in  a game about finding better loot.* Speaking of loot, I had a really hard time parsing the loot in this game. The depth of customization is cool but I didn't feel a meaningful trade-off between certain guns. The AR did a good enough job taking out enemies at mid and close range. I occasionally switched to the SMG but found myself quickly swapping back to the AR once I'd killed whatever was close. The shotguns were incredibly disappointing - the options were either a double-barrel breach-loader OR a pump-action that doesn't feel particularly powerful. The revolvers felt similarly weak for what they are.* You get a dog but it feels super squishy and doesn't seem terribly useful. Your dog's not with you all the time, you have to summon it. Once summoned it runs around for a bit, usually grabs a guy, and then de-spawns for you to summon it again on cooldown.

_childDocuments_.review: - Lovingly crafted Necromunda visual- Incredibly detailed maps (ruined by cons)- Weapon variety (ruined by cons)- Weapon customisation could be neat (ruined by cons)- A not mediocre soundtrack- Wants to be Doom so badly, but fails to emulate it effectively- The huge variety of weapons means little as half of them are useless in the mindless close quarter combat, the ♥♥♥♥ am I going to use a max-zoom long-las for?- A very lazy approach to enemy spawning where you craft a map first and then try to jam gameplay in to it afterwards- Enemy AI spot you instantly, charge you, fire constantly and that's it- The health system is a constant tug'o'war of searching the rafters for energy cells and masochistically exchanging fire with enemies for health and hoping you die last- Visual clutter forces the game to need to highlight enemies for you- Physical clutter voids most of your evasion mechanics like wall running, a game where standing still means death should not have so many static wall/floor obstructions- The game feels like it is moving about 25% faster than it should be, just for the sake of frenetic gameplay- Needlessly confusing and janky inventory system, why are you trying to reinvent the wheel so poorly- It's a looter shooter that hates you collecting loot and forces you to ditch it constantly- Your dog is just a gimmicky activated ability that zooms around the arena ridiculously or sits still doing nothing- Bafflingly useless default keyboard scheme with ridiculous positioning- Narrative/NPC interaction is badly executed, confusing and provides no exposition for anyone not already deeply versed in Necromunda lore- Levelling up seems to mean nothing- You can unlock all available powers almost immediately and from then on it is unsatisfying incremental upgrades like "make an ability last 0.1 seconds longer"I want to like this game but it is a real hot mess, frankly, with a whole bunch of on-paper good ideas mashed together very clumsily. There are layers of different games in here that just don't work together very well and are just kind of there, for instance wall running for traversal becomes pointless once you get a grapple almost immediately. Pick one.It's going for "ballet of death" but all it ends up with is "noisy cluster ♥♥♥♥", wasting its potential. It took a very high level look at Doom and copied it across without appreciating any of the nuances that stopped Doom's gameplay from just turning in to a tangled heap of explosions and viscera.

_childDocuments_.review: As a living creature, your time is priceless. Don't waste it playing this game. I really wanted to love Hired Gun but I just can't. Pro : art-wise, it's a hit. Looks great. Nails the atmosphere.Cons : nothing else comes together. The quality of this game is even lower (far lower) than E.Y.E, if you can believe it, and E.Y.E was a heap of jank built on a piece of string and a wooden board with two nails stuck in it. Games you can play instead : Dusk, Nightmare Reaper, Amid Evil, Forgive Me Father, Wrath : Aeon of RuinBiggest grievances :- ENEMIES RESPAWN OUT OF THIN AIR RIGHT IN FRONT OF YOUR FACE, OR WORSE, BEHIND YOU, WITH NO SOUND CUE. That is the worst part of this experience. Not only does it shatter the immersion into pieces, it also becomes cheap, irritating, and absurd. You can kill a clump of 5 goons and watch them all repop a literal second later right where you killed them. They don't even produce sound when moving. - The general gameplay balance is a complete joke. It's way too hard, and not in fun ways, with a lot of excessively accurate hitscan arrayed against you, your run speed feels juuuuust a tad too slow, etc. Highest difficulty is just a meme. Melee enemies damage you instantly. Shielded enemies are utterly absurd. - The animations are trash. Nothing feels right. The takedowns are horrendous to look at, with screen shake galore and misplaced objects, eg, stabbing thin air. Feedback when hitting enemies is non-existent. - Many of the visual effects are totally obnoxious. Plasma guns, for example, blind you when you fire them, and you just can't even see what you're shooting at. - Guns feel eh. Not good for an FPS. This is just a complete shame. This game could have been amazing with a few heavy patches. But as it is, it's not worth playing even on sale, because you are a mortal creature with a limited lifespan (if you'll allow me to presume)I had 66 hours on E.Y.E, because it was playable. This isn't playable, this is W40k-skinned ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥.

_childDocuments_.review: 6.5/10.This is a game of two halves.The actual mechanics are good. Environments are excellent, the detail is fantastic, guns work as they should for anyone that knows the lore. The upgrade portion is fantastic, gives you a little something to strive for and carry on. Combat is great once you get the hang of it. As long as you don't play the new DOOM games beforehand. They tried to do that and ended up with a watered-down version.It fails on just about everything else, though. The story is very average, a poor effort when such care was put into the detail. The side missions are instantly immersion breaking, pulling down the quality of the main plot. Without these, the story might be more interesting, but such is the feeling  of just grinding for money that the entire game just loses something.While those main missions are relatively interesting, there is nothing to care about, nothing to get you invested in what's happening. The main character is an a**, the side characters aren't really of much interest either.And they could have been.Spoiler Warning.If they had access to the Kal Jerico IP, why in the hell wasn't HE the MC? There is a character that is likeable, interesting and comes with his own universe and cast of characters. I'd have paid double for a Kal Jerico game with this sort of production value, instead we got this mess. Jerico is a bit player and shows none of the roguish charm that so defined the original stories.There were genestealers... once. That could have been a hell of a big-bad, instead we got a generic gang member. Necromunda, in its various incarnations, has included, in no particular order: flame-wielding fanatics, mega-spiders, necromancer psykers, ultra-fascists, Lovecraftian monsters and more. We get none of those, none of the whacky flavour that so defines the 40k universe.We get an antihero hunting for money. Something that's been done a dozen times. Vanilla in a universe of potential flavours.God the sheer waste of this opportunity makes me want to spit. It could have been so magnificent, they clearly had the budget to make something unique, but all we got was the same old shooter with different skin and a couple of gimmicks.Buy if it's on sale. Or if you don't know anything about 40k and haven't played Doom or Doom Eternal.
